LESSONS.title: The human brain
LESSONS.hook: A 1.4-kilogram organ with 86 billion nerve cells, running on about the power of a dim light bulb.

sections.key: The brain is about 2% of body weight but uses about 20% of its energy.
sections.b: The adult human brain weighs about 1.3 to 1.4 kilograms, around 2% of your body weight, yet it uses about 20% of your body's energy, even at rest. That's roughly 20 watts, about the power of a dim light bulb, which is remarkably efficient compared with computers doing far less. It's about 75% water, with the consistency of soft tofu, which is why it floats in protective fluid inside the skull. It has no pain receptors of its own, which is why some brain surgery can be done while the patient is awake.

sections.key: About 86 billion neurons communicate across synapses, forming trillions of connections.
sections.b: The brain contains roughly 86 billion nerve cells called neurons, and a similar number of supporting glial cells. Neurons communicate using electrical signals that travel along their length, and chemical messengers called neurotransmitters, such as dopamine and serotonin, that cross tiny gaps between cells called synapses. Each neuron can connect with thousands of others, creating an estimated 100 trillion or more connections. Thoughts, memories and feelings are patterns of activity across these networks.

sections.key: Cerebrum: thinking and movement. Cerebellum: coordination. Brainstem: breathing and heart rate.
sections.b: The cerebrum, the large wrinkled outer part, handles thinking, language, memory, senses and voluntary movement. Its wrinkles pack more surface area into the skull. The cerebellum, tucked at the back underneath, fine-tunes balance, coordination and learned movements like riding a bike. The brainstem, connecting the brain to the spinal cord, controls automatic functions you don't think about, like breathing, heart rate, swallowing and sleep cycles.

sections.key: Frontal (planning, self-control), parietal (touch, space), temporal (hearing, memory), occipital (vision).
sections.b: Each side of the cerebrum has four lobes. The frontal lobes, behind your forehead, handle planning, decision-making, self-control and personality; they're the last part to fully mature, in the mid-20s. The parietal lobes process touch and help you sense where things are in space. The temporal lobes, near your ears, handle hearing, language and memory, and contain the hippocampus, vital for forming new memories. The occipital lobes, at the back, process vision.

sections.key: Each hemisphere controls the opposite side of the body; 'left-brained' personalities are a myth.
sections.b: The brain has two hemispheres connected by a thick bundle of fibres. Each side mostly controls the opposite side of the body. Some functions lean to one side; in most people, language is mainly processed on the left. But the popular idea that people are 'left-brained' (logical) or 'right-brained' (creative) is a myth. A large 2013 study scanning over 1,000 people found no evidence that individuals use one side more overall. Both sides work together constantly.

sections.key: We use virtually all of our brain, not just 10%.
sections.b: You've probably heard that we only use 10% of our brains. It's false. Brain scans show activity across nearly every region over the course of a day, even during sleep. Damage to almost any area, from a stroke or injury, causes noticeable problems. And it would make no evolutionary sense to maintain such an energy-hungry organ if 90% of it did nothing. The myth probably came from misquoted early psychology and has been kept alive by movies and self-help marketing.

sections.key: Neuroplasticity is the brain's ability to change with experience, throughout life.
sections.b: Your brain physically changes with experience, a property called neuroplasticity. Every time you learn something, connections between neurons strengthen or form. Scientists once thought the adult brain was fixed, but we now know it keeps changing throughout life. In a well-known study, London taxi drivers who spent years memorising the city's 25,000 streets had a larger rear hippocampus than bus drivers who followed set routes. After strokes, other areas can sometimes take over lost functions with rehabilitation.

sections.key: Exercise, sleep, social connection, learning and heart health all support brain health.
sections.b: Brain health is closely tied to overall health. Regular physical exercise increases blood flow to the brain and is one of the best-supported ways to protect thinking skills as we age. Sleep clears waste and consolidates memories. Social connection and continuing to learn new things are linked to lower dementia risk. Protecting your heart, by managing blood pressure, not smoking and limiting alcohol, protects your brain too. Wearing a helmet when cycling protects it more directly.

quiz.q: Roughly what share of the body's energy does the brain use?
quiz.e: About 20%, despite being about 2% of body weight.

quiz.q: What are synapses?
quiz.e: Neurotransmitters cross these gaps.

quiz.q: Which part of the brain controls breathing and heart rate?
quiz.e: The brainstem runs automatic functions.

quiz.q: Which lobe handles planning and self-control, and matures last?
quiz.e: The frontal lobes mature in the mid-20s.

quiz.q: What is neuroplasticity?
o: The brain's ability to change with experience
quiz.e: Learning physically reshapes the brain.

LESSONS.title: Why we sleep
LESSONS.hook: You'll spend about a third of your life asleep. Here's what your brain is doing, and how to sleep better.

sections.key: Sleep is active maintenance for body and brain, not wasted time.
sections.b: You'll spend roughly a third of your life asleep, around 25 years for most people. Far from being wasted time, sleep is when your body and brain do essential maintenance: repairing tissue, consolidating memories, regulating hormones and supporting the immune system. Every animal studied so far sleeps in some form, even fruit flies and jellyfish, which suggests it serves fundamental purposes. Going without it quickly affects mood, attention and judgement.

sections.key: Sleep runs in ~90-minute cycles of light, deep and REM sleep.
sections.b: Each night you move through cycles of roughly 90 minutes. Each cycle includes light sleep, deep sleep (also called slow-wave sleep) and REM, or rapid eye movement, sleep. Deep sleep dominates the first half of the night and is important for physical recovery. REM sleep, when most vivid dreaming happens, becomes longer towards morning. During REM, your brain is highly active but most of your muscles are temporarily paralysed, which stops you acting out your dreams.

sections.key: Sleep strengthens the day's memories and moves them into long-term storage.
sections.b: During sleep, the brain replays and strengthens memories from the day, helping move them into long-term storage. Studies show people remember new facts and skills better after sleeping on them than after the same time awake. Both deep sleep and REM seem to contribute in different ways. Sleep also helps with creative problem-solving: people are more likely to spot hidden patterns after a night's sleep. It's one more reason spaced learning beats an all-night cram.

sections.key: Research in mice suggests the brain clears waste more actively during sleep.
sections.b: In 2013, researchers studying mice found that the brain's 'glymphatic' system, which flushes fluid through brain tissue, becomes much more active during sleep, clearing waste products including proteins linked to Alzheimer's disease. Scientists are still working out exactly how this applies to humans, but it may be one reason chronic poor sleep is associated with a higher risk of cognitive decline. It's a vivid reminder that sleep is active work, not just switching off.

sections.key: The circadian rhythm is a ~24-hour body clock set by light; melatonin rises in the evening.
sections.b: A master clock in the brain, in a region called the suprachiasmatic nucleus, runs your circadian rhythm, a roughly 24-hour cycle controlling sleepiness, body temperature and hormones. Light is its main timekeeper. Morning daylight tells it the day has begun; as evening falls, the hormone melatonin rises to prepare you for sleep. Bright light, including from screens, late at night can delay that signal. Jet lag and shift work are hard because they force you out of sync with your clock.

sections.key: Adenosine builds sleep pressure during the day; caffeine blocks it for hours.
sections.b: While you're awake, a chemical called adenosine builds up in the brain, creating 'sleep pressure' that makes you drowsy. Sleep clears it. Caffeine works by blocking adenosine receptors, masking tiredness. But it lingers: caffeine has a half-life of about five hours in most adults, so half the caffeine from a 3 pm coffee may still be in your system at 8 pm. Even if you can fall asleep, it can reduce deep sleep. Many sleep experts suggest avoiding caffeine for 8 hours or more before bed.

sections.key: Most adults need 7–9 hours; regular short sleep has real costs.
sections.b: Most adults need 7 to 9 hours of sleep a night; teenagers need more, around 8 to 10. Very few people genuinely thrive on less than 6. Regularly getting too little is linked to poorer concentration, mood and immune function, weight gain and higher risks of heart disease and diabetes. Tiredness is also dangerous on the roads: being awake for 17 hours affects driving roughly as much as a blood alcohol concentration of 0.05. Surveys suggest many Australians regularly don't get enough sleep.

sections.key: Keep a consistent schedule, get morning light, and keep the bedroom cool, dark and quiet.
sections.b: The most effective habit is consistency: going to bed and getting up at similar times every day, including weekends. Get daylight in the morning. Keep your bedroom cool, dark and quiet, and use the bed mainly for sleep. Wind down with a routine and dim lights in the hour before bed. Limit caffeine later in the day and alcohol at night; alcohol may help you nod off but fragments sleep later. If you regularly struggle with sleep or snore heavily, talk to a doctor, as conditions like sleep apnoea are common and treatable.

quiz.q: About how long is one sleep cycle?
quiz.e: Cycles last about 90 minutes.

quiz.q: When does most vivid dreaming happen?
quiz.e: REM sleep increases towards morning.

quiz.q: Which hormone rises in the evening to prepare you for sleep?
quiz.e: Melatonin rises as it gets dark.

quiz.q: How does caffeine keep you awake?
o: It blocks adenosine, the sleep-pressure chemical
quiz.e: It masks tiredness rather than removing it.

quiz.q: Being awake for 17 hours affects driving about as much as what?
quiz.e: Fatigue is a serious road safety risk.

LESSONS.title: How your immune system works
LESSONS.hook: Right now, an army of cells is patrolling your body, learning, remembering and fighting invaders you'll never notice.

sections.key: The immune system defends against pathogens using barriers, fast general defences and targeted responses.
sections.b: Every day your body encounters bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites, called pathogens. Most never make you sick, thanks to your immune system: a network of cells, tissues and organs spread throughout your body, including the bone marrow, thymus, spleen, lymph nodes and tonsils. It works in layers: physical barriers keep most invaders out, fast general defences attack anything suspicious, and a slower, targeted system learns to recognise specific threats and remembers them.

sections.key: Skin, mucus, stomach acid and friendly bacteria stop most pathogens getting in.
sections.b: The first line of defence is simply keeping invaders out. Your skin is a tough physical barrier. Mucus in your nose and airways traps particles, and tiny hairs called cilia sweep it out. Tears and saliva contain enzymes that break down bacteria. Stomach acid kills many microbes you swallow. And the trillions of friendly bacteria living on your skin and in your gut take up space and resources that harmful microbes would otherwise use.

sections.key: The innate immune system responds fast to any invader, causing inflammation and fever.
sections.b: When something gets past the barriers, the innate immune system responds within minutes to hours. White blood cells such as neutrophils and macrophages rush to the site and engulf invaders. They release chemical signals that cause inflammation, the redness, heat, swelling and pain around a cut, which brings more blood and immune cells to the area. Fever is also part of the response; a higher body temperature makes it harder for many pathogens to multiply and speeds up immune reactions.

sections.key: The adaptive immune system uses B cells (antibodies) and T cells to target specific invaders.
sections.b: The adaptive immune system is slower, taking days, but highly targeted. It relies on two types of white blood cells called lymphocytes. B cells make antibodies, Y-shaped proteins that lock onto a specific pathogen, neutralising it or flagging it for destruction. T cells come in different kinds: some coordinate the immune response, while killer T cells destroy infected cells directly. Your body can produce a vast variety of antibodies, enough to recognise almost any invader it might meet.

sections.key: After an infection, memory cells let the body respond faster and stronger next time.
sections.b: After fighting off an infection, some B and T cells become long-lived memory cells. If the same pathogen returns, they recognise it and mount a faster, stronger response, often clearing it before you feel sick. That's why you usually only get diseases like chickenpox once. Some viruses, like flu and the common cold, keep changing their outer proteins or come in many varieties, so your memory cells don't recognise the new versions, and you can catch them again.

sections.key: Vaccines train immune memory safely, without you having to get sick first.
sections.b: Vaccines give your immune system a safe preview of a pathogen, using a weakened or inactivated form, a piece of it, or instructions for making a piece, as mRNA vaccines do. Your body builds memory cells without you having to suffer the disease. Vaccines have been extraordinarily successful: smallpox, which killed hundreds of millions of people, was declared eradicated in 1980. When enough people are immune, disease struggles to spread, protecting those who can't be vaccinated, an effect called herd immunity.

sections.key: Allergies are overreactions to harmless things; autoimmune diseases attack the body itself.
sections.b: The immune system isn't perfect. In allergies, it overreacts to harmless substances like pollen, dust mites or certain foods. Australia has one of the highest rates of food allergy in the world, especially among children. In autoimmune diseases, such as type 1 diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis and coeliac disease, the immune system mistakenly attacks the body's own tissues. Scientists are still unravelling why, but genetics and environment both play roles.

sections.key: Sleep, exercise, a balanced diet, vaccination and hygiene support immunity; 'boosting' products mostly don't.
sections.b: You can't 'boost' a healthy immune system into overdrive, and you wouldn't want to, since an overactive immune system causes problems. But you can support it. Regular sleep, physical activity, a balanced diet with plenty of vegetables and fruit, not smoking and moderating alcohol all help it work well. Staying up to date with vaccinations and washing your hands prevent infections in the first place. Be sceptical of supplements and products that promise to 'boost immunity'; for most people, the evidence is weak.

quiz.q: Which of these is part of the body's first line of defence?
quiz.e: Barriers keep most invaders out.

quiz.q: Why does inflammation happen around a cut?
o: To bring more blood and immune cells to the area
It's a sign of infection only
quiz.e: Redness and swelling are part of the rapid response.

quiz.q: What do B cells make?
quiz.e: Antibodies lock onto specific pathogens.

quiz.q: How do vaccines protect you?
o: They train immune memory without you getting sick
quiz.e: Your body builds memory cells safely.

quiz.q: What happens in an autoimmune disease?
o: The immune system attacks the body's own tissues
quiz.e: Examples include type 1 diabetes and coeliac disease.

LESSONS.title: Nutrition: what the evidence actually says
LESSONS.hook: Ignore the fads. The science of eating well is simpler, and less exciting, than the internet suggests.

sections.key: Nutrition science is hard, so single studies and fads mislead; look at the big picture.
sections.b: One week coffee is bad for you, the next it's good. Nutrition seems confusing partly because it's genuinely hard to study: we can't lock people in labs for decades, so much evidence comes from observational studies, which show links but not always causes. Headlines amplify single small studies, and influencers sell fads. The reassuring news is that when you look at the big picture, decades of research and official guidelines around the world agree on a fairly simple core.

sections.key: Eat a wide variety from the five food groups, and limit foods high in saturated fat, added salt and sugar.
sections.b: The Australian Dietary Guidelines, based on a large review of evidence, recommend enjoying a wide variety of foods from five groups: vegetables and legumes; fruit; grain foods, mostly wholegrain; lean meats, fish, eggs, tofu, nuts and legumes; and milk, yoghurt, cheese or alternatives. They also recommend limiting foods high in saturated fat, added salt, added sugars and alcohol, and drinking plenty of water. It's not glamorous, but it's backed by a mountain of evidence.

sections.key: Fewer than 1 in 10 Australian adults eat the recommended serves of vegetables.
sections.b: Adults are advised to eat five to six serves of vegetables and two serves of fruit a day. A serve of vegetables is about half a cup of cooked vegetables or a cup of salad. Yet fewer than one in ten Australian adults eat enough vegetables. Vegetables, fruit and legumes provide fibre, vitamins, minerals and a huge range of beneficial plant compounds, and they're consistently linked with lower risks of heart disease, stroke and some cancers. For most people, eating more of them is the single most useful change.

sections.key: Fibre feeds gut bacteria and supports heart and bowel health; most people don't get enough.
sections.b: Fibre is the part of plant foods that your body can't fully digest. That's exactly why it's useful. It keeps your bowels regular, helps you feel full, slows the absorption of sugar and feeds the beneficial bacteria in your gut. Diets high in fibre are linked with lower risks of heart disease, type 2 diabetes and bowel cancer. Recommended intakes are about 25 grams a day for women and 30 for men, and many people fall short. Wholegrains, legumes, vegetables, fruit, nuts and seeds are the best sources.

sections.key: Ultra-processed foods make up a large share of Australian diets and are linked with poorer health.
sections.b: Ultra-processed foods are industrially made products, often containing ingredients you wouldn't use at home, like flavour enhancers, emulsifiers and modified starches. Think soft drinks, packaged snacks, confectionery, many breakfast cereals and reconstituted meats. They make up around 40% of the energy in the average Australian diet. Large studies link high intakes with higher risks of obesity, heart disease, type 2 diabetes and depression. Scientists are still debating exactly why, but eating more minimally processed food is a sensible direction.

sections.key: Use the 'per 100 g' column to compare products; the Health Star Rating is a quick guide.
sections.b: Packaged foods in Australia must have a nutrition information panel. To compare similar products, use the 'per 100 g' column, since serving sizes vary between brands. Ingredients are listed from most to least by weight, so if sugar is near the top, there's a lot of it; watch for its many aliases, like glucose syrup or dextrose. Energy is shown in kilojoules; one food Calorie (a kilocalorie) is about 4.2 kJ. The Health Star Rating on the front offers a quick comparison between similar products, but it's not perfect.

sections.key: Most people don't need supplements, 'detoxes', or exactly eight glasses of water.
sections.b: Some popular beliefs don't hold up. 'Detox' products are unnecessary; your liver and kidneys do that job. Most healthy people eating a varied diet don't need vitamin supplements, though some groups do, such as people who are pregnant or have specific deficiencies; ask a doctor. There's no need to drink exactly eight glasses of water a day; fluid needs vary, food provides some, and thirst is a reasonable guide for most healthy adults. No single 'superfood' transforms your health; patterns matter more than individual foods.

sections.key: Small, lasting changes beat strict diets; focus on adding good foods, not just cutting.
sections.b: The best eating pattern is one you can keep up. Strict diets often fail because they're hard to sustain. Small changes add up: add a vegetable to every meal, swap sugary drinks for water, choose wholegrain bread, keep fruit where you'll see it, cook at home a bit more. Focusing on what to add, rather than only what to cut, tends to feel better and works well. For personalised advice, especially with a health condition, an Accredited Practising Dietitian is the qualified professional to see.

quiz.q: How many serves of vegetables are adults advised to eat each day?
quiz.e: Fewer than 1 in 10 Australian adults manage this.

quiz.q: Which is a benefit of fibre?
quiz.e: It also supports bowel and heart health.

quiz.q: About what share of energy in the average Australian diet comes from ultra-processed foods?
quiz.e: High intakes are linked with poorer health.

quiz.q: Which column should you use to compare similar packaged foods?
quiz.e: Serving sizes vary between brands.

quiz.q: Do most healthy people need 'detox' products?
o: No, the liver and kidneys do that job
quiz.e: Detox products are unnecessary.

LESSONS.title: What exercise does for you
LESSONS.hook: If exercise were a pill, it would be the most prescribed medicine in the world. You need less than you might think.

sections.h: The closest thing to a wonder drug
sections.key: Regular activity lowers the risk of heart disease, diabetes, some cancers, depression and dementia.
sections.b: Regular physical activity is one of the most powerful things you can do for your health. It lowers the risk of heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, several cancers including bowel and breast cancer, depression, anxiety and dementia. It strengthens bones and muscles, improves sleep and helps manage weight and blood pressure. Researchers often say that if exercise were a pill, it would be the most prescribed medicine in the world. And many benefits begin with even modest amounts.

sections.key: Short bursts of vigorous everyday activity, even a minute at a time, are linked with real health benefits.
sections.b: You don't need a gym session for movement to count. Guidelines once said activity only mattered in blocks of at least ten minutes, but the World Health Organization dropped that rule in 2020 because the evidence showed every bit counts. A 2022 study led by Emmanuel Stamatakis at the University of Sydney used wrist-worn trackers on more than 25,000 UK adults who didn't exercise. Those who did three or four short bursts of vigorous activity a day, like charging up stairs, power walking to the shops or running for the bus, had up to 40% lower risk of dying early than those who did none. It's an observational study, so it can't prove cause, but 'exercise snacks' are an easy place to start.

sections.key: Use the talk test: moderate means you can talk but not sing; vigorous means only a few words.
sections.b: How do you know how hard you're working? Use the talk test. During moderate activity, your breathing and heart rate rise, and you can talk but not sing. Brisk walking, dancing, mowing the lawn and easy cycling count. During vigorous activity, you're breathing hard and can only say a few words without pausing, as with running, fast cycling, swimming laps or competitive sport. As a rough rule, one minute of vigorous activity gives similar benefits to two minutes of moderate activity.

sections.h: Can you outrun a bad diet?
sections.key: Exercise on its own usually brings only modest weight loss, but its health benefits don't depend on the scales.
sections.b: Many people start exercising to lose weight and are disappointed. Research by anthropologist Herman Pontzer helps explain why. In a 2012 study, he measured the daily energy use of the Hadza, hunter-gatherers in Tanzania who walk and work physically all day. Once body size was accounted for, they burned about the same number of calories as office workers in Europe and the United States. Pontzer argues the body adapts, trimming energy spent elsewhere when we're very active, and many people also eat a little more after exercise. So for losing weight, what you eat usually matters more. But activity helps people keep weight off, and it improves fitness, blood pressure, blood sugar and mood at any size.

sections.key: 10,000 steps began as marketing; benefits start well below it and level off around 7,000–10,000.
sections.b: The famous 10,000-steps target didn't come from science. It traces back to a pedometer sold in Japan in the 1960s called the manpo-kei, meaning '10,000-step meter'. Research since then has found that health benefits increase with steps but begin well below 10,000. Large studies suggest that about 7,000 steps a day is linked with substantially lower risks of early death and many diseases compared with 2,000, with gains flattening out beyond that for many people. Every extra bit of movement helps.

sections.key: Long periods of sitting carry health risks; break them up regularly.
sections.b: Many of us sit for most of the day: commuting, working and relaxing. Long, uninterrupted sitting is linked with poorer health, somewhat independently of how much you exercise. The guidelines recommend minimising prolonged sitting and breaking it up as often as possible. Simple habits help: stand for phone calls, take the stairs, walk to talk to a colleague instead of emailing, set a reminder to get up every 30 to 60 minutes, or use a standing desk for part of the day.

sections.key: Exercise improves mood and can be an effective part of treatment for depression.
sections.b: The mental benefits are as striking as the physical ones. Exercise reduces symptoms of anxiety and depression, and a 2024 review in the BMJ found activities like walking, jogging, yoga and strength training were effective treatments for depression, especially at higher intensity. It improves sleep, lifts mood, and boosts attention and memory, partly by increasing blood flow and growth factors in the brain. Exercising outdoors or with other people adds extra benefits from nature and social connection.

sections.key: Choose activities you enjoy, start small, schedule it and make it social.
sections.b: The best exercise is the one you'll actually do. Choose activities you enjoy, whether that's walking with a podcast, dancing, swimming, gardening, a team sport or lifting weights. Start small, even ten minutes a day, and build gradually to avoid injury and burnout. Schedule it like an appointment. Exercising with a friend or group makes you more likely to turn up. If you have a health condition or haven't exercised in a long time, check with your doctor first; an accredited exercise physiologist can also help.

quiz.q: What does research suggest about long, uninterrupted sitting?
o: It's harmless if you exercise daily
It's linked with poorer health, somewhat independently of exercise
quiz.e: Break it up every 30 to 60 minutes.

quiz.q: In a 2022 study of adults who didn't exercise, how many short bursts of vigorous everyday activity a day were linked with up to 40% lower risk of early death?
quiz.e: Charging up stairs or running for the bus, a minute or so at a time, three or four times a day was linked with big benefits.

quiz.q: Using the talk test, what does moderate activity feel like?
o: You can talk but not sing
quiz.e: Vigorous means only a few words at a time.

quiz.q: Where did the 10,000-steps target come from?
quiz.e: Benefits begin well below 10,000.

quiz.q: What did a 2024 review find about exercise and depression?
o: It can be an effective treatment
quiz.e: Walking, jogging, yoga and strength training all helped.

LESSONS.title: Stress: friend and foe
LESSONS.hook: Stress can sharpen you or wear you down. The difference is how long it lasts and what you do with it.

sections.key: Stress triggers adrenaline and cortisol, preparing the body for action (fight or flight).
sections.b: When your brain perceives a threat, whether a snake, a looming deadline or a tense conversation, it triggers the stress response. The adrenal glands release adrenaline, which speeds up your heart and breathing, and cortisol, which releases energy into the bloodstream. Blood flow shifts to muscles, senses sharpen and digestion slows. This fight-or-flight response evolved to help our ancestors escape predators. It's fast and powerful, and it still switches on for modern, non-physical threats.

sections.key: Short-term stress can improve performance; too little or too much performance suffers.
sections.b: Stress isn't all bad. Short bursts can sharpen focus, boost energy and improve performance, which is why a little pressure before an exam or match can help. In 1908, psychologists Robert Yerkes and John Dodson described what's now drawn as an inverted-U curve: performance improves with arousal up to a point, then declines when stress becomes too much. Challenges that stretch you, like learning a new skill or exercising, involve a healthy kind of stress that helps you grow.

sections.key: Chronic stress keeps the system switched on, affecting sleep, mood, immunity and heart health.
sections.b: The stress response is designed to switch off once the threat passes. The problem comes when it doesn't: ongoing work pressure, money worries, caring responsibilities or conflict can keep it switched on for weeks or months. Chronic stress is linked with poor sleep, anxiety, depression, headaches, digestive problems, a weaker immune response and a higher risk of high blood pressure and heart disease. It also tends to push people towards unhealthy coping, like extra alcohol, junk food and less exercise.

sections.key: Seeing the stress response as helpful can change how your body and performance respond.
sections.b: How you think about stress can change how it affects you. In experiments at Harvard, people taught to view their racing heart and fast breathing as their body preparing them to perform, rather than as a sign of failure, showed healthier cardiovascular responses and performed better under pressure. Stanford psychologist Kelly McGonigal popularised this 'stress mindset' idea. It doesn't mean pretending stress is fine, but seeing it as a sign that something matters to you can make it more useful and less harmful.

sections.key: Slow breathing with long exhales activates the body's calming system.
sections.b: Breathing is one of the few parts of the stress response you can directly control. Slow breathing with long exhales activates the parasympathetic nervous system, the body's 'rest and digest' mode, lowering heart rate. One technique is cyclic sighing: two inhales through the nose, the second topping up the lungs, then a long, slow exhale through the mouth. In a 2023 Stanford study, five minutes a day of cyclic sighing lifted positive mood more than a similar amount of mindfulness meditation, and both practices reduced anxiety.

sections.key: Exercise, sleep, time outdoors and social connection are among the most effective ways to manage stress.
sections.b: Some of the best-supported stress relievers are simple. Physical activity burns off stress hormones and lifts mood. Sleep helps regulate the stress system, while poor sleep makes you more reactive. Time in nature, even a short walk in a park, is linked with lower stress. Social connection is powerful: talking to someone you trust, or simply spending time with people, buffers the effects of stress. Limiting caffeine, alcohol and doomscrolling helps too.

sections.key: Where possible, tackle the source of stress: plan, set boundaries and ask for help.
sections.b: Coping techniques help, but where you can, it's worth tackling the source. Break overwhelming problems into small next steps. Write down what's worrying you; getting it out of your head and onto paper can reduce its power. Separate what you can control from what you can't, as the Stoics advised. Set boundaries on work hours and commitments. Ask for help at work or at home. For money stress, the free National Debt Helpline (1800 007 007) offers confidential financial counselling.

sections.key: If stress is overwhelming or persistent, talk to a GP; support lines are available 24/7.
sections.b: If stress feels overwhelming, lasts for weeks, or is affecting your sleep, work, relationships or health, it's worth talking to your GP, who can discuss options including a mental health treatment plan with Medicare-subsidised psychology sessions. Support is also available any time: Beyond Blue on 1300 22 4636 and Lifeline on 13 11 14, which is available 24 hours a day. Asking for help early is a sign of good sense, not weakness.

quiz.q: Which hormones are central to the stress response?
quiz.e: They prepare the body for action.

quiz.q: What does the Yerkes–Dodson curve show?
o: Performance improves with stress up to a point, then declines
quiz.e: It's an inverted U.

quiz.q: Which is linked with chronic stress?
o: Higher risk of high blood pressure and heart disease
quiz.e: Staying 'switched on' takes a toll.

quiz.q: In Harvard experiments, what helped people perform better under pressure?
o: Seeing a racing heart as the body preparing to perform
quiz.e: Seeing stress as helpful led to healthier cardiovascular responses.

quiz.q: Which line offers 24-hour crisis support in Australia?
quiz.e: Beyond Blue (1300 22 4636) also offers support.

LESSONS.title: Sun, UV and skin cancer
LESSONS.hook: Australia has one of the highest skin cancer rates in the world. Most of it is preventable, and it's not about the temperature.

sections.key: Australia and New Zealand have the world's highest melanoma rates; about 2 in 3 Australians get skin cancer by 70.
sections.b: Australia and New Zealand have the highest rates of melanoma in the world. The Cancer Council estimates that about two in three Australians will be diagnosed with some form of skin cancer by the age of 70. Skin cancer is the most common cancer in the country, and melanoma, the most dangerous type, kills over a thousand Australians each year. Our high UV levels, outdoor lifestyle and a largely fair-skinned population make the risk unusually high. The good news: most skin cancers are preventable.

sections.key: UV radiation, not temperature, causes sunburn; you can burn on cool or cloudy days.
sections.b: Sunburn and skin cancer are caused by ultraviolet (UV) radiation, not heat. UV can't be seen or felt, and it's not related to temperature. You can get badly burnt on a cool, cloudy or windy day, because UV passes through cloud and a breeze makes you feel cooler than you are. UV is strongest in the middle of the day and in summer, but in much of Australia it reaches damaging levels for most of the year, including winter in the north.

sections.key: Protect yourself whenever the UV index is 3 or above.
sections.b: The UV index measures the strength of UV radiation on a scale that starts at 0 and has no upper limit; 11 and above is classed as extreme. When the UV index is 3 or above, it's strong enough to damage your skin, and sun protection is recommended. In many parts of Australia, the index hits 3 or above most days of the year. The free SunSmart app and the Bureau of Meteorology show daily sun protection times for your location, telling you exactly when to protect yourself.

sections.key: Clothing, sunscreen, a hat, shade and sunglasses: use all five together.
sections.b: Australia's famous sun safety campaign began in 1981 with 'Slip, Slop, Slap', sung by an animated seagull, and later grew into SunSmart. Two more steps have since been added. Slip on sun-protective clothing that covers as much skin as possible. Slop on SPF50 or higher broad-spectrum, water-resistant sunscreen. Slap on a broad-brimmed hat that shades your face, ears and neck. Seek shade. Slide on sunglasses that meet the Australian standard. No single measure is enough on its own; use them together.

sections.key: Apply generously 20 minutes before going out and reapply every two hours.
sections.b: Most people apply far less sunscreen than they need, getting only a fraction of the protection on the label. Adults need about a teaspoon for each arm, each leg, the front and back of the body, and the face, neck and ears: roughly 35 millilitres, or seven teaspoons, for the whole body. Apply it about 20 minutes before going outside and reapply every two hours, and after swimming, sweating or towelling off. Check the expiry date. Sunscreen should never be used to extend time in the sun.

sections.key: A tan is a sign of skin damage; commercial solariums are banned in Australia.
sections.b: There's no such thing as a safe tan from UV. Tanning is your skin's response to damage, as it produces extra pigment to try to protect itself. Every sunburn increases your risk of skin cancer, especially in childhood and adolescence. Solariums expose skin to intense UV and significantly increase melanoma risk, which is why commercial solariums have been banned across Australia since 2015. If you like the look of a tan, fake tan products are a safer option, though they don't protect against UV.

sections.key: Short sun exposure provides vitamin D; most Australians need only a few minutes in summer.
sections.b: Sunlight also helps your body make vitamin D, which is important for bones and muscles. The balance matters. In summer, most fair-skinned Australians get enough vitamin D from just a few minutes of sun on their arms and hands on most days, outside the peak UV times. In winter, in southern parts of Australia where UV is lower, you may need more time outdoors. People with naturally very dark skin need more sun exposure. If you're concerned, talk to your GP.

sections.key: Check your skin regularly and see a doctor about any new or changing spot (ABCDE).
sections.b: Skin cancers found early are usually easy to treat. Get to know your skin, including areas you can't easily see, using a mirror or a partner. See a doctor promptly about any new spot, or any spot that changes in size, shape or colour, bleeds, itches or doesn't heal. The ABCDE guide can help identify suspicious moles: Asymmetry, irregular Border, uneven Colour, Diameter larger than about 6 millimetres, and Evolving, meaning changing over time. When in doubt, get it checked.

quiz.q: What causes sunburn and skin cancer?
quiz.e: UV isn't related to temperature.

quiz.q: From what UV index level is sun protection recommended?
quiz.e: At 3 or above, UV can damage skin.

quiz.q: What does 'slide' stand for in the SunSmart campaign?
quiz.e: Slip, slop, slap, seek, slide.

quiz.q: How often should you reapply sunscreen?
o: Every two hours, and after swimming or sweating
quiz.e: Most people also apply too little.

quiz.q: In the ABCDE guide, what does 'E' stand for?
quiz.e: Any change is a reason to see a doctor.

LESSONS.title: Ancient Egypt
LESSONS.hook: A civilisation that lasted 3,000 years, built by a river in the desert.

sections.key: The Nile's yearly floods left fertile soil that made Egyptian civilisation possible.
sections.b: Ancient Egypt grew up along the Nile, a ribbon of green through one of the driest deserts on Earth. Every summer, rains far to the south swelled the river and it flooded, leaving behind a layer of rich black silt. Egyptians called their land Kemet, 'the black land', after that soil, and the surrounding desert Deshret, 'the red land'. Reliable harvests of wheat and barley fed a large population and freed people to become builders, scribes, priests and artisans. The Greek historian Herodotus called Egypt 'the gift of the Nile'.

sections.key: Ancient Egypt lasted about 3,000 years, from around 3100 BC to 30 BC.
sections.b: Egypt was first unified under a single king around 3100 BC, traditionally by a ruler called Narmer or Menes. It remained a major civilisation for about 3,000 years. Historians divide it into the Old Kingdom (the age of the great pyramids), the Middle Kingdom and the New Kingdom (the age of Tutankhamun and Ramesses II), separated by periods of disorder. It ended as an independent kingdom when Rome took over after the death of Cleopatra in 30 BC. Cleopatra actually lived closer in time to us than to the building of the Great Pyramid.

sections.key: Pharaohs were seen as god-kings who kept order and balance, called ma'at.
sections.b: The pharaoh was seen as a god on earth, a link between people and the divine. His most important job was keeping ma'at: cosmic order, truth, justice and balance. Egyptians worshipped hundreds of gods, many with animal features, including Ra the sun god, Osiris god of the afterlife, his wife Isis, and Anubis, the jackal-headed guardian of the dead. Temples were run by powerful priesthoods, and religion shaped everything from farming to law.

sections.key: The Great Pyramid was built for Khufu around 2560 BC, most likely by paid workers.
sections.b: The Great Pyramid of Giza was built for the pharaoh Khufu around 2560 BC, from roughly 2.3 million stone blocks. It was the tallest human-made structure on Earth for more than 3,800 years. How it was built is still studied, but ramps, sledges, levers and huge organised workforces were involved. Archaeologists have found the nearby workers' town, with bakeries, breweries and cemeteries, as well as a papyrus logbook kept by an official who shipped limestone for the pyramid. The evidence suggests it was built by organised, paid labourers, not slaves.

sections.key: Mummification preserved the body so the soul could live on.
sections.b: Egyptians believed a person's soul could live on after death, but it needed the body. Mummification took around 70 days. Embalmers removed the brain and most organs, dried the body with natron, a natural salt, then wrapped it in hundreds of metres of linen. Organs were stored in canopic jars. In the afterlife, the dead person's heart was weighed against the feather of ma'at; a heart heavy with wrongdoing was devoured by a monster. Tombs were stocked with food, furniture and even board games for the journey.

sections.key: Most Egyptians were farmers; women had notable legal rights for the ancient world.
sections.b: Most Egyptians weren't pharaohs or priests but farmers, living in mud-brick houses and working the fields around the flood. They ate bread, onions, fish and a thick, nutritious beer. Children played with toys and board games like senet. By ancient standards, women had notable rights: they could own and inherit property, run businesses, sign contracts and bring cases to court. People also cared about appearance; both men and women wore eye make-up, which may have helped protect against sun glare and eye infections.

sections.key: The craftsmen who built royal tombs lived at Deir el-Medina, where around 1150 BC they staged the first recorded strike.
sections.b: The artisans who cut and decorated the royal tombs in the Valley of the Kings lived in their own walled village, Deir el-Medina, across the Nile from modern Luxor. Many could read and write, and they left thousands of notes scribbled on flakes of limestone and broken pottery, giving a rare close-up view of ordinary lives. One work register records reasons for missing work, including being stung by a scorpion and brewing beer. Around 1150 BC, under Ramesses III, the workers' grain rations were weeks late, so they downed tools and staged sit-ins at nearby temples until they were paid. It's the earliest strike on record, preserved on a papyrus now in Turin, Italy.

sections.key: Tutankhamun's nearly intact tomb was found in 1922; Egypt gave us calendars, medicine and more.
sections.b: Tutankhamun was a fairly minor boy king who died at about 19. He's famous because his tomb, discovered by Howard Carter in 1922, was nearly intact, packed with more than 5,000 objects including his solid gold burial mask. Egypt's legacy runs deep: a 365-day calendar, early medical texts describing injuries and treatments, papyrus, advances in maths and engineering, and some of the world's most recognisable art. It still shapes how we imagine the ancient world.

quiz.q: Why was the Nile so important to ancient Egypt?
o: Its yearly floods left fertile soil
quiz.e: The floods deposited rich soil, making reliable farming possible.

quiz.q: Roughly how long did ancient Egyptian civilisation last?
quiz.e: From about 3100 BC to 30 BC.

quiz.q: Which pharaoh was the Great Pyramid built for?
quiz.e: It was built for Khufu around 2560 BC.

quiz.q: Which right did women in ancient Egypt have?
o: They could own property and run businesses
quiz.e: Women had notable legal rights for the ancient world.

quiz.q: What did the tomb builders of Deir el-Medina do when their grain rations were weeks late?
o: Staged the earliest strike on record
quiz.e: Around 1150 BC they downed tools and held sit-ins until they were paid.

LESSONS.title: World War II: how it began and ended
LESSONS.hook: The deadliest conflict in human history, and how it still shapes the world you live in.

sections.key: World War II (1939–1945) was the deadliest conflict in history, killing 70–85 million people.
sections.b: World War II ran from 1939 to 1945 and drew in most of the world's nations, including every great power. It was fought across Europe, Africa, Asia and the Pacific, on land, at sea and in the air. It was the deadliest conflict in human history, with an estimated 70 to 85 million deaths, most of them civilians. Around a million Australians served, out of a population of about seven million, and nearly 40,000 died.

sections.key: After WWI and the Depression, Hitler rose to power; Britain and France first tried appeasement.
sections.b: After World War I, Germany faced harsh peace terms under the Treaty of Versailles, including losing territory and paying reparations. Then the Great Depression of the 1930s brought mass unemployment. Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party exploited the anger and took power in 1933, then built a dictatorship, rearmed and began expanding Germany's borders. Britain and France, desperate to avoid another war, tried appeasement: giving in to some demands, such as letting Germany take part of Czechoslovakia in 1938, in the hope of keeping the peace.

sections.key: Germany's invasion of Poland on 1 September 1939 started the war in Europe.
sections.b: In August 1939, Germany and the Soviet Union signed a pact not to attack each other, secretly agreeing to divide Poland. On 1 September 1939, Germany invaded Poland. Two days later, Britain and France declared war, and Prime Minister Robert Menzies announced that Australia was at war too. Using fast-moving tanks and aircraft, Germany swept through Denmark, Norway, the Netherlands, Belgium and France, which fell in June 1940. Britain held out through the Battle of Britain in the air.

sections.key: Germany invaded the USSR in 1941; Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor brought the US in.
sections.b: In June 1941, Hitler broke the pact and invaded the Soviet Union, opening the war's largest and bloodiest front. In December 1941, Japan attacked the US naval base at Pearl Harbor in Hawaii and swept through South-East Asia. Singapore fell in February 1942, and around 15,000 Australians were among those taken prisoner; Darwin was bombed days later. The main Allies were Britain and its Commonwealth, the Soviet Union and the US; the Axis powers were Germany, Italy and Japan.

sections.key: The Nazi regime murdered around six million Jews and millions of others.
sections.b: The Nazi regime systematically murdered around six million Jews, about two thirds of Europe's Jewish population, in what is known as the Holocaust or Shoah. Millions of others were also killed, including Roma, disabled people, Soviet prisoners of war, Poles and political opponents. Victims were shot in mass executions or murdered in death camps such as Auschwitz-Birkenau. The Holocaust led directly to new international laws on genocide and human rights after the war.

sections.key: Midway, Stalingrad, Kokoda and El Alamein turned the war; D-Day opened a Western front in 1944.
sections.b: In 1942 and 1943 the tide turned. The US defeated Japan's navy at the Battle of Midway in June 1942. Australian troops halted the Japanese advance on the Kokoda Track in Papua. British and Commonwealth forces, including Australians, won at El Alamein in Egypt. And the Soviet victory at Stalingrad in early 1943 destroyed an entire German army. On 6 June 1944, D-Day, Allied troops landed in Normandy, France, opening a second front in the west.

sections.key: Germany surrendered in May 1945; Japan surrendered after the atomic bombings, formally on 2 September 1945.
sections.b: Squeezed between Soviet forces in the east and the Western Allies, Germany collapsed. Hitler took his own life in Berlin, and Germany surrendered in May 1945. In the Pacific, the US dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945, killing well over 100,000 people, and the Soviet Union declared war on Japan. Japan announced its surrender on 15 August, now marked in Australia as Victory in the Pacific Day, and signed formally on 2 September 1945.

sections.key: WWII led to the UN, the Cold War, decolonisation and a surge of postwar migration to Australia.
sections.b: The war reshaped the world. The United Nations was founded in 1945 to prevent another global conflict. The US and Soviet Union emerged as rival superpowers, beginning the Cold War. European empires weakened, and many colonies in Asia and Africa soon gained independence. In Australia, the war shifted the country's main alliance from Britain towards the US, and a huge postwar migration program, under the slogan 'populate or perish', brought millions of people from Europe and later the world.

quiz.q: Which event started World War II in Europe?
quiz.e: Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939.

quiz.q: What was 'appeasement'?
o: Giving in to some demands to avoid war
The peace treaty after the war
quiz.e: Britain and France conceded to Hitler hoping to prevent war.

quiz.q: What brought the United States into the war?
quiz.e: Japan attacked Pearl Harbor in December 1941.

quiz.q: Where did Australian troops halt the Japanese advance in Papua?
quiz.e: The Kokoda campaign was fought in 1942.

quiz.q: Which international organisation was founded in 1945?
quiz.e: The UN was created to prevent future world wars.

LESSONS.title: The printing press changed everything
LESSONS.hook: One goldsmith's invention sparked religious revolutions, modern science and, eventually, the idea of news.

sections.key: Before the printing press, European books were copied by hand and were rare and expensive.
sections.b: Before the mid-1400s, books in Europe were copied by hand, often by monks working in monasteries. A single Bible could take a scribe more than a year. Copying introduced errors, and books were so rare and expensive that a library of a few hundred volumes was a treasure. Most people never owned a book, and most couldn't read. Knowledge was concentrated in churches, universities and the homes of the wealthy.

sections.key: Around 1440, Gutenberg developed a press with reusable movable metal type.
sections.b: Around 1440, Johannes Gutenberg, a goldsmith in Mainz, Germany, developed a printing system using movable metal type. He cast individual letters from a metal alloy using a hand mould, so they could be arranged into pages, inked, printed and then reused. He adapted the screw press used for making wine and olive oil, and developed an oil-based ink that stuck to metal. His famous Bible, printed around 1455, is still considered one of the most beautiful books ever made. About 49 copies survive.

sections.key: Movable type was invented earlier in China (around 1040) and Korea was using metal type by the 1200s.
sections.b: Printing wasn't new everywhere. China had woodblock printing centuries earlier; the Diamond Sutra, printed in 868, is the oldest dated printed book. Around 1040, Bi Sheng invented movable type made from baked clay. Korea was printing with movable metal type by the 1200s, and its Jikji of 1377 is the oldest surviving book printed that way, decades before Gutenberg. But Chinese writing uses thousands of characters, which made movable type harder to use. Gutenberg's system suited Europe's small alphabet, and combined with a trading economy hungry for books, it spread explosively.

sections.key: Print made books cheaper and let ideas spread across Europe in months instead of years.
sections.b: Printing spread astonishingly fast. By 1500, presses were running in more than 200 European towns, and historians estimate millions of books had been printed. Prices fell dramatically, so merchants, lawyers and craftspeople could afford books. Ideas that once took years to spread by hand could now travel across the continent in months, in identical copies. Mistakes could be corrected in the next edition rather than multiplied by tired copyists.

sections.key: Print fuelled the Protestant Reformation as Luther's writings spread in huge numbers.
sections.b: In 1517, German monk Martin Luther wrote his 95 Theses criticising the Catholic Church's sale of indulgences. Thanks to the printing press, his writings spread across Germany within weeks, and he became one of the best-selling authors of his time. He translated the Bible into German so ordinary people could read it themselves. The resulting Protestant Reformation split Western Christianity and reshaped politics, war and culture across Europe for centuries. It's hard to imagine without print.

sections.key: Print let scientists share, check and build on each other's work, fuelling the Scientific Revolution.
sections.b: Science depends on sharing results so others can check and build on them. Printed books and, later, scientific journals made this possible on a large scale. Accurate printed diagrams, maps and tables could be copied exactly, which hand copying never managed. Copernicus's book arguing that the Earth orbits the Sun was printed in 1543, and works by Galileo, Kepler and Newton followed. The world's first scientific journals appeared in 1665. The Scientific Revolution rode on the printing press.

sections.key: Print boosted literacy, standardised languages and eventually created newspapers.
sections.b: As books got cheaper, more people learned to read, and literacy rates rose steadily over the following centuries. Printers needed consistent spelling and grammar to sell to wide audiences, which helped standardise languages like English and German. Printed pamphlets, and eventually newspapers from the early 1600s, created something new: the public sphere, where ordinary people could read about and debate current events. Governments and churches quickly realised this was dangerous, and censorship followed.

sections.key: Like print, the internet made publishing cheap and spread both knowledge and misinformation.
sections.b: Historians often compare the printing press with the internet. Both made publishing dramatically cheaper and faster. Both spread knowledge, but also propaganda, scandal and misinformation; early printers churned out sensational pamphlets about witches and monsters. Both shifted power away from traditional gatekeepers and provoked anxious debates about information overload. It took societies generations to develop norms, like editors, libraries and reputable publishers, to cope with print. We're still working out the equivalent for the internet.

quiz.q: How were most European books made before the printing press?
quiz.e: Scribes, often monks, copied books by hand.

quiz.q: What was Gutenberg's key innovation?
quiz.e: Reusable metal type made printing fast and cheap.

quiz.q: Where was movable type first invented?
quiz.e: Bi Sheng invented movable clay type in China around 1040.

quiz.q: Which movement spread rapidly through print after 1517?
quiz.e: Luther's writings spread in huge numbers.

quiz.q: Why do historians compare the printing press with the internet?
o: Both made publishing cheap and spread knowledge and misinformation
quiz.e: Each transformed who could publish and how fast ideas spread.

LESSONS.title: The Renaissance
LESSONS.hook: How a handful of Italian cities rediscovered the ancient world and reinvented art, science and what it means to be human.

sections.key: The Renaissance ('rebirth') was a cultural revival from about the 14th to 17th century, starting in Italy.
sections.b: The Renaissance, French for 'rebirth', was a period of cultural revival in Europe from roughly the 14th to the 17th century. It began in the wealthy city-states of Italy, especially Florence, and spread north to France, the Netherlands, Germany and England. People at the time felt they were reviving the glories of ancient Greece and Rome after a long decline. Historians now see the 'Dark Ages' as less dark than Renaissance writers claimed, but the period was genuinely a burst of creativity.

sections.key: Trade wealth, ancient ruins and competing city-states made Italy the Renaissance's birthplace.
sections.b: Italy had advantages. Its cities, such as Florence, Venice and Milan, grew rich through trade, banking and manufacturing. Ancient Roman ruins were all around, a daily reminder of past greatness. Italy was divided into competing city-states whose rulers used art and architecture to show off their power. And after the fall of Constantinople to the Ottomans in 1453, Greek scholars fled to Italy, bringing ancient manuscripts with them.

sections.key: Rediscovering Greek and Roman texts inspired humanism, which celebrated human potential.
sections.b: Scholars hunted through monastery libraries for lost Greek and Roman writing on philosophy, history, science and poetry. This inspired humanism, an outlook that celebrated human potential, reason and achievement alongside religious devotion. Humanists believed a well-rounded education in subjects like grammar, rhetoric, history and moral philosophy produced better citizens. The poet Petrarch, often called the father of humanism, helped launch this revival in the 1300s. Our idea of the 'humanities' comes from it.

sections.key: Wealthy patrons like the Medici of Florence funded artists and scholars.
sections.b: Art needed money, and the Renaissance ran on patronage. The Medici family of Florence, who made their fortune in banking, paid artists, architects and scholars for generations. Popes in Rome commissioned huge projects, including the rebuilding of St Peter's Basilica. Guilds and wealthy merchants paid for church decorations to display both piety and status. Artists competed fiercely for these commissions, which pushed standards higher and higher.

sections.key: Artists mastered linear perspective and anatomy for realistic, deep-looking images.
sections.b: Around 1415, the architect Filippo Brunelleschi demonstrated linear perspective, a mathematical way of creating the illusion of depth on a flat surface, with lines converging on a vanishing point. Painters quickly adopted it. Artists also studied anatomy, sometimes by dissecting corpses, to paint realistic bodies, and used light and shadow to create volume. Leonardo da Vinci painted the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper; Michelangelo sculpted David and painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling; Raphael painted The School of Athens.

sections.key: Leonardo da Vinci embodied the 'Renaissance man', skilled in many fields.
sections.b: Leonardo da Vinci was a painter, engineer, anatomist, inventor and scientist. His notebooks, written in mirror script, contain designs for flying machines, armoured vehicles and diving suits, along with remarkably accurate anatomical drawings. He embodies the 'Renaissance man': someone skilled across many fields. The ideal was that a cultivated person should be able to discuss art, science, poetry and politics, not just specialise in one thing.

sections.key: The Renaissance fed the Scientific Revolution and the age of European exploration.
sections.b: The Renaissance spirit of questioning and observation spilled into science and exploration. In 1494 the mathematician Luca Pacioli, a friend of Leonardo, published the first printed explanation of double-entry bookkeeping, still the basis of accounting today. Mapmakers constantly redrew the world as new reports arrived. European navigators sailed to the Americas, around Africa and across the Pacific. These voyages brought wealth and knowledge to Europe, but also colonisation, conquest and devastating consequences for Indigenous peoples in the Americas and elsewhere.

sections.key: The printing press spread Renaissance ideas and paved the way for the modern world.
sections.b: The printing press, arriving in the mid-1400s, helped Renaissance ideas spread quickly. Books on art, architecture and ancient philosophy reached readers across Europe, and artists' engravings circulated widely. The period laid foundations for the Scientific Revolution, the Enlightenment and modern ideas about education and individual achievement. Walk through almost any old European city, or look at many grand public buildings in Australia with their columns and domes, and you'll see its influence.

quiz.q: What does 'Renaissance' mean?
quiz.e: It's French for 'rebirth'.

quiz.q: Which of these helped make Italy the birthplace of the Renaissance?
quiz.e: Trade and banking funded the arts.

quiz.q: What was humanism?
o: An outlook celebrating human potential and learning
quiz.e: Humanism celebrated human potential, inspired by ancient texts.

quiz.q: Which Florentine family were famous patrons of the arts?
quiz.e: The Medici funded many artists and scholars.

quiz.q: Which technique created the illusion of depth in paintings?
quiz.e: Brunelleschi demonstrated it around 1415.

LESSONS.title: Ancient Rome: from village to empire
LESSONS.hook: How a small town on the Tiber built an empire of tens of millions, and why you still use its words, laws and calendar.

sections.key: Rome was traditionally founded in 753 BC and became a republic in 509 BC.
sections.b: According to legend, Rome was founded in 753 BC by Romulus, who with his twin brother Remus had been raised by a she-wolf. In reality, it grew from a cluster of farming villages on hills beside the River Tiber in central Italy. For its first centuries it was ruled by kings. In 509 BC, the Romans expelled their last king and founded a republic, a system in which elected officials ran the state. They hated the idea of kings so much that the word 'king' remained an insult for centuries.

sections.key: The Republic had elected consuls and a Senate, with checks to stop any one person taking total power.
sections.b: The Roman Republic was designed to stop any one person grabbing total power. Two consuls were elected each year and could block each other. The Senate, made up of experienced former officials, advised and controlled finances. Citizen assemblies voted on laws and elected officials. Ordinary citizens, the plebeians, fought long political battles with the aristocratic patricians to win more rights. This system of checks inspired the founders of the United States and many modern democracies, including ideas behind Australia's Senate.

sections.key: Rome's disciplined legions and alliances let it conquer the Mediterranean world.
sections.b: Over several centuries, Rome conquered Italy, then defeated its great rival Carthage in the Punic Wars, including Hannibal, who famously crossed the Alps with elephants. Its armies were disciplined, well organised and relentless, and Rome was skilled at turning defeated enemies into allies and eventually citizens. At its height, around 117 AD under the emperor Trajan, the empire stretched from northern England to Egypt and from Spain to Iraq, home to perhaps 60 million people.

sections.h: Caesar and the fall of the Republic
sections.key: Julius Caesar seized power and was assassinated in 44 BC; the Republic collapsed into civil war.
sections.b: Conquest brought enormous wealth, but also inequality and ambitious generals with loyal armies. In 49 BC, Julius Caesar crossed the Rubicon river with his army, breaking Roman law and starting a civil war. He won and was made dictator for life. Fearing he'd become a king, a group of senators stabbed him to death on the Ides of March, 15 March 44 BC. Rather than saving the Republic, the murder triggered more civil wars.

sections.key: Augustus became the first emperor in 27 BC, beginning about two centuries of relative peace.
sections.b: Caesar's adopted heir, Octavian, won the civil wars and in 27 BC became Augustus, the first Roman emperor, though he was careful to keep the trappings of the Republic. His reign began the Pax Romana, about two centuries of relative peace and prosperity. Later emperors ranged from capable rulers like Trajan and Marcus Aurelius to notorious ones like Caligula and Nero. The month of August is named after Augustus, and July after Julius Caesar.

sections.key: Romans built vast road networks, aqueducts and concrete structures like the Pantheon.
sections.b: Romans were superb engineers. They built more than 80,000 kilometres of paved roads, allowing armies, traders and messages to move quickly; the phrase 'all roads lead to Rome' was nearly literal. Aqueducts carried fresh water many kilometres into cities for fountains, public baths and even toilets. Roman concrete was remarkably durable, and the dome of the Pantheon, completed around 125 AD, is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world.

sections.key: The Western Empire fell in 476 AD; the Eastern (Byzantine) Empire lasted until 1453.
sections.b: From the 200s AD, the empire faced civil wars, economic trouble, plague and pressure from peoples along its borders. It was eventually split into western and eastern halves. In 476 AD, the last western emperor, a teenager called Romulus Augustulus, was deposed by a Germanic general, a date often used to mark the fall of Rome. But the eastern half, based in Constantinople and later called the Byzantine Empire, survived for nearly another thousand years, until the Ottomans captured the city in 1453.

sections.key: Rome's legacy includes Latin-based languages, legal ideas, the calendar and Christianity's spread.
sections.b: Rome's influence is everywhere. Latin evolved into Italian, Spanish, French, Portuguese and Romanian, and supplies a huge share of English vocabulary. Roman law shaped the legal systems of much of Europe and concepts still used today. Our calendar descends from Julius Caesar's reforms. Christianity, adopted by the emperor Constantine in the 300s, spread across Europe partly through Roman networks. Even words like senate, republic, citizen and veto are Roman.

quiz.q: In what year did Rome traditionally become a republic?
quiz.e: Romans expelled their last king in 509 BC.

quiz.q: What happened on the Ides of March, 44 BC?
quiz.e: Senators killed Caesar, fearing he'd become king.

quiz.q: Who was the first Roman emperor?
quiz.e: Augustus took power in 27 BC.

quiz.q: What is special about the Pantheon's dome?
o: It's still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world
quiz.e: Roman concrete was remarkably durable.

quiz.q: When did the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire finally fall?
quiz.e: The Ottomans captured Constantinople in 1453.

LESSONS.title: The Black Death
LESSONS.hook: A plague that killed a third to a half of Europe, and accidentally helped end the medieval world.

sections.key: The Black Death reached Europe in 1347, probably via trade routes from Central Asia.
sections.b: In October 1347, trading ships docked at Messina in Sicily. Many aboard were dead or dying. The plague had travelled along trade routes from Central Asia, and within four years it swept across Europe, the Middle East and North Africa. People called it the great mortality or the pestilence; the name Black Death came later. Nothing in living memory had prepared them for it.

sections.key: The plague was caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, spread by fleas and, in some forms, person to person.
sections.b: We now know the Black Death was caused by a bacterium, Yersinia pestis, confirmed by DNA recovered from plague burial pits. It is usually spread by fleas that live on rats and other rodents. The bubonic form causes painful swollen lymph nodes, called buboes, in the groin, armpits and neck. When the infection reaches the lungs, it becomes pneumonic plague, which can spread from person to person through coughing and is almost always fatal without treatment. Some historians argue human fleas and lice also played a big role.

sections.key: Estimates suggest 30–50% of Europe's population died between 1347 and 1351.
sections.b: The scale is hard to imagine. Historians estimate that between 30% and 50% of Europe's population died between 1347 and 1351, perhaps 25 to 50 million people, with many more across Asia and Africa. Some towns lost more than half their people; some villages were abandoned entirely. Cities dug mass graves when churchyards filled. It took Europe's population around two centuries to recover, and the plague kept returning in waves for hundreds of years.

sections.key: Without understanding the cause, people blamed sin, bad air and outsiders, leading to terrible persecution.
sections.b: No one understood germs. Many believed the plague was God's punishment for sin, and groups of flagellants whipped themselves in public penance. Doctors blamed 'miasma', poisonous bad air, and carried sweet-smelling herbs. Terrifyingly, some communities blamed outsiders. Jewish people were falsely accused of poisoning wells, and in many towns across Europe, Jewish communities were massacred. It's a grim reminder of how fear during epidemics can turn into scapegoating.

sections.key: The word quarantine comes from the 40 days ships were isolated in Venice-controlled ports.
sections.b: Some responses were remarkably modern. In 1377, the city of Ragusa, now Dubrovnik in Croatia, required arriving ships and travellers to isolate for 30 days before entering. Venice and other ports later extended it to 40 days. The word quarantine comes from the Italian quaranta giorni, meaning 40 days. Cities also set up health boards, isolated the sick in special hospitals and restricted travel from infected areas, ideas still used in public health today.

sections.key: Labour shortages after the plague raised wages and weakened the feudal system.
sections.b: The survivors inherited a changed world. With so many workers dead, labour became scarce and valuable. Peasants demanded higher wages and better conditions, and many moved to wherever pay was best. Landowners and governments tried to freeze wages by law, such as England's Statute of Labourers in 1351, which fuelled anger that later exploded in the Peasants' Revolt of 1381. Over time, the old feudal system, where peasants were tied to a lord's land, weakened.

sections.key: The plague shaped art, religion and medicine, and some historians link it to the Renaissance.
sections.b: Art became preoccupied with death, with images of skeletons dancing with people of every rank. Faith in the Church was shaken because prayer seemed useless. Medicine began, slowly, to rely more on observation. Some historians argue that higher wages and wealth concentrated in fewer hands helped fund the Renaissance. Others link labour shortages to experiments with labour-saving technology. Big historical shocks often have consequences no one could predict at the time.

sections.key: Plague still exists but is rare and treatable with antibiotics.
sections.b: Plague hasn't disappeared. It still lives in wild rodent populations in parts of Africa, Asia and the Americas, including the western United States, and there are a few hundred to a few thousand human cases worldwide each year. The difference is that it can now be treated with common antibiotics if caught early. Studying the Black Death helped scientists understand how diseases spread along trade routes, lessons that became very relevant again during COVID-19.

quiz.q: What caused the Black Death?
quiz.e: DNA from burial pits confirmed Yersinia pestis.

quiz.q: Roughly what share of Europe's population died?
quiz.e: Estimates range from about a third to a half.

quiz.q: Which city first required arriving ships and travellers to isolate before entering, in 1377?
quiz.e: Ragusa required 30 days of isolation; Venice and other ports later extended it to 40.

quiz.q: What happened to wages after the plague?
o: They rose because workers were scarce
quiz.e: Labour shortages gave surviving workers bargaining power.

quiz.q: How is plague treated today?
quiz.e: Common antibiotics work if given early.

LESSONS.title: The Industrial Revolution
LESSONS.hook: For most of history, almost everyone was a farmer. Then, in about a century, machines changed everything.

sections.key: Starting in Britain around 1760, machines and fossil fuels transformed how people worked and lived.
sections.b: For thousands of years, most people lived in villages and worked the land, and living standards barely changed from one century to the next. Starting in Britain around 1760, that began to change. Machines powered first by water and then by coal-fired steam replaced hand tools. Production moved from homes into factories. Over the next century, the change spread to Europe, North America and beyond. Historians often call it the most important change in human life since the invention of farming.

sections.key: Britain had coal, capital, colonies, inventors and a large trading market.
sections.b: Britain had a combination of advantages. It had plentiful coal and iron ore, often close together. It had banks and investors willing to fund new ventures, a large trading empire supplying raw materials like cotton and buying finished goods, and relatively stable politics. Wages in Britain were high and coal was cheap, which made labour-saving machines especially worth inventing. Much of the cotton came from plantations worked by enslaved people in the Americas, a dark foundation of the new wealth.

sections.key: Textile machines like the spinning jenny and water frame created the first factories.
sections.b: The revolution began in textiles. Inventions like James Hargreaves' spinning jenny (around 1764) and Richard Arkwright's water frame let one worker spin many threads at once. Arkwright's mill at Cromford, opened in 1771, is often called the first modern factory, with workers arriving for set shifts to tend machines. Output soared and cloth became cheap. For workers, it meant long hours, strict discipline and dangerous machinery.

sections.key: Smelting iron with coke instead of charcoal, pioneered by Abraham Darby in 1709, made iron cheap and plentiful.
sections.b: Iron was the backbone of the new machines, but traditional ironmaking needed charcoal, and Britain's woodlands were running short. In 1709 Abraham Darby, a Quaker ironmaster at Coalbrookdale in Shropshire, succeeded in smelting iron with coke, coal that has been baked to drive off impurities. Britain had coal in abundance, so iron could now be made on a far larger scale and more cheaply. In 1779 his grandson, Abraham Darby III, built the world's first major cast-iron bridge across the River Severn nearby; it still stands, and gave the town of Ironbridge its name. Cheap iron went into engines, machinery, rails and ships, and deep coal mining boomed to feed the furnaces.

sections.key: Railways, from the 1820s–30s, made travel and transport dramatically faster and cheaper.
sections.b: The Stockton and Darlington Railway opened in 1825, and the Liverpool and Manchester Railway in 1830 became the first to run regular passenger services entirely by steam. Within decades, railways crossed Britain, Europe and America. Journeys that took days by horse took hours. Goods, food, mail and newspapers moved quickly and cheaply. Railways even standardised time: towns had kept their own local time until timetables demanded a single national time.

sections.key: Rapid urbanisation brought crowded slums, child labour and disease, followed by reforms.
sections.b: People poured from the countryside into cities like Manchester, which grew from a market town to one of the world's first industrial cities. Housing was cramped, dirty and poorly built; diseases like cholera spread through contaminated water. Children as young as five or six worked in mills and mines. Over time, reformers pushed back. Britain's Factory Acts from 1833 limited child labour, public health laws brought sewers and clean water, and trade unions fought for better wages and shorter hours.

sections.key: Living standards were mixed at first but rose dramatically over the long run.
sections.b: Historians still debate how quickly ordinary people benefited. For the first generations, wages rose slowly while conditions in cities were often grim, and life expectancy in industrial towns was low. But over the long run, the gains were enormous. Productivity kept climbing, goods became cheaper, and incomes in industrialised countries rose many times over. Most of the extraordinary rise in global living standards since 1800 traces back to the processes that started in those British mills.

sections.key: Industrialisation created modern prosperity and also began large-scale fossil fuel emissions.
sections.b: The Industrial Revolution created the modern world: factories, cities, mass-produced goods, railways, the middle class, and eventually electricity, cars and computers. It also began the large-scale burning of coal, then oil and gas. Carbon dioxide in the atmosphere has risen from about 280 parts per million before industrialisation to over 420 today, driving climate change. Many argue we're now living through the next great transition: from fossil fuels to clean energy.

quiz.q: Where and roughly when did the Industrial Revolution begin?
quiz.e: It started in Britain in the second half of the 1700s.

quiz.q: Which industry led the early Industrial Revolution?
quiz.e: Spinning and weaving machines came first.

quiz.q: What did Abraham Darby use to smelt iron at Coalbrookdale from 1709?
quiz.e: Coke let Britain use its plentiful coal, making iron far cheaper.

quiz.q: Which railway first ran regular passenger services entirely by steam?
quiz.e: It opened in 1830.

quiz.q: About how much CO₂ was in the atmosphere before industrialisation?
quiz.e: It has risen from about 280 to over 420 parts per million.

LESSONS.title: World War I and the ANZACs
LESSONS.hook: The war that was meant to be over by Christmas lasted four years, killed millions and shaped Australia's sense of itself.

sections.key: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand on 28 June 1914 triggered the war.
