sections.b: On 28 June 1914, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary, was shot dead in Sarajevo by Gavrilo Princip, a young Bosnian Serb nationalist. Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia and declared war a month later. Within days, a chain reaction dragged in the great powers of Europe. What began as a regional crisis became a world war, fought from Belgium to the Middle East and across the oceans.

sections.key: Alliances, militarism, imperial rivalry and nationalism turned a local crisis into a world war.
sections.b: Historians point to several underlying causes. Europe was divided into two alliance blocs: Germany and Austria-Hungary on one side; France, Russia and Britain on the other. Countries had built up huge armies and detailed war plans that relied on mobilising quickly. Empires competed for colonies and naval power, and nationalism ran high. Russia backed Serbia, Germany backed Austria-Hungary, and when Germany invaded neutral Belgium to attack France, Britain declared war. As part of the British Empire, Australia was automatically at war.

sections.key: On the Western Front, trench warfare created a deadly stalemate for years.
sections.b: Everyone expected a short war. Instead, by late 1914 the Western Front had become a line of trenches stretching from the Belgian coast to Switzerland. Machine guns, barbed wire and artillery made attacking across 'no man's land' suicidal, and huge offensives gained only a few kilometres at enormous cost. On the first day of the Battle of the Somme in 1916, the British Army suffered about 57,000 casualties. Soldiers lived with mud, rats, lice, disease and constant shelling.

sections.key: On 25 April 1915, ANZAC troops landed at Gallipoli; about 8,700 Australians died there.
sections.b: In 1915, the Allies tried to knock the Ottoman Empire out of the war by seizing the Dardanelles strait. On 25 April, troops of the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps, the ANZACs, landed at what became known as Anzac Cove on the Gallipoli peninsula. They faced steep cliffs and determined Ottoman defenders. The campaign dragged on for eight months before the Allies withdrew in December. About 8,700 Australians died there. The day of the landing became Anzac Day.

sections.key: About 417,000 Australians enlisted from under 5 million people; around 60,000 died.
sections.b: Australia had fewer than five million people, yet about 417,000 men enlisted, all volunteers; two referendums on conscription were narrowly defeated. More than 60,000 Australians died and around 156,000 were wounded, gassed or taken prisoner, among the highest casualty rates of any army in the war. Most Australian deaths came on the Western Front in France and Belgium, at places like Pozières, Fromelles and Passchendaele. More than 1,000 Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander men served too, despite facing discrimination at home.

sections.key: WWI introduced poison gas, tanks, aircraft and submarines to large-scale warfare.
sections.b: The war was an industrial conflict that introduced terrible new weapons. Poison gas, first used on a large scale in 1915, caused blindness, burns and suffocation. Tanks appeared at the Somme in 1916. Aircraft moved from scouting to dogfights and bombing. German submarines sank merchant ships, and their attacks on shipping helped bring the United States into the war in 1917. Medicine advanced too, with blood transfusions, better surgery and new understanding of what was then called 'shell shock'.

sections.key: The armistice took effect at 11 am on 11 November 1918; about 20 million people died.
sections.b: In 1917, Russia collapsed into revolution and left the war, but American troops and resources tipped the balance towards the Allies. Germany's final offensives in 1918 failed, its allies surrendered and its people were starving. An armistice took effect at 11 am on 11 November 1918, the 'eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month', now marked as Remembrance Day. Around 20 million soldiers and civilians had died, and the flu pandemic that followed killed tens of millions more.

sections.key: The Treaty of Versailles punished Germany and helped set the stage for WWII.
sections.b: The 1919 Treaty of Versailles forced Germany to accept blame, give up territory and colonies, limit its army and pay heavy reparations. Australian Prime Minister Billy Hughes was there and fought for Australia to control German New Guinea. Four empires, the German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman, had collapsed, redrawing maps across Europe and the Middle East. Many Germans resented the treaty bitterly, and that resentment helped fuel the rise of Hitler and a second, even deadlier world war just 20 years later.

quiz.q: Which event triggered World War I?
o: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand
quiz.e: He was shot in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914.

quiz.q: When did the ANZACs land at Gallipoli?
quiz.e: 25 April is now Anzac Day.

quiz.q: About how many Australians died in World War I?
quiz.e: More than 60,000, from a population under five million.

quiz.q: What made attacking on the Western Front so deadly?
o: Machine guns, barbed wire and artillery
quiz.e: Defensive weapons made trench attacks suicidal.

quiz.q: At what time did the WWI armistice take effect?
quiz.e: The eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month.

LESSONS.title: The Cold War
LESSONS.hook: For over 40 years, two superpowers came close to destroying the world without ever fighting each other directly.

sections.key: After WWII, the US and Soviet Union became rival superpowers with opposing systems.
sections.b: The United States and the Soviet Union fought on the same side in World War II, but they had little else in common. The US was a capitalist democracy; the USSR was a communist one-party state. As the war ended, Soviet forces controlled Eastern Europe and installed communist governments there. In 1946, Winston Churchill warned that an 'iron curtain' had descended across Europe. The Cold War, roughly 1947 to 1991, was called 'cold' because the two superpowers never fought each other directly.

sections.key: Germany was split, NATO and the Warsaw Pact formed, and the Berlin Wall stood from 1961 to 1989.
sections.b: Germany was split into a democratic West and communist East. Berlin, deep inside East Germany, was split too. In 1948–49, the Soviets blockaded West Berlin, and the Western allies supplied the city entirely by air for almost a year. In 1949, the US and Western European countries formed the NATO military alliance; the Soviet bloc answered with the Warsaw Pact in 1955. In 1961, East Germany built the Berlin Wall to stop its citizens fleeing west. It stood until 1989.

sections.key: Both sides built tens of thousands of nuclear weapons under the logic of mutually assured destruction.
sections.b: The US had used atomic bombs in 1945; the Soviet Union tested its own in 1949. Both sides then raced to build more and bigger weapons, including hydrogen bombs thousands of times more powerful than the Hiroshima bomb. At the peak in the mid-1980s, there were around 70,000 nuclear warheads in the world. The strategy of mutually assured destruction, aptly abbreviated MAD, held that neither side would attack because it would be destroyed in return. Schoolchildren practised 'duck and cover' drills.

sections.key: In October 1962, Soviet missiles in Cuba brought the world closer to nuclear war than ever.
sections.b: In October 1962, US spy planes discovered Soviet nuclear missiles being installed in Cuba, just 145 kilometres from Florida. For thirteen tense days, the world stood on the edge of nuclear war. President John F. Kennedy ordered a naval blockade of Cuba. Eventually Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles in exchange for a US promise not to invade Cuba and a secret deal to remove US missiles from Turkey. Afterwards, a direct hotline was set up between Washington and Moscow.

sections.key: The superpowers fought indirectly through proxy wars, including Korea and Vietnam, where Australians served.
sections.b: Instead of fighting each other, the superpowers backed opposing sides in conflicts around the world. The Korean War (1950–53) ended in a stalemate that still divides the peninsula. In the Vietnam War, the US fought to stop the communist North taking over the South; about 60,000 Australians served there between 1962 and 1973, and 523 died. The war sparked huge protests in Australia, including over conscription. Proxy conflicts also raged in Afghanistan, Angola and Latin America.

sections.key: The USSR launched Sputnik (1957) and Gagarin (1961); the US landed on the Moon in 1969.
sections.b: Rivalry extended into space. In 1957, the Soviet Union shocked the world by launching Sputnik, the first artificial satellite. In 1961, Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space. The US poured money into NASA, and on 20 July 1969, Apollo 11 landed Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin on the Moon, with the world watching on television. Australia played a part: tracking stations at Honeysuckle Creek and the Parkes radio telescope helped broadcast those first pictures.

sections.h: The end of the Cold War
sections.key: Reforms under Gorbachev, the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989 and the USSR's dissolution in 1991 ended it.
sections.b: By the 1980s, the Soviet economy was struggling. Mikhail Gorbachev, who became Soviet leader in 1985, introduced reforms known as glasnost (openness) and perestroika (restructuring), and signed arms reduction treaties with US President Ronald Reagan. In 1989, peaceful revolutions swept Eastern Europe, and on 9 November crowds began tearing down the Berlin Wall. Germany reunified in 1990, and on 26 December 1991 the Soviet Union officially dissolved into 15 separate countries.

sections.key: Cold War legacies include NATO, nuclear arsenals, space technology and today's geopolitical tensions.
sections.b: The Cold War's legacy is all around us. NATO still exists and has expanded. Thousands of nuclear weapons remain, though far fewer than at the peak. Technologies developed for the rivalry, such as satellites, GPS and the early internet, now run everyday life. Many of today's tensions, from Ukraine to Korea, have roots in Cold War divisions. Understanding it helps make sense of the news.

quiz.q: Why was it called the 'Cold' War?
o: The superpowers never fought each other directly
It took place in the Arctic
quiz.e: They competed through arms races and proxy wars instead.

quiz.q: When did the Berlin Wall fall?
quiz.e: Crowds began tearing it down on 9 November 1989.

quiz.q: What does MAD stand for?
quiz.e: Neither side would attack because it would be destroyed in return.

quiz.q: What was Sputnik?
quiz.e: Launched by the USSR in 1957.

quiz.q: When did the Soviet Union dissolve?
quiz.e: On 26 December 1991.

LESSONS.title: The world's oldest continuous cultures
LESSONS.hook: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have lived in Australia for tens of thousands of years. Here's what that history includes.

sections.key: Aboriginal people have lived in Australia for at least 50,000 years, possibly 65,000.
sections.b: Aboriginal people have lived on the Australian continent for at least 50,000 years, and excavations at Madjedbebe in Arnhem Land suggest people may have been there around 65,000 years ago. That makes Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cultures among the oldest continuous living cultures on Earth. To put it in perspective, people were living in Australia tens of thousands of years before the last Ice Age ended, and long before the pyramids, farming in the Middle East or the first cities.

sections.key: The first Australians crossed open sea from South-East Asia, among the earliest ocean voyages known.
sections.b: During the Ice Age, sea levels were much lower, and Australia, New Guinea and Tasmania were joined in one landmass called Sahul. But even then, reaching it from South-East Asia required crossing open sea. That makes the arrival of the first Australians one of the earliest known deliberate ocean voyages by humans anywhere. Over thousands of years, people spread across the entire continent, adapting to rainforests, deserts, coasts, alpine areas and tropical islands.

sections.key: Before 1788 there were more than 250 languages and hundreds of distinct nations or clan groups.
sections.b: Aboriginal Australia was never one culture. Before British colonisation in 1788, there were hundreds of distinct nations or clan groups, each with its own country, laws, customs and kinship systems. More than 250 languages were spoken, with around 800 dialects. The Torres Strait Islands, between Cape York and Papua New Guinea, have their own distinct Melanesian cultures. Many Aboriginal words are now part of Australian English, like kangaroo, koala, billabong, yakka and boomerang.

sections.key: Connection to Country is central; cultural burning (fire-stick farming) shaped landscapes for millennia.
sections.b: For Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, Country means much more than land. It includes waters, skies, plants, animals, ancestors and stories, all connected, with responsibilities to care for it. People managed landscapes skilfully, for example through cultural burning, sometimes called fire-stick farming: frequent small, cool fires that reduced fuel, encouraged fresh growth and attracted game. Today, fire agencies increasingly work with Traditional Owners to bring cultural burning back as a way of reducing bushfire risk.

sections.key: Sites like the Budj Bim eel traps show sophisticated engineering thousands of years old.
sections.b: At Budj Bim in western Victoria, the Gunditjmara people built a system of channels, weirs and ponds to trap and farm short-finned eels, dating back at least 6,600 years. It's one of the oldest known aquaculture systems in the world and was listed as World Heritage in 2019. Stone fish traps at Brewarrina in New South Wales are also thought to be extremely old. Knowledge of seasons, plants, medicine and the night sky was passed down through generations.

sections.key: Songlines encode maps, laws and knowledge in song, story, dance and art.
sections.b: Aboriginal cultures kept knowledge not in books but in song, story, dance and art. Songlines, also called dreaming tracks, trace the journeys of ancestral beings across the land. They work as maps, laws, histories and guides to water and food, and some stretch across the continent, linking many different language groups. Researchers have found that some oral traditions accurately describe events such as rising sea levels at the end of the Ice Age, suggesting stories passed down for thousands of years.

sections.key: British colonisation from 1788 brought dispossession, disease, frontier violence and the Stolen Generations.
sections.b: In 1788, Britain established a colony at Sydney Cove on the basis that the land belonged to no one, a legal idea known as terra nullius. Colonisation brought devastating consequences: introduced diseases like smallpox, loss of land and water, frontier violence including massacres, and laws that controlled where Aboriginal people could live and work. Throughout much of the 20th century, many children were removed from their families by governments and churches. They are known as the Stolen Generations.

sections.key: Key moments include the 1967 referendum, Mabo (1992) and the 2008 National Apology.
sections.b: Change came through decades of activism. In the 1967 referendum, over 90% of Australians voted to count Aboriginal people in the census and let the federal government make laws for them. In 1992, the High Court's Mabo decision, won by Torres Strait Islander Eddie Mabo, rejected terra nullius and recognised native title. In 2008, Prime Minister Kevin Rudd delivered a National Apology to the Stolen Generations. Today, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cultures are living cultures, and gaps in areas like health and life expectancy remain a national focus.

quiz.q: For at least how long have Aboriginal people lived in Australia?
quiz.e: At least 50,000 years, possibly around 65,000.

quiz.q: About how many languages were spoken in Australia before 1788?
quiz.e: More than 250 languages, with around 800 dialects.

quiz.q: What is cultural burning?
o: Frequent small, cool fires to manage the land
quiz.e: It reduces fuel and encourages new growth.

quiz.q: What are the Budj Bim structures used for?
quiz.e: An eel aquaculture system at least 6,600 years old.

quiz.q: What did the 1992 Mabo decision do?
o: Rejected terra nullius and recognised native title
quiz.e: It recognised that Indigenous people had rights to land before colonisation.

LESSONS.title: How to negotiate
LESSONS.hook: Salaries, rent, car prices, bedtimes: life is full of negotiations. A few principles reliably change the outcome.

sections.key: Negotiation is two sides working out an agreement; a few principles make a big difference.
sections.b: Negotiation is simply two or more sides working out an agreement. Whether it's a pay rise, a second-hand car, a phone bill or who does the dishes, you're negotiating. Many people avoid it because it feels awkward or confrontational, and they leave real money on the table. Studies of salary offers find that people who negotiate often get more, and employers generally expect it. A handful of principles, most from the Harvard Negotiation Project, make a big difference.

sections.key: Research the market, know what you want and plan your walk-away point before you start.
sections.b: Most negotiations are won before they start. Research the market: what do similar jobs pay, what have similar cars sold for, what are competitors offering? Websites, job ads and industry salary surveys help. Decide your target, the outcome you're aiming for, and your walk-away point, the worst deal you'll accept. Anticipate the other side's concerns and questions. Preparation gives you confidence and stops you making decisions on the spot under pressure.

sections.key: Your BATNA is your best alternative if no deal is reached; a strong one gives you power.
sections.b: Your BATNA is your 'best alternative to a negotiated agreement': what you'll do if this deal falls through. The term comes from the 1981 book Getting to Yes by Roger Fisher and William Ury. If you have another job offer, your BATNA is strong; if you'd be unemployed, it's weak. The stronger your alternative, the more confidently you can push, and the more clearly you'll know when to walk away. Improving your BATNA, for example by getting another quote, is often the smartest move.

sections.key: A position is what someone asks for; an interest is why. Find the interests.
sections.b: A position is what someone says they want. An interest is why they want it. The classic story: two sisters argue over one orange and finally cut it in half. One eats the fruit and throws away the peel; the other uses the peel for baking and throws away the fruit. If they'd asked why, both could have had all they needed. Asking 'What's most important to you here?' uncovers room for creative deals, like a later start date in exchange for a higher salary.

sections.key: A well-researched first offer anchors the conversation; back it with a reason.
sections.b: The first number on the table tends to anchor the whole conversation. If you've done your research, it often pays to make the first offer, aiming ambitious but defensible, and to back it with a reason: 'Similar roles pay $95,000 to $105,000, and I bring X, so I'm looking for $102,000.' Reasons make numbers feel legitimate. If the other side anchors first with an unreasonable figure, don't argue about it; calmly re-anchor with your own researched number.

sections.key: Ask open questions, name the other side's feelings, and get comfortable with silence.
sections.b: Former FBI negotiator Chris Voss recommends 'labelling': naming the other side's feelings, like 'It sounds like budgets are tight this year.' It shows you're listening, builds trust and often draws out useful information. Ask open questions: 'How am I supposed to do that?' invites them to solve your problem. After making an offer, stop talking. Silence feels uncomfortable, and the other person will often fill it, sometimes with a better offer.

sections.key: Never give something for nothing; trade concessions and look beyond price.
sections.b: Avoid simply splitting the difference or giving ground for nothing. Every concession should buy something: 'I can do that price if you include delivery.' Look beyond the headline number. In a job negotiation, there's leave, flexibility, training, title and start date. When buying a car, there are accessories, servicing and warranty. Give ground on what's cheap for you but valuable to them, and ask for things that are cheap for them but valuable to you.

sections.h: A deal both can live with
sections.key: Aim for agreements both sides can live with; resentful deals fall apart.
sections.b: If the other side feels cheated, they may not follow through, may resent you in a job you'll hold for years, or may never deal with you again. Most negotiations are with people we'll meet again, so relationships matter. Aim for an agreement both sides can live with, be firm on substance and friendly with people, and get the final deal in writing. And remember your walk-away point: sometimes the best negotiation is the one where you politely say no.

quiz.q: What is a BATNA?
o: Your best alternative if no deal is reached
quiz.e: It's your fallback and your source of leverage.

quiz.q: What's the difference between a position and an interest?
o: A position is what you ask for; an interest is why you want it
quiz.e: Interests reveal creative solutions.

quiz.q: Why can it help to make the first offer?
quiz.e: First numbers pull later ones towards them.

quiz.q: What should you usually do right after making an offer?
o: Stay quiet and let them respond
quiz.e: Silence often works in your favour.

quiz.q: What's the principle behind 'trade, don't just concede'?
o: Every concession should get something in return
quiz.e: Give ground on what's cheap for you and valuable to them.

LESSONS.title: How scams work, and how to beat them
LESSONS.hook: Australians lose billions to scams. Scammers aren't targeting the gullible; they're targeting everyone, using the same few tricks.

sections.key: Scams target everyone; they succeed through pressure and emotion, not stupidity.
sections.b: Australians reported losing about $2.18 billion to scams in 2025, and many losses go unreported. Scams aren't only aimed at the elderly or naive; young adults are frequently targeted, especially through social media and job and investment scams. Scammers are organised, professional and constantly adapting. They succeed not because victims are foolish but because they exploit universal emotions: fear, urgency, greed, love and the desire to help. Knowing the patterns is the best defence.

sections.key: Scammers pretend to be banks, government agencies, delivery firms or family members.
sections.b: Most scams start with impersonation. Scammers pretend to be your bank, the ATO, myGov, Australia Post, a toll company, a phone provider or the police. Until mid-2026, scam texts could even land in the same thread as genuine messages by spoofing sender names; since July 2026, texts using an unregistered sender name are marked 'Unverified', but scammers keep adapting, so don't rely on that alone. A notorious version is the 'Hi Mum' scam, where someone claims to be your child on a new number and urgently needs money. Always verify using contact details you find yourself, never the ones in the message.

sections.key: Urgency, secrecy, unusual payment methods and requests for codes or passwords are red flags.
sections.b: Scams share tell-tale signs. You're rushed: act now or your account will be closed, you'll be arrested, the offer disappears. You're asked to keep it secret. You're asked to pay in unusual ways: gift cards, cryptocurrency, wire transfers or to a 'safe account'. You're asked for passwords, one-time codes or remote access to your computer. The deal seems too good to be true. Any one of these should make you stop. Genuine organisations won't pressure you this way.

sections.key: Investment scams promise high, guaranteed returns, often via social media, fake ads or 'mentors'.
sections.b: Investment scams cause the biggest losses. They often start with fake ads featuring celebrities or well-known Australians, or a friendly stranger on social media or a dating app who shares their 'success' trading crypto. Victims are shown professional-looking platforms with fake profits, encouraged to invest more, then find they can't withdraw. Warning signs: guaranteed high returns, pressure to invest quickly, and unlicensed operators. Check whether a company holds an Australian Financial Services licence on ASIC's professional register.

sections.key: Romance scammers build trust over weeks before asking for money; fake jobs demand upfront payments.
sections.b: Romance scammers build relationships online over weeks or months, often claiming to work overseas, in the military or on oil rigs. They avoid video calls, then eventually ask for money for an emergency, travel or an investment opportunity. Job scams offer easy money for simple online tasks like rating products, then ask you to deposit money to 'unlock' earnings. Rule of thumb: never send money to someone you've only met online, and a real job never asks you to pay to work.

sections.key: Never let a caller access your device, and banks never ask you to move money to a 'safe account'.
sections.b: In remote access scams, a caller claims to be from your telco, bank or a tech company, says your computer or account has been hacked, and asks you to install software so they can 'fix' it. Once in, they can access your banking. In 'safe account' scams, a fake bank officer says your money is at risk and must be moved to a new account, which they control. No genuine bank or tech company will ask you to do either. Hang up and call the organisation yourself.

sections.key: Stop and slow down, check independently, and protect yourself by acting fast if something's wrong.
sections.b: Australia's National Anti-Scam Centre recommends three steps. Stop: don't give money or information if you're unsure; scammers rely on rushing you. Check: ask yourself if the message could be fake, and contact the organisation using details from its official website or app, not the message. Talk to someone you trust; a second opinion breaks the spell. Protect: act quickly if something feels wrong. Use two-factor authentication and strong, unique passwords to reduce the damage if details leak.

sections.key: Contact your bank immediately, then report to Scamwatch and ReportCyber; IDCARE can help.
sections.b: If you've been scammed, act fast and don't be embarrassed; it happens to smart people every day. Contact your bank or card provider immediately; they may be able to stop or recover payments. Change compromised passwords. Report it to Scamwatch (scamwatch.gov.au), and cybercrime to ReportCyber (cyber.gov.au). If your identity documents were exposed, contact IDCARE (1800 595 160), a free national support service. Beware of 'recovery' scammers who contact victims promising to get their money back for a fee.

quiz.q: Which of these is a classic scam red flag?
o: A request to pay by gift card or crypto
quiz.e: Unusual payment methods are a major warning sign.

quiz.q: What's the 'Hi Mum' scam?
o: A scammer pretends to be your child on a new number
quiz.e: Always verify on a number you already know.

quiz.q: Where can you check whether an investment company is licensed?
quiz.e: Legitimate advisers and dealers hold an AFS licence.

quiz.q: Your 'bank' calls asking you to move money to a safe account. What should you do?
o: Hang up and call your bank on its official number
quiz.e: Banks never ask you to do this.

quiz.q: What should you do first if you've been scammed?
quiz.e: Speed can help stop or recover payments.

LESSONS.title: Stay safe online
LESSONS.hook: A few simple habits stop the vast majority of account takeovers, and most take only minutes to set up.

sections.key: Attackers target everyone automatically; your accounts, data and identity all have value.
sections.b: Many people think, 'Why would a hacker want my stuff?' But most attacks aren't personal. Criminals use automated tools to try millions of stolen passwords, send millions of phishing messages and scan for unpatched devices. Your email account alone can be used to reset passwords for your bank, shopping and social media. Stolen identities are sold and used for fraud. Australia has seen major data breaches, like Optus and Medibank in 2022, exposing millions of people's details.

sections.key: Use long passphrases and never reuse a password.
sections.b: Length beats complexity. A passphrase of four or more random words, like 'purple-kettle-marathon-cactus', is easier to remember and much harder to crack than a short jumble like P@ssw0rd1. The most important rule is never reuse passwords. When one website is breached, attackers automatically try the same email and password on banks, email and shopping sites, a technique called credential stuffing. Your email password is the most important of all; make it unique and strong.

sections.key: A password manager creates and stores a unique strong password for every account.
sections.b: Nobody can remember 100 unique strong passwords. A password manager solves this: it generates a random password for each site, stores them securely, and fills them in for you. You only remember one strong master password. Good password managers are built into Apple and Google devices and browsers, and dedicated apps are also available. They also help protect against phishing, because they won't autofill your password on a fake website with the wrong address.

sections.key: Two-factor authentication adds a second login step, so a stolen password isn't enough.
sections.b: Two-factor (or multi-factor) authentication, often called 2FA or MFA, adds a second step when you log in, such as a code from an authenticator app, a text message code, a fingerprint or a security key. Even if someone steals your password, they can't get in without that second factor. Turn it on for your email, banking, myGov, social media and shopping accounts. Authenticator apps are more secure than text messages. And never share a code with anyone who asks for it.

sections.key: Phishing uses urgency, threats and fake links; go to the official site or app directly.
sections.b: Phishing messages pretend to come from organisations you trust to trick you into clicking a link, opening an attachment or entering details. Warning signs include urgency or threats, generic greetings, odd sender addresses, spelling mistakes and links that don't match the real website. But modern phishing can look flawless. The safest habit: don't click links in unexpected messages. Instead, open the official app or type the website address yourself. myGov, for example, says it will never send you a link to sign in.

sections.key: Automatic updates patch security holes attackers already know about.
sections.b: Software updates often patch security holes that attackers already know about and actively exploit. The Australian Signals Directorate lists patching applications and operating systems among its most important cyber security strategies. Turn on automatic updates for your phone, computer, browser and apps. Don't ignore update prompts for weeks. Old devices that no longer receive security updates, like very old phones and routers, are a risk and worth replacing when practical.

sections.key: Back up important files, lock your devices and be careful on public Wi-Fi.
sections.b: Ransomware and device failure can wipe out photos and documents. Back up important files regularly, ideally automatically to the cloud and to an external drive. Lock your phone and computer with a PIN, password or biometrics, and turn on 'find my device' so you can locate or wipe a lost one. Public Wi-Fi is less risky than it used to be, since most websites are encrypted, but avoid banking on unknown networks and use your mobile data when in doubt.

sections.key: Limit what you share publicly; details like birthdays and pet names help scammers.
sections.b: Scammers and identity thieves piece together information from social media: your birthday, hometown, school, pet's name and holiday dates. These are often the answers to security questions or useful for impersonation. Review your privacy settings, limit what's public and think before posting in real time that you're away from home. Be sceptical of quizzes asking for personal details. If an organisation you use suffers a data breach, change that password and watch for follow-up scams.

quiz.q: Which is the strongest password?
o: A long passphrase of random words
quiz.e: Length beats complexity.

quiz.q: Why shouldn't you reuse passwords?
o: A breach at one site exposes other accounts
quiz.e: Attackers try leaked logins everywhere (credential stuffing).

quiz.q: What does two-factor authentication add?
o: A second step, like an app code, when logging in
quiz.e: A stolen password alone isn't enough.

quiz.q: What's the safest response to an unexpected message with a login link?
o: Open the official app or type the address yourself
quiz.e: Never log in through links in unexpected messages.

quiz.q: Why install updates promptly?
quiz.e: Unpatched software is an easy target.

LESSONS.title: First aid basics: DRSABCD
LESSONS.hook: The seven steps that could help you save a life. An overview to build confidence, not a replacement for a proper course.

sections.key: Australian first aid follows DRSABCD; a hands-on course is the best way to learn.
sections.b: Knowing what to do in the first few minutes of an emergency can save a life. When someone's heart stops, every minute without CPR sharply reduces their chance of survival, and ambulances can take several minutes or more to arrive. In Australia, first aid follows an action plan called DRSABCD, from the Australian Resuscitation Council. This lesson is an overview only. A hands-on course, from organisations such as St John Ambulance or Australian Red Cross, is the best way to learn properly and practise on a manikin.

sections.key: Check for danger to yourself, bystanders and the casualty before approaching.
sections.b: Before rushing in, check for danger to yourself, bystanders and the injured person: traffic, fire, electricity, deep water, falling objects or aggressive people. You can't help anyone if you become a casualty yourself. If it's safe, approach. If not, and you can't make it safe, call for help and keep your distance. Wear gloves if available when dealing with blood or bodily fluids.

sections.key: Check for a response by talking to the person and squeezing their shoulders.
sections.b: Check whether the person responds. Use the COWS approach: can you hear me, open your eyes, what's your name, squeeze my hand. Speak loudly and firmly squeeze their shoulders. If they respond, they're conscious: make them comfortable, check for injuries, call for help if needed and monitor them. If there's no response, move straight on to getting help and checking their airway and breathing.

sections.key: Call Triple Zero (000); the operator will guide you. 112 also works from mobiles.
sections.b: If the person is unresponsive, call Triple Zero (000), or ask a bystander to call while you help. From a mobile, 112 also works. Ask for an ambulance and put the phone on speaker. The operator will ask questions and can guide you step by step through what to do, including CPR, so you're not alone. If there's an AED (defibrillator) nearby, send someone to get it immediately; many are listed on apps and at shopping centres, gyms and sporting clubs.

sections.key: Open the mouth, check for blockages and roll the person onto their side to clear them if needed.
sections.b: Open the person's mouth and look for anything blocking the airway, such as vomit, blood, food or loose teeth. If there's something there, roll them onto their side and clear it with your fingers. Then, with the person on their back, open the airway by gently tilting the head back and lifting the chin. For babies, keep the head in a neutral position rather than tilting it back.

sections.key: Look, listen and feel for normal breathing for up to 10 seconds; if breathing, use the recovery position.
sections.b: Look for the chest rising and falling, listen for breathing and feel for breath on your cheek, for up to 10 seconds. Occasional gasping is not normal breathing and can happen in the first minutes after cardiac arrest. If the person is breathing normally, place them in the recovery position, on their side with the top leg bent, which keeps the airway clear, and keep watching them until help arrives. If they're not breathing normally, start CPR.

sections.key: If the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally, start CPR straight away.
sections.b: CPR, short for cardiopulmonary resuscitation, is the C in DRSABCD. It combines chest compressions with rescue breaths to keep some oxygen-carrying blood flowing to the brain and heart. CPR on its own rarely restarts a stopped heart, but it buys precious time until a defibrillator or paramedics arrive. Start as soon as you've found that the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally. Starting quickly matters more than perfect technique. The CPR lesson walks you through exactly how to do it, including rescue breaths and how to adjust for children and babies.

sections.key: Attach an AED (defibrillator) as soon as one is available and follow its instructions.
sections.b: The final D is defibrillation: an electric shock that can reset a heart whose rhythm has become chaotic. An automated external defibrillator, or AED, is built for untrained bystanders. It analyses the heart rhythm itself and tells you what to do at every step. Attach it the moment it arrives, keeping CPR going while it's set up. It's worth noticing where AEDs are kept at your workplace, gym, sports club or local shops, usually marked by a green sign with a heart and lightning bolt. The CPR lesson covers using one step by step.

quiz.q: What does the first D in DRSABCD stand for?
quiz.e: Always check for danger first.

quiz.q: What number do you call in an emergency in Australia?
quiz.e: Triple Zero (000). 112 also works from mobiles.

quiz.q: Someone unresponsive is breathing normally. What should you do?
o: Place them in the recovery position and monitor them
quiz.e: The recovery position keeps the airway clear.

quiz.q: What does CPR do for someone whose heart has stopped?
o: It always restarts the heart on its own
It keeps some oxygen-carrying blood flowing until a defibrillator or paramedics arrive
It replaces the need to call Triple Zero
quiz.e: CPR buys time; defibrillation is usually what restarts the heart's rhythm.

quiz.q: When should you attach an AED?
o: Only if a doctor is present
As soon as one is available, keeping CPR going while it's set up
quiz.e: AEDs are designed for bystanders and talk you through each step.

LESSONS.title: Speak with confidence
LESSONS.hook: The nerves never fully go away, even for professionals. These habits make them work for you.

sections.key: Fear of public speaking is extremely common; the body's stress response is natural.
sections.b: Fear of public speaking is one of the most common fears there is; surveys regularly rank it alongside heights and spiders. The racing heart, dry mouth, shaky hands and sweaty palms are your body's fight-or-flight response, releasing adrenaline to prepare you for action. Even experienced speakers, actors and politicians feel it. The goal isn't to eliminate nerves but to manage them, and to understand that the audience notices them far less than you think, an effect psychologists call the illusion of transparency.

sections.key: Telling yourself you're excited, rather than trying to calm down, can improve performance.
sections.b: Anxiety and excitement feel remarkably similar in the body: both involve a racing heart and a surge of energy. Harvard researcher Alison Wood Brooks found that people who said 'I am excited' out loud before a speech or a stressful task performed better than those who tried to tell themselves to calm down. Calming down is hard when your body is revved up. Relabelling the feeling as excitement is easier and channels the energy into enthusiasm. Slow breathing, with long exhales, also helps settle the body.

sections.key: Build the talk around one clear message you can say in a sentence.
sections.b: Audiences remember surprisingly little of what they hear. Decide the single message you want people to leave with, and build everything around it. If you can't say it in one sentence, it isn't clear yet, to you or to them. Then cut ruthlessly: anything that doesn't support the big idea is a distraction, however interesting. Most talks improve by being shorter. Nobody has ever complained that a good presentation finished five minutes early.

sections.key: Tell them what you'll say, say it, sum up; stories and examples beat lists of facts.
sections.b: A simple structure works for almost any talk: open with a hook that grabs attention, like a question, a surprising fact or a short story; tell them what you'll cover; cover it in two or three main points; then sum up and finish with a clear takeaway or call to action. Stories and concrete examples stick far better than lists of facts or abstract ideas, because our brains are wired for narrative. One vivid example often does more than ten statistics.

sections.key: Slides should support you, not be your script: few words, big visuals.
sections.b: Slides should support what you're saying, not repeat it. People can't read dense text and listen to you at the same time, so they'll end up doing neither well. Use few words, large fonts, and images or simple charts that make a point at a glance. One idea per slide is a good rule. Never read your slides aloud. If the projector died, you should still be able to give the talk; if you couldn't, you're relying on the slides too much.

sections.key: Rehearse aloud, standing, and record yourself once to spot filler words.
sections.b: Reading your notes silently is not practice. Rehearse the whole talk out loud, ideally standing up, at least three times. Time it; most people run long. Record yourself once on your phone and watch it back. It's uncomfortable, but you'll spot filler words like 'um', 'like' and 'you know', nervous habits like swaying, and the parts where you rush. Know your opening lines especially well, since that's when nerves peak; after the first minute, most people settle.

sections.key: Deliberate pauses sound confident and replace filler words.
sections.b: Nervous speakers rush. Deliberately slow down, and use pauses: before an important point, after a question, when moving to a new section. A pause feels like an eternity to you but reads as confidence to the audience, gives them time to think and naturally replaces filler words. Look at real people, one at a time, for a sentence or so each, rather than scanning the back wall or staring at your notes. Friendly faces help; find a few and return to them.

sections.key: Repeat questions, it's fine to say 'I don't know', and keep going after a slip.
sections.b: When taking questions, repeat or paraphrase each question so everyone hears it and you gain a moment to think. It's perfectly fine to say, 'I don't know, but I'll find out and get back to you.' If you lose your place or make a mistake, pause, glance at your notes and carry on; audiences rarely notice and are almost always on your side. Every talk you give makes the next one easier, so look for low-stakes chances to practise, like team meetings or a Toastmasters club.

quiz.q: What can help with nerves before a talk, according to research?
quiz.e: Anxiety and excitement feel similar in the body.

quiz.q: How many core messages should a talk aim for?
quiz.e: One idea people can remember.

quiz.q: What makes a good slide?
o: Lots of text so you can read it
Few words and a clear visual
quiz.e: Slides should support you, not be your script.

quiz.q: Why record yourself practising?
o: To spot filler words and rushed parts
quiz.e: You'll hear what the audience hears.

quiz.q: What does a deliberate pause do?
o: Makes you sound confident and replaces filler words
quiz.e: Pauses signal control.

LESSONS.title: How to really listen (and be heard)
LESSONS.hook: Most arguments aren't about what they seem to be about. Better communication starts with listening.

sections.key: Most people listen to reply rather than to understand.
sections.b: In most conversations, we're not really listening. We're waiting for our turn to talk, planning our response, or relating everything back to ourselves. Author Stephen Covey put it simply: most people listen with the intent to reply, not to understand. The other person can tell. Feeling genuinely heard is one of the most powerful things you can give someone, and it's the foundation for resolving disagreements, building trust and being heard in return.

sections.key: Active listening means full attention, reflecting back what you heard and asking open questions.
sections.b: Active listening is a set of simple skills. Give your full attention: phone away, eye contact, no interrupting. Reflect back what you heard in your own words: 'So you're frustrated because you felt left out of the decision?' This shows you understood and lets them correct you if you didn't. Ask open questions that start with what, how or tell me, rather than yes-or-no questions. And resist the urge to jump in with solutions; often people want to be understood before they want advice.

sections.key: Acknowledging emotions ('That sounds really stressful') calms conversations.
sections.b: Emotions drive most difficult conversations. Simply naming what someone seems to feel, like 'That sounds really stressful' or 'You seem disappointed', tends to lower the temperature. Brain-imaging research by psychologist Matthew Lieberman found that putting feelings into words reduced activity in the amygdala, a brain region involved in threat responses. You don't have to agree with someone to acknowledge how they feel. Validation says 'your feelings make sense', not 'you're right'.

sections.key: 'I' statements describe your experience without blaming, making defensiveness less likely.
sections.b: When raising a problem, how you start matters. 'You never help around the house' is an attack, and the other person will defend themselves. An 'I' statement describes your experience instead: 'I feel overwhelmed when I do the dishes every night on my own. Could we take turns?' A useful formula: I feel [emotion] when [specific situation], because [why it matters]. Could we [specific request]? It focuses on behaviour and needs, not character.

sections.key: Criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling predict relationship breakdown.
sections.b: Psychologist John Gottman studied thousands of couples and identified four communication patterns he called the four horsemen, because they predict relationship breakdown. Criticism attacks the person rather than the behaviour. Contempt, including sarcasm, eye-rolling and mockery, is the most damaging of all. Defensiveness means making excuses and refusing responsibility. Stonewalling is shutting down and withdrawing. The antidotes: complain without blame, express appreciation, take responsibility for your part, and take a break to calm down.

sections.key: When flooded with emotion, pause for 20+ minutes before continuing.
sections.b: When an argument escalates, your heart rate climbs and your body floods with stress hormones. In this state, called flooding, it's very hard to think clearly or listen, and people say things they regret. Gottman's research suggests taking a break of at least 20 minutes, doing something calming, not rehearsing your arguments. Agree on a time to come back to it. Pausing isn't avoiding the issue; it's giving both of you the chance to discuss it productively.

sections.key: Use Situation–Behaviour–Impact: specific, factual and about effects, not character.
sections.b: Feedback at work or home lands better when it's specific. The Situation–Behaviour–Impact model is simple. Describe the situation: 'In this morning's meeting…'. Describe the specific behaviour, not your interpretation: '…you interrupted Sam twice while she was presenting…'. Then the impact: '…and she didn't finish her point, so we missed her idea.' Then ask for their view. Give positive feedback the same way; 'Great job' is nice, but specific praise tells people what to repeat.

sections.key: Put the phone away, remember details, and express appreciation often.
sections.b: Good communication is built from small habits. Put your phone out of sight in conversations; research suggests even a visible phone can make conversations feel less close. Remember details people tell you and ask about them later. Express appreciation out loud and often; Gottman found that stable couples have around five positive interactions for every negative one during conflict. And when you get it wrong, which everyone does, a sincere, specific apology without 'but' goes a long way.

quiz.q: Which is a key part of active listening?
o: Planning your reply while they talk
quiz.e: Reflecting shows you understood and lets them correct you.

quiz.q: Which is an 'I' statement?
o: I feel overwhelmed when I do the dishes alone
quiz.e: It describes your experience without blame.

quiz.q: What does Gottman suggest as the antidote to criticism?
o: Complaining about the behaviour without blaming the person
Using sarcasm to lighten the mood
quiz.e: Criticism attacks the person; a complaint without blame focuses on the behaviour.

quiz.q: How long a break does Gottman suggest when flooded with emotion?
quiz.e: Enough for your body to calm down.

quiz.q: In the SBI feedback model, what does the 'B' stand for?
quiz.e: Situation, Behaviour, Impact.

LESSONS.title: Time management that works
LESSONS.hook: You can't make more time. But you can stop losing it to the wrong things.

sections.key: The Eisenhower matrix sorts tasks by urgency and importance; important-not-urgent work matters most.
sections.b: In a 1954 speech, US President Dwight Eisenhower quoted a former college president: 'I have two kinds of problems, the urgent and the important. The urgent are not important, and the important are never urgent.' The Eisenhower matrix sorts tasks into four boxes. Urgent and important: do it now (a crisis, a deadline). Important but not urgent: schedule it (exercise, planning, relationships, learning). Urgent but not important: delegate or minimise (most interruptions and many emails). Neither: drop it. Most people live in the urgent boxes. The biggest gains come from protecting time for important-but-not-urgent work.

sections.key: Parkinson's law: work expands to fill the time available, so set tighter limits.
sections.b: In 1955, British historian C. Northcote Parkinson wrote that 'work expands so as to fill the time available for its completion.' Give yourself a week to write a report and it takes a week; give yourself a day and it often takes a day. Setting your own shorter deadlines, or timeboxing, allocating a fixed block of time to a task, uses this to your advantage. It also helps to decide what 'good enough' looks like before you start, so perfectionism doesn't swallow the extra time.

sections.key: The planning fallacy makes us underestimate how long tasks take; add a buffer.
sections.b: Psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky named the planning fallacy: we consistently underestimate how long tasks will take, even when we know similar tasks took longer in the past. We imagine the best-case scenario and forget interruptions and problems. Sydney's Opera House is the classic example: due to open in early 1963, it opened in 1973, ten years late and hugely over budget. Fix it by checking how long similar tasks actually took and adding a buffer, often 50% or more.

sections.key: Schedule your important tasks in your calendar like appointments.
sections.b: A to-do list tells you what to do, not when. Time blocking means scheduling your tasks in your calendar as if they were meetings: 9 to 10.30 am, write proposal; 2 to 2.30 pm, emails. It forces you to confront how much time you really have, reduces decision fatigue and protects focus. Put your most demanding work in your peak energy hours; for many people that's the morning. Leave buffer blocks for the unexpected, because something always comes up.

sections.key: Multitasking is task-switching, and each switch costs time and focus.
sections.b: Multitasking is mostly a myth. The brain doesn't do two demanding things at once; it switches between them, and each switch costs time and attention. Research on interruptions suggests it can take many minutes to fully refocus on a complex task after a distraction. Batch similar small tasks, like emails and calls, into set times rather than responding to every notification. Turn off non-essential alerts. Even an hour of genuinely uninterrupted work can achieve more than a whole distracted afternoon.

sections.key: If something takes less than two minutes, do it now.
sections.b: David Allen, author of Getting Things Done, suggests a simple rule: if a task takes less than two minutes, do it immediately rather than writing it down or putting it off. Reply to the quick email, file the document, book the appointment. It stops small tasks piling up into a mental burden. Allen's broader insight is that your mind is for having ideas, not holding them: capture every task in one trusted list or app so your brain can stop trying to remember everything.

sections.key: Every yes is a no to something else; protect time for your priorities.
sections.b: Every time you say yes to something, you're saying no to something else, even if you don't notice it. Before agreeing to a new commitment, ask what it will replace. You can decline politely without a long excuse: 'Thanks for thinking of me, but I can't take that on right now.' Some people use a rule: if it's not a clear yes, it's a no. Saying no to less important things is how you make room for what matters most to you.

sections.key: A short weekly review keeps your plans on track and your mind clear.
sections.b: Once a week, often Friday afternoon or Sunday evening, spend 20 to 30 minutes reviewing. Look at what you got done, what's still open and what's coming up. Clear your inboxes and notes into your task list. Choose your three most important priorities for the next week and block time for them. It's a small investment that stops tasks slipping through the cracks and turns vague stress into a clear plan. Many productive people say it's their single most useful habit.

quiz.q: In the Eisenhower matrix, what should you do with important but not urgent tasks?
quiz.e: These tasks deliver the biggest long-term gains.

quiz.q: What does Parkinson's law say?
o: Work expands to fill the time available
quiz.e: Tighter time limits can make you more efficient.

quiz.q: What is the planning fallacy?
o: Underestimating how long tasks will take
quiz.e: The Sydney Opera House ran ten years late.

quiz.q: What really happens when you 'multitask' on demanding work?
o: You switch between tasks, losing time and focus
quiz.e: Each switch has a cost.

quiz.q: What is the two-minute rule?
o: Take a two-minute break every hour
If a task takes under two minutes, do it now
Work for two minutes at a time
Reply to emails in two minutes
quiz.e: It stops small tasks piling up.

LESSONS.title: Cooking fundamentals
LESSONS.hook: You don't need recipes to cook well. You need to understand salt, fat, acid, heat and a few core techniques.

sections.key: Understanding principles lets you cook without recipes and fix dishes as you go.
sections.b: Recipes are useful, but people who cook confidently understand principles, not just steps. Chef and author Samin Nosrat boiled good cooking down to four elements in her book Salt Fat Acid Heat: salt enhances flavour, fat carries flavour and creates texture, acid balances and brightens, and heat transforms food. Once you understand these, you can improvise, rescue a bland dish and cook with whatever's in the fridge. The single best habit? Taste as you go.

sections.key: Salt enhances flavour; season in stages and taste as you go.
sections.b: Salt doesn't just make food salty; used well, it makes food taste more like itself and reduces bitterness. Season in stages rather than all at the end, because salt added early has time to penetrate. Salt pasta and vegetable cooking water generously. Salting meat ahead of time, even 40 minutes to a day before cooking, helps it stay juicy and seasoned throughout. If a dish tastes flat or dull, it often needs a pinch more salt before anything else. Health guidelines still recommend moderating overall salt intake, much of which comes from processed foods.

sections.key: Butter burns early because of its milk solids, and smoke point alone doesn't tell you how stable a cooking oil is.
sections.b: Different fats suit different jobs. Butter tastes wonderful, but its milk solids start to burn at around 150°C, so for high-heat searing add it near the end, or use ghee, clarified butter with the milk solids removed, which copes with far more heat. Neutral oils such as peanut or canola suit woks and deep-frying. Smoke point isn't the whole story, though: a 2018 test by an Australian olive oil laboratory, heating ten supermarket oils, found extra virgin olive oil among the most stable despite its modest smoke point, likely helped by its natural antioxidants. Fat also builds texture: cold butter rubbed into flour makes flaky pastry. And never pour used oil down the sink, where it sets and clogs pipes.

sections.key: Tough, collagen-rich cuts turn tender with long, gentle, moist cooking, while lean cuts suit fast, hot cooking.
sections.b: Choosing the right heat starts with the cut. Lean, tender cuts such as fillet, loin and chicken breast have little connective tissue, so they suit quick, hot methods like grilling and pan-frying, and dry out if cooked too long. Hard-working muscles such as beef shin, chuck, brisket and lamb shoulder are full of collagen, a tough connective protein. Cooked gently in liquid for hours, collagen slowly melts into gelatine, giving meat that falls apart and a silky sauce. Keep a braise at a bare simmer rather than a rolling boil, which tightens the muscle fibres and dries the meat. If a stew is still tough, it usually needs more time, not more heat.

sections.key: Read the recipe through and prepare everything before you turn on the heat.
sections.b: Mise en place is French for 'everything in its place', and it's the habit that separates calm cooks from frantic ones. Before any heat goes on, read the whole recipe, then wash, chop, measure and line up every ingredient and tool. The late chef Anthony Bourdain called it the religion of all good line cooks. It matters most for fast cooking like stir-fries, where there's no time to mince garlic while the onions scorch. Reading ahead also catches surprises, such as meat that needs marinating overnight or an oven that needs preheating. Set out small bowls or a plate to hold prepped ingredients, plus a bin bowl for scraps, and cleaning up as you go becomes easier too.

sections.key: Meat keeps cooking after it leaves the heat, so take it off a little early and let it rest.
sections.b: Food doesn't stop cooking the moment you take it off the heat. The hot outer layers keep pushing heat inward, so the centre of a steak can climb a few more degrees as it sits, and a big roast even more. This is called carryover cooking, and it's why cooks take meat off slightly before it reaches their target. Resting also helps with juiciness: meat sliced straight from the pan tends to lose more of its juices onto the board. Rest a steak for about five minutes and a roast for ten to twenty, loosely covered with foil so it doesn't sweat and lose its crust. A meat thermometer takes the guesswork out of all of this.

sections.key: Stir pasta early, cook it just shy of done, and finish it in the sauce with a splash of its cooking water.
sections.b: A few simple habits transform everyday pasta. Adding oil to the water doesn't stop sticking; it mostly makes the sauce slide off later. Instead, stir well in the first minute or two, when the surface starch is stickiest. Start tasting a couple of minutes before the packet time and stop when it's al dente, Italian for 'to the tooth': tender with a slight bite. Before draining, scoop out a cup of the cloudy cooking water. Then finish the pasta in the pan with the sauce for a minute, adding splashes of that starchy water. The starch helps the sauce turn glossy and cling to every strand. And don't rinse cooked pasta, unless you're making a cold salad.

sections.h: A few meals you can riff on
sections.key: Master a few flexible templates: a stir-fry, a tray bake, a soup and eggs.
sections.b: Rather than collecting hundreds of recipes, master a few flexible templates. A stir-fry: hot pan, protein, vegetables, a sauce of soy, garlic, ginger and something sweet or sour. A tray bake: chopped vegetables and protein, oil, salt and spices, roasted at about 200°C. A soup: soften onion and garlic, add vegetables, stock and beans or lentils, simmer and season. And eggs, which can become a quick dinner in countless ways. Swap ingredients freely and taste as you go.

quiz.q: What are the four elements in Samin Nosrat's approach to cooking?
quiz.e: Understanding them lets you cook without recipes.

quiz.q: Why does butter burn more easily than ghee in a hot pan?
o: Butter's milk solids start to burn at around 150°C
quiz.e: Ghee is clarified butter with the milk solids removed, so it copes with higher heat.

quiz.q: Why do cuts like beef shin and chuck suit long, slow cooking?
o: Their collagen slowly melts into gelatine
quiz.e: Gentle, moist heat over hours turns tough connective tissue tender.

quiz.q: Why is it worth salting meat 40 minutes to a day before cooking?
o: It helps the meat stay juicy and seasoned throughout
It makes it cook twice as fast
quiz.e: Salt added early has time to penetrate.

quiz.q: What does the lesson suggest instead of collecting hundreds of recipes?
o: Mastering a few flexible templates, like a stir-fry, tray bake and soup
Following one recipe exactly each night
quiz.e: Learn the pattern, then swap ingredients freely.

LESSONS.title: Home maintenance basics
LESSONS.hook: Ten minutes a month and a few checks a year prevent the expensive, and dangerous, problems. Renters, this is for you too.

sections.key: Know where your water main, switchboard and gas meter are before you need them.
sections.b: The time to find your water shut-off valve is not when a pipe has burst and water is pouring through the ceiling. Locate three things now: the water main tap, usually near the water meter at the front of the property; the electrical switchboard and main switch; and, if you have gas, the gas meter and its shut-off valve. Show everyone in the household. Keep a torch that works somewhere you can find it in the dark.

sections.key: Test smoke alarms monthly and replace them every 10 years; photoelectric types are recommended.
sections.b: Working smoke alarms save lives, and they're required by law in Australian homes. Test each alarm monthly by pressing the test button. Vacuum dust from the vents occasionally. Replace alarms that are 10 years old or more; the date is usually printed on the alarm. Fire services recommend photoelectric alarms, ideally interconnected so they all sound together, installed in bedrooms, hallways and every level. Rules differ by state; Queensland, for example, is phasing in interconnected photoelectric alarms in every bedroom.

sections.key: Test safety switches (RCDs) every three months by pressing the test button.
sections.b: A safety switch, or residual current device (RCD), cuts power in a fraction of a second if it detects electricity leaking, for example through a person, preventing many electrocutions. Most homes have them on the switchboard. Test them every three months by pressing the 'T' or test button; power to those circuits should cut off, then you flip the switch back up. If it doesn't trip, call a licensed electrician. Remember: in Australia, most electrical work must legally be done by a licensed electrician.

sections.key: Check for leaks with your water meter, and fix drips early to avoid damage and bills.
sections.b: A dripping tap can waste thousands of litres a year, and a hidden leak can cause major damage. To check for hidden leaks, turn off every tap in the house, note the reading on your water meter, wait an hour without using water and check again. If it's moved, you have a leak somewhere. Watch for warning signs like damp patches, bubbling paint, musty smells or unusually high water bills. Silicone around showers and baths wears out; replacing it stops water getting behind tiles.

sections.key: Mould thrives on moisture; ventilate bathrooms and fix leaks to prevent it.
sections.b: Mould loves moisture and poor airflow, and it's common in humid parts of Australia. It can trigger allergies and breathing problems. Prevention is mostly about moisture: run the bathroom exhaust fan during and after showers, open windows when you can, dry clothes outside or in a vented dryer, and fix leaks promptly. Small patches can be cleaned with a diluted white vinegar solution. Large or recurring outbreaks may indicate a hidden leak or damp problem that needs a professional.

sections.key: Clean gutters before storm and bushfire seasons and clear dryer lint every load.
sections.b: Some jobs are seasonal. Clean gutters and downpipes before storm season, since blocked gutters overflow into roofs and walls, and before bushfire season, since dry leaves are a major ignition risk from embers. Check the roof for loose tiles or sheets after big storms, from the ground with binoculars rather than climbing up. Clean the air-conditioner filters every few months. And clear the clothes dryer's lint filter every load; lint build-up is a common cause of house fires.

sections.h: Know when to call a pro
sections.key: Electrical, gas and major plumbing work need licensed trades; homes built before 1990 may contain asbestos.
sections.b: Plenty of jobs are fine to DIY: painting, changing tap washers, patching small holes, assembling furniture. But electrical work, gas fitting and most plumbing must be done by licensed tradespeople in Australia, for good safety reasons. Be especially careful with renovations in homes built before 1990, which may contain asbestos in walls, eaves, floors and roofing. Disturbing it can release deadly fibres. If you're not sure, get it tested before drilling, cutting or sanding. And always check for underground services through Before You Dig Australia before digging.

sections.key: Renters should report repairs in writing; urgent repairs must be fixed promptly.
sections.b: If you rent, most repairs are the landlord's responsibility, but you need to report them. Always report problems in writing, such as by email, and keep copies. Every state distinguishes urgent repairs, like a burst water pipe, gas leak, dangerous electrical fault or broken hot water system, which must be fixed quickly, from general repairs, which must be done within a reasonable time. Take dated photos at the start of your lease for your condition report. Your state's tenancy authority has free guides and advice.

quiz.q: How often should you test smoke alarms?
quiz.e: And replace them every 10 years.

quiz.q: How often should you test your safety switch (RCD)?
quiz.e: Press the test button; power should cut off.

quiz.q: How can you check for a hidden water leak?
o: Turn off all taps and see if the water meter moves
quiz.e: If the meter moves with no water in use, there's a leak.

quiz.q: Why should you clear the dryer's lint filter every load?
o: Lint build-up is a fire risk
quiz.e: Lint is highly flammable.

quiz.q: Homes built before roughly which year may contain asbestos?
quiz.e: Get it tested before drilling or sanding.

LESSONS.title: Car basics everyone should know
LESSONS.hook: A few simple checks keep you safer, save money on fuel and repairs, and stop you being stranded on the side of the road.

sections.key: Check tyre pressure monthly when cold, using the placard on the driver's door.
sections.b: Tyres are your only contact with the road, so they matter enormously for braking and handling. Check the pressure at least once a month and before long trips, when the tyres are cold. The correct pressure is on a placard, usually inside the driver's door or fuel flap, not the maximum printed on the tyre. Most service stations have free air machines. Under-inflated tyres wear faster, increase fuel use and can overheat; over-inflated tyres reduce grip.

sections.key: Legal minimum tread depth is 1.5 mm in most of Australia; check wear indicators.
sections.b: Tread channels water away so the tyre can grip wet roads. In most of Australia, the legal minimum tread depth is 1.5 millimetres. Tyres have small raised bars in the grooves called tread wear indicators; when the tread is level with them, it's time to replace the tyre. Also look for cracks, bulges or uneven wear, which can signal alignment or suspension problems. And know where your spare tyre and jack are, and how to use them, before you need them.

sections.key: Red warning lights mean stop safely soon; amber means get it checked.
sections.b: Dashboard warning lights generally follow a colour code. Red means a potentially serious problem: stop when it's safe and investigate, for example for the oil pressure, engine temperature, brake or battery warnings. Amber or orange means something needs attention soon, such as the check engine light, low tyre pressure or ABS warning. Green or blue lights are just information, like headlights on. Your owner's manual explains every symbol; it's worth keeping in the glovebox or finding online.

sections.key: Regularly check engine oil, coolant, brake fluid and washer fluid.
sections.b: Every month or so, with the engine cold and the car on level ground, check the engine oil using the dipstick; it should sit between the minimum and maximum marks. Check the coolant level in the overflow reservoir, but never open a radiator cap on a hot engine, as scalding liquid can spray out. Check brake fluid and top up the windscreen washer fluid. A sudden drop in any fluid can indicate a leak that needs a mechanic.

sections.key: Follow the logbook service schedule; skipping services costs more in the long run.
sections.b: Your car's logbook sets out when it needs servicing, usually by time or distance, such as every 12 months or 15,000 kilometres. Regular servicing replaces oil and filters, checks brakes, belts and other parts, and catches problems early, when they're cheaper to fix. You don't have to use the dealer to keep your new-car warranty in Australia, as long as the service follows the manufacturer's specifications and uses suitable parts. Keep records; a full service history also helps resale value.

sections.key: Car batteries last about 3–5 years; roadside assistance is worth having.
sections.b: Car batteries typically last around three to five years, often less in hot climates. Warning signs include a slow, sluggish start and dim lights. Many auto shops test batteries for free. Roadside assistance membership, through state motoring clubs like the RACQ or NRMA, or some insurers and new-car warranties, can be worth it for breakdowns, flat batteries and lockouts. If you break down, pull over as far off the road as possible, turn on hazard lights and stay safe, usually away from traffic.

sections.key: Smooth driving, correct tyre pressure and less weight all cut fuel use.
sections.b: How you drive makes a big difference to fuel use. Accelerate smoothly, look ahead to avoid unnecessary braking and keep to steady speeds. Driving at 110 km/h uses noticeably more fuel than at 90 or 100. Correct tyre pressure, removing roof racks when not in use and clearing heavy junk from the boot all help. Fuel prices in many Australian cities follow a regular cycle; fuel price apps and state government websites show where it's cheapest nearby.

sections.key: After a crash: stop, check for injuries, call 000 if needed and exchange details.
sections.b: If you're in a crash, you must stop. Turn on hazard lights, check yourself and others for injuries, and call Triple Zero (000) if anyone is hurt, if there's a danger such as fire or leaking fuel, or if a driver leaves without exchanging details. Exchange names, addresses, registration numbers and insurance details with other drivers. Take photos of the scene and damage. Don't admit fault at the scene. Reporting requirements to police vary by state, so check your state's rules.

quiz.q: Where do you find the correct tyre pressure for your car?
o: The number on the tyre wall
The placard on the driver's door or fuel flap
It's the same for all cars
quiz.e: The tyre wall shows the maximum, not the recommended pressure.

quiz.q: What is the legal minimum tread depth in most of Australia?
quiz.e: Check the tread wear indicators.

quiz.q: What does a red dashboard warning light usually mean?
quiz.e: Red signals a potentially serious problem.

quiz.q: Why should you never open a radiator cap on a hot engine?
quiz.e: The cooling system is under pressure when hot.

quiz.q: About how long do car batteries typically last?
quiz.e: Often less in hot climates.

LESSONS.title: How compound interest works
LESSONS.hook: Interest that earns interest. It's the most powerful force in personal finance, working for you or against you.

sections.key: Compound interest is interest paid on your original money plus the interest already earned.
sections.b: Interest is the price of money: what a bank pays you for keeping your savings, or what a lender charges you for borrowing. Simple interest is paid only on your original amount, called the principal. Compound interest is paid on the principal plus any interest you've already earned. Your money earns money, and then that money earns money too. It starts slowly, then snowballs. The same maths applies to investments that grow and reinvest their returns, not just bank accounts.

sections.key: $10,000 at 5% becomes $10,500, then $11,025, and about $43,000 after 30 years.
sections.b: Put $10,000 in an account paying 5% a year and leave the interest in. After one year, you have $10,500. In year two, you earn 5% on $10,500, not $10,000, so you gain $525 and have $11,025. The extra $25 is interest on interest. It seems trivial at first, but it grows every year. After 10 years you'd have about $16,300; after 20, about $26,500; and after 30 years, about $43,200, more than four times the original, without adding another dollar.

sections.key: Compound growth starts slowly and accelerates; most of the gain comes late.
sections.b: Compound growth doesn't rise in a straight line; it curves upward, gently at first, then steeply. In the example above, the first 10 years added about $6,300. The last 10 years added about $16,700, from the same starting $10,000. This is why patience matters so much. Many people give up on saving or investing in the early years because progress feels slow, just before the curve starts to bend upwards.

sections.key: Starting early often matters more than how much you invest.
sections.b: Here's a famous comparison. At a 7% annual return, Alex invests $5,000 a year from age 25 to 35, then stops completely: $50,000 in total. Sam starts at 35 and invests $5,000 every year until 65: $150,000 in total. At 65, Alex ends up with more money than Sam, despite contributing a third as much, because Alex's money had an extra decade to compound. The lesson isn't that it's ever too late, but that small amounts started early are extraordinarily powerful.

sections.key: Divide 72 by the interest rate to estimate how many years it takes to double.
sections.b: A handy shortcut: divide 72 by the annual rate to estimate how many years it takes to double your money. At 6%, it doubles in about 12 years. At 9%, about 8 years. At 2%, a typical savings rate in some years, about 36 years. It works in reverse too: to double your money in 10 years, you'd need about a 7.2% return. The rule is an approximation, but it's accurate enough for rates between about 2% and 15%.

sections.key: More frequent compounding increases returns slightly; compare accounts by their effective annual rate.
sections.b: Interest can be added annually, monthly or even daily. The more often it's added, the sooner it starts earning interest itself. At the same 5% rate, monthly compounding gives an effective annual return of about 5.12%, compared with 5% for yearly compounding. The difference is small, but it adds up over decades. When comparing savings accounts, look for the effective annual rate, and watch for 'bonus' rates that only apply if you meet conditions each month.

sections.key: Compounding also makes high-interest debt grow fast.
sections.b: Compounding is just as powerful in reverse. Credit cards in Australia often charge around 20% interest a year. By the rule of 72, an unpaid balance would roughly double in under four years. Paying only the minimum each month can stretch a modest debt out for a decade or more, costing far more in interest than the original purchase. That's why paying down high-interest debt is often one of the best 'returns' you can get: it's a guaranteed saving at that rate.

sections.key: Fees and inflation also compound, quietly eating long-term returns.
sections.b: Anything expressed as a yearly percentage compounds, including things that work against you. A super or investment fund charging 1% more in fees each year doesn't sound like much, but over 30 years it can reduce your final balance by tens of thousands of dollars. Inflation compounds too, shrinking what your money can buy. The takeaway: start early, be patient, keep fees low, pay off expensive debt, and let time do the heavy lifting.

quiz.q: What makes compound interest different from simple interest?
o: You earn interest on your interest
quiz.e: Interest is added to your balance, so it earns interest too.

quiz.q: $10,000 at 5% a year compounds to how much after two years?
What's the most powerful ingredient in compound growth?
quiz.e: The longer money compounds, the faster it grows.

quiz.q: Using the rule of 72, how long does money take to double at 8%?
quiz.e: 72 ÷ 8 = 9 years.

quiz.q: Why is a 20% credit card balance so dangerous?
o: It roughly doubles in under four years if unpaid

LESSONS.title: How the stock market works
LESSONS.hook: What you're actually buying when you buy a share, why prices jump around, and how ordinary people build wealth with it.

sections.key: A share is a small slice of ownership in a company.
sections.b: A share, or stock, is a small slice of ownership in a company. If a company has a million shares and you own 1,000, you own 0.1% of it, including a claim on 0.1% of its future profits. Companies sell shares to raise money to grow, without having to borrow. Shareholders can usually vote on some big decisions, like electing the board of directors. If the company does well, your slice becomes more valuable; if it fails, it can become worthless.
