sections.key: Exchanges like the ASX are where shares are traded; an IPO is a company's first sale to the public.
sections.b: A stock exchange is a marketplace where shares are bought and sold. Australia's main one is the ASX, founded in 1987 from the merger of earlier state exchanges; the biggest in the world are in New York. Most trading today is electronic, through brokers and investing apps. When a company first sells shares to the public, it's called an initial public offering, or IPO, and it's then 'listed'. After that, investors trade shares with each other; the company doesn't get the money from those trades.

sections.key: Prices move with supply and demand, driven by expectations of future profits.
sections.b: Share prices move with supply and demand. If more people want to buy than sell, the price rises. Underneath, buyers are betting on a company's future profits: a share is worth what investors expect the business to earn over time. So prices react to earnings reports, new products, scandals, interest rates, the economy and even general mood. In the short term, prices can be driven by fear and excitement; in the long run, they tend to follow real profits.

sections.key: Investors earn through capital gains (selling higher) and dividends (shared profits).
sections.b: There are two main ways to make money from shares. If the price rises and you sell for more than you paid, that's a capital gain. And many companies pay part of their profits to shareholders as dividends, usually twice a year in Australia. Australian companies often attach franking credits to dividends, representing company tax already paid, which can reduce the tax you owe. Reinvesting dividends to buy more shares is a powerful way to compound growth.

sections.key: An index tracks a group of stocks; an index fund buys them all to spread risk cheaply.
sections.b: An index tracks a group of stocks to show how part of the market is doing. The ASX 200 tracks the 200 largest companies on the ASX; the S&P 500 tracks 500 large US companies. An index fund, often bought as an exchange-traded fund (ETF), simply buys all the companies in an index. With one purchase, you own a tiny slice of hundreds of businesses, at low cost. Most professional fund managers fail to beat their index over the long term, once fees are included.

sections.key: Bull markets rise, bear markets fall 20% or more; crashes happen but markets have historically recovered.
sections.b: A rising market is called a bull market, and a fall of 20% or more from a peak is a bear market. Crashes are a normal part of investing. Markets fell sharply in 1987, during the global financial crisis of 2008–09, and briefly in early 2020 when COVID-19 hit, when the ASX lost over a third of its value in about a month. Broad markets have historically recovered and gone on to new highs, though recovery can take years, and past performance never guarantees the future.

sections.key: Listed companies must announce price-sensitive news promptly, and trading on inside information is a crime.
sections.b: A fair market needs everyone to have access to the same important information. Under the ASX's continuous disclosure rules, a listed company must immediately announce anything a reasonable person would expect to have a material effect on its share price, such as a big new contract, a profit downgrade or a takeover offer. If news is about to break, a company can ask for a trading halt so no one trades on half the story. Buying or selling shares using price-sensitive information that isn't public, or tipping someone else off, is insider trading. It's a serious crime in Australia, carrying up to 15 years' jail, and the corporate regulator, ASIC, investigates suspicious trades.

sections.key: Long-term diversified investing differs from short-term trading and speculation.
sections.b: Buying a broad index fund and holding it for decades is very different from day-trading individual stocks or chasing tips on social media. Studies of day traders consistently find that most lose money over time, after costs. Useful principles for most people: invest for the long term, diversify, keep fees low, don't try to time the market, and never invest money you might need soon or can't afford to lose. This is general information, not personal advice; a licensed adviser can help with your situation.

quiz.q: What does owning a share mean?
o: You've lent money to a company
You own a small part of a company
quiz.e: A share is part-ownership of the business.

quiz.q: What is an IPO?
o: A company's first sale of shares to the public
quiz.e: An initial public offering lists a company.

quiz.q: What is a dividend?
o: A share of profits paid to shareholders
quiz.e: Companies share profits with shareholders.

quiz.q: When COVID-19 hit in early 2020, roughly how much did the ASX fall in about a month?
quiz.e: Broad markets later recovered, though recoveries can take years.

quiz.q: What is insider trading?
o: Buying shares through a licensed broker
Trading shares using price-sensitive information that isn't public
Owning shares in the company you work for
Buying every company in an index
quiz.e: It's a serious crime in Australia, investigated by the corporate regulator, ASIC.

LESSONS.title: What inflation really is
LESSONS.hook: Why a dollar buys less every year, what the Reserve Bank does about it and what it means for your money.

sections.key: Inflation is the general rise in prices, so each dollar buys a bit less.
sections.b: Inflation is the general rise in prices across the economy over time. When inflation is 3%, something that cost $100 last year costs about $103 today. Put another way, each dollar buys a little less. Individual prices always move around; petrol might jump while TVs get cheaper. Inflation is about the overall level. Over decades it adds up: something that cost $1 in 1990 costs well over $2 today.

sections.key: Australia measures inflation with the Consumer Price Index (CPI), a basket of everyday goods.
sections.b: The Australian Bureau of Statistics tracks the prices of a 'basket' of goods and services a typical household buys, from bread, petrol and electricity to rent, insurance and haircuts. The change in the cost of this basket is the Consumer Price Index, or CPI. Each item is weighted by how much households spend on it, so housing counts for far more than, say, tea. Since late 2025, the ABS has published a complete CPI every month, replacing the quarterly figure as the headline measure of inflation.

sections.key: Inflation comes from demand outstripping supply (demand-pull) or rising costs (cost-push).
sections.b: Inflation has two classic causes. Demand-pull inflation happens when people and businesses want to buy more than the economy can produce, so sellers raise prices. Cost-push inflation happens when the cost of making things rises, such as wages, energy or shipping, and businesses pass it on. The surge of inflation after COVID-19 was both: supply chains were disrupted and energy prices spiked, while demand bounced back strongly. Australia's inflation peaked at 7.8% in late 2022.

sections.key: Central banks aim for low, stable inflation because falling prices (deflation) can be harmful.
sections.b: Why not aim for zero? A little inflation is considered healthy. It gives central banks room to cut interest rates in a downturn and helps wages and prices adjust. Deflation, a general fall in prices, sounds nice but can be damaging: people delay purchases expecting lower prices, businesses cut jobs and debts become harder to repay. Japan struggled with low growth and deflation for years. Very high inflation, though, erodes savings and makes planning difficult.

sections.key: The RBA targets 2–3% inflation and raises interest rates to cool it.
sections.b: The Reserve Bank of Australia aims to keep inflation between 2% and 3%, focusing on the 2.5% midpoint. Its main tool is the cash rate, the interest rate on overnight loans between banks, which flows through to mortgage, loan and savings rates. When inflation is too high, the RBA raises rates. Borrowing becomes more expensive, people with mortgages have less to spend, businesses invest less, and demand cools. When the economy is weak, it cuts rates to encourage spending. Changes take a year or more to fully work through.

sections.key: Inflation hurts savers earning low interest and can help borrowers; wages may lag.
sections.b: Inflation doesn't hit everyone equally. Savers lose out when inflation runs higher than the interest they earn, because their money's real buying power shrinks. People on fixed incomes, or whose wages rise slower than prices, see their living standards fall. Borrowers with fixed debts can benefit, because the real value of what they owe shrinks over time. Economists talk about 'real' figures, meaning adjusted for inflation: a 4% pay rise with 5% inflation is actually a 1% real pay cut.

sections.key: Hyperinflation is extreme, runaway inflation, as in Germany in 1923 and Zimbabwe in the late 2000s.
sections.b: Extreme, runaway inflation is called hyperinflation, often defined as prices rising more than 50% in a month. It usually happens when governments print money to pay debts. In Germany in 1923, prices rose so fast that people carted cash around in wheelbarrows and workers were paid twice a day. Zimbabwe's hyperinflation peaked in 2008, and it went on to print a 100 trillion dollar note. Hyperinflation wipes out savings and can destabilise entire societies.

sections.key: Beat inflation by earning more than it on savings and investments, and reviewing pay and bills.
sections.b: You can't control inflation, but you can soften its effect. Keep an emergency fund in a high-interest savings account rather than a zero-interest transaction account. For long-term money, investments like shares and property have historically outpaced inflation over long periods, though with more risk. Review your pay regularly, since employers may not raise it automatically. And shop around on big recurring bills like insurance, energy and phone plans, which often creep up when you stay with the same provider.

quiz.q: If inflation is 3%, what does $100 of groceries cost a year later?
quiz.e: Prices rise about 3%.

quiz.q: In Australia, what measures inflation?
quiz.e: The ABS publishes the CPI.

quiz.q: How does the Reserve Bank usually fight high inflation?
quiz.e: Higher rates cool spending.

quiz.q: You get a 4% pay rise but inflation is 5%. What's your real pay change?
quiz.e: Prices rose faster than your pay.

quiz.q: What is hyperinflation?
quiz.e: Like Germany in 1923 or Zimbabwe in the late 2000s.

LESSONS.title: Budgeting that actually works
LESSONS.hook: A budget isn't a diet for your money. It's a plan that gives every dollar a job, and it takes about 20 minutes to set up.

sections.key: A budget is a plan for your money that reduces stress and helps you reach goals.
sections.b: A budget is simply a plan for your money: deciding in advance where it goes instead of wondering afterwards where it went. It's not about never spending on fun; it's about spending on what matters to you and cutting what doesn't. Surveys consistently find money is one of the biggest sources of stress for Australians. Knowing your numbers, even roughly, replaces vague anxiety with a plan.

sections.key: Start by tracking where your money currently goes for a month.
sections.b: Before planning, look at reality. Most banking apps now automatically sort your spending into categories like groceries, transport and entertainment. Look back over the last one to three months. Many people are surprised by the total of small, regular purchases: coffees, takeaway, delivery fees and subscriptions they'd forgotten about. Don't judge yet; just get the facts. Include irregular costs like car rego, insurance and Christmas by dividing their yearly cost by 12.

sections.key: About 50% on needs, 30% on wants, 20% on savings and extra debt repayments.
sections.b: A simple starting framework, popularised by US senator and former Harvard professor Elizabeth Warren, is the 50/30/20 rule. About 50% of after-tax income goes on needs: rent or mortgage, groceries, utilities, transport and insurance. About 30% goes on wants: eating out, entertainment, hobbies and holidays. And 20% goes on savings and paying down debt faster. In high-cost cities, needs often take more than half, so treat the numbers as a guide and adjust them to fit your life.

sections.key: Automatically move savings out on payday, before you can spend it.
sections.b: The most effective budgeting habit is automation. Set up an automatic transfer to a separate savings account on payday, before you have a chance to spend it. Money you never see in your everyday account is much easier not to spend. Many Australians use multiple accounts, sometimes called 'buckets': one for bills, one for everyday spending, one for savings goals and one for emergencies. Several banks let you open these free and nickname them.

sections.key: Aim for 3–6 months of essential expenses in an easy-access account.
sections.b: Life guarantees surprises: a car repair, a vet bill, a broken phone or a job loss. An emergency fund turns these from crises into inconveniences. A common target is three to six months of essential expenses, kept in an easy-access, high-interest savings account. That sounds like a lot, so start with a smaller goal, like $1,000, which covers many common emergencies. Without a buffer, unexpected costs tend to end up on a credit card, where they grow.

sections.key: Avalanche (highest rate first) saves most; snowball (smallest first) builds momentum.
sections.b: Credit cards often charge around 20% interest, so paying one off is like earning a guaranteed 20% return. Two popular methods: the avalanche, where you pay the minimum on everything and throw extra money at the debt with the highest interest rate, saves the most money. The snowball, where you clear the smallest balance first, builds momentum through quick wins. Also be wary of buy now, pay later services: they're convenient, but missed payments bring fees and they make it easy to overspend.

sections.key: Review subscriptions and shop around on insurance, energy and phone plans each year.
sections.b: The easiest savings are often recurring costs you've stopped noticing. Go through your statements and cancel subscriptions you don't use. Once a year, compare your energy, insurance, internet and phone plans; loyalty is rarely rewarded, and switching can save hundreds of dollars. The Australian Government's Energy Made Easy website compares electricity and gas offers for free (in Victoria, use Victorian Energy Compare). Small recurring savings compound: $50 a month is $600 a year, every year.

sections.key: Review monthly, allow fun money and focus on goals, not perfection.
sections.b: The best budget is one you'll actually keep. Include some guilt-free fun money, or you'll eventually rebel against it. Check in once a month for 15 minutes to see how you're tracking and adjust. Give your savings a purpose, like a holiday, a house deposit or freedom from debt, because goals motivate more than numbers. And expect imperfect months. This is general information, not personal financial advice; free services like the National Debt Helpline (1800 007 007) can help if debts feel overwhelming.

quiz.q: What's the first step in making a budget?
o: Track where your money currently goes
quiz.e: You can't plan until you know where the money goes.

quiz.q: In the 50/30/20 rule, what's the 20% for?
quiz.e: 50 needs, 30 wants, 20 savings and debt.

quiz.q: What does 'pay yourself first' mean?
o: Move money to savings automatically before spending
quiz.e: Savings come out first, automatically.

quiz.q: What's a typical emergency fund target?
quiz.e: Enough to ride out a job loss or big repair.

quiz.q: Which debt payoff method saves the most interest?
quiz.e: Tackling the highest rate first minimises interest.

LESSONS.title: Superannuation explained
LESSONS.hook: It's probably your second-biggest asset after a home, and most people barely look at it. Ten minutes here could be worth tens of thousands.

sections.key: Super is money set aside during your working life, invested to fund your retirement.
sections.b: Superannuation, or super, is money set aside from your pay during your working life and invested to support you in retirement. It became compulsory for most employees in 1992, and Australia's super system now holds more than $4 trillion, one of the largest retirement savings pools in the world. The idea is simple: small amounts invested over 40-odd years, compounding the whole time, grow into a large sum. Because it's locked away, it's protected from being spent early.

sections.key: Employers must pay super on top of wages; the rate is 12% from July 2025.
sections.b: If you're an employee, your employer must pay a percentage of your ordinary earnings into your super fund, on top of your wages. This is called the Super Guarantee, and it rose to 12% on 1 July 2025. So on a $70,000 salary, your employer adds $8,400 a year. Check your payslips and your fund account to make sure it's actually being paid; unpaid super can be reported to the ATO. Self-employed people aren't covered, so they need to make their own contributions.

sections.key: Super is invested, mostly in shares and property, and compounds over decades.
sections.b: Your super isn't sitting in a bank account. Your fund invests it in a mix of Australian and international shares, property, infrastructure, bonds and cash. Most people are in their fund's default 'balanced' or 'growth' option, often a MySuper product. Because it's invested for 40 years or more, compounding does enormous work: much of your final balance will come from investment returns, not contributions. Balances will fall in some years when markets drop, but it's a very long game.

sections.key: Small differences in fees compound into large differences at retirement.
sections.b: Fees are charged as a dollar amount, a percentage of your balance, or both. A difference of just 0.5% or 1% a year sounds tiny, but over a working lifetime it can mean tens of thousands of dollars less in retirement. The ATO's free YourSuper comparison tool lets you compare MySuper products by fees and past returns. The regulator, APRA, also tests these products each year, and funds that fail the performance test must tell their members.

sections.key: Consolidate multiple super accounts to avoid paying fees and insurance premiums several times.
sections.b: Many people have several super accounts from different jobs, each charging fees and often insurance premiums. Since 2021, your existing fund is generally 'stapled' to you and follows you to new jobs, which helps. You can find all your accounts, including lost super, by linking the ATO to your myGov account, and consolidate them online in minutes. Before closing an account, check whether it holds insurance you want to keep, as that cover ends when the account closes.

sections.key: Most funds include default life, TPD and sometimes income protection insurance.
sections.b: Most super funds automatically include insurance: life cover (paid to your beneficiaries if you die), total and permanent disability (TPD) cover and sometimes income protection. Premiums come out of your balance. It can be good value and is often the only life insurance people have. But check whether the amount suits your situation, and make sure you've nominated who should receive your super if you die. A binding nomination gives you more certainty.

sections.key: Super is taxed at a low rate, and extra contributions can reduce tax, within yearly caps.
sections.b: Super is taxed lightly to encourage saving. Contributions from your employer are generally taxed at 15%, which is lower than most people's income tax rate, and investment earnings are generally taxed at no more than 15%, though extra tax applies from July 2026 on earnings for balances above $3 million. You can add extra through salary sacrifice or personal contributions you claim as a tax deduction, up to the concessional cap, $32,500 a year from July 2026, including employer contributions. Lower-income earners may qualify for government co-contributions. Rules have limits and exceptions, so check the ATO website.

sections.key: You generally access super after reaching preservation age (60) and retiring, or at 65.
sections.b: Super is locked away until you meet a 'condition of release'. For anyone born on or after 1 July 1964, the preservation age is 60: you can generally access your super once you're 60 and retire, or at 65 even if you keep working. Early access is only allowed in narrow situations, such as severe financial hardship or certain medical conditions. Be wary of anyone offering to help you access super early; illegal early release schemes can bring heavy penalties.

quiz.q: What is the Super Guarantee rate from 1 July 2025?
quiz.e: Employers must pay 12% of ordinary earnings.

quiz.q: Why do small differences in super fees matter so much?
quiz.e: 0.5–1% a year can cost tens of thousands by retirement.

quiz.q: How can you find lost or multiple super accounts?
quiz.e: Link the ATO to myGov to see all your accounts.

quiz.q: What is the concessional contributions cap?
quiz.e: From 1 July 2026. It includes employer contributions.

quiz.q: What is the preservation age for people born on or after 1 July 1964?
quiz.e: Generally you can access super at 60 once retired, or at 65.

LESSONS.title: How tax works in Australia
LESSONS.hook: The pay rise that 'pushes you into a higher bracket' won't leave you worse off. Here's how income tax actually works.

sections.key: Income tax funds services like health, education, welfare and defence.
sections.b: Income tax is the Australian Government's biggest source of revenue. It funds services like Medicare and hospitals, schools and universities, the pension and other welfare payments, defence, roads and much more. Other taxes include the 10% GST on most goods and services, company tax and excise on fuel, alcohol and tobacco. The financial year runs from 1 July to 30 June, and the Australian Taxation Office, the ATO, collects the money.

sections.key: Australia uses progressive tax brackets: higher rates apply only to income above each threshold.
sections.b: Australia has a progressive income tax system: the more you earn, the higher the rate on the extra dollars. For Australian residents in 2026–27, the first $18,200 is tax-free. Income from $18,201 to $45,000 is taxed at 15%, from $45,001 to $135,000 at 30%, from $135,001 to $190,000 at 37%, and above $190,000 at 45%. The 15% rate is legislated to fall to 14% from July 2027. Most people also pay a 2% Medicare levy.

sections.key: Tax brackets never make a pay rise reduce your take-home pay; only the extra dollars are taxed at the higher rate.
sections.b: A common myth says a pay rise can 'push you into a higher tax bracket' and leave you worse off. It can't. Each rate applies only to the income within that bracket. If you earn $136,000, only the $1,000 above $135,000 is taxed at 37%; the rest is taxed exactly as before. So, as far as brackets go, a pay rise always increases your take-home pay. Your marginal rate is the rate on your next dollar; your average rate, the share of your total income paid in tax, is always lower.

sections.key: Employers withhold tax from each pay; your return settles the difference.
sections.b: If you're an employee, your employer withholds tax from each pay under the Pay As You Go (PAYG) system and sends it to the ATO. They use your tax file number and whether you claim the tax-free threshold, which you should normally only claim from one job at a time. At the end of the financial year, your tax return works out exactly what you owed. If too much was withheld, you get a refund; if too little, you pay the difference.

sections.key: Lodge by 31 October if doing it yourself; much of it is pre-filled via myGov.
sections.b: If you lodge your own tax return, it's due by 31 October. Registered tax agents can often lodge later for their clients. Most people lodge online through myTax in myGov, where much of the information, like your income, bank interest and private health insurance details, is pre-filled from late July. It's worth waiting until early August for the pre-filling to be complete. Double-check everything; you're responsible for what you lodge, even if it's pre-filled.

sections.key: You can claim work-related expenses you paid, that relate to earning income, with records.
sections.b: Deductions reduce your taxable income. You can generally claim expenses directly related to earning your income, such as work tools, uniforms with a logo, professional memberships and some work-from-home costs. The ATO's three golden rules: you must have spent the money yourself and not been reimbursed; it must directly relate to earning your income; and you need a record, like a receipt. A $100 deduction doesn't save you $100; it saves you $100 multiplied by your marginal tax rate.

sections.key: GST (10%), capital gains tax and HECS-HELP repayments also affect many people.
sections.b: GST, a 10% tax on most goods and services, is built into prices, though basic food, most health care and education are exempt. If you sell an investment such as shares or an investment property for a profit, capital gains tax applies. Currently there's a 50% discount if you held the asset for more than a year; for gains that build up after 1 July 2027, this is legislated to be replaced by indexing the cost for inflation, with a 30% minimum tax rate on gains. Your main home is generally exempt. If you have a HECS-HELP student debt, compulsory repayments are collected through the tax system once your income passes a threshold.

sections.key: Keep records, use official sources and beware of tax scams impersonating the ATO.
sections.b: Keep receipts and records for five years, since the ATO can review your return. Use official sources like ato.gov.au for rates and rules, which change regularly. Be very wary of scams: fake ATO texts, emails and calls threatening arrest or demanding payment in gift cards or cryptocurrency are common. The ATO won't threaten you with immediate arrest or ask for payment that way. If unsure, contact the ATO directly using the number on its official website. This is general information only.

quiz.q: How much income is tax-free for Australian residents?
quiz.e: The tax-free threshold is $18,200.

quiz.q: You earn $136,000. How much is taxed at the 37% rate?
quiz.e: Each rate applies only to income within its bracket.

quiz.q: Can a pay rise leave you with less take-home pay because of tax brackets?
o: No, only the extra dollars are taxed at the higher rate
quiz.e: The bracket myth is false.

quiz.q: When is your tax return due if you lodge it yourself?
quiz.e: Tax agents can often lodge later.

quiz.q: Which is one of the ATO's golden rules for deductions?
o: You must have a record, like a receipt
quiz.e: You also must have paid it and it must relate to earning income.

LESSONS.title: How credit scores work
LESSONS.hook: A three- or four-digit number can decide whether you get a loan, and at what rate. Here's how to see yours for free.

sections.key: A credit score summarises how reliably you've handled credit, to help lenders assess risk.
sections.b: When you apply for a loan, credit card, phone plan or sometimes even a utility account, the provider checks your credit history to judge how likely you are to repay. A credit score boils that history down to a single number. A higher score suggests lower risk, which can mean easier approval and sometimes better interest rates. A low score doesn't mean you'll be rejected everywhere, but it can limit your options.

sections.key: In Australia, Equifax, Experian and illion are the main credit reporting bodies.
sections.b: In Australia, credit reports are kept by credit reporting bodies, mainly Equifax, Experian and illion. Each may hold slightly different information and calculates its own score on its own scale: Equifax uses 0 to 1,200, while Experian and illion use 0 to 1,000. So your score can differ between them. Lenders may check one or more of these bureaus when you apply.

sections.key: Reports include your credit accounts, enquiries, 24 months of repayment history and defaults.
sections.b: Your credit report includes personal details, the credit accounts you hold and their limits, and every time you've applied for credit, called an enquiry. Since comprehensive credit reporting began in 2014, reports also include up to 24 months of repayment history, showing whether you paid on time each month. Defaults (overdue debts of $150 or more that a lender has reported), court judgments and bankruptcies can also appear, and generally stay for years.

sections.key: Paying on time, keeping limits sensible and applying for credit rarely all help.
sections.b: The single biggest factor is paying bills and loan repayments on time, every time. Setting up direct debits for at least the minimum payment helps avoid accidental misses. Keeping credit card limits no higher than you need can help, since lenders consider your total available credit, not just what you've used. A long, steady history of well-managed accounts also works in your favour.

sections.key: Late payments, defaults and many credit applications in a short time lower your score.
sections.b: Missing repayments, especially by more than 14 days, can show up in your repayment history. Defaults are more serious and can remain on your report for five years even after you pay them. Applying for lots of credit in a short period can also lower your score, because it can look like financial stress. Buy now, pay later services became regulated as credit in 2025, so providers may now check and report to credit bureaus.

sections.key: You're entitled to a free credit report from each bureau every three months.
sections.b: You have the right to get your credit report free from each credit reporting body every three months, and also if you've been refused credit recently. Request it directly from Equifax, Experian and illion; look for the free option, as some services try to sell paid subscriptions. Checking your own report doesn't hurt your score. It's worth doing once a year, and before applying for a big loan like a mortgage.

sections.key: Incorrect information can be corrected free of charge through the bureau or lender.
sections.b: Credit reports sometimes contain mistakes, such as a debt that isn't yours, a default already paid or a sign of identity fraud. You can ask the credit reporting body or the lender to correct it, free of charge. If they don't resolve it, you can complain to the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA). Be wary of 'credit repair' companies that charge large fees for things you can do yourself for free. Legitimate negative information can't simply be removed.

sections.key: Unexpected enquiries may signal identity theft; you can request a ban on your credit file.
sections.b: Identity thieves sometimes use stolen details to apply for credit in your name, which damages your report. Warning signs include enquiries you didn't make or accounts you don't recognise. If you think your identity has been stolen, you can ask the credit reporting bodies to place a ban on your credit file, stopping anyone accessing it for 21 days (extendable). IDCARE, a free national service, can help you respond. Guard your licence, passport and Medicare details carefully.

quiz.q: Which of these is an Australian credit reporting body?
quiz.e: Equifax, Experian and illion are the main ones.

quiz.q: How many months of repayment history can appear on your report?
quiz.e: Comprehensive credit reporting includes up to 24 months.

quiz.q: What's the biggest thing you can do to help your score?
o: Pay bills and repayments on time
quiz.e: On-time repayments matter most.

quiz.q: How often can you get a free credit report from each bureau?
quiz.e: And checking it doesn't hurt your score.

quiz.q: What can you request if you suspect identity theft?
o: A ban on your credit file
quiz.e: It stops anyone accessing your credit file for a period.

LESSONS.title: How home loans work
LESSONS.hook: Over a 30-year loan, you can pay more in interest than you originally borrowed. Understanding a few features can save you tens of thousands.

sections.key: A home loan is borrowed money secured against the property, repaid with interest over decades.
sections.b: A home loan, or mortgage, is money borrowed from a lender to buy a property, which serves as security: if you can't repay, the lender can sell it to recover the debt. Most Australian home loans run for 25 to 30 years. You repay the amount borrowed, called the principal, plus interest. Because the sums are so large and the timeframes so long, small differences in interest rates and features make an enormous difference.

sections.key: Early repayments are mostly interest; the interest bill over 30 years can exceed the loan itself.
sections.b: Take a $500,000 loan at 6% interest over 30 years. The monthly repayment is about $3,000. Over the life of the loan, you'd repay around $1.08 million, meaning roughly $580,000 in interest, more than the amount borrowed. Early on, most of each repayment goes on interest; only a small slice reduces the principal. As the balance falls, that balance shifts. This is why extra repayments in the early years are so powerful.

sections.key: Borrowing more than 80% of the property's value usually means paying lenders mortgage insurance.
sections.b: Your deposit is the share of the price you pay yourself. Lenders look at the loan-to-value ratio (LVR): a $600,000 loan on a $750,000 home is an 80% LVR. If you borrow more than 80%, lenders usually charge lenders mortgage insurance (LMI), which can cost thousands or tens of thousands of dollars. Note that LMI protects the lender, not you. Government schemes such as the Home Guarantee Scheme can let eligible first-home buyers purchase with a smaller deposit without paying LMI.

sections.key: Variable rates move with the market; fixed rates lock in certainty but reduce flexibility.
sections.b: A variable rate moves up or down over time, usually following the Reserve Bank's cash rate. A fixed rate stays the same for a set period, often one to five years, giving certainty about repayments. Fixed loans often limit extra repayments and can charge break fees if you exit early. Many people split their loan, part fixed and part variable, to balance certainty and flexibility. When a fixed period ends, the loan usually rolls onto a variable rate, often not the lender's best one.

sections.key: An offset account reduces the balance you pay interest on; every dollar in it saves interest at your loan rate.
sections.b: An offset account is a transaction or savings account linked to your loan. The balance in it is subtracted from your loan balance when interest is calculated. With $30,000 in offset against a $500,000 loan, you pay interest on only $470,000. Every dollar in offset effectively 'earns' your mortgage rate, tax-free. A redraw facility lets you take back extra repayments you've made. Both reward keeping spare cash working against your loan.

sections.key: Extra repayments, especially early, can cut years and tens of thousands off a loan.
sections.b: Because interest is calculated on the outstanding balance, every extra dollar you repay reduces all the interest that dollar would have attracted for the rest of the loan. On the $500,000 example, paying an extra $200 a month from the start would cut about four and a half years off the loan and save roughly $100,000 in interest. Switching from monthly to fortnightly repayments of half the monthly amount also helps, because it adds up to one extra monthly payment each year.

sections.key: Compare using the comparison rate, and check features and fees, not just the headline rate.
sections.b: Advertised rates can hide fees, so Australian lenders must also show a comparison rate, which combines the interest rate with most fees into a single figure. Compare features too: offset, redraw, extra repayments and fees. Mortgage brokers can compare many lenders for you; they're usually paid by the lender, and must act in your best interests by law. Also check how much you can comfortably afford, not just how much a lender will offer, since lenders test whether you could cope if rates rose.

sections.key: Existing customers are often charged more than new ones; ask for a better rate or refinance.
sections.b: Banks often offer their best rates to new customers while existing customers drift onto higher ones, sometimes called the loyalty tax. Every year or two, check what rate new customers are being offered. Call your lender and ask for a better rate; many will match competitors to keep you. If not, consider refinancing to another lender, weighing up any switching costs. Even a 0.3% cut on a $500,000 loan saves about $1,500 a year. This is general information only.

quiz.q: Early in a home loan, where does most of each repayment go?
quiz.e: Most early repayments cover interest.

quiz.q: Above what LVR do lenders usually charge LMI?
quiz.e: Borrowing more than 80% usually triggers LMI.

quiz.q: Who does lenders mortgage insurance protect?
quiz.e: Despite you paying for it.

quiz.q: What does an offset account do?
o: Reduces the balance you're charged interest on
quiz.e: Money in offset saves interest at your loan rate.

quiz.q: What does the comparison rate include?
o: The interest rate plus most fees
quiz.e: It helps compare loans with different fees.

LESSONS.title: Index funds and ETFs
LESSONS.hook: The boring, low-cost way to invest that beats most professional fund managers over time.

sections.key: An index fund buys every company in an index, instead of trying to pick winners.
sections.b: Most investment funds are actively managed: professionals try to pick shares that will beat the market. An index fund does something simpler. It buys every company in a market index, like the ASX 200 or the S&P 500, in proportion to its size, and just holds them. You don't try to beat the market; you are the market. The first index fund for ordinary investors was launched in 1976 by John Bogle, founder of Vanguard. Critics called it 'Bogle's folly'. It turned out to change investing.

sections.key: Most active funds underperform their index over the long run after fees.
sections.b: It seems obvious that experts should beat a fund that simply buys everything. But year after year, studies such as S&P's SPIVA reports find that most actively managed funds underperform their benchmark index over 10 to 15 years, once fees are counted. Part of the reason is simple maths: before costs, the average investor earns the market return, so after higher costs, the average active investor must do worse. It's also very hard to identify in advance which managers will be the lucky few who win.

sections.key: Low fees are one of the few things investors control, and they compound over decades.
sections.b: Index funds are cheap because they don't pay teams of analysts to pick stocks. Broad index funds and ETFs often charge between about 0.03% and 0.3% a year, while active funds commonly charge 1% or more. On a $100,000 investment over 30 years, earning 6% a year after fees instead of 7% leaves you with about $187,000 less. You can't control market returns, but you can control costs.

sections.key: An ETF is a fund that trades on the stock exchange like a share; many track indexes.
sections.b: An exchange-traded fund, or ETF, is a fund that's bought and sold on the stock exchange like a share. Many ETFs track an index, so buying one unit gives you a slice of hundreds or thousands of companies. You can buy them through any online broker, often with small amounts. There are ETFs for Australian shares, global shares, bonds, property and more. Some ETFs are narrow or complex, like those focused on a single theme or using leverage; broad, simple ones suit most long-term investors.

sections.key: Warren Buffett's 10-year bet showed an S&P 500 index fund beating a set of hedge funds.
sections.b: In 2007, Warren Buffett, one of history's most successful investors, bet $1 million that a simple S&P 500 index fund would beat a selection of hedge funds chosen by professionals over the following 10 years. A fund firm took the bet. By the end of 2017, the index fund had returned about 7% a year on average, while the hedge funds' average was about 2%. Buffett has said most people would be best served by low-cost index funds.

sections.key: Australian shares are a small slice of global markets; global funds add diversification.
sections.b: Australian shares make up only about 2% of the world's share markets, and the ASX is dominated by banks and miners. Many Australians have a 'home bias', holding mostly local shares. A diversified portfolio often includes international shares too, giving exposure to industries like technology and healthcare that are smaller here. Some diversified ETFs hold a mix of Australian and global shares and bonds in a single fund, rebalancing automatically.

sections.key: Regular investing and staying invested beat trying to time the market.
sections.b: Nobody reliably predicts short-term market moves, and some of the best days often come shortly after the worst ones, so jumping in and out can mean missing the recovery. Many investors use dollar-cost averaging: investing a fixed amount regularly, such as monthly, which means buying more units when prices are low and fewer when they're high. It also removes the stress of deciding when to invest. The old saying holds: time in the market beats timing the market.

sections.key: Index investing suits long-term money; short-term savings belong somewhere safer.
sections.b: Index funds invested in shares suit money you won't need for at least five to seven years, because markets can fall sharply in the short term. Before investing, it's wise to have an emergency fund and clear high-interest debt. Remember that your super is probably already invested in shares, possibly including index funds. This is general information, not personal advice; ASIC's Moneysmart website has free, independent guides, and a licensed financial adviser can help with your circumstances.

quiz.q: What does an index fund do?
o: Buys every company in an index
quiz.e: It aims to match the market, not beat it.

quiz.q: Over 10–15 years, how do most active funds perform against their index after fees?
quiz.e: SPIVA reports consistently find this.

quiz.q: What is an ETF?
o: A fund traded on the stock exchange like a share
quiz.e: Exchange-traded fund.

quiz.q: What did Warren Buffett's famous bet show?
o: An S&P 500 index fund beat a set of hedge funds
quiz.e: About 7% a year versus about 2%.

quiz.q: What is dollar-cost averaging?
o: Investing a fixed amount at regular intervals
quiz.e: It removes the stress of timing the market.

LESSONS.title: Supply and demand: why things cost what they do
LESSONS.hook: Why avocados are cheap one month and pricey the next, why concert tickets vanish in minutes, and why rents keep rising.

sections.key: In a market, prices carry information about scarcity and desire.
sections.b: Every price you see is a signal. In a market economy, prices aren't set by a central planner; they emerge from millions of decisions by buyers and sellers. A high price signals that something is scarce or much wanted, encouraging producers to make more and buyers to use less. A low price signals the opposite. Economist Friedrich Hayek argued this is one of the market's most remarkable features: prices coordinate the actions of millions of people who've never met and don't know why things changed.

sections.key: Demand: the lower the price, the more people generally want to buy.
sections.b: Demand describes how much of something people want to buy at different prices. Generally, the lower the price, the more people buy; the higher the price, the less. That's the law of demand. Demand also shifts for reasons other than price: income, tastes, the price of alternatives, expectations and population. When avocado toast became a café trend, demand for avocados rose at every price. When interest rates rise, demand for houses falls, because borrowing costs more.

sections.key: Supply: the higher the price, the more producers are generally willing to sell.
sections.b: Supply describes how much sellers are willing to produce at different prices. Generally, higher prices encourage more supply, because producing becomes more profitable; lower prices discourage it. Supply shifts with production costs, technology, weather and the number of producers. A cyclone that wipes out Queensland banana crops cuts supply sharply. After Cyclone Larry in 2006, banana prices in Australia soared to around $12 or more a kilogram.

sections.key: The market price settles where supply equals demand (equilibrium).
sections.b: Put supply and demand together and the price tends to settle where the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers offer. Economists call this the equilibrium. If the price is above it, sellers have unsold stock and cut prices. If it's below it, buyers compete for too few goods and prices rise. This constant push and pull explains everyday price changes: strawberries are cheap in peak season when supply floods in, and dear in the off-season when they're scarce.

sections.key: When demand suddenly jumps and prices don't rise, shortages follow.
sections.b: In March 2020, as COVID-19 spread, Australians rushed to buy toilet paper. Demand suddenly spiked while supply couldn't adjust overnight, and shelves emptied. Supermarkets kept prices steady and imposed purchase limits instead, a form of rationing. There was never a real shortage of toilet paper production in Australia; the problem was a sudden surge in demand driven by fear, which fuelled more fear. Within weeks, supply caught up and shelves refilled.

sections.key: Elasticity measures how much demand changes when price changes; essentials are often inelastic.
sections.b: Some things you'll buy almost regardless of price, at least in the short term, like petrol to get to work, electricity or essential medicines. Demand for these is called inelastic. Other things you can easily skip or swap, like a particular brand of chips or a restaurant meal, so demand is elastic: a price rise sends buyers elsewhere. Elasticity explains why governments tax items like tobacco and fuel, which people keep buying, and why businesses fight so hard over competitive products.

sections.key: Underpriced tickets create excess demand; dynamic pricing and scalping are responses to it.
sections.b: When a hugely popular artist tours, tickets are often priced below what fans are willing to pay. Demand far exceeds supply, so tickets sell out in minutes, and scalpers buy them to resell at much higher prices. Some sellers now use dynamic pricing, raising prices in real time with demand, as airlines and rideshare apps do. It captures more money for the seller but often angers fans. Several Australian states have laws capping ticket resale prices to limit scalping.

sections.key: When housing supply doesn't keep up with population and demand, prices and rents rise.
sections.b: Housing shows supply and demand in action. When population grows and incomes and borrowing capacity rise, demand for homes increases. If building new homes doesn't keep pace, because of land availability, planning rules, construction costs or labour shortages, prices and rents climb. Low vacancy rates, where few rentals are empty, give landlords more pricing power. Economists debate the balance of causes, but most agree that building more homes in places people want to live is a key part of improving affordability.

quiz.q: According to the law of demand, what usually happens when prices fall?
quiz.e: Lower prices generally increase the quantity demanded.

quiz.q: What happened to banana prices after Cyclone Larry in 2006?
quiz.e: A supply shock raised prices dramatically.

quiz.q: What is the equilibrium price?
o: Where the amount demanded equals the amount supplied
quiz.e: Where supply and demand meet.

quiz.q: Demand for petrol in the short term is usually...
quiz.e: People still need to get to work.

quiz.q: What tends to happen when housing supply doesn't keep up with demand?
quiz.e: Scarcity pushes prices up.

LESSONS.title: The alien intelligence of octopuses
LESSONS.hook: An animal that thinks with its arms, tastes with its suckers, changes colour while colour-blind and escapes from aquariums.

sections.key: Octopuses evolved intelligence completely separately from vertebrates like us.
sections.b: Octopuses are molluscs, related to snails and clams. Our last common ancestor with them was probably a small worm-like creature that lived over 500 million years ago. That means octopus intelligence evolved completely independently of ours. Philosopher Peter Godfrey-Smith, who spent years diving with octopuses off Sydney, describes them as the closest thing we'll meet to an intelligent alien. Studying them helps scientists understand what minds are, and the different ways they can be built.

sections.key: Octopuses have ~500 million neurons, about two thirds of them in their arms.
sections.b: An octopus has around 500 million neurons, similar to a dog. But about two thirds of them are in its eight arms, not its central brain. Each arm has its own cluster of neurons that can process information and control movement semi-independently. An arm can explore a crevice, taste what it finds and decide to grab something, while the central brain focuses elsewhere. Even an arm that has been severed can react to touch and grasp food for a while.

sections.key: Octopus suckers can taste and smell by touch.
sections.b: Each of an octopus's suckers, up to around 2,000 on a common octopus, is packed with chemical receptors. So octopuses 'taste' what they touch. In 2020, researchers discovered special receptors in the suckers that let them detect chemicals on surfaces and identify prey hidden in cracks without seeing it. Imagine reaching into a dark cupboard and tasting everything your fingertips brushed against.

sections.key: Octopuses have three hearts and blue, copper-based blood.
sections.b: Octopuses have three hearts. Two pump blood through the gills to pick up oxygen; the third pumps it around the rest of the body. That third heart stops beating when the octopus swims, which is partly why they tire quickly and prefer crawling. Their blood uses a copper-based protein called haemocyanin to carry oxygen, which makes it blue. Haemocyanin works well in cold, low-oxygen water.

sections.key: Octopuses change colour and texture using chromatophores, despite appearing to be colour-blind.
sections.b: Octopuses can change colour, pattern and even skin texture in a fraction of a second. Thousands of pigment cells called chromatophores, each controlled by tiny muscles and nerves, expand or shrink to show colour. Other cells reflect light to create shimmering or white effects, and muscles raise bumps and spikes to mimic rocks or seaweed. Remarkably, octopuses appear to be colour-blind, having only one type of light receptor. Scientists are still working out how they match colours so well.

sections.key: With no bones, an octopus can squeeze through any gap bigger than its beak.
sections.b: An octopus has no bones; its only hard part is its parrot-like beak. So it can squeeze through any gap larger than the beak, sometimes just a couple of centimetres. Aquarium keepers know them as escape artists. In 2016, an octopus named Inky escaped from New Zealand's National Aquarium by slipping out of a gap in his tank, crossing the floor and sliding down a drainpipe into the sea. Others have been caught sneaking into neighbouring tanks for a snack.

sections.key: Octopuses unscrew jars, solve mazes and carry coconut shells as portable shelters.
sections.b: Octopuses can learn to unscrew jar lids, even from the inside, navigate mazes and recognise individual humans, sometimes squirting water at people they dislike. In Indonesia, veined octopuses have been filmed collecting discarded coconut shell halves, carrying them awkwardly across the sea floor, and assembling them into portable shelters, one of the few known examples of tool use by an invertebrate. Off the New South Wales coast, researchers have found gloomy octopuses living in small communities nicknamed Octopolis and Octlantis.

sections.key: Most octopuses live only one to two years and die soon after breeding.
sections.b: Despite their intelligence, most octopuses live only one to two years. Many species breed once and then die. A female guards her eggs, sometimes for months, without eating, and dies soon after they hatch. One deep-sea octopus was observed brooding her eggs for four and a half years, the longest known of any animal. Their short lives puzzle scientists: why evolve a big, costly brain if you won't live long enough to learn much? It's one of the many mysteries these creatures still hold.

quiz.q: Where are most of an octopus's neurons?
quiz.e: About two thirds are in the arms.

quiz.q: What can octopus suckers do?
quiz.e: They're packed with chemical receptors.

quiz.q: Why is octopus blood blue?
quiz.e: Our blood uses iron-based haemoglobin.

quiz.q: What limits the size of gap an octopus can squeeze through?
quiz.e: The beak is its only hard part.

quiz.q: How long do most octopuses live?
quiz.e: Many die soon after breeding.

LESSONS.title: Why bees matter
LESSONS.hook: About a third of what we eat depends on pollinators. Australia has around 2,000 native bee species most people have never noticed.

sections.key: Pollinators carry pollen between flowers, letting many plants produce fruit and seeds.
sections.b: Many flowering plants can't make fruit or seeds unless pollen moves from one flower to another. Wind does the job for some, like wheat and rice, but many others rely on animals, mostly insects, that visit flowers for nectar and pollen and carry pollen with them. Bees are the most important pollinators. The UN Food and Agriculture Organization estimates that about three quarters of the world's leading food crops benefit at least partly from animal pollination.

sections.key: Crops like almonds, apples, berries and avocados depend heavily on pollinating insects.
sections.b: Without pollinators, supermarket shelves would look very different. Almonds depend almost entirely on bees; Australia's almond industry hires hundreds of thousands of beehives each winter to pollinate its orchards. Apples, cherries, blueberries, avocados, melons, pumpkins and many vegetable seeds also rely heavily on them. Staple grains like wheat, rice and corn don't, so we wouldn't starve, but our diets would be far less varied and nutritious, and many foods would become much more expensive.

sections.key: European honey bees were introduced to Australia in 1822 and live in large, organised colonies.
sections.b: The honey bee most people know isn't native to Australia. European honey bees were introduced in 1822. A hive can hold tens of thousands of bees: one queen who lays eggs, a few hundred male drones, and thousands of female workers who build comb, feed young, guard the hive and forage. To make about half a kilogram of honey, bees may visit around two million flowers. Honey bees are vital for commercial pollination, and there are also large feral populations in the bush.

sections.key: Honey bees communicate the direction and distance of food using the waggle dance.
sections.b: When a forager finds a good patch of flowers, she returns to the hive and performs a 'waggle dance' on the honeycomb. The angle of her waggle run relative to vertical shows the direction of the food relative to the Sun, and the length of the waggle indicates distance. Other bees follow her movements and fly straight to the flowers. Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch decoded the dance and shared the 1973 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

sections.key: Australia has around 2,000 native bee species, most of them solitary.
sections.b: Australia has around 2,000 native bee species, many still not formally described. Most are solitary: each female builds her own nest in the ground, in wood or in plant stems, and doesn't live in a hive. They come in striking forms, like the blue-banded bee, which pollinates tomatoes by 'buzz pollination', vibrating flowers to shake pollen loose, something honey bees can't do. About a dozen species are social stingless bees, found mainly in warmer areas, which make small amounts of tangy 'sugarbag' honey that Aboriginal people have long harvested.

sections.key: Bees face habitat loss, pesticides, disease, parasites like varroa and climate change.
sections.b: Bees face many pressures: loss of flowering habitat, some pesticides, diseases and parasites, and climate change shifting when flowers bloom. The varroa mite, a parasite that has devastated honey bee colonies worldwide, was detected in Newcastle, NSW, in 2022. After a major effort, authorities concluded in 2023 that eradication was no longer feasible, and the focus shifted to managing it. Australia had been the last inhabited continent free of varroa. Native bees aren't affected by varroa but face their own habitat pressures.

sections.key: Flies, beetles, moths, butterflies, birds, bats and even possums also pollinate.
sections.b: Bees aren't the only pollinators. Hoverflies, beetles, moths and butterflies all move pollen. In Australia, birds such as honeyeaters and lorikeets pollinate many native plants like banksias, grevilleas and eucalypts. Flying foxes pollinate eucalypts as they travel long distances at night, spreading pollen across the landscape. Even small marsupials like the honey possum, which feeds almost entirely on nectar and pollen, act as pollinators.

sections.key: Plant diverse flowers, avoid unnecessary pesticides and provide water and nesting spots.
sections.b: You can help pollinators even in a small backyard or on a balcony. Plant a variety of flowering plants, especially native ones, so something is blooming across the seasons. Herbs like lavender, basil and rosemary are popular with bees when they flower. Avoid spraying pesticides, especially on flowering plants. Leave a shallow dish of water with pebbles for landing. Leave some bare ground, or build a simple 'bee hotel' from drilled wood blocks, for native solitary bees to nest in.

quiz.q: About what share of the world's leading food crops benefit from animal pollination?
quiz.e: According to the UN FAO.

quiz.q: When were European honey bees introduced to Australia?
quiz.e: They're not native to Australia.

quiz.q: What does the honey bee waggle dance communicate?
quiz.e: Decoded by Karl von Frisch.

quiz.q: What can blue-banded bees do that honey bees can't?
o: Buzz pollinate flowers such as tomatoes
Live in hives of tens of thousands
quiz.e: They vibrate flowers to shake the pollen loose.

quiz.q: What parasite of honey bees was detected in NSW in 2022?
quiz.e: Eradication was later judged no longer feasible.

LESSONS.title: Australia's 'deadly' animals, in perspective
LESSONS.hook: Snakes, spiders, sharks and crocs get the headlines. The numbers tell a very different, and reassuring, story.

sections.key: Australia is famous for dangerous animals, but deaths from them are rare.
sections.b: Australia has a fearsome reputation: venomous snakes, deadly spiders, box jellyfish, crocodiles and sharks. It's true that many of the world's most venomous snakes live here. But the chance of being killed by any wild animal in Australia is extremely low. A study of hospital and coronial data from 2000 to 2013 found that about 20 to 30 people died from animal-related causes in Australia each year, and most of those deaths weren't from the animals you'd expect.

sections.key: Horses and cattle cause more deaths than venomous snakes or spiders.
sections.b: That same study found that horses and cattle were responsible for more deaths than any wild animal, through falls, kicks and crushing. Bees and wasps, through severe allergic reactions called anaphylaxis, caused about as many deaths as snakes. The lesson: familiar animals cause far more harm than the exotic ones we fear, simply because we're around them so much more.

sections.key: Australia averages around 2 snakebite deaths a year; the pressure immobilisation bandage saves lives.
sections.b: Australia has some of the most venomous snakes in the world, including the inland taipan and the eastern brown snake. Yet on average only about two people die from snakebite each year, thanks to antivenom, fast emergency care and good first aid. Australian researchers developed the pressure immobilisation technique: call 000, keep the person still, and wrap a firm bandage over the bite and up the whole limb, then splint it. Don't wash the bite, cut it or apply a tourniquet. Most bites happen when people try to catch or kill snakes.

sections.key: No one has died from a confirmed spider bite in Australia since antivenoms became available.
sections.b: Sydney funnel-web and redback spiders can be dangerous, but no one has died from a confirmed spider bite in Australia since the funnel-web antivenom was introduced in 1981; redback antivenom has been available since the 1950s. The funnel-web antivenom is made using venom 'milked' from spiders, some collected by members of the public and handed in to the Australian Reptile Park. For a suspected funnel-web bite, use pressure immobilisation and call 000.

sections.key: Fatal shark and crocodile attacks are rare, averaging a few a year combined.
sections.b: Shark attacks get enormous media attention, but fatal attacks in Australia average only a few a year, while millions of people swim and surf. Drowning kills far more beachgoers: around 300 people drown in Australia each year across all waterways. Saltwater crocodiles in northern Australia are genuinely dangerous and cause roughly one or two deaths a year, usually when people ignore warning signs. In croc country, stay well back from the water's edge and never swim where crocodiles may be present.

sections.key: Box jellyfish and irukandji are a risk in tropical waters in summer; swim at patrolled beaches.
sections.b: In tropical northern waters, box jellyfish and tiny irukandji jellyfish are a serious risk during the warmer months, roughly October to May. Box jellyfish stings can be fatal. Swim at patrolled beaches, inside stinger nets where provided, and wear a full-body stinger suit. For a box jellyfish sting, call 000 and pour vinegar over the sting for at least 30 seconds; vinegar is not recommended for bluebottle stings, which are best treated with hot water. Always swim between the flags.

sections.key: Magpies swoop in spring to protect their nests; walk away calmly and protect your head.
sections.b: Every spring, some Australian magpies swoop people who come near their nests. It's the male bird protecting his chicks, usually for about six weeks. Most swoops are warnings, but they can cause eye injuries. Avoid known swooping areas if you can, walk rather than run, wear a hat and sunglasses, and cyclists should dismount and walk through. Interestingly, research shows magpies can recognise individual human faces and are less likely to swoop people who've been kind to them.

sections.key: The biggest outdoor dangers are drowning, heat, sun and roads, not wildlife.
sections.b: Australia's genuinely big outdoor killers are far less exotic: drowning, road crashes, extreme heat and, over the long run, skin cancer from UV. Heatwaves kill more Australians than any other natural hazard. So by all means respect the wildlife, learn basic snakebite first aid and heed croc and stinger warnings. But the most life-saving habits are swimming between the flags, being sun smart, staying hydrated in heatwaves and driving safely.

quiz.q: Which animals caused more deaths in Australia than venomous snakes in the 2000–2013 study?
quiz.e: Familiar animals cause most harm.

quiz.q: On average, about how many people die from snakebite in Australia each year?
quiz.e: Antivenom, fast emergency care and good first aid save nearly everyone.

quiz.q: Since when has no one died from a confirmed spider bite in Australia?
quiz.e: Redback antivenom dates from the 1950s.

quiz.q: What kills far more Australian beachgoers than sharks?
quiz.e: Around 300 people drown in Australia each year.

quiz.q: Which natural hazard kills the most Australians?
quiz.e: Heat is the deadliest natural hazard.

LESSONS.title: The strange story of English
LESSONS.hook: Why is English spelling so chaotic? Why do we eat 'beef' from a 'cow'? Blame invaders, printers and a mysterious vowel shift.

sections.key: English began with Germanic tribes settling Britain in the 5th century.
sections.b: English began in the 5th century, when Germanic tribes, the Angles, Saxons and Jutes, crossed the North Sea and settled in Britain. Their language, Old English, would be unreadable to most of us today; the epic poem Beowulf looks almost like a foreign language. But many of our most basic, everyday words come from it: house, water, bread, eat, sleep, mother, love, and the word 'English' itself, from the Angles.

sections.key: Viking settlers added Norse words like sky, egg, knife and even 'they'.
sections.b: From the late 700s, Viking raiders and then settlers from Scandinavia arrived in England. Old Norse was related to Old English, so the two mixed easily. English borrowed hundreds of everyday words from Norse, including sky, egg, knife, window, skin, skull, husband, law and even the pronouns they, them and their. Words starting with 'sk', like skirt and sky, often have Norse origins, while their older English equivalents, like shirt, survived alongside them with different meanings.

sections.key: After the Norman Conquest, French flooded English, especially in law, government and food.
sections.b: In 1066, William of Normandy conquered England, and for around 300 years the ruling class spoke Norman French. English survived among ordinary people, but it absorbed around 10,000 French words, especially related to power: government, parliament, court, judge, jury, crime, army and nobility. This created a class divide that still shows in food: the animals, tended by English-speaking peasants, kept English names like cow, pig and sheep, while the meat served to French-speaking nobles took French names: beef, pork and mutton.

sections.key: The Great Vowel Shift changed pronunciation after spelling had started to settle, leaving mismatches.
sections.b: Between roughly 1400 and 1700, English went through the Great Vowel Shift, a major change in how long vowels were pronounced. 'Bite' had sounded like 'beet' and 'house' like 'hoose'. But spelling, influenced by the arrival of printing in England in 1476, was starting to settle during this time, so many words kept spellings that matched old pronunciations. Printers, some of them Dutch, added quirks too. Words like 'knight', where the k and gh were once pronounced, are fossils of older English.

sections.key: Shakespeare's works include the first recorded uses of many words and phrases still in use.
sections.b: William Shakespeare's works contain the first recorded uses of many words and phrases that are still common, though some were probably already in speech. Phrases include 'the be-all and end-all', 'wild-goose chase', 'heart of gold', 'in a pickle' and 'wear my heart upon my sleeve'. The 1611 King James Bible also shaped the language with phrases like 'the salt of the earth' and 'a drop in the bucket'. Samuel Johnson's influential dictionary of 1755 helped standardise meanings and spellings.

sections.key: English has borrowed words from hundreds of languages around the world.
sections.b: English is a magpie language, borrowing freely from others. From Latin and Greek came thousands of scientific and academic words. Trade and empire brought words from around the world: shampoo, bungalow and pyjamas from Indian languages; tea and ketchup from Chinese; algebra and coffee via Arabic; tsunami and emoji from Japanese; chocolate and tomato from Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs. This is one reason English has such a huge vocabulary, often with several words for similar ideas.

sections.key: Australian English has its own accent, slang and words borrowed from Aboriginal languages.
sections.b: Australian English developed from the mix of accents brought by convicts and settlers, mainly from southern England and Ireland, and soon had a distinct accent. It borrowed around 400 words from Aboriginal languages, including kangaroo, koala, wombat, dingo, billabong, yakka and boomerang. It's famous for shortening words: arvo, brekkie, servo, barbie and ambo. Australian spelling mostly follows British conventions, with some exceptions. The Macquarie Dictionary, first published in 1981, records Australian English.

sections.key: English is spoken by about 1.5 billion people, most of them as a second language.
sections.b: Today, around 1.5 billion people speak English, but only about 380 million as a first language. It's the dominant language of international business, science, aviation and the internet, a result of British colonial history and later American economic and cultural influence. As it spreads, English keeps changing, with new varieties, slang and words emerging all the time. Dictionaries now add hundreds of new words each year. Language is always a work in progress.

quiz.q: Which groups brought the earliest form of English to Britain?
quiz.e: Germanic tribes in the 5th century.

quiz.q: Which everyday pronoun did English borrow from Old Norse?
quiz.e: Along with them and their.

quiz.q: Why do we call cow meat 'beef'?
o: French-speaking nobles ate it after 1066, and 'beef' comes from French
quiz.e: The animal kept its English name; the meat took the French one.

quiz.q: What was the Great Vowel Shift?
o: A change in vowel pronunciation from about 1400–1700
quiz.e: Spelling didn't keep up with the new sounds.

quiz.q: Which of these words comes from an Aboriginal language?
quiz.e: Along with koala, wombat and billabong.

LESSONS.title: Cognitive biases: the shortcuts that fool you
LESSONS.hook: Your brain makes the same mistakes again and again, in ways psychologists can predict. Once you know them, you'll spot them everywhere.

sections.key: Cognitive biases are predictable errors caused by the brain's mental shortcuts.
sections.b: Your brain handles an enormous amount of information every second. To cope, it relies on mental shortcuts called heuristics. Most of the time they work well enough: you don't need to calculate the odds before crossing a quiet street. But in certain situations the same shortcuts lead to the same mistakes, again and again. Psychologists call these systematic errors cognitive biases. The idea was popularised in the 1970s by Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, whose work later earned Kahneman a Nobel Prize in economics. The key word is systematic: biases aren't random slips, they push everyone's thinking in the same predictable direction.

sections.key: System 1 is fast and automatic; System 2 is slow and deliberate. Biases live mostly in System 1.
sections.b: In his 2011 book Thinking, Fast and Slow, Kahneman described two modes of thought. System 1 is fast, automatic and effortless: it reads a face, finishes the phrase 'bread and…', and gives you a gut feeling. System 2 is slow, deliberate and tiring: it's what you use to multiply 17 by 24 or fill in a tax return. System 1 runs the show most of the day, and System 2 is lazy, happily accepting System 1's answers. Most biases come from System 1 jumping to conclusions that System 2 never bothers to check. The practical lesson: for decisions that matter, deliberately slow down.

sections.key: Confirmation bias is favouring information that supports what you already believe.
sections.b: We tend to notice, search for and remember information that supports what we already believe, and to dismiss what doesn't. Two people can read the same news story and each come away more convinced they were right. It also shapes how we search: type 'is coffee bad for you' and you'll find reasons to worry; type 'benefits of coffee' and you'll feel reassured. Social media amplifies this by showing us more of what we already engage with. It's one reason facts alone rarely change someone's mind, and why the most useful question you can ask is: what would convince me I'm wrong?

sections.key: Anchoring is when the first number you see skews your later estimates.
sections.b: The first number you hear pulls your later judgements towards it, even when it's irrelevant. In a famous experiment, people spun a rigged wheel of fortune that landed on either 10 or 65, then estimated the percentage of African countries in the United Nations. Those who saw 65 gave much higher estimates. Anchors are everywhere in shopping: a 'was $199' price next to '$129' makes the deal feel better, and a $90 bottle on a wine list makes the $45 one seem reasonable. In salary negotiations, the first number mentioned often sets the range for everything that follows.

sections.key: The availability heuristic is judging how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind.
sections.b: We judge how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind. Plane crashes are vivid and widely reported, so many people fear flying more than driving, even though driving is far more dangerous per kilometre travelled. Shark attacks get headlines, while drownings and road deaths rarely do. After a friend's house is burgled, you'll overestimate the chance of burglary for weeks. The fix is to ask for base rates: how often does this actually happen, out of how many? Statistics feel boring, but they're a much better guide than whatever is most memorable.

sections.key: Loss aversion means losses feel roughly twice as strong as equal gains.
sections.b: Losing something feels worse than gaining the same thing feels good. Research suggests losses weigh roughly twice as heavily as equivalent gains, so most people won't accept a coin flip that wins $100 or loses $100. Loss aversion explains why people hold on to falling investments too long, hoping to 'get back to even', and why free trials work so well: once something feels like yours, cancelling feels like a loss. Marketers know this, which is why 'Don't miss out' and 'Last chance' are among the most powerful phrases in advertising.

sections.key: The sunk cost fallacy is continuing something because of what you've already put in, not what's ahead.
sections.b: A sunk cost is money, time or effort you've already spent and can't get back. The fallacy is letting it drive future decisions. You sit through a terrible movie because you paid for the ticket. A company keeps funding a failing project because it has already spent millions. A person stays in a job they hate because of the years they've invested. The rational question is only about the future: from here, is continuing worth it? What's gone is gone either way. Asking 'If I were starting fresh today, would I choose this?' cuts through the fallacy.

sections.key: Most people overrate their own abilities; the less skilled often overrate themselves most.
sections.b: Most of us think we're better than average. In a classic 1981 survey, the large majority of American drivers rated themselves as safer than the median driver, which can't be true for everyone. In 1999, psychologists David Dunning and Justin Kruger found that people who scored lowest on tests of logic and grammar overestimated their performance the most. Researchers still debate how much of that pattern is a statistical quirk, but overconfidence itself is well documented. It shows up in planning too: we routinely underestimate how long projects will take, even when we've been late before.

sections.key: Slow down, look for evidence against your view, and set your own estimate first.
sections.b: You can't switch biases off, and knowing about them doesn't make you immune. But you can build habits that catch them. Before a big decision, deliberately look for evidence against your view. Write down your own estimate before hearing anyone else's number. Ask how you'd feel if the same choice were framed as a gain instead of a loss. Check base rates rather than trusting vivid stories. And for plans, look at how long similar projects actually took. Small speed bumps like these give your slow, careful System 2 a chance to step in.

quiz.q: What are cognitive biases?
o: Predictable errors caused by mental shortcuts
Beliefs you learned from your parents
quiz.e: They're systematic, predictable errors that come from the brain's shortcuts (heuristics).

quiz.q: A car is listed at $40,000, then 'reduced' to $32,000. Which bias makes it feel like a bargain?
quiz.e: The original $40,000 acts as an anchor, making $32,000 look cheap by comparison.

quiz.q: What's the best antidote to the availability heuristic?
o: Ask for base rates: how often it actually happens
quiz.e: Base rates are a far better guide than whatever is most memorable.

quiz.q: You keep watching a boring movie because you paid for the ticket. What is this?
quiz.e: The ticket money is gone either way. Only future enjoyment should count.

quiz.q: In Kahneman's model, how does System 2 usually treat System 1's quick answers?
o: It lazily accepts most of them
quiz.e: System 2 is lazy, so System 1's snap judgements often go unchecked.

LESSONS.title: The psychology of persuasion
LESSONS.hook: Most attempts to persuade you pull on the same few levers. Once you see them, you can't unsee them.

sections.key: Psychologist Robert Cialdini identified core principles that make people say yes.
sections.b: In 1984, psychologist Robert Cialdini published Influence after years studying salespeople, fundraisers and advertisers, even taking jobs undercover to learn their techniques. He found that most persuasion relies on a handful of principles that trigger fairly automatic responses. These shortcuts usually serve us well: following experts or returning favours is often sensible. The trouble is that anyone who knows the shortcuts can trigger them on purpose. Knowing the principles helps you persuade honestly and notice when someone is pushing your buttons.

sections.key: Reciprocity: we feel obliged to repay what we're given.
sections.b: People feel obliged to return favours. It's a deep social rule found in every culture, and it's powerful enough that an uninvited gift still creates a sense of debt. Free samples at the supermarket, a 'complimentary' drink before a sales pitch and charity letters that include a small gift all rely on it. Restaurants that bring mints with the bill tend to get slightly bigger tips. The defence isn't to refuse every gift. It's to recognise when a gift is really a sales technique, and to feel free to accept it without owing anything.

sections.key: Consistency: once we commit to something small, a bigger yes becomes more likely.
sections.b: Once we commit to something, especially publicly or in writing, we want to act consistently with it. Being inconsistent feels uncomfortable and looks unreliable. Salespeople use the 'foot in the door' technique: get a small yes first, like signing a petition or agreeing to a free trial, and a bigger yes becomes more likely. The same principle can work for you. Writing a goal down, or telling a friend about it, makes you more likely to follow through.
