Just watch out for small agreements that are designed to lead somewhere you didn't intend to go.

sections.key: Social proof: when we're unsure, we copy what other people do.
sections.b: When we're unsure, we look at what others are doing. It's why a busy restaurant seems more appealing than an empty one, and why reviews, star ratings and 'bestseller' labels are so effective. In one well-known hotel study, a card saying most guests reused their towels worked better than a card about saving the environment. Social proof is strongest when the people are similar to us. The catch is that crowds can be wrong, and fake reviews and bought followers exploit exactly this instinct.

sections.key: Authority: we tend to follow credible experts and symbols of expertise.
sections.b: We tend to follow credible experts, and we respond to the symbols of expertise, not just the real thing. Uniforms, titles, lab coats and confident delivery all increase compliance. Ads feature people who look like doctors or scientists for a reason. Following genuine experts in their field is usually wise. The problem is when authority is borrowed: a celebrity talking about medicine, or a finance influencer with no qualifications. Ask two questions: is this person truly an expert in this topic, and do they gain anything if I agree?

sections.key: Liking: we say yes more easily to people we like and who seem similar to us.
sections.b: We're more easily persuaded by people we like, and we like people who are similar to us, who pay us compliments and who cooperate with us. That's why salespeople look for common ground ('Oh, you're from Brisbane too?'), and why products are often sold through friends at parties. Attractive or familiar faces work too. A useful habit is to separate the person from the deal: would this offer still look good if a stranger you didn't warm to were making it?

sections.key: Scarcity: things seem more valuable when they're rare or running out.
sections.b: Things seem more valuable when they're rare or running out. 'Only 3 left', 'offer ends tonight' and 'limited edition' all tap into this. Scarcity connects to loss aversion: missing out feels like losing something. It also cuts our thinking time, which is often the point. When you notice urgency, treat it as a signal to slow down. Genuine bargains rarely vanish the moment you take a day to think. If a seller won't let you sleep on it, that tells you something.

sections.key: Unity: we say yes to people we see as part of our group. Use persuasion honestly.
sections.b: In 2016, Cialdini added a seventh principle, unity: we're more easily influenced by people we see as part of 'us', whether that's family, a team, a hometown or a shared identity. Brands build communities for this reason. All seven principles can be used honestly. If you genuinely offer value, give something first, show real reviews, cite real expertise and give people a true deadline, you're persuading ethically. The line is crossed when the pressure is manufactured. A simple test: would you be comfortable if the other person knew exactly what you were doing?

quiz.q: Who wrote Influence, the classic book on persuasion?
quiz.e: Robert Cialdini published Influence in 1984.

quiz.q: A shop gives you a free coffee, and you feel you should buy something. Which principle is at work?
quiz.e: The free gift creates a sense of debt. That's reciprocity.

quiz.q: What is the 'foot in the door' technique?
o: Getting a small yes before asking for a bigger one
Wearing a uniform to seem official
quiz.e: A small commitment makes people want to stay consistent and agree to more.

quiz.q: When is social proof at its most persuasive?
o: When the people are similar to us
When the crowd is very small
When the people are very different from us
quiz.e: We're most influenced by what people like us are doing.

quiz.q: Why does scarcity make things seem more valuable?
o: Rare things are always better quality
Missing out feels like losing something
Sellers must prove stock is limited
It gives us more time to think
quiz.e: Scarcity taps into loss aversion, and it also cuts our thinking time.

LESSONS.title: Classical and operant conditioning
LESSONS.hook: Why does your heart jump when your phone buzzes? Blame a Russian scientist, his dogs and a man who trained pigeons.

sections.key: Pavlov discovered dogs learned to drool in anticipation of food.
sections.b: Around 1900, Russian physiologist Ivan Pavlov was studying digestion in dogs, work that won him a Nobel Prize in 1904. He was measuring how much saliva the dogs produced when fed. But he noticed something odd: the dogs started drooling before the food arrived, at the sight of the assistants who usually fed them, or at the sound of their footsteps. Their bodies had learned to predict food. Pavlov realised he had stumbled on one of the most basic forms of learning, and he spent decades studying it.

sections.key: Classical conditioning is learning to link a neutral signal with something that triggers a response.
sections.b: Pavlov paired a neutral sound, such as a metronome or buzzer, with food. At first the sound meant nothing to the dogs. After repeated pairings, the sound alone made them salivate. In the jargon, the food is an unconditioned stimulus (it naturally causes drooling), and the sound becomes a conditioned stimulus (it causes drooling only after learning). This is classical conditioning: learning to link two things that happen together, so that one starts to trigger the response to the other.

sections.key: Many everyday reactions to sounds, places and brands are conditioned.
sections.b: Feel a jolt when your phone buzzes? Get hungry at the rustle of a chip packet? Feel tense in a dentist's waiting room, even before anything happens? These are conditioned responses. Your brain has linked a cue with an outcome. Advertisers pair products with upbeat music, attractive people and happy scenes, hoping the good feelings rub off on the brand. And fears can be conditioned too: a bad experience in a lift can make lifts feel frightening for years.

sections.key: Extinction: a conditioned response fades if the cue keeps appearing without the outcome.
sections.b: Conditioned links can fade. If Pavlov kept sounding the buzzer without ever bringing food, the drooling gradually stopped. This is called extinction. It's the basis of exposure therapy, one of the most effective treatments for phobias: by meeting the feared cue repeatedly in safe conditions, the brain learns it no longer predicts danger. Interestingly, extinguished responses can suddenly return after a break, called spontaneous recovery, which is why old habits and fears sometimes resurface.

sections.key: Operant conditioning is learning from consequences: rewards and punishments shape behaviour.
sections.b: In the 1930s, American psychologist B. F. Skinner studied a different kind of learning: how consequences shape behaviour. Behaviour followed by a reward becomes more likely. Behaviour followed by something unpleasant becomes less likely. Using boxes fitted with levers and food dispensers, he trained rats to press levers and pigeons to peck keys, and even taught pigeons to play a simple version of ping-pong. Classical conditioning is about linking signals; operant conditioning is about learning which actions pay off.

sections.key: Reinforcement increases behaviour; punishment decreases it. 'Negative' means taking something away.
sections.b: Skinner's terms confuse many people. Reinforcement makes a behaviour more likely; punishment makes it less likely. 'Positive' means adding something, and 'negative' means removing something. So a treat for a sitting dog is positive reinforcement. A seatbelt beep that stops when you buckle up is negative reinforcement: removing the annoying noise rewards buckling. Being scolded for running late is positive punishment, and a parking fine or losing screen time is negative punishment. In general, rewarding what you want works better and lasts longer than punishing what you don't.

sections.key: Unpredictable (variable) rewards create the most persistent behaviour.
sections.b: Skinner found that rewards given unpredictably, on a variable schedule, produce the most persistent behaviour. If a pigeon gets food every tenth peck, it pecks steadily. If food arrives after a random number of pecks, it pecks relentlessly, and keeps going long after the food stops. It's the logic of poker machines and social media feeds: you never know when the next reward is coming, so you keep checking. It's also why Golden Lessons in this app appear at random.

sections.key: Make good habits rewarding, bad ones harder, and notice the cues that trigger you.
sections.b: You can use conditioning deliberately. Pair a habit you want with something you enjoy, like only listening to a favourite podcast while exercising. Reward yourself immediately after the behaviour, not days later. Notice the cues that trigger habits you don't want, like the phone on your bedside table, and remove or change them. And be aware of variable rewards in the apps you use: turning off notifications breaks the cue, and moving apps off your home screen adds friction to the loop.

quiz.q: What was Pavlov originally studying?
quiz.e: He was researching digestion when he noticed the dogs drooling early.

quiz.q: Your mouth waters when you hear a chip packet open. This is an example of...
quiz.e: You've linked the sound with food: classical conditioning.

quiz.q: What happens if a conditioned cue keeps appearing without the outcome?
quiz.e: That's extinction, the basis of exposure therapy.

quiz.q: A car beeps until you buckle your seatbelt. What is the beep stopping an example of?
quiz.e: Removing something unpleasant to reward a behaviour is negative reinforcement.

quiz.q: Which reward schedule creates the most persistent behaviour?
quiz.e: Variable, unpredictable rewards keep people (and pigeons) coming back.

LESSONS.title: How habits really work
LESSONS.hook: Around 40% of what you do each day happens on autopilot. Here's how to take control of the autopilot.

sections.key: A large share of daily behaviour is habitual, done automatically in familiar contexts.
sections.b: Studies that asked people to log what they were doing throughout the day found that roughly 40% of their actions were repeated almost daily, in the same place, often while they were thinking about something else. That's the power of habits: they free your conscious mind for other things. You don't decide how to brush your teeth or which route to drive to work. The downside is that bad habits run on the same autopilot, which is why willpower alone so often fails to change them.

sections.key: Habits follow a loop: cue, routine, reward.
sections.b: Researchers describe habits as a loop. A cue triggers the behaviour: a time, a place, a feeling, a person or a preceding action. Then comes the routine, the behaviour itself. Finally there's a reward, something that makes the brain want to repeat the loop. Finishing a coffee (cue) leads to checking your phone (routine), which delivers a hit of novelty (reward). The writer Charles Duhigg popularised this model in The Power of Habit, and James Clear expanded it in Atomic Habits. To change a habit, you work on each part of the loop.

sections.h: How long does a habit take?
sections.key: Forming a habit took 66 days on average in one study, with a huge range.
sections.b: You may have heard that habits take 21 days. That figure doesn't come from habit research. In a 2009 study at University College London, volunteers chose a new daily behaviour, like drinking water with lunch or doing sit-ups before dinner. On average it took 66 days for the behaviour to feel automatic, but the range was huge, from 18 to 254 days depending on the person and the habit. Encouragingly, missing a single day didn't derail progress. Consistency matters more than perfection.

sections.key: Tie a new habit to a clear cue, like 'After I pour my coffee, I will…'.
sections.b: Vague intentions like 'I'll exercise more' rarely stick. Specific plans work far better. Psychologists call these implementation intentions: 'I will do X at time Y in place Z.' A powerful version is habit stacking, where you attach a new habit to an existing one: 'After I pour my morning coffee, I'll write down three priorities for the day.' The existing habit becomes the cue. You can also design your surroundings: put the book on your pillow, the running shoes by the door and the fruit bowl on the bench.

sections.key: Shrink new habits until they're almost too easy to skip; add friction to bad ones.
sections.b: The biggest enemy of a new habit is friction. Start ridiculously small: one push-up, one page, two minutes of tidying. The point isn't the push-up; it's becoming someone who shows up every day. Once the habit exists, you can grow it. Flip the principle for bad habits: add friction. Log out of social media so you have to sign in each time. Keep snacks in a high cupboard. Leave your credit card out of your online shopping accounts. Small obstacles are surprisingly effective because habits run on the path of least resistance.

sections.key: Immediate rewards reinforce habits; delayed benefits don't motivate the brain much.
sections.b: The benefits of many good habits, like fitness or savings, come months or years later, and our brains don't value distant rewards much. So add an immediate one. Tick a box on a calendar and enjoy watching the chain grow. Pair the habit with something you enjoy. Transfer $5 to a 'treat' account each time you skip takeaway. Streaks work for the same reason, which is why this app has one. The satisfaction has to arrive right after the behaviour to strengthen the loop.

sections.key: Keep the cue and reward but swap the routine; or remove the cue altogether.
sections.b: You rarely delete a habit; you replace it. Work out what reward the bad habit actually gives you. Is afternoon snacking about hunger, boredom or a break from work? Then keep the cue and reward but change the routine: when the 3 pm slump hits, take a five-minute walk and chat to a colleague instead. Where possible, remove the cue entirely. People who successfully quit smoking often change routines linked to cigarettes, like the morning coffee spot, because context is such a strong trigger.

sections.key: Habits stick best when they reflect who you want to be, not just a target to hit.
sections.b: Goals are useful for direction, but they end: you run the marathon, then stop running. Habits that last are often tied to identity. 'I'm trying to quit smoking' is weaker than 'I'm not a smoker.' 'I want to read more' is weaker than 'I'm a reader.' Every time you do the behaviour, you cast a small vote for that identity. Start with who you want to become, then choose the tiny daily actions that person would take, and let the results follow.

quiz.q: What are the three parts of the habit loop?
quiz.e: A cue triggers a routine, and a reward reinforces it.

quiz.q: In the 2009 UCL study, how long did it take on average for a habit to feel automatic?
quiz.e: 66 days on average, ranging from 18 to 254.

quiz.q: 'After I pour my coffee, I'll write my three priorities.' What's this technique called?
quiz.e: Attaching a new habit to an existing one makes the old habit the cue.

quiz.q: What's the best way to discourage a bad habit?
o: Add friction to make it harder
Do it more to get bored
quiz.e: Habits follow the easiest path, so obstacles work.

quiz.q: How do you usually break a bad habit most effectively?
o: Keep the cue and reward but swap the routine
quiz.e: Replace the routine while still meeting the underlying need.

LESSONS.title: Why we procrastinate
LESSONS.hook: Procrastination isn't laziness or poor time management. It's an emotion problem, and that's good news.

sections.key: Procrastination is mainly about avoiding unpleasant feelings, not poor time management.
sections.b: Around one in five adults describe themselves as chronic procrastinators, and nearly everyone does it sometimes. It's tempting to blame laziness or a lack of organisation, but research by psychologists such as Tim Pychyl and Fuschia Sirois suggests something different. Procrastination is mostly about emotions. We delay tasks that make us feel bored, anxious, confused, overwhelmed or insecure. Putting them off gives instant relief. Unfortunately, it's a short-term fix that creates a long-term problem, and the relief rewards the delay, making it a habit.

sections.key: We discount future rewards and treat our future self almost like a stranger.
sections.b: Economists call it present bias or temporal discounting: rewards now feel much bigger than rewards later. The satisfaction of a finished report next week can't compete with the pleasure of scrolling right now. Brain-imaging studies have even found that when people think about their future selves, their brain activity looks more like thinking about a stranger than about themselves. So we happily hand future-us the hard work, as if it were somebody else's problem. Strategies that make the future feel closer, or the present more rewarding, help.

sections.key: Fear of doing something imperfectly is a major driver of delay.
sections.b: Many procrastinators aren't lazy at all; they care a lot. If a task feels like a test of your ability, starting risks proving you're not good enough, so delaying protects your self-image. There's even an excuse built in: 'I only did badly because I left it too late.' The antidote is to lower the stakes of starting. Give yourself permission to write a terrible first draft. Call it 'version zero'. Perfection is something you might aim for at the end, never at the beginning.

sections.key: Commit to starting for just a few minutes; starting is the hardest part.
sections.b: The feeling of dread is usually worst before you begin. Once you start, it often fades. So make starting tiny: commit to two minutes, one paragraph or opening the document and writing the heading. You're allowed to stop after that, but you often won't. This works partly because unfinished tasks tend to stay on your mind, pulling you back. Even if you only do the two minutes, you've broken the avoidance loop and proved to yourself the task is survivable.

sections.key: Vague, huge tasks invite avoidance; turn them into small, concrete next actions.
sections.b: 'Do tax' or 'Plan the wedding' is overwhelming because it's vague. Your brain can't picture the first step, so it avoids the whole thing. Turn big tasks into concrete next actions that start with a verb: 'Find last year's tax return', 'Email three venues for quotes'. Productivity writer David Allen calls this identifying the 'next action'. Each small step is less threatening, gives a small win and builds momentum. A long list of tiny actions is far less scary than one giant task.

sections.key: Work in short, focused blocks with breaks, such as 25 minutes on, 5 off.
sections.b: The Pomodoro Technique, created by Francesco Cirillo in the late 1980s and named after a tomato-shaped kitchen timer, is simple: work for 25 minutes on one task, then take a 5-minute break. After four rounds, take a longer break. A deadline 25 minutes away is easy to face, and the break is a built-in reward. A related idea is timeboxing: put the task in your calendar like an appointment. Deciding exactly when you'll do something removes one more decision that feeds delay.

sections.key: Remove temptations from your environment rather than relying on willpower.
sections.b: Willpower is unreliable, especially when you're tired. It's far easier to change your surroundings. Put your phone in another room or in a drawer; even having it face-down on the desk can pull at your attention. Use website blockers for your worst time-wasters. Close extra tabs. Work somewhere you associate with focus, like a library. Tell someone what you'll finish by a certain time; a little accountability goes a long way. Remove the easy escape routes, and the task becomes the path of least resistance.

sections.key: Self-compassion after procrastinating reduces future procrastination.
sections.b: Beating yourself up feels like it should help, but it usually makes things worse, because guilt is another unpleasant feeling to avoid. In a study of university students, those who forgave themselves for procrastinating before their first exam procrastinated less before the next one. Self-compassion isn't letting yourself off the hook; it's treating yourself like a friend who stumbled. Acknowledge it, work out what made the task feel hard, and choose the next small step. Then take it.

quiz.q: According to research, what is procrastination mainly about?
quiz.e: We delay tasks to escape feelings like anxiety or boredom.

quiz.q: Why do we hand hard tasks to 'future us'?
o: We value present rewards more and treat our future self like a stranger
quiz.e: Present bias makes immediate pleasure feel bigger.

quiz.q: What's the idea behind 'just start for two minutes'?
o: Starting is the hardest part, and dread usually fades once you begin
Two minutes is enough to finish anything
quiz.e: Tiny starts break the avoidance loop.

quiz.q: Why do short, timed work blocks help procrastinators?
o: They make the task finish itself
A deadline minutes away is easy to face, and the break is a built-in reward
They remove the need for breaks
quiz.e: Short blocks lower the dread of starting and reward you quickly.

quiz.q: What happened to students who forgave themselves for procrastinating?
quiz.e: Self-compassion reduced later procrastination.

LESSONS.title: The memory palace
LESSONS.hook: The 2,500-year-old technique memory champions use to remember almost anything, and how to build your own tonight.

sections.key: The memory palace (method of loci) dates to ancient Greece and was used by Roman orators.
sections.b: The memory palace, or method of loci ('loci' is Latin for places), dates back to ancient Greece. Legend says the poet Simonides stepped out of a banquet moments before the hall collapsed. The victims were unrecognisable, but Simonides identified them by remembering where each person had been sitting. He realised that memory for places is remarkably strong. Roman orators like Cicero and Quintilian later described using the technique to deliver long speeches without notes, walking through an imagined building where each room held the next point.

sections.key: Human spatial memory is extremely strong, so linking facts to places makes them stick.
sections.b: Our ancestors needed to remember where water, food and danger were, so human brains became extraordinarily good at remembering places and routes. Think about it: you can probably walk through your childhood home in your mind and describe each room, but you'd struggle to recall a list of ten random words you read yesterday. The memory palace borrows that strong spatial memory and uses it to store things our brains are bad at holding, like lists, numbers and abstract facts. The hippocampus, a brain region important for navigation, is also central to forming new memories.

sections.key: Choose a familiar place and a fixed route of distinct spots.
sections.b: Pick a place you know well, like your home, your workplace or your walk to the shops. Now choose a route through it and pick out distinct spots in order: front door, hallway mirror, lounge, TV, kitchen bench, fridge, back door. Always walk the route in the same direction. Start with about ten spots. Rehearse the route a couple of times until you can list the spots easily. That route is your palace, and you can reuse it again and again for different lists.

sections.key: Turn each item into a bizarre, exaggerated, multi-sensory image placed at a spot.
sections.b: Now turn each item you want to remember into a vivid image and place it at a spot. The stranger, funnier and more exaggerated, the better. To remember 'milk, eggs, batteries', picture a giant cow blocking your front door, eggs exploding against the hallway mirror and batteries fizzing and sparking all over the lounge. Add sound, smell and movement. Make images interact with the location. Ordinary images fade; absurd ones stick, because the brain pays attention to things that are surprising or emotional.

sections.key: Recall by mentally walking the route; the order comes back automatically.
sections.b: To recall the list, simply walk the route in your mind and see what's waiting at each spot. Because the route is fixed, you also get the order for free, and you can even recall the list backwards. If a spot is empty, you know exactly which item you've forgotten, which is handy for speeches. The first few attempts feel slow and silly, but after a little practice, placing images takes a few seconds each.

sections.key: Convert abstract ideas and numbers into concrete images before placing them.
sections.b: Lists of objects are easy, but what about ideas or numbers? Convert them into something you can picture. For a speech point about 'rising costs', imagine a price tag growing into a balloon and lifting off the couch. For names, link the name to an image: 'Rose' becomes a rose; 'Barker' becomes a barking dog. For numbers, memory athletes use systems that turn digits into images, such as 1 = a candle (it looks like one) and 2 = a swan. Anything can be remembered once it becomes a picture.

sections.key: In a 2017 study, six weeks of training more than doubled word-list recall.
sections.b: Yes. Competitive memory athletes use the method to memorise shuffled decks of cards in under a minute and thousands of digits of pi. In a 2017 study published in the journal Neuron, ordinary volunteers trained with the technique for 30 minutes a day over six weeks. Their recall of a 72-word list more than doubled, and their brain connectivity shifted to resemble that of memory champions. Four months later, much of the improvement was still there.

sections.key: Use memory palaces for shopping lists, speeches, key points and names; combine with spaced review.
sections.b: Everyday uses include shopping lists, the key points of a presentation, a set of instructions, the order of topics in an exam essay, or the names of people at a meeting. You can build multiple palaces from places you know: your gym, your parents' house, your favourite café. The technique helps you get information in. To keep it for months, combine it with spaced review, walking through the palace again a day later, then a few days later, then a week later.

quiz.q: What's another name for the memory palace?
quiz.e: Loci is Latin for 'places'.

quiz.q: Why does the technique work so well?
o: It uses our very strong spatial memory
quiz.e: We're naturally very good at remembering places.

quiz.q: What kind of images work best?
quiz.e: Unusual, emotional images grab attention and stick.

quiz.q: How do you remember an abstract idea with a memory palace?
o: Turn it into a concrete image first
quiz.e: Anything can be stored once it becomes a picture.

quiz.q: In the 2017 study, what happened after six weeks of training?
quiz.e: Ordinary volunteers more than doubled their recall.

LESSONS.title: Mnemonics, chunking and how memory works
LESSONS.hook: Simple tricks that make information stick, from ROY G BIV to phone numbers, and the science of why they work.

sections.key: Memory involves encoding, storage and retrieval; most forgetting is a failure at one of these.
sections.b: Remembering something involves three stages. Encoding is getting information into memory in the first place. Storage is keeping it there over time. Retrieval is getting it back out when you need it. Most 'bad memory' is really poor encoding: you never properly paid attention, like forgetting a name seconds after hearing it because you were thinking about what to say. Mnemonics mostly help with encoding, making information meaningful and memorable, and they also give you a hook to pull it back out later.

sections.key: Short-term (working) memory holds only about four chunks at once.
sections.b: Your working memory, the mental scratchpad you use to hold information right now, is surprisingly small. In 1956, psychologist George Miller famously suggested it holds about 'seven, plus or minus two' items. More recent research by Nelson Cowan and others puts the true limit closer to four meaningful chunks. That's why you can lose track of a phone number between reading it and dialling it, and why too many instructions at once go in one ear and out the other.

sections.key: Grouping information into meaningful chunks multiplies what you can hold.
sections.b: The way around the limit is chunking: grouping items into meaningful units. 0412345678 is ten items, but 0412 345 678 is three chunks. FBICIAABC is nine letters, but FBI, CIA, ABC is three familiar acronyms. Chess masters can recall a whole board at a glance, but only if the pieces are in positions from real games, because they see patterns rather than individual pieces. Chunking is one reason experts seem to have super memories: their knowledge lets them group new information into bigger chunks.

sections.key: Acronyms and first-letter sentences compress lists into one memorable item.
sections.b: Acronyms turn a list into a single word. ROY G BIV gives the colours of the rainbow: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet. Many first-aid courses teach DRSABCD for the emergency action plan. When the first letters don't form a word, make a sentence: 'My Very Educated Mother Just Served Us Noodles' gives the planets in order from the Sun. Silly or personal sentences are the most memorable. Make up your own; they work better than borrowed ones.

sections.key: Rhyme and rhythm make information easier to recall.
sections.b: Rhyme and rhythm give the brain extra cues. 'Thirty days hath September, April, June and November' has helped people for centuries. Advertising jingles stick for decades for the same reason. Songs work too: many people learned the alphabet through a song and still hum it to find a letter. Setting information to a familiar tune, or chanting it with a beat, can help with lists like the states and capitals or a sequence of steps you need to follow.

sections.key: Linking new information to what you already know, and asking 'why', deepens memory.
sections.b: The more connections a memory has, the easier it is to find. Link new facts to things you already know: the capital of Australia is Canberra, which sounds like 'can, bra', so picture a bra in a can. When meeting someone called Rose with rosy cheeks, notice the link. Even better is elaboration: asking why and how something is true, and explaining it in your own words. Research shows that thinking about the meaning of information produces much stronger memories than simply repeating it.

sections.key: To learn a foreign word, link its sound to a familiar keyword, then picture the two together.
sections.b: The keyword method is a powerful mnemonic for vocabulary. First find a familiar word that sounds like the foreign one: the Spanish 'pato', meaning duck, sounds like 'pot'. Then create an image joining the keyword to the meaning, such as a duck wearing a pot on its head. When you see 'pato', 'pot' springs to mind, and the image hands you 'duck'. In 1975 psychologists Richard Atkinson and Michael Raugh tested the technique on Russian vocabulary and found that learners using it remembered far more words than those who simply rehearsed. It works for names, medical terms and anything else that sounds foreign at first.

sections.key: Drawing a word or idea, even badly, makes it more memorable than writing it out.
sections.b: One of the simplest memory boosters is to draw what you want to remember. In 2016, researchers at the University of Waterloo in Canada gave volunteers lists of simple words and about 40 seconds for each, asking them either to draw the word or to write it out repeatedly. Drawn words were remembered far better, in some experiments about twice as often, and artistic skill made no difference. Drawing seems to work because it combines thinking about meaning, making a picture and moving your hand. Quick sketches in the margins of your notes, or a rough diagram of how a process works, can turn a forgettable page into a memorable one.

quiz.q: Roughly how many chunks can working memory hold at once?
quiz.e: Recent research puts it around four meaningful chunks.

quiz.q: Why are phone numbers split into groups?
o: Chunking makes them easier to remember
quiz.e: Three chunks are easier than ten loose digits.

quiz.q: What does ROY G BIV help you remember?
quiz.e: Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.

quiz.q: Using the keyword method, how might you learn that the Spanish 'pato' means duck?
o: Picture a duck wearing a pot, since 'pato' sounds like 'pot'
Only ever see it in a sentence
quiz.e: A sound-alike keyword plus a vivid image links the new word to its meaning.

quiz.q: What did the 2016 University of Waterloo 'drawing effect' studies find?
o: Drawing words helped people remember them better than writing them out
Drawing distracted people and hurt memory
Writing words out repeatedly worked best
quiz.e: Even rough drawings boosted recall, regardless of artistic skill.

LESSONS.title: The placebo effect
LESSONS.hook: A sugar pill can make you feel better. Even when you know it's a sugar pill.

sections.key: A placebo is a treatment with no active ingredient; the placebo effect is the improvement people feel anyway.
sections.b: A placebo is a treatment with no active ingredient: a sugar pill, a saline injection or even a fake procedure. The placebo effect is the real improvement people often feel after receiving one. The word comes from Latin for 'I shall please'. Placebos are essential in medical research: to prove a drug works, scientists compare it with a placebo. If people taking the real drug don't improve more than those taking the dummy, the drug isn't doing much.

sections.key: Placebo effects involve real brain chemistry, such as the release of natural painkillers.
sections.b: Placebo effects aren't imaginary. Brain-imaging studies show that when people expect pain relief from a placebo, their brains release endorphins, the body's natural painkillers. In one classic experiment, a drug that blocks endorphins also blocked the placebo's pain relief. Expectation changes how the brain processes signals like pain, nausea and fatigue. That said, placebos work mainly on symptoms we perceive, not on the underlying disease: a sugar pill won't shrink a tumour or cure an infection.

sections.key: Price, colour, injections and a caring clinician can all strengthen placebo effects.
sections.b: Strangely, the details matter. In studies, expensive placebos relieved pain better than cheap ones. Two pills tend to beat one. Injections tend to beat pills, and fake surgery can be surprisingly powerful. Colour plays a role too: blue pills are often perceived as calming. A warm, confident, attentive doctor boosts the effect. In one study of irritable bowel syndrome, patients given placebo treatment with a warm, attentive practitioner improved more than those given the same treatment in a brisk, impersonal manner.

sections.key: Open-label placebos can help some conditions even when patients know they're fake.
sections.b: Here's the strangest part. In a 2010 Harvard study, people with irritable bowel syndrome were given pills openly labelled as placebos, 'like sugar pills', and told they'd been shown to help through mind-body processes. They still reported significantly more improvement than a group who got no pills. Later studies found similar results for chronic back pain and fatigue. Researchers think the ritual of taking a treatment, and the expectation it creates, can work even without deception.

sections.key: The nocebo effect is negative expectations causing real symptoms.
sections.b: The placebo effect has a dark twin: the nocebo effect. If people expect side effects, they often get them, even from a dummy pill. In drug trials, people on placebo commonly report headaches, fatigue and nausea, especially after reading a long list of possible side effects. In a 2021 study of people who had stopped taking cholesterol-lowering statins because of side effects, much of the discomfort they reported also appeared when they took placebo tablets. Expectations shape how we feel in both directions.

sections.key: Sham-surgery trials have shown that some common operations work no better than a placebo procedure.
sections.b: Surgery carries a powerful placebo effect of its own, which only trials using sham operations can reveal. In a 2002 US study of keyhole knee surgery for osteoarthritis, patients who received only skin incisions, without the real procedure, reported as much improvement in pain and function over two years as those who had the full operation. A 2013 Finnish trial found much the same for a common keyhole operation on worn knee cartilage in middle-aged people. A 2014 review found that in about half of sham-controlled surgical trials, the real operation did no better than the fake. Results like these have led guidelines to advise against routine keyhole knee surgery for osteoarthritis.

sections.key: Pairing a real drug with a cue can train the body to respond to the cue alone.
sections.b: In 1975, psychologist Robert Ader gave rats saccharin-sweetened water together with a drug that suppresses the immune system. Later, the sweet water on its own suppressed their immune responses. Much as Pavlov's dogs learned to salivate at a sound, their bodies had learned to link a cue with a drug's effect. Researchers are now testing this in people. In small trials with children taking medication for ADHD, pairing each dose with a placebo pill, then cutting the real dose while the placebo pills continued, kept much of the benefit on a lower dose. This 'conditioned placebo' approach may one day help reduce doses and side effects.

sections.key: Expectations affect how you feel, but don't swap proven treatments for placebos.
sections.b: The placebo effect shows that the mind has real influence over how we experience symptoms, especially pain, nausea and fatigue. Positive expectations, trusted care and good routines can genuinely help you feel better. But it's no substitute for effective treatment, and it's often exploited by products that rely on it. When judging any remedy, ask whether it has been tested against a placebo in a blinded trial. If not, you can't know whether it's doing anything beyond what belief and time would do.

quiz.q: What is a placebo?
o: A treatment with no active ingredient
quiz.e: Such as a sugar pill or saline injection.

quiz.q: What has brain imaging shown about placebo pain relief?
quiz.e: Expectation triggers real brain chemistry.

quiz.q: What did the 2010 open-label placebo study find?
o: Placebos only work if you're deceived
People improved even when told the pills were placebos
quiz.e: Improvement happened without deception.

quiz.q: What is the nocebo effect?
quiz.e: Expecting side effects can produce them.

quiz.q: What did a 2002 sham-controlled study of keyhole knee surgery for osteoarthritis find?
o: The real operation worked far better
Patients given only skin incisions improved as much as those who had the real operation
quiz.e: Only a sham-controlled trial could show how much of the benefit came from expectation.

LESSONS.title: How to make better decisions
LESSONS.hook: Practical tools from psychology and economics for the choices that actually matter.

sections.key: Match effort to stakes: decide small, reversible things quickly.
sections.b: We make thousands of decisions a day, and treating them all seriously is exhausting. A useful filter, popularised by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, is to ask whether a decision is a 'one-way door' or a 'two-way door'. One-way doors, like selling a house or quitting a career, are hard to reverse and deserve careful thought. Two-way doors, like trying a new gym or ordering a dish, can be undone, so decide quickly and learn from the result. Most decisions are two-way doors.

sections.key: Satisficers pick 'good enough' and tend to be happier than maximisers who seek the best.
sections.b: Psychologist Barry Schwartz describes two decision styles. Maximisers try to find the very best option, comparing everything. Satisficers set criteria and pick the first option that meets them. In studies, maximisers sometimes land slightly better outcomes, such as higher starting salaries, but they tend to feel less satisfied and more regretful. For most choices, like a toaster, a streaming show or a restaurant, deciding what 'good enough' means before you look, then stopping when you find it, saves time and happiness.

sections.key: More choice can make deciding harder and less satisfying.
sections.b: In a famous 2000 study, shoppers who saw a display of 24 jams were more likely to stop, but far less likely to buy, than those who saw only 6. Later research found the 'choice overload' effect isn't universal: it depends on how complex the options are and how clear your preferences are. But the practical lesson holds. When faced with too many options, narrow them fast. Decide your top two or three criteria, eliminate anything that fails them, and compare only the finalists.

sections.key: The real cost of a choice includes the best alternative you give up.
sections.b: Every choice has an opportunity cost: the value of the best alternative you give up. The cost of a $60,000 car isn't just $60,000; it's also what that money could have become if invested, or the holiday you won't take. The cost of an evening scrolling is the book not read or the friend not called. People often forget opportunity costs because they're invisible. Asking 'What else could I do with this money or time?' makes them visible and sharpens almost any decision.

sections.h: Write down the pros, cons and weights
sections.key: Listing factors and weighting what matters most beats juggling it all in your head.
sections.b: Our working memory can hold only a few items at once, so big decisions juggled in our heads get dominated by whichever factor feels loudest right now. Writing things down helps. Charles Darwin famously listed the pros and cons of marriage before proposing. An upgrade is to weight each factor: score how much each one matters to you from 1 to 5, and how well each option performs. You don't have to follow the numbers blindly, but the process often reveals what you really care about.

sections.key: Decide in advance what would make you stop or rethink, so sunk costs don't trap you later.
sections.b: Many decisions go wrong not at the start but months later, when we keep pushing on after the evidence has turned, partly because of the time and money already spent. Brothers Chip and Dan Heath, in their 2013 book Decisive, suggest setting tripwires: before committing, write down the signals that would make you stop or reconsider. 'If the renovation runs 20% over budget, we pause and rethink.' 'If this job still feels wrong in six months, I start looking.' Drawing the line while you're calm makes it far easier to act later, when pride and money already spent are urging you to keep going.

sections.key: Consider how you'll feel in 10 minutes, 10 months and 10 years, and ask what you'd advise a friend.
sections.b: Emotions in the moment can hijack decisions. Writer Suzy Welch suggests the 10/10/10 test: how will I feel about this in 10 minutes, 10 months and 10 years? It separates short-term discomfort from long-term value. Another trick is to take the outsider view: ask 'What would I tell my best friend to do?' Research suggests we often reason more wisely about other people's problems than our own, because we're less emotionally tangled up.

sections.key: Good decisions can have bad outcomes because of luck; judge the process.
sections.b: Former poker champion Annie Duke warns against 'resulting': judging a decision by how it turned out. A good decision can have a bad outcome because of luck, and a reckless one can work out fine. If you drive home drunk and arrive safely, it was still a bad decision. Instead, judge the process: did you have reasonable information, consider alternatives and think about risks? Keeping a simple decision journal, noting what you decided and why, helps you learn from both luck and skill over time.

quiz.q: What's a 'two-way door' decision?
o: One that can never be undone
quiz.e: Reversible decisions deserve less deliberation.

quiz.q: Compared with maximisers, satisficers tend to be...
quiz.e: 'Good enough' often leads to more happiness.

quiz.q: Why do people often overlook opportunity costs?
o: They are invisible: the alternative you gave up never shows on a receipt
They are already included in the price tag
quiz.e: Asking 'What else could I do with this money or time?' makes the hidden cost visible.

quiz.q: What is a 'tripwire' in decision-making?
o: A signal chosen in advance that will make you stop or rethink
A deadline set by your boss
A coin toss to break a tie
quiz.e: Deciding the exit point while you're calm counters the pull of sunk costs.

quiz.q: What is 'resulting'?
o: Judging a decision only by its outcome
quiz.e: Luck means outcomes don't always reflect decision quality.

LESSONS.title: How evolution works
LESSONS.hook: No designer, no plan, just time, variation and small differences adding up over millions of years.

sections.key: Darwin (and Wallace) proposed that species change over generations through natural selection.
sections.b: In 1859, Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species. Drawing on years of observation, including his voyage on HMS Beagle, which stopped in Sydney and Hobart in 1836, he argued that living things change over many generations through a process he called natural selection. Alfred Russel Wallace, working in South-East Asia, reached the same idea independently, and their work was presented together in 1858. It has since become the foundation of modern biology.

sections.key: Individuals vary, and much of that variation comes from genes passed to offspring.
sections.b: No two individuals are exactly alike. Some giraffes have slightly longer necks; some moths are slightly darker; some bacteria are slightly more resistant to a drug. Much of this variation comes from differences in genes, which are passed from parents to offspring. New variation arises from mutations, small random changes in DNA, and from the reshuffling of genes that happens with sexual reproduction. Most mutations are neutral or harmful, but occasionally one is helpful.

sections.key: Individuals with traits that suit their environment leave more offspring, so those traits spread.
sections.b: Every species produces more offspring than can survive. A cod can release millions of eggs, and even slow-breeding elephants would overrun the planet if every calf survived. So there's competition for food, mates and safety. Individuals whose traits suit their environment are slightly more likely to survive and have young, passing those traits on. Over many generations, helpful traits become more common and unhelpful ones less so. That's natural selection: simple, relentless and unguided.

sections.key: Dark peppered moths spread when soot blackened trees, because birds spotted pale moths more easily.
sections.b: Peppered moths in England were mostly pale, speckled like the lichen on tree bark. During the Industrial Revolution, soot killed the lichen and blackened the trees. Within decades, dark moths became far more common around industrial cities, because birds spotted and ate pale moths more easily. When clean-air laws reduced pollution in the late 20th century, pale moths bounced back. Scientists have since tracked the gene responsible, making it one of the best-documented examples of evolution in action.

sections.key: Antibiotic resistance is evolution happening fast, right now.
sections.b: Evolution isn't only ancient history. Bacteria reproduce so quickly, sometimes every 20 minutes, that they can evolve within weeks. When antibiotics kill most bacteria in an infection, any with a lucky mutation that helps them survive are left to multiply. Repeat that often enough and you get resistant 'superbugs'. It's also why doctors say to take antibiotics exactly as prescribed and not to use them for viral infections like colds. Insects evolving resistance to pesticides works the same way.

sections.key: 'Fittest' means best suited to an environment, not strongest; evolution has no goal.
sections.b: 'Survival of the fittest' is a phrase coined by philosopher Herbert Spencer, and it's often misunderstood. It doesn't mean the strongest survive. It means those best suited to a particular environment leave the most offspring. Sometimes that's the fastest, but it might be the best camouflaged, the most cooperative or the one that needs the least food. A trait that helps in one place can hurt in another. And evolution has no goal or direction; it simply keeps whatever works well enough, right now.

sections.key: Fossils, DNA, anatomy and observed change all independently support evolution.
sections.b: Evolution is supported by several independent lines of evidence. Fossils show changing life forms through time, including transitional species like early whales with legs. DNA comparisons show how closely species are related; humans and chimpanzees share about 98.8% of their DNA. Anatomy reveals shared designs, like the same bones in a human arm, a bat wing and a whale flipper. And we observe evolution directly in bacteria, insects and even Darwin's finches in the Galápagos.

sections.key: Earth is about 4.5 billion years old; humans share common ancestors with all life.
sections.b: Earth is about 4.5 billion years old, and life appeared at least 3.5 billion years ago. That's enough time for small changes to add up to the enormous variety of life today. Humans didn't evolve from modern chimpanzees; we share a common ancestor that lived roughly 6 to 7 million years ago. Our own species, Homo sapiens, appeared in Africa around 300,000 years ago. Go back far enough and every living thing, from koalas to mushrooms, shares a common ancestor.

quiz.q: Who published On the Origin of Species in 1859?
quiz.e: Charles Darwin published it in 1859.

quiz.q: In natural selection, which individuals pass on their traits most?
o: Those best suited to their environment
quiz.e: Better-suited individuals survive and reproduce more.

quiz.q: Why is antibiotic resistance an example of evolution?
o: Bacteria that survive the drug multiply and pass on resistance
quiz.e: The drug selects for resistant survivors.

quiz.q: What does 'fittest' mean in evolution?
quiz.e: Fitness means how well suited an organism is to its environment.

quiz.q: What is the relationship between humans and chimpanzees?
o: We share a common ancestor from millions of years ago
quiz.e: Our lineages split roughly 6 to 7 million years ago.

LESSONS.title: Water is weird
LESSONS.hook: The most ordinary liquid on Earth breaks almost every rule in chemistry, and life depends on it.

sections.key: Water (H₂O) is a bent, polar molecule: one oxygen and two hydrogens.
sections.b: A water molecule is one oxygen atom bonded to two hydrogen atoms, in a bent shape like a wide 'V', with an angle of about 104.5 degrees. Oxygen pulls the shared electrons towards itself, making the oxygen end slightly negative and the hydrogen ends slightly positive. That uneven charge makes water polar, a bit like a tiny magnet. Almost everything strange about water follows from this one simple fact.

sections.key: Hydrogen bonds are weak attractions between water molecules that explain most of its oddness.
sections.b: The positive hydrogen end of one water molecule is attracted to the negative oxygen end of its neighbour. These weak links are called hydrogen bonds. In liquid water they constantly form and break, trillions of times a second. They make water molecules cling to each other far more than you'd expect for such small molecules. Without hydrogen bonds, water would boil at around minus 80°C, and Earth would have no liquid oceans at all.

sections.key: Ice floats because freezing locks molecules into an open lattice about 9% less dense than liquid water.
sections.b: Most substances are densest as solids: solid wax sinks in melted wax. Water does the opposite. When it freezes, hydrogen bonds lock the molecules into an open, hexagonal lattice, which takes up more space. Ice is about 9% less dense than liquid water, so it floats. That's why pipes burst in freezing weather and why icebergs show only about a tenth of their bulk above the surface. Water is actually densest at about 4°C.

sections.key: Because ice floats, lakes freeze from the top, insulating life beneath.
sections.b: If ice sank, lakes and seas in cold regions would freeze from the bottom up, and many would freeze solid every winter, killing most life in them. Instead, floating ice forms an insulating lid on top. The water beneath stays liquid, often at around 4°C, and fish, plants and other creatures survive the winter underneath. This quirk of chemistry has helped life on Earth persist through ice ages.

sections.key: Water's high heat capacity keeps coastal climates mild and body temperature stable.
sections.b: Water has a very high heat capacity: it takes a lot of energy to warm it up, and it releases that energy slowly as it cools. That's why the sea is still cold in early summer and still warm in autumn, and why coastal cities like Sydney have milder temperatures than inland towns like Dubbo. The oceans absorb enormous amounts of heat, moderating global climate. Your body, which is around 60% water, uses the same property to hold a steady temperature.

sections.key: Evaporating water carries away lots of heat, which is how sweating cools you.
sections.b: Turning liquid water into vapour also takes a lot of energy, because hydrogen bonds must be broken. When sweat evaporates from your skin, it carries that heat away, cooling you down. That's why a breeze feels so good on a hot day, and why humid days feel worse: when the air is already full of moisture, sweat evaporates more slowly. Evaporative coolers, common in drier parts of Australia, work on the same principle.

sections.key: Hydrogen bonds give water strong surface tension, letting insects walk on it.
sections.b: At the surface of water, molecules are pulled inwards by their neighbours below, creating a kind of elastic skin called surface tension. It's strong enough for insects like water striders to walk on ponds and for a carefully placed paper clip to float. Surface tension also helps water climb up narrow tubes, called capillary action, which is part of how plants draw water from their roots up to their leaves.

sections.key: Because it's polar, water dissolves more substances than almost any other liquid.
sections.b: Because it's polar, water pulls apart and surrounds many other charged or polar molecules, dissolving them. It dissolves more substances than almost any other liquid, which is why it's called the universal solvent. It carries nutrients in your blood, minerals from rocks into rivers, and salt into the sea. It's also why water is so hard to keep pure. Every chemical reaction that keeps you alive happens in water, which is why scientists searching for life elsewhere start by looking for it.

quiz.q: What is a water molecule made of?
o: Two oxygen atoms and one hydrogen
One oxygen atom and two hydrogens
quiz.e: H₂O: two hydrogens and one oxygen.

quiz.q: What are hydrogen bonds?
o: Bonds between salt and water only
quiz.e: They're weak attractions between charged ends of neighbouring molecules.

quiz.q: Why does ice float?
o: Its molecules lock into an open, less dense pattern
quiz.e: The open lattice makes ice about 9% less dense.

quiz.q: Why do coastal cities have milder temperatures than inland ones?
o: Water has a high heat capacity
quiz.e: The sea absorbs and releases heat slowly.

quiz.q: Why do humid days feel hotter?
o: Sweat evaporates more slowly, so it cools you less
quiz.e: Evaporation is what carries heat away.

LESSONS.title: Quantum mechanics, simply
LESSONS.hook: The physics of the very small breaks every everyday rule. Yet it's the most tested theory in science, and it runs your phone.

sections.h: The physics of the very small
sections.key: Quantum mechanics describes how atoms and particles behave; it's behind lasers, chips and MRI.
sections.b: Quantum mechanics describes how things behave at the scale of atoms and subatomic particles, like electrons and photons. At that size, the everyday rules of cause and effect you're used to stop working the way you'd expect. It sounds like science fiction, yet it's one of the most precisely tested theories in science, with predictions confirmed to many decimal places. It's also practical: without it, we'd have no transistors, computer chips, lasers, LEDs, solar panels or MRI machines.

sections.key: Energy comes in fixed packets called quanta; packets of light are photons.
sections.b: In 1900, German physicist Max Planck was trying to explain the colours of light given off by hot objects. He found the maths only worked if energy was given off in tiny fixed amounts, which he called quanta. In 1905, Albert Einstein showed that light itself comes in packets, now called photons, to explain how light knocks electrons out of metal. That discovery, not relativity, won him his Nobel Prize. 'Quantum' simply means a fixed amount.

sections.key: Electrons in atoms can only have certain energy levels and jump between them.
sections.b: In 1913, Niels Bohr proposed that electrons in an atom can only have certain fixed energy levels, like steps on a ladder rather than a ramp. They jump between levels, absorbing or giving off exactly the right amount of energy as light. That's why each element glows with its own unique set of colours, which astronomers use to work out what distant stars are made of. Ironically, a 'quantum leap' in physics is incredibly tiny, not huge.

sections.key: Particles like electrons behave as both waves and particles (the double-slit experiment).
sections.b: Light and matter behave like particles in some experiments and like waves in others. In the famous double-slit experiment, electrons are fired one at a time at a barrier with two narrow slits. Each electron lands as a single dot on the screen behind, like a particle. But over time, the dots build up a striped interference pattern, which only waves make, as if each electron passed through both slits at once. Try to detect which slit each electron goes through, and the pattern disappears.

sections.key: Quantum theory predicts probabilities; before measurement a particle can be in a superposition.
sections.b: Quantum mechanics doesn't tell you exactly where a particle is or what it will do. It gives probabilities. Before it's measured, a particle can be in a 'superposition' of several possible states at once. Measuring it produces one definite result, with odds the theory predicts precisely. Erwin Schrödinger's famous thought experiment, a cat that is somehow both alive and dead until the box is opened, was meant to show how strange this seems when scaled up.

sections.key: You can't know a particle's exact position and momentum at the same time.
sections.b: In 1927, Werner Heisenberg showed that you can't know both a particle's exact position and its exact momentum at the same time. The more precisely you pin down one, the fuzzier the other becomes. This isn't a flaw in our instruments; it's built into nature. It's also why atoms don't collapse: an electron squeezed into the tiny nucleus would have enormous uncertainty in its momentum, so it spreads out in a cloud around it instead.

sections.key: Entangled particles have linked measurements; tunnelling lets particles pass through barriers.
sections.b: Two particles can become entangled, so that measuring one instantly tells you about the other, however far apart they are. Einstein called it 'spooky action at a distance' and doubted it, but experiments have confirmed it repeatedly, and that work won the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics. Another quantum effect, tunnelling, lets particles pass through barriers they classically shouldn't be able to cross. Tunnelling helps power the Sun's nuclear fusion and is used in some computer memory.

sections.key: Quantum physics powers today's electronics; quantum computers use superposition for certain problems.
sections.b: The first quantum revolution gave us transistors, lasers and much of modern electronics. A second is under way. Quantum computers use qubits, which can be in superpositions of 0 and 1, to tackle certain problems, such as simulating molecules for new medicines, that would take ordinary computers far too long. They're still experimental and error-prone. Australia is a notable player in the field, with major research groups at universities in Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane.

quiz.q: What is a photon?
o: A heavy particle in the nucleus
quiz.e: Light comes in packets called photons.

quiz.q: In physics, how big is a 'quantum leap'?
quiz.e: It's an electron jumping between energy levels in an atom.

quiz.q: In the double-slit experiment, what do single electrons build up over time?
quiz.e: The interference pattern reveals their wave-like behaviour.

quiz.q: What does the uncertainty principle say?
o: You can't know exact position and momentum at the same time
quiz.e: Pinning down one makes the other less certain.

quiz.q: What did Einstein call entanglement?
quiz.e: He was sceptical, but experiments proved it real.

LESSONS.title: Climate change: the basics
LESSONS.hook: The physics has been understood since the 1800s. Here's what's actually happening, what it means for Australia and what's being done.

sections.key: Greenhouse gases trap heat that would otherwise escape to space, keeping Earth warm.
sections.b: Sunlight passes through the atmosphere and warms the Earth's surface. The surface then gives off heat as infrared radiation. Certain gases, especially water vapour, carbon dioxide (CO₂) and methane, absorb some of that infrared and send it back down, like a blanket. This natural greenhouse effect is essential: without it, Earth's average temperature would be around minus 18°C instead of about 15°C. The problem isn't the greenhouse effect itself, but thickening the blanket.

sections.key: Scientists showed CO₂ traps heat in the 1850s; the link to fossil fuels was predicted in 1896.
sections.b: This isn't new science. In 1856, American scientist Eunice Foote showed that a glass cylinder filled with CO₂ heated up more in sunlight than one filled with ordinary air. In 1859, John Tyndall in Britain measured how different gases absorb heat. In 1896, Swedish chemist Svante Arrhenius calculated that burning coal could eventually warm the planet. The basic physics has been settled for over a century; modern research focuses on how much warming, how fast and with what effects.

sections.key: CO₂ has risen from about 280 ppm before industrialisation to over 420 ppm, mainly from fossil fuels.
sections.b: Since the Industrial Revolution, humans have burned vast amounts of coal, oil and gas, and cleared forests. Atmospheric CO₂ has risen from about 280 parts per million before industrialisation to over 420 today, higher than at any time in at least 800,000 years, based on air bubbles trapped in Antarctic ice. We know the extra carbon comes from fossil fuels because it carries a distinctive chemical signature: fossil carbon is depleted in certain isotopes, and that signature shows up in the air.

sections.key: The world has warmed about 1.3–1.4°C since pre-industrial times; Australia about 1.5°C since 1910.
sections.b: The global average surface temperature has risen by roughly 1.3 to 1.4°C since the late 1800s, and the last decade was the warmest on record. In 2024, the global average for a single year exceeded 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels for the first time. Australia's climate has warmed by about 1.5°C since national records began in 1910, according to the Bureau of Meteorology and CSIRO. Land warms faster than oceans, which is why Australia's figure is higher than the global average.

sections.key: Australia faces more extreme heat, longer fire seasons, marine heatwaves and rising seas.
sections.b: For Australia, the effects include more frequent and intense heatwaves, longer and more dangerous bushfire seasons in the south and east, heavier downpours in some areas and less cool-season rain in the south-west and south-east. Oceans around Australia have warmed and become more acidic, and the Great Barrier Reef has suffered several mass bleaching events since 2016 during marine heatwaves. Global sea level has risen by more than 20 centimetres since 1900, and the rate is increasing.

sections.key: Most emissions come from electricity, transport, industry and agriculture.
sections.b: Globally, the largest sources of greenhouse gases are generating electricity and heat, industry (such as steel and cement), transport, agriculture and land clearing, and buildings. Methane, from livestock, landfill and gas leaks, is a powerful short-lived greenhouse gas. In Australia, electricity has historically been the biggest source because of the country's reliance on coal, followed by other stationary energy (fuel burned directly in industry, mining and buildings), transport and agriculture. Australia's emissions per person are among the highest in the developed world.

sections.key: Under the 2015 Paris Agreement, countries aim to keep warming well below 2°C, ideally 1.5°C.
sections.b: In the 2015 Paris Agreement, nearly every country agreed to aim to keep warming well below 2°C and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C. Scientists say that requires global emissions to fall steeply this decade and reach net zero, where any remaining emissions are balanced by removals, around mid-century. Every fraction of a degree matters: the difference between 1.5°C and 2°C means noticeably more extreme heat, more species loss and far more damage to coral reefs.

sections.key: Renewables are growing fast; solar is now among the cheapest electricity ever built.
sections.b: The good news is that solutions are scaling quickly. The cost of solar power fell by around 90% in the 2010s, and wind and solar are now among the cheapest sources of new electricity. Australia has more than four million rooftop solar systems, among the highest per person in the world, and renewables now provide around 40% of the country's electricity. Batteries, electric vehicles and heat pumps are spreading fast. Individuals can help most through big decisions: how they heat and power their homes, how they travel and how they vote.

quiz.q: What would Earth's average temperature be without any greenhouse effect?
quiz.e: The natural greenhouse effect keeps us about 33°C warmer.

quiz.q: When did scientists first show that CO₂ traps heat?
quiz.e: Eunice Foote (1856) and John Tyndall (1859).

quiz.q: How do scientists know the extra CO₂ comes from fossil fuels?
o: It carries a distinctive isotope signature
It is warmer than other CO₂
quiz.e: Fossil carbon is depleted in certain isotopes, and that fingerprint shows up in the air.

quiz.q: About how much has Australia's climate warmed since 1910?
quiz.e: According to the Bureau of Meteorology and CSIRO.

quiz.q: What temperature goals did the Paris Agreement set?
quiz.e: Countries agreed to pursue 1.5°C.

LESSONS.title: Antibiotics and superbugs
LESSONS.hook: A mouldy dish in 1928 changed medicine forever. Now the bugs are fighting back.

sections.key: Before antibiotics, minor infections were often deadly.
sections.b: It's easy to forget how dangerous life was before antibiotics. A scratch from a rose thorn, an infected tooth or a cut from farm work could turn into a fatal infection. Pneumonia, tuberculosis, meningitis and infections after childbirth killed huge numbers of people. Surgery was risky largely because of infection afterwards. In World War I, infected wounds killed many soldiers who would survive today.

sections.key: Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928 when mould killed bacteria on a dish.
sections.b: In September 1928, Scottish scientist Alexander Fleming returned from holiday to his London laboratory and noticed that one of his dishes of Staphylococcus bacteria had been contaminated by a mould. Around the mould, the bacteria had died. The mould was Penicillium, and Fleming named the bacteria-killing substance penicillin. But he struggled to purify it, and for about a decade it remained a laboratory curiosity.

sections.key: Adelaide-born Howard Florey and his team turned penicillin into a usable medicine in the 1940s.
sections.b: The breakthrough came at Oxford University, led by Howard Florey, who was born in Adelaide, with biochemist Ernst Chain and a talented team including Norman Heatley. Around 1940 they purified penicillin, showed it cured infected mice and then treated the first human patients. With American help, production was scaled up massively during World War II, saving countless wounded soldiers. Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the 1945 Nobel Prize in Medicine. Florey's portrait later appeared on Australia's $50 note.

sections.key: Antibiotics target structures bacteria have but human cells don't, such as cell walls.
sections.b: Antibiotics work by attacking features bacteria have but human cells don't. Penicillin and its relatives stop bacteria from building their cell walls, so they burst. Others block the tiny machines bacteria use to make proteins, or interfere with how they copy their DNA. Because they target bacteria specifically, they can kill an infection without harming your own cells, though they also affect the helpful bacteria in your gut, which is why they sometimes cause stomach upsets.

sections.key: Antibiotics don't work on viruses, like colds and flu.
sections.b: Viruses are completely different from bacteria. They have no cell walls or protein-making machinery of their own; they hijack your cells instead. So antibiotics do nothing against colds, flu, COVID-19 or most sore throats and coughs, which are usually viral. Taking antibiotics for a cold won't make you better faster, but it will expose the bacteria in your body to the drug, which can help resistance develop. Antivirals and vaccines are the tools for viruses.

sections.key: Overuse of antibiotics drives resistance; drug-resistant infections kill over a million people a year.
sections.b: Every time antibiotics are used, bacteria that happen to survive can multiply and spread their resistance, even swapping resistance genes with other bacteria. Overuse in humans and animals speeds this up. The result is superbugs: infections that some or most antibiotics can no longer treat. A major study estimated that in 2019, drug-resistant bacterial infections directly caused about 1.27 million deaths worldwide. Fleming himself warned in his 1945 Nobel lecture that misuse could lead to resistance.

sections.key: Only use antibiotics when prescribed, take them as directed and never share them.
sections.b: Everyone can help keep antibiotics working. Only take them when a doctor prescribes them, and don't pressure doctors for them for colds or flu. Take them exactly as directed. Never share antibiotics or use leftover ones. Return unused medicines to a pharmacy for safe disposal. Keep up to date with vaccinations, which prevent infections in the first place. And wash your hands well, which remains one of the most effective ways to stop infections spreading.

sections.key: Scientists are searching for new antibiotics and alternatives like bacteriophages.
sections.b: Very few new classes of antibiotics have been discovered in recent decades, partly because developing them is expensive and less profitable than drugs taken every day. Scientists are searching soil, oceans and even the human body for new compounds, and using AI to screen millions of molecules. They're also exploring alternatives, like bacteriophages, viruses that infect and kill specific bacteria, which have been used experimentally to treat otherwise untreatable infections.

quiz.q: Who discovered penicillin in 1928?
quiz.e: Fleming noticed mould killing bacteria on a dish.

quiz.q: Which Adelaide-born scientist helped turn penicillin into a usable medicine?
quiz.e: Florey led the Oxford team in the 1940s.

quiz.q: Why won't antibiotics cure a cold?
quiz.e: Antibiotics only work on bacteria.

quiz.q: What drives antibiotic resistance?
quiz.e: Every use gives resistant bacteria a chance to multiply.

quiz.q: What should you do with leftover antibiotics?
quiz.e: Pharmacies dispose of medicines safely.

LESSONS.title: DNA: your body's instruction manual
LESSONS.hook: Two metres of code in every cell, written in a four-letter alphabet.

sections.key: DNA carries the instructions for building and running living things.
sections.b: DNA, short for deoxyribonucleic acid, is the molecule that carries the instructions for building and running almost every living thing, from bacteria to blue whales. It's found inside nearly every cell in your body. If you unwound all the DNA in a single human cell and laid it end to end, it would stretch about two metres, yet it's packed into a nucleus far too small to see without a microscope.

sections.key: DNA's double-helix structure was revealed in 1953, using Rosalind Franklin's X-ray images.
sections.b: In 1953, James Watson and Francis Crick published the structure of DNA: a double helix, like a twisted ladder. Their model relied heavily on X-ray images taken by Rosalind Franklin, especially the famous 'Photo 51', and on data from Maurice Wilkins. Watson, Crick and Wilkins received the Nobel Prize in 1962. Franklin had died of cancer in 1958, aged 37, and Nobel Prizes aren't awarded posthumously. Her crucial role is now widely recognised.

sections.key: DNA's code uses four bases: A, T, C and G. A pairs with T, and C with G.
sections.b: The rungs of the DNA ladder are made of four chemical bases: adenine (A), thymine (T), cytosine (C) and guanine (G). A always pairs with T, and C always pairs with G. That pairing means each strand is a complementary template for the other, so a cell can copy its DNA by unzipping the ladder and building new partner strands. The human genome contains about 3 billion of these base pairs. Printed out, it would fill about 100 large encyclopedia volumes.

sections.key: Cells copy a gene into messenger RNA, then read it three letters at a time to string amino acids into a protein.
sections.b: To use a gene, a cell first copies it into a similar molecule called messenger RNA, which carries the instructions out of the nucleus to tiny protein-building machines called ribosomes. Ribosomes read the message three letters at a time. Each three-letter 'word', called a codon, calls for one of 20 amino acids, the building blocks of proteins, or signals where to stop. Four letters give 64 possible codons, so most amino acids have several, which means some spelling changes make no difference to the finished protein. In 1961 American biochemist Marshall Nirenberg and his colleague Heinrich Matthaei decoded the first codon, starting a race that cracked the whole code by the mid-1960s.

sections.key: Mutations are changes in DNA; most are harmless, some cause disease, a few are useful.
sections.b: Every time a cell divides, it copies its 3 billion letters, and occasionally makes a mistake. Radiation, like UV from the sun, and chemicals, like those in tobacco smoke, can also damage DNA. These changes are called mutations. Most are harmless or quickly repaired. Some cause disease, including many cancers, which is one reason sun protection matters so much in Australia. Occasionally a mutation is useful, and over generations those changes are the raw material for evolution.

sections.key: Any two people share about 99.9% of their DNA.
sections.b: Any two people share about 99.9% of their DNA. The remaining 0.1%, around 3 million letters, accounts for differences in appearance, some disease risks and more. There's actually more genetic variation within any so-called racial group than between groups, which is why scientists consider race a social idea rather than a clear biological category. You inherit half your DNA from each parent, which is why ancestry and paternity tests work.

sections.key: The Human Genome Project finished in 2003; sequencing now costs a tiny fraction of the original.
sections.b: The Human Genome Project, an international effort to read an entire human genome, was completed in 2003 after 13 years at a cost of about US$2.7 billion. Today, a human genome can be sequenced in about a day for a few hundred dollars. That has transformed medicine: doctors can diagnose rare genetic diseases in babies, match cancer treatments to the mutations in a tumour, and track the spread of viruses in real time, as happened during the COVID-19 pandemic.

sections.key: In 1984 Alec Jeffreys discovered DNA fingerprinting, which soon transformed family testing and criminal investigations.
sections.b: In 1984, British geneticist Alec Jeffreys, at the University of Leicester, noticed that certain repeated stretches of DNA vary so much between people that they form a pattern almost unique to each person, identical twins aside. He called it DNA fingerprinting. In 1985 it settled an immigration case by proving a boy really was his mother's son. Soon after, in a murder investigation, it cleared an innocent man who had confessed and then, in 1988, helped convict the real killer. Modern forensic profiles compare short repeated sequences at around 20 places in the genome. Because relatives share DNA, profiles are also used to identify disaster victims and reunite families.

quiz.q: Whose X-ray images were crucial to discovering DNA's structure?
quiz.e: Her 'Photo 51' was key evidence for the double helix.

quiz.q: Which base pairs with adenine (A)?
quiz.e: A pairs with T, and C pairs with G.

quiz.q: What is a codon?
o: A three-letter sequence that codes for an amino acid or a stop signal
quiz.e: Ribosomes read messenger RNA one codon at a time.

quiz.q: Roughly how much DNA do any two people share?
quiz.e: The 0.1% difference is about 3 million letters.

quiz.q: What did Alec Jeffreys discover in 1984?
quiz.e: Repeated stretches of DNA vary so much between people that they form a near-unique pattern.

LESSONS.title: How black holes work
LESSONS.hook: Places where gravity wins completely, time slows down and even light can't escape.

sections.key: A black hole is a region where gravity is so strong that not even light can escape.
sections.b: A black hole is a region of space where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape. It forms when a huge amount of mass is squeezed into a tiny space. Every object has an 'escape velocity', the speed you need to break free of its gravity: about 11 kilometres per second for Earth. For a black hole, the escape velocity is greater than the speed of light, about 300,000 kilometres per second, and since nothing can travel faster than light, nothing gets out.

sections.key: Black holes were predicted by Einstein's general relativity and were once thought purely theoretical.
sections.b: In 1783, English clergyman John Michell imagined 'dark stars' so massive that light couldn't escape. The modern idea came from Albert Einstein's general theory of relativity (1915), which describes gravity as the bending of space and time by mass.
