Within months, Karl Schwarzschild found that Einstein's equations allowed for regions from which nothing could escape. For decades many physicists, including Einstein, doubted they really existed. The name 'black hole' was popularised in the late 1960s.

sections.key: Stellar black holes form when the core of a very massive star collapses.
sections.b: Stellar black holes form when a very massive star, typically at least about 20 times the mass of our Sun, runs out of fuel. Without the outward push of nuclear fusion, the core collapses under its own gravity in a fraction of a second, often triggering a supernova explosion that blasts away the outer layers. What remains is crushed into a black hole. Our Milky Way probably contains tens of millions of these stellar-mass black holes, most of them invisible.

sections.key: The event horizon is the boundary beyond which nothing can escape.
sections.b: The boundary around a black hole is called the event horizon. Outside it, a powerful enough rocket could still escape. Once inside, escape is impossible, because every possible path leads further in. A black hole with the mass of our Sun would have an event horizon only about 6 kilometres across. If Earth were somehow squeezed into a black hole, it would be about the size of a marble. At the centre, general relativity predicts a 'singularity', where our current physics breaks down.

sections.key: Near a small black hole, uneven gravity would stretch you like spaghetti.
sections.b: Gravity gets stronger the closer you are to a mass. Near a small black hole, the pull on your feet would be enormously stronger than on your head, stretching you out like a noodle while squeezing you from the sides. Scientists really do call this spaghettification. Strangely, near a supermassive black hole the stretching at the event horizon is gentler, so you could cross it without noticing, though you'd still never come back out.

sections.key: General relativity says time passes more slowly in strong gravity.
sections.b: Einstein's general relativity predicts that time passes more slowly in stronger gravity. It's not just theory: clocks on GPS satellites, in weaker gravity high above Earth, tick slightly faster than clocks on the ground, and the system must correct for it. Near a black hole the effect becomes extreme. To a distant observer, a clock falling towards a black hole would appear to tick slower and slower as it approached the event horizon, its light growing dimmer and redder.

sections.key: Supermassive black holes, millions to billions of Suns in mass, sit at the centres of most large galaxies.
sections.b: Most large galaxies have a supermassive black hole at their centre, weighing millions to billions of times as much as the Sun. Ours is Sagittarius A*, about 4 million times the Sun's mass, around 26,000 light-years away. Astronomers proved it was there by tracking stars whipping around an invisible object at enormous speeds, work that won the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics. Gas falling into supermassive black holes can heat up and shine brighter than whole galaxies, creating quasars.

sections.key: The Event Horizon Telescope imaged M87's black hole (2019) and Sagittarius A* (2022); LIGO detected black hole collisions (2015).
sections.b: Black holes can't be seen directly, but their surroundings can. In 2015, the LIGO detectors in the US picked up gravitational waves, tiny ripples in space itself, from two black holes colliding over a billion light-years away. In 2019, the Event Horizon Telescope, a network of radio telescopes working as one Earth-sized dish, released the first image of a black hole's shadow, in the galaxy M87. In 2022 it imaged Sagittarius A*, at the heart of our own galaxy.

quiz.q: What makes a black hole 'black'?
o: Not even light can escape its gravity
It's too far away to see
quiz.e: Its escape velocity exceeds the speed of light.

quiz.q: How do stellar black holes usually form?
o: A galaxy runs out of gas
quiz.e: When a massive star runs out of fuel, its core collapses.

quiz.q: What is the event horizon?
o: The centre of a black hole
The boundary beyond which nothing can escape
quiz.e: Past it, escape would require going faster than light.

quiz.q: How do GPS satellites show that gravity affects time?
o: Their clocks tick slightly faster than ground clocks
quiz.e: Weaker gravity up there means time runs slightly faster.

quiz.q: What sits at the centre of the Milky Way?
o: A supermassive black hole called Sagittarius A*
quiz.e: About 4 million times the Sun's mass.

LESSONS.title: The life and death of stars
LESSONS.hook: How stars are born, why their mass decides their fate, and why many of them don't shine alone.

sections.key: Stars form in nebulae when gravity pulls gas together until it ignites.
sections.b: Stars form inside giant, cold clouds of gas and dust called nebulae, made mostly of hydrogen. Something, perhaps a nearby supernova or a collision between clouds, disturbs the gas. Gravity pulls denser clumps together, and as they shrink they heat up. When the core reaches about 10 million degrees, nuclear fusion ignites and a star is born. The Orion Nebula, visible to the naked eye as a fuzzy patch in Orion's 'sword' (the handle of the Saucepan in Australian skies), is a stellar nursery.

sections.key: Stars shine by fusing hydrogen into helium, which balances gravity pulling inwards.
sections.b: In a star's core, hydrogen nuclei are squeezed together so hard that they fuse into helium, converting a tiny amount of mass into a huge amount of energy, as described by Einstein's E = mc². The Sun converts about 4 million tonnes of matter into energy every second. That energy pushes outwards, balancing gravity pulling inwards. For most of a star's life, these two forces are locked in a stable balance.

sections.key: The Sun is an ordinary middle-aged star about 4.6 billion years old.
sections.b: The Sun is a fairly ordinary star, about 1.4 million kilometres across and 4.6 billion years old, roughly halfway through its life. Its surface is about 5,500°C and its core about 15 million °C. Energy released in the core can take tens of thousands of years or more to work its way out through the Sun's dense interior, but once it leaves the surface, the light reaches Earth in about eight minutes.

sections.key: Small stars live longest; massive stars burn out in millions of years.
sections.b: A star's mass decides almost everything about it: its colour, brightness and lifespan. Small, cool red dwarfs use fuel so slowly they can shine for trillions of years, far longer than the universe has existed. Massive blue stars burn hot and fast, lasting only a few million years. It seems backwards, but more fuel means a shorter life, because heavier stars burn it at a vastly faster rate. Most stars in the galaxy are red dwarfs, too faint to see with the naked eye.

sections.h: The death of a Sun-like star
sections.key: The Sun will become a red giant, then a white dwarf, in about 5 billion years.
sections.b: In about 5 billion years, when the Sun runs low on hydrogen in its core, it will swell into a red giant, perhaps large enough to engulf Mercury, Venus and possibly Earth. Well before then, in about a billion years, its growing brightness will have boiled away Earth's oceans. Eventually the Sun will puff off its outer layers into a glowing shell called a planetary nebula. What's left will be a white dwarf: a dense, Earth-sized ember that slowly cools over trillions of years.

sections.key: Massive stars explode as supernovae, leaving neutron stars or black holes.
sections.b: Massive stars end far more violently. They fuse heavier and heavier elements in their cores, up to iron. Fusing iron doesn't release energy, so the core collapses in less than a second, rebounding in a supernova, an explosion that can briefly outshine an entire galaxy of billions of stars. The collapsed core becomes a neutron star, so dense that a teaspoon would weigh billions of tonnes, or, if massive enough, a black hole.

sections.key: Close to half of Sun-like stars have a companion, and an exploding white dwarf in a pair makes a useful cosmic measuring stick.
sections.b: Our solitary Sun is a little unusual: close to half of Sun-like stars have at least one companion. Some pairs give themselves away by eclipses. Algol, in the constellation Perseus, noticeably dims every 2.9 days as a fainter partner passes in front of the brighter star. Sirius is circled by a small, faint companion, Sirius B, a white dwarf. Pairs can also be destructive. When a white dwarf pulls enough gas from a close partner, or merges with another white dwarf, it can blow apart in a type Ia supernova. These reach a predictable peak brightness, so astronomers use them to measure distances across the universe, work that earned ANU astronomer Brian Schmidt a share of the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics.

sections.key: A star's colour reveals its temperature, and starlight is a view into the past.
sections.b: Next time you're somewhere dark, look for colours. Reddish stars like Antares, in Scorpius, are cooler; blue-white stars like Rigel, in Orion, are hotter. Remember that starlight is old: light from the brightest star in the night sky, Sirius, left it about 8.6 years ago. Australia's dark outback skies are among the best in the world, and in 2016 Warrumbungle National Park in NSW became Australia's first Dark Sky Park.

quiz.q: Where are stars born?
o: In clouds of gas and dust called nebulae
quiz.e: Gravity collapses clumps of gas inside nebulae.

quiz.q: What powers a star?
o: Nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium
quiz.e: Fusion converts mass into energy.

quiz.q: Which stars live the longest?
quiz.e: They burn fuel so slowly they can last trillions of years.

quiz.q: What will the Sun eventually become?
quiz.e: It's not massive enough to explode.

quiz.q: What can happen to a white dwarf in a close pair of stars?
o: It turns back into a Sun-like star
It can explode as a type Ia supernova
It swells into a red giant again
quiz.e: These explosions reach a predictable brightness, making them useful distance markers.

LESSONS.title: The Big Bang
LESSONS.hook: 13.8 billion years ago, everything you can see was packed into a space smaller than an atom. How do we know?

sections.key: The Big Bang was the rapid expansion of space itself, not an explosion into existing space.
sections.b: The Big Bang theory describes how the universe expanded from an extremely hot, dense state about 13.8 billion years ago. The name is misleading. It wasn't an explosion in a particular place, flinging matter outwards into empty space. It was the expansion of space itself, happening everywhere at once. There's no centre and no edge to point to. The name was coined, somewhat mockingly, by astronomer Fred Hoyle in a 1949 radio broadcast; he preferred a rival theory.

sections.key: In 1929, Edwin Hubble showed galaxies are moving away from us, faster the further they are.
sections.b: In the 1920s, astronomers were still arguing about whether other galaxies even existed. Edwin Hubble settled that and then, in 1929, showed something astonishing: nearly all galaxies are moving away from us, and the further away they are, the faster they recede. That's exactly what you'd expect if space itself is stretching. Picture raisins in rising bread dough: every raisin moves away from every other, and distant ones separate faster. Run the film backwards and everything converges.

sections.key: The cosmic microwave background, discovered in 1965, is leftover heat from the early universe.
sections.b: If the universe began hot and dense, some of that heat should still be around, stretched into faint microwaves by billions of years of expansion. In 1965, Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, working at Bell Labs, found a mysterious hiss in their radio antenna coming from every direction. At first they suspected pigeon droppings. It turned out to be the cosmic microwave background: light released about 380,000 years after the Big Bang. It won them a Nobel Prize and is some of the strongest evidence for the theory.

sections.key: In the first few minutes, the universe made hydrogen, helium and a little lithium.
sections.b: In the first fraction of a second, the universe was far too hot for atoms to exist. As it expanded and cooled, basic particles formed, and within about three minutes, protons and neutrons fused into the nuclei of the lightest elements. The theory predicts the universe should have started out about three-quarters hydrogen and a quarter helium by mass, with a trace of lithium. That's almost exactly what astronomers observe in the oldest stars and gas clouds.

sections.key: After about 380,000 years atoms formed and light travelled freely; the first stars formed within a few hundred million years.
sections.b: For its first 380,000 years, the universe was a glowing fog of charged particles that scattered light. When it cooled enough for electrons to join nuclei and form atoms, the fog cleared and light could travel freely. That's the light we see as the cosmic microwave background. Then came a long 'dark age' until gravity pulled gas into the first stars and galaxies, within a few hundred million years. The James Webb Space Telescope, launched in 2021, is now spotting galaxies from this early era.

sections.key: Ordinary matter is only about 5% of the universe; dark matter and dark energy make up the rest.
sections.b: Everything we can see, stars, planets, gas and people, makes up only about 5% of the universe's contents. About 27% is dark matter, invisible material we detect only through its gravity, which holds galaxies together. The remaining 68% or so is dark energy, a mysterious effect causing the expansion of the universe to speed up, discovered in 1998. We don't yet know what either of them actually is. They're among the biggest open questions in science.

sections.key: What came 'before', and why, are open questions; the theory describes what happened after.
sections.b: The Big Bang theory describes how the universe evolved from an early hot, dense state. It doesn't explain what caused that state or whether anything came 'before'. Time itself may have begun with the Big Bang, making 'before' meaningless, much like asking what's north of the North Pole. Some physicists explore ideas such as cosmic inflation, a brief burst of extreme expansion in the first instant, or even multiple universes. These are active areas of research, not settled science.

sections.key: The observable universe is about 93 billion light-years across and holds hundreds of billions of galaxies, perhaps more.
sections.b: Because space has expanded while light travelled, the observable universe is about 93 billion light-years across, even though it's 13.8 billion years old. It may contain hundreds of billions of galaxies, perhaps as many as two trillion, each with billions of stars. The universe beyond what we can observe may be much larger, possibly infinite. On a clear night away from city lights, the faint smudge of the Large Magellanic Cloud, visible from Australia, is another galaxy whose light left it around 160,000 years ago.

quiz.q: How old is the universe, according to the Big Bang theory?
quiz.e: About 13.8 billion years.

quiz.q: What did Edwin Hubble discover in 1929?
o: Galaxies are moving away from us, faster the further they are
quiz.e: That's the signature of an expanding universe.

quiz.q: What is the cosmic microwave background?
o: Leftover heat from the early universe
quiz.e: Light released about 380,000 years after the Big Bang.

quiz.q: Roughly what share of the universe is ordinary matter?
quiz.e: Dark matter and dark energy make up the rest.

quiz.q: Does the Big Bang theory explain what caused the Big Bang?
o: No, it describes what happened after
quiz.e: What came before, if anything, is still an open question.

LESSONS.title: The Moon: our strange companion
LESSONS.hook: It was born in a collision, it's slowly drifting away, and it controls the tides at your local beach.

sections.key: The Moon most likely formed when a Mars-sized body hit the young Earth.
sections.b: The leading explanation for the Moon's origin is the giant-impact hypothesis. About 4.5 billion years ago, when Earth was young, a Mars-sized body, sometimes called Theia, smashed into it. The collision flung molten rock into orbit, which gradually clumped together to form the Moon. Evidence includes the Moon's small iron core and the remarkable similarity between Moon rocks brought back by Apollo astronauts and rocks on Earth.

sections.key: The Moon is tidally locked, so the same side always faces Earth.
sections.b: The Moon spins once on its axis in exactly the time it takes to orbit Earth, about 27 days. So the same side always faces us. This isn't a coincidence: Earth's gravity gradually slowed the Moon's spin until it locked into step, a process called tidal locking. The far side isn't permanently dark; it gets just as much sunlight. We simply never see it from Earth. Humans first saw it in 1959, in photos from a Soviet probe.

sections.key: Moon phases come from seeing different amounts of its sunlit half as it orbits.
sections.b: The Moon makes no light of its own; it reflects sunlight. Half of it is always lit by the Sun. As it orbits Earth, we see different amounts of that lit half, producing the phases: new moon, crescent, first quarter, gibbous and full, then back again, in a cycle of about 29.5 days. The word 'month' comes from 'moon'. From Australia, the Moon appears 'upside down' compared with northern hemisphere pictures, so a waxing crescent is lit on the left rather than the right.

sections.key: The Moon's gravity creates two tidal bulges, giving most coasts two high tides a day.
sections.b: The Moon's gravity pulls on Earth's oceans. It pulls hardest on the side facing it, creating a bulge of water, and least on the far side, where another bulge forms because the water is effectively left behind. As Earth rotates through the two bulges, most coasts get two high tides and two low tides each day. The Sun helps too: when Sun and Moon line up at full and new moon, we get extra-large spring tides. Australia's north-west has some of the largest tides in the world, over 10 metres.

sections.key: A solar eclipse happens when the Moon blocks the Sun; a lunar eclipse when Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.
sections.b: By a remarkable coincidence, the Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and about 400 times further away, so they look almost exactly the same size in our sky. When the Moon passes directly in front of the Sun, it can block it completely in a total solar eclipse. When Earth passes between the Sun and Moon, its shadow falls on the Moon, often turning it red, in a lunar eclipse. Eclipses don't happen every month because the Moon's orbit is tilted slightly.

sections.key: The Moon is moving away from Earth at about 3.8 cm a year.
sections.b: Apollo astronauts left mirrors on the Moon. Scientists fire lasers at them and time the reflection, measuring the distance to within millimetres. They've found the Moon is drifting away by about 3.8 centimetres a year, roughly the rate your fingernails grow. Tidal forces are also slowly lengthening Earth's day: hundreds of millions of years ago, a day was only around 22 hours long. Far in the future, total solar eclipses will no longer be possible, because the Moon will look too small to cover the Sun.

sections.key: The Moon's dark patches, called maria or 'seas', are plains of ancient solidified lava.
sections.b: The dark patches you can see with the naked eye are called maria, Latin for 'seas', because early astronomers thought they might be oceans. They are actually vast plains of solidified lava that flooded huge impact basins roughly 3 to 3.9 billion years ago. The brighter highlands are older, made of paler rock and packed with craters. Almost all the maria are on the near side, which is one reason the far side looks so different in photos. With no wind, rain or moving plates to wear them away, craters last billions of years. At full moon, binoculars show bright rays of debris spreading from young craters like Tycho.

sections.key: Under the 1967 Outer Space Treaty no country can claim the Moon, but plans to mine it raise new questions.
sections.b: Officially, nobody owns the Moon. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty, joined by Australia and more than 100 other countries, says no nation can claim the Moon or any other celestial body, and that space should be used for peaceful purposes. But plans to mine lunar water ice raise a new question: can a company own what it digs up? In 2020 Australia was one of eight founding signatories of the Artemis Accords, US-led principles that support using space resources and call for protecting historic sites such as the Apollo landing areas. Dozens more countries have since signed, while China and Russia are planning their own lunar research station instead.

quiz.q: How did the Moon most likely form?
o: A Mars-sized body collided with Earth
quiz.e: The giant-impact hypothesis.

quiz.q: Why do we always see the same side of the Moon?
o: The far side is always dark
quiz.e: Its spin matches its orbit.

quiz.q: What causes ocean tides?
quiz.e: The Sun contributes too.

quiz.q: How fast is the Moon drifting away from Earth?
quiz.e: Measured by bouncing lasers off Apollo mirrors.

quiz.q: What are the Moon's dark 'seas', or maria?
quiz.e: Lava flooded huge impact basins roughly 3 to 3.9 billion years ago.

LESSONS.title: How the internet works
LESSONS.hook: What actually happens in the second between tapping a link and seeing a page.

sections.key: The internet is a global network of networks that grew from ARPANET (1969).
sections.b: The internet is a global network of networks: billions of computers, phones and servers owned by millions of different organisations, linked by cables, fibre optics, radio and satellites. Nobody owns it as a whole. It grew from ARPANET, a US research network that sent its first message in October 1969; the system crashed after two letters, so the first message was 'lo'. Australia's first international internet connection came in 1989, linking the University of Melbourne to Hawaii.

sections.key: Data is split into packets that travel separately and are reassembled at the destination.
sections.b: When you send a photo, email or video call, the data is chopped into small chunks called packets, typically around 1,500 bytes each. Each packet carries addressing information, like an envelope, and travels independently, possibly by different routes. At the destination they're reassembled in the right order. If a packet goes missing, only that piece needs resending. This design, called packet switching, makes the network resilient: if one route fails, packets simply take another.

sections.key: An IP address tells routers where to deliver packets, like a street address.
sections.b: Every device on the internet needs an address so packets can find it. That's its IP address, for Internet Protocol. The older IPv4 system uses addresses like 203.0.113.42, allowing about 4.3 billion combinations, which ran out as the internet grew. The newer IPv6 allows an almost unimaginable number. Routers, specialised computers across the network, read each packet's destination address and pass it one step closer, hop by hop, often across a dozen or more routers.

sections.key: DNS translates names like wikipedia.org into IP addresses.
sections.b: People remember names like abc.net.au, but computers need numbers. The Domain Name System, or DNS, translates names into IP addresses. When you type a web address, your device asks a DNS server, which looks it up, sometimes asking other servers in a chain, and returns the address, usually in a fraction of a second. If DNS fails, websites seem to vanish even though they're still running, which is behind some major outages.

sections.h: TCP and the rules of the road
sections.key: Protocols like TCP/IP set the rules; TCP checks that everything arrives correctly.
sections.b: The internet works because everyone follows shared rules, called protocols. The two most important were designed in the 1970s by Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn: IP handles addressing and routing, and TCP makes sure data arrives completely and in order, requesting resends of anything lost. Together, TCP/IP was adopted across ARPANET on 1 January 1983, often called the internet's birthday. Other protocols sit on top, like HTTP for web pages and SMTP for email.

sections.key: Most data between continents travels through undersea fibre-optic cables.
sections.b: It's easy to imagine data flying through space, but around 99% of international internet traffic travels through undersea fibre-optic cables. Hundreds of these cables criss-cross the ocean floors, many only about as thick as a garden hose, carrying data as pulses of light. Australia is connected by cables landing mainly in Sydney and Perth, linking to Asia, the US and New Zealand. Occasionally cables are damaged by ship anchors, earthquakes and even sharks biting them.

sections.key: Your connection to the network (NBN, 5G, satellite) is often the slowest link.
sections.b: The part of the network connecting your home to the wider internet is called the last mile, and it's often the slowest link. In Australia, most homes connect through the NBN using fibre to the premises, fibre to the node with copper for the last stretch, cable or fixed wireless. Mobile networks like 4G and 5G carry data by radio to nearby towers. Remote areas increasingly use satellites, including low-Earth-orbit satellites that orbit much closer than older ones, reducing delay.

sections.key: The World Wide Web (1989, Tim Berners-Lee) is one service that runs on the internet.
sections.b: The internet and the web aren't the same thing. The internet is the network. The World Wide Web, proposed by Tim Berners-Lee at the physics lab CERN in 1989, is one service running on it, made of web pages linked together and viewed in a browser. Email, video calls, online games and streaming are other services using the same network. Berners-Lee chose not to patent the web, making it free for anyone to use, which helped it spread worldwide.

quiz.q: What happens to data when it's sent over the internet?
o: It travels as one big file
quiz.e: Packets travel independently and are reassembled.

quiz.q: What is an IP address for?
quiz.e: It works like a street address.

quiz.q: What does DNS do?
o: Translates website names into IP addresses
quiz.e: DNS is the internet's phone book.

quiz.q: How does most data travel between continents?
quiz.e: Around 99% of international traffic.

quiz.q: Who invented the World Wide Web?
quiz.e: At CERN in 1989. Vint Cerf co-designed TCP/IP.

LESSONS.title: How encryption keeps secrets
LESSONS.hook: The maths behind the padlock in your browser, and why it protects nearly everything you do online.

sections.key: Encryption uses a key to turn readable plaintext into scrambled ciphertext.
sections.b: Encryption turns readable information, called plaintext, into scrambled data, called ciphertext, using a key. Only someone with the right key can turn it back. It protects your messages, passwords, banking, medical records and card payments every day, usually without you noticing. Without encryption, anyone able to intercept internet traffic, such as someone on the same public Wi-Fi, could read what you send.

sections.key: The Caesar cipher shifted each letter along the alphabet and is easy to crack.
sections.b: Secret codes are ancient. Julius Caesar is said to have shifted each letter three places along the alphabet, so A became D and B became E. Simple substitution ciphers like this are easy to crack by frequency analysis: in English, E is the most common letter, so the most common symbol in a long message probably stands for E. The Arab scholar al-Kindi described this technique in the 9th century.

sections.key: Breaking Germany's Enigma cipher in WWII shortened the war and helped launch computing.
sections.b: In World War II, Germany used the Enigma machine, whose rotating wheels scrambled each letter differently, creating an astronomical number of possible settings. Building on earlier work by Polish mathematicians, British codebreakers at Bletchley Park, including Alan Turing, built machines to find the daily settings. The intelligence helped the Allies win the Battle of the Atlantic and is thought to have shortened the war. The effort also helped lay foundations for modern computing.

sections.key: Symmetric encryption uses one shared key; it's fast, but sharing the key safely is hard.
sections.b: In symmetric encryption, the same key locks and unlocks the data. Modern symmetric ciphers, like the widely used AES standard, are fast and extremely secure. They're used to encrypt files, phones and most internet traffic. The problem is the key itself: how do you share it with someone far away without anyone else intercepting it? For centuries, keys had to be delivered physically, by couriers or in person.

sections.key: Public-key encryption uses a shareable public key to lock and a secret private key to unlock.
sections.b: In 1976, Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman published a revolutionary idea, and in 1977 Rivest, Shamir and Adleman created the RSA system. Public-key encryption uses two mathematically linked keys. Your public key can be shared with anyone and used to lock messages to you. Only your matching private key can unlock them. Think of a padlock anyone can snap shut, but only you have the key to open. It solved the key-sharing problem and made secure online shopping possible.

sections.key: HTTPS uses public-key encryption to agree on a key, then fast symmetric encryption.
sections.b: When you see HTTPS and a padlock in your browser, a protocol called TLS is protecting the connection. Your browser checks the website's digital certificate, issued by a trusted authority, to confirm you're talking to the real site. Then the two use public-key techniques to agree on a shared secret key, and switch to fast symmetric encryption for the rest of the session. Note that the padlock means the connection is encrypted, not that the website is trustworthy; scam sites can have padlocks too.

sections.key: Modern encryption relies on maths that's easy one way and extremely hard to reverse.
sections.b: Modern encryption relies on maths problems that are easy to do one way and extremely hard to reverse. Multiplying two huge prime numbers is easy for a computer; working out which two primes produced the result is enormously hard. Guessing a 256-bit symmetric key by brute force would take longer than the age of the universe with today's computers. In practice, attackers rarely break the maths; they steal passwords, trick people or exploit software bugs instead.

sections.key: End-to-end encryption means only sender and recipient can read messages; quantum computing is prompting new standards.
sections.b: Messaging apps like Signal, WhatsApp and iMessage use end-to-end encryption, meaning only the sender and recipient can read messages, not even the company running the service. Phones encrypt their storage, protecting data if the device is lost. Governments periodically debate whether police should have special access, while security experts warn any 'back door' could be exploited by criminals. Future quantum computers could break some of today's public-key systems, so new 'post-quantum' standards were published in 2024.

quiz.q: What is ciphertext?
quiz.e: Ciphertext is encryption's scrambled output.

quiz.q: How can simple substitution ciphers be cracked?
quiz.e: E is the most common letter in English.

quiz.q: Where did Alan Turing and colleagues break Enigma?
quiz.e: The work helped shorten World War II.

quiz.q: In public-key encryption, what unlocks a message sent to you?
quiz.e: Only your private key can decrypt it.

quiz.q: What does the padlock in your browser tell you?
quiz.e: Scam sites can have padlocks too.

LESSONS.title: How GPS knows where you are
LESSONS.hook: Your phone finds you to within a few metres by listening to ultra-precise clocks orbiting high above the Earth.

sections.key: GPS works by measuring how long signals take to arrive from multiple satellites.
sections.b: The Global Positioning System is run by the US and uses a constellation of around 31 satellites orbiting about 20,200 kilometres above Earth. Each satellite constantly broadcasts a signal saying, in effect, 'I'm this satellite, here's my position, and this is the exact time.' Your phone doesn't send anything back. It just listens. By measuring how long each signal took to arrive, it can work out how far away each satellite is.

sections.key: Knowing distances to four or more satellites pins down your position and the time.
sections.b: If you know you're exactly 20,500 km from one satellite, you could be anywhere on a giant sphere around it. A second satellite narrows it to a circle where two spheres meet; a third narrows it to two points, one of which is usually far off in space. A fourth satellite is needed to correct for the fact that your phone's clock isn't perfectly accurate. This process is called trilateration. Your device usually uses signals from many more satellites for better accuracy.

sections.key: Signals travel at light speed, so tiny timing errors mean big position errors.
sections.b: GPS signals travel at the speed of light, about 300,000 kilometres per second. That means a timing error of just one millionth of a second would put your position out by about 300 metres. So each GPS satellite carries extremely precise atomic clocks, accurate to billionths of a second. The whole system is really a way of distributing precise time from space, which is why it's also used to synchronise phone networks, power grids and financial transactions.

sections.key: Until May 2000 the US deliberately degraded civilian GPS accuracy; switching this off made positions about ten times more precise.
sections.b: GPS began as a US military project. The first satellite was launched in 1978, and the full system was declared operational in 1995. For years the military deliberately added errors to the civilian signal, a feature called Selective Availability, so ordinary receivers were only accurate to around 100 metres while military users got precise positions. In May 2000, on the orders of President Bill Clinton, it was switched off, and civilian accuracy improved roughly tenfold overnight. That single change helped spark the boom in car navigation, fitness trackers and eventually smartphone maps. The US later announced that newer GPS satellites would be built without the ability to degrade the signal at all.

sections.key: Phones use several satellite systems (GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, BeiDou), known together as GNSS.
sections.b: GPS isn't the only satellite navigation system. Russia runs GLONASS, the European Union runs Galileo, and China runs BeiDou. Together they're called GNSS, global navigation satellite systems. Most modern phones use several at once, seeing more satellites and getting faster, more accurate fixes. Australia is building SouthPAN, a system that improves positioning accuracy across Australia and New Zealand, useful for farming, mining, aviation and emergency services.

sections.key: Phones also use Wi-Fi, mobile towers and downloaded data to find you quickly.
sections.b: A standalone GPS receiver can take a while to lock on, because it has to download satellite position data slowly from space. Your phone cheats a little: it downloads that data over the internet, and it also estimates your location from nearby mobile towers and Wi-Fi networks, whose locations are stored in huge databases. That's why your phone can find you almost instantly, and even indoors where satellite signals are weak.

sections.key: Tall buildings, tunnels and dense trees can reflect or block signals, reducing accuracy.
sections.b: GPS signals are weak by the time they reach Earth and can't pass through buildings or ground. In city centres, signals bounce off tall buildings, confusing receivers and making your blue dot jump around; this is called the urban canyon effect. Tunnels and dense forest can block signals entirely. Ordinary phones are typically accurate to within about five metres in open sky. Specialised equipment used in surveying and farming can reach centimetre accuracy.

sections.key: GPS underpins navigation, aviation, farming, emergency services and precise timing everywhere.
sections.b: Beyond getting you to a café, GPS guides planes and ships, helps emergency services find people, tracks deliveries and lets tractors drive themselves in straight lines to save fuel and fertiliser. Its timing signals keep mobile networks, power grids and stock exchanges in sync. The US opened GPS to civilian use after a Korean Air Lines passenger plane strayed into Soviet airspace and was shot down in 1983. Today it's so embedded in daily life that an outage would disrupt far more than maps.

quiz.q: Does your phone send signals to GPS satellites?
quiz.e: It calculates position from signals it receives.

quiz.q: Why is a fourth satellite needed?
o: To correct for errors in your phone's clock
quiz.e: Time is one of the unknowns being solved.

quiz.q: About how far off would a one-millionth-of-a-second timing error put you?
quiz.e: Light travels about 300 metres in a microsecond.

quiz.q: What was GPS 'Selective Availability'?
o: A deliberate degrading of civilian GPS accuracy, switched off in 2000
A way for phones to choose the nearest satellites
A backup system for power blackouts
quiz.e: Turning it off made civilian positions roughly ten times more precise.

quiz.q: What is the European Union's satellite navigation system called?
quiz.e: GNSS is the umbrella term for all of them.

LESSONS.title: Blockchain, simply
LESSONS.hook: What a blockchain actually is, what it's good for, and what it isn't, without the crypto hype.

sections.key: Blockchains let strangers agree on a shared record without trusting a central authority.
sections.b: Normally, when you send money online, a trusted middleman, like your bank, keeps the official record of who owns what. Digital files are easy to copy, so without that middleman, how would anyone stop you spending the same digital dollar twice? A blockchain is a way for many people who don't know or trust each other to agree on a shared record, without any central authority in charge.

sections.key: A blockchain is a record of transactions that many computers keep matching copies of.
sections.b: A blockchain is a list of records, usually transactions, that thousands of computers around the world keep identical copies of. It's often called a distributed ledger. Anyone can check it, and no single person or company controls it. When a new transaction happens, it's broadcast to the network, and the computers work together to add it to everyone's copy in the same order. Because so many copies exist, you can't quietly change the history in one place.

sections.key: Each block contains a hash of the previous block, so changing old data breaks the chain.
sections.b: Transactions are grouped into blocks. Each block includes a hash of the block before it. A hash is a kind of digital fingerprint: a short code calculated from the data, which changes completely if even one character of the data changes. Because each block contains the fingerprint of the previous one, they're linked into a chain. Change anything in an old block and its fingerprint changes, breaking every link after it, which everyone else would immediately notice.

sections.key: Networks agree on new blocks through proof of work or proof of stake.
sections.b: The network needs a way to decide who adds the next block. Bitcoin uses proof of work: computers called miners compete to solve a hard mathematical puzzle, and the winner adds the block and earns new bitcoin. It's deliberately expensive, which makes cheating costly. Ethereum switched in 2022 to proof of stake, where participants lock up their own coins as a guarantee of good behaviour and risk losing them if they cheat. That change cut Ethereum's energy use by more than 99%.

sections.key: Bitcoin (2009) was the first blockchain; Ethereum added smart contracts.
sections.b: Bitcoin, launched in 2009 by the pseudonymous Satoshi Nakamoto, was the first blockchain, designed as digital money without banks. Its supply is capped at 21 million coins. Ethereum, launched in 2015, added smart contracts: programs stored on the blockchain that automatically carry out an agreement when set conditions are met. Thousands of other cryptocurrencies, or tokens, exist. Many have collapsed, and some were outright scams.

sections.key: Blockchains suit situations needing a shared, tamper-resistant record without a trusted middleman.
sections.b: Blockchains are genuinely useful when many parties need a shared, tamper-resistant record and don't want to trust one middleman: sending money across borders, tracking supply chains, or proving ownership of a digital item. They've been trialled for trade finance and property records. But many proposed uses would work just as well, or better, with an ordinary database run by a trusted organisation. A useful question to ask about any blockchain project is: why does this need a blockchain?

sections.key: Blockchains remove middlemen but can be slow, energy-hungry and irreversible.
sections.b: Removing the middleman has costs. Public blockchains can be slow and expensive compared with card networks. Proof-of-work systems use enormous amounts of electricity; Bitcoin's annual use has been estimated to be comparable to that of a mid-sized country. Transactions generally can't be reversed, so mistakes and thefts are often permanent. And there's no customer service to call if you lose the password, or 'private key', to your wallet: your coins are gone.

sections.key: Cryptocurrencies are highly volatile, and crypto is a common vehicle for scams.
sections.b: Cryptocurrency prices are extremely volatile; a coin can lose most of its value within weeks, and unlike bank deposits, money held on a crypto exchange isn't protected by the government's Financial Claims Scheme. In 2025 AUSTRAC, Australia's financial crime regulator, imposed a $5,000 cash limit on crypto ATMs after finding they were heavily used by scam victims, many of them older Australians. Crypto is also the payment method of choice for many scams, because transfers are fast and hard to reverse. If you choose to invest, only use money you can afford to lose, use reputable Australian-registered exchanges, and be deeply sceptical of anyone promising guaranteed returns. This is general information only.

quiz.q: What is a blockchain?
o: A record that many computers keep matching copies of
quiz.e: It's a shared, distributed ledger.

quiz.q: What links each block to the one before it?
o: A hash of the previous block
quiz.e: The hash acts like a fingerprint.

quiz.q: What did Ethereum's 2022 switch to proof of stake achieve?
o: Cut energy use by more than 99%
quiz.e: No more energy-hungry mining.

quiz.q: What is Bitcoin's maximum supply?
quiz.e: It's capped at 21 million coins.

quiz.q: What happens if you lose the private key to your crypto wallet?
o: You usually lose access to your coins permanently
quiz.e: There's no one to call.

LESSONS.title: How AI chatbots work
LESSONS.hook: They can write essays and code, yet they sometimes invent facts with total confidence. Understanding how they work explains both.

sections.key: Large language models generate text by repeatedly predicting the most likely next piece of text.
sections.b: AI chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini are built on large language models, or LLMs. At their core, they do something that sounds simple: given some text, they predict what text is likely to come next. They generate replies one small piece at a time, called a token, which is often part of a word, each time predicting the next token based on everything before it. Doing this extremely well, at enormous scale, produces surprisingly capable writing, reasoning and conversation.

sections.h: Learning from vast amounts of text
sections.key: Models learn patterns from huge amounts of text during training, adjusting billions of parameters.
sections.b: To learn, a model is trained on a huge collection of text, such as books, websites and code. During training, it repeatedly tries to predict missing or next words and adjusts itself when it's wrong. It does this by tuning billions of internal numbers, called parameters, inside a network loosely inspired by the brain. Over trillions of examples, it picks up grammar, facts, reasoning patterns and writing styles. Nobody writes explicit rules; the patterns are learned from data.

sections.key: The 2017 'transformer' design lets models weigh how words relate across long passages.
sections.b: Modern language models are based on the transformer, a design introduced by Google researchers in a 2017 paper titled 'Attention Is All You Need'. Its key idea, attention, lets the model weigh how every word in a passage relates to every other word, so it can keep track of context, like what 'it' refers to several sentences back. Transformers also train efficiently on powerful chips, which made it practical to build much larger models. ChatGPT's release in November 2022 brought this technology to the public.

sections.key: After initial training, models are fine-tuned with human feedback to be helpful and safe.
sections.b: A model trained only to predict text isn't automatically a helpful assistant; it might just continue your question with more questions. So developers fine-tune it on examples of good conversations, and use feedback, often from people rating different answers, to reward responses that are helpful, honest and harmless. This technique is known as reinforcement learning from human feedback, or RLHF, and variations of it. It's also how developers try to reduce harmful or biased outputs.

sections.key: Models can produce confident, plausible-sounding but false information, called hallucinations.
sections.b: Because language models generate what sounds plausible, they can produce confident, fluent answers that are simply wrong, including made-up facts, quotes, statistics or references. This is often called hallucination. A model isn't looking things up in a database of facts unless it's connected to search tools; it's producing likely text based on patterns. Newer systems hallucinate less and can search the web or cite sources, but errors still happen, especially on obscure topics, precise numbers and recent events.

sections.key: Because models see text as tokens rather than letters, they can stumble on tasks that seem trivially easy.
sections.b: Models don't read letters the way you do. Text is chopped into tokens, so a word like 'strawberry' may reach the model as a couple of chunks rather than ten letters. That's one reason chatbots famously miscounted the r's in 'strawberry' and fumbled simple arithmetic while writing fluent essays. Since 2024, 'reasoning' models have been trained to work through problems step by step before answering, which has greatly improved their maths and logic, and many assistants now hand calculations to built-in tools. Still, a model's fluency in one area says little about its reliability in another, so judge each answer on its merits.

sections.key: A model's built-in knowledge stops at a training cut-off, and it can only consider so much text at once.
sections.b: A language model doesn't update its knowledge while you chat. What it knows comes from training data collected up to a cut-off date, often many months before you use it, so without a search tool it may not know recent news, prices or who currently holds an office. Within a conversation, it can only consider a limited amount of text at once, called its context window. Modern context windows can hold hundreds of pages, but very long chats can still lose track of early details. Some apps add 'memory' features that save notes about you between chats; these can usually be viewed and switched off in settings.

sections.key: AI raises big questions about jobs, misinformation, energy use and safety.
sections.b: AI is changing how people work, learn and create, and it raises serious questions. How will jobs change? How do we deal with convincing AI-generated fake images, audio and video? Training and running large models uses significant energy and water. Who's responsible when AI makes a harmful mistake? And how do we make increasingly capable systems reliably safe? Governments, including Australia's, are developing rules. Understanding the basics helps you use these tools wisely and join the conversation.

quiz.q: At their core, what do large language models do?
o: Look up answers in a database
Predict the next piece of text
quiz.e: They generate text one token at a time.

quiz.q: What 2017 design underpins modern language models?
quiz.e: From the paper 'Attention Is All You Need'.

quiz.q: What is RLHF used for?
o: Fine-tuning models using human feedback to be more helpful and safe
quiz.e: People rate answers to guide the model.

quiz.q: Why can a chatbot state a made-up fact with total confidence?
o: It generates plausible-sounding text rather than checking facts, unless it's connected to tools like search
It copies the first website it finds
It makes mistakes on purpose to test users
quiz.e: Fluent text and true text aren't the same thing, so important claims need checking.

quiz.q: Why might a chatbot without web search give out-of-date answers about current events?
o: Its built-in knowledge stops at a training cut-off date
It can only read printed books
It forgets everything after each word
quiz.e: Without a search tool, it only knows what was in its training data.

LESSONS.title: Correlation vs causation
LESSONS.hook: Ice-cream sales and drownings rise together. Does ice cream kill? The most useful idea for reading any headline.

sections.key: A correlation means two things tend to change together, not that one causes the other.
sections.b: A correlation means two things tend to change together. As ice-cream sales rise, so do drownings. Countries that eat more chocolate win more Nobel Prizes per person. People who carry lighters get lung cancer more often. All of these correlations are real. But in none of them does the first thing cause the second. 'Correlation doesn't imply causation' is one of the most important phrases in science, and one of the most ignored in headlines and advertising.

sections.key: A confounding variable is a hidden factor that drives both things.
sections.b: Often a third factor, called a confounding variable, is driving both things. Hot weather makes people buy ice cream and go swimming, which leads to more drownings. Wealthier countries eat more chocolate and also fund more research. Smoking causes people to carry lighters and causes lung cancer. Whenever you see a link, ask: what else could explain this? Is there something that might cause both?

sections.key: Sometimes the cause runs the other way from what you'd assume.
sections.b: Sometimes the arrow points the opposite way. People who use walking sticks tend to be less mobile, but the sticks don't cause it; poor mobility leads people to use sticks. A study might find that people who drink diet soft drinks are more likely to be overweight. Does diet soft drink cause weight gain, or are people who are already concerned about their weight more likely to choose diet drinks? Always consider whether the effect might actually be the cause.

sections.key: With enough data, some things line up by pure chance.
sections.b: With enough data, some things line up by pure chance. For about a decade, the number of films Nicolas Cage appeared in each year closely tracked the number of people who drowned by falling into US swimming pools. Per capita cheese consumption tracked the number of people who died by becoming tangled in their bedsheets. The writer Tyler Vigen collects these 'spurious correlations'. If you compare enough random things, some will match beautifully, meaning nothing.

sections.key: Observational studies find links but can't easily prove cause; they must account for confounders.
sections.b: Many health headlines come from observational studies, where researchers observe what people do and track what happens to them, rather than assigning treatments. They're valuable and sometimes the only ethical option: you can't randomly assign people to smoke. But they can't easily prove causation because people who choose to do something differ in other ways. Good studies try to adjust for known confounders, like age, income and smoking, but unknown ones can still mislead.

sections.key: Randomised controlled trials balance hidden factors, so they can show cause.
sections.b: The gold standard for testing cause and effect is the randomised controlled trial. Participants are randomly assigned to groups, for example one gets a new drug and one gets a placebo. Randomisation means both groups should be similar in every way, including factors nobody thought to measure, so the only systematic difference is the treatment. If the groups end up differing, the treatment is the likely cause. Blinding, where people don't know which group they're in, further reduces bias.

sections.key: Without trials, causation can still be established through strong, consistent evidence (e.g. smoking).
sections.b: Sometimes causation can be established without trials. The link between smoking and lung cancer was proven through overwhelming, consistent evidence: the link was very strong, it appeared in study after study and in different populations, more smoking meant more risk, quitting reduced the risk, smoking came before the cancer, and laboratory research showed how tobacco smoke damages cells. Epidemiologist Austin Bradford Hill set out these kinds of criteria in 1965, and they're still used today.

sections.key: Watch for causal words in headlines about observational studies; ask what else could explain it.
sections.b: Headlines often turn correlations into causes: 'Coffee makes you live longer!' when the study only found that coffee drinkers lived longer. Watch for words like 'causes', 'boosts', 'prevents' and 'makes you'. Ask three questions: Was this an observational study or a randomised trial? What else could explain the link? Could the cause run the other way? These simple questions will protect you from a huge amount of misleading information.

quiz.q: What does a correlation show?
o: That two things tend to change together
quiz.e: It's a link, not proof of cause.

quiz.q: What is a confounding variable?
o: A hidden third factor affecting both things
quiz.e: Like hot weather behind ice cream and drownings.

quiz.q: 'Hospitals are full of sick people, so hospitals make people sick.' What's the error?
quiz.e: Sickness sends people to hospital.

quiz.q: Why do randomised controlled trials help show cause?
o: Random groups balance out hidden factors
quiz.e: Randomisation removes systematic differences.

quiz.q: How was smoking proven to cause lung cancer without randomised trials?
o: Strong, consistent evidence from many angles
quiz.e: Bradford Hill's criteria describe that kind of evidence.

LESSONS.title: Logical fallacies
LESSONS.hook: The tricks that make weak arguments sound strong. You'll hear at least three of these in the next news bulletin.

sections.key: A fallacy is a reasoning flaw that makes an argument seem stronger than it is.
sections.b: A logical fallacy is a flaw in reasoning that makes an argument seem more convincing than it really is. Fallacies are everywhere: in politics, advertising, social media arguments and family dinners. Sometimes they're deliberate manipulation; often they're honest mistakes. Learning to name them helps you think more clearly, argue more fairly and resist being manipulated. Here are some of the most common.

sections.key: Ad hominem attacks the person instead of their argument.
sections.b: An ad hominem attacks the person making an argument instead of the argument itself. 'Why would we listen to her views on the economy? She's never run a business.' Whether she's run a business doesn't determine whether her argument is right. A related trick is 'whataboutism': answering criticism by pointing to someone else's faults ('What about when your side did it?'), which dodges the actual issue.

sections.key: A straw man twists someone's argument into a weaker version that's easier to attack.
sections.b: A straw man misrepresents someone's position as something weaker or more extreme, then knocks down that version. Someone says, 'We should reduce sugar in school canteens,' and the reply is, 'So you want to ban birthday cake and control what kids eat!' The opposite, and much fairer, approach is called a steel man: restating the other side's argument in its strongest form before responding to it.

sections.key: A false dilemma presents only two options when more exist.
sections.b: A false dilemma, or false dichotomy, presents only two options when there are actually more. 'You're either with us or against us.' 'Either we build this road or the town dies.' Real life usually has a range of options and trade-offs. When someone presents just two choices, especially when one is obviously bad, ask what other options are being left out.

sections.key: A slippery slope claims one step will inevitably lead to disaster, without evidence.
sections.b: A slippery slope argument claims that one small step will inevitably lead to a chain of events ending in disaster, without showing why each step would follow. 'If we let students use phones for research, soon they'll be on TikTok all lesson and nobody will learn anything.' Some chains of consequences are real, but each link needs evidence. When you hear a dramatic chain reaction, ask what makes each step likely.

sections.key: Popularity isn't proof, and authority only counts within someone's real expertise.
sections.b: The bandwagon fallacy says something must be true or good because many people believe or do it: 'Millions of people use this remedy.' Popularity isn't evidence; plenty of widely held beliefs have been wrong. The appeal to authority cites someone as proof, but it's only reasonable when that person is a genuine expert in the relevant field and represents expert consensus. A famous actor's opinion on vaccines, or a single doctor contradicting thousands of others, isn't strong evidence.

sections.key: Circular reasoning assumes its conclusion; hasty generalisations leap from too few examples.
sections.b: Circular reasoning assumes what it's trying to prove: 'This news site is trustworthy because it says it only reports the truth.' The conclusion is hidden in the premise. A hasty generalisation draws a broad conclusion from too little evidence: 'I got a rude driver twice; all rideshare drivers are rude.' Both are easy to fall into when we already believe the conclusion.

sections.key: A fallacy shows an argument is weak, not that its conclusion is false.
sections.b: Pointing out a fallacy doesn't prove the conclusion is false; it only shows that this particular argument for it is weak. Someone can argue badly for something true. Assuming a claim is false because it was argued badly is itself an error, sometimes called the fallacy fallacy. And shouting 'Straw man!' in an argument rarely changes minds. The real value of knowing fallacies is checking your own reasoning, and asking better questions of others.

quiz.q: 'Don't listen to his views on climate, he dropped out of uni.' Which fallacy?
quiz.e: It attacks the person, not the argument.

quiz.q: What does a straw man do?
o: Twists an argument into a weaker version
quiz.e: It knocks down an argument nobody made.

quiz.q: 'Either we ban all cars in the city or accept pollution forever.' Which fallacy?
quiz.e: There are many options in between.

quiz.q: 'This site is trustworthy because it says so.' Which fallacy?
quiz.e: The conclusion is assumed in the premise.

quiz.q: If an argument contains a fallacy, what does that prove?
o: The argument for it is weak
quiz.e: Bad arguments can still reach true conclusions.

LESSONS.title: How to judge a claim
LESSONS.hook: 'Scientists say…', 'A study found…'. A practical checklist for deciding what to believe.

sections.key: Evidence has a hierarchy: systematic reviews near the top, anecdotes near the bottom.
sections.b: Anecdotes, expert opinions, single studies and large reviews all count as 'evidence', but they're not equally reliable. Scientists often rank them in a hierarchy. Near the bottom sit personal stories and opinions. Above them come observational studies, then randomised controlled trials. Near the top are systematic reviews and meta-analyses, which combine the results of many good studies. One study rarely settles a question; the weight of evidence does.

sections.key: Small studies can produce dramatic results by chance.
sections.b: Small studies can produce dramatic results purely by chance. If you flip a coin 10 times, getting 7 heads isn't unusual; getting 7,000 heads in 10,000 flips would be astonishing. A treatment that 'worked for 8 of 10 people' is far less convincing than one tested on thousands. Surprising findings from small studies often shrink or vanish when larger studies are done, a pattern sometimes called the decline effect.

sections.key: Without a comparison group, you can't separate the treatment from placebo or natural recovery.
sections.b: Without a comparison group, you can't tell whether an improvement came from the treatment, the placebo effect or people simply getting better on their own. The choice of comparison matters too. A new drug that beats a sugar pill may still be worse than the treatment doctors already use, so the most useful trials test new options against standard care. Be wary of comparisons with patients from years earlier, or with people who chose not to take part, since they may differ in many ways. When you read about a study, ask: compared with what?

sections.key: Always ask 'out of how many?': relative risks can hide tiny absolute changes.
sections.b: 'Doubles your risk' sounds alarming, but if the risk goes from 1 in 100,000 to 2 in 100,000, the absolute change is tiny. That's a 100% relative increase but only 0.001 percentage points in absolute terms. Headlines and ads prefer relative numbers because they sound bigger. The same trick flatters treatments: 'cuts risk by 50%' might mean 2 in 1,000 falling to 1 in 1,000. Always ask: out of how many people?

sections.key: When something is rare, even accurate tests give many false positives.
sections.b: When something is rare, even accurate tests produce many false alarms. Imagine a disease that affects 1 in 1,000 people, and a test that's 99% accurate. Test 1,000 people: about 1 has the disease and tests positive, but about 10 of the 999 healthy people also test positive by mistake. So if you test positive, there's only about a 1 in 11 chance you actually have it. That's why doctors often confirm results with a second test, and why screening rare conditions is tricky.

sections.key: Ask who funded the research and who benefits; look for independent confirmation.
sections.b: Ask who's making the claim and what they gain if you believe it. Research funded by companies with a stake in the result isn't automatically wrong, but it's more likely to favour the sponsor, so independent confirmation matters. Be wary of claims that appear only on sites selling a product. Check whether the source is a peer-reviewed journal, a reputable organisation like the CSIRO or a university, or a press release, blog or social media post.

sections.key: Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence; be wary of miracle cures and 'secret' knowledge.
sections.b: Astronomer Carl Sagan popularised the principle that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence. If something would overturn well-established science, cure everything, or reveal what 'they' don't want you to know, the bar for evidence should be very high. Warning signs include claims of a miracle breakthrough, testimonials instead of data, attacks on mainstream experts, and pressure to buy now. Real breakthroughs are usually cautious and replicated by independent teams.

sections.key: Check the source, study type, size, comparison group, absolute numbers and expert consensus.
sections.b: Next time you meet a claim, run through six questions. What's the source, and could they be biased? What kind of evidence is it: anecdote, observational study or trial? How many people were studied? Compared with what? What are the absolute numbers? And what do most experts in the field think? You won't always have time to check everything, but even asking two or three of these questions will make you far harder to fool.

quiz.q: What usually sits at the top of the evidence hierarchy?
o: A systematic review of many good studies
quiz.e: Reviews combine the results of many studies.

quiz.q: Why are small studies risky?
quiz.e: Small samples swing wildly.

quiz.q: A risk rises from 1 in 100,000 to 2 in 100,000. What's the absolute increase?
quiz.e: Relative risk doubled; absolute risk barely moved.

quiz.q: Why can a positive result on an accurate test still be likely false?
o: When a condition is rare, false positives outnumber true ones
quiz.e: That's the base-rate effect.

quiz.q: What did Carl Sagan say about extraordinary claims?
quiz.e: The bigger the claim, the higher the bar.

LESSONS.title: Probability for everyday life
LESSONS.hook: Why the pokies always win, why a streak of heads means nothing, and how to think clearly about risk.

sections.key: Probability runs from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain), and can be expressed as percentages or odds.
sections.b: Probability measures how likely something is, from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). A 50% chance is 0.5; a 1 in 4 chance is 0.25. Weather forecasts use it: a 70% chance of rain means that on days with similar conditions, it rained about 70% of the time. Humans aren't naturally good at probability; our intuitions evolved for small groups and immediate dangers, not for statistics. Learning a few core ideas makes a big difference to everyday decisions.

sections.key: Independent events have no memory; past results don't change future odds.
sections.b: A fair coin lands heads five times in a row. What's the chance of heads next time? Still 50%. The coin has no memory. Believing that tails is now 'due' is the gambler's fallacy. In 1913 at the Monte Carlo casino, a roulette ball landed on black 26 times in a row, and gamblers lost millions betting that red must come up next. Each spin was independent. The same applies to lotto numbers, poker machine spins and the sex of a family's next baby.

sections.key: Expected value is the average outcome over many tries; gambling has negative expected value.
sections.b: Expected value is the average result you'd get if you repeated something many times. If a game costs $1 and gives a 1 in 10 chance of winning $5, you'd win $5 about once every 10 plays, spending $10: an expected loss of 50 cents a play. Every casino game, poker machine and lottery is designed to have negative expected value for players; that's how they make money. Poker machines in NSW, for example, must return at least 85% of money wagered over time, meaning players lose around 15% on average.

sections.key: Big lottery jackpots have odds of over 100 million to one.
sections.b: The odds of winning division one in Australia's Powerball are about 1 in 134 million per game. To picture it: if you bought one game every week, you'd expect to wait around 2.5 million years for a jackpot on average. You're far more likely to be struck by lightning. Buying a ticket for fun is fine, but it's worth understanding that it's entertainment, not a financial plan. Our brains struggle with very large numbers, so 'someone has to win' feels more meaningful than it is.

sections.key: Surprising coincidences are likely when there are many chances for them; e.g. the birthday paradox.
sections.b: How many people need to be in a room for there to be a better-than-even chance that two share a birthday? Just 23. With 70 people, it's over 99%. This birthday paradox surprises people because we think about our own birthday matching someone's, rather than any pair of people matching. With so many possible pairs, coincidences become likely. In a country of 27 million people, a 'one in a million' event happens to around 27 people. Unlikely things happen all the time; they just don't happen to any particular person often.

sections.key: Probabilities change with information, and flipping a conditional probability can cause disastrous errors.
sections.b: Probabilities change with information. The chance that a randomly chosen person is over 190 cm tall is small; the chance that a professional basketball player is over 190 cm is huge. This is conditional probability, and confusing its direction causes serious errors. In 1999, English solicitor Sally Clark was convicted of murdering her two baby sons, helped by an expert's claim that two cot deaths in one family had a 1 in 73 million chance. That figure was flawed, and it answered the wrong question, because double murder is also extremely rare. Her conviction was overturned in 2003.

sections.key: We underweight risks we choose and control, and overweight unfamiliar or imposed ones.
sections.b: Our sense of risk is shaped by emotion and familiarity more than numbers. Risks we choose and feel in control of, like driving, feel smaller than ones imposed on us, like a new phone tower or a food additive, even when the numbers point the other way. In Australia, you're vastly more likely to die in a car crash than from a shark or snake. A useful habit when weighing a risk is to ask for the actual numbers: out of how many people, over what time period, compared with what alternative?

sections.key: Think in probabilities and ranges, not certainties; consider both likelihood and impact.
sections.b: Good decision-makers think in probabilities rather than certainties. Instead of 'this will work' or 'this won't work', try 'there's maybe a 70% chance this works'. It encourages you to plan for the other 30%. For risks, consider both likelihood and impact: something unlikely but catastrophic, like a house fire, is worth insuring against, while something likely but minor, like a scratched phone, often isn't. Insurance makes sense for losses you couldn't afford, not ones you could easily cover yourself.

quiz.q: A fair coin lands heads five times in a row. What's the chance of heads next?
quiz.e: Believing otherwise is the gambler's fallacy.

quiz.q: What is the expected value of casino games for players?
quiz.e: That's how casinos make money.

quiz.q: Roughly what are the odds of winning Powerball division one?
quiz.e: You'd wait millions of years on average.

quiz.q: How many people are needed for a better-than-even chance that two share a birthday?
quiz.e: It's the birthday paradox.

quiz.q: When does insurance make the most sense?
o: For losses you couldn't afford to cover yourself
quiz.e: Consider both likelihood and impact.

LESSONS.title: How statistics can mislead
LESSONS.hook: The numbers can be true and still tell a false story. Here's how to spot the tricks.

sections.key: Accurate statistics can still mislead through selection, framing and presentation.
sections.b: Statistics are powerful tools for understanding the world, which is why they're also powerful tools for persuasion. Most misleading statistics aren't lies; the numbers are accurate. The deception is in what's included, what's left out, how it's compared and how it's shown. The 1954 book How to Lie with Statistics by Darrell Huff became a bestseller because its tricks were so common. Most of them still are.

sections.key: The median is often more representative than the mean when data is skewed.
sections.b: The 'average' usually means the mean: add everything up and divide. But means can be dragged around by extremes. If a billionaire walks into a café, the mean wealth of the customers soars, though nobody else got richer. The median, the middle value when everything is lined up, is often more representative for skewed data like incomes and house prices. That's why you'll usually see median house prices and median incomes reported. When someone quotes an average, ask which one.

sections.key: A rise from 10% to 15% is 5 percentage points but a 50% increase.
sections.b: If an interest rate rises from 4% to 5%, it went up by one percentage point, but that's a 25% increase in the rate. If support for something rises from 10% to 15%, that's 5 percentage points, or a 50% increase. Both descriptions are correct, and people choose whichever sounds more impressive for their argument. Percentages of small numbers are especially slippery: a 200% increase in something rare might mean going from 1 case to 3.

sections.key: Truncated axes, cherry-picked timeframes and distorted visuals exaggerate changes.
sections.b: Graphs can mislead at a glance. The most common trick is a truncated y-axis: starting the vertical axis at, say, 95 instead of 0 makes a small change look like a dramatic leap. Choosing a convenient start and end date can make a trend look up or down. Two lines on different scales can seem connected. Pictures scaled in two dimensions exaggerate differences. Always check the axis labels, the starting point and the timeframe before reacting to a chart.

sections.key: Results only apply to the population actually sampled; self-selected polls are unreliable.
sections.b: A statistic is only as good as the sample it came from. Online polls where anyone can vote attract people with strong opinions and can be flooded by campaigns, so they tell you little about the public. A famous example: in 1936, the Literary Digest magazine polled over two million people, drawn largely from car owners and telephone directories, and predicted a landslide defeat for President Roosevelt. He won by a landslide. A well-designed random sample of around 1,000 people is usually far more accurate than a huge biased one.

sections.key: Looking only at successes, not failures, gives a distorted picture.
sections.b: In World War II, the US military studied returning bombers to decide where to add armour, focusing on areas with the most bullet holes. Statistician Abraham Wald pointed out the flaw: they were only seeing planes that survived. The areas without holes, like the engines, were where hits brought planes down. The armour belonged there. We make the same mistake when we study only successful businesses, famous dropouts or old buildings that are still standing ('they built things better back then').

sections.key: A trend can appear in groups but reverse when the groups are combined.
sections.b: Sometimes a trend that appears in every subgroup reverses when the data is combined. In a well-known 1973 case, the University of California, Berkeley appeared to admit men at a higher rate than women overall. But when researchers looked department by department, women were admitted at similar or higher rates in most departments. The overall difference arose because women applied more often to highly competitive departments. The lesson: how data is grouped can completely change its story.

sections.key: Ask who collected the data, how, compared with what, and what's missing.
sections.b: When you meet a striking statistic, ask: Who collected it, and do they have an agenda? How was the sample chosen, and how big was it? Is it an average, and which kind? Is it a relative or absolute change? Compared with what, and over what time period? What's left out? Reputable sources, like the Australian Bureau of Statistics, publish their methods so you can check. You don't need to be a mathematician to ask good questions about numbers.

quiz.q: Why are median incomes often reported instead of mean incomes?
o: The median is easier to calculate
The mean can be dragged up by a few very high earners
quiz.e: Medians better represent a typical person with skewed data.

quiz.q: An interest rate rises from 4% to 5%. Which is true?
o: It rose 1 percentage point, a 25% increase
quiz.e: Percentage points and percentages differ.

quiz.q: What's the most common trick in misleading graphs?
o: Starting the vertical axis above zero
quiz.e: A truncated axis exaggerates small changes.

quiz.q: What did Abraham Wald realise about the bombers?
o: Armour where there were no holes, since planes hit there didn't return
quiz.e: Classic survivorship bias.

quiz.q: Why did the 1936 Literary Digest poll fail despite 2 million responses?
quiz.e: Car and phone owners weren't representative.

LESSONS.title: How to spot misinformation
LESSONS.hook: False stories spread faster than true ones. Professional fact-checkers use a few simple habits you can copy in 30 seconds.

sections.key: False news spreads faster and further than true news, largely driven by people, not bots.
sections.b: A major 2018 MIT study of millions of tweets found that false news stories spread further, faster and deeper than true ones, and were about 70% more likely to be retweeted. The researchers found people, not bots, were mainly responsible. False stories tend to be more novel and emotionally charged, triggering surprise, fear or disgust, and that's exactly what makes us want to share. Misinformation isn't a problem only 'other people' fall for; it's designed to exploit everyone's instincts.

sections.key: Misinformation is false info shared by mistake; disinformation is spread deliberately to deceive.
sections.b: Misinformation is false or misleading information shared by people who believe it, like a relative forwarding a fake health tip. Disinformation is false information spread deliberately to deceive, for profit, politics or to cause chaos. There's also malinformation: true information used out of context to mislead, like an old photo presented as happening today. Much of what spreads online is a mix: a kernel of truth wrapped in exaggeration or missing context.

sections.key: Strong emotional reactions are a cue to pause before believing or sharing.
sections.b: If a post makes you instantly furious, frightened or triumphant, that's a signal to slow down. Misleading content is often engineered to provoke strong emotion, because emotion bypasses careful thinking and drives shares. Watch especially for content that confirms what you already believe about people you disagree with; that's when we're least likely to check. A simple rule: the stronger your emotional reaction, the more worthwhile it is to spend 30 seconds checking before sharing.

sections.key: SIFT: Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, Trace claims to the original.
sections.b: Digital literacy expert Mike Caulfield developed a simple four-step method called SIFT. Stop: pause before reacting or sharing. Investigate the source: who's behind this, and what's their expertise and agenda? Find better coverage: look for what trusted news outlets or fact-checkers say about the claim. Trace claims, quotes and media to their original context: was the quote real, and is the photo from the event described? Most checks take under a minute.

sections.key: Fact-checkers open new tabs to check who's behind a source rather than judging the site itself.
sections.b: When Stanford researchers compared how professional fact-checkers, historians and students evaluated websites, the fact-checkers were fastest and most accurate.
