sections.b: The English words 'Dreamtime' and 'Dreaming' were popularised by anthropologists in the late 1800s, translating an Arrernte word from Central Australia that is often written altyerre. Many Aboriginal people and scholars feel the translation is clumsy, because it suggests something imaginary or unreal, when these beliefs describe what is most real. Other communities have their own terms. The Anangu people of Uluru speak of Tjukurpa, and the Warlpiri of the Tanami Desert speak of Jukurrpa. In the 1950s the anthropologist W. E. H. Stanner described the Dreaming as an 'everywhen', a phrase that is still widely quoted. He meant that ancestral events are not only in the past: they continue to shape the present and the future.

sections.key: Ancestral beings shaped the land, and their presence remains in it.
sections.b: In many Dreaming accounts, ancestral beings travelled across a formless or sleeping land, and their actions created its features. A waterhole may mark where an ancestor rested, a ridge where one lay down, a rock formation where a battle took place. These beings took many forms: animals, plants, people, stars, and powerful figures like the Rainbow Serpent, which appears in different ways in stories across much of the continent and is often associated with water and fertility. Because ancestors are believed to remain present in the land, country is not just scenery or property. It is family, history and law all at once. Many Aboriginal people speak of belonging to country, rather than country belonging to them.

sections.key: Songlines are routes across the land that carry stories, law and practical knowledge.
sections.b: The journeys of ancestral beings are often remembered as songlines, sometimes called Dreaming tracks. A songline can stretch hundreds or even thousands of kilometres, crossing the lands of many nations, with each group holding responsibility for its own section of the song. Singing the verses in order works like a map: it names waterholes, landmarks and food sources in sequence, which could help people travel safely through dry country. Songlines also carry law, kinship rules and seasonal knowledge, and some follow patterns in the stars. Researchers studying memory have taken a keen interest in how songs, places and stories together can hold huge amounts of information without writing. For the custodians, though, songlines are first and foremost sacred.

sections.h: Not every story is for everyone
sections.key: Some Dreaming knowledge is restricted, and sharing it needs the right authority.
sections.b: A key point for outsiders is that Dreaming knowledge is not public property. Some stories are open, often told to children and visitors. Others are restricted to people who have gone through certain ceremonies, or are known as men's business or women's business and kept within those groups. Certain sites are sacred and should not be photographed or entered. Rights to tell a story, paint its designs or sing its songs belong to particular custodians, who inherit that responsibility through kinship. This is why respectful books, galleries and tourism operators work with traditional owners and seek permission. It is also why this lesson does not retell specific sacred stories: the respectful way to hear them is from the people who hold them.

sections.key: At Uluru, Anangu law guided the 2019 decision to close the climb.
sections.b: Uluru in the Northern Territory shows how the Dreaming shapes modern life. For the Anangu traditional owners, Uluru is a place where Tjukurpa is present, and the route visitors once climbed has deep spiritual significance. For decades, signs at the base politely asked tourists not to climb, and many did anyway. After the park was handed back to Anangu ownership in 1985 and leased to the national parks agency, the joint management board eventually voted to end the climb, and it closed permanently in October 2019. Today visitors walk around the base instead, where guides share stories that are open to the public. Rangers explain which areas are sensitive and why some features should not be photographed.

sections.key: The Dreaming continues today through ceremony, art, language and care for country.
sections.b: It is a mistake to describe the Dreaming in the past tense. Colonisation caused enormous harm: dispossession, the loss of many languages and the removal of children from families broke many lines of transmission. Yet ceremony, song and story have survived, and many communities are working hard to revive languages and pass knowledge on. Art has become one of the most visible bridges. Since the 1970s, painters from places like Papunya in the Western Desert have used acrylic paint to share permitted aspects of their Dreamings, creating a world famous art movement. Ranger programs blend traditional knowledge with modern land management. When you hear a Welcome to Country, you are hearing a small part of a very old relationship with land.

quiz.q: Which description of the Dreaming is most accurate?
o: A single shared story told the same way across Australia
A system linking creation, law, kinship, land and responsibility
A belief that ended with colonisation
quiz.e: The Dreaming is a whole framework of law, belief and knowledge, and it differs between nations.

quiz.q: Who described the Dreaming as an 'everywhen'?
quiz.e: The anthropologist W. E. H. Stanner used the term in the 1950s to convey that ancestral events continue into the present.

quiz.q: What is one practical function of a songline?
o: It names landmarks and waterholes in order, like a map
It sets the dates of school holidays
quiz.e: Sung in order, a songline names places and resources along a route, helping people navigate country.

quiz.q: Why might a respectful book avoid retelling certain Dreaming stories?
o: Some knowledge is restricted and belongs to particular custodians
They are only told in English
quiz.e: Some stories are restricted, and the right to share them belongs to specific custodians.

quiz.q: When did the climb at Uluru permanently close?
quiz.e: The climb closed permanently in October 2019, following a decision by the park's board, which has an Anangu majority.

LESSONS.title: Gilgamesh: the world's oldest great story
LESSONS.hook: A tyrant king, a wild man from the steppe and a desperate quest to cheat death. Written on clay over 3,000 years ago, Gilgamesh still feels startlingly modern.

sections.key: Gilgamesh was rediscovered in the 1800s on clay tablets from ancient Nineveh.
sections.b: In 1872 a young assistant at the British Museum named George Smith was piecing together broken clay tablets dug up in the ruins of Nineveh, in modern Iraq. Reading the wedge shaped cuneiform script, he found a story of a great flood, a man who built a boat, and a bird sent out to look for dry land. It looked strikingly like the story of Noah. According to a well known account, Smith was so excited he leapt up and began rushing around the room. The tablets came from the library of the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal, from the 600s BCE. They held the Epic of Gilgamesh, a poem whose roots go back far earlier, and it caused a sensation.

sections.h: A king who might have been real
sections.key: Gilgamesh may have been a real king of Uruk, later turned into a legend.
sections.b: The story is set in Uruk, one of the first great cities, in southern Mesopotamia. Ancient king lists name Gilgamesh as one of its rulers, and many historians think a real king of that name may have reigned around 2700 BCE, though there is no direct proof. Over the centuries he grew into a figure of legend, described as two thirds god and one third human. Poems about him were first written in Sumerian, probably around 2100 BCE, and later woven into a longer Babylonian epic. The best known version, spread over twelve tablets, is traditionally credited to a scholar named Sin leqi unninni. In other words, Gilgamesh is part history, part myth and part great literature.

sections.h: The tyrant and the wild man
sections.key: The gods create Enkidu to balance Gilgamesh, and the two become close friends.
sections.b: The epic opens with a problem. Gilgamesh is magnificent but arrogant, and he oppresses the people of Uruk, who cry out to the gods. The gods respond by creating Enkidu, a wild man who lives among the animals of the steppe, eating grass and drinking at waterholes. A woman named Shamhat is sent to bring him into human society, and he learns to eat bread, drink beer and wear clothes. When Enkidu finally confronts Gilgamesh, the two wrestle fiercely in the street. Neither can fully defeat the other, and their struggle turns into a deep friendship. Many readers see in this a story about civilisation and nature, and about how friendship can tame pride.

sections.key: Gilgamesh and Enkidu kill the guardian of the Cedar Forest and the Bull of Heaven.
sections.b: Seeking lasting fame, Gilgamesh persuades Enkidu to travel to the distant Cedar Forest and kill its fearsome guardian, Humbaba. With help from the sun god Shamash, they succeed and cut down the great cedars. Back in Uruk, the goddess Ishtar is so impressed by Gilgamesh that she proposes marriage. He rejects her rudely, listing the sad fates of her previous lovers. Furious, she sends the Bull of Heaven to ravage the land, and the two heroes slay it too. Enkidu even throws a piece of the bull at the goddess. It is thrilling adventure, but the gods take note. They decide that one of the friends must die for these offences, and the lot falls on Enkidu.

sections.h: Grief and the fear of death
sections.key: Enkidu's death turns the epic into a meditation on mortality.
sections.b: Enkidu falls ill and dies after days of suffering, and Gilgamesh is shattered. He refuses to let his friend be buried until, in a famously grim detail, a worm falls from Enkidu's nose. The mighty king suddenly understands that he too will die. This is the emotional heart of the epic, and it is what makes Gilgamesh feel so human more than 3,000 years later. He tears off his fine clothes, dresses in animal skins and wanders the wilderness, consumed by grief and terror. His question is one every reader recognises: is there any way to escape death? He sets out to find the one man who is said to have been granted eternal life.

sections.key: Utnapishtim tells Gilgamesh how he survived a great flood sent by the gods.
sections.b: After a long journey, including crossing the waters of death, Gilgamesh reaches Utnapishtim, a wise man who lives with his wife at the edge of the world. Utnapishtim tells his story. The gods decided to destroy humanity with a flood, but the god Ea secretly warned him to build a huge boat and load it with his family, craftsmen and animals. The storm raged for days. When it ended, the boat came to rest on a mountain, and Utnapishtim released a dove, a swallow and then a raven, which did not return because it had found land. Grateful, he made an offering, and the gods granted him and his wife immortality. Scholars still discuss how this story relates to the biblical flood.

sections.h: The plant, the snake and the wall
sections.key: Gilgamesh loses his chance at youth, and returns home to find a different kind of immortality.
sections.b: Utnapishtim tests Gilgamesh by challenging him to stay awake for a week, and the exhausted king immediately falls asleep. Out of kindness, Utnapishtim tells him of a plant at the bottom of the sea that restores youth. Gilgamesh ties stones to his feet, dives down and gets it. But on the way home, while he bathes in a pool, a snake slithers up and eats the plant, shedding its skin as it goes. Gilgamesh weeps. He returns to Uruk empty handed, and the epic ends with him showing a companion the city's mighty walls and brickwork. The message many readers take is that we cannot live forever, but our work, our cities and our stories can outlast us.

quiz.q: What did George Smith discover in 1872?
o: A flood story on tablets from Nineveh
quiz.e: Smith found a flood story in the Gilgamesh tablets from Ashurbanipal's library at Nineveh.

quiz.q: How do Gilgamesh and Enkidu become friends?
o: They wrestle, neither fully wins, and they bond
quiz.e: Their fierce wrestling match ends in mutual respect and a deep friendship.

quiz.q: Why do the gods decide one hero must die?
o: For killing Humbaba and the Bull of Heaven
For stealing the plant of youth
quiz.e: Killing the forest guardian and the Bull of Heaven offended the gods, and Enkidu is chosen to die.

quiz.q: Which bird did not return to Utnapishtim's boat?
quiz.e: The raven did not come back, showing that it had found dry land.

quiz.q: What happens to the plant that restores youth?
o: Gilgamesh eats it and lives forever
A snake eats it while Gilgamesh bathes
quiz.e: A snake eats the plant and sheds its skin, and Gilgamesh loses his chance at renewed youth.

LESSONS.title: The great flood stories
LESSONS.hook: Noah's ark is famous, but it is one of many. From Mesopotamia to India, Greece and China, cultures have told of a world drowned and begun again.

sections.key: Flood stories appear in many cultures, each with its own meaning.
sections.b: Imagine rain that does not stop, rivers that swallow fields, then a single boat afloat on an endless sea. Versions of this image appear in sacred stories around the world. In the Hebrew Bible, Noah builds an ark for his family and the animals. In ancient Mesopotamia, several heroes survive a flood sent by the gods. In Hindu tradition, a fish warns the first man of a coming deluge. Greek, Chinese and many Indigenous traditions have their own versions. For believers, some of these accounts carry deep religious meaning. For historians, the pattern raises interesting questions about shared memories, borrowed stories and the experience of living beside water. This lesson looks at both, without assuming any single answer.

sections.key: The oldest written flood stories come from ancient Mesopotamia.
sections.b: The earliest known written flood stories come from Mesopotamia, the land between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers in modern Iraq. A Sumerian account tells of a king named Ziusudra who survives a flood. A Babylonian poem, the Atrahasis epic, explains that the gods sent the flood because humans had become too numerous and noisy, disturbing their rest. The wise Atrahasis is secretly warned by the god Enki and builds a boat. The same story appears in the Epic of Gilgamesh, where the survivor is called Utnapishtim. These tablets date back to roughly the early second millennium BCE. In a region where great rivers regularly burst their banks and flat land stretched for kilometres, a catastrophic flood was a very real fear.

sections.key: In Genesis, the flood is about human wrongdoing, judgment and a new promise.
sections.b: The story of Noah appears in the Book of Genesis and is shared by Judaism and Christianity, with a version in the Quran, where Noah is known as Nuh. In Genesis, God sees that the earth is filled with violence and decides to send a flood, but chooses the righteous Noah to survive with his family and pairs of animals. After the waters recede, Noah sends out a raven and a dove, and the dove returns with an olive leaf. God then makes a covenant, or solemn promise, never again to destroy the earth by flood, with the rainbow as its sign. For many believers, the story is about faithfulness, justice and mercy, whatever view they take on its historical detail.

sections.key: Scholars note close parallels between Genesis and Mesopotamian accounts, alongside big differences.
sections.b: When George Smith translated the Gilgamesh flood tablet in 1872, readers were struck by the parallels with Noah: a warning from the divine, a great boat, animals aboard, a landing on a mountain, birds sent out to find land and a sacrifice afterwards. Many scholars think the Genesis account and the Mesopotamian stories draw on a shared regional tradition, since the Israelites lived in the same wider cultural world. But the differences matter just as much. In the Mesopotamian versions, many quarrelsome gods send the flood for reasons that can seem petty. In Genesis, one God acts in response to moral wrongdoing and ends with a promise. Same shape, very different message, which is often how traditions reshape shared stories.

sections.key: Hindu, Greek and Chinese flood stories each have their own twist.
sections.b: In Hindu tradition, the first man, Manu, finds a tiny fish that asks for protection. He cares for it as it grows huge, and it turns out to be the god Vishnu in his fish form, Matsya. The fish warns of a flood and tows Manu's boat to safety. In Greek myth, Deucalion and his wife Pyrrha survive a flood sent by Zeus, then repopulate the world by throwing stones over their shoulders, which become people. Chinese tradition tells of Yu the Great, who succeeded where his father had failed. Instead of building dams to block the water, Yu dug channels to guide it to the sea. The Chinese story is less about divine punishment and more about wise human effort.

sections.key: Some flood stories may preserve real memories of changing coastlines.
sections.b: Could some flood stories remember real events? At the end of the last Ice Age, melting ice sheets raised global sea levels by well over 100 metres, a process that largely ended around 7,000 years ago. Coastlines around the world moved inland. In Australia, researchers including linguist Nicholas Reid and geographer Patrick Nunn have studied Aboriginal stories from many coastal areas that describe the sea rising and land being lost, and argue that some may preserve memories from that time. Other researchers have proposed that a sudden flooding of the Black Sea inspired ancient legends, though that idea remains debated. These theories are interesting but not settled, and none of them proves or disproves any particular religious account.

sections.key: Flood stories speak to fear, renewal and the hope of a fresh start.
sections.b: There are practical reasons flood stories are so widespread. Most early civilisations grew along rivers or coasts, where floods were both a threat and a source of fertile soil, so disaster was a shared experience worth remembering. But the stories endure for deeper reasons too. A flood wipes the slate clean, so it lets a tradition ask big questions. Why do bad things happen? What do we owe each other and the divine? Who deserves to survive, and why? The survivors usually start a new world, so the stories are as much about hope as about destruction. In a time of climate change and rising seas, these ancient tales can feel surprisingly relevant to people of every belief.

quiz.q: According to the Atrahasis epic, why did the gods send a flood?
o: Humans had become too numerous and noisy
A king had insulted the sun god
The rivers needed to be refilled
quiz.e: In Atrahasis, the gods are disturbed by the noise of an overpopulated humanity.

quiz.q: In Genesis, what is the sign of God's covenant after the flood?
quiz.e: The rainbow is given as the sign of the promise never again to destroy the earth by flood.

quiz.q: What is a key difference between Genesis and the Mesopotamian flood accounts?
o: In Genesis one God acts in response to moral wrongdoing
quiz.e: Mesopotamian versions feature many gods with sometimes petty motives, while Genesis centres on one God, wrongdoing and a promise.

quiz.q: How did Yu the Great tame the flood in Chinese tradition?
o: By praying to the dragon king
By digging channels to guide water to the sea
quiz.e: Yu succeeded by channelling the water, where his father's dams had failed.

quiz.q: What real event might some Aboriginal coastal stories remember, according to some researchers?
o: Sea level rise after the last Ice Age
The flooding of the Murray in 1956
quiz.e: Researchers have argued some stories may preserve memories of coastlines lost as seas rose after the last Ice Age.

LESSONS.title: Zoroastrianism: the fire and the choice
LESSONS.hook: Once the faith of Persian empires, now held by a small community, Zoroastrianism asks every person to pick a side in a cosmic battle between good and evil.

sections.h: The flame that never goes out
sections.key: Zoroastrian fire temples keep sacred fires burning as symbols of purity.
sections.b: In the Iranian city of Yazd, inside a fire temple, a flame burns in a large metal vessel behind glass. According to the community, it has been kept alight for many centuries, tended carefully by priests who add sandalwood and recite prayers. Outsiders sometimes call Zoroastrians 'fire worshippers', but that is a misunderstanding. For Zoroastrians, fire is a powerful symbol of purity, light and the presence of the divine, and prayers are said in the presence of fire rather than to it. Zoroastrianism is one of the world's oldest living religions. It shaped the beliefs of ancient Persian empires and, many scholars think, influenced other faiths. Today its followers number only in the low hundreds of thousands worldwide.

sections.key: Zoroastrianism traces back to the prophet Zarathustra, whose dates are uncertain.
sections.b: The religion takes its name from its prophet, Zarathustra, known to the Greeks as Zoroaster. Very little is certain about his life. Scholars disagree about when he lived, with estimates ranging from around 1500 BCE to about 600 BCE, and many favour an early date based on the language of his hymns. Those hymns, called the Gathas, are written in an ancient language known as Avestan and are the oldest part of the Zoroastrian scripture, the Avesta. In them, Zarathustra speaks directly and personally to God, asking questions about justice, truth and how a person should live. Tradition says he was a priest who received a vision, then faced strong opposition before winning the support of a local king.

sections.h: Wise Lord and the destructive spirit
sections.key: Zoroastrians worship Ahura Mazda, the Wise Lord, who is opposed by a destructive spirit.
sections.b: Zoroastrians worship one supreme God, Ahura Mazda, whose name means Wise Lord. Ahura Mazda is entirely good and is the creator of all that is good. Opposed to him is Angra Mainyu, the destructive or hostile spirit, the source of evil, sickness and death. The world is the scene of a struggle between asha, meaning truth and right order, and druj, meaning the lie or disorder. Scholars debate whether this makes the faith dualistic, with two opposing powers, or monotheistic with a powerful adversary, and Zoroastrians themselves generally describe their faith as monotheistic. Either way, the key idea is that evil is not part of God's nature. It is something that will ultimately be defeated.

sections.h: Good thoughts, good words, good deeds
sections.key: Every person has free will and must choose to side with good.
sections.b: At the heart of Zoroastrian ethics is a simple three part motto: good thoughts, good words, good deeds. Because the world is a battleground, every human choice counts. People are not born sinful; they have free will and can strengthen the side of good through honesty, kindness, hard work and care for the natural world. Zoroastrians also place great value on purity, including keeping earth, water and fire clean. Young people are initiated in a ceremony called the navjote, where they receive a white undershirt, the sudreh, and a sacred cord, the kusti, which is tied around the waist. Many Zoroastrians retie the kusti several times a day while saying prayers, a regular reminder to choose good.

sections.key: Zoroastrian teaching describes judgment after death and a final renewal of the world.
sections.b: Zoroastrianism has a vivid picture of what happens after death. Tradition teaches that on the third night after a person dies, the soul crosses the Chinvat Bridge. For the righteous, the bridge is wide and they pass to the House of Song, a paradise. For the wicked it narrows like a blade, and they fall into a place of suffering. At the end of time, a saviour figure called the Saoshyant will appear, the dead will be raised, evil will be defeated and the world will be renewed in perfection. Many scholars think these ideas of individual judgment, heaven and hell, resurrection and a final saviour influenced Judaism, Christianity and Islam, though the extent of that influence is still debated.

sections.key: Zoroastrianism was closely tied to the great Persian empires.
sections.b: Zoroastrian beliefs were bound up with Persian power for over a thousand years. Inscriptions of the Achaemenid king Darius the Great, who ruled from about 522 BCE, credit his rule to Ahuramazda, a form of Ahura Mazda. The Sasanian empire, from the 200s CE, made Zoroastrianism its official religion, with a powerful priesthood and grand fire temples. Many people believe the Magi who visit the infant Jesus in the Gospel of Matthew were Zoroastrian priests, as magi was a term for that priestly class, though the Gospel does not say so directly. After the Arab conquest of Persia in the 600s CE, Islam gradually became the majority faith, and Zoroastrians became a shrinking minority in their homeland.

sections.h: The Parsis and a small community today
sections.key: Many Zoroastrians today are Parsis, descendants of migrants to India.
sections.b: According to tradition, a group of Zoroastrians left Persia and sailed to the coast of Gujarat in India, perhaps around the 700s to 900s CE, seeking freedom to practise their faith. Their descendants are called Parsis, meaning Persians. Many later settled in Mumbai, where Parsis became prominent in business, law and philanthropy; the Tata family is a famous example. The rock star Freddie Mercury, born Farrokh Bulsara, came from a Parsi family. Traditionally Parsis placed the dead in Towers of Silence to be exposed to vultures, to avoid polluting earth or fire, though this is changing. The community is small and ageing, and debates about intermarriage and conversion are lively. Iran's festival of Nowruz has Zoroastrian roots.

quiz.q: How do Zoroastrians understand the sacred fire?
o: As a god to be worshipped
As a symbol of purity and the divine, in whose presence they pray
As a way to cook offerings
quiz.e: Fire is a symbol of purity and divine presence; prayers are said before it, not to it.

quiz.q: What does the name Ahura Mazda mean?
quiz.e: Ahura Mazda means Wise Lord, the supreme and wholly good God.

quiz.q: What is the Zoroastrian three part motto?
o: Good thoughts, good words, good deeds
quiz.e: Good thoughts, good words and good deeds sum up Zoroastrian ethics.

quiz.q: What happens at the Chinvat Bridge, according to tradition?
quiz.e: The soul crosses the Chinvat Bridge after death, and it widens for the righteous and narrows for the wicked.

quiz.q: Who are the Parsis?
o: Descendants of Zoroastrians who migrated to India
Followers of a breakaway Islamic sect
quiz.e: Parsis descend from Zoroastrians who, by tradition, sailed from Persia to Gujarat in India.

LESSONS.title: Daoism: the way of water
LESSONS.hook: A short ancient book, a sage who may never have existed and the idea that doing less can achieve more. Daoism has shaped Chinese life for over 2,000 years.

sections.h: The softest thing in the world
sections.key: Daoism often uses water as an image of quiet, yielding strength.
sections.b: Watch a river carve a canyon. Water does not fight the rock; it flows around it, finds the low places and, over enough time, wears down stone. Few images capture Daoism better. The Daodejing, Daoism's most famous text, praises water again and again: it benefits all things without competing, settles in places others avoid and yet nothing can withstand it. Daoism, sometimes spelled Taoism, is one of China's great traditions, alongside Confucianism and Buddhism. It is both a philosophy about living in harmony with the natural flow of things and an organised religion with temples, priests and rituals. Many people in China, Taiwan and elsewhere draw on its ideas without calling themselves Daoists at all.

sections.h: The Dao that cannot be named
sections.key: The Dao, or the Way, is the ultimate source and pattern of all things.
sections.b: Dao means 'way' or 'path'. In Daoism it refers to the ultimate reality behind everything: the source from which the universe arises and the natural pattern by which it unfolds. The Daodejing opens with a famous warning, usually translated along the lines of 'the Dao that can be spoken of is not the eternal Dao'. In other words, words and concepts can point towards it, but never fully capture it. The Dao is not a god who issues commands or judges people. It is more like the grain of the universe. The wise person, in this view, does not try to master or fight the world, but learns to recognise its patterns and move with them.

sections.key: Laozi is the legendary author of the Daodejing, though historians doubt the story.
sections.b: Tradition credits the Daodejing to Laozi, whose name means 'Old Master'. A famous legend says he was a record keeper at the royal court of the Zhou dynasty. Weary of the decline of society, he rode west on a water buffalo to leave China. At the border pass, a gatekeeper recognised his wisdom and begged him to write down his teachings before departing. Laozi wrote a short book of about five thousand characters, handed it over and was never seen again. Most historians today think the Daodejing was compiled from earlier sayings, probably around the 300s or 400s BCE, and that Laozi may be partly or wholly legendary. The book is now one of the most translated texts in the world.

sections.key: Wu wei means acting naturally and without strain, not doing nothing.
sections.b: One of Daoism's central ideas is wu wei, often translated as 'non action' but better understood as effortless or natural action. It does not mean being lazy. It means acting in harmony with circumstances rather than forcing them, like a skilled swimmer who uses the current instead of thrashing against it. A well known story from the Zhuangzi, another key Daoist text, describes a cook who carves an ox so skilfully that his knife never dulls, because he follows the natural spaces between the joints. Daoist writing applies the same idea to rulers: the best leaders, it suggests, govern so lightly that people barely notice them. Modern ideas about being in the 'flow' echo this ancient thought.

sections.key: Zhuangzi's playful writings question how sure we can be about reality.
sections.b: The second great Daoist thinker, Zhuangzi, lived around the 300s BCE and wrote with humour and imagination. In his most famous passage, he dreams he is a butterfly, fluttering happily with no idea he is Zhuangzi. Then he wakes and is unmistakably himself. But now he wonders: was he Zhuangzi dreaming of being a butterfly, or is he a butterfly now dreaming of being Zhuangzi? The story is less a riddle to solve than an invitation to hold our fixed ideas lightly. Zhuangzi loved stories that turn conventional values upside down: useless trees that survive because no carpenter wants them, and outcasts who turn out to be wiser than kings. His book remains one of the most enjoyable works of ancient philosophy.

sections.key: Religious Daoism includes temples, gods, rituals and the search for long life.
sections.b: The ideas of yin and yang, though older than Daoism, are closely linked to it, and the black and white yin yang symbol has become one of its best-known emblems. Yin, the dark, receptive side, and yang, the bright, active side, are not good and evil but complementary forces, each holding a seed of the other. Around the 100s CE, Daoism also developed as an organised religion, often traced to a movement called the Way of the Celestial Masters. Religious Daoism has priests, temples, scriptures, colourful festivals and a large family of deities and immortals, such as the popular Eight Immortals. Some Daoists sought long life or even immortality through meditation, breathing exercises, diet and, in earlier times, alchemy. Some alchemical elixirs contained toxic substances like mercury, with deadly results.

sections.key: Daoist ideas live on in tai chi, Chinese medicine and popular culture.
sections.b: You may already have met Daoism without knowing it. Tai chi, the slow, flowing exercise practised in parks around the world, including many Australian ones, draws on Daoist ideas about balance and the flow of qi, or life energy. Traditional Chinese medicine and feng shui share some of the same concepts. In China, people often blend Confucian values about family and duty, Buddhist ideas about suffering and Daoist practices without seeing any contradiction, a mix sometimes called the 'three teachings'. In the West, Daoist ideas have influenced writers, poets and even a popular book, The Tao of Pooh, which explains Daoism through Winnie the Pooh. The core message travels well: slow down, notice nature and stop forcing things.

quiz.q: Which natural image does the Daodejing often use for yielding strength?
quiz.e: Water yields and flows yet wears down stone, a favourite Daoist image.

quiz.q: What does the word Dao mean?
quiz.e: Dao means way or path, referring to the ultimate source and pattern of all things.

quiz.q: What is the best description of wu wei?
quiz.e: Wu wei means effortless action in harmony with circumstances, not doing nothing.

quiz.q: What does Zhuangzi wonder after his butterfly dream?
o: Whether he is a man who dreamt of being a butterfly or a butterfly dreaming of being a man
quiz.e: The famous story questions how certain we can be about which state is real.

quiz.q: How do Daoists view yin and yang?
o: As good and evil at war
As complementary forces, each containing the other
quiz.e: Yin and yang are complementary, not opposing moral forces.

LESSONS.title: Māui and the myths of Polynesia
LESSONS.hook: He fished up islands, slowed the sun and stole fire. Māui, the trickster demigod, is a hero across thousands of kilometres of Pacific Ocean.

sections.h: A hero of the whole Pacific
sections.key: Māui appears in stories from Aotearoa New Zealand to Hawaiʻi.
sections.b: Spread your fingers across a map of the Pacific: from Aotearoa New Zealand in the south west to Hawaiʻi in the north and Rapa Nui, or Easter Island, in the east, lies the vast triangle of Polynesia. Across this huge ocean, island peoples who share ancestral roots tell stories of the same mischievous hero: Māui. The details change from place to place, but he is almost always clever, cheeky, brave and a little reckless. He is a demigod, part divine and part human, and his adventures explain features of the world. In many versions he is the youngest of several brothers, often underestimated, which makes his triumphs all the sweeter. This lesson focuses mostly on Māori versions, with a few others for comparison.

sections.key: In Māori tradition, the baby Māui was cast into the sea and raised by the gods.
sections.b: In a well known Māori telling, Māui was born early and his mother, Taranga, thinking he would not survive, wrapped him in her topknot of hair and cast him into the sea. Seaweed and jellyfish protected him, and he was rescued and raised by a sky ancestor, Rangi. As a boy he found his way back to his mother's house and announced himself to his surprised family. His full name in some versions is Māui Tikitiki a Taranga, a reference to that topknot. The story establishes a pattern: Māui begins as an outsider who has to prove himself. Many listeners have found that idea powerful, because it suggests that unlikely beginnings can lead to remarkable lives.

sections.key: Māori tradition says Māui hauled up the North Island like a giant fish.
sections.b: The most famous Māui story in Aotearoa tells how he hid in the bottom of his brothers' canoe when they went fishing. Far out to sea, he revealed himself and lowered a magical hook made from the jawbone of his grandmother, Murirangawhenua. He caught something enormous and hauled it up: a vast fish, which became the North Island. Its Māori name, Te Ika a Māui, means the fish of Māui. His brothers began hacking at the fish before it had settled, which is said to explain the North Island's mountains and valleys. The South Island is often known as Te Waka a Māui, his canoe, and Stewart Island as Te Punga a Māui, its anchor stone.

sections.key: Māui snares the sun so that days are long enough to live and work.
sections.b: In Māui's time, the stories say, the sun raced across the sky so quickly that people did not have enough daylight to fish, farm and cook. Māui decided to fix this. With his brothers he plaited strong ropes and travelled to the place where the sun rose. They set a noose and, when the sun climbed out, they snared it. Māui beat the struggling sun with his grandmother's jawbone until it agreed to travel more slowly. In Hawaiian tradition, a similar feat happens on the summit of Haleakalā, whose name is often translated as 'house of the sun', on the island of Maui, which bears his name. The story neatly explains why the days are as long as they are.

sections.key: Māui tricks the fire goddess and fire ends up hidden in trees.
sections.b: Another Māori story tells how Māui, curious about where fire came from, put out all the fires in the village one night. He then went to the underworld to visit Mahuika, the fire goddess and his ancestor, who kept fire in her fingernails. She gave him one fingernail of flame, but he deliberately put it out and returned for another, again and again, until she had only one left. Furious, she threw it at him and set the land ablaze. Māui called on rain to quench the flames, and the last sparks escaped into certain trees, such as the kaikōmako. That is why, the story says, people can make fire by rubbing sticks of those woods together.

sections.key: Māui's attempt to win immortality for humans ends in his death.
sections.b: Māui's final adventure is his most daring. He wanted to defeat death itself, so that people could live forever. Death was personified by Hine nui te pō, the great woman of the night, a guardian of the underworld. Māui planned to crawl through her body while she slept, which would reverse the course of death. He took birds with him and warned them to keep quiet. But as he crawled, the sight was so comical that a little fantail, the pīwakawaka, burst into laughter. Hine nui te pō woke and crushed Māui, and so all people remain mortal. Like Gilgamesh, the hero fails to escape death, and the story asks listeners to accept mortality as part of life.

sections.key: Polynesian myths remain living culture, from Matariki to debates about film.
sections.b: These stories are not museum pieces. Many Māori trace their whakapapa, or genealogy, back through gods and ancestors, so myths and family history are deeply connected. Māori creation traditions describe the sky father Ranginui and earth mother Papatūānuku, pushed apart by their son Tāne to let light into the world. Matariki, the Māori new year marked by the rising of the Pleiades star cluster, became a New Zealand public holiday in 2022. Māui reached a global audience in Disney's 2016 film Moana. Many people enjoyed it, while some Pacific voices criticised the way Māui was portrayed and argued that sacred figures should be depicted with care. That debate shows how much these stories still matter to the people who own them.

quiz.q: Where are Māui stories told?
o: Across much of Polynesia, including Hawaiʻi
quiz.e: Māui is a hero across Polynesia, with versions from Aotearoa to Hawaiʻi.

quiz.q: What does Te Ika a Māui, a name for the North Island, mean?
quiz.e: Te Ika a Māui means the fish of Māui, recalling the story of him hauling up the land.

quiz.q: Why did Māui snare the sun?
o: To make it travel more slowly so days were longer
quiz.e: The sun raced across the sky, so Māui slowed it to give people enough daylight.

quiz.q: Which bird's laughter woke Hine nui te pō?
quiz.e: The fantail laughed at the sight of Māui crawling, waking the guardian of death.

quiz.q: What is Matariki?
o: The Māori new year, marked by the rising of the Pleiades
quiz.e: Matariki marks the Māori new year and became a New Zealand public holiday in 2022.

LESSONS.title: Your skin: the organ you wear
LESSONS.hook: It is waterproof, self-repairing, temperature-controlled and covered in sensors, and you are wearing it right now. Meet the most underrated organ you have.

sections.key: Skin is your largest organ, doing far more than simply holding you in.
sections.b: Picture unpacking an adult's skin and laying it flat. It would cover roughly two square metres, about the size of a single bed sheet, and weigh several kilograms. That makes it the largest organ in the body, even though we rarely think of it as an organ at all. Yet skin does an astonishing amount of work. It keeps water in and germs out, shields you from sunlight, helps control your temperature, makes vitamin D, and feeds your brain a constant stream of information about touch, pressure, heat and pain. It also heals itself after cuts and scrapes, usually without leaving much trace. Every square centimetre is a busy, living system, packed with blood vessels, nerves, glands and cells that are constantly being replaced.

sections.key: The epidermis protects, the dermis supports and senses, and the fat layer below cushions and insulates.
sections.b: Skin is built in layers, a bit like a well-made jacket. The outermost layer, the epidermis, is surprisingly thin, in most places thinner than a sheet of paper, but it is the part that faces the world. Its top is made of flattened dead cells packed with a tough protein called keratin, which forms a waterproof, germ-resistant barrier. Beneath it lies the dermis, a thicker layer woven from collagen and elastin fibres that give skin its strength and stretch. The dermis holds the blood vessels, nerve endings, hair roots and sweat glands. Below that is the subcutaneous layer, mostly fat, which cushions you against bumps, stores energy and helps hold in body heat. Thickness varies hugely: the skin on your eyelids is delicate, while the soles of your feet are thick and rugged.

sections.key: You shed skin cells constantly and grow a fresh outer layer every few weeks.
sections.b: Deep at the base of the epidermis, cells are dividing all the time. As new cells form, older ones are pushed upwards towards the surface. On the way they fill with keratin, flatten out and die, so the surface you touch is essentially a layer of dead cells doing a protective job. Eventually they flake away, often too small to notice. This journey from bottom to top takes roughly a month, so in a sense you grow a new outer skin many times a year. You lose a huge number of skin cells every day. A popular claim says most household dust is dead skin, but research suggests a lot of indoor dust actually comes in from outside, so skin is only part of the story.

sections.key: Skin colour comes mainly from melanin, a natural pigment that helps protect against ultraviolet light.
sections.b: Scattered through the bottom of the epidermis are cells called melanocytes, which make a pigment called melanin. People of all skin tones have broadly similar numbers of melanocytes. What differs is how much melanin they produce and what type. More melanin, especially the darker form, gives deeper skin tones and stronger natural protection against ultraviolet radiation. When skin is exposed to the sun, melanocytes ramp up production, which is what a tan is: a sign that skin has been damaged and is trying to defend itself. Scientists think human skin colour varies so much because our ancestors lived under very different levels of sunlight, balancing protection from UV against the need to make vitamin D. In a high-UV country like Australia, that protection matters for everyone.

sections.key: Sweat cools you down, blood vessels redirect heat, and goosebumps are a leftover from furrier ancestors.
sections.b: Go for a brisk walk on a hot Brisbane afternoon and your skin becomes a cooling system. Millions of small sweat glands release watery sweat, and as it evaporates it carries heat away. Meanwhile, blood vessels near the surface widen, sending warm blood close to the skin so heat can escape, which is why your face flushes. In the cold, the reverse happens: those vessels narrow to keep warmth near your core. A second type of sweat gland, found mainly in the armpits and groin, releases a thicker sweat. It is odourless at first, and the smell comes from skin bacteria breaking it down. Goosebumps are made by tiny muscles that pull hairs upright. In furry animals this traps insulating air or makes them look bigger; in us, it is mostly a curious leftover.

sections.key: Skin contains several kinds of touch receptors, and your fingertips are among the most sensitive spots.
sections.b: Close your eyes and run a finger over a coin. You can feel the ridges, the edge and the coolness of the metal, all thanks to specialised nerve endings in your skin. Some respond to light touch, others to vibration, deep pressure, stretching, heat, cold or damage. They are not spread evenly. Your fingertips, lips and tongue are packed with receptors, while your back has far fewer, which is why it is hard to tell whether one or two pencil points are pressing on it. The ridges that make up your fingerprints form before birth and seem to help with grip and with sensing fine texture. Even identical twins, who share the same DNA, have different fingerprints, because small variations in the womb shape how the ridges form.

sections.key: Sun protection matters most, and the changes that come with age are mostly driven by collagen loss and UV exposure.
sections.b: As we age, skin makes less collagen and elastin, grows thinner, and holds less moisture, which is why wrinkles and sagging appear. But much of what people think of as ageing skin is actually sun damage. Compare the skin on someone's forearm with the skin on their inner upper arm and the difference can be striking. Australia has some of the highest rates of skin cancer in the world, so sun protection is the single most useful habit: shade, clothing, a broad-brimmed hat, sunglasses and sunscreen, especially when the UV index is 3 or above. Getting to know your own skin and checking for new or changing spots is also worthwhile. This is general information, not medical advice, so for any concern see a doctor or visit healthdirect.

quiz.q: Roughly how much area would an adult's skin cover if laid flat?
quiz.e: An adult's skin covers roughly two square metres, making it the body's largest organ.

quiz.q: Which layer of skin contains collagen fibres, blood vessels and hair roots?
quiz.e: The dermis is the thicker middle layer that holds structural fibres, vessels, nerves and glands.

quiz.q: What do people with different skin tones mainly differ in?
o: The amount and type of melanin produced
quiz.e: People have broadly similar numbers of melanocytes; it is melanin production that varies.

quiz.q: Why does armpit sweat develop a smell?
o: It is made by the kidneys
quiz.e: This sweat is odourless at first; bacteria on the skin create the smell as they break it down.

quiz.q: Why do identical twins have different fingerprints?
o: Small variations in the womb shape the ridges
Fingerprints come only from the father
quiz.e: Fingerprints form before birth and are shaped by tiny differences in the womb environment, not DNA alone.

LESSONS.title: How breathing works
LESSONS.hook: You will take more than 20,000 breaths today without thinking about any of them. Here is the clever machinery that keeps the air moving.

sections.key: Breathing runs on autopilot, but you can take manual control whenever you like.
sections.b: Right now, while you read this, you are breathing roughly 12 to 20 times a minute. Over a day that adds up to tens of thousands of breaths, almost none of which you choose to take. Breathing is one of the few body functions that runs automatically yet can also be taken over by will. You can hold your breath, speed it up, sing a long note or blow out birthday candles. Then, the moment you stop paying attention, your brain quietly takes the controls back. That handover is managed by the brainstem, an ancient part of the brain at the top of the spinal cord. Every breath delivers oxygen your cells need to release energy from food, and carries away the carbon dioxide they produce as waste.

sections.key: Breathing in happens when the diaphragm and rib muscles enlarge the chest, letting air rush in.
sections.b: Lungs have no muscles of their own to pull in air. Instead, the work is done by the diaphragm, a dome-shaped sheet of muscle beneath the lungs. When it contracts, it flattens and moves downwards, while muscles between the ribs lift the ribcage up and out. The chest gets bigger, the pressure inside the lungs drops slightly below the pressure of the air outside, and air flows in to fill the space. Breathing out at rest is mostly passive: the diaphragm relaxes, the elastic lungs spring back, and air is pushed out. When you exercise hard, extra muscles in your neck, chest and belly join in to move air faster. Hiccups, by the way, are sudden involuntary spasms of the diaphragm, with a snap of the vocal cords closing.

sections.key: Air travels through ever-smaller branching tubes to reach hundreds of millions of tiny air sacs.
sections.b: Air enters through your nose or mouth, passes the voice box and travels down the windpipe, or trachea. From there the airways split into two main branches, one for each lung, then keep dividing again and again, like an upside-down tree. The smallest twigs end in clusters of tiny balloon-like sacs called alveoli. There are hundreds of millions of them, and because they are so numerous and so small, their combined inner surface is enormous, often compared to around half a tennis court. The two lungs are not identical either. The right lung has three sections, called lobes, while the left has only two, leaving room for the heart. The nose matters too: it warms, moistens and filters air before it reaches these delicate surfaces.

sections.key: In the alveoli, oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out, across walls thinner than a hair.
sections.b: The real business of breathing happens in the alveoli. Each tiny sac is wrapped in a mesh of hair-thin blood vessels called capillaries, and the barrier between air and blood is astonishingly thin. Oxygen drifts across into the blood, where it latches onto haemoglobin, an iron-rich protein inside red blood cells. At the same time, carbon dioxide moves the other way, out of the blood and into the air sacs, ready to be breathed out. The air you breathe in is about 21 per cent oxygen, and the air you breathe out still contains roughly 16 per cent. Your body uses only a fraction on each breath. That leftover oxygen is one reason rescue breaths during CPR can still help someone who is not breathing.

sections.h: The urge comes from carbon dioxide
sections.key: Your drive to breathe is triggered mainly by rising carbon dioxide, not falling oxygen.
sections.b: Hold your breath and after a while the urge to breathe becomes overwhelming. Surprisingly, that urge is not mainly caused by running low on oxygen. Sensors in the brainstem and in major arteries track the level of carbon dioxide in the blood, which also changes the blood's acidity. When carbon dioxide rises, these sensors push you hard to breathe. This has an important safety lesson. Some swimmers and divers hyperventilate before going underwater, breathing rapidly to blow off carbon dioxide so they can stay down longer. The urge to breathe is delayed, but oxygen keeps falling, and a person can black out without warning. This is a known cause of drowning, even among strong swimmers, so hyperventilating before breath-holding in the water is dangerous and should be avoided.

sections.key: A layer of mucus and tiny beating hairs constantly sweeps dust and germs out of your airways.
sections.b: Every day you breathe in dust, pollen, smoke particles and microbes. To deal with them, your airways are lined with sticky mucus that traps particles, and with millions of microscopic hair-like structures called cilia. The cilia beat in coordinated waves, moving the mucus upwards towards the throat, where it is usually swallowed without you noticing. Scientists sometimes call this the mucociliary escalator. Coughing and sneezing are the emergency backups, blasting out irritants at high speed. Cigarette smoke damages and slows the cilia, which is one reason people who smoke often develop a persistent cough: the body has to cough up what the escalator can no longer clear. Bushfire smoke is also hard on airways, so on smoky days it makes sense to follow local health advice.

sections.key: Slow, steady breathing can help you feel calmer, and your lungs reward regular exercise.
sections.b: Breathing is closely tied to the nervous system. When you are anxious, breathing tends to become fast and shallow, and when you are relaxed it slows down. The link works in both directions, so deliberately slowing your breath, especially with a long, unhurried breath out, can help many people feel calmer. Exercise does not grow new lung tissue, but it trains the breathing muscles, the heart and the muscles that use oxygen, so everyday activity feels easier. Lung function naturally declines a little with age, and smoking speeds that decline sharply. Breathlessness that is new, sudden or worsening deserves attention. This lesson is general information rather than medical advice, so if you are worried about your breathing, talk to a doctor or check healthdirect, and in an emergency call triple zero.

quiz.q: What happens when the diaphragm contracts?
o: It flattens and moves down, enlarging the chest
It pushes up and squeezes the lungs
It pumps blood into the lungs
quiz.e: Contracting flattens the diaphragm, lowering pressure in the chest so air flows in.

quiz.q: Why does the left lung have fewer lobes than the right?
o: It is used only during exercise
It leaves room for the heart
quiz.e: The left lung has two lobes rather than three, making space for the heart.

quiz.q: Roughly how much oxygen is in the air you breathe out?
quiz.e: Exhaled air still contains around 16 per cent oxygen, compared with about 21 per cent going in.

quiz.q: Why is hyperventilating before breath-hold swimming dangerous?
o: It fills the lungs with water
It raises carbon dioxide too high
It delays the urge to breathe while oxygen keeps falling
quiz.e: Blowing off carbon dioxide postpones the warning signal, so a swimmer can black out without feeling the need to surface.

quiz.q: What job do the cilia in your airways do?
o: Sweep mucus and trapped particles up towards the throat
Produce the sound of your voice
Warm the air to body temperature
quiz.e: Cilia beat in waves to move mucus and trapped particles out of the airways.

LESSONS.title: Hormones: the body's chemical messengers
LESSONS.hook: A tiny drop of the right chemical can make your heart race, your stomach growl or a child grow taller. Hormones are the body's slow but powerful postal service.

sections.key: Hormones are chemicals released into the blood that change how distant cells behave.
sections.b: Imagine you nearly step on a snake on a bush track. Within seconds your heart is pounding, your breathing is fast and your muscles feel ready to spring. Part of that response comes from nerves, which act almost instantly, but part comes from hormones. A hormone is a chemical messenger made in one place and carried in the blood to cells elsewhere, where it changes what those cells do. Only cells with the matching receptor respond, a bit like a letter that can only be opened by the right key. Nerves are like phone calls: fast, targeted and brief. Hormones are more like a broadcast: slower to arrive, but able to reach the whole body at once and to keep working for minutes, hours or even years.

sections.key: Hormones come from endocrine glands, coordinated by the hypothalamus and pituitary in the brain.
sections.b: The organs that release hormones directly into the blood make up the endocrine system. Key players include the thyroid in your neck, the adrenal glands perched on top of the kidneys, the pancreas, and the ovaries or testes. Fat tissue, the gut, the heart and the kidneys release hormones too. Overseeing much of this is a partnership in the brain. The hypothalamus monitors the body's state and sends signals to the pituitary gland, a pea-sized structure just below it. The pituitary then releases hormones that instruct other glands to speed up or slow down. Because it directs so many other glands, the pituitary is often called the master gland, although it takes its own orders from the hypothalamus.

sections.key: Most hormone levels are held steady by negative feedback, much like a thermostat.
sections.b: Think of the thermostat on an air conditioner. When the room warms past the set point, the cooling switches on; once it is cool enough, the cooling switches off. Many hormones work the same way, through negative feedback. Take the thyroid. When thyroid hormone levels fall, the hypothalamus and pituitary sense it and send signals urging the thyroid to make more. When levels rise high enough, those signals are turned down. This keeps things within a healthy range. The thyroid needs iodine to make its hormones, and iodine deficiency was once a widespread problem in parts of Australia. Since 2009, iodised salt has been required in most commercial bread here, a simple measure designed to top up iodine levels across the population.

sections.key: Adrenaline gives an instant boost, while cortisol manages longer-term energy and follows a daily rhythm.
sections.b: When you get a fright, your adrenal glands release adrenaline, also called epinephrine. It quickens the heart, widens the airways, sends more blood to the muscles and releases stored fuel into the blood, preparing you to fight or flee. The adrenals also make cortisol, often labelled the stress hormone, though that undersells it. Cortisol helps regulate blood sugar, blood pressure, inflammation and the body's use of energy. It also follows a daily rhythm, typically rising in the early morning to help you wake and falling towards night. Short bursts of these hormones are useful and normal. Problems are more likely when stress is intense and long-lasting, which is one reason sleep, exercise and rest matter for the whole body, not just the mind.

sections.key: Insulin controls blood sugar, and its discovery in Canada in the early 1920s transformed type 1 diabetes.
sections.b: After a meal, sugar from your food enters the blood. The pancreas responds by releasing insulin, which signals cells in the muscles, liver and fat to take that sugar in, bringing blood levels back down. Between meals, another hormone, glucagon, does the reverse. In type 1 diabetes, the body's immune system destroys the cells that make insulin. Before the 1920s, this meant a grim and usually short life. Then, in 1921, Frederick Banting and Charles Best, working at the University of Toronto with colleagues, managed to extract insulin. In early 1922 a teenage boy named Leonard Thompson became the first person to receive it as a treatment, and his condition improved. Within a few years insulin was being produced on a large scale, saving countless lives worldwide.

sections.key: Hormones such as ghrelin, leptin, melatonin and oxytocin shape appetite, sleep and connection.
sections.b: Hormones influence everyday feelings more than many people realise. Ghrelin, made mainly in the stomach, tends to rise before meals and helps stir up hunger. Leptin, released by fat tissue, helps signal to the brain how much energy is stored. Melatonin, produced by the pineal gland deep in the brain, rises in the evening as light fades and helps signal that it is time for sleep, which is one reason bright screens late at night can make it harder to drift off. Oxytocin plays key roles in childbirth and breastfeeding, and it is involved in social bonding and trust. It is sometimes nicknamed the love hormone, but scientists caution that its effects are complex and depend heavily on context, so the nickname is a big oversimplification.

sections.key: The term hormone dates from 1905, and hormones remain central to modern medicine.
sections.b: The idea of chemical messengers is surprisingly recent. In 1902 two physiologists in London, William Bayliss and Ernest Starling, discovered that a substance from the gut, which they called secretin, could trigger the pancreas through the blood rather than through nerves. In 1905 Starling popularised the word hormone, from a Greek word meaning to set in motion or to excite. Since then, hormones have become central to medicine, from treating thyroid conditions to fertility treatment and contraception. Because hormones affect so many systems, symptoms of hormone problems can be vague, such as tiredness, weight changes or feeling unusually hot or cold. This lesson is general information, not medical advice. If something feels off, a GP can arrange tests, and healthdirect is a reliable starting point.

quiz.q: How do hormones mainly travel to their target cells?
quiz.e: Hormones are released into the blood and carried to cells with the matching receptors.

quiz.q: Which gland is often called the master gland?
quiz.e: The pituitary directs many other glands, although it takes its cues from the hypothalamus.

quiz.q: Why has iodised salt been required in most Australian bread since 2009?
o: To help the thyroid by boosting iodine intake
quiz.e: The thyroid needs iodine to make its hormones, and the measure aimed to reduce iodine deficiency.

quiz.q: What does insulin do after a meal?
o: Signals cells to take sugar from the blood
Releases stored sugar into the blood
quiz.e: Insulin helps cells absorb sugar, bringing blood sugar levels back down.

quiz.q: Which hormone rises in the evening as light fades and helps signal sleep?
quiz.e: Melatonin from the pineal gland rises in darkness and helps prepare the body for sleep.

LESSONS.title: The liver: your chemical factory
LESSONS.hook: Quietly tucked under your ribs is an organ that stores fuel, builds proteins, breaks down toxins and can even regrow itself. Meet the liver.

sections.key: The liver is a remarkable regenerating organ, a fact that echoes an ancient Greek story.
sections.b: In Greek mythology, Prometheus stole fire from the gods and was punished by being chained to a rock. Each day an eagle ate his liver, and each night it grew back. Whether the ancient storytellers knew it or not, they picked exactly the right organ. The liver is famous among doctors for its ability to regenerate. If a large part is removed, the remaining tissue can grow and restore much of the organ's size and function within weeks to months. This is what makes living donor liver transplants possible: part of a healthy adult's liver can be given to someone else, and both pieces can grow. Few organs can do anything like it, and it is only one of the liver's many talents.

sections.key: The liver is the largest internal organ and receives blood from two sources.
sections.b: Your liver sits in the upper right of your abdomen, mostly tucked behind the lower ribs. In an adult it weighs around one and a half kilograms, making it the largest solid organ inside the body. It is also unusually well supplied with blood. Like other organs, it receives oxygen-rich blood through an artery. But most of its blood arrives through a second route, the hepatic portal vein, which carries blood straight from the stomach and intestines. That means nearly everything you absorb from a meal, nutrients, alcohol, medicines and the odd unwanted chemical, passes through the liver before it reaches the rest of your body. The liver gets first look at it all, and gets to decide what to store, change, use or send on.

sections.key: The liver stores sugar as glycogen and releases it to keep blood sugar steady between meals.
sections.b: After a meal, your blood carries a flood of sugar. With help from insulin, the liver takes some of it in and links the sugar molecules together into a storage form called glycogen. Hours later, when you have not eaten and blood sugar starts to dip, the liver breaks glycogen back down and releases sugar into the blood. This keeps your brain, which relies heavily on sugar for fuel, running smoothly overnight and between meals. When glycogen runs low, during a long fast for example, the liver can make new sugar from other building blocks. It also handles fats, packaging them for transport around the body, and makes cholesterol, which the body uses to build cell membranes and some hormones. Think of the liver as both pantry and kitchen.

sections.key: The liver makes many vital blood proteins, including those that help your blood clot.
sections.b: Cut your finger and, within minutes, the bleeding slows and stops. That depends partly on clotting factors, proteins that work together to form a clot, and the liver makes most of them. It also produces albumin, the most abundant protein in blood plasma, which helps keep fluid inside blood vessels and carries hormones and medicines around the body. Many other transport proteins and parts of the immune system are made here too. Because of this, a liver that is not working well can cause problems that seem to have nothing to do with the liver, such as easy bruising or swelling in the legs. Doctors often check liver function with a blood test that measures some of these proteins along with enzymes that leak out when liver cells are damaged.

sections.h: Bile and the colour of things
sections.key: The liver makes bile to help digest fat, and recycled red blood cells give bile its colour.
sections.b: Every day your liver produces bile, a greenish-yellow fluid that drains into the gallbladder for storage. When you eat a fatty meal, the gallbladder squeezes bile into the small intestine, where it breaks fat into tiny droplets, a bit like washing-up liquid on a greasy pan, so digestive enzymes can work on it. Bile is also a way of getting rid of waste. When old red blood cells are broken down, their haemoglobin is converted into a yellow substance called bilirubin. The liver processes it and sends it out in bile. Gut bacteria then change it further, and that is what gives poo its brown colour. If bilirubin builds up in the blood instead, the skin and the whites of the eyes can turn yellow, a sign called jaundice.

sections.key: The liver changes harmful substances, including ammonia and alcohol, into forms the body can remove.
sections.b: Your cells constantly produce waste, and some of it is toxic. When proteins are broken down, they release ammonia, which is harmful to the brain at high levels. The liver converts it into urea, a much safer substance that the kidneys then flush out in urine. The liver also chemically alters many medicines, hormones and foreign substances, often making them easier to excrete. Alcohol is a major example. The liver breaks it down at a fairly fixed pace, often estimated at around one standard drink an hour, and nothing such as coffee or a cold shower speeds this up. This is also why so-called detox teas and cleanses are unnecessary for healthy people: the liver and kidneys already do this job continuously, and they do it well.

sections.key: Liver problems often cause no symptoms early on, so prevention and checks matter.
sections.b: The liver has few pain nerves inside it and a lot of spare capacity, so it can be quite damaged before a person feels unwell. One of the most common liver problems today is a build-up of fat in the liver, often linked with being overweight, type 2 diabetes and inactivity. It frequently causes no symptoms at first, and it can often improve with changes to diet, activity and weight. Heavy drinking and viral hepatitis are other major causes of liver damage. Australia offers vaccination against hepatitis B, and effective treatments now exist for hepatitis C. Remember that this is general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns about your liver, talk to your GP, who can arrange simple blood tests, and see healthdirect for reliable background.

quiz.q: Why are living donor liver transplants possible?
o: The liver can regenerate after part is removed
The liver is not essential for life
quiz.e: Part of a healthy liver can be donated and both portions can regrow.

quiz.q: What does the hepatic portal vein carry to the liver?
o: Blood straight from the stomach and intestines
quiz.e: Most of the liver's blood comes from the gut, so absorbed substances pass through the liver first.

quiz.q: In what form does the liver store sugar?
quiz.e: The liver links sugar molecules into glycogen and breaks it down again when blood sugar drops.

quiz.q: What gives poo its typical brown colour?
o: Bilirubin from old red blood cells, changed by gut bacteria
quiz.e: Bilirubin from recycled red blood cells is sent out in bile and altered by gut bacteria.

quiz.q: What does the liver convert ammonia into?
quiz.e: Ammonia is turned into urea, which the kidneys then remove in urine.

LESSONS.title: Your kidneys: the body's master filters
LESSONS.hook: Two fist-sized organs filter your entire blood supply many times a day, balancing water, salt and acid with exquisite precision.

sections.key: Your kidneys filter around 180 litres of fluid a day but make only about one and a half litres of urine.
sections.b: Each kidney is roughly the size of a fist and shaped, unsurprisingly, like a kidney bean. They sit against the back wall of the abdomen, partly protected by the lower ribs. Despite their modest size, they receive about a fifth of all the blood the heart pumps. Every day they filter something like 180 litres of fluid out of the blood, enough to fill a large bathtub. Yet a typical adult produces only around one and a half litres of urine. That means the kidneys reclaim about 99 per cent of what they filter, carefully choosing what to keep and what to throw away. The kidneys' real skill is not simply removing waste, but deciding, moment by moment, exactly how much of everything the body should hold onto.

sections.key: Each kidney contains around a million tiny filtering units called nephrons.
sections.b: The working unit of the kidney is the nephron, and each kidney has roughly a million of them, though the number varies a lot between people. A nephron begins with a glomerulus, a tiny tangle of capillaries where blood pressure pushes water and small molecules through a fine filter, while blood cells and most proteins stay behind. The filtered fluid then flows into a long, twisting tube. Along its length, cells lining the tube pull back the useful things, such as sugar, salts, amino acids and most of the water, and return them to the blood. They also actively push some extra wastes and excess substances into the tube. What remains at the end becomes urine, which drains into collecting ducts and then out of the kidney towards the bladder.

sections.key: A hormone from the brain tells the kidneys how much water to save, which is why urine colour changes.
sections.b: Spend a long, hot day working outdoors in the Pilbara without drinking enough, and your urine becomes darker and smaller in volume. Drink a lot of water on a cool day, and it becomes pale and plentiful. The kidneys are responding to instructions. When your blood becomes too concentrated, sensors in the brain trigger the release of antidiuretic hormone, also called vasopressin, from the pituitary gland. This hormone makes the final parts of the nephron more permeable to water, so more is reabsorbed and urine becomes concentrated. Alcohol suppresses this hormone, which is partly why drinking makes people urinate more and can leave them dehydrated. Urine colour is a handy rough guide to hydration, though some vitamins, foods and medicines can change it too.

sections.key: By adjusting how much sodium and water they keep, the kidneys help set long-term blood pressure.
sections.b: Sodium and potassium are essential for nerves and muscles, including the heart, and their levels must be kept in a fairly narrow range. The kidneys fine-tune both. They are also central to blood pressure. When blood flow to the kidneys falls, they release an enzyme called renin, which starts a chain of reactions involving a hormone system that narrows blood vessels and signals the body to retain salt and water. More fluid in the circulation means higher pressure. This system is useful after blood loss, but it is also why several common blood pressure medicines work by acting on this pathway or on the kidneys' handling of salt. The link runs both ways too: long-term high blood pressure can damage the delicate filters inside the kidneys.

sections.key: The kidneys also manage the blood's acidity, activate vitamin D and signal the body to make red blood cells.
sections.b: Filtering is only part of the job. Your metabolism constantly produces acids, and the kidneys help keep the blood's acidity in a tight range by getting rid of acid and holding onto bicarbonate, a natural buffer. The kidneys also act as hormone factories. When oxygen levels in the kidney fall, as they do at high altitude or after significant blood loss, the kidneys release erythropoietin, often shortened to EPO, which tells the bone marrow to make more red blood cells. A synthetic version is a vital medicine for some patients, and it became notorious when misused as a doping drug in endurance sport. The kidneys also complete the activation of vitamin D, which the body needs to absorb calcium, so healthy kidneys matter for healthy bones.

sections.key: Kidney stones form when minerals crystallise in urine, and dehydration is a common contributor.
sections.b: Kidney stones are hard deposits that form when minerals in urine, most often calcium combined with oxalate, become concentrated enough to crystallise. Small stones may pass unnoticed, but a stone moving down the narrow tube to the bladder can cause sudden, severe pain that people often rank among the worst they have experienced. Being dehydrated is a common contributor, which is relevant in hot parts of Australia. Kidneys can also be gradually harmed by long-term diabetes and high blood pressure, two of the leading causes of chronic kidney disease. Because the kidneys have so much reserve, chronic kidney disease often causes no symptoms until a lot of function has been lost. Simple blood and urine tests can pick it up early, when steps to protect the kidneys are most effective.

sections.h: Living with one, or with none
sections.key: People can live well with one kidney, and dialysis or a transplant can replace failed kidneys.
sections.b: Because the kidneys have so much spare capacity, most people can live a normal life with just one, which is why living kidney donation is possible. The first successful kidney transplant took place in Boston in 1954, between identical twins, which avoided the problem of rejection. When both kidneys fail, a person needs either dialysis, where a machine or the lining of the abdomen is used to filter the blood, or a transplant. In Australia you can register your decision to be an organ and tissue donor through the Australian Organ Donor Register, which is run by Services Australia, and talking about your wishes with family is important too. This lesson is general information, not medical advice. For questions about kidney health, speak with your GP or visit healthdirect.

quiz.q: About what proportion of the fluid they filter do the kidneys reclaim?
quiz.e: Of roughly 180 litres filtered daily, only about one and a half litres leaves as urine.

quiz.q: What is the glomerulus?
o: A tangle of capillaries where blood is first filtered
The tube that carries urine to the bladder
quiz.e: The glomerulus is the filtering start of each nephron, where pressure pushes fluid out of the blood.

quiz.q: Why can alcohol leave people dehydrated?
o: It suppresses antidiuretic hormone, so less water is reabsorbed
It makes the kidneys release EPO
quiz.e: With less antidiuretic hormone, the kidneys save less water and more urine is produced.

quiz.q: What does erythropoietin (EPO) from the kidneys do?
o: Tells bone marrow to make more red blood cells
quiz.e: When oxygen in the kidney is low, EPO signals the bone marrow to boost red blood cell production.

quiz.q: Why was the first successful kidney transplant, in 1954, between identical twins?
o: It avoided the problem of rejection
quiz.e: Identical twins are genetically matched, so the recipient's immune system did not reject the organ.

LESSONS.title: Your microbiome: the trillions living inside you
LESSONS.hook: You are not just you. Your gut is home to a vast, bustling community of microbes that digest food you cannot, train your immune system and may even chat with your brain.

sections.key: Your large intestine hosts a vast, diverse ecosystem of microbes, mostly bacteria.
sections.b: If you could shrink down and wander into your large intestine, you would find something like a rainforest: crowded, warm, dark and teeming with life. Living there are trillions of microorganisms, mostly bacteria, along with archaea, fungi and viruses. Together they are called the gut microbiota, and their combined genes are often called the microbiome. Hundreds of different species may live in one person's gut, and the mix is so individual that it is sometimes compared to a fingerprint. Most of these microbes are not germs in the frightening sense. They are long-term residents that have evolved alongside humans, and many of them are helpful or harmless. In total, the microbes in your gut weigh perhaps a couple of hundred grams, roughly the weight of a mango.

sections.key: An old claim of ten microbes for every human cell has been revised to roughly one to one.
sections.b: For decades, textbooks and popular articles repeated a striking claim: microbial cells in the body outnumber human cells by about ten to one. It made a great headline, but it was based on a rough estimate from the 1970s. In 2016, researchers recalculated the numbers more carefully and concluded the ratio is closer to one to one, with tens of trillions of each. The exact figure shifts with every trip to the toilet, since faeces contain a large share of gut bacteria. The lesson here is a good one for any curious reader: catchy statistics sometimes survive long after the evidence for them has been questioned. Even at one to one, though, the microbes in and on your body form an enormous and important community.

sections.key: Gut microbes ferment fibre that human enzymes cannot digest, producing useful short-chain fatty acids.
sections.b: Humans make enzymes that digest sugars, starches, proteins and fats, but we lack the enzymes to break down many types of dietary fibre, such as those in legumes, oats, wholegrains, vegetables and fruit. That fibre travels largely intact to the large intestine, where gut microbes take over. They ferment it, producing gases, which explains why a big serve of baked beans can have noisy consequences, and also substances called short-chain fatty acids. One of these, butyrate, is a key fuel for the cells lining the colon. Short-chain fatty acids also appear to influence inflammation and metabolism elsewhere in the body. Gut bacteria help make some vitamins too, including vitamin K. In a real sense, eating fibre is a way of feeding the microbes that help feed you.

sections.key: Gut microbes help educate the immune system and crowd out harmful invaders.
