A cheap fridge thermometer is the easiest way to check. Fridges run all day, every day, so they are among the bigger energy users in a home. In Australia, new fridges carry an Energy Rating label showing stars and an estimate of yearly energy use, which makes it easier to compare models. A fridge that is too big for your needs, has worn door seals or is jammed against a wall with no room to release heat will use more power. An old second fridge humming away in the garage can quietly add to your power bill.

quiz.q: What was Frederic Tudor known as?
quiz.e: Tudor built a large trade shipping natural pond ice around the world.

quiz.q: Why does the back of a fridge feel warm?
o: Heat removed from inside is released there
Warm air leaks through the door
quiz.e: A fridge moves heat from inside the cabinet to the outside.

quiz.q: Which industry was an early user of James Harrison's ice machines?
quiz.e: Breweries needed reliable cold to make lager style beer.

quiz.q: What problem was later found with CFCs?
quiz.e: CFCs were phased out under the 1987 Montreal Protocol because they destroyed ozone.

quiz.q: What temperature do Australian food safety authorities recommend for your fridge?
quiz.e: At 5°C or below, most food poisoning bacteria grow slowly.

LESSONS.title: Flushing toilets and the Great Stink
LESSONS.hook: Few inventions have saved as many lives as the humble toilet and the sewer pipe behind it. Their story involves a smelly river, a deadly pump and a lot of bricks.

sections.key: In 1858 the stench from the sewage-filled Thames pushed Parliament to act.
sections.b: The summer of 1858 in London was unusually hot, and the River Thames was full of human waste. The smell became so overpowering that it was nicknamed the Great Stink. In the new Houses of Parliament, beside the river, curtains were reportedly soaked in chemicals to mask the odour, and politicians considered moving elsewhere. For years engineers had warned that London's drains were failing, but nothing much had happened. Now the people in charge could smell the problem for themselves. Within weeks Parliament passed a law giving the city's new Metropolitan Board of Works the power and money to build a proper sewer system. It became one of the great engineering projects of the Victorian age.

sections.key: For most of history, waste went into pots, pits and the street.
sections.b: Some ancient cities managed waste impressively. Homes in the Indus Valley cities had drains connected to covered channels, and Rome had large sewers, including the Cloaca Maxima, which still exists. But in many later towns, people used chamber pots, emptied the contents into cesspits or simply tipped them into the street or a nearby river. Workers called nightsoil men collected waste after dark and carted it away, sometimes to sell as fertiliser. As cities grew during the Industrial Revolution, cesspits overflowed and seeped into wells. Rivers that supplied drinking water also carried away sewage. Few people understood the danger, because the dominant theory blamed disease on bad air, or miasma, rather than on contaminated water.

sections.key: An Elizabethan courtier designed an early flush toilet, but the key S-bend came later.
sections.b: Around 1596 Sir John Harington, a godson of Queen Elizabeth I, described a flushing toilet with a water tank and a valve, and he is said to have installed one for the Queen. It did not catch on. The crucial improvement came in 1775, when the Scottish watchmaker Alexander Cumming patented a design with an S-shaped bend in the pipe below the bowl. Water sitting in the bend forms a seal that blocks smelly gases from rising back into the room, an idea still used today. And what about Thomas Crapper? He was a real Victorian plumber who ran a successful business and made improvements to toilets, but he did not invent the flush toilet, despite the popular myth.

sections.key: In 1854 John Snow traced a cholera outbreak to a contaminated water pump.
sections.b: Cholera struck London several times in the 1800s, killing tens of thousands. In 1854 a terrible outbreak hit Soho. The doctor John Snow doubted the miasma theory and suspected cholera spread through water. He mapped where the victims lived and found they clustered around a public water pump on Broad Street. He persuaded local officials to remove the pump's handle, and the outbreak, which was already declining, came to an end. Later investigation suggested the well had been contaminated by a nearby cesspit. Snow's map became a classic of public health and epidemiology. His ideas were not widely accepted at the time, but they helped show that clean water and safe sewage disposal were matters of life and death.

sections.key: Joseph Bazalgette built London's sewer network, planning generously for the future.
sections.b: The engineer given the job of fixing London was Joseph Bazalgette. From 1859 his teams built a vast network of brick sewers, with large intercepting sewers running alongside the Thames to carry waste east, away from the centre, to be released further downstream. In all, the system included around 1,800 kilometres of street sewers and main lines. Bazalgette is often praised for his foresight: when calculating the pipe sizes he needed, he reportedly doubled them, allowing for the city's growth. Parts of the network still work today. The project also created the Victoria Embankment and other riverside roads. Cholera outbreaks in the city declined, and Bazalgette's work is credited with saving countless lives.

sections.key: Australian cities faced the same problems, and Melbourne's stink earned it a rude nickname.
sections.b: Australia's booming cities were no better. In the 1880s Melbourne was one of the richest cities in the world, but its waste drained into open gutters, cesspits and the Yarra River. Critics punned on its nickname Marvellous Melbourne and called it Marvellous Smellbourne. Typhoid was a constant threat. In 1891 the Melbourne and Metropolitan Board of Works was created, and later that decade the first homes were connected to a sewer system, with waste pumped to a treatment farm at Werribee. Sydney built its own sewers through the late 1800s. Australia later made its own contribution to toilet design: the dual flush toilet, developed by Australian company Caroma around 1980, which helps save large amounts of water.

sections.key: Safe toilets are one of the greatest health advances, yet billions still lack them.
sections.b: In 2007 readers of the British Medical Journal voted sanitation the most important medical milestone since 1840, ahead of antibiotics and vaccines. Safe disposal of human waste stops the spread of diseases such as cholera, typhoid and many causes of diarrhoea, which still kill large numbers of young children worldwide. According to United Nations estimates, around 3.5 billion people still lack safely managed sanitation, meaning a toilet whose waste is safely contained and treated. Many still have no toilet at all. The UN marks World Toilet Day each year on 19 November to draw attention to the problem. Next time you flush and forget, it is worth remembering how recently, and how hard, that simple convenience was won.

quiz.q: What was the Great Stink of 1858?
o: A foul smell from London's sewage-filled Thames
A rotting whale on a beach
quiz.e: The stench pushed Parliament to fund a proper sewer system.

quiz.q: What did Alexander Cumming's S-bend do?
o: Held water to block smells rising from the pipe
Allowed toilets to be built upstairs
quiz.e: Water trapped in the bend seals out sewer gases.

quiz.q: How did John Snow help end the 1854 Soho outbreak?
o: He had a water pump's handle removed
quiz.e: Snow linked cholera cases to a contaminated pump on Broad Street.

quiz.q: What is Joseph Bazalgette often praised for?
o: Building sewers larger than first calculated to allow for growth
quiz.e: He reportedly doubled his pipe sizes, and parts of his system still work.

quiz.q: What Australian innovation helps toilets save water?
quiz.e: Caroma developed the dual flush toilet around 1980.

LESSONS.title: Burke and Wills: the expedition that went wrong
LESSONS.hook: In 1860 a lavishly equipped expedition left Melbourne cheered by thousands. Within a year its leaders were dead, starving beside a creek where others had lived for millennia.

sections.key: The Victorian Exploring Expedition set out in 1860 to cross Australia from south to north.
sections.b: On 20 August 1860, crowds gathered in Royal Park, Melbourne, to farewell the Victorian Exploring Expedition. Its goal was to cross the continent from Melbourne to the Gulf of Carpentaria, a journey of more than 3,000 kilometres through country few colonists had seen. Organised by the Royal Society of Victoria and funded by the colony's government and private donors, it was one of the best equipped expeditions in Australian history. It set off with around nineteen men, horses, wagons and about two dozen camels imported specially from India, along with huge amounts of supplies. Victoria, rich from the gold rushes, wanted the glory of being first across, and perhaps to find a route for a telegraph line linking Australia to the world.

sections.key: Robert O'Hara Burke was brave and ambitious but had no experience of exploring.
sections.b: The leader chosen was Robert O'Hara Burke, an Irish-born police officer. He was known for courage and charm but had no experience of exploration, navigation or the inland. His third in command, and later second, was William John Wills, a young English-born surveyor and astronomer responsible for navigation and scientific records. Problems began almost immediately. The expedition was overloaded and moved slowly, and quarrels broke out among the men. At Menindee, on the Darling River, the original second in command, George Landells, resigned after clashing with Burke. Burke, worried that a rival expedition from South Australia led by John McDouall Stuart might beat him, grew impatient and began splitting his party to move faster.

sections.key: Burke took a small party from Cooper Creek to the north coast, leaving others to wait.
sections.b: Burke established a depot at Cooper Creek, in what is now south-west Queensland. In December 1860, with summer heat building, he set out for the Gulf with just three companions: Wills, Charles Gray and John King, along with a horse and six camels. He left William Brahe in charge of the depot, with instructions to wait for about three months, or longer if possible. The small party travelled north quickly. By around February 1861 they reached the tidal channels and mangroves near the Flinders River. Thick swamps blocked them from seeing the open sea, but they had effectively crossed the continent. Now they had to get back, with food running low and the wet season turning the ground to mud.

sections.key: Starving and exhausted, the party struggled back towards Cooper Creek.
sections.b: The return was a grim march. Supplies were running out, and the men killed and ate several of their camels and their horse. Heavy rain and heat sapped their strength. Charles Gray became ill and weak, and Burke at first suspected him of pretending. When Gray was caught taking extra flour, Burke reportedly hit him. Gray died in April 1861, and the survivors lost a day burying him. Every delay mattered, because they were relying on Brahe's party still being at the depot. Back at Cooper Creek, Brahe's men had waited longer than the three months Burke had asked for. Some were sick with scurvy, no relief party had arrived, and they had no word from Burke.

sections.key: The survivors reached the depot on the very day Brahe's party had left.
sections.b: On the evening of 21 April 1861, Burke, Wills and King staggered back into the Cooper Creek depot. It was empty. Brahe's party had left that same morning, only hours earlier. On a coolibah tree, Brahe's men had carved a message telling them to dig. Buried beneath were supplies and a note. The tree, now known as the Dig Tree, still stands beside the creek. Too weak to catch up with Brahe, Burke decided to head south-west towards Mount Hopeless, a South Australian police outpost, rather than follow the known route home. In a cruel twist, Brahe later returned briefly to the depot, but did not notice signs that Burke had been there, and left again.

sections.key: Local Aboriginal people fed the starving explorers, and only King survived.
sections.b: The three men never reached Mount Hopeless. They wandered along Cooper Creek, growing weaker. The Yandruwandha people, who had lived in the area for thousands of years, gave them fish and cakes made from nardoo, a fern whose spore cases can be ground into flour. Burke at one point fired a pistol to drive them away, and the explorers tried preparing nardoo themselves. Historians think they did not prepare it the traditional way, which removes a substance that destroys vitamin B1, and this may have worsened their starvation. Burke and Wills died around the end of June 1861. King survived by staying with the Yandruwandha, who cared for him until a rescue party led by Alfred Howitt found him in September.

sections.key: The expedition became a national legend and a lesson about ignoring local knowledge.
sections.b: News of the deaths shocked the colony. A Royal Commission criticised Burke's judgement as well as the expedition's organisers and other members. In 1863 Burke and Wills were given a grand public funeral in Melbourne, and statues and memorials followed. The relief expeditions sent to find them mapped large areas of the inland, so the disaster did add to colonial knowledge of the country. Meanwhile John McDouall Stuart's party successfully crossed from south to north and returned in 1862, and the Overland Telegraph later followed close to his route. Today the story is often retold as a lesson in poor leadership and in the cost of ignoring Aboriginal people, whose knowledge kept King alive in country where the explorers starved.

quiz.q: Where did the Burke and Wills expedition aim to reach?
quiz.e: The goal was to cross from Melbourne to the Gulf of Carpentaria in the north.

quiz.q: What was a major weakness of Robert O'Hara Burke as leader?
o: He had no experience of exploration
He could not ride a horse
quiz.e: Burke was a brave police officer but had never led an exploring expedition.

quiz.q: What happened when the survivors returned to Cooper Creek?
o: They found Brahe waiting with fresh supplies
The depot had been destroyed by floods
They found the depot abandoned only hours earlier
A rescue party had just arrived
quiz.e: Brahe's party had left that very morning, leaving supplies buried under the Dig Tree.

quiz.q: Who kept John King alive after Burke and Wills died?
quiz.e: King lived with the Yandruwandha until Howitt's rescue party found him.

quiz.q: Whose expedition successfully crossed the continent and returned in 1862?
quiz.e: Stuart's route was later closely followed by the Overland Telegraph.

LESSONS.title: Ibn Battuta: the greatest traveller of the Middle Ages
LESSONS.hook: In 1325 a young Moroccan set off on a pilgrimage to Mecca. He came home almost a quarter of a century later, having seen more of the world than anyone of his age.

sections.key: Ibn Battuta left Morocco at 21 on the pilgrimage to Mecca and kept travelling for decades.
sections.b: In June 1325, a 21-year-old named Ibn Battuta left his home in Tangier, in what is now Morocco, to make the hajj, the pilgrimage to Mecca that Muslims aim to complete at least once in their lives. He came from a family of legal scholars and was trained in Islamic law. He set out alone, and later described feeling such grief at leaving his parents that he wept. He expected the journey to take perhaps a year or two. Instead, he would not return home for around 24 years. His travels took him across North Africa, the Middle East, East Africa, Central Asia, India, South-East Asia and, by his account, China, a distance often estimated at well over 100,000 kilometres.

sections.key: A shared religion, language and legal system let Ibn Battuta travel and find work far from home.
sections.b: How could a young man travel so far in the 1300s? Much of the answer lies in the world he lived in. Islam had spread across a vast region, from Spain and West Africa to India and parts of South-East Asia. Across this world, educated Muslims shared Arabic as a language of learning, followed the same broad body of Islamic law and recognised each other's scholarship. A trained legal scholar like Ibn Battuta could arrive in a distant city and be welcomed by rulers and religious leaders, who often gave travellers gifts, lodging and sometimes jobs. Pilgrim caravans, trade routes and religious lodges provided support along the way. It was a network as much as a map.

sections.h: From Mecca to the coast of Africa
sections.key: After his first pilgrimage he explored the Middle East and sailed down the East African coast.
sections.b: Ibn Battuta reached Mecca in 1326, but rather than heading home he kept exploring. He travelled through Iraq and Persia, returned to Mecca, and spent time studying there. Around 1330, he sailed down the Red Sea and along the coast of East Africa, visiting trading cities such as Mogadishu, Mombasa and Kilwa. He described the wealth of these ports, which traded gold, ivory and other goods across the Indian Ocean. He later journeyed through Anatolia, in modern Turkey, and onto the steppes of Central Asia, where he joined the court of a Mongol khan. He says he travelled with one of the khan's wives, a Byzantine princess, to visit Constantinople, the great Christian capital.

sections.key: He spent years serving the unpredictable Sultan of Delhi as a judge.
sections.b: Ibn Battuta's next goal was India, where the Sultan of Delhi, Muhammad bin Tughluq, was famous for his generosity to foreign scholars. After a hard journey through Afghanistan, he arrived in the 1330s and was appointed a qadi, or judge, with a large salary. He stayed for about eight years. But the Sultan was also notorious for sudden cruelty, and courtiers could fall from favour without warning. Ibn Battuta himself fell under suspicion at one point and feared for his life. So when the Sultan chose him to lead an embassy to the Mongol emperor of China, he must have been relieved. The journey began badly: his party was attacked, and the ships meant to carry the gifts were wrecked.

sections.h: Islands and the road to China
sections.key: He worked in the Maldives, visited Sri Lanka and says he reached China.
sections.b: Having lost the embassy, and afraid to return to Delhi, Ibn Battuta made his way to the Maldives. There he served as a judge for around a year, married several times and tried, with mixed success, to impose stricter religious law on the islanders. He then visited Sri Lanka, where he climbed the sacred mountain known as Adam's Peak, before continuing to Bengal and South-East Asia. By his account he finally reached China in the 1340s, describing its ports, paper money and porcelain. Some historians doubt how far into China he really went, because parts of this section are vague or seem borrowed from other sources. Even so, his descriptions show a world joined by busy sea trade.

sections.key: Back in Morocco, he set out again, crossing the Sahara to the Mali Empire.
sections.b: Ibn Battuta returned to Morocco in 1349, only to learn that his mother had died of the plague that was sweeping the region. Remarkably, he was soon travelling again. He visited Granada in Muslim Spain, then in the early 1350s joined a camel caravan across the Sahara to the Mali Empire, one of the richest states in Africa, famous for its gold. He visited the court of the ruler, Mansa Sulayman, and travelled to Timbuktu. He admired the safety of travel in Mali and the devotion of its people to prayer, but was disappointed by the gifts he received and disapproved of some local customs, revealing his own biases as clearly as anything about the places he visited.

sections.key: His travels survive in the Rihla, a book dictated to a court scholar.
sections.b: When Ibn Battuta finally settled in Morocco, the Sultan of Fez asked him to record his journeys. He dictated his memories to a young scholar named Ibn Juzayy, who shaped them into a book completed around 1355. Its title is long, but it is usually just called the Rihla, meaning journey. Historians treat it with care. It was written from memory years later, some passages appear to be copied from earlier writers, and a few journeys may be exaggerated. Yet it remains one of the richest records of the fourteenth century world, describing food, customs, rulers and trade from Spain to Asia. Ibn Battuta is still celebrated in Morocco, and even a crater on the Moon bears his name.

quiz.q: Why did Ibn Battuta first leave Tangier in 1325?
o: To make the pilgrimage to Mecca
quiz.e: He set out on the hajj, then kept travelling for decades.

quiz.q: What helped Ibn Battuta find work and welcome so far from home?
o: Royal letters from the King of France
A shared religion, legal tradition and language of learning
quiz.e: As a trained legal scholar, he was valued across the Muslim world.

quiz.q: What role did Ibn Battuta hold in Delhi?
quiz.e: He served the Sultan Muhammad bin Tughluq as a qadi for about eight years.

quiz.q: Which wealthy African empire did he visit after crossing the Sahara?
quiz.e: He visited the court of Mansa Sulayman and travelled to Timbuktu.

quiz.q: Why do historians read the Rihla with care?
o: It was dictated from memory years later and borrows some passages
It was written by his enemies
quiz.e: Despite its flaws, it remains a rich record of the fourteenth century world.

LESSONS.title: How photography was invented
LESSONS.hook: For thousands of years, people could watch an image of the world appear in a darkened room but had no way to keep it. Then chemistry caught up.

sections.h: A picture in a dark room
sections.key: The camera obscura projected images long before anyone could capture them.
sections.b: If you darken a room completely and make a small hole in one wall, an upside-down image of the outside world appears on the opposite wall. This effect, called the camera obscura, Latin for dark room, was described by thinkers in ancient China and Greece and studied carefully by the Arab scholar Ibn al-Haytham around 1,000 years ago. By the Renaissance, portable versions with lenses and mirrors helped artists trace scenes accurately. But the image vanished the moment the light changed. Capturing it permanently needed a material that changed when light hit it, and a way to stop that change once the picture was made. Solving those two problems took until the nineteenth century.

sections.key: Nicéphore Niépce made the oldest surviving camera photograph in the 1820s, with an exposure of many hours.
sections.b: In about 1826 or 1827, the French inventor Nicéphore Niépce placed a pewter plate coated with a kind of bitumen in a camera at a window of his country house. Bitumen hardens when exposed to light. After a very long exposure, probably many hours and possibly days, he washed away the unhardened parts, leaving a faint image of buildings and rooftops. Called View from the Window at Le Gras, it is the oldest surviving photograph taken with a camera. It is now held at the University of Texas in Austin. Because the sun moved across the sky during the exposure, buildings on both sides of the scene appear lit, an eerie clue to how slow the process was.

sections.key: Louis Daguerre's 1839 process made sharp, unique images on silvered copper plates.
sections.b: Niépce teamed up with Louis Daguerre, a Parisian showman famous for theatrical scenery. After Niépce died in 1833, Daguerre kept experimenting and developed a much faster process. A silver-coated copper plate was made light-sensitive with iodine fumes, exposed in a camera, then developed with mercury vapour, which was later recognised as highly toxic. The result was a stunningly detailed image, but each one was unique and could not be copied. In 1839 the French government acquired the rights and announced the process to the world, granting Daguerre and Niépce's son pensions. Daguerreotype studios soon opened across Europe and America. One of Daguerre's street scenes captured what are often called the first people ever photographed: a man having his boots polished.

sections.key: William Henry Fox Talbot's paper negatives allowed many prints from one image.
sections.b: In England, William Henry Fox Talbot was working on his own method at the same time. He used paper soaked in silver salts, which darkened in light, to make negatives, images where light and dark were reversed. By shining light through a negative onto another sheet of sensitive paper, he could make a positive print, and he could do it again and again. His improved process, the calotype, was patented in 1841. Calotypes were softer and less detailed than daguerreotypes, but the negative and positive principle was the future. Almost all film photography for the next 150 years followed Talbot's idea. One of his earliest surviving negatives, from 1835, shows a window at his home, Lacock Abbey.

sections.key: Faster processes brought photography to wars, families and colonial Australia.
sections.b: In 1851 Frederick Scott Archer introduced the wet collodion process, using glass plates that combined fine detail with the ability to make copies. Exposures dropped to seconds. Photographers had to coat, expose and develop each plate while it was still wet, so they hauled portable darkrooms with them. Photography soon recorded war, from the Crimean War to the American Civil War, bringing distant conflict home to the public in a new way. Portrait studios spread rapidly, and many families could afford a likeness for the first time. In Australia, a daguerreotype of the Sydney politician and doctor William Bland, taken in 1845, is thought to be the oldest surviving photograph made in the country.

sections.key: George Eastman's Kodak camera turned photography into a hobby for everyone.
sections.b: Photography was still fiddly and expensive until an American businessman, George Eastman, made it simple. In 1888 his company launched the Kodak camera, sold already loaded with a roll of film for about 100 pictures. When it was full, customers posted the whole camera back to the company, which developed the prints, reloaded the camera and returned it. The famous slogan was 'You press the button, we do the rest.' In 1900 Kodak released the Brownie, a simple box camera priced at one dollar in the United States, putting photography within reach of children and ordinary families. Holiday snaps, birthday photos and the family album were born, and taking pictures became part of everyday life.

sections.key: Colour film arrived in the twentieth century, then digital sensors changed everything.
sections.b: Early colour photography was difficult. The French Lumière brothers released the Autochrome process in 1907, which used dyed grains of potato starch to produce dreamy colour images on glass. Easier colour film, such as Kodachrome, launched in 1935. Then came a bigger shift. In 1975 Kodak engineer Steven Sasson built an experimental digital camera. It was about the size of a toaster, captured black and white images of just 0.01 megapixels and recorded them onto cassette tape. Kodak did not push the technology hard, partly because film was so profitable, and the company filed for bankruptcy protection in 2012. Today billions of people carry a camera in their phone, and more photos are taken every year than in all earlier history.

quiz.q: What does camera obscura mean?
quiz.e: The Latin phrase describes the darkened room in which an image is projected.

quiz.q: Why do buildings on both sides of Niépce's first photograph look sunlit?
o: The exposure lasted so long that the sun moved across the sky
It was taken at noon in summer
quiz.e: The exposure took many hours, possibly days.

quiz.q: What was a major limitation of the daguerreotype?
o: Each image was unique and could not be copied
It needed a huge glass lens
It could only be used outdoors
quiz.e: The detail was stunning, but there was no negative to make prints from.

quiz.q: What was Fox Talbot's key contribution?
o: A negative that could make many positive prints
quiz.e: His negative and positive principle guided film photography for 150 years.

quiz.q: What did Kodak's slogan promise customers in 1888?
o: You press the button, we do the rest
quiz.e: Customers sent the camera back and Kodak developed the film for them.

LESSONS.title: The bicycle: a simple machine that changed society
LESSONS.hook: Two wheels, a frame and a chain. The bicycle looks so obvious it is hard to believe it took the best part of a century to get right, or that it helped change the lives of women.

sections.key: The first two-wheeler, built by Karl Drais in 1817, had no pedals at all.
sections.b: In 1817 a German forestry official named Karl Drais rode a strange new machine near the city of Mannheim. It had two wheels in a line, a wooden frame and a seat, and he pushed it along by striding with his feet on the ground, much like a modern children's balance bike. He called it a Laufmaschine, or running machine, and it became known as the draisine or dandy horse. Some historians link the invention to 1816, the so-called Year Without a Summer, when a huge volcanic eruption in Indonesia had disrupted the climate and crop failures made feeding horses expensive. The craze for dandy horses faded quickly, but the idea of balancing on two wheels had arrived.

sections.key: In the 1860s, French makers added pedals to the front wheel.
sections.b: Nearly half a century passed before the next big step. In the 1860s in France, makers attached pedals and cranks directly to the front wheel, so riders could keep their feet off the ground. Who did it first is disputed, with credit usually given to the Michaux family business in Paris or to a mechanic named Pierre Lallement. These machines, called velocipedes, had iron frames and wooden wheels with iron rims. On the rough roads of the day they rattled so badly that English speakers nicknamed them boneshakers. Even so, they were wildly popular for a time. Riding schools opened, races were held and people began to imagine bicycles as practical transport rather than a toy.

sections.key: Giant front wheels made bikes faster but dangerously high.
sections.b: With pedals fixed to the front wheel, each turn of the pedals moved the bike only as far as that wheel's circumference. The way to go faster was to make the front wheel bigger. By the 1870s, high wheelers had front wheels well over a metre across, with a tiny wheel behind. Later they were nicknamed penny-farthings, after the large penny and small farthing coins of Britain. Solid rubber tyres and wire spokes made them lighter and smoother than boneshakers, and they were fast. But the rider sat high above the front wheel, and hitting a rock or pothole could pitch them head first over the handlebars. Riding one was an athletic, risky hobby mostly for young men.

sections.key: Chain drive and equal wheels in the 1880s created the bicycle we know today.
sections.b: The breakthrough came in 1885, when the English inventor John Kemp Starley launched the Rover. It had two wheels of similar size and a chain driving the back wheel. Gears in the chain drive meant a small wheel could still travel fast, and the rider sat low enough to put a foot down. It was called a safety bicycle, and its basic layout is still used today. A few years later came comfort. In 1888 John Boyd Dunlop, a Scottish vet living in Belfast, developed an air-filled tyre for his young son's tricycle. Pneumatic tyres made riding far smoother and faster, and Dunlop's name became a famous brand. By the 1890s, the modern bicycle was essentially complete.

sections.key: The 1890s bicycle boom gave many women new independence.
sections.b: The 1890s saw a worldwide bicycle craze, and its effects went far beyond transport. For many women, the bicycle offered a new kind of freedom: the ability to travel independently, without a chaperone or a horse and carriage. Cycling also encouraged dress reform. Heavy, long skirts and tight corsets were impractical on a bike, and some women adopted divided skirts or loose trousers called bloomers, to the outrage of critics. The American campaigner for women's voting rights Susan B. Anthony said in an 1896 interview that the bicycle had done more to emancipate women than anything else in the world. The bicycle became a symbol of the 'New Woman', confident, active and moving about on her own terms.

sections.key: In the 1890s, Australians cycled across the outback and around the continent.
sections.b: Australia caught the bicycle craze in the 1890s, and bikes were put to surprisingly tough work. During the gold rushes in Western Australia, cyclists carried messages and mail across long distances to and from the goldfields. Shearers in the outback rode between sheep stations, and some cyclists made epic overland journeys, including rides around the whole continent, on dirt tracks with no support. Bikes were cheaper than horses and did not need feed or water, a big advantage in dry country. Later, cycling became a popular sport, and Hubert Opperman became a national hero for his endurance riding in the 1920s and 1930s. In 1990 Victoria became the first place in the world to make bicycle helmets compulsory.

sections.key: Bicycle technology helped give rise to cars and aeroplanes, and bikes are still among the most efficient ways to travel.
sections.b: The bicycle's influence spread into other machines. Bicycle makers developed and refined ball bearings, chain drives, pneumatic tyres and lightweight steel tubing, all of which fed into early cars and motorcycles. The campaign for better roads in some countries began with cyclists, before motorists took it over. Most famously, Wilbur and Orville Wright ran a bicycle shop in Dayton, Ohio, and used its skills, tools and profits to build the aeroplane they flew in 1903. Today the bicycle remains one of the most energy-efficient ways for a person to travel. In cities from Amsterdam to Copenhagen, bikes are used for a large share of daily trips, and cities around the world are building bike lanes to follow their lead.

quiz.q: How did riders move Karl Drais's 1817 running machine?
o: By pushing along the ground with their feet
With pedals on the back wheel
quiz.e: The draisine had no pedals, like a modern balance bike.

quiz.q: Why did penny-farthings have such large front wheels?
o: To make them easier to climb on
So each pedal turn covered more distance
quiz.e: With pedals fixed to the front wheel, a bigger wheel meant more speed.

quiz.q: What did John Boyd Dunlop develop in 1888?
quiz.e: He made a pneumatic tyre for his son's tricycle, making rides far smoother.

quiz.q: How did the bicycle change life for many women in the 1890s?
o: It was banned for women everywhere
It replaced sewing as a hobby
It was mainly used for deliveries
It offered independent travel and encouraged dress reform
quiz.e: Bikes gave women new freedom and helped loosen restrictive clothing.

quiz.q: Which famous inventors ran a bicycle shop?
quiz.e: The Wright brothers used their bicycle shop's skills to build their aeroplane.

LESSONS.title: Coffee: from goat legend to flat white
LESSONS.hook: Every morning, billions of people drink the roasted seeds of a cherry from the Ethiopian highlands. Here is how that seed conquered the world, and what actually happens between the farm and your cup.

sections.key: Coffee's origin legend is charming, but its real roots lie in Ethiopia and Yemen.
sections.b: The most famous coffee story tells of Kaldi, an Ethiopian goatherd who noticed his goats prancing about after nibbling red berries from a shrub. He tried them himself, felt wonderfully alert, and the rest is history. Sadly, the tale was first written down many centuries after it supposedly happened, so historians treat it as legend. What we do know is that the arabica coffee plant grows wild in the highland forests of Ethiopia. The first solid evidence of people drinking coffee comes from Yemen in the fifteenth century, where Sufi religious communities brewed it to stay awake during night-time prayers. From the Yemeni port of Mocha, whose name still lives on in cafe menus, coffee began its journey across the Islamic world.

sections.key: Coffeehouses became places where news, business and ideas were traded.
sections.b: By the sixteenth century, coffeehouses were thriving in cities such as Cairo and Istanbul, and some rulers tried to ban them, worried about the gossip and political talk they encouraged. Coffee reached Europe in the seventeenth century and the pattern repeated. In London, coffeehouses were nicknamed 'penny universities' because for the price of a cup you could sit for hours reading newspapers and arguing with strangers. Particular coffeehouses attracted particular crowds. Merchants and ship owners gathered at Edward Lloyd's coffeehouse to swap shipping news, and that meeting place grew into Lloyd's of London, the famous insurance market. Unlike beer and wine, the usual everyday drinks of the time, coffee sharpened people rather than dulling them, which may help explain why it became linked with commerce and debate.

sections.key: Two species dominate the world's coffee, and they taste quite different.
sections.b: Almost all the coffee people drink comes from two species. Arabica is the prized one: it grows best at higher altitudes, produces sweeter, more complex flavours and makes up the larger share of world production. Robusta, as the name hints, is a tougher plant that tolerates heat and disease and grows at lower altitudes. Its beans contain roughly twice as much caffeine, which partly acts as a natural pesticide, and they taste more bitter and earthy. Robusta is common in instant coffee and in many espresso blends, where it adds body and a thick crema. Today Brazil is the world's biggest coffee producer by a wide margin, while Vietnam, a robusta powerhouse, is usually second. Climate change worries growers, because arabica in particular is fussy about temperature.

sections.key: A coffee bean is the seed of a fruit, and how that fruit is processed shapes the flavour.
sections.b: On the plant, coffee grows as small cherries that ripen from green to deep red. Inside each cherry are usually two seeds, the beans. After picking, farmers must remove the fruit, and the method matters. In washed processing, the skin and most of the sticky flesh are stripped off and the beans are soaked so microbes break down the rest, giving clean, bright flavours. In natural processing, the whole cherry is dried in the sun before the fruit is removed, which can add fruity, wine-like notes. Either way, the result is a hard, pale green bean that smells grassy rather than anything like coffee. Green beans keep well for months, which is why coffee is shipped around the world in this state and roasted closer to where it is drunk.

sections.key: Roasting turns a grassy seed into something with hundreds of aroma compounds.
sections.b: Roasting is where coffee's flavour is created. Green beans are tumbled in hot air, usually reaching around 200 degrees Celsius. First they dry out and turn yellow, smelling a bit like bread. Then the browning reactions kick in: sugars caramelise, and amino acids react with sugars in the Maillard reaction, the same chemistry that browns toast and seared steak. Pressure builds inside the bean until it cracks audibly, rather like popcorn. Scientists have identified hundreds of aroma compounds in roasted coffee. Light roasts keep more of the bean's origin character, often tasting fruity or floral and more acidic. Dark roasts taste more of the roast itself: smoky, bitter and chocolatey. Once roasted, beans start to go stale within weeks as aromas escape, so freshness really does matter.

sections.key: Making coffee is about dissolving the right amount of flavour out of the grounds.
sections.b: Whatever your method, brewing is extraction: water dissolves flavour compounds from ground coffee. The trick is getting the amount right. Acids dissolve first, then sweeter compounds, and bitter ones last. Pull too little and the coffee tastes sour and thin; pull too much and it turns harsh and bitter. Grind size, water temperature, contact time and the ratio of coffee to water are the levers. Espresso uses very fine grounds and forces hot water through them at high pressure, typically around nine bars, for roughly half a minute, producing a small, intense shot topped with crema, a foam of oils and gases. Plunger coffee uses coarse grounds steeped for several minutes. Cold brew steeps in cold water for many hours, giving a smoother, less acidic drink.

sections.key: Post-war migrants helped turn Australia into a nation of espresso lovers.
sections.b: For much of the twentieth century, Australia was a tea-drinking country, and coffee often meant a spoonful of instant. That changed after the Second World War, when Italian and Greek migrants opened cafes and brought espresso machines with them, especially in Melbourne and Sydney. Over the following decades, a distinctive cafe culture grew, built around milk-based espresso drinks and independent cafes rather than big chains. The flat white became an Australian favourite, although New Zealanders also claim to have invented it, and the argument shows no sign of ending. Caffeine works by blocking adenosine, a chemical that builds up in the brain and makes us feel sleepy. Most healthy adults can enjoy a few cups a day, but this is general information, so check healthdirect for guidance on caffeine limits.

quiz.q: Where did people first clearly drink coffee as a beverage?
quiz.e: The earliest solid evidence of coffee drinking comes from fifteenth-century Yemen, where Sufi communities brewed it to stay awake.

quiz.q: Which famous institution grew out of a London coffeehouse?
quiz.e: Merchants met at Edward Lloyd's coffeehouse to share shipping news, and it grew into the Lloyd's insurance market.

quiz.q: How does robusta compare with arabica?
o: It has roughly twice the caffeine and tastes more bitter
It grows only at very high altitudes
It contains no caffeine at all
It is the sweeter, more delicate species
quiz.e: Robusta is hardier, contains around twice the caffeine and has a more bitter, earthy taste.

quiz.q: Which chemical reaction, also used to brown toast, helps create coffee's flavour during roasting?
quiz.e: The Maillard reaction between amino acids and sugars produces many of roasted coffee's flavours and aromas.

quiz.q: What usually causes a coffee to taste sour and thin?
quiz.e: Acids dissolve first, so pulling too little from the grounds leaves coffee sour and thin.

LESSONS.title: Chocolate: from bitter drink to sweet bar
LESSONS.hook: For thousands of years, chocolate was a frothy, bitter drink for rulers and gods. It became the solid, sweet bar we know only in the last two centuries.

sections.key: Cacao has been used in the Americas for more than 5,000 years.
sections.b: Chocolate begins with the cacao tree, whose scientific name, Theobroma cacao, means 'food of the gods'. The tree is native to the tropical Americas, and archaeologists have found traces of cacao on pottery in Ecuador more than 5,000 years old. Later, the Olmec, Maya and Aztec peoples of Mexico and Central America made it central to their cultures. They did not eat chocolate bars. Instead they ground roasted cacao beans into a paste, mixed it with water, and often added chilli, maize or flowers, then poured it from a height to create a prized layer of foam. The drink was bitter, not sweet. It featured in religious ceremonies, feasts and marriages, and the Aztecs valued the beans so highly they used them as a form of money.

sections.key: Europeans sweetened cacao with sugar and turned it into a fashionable luxury.
sections.b: Spanish invaders encountered cacao in the sixteenth century and brought it back to Spain. At first Europeans found the bitter drink strange, but once it was sweetened with sugar and flavoured with spices such as cinnamon and vanilla, it caught on. For a long time, drinking chocolate was an expensive luxury for royal courts and the wealthy, spreading from Spain to Italy, France and England. Chocolate houses opened in London alongside the coffeehouses. Because sugar and cacao both came from plantations in the colonies, the European taste for chocolate was tied to colonial trade and the forced labour of enslaved people. It is a reminder that many everyday foods we now take for granted have complicated and sometimes painful histories behind them.

sections.h: The inventions that made the bar
sections.key: A handful of nineteenth-century inventions created modern chocolate.
sections.b: Chocolate as we know it is surprisingly recent. In 1828, the Dutch chocolate maker Casparus van Houten patented a press that squeezed much of the fat, called cocoa butter, out of ground cacao, leaving a powder that mixed easily into drinks. (The invention is often credited to his son Coenraad.) That cocoa butter turned out to be useful. In 1847, the English firm J. S. Fry and Sons combined cocoa powder, sugar and extra cocoa butter to make a mouldable paste, often credited as the first modern chocolate bar. In Switzerland, Daniel Peter used condensed milk developed by his neighbour Henri Nestle to create milk chocolate in the 1870s. Soon after, Rodolphe Lindt invented the conche, a machine that stirs chocolate for hours or days, making it far smoother than the gritty bars before it.

sections.key: The flavour of chocolate starts with fermentation on the farm.
sections.b: Cacao trees grow large, rugby-ball-shaped pods directly from their trunks and thick branches. Inside each pod are dozens of beans surrounded by sweet, white pulp. After harvest, farmers scoop out the beans and pulp and pile them up, often covered with banana leaves, for several days. Yeasts and bacteria feast on the pulp, the pile heats up, and chemical changes inside the beans begin to develop chocolate flavour. Without fermentation, cacao would taste astringent and flat. The beans are then dried in the sun and shipped to chocolate makers. There, they are roasted, cracked and winnowed to remove the shells, leaving pieces called nibs. Grinding the nibs produces a thick liquid known as cocoa mass or cocoa liquor, though it contains no alcohol at all.

sections.h: The secret of snap and shine
sections.key: Tempering controls how cocoa butter crystallises, giving chocolate its gloss and snap.
sections.b: Good chocolate breaks with a clean snap, shines like glass and melts smoothly on the tongue. The secret is cocoa butter, a fat that can solidify into several different crystal forms. Only one of them gives that perfect texture. Tempering is the process of heating, cooling and gently reheating chocolate so the right crystals form and spread. Chocolatiers do it by hand on marble slabs or with machines. If chocolate is poorly tempered, or if a bar gets warm and then cools again, you may see white or grey streaks on the surface. This is called bloom, and it is either cocoa butter or sugar that has moved to the surface. It looks unappealing and the texture suffers, but bloomed chocolate is still safe to eat.

sections.key: Most of the world's cacao comes from small farms in West Africa.
sections.b: Cacao only thrives in a narrow band of hot, humid land near the equator. Although the tree comes from the Americas, today most of the world's cacao is grown in West Africa, with Cote d'Ivoire and Ghana together producing well over half of global supply. Much of it comes from millions of small family farms. Many cacao farmers earn very little, and investigations have repeatedly found child labour on farms in the region. Certification schemes and company programmes aim to improve conditions, with mixed results. Cacao is also vulnerable to plant diseases and changing weather. When harvests failed in West Africa in 2023 and 2024, cocoa prices shot to record highs, and shoppers around the world noticed chocolate becoming more expensive or bars getting smaller.

sections.key: Dark chocolate contains interesting compounds, but it is still a treat.
sections.b: Cacao contains plant compounds called flavanols, which researchers have studied for possible benefits to blood vessels, and theobromine, a mild stimulant related to caffeine. These findings are often turned into headlines claiming chocolate is a health food. In reality, most chocolate is also high in sugar and fat, and processing can strip out many of the flavanols, so it is best enjoyed as a treat. This is general information, and healthdirect is a good place for advice about diet. One important warning concerns pets. Dogs break down theobromine far more slowly than people do, so chocolate can be poisonous to them, and dark chocolate and cooking chocolate are the most dangerous. If a dog eats chocolate, call a vet promptly, especially around Easter and Christmas.

quiz.q: How did the Aztecs and Maya usually consume cacao?
quiz.e: In Mesoamerica cacao was ground and mixed with water, often with chilli or maize, and drunk as a foamy, bitter beverage.

quiz.q: What did the van Houten family's 1828 cocoa press do?
o: Removed much of the cocoa butter to make cocoa powder
quiz.e: The press squeezed out cocoa butter, leaving a powder that mixed easily into drinks.

quiz.q: Why are cacao beans fermented after harvest?
o: To develop chocolate flavour and reduce astringency
quiz.e: Fermentation by yeasts and bacteria triggers changes inside the beans that develop chocolate flavour.

quiz.q: What are the white streaks called bloom?
o: Cocoa butter or sugar that has moved to the surface
quiz.e: Bloom is fat or sugar migrating to the surface; it affects texture but the chocolate is still safe.

quiz.q: Why is chocolate dangerous for dogs?
o: They process theobromine far more slowly than people
quiz.e: Dogs break down theobromine slowly, so it can build up to toxic levels, especially from dark chocolate.

LESSONS.title: Tea: one plant, a thousand cups
LESSONS.hook: Green, black, white and oolong tea all come from the same shrub. The differences lie in what happens to the leaves after picking, and the story of how tea spread reshaped empires.

sections.key: All true tea comes from Camellia sinensis; processing creates the different types.
sections.b: It surprises many people that green tea, black tea, white tea and oolong all come from a single plant, an evergreen shrub called Camellia sinensis. The differences come from how the leaves are handled after picking. Drinks made from other plants, such as peppermint, chamomile or rooibos, are not technically tea at all. They are herbal infusions, sometimes called tisanes. There are two main varieties of the tea plant. The Chinese type has smaller leaves and copes with cooler mountain climates. The Assam type, found growing wild in north-east India, has bigger leaves and suits hot, wet lowlands, and it gives many strong black teas their malty character. Growing conditions, altitude, season and the skill of the tea maker all shape the final flavour in the cup.

sections.key: Tea has been drunk in China for more than 2,000 years.
sections.b: Chinese legend credits the emperor Shennong with discovering tea when leaves blew into his pot of boiling water, but this is a myth. The hard evidence is still impressively old. Archaeologists found tea leaves buried in the tomb of a Han dynasty emperor who died in 141 BCE, showing tea was valued more than 2,000 years ago. At first it was often treated as a medicine. During the Tang dynasty, a writer named Lu Yu produced 'The Classic of Tea' in the eighth century, a detailed guide to growing, preparing and appreciating it, and tea became an art. Buddhist monks carried tea to Japan, where powdered green tea, now known as matcha, became the heart of the Japanese tea ceremony, with its careful, meditative rituals.

sections.key: Tea arrived in Europe in the 1600s and became a British obsession.
sections.b: Dutch traders brought tea to Europe in the early seventeenth century. In England it got a fashionable boost from Catherine of Braganza, the Portuguese princess who married King Charles II in 1662 and was already a tea drinker. At first tea was expensive and heavily taxed, so smuggling was widespread. As prices fell, tea spread from the upper classes to working people, and sugared tea became a staple of the British diet. Tea also carried politics. In 1773, protesters in Boston dumped a cargo of East India Company tea into the harbour in protest against British taxation, an event that fed into the American Revolution. Britain bought so much tea from China that it ran short of silver to pay for it, a problem that helped lead to the Opium Wars.

sections.key: Britain broke China's control of tea by moving production to India.
sections.b: For centuries, China kept the secrets of growing and processing tea to itself, and Britain wanted its own supply. Two things changed the picture. In the 1820s and 1830s, the Assam variety of the tea plant was identified growing in north-east India, and the British began plantations there. Then, between 1848 and 1851, the Scottish botanist Robert Fortune travelled in China, sometimes in disguise, and smuggled out thousands of tea plants and seeds, along with knowledge of how tea was made and even skilled workers. Plantations spread across India and Ceylon, now Sri Lanka. They made tea cheap, but the plantation system relied on poorly paid labourers working in harsh conditions. Today India, Sri Lanka and Kenya are major exporters alongside China, which remains the biggest producer.

sections.key: Black tea is oxidised, green tea is not, and oolong sits in between.
sections.b: Once tea leaves are picked, enzymes inside them start reacting with oxygen, much as a cut apple turns brown. This process is called oxidation, and controlling it is the key to tea making. For green tea, leaves are heated soon after picking, by steaming in Japan or pan-firing in China, which stops the enzymes and keeps the leaves green and grassy. For black tea, leaves are withered, then rolled or crushed to break their cells, and left to oxidise fully. Compounds called catechins turn into darker, richer molecules, giving black tea its colour, briskness and depth. Oolong is only partly oxidised, so it can range from flowery and light to toasty and dark. White tea is minimally processed, usually made from young buds and leaves that are simply withered and dried.

sections.key: Water temperature and steeping time make a big difference.
sections.b: Because different teas are processed differently, they like to be brewed differently. Black tea generally suits water just off the boil and a steep of three to five minutes. Green tea is more delicate, and boiling water can scorch its flavour and pull out bitterness, so many people use water that has cooled to roughly 70 to 80 degrees Celsius and steep it for a shorter time. Oolongs often reward several short infusions from the same leaves. Tea contains caffeine, usually less per cup than coffee, along with an amino acid called L-theanine, which some research links to a calm, focused feeling. Tea bags spread widely in the twentieth century. A popular story says they began when a New York merchant sent samples in small silk bags, though the history is fuzzier.

sections.key: Tea was Australia's national drink long before the espresso arrived.
sections.b: For most of Australia's colonial and early national history, tea was the drink of choice. It travelled well, was easy to brew over a campfire, and the billy, a simple tin can for boiling water, became an icon of bush life, celebrated in songs and stories. Tea was included in rations for convicts, soldiers and workers, and for much of the twentieth century Australians drank far more tea than coffee. Although Australia imports most of its tea, small amounts are grown here, mainly in the wet tropics of far north Queensland. Tea drinking has since been overtaken by the cafe espresso, but it remains hugely popular, and a new wave of specialty tea shops, bubble tea bars and Chinese and Indian tea traditions has given it fresh life.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT made from the tea plant Camellia sinensis?
quiz.e: Peppermint is a herbal infusion; true teas all come from Camellia sinensis.

quiz.q: What is the oldest firm archaeological evidence of tea mentioned here?
o: Leaves in a Han dynasty emperor's tomb from about 141 BCE
A painting in an Egyptian pyramid
Seeds found in a Viking grave
quiz.e: Tea leaves found in a Han emperor's tomb show tea was valued in China more than 2,000 years ago.

quiz.q: What did Robert Fortune do between 1848 and 1851?
o: Smuggled tea plants and know-how out of China
quiz.e: Fortune smuggled thousands of plants and seeds, plus processing knowledge, to help establish tea in India.

quiz.q: What mainly makes black tea different from green tea?
o: It comes from a different species
It is grown in the dark
It is always flavoured with bergamot
Its leaves are allowed to oxidise fully
quiz.e: Black tea leaves are oxidised fully, while green tea is heated early to stop oxidation.

quiz.q: Why do many people brew green tea with water below boiling?
o: Boiling water can scorch it and draw out bitterness
It makes the tea turn black
Green tea will not dissolve in hot water
quiz.e: Green tea is delicate, so slightly cooler water gives a smoother, less bitter cup.

LESSONS.title: Bush foods: Australia's native pantry
LESSONS.hook: Long before supermarkets, this continent was a pantry of seeds, fruits, nuts and greens known intimately by First Nations peoples. Many are now finding their way onto restaurant menus.

sections.key: First Nations peoples have used thousands of native foods over tens of thousands of years.
sections.b: When Europeans arrived in Australia, many assumed the land offered little to eat. They were badly mistaken. First Nations peoples had lived here for tens of thousands of years, and over that time they built up deep knowledge of thousands of plants and animals: which ones were edible, when they were ripe, how to prepare them and how to look after the places where they grew. That knowledge was passed down through generations and differed from Country to Country, from tropical rainforests to deserts and coasts. Food was tied to seasons, ceremony, law and trade. Today the term bush food, or bush tucker, covers native ingredients from this long tradition. Many are being rediscovered by chefs and home cooks, but they were never lost to the communities who knew them.

sections.key: Grinding stones show Aboriginal people were processing seeds into flour very early.
sections.b: In dry inland Australia, seeds from native grasses, acacias and other plants were an important food. Collecting and processing them was skilled, laborious work. Seeds were winnowed, then ground between a large flat stone and a smaller hand stone, mixed with water and baked as cakes in hot ashes. Archaeologists have found grinding stones in Australia that are tens of thousands of years old, among the oldest evidence of seed grinding anywhere in the world. That suggests Aboriginal people were making a kind of bread long before farming began in the Middle East. Today, some growers and researchers are exploring native grains again because many of these grasses are perennial and adapted to Australian conditions, meaning they may need less water and fertiliser than imported crops.

sections.key: Some native flavours are now used in kitchens around the world.
sections.b: Wattleseed comes from certain species of acacia, the wattles whose golden flowers are Australia's floral emblem. When roasted and ground, the seeds have a rich, nutty flavour often compared to coffee, chocolate and hazelnut, and they turn up in bread, ice cream and desserts. Only particular species are used for food, and some acacias are toxic, so this is not something to experiment with on your own. Lemon myrtle is a rainforest tree from Queensland whose leaves are packed with citral, the compound that makes lemons smell lemony. Many people find it more intensely lemony than lemon itself. It is used in teas, biscuits, marinades and cheesecakes. Pepperberry and pepperleaf from the Tasmanian mountain pepper add a hot, spicy bite that some cooks use instead of black pepper.

sections.h: Fruits of the rainforest and desert
sections.key: Finger limes, quandongs and Kakadu plums are prized for flavour and nutrition.
sections.b: Australia has some remarkable native fruits. The finger lime grows wild in the rainforests near the border of New South Wales and Queensland. Slice one open and out tumble tiny pearls of juice, earning it the nickname 'citrus caviar', and chefs love it with seafood. The quandong, sometimes called the desert peach, grows in arid regions and has tart red flesh used in jams and pies, while its hard seed was used to make jewellery and games. The Kakadu plum, also known as gubinge, is a small green fruit from northern Australia that is famous for having one of the highest vitamin C contents of any fruit in the world. Aboriginal communities have harvested it for generations, and it is now sold in powders and skincare.

sections.key: Australia's best-known native food crop was commercialised overseas first.
sections.b: The macadamia is the most commercially successful Australian native food. The trees come from the rainforests of south-east Queensland and northern New South Wales, where Aboriginal people had long eaten the nuts. Ironically, the first big macadamia industry grew in Hawaii in the twentieth century, using trees taken from Australia, and for decades many people assumed the nut was Hawaiian. Australia later built its own large industry and is now one of the world's leading producers. Genetic research suggests that most Hawaiian commercial trees may descend from a very small number of Queensland trees, possibly even a single one. That narrow genetic base makes the crop more vulnerable to disease, so scientists are working to protect the remaining wild macadamias, several species of which are now threatened.

sections.key: Some bush foods were the centre of great seasonal gatherings.
sections.b: Warrigal greens, a native leafy plant also called New Zealand spinach, grow along coasts and were eaten by Captain Cook's crew to ward off scurvy. They contain oxalates, so they should be blanched briefly before eating, much like ordinary spinach is sometimes treated. In the Bunya Mountains of Queensland, huge bunya pines drop enormous cones packed with starchy nuts. In years of heavy crops, many Aboriginal groups travelled long distances to gather there for weeks of feasting, ceremony, trade, marriage arrangements and settling disputes. These bunya gatherings show how food could bring together people from across a vast region. Today bunya nuts are eaten boiled or roasted, and they have a texture somewhere between a chestnut and a potato, with a mild, earthy flavour.

sections.key: Growing interest in bush foods raises questions about who benefits.
sections.b: The native food industry has grown quickly, but research has found that only a small share of it is owned or led by First Nations people, even though it rests on their knowledge. Many communities and organisations are working to change that, through Aboriginal-owned businesses, fair partnerships and protections for traditional knowledge. When buying bush foods, you can look for products that name the communities involved or come from Indigenous-owned enterprises. A word of caution: foraging for wild plants without expert knowledge is risky, because some native plants are toxic or need careful preparation. Buy from reputable suppliers, and learn from First Nations guides where possible. Try a pinch of wattleseed in pancakes or lemon myrtle in a cup of tea for an easy first taste.

quiz.q: What do ancient grinding stones in Australia suggest?
o: Aboriginal people ground seeds into flour very early
Wheat was grown in Australia 50,000 years ago
Stones were only used for weapons
Bread came to Australia with the First Fleet
quiz.e: Grinding stones tens of thousands of years old are among the oldest evidence of seed grinding anywhere.

quiz.q: Which compound gives lemon myrtle its strong lemony scent?
quiz.e: Lemon myrtle leaves are rich in citral, the compound responsible for lemon aroma.

quiz.q: Which native fruit is famous for an extremely high vitamin C content?
quiz.e: The Kakadu plum, or gubinge, has one of the highest vitamin C levels of any fruit.

quiz.q: Where did the first large commercial macadamia industry develop?
quiz.e: The industry first boomed in Hawaii using trees taken from Australia.

quiz.q: What is sensible advice for trying bush foods?
o: Forage any berry that looks ripe
Buy from reputable suppliers rather than foraging unknown plants
Eat acacia seeds from any wattle tree
quiz.e: Some native plants are toxic or need preparation, so buy from reputable sources or learn from experts.

LESSONS.title: Fermentation: cooking with microbes
LESSONS.hook: Bread, cheese, yoghurt, soy sauce, kimchi, vinegar and Vegemite all depend on tiny living helpers. Fermentation is one of humanity's oldest and cleverest food technologies.

sections.key: Fermentation is microbes transforming food in ways we find useful.
sections.b: Leave a bowl of fruit on the bench and microbes will eventually spoil it. Fermentation is what happens when we steer that process instead. By controlling things like salt, temperature, moisture and oxygen, cooks encourage helpful microbes and keep harmful ones out. The helpful microbes eat sugars and other nutrients in food and produce by-products such as alcohol, carbon dioxide and acids. Those by-products change flavour and texture, and often make food last longer. People fermented food for thousands of years without knowing microbes existed. Chemical traces in pottery from Jiahu in China suggest people there brewed a drink from rice, honey and fruit about 9,000 years ago. In the 1850s and 1860s, Louis Pasteur showed that living microorganisms were responsible for fermentation, transforming our understanding of food and disease.

sections.key: Yeasts turn sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide.
sections.b: The best-known fermenting microbe is yeast, a single-celled fungus. When yeast feeds on sugar without much oxygen around, it produces two main by-products: alcohol and carbon dioxide gas. Brewers and winemakers want the alcohol. In wine, yeast ferments the sugars in grape juice. In beer, grains such as barley are first malted and mashed so their starches break down into sugars that yeast can use. Bakers want the gas. In bread dough, carbon dioxide bubbles get trapped in a stretchy network of gluten, making the loaf rise, and the small amount of alcohol produced bakes off in the oven. Sourdough uses a starter, a living culture of wild yeasts and bacteria, which gives a tangier flavour than bread made with commercial baker's yeast.

sections.key: Bacteria that make lactic acid give us yoghurt, sauerkraut and kimchi.
sections.b: Lactic acid bacteria are the quiet workhorses of fermentation. They convert sugars into lactic acid, which makes food tangy and creates an acidic environment where many spoilage and disease-causing microbes struggle to survive. Yoghurt is made by adding specific bacteria to warm milk. As they produce acid, milk proteins tighten and the milk thickens into a soft gel. Sauerkraut and kimchi rely on bacteria that live naturally on vegetables. Cabbage is salted, which draws out water and favours salt-tolerant lactic acid bacteria over other microbes. Over days or weeks, the vegetables sour and soften. Kimchi in its familiar red form is a newer invention than many people assume, because chillies only reached Korea from the Americas a few centuries ago, after European traders spread them across Asia.

sections.key: Moulds such as koji are behind soy sauce, miso and sake.
sections.b: Not all fermenting microbes are yeasts or bacteria. Some are moulds. In East Asian cooking, the most important is koji, a mould with the scientific name Aspergillus oryzae. Grown on steamed rice, soybeans or barley, koji produces powerful enzymes that break starches into sugars and proteins into amino acids. That makes it the starting point for soy sauce, miso, mirin and sake. Soy sauce is traditionally made by mixing koji-covered soybeans and wheat with brine and leaving the mixture to ferment for months. The amino acids released, especially glutamate, give these foods their deep savoury taste, often called umami. In Europe, moulds also play a role: blue cheeses such as Roquefort get their veins from Penicillium moulds, and white rinds on brie and camembert come from moulds too.

sections.key: Cheese and vinegar show how fermentation can be layered in steps.
sections.b: Many fermented foods involve more than one step and more than one microbe. Cheese begins when milk is soured by bacteria and then curdled, usually with rennet, an enzyme that makes milk proteins clump into curds. The liquid whey is drained off, and the curds are salted, pressed and often aged. During ageing, bacteria and moulds slowly break down fats and proteins, creating the huge range of cheese flavours and textures. Vinegar is a two-stage fermentation. First, yeast turns sugars in fruit or grain into alcohol, making wine, cider or beer. Then acetic acid bacteria, which need oxygen, convert that alcohol into acetic acid. The word vinegar comes from the French for 'sour wine', which is a pretty accurate description of what it is.

sections.key: Before refrigeration, fermentation helped food last through winters and voyages.
sections.b: Before refrigerators, fermentation was one of the most important ways to stop food from spoiling. Acid, alcohol and salt all make life difficult for harmful microbes, so fermented foods could be stored for months. Communities relied on them to get through winters and lean seasons, and sailors relied on them at sea. On his voyages in the eighteenth century, including the one that reached Australia's east coast in 1770, James Cook carried large quantities of sauerkraut, partly in the hope of preventing scurvy. Fermentation also turns waste into food. Vegemite, created in Melbourne in the early 1920s by the chemist Cyril Callister, is made from spent brewer's yeast left over from beer making, which is mixed with salt and vegetable extracts and turned into the famous dark spread.

sections.key: Home fermenting is rewarding, but safety depends on following tested methods.
sections.b: Fermenting at home has become popular, and sauerkraut, yoghurt, kombucha and sourdough are good places to start. The general principles are simple: use clean equipment, get the salt or acidity right, keep air out when the recipe says to, and trust your senses. Healthy ferments smell sour, yeasty or pleasantly funky. Fuzzy coloured mould, slime or a rotten smell are signs to throw a batch out. Low-acid foods stored without oxygen can carry a risk of botulism, a rare but dangerous illness, so follow reliable, tested recipes rather than improvising. Fermented foods are often promoted for gut health, and some contain live microbes, but the evidence for specific benefits is still developing. This is general information, so see Food Standards Australia New Zealand and healthdirect for more.

quiz.q: Who showed in the mid-1800s that living microbes cause fermentation?
quiz.e: Pasteur's work in the 1850s and 1860s showed microorganisms were responsible for fermentation.

quiz.q: In bread making, which product of yeast fermentation makes the dough rise?
quiz.e: Carbon dioxide bubbles get trapped in the gluten network and make the dough rise.

quiz.q: Why is salt added when making sauerkraut?
o: To favour salt-tolerant lactic acid bacteria
quiz.e: Salt draws out water and gives salt-tolerant lactic acid bacteria an advantage over other microbes.

quiz.q: Koji, used for soy sauce and miso, is what kind of organism?
quiz.e: Koji is the mould Aspergillus oryzae, which produces enzymes that break down starches and proteins.

quiz.q: What is Vegemite made from?
quiz.e: Vegemite was developed in the 1920s using spent yeast left over from brewing beer.

LESSONS.title: The spice trade: flavours that built empires
LESSONS.hook: Pepper, cloves and nutmeg were once worth fighting and dying for. The hunt for spices sent ships around the world, made fortunes and caused terrible violence.

sections.key: Many of the most valuable spices came from small parts of South and South-East Asia.
sections.b: Today you can buy a jar of nutmeg for a few dollars, but for most of history spices were luxury goods, partly because they grew in so few places. Black pepper came from the Malabar Coast of south-west India, in what is now Kerala. True cinnamon came from Sri Lanka. Cloves grew on a handful of islands in the northern Moluccas, now part of Indonesia, and nutmeg and its lacy covering, mace, came almost entirely from the tiny Banda Islands. These goods passed through many hands, carried by Indian, Arab, Malay, Chinese and other merchants over sea and land. Each trader added a markup, so by the time spices reached a European or Middle Eastern market they could be astonishingly expensive, and their origins were often shrouded in tall tales.

sections.key: The ancient Romans imported huge quantities of Indian pepper.
sections.b: The spice trade is ancient. Romans developed a serious taste for black pepper, and merchants learned to use the monsoon winds to sail between Egypt's Red Sea ports and India, crossing the Arabian Sea in weeks. Roman coins have been found in southern India, evidence of the trade's scale. Roman recipes from a cookbook attributed to Apicius use pepper constantly. According to ancient accounts, when the Gothic leader Alaric besieged Rome in 408, his demands included thousands of pounds of pepper along with gold and silver. A popular modern belief holds that medieval Europeans used spices to hide the taste of rotting meat. Most historians reject this, pointing out that spices often cost far more than fresh meat, and that they were prized for flavour, medicine and status.

sections.h: The race for a sea route
sections.key: The desire to reach spice markets directly drove European voyages of exploration.
sections.b: In the medieval period, much of the spice trade into Europe flowed through Middle Eastern routes and then through Italian cities such as Venice, which grew rich as middlemen. Other European powers wanted to cut out those middlemen. Portugal pushed down the coast of Africa, and in 1498 Vasco da Gama rounded the Cape of Good Hope and reached Calicut in India by sea. Christopher Columbus, sponsored by Spain, sailed west in 1492 hoping to reach Asia. He reached the Caribbean instead, where he encountered chillies and allspice, and he called the chillies 'peppers', a name that has confused people ever since. Ferdinand Magellan's expedition, which completed the first circumnavigation of the globe in 1522, was also largely a search for a route to the spice islands.

sections.key: The Dutch East India Company used extreme violence to control nutmeg and cloves.
sections.b: In the seventeenth century, the Dutch East India Company, known by its initials VOC, set out to control the most valuable spices completely. Its methods were brutal. In 1621, forces under the governor-general Jan Pieterszoon Coen conquered the Banda Islands, the world's only real source of nutmeg. Most of the Bandanese population was killed, enslaved or driven away, and the islands were turned into plantations worked by enslaved people. The Dutch also restricted clove trees to particular islands and destroyed trees elsewhere to keep prices high. When England and the Netherlands made peace in 1667, the Dutch kept Run, a tiny nutmeg island the English had held, while England kept New Amsterdam, which it had seized and renamed New York. In hindsight, the deal looks rather different.

sections.key: Smuggled plants and changing tastes made spices cheap and ordinary.
sections.b: Monopolies over living plants are hard to keep forever. In the 1770s, a French official named Pierre Poivre organised expeditions that smuggled clove and nutmeg seedlings out of the Dutch-controlled islands and planted them on Mauritius and other French colonies. During the Napoleonic Wars, the British also took spice plants and spread them to places such as Ceylon and the Caribbean island of Grenada, which still features a nutmeg on its flag. Clove growing became a major industry on Zanzibar, worked by enslaved people. As spices were grown in more places, prices fell. At the same time, European tastes shifted towards sugar, coffee, tea and chocolate. Spices that had once been worth a fortune became ordinary kitchen staples, sold cheaply in jars all over the world.

sections.key: The priciest spices today are labour-intensive rather than rare.
sections.b: Some spices are still expensive, mostly because they take so much work. Saffron, usually the most expensive spice by weight, is made from the thread-like stigmas of a crocus flower. Each flower has only three, and they must be picked by hand, so a single kilogram requires well over a hundred thousand flowers. Iran grows most of the world's saffron, and small amounts are grown in Tasmania. Vanilla, the cured pods of a climbing orchid from Mexico, is another luxury. Outside Mexico, its natural pollinators are missing, so for a long time plants grown elsewhere produced few pods. In 1841, Edmond Albius, a twelve-year-old enslaved boy on the island of Reunion, worked out a quick method for hand-pollinating vanilla flowers, a technique still used on plantations today.

sections.key: The spice trade reshaped cuisines and left a lasting, complicated legacy.
sections.b: The spice trade did more than move goods. It moved plants, people and ideas, and it reshaped cooking everywhere. Chillies from the Americas became central to Indian, Thai, Sichuan and Korean food within a few centuries. Black pepper became so common in Western kitchens that it sits beside salt on almost every table. Words travelled too: the word pepper ultimately traces back to a Sanskrit word for long pepper. The trade also left a darker legacy of colonial conquest, monopoly, slavery and environmental change in the places where spices grew. Next time you grind pepper over your dinner or sprinkle cinnamon on toast, it is worth remembering that these ordinary flavours once drove some of the biggest and most violent upheavals in world history.

quiz.q: Where did nutmeg and mace come from almost exclusively?
quiz.e: Nutmeg and mace came almost entirely from the tiny Banda Islands in present-day Indonesia.

quiz.q: Why do most historians reject the idea that spices hid rotten meat?
o: Spices were banned in medieval Europe
Spices often cost far more than fresh meat
Spices were only used in drinks
quiz.e: Spices were expensive status goods, so using them to rescue spoiled meat makes little sense.

quiz.q: What did Columbus call the chillies he found in the Caribbean?
quiz.e: Columbus called chillies peppers, a name that has caused confusion ever since.

quiz.q: What happened in the Banda Islands in 1621?
o: Nutmeg trees were first planted there
Portugal and Spain divided them by treaty
Dutch forces conquered them and most of the population was killed, enslaved or driven away
