quiz.e: Under Jan Pieterszoon Coen, the VOC conquered Banda in a brutal campaign to control nutmeg.

quiz.q: What did Edmond Albius discover in 1841?
o: How to grow saffron in Tasmania
A quick way to hand-pollinate vanilla flowers
quiz.e: Albius, an enslaved twelve-year-old on Reunion, devised the hand-pollination method still used for vanilla.

LESSONS.title: Umami and the MSG story
LESSONS.hook: A Japanese chemist tasting his soup discovered a fifth basic taste. The seasoning he created went on to become one of the most misunderstood ingredients in the world.

sections.key: In 1908, Kikunae Ikeda identified the taste he called umami.
sections.b: In 1908, the Japanese chemist Kikunae Ikeda was enjoying a bowl of dashi, a broth made with kombu seaweed, when he wondered about its distinctive savoury taste. It was not sweet, sour, salty or bitter, the four tastes scientists recognised at the time. Ikeda set out to find what caused it. Working with large quantities of kombu, he isolated crystals of glutamic acid, an amino acid, and showed that its salts carried the savoury taste. He named the sensation umami, from a Japanese word for delicious, roughly meaning 'savoury deliciousness'. Ikeda then worked out how to produce a stable, easy-to-use seasoning based on his discovery: monosodium glutamate, or MSG. Together with a business partner, he launched it commercially in Japan in 1909 under the brand name Ajinomoto.

sections.key: Glutamate occurs naturally in many foods, especially ripe, aged and fermented ones.
sections.b: MSG sounds like an industrial invention, but glutamate is one of the most common amino acids in nature. Our bodies make it, and it is found in many foods, including human breast milk. Usually glutamate is locked up in proteins, where we cannot taste it. When proteins break down, through ripening, ageing, drying, cooking or fermenting, free glutamate is released and umami appears. That explains why ripe tomatoes taste more savoury than green ones, why parmesan and other aged cheeses are so moreish, and why soy sauce, fish sauce, miso, mushrooms, anchovies and cured meats are prized for adding depth. Vegemite and Marmite, made from yeast extract, are also rich in glutamate. Cooks were using umami for thousands of years before anyone had a name for it.

sections.key: Certain compounds team up with glutamate to multiply umami.
sections.b: After Ikeda, other Japanese scientists found more umami substances. In 1913 his student Shintaro Kodama identified inosinate in dried bonito flakes, and in the 1950s Akira Kuninaka identified guanylate, which is abundant in dried shiitake mushrooms. These compounds, called nucleotides, have an extraordinary property. When combined with glutamate, they do not simply add to the umami taste, they multiply it, so the combination tastes far stronger than either alone. Traditional cooking had stumbled on this long before the chemistry was understood. Japanese dashi combines kombu, rich in glutamate, with bonito flakes, rich in inosinate. Western cooks do something similar when they pair tomatoes or parmesan with meat, or add anchovies to a beef stew. This synergy is one reason some dish combinations feel so deeply satisfying.

sections.key: Scientists eventually found taste receptors dedicated to umami.
sections.b: For decades, many Western scientists doubted that umami was a separate taste. They argued it was just a blend of other tastes or an effect of smell. The debate shifted in the early 2000s, when researchers identified taste receptors on the tongue that respond specifically to glutamate, giving umami a clear biological basis. Today it is widely accepted as the fifth basic taste alongside sweet, sour, salty and bitter. Why would we evolve to detect it? A common explanation is that umami signals protein. Since glutamate is released when protein-rich foods are cooked or aged, a taste that rewards it could steer us towards nourishing food. Sweetness, by comparison, signals energy from sugars, while bitterness may warn of toxins and sourness of unripe or spoiled food.

sections.key: A 1968 letter sparked decades of fear about MSG.
sections.b: For its first half-century, MSG was used widely with few complaints. In 1968, a doctor wrote a letter to a prominent medical journal describing symptoms such as numbness and palpitations after eating at Chinese restaurants in the United States, wondering whether cooking wine, sodium or MSG might be to blame. The letter prompted a flood of responses and the term 'Chinese restaurant syndrome' spread through newspapers. MSG became a villain, and restaurants began displaying 'no MSG' signs. Many people now see this panic as tinged with prejudice, because ingredients such as parmesan, tomatoes and stock were rarely blamed, despite their natural glutamate. The idea stuck so firmly that many people still report avoiding MSG today, often without knowing that much of their favourite food is naturally rich in glutamate.

sections.key: Food regulators consider MSG safe for the general population.
sections.b: Since the 1970s, researchers have run many studies on MSG, including double-blind trials in which neither participants nor researchers know who has eaten MSG and who has had a placebo. These studies have generally failed to find consistent reactions at the amounts used in normal food. Some people report mild, short-lived symptoms after large doses taken without food, but the evidence is weak. Food Standards Australia New Zealand considers MSG safe for the general population. In Australia, MSG appears on ingredient lists by name or as flavour enhancer 621. A product labelled 'no added MSG' may still contain plenty of natural glutamate from ingredients like yeast extract or tomato. This is general information, so anyone with concerns about reactions to food should speak with a doctor.

sections.key: A little umami can add depth and even help reduce salt.
sections.b: MSG today is mostly made by fermentation: bacteria feed on sugars from crops such as sugarcane, corn or cassava and produce glutamate, which is purified and crystallised. It looks like fine white salt and has a mild taste on its own, but it lifts savoury dishes such as soups, stir-fries, stews and dressings. MSG contains roughly a third as much sodium as table salt, so swapping some salt for a little MSG can reduce sodium in a dish without losing flavour. You do not need the crystals to cook with umami, though. A splash of soy or fish sauce, a spoonful of tomato paste, a grating of parmesan, a few dried mushrooms or a dab of Vegemite in gravy can all deepen flavour in exactly the same way.

quiz.q: What was Kikunae Ikeda eating when he set out to identify umami?
o: Dashi broth made with kombu seaweed
quiz.e: Ikeda investigated the savoury taste of kombu dashi and isolated glutamate from the seaweed.

quiz.q: Why do ripe tomatoes and aged cheeses taste strongly of umami?
o: Breaking down proteins releases free glutamate
quiz.e: Ripening and ageing break down proteins, releasing free glutamate that we can taste.

quiz.q: What happens when glutamate is combined with nucleotides like inosinate?
quiz.e: Glutamate and nucleotides work synergistically, making umami far stronger than either alone.

quiz.q: What firmly established umami as a basic taste in the early 2000s?
o: The discovery of taste receptors that respond to glutamate
quiz.e: Identifying dedicated receptors gave umami a clear biological basis.

quiz.q: How does MSG's sodium content compare with table salt?
o: It has about three times as much
It has roughly a third as much
It has exactly the same amount
quiz.e: MSG contains roughly a third of the sodium of table salt, so it can help cut salt.

LESSONS.title: Why chillies burn: the science of heat
LESSONS.hook: Chilli heat is not a taste at all. It is a clever chemical trick that fools your pain sensors, and the story of how it conquered the world's kitchens is just as surprising.

sections.key: Chillies are American plants that spread across the globe after 1492.
sections.b: It is hard to imagine Thai, Indian, Sichuan or Korean food without chillies, yet every one of these cuisines learned to use them only in the last five centuries. Chillies belong to the genus Capsicum and originated in the Americas. They were domesticated in Mexico thousands of years ago and were a central part of cooking across the region. After Columbus's voyages, Spanish and especially Portuguese traders carried chillies around the world. Unlike many crops, chillies were easy to grow from seed, thrived in warm climates and offered a cheap, intense flavour, so they spread with remarkable speed. Within about a century they were being grown in India, Africa and South-East Asia, and local cooks soon made them their own, often replacing or supplementing black pepper.

sections.key: Capsaicin triggers the same nerve receptor that detects painful heat.
sections.b: The burn of chilli comes mainly from a group of compounds called capsaicinoids, the most important being capsaicin. Capsaicin is not detected by taste buds. Instead it binds to a protein on pain-sensing nerve endings called TRPV1. This receptor's normal job is to detect dangerous heat, and it switches on at temperatures above roughly 43 degrees Celsius. When capsaicin latches on, it flips the same switch, so your brain receives the message that your mouth is being burned, even though the temperature has not changed. That is why chilli can make you sweat, flush and feel genuinely hot. Work on how TRPV1 and related receptors sense temperature and pain earned the American scientist David Julius a share of the 2021 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

sections.key: Capsaicin seems to deter mammals and fungi while sparing seed-spreading birds.
sections.b: Why would a plant produce something that burns? One leading explanation is called directed deterrence. Mammals that chew chilli fruits tend to crush the seeds, while birds swallow them whole and spread them far and wide in their droppings. Crucially, birds' version of the TRPV1 receptor is insensitive to capsaicin, so they can eat the hottest chillies without discomfort. Capsaicin therefore discourages the animals that destroy seeds while allowing the ones that disperse them. There is also evidence that capsaicin protects fruits from fungi. Studies of wild chillies in Bolivia found that plants in wetter areas, where fungal attack was more common, tended to be hotter. As with many evolutionary explanations, scientists continue to debate the relative importance of these factors, and both may play a part.

sections.key: The Scoville scale began with human tasters and now uses lab instruments.
sections.b: In 1912, the American pharmacist Wilbur Scoville devised a way to compare chilli heat. He dissolved an extract of dried chilli in alcohol, diluted it in sugar water and asked a panel of tasters to report when they could no longer detect any heat. The more dilution required, the hotter the chilli, and the result was expressed in what became known as Scoville heat units. A bell pepper scores zero, a jalapeno typically scores a few thousand, and the hottest varieties bred by enthusiasts now exceed two million. Because human tasters vary and tire quickly, modern labs instead use a technique called high-performance liquid chromatography to measure capsaicinoid concentrations directly. The results are then converted into Scoville units, so the familiar scale survives even though its original method has largely been retired.

sections.key: Capsaicin is concentrated in the pale pith, and it dissolves in fat, not water.
sections.b: Many people believe the seeds are the hottest part of a chilli. In fact, capsaicin is made mostly in the pale, spongy tissue called the placenta, the ribs inside the fruit to which the seeds are attached. Seeds can taste hot because they sit pressed against it. Removing the ribs and seeds therefore tames a chilli considerably. Chemistry also explains why water does little to cool a burning mouth. Capsaicin is an oily molecule that dissolves poorly in water but well in fats and alcohol. Gulping water mostly spreads it around. Dairy products such as milk and yoghurt help, probably because their fat and a protein called casein help carry capsaicin away. Starchy foods like rice or bread can also provide some relief by physically mopping up the oil.

sections.key: Wasabi, mustard, black pepper and Sichuan pepper each trigger different sensations.
sections.b: Not every pungent spice works the way chilli does. Black pepper gets its bite from piperine, which also activates TRPV1, along with a related receptor, though its burn is milder. Wasabi, horseradish and mustard rely on compounds called isothiocyanates, which are volatile, so the heat rushes up the nose and fades quickly. They activate a different receptor, TRPA1, which responds to irritants such as the fumes from cut onions. Sichuan pepper, from the dried husks of a prickly ash shrub unrelated to chillies or black pepper, does something stranger still. A compound called hydroxy-alpha-sanshool produces a tingling, buzzing numbness that researchers have compared to a mild vibration on the lips. Sichuan cooking combines this numbing sensation with chilli heat in a famous pairing called mala, meaning numbing and spicy.

sections.key: Chilli lovers may enjoy a safe thrill, and tolerance builds with exposure.
sections.b: Humans are one of very few animals that seek out chilli's burn on purpose. One idea, developed by the psychologist Paul Rozin, is called benign masochism: we enjoy experiences that feel threatening while our brain knows we are actually safe, much like riding a roller coaster or watching a horror film. Pain may also trigger the release of endorphins, adding to the pleasure, although how much this contributes is uncertain. Tolerance is real. Repeated exposure to capsaicin makes the nerve endings less responsive for a while, which is why regular chilli eaters can handle more heat. Capsaicin is also the active ingredient in some pain-relief creams and in pepper spray. Handle very hot chillies with gloves, avoid touching your eyes, and take extreme chilli challenges cautiously.

quiz.q: Where did chillies originally come from?
quiz.e: Chillies are native to the Americas and spread worldwide after Columbus's voyages.

quiz.q: Which receptor does capsaicin activate to create the sensation of heat?
quiz.e: Capsaicin binds TRPV1, the receptor that normally detects painful heat above about 43 degrees Celsius.

quiz.q: Why can birds eat very hot chillies without discomfort?
o: Their stomach acid destroys capsaicin instantly
Their version of TRPV1 is insensitive to capsaicin
quiz.e: Birds' TRPV1 does not respond to capsaicin, so they eat chillies and spread the seeds intact.

quiz.q: Why does milk soothe chilli burn better than water?
o: Capsaicin dissolves in fat and is carried away by milk's fat and casein
quiz.e: Capsaicin dissolves poorly in water but is helped away by fats and the protein casein in dairy.

quiz.q: Which compound produces the tingling numbness of Sichuan pepper?
quiz.e: Hydroxy-alpha-sanshool causes the buzzing, numbing sensation unique to Sichuan pepper.

LESSONS.title: Uluru and Kata Tjuta: the rocks at the heart of Australia
LESSONS.hook: A single rock rising out of a flat red plain looks like it was dropped from the sky. The real story involves vanished mountains, half a billion years and a culture that has known this place for tens of thousands of years.

sections.key: Uluru is a huge sandstone monolith whose colour changes with the light.
sections.b: Stand on the plain at sunset and Uluru seems to catch fire. Its surface shifts from ochre to orange to a deep, burning red, then fades to purple as the light goes. The rock rises about 348 metres above the surrounding desert, higher than the Eiffel Tower, and it takes most people around three hours to walk the base track of roughly ten kilometres. It sits in the south of the Northern Territory, about 450 kilometres by road from Alice Springs. What makes it so striking is the isolation: for kilometres in every direction the land is almost flat, covered in red sand, spinifex and desert oaks. Then this enormous, smooth shape appears, as if it does not belong to the landscape around it at all.

sections.key: Uluru's sand came from mountains that eroded away more than 500 million years ago.
sections.b: The story of Uluru begins with mountains that no longer exist. More than 500 million years ago, a range in central Australia was being worn down by water and weather. Rivers carried the debris away and dumped it in great fans of sand and gravel at the foot of the mountains. Over time those fans were buried under a shallow sea, and the weight of the layers above pressed the loose grains into solid rock. The coarse sand became the sandstone of Uluru, rich in a mineral called feldspar. The pebbles and boulders became the conglomerate of Kata Tjuta, about 30 kilometres to the west. So the two landmarks are siblings, made from the same ancient mountains but sorted by the rivers into different sizes of stone.

sections.key: Huge earth movements tilted Uluru's rock layers until they stand almost vertical.
sections.b: Look closely at Uluru and you can see faint parallel lines running up its sides. These are the original layers of sand, and they should be lying flat. Instead they stand nearly upright. Hundreds of millions of years ago, slow and powerful movements of the Earth's crust squeezed central Australia, folding and tilting the buried rock. Uluru's layers were tipped by close to 90 degrees, while Kata Tjuta's were tilted only gently. Then erosion went to work again, stripping away the softer rock around them and leaving the tougher, more tightly packed stone standing proud. Geologists think much of the rock continues underground, so the part we see may be only a fraction of the whole body, like the visible tip of a buried slab.

sections.key: Uluru's red skin is rust, and the rock underneath is grey.
sections.b: If you could break a piece off Uluru, which you must not, you would find something surprising. Fresh rock inside is a dull grey. The famous red is only a thin outer coating. Uluru's sandstone contains iron-bearing minerals, and when these are exposed to air and occasional rain, the iron oxidises. In plain language, the surface of the rock has rusted. The same chemistry gives much of the outback its red soil. The colour changes during the day because the low sun at dawn and dusk shines through more of the atmosphere, which scatters away blue light and leaves warm reds and oranges. After rare heavy rain, Uluru turns silvery and dark, and waterfalls pour down its gullies, a sight many locals say is the most beautiful of all.

sections.key: For the Anangu, Uluru and Kata Tjuta are living places shaped by ancestral beings.
sections.b: Long before any geologist arrived, the Anangu people knew this country intimately. Anangu are the Traditional Owners of the area, and Aboriginal people have lived in central Australia for many tens of thousands of years. For Anangu, the landscape is explained through Tjukurpa, a body of law, knowledge and story that describes how ancestral beings travelled across the land and created its features. Marks, caves and waterholes around Uluru are linked to these stories and to rules for living. Some places are sacred and are not to be photographed or visited by outsiders, which is why certain parts of the base walk carry signs asking visitors to respect them. To Anangu, Uluru is not a scenic backdrop but a place of law, family and responsibility.

sections.h: Ayers Rock, handback and the climb
sections.key: The park was handed back to Anangu in 1985 and the climb closed in 2019.
sections.b: In 1873 the explorer William Gosse saw the rock and named it Ayers Rock after Sir Henry Ayers, a South Australian politician. For about a century tourism grew, and many visitors climbed a steep route up one side, despite Anangu asking people not to. On 26 October 1985, ownership of the national park was formally handed back to Anangu, who then leased it to the federal government to be jointly managed. The park was later World Heritage listed for both its natural and cultural values. The name Uluru came first in official use from 2002. After years of discussion, the park board decided to end the climb, and it closed permanently on 26 October 2019, exactly 34 years after the handback.

sections.key: Kata Tjuta is a cluster of rounded domes that is taller than Uluru.
sections.b: Many visitors are surprised to learn that Kata Tjuta, once called the Olgas, is actually taller than Uluru. Its highest dome rises around 546 metres above the plain. Kata Tjuta means 'many heads' in the local language, and the name fits: there are 36 rounded domes separated by deep valleys and narrow gorges. Because it is made of conglomerate, a jumble of pebbles and boulders cemented together, it weathers differently from Uluru and has broken into many separate shapes. The Valley of the Winds walk winds between the domes, where the temperature drops and sounds echo strangely. Seen together from a distance at dawn, the two formations show how one ancient landscape, worked on by patient forces over unimaginable time, can produce two utterly different works of natural sculpture.

quiz.q: What kind of rock is Uluru mainly made of?
quiz.e: Uluru is sandstone, formed from sand washed off ancient mountains and pressed into rock.

quiz.q: Why do the faint lines on Uluru's sides run almost vertically?
o: Rain cut grooves down the rock
Earth movements tilted the original layers by close to 90 degrees
quiz.e: The rock layers were once flat but were tipped nearly upright by movements of the crust.

quiz.q: What gives Uluru its red colour?
o: A thin coating of oxidised iron, essentially rust
The rock is red all the way through
quiz.e: The inside is grey; only the surface has rusted to red.

quiz.q: When was the Uluru climb permanently closed?
quiz.e: It closed on 26 October 2019, 34 years to the day after the park was handed back to Anangu.

quiz.q: What does the name Kata Tjuta mean?
quiz.e: Kata Tjuta means 'many heads', a fitting name for its 36 rounded domes.

LESSONS.title: Lightning: how storms make electricity
LESSONS.hook: Somewhere on Earth, lightning strikes dozens of times every second. Here is how a cloud builds up enough electricity to light the sky, why thunder follows, and how to stay safe.

sections.h: A flash hotter than the Sun
sections.key: A lightning bolt heats the air to several times the temperature of the Sun's surface.
sections.b: On a summer afternoon a dark cloud piles up over the suburbs, the air goes strangely still, and then a jagged white line splits the sky. In that instant, a channel of air only a few centimetres wide is heated to roughly 30,000 degrees Celsius, about five times hotter than the visible surface of the Sun. Lightning is one of the most common dramatic events on the planet. Satellite measurements suggest there are somewhere around 40 to 50 flashes every second worldwide, adding up to more than a billion a year. Most of them happen over land in the tropics, where warm, moist air rises fastest. Yet for something so ordinary, the exact physics of how a flash begins is still an active area of research.

sections.key: Collisions between ice particles inside a storm cloud separate electric charge.
sections.b: A thunderstorm is a giant vertical engine. Warm, humid air rushes upward, cools and condenses into water droplets, and near the top of the cloud the droplets freeze. Inside, the cloud is a chaos of tiny ice crystals, supercooled water and soft pellets of ice called graupel, all being thrown around by powerful updrafts. When ice crystals and graupel collide, electric charge is transferred between them. The lighter crystals, generally carrying positive charge, are swept to the top of the cloud, while the heavier graupel, usually negative, gathers lower down. The result is a cloud that works like an enormous battery, with opposite charges separated by kilometres of air. Air is normally a good insulator, so the charge keeps building until the insulation finally breaks down.

sections.key: A faint stepped leader creeps down, then a brilliant return stroke races back up.
sections.b: Most lightning never reaches the ground. It jumps within a cloud or between clouds. When a bolt does head for the ground, it begins with something you cannot easily see: a faint, branching channel of charged air called a stepped leader, which zigzags downward in short jumps. As it gets close, the ground and tall objects respond by sending up their own small streamers. When a leader and a streamer meet, the circuit is complete and an enormous current surges along the path. This is the return stroke, the blinding flash we actually see, and it travels upward from the ground into the cloud. Several strokes often follow the same channel in quick succession, which is why lightning sometimes appears to flicker.

sections.key: Thunder is the sound of air expanding explosively around the hot lightning channel.
sections.b: Thunder is lightning's sonic boom. When the channel suddenly heats to tens of thousands of degrees, the air inside it expands so quickly that it creates a shock wave, which spreads out as the crack and rumble we hear. A nearby strike sounds like a sharp, ripping explosion. A distant one rolls and grumbles, because sound from different parts of a long, twisting channel reaches you at slightly different times and echoes off hills and buildings. Light travels almost instantly, but sound moves at only about a third of a kilometre per second. That gives a handy rule: count the seconds between the flash and the thunder, then divide by three to estimate the distance in kilometres. If the gap is short, the storm is close.

sections.key: Lightning can strike the same place twice, and car tyres are not what protects you.
sections.b: Several popular beliefs about lightning are simply wrong. The idea that it never strikes the same place twice is false: tall buildings are hit again and again, and the Empire State Building in New York is struck many times every year. Another myth is that rubber tyres make a car safe. In fact a hard-topped car protects you because its metal body carries the current around the outside and into the ground, while the people inside stay clear of the path. Lying flat on the ground is also poor advice, because current can spread across the surface. Sheltering under a lone tree is one of the worst choices of all, since the tree is a likely target and the current can jump sideways to anyone standing beneath it.

sections.key: If you can hear thunder, you are close enough to be struck, so get inside.
sections.b: The simplest safety rule is often summed up as 'when thunder roars, go indoors'. If you can hear thunder, the storm is close enough for lightning to reach you, because strikes can land many kilometres from the main storm. The safest places are solid buildings with wiring and plumbing, or a hard-topped vehicle with the windows up. Inside, avoid using corded phones, running water and touching appliances plugged into the wall, since current can travel through wiring and pipes. Experts generally suggest waiting around 30 minutes after the last thunder before heading back outside. This is general information rather than personal advice, and during severe weather it is worth checking warnings from the Bureau of Meteorology and following any instructions from your state emergency service.

sections.key: Lake Maracaibo in Venezuela sees more lightning than almost anywhere on Earth.
sections.b: Some places are lightning magnets. Over Lake Maracaibo in Venezuela, warm moist air from the lake meets cool winds tumbling off the surrounding mountains, and night after night storms erupt over the water. Satellite studies rank it as one of the most lightning-rich spots on the planet, and the silent, flickering display has been used by sailors as a natural lighthouse for centuries. Central Africa, especially the Congo basin, is another hotspot. In Australia, the tropical north sees spectacular storms in the build-up to the wet season, and Darwin is famous for its evening light shows. Lightning also matters for life: the extreme heat of a strike joins nitrogen and oxygen in the air into compounds that rain washes into the soil, where plants can use them.

quiz.q: What separates electric charge inside a storm cloud?
o: Collisions between ice crystals and soft ice pellets called graupel
quiz.e: Collisions between ice particles transfer charge, and updrafts separate the light and heavy particles.

quiz.q: What is the bright flash we actually see in a lightning strike?
quiz.e: The return stroke surges along the completed channel, producing the brilliant flash.

quiz.q: You count 9 seconds between a flash and its thunder. Roughly how far away is the strike?
quiz.e: Sound travels about a third of a kilometre per second, so divide the seconds by three.

quiz.q: Why is a hard-topped car fairly safe in a lightning storm?
o: The rubber tyres insulate it from the ground
The metal body carries current around the outside to the ground
Cars are too low to be struck
quiz.e: It is the metal shell, not the tyres, that steers current around the occupants.

quiz.q: Which place is famous for having some of the most frequent lightning on Earth?
quiz.e: Lake Maracaibo has storms on most nights and ranks among the world's lightning hotspots.

LESSONS.title: Rainforests: Earth's richest places
LESSONS.hook: Rainforests cover only a small slice of the planet's land, yet they are home to a huge share of its living things. Australia has some of the oldest on Earth.

sections.key: Rainforests are dense, wet forests packed with an extraordinary variety of life.
sections.b: Walk into the Daintree in far north Queensland and the world closes over you. Sunlight drips through layer after layer of leaves, the air is thick and warm, and everything seems to be growing on something else: ferns on trunks, vines on branches, mosses on ferns. Somewhere a bird calls, and a lizard flicks across the leaf litter. A rainforest is, broadly, a forest that receives heavy and reliable rainfall and has a closed canopy, meaning the treetops join to shade the ground. Tropical rainforests grow near the equator, but there are temperate rainforests too, in cool, wet places such as Tasmania and New Zealand. Together they cover only a small fraction of the Earth's land, yet scientists think they hold a large share of all land species.

sections.key: Rainforests are built in storeys, each with its own climate and residents.
sections.b: A tropical rainforest is less like a single forest and more like a tall apartment building. At the very top, scattered giant trees called emergents poke above everything else, battered by sun and wind. Below them is the canopy, a dense roof of leaves and branches where much of the forest's life is concentrated: birds, insects, possums, fruit bats and countless plants that never touch the ground. Under the canopy is the understorey, a dim world of young trees, palms and shrubs waiting for a gap to open above them. Finally there is the forest floor, where only a few per cent of the sunlight may reach. When a big tree falls, light floods in and a frantic race begins as seedlings compete to fill the gap.

sections.key: Tropical rainforest soils are often thin because nutrients are locked up in living things.
sections.b: You might expect such lush forests to grow in rich, deep soil. Often the opposite is true. In many tropical rainforests, constant heat and rain break down fallen leaves within weeks, and heavy downpours wash nutrients out of the ground. The forest survives by recycling at speed. Fungi and roots spread through the leaf litter and grab nutrients almost as soon as they are released, so most of the forest's wealth is stored in the living plants rather than in the soil. This is why clearing rainforest for farming can be so disappointing. Once the trees are cut and burned, the land may produce good crops for a few years, then the thin soil is exhausted. A forest that took centuries to build can be very hard to bring back.

sections.h: Forests that make their own rain
sections.key: Rainforests pump water into the sky, helping to create the rain they need.
sections.b: Rainforests do not just receive rain; they help make it. Trees draw water up from the soil and release it as vapour through tiny pores in their leaves, a process called transpiration. Across a forest the size of the Amazon, the amount is staggering. Moist air rising from the canopy forms clouds that drop rain further inland, where the water is drawn up and released again. Scientists sometimes describe these moving streams of moisture as 'flying rivers'. Research suggests a large part of the Amazon's rainfall is recycled in this way, and that moisture from the forest helps water farmland far to the south. It also explains a worry: if too much forest is cleared, parts of the system could dry out and struggle to sustain rainforest at all.

sections.key: Some Australian rainforests preserve plant families from the days of Gondwana.
sections.b: Australia is famous for deserts, but it also holds some of the oldest rainforests on Earth. The Wet Tropics of Queensland, including the Daintree, were World Heritage listed in 1988, partly because they preserve an exceptional record of plant evolution. Many flowering plant families that appeared early in their history still grow there. Further south, the Gondwana Rainforests of Australia stretch across parts of New South Wales and southern Queensland. They are remnants of forests that once covered much of the ancient supercontinent Gondwana, which included Australia, Antarctica, South America, Africa and India. As Australia drifted north and dried out over millions of years, rainforest retreated to moist pockets along the east coast and the ranges, where it survives today like a living museum.

sections.key: Many rainforest plants depend on animals to spread their seeds.
sections.b: In the Queensland rainforest, one of the most important gardeners is a bird taller than many people. The southern cassowary swallows fallen fruit whole, including some fruits too large for any other native animal to eat, and later deposits the seeds in a pile of dung, often far from the parent tree. Some plants appear to rely heavily on the cassowary to spread. Rainforests are full of partnerships like this. Fig trees depend on tiny wasps to pollinate their hidden flowers, while fruit bats carry seeds and pollen across long distances at night. Strangler figs begin life high in the canopy, dropped there by a bird, and send roots down to the ground that eventually encircle the host tree. Every species is tangled up with others.

sections.key: Rainforests store carbon, influence climate and supply medicines and foods.
sections.b: Rainforests matter even if you never set foot in one. They store vast amounts of carbon in their trunks, roots and soils, so clearing and burning them releases carbon dioxide and adds to climate change. They influence rainfall patterns across whole regions. Many everyday foods, including coffee, cocoa, bananas and vanilla, have origins in tropical forests, and a number of medicines have come from rainforest plants. The macadamia, Australia's best-known native food crop, comes from the rainforests of south-east Queensland and northern New South Wales. Large areas of tropical rainforest are still being cleared each year, mostly for farming and grazing. The good news is that protection works when it is enforced, and places such as the Daintree show that rainforest and tourism can thrive together.

quiz.q: Which rainforest layer is the dense 'roof' where much of the forest's life is concentrated?
quiz.e: The canopy is the thick roof of joined treetops where most rainforest life lives.

quiz.q: Why are many tropical rainforest soils surprisingly poor?
o: Nutrients are quickly recycled into living plants and washed out by rain
It is too cold for decomposition
quiz.e: Most nutrients are held in living things, not in the thin, heavily leached soil.

quiz.q: What is transpiration?
o: Plants releasing water vapour through pores in their leaves
quiz.e: Transpiration lets forests pump moisture into the air, helping to create rain.

quiz.q: The Gondwana Rainforests of Australia are remnants of forests from which ancient landmass?
quiz.e: They survive from forests that once covered the supercontinent Gondwana.

quiz.q: Why is the southern cassowary important to Queensland's rainforest?
o: It spreads the seeds of large fruits through its dung
quiz.e: Cassowaries swallow large fruits whole and deposit the seeds far from the parent tree.

LESSONS.title: How beaches and coastlines are made
LESSONS.hook: A beach looks permanent, but it is really a river of sand that never stops moving. Here is how waves build, shift and carve Australia's coastlines.

sections.h: A beach is on the move
sections.key: Every beach is a temporary pile of sand that waves are constantly rearranging.
sections.b: Picture your favourite beach on a calm summer morning: a wide sweep of golden sand, gentle waves, children digging holes. Now picture the same beach after a big winter storm, with the sand stripped back to a steep scarp and rocks exposed that nobody had seen in years. Both are the same beach. Coastlines are among the most active landscapes on Earth, reshaped every day by waves, tides, currents and wind. Sand that seems solid underfoot is really in transit, arriving from rivers and cliffs, being pushed along the shore and sometimes lost offshore or blown inland. Australia, with tens of thousands of kilometres of mainland coast and thousands of beaches, is a superb place to watch these forces at work.

sections.key: Most waves are made by wind blowing over the sea, often far away.
sections.b: The waves breaking at your feet may have been born days earlier, thousands of kilometres away. Most ocean waves are created by wind. As wind blows across the water, friction ruffles the surface and transfers energy into it. The size of the waves depends on three things: how strong the wind is, how long it blows and the distance of open water it blows across, known as the fetch. Great storms in the Southern Ocean, with enormous fetch and fierce winds, send long, powerful swells north to Australia's southern and western coasts. Out at sea, the water in a wave mostly moves in circles rather than travelling forward. It is the energy that crosses the ocean. Only when the wave reaches shallow water does it slow, steepen and finally break.

sections.key: Beach sand is mostly worn-down rock, especially quartz, mixed with shell.
sections.b: Scoop up a handful of beach sand and you are holding a sample of the land behind it. On many Australian beaches the grains are mostly quartz, a hard mineral that survives long after softer minerals have been ground away. Rivers carry it down from eroding mountains, and waves sort it by size. Other beaches tell different stories. Some tropical beaches are made largely of broken shell and coral, pale and crunchy underfoot. Black sand beaches form where waves wear down dark volcanic rock. At Whitehaven Beach in the Whitsundays the sand is famously white and fine because it is extremely pure silica. Gold and other heavy minerals sometimes collect in darker streaks, and some Australian beaches have been mined for minerals such as rutile and zircon.

sections.h: Rivers of sand along the shore
sections.key: Longshore drift moves sand along the coast like a slow conveyor belt.
sections.b: Waves rarely hit a beach dead straight. They usually arrive at a slight angle, pushing sand up the beach on a slant, while the backwash drags it straight back down the slope. Each wave moves grains a little further along the shore, and over months and years enormous volumes of sand travel along the coast. This process is called longshore drift. On much of Australia's east coast, the overall drift runs northward, carrying sand up from New South Wales towards Queensland. Where that river of sand meets a headland or a change in the coast, it can pile up into sand spits and huge dune systems. K'gari, formerly called Fraser Island, is widely described as the largest sand island in the world, built in part from sand delivered this way.

sections.key: Waves carve headlands into caves, then arches, then lonely stacks.
sections.b: On rocky coasts, waves act like a slow chisel. They pound weaknesses in a cliff, such as cracks and softer layers, and hurl sand and pebbles against the rock. Over time a crack becomes a sea cave. If caves form on both sides of a narrow headland, they may meet to make an arch. Eventually the arch roof falls, leaving a pillar of rock standing alone in the sea, known as a stack, which itself is slowly worn down to a stump. Victoria's Twelve Apostles, limestone stacks along the Great Ocean Road, are a famous example. Nearby, a formation once called London Bridge was a double arch until its inner span collapsed in 1990, leaving two startled tourists stranded on the outer section until they were rescued by helicopter.

sections.key: Rip currents are strong channels of water flowing back out to sea.
sections.b: The biggest everyday hazard on Australian beaches is not sharks but rip currents. When waves push water up onto the beach, it has to return to the sea somehow. Often it flows back through a channel between sandbars, forming a narrow, fast current running away from shore. Rips can look deceptively calm: a darker, flatter gap in the breaking waves, sometimes with rippled or sandy water. Swimmers caught in one can be carried out quickly and exhaust themselves fighting it. The safest choice is to swim between the red and yellow flags at a patrolled beach. If caught, safety advice generally says to stay calm, float, raise an arm to signal for help, and swim parallel to the shore if you can. Surf Life Saving Australia has detailed guidance.

sections.key: Coastlines respond to storms, sea level and human building.
sections.b: Beaches naturally breathe in and out with the seasons. Big winter storms tend to drag sand offshore into bars, and gentler summer swells push it back. Problems arise when we build too close to the moving edge. In 1974, a series of powerful storms struck the New South Wales coast and badly eroded beaches such as Collaroy and Narrabeen in Sydney, and the same stretch suffered serious damage again in 2016. Seawalls can protect property, but they can also starve neighbouring beaches of sand. Rising sea levels, caused mainly by warming oceans and melting ice, are expected to push shorelines inland in many places. Coastal scientists increasingly argue that the best defence is to give beaches room to move, with healthy dunes acting as a natural sand bank for storms.

quiz.q: What is 'fetch' when talking about waves?
o: The distance of open water the wind blows across
The angle a wave hits the beach
quiz.e: Fetch, along with wind strength and duration, controls how big waves can grow.

quiz.q: What mineral makes up most of the sand on many Australian beaches?
quiz.e: Quartz is hard and long lasting, so it survives after softer minerals wear away.

quiz.q: What is longshore drift?
o: The movement of sand along the coast by waves arriving at an angle
quiz.e: Angled waves move sand step by step along the shore, like a slow conveyor belt.

quiz.q: What is the usual order as waves erode a headland?
quiz.e: Caves become arches, arches collapse into stacks, and stacks wear down to stumps.

quiz.q: What is the safest way to avoid rip currents at the beach?
o: Swim between the red and yellow flags
Swim where the water looks flattest
quiz.e: Patrolled flags mark the safest area, and calm-looking gaps can actually be rips.

LESSONS.title: Tropical cyclones: anatomy of a monster storm
LESSONS.hook: Cyclones, hurricanes and typhoons are the same storm with different names. Learn how warm oceans power them, why they spin, and what Cyclone Tracy taught Australia.

sections.key: Cyclone Tracy flattened much of Darwin and changed how Australia builds.
sections.b: On Christmas Eve 1974, Darwin went to bed expecting a stormy night. Cyclone Tracy was small, but in the early hours of Christmas Day it struck the city with ferocious winds. By morning, most of Darwin's homes had been destroyed or badly damaged, and dozens of people had been killed, with figures of around 66 to 71 deaths commonly cited. Most of the population was evacuated in the days that followed, one of the largest peacetime airlifts in Australian history. Tracy became a turning point. Investigations found that many houses had simply come apart in the wind, and building codes in cyclone-prone regions were strengthened dramatically. Northern Australian homes are now built to hold together under forces that would once have torn them apart.

sections.key: Cyclone, hurricane and typhoon all describe the same kind of tropical storm.
sections.b: Whether a storm is called a hurricane, a typhoon or a cyclone depends on where it forms, not what it is. In the North Atlantic and north-east Pacific it is a hurricane. In the north-west Pacific, near Japan and the Philippines, it is a typhoon. In the Indian Ocean and around Australia it is a tropical cyclone. All are rotating storm systems that form over warm tropical seas, with a calm centre and bands of thunderstorms spiralling around it. In Australia, the Bureau of Meteorology names cyclones from a rotating list, alternating between male and female names. When a storm is especially deadly or destructive, its name is retired so it will never be used again, which is why there will never be another Cyclone Tracy.

sections.key: Cyclones draw their energy from warm seas, usually above about 26 degrees Celsius.
sections.b: A tropical cyclone is essentially a heat engine fuelled by the ocean. It needs sea surface temperatures of roughly 26 to 27 degrees Celsius or more, through a reasonably deep layer of water. Warm water evaporates into the air above, and as that moist air rises and cools, the vapour condenses into cloud and rain. Condensation releases heat, which warms the surrounding air, makes it rise even faster, and draws in more moist air from below. This feedback loop is what allows a cluster of thunderstorms to organise into a cyclone. It also explains why cyclones weaken quickly after crossing the coast or moving over cooler water: they are cut off from their fuel supply, although the rain they carry inland can still cause severe flooding.

sections.key: The Earth's rotation makes cyclones spin clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere.
sections.b: As air rushes inward towards the low pressure at a storm's centre, the rotation of the Earth deflects its path. This effect, named after the French scientist Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis, bends moving air to the left in the Southern Hemisphere and to the right in the Northern Hemisphere. The result is that Australian cyclones spin clockwise, while hurricanes in the United States spin anticlockwise. The Coriolis effect is almost zero right at the equator, which is why cyclones very rarely form within about five degrees of it. That is also why the popular claim that toilets flush in opposite directions in each hemisphere is a myth: in something as small as a bowl, the shape and the water jets matter far more than the Earth's spin.

sections.key: The calm eye is surrounded by the eyewall, where the strongest winds are found.
sections.b: Seen from a satellite, a mature cyclone is a vast pinwheel of cloud, often several hundred kilometres across. At its centre sits the eye, a region typically a few tens of kilometres wide where air sinks, skies may be clear and winds are light. People caught as the eye passes over them sometimes think the storm is over, only for the winds to return suddenly from the opposite direction. Around the eye is the eyewall, a ring of towering thunderstorms where the most violent winds and heaviest rain are concentrated. Beyond that, spiral rainbands sweep outward, bringing bursts of squalls. Australia rates cyclones from category 1 to category 5 based on their strongest wind gusts, with category 5 storms capable of gusts well over 280 kilometres per hour.

sections.key: Storm surge and flooding often cause more harm than the wind itself.
sections.b: Wind grabs the headlines, but water is often the greatest danger in a cyclone. As the storm approaches land, its winds pile seawater up against the coast, and the low pressure lets the sea bulge upward. This storm surge can push the ocean far inland, especially when it arrives at high tide over low-lying land. Some of the deadliest tropical cyclones in history, including disasters in Bangladesh and Myanmar, killed most of their victims through surge. Heavy rain is the other hazard, with flooding sometimes continuing for days after landfall as the remains of the storm drift inland. This is general information, not personal advice: if you live in a cyclone area, follow Bureau of Meteorology warnings and your state emergency service's instructions, including any evacuation orders.

sections.key: Scientists expect fewer but stronger cyclones in Australia's region, on balance.
sections.b: Will climate change mean more cyclones? The answer is more nuanced than many people expect. Research for the Australian region suggests the overall number of tropical cyclones has declined somewhat in recent decades, and climate models generally project that trend may continue. However, warmer oceans and a moister atmosphere are expected to make a larger share of cyclones intense, with heavier rainfall. Rising sea levels also add to the height of storm surges, so a storm of the same strength can do more damage at the coast. Some studies suggest cyclones may also form or travel further from the tropics than in the past, though this remains uncertain. For people living along the northern coast, the practical message is the same: preparation, strong buildings and early warnings save lives.

quiz.q: What is a tropical cyclone called in the north-west Pacific near Japan?
quiz.e: The same type of storm is called a typhoon in the north-west Pacific.

quiz.q: Roughly what sea surface temperature do tropical cyclones usually need?
o: About 26 to 27 degrees Celsius or more
quiz.e: They need warm water, generally around 26 to 27 degrees or more, to fuel them.

quiz.q: Which way do cyclones spin in the Southern Hemisphere?
quiz.e: The Coriolis effect makes Southern Hemisphere cyclones spin clockwise.

quiz.q: Where are the strongest winds in a cyclone found?
quiz.e: The eyewall, the ring of thunderstorms around the eye, has the most violent winds.

quiz.q: What is a storm surge?
o: A rise in sea level pushed onto the coast by the storm
quiz.e: Winds and low pressure pile up seawater, which can flood far inland.

LESSONS.title: Glaciers: rivers of ice
LESSONS.hook: Glaciers look frozen in place, but they flow, grind and carve like slow-motion rivers. They shaped many of the world's most beautiful landscapes, including some in Tasmania.

sections.key: A glacier is a mass of ice so heavy that it flows under its own weight.
sections.b: Stand beside a glacier in New Zealand or Alaska and you will hear it before you understand it. It creaks, groans and occasionally cracks like a gunshot, because it is moving. A glacier is a large body of ice that forms on land and flows downhill or outward under its own weight. Most move slowly, perhaps tens of centimetres to a few metres a day, though some outlet glaciers in Greenland and Antarctica race along at many kilometres a year. Glaciers and ice sheets together hold most of the planet's fresh water, around two thirds by common estimates. They exist on every continent except mainland Australia, from tropical mountain peaks in South America and Africa to the vast ice of the polar regions.

sections.key: Over years, buried snow is squeezed into dense, blue glacier ice.
sections.b: Every glacier begins as falling snow. In places where more snow falls in winter than melts in summer, it builds up year after year. Fresh snowflakes are delicate and full of air, but as new layers pile on top, the older snow is compressed. The flakes lose their points and become rounded grains, forming a dense, granular material called firn. Over years to centuries, depending on the climate, the firn is squeezed further until the air spaces are closed off as tiny bubbles and it becomes solid glacier ice. Thick, dense ice absorbs red light and lets blue light travel further, which is why deep crevasses and fresh icebergs glow an intense blue. Those trapped bubbles are valuable too: they preserve samples of ancient air.

sections.key: Glaciers move by the ice slowly deforming and by sliding over their beds.
sections.b: It seems impossible that solid ice could flow, but under enough pressure it behaves a little like very stiff toffee. Deep inside a thick glacier, the weight of the ice above makes the crystals slowly deform and slide past one another, so the whole mass creeps downhill. Many glaciers also slide along their base, especially where meltwater collects underneath and acts like a lubricant. The top layer of ice is brittle, though. As the glacier flows over bumps or around bends, the surface cracks into deep crevasses that can be tens of metres deep and hidden under snow bridges, making glacier travel dangerous. Where a glacier spills over a steep drop, it shatters into a chaotic jumble of ice blocks called an icefall.

sections.key: Glaciers carve U-shaped valleys, sharp peaks and deep fjords.
sections.b: As a glacier moves, it plucks rocks from its bed and drags them along, using them like sandpaper to scour the landscape. A river usually cuts a narrow V-shaped valley, but a glacier widens and deepens it into a broad U shape with steep walls. At the head of a glacier, ice gouges out a bowl-shaped hollow called a cirque, which often holds a lake after the ice melts. Where several cirques eat into a mountain from different sides, they leave a sharp pyramid peak, as with the Matterhorn in the Alps. When glaciers carve valleys below sea level and the ice later retreats, the sea floods in, creating fjords like those of Norway and Fiordland in New Zealand.

sections.key: Moraines and erratic boulders are clues that ice once covered a landscape.
sections.b: Glaciers are messy. Everything they carry, from fine rock flour to boulders the size of houses, is eventually dumped where the ice melts. Ridges of this jumbled debris are called moraines, and they mark the sides and furthest reach of old glaciers. Huge lone boulders sitting in fields far from any matching rock are known as glacial erratics. In the 1800s, scientists such as Louis Agassiz used clues like these to argue that much of Europe had once been buried under ice, an idea that was startling at the time. Glacial meltwater is milky with fine rock flour, which is why glacier-fed lakes often have a striking turquoise colour, as at Lake Tekapo in New Zealand and Lake Louise in Canada.

sections.key: Tasmania's high country was carved by glaciers during the last ice age.
sections.b: Mainland Australia has no glaciers today, and the mainland saw only small ones in the Snowy Mountains during the last ice age. Tasmania tells a different story. During cold periods, ice caps and glaciers covered parts of its Central Highlands and West Coast ranges. Many of Tasmania's most loved landscapes are glacial handiwork. Dove Lake, beneath Cradle Mountain, sits in a basin carved by ice, and the area is dotted with cirques, moraines and small glacial lakes. Lake St Clair, Australia's deepest freshwater lake, was also shaped by glaciers. Australia does still have active glaciers in its territory: Heard Island, an external territory in the Southern Ocean, is home to an active volcano called Big Ben, much of it covered in glaciers.

sections.key: Most of the world's glaciers are shrinking as the climate warms.
sections.b: Around the world, most mountain glaciers are losing ice. Comparing old photographs with the same view today can be startling: valleys once filled with ice now hold bare rock and meltwater lakes. Scientists measure glaciers using field surveys, aerial photographs and satellites, and the long-term picture shows widespread retreat linked to rising temperatures. This matters well beyond the mountains. Meltwater from glaciers feeds rivers that supply water to many millions of people, especially in Asia and South America, and shrinking glaciers may eventually mean lower summer flows. Melting glaciers and ice sheets also add water to the oceans, contributing to sea level rise. In 2019, Iceland held a memorial for Okjökull, a glacier that had lost so much ice it was no longer considered a glacier.

quiz.q: What is firn?
o: Compressed, granular snow on its way to becoming glacier ice
quiz.e: Firn is old snow squeezed into rounded grains, partway between snow and glacier ice.

quiz.q: Why do crevasses form at the surface of a glacier?
o: The top ice is brittle and cracks as the glacier flows
Sunlight melts holes in the ice
quiz.e: Deep ice deforms slowly, but brittle surface ice cracks as it moves over bumps and bends.

quiz.q: What shape of valley is typically carved by a glacier?
quiz.e: Glaciers widen and deepen valleys into a broad U shape with steep sides.

quiz.q: What is a glacial erratic?
o: A large boulder carried and dropped far from its source by ice
quiz.e: Erratics are boulders left by melting ice, often far from any matching rock.

quiz.q: Which Tasmanian lake sits in a basin carved by glaciers beneath Cradle Mountain?
quiz.e: Dove Lake lies in a glacially carved basin below Cradle Mountain.

LESSONS.title: Caves: the hidden world beneath our feet
LESSONS.hook: Under quiet paddocks and plains lie vast cave systems, sculpted drop by drop over hundreds of thousands of years. Here is how rain dissolves rock, and what caves preserve.

sections.key: Beneath some landscapes lie huge networks of caves carved by water.
sections.b: Drive across the Nullarbor Plain and you see almost nothing: a flat, treeless expanse stretching to the horizon. Fittingly, the name comes from Latin for 'no tree'. Yet beneath that empty surface lies one of the largest areas of limestone on Earth, riddled with caves, some holding long underground lakes of clear water explored by cave divers. Landscapes like this are called karst, after a limestone region in Slovenia where scientists first studied them closely. Karst country is full of surprises. Rivers vanish into the ground, springs burst from hillsides, and holes suddenly open in fields. It covers a significant share of the world's land, and in some regions karst aquifers supply drinking water to large numbers of people, often without them knowing it.

sections.key: Slightly acidic rainwater slowly dissolves limestone, opening up caves.
sections.b: Most caves are made by water dissolving rock, and the key ingredient is carbon dioxide. As rain falls, it absorbs a little carbon dioxide from the air, and much more as it soaks through soil full of decaying plants. This forms a weak acid called carbonic acid, the same acid that puts the fizz in soft drinks. When this slightly acidic water seeps into limestone, which is made mostly of calcium carbonate, it slowly dissolves the rock. The water follows cracks and layers, widening them over tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of years into passages and chambers. Eventually the water table may drop, leaving the passages filled with air. The result is a cave system shaped like the plumbing of the landscape.

sections.key: Cave formations grow as dripping water leaves behind tiny amounts of calcite.
sections.b: Once a cave fills with air, a new kind of sculpture begins. Water dripping from the ceiling carries dissolved limestone. When it reaches the cave air, it releases some of its carbon dioxide, and a tiny amount of the mineral calcite is left behind. Drip by drip, a thin hollow tube called a straw forms, which can thicken into an icicle-like stalactite hanging from the roof. Where the drops land, calcite builds upward into a stalagmite. A simple way to remember: stalactites hold 'tight' to the ceiling, while stalagmites 'might' reach up one day. When the two meet they form a column. Growth is usually extraordinarily slow, often a fraction of a millimetre a year, so touching formations is discouraged because skin oils can stop them growing.

sections.key: Jenolan, Naracoorte and the Nullarbor caves are among Australia's underground treasures.
sections.b: Australia's best-known show caves are the Jenolan Caves in the Blue Mountains region of New South Wales, where visitors have been exploring lit chambers since the 1800s. Scientific dating has suggested that the caves are very old indeed, possibly hundreds of millions of years, making them among the oldest known open caves in the world. In South Australia, the Naracoorte Caves act as natural traps. For hundreds of thousands of years, animals fell through openings in the ground and could not climb out, leaving a remarkable fossil record that includes Australia's extinct megafauna. Together with Riversleigh in Queensland, Naracoorte was World Heritage listed in 1994. In north Queensland, the Undara lava tubes are a different kind of cave altogether, formed by flowing lava rather than water.

sections.key: When a cave roof collapses, the ground can suddenly open up.
sections.b: As caves grow, their roofs can become thin and unstable. Eventually the roof may collapse, opening a hole at the surface called a sinkhole or doline. Some form slowly as the ground sags; others appear suddenly, swallowing roads, cars and occasionally buildings. Mount Gambier in South Australia is famous for its water-filled sinkholes, including the sunken gardens of the Umpherston Sinkhole. On Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula, sinkholes known as cenotes open into water-filled cave systems. The ancient Maya relied on them for fresh water in a land with almost no surface rivers, and some cenotes were sacred places where offerings were made. Today cave divers explore the enormous flooded passages that link them, some of which stretch for hundreds of kilometres.

sections.key: Vietnam's Son Doong has some of the largest cave passages known, and Kentucky's Mammoth Cave is the longest known system.
sections.b: Caves come in staggering sizes. Mammoth Cave in Kentucky in the United States is the longest known cave system in the world, with more than 600 kilometres of mapped passages, and explorers keep adding more. For sheer volume, Son Doong in Vietnam is extraordinary. A local man found its entrance around 1990, but it was not explored by a British and Vietnamese caving team until 2009. Parts of its main passage are big enough to hold city buildings, and where the roof has collapsed, sunlight pours in and a jungle grows inside the cave, complete with its own clouds. Many caves remain unexplored, and new passages are still being discovered around the world, including in Australia, by volunteers squeezing through tight gaps.

sections.key: Cave animals have evolved to live without light, often losing their eyes and colour.
sections.b: Deep caves are dark, damp and short of food, yet life has moved in. Animals that live their whole lives in caves often look strange to us. Over many generations, many have lost their eyes and pigment, since neither is useful in total darkness, and have developed long antennae or legs and sharp senses of touch and smell. The olm, a pale salamander from the caves of south-eastern Europe, can live for many decades and survive for years without eating. Australia has its own hidden cave fauna, including blind fish and shrimp in the underground waters of Cape Range in Western Australia. Caves also preserve climate records in their formations, so they help scientists read the past. They are fragile places worth protecting.

quiz.q: What acid is mainly responsible for dissolving limestone to form caves?
quiz.e: Rainwater absorbs carbon dioxide to form weak carbonic acid, which dissolves limestone.

quiz.q: Which cave formation grows upward from the floor?
quiz.e: Stalagmites build up from the floor where drips land; stalactites hang from the ceiling.

quiz.q: Why are the Naracoorte Caves so important to scientists?
o: They contain the world's longest underground river
They acted as natural traps, preserving a rich fossil record including megafauna
They hold the world's largest stalactite
quiz.e: Animals fell in and could not escape, leaving fossils spanning hundreds of thousands of years.

quiz.q: What are cenotes?
o: Water-filled sinkholes, famously in Mexico's Yucatán
quiz.e: Cenotes are sinkholes opening into flooded caves, vital to the ancient Maya for water.

quiz.q: Why have many cave animals lost their eyes and colour?
o: Eyes and pigment are of little use in total darkness
They were born without them by accident
quiz.e: Over many generations, traits with no use in darkness have faded away.

LESSONS.title: Jet streams: the rivers of wind above us
LESSONS.hook: High above the clouds, narrow bands of wind race around the planet at hundreds of kilometres an hour. They steer our weather, speed up flights and once carried balloon bombs across an ocean.

sections.key: Jet streams can push an aircraft along so fast that flights arrive early.
sections.b: Every so often a long-haul flight lands well ahead of schedule, and the pilot mentions a strong tailwind. That boost comes from a jet stream, a narrow, fast-flowing band of air high in the atmosphere. Jet streams usually sit about 9 to 16 kilometres above the ground, near the top of the lowest layer of the atmosphere, called the troposphere. Their core winds commonly exceed 100 kilometres per hour, and in strong winter jets they can reach well over 300. They mostly blow from west to east. That is why flights heading east across the Pacific or North Atlantic are often noticeably quicker than the return journey, and why airlines plan routes each day to ride the jet one way and avoid it the other.

sections.key: A Japanese meteorologist measured the jet stream in the 1920s, but few noticed.
sections.b: In the 1920s, the Japanese meteorologist Wasaburo Oishi released weather balloons from near Mount Fuji and tracked them as they rose. He found remarkably strong westerly winds high above Japan and published his results, but largely in Esperanto, and his work attracted little attention outside Japan. During the Second World War, American B-29 bomber crews flying high over Japan ran into fierce headwinds that slowed them almost to a crawl, and the jet stream became widely known. Japan, meanwhile, made use of Oishi's findings. From late 1944, it launched thousands of hydrogen balloons carrying bombs, designed to ride the jet stream across the Pacific to North America. Most failed or landed harmlessly, but one killed six people on a picnic in Oregon in 1945.

sections.key: Jet streams form where warm and cold air masses meet, steered by the Earth's spin.
sections.b: Jet streams are born from temperature differences. The tropics receive far more heat from the Sun than the poles, so the atmosphere is constantly trying to move heat towards the poles. Where a mass of warm air sits beside cold air, the difference in temperature creates a steep difference in air pressure at high altitude, and air begins to flow. The Earth's rotation then deflects that flow, through the Coriolis effect, until it runs mostly from west to east, parallel to the boundary. The sharper the temperature contrast, the faster the wind. Each hemisphere generally has two main jets: a polar front jet, which sits above the boundary between polar and mid-latitude air, and a subtropical jet, which sits closer to the tropics and higher up.

sections.key: Jet streams meander in giant loops called Rossby waves, which shape weather systems.
sections.b: A jet stream is rarely a neat straight band. It snakes around the globe in huge meanders, often thousands of kilometres long, known as Rossby waves after the Swedish American meteorologist Carl-Gustaf Rossby, who explained them in the late 1930s. These waves matter enormously for the weather on the ground. Where the jet bulges towards the pole, warm air pushes poleward behind it. Where it dips towards the equator, cold air follows. The swirling high and low pressure systems on weather maps are closely linked to these loops, and the jet tends to steer storms along its path. Forecasters watch the jet stream closely, because changes in its shape a few days ahead often signal major shifts in temperature and rainfall at the surface.

sections.key: A stalled, wavy jet stream can lock weather in place for days or weeks.
sections.b: Usually the jet stream's waves travel steadily eastward, and weather systems move along with them. Sometimes, though, the pattern stalls. A large high pressure system can become wedged in place, forcing the jet to flow around it in a giant loop. Meteorologists call this a blocking pattern. While a block persists, the same weather can sit over a region for days or even weeks: one area bakes in a heatwave or drought while another suffers repeated rain and flooding. Severe European heatwaves have been linked to blocking highs. In Australia, a related feature is the cut-off low, a pocket of cold air that breaks away from the main flow and lingers, sometimes bringing very heavy rain to the south-east of the continent.

sections.key: The subtropical jet and the westerlies strongly influence southern Australian weather.
sections.b: Australia sits beneath some of the most important jet stream features in the Southern Hemisphere. The subtropical jet often runs across the continent, especially in winter, and it can carry high cloud and moisture from the Indian Ocean diagonally across the country in long bands. Meteorologists call these northwest cloud bands, and they can deliver valuable rain to inland farming areas. Further south, the polar front jet sits above the belt of strong westerly winds over the Southern Ocean that sailors nicknamed the Roaring Forties and Furious Fifties. In winter this belt tends to shift north, sending cold fronts across southern Australia and bringing much of the winter rain to places such as Perth, Adelaide and Melbourne. When the belt stays further south, those regions can be noticeably drier.

sections.key: Jet streams cause clear-air turbulence, and climate change may be altering them.
sections.b: Jet streams are a headache as well as a help for aviation. Where fast-moving air in the jet shears past slower air nearby, it can create clear-air turbulence, invisible bumps that cannot be seen on weather radar because there is no cloud. Pilots rely on forecasts and reports from other aircraft to avoid the worst patches, which is one reason it is sensible to keep your seatbelt fastened while seated. Scientists are also studying how a warming climate affects the jets. Some research suggests that clear-air turbulence over the North Atlantic has increased in recent decades. Other researchers have argued that rapid Arctic warming could make the northern jet wavier and more prone to blocking, but this idea is still debated and the evidence remains mixed.

quiz.q: How did Japan use the jet stream during the Second World War?
o: To launch balloon bombs towards North America
To spread propaganda leaflets over Australia
quiz.e: Japan launched thousands of balloon bombs designed to ride the jet stream across the Pacific.

quiz.q: What mainly drives the formation of jet streams?
o: Temperature contrasts between air masses, plus the Earth's rotation
quiz.e: Warm and cold air side by side create pressure differences, and the Coriolis effect turns the flow eastward.

quiz.q: What are the large meanders in a jet stream called?
quiz.e: They are named after Carl-Gustaf Rossby, who explained them in the late 1930s.

quiz.q: What is a blocking pattern?
o: A storm that blocks out the Sun
A stalled weather pattern that holds the same weather in place for days or weeks
quiz.e: When a large high gets stuck, the jet flows around it and weather stalls.

quiz.q: Why can clear-air turbulence be hard for pilots to avoid?
o: It is invisible on weather radar because there is no cloud
It is caused by other aircraft
quiz.e: Without cloud or rain to detect, pilots rely on forecasts and reports from other planes.

LESSONS.title: The Spanish Armada, 1588
LESSONS.hook: The most powerful empire on Earth sent a giant fleet to conquer England. Fireships, bad maps and brutal storms decided what happened next.

sections.key: The Armada grew out of a long religious and political feud between Catholic Spain and Protestant England.
sections.b: Picture two rulers who had once been in-laws. Philip II of Spain had been married to Mary I of England, Elizabeth I's older half-sister. After Mary died, Elizabeth steered England firmly towards Protestantism, while Philip saw himself as the champion of Catholic Europe. The quarrel deepened for decades. English privateers such as Francis Drake raided Spanish treasure ships and colonies, and Elizabeth sent soldiers to help Dutch Protestants rebelling against Spanish rule. The breaking point came in 1587, when Elizabeth allowed the execution of Mary, Queen of Scots, the Catholic cousin many hoped would replace her. To Philip, invading England now looked like a matter of faith, security and honour all at once. He began assembling the largest fleet his kingdom had ever sent north.

sections.key: Spain's fleet was meant to escort an invasion army across the Channel, not to win England alone.
sections.b: The Armada that sailed in 1588 numbered around 130 ships, carrying sailors, soldiers, priests, horses and enormous quantities of supplies. Its commander was the Duke of Medina Sidonia, a wealthy nobleman with little experience at sea, who had reportedly tried to decline the job. The fleet was not supposed to conquer England by itself. Its task was to sail up the English Channel, link up with the Duke of Parma's veteran army waiting in the Spanish Netherlands, and protect the barges carrying those troops across to Kent. The flaw was obvious in hindsight. There was no deep water port where the big ships and Parma's barges could safely meet, and messages between the two dukes travelled slowly. Coordinating them under enemy fire would prove almost impossible.

sections.h: Cat and mouse in the Channel
sections.key: For a week the English harassed the Armada but could not break its tight formation.
sections.b: In late July 1588 the Spanish ships were sighted off Cornwall, and warning beacons flared along the coast. The Armada moved up the Channel in a disciplined crescent formation, with the strongest warships protecting the slower supply vessels at the centre. The English fleet, led by Lord Howard of Effingham with Drake as one of his senior captains, had faster, nimbler ships and longer range guns. Spanish tactics relied on closing in, grappling and boarding, turning a sea fight into an infantry battle. The English refused to let them get close. Over several days the two fleets exchanged long range fire off Plymouth, Portland and the Isle of Wight. Both sides burned through gunpowder and shot, but the Armada stayed largely intact as it anchored off Calais.

sections.key: A night attack with burning ships broke the Armada's formation and opened the way to a decisive battle.
sections.b: Anchored off Calais, the Armada was vulnerable. Parma's army was not ready, and the Spanish had nowhere safe to wait. On the night of 7 to 8 August, by the modern calendar, the English packed eight old ships with tar, pitch and anything that would burn, set them alight and let wind and tide carry them towards the anchored fleet. Fireships terrified wooden navies, and many Spanish captains cut their anchor cables and scattered into the darkness. By morning the famous crescent was gone. The English attacked off Gravelines, close to the Flemish coast, and this time they came in closer. Several Spanish ships were wrecked or captured, many were badly damaged, and the wind pushed the rest away from Parma's waiting army.

sections.key: Storms and shipwrecks on the voyage around Scotland and Ireland cost Spain far more than English guns did.
sections.b: With the wind blowing from the south and the English fleet behind them, the Spanish could not turn back down the Channel. Medina Sidonia chose to sail north around Scotland and down the west coast of Ireland, a huge detour through unfamiliar, stormy waters. The ships were battered, short of water and food, and their charts of those coasts were poor. Autumn gales drove many onto the rocks of Ireland and Scotland. Thousands of men drowned, and many who reached shore were killed or captured. Historians think roughly a third or more of the fleet never made it back to Spain, and a far larger share of the men died. Most of those losses came from weather, disease and hunger rather than from battle.

sections.key: The Armada crisis helped turn Elizabeth I into a national legend.
sections.b: While the danger was still real, Elizabeth travelled to Tilbury, on the Thames, to review troops gathered to resist an invasion. Accounts written afterwards record her saying that she had the body of a weak and feeble woman, but the heart and stomach of a king, and of a king of England too. Historians debate exactly what she said, because the best known version was written down years later, but the image stuck. After the victory, English propaganda presented the Armada's defeat as a sign of God's favour, describing the storms as a Protestant wind. Medals celebrated the event and portraits showed Elizabeth with the wrecked fleet behind her. For centuries the story was told as proof that a small island could defy a superpower.

sections.key: The Armada did not end Spanish power, but it helped shape how England saw itself.
sections.b: Popular history often treats 1588 as the moment England became a great sea power and Spain began to decline. The reality is messier. The war dragged on until 1604. An English counter attack on Spain and Portugal in 1589 failed badly, and Philip sent further armadas in the 1590s, which were scattered by storms before they could land. Spain remained the dominant power in Europe for decades and rebuilt its navy quickly. Yet the Armada's failure mattered. It kept Protestant England independent, encouraged the Dutch revolt, and gave English sailors confidence for later ventures across the oceans. Perhaps its biggest legacy was a national story about plucky defiance against invasion, one that would be retold in 1805, 1940 and beyond.

quiz.q: Which event in 1587 pushed Philip II to finally launch the invasion?
o: The execution of Mary, Queen of Scots
quiz.e: Elizabeth allowed Mary, Queen of Scots, a Catholic claimant to the throne, to be executed in 1587.

quiz.q: What was the Armada's main job?
o: To escort the Duke of Parma's army across to England
To seize the English treasure fleet
quiz.e: The fleet was meant to link up with Parma's army in the Netherlands and protect its crossing.

quiz.q: What broke up the Armada's formation off Calais?
quiz.e: Burning ships sent in at night made Spanish captains cut their anchors and scatter.

quiz.q: What caused most of the Armada's losses?
o: Storms, shipwrecks, hunger and disease on the way home
quiz.e: The voyage around Scotland and Ireland in autumn gales was far deadlier than the fighting.

quiz.q: What happened after 1588?
