o: The war continued until 1604 and Spain sent more armadas
quiz.e: The war dragged on, and later Spanish fleets were also scattered by storms.

LESSONS.title: The Great Fire of London
LESSONS.hook: In September 1666 a small fire in a bakery grew into a firestorm that swallowed a medieval city. What rose from the ashes still shapes London today.

sections.key: The fire began in the early hours of 2 September 1666 at a bakery near London Bridge.
sections.b: Sometime after midnight on Sunday 2 September 1666, a fire started in the bakery of Thomas Farriner on Pudding Lane, a narrow street close to London Bridge. Farriner later insisted he had put out his oven before bed, but the house was soon ablaze and the family escaped across the rooftops. Fires were common in seventeenth century London, so at first few people panicked. The Lord Mayor, Sir Thomas Bludworth, was woken and reportedly decided the blaze was not worth demolishing neighbouring houses for. It was a costly misjudgement. The summer had been long and dry, the timber buildings were tinder, and a strong east wind was blowing. By morning the fire had reached the warehouses along the Thames, packed with oil, tallow, coal and brandy.

sections.key: Crowded timber houses, narrow lanes and riverside warehouses gave the fire everything it needed.
sections.b: London in 1666 was still largely a medieval city within its old Roman and medieval walls. Houses were made of timber and plaster, often with overhanging upper storeys called jetties that almost touched across the narrow streets, so flames could leap from one side to the other. Rubbish, hay and firewood were stored everywhere. Firefighting technology was basic: leather buckets, axes, simple hand pumps and long hooks for pulling down buildings. There was no organised fire brigade. The city had also just been through the Great Plague of 1665, which killed perhaps a fifth of its population, so many Londoners were already exhausted and frightened. When the fire reached the riverfront, the warehouses acted like fuel depots, and the blaze became too hot for anyone to approach.

sections.key: The fire raged from Sunday to Wednesday, driven by wind and checked at last by firebreaks.
sections.b: For about four days the fire swept west and north across the city. People fled with whatever they could carry, piling belongings into carts and boats, and prices for transport soared. The heat was so intense that St Paul's Cathedral, which was covered in wooden scaffolding for repairs, caught fire; its lead roof melted and reportedly ran down the streets. King Charles II and his brother James, Duke of York, took charge, joining the effort to create firebreaks by pulling down or blowing up houses with gunpowder. On Tuesday night the wind finally eased. Combined with the firebreaks, this allowed the fire to be brought under control by Wednesday and Thursday, though cellars and rubble smouldered for weeks afterwards.

sections.key: Eyewitness diaries give us vivid, human details of the disaster.
sections.b: Much of what we know comes from two famous diarists, Samuel Pepys and John Evelyn. Pepys, a naval administrator, watched from a boat on the Thames and described pigeons hanging around their homes until their wings caught fire. He hurried to warn the king and urged that houses be pulled down. Like many Londoners he also worried about his valuables. He records digging a pit in his garden with a colleague to bury wine and his parmesan cheese, along with official papers. Evelyn described the sky glowing red for miles and the ground so hot it was hard to walk on. These diaries show not only the scale of the fire but also the confusion, fear and everyday practicality of people caught in it.

sections.key: The fire destroyed most of the old city, though the recorded death toll was surprisingly low.
sections.b: When the smoke cleared, around 13,000 houses had been destroyed, along with 87 parish churches, St Paul's Cathedral, the Guildhall and many other public buildings. Tens of thousands of people were homeless, camping in the fields north of the city. Only a handful of deaths were officially recorded, but historians think the true number was higher, since the deaths of poor people and anyone consumed by the intense heat may never have been counted. People wanted someone to blame. Foreigners and Catholics were attacked in the streets. A French watchmaker named Robert Hubert confessed to starting the fire and was hanged, even though evidence later suggested he had not even been in London when it began. An inquiry eventually concluded the fire was an accident.

sections.key: Grand plans for a new city lost out to practical rebuilding, but with new safety rules.
sections.b: Within days, architects including Christopher Wren and John Evelyn presented plans for a new London with wide boulevards and open piazzas, rather like a European capital. None was adopted. Property owners wanted their land back quickly, and sorting out who owned what was hard enough already. Instead, the city was rebuilt largely along its old street pattern, but with important changes. New laws required buildings to be made of brick or stone, set limits on heights and widened some streets. Wren designed the new St Paul's Cathedral, with its famous dome, which took several decades to complete, along with dozens of new city churches. A special Fire Court settled disputes between landlords and tenants so rebuilding could get moving.

sections.key: From insurance to a famous column, the Great Fire left lasting marks on modern life.
sections.b: Near Pudding Lane stands the Monument, a tall stone column designed by Wren and Robert Hooke. It is 202 feet high, roughly 61 metres, and sits about 202 feet from where the bakery stood. The fire also helped launch modern property insurance: in the following years, businesses began offering cover against fire, and some ran their own teams of firefighters to protect insured buildings. A popular story says the fire ended the plague by burning the rats, but historians are doubtful, because the plague was already declining and also faded in areas the fire never touched. What is certain is that the disaster changed how cities thought about fire safety, building materials and planning, lessons that later shaped building codes around the world, including in Australia.

quiz.q: Where did the Great Fire of London start?
o: In a bakery on Pudding Lane
In a theatre on the South Bank
quiz.e: It began in Thomas Farriner's bakery on Pudding Lane, near London Bridge.

quiz.q: Why did flames spread so easily between houses?
o: The houses were timber, with upper storeys that nearly touched across narrow lanes
The streets were paved with wood
quiz.e: Overhanging timber jetties let fire leap across the narrow streets.

quiz.q: What did Samuel Pepys famously bury in his garden?
quiz.e: Pepys records burying wine, official papers and his parmesan cheese.

quiz.q: What did new building rules require after the fire?
o: Houses no taller than one storey
Buildings made of brick or stone
quiz.e: Rebuilding laws required brick or stone construction and set height limits.

quiz.q: What is notable about the Monument's height?
o: It matches its distance from the site of the bakery
It is the tallest structure in Europe
It is exactly as tall as St Paul's
It was built in a single day
quiz.e: The column is 202 feet tall and stands about 202 feet from where the fire started.

LESSONS.title: The East India Company: a business that ruled
LESSONS.hook: It began as a group of London merchants chasing pepper. Within two centuries it had its own army and ruled millions of people across India.

sections.key: The East India Company began in 1600 as a trading venture backed by investors and a royal monopoly.
sections.b: On the last day of 1600, Elizabeth I granted a charter to a group of London merchants, giving them the sole English right to trade with Asia. Their target was spices, especially pepper, which earned huge profits in Europe. The Company was an early joint stock venture: investors pooled money to fund risky voyages and shared the returns. Its great rival, the Dutch East India Company, founded in 1602, was richer and more aggressive, and soon pushed the English out of the most lucrative spice islands in what is now Indonesia. So the English turned to India instead. There they found something even more valuable than pepper: cotton textiles. Bright, washable Indian calicoes and chintzes became a fashion craze back home.

sections.key: For over a century the Company was a trader that depended on the favour of Indian rulers.
sections.b: In its early years the Company was a junior player in a rich, powerful region. Much of India was ruled by the Mughal Empire, one of the wealthiest states in the world. The Company negotiated with emperors and local governors for permission to trade, setting up trading posts called factories. Its main bases grew into Madras, now Chennai, in the south; Bombay, now Mumbai, which came to England as part of Charles II's marriage settlement and was handed to the Company; and Calcutta, now Kolkata, in Bengal. These posts were fortified and guarded by small private forces. As Mughal power weakened in the eighteenth century and regional rulers competed for control, the Company began to use its soldiers and money to play politics as well as trade.

sections.h: Plassey: a battle and a betrayal
sections.key: In 1757 the Company won control of Bengal more through intrigue than fighting.
sections.b: Bengal was one of the richest provinces in India, and in 1756 its young ruler, the Nawab Siraj ud-Daulah, captured Calcutta after the Company strengthened its fortifications without permission. A Company officer, Robert Clive, sailed north to take it back. Clive was ambitious and ruthless, and he found allies among Bengal's elite who wanted the Nawab gone, including his army commander Mir Jafar. At the Battle of Plassey in 1757, Clive's much smaller force faced the Nawab's army, but much of that army never fought because its commanders had already agreed to switch sides. Siraj ud-Daulah was later killed and Mir Jafar was installed as a puppet ruler. Huge sums flowed to the Company and to Clive personally, who returned to Britain extremely rich.

sections.key: Winning the right to collect Bengal's taxes turned the Company into a government.
sections.b: The real turning point came in 1765. After further fighting, the weakened Mughal emperor granted the Company the diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa: the right to collect land revenue across a vast and populous region. Instead of bringing silver from Britain to buy Indian goods, the Company could now use Indian taxes to pay for them, and for its growing army. Its officials were poorly supervised and often grew rich through private trade and bribes, earning the mocking nickname 'nabobs' back in Britain. In 1770 a devastating famine struck Bengal. Millions died, possibly as much as a third of the population in the worst areas, and critics accused the Company of making things worse by keeping up harsh tax collection while people starved.

sections.key: Britain's government stepped in when the Company's power and debts became a national problem.
sections.b: By the early 1770s the Company was both mighty and in financial trouble, and Parliament grew alarmed that a private business was running an empire. The Regulating Act of 1773 began bringing it under government oversight, and later laws went further, creating a government board to supervise its political decisions. Also in 1773, the Tea Act tried to help the struggling Company sell surplus tea in the American colonies, which led directly to the Boston Tea Party. In Britain, Warren Hastings, the first Governor General of Bengal, was impeached for corruption and abuse of power in a famous trial that ran for seven years. He was eventually acquitted, but the trial showed how uneasy many Britons felt about the Company's conduct in India.

sections.h: An army with a company attached
sections.key: By the early 1800s the Company commanded an army larger than Britain's own.
sections.b: Through the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries the Company fought a series of wars against Indian powers, including the Kingdom of Mysore and the Maratha Confederacy. Most of its soldiers were Indian troops known as sepoys, led by British officers. Historians estimate its armies numbered in the hundreds of thousands at their peak, larger than the regular British Army at the time. By the 1850s the Company directly ruled much of the subcontinent and controlled many princely states through treaties. It also grew opium in India and sold it to traders who smuggled it into China, helping to pay for its purchases of Chinese tea. Meanwhile, Parliament stripped away its trading monopolies, leaving it more a government than a business.

sections.key: After the uprising of 1857, the British Crown took over, and the Company faded away.
sections.b: In 1857 a mutiny by sepoys at Meerut spread into a widespread rebellion across northern India, fuelled by many grievances, from annexations and taxes to fears about religious interference. The fighting was brutal on both sides, and the British response was savage. Afterwards, Parliament decided the Company could no longer be trusted with India. In 1858 the British Crown took direct control, beginning the period known as the Raj, and the Company was formally dissolved in 1874. Its legacy is debated to this day. It left behind cities, railways planned in its final years and words such as 'loot', borrowed from Hindi. It also stands as a warning about what can happen when a profit seeking corporation holds unchecked political and military power.

quiz.q: What did the East India Company first come to Asia for?
quiz.e: The Company's founders were chasing the hugely profitable spice trade.

quiz.q: How did Robert Clive win at Plassey in 1757?
o: Because key commanders in the Nawab's army had agreed to switch sides
quiz.e: Mir Jafar and others had secretly agreed to betray Siraj ud-Daulah, so much of his army did not fight.

quiz.q: What was the diwani the Company gained in 1765?
o: The right to collect land revenue in Bengal and nearby regions
A seat in the Mughal court
quiz.e: The diwani let the Company collect taxes, turning it into a governing power.

quiz.q: Which American event was linked to the Company's troubles?
quiz.e: The 1773 Tea Act, meant to help the Company sell tea, sparked the Boston Tea Party.

quiz.q: What happened to India after the 1857 rebellion?
o: The British Crown took direct control
quiz.e: In 1858 the Crown took over from the Company, beginning the Raj.

LESSONS.title: Meiji Japan: the great makeover
LESSONS.hook: In about forty years, Japan went from a closed realm of samurai and shoguns to an industrial power that defeated a European empire. How did it happen so fast?

sections.key: For more than two centuries Japan strictly limited contact with the outside world.
sections.b: In the early 1600s the Tokugawa family unified Japan after long civil wars and ruled as shoguns, military leaders who held real power while the emperor lived in ceremonial seclusion in Kyoto. Worried about Christian missionaries and European influence, the shoguns restricted foreign contact. Japanese people were generally forbidden to travel abroad, and European trade was limited to the Dutch, confined to a small artificial island called Dejima in Nagasaki harbour. Trade with China and Korea continued under controls. Inside these walls Japan was not frozen. Cities such as Edo, now Tokyo, grew huge, literacy was relatively high and arts like kabuki theatre and woodblock prints flourished. But Japan's rulers had little idea how quickly Western industry and military technology were changing.

sections.key: American warships in 1853 forced Japan to open up and exposed the shogunate's weakness.
sections.b: In July 1853 four American ships steamed into Edo Bay under Commodore Matthew Perry. Two were steam powered, belching black smoke, and the Japanese called them the black ships. Perry carried a letter demanding that Japan open its ports to American ships for supplies and trade, and he made it clear he would return. When he came back in 1854 with a larger squadron, the shogunate signed the Treaty of Kanagawa. Agreements with other Western powers soon followed, including 'unequal treaties' that fixed low tariffs and let foreigners be tried in their own courts rather than Japanese ones. Many Japanese were humiliated. The shogun seemed unable to protect the country, and his critics began rallying around the emperor instead.

sections.key: In 1868 rebel samurai toppled the shogunate and ruled in the name of a teenage emperor.
sections.b: Through the 1860s, ambitious samurai from southwestern domains, especially Satsuma and Choshu, plotted against the Tokugawa. Their early slogan was 'revere the emperor, expel the barbarians', but clashes with Western warships taught them that expelling foreigners was impossible. They concluded Japan would have to learn from the West to resist it. In late 1867 and early 1868 the last shogun gave up power, and after a short civil war the new leaders declared the emperor restored to direct rule. The emperor was a teenager named Mutsuhito, and his reign took the name Meiji, usually translated as 'enlightened rule'. In practice a small group of young oligarchs governed in his name. The imperial court moved to Edo, which was renamed Tokyo, meaning 'eastern capital'.

sections.key: Japan's new leaders dismantled the old class system, even though most of them were samurai themselves.
sections.b: The new government moved astonishingly fast. In 1871 it abolished the old feudal domains and replaced them with prefectures run from Tokyo. The rigid class system was dismantled, and samurai lost their hereditary stipends, which were converted into government bonds. A conscript army of ordinary men replaced the samurai's monopoly on fighting, and in 1876 the wearing of swords in public was largely banned. Many samurai adapted, becoming officials, teachers, police officers or businessmen. Others resisted. The biggest uprising was the Satsuma Rebellion of 1877, led by Saigo Takamori, once a hero of the restoration. The new conscript army crushed it, and Saigo died in the final battle. He became a romantic legend, loosely echoed much later in the Hollywood film The Last Samurai.

sections.key: Japan studied Western nations closely and adopted what it thought worked best.
sections.b: In 1871 a large government delegation known as the Iwakura Mission set off to visit the United States and Europe. It spent well over a year touring factories, schools, parliaments, shipyards and prisons, taking careful notes. Japan then borrowed selectively: a navy modelled on Britain's, an army influenced first by France and later by Germany, legal codes drawing on French and German law, and a school system with ideas from several countries. The government hired thousands of foreign experts, then gradually replaced them with Japanese graduates. A popular slogan captured the goal: 'rich country, strong army'. Another phrase described the balance many hoped for, Japanese spirit with Western techniques. Clothing, hairstyles and even the calendar changed, as Japan adopted the Western solar calendar from 1873.

sections.key: Industry, education and a new constitution turned Japan into a modern state.
sections.b: Japan's first railway, between Tokyo and Yokohama, opened in 1872, and lines soon spread across the country. The government built model factories, including a large silk mill at Tomioka, then sold many enterprises cheaply to private businesses, helping create powerful family conglomerates known as zaibatsu, such as Mitsubishi and Mitsui. Silk exports earned the foreign currency Japan needed to buy machinery and warships. Primary schooling became compulsory, and literacy climbed even higher. In 1889 the emperor granted a written constitution, influenced by Prussia's, which created an elected parliament called the Diet. Voting was restricted to a small minority of wealthy men, and the emperor was declared sacred and inviolable, but it made Japan the first East Asian nation with a Western style constitution.

sections.h: A new power, and a warning
sections.key: Victories over China and Russia made Japan a great power, but also set it on the road to empire.
sections.b: Japan's transformation was tested in war. In 1894 to 1895 it defeated China and took Taiwan as a colony. Then, in 1904 to 1905, it shocked the world by defeating Russia on land and at sea, the first time in modern history that an Asian nation had beaten a European great power in a major war. Japan had already won agreement in 1894 to end foreign extraterritoriality, and it regained full control of its tariffs in 1911. When the Meiji emperor died in 1912, Japan was an industrial and colonial power that had annexed Korea in 1910. The Meiji era is often held up as a model of rapid modernisation. But the same drive for national strength, and the army's growing political power, helped set Japan on a path towards militarism, expansion in Asia and, eventually, the Pacific War.

quiz.q: Which Europeans could still trade with Tokugawa Japan?
o: The Dutch, on the island of Dejima
quiz.e: Dutch traders were confined to Dejima in Nagasaki harbour.

quiz.q: What did Commodore Perry's 1853 visit demand?
o: That Japan open its ports to American ships
quiz.e: Perry demanded access to Japanese ports for supplies and trade.

quiz.q: What was the Satsuma Rebellion of 1877?
o: A peasant revolt over rice prices
A samurai uprising crushed by the new conscript army
quiz.e: Saigo Takamori led samurai against the government, and the conscript army defeated them.

quiz.q: What did the 1889 constitution create?
o: Full voting rights for all adults
An elected parliament called the Diet
quiz.e: It established the Diet, though only a small minority of men could vote.

quiz.q: Why was Japan's victory over Russia in 1904 to 1905 so significant?
o: It was the first modern defeat of a European great power by an Asian nation in a major war
It gave Japan control of China
quiz.e: The victory stunned the world and confirmed Japan as a great power.

LESSONS.title: The Opium Wars and China's century of humiliation
LESSONS.hook: Britain went to war so its merchants could keep selling a drug China had banned. The consequences still shape China's view of the West.

sections.key: Britain's thirst for Chinese tea created a trade imbalance that opium was used to fix.
sections.b: By the late 1700s the British were drinking enormous amounts of tea, and almost all of it came from China. The trouble was that China wanted very little that Britain made. The Qing government also strictly controlled foreign trade, confining Western merchants to the port of Canton, now Guangzhou, where they dealt through licensed Chinese merchants. So the British paid in silver, and silver flowed steadily out of Britain towards China. The East India Company found a solution in the fields of Bengal, which it controlled. It grew opium there and sold it at auction in Calcutta to private traders. Those traders carried it to the Chinese coast and smuggled it ashore, keeping the Company's own hands technically clean. Silver began flowing the other way.

sections.h: A nation in the grip of a drug
sections.key: Opium smuggling exploded in the early 1800s, alarming the Qing government.
sections.b: China had banned opium smoking and imports, but the bans were widely ignored. Smugglers worked with corrupt officials, and by the 1830s tens of thousands of chests were arriving each year. Addiction spread from the wealthy to soldiers, officials and labourers, and opium dens appeared in many cities. For the government, the crisis was both moral and financial. Officials worried about the damage to people and to the army, and about the drain of silver out of the country, which was pushing up the cost of silver and making taxes harder for ordinary farmers to pay. In Beijing there was a fierce debate over whether to legalise and tax the trade or to crush it. The Daoguang Emperor chose to crush it.

sections.key: In 1839 Lin Zexu seized and destroyed a vast stockpile of foreign opium.
sections.b: The emperor sent an incorruptible official, Lin Zexu, to Canton in 1839 with orders to end the trade. Lin arrested Chinese dealers, pressured smokers to give up the drug and then blockaded the foreign merchants in their warehouses until they surrendered their stocks. The British superintendent of trade, Charles Elliot, persuaded the merchants to hand over more than 20,000 chests, promising that the British government would compensate them. Lin had the opium mixed with lime and salt in large trenches at Humen and flushed out to sea, a process that took weeks. He also wrote a letter addressed to Queen Victoria, asking how Britain could allow a poison it banned at home to be sold to China. Historians doubt she ever read it.

sections.key: Britain sent warships, and modern firepower overwhelmed Qing forces.
sections.b: News of the seized opium caused uproar among British merchants, who lobbied for war. In Parliament some members, including a young William Gladstone, condemned the idea as unjust and shameful, but the government sent a naval force anyway. The war that began in 1839 and ran until 1842 was lopsided. British warships, including the iron steamship Nemesis, which could navigate shallow rivers, destroyed Chinese war junks and coastal forts. British forces captured key cities and finally threatened Nanjing, the old southern capital. The Qing armies fought bravely in places but were outgunned and badly coordinated. Officials sometimes sent misleading reports to Beijing, so the emperor did not fully grasp how badly things were going until it was too late.

sections.key: The peace of 1842 began a series of unequal treaties forced on China.
sections.b: The Treaty of Nanking, signed in 1842, was the first of what Chinese later called the unequal treaties. China paid a large indemnity, including compensation for the destroyed opium. It handed Hong Kong Island to Britain and opened five ports, including Shanghai, to British trade and residence. Supplementary agreements gave British subjects extraterritoriality, meaning they would be tried under British law rather than Chinese law, and guaranteed Britain any privileges China granted to other nations. The United States and France soon secured similar treaties. Strikingly, the treaty did not mention opium. The drug trade carried on and grew. Foreign concessions in the treaty ports became small enclaves where Chinese authority barely reached, and Shanghai grew into a booming international city.

sections.key: A second war, fought by Britain and France, ended with the burning of the emperor's summer palace.
sections.b: Western powers wanted still more access, including diplomats in Beijing and trade inland. In 1856 Chinese officials boarded the Arrow, a ship registered in Hong Kong, and Britain used the incident to go to war again, this time alongside France. The Second Opium War dragged on until 1860. When Qing officials detained and mistreated a British and French negotiating party, some of whom died, the British envoy Lord Elgin ordered the destruction of the Old Summer Palace outside Beijing, a vast complex of gardens and pavilions. Troops looted its treasures, many of which remain in Western collections, and burned it. The treaties that followed opened more ports, allowed foreign envoys in Beijing, ceded Kowloon to Britain and effectively legalised the opium trade.

sections.key: The Opium Wars remain central to how China understands its modern history.
sections.b: The wars weakened the Qing dynasty at a terrible time. The Taiping Rebellion, which began in 1850, killed perhaps 20 million people or more, and further defeats and concessions followed for decades. In 1898 Britain leased the New Territories next to Kowloon for 99 years, which is why Hong Kong returned to Chinese rule in 1997. In China, the period from 1839 to the founding of the People's Republic in 1949 is often called the century of humiliation, and it features heavily in school textbooks and national messaging. Many in the West know little about the Opium Wars. Understanding them helps explain why China's leaders talk so often about sovereignty, foreign interference and national rejuvenation, and why history remains a sensitive subject in relations today.

quiz.q: Why did Britain begin selling opium to China?
o: To pay for tea without sending so much silver
quiz.e: Opium sales reversed the flow of silver that buying Chinese tea had created.

quiz.q: What did Commissioner Lin Zexu do with the seized opium?
o: Mixed it with lime and salt and flushed it out to sea
quiz.e: More than 20,000 chests were destroyed in trenches at Humen.

quiz.q: What advantage helped Britain win the First Opium War?
o: Superior naval firepower, including the steamship Nemesis
Support from the Qing emperor's rivals
quiz.e: Modern warships, including the iron steamer Nemesis, overwhelmed Chinese defences.

quiz.q: Which territory did China cede to Britain in 1842?
quiz.e: The Treaty of Nanking handed Hong Kong Island to Britain.

quiz.q: Why did Hong Kong return to China in 1997?
o: The 99 year lease on the New Territories expired
The Treaty of Nanking set that date
quiz.e: The 1898 lease ran out in 1997, and Britain returned the whole colony.

LESSONS.title: The Thirty Years' War
LESSONS.hook: It began with three men thrown from a castle window and became one of the deadliest wars in European history. Its peace treaties helped shape the idea of the modern state.

sections.key: The war began with a dramatic act of defiance in Prague in 1618.
sections.b: In May 1618, a group of angry Protestant nobles stormed into Prague Castle, seized two Catholic officials representing the Habsburg emperor, along with their secretary, and threw them out of a high window. Remarkably, all three survived the fall. Catholics claimed angels had saved them; Protestants mocked that they had landed in a dung heap. The event, known as the Defenestration of Prague, was a protest against the Habsburgs, who ruled Bohemia and were restricting Protestant rights there. The Bohemian nobles then rejected their Habsburg king and offered the crown to a Protestant prince, Frederick V of the Palatinate. A local revolt was about to grow into a conflict that would drag in most of Europe's major powers for three decades.

sections.key: The Holy Roman Empire's complex politics made the conflict hard to contain.
sections.b: To understand the war, picture central Europe as a patchwork. The Holy Roman Empire covered much of what is now Germany, Austria, the Czech Republic and more, but it was not a unified country. It contained hundreds of states, from large principalities to tiny territories and free cities, each with its own ruler. The emperor, usually a Habsburg, had real but limited authority. Since the Peace of Augsburg in 1555, each ruler could choose whether their territory was Lutheran or Catholic, a principle later summed up as 'whose realm, his religion'. Calvinism, a growing Protestant movement, had not been included in that settlement. Religious tensions, rival dynasties and foreign powers eager to weaken the Habsburgs made the empire a tinderbox waiting for a spark.

sections.key: The Catholic Habsburgs crushed the Bohemian revolt and then pushed north, alarming Protestant Europe.
sections.b: Frederick V's reign in Bohemia was so brief that he became known as the Winter King. In 1620 imperial and Catholic League forces crushed his army at the Battle of White Mountain, outside Prague. Bohemia was forcibly returned to Catholicism, Protestant nobles were executed or driven out, and their lands were handed to loyal supporters. The war then spread. King Christian IV of Denmark, a Lutheran who also held lands within the empire, intervened in 1625 but was defeated. The emperor's armies were now led partly by Albrecht von Wallenstein, a brilliant and enormously wealthy military entrepreneur who raised his own huge army and paid for it by forcing occupied regions to supply money and food. By the late 1620s the Catholic side seemed close to total victory.

sections.key: Sweden's King Gustavus Adolphus transformed the war before dying in battle.
sections.b: In 1630 a new force landed on the German coast: King Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden, a Lutheran with a highly trained, disciplined army and modern tactics, including mobile field artillery and flexible infantry formations. Nicknamed the Lion of the North, he defeated the imperial army decisively at Breitenfeld in 1631 and swept deep into southern Germany. His campaign was funded partly by Catholic France, which cared more about weakening the Habsburgs than about religion. In 1632 Gustavus was killed at the Battle of Lützen, though the Swedes won the battle itself. Two years later Wallenstein, suspected by the emperor of secret negotiations and disloyalty, was assassinated by his own officers. The war had lost its most famous commanders but showed no sign of ending.

sections.key: When France entered openly in 1635, the war became a struggle for power more than for faith.
sections.b: In 1635 France, guided by its chief minister Cardinal Richelieu, openly declared war on Spain and soon fought the Austrian Habsburgs too. This was a striking moment: a Catholic kingdom, led by a cardinal of the Catholic Church, fighting alongside Protestant Sweden and German princes against the Catholic Habsburgs. It showed that the war had become mainly about power and the balance of Europe. France feared being encircled by Habsburg lands in Spain, Italy, the Netherlands and Germany. The fighting spread across many fronts and grew increasingly about who would dominate the continent. Meanwhile, armies on all sides lived off the land, marching back and forth across the same German territories, plundering towns and villages again and again.

sections.key: Civilians suffered most, through massacre, famine and disease.
sections.b: The worst single atrocity was the sack of Magdeburg in 1631, when imperial troops stormed the Protestant city and it burned. Historians estimate that about 20,000 people died, and the city was left almost empty. Yet most deaths in the war came not from battles but from what armies brought with them. Soldiers seized crops and livestock, burned farms and spread diseases such as typhus and plague. Refugees crowded into towns where hunger and sickness followed. Estimates vary, but many historians think the German lands lost roughly a fifth or more of their population, with some regions losing far more. Artists recorded the horror, notably Jacques Callot in his etchings The Miseries of War, and the novel Simplicius Simplicissimus captured the chaos through a wandering soldier's eyes.

sections.key: The peace of 1648 redrew Europe's map and helped define how states deal with each other.
sections.b: Peace talks dragged on for years in two Westphalian towns, Münster and Osnabrück, with delegations from across Europe. The resulting Peace of Westphalia in 1648 recognised the independence of the Dutch Republic from Spain and of the Swiss Confederation, gave territory to France and Sweden, and allowed German princes greater freedom to run their own affairs. Calvinism was finally recognised alongside Lutheranism and Catholicism. Political scientists often describe 'Westphalian sovereignty', the idea that states are equal and should not interfere in each other's internal affairs, as born here. Historians point out that this is partly a later myth, since the treaties themselves were more complicated. Even so, Westphalia marked a shift away from wars fought mainly over religion towards a Europe of competing sovereign states.

quiz.q: What was the Defenestration of Prague?
o: Protestant nobles throwing Habsburg officials from a castle window
The execution of the Bohemian king
A siege of Prague by Sweden
quiz.e: In 1618 Protestant nobles threw two officials and their secretary out of a window, and all three survived.

quiz.q: Which Protestant group had been left out of the Peace of Augsburg in 1555?
quiz.e: Augsburg let rulers choose Lutheranism or Catholicism, but Calvinism was not included.

quiz.q: What happened to Gustavus Adolphus in 1632?
o: He was killed at the Battle of Lützen
He signed a peace with France
He was assassinated by his officers
quiz.e: He died at Lützen, although the Swedes won the battle.

quiz.q: Why was France's entry into the war in 1635 so striking?
o: France was led by a Protestant king
A Catholic kingdom fought against the Catholic Habsburgs
quiz.e: Led by Cardinal Richelieu, France fought the Habsburgs to protect its own power.

quiz.q: Which country's independence did the Peace of Westphalia recognise?
quiz.e: The 1648 settlement recognised the Dutch Republic's independence from Spain.

LESSONS.title: Kokoda: the track that shaped a nation
LESSONS.hook: In 1942, on a muddy jungle path in Papua, young Australian soldiers fought to stop a Japanese advance on Port Moresby. Kokoda became one of Australia's defining wartime stories.

sections.key: In 1942 Japan's rapid advance brought the war close to Australia's doorstep.
sections.b: Early in 1942, Japan seemed unstoppable. Singapore fell in February, and thousands of Australian soldiers became prisoners of war. Days later Darwin was bombed. Papua, on the island of New Guinea, was then an Australian territory, and its capital, Port Moresby, lay just across the Torres Strait from Queensland. Japanese commanders wanted to capture it as a base that could threaten northern Australia and cut its links with the United States. An attempt to reach Port Moresby by sea was turned back after the Battle of the Coral Sea in May 1942. So in July Japanese forces landed on Papua's northern coast, near Buna and Gona, planning to march overland across the rugged Owen Stanley Range and seize the town from behind.

sections.key: The Kokoda Track was a narrow, steep path through some of the world's toughest terrain.
sections.b: The Kokoda Track runs for about 96 kilometres between the outskirts of Port Moresby and the village of Kokoda, which had a small airstrip. It is not a road but a footpath, used for generations by local people, climbing and plunging over steep ridges and through dense rainforest. Soldiers described climbing slippery slopes on hands and knees, crossing fast rivers and sleeping in mud as rain fell day after day. It was hot and humid in the valleys and cold at night on the high ridges. Malaria, dysentery and exhaustion struck everyone. Every bullet, tin of food and stretcher had to be carried in on someone's back. Historians often say the terrain itself was as much an enemy as the opposing army.

sections.key: Poorly trained militia troops were the first to face the Japanese advance.
sections.b: When the Japanese landed, the only Australian troops in their path were a small force of local Papuan police and soldiers, and the 39th Battalion. The 39th was a militia unit made up of young, mostly inexperienced volunteers and conscripts, many still in their teens. Some regular soldiers had mocked militia troops as 'chocos', or chocolate soldiers, who would melt under pressure. On Kokoda they did nothing of the sort. Heavily outnumbered, they fought a series of desperate actions around Kokoda village, losing and briefly retaking it before being forced back. In August, under a new commander, Lieutenant Colonel Ralph Honner, they held on at Isurava until reinforcements arrived. Their stand became one of the proudest stories in Australian military history.

sections.key: Experienced AIF battalions joined the fight, slowing the Japanese at a heavy cost.
sections.b: In late August, battle hardened soldiers of the Second Australian Imperial Force, veterans of fighting in the Middle East, reached the front. The 2/14th and 2/16th Battalions joined the 39th in a fierce battle at Isurava against a much larger Japanese force. During this fighting, Private Bruce Kingsbury charged forward firing a Bren gun from the hip, breaking up an enemy attack before he was killed by a sniper. He was awarded the Victoria Cross after his death, the first awarded for action on Australian territory. The Australians could not hold Isurava, but they made the Japanese pay for every ridge. Over the following weeks they conducted a fighting withdrawal back along the track towards Port Moresby, exhausted, hungry and sick.

sections.key: Papuan carriers moved supplies forward and carried the wounded back, saving countless lives.
sections.b: The campaign could not have been fought without thousands of Papuan men recruited, some under pressure, to work as carriers. They hauled heavy loads of food and ammunition up the mountains and, most famously, carried wounded Australians on stretchers for days through the jungle, sheltering them at night and treating them with great care. Soldiers wrote with deep gratitude about their kindness. A poem by an Australian sapper, Bert Beros, called them the Fuzzy Wuzzy Angels, and the name stuck for decades, though some now consider it outdated. The carriers were poorly paid and often worked in harsh conditions themselves. In recent years Australia has done more to recognise their contribution, which many veterans believed had never been properly honoured.

sections.key: By late 1942 the Japanese had been ordered back, and Australians pushed them to the coast.
sections.b: By mid September the Japanese had reached Ioribaiwa Ridge, within sight of the lights of Port Moresby, according to many accounts. But they were starving and stretched thin at the end of a long supply line. Japan had also suffered setbacks elsewhere, including defeat by Australian forces at Milne Bay, on Papua's eastern tip, and heavy fighting with the Americans at Guadalcanal. The Japanese were ordered to withdraw. Australian troops then pursued them back along the track, fighting hard battles at places such as Eora Creek and Oivi to Gorari, and recaptured Kokoda on 2 November 1942. The campaign ended with bloody battles alongside American troops at Buna, Gona and Sanananda, which lasted into January 1943.

sections.key: Kokoda has become a pilgrimage site and a central part of how Australians remember the war.
sections.b: More than 600 Australians were killed on the Kokoda Track and over a thousand were wounded, with many more struck down by disease. Japanese losses were much greater, many from starvation and illness. Cameraman Damien Parer filmed the campaign, and his newsreel Kokoda Front Line! won an Academy Award, bringing the jungle war home to cinema audiences. For decades Kokoda received less attention than Gallipoli, but that began to change. In 1992 Prime Minister Paul Keating knelt and kissed the ground at Kokoda, arguing that Australians had fought there to defend their own country. Today thousands of Australians walk the track each year with Papuan guides, a hard trek that ends at memorials honouring both the soldiers and the carriers.

quiz.q: Why did Japanese forces want to capture Port Moresby?
o: To use it as a base threatening Australia and its links with the United States
To reach the gold fields of Papua
To build a railway to Darwin
quiz.e: Port Moresby would have given Japan a base close to northern Australia.

quiz.q: Which Australian unit first fought the Japanese on the track?
quiz.e: The young militiamen of the 39th faced the early Japanese advance.

quiz.q: Who was awarded a Victoria Cross for his actions at Isurava?
quiz.e: Private Bruce Kingsbury was awarded the VC after his death, the first for action on Australian territory.

quiz.q: What role did Papuan carriers play?
o: They carried supplies forward and wounded soldiers back
They built the airstrip at Darwin
quiz.e: Papuan carriers moved vital supplies and carried the wounded for days through the jungle.

quiz.q: What did Paul Keating do at Kokoda in 1992?
quiz.e: Keating kissed the ground, highlighting Kokoda's place in Australian memory.

LESSONS.title: Chernobyl: the night a reactor exploded
LESSONS.hook: In April 1986 a late night safety test went catastrophically wrong in Soviet Ukraine. The disaster spread radiation across Europe and shook the Soviet Union to its core.

sections.h: A test in the middle of the night
sections.key: The disaster began during a poorly managed safety test at reactor number 4.
sections.b: The Chernobyl nuclear power plant stood in the north of Soviet Ukraine, near the new town of Pripyat, home to tens of thousands of workers and their families. In the early hours of 26 April 1986, operators at reactor number 4 were running a test. They wanted to check whether the spinning turbines could keep supplying power to cooling pumps for a short time if the electricity supply failed. The test had already been delayed, so a night shift that had not prepared for it carried it out. To run it, operators reduced the reactor's power and disabled several safety systems. The reactor became unstable at low power, and operators withdrew most of the control rods to try to keep it running. It was a deadly combination.

sections.key: Design flaws in the Soviet RBMK reactor combined with operator errors to cause an explosion.
sections.b: Chernobyl used a Soviet design known as the RBMK, which had dangerous features that operators were not fully told about. In this design, if cooling water turned to steam, the reactor's power could increase rather than fall, a feedback loop that can run out of control. When the test began, power started to rise. An operator pressed the emergency shutdown button, sending control rods back into the core. But a flaw in the rods meant that, for a few seconds, their tips actually boosted the reaction in parts of the core. Power surged enormously. Steam explosions blew apart the reactor and threw off its heavy lid. The graphite inside caught fire, sending radioactive material high into the sky for days.

sections.key: Firefighters and plant workers fought the blaze, many unaware of the danger they faced.
sections.b: Firefighters raced to the plant within minutes, fighting fires on the roof and around the reactor building. Few understood how intense the radiation was. Some reportedly picked up chunks of graphite thrown from the core. Two plant workers died on the night of the explosion, and in the following weeks and months around 28 more, mostly firefighters and staff, died from acute radiation sickness. Many were flown to a specialist hospital in Moscow, where doctors could do little. Over the following days, helicopters dropped thousands of tonnes of sand, clay, lead and other materials onto the burning reactor to smother it. Later, miners dug beneath the reactor to install cooling, and huge numbers of workers known as liquidators were brought in for the cleanup.

sections.key: Residents of Pripyat were evacuated after about a day and a half and never returned.
sections.b: On the day after the explosion, life in Pripyat continued almost as normal. Children played outside and a wedding went ahead. Then, roughly 36 hours after the accident, residents were told to pack for a short evacuation and boarded a long line of buses. About 49,000 people left the town, believing they would return within days. They never did. Over the following weeks the evacuation zone was widened to a radius of about 30 kilometres, and more than 100,000 people were eventually moved from the area. Today Pripyat is a ghost town, its apartment blocks crumbling and trees growing through the floors. Its unused amusement park, with a Ferris wheel that was due to open days later, has become a haunting symbol of the disaster.

sections.key: The Soviet government admitted the accident only after radiation was detected in Sweden.
sections.b: At first the Soviet authorities said almost nothing publicly. The breakthrough came from Sweden. On 28 April, workers arriving at the Forsmark nuclear plant, more than 1,000 kilometres away, set off radiation alarms. Swedish experts checked their own plant, found nothing wrong and traced the radioactive particles to winds blowing from the Soviet Union. Under pressure, Soviet state media issued a short statement that evening acknowledging an accident. Radioactive fallout drifted across Belarus, Ukraine and Russia, and on to much of Europe, with rain bringing it down unevenly. Farmers in places as distant as Wales and Scandinavia faced restrictions on sheep and reindeer for years. The Soviet leader, Mikhail Gorbachev, later suggested that Chernobyl was a turning point that exposed the failings of the Soviet system.

sections.key: The long term death toll is still debated, but thyroid cancer in children is a clear consequence.
sections.b: The full human cost of Chernobyl is hard to measure. Its clearest health effect was a sharp rise in thyroid cancer among people who were children at the time, mainly because radioactive iodine got into milk from cows grazing on contaminated grass. Thousands of cases were diagnosed, although with treatment most patients survived. Estimates of eventual cancer deaths vary widely. A major United Nations led review in 2005 estimated that up to about 4,000 deaths might eventually result among the most heavily exposed groups, while some other studies give much higher figures for Europe as a whole. Many evacuees also suffered serious stress, anxiety and upheaval. The economic cost to Ukraine, Belarus and Russia ran into hundreds of billions of dollars over the following decades.

sections.key: A giant steel shelter now covers the reactor, and wildlife has returned to the exclusion zone.
sections.b: Within months of the disaster, workers built a concrete shelter, nicknamed the sarcophagus, over the shattered reactor. It was rushed and began to deteriorate, so an international project built an enormous arched steel structure called the New Safe Confinement, which was slid into place over the old shelter in 2016. The plant's last working reactor was shut down in 2000. With people gone, the exclusion zone has become an unexpected wildlife refuge, home to wolves, elk, deer and a herd of rare Przewalski's horses, though scientists still debate radiation's effects on the animals. In 2022 Russian troops occupied the site for several weeks during the invasion of Ukraine, a reminder that the legacy of Chernobyl is still tied to today's politics.

quiz.q: What were operators doing when the Chernobyl accident began?
o: Running a safety test on power supply to cooling pumps
Testing a new type of fuel
quiz.e: The night shift was testing whether turbines could power cooling pumps during an electricity failure.

quiz.q: What flaw made the emergency shutdown backfire?
o: The tips of the control rods briefly boosted the reaction
The alarm system was switched off
The reactor had no control rods
quiz.e: A design flaw meant the rods' tips increased power for a few seconds as they entered the core.

quiz.q: Roughly how long after the accident was Pripyat evacuated?
quiz.e: Around 49,000 residents left Pripyat by bus roughly a day and a half after the explosion.

quiz.q: How did the outside world first learn of the disaster?
o: Radiation alarms at a Swedish nuclear plant
quiz.e: Workers at Forsmark in Sweden detected radiation and traced it to the Soviet Union.

quiz.q: What was the clearest health effect of Chernobyl?
o: A rise in thyroid cancer among people exposed as children
A rise in heart disease across Europe
quiz.e: Radioactive iodine in milk led to thousands of thyroid cancer cases among those exposed as children.

LESSONS.title: Medicare and finding a GP you trust
LESSONS.hook: Most Australians carry a green card in their wallet without really knowing what it does. Here is how Medicare works in practice, and how to find a doctor who will know you by name.

sections.key: Medicare pays a set rebate for many medical services and free treatment as a public patient in public hospitals.
sections.b: Picture two people seeing the same GP on the same morning. One walks out paying nothing, the other pays at the desk and gets part of it back a day later. Both are using Medicare. Medicare is Australia's public health scheme, and it does two main things. It pays a rebate for a long list of out of hospital services, such as GP visits, many specialist consultations, blood tests and scans, based on a fee set by the government. It also covers treatment as a public patient in a public hospital at no cost. It does not cover most dental care, glasses, ambulance trips in most states or private hospital accommodation. This is general information, and the details are on servicesaustralia.gov.au.

sections.h: Getting your card and the app
sections.key: Enrol through Services Australia, then use the Express Plus Medicare app or your myGov account to manage it.
sections.b: Citizens and permanent residents can enrol in Medicare, as can some visitors from countries with reciprocal agreements. Most Australians are enrolled as babies on a parent's card, and you can apply for your own card from age 15. Once enrolled, you can link Medicare to your myGov account, which lets you see your claims history, update bank details so rebates land in your account, and download a digital copy of your card. The Express Plus Medicare app does much the same on your phone. Keep your bank details current: if the clinic charges you upfront, the rebate is often paid straight back to you, sometimes within minutes. Check who is on your card too, so a teenager heading off to university has their own.

sections.h: Bulk billing versus paying a gap
sections.key: Bulk billing means the doctor accepts the Medicare rebate as full payment; otherwise you pay the difference.
sections.b: When a GP bulk bills, they claim the rebate directly from Medicare and you pay nothing. When they do not, they charge their own fee, and you pay the gap between that fee and the rebate. Gaps vary widely between clinics and even between doctors in the same clinic, so it is worth asking at the desk before you book, not after. Many practices bulk bill some groups, such as children or concession card holders, while charging others. The government has expanded incentives for bulk billing in recent years, so the picture is changing. The quickest way to check is simply to ring and ask: 'Do you bulk bill, and if not, what will I be out of pocket for a standard consult?'

sections.h: The safety net for heavy years
sections.key: If your out of pocket costs pile up in a calendar year, the Medicare Safety Net can raise your rebates.
sections.b: Some years are expensive. A run of specialist visits, scans and tests can add up quickly, especially for out of hospital care. The Medicare Safety Net is designed for this. Once your gap payments for eligible services pass a threshold in a calendar year, Medicare pays a higher rebate for the rest of that year. Individuals are registered automatically, but couples and families need to register together so their costs are combined, and many people forget. You can do this through your Medicare online account in myGov. The thresholds change each year, so check the current figures on the Services Australia website rather than relying on an old number you heard from a friend.

sections.key: Seeing the same GP over time means better care, because they know your history and notice changes.
sections.b: A GP who has seen you for years remembers that your blood pressure crept up last winter, that your father had heart trouble and that you hate taking tablets. That memory is valuable. Continuity of care is linked with better management of long term conditions and fewer unnecessary tests. Australia now has MyMedicare, a voluntary scheme where you formally register with one practice. Registration can unlock longer telehealth consultations with that practice and helps the clinic plan your care. Even without registering, try to stick with one clinic and, where possible, one doctor. Ask for a longer appointment when you have several issues, rather than squeezing everything into a standard visit and leaving the important question until the door handle.

sections.h: How to find a good one
sections.key: Look for a GP who listens, explains clearly and works with you, and do not be afraid to try another.
sections.b: Start with healthdirect's Service Finder at healthdirect.gov.au, which lists practices near you along with their opening hours and whether they bulk bill. Friends and neighbours are another good source: ask what they like about their doctor, not just whether the clinic is convenient. On your first visit, notice whether the GP listens without rushing, explains things in plain language and asks what matters to you. Some people prefer a doctor of a particular gender, or one who speaks their language, and clinics can usually tell you this. If the fit is not right after a visit or two, it is perfectly fine to move on. You can ask the old practice to transfer your records to the new one.

sections.h: After hours and when to go elsewhere
sections.key: Know your options outside clinic hours, and call triple zero in an emergency.
sections.b: Illness rarely keeps business hours. For advice at any time, the healthdirect helpline on 1800 022 222 connects you with a registered nurse who can help you decide whether to see a GP, go to an urgent care clinic or head to hospital. Many areas now have Medicare Urgent Care Clinics, which treat urgent but not life threatening problems, such as minor fractures or cuts needing stitches, often without an appointment and without a fee. Telehealth GP services can handle many simple issues by phone or video. For chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of stroke or serious injury, call triple zero (000) straight away. Saving these options in your phone now means you will not be searching in a panic later.

quiz.q: Which of these does Medicare generally NOT cover?
o: Public patient treatment in a public hospital
quiz.e: Most dental care, glasses and private hospital accommodation sit outside Medicare.

quiz.q: What does bulk billing mean?
o: The doctor charges a discounted private fee
The doctor accepts the Medicare rebate as full payment
You pay upfront and claim later
Your health fund pays the bill
quiz.e: With bulk billing the doctor claims the rebate directly and you pay nothing.

quiz.q: Why should couples and families register for the Medicare Safety Net?
o: So their costs are combined toward the threshold
So they get a free GP
It is required for a Medicare card
So they can skip waiting lists
quiz.e: Individuals are registered automatically, but families must register so their costs count together.

quiz.q: What is MyMedicare?
o: A voluntary scheme to register with one regular practice
A new kind of Medicare card
quiz.e: MyMedicare lets you formally register with one practice to support continuity of care.

quiz.q: Which service lets you speak to a registered nurse at any hour?
quiz.e: The healthdirect helpline, 1800 022 222, connects you with a registered nurse.

LESSONS.title: myGov without the headache
LESSONS.hook: One login for Centrelink, Medicare, the tax office and more sounds simple, until you are stuck on hold. Here is how to make the system work for you.

sections.key: myGov is a single secure account that links many federal government services.
sections.b: Imagine you have just moved house. In the old days you might have filled in separate forms for the tax office, Medicare and Centrelink. With myGov, you sign in once at my.gov.au and update your details for several services together. myGov is not a service itself, more like a front door with a set of keys. Behind it sit linked services such as the Australian Taxation Office, Medicare, Centrelink, Child Support, My Health Record and the Department of Veterans' Affairs, along with some state services. You choose which ones to link. Each service still holds its own records, so linking simply lets you reach them all from one place and receive their letters in one inbox.

sections.key: Create your account with a personal email, strong sign-in and your own details, never someone else's.
sections.b: Go directly to my.gov.au by typing the address yourself, and create an account using an email address only you can access. Avoid a shared family email or a work address you might lose when you change jobs. You will then choose how to sign in. Options have included a code sent by text, an authenticator app, passkeys and the myID app, which is the government's Digital ID. Stronger options make it much harder for someone else to break in. Each adult in a household should have their own account, even couples who share everything else. Some services require you to prove your identity before linking, so have documents such as your driver licence, passport or Medicare card handy.

sections.key: To link a service you answer questions only you should know, using details from your records.
sections.b: Linking is where many people get stuck. When you link the ATO, for instance, you may be asked for details from a past tax return or payment summary. Linking Medicare asks for your card number and recent claim details. Centrelink can generate a linking code if you call or visit, which is handy when you cannot answer the questions. These checks exist to stop impostors, so treat them as protection rather than a nuisance. Before you start, gather a recent payslip, your tax file number, your Medicare card and any letters from the agency. Doing it in one sitting at a desk, rather than on a phone in a car park, saves a lot of frustration.

sections.key: Government letters now arrive in your myGov inbox, so turn on notifications and check them.
sections.b: Once services are linked, many will stop posting paper letters and send them to your myGov inbox instead. That includes notices about payments, debts, tax assessments and reviews, some with deadlines. Missing one can be costly, for example if Centrelink asks you to confirm your income and your payment is paused when you do not reply. Turn on email or text notifications so you know when something arrives, but remember that the notification will never contain a link to sign in. Make a habit of opening the inbox whenever you are alerted, reading the letter in full and saving important ones as PDFs. A simple folder on your computer for government letters makes tax time and disputes far easier.

sections.key: Scammers copy myGov branding, so never sign in through a link in a text or email.
sections.b: myGov is a favourite disguise for scammers. A text might say you are owed a refund or that your account has been suspended, with a link to a convincing fake site that steals your login. Services Australia has said that myGov texts and emails will not contain links asking you to sign in. The safe habit is simple: whatever the message says, close it, open your browser and type my.gov.au yourself, or use the official app. If you have entered your details on a fake page, change your password straight away, and contact Services Australia for help securing your account. You can also report scam messages to Scamwatch, run by the ACCC, at scamwatch.gov.au.

sections.key: Use online options first, and prepare before you call so one call does the job.
sections.b: Most routine tasks, such as updating an address, reporting income or claiming a Medicare rebate, can be done online or in the app, often faster than waiting on the phone. When you do need a person, prepare before you dial. Have your customer reference number, your myGov sign-in, and a short note of what you need and what has happened so far. Calls are usually quieter early in the morning and later in the week, though this varies. Write down the date, the name or identifier of the person you spoke to and what they said. Service centres can help in person, and Services Australia also offers interpreter services and support for people who are not comfortable online.

sections.key: If you disagree with a decision, ask for an explanation, then a formal review, and keep records.
sections.b: Government decisions are not always right. If Centrelink cuts a payment or raises a debt you think is wrong, you have options. First, ask for an explanation of how the decision was made. You can then request a formal review, where someone not involved in the original decision looks again. Time limits can apply, especially if you want any back pay, so act quickly. Beyond that, independent bodies such as the Administrative Review Tribunal can review many decisions, and the Commonwealth Ombudsman investigates complaints about how agencies have treated you. Free legal help is available through community legal centres and Economic Justice Australia's network. This is general information; check the details for your situation on servicesaustralia.gov.au.

quiz.q: What is myGov best described as?
o: A single front door linking many government services
quiz.e: myGov is one secure account that links services like the ATO, Medicare and Centrelink.

quiz.q: Which email is best for a myGov account?
o: A personal address only you can access
Any address, it does not matter
quiz.e: A personal email you control avoids losing access or sharing it with others.

quiz.q: Why should you turn on myGov inbox notifications?
o: So you never miss letters that may have deadlines
Because paper letters are illegal now
quiz.e: Many agencies send important letters only to the inbox, some with deadlines.

quiz.q: A text says your myGov account is suspended and gives a link. What should you do?
o: Ignore the link and type my.gov.au yourself
quiz.e: Official myGov messages will not include sign-in links, so go to the site directly.

quiz.q: If you disagree with a Centrelink decision, what is usually the first formal step after asking for an explanation?
o: Go straight to the High Court
quiz.e: A formal review by someone not involved in the original decision is the usual next step.

LESSONS.title: Buying a used car without getting burned
LESSONS.hook: A shiny paint job can hide a lot. With a few checks and a cool head, you can buy a second hand car that is exactly what it seems.

sections.key: Set a total budget and a shortlist of models before you look at a single listing.
sections.b: Scrolling car listings late at night is a fast way to fall in love with the wrong vehicle. Start instead with a plan. Work out what you need the car to do: daily commuting, towing, long country drives or squeezing into tight city parks. Then set a total budget that includes transfer costs, stamp duty, insurance and a buffer for early repairs, not just the sticker price. Research a shortlist of reliable models in that range using independent reviews and safety ratings from ANCAP, the Australasian New Car Assessment Program. Also check running costs such as fuel use, servicing and insurance premiums. When you know which three or four models suit you, every listing becomes easier to judge calmly.

sections.key: Each way of buying carries different protections, prices and risks.
sections.b: Licensed dealers usually charge more, but you get extra protection. In several states, dealers must provide a statutory warranty on cars under a certain age and kilometres, and some states give a short cooling-off period on dealer sales. Consumer guarantees under Australian Consumer Law also apply. Private sales are often cheaper, but you have far fewer rights: the car is largely sold as it is, and there is generally no cooling-off period. Auctions can offer bargains, yet you usually cannot test drive and your recourse is limited. The rules differ by state, so check your state's fair trading or consumer affairs website before you buy. This is general information, not legal advice.

sections.key: A PPSR search shows whether a car has money owing, has been written off or is reported stolen.
sections.b: Here is a nasty surprise some buyers get: months after buying a car privately, a finance company turns up to repossess it because the seller still owed money on a loan secured against it. The Personal Property Securities Register exists to prevent this. For a small fee, a search at ppsr.gov.au using the car's VIN (vehicle identification number) tells you whether there is security interest registered over the car, and whether it has been recorded as written off or stolen. Do the search on the day you pay, because a seller could take out a loan between your first look and the sale. Save the certificate. Make sure the VIN on the paperwork matches the one stamped on the car itself.

sections.key: View the car in daylight, start it cold and look for signs that do not match the story.
sections.b: Arrange to see the car in daylight, at the seller's home if it is a private sale, so you know where they live. Ask the seller not to start the engine before you arrive, because a cold start can reveal rattles, smoke and hard starting that disappear once it is warm. Look for uneven panel gaps or paint that does not quite match, which can point to accident repairs. Check tyre wear, under the oil cap for milky residue and under the car for leaks. Ask for the service book and receipts, and make sure the kilometres and dates make sense. Compare the name on the registration papers with the seller's licence. If anything feels rushed or evasive, walk away.

sections.key: Drive on a mix of roads and listen, feel and test everything, from brakes to air conditioning.
sections.b: A good test drive lasts at least twenty minutes and covers suburban streets, a stretch of highway and, ideally, a hill. Turn the radio off. Listen for knocks over bumps, whining from the gearbox and squealing brakes. Notice whether the car pulls to one side when you brake hard on a clear, safe road or let go of the wheel briefly on a straight. Automatic gear changes should be smooth, and a manual clutch should not slip. Test every switch: windows, lights, wipers, air conditioning, heating, reversing camera and locks. Check that warning lights come on briefly at start-up and then go out, since a light that never appears may have been disconnected.

sections.key: A pre-purchase inspection by an independent mechanic is cheap insurance on an expensive purchase.
sections.b: Even confident car people miss things. An independent pre-purchase inspection, from a mechanic you choose or a motoring club such as the NRMA, RACV or RACQ, typically costs a few hundred dollars and can uncover rust, hidden accident damage, worn suspension or engine problems. That report is also a powerful negotiating tool: if it finds worn brake pads and an overdue timing belt, you can reasonably ask for the cost to come off the price. Never let the seller choose the mechanic. If a seller refuses to allow an inspection, treat that as a red flag. Remember to also check registration status and what safety or roadworthy certificate your state requires before transfer.

sections.key: Pay securely, get a written receipt and lodge the transfer with your state's transport agency promptly.
sections.b: Online car scams often follow a pattern: a great price, a seller who is overseas or in the army, and a request for a deposit before you can see the car. Never pay for a car you have not inspected in person. When you are ready to buy, pay by bank transfer or bank cheque rather than carrying large amounts of cash, and get a written receipt with both names, the date, the price, the VIN and the registration number. Both buyer and seller usually have to complete a transfer form, and you will pay stamp duty and a transfer fee within a set number of days. Arrange insurance before you drive away, not the next morning.

quiz.q: What can a PPSR search reveal about a used car?
o: Whether money is owing, or it is written off or stolen
quiz.e: The PPSR shows registered security interests and written off or stolen status.

quiz.q: Compared with buying from a dealer, a private sale usually gives you
o: Fewer rights, as the car is largely sold as is
quiz.e: Private sales are often cheaper but carry far fewer protections.

quiz.q: Why ask the seller not to start the car before you arrive?
o: A cold start can reveal problems that disappear once warm
quiz.e: Rattles, smoke and hard starting are easier to spot from cold.

quiz.q: Who should choose the mechanic for a pre-purchase inspection?
quiz.e: An inspector you choose is independent of the seller.

quiz.q: A seller says they are overseas and asks for a deposit before you can see the car. This is
quiz.e: Never pay for a car you have not inspected in person.

LESSONS.title: Travelling overseas without the drama
LESSONS.hook: The best trips start long before the airport. A little preparation with your passport, the right insurance and official travel advice can save you a world of trouble.

sections.key: Many countries want your passport valid for months beyond your trip, so check the expiry date early.
sections.b: Every year some travellers arrive at the check-in desk only to be turned away because their passport expires too soon. Many countries require your passport to be valid for at least six months beyond the date you arrive or leave, and some also need blank pages for stamps. So the first job, ideally months before you fly, is to find your passport and look at the expiry date. Australian passports are issued by the Australian Passport Office, and you can apply or renew through passports.gov.au. Processing times vary and can stretch during busy seasons, so leave plenty of time. Paying for priority processing is possible but costs extra and is not always available.

sections.key: Check entry rules for every country you visit, including those you only pass through.
sections.b: Australian passport holders can visit many countries without a visa, but not all, and the rules change. Some places require an electronic travel authorisation applied for online before departure, such as the United States ESTA or the United Kingdom's ETA. Others need a full visa from an embassy. Do not forget countries where you only change planes, as some transit stops have their own rules. The safest source is the official government website of the country you are visiting, linked from its Smartraveller page. Be wary of third party websites that look official but charge large fees to submit a form you could lodge yourself. Also check rules about medicines you plan to carry, since some common ones are restricted overseas.

sections.key: Smartraveller is the Australian government's travel advice service, with a level for every destination.
sections.b: Smartraveller, at smartraveller.gov.au, is run by the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade. Each destination has a travel advice page with an overall advice level, from 'Exercise normal safety precautions' through 'Exercise a high degree of caution' and 'Reconsider your need to travel' to 'Do not travel'. Different regions within a country can carry different levels. The pages also cover local laws, health risks, scams, natural hazards and entry requirements. Read the advice for every country before you book and again before you leave, since it can change quickly. You can subscribe to email updates for your destinations. Insurers may refuse to cover you in places marked 'Do not travel', so the level matters for your policy too.

sections.key: Get insurance when you book, and read what it excludes, especially pre-existing conditions and activities.
sections.b: Smartraveller puts it bluntly: if you cannot afford travel insurance, you cannot afford to travel. Medical treatment overseas can cost tens of thousands of dollars, and an evacuation flight home far more. Buy cover as soon as you book, so cancellation cover protects you if something goes wrong before you leave. Then read the product disclosure statement, not just the brochure. Check how pre-existing medical conditions are handled, the excess you pay per claim, and exclusions for things such as riding a scooter without the right licence, extreme sports, or incidents involving alcohol. Credit card insurance can be useful but often has strict conditions. This is general information, so compare policies carefully for your situation.

sections.key: Tell your bank you are travelling, sort out phone roaming and keep copies of key documents.
sections.b: A card blocked for suspicious overseas activity can leave you stranded at a hotel desk. Check whether your bank wants to know your travel plans, and carry at least two ways to pay, kept in different places. Compare fees: some cards charge international transaction fees on every purchase, while travel cards and some bank accounts do not. Before you leave, check your phone plan's roaming charges, which can be huge, or plan to buy a local SIM or eSIM. Save digital copies of your passport, insurance policy and bookings somewhere you can reach from any device, and share them with someone at home. A printed copy of your insurer's emergency number in your wallet is a smart backup.

sections.key: See a GP or travel clinic well before departure for vaccinations and medicine advice.
sections.b: Some vaccinations need several weeks to take effect, or more than one dose, so book a GP or travel clinic six to eight weeks before departure if you can. Bring a list of medicines and a letter from your doctor describing them, and keep them in original labelled packaging. Australia has reciprocal health care agreements with some countries, including the United Kingdom, New Zealand and Ireland, which can cover medically necessary treatment, but they are limited and do not replace insurance. On long flights, move around and drink water. Healthdirect and Smartraveller both have practical pages on travel health. This is general information, not medical advice, so talk to a health professional about your own needs.

sections.key: Know what the Australian government can and cannot do for you overseas.
sections.b: If your passport is stolen, report it to local police and contact the nearest Australian embassy or consulate for an emergency travel document. If you are arrested, seriously ill or caught in a crisis, consular staff can help, and the 24 hour Consular Emergency Centre can be reached from anywhere. Smartraveller lists the numbers. But the Consular Services Charter is clear about limits. The government cannot pay your medical bills or legal fees, get you out of jail or override local laws. That is exactly why insurance and good preparation matter. Before you leave, make sure someone at home has your itinerary and knows how to reach you, and check in with them regularly.

quiz.q: Why check your passport expiry well before travel?
o: Many countries require validity for months beyond your trip
Airlines charge more for older passports
It is needed for travel insurance
quiz.e: Many countries want at least six months' validity remaining.

quiz.q: What is the highest Smartraveller advice level?
o: Exercise a high degree of caution
quiz.e: 'Do not travel' is the most serious of the four advice levels.

quiz.q: When is the best time to buy travel insurance?
quiz.e: Buying early means cancellation cover protects you before departure.

quiz.q: What do reciprocal health care agreements do?
o: Cover some medically necessary care in certain countries
quiz.e: They provide limited cover in some countries and do not replace insurance.

quiz.q: Which of these can the Australian government NOT do for you overseas?
quiz.e: The Consular Services Charter says the government cannot pay medical or legal bills.

LESSONS.title: Making a will, and why it matters
