LESSONS.hook: Nobody likes thinking about it, but a will is one of the kindest things you can leave the people you love. Here is what it does and how to get one right.

sections.key: If you die without a valid will, the law decides who gets what, using a fixed formula.
sections.b: Imagine a couple who have lived together for years but never married, with a child from an earlier relationship. One dies suddenly without a will. Their partner may face a slow and stressful process to prove the relationship, while assets are divided according to a formula set out in state or territory law, not by what the person would have wanted. Dying without a will is called dying intestate. The rules generally favour spouses, partners, children and close relatives in a set order, and they do not cover friends, charities or stepchildren in the way many people expect. A clear will spares your family guesswork, delay and, often, conflict at the worst possible time.

sections.key: A will names who receives your property, who manages your estate and who should care for young children.
sections.b: At its simplest, a will is a written document setting out what happens to your estate, meaning the property you own when you die. It names beneficiaries, the people or organisations who inherit, and says what each receives. It names an executor, the person responsible for gathering your assets, paying debts and distributing what is left. If you have children under 18, it can also name a guardian you would like to care for them. A will can include specific gifts, such as a ring to a niece, as well as the 'residue', which is everything else. It can also set out wishes about funerals, though these are not always legally binding.

sections.key: Pick someone trustworthy and organised, and ask them first, because the role is real work.
sections.b: Being an executor is not an honour you frame on the wall. It can mean months of paperwork: locating documents, dealing with banks, possibly applying to the Supreme Court for a grant of probate, selling property and paying tax obligations. Choose someone you trust, who is organised and likely to outlive you, and ask them before naming them. Many people pick a partner or adult child, often with a backup in case the first cannot act. Some appoint a professional, such as a solicitor or the state trustee organisation, which charges fees but brings experience and neutrality. Naming two people who do not get along as joint executors can cause exactly the conflict you hoped to avoid.

sections.key: A will must generally be in writing, signed by you and witnessed by two adults present together.
sections.b: The formal rules vary a little between states and territories, but the core is similar. The will must be in writing, signed by the person making it, and signed by two adult witnesses who are both present when you sign. A witness who is also a beneficiary, or a beneficiary's partner, can create problems, and in some places the gift to them may be at risk, so use independent witnesses. Courts can sometimes accept informal documents, even unsigned notes or videos, but proving them is slow and expensive. Do-it-yourself will kits exist and can work for very simple situations, yet small mistakes are common. This is general information, not legal advice.

sections.h: Things a will does not control
sections.key: Superannuation and jointly owned assets often pass outside your will, so plan them separately.
sections.b: Many Australians are surprised to learn that their superannuation does not automatically follow their will. Super is held in trust, and the fund trustee decides who receives it unless you have made a valid binding death benefit nomination. Some binding nominations lapse after a few years unless renewed, so check with your fund. Life insurance held inside super follows the same path. Property owned as joint tenants, such as a home held jointly by a couple, usually passes straight to the surviving owner regardless of the will. Bank accounts held jointly can work the same way. Reviewing these alongside your will is essential, or your careful plan may only cover a fraction of what you own.

sections.h: Getting help and keeping it current
sections.key: Solicitors and state public trustees can prepare wills, and life changes mean it is time to review.
sections.b: For most people, a will prepared by a solicitor is money well spent, particularly with blended families, a business, overseas assets or a family member who may contest. Each state and territory also has a public trustee or state trustee organisation that can prepare wills, sometimes at low cost. Once it is signed, store the original somewhere safe and tell your executor where. Then review it whenever life changes. In most states, getting married revokes an existing will unless it was made in contemplation of that marriage, and divorce can cancel gifts to a former spouse. Having children, separating, buying property or a beneficiary dying are all good reasons to check that the will still says what you mean.

sections.key: An enduring power of attorney and an advance care directive cover decisions while you are alive.
sections.b: A will only speaks after death. If an accident or illness left you unable to make decisions, a will would not help. That is the job of two other documents. An enduring power of attorney lets someone you trust manage your financial and legal affairs if you cannot. An enduring guardianship or similar appointment, along with an advance care directive, covers health and lifestyle decisions and records your wishes about medical treatment. The names and forms differ between states, so look up the official forms for where you live, or ask a solicitor. Talking openly with your family about your wishes is uncomfortable for a few minutes and an enormous gift for years.

quiz.q: What is it called when someone dies without a valid will?
quiz.e: Dying without a valid will is called dying intestate, and a legal formula applies.

quiz.q: What does an executor do?
quiz.e: The executor gathers assets, pays debts and distributes what remains.

quiz.q: Why should will witnesses usually not be beneficiaries?
o: It can put their gift at risk
It makes the will too long
quiz.e: A beneficiary witness can cause problems and may jeopardise their gift.

quiz.q: What controls who receives your superannuation when you die?
o: The fund trustee, guided by any valid binding nomination
quiz.e: Super is held in trust and does not automatically follow your will.

quiz.q: In most Australian states, what happens to an existing will when you marry?
o: It is usually revoked unless made in contemplation of the marriage
It automatically names your spouse executor
quiz.e: Marriage generally revokes a will unless it was made with that marriage in mind.

LESSONS.title: Making a complaint that actually gets results
LESSONS.hook: Knowing your rights is one thing; getting a business to honour them is another. Here is the step by step path from polite email to independent ombudsman.

sections.key: Before you complain, decide exactly what outcome you want and what the law says you are entitled to.
sections.b: Consider a washing machine that dies a fortnight after its warranty ends. Angry phone calls get nowhere. What works is clarity. Before you contact the business, write down what went wrong, when, and what you want: a repair, a replacement, a refund or compensation. Then check what Australian Consumer Law says. Its consumer guarantees mean goods must be of acceptable quality and last a reasonable time, regardless of any manufacturer's warranty, and a major failure gives you a choice of remedy. The ACCC's website, accc.gov.au, explains the guarantees in plain English. Knowing your rights lets you ask calmly for something specific, which is far harder to dismiss than general frustration. This is general information, not legal advice.

sections.key: Receipts, photos, dates and names turn a story into a case.
sections.b: Complaints succeed on evidence. Collect proof of purchase, such as a receipt, bank statement or order confirmation. Photograph or video the fault, ideally showing it happening. Keep the original packaging and any warranty documents if you still have them. Most importantly, start a simple log: every call, email and visit, with the date, the person you dealt with and what they said or promised. If a salesperson made a claim about what the product could do, note it, because misleading representations are a separate problem under the law. This record does two jobs. It makes your complaint precise, and if you later need an ombudsman or tribunal, it shows that you tried reasonably to resolve things first.

sections.h: Complain to the business in writing
sections.key: Contact the business first, then follow up in writing so there is a clear record.
sections.b: Most problems are fixed at the first step, so give the business a genuine chance. Ask to speak with someone who can make decisions, often a manager or the complaints team rather than front counter staff. Be polite, specific and firm. If that does not work, put your complaint in writing by email or letter. Briefly set out what you bought, the problem, what you have done so far and the remedy you want. Refer to the consumer guarantees if relevant, and give a reasonable deadline, such as 14 days, for a response. Many large businesses must have an internal dispute resolution process, and asking for your complaint to be formally logged often moves it to more senior people.

sections.key: If the business will not budge, go to your state fair trading agency or the relevant ombudsman.
sections.b: Where you go next depends on the industry. For most goods and services, contact the fair trading or consumer affairs agency in your state or territory, such as NSW Fair Trading or Consumer Affairs Victoria. They can give advice and may contact the business on your behalf. The ACCC enforces the law across Australia but generally does not resolve individual disputes, though reporting to it helps reveal patterns. Several industries have their own free, independent ombudsman schemes. The Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman handles phone and internet complaints, the Australian Financial Complaints Authority covers banks, insurers and super funds, and each state has an energy and water ombudsman. Most require you to complain to the business first.

sections.key: Ombudsmen are free for consumers and can make binding decisions on member businesses.
sections.b: An ombudsman scheme is a free, independent service that tries to resolve disputes between consumers and businesses in a particular industry. You lodge a complaint, usually online, and the scheme refers it back to the business's senior staff for a final chance to fix it. Many complaints settle at this point, because businesses often pay fees when complaints progress. If not, the scheme investigates and may recommend or decide an outcome. In schemes like AFCA, a decision you accept can bind the business, while you remain free to go to court instead if you reject it. Time limits apply, so lodge promptly. The process is designed for ordinary people, and you do not need a lawyer.

sections.key: Small claims tribunals and card chargebacks are powerful tools when other steps fail.
sections.b: If no ombudsman covers the business and the fair trading agency cannot resolve it, a state tribunal or local court can hear consumer claims. Examples include NCAT in New South Wales, VCAT in Victoria and QCAT in Queensland. Small claims processes are designed to be cheaper and less formal than ordinary courts, though there is usually a filing fee and you present your own case with your evidence. Separately, if you paid by credit or debit card and the goods never arrived or the business has collapsed, ask your bank about a chargeback. Card schemes have rules for disputed transactions, and banks set time limits for requests, so contact them as soon as you realise there is a problem.

sections.key: Stay calm, factual and persistent, and be open to a fair compromise.
sections.b: The most effective complainers are rarely the loudest. Staff who are shouted at tend to follow the script; staff who are treated respectfully often look for a way to help. Keep your messages short and factual, repeat your requested remedy clearly, and do not accept vague promises without a date. If you are offered something less than you asked for, consider whether it is fair rather than rejecting it on principle, since time and stress have costs too. Public reviews and social media posts can attract attention, but stick to accurate facts to avoid defamation risks. Finally, report scams and misleading conduct to the ACCC or Scamwatch, even if you get your money back. It helps protect the next customer.

quiz.q: Under the consumer guarantees, when can you get a remedy for a faulty product?
o: When goods fail to be of acceptable quality, even after the warranty ends
quiz.e: Consumer guarantees apply regardless of any manufacturer's warranty period.

quiz.q: Why keep a log of calls and emails?
o: To make the complaint precise and show you tried to resolve it
quiz.e: A log strengthens your case at every later step.

quiz.q: Which body handles phone and internet complaints?
quiz.e: The TIO is the free ombudsman for telco disputes.

quiz.q: What do most ombudsman schemes require before they will take your complaint?
o: That you first complained to the business
quiz.e: You usually need to give the business a chance to fix it first.

quiz.q: If you paid by card and the goods never arrived, what can you ask your bank for?
quiz.e: Card schemes have chargeback rules for disputed transactions, with time limits.

LESSONS.title: Building a better sleep routine
LESSONS.hook: Good sleep is less about a magic pill and more about a handful of habits done consistently. Here is a practical routine you can start tonight.

sections.key: Getting up at the same time every day is the single strongest lever for steadier sleep.
sections.b: Many people try to fix bad sleep by going to bed earlier, then lie awake staring at the ceiling. A more reliable starting point is the other end of the night. Your body clock, the circadian rhythm, runs on a roughly 24 hour cycle and is set largely by when you wake and see light. Choose a wake time you can keep seven days a week, within about half an hour, including weekends. Big Saturday sleep-ins shift your clock later, which is part of why Monday mornings feel brutal. After a week or two of a steady wake time, many people find they naturally feel sleepy at a more regular hour. This is general information, not medical advice.

sections.key: Bright light in the morning and dim light at night help your body know what time it is.
sections.b: Light is the main signal your brain uses to set its clock. Getting outside within an hour or so of waking, even on a cloudy day, gives a much stronger signal than indoor lighting. A short walk, breakfast on the balcony or a coffee by an open window all count. In the evening, the opposite helps. Dimming the house lights an hour or two before bed, using lamps instead of bright overheads, and lowering screen brightness all send the message that night is coming. Many phones and computers have a night mode that warms the colour of the screen. In Australian summers, block-out curtains can stop early sunrise from waking you before you are ready.

sections.key: Caffeine lingers for hours and alcohol fragments sleep, so time them carefully.
sections.b: That 3 pm flat white may feel harmless, but caffeine stays in your system for several hours, and for some people much longer. It blocks the brain's receptors for adenosine, a chemical that builds up while you are awake and makes you feel sleepy. A common suggestion is to have your last caffeine around midday or early afternoon, and to remember hidden sources such as energy drinks, cola, some teas and dark chocolate. Alcohol is trickier because it can make you drowsy at first. Later in the night, though, it tends to disrupt sleep, causing lighter, more broken rest and more trips to the bathroom. Heavy meals close to bedtime can also cause discomfort, so try to eat dinner a few hours before bed.

sections.key: A predictable 30 to 60 minute routine before bed tells your brain it is time to switch off.
sections.b: Children have bedtime routines for good reason: bath, book, lights out. Adults benefit from the same idea. Pick a few calm activities and do them in roughly the same order each night for the last half hour to an hour before bed. That might be tidying the kitchen, a warm shower, setting out tomorrow's clothes, reading a paper book and some slow breathing. Keep work emails and gripping news out of this window, since they can switch your brain back into problem solving mode. If worries race through your head, try writing a quick to-do list for tomorrow before you start winding down. Getting tasks onto paper can make them easier to let go of.

sections.key: A cool, dark, quiet and comfortable room makes sleep easier to start and keep.
sections.b: Your bedroom works best when it is mainly for sleep. Most people sleep better in a slightly cool room, so in hot Australian summers a fan, air conditioning set to a comfortable level or lighter bedding can make a real difference. Darkness helps too: block-out curtains or an eye mask can cut light from street lamps and early dawn. For noise, earplugs or a steady background sound such as a fan can mask barking dogs and traffic. Check that your mattress and pillow still support you, since both wear out. Finally, consider charging your phone outside the bedroom and using a cheap alarm clock instead, which removes the temptation to scroll at midnight.

sections.key: If you are awake for a long while, get up and do something calm until you feel sleepy.
sections.b: Lying in bed for an hour willing yourself to sleep can teach your brain to link bed with frustration. Sleep specialists often suggest a different approach. If you have been awake for what feels like twenty minutes or so, without clock watching, get up and go to another dim room. Do something quiet and boring, such as reading or folding washing, then return to bed only when you feel sleepy. Repeat if needed. It feels counterintuitive, but over time it rebuilds the connection between bed and sleep. Keep naps short, ideally under half an hour and before mid afternoon, so they do not steal sleep from the night. Avoid looking at the time repeatedly, which tends to increase anxiety.

sections.key: Ongoing poor sleep, loud snoring or gasping, or daytime sleepiness are reasons to see a GP.
sections.b: Most adults are thought to need roughly seven to nine hours of sleep, though individuals vary. Occasional bad nights are normal, but persistent trouble is worth taking seriously. See your GP if poor sleep lasts for weeks and affects your daytime life, if a partner notices loud snoring, pauses in breathing or gasping, if you feel very sleepy during the day, especially while driving, or if you have strong urges to move your legs at night. These can point to treatable sleep conditions. Effective help exists, including a structured talking therapy for insomnia known as CBT-I. The Sleep Health Foundation and healthdirect have reliable information, and this lesson is general information, not medical advice.

quiz.q: What is suggested as the strongest lever for steadier sleep?
o: Keeping a consistent wake time every day
quiz.e: A steady wake time anchors your body clock.

quiz.q: Why get outside soon after waking?
o: Morning light strongly sets your body clock
quiz.e: Bright morning light is the main signal that sets the circadian rhythm.

quiz.q: What does alcohol tend to do to sleep later in the night?
o: Disrupt it, making it lighter and more broken
quiz.e: Alcohol may cause drowsiness at first but fragments sleep later.

quiz.q: If you have been awake in bed for a long while, what is often suggested?
o: Get up, do something calm in dim light, and return when sleepy
quiz.e: This helps rebuild the link between bed and sleep.

quiz.q: Which of these is a reason to see a GP about sleep?
o: One bad night before an exam
Snoring with pauses in breathing or gasping
Waking once to use the bathroom
quiz.e: Pauses in breathing or gasping can signal a treatable sleep condition.

LESSONS.title: Private health insurance, decoded
LESSONS.hook: Gold, Silver, Bronze, extras, excesses and a mysterious loading after 30. Here is how private health insurance really works in Australia, so you can decide what you need.

sections.key: Private cover sits on top of Medicare, mainly for choice of doctor, timing and private hospital care.
sections.b: Every Australian resident enrolled in Medicare can be treated free as a public patient in a public hospital. So why do roughly half of Australians hold private hospital cover? Mostly for choice and timing. As a private patient you can usually choose your specialist and hospital, and elective surgery such as a knee reconstruction may happen sooner than on a public waiting list. Private cover can also help with services Medicare does not cover, such as dental, physiotherapy and glasses, through extras policies. There are tax rules that push some people towards cover as well. Whether it is worth it depends on your health, age, income and priorities. This is general information, not financial advice.

sections.key: Hospital policies are sorted into Gold, Silver, Bronze and Basic tiers based on what treatments they must cover.
sections.b: Hospital cover pays towards your costs as a private patient in hospital, such as accommodation, theatre fees and part of the doctors' fees. Since reforms in 2019, policies are grouped into four tiers: Gold, Silver, Bronze and Basic. Each tier must cover a minimum list of clinical categories. Gold covers every category, including pregnancy and birth, joint replacements and assisted reproductive services. Lower tiers cover fewer categories, so a cheap Basic policy may cover very little. Some policies are labelled 'plus', meaning they cover extra categories above their tier's minimum. When comparing policies, look at the specific treatments you might realistically need in the next few years, rather than just the tier name or the price.

sections.key: Extras policies pay benefits for things like dental and physio, but limits and gaps mean you rarely get full cost back.
sections.b: Extras, sometimes called general treatment, pays part of the cost of services outside hospital such as dental check-ups, physiotherapy, optical, chiropractic and remedial massage. It is sold separately or combined with hospital cover. The catch is that extras rarely pays the full bill. Each service has a benefit amount and an annual limit, and you pay the rest. A quick test is to add up what you actually spend on these services in a typical year, then compare it with the premium plus the gaps you would still pay. For some people, especially those with regular dental or physio needs, it comes out ahead. For others, putting the premium into a savings account works better.

sections.key: Know what you pay at the time of treatment and how long before you can claim.
sections.b: Two policies with the same tier can cost very different amounts because of the excess, the amount you agree to pay upfront if you are admitted to hospital. A higher excess lowers your premium but raises your bill when you need care. You may also face a gap, the difference between what doctors charge and what Medicare and your insurer pay. Ask your specialist and hospital about likely gaps before treatment, and ask whether they have an arrangement with your fund. Waiting periods apply when you first take out cover or upgrade. They are commonly up to 12 months for pre-existing conditions and pregnancy, and shorter for most other hospital treatment. Check the specifics before you need them.

sections.key: If you take out hospital cover later in life, you may pay an extra loading on your premium for years.
sections.b: Lifetime Health Cover is designed to encourage people to take out hospital cover earlier. If you do not hold private hospital cover by 1 July following your 31st birthday, a loading of 2 per cent is added to your hospital premium for every year you are over 30 when you eventually take it out, up to a maximum of 70 per cent. So someone first joining at 40 would typically pay around 20 per cent more than someone who joined at 30. The loading is removed after you have held hospital cover continuously for 10 years. There are some exceptions, including for people who arrived in Australia later in life. Extras-only cover does not count towards avoiding the loading.

sections.h: The Medicare Levy Surcharge and rebate
sections.key: Higher earners without hospital cover may pay an extra tax, and the government rebate on premiums is income tested.
sections.b: The Medicare Levy Surcharge is an extra tax charged to people whose income is above a threshold and who do not hold an appropriate level of private hospital cover. It is separate from the ordinary Medicare levy most taxpayers pay. For some people on higher incomes, the surcharge would cost more than a basic hospital policy, which is why some buy cover mainly for tax reasons. Separately, the Australian Government Rebate reduces premiums for many people, with the amount depending on income and age. Thresholds and percentages change regularly, so check the current figures on the ATO website, ato.gov.au, rather than relying on old numbers. A tax agent can help you apply the rules to your own situation.

sections.key: Use the government's comparison site, compare like with like, and review your cover regularly.
sections.b: Insurers have thousands of policies, and the names alone tell you very little. The government run website privatehealth.gov.au, managed by the Commonwealth Ombudsman, lets you compare policies from all registered funds, and every policy has a standard information statement summarising what it covers. Commercial comparison sites can be useful, but they may not include every fund. You can switch funds, and if you move to an equivalent level of hospital cover you generally will not serve the same waiting periods again, though upgrades may attract new ones. Review your cover each year, especially when life changes, such as planning a family or retiring. If you have a dispute with your fund, the Private Health Insurance Ombudsman can help, free of charge.

quiz.q: What is a main reason people hold private hospital cover?
o: Choice of doctor and timing for elective care
To avoid all costs in public hospitals
quiz.e: Private cover mainly offers choice of specialist and hospital, and often shorter waits.

quiz.q: Which hospital tier must cover every clinical category?
quiz.e: Gold policies cover all clinical categories, including pregnancy and joint replacements.

quiz.q: What is the effect of choosing a higher excess?
o: Lower premiums but a bigger bill when admitted
quiz.e: A higher excess trades a lower premium for more upfront cost when you need care.

quiz.q: Under Lifetime Health Cover, what loading applies for each year you are over 30 when you first take hospital cover?
quiz.e: The loading is 2 per cent a year, capped at 70 per cent, and removed after 10 years.

quiz.q: Which website lets you compare policies from all registered funds?
quiz.e: privatehealth.gov.au, run by the Commonwealth Ombudsman, covers all registered funds.

LESSONS.title: Cleaning smarter: the science of stains
LESSONS.hook: Hot water can set a bloodstain for good, and vinegar can wreck a marble benchtop. Learn what is really happening when you clean, and you will clean faster with fewer products.

sections.key: Detergents grab grease with one end of the molecule and water with the other.
sections.b: Rinse a greasy frying pan under the tap and the water simply beads and runs off, leaving the oil behind. Oil and water do not mix, which is why plain water is a poor cleaner. Soaps and detergents solve this with clever molecules called surfactants. One end of each molecule is attracted to water, and the other end is attracted to oil and grease. When you scrub, millions of these molecules surround tiny droplets of grease, oily tails pointing inwards and water loving heads pointing out. The grease is now wrapped in little parcels that rinse away in the water. Warm water helps because it softens fats, and scrubbing helps because it breaks the grime into smaller pieces for the surfactants to grab.

sections.key: Clean top to bottom and dry to wet, so you never redo a finished job.
sections.b: Imagine wiping the kitchen bench until it gleams, then dusting the rangehood above it and watching crumbs and dust drift down onto your clean surface. Professional cleaners avoid this with two simple rules. First, work from top to bottom, so gravity carries dirt onto areas you have not cleaned yet: high shelves and light fittings first, floors last. Second, work dry to wet: dust and vacuum before you mop or wipe, because wet cloths turn loose dust into smeared mud. It also pays to spray a product and walk away for a few minutes while you do something else. Many cleaners need contact time to loosen grime, so letting them sit means less scrubbing. Finally, clean one room completely before moving on, so you can see your progress.

sections.key: Cleaning removes dirt and most germs; disinfectants only work properly on surfaces that are already clean.
sections.b: Wiping a chopping board with a damp cloth and spraying it with disinfectant can look like the same job, but they do different things. Cleaning with detergent and water physically lifts off dirt, grease and most of the germs riding on them. Disinfecting uses chemicals to kill germs that remain. Disinfectants work poorly through a layer of grime, so the rule is clean first, then disinfect if needed. Most disinfectants also need to stay wet on the surface for a set time, often several minutes, to work as claimed; check the label. For most of the home, ordinary cleaning is enough. Disinfecting matters more for high risk spots, such as benches after raw meat, toilets, and surfaces touched by someone with a stomach bug.

sections.h: Acids, alkalis and what to use where
sections.key: Acids dissolve mineral deposits; alkalis cut grease; neither suits every surface.
sections.b: Look at a shower screen in a hard water area and you will see a chalky white crust. That crust is mostly alkaline mineral deposit, and a mild acid such as white vinegar or citric acid dissolves it. Greasy kitchen grime is different: it responds better to alkaline products such as bicarbonate of soda or dishwashing detergent. Knowing this saves you buying a cupboard full of special sprays. It also protects your surfaces. Acids etch natural stone such as marble and limestone, leaving dull patches, so use a pH neutral cleaner there. And mixing vinegar with bicarb, a popular online trick, mostly cancels them out: the fizz is carbon dioxide, and what remains is largely salty water. Use them separately, each for the job it does best.

sections.key: Mixing bleach with ammonia or acids can release toxic gases.
sections.b: Some cleaning mistakes leave streaks. Others put people in hospital. Bleach, which contains sodium hypochlorite, is the most dangerous product to combine. Mixed with ammonia, found in some glass and multipurpose cleaners, it releases chloramine gases. Mixed with acids, including vinegar and some toilet and descaling cleaners, it can release chlorine gas. Both irritate the eyes and lungs and can cause serious breathing problems. Even mixing two different brands of toilet cleaner can be risky if you do not know what is in them. The safe habits are simple: use one product at a time, rinse between products, keep products in their original labelled bottles, and open a window when you clean. If someone feels unwell after exposure, call the Poisons Information Centre on 13 11 26 for advice.

sections.key: Protein, tannin, grease and dye stains each need a different approach.
sections.b: A splash of red wine, a smear of butter and a grass stain on school pants may all look like stains, but chemically they are different problems. Protein stains, such as blood, egg, milk and sweat, need cold water first, because heat cooks the proteins and bonds them to the fibres; enzyme pre-treatments then break them down. Tannin stains, such as tea, coffee, wine and fruit juice, usually respond to prompt rinsing and laundry detergent, though some need an oxygen bleach soak. Grease and oil stains need something to dissolve the oil, such as dishwashing liquid rubbed in before washing in warm water. Dye stains, such as ink or a bleeding red sock, are the hardest and may need specialist removers. Identify the stain first, then choose your weapon.

sections.key: Act fast, blot, work from the outside in, and check before you dry.
sections.b: When coffee hits the carpet, your first instinct may be to scrub hard. Resist it. Scrubbing pushes the stain deeper and spreads it wider. Instead, blot with a clean cloth to lift as much liquid as you can. Work from the outer edge towards the centre so the stain shrinks rather than grows. Test any product on a hidden spot first, such as inside a hem or under a couch, to check it does not bleach or damage the fabric. Give the treatment time to work, then rinse it out, because leftover product can attract dirt. Most importantly, check that a stain has gone before putting the item in a clothes dryer or ironing it. Heat can fix a faint stain permanently, while a second treatment might have removed it completely.

quiz.q: How do detergent molecules remove grease?
o: They make water heavier than oil
One end grabs oil and the other end is attracted to water
They dissolve the fabric around the grease
They freeze the grease so it cracks
quiz.e: Surfactants wrap grease in tiny parcels that water can carry away.

quiz.q: Why should you clean a surface before disinfecting it?
o: Disinfectants work poorly through a layer of grime
Cleaning is only needed on floors
quiz.e: Dirt and grease shield germs, so clean first and then disinfect.

quiz.q: What is the best choice for cleaning a marble benchtop?
quiz.e: Acids etch natural stone, so a pH neutral cleaner is the safe option.

quiz.q: What can happen if bleach is mixed with vinegar?
o: It becomes a stronger, safer disinfectant
Nothing, they cancel each other out
quiz.e: Acids mixed with bleach can release toxic chlorine gas.

quiz.q: Why should a bloodstain be rinsed in cold water first?
o: Heat sets protein stains into the fibres
Hot water dissolves the fabric dye
quiz.e: Heat cooks proteins such as blood and bonds them to the fabric.

LESSONS.title: Laundry done right
LESSONS.hook: Shrunken jumpers, pink socks and towels that smell faintly of damp are all avoidable. A few habits will make your clothes last longer and your washing cheaper.

sections.key: Care labels tell you the safest temperature, wash cycle and drying method.
sections.b: Flip a shirt inside out and you will find a small label covered in symbols: a tub of water, a triangle, a square with a circle in it. Most people ignore it, which is how a favourite wool jumper ends up fitting a child. The tub shows washing instructions, with a number or dots for the maximum temperature and a hand for hand washing. The triangle covers bleaching, the square covers drying, the iron covers ironing, and a circle on its own means dry cleaning. A cross through any symbol means do not. You do not need to memorise every variation: a quick search for laundry symbols will give you a chart. Just glance at the label the first time you wash something new, especially wool, silk, rayon and anything with embellishments.

sections.key: Sort by colour, then by fabric weight and how dirty things are.
sections.b: One new red t-shirt can turn a load of white undies a gentle shade of pink. Dye transfer is the classic laundry disaster, and it is why sorting matters. Start by separating whites, lights and darks, and wash brand new dark or bright items on their own for the first few washes, since that is when excess dye is most likely to run. Next, think about fabric weight. Heavy towels and jeans rub against delicate items and wear them out faster, and they take longer to dry. Finally, keep heavily soiled work clothes or sports gear apart from everyday clothes. Before anything goes in, empty the pockets, because a single tissue can coat a whole load in white fluff. Zip up zips and close hooks so they do not snag other garments.

sections.h: Cold water and how much detergent
sections.key: Cold washing saves energy, and more detergent does not mean cleaner clothes.
sections.b: Most of the energy a washing machine uses on a warm or hot cycle goes into heating the water. Modern detergents are designed to work well in cold water, so for everyday loads a cold wash is usually enough and costs much less to run. Save warm or hot washes for greasy stains, towels, bedding and items that need extra hygiene, if the care label allows. Detergent is another place to save. It is tempting to add an extra splash for good measure, but too much detergent does not rinse out properly. It can leave clothes stiff, dull and itchy, and the residue can build up inside the machine and cause smells. Follow the dose on the pack, adjusting for load size and how dirty things are, and use detergent made for your machine type.

sections.key: Clothes need room to move, so do not overload the drum.
sections.b: Washing machines clean by tumbling or agitating clothes through soapy water, so the clothes need space to move. Cram the drum to bursting and the result is often patchy cleaning, detergent marks and extra creasing. A rough guide for a front loader is to leave a hand's width of space at the top of the drum, though your manual is the best reference. At the other extreme, running tiny half loads wastes water and electricity, so wait until you have a sensible load or use a smaller load setting if your machine has one. Wash delicate items such as bras and tights in a mesh laundry bag to stop them stretching or tangling. Turn dark clothes, printed t-shirts and jeans inside out to reduce fading and protect the print.

sections.key: Line drying is cheap and gentle; dryers are convenient but harder on fabric.
sections.b: Australia's sunshine makes the clothesline one of the best appliances in the house, and it costs nothing to run. Sunlight helps freshen whites, though strong sun can fade dark and bright colours, so hang those inside out or in the shade. Shake clothes out and hang them by their strongest seams to cut down on ironing. Dry knitted wool flat on a towel, because hanging it wet can stretch it out of shape. Clothes dryers are handy on wet days, but heat and tumbling are the main causes of shrinkage and wear, and dryers use a lot of electricity. If you use one, clean the lint filter every single load: built up lint makes the dryer work harder and is a recognised fire risk. Heat pump dryers use considerably less power than standard vented ones.

sections.key: Leave the door open, clean the seal and run a hot maintenance wash.
sections.b: If your clean washing smells musty, the problem may be the machine rather than the clothes. Front loaders in particular have rubber door seals that trap water, lint and detergent, creating a cosy home for mould and bacteria. After each wash, leave the door and detergent drawer slightly open so the inside can dry out. Wipe the door seal regularly, checking the folds for hair, coins and grime. Every month or so, run an empty hot wash, using a washing machine cleaner if you like; many machines have a dedicated drum clean cycle. Clean the filter too, if your machine has an accessible one, following the manual. And take wet clothes out promptly: washing left sitting in the drum for hours is a fast route to that damp, sour smell.

sections.key: Some laundry mishaps can be partly reversed if you act quickly.
sections.b: Even careful people end up with a pink load now and then. If dye has run, do not put the clothes in the dryer. Rewash them straight away in cold water, or use a colour run remover from the supermarket, following the instructions and checking the care labels first. White items can often be soaked in an oxygen bleach solution. Shrunken wool is harder: heat and agitation lock wool fibres together in a process called felting, which is permanent. Soaking the garment in lukewarm water with a little hair conditioner and gently stretching it while damp can sometimes win back a little size, but there are no guarantees. For stubborn smells in towels and sportswear, a hot wash with less detergent, plus thorough drying in the sun, often does more than adding fragrance.

quiz.q: What does a cross through a care label symbol mean?
o: Only do it in cold water
quiz.e: A cross through any laundry symbol means that treatment should be avoided.

quiz.q: When are new dark clothes most likely to run dye?
quiz.e: Excess dye washes out early, so wash new darks separately at first.

quiz.q: Where does most of the energy go in a warm or hot wash?
quiz.e: Heating the water is the main energy cost, which is why cold washes save money.

quiz.q: How often should you clean a clothes dryer's lint filter?
quiz.e: Built up lint makes the dryer work harder and is a fire risk.

quiz.q: Why is shrunken wool so hard to fix?
o: The fibres have locked together through felting
quiz.e: Heat and agitation felt wool fibres together, which is largely permanent.

LESSONS.title: Cutting your power and water bills
LESSONS.hook: Your energy bill is a story about heat: heating rooms, heating water and keeping food cold. Read it properly and you can find real savings without living in the dark.

sections.h: Read your bill like a detective
sections.key: Bills combine a daily supply charge with a price for each kilowatt hour you use.
sections.b: Pull out your last electricity bill and look past the total. You will usually find two main parts. The daily supply charge is a fixed amount you pay just to be connected, whether you use any power or not. The usage charge is a price per kilowatt hour, or kWh, the unit your meter counts. One kilowatt hour is the energy used by a 1,000 watt appliance running for one hour, such as a small heater, or a 10 watt LED globe running for 100 hours. Some plans have a single flat rate, while time of use plans charge more at peak times and less overnight or in the middle of the day. Your bill will also usually show your average daily use, which is the number to watch as you make changes.

sections.key: Heating, cooling and hot water usually dwarf lights and gadgets.
sections.b: People often start saving energy by unplugging phone chargers, which is a bit like saving money by skipping a mint while still buying a new car. In most Australian homes, the biggest energy users are heating and cooling, followed by water heating, then appliances such as fridges, dryers and pool pumps. Lighting and small electronics are usually a smaller share. A quick way to find your big users is to look at an appliance's wattage, often on a sticker or in the manual, and multiply by the hours it runs. A 2,400 watt portable heater running five hours a night uses 12 kWh, every night. Some energy retailers and smart meters show usage by half hour, which helps you see spikes. Target the large loads first.

sections.key: Reverse cycle air conditioners, sensible thermostat settings and draught sealing cut the biggest costs.
sections.b: A reverse cycle air conditioner is a heat pump: rather than turning electricity directly into heat, it moves heat from outside to inside. That means it can deliver several units of heat for each unit of electricity it uses, which typically makes it far cheaper to run than a plug in bar or fan heater. The thermostat setting matters too. Australian energy agencies commonly suggest around 18 to 20 degrees in winter and 25 to 27 degrees in summer, and each extra degree adds noticeably to running costs. Heat or cool only the rooms you are using, and close doors. Seal draughts around doors and windows with weather strips and door snakes. Close curtains on winter nights and block hot summer sun with external shading, which works better than internal blinds.

sections.key: Shorter showers, efficient showerheads and a well set fridge are easy wins.
sections.b: Every hot shower costs you twice: once for the water and again to heat it. That makes the shower one of the best places to save. A water efficient showerhead with a good Water Efficiency Labelling and Standards (WELS) star rating uses less hot water while still feeling comfortable, and cutting a shower by a couple of minutes adds up over a year. Fix dripping hot taps quickly. Wash clothes in cold water. Your fridge runs all day, every day, so make it efficient: keep it at around 3 to 4 degrees and the freezer around minus 18, check the door seals by closing the door on a sheet of paper to see if it holds, and leave space behind it for air to circulate. An old second fridge in the garage can be surprisingly expensive to run.

sections.key: Use energy star ratings when buying, and switch off devices that sit on standby.
sections.b: Walk through your home at night with the lights off and count the little glowing lights. Each one is a device on standby, drawing a small amount of power around the clock. Individually they are minor, but together they can add up, so switch off things like game consoles, entertainment units and spare devices at the wall when you are not using them. Bigger savings come when you replace appliances. The Energy Rating Label shows a star rating and an estimated yearly energy use in kWh, and that kWh figure is the most useful number for comparing models of a similar size. A cheaper appliance with a poor rating can cost more over its life than a pricier efficient one. Check the government Energy Rating website for calculators that compare running costs.

sections.key: Leaks, toilets and gardens are where hidden water waste usually hides.
sections.b: A toilet with a slow leak into the bowl can waste a large amount of water without anyone noticing. Test yours by adding a few drops of food colouring to the cistern and waiting about 15 minutes without flushing. If colour appears in the bowl, the cistern is leaking and needs repair. Remember that in Australia most plumbing work must be done by a licensed plumber. Use the half flush button where you have one. Run dishwashers and washing machines only when full, and look for good WELS star ratings when buying them. Outside, water the garden early in the morning or in the evening so less is lost to evaporation, and use mulch to keep soil moist. Check your local water authority for any current restrictions and rebates.

sections.key: Compare plans regularly, check for concessions, and treat this as general information.
sections.b: Many households stay on the same energy plan for years and pay more than they need to. Retailers change their offers often, so it is worth comparing plans every year or so. The government's Energy Made Easy website, energymadeeasy.gov.au, compares offers in most states and territories, and Victoria has its own Victorian Energy Compare site. Have a recent bill handy so you can enter your actual usage. Ask your current retailer if they have a better plan, as they often do. If you hold a pension, health care or other concession card, check with your retailer and state government about energy concessions and rebates. If you are struggling to pay, contact your retailer early to ask about hardship programs. This lesson is general information only, so check official sources for your situation.

quiz.q: What is a kilowatt hour?
o: The energy a 1,000 watt appliance uses in one hour
The daily cost of being connected
The maximum power your house can draw
quiz.e: One kilowatt hour equals 1,000 watts used for one hour.

quiz.q: Which usually uses the most energy in an Australian home?
quiz.e: Heating and cooling are typically the largest energy users at home.

quiz.q: Why is a reverse cycle air conditioner cheap to heat with?
o: It moves heat from outside rather than making it directly
It only heats one small spot
quiz.e: As a heat pump, it delivers several units of heat per unit of electricity.

quiz.q: How can you check a fridge door seal?
o: Measure the fridge with a tape measure
Close the door on a sheet of paper and see if it holds
quiz.e: If the paper slides out easily, the seal may be leaking cold air.

quiz.q: How can you test a toilet cistern for a leak?
o: Add food colouring to the cistern and wait without flushing
Turn off the water main for a week
quiz.e: Colour appearing in the bowl means water is leaking from the cistern.

LESSONS.title: DIY basics: your toolkit and first fixes
LESSONS.hook: Hanging a mirror, patching a hole and fixing a sticking door are well within reach. Knowing which jobs to leave to a licensed tradie is just as important.

sections.key: A small set of quality tools handles most household jobs.
sections.b: You do not need a shed full of gear to look after a home. A good starter kit fits in one toolbox. Include a claw hammer, a set of screwdrivers with both flat and Phillips heads, a tape measure, a spirit level, a utility knife with spare blades, pliers and an adjustable spanner. A cordless drill driver is the single most useful power tool, since it both drills holes and drives screws. Add a stud finder, a pencil, some sandpaper, a putty knife and a selection of screws and wall plugs. Safety gear belongs in the kit too: safety glasses, gloves and a dust mask. Buy decent quality basics rather than a giant bargain set of flimsy tools, and keep everything together so you are not hunting for the hammer every time.

sections.key: Protect your eyes, use ladders carefully, and beware of asbestos in older homes.
sections.b: Most DIY injuries come from ordinary moments: a slip on a ladder, a chip of masonry in the eye, a knife sliding off a box. Wear safety glasses whenever you drill, hammer or cut. Set ladders on firm, level ground, keep three points of contact, and do not stand on the top rungs; for high work, have someone steady the ladder. Unplug or remove the battery from power tools before changing bits or blades. In Australian homes built before about 1990, some building materials may contain asbestos, including some wall and ceiling sheeting, eaves and vinyl floor tiles. Do not drill, cut or sand anything you suspect might contain asbestos. You cannot identify it by looking, so get it tested, and check your state's asbestos information website for guidance.

sections.h: Leave these jobs to licensed tradies
sections.key: Electrical, gas and most plumbing work must be done by licensed professionals in Australia.
sections.b: In some countries, homeowners rewire their own light switches. Australia is much stricter, for good reason. In every state and territory, electrical wiring work must be done by a licensed electrician, and that includes jobs that seem simple, such as replacing a power point or light switch. Gas fitting must be done by a licensed gasfitter, because a small leak can cause a fire, explosion or carbon monoxide poisoning. Most plumbing and drainage work also needs a licensed plumber; the rules for very minor jobs differ between states, so check with your state regulator before attempting anything. Unlicensed work can be dangerous, illegal and may affect your home insurance. What you can do is change light globes, test safety switches, and describe problems clearly so the tradie can quote accurately.

sections.key: Find studs, avoid hidden pipes and cables, and choose the right fixing.
sections.b: Before you drill, picture what lies behind the wall. Most Australian homes have plasterboard walls fixed to timber or steel studs, commonly spaced about 450 or 600 millimetres apart. Pipes and electrical cables also run inside. Cables often travel straight up or down from power points and switches, so avoid drilling directly above or below them. A stud finder with cable detection helps, but it is not foolproof, so drill carefully and stop if you hit something unexpected. For heavy items such as shelves, mirrors and wall mounted televisions, screw into the studs where possible. Where there is no stud, use plasterboard anchors rated for the weight, as an ordinary screw will simply pull out. Brick and concrete walls need a masonry drill bit and wall plugs.

sections.key: Fill, let dry, sand smooth and paint for an almost invisible repair.
sections.b: A doorknob that bangs into the wall, or the screw holes left after taking down a picture, are some of the most common repair jobs, and among the easiest. For small holes and dents in plasterboard, use a ready mixed filler from a hardware store. Clean away loose crumbs, then press filler into the hole with a putty knife, scraping it level with the wall. Many fillers shrink slightly as they dry, so a second thin coat may be needed. Once completely dry, sand gently until smooth, wipe off the dust, and paint to match. Holes bigger than a coin need a self adhesive mesh patch before filling. Renters should check their lease and talk to their landlord before making holes, since repair expectations at the end of a tenancy vary.

sections.key: Most squeaks and sticks come from loose screws or a lack of lubrication.
sections.b: A door that squeals every time you open it is usually asking for lubricant. Spray a little onto the hinge pin, swing the door back and forth, and wipe off any drips. If a door sticks or will not latch, look at the hinges before reaching for a plane. Loose hinge screws let the door sag so it rubs against the frame. Tighten them, and if a screw just spins, the hole is stripped: pack it with wooden matchsticks or toothpicks and a little wood glue, snap them off flush, and drive the screw back in. Sticking drawers often have worn runners or something jammed behind them. Cabinet doors that hang crooked usually have adjustable hinges, with small screws that move the door up, down or sideways.

sections.key: Fresh silicone around wet areas keeps water out and mould away.
sections.b: Look closely at the line of sealant where your bath or shower meets the wall. If it is black with mould, cracked or peeling away, water can seep behind it and damage the wall and floor. Resealing is a satisfying weekend job. Cut away the old sealant with a sharp blade or a dedicated removal tool, clean the joint thoroughly and let it dry completely. Apply masking tape on either side of the joint for a clean edge, then run a steady bead of mould resistant bathroom silicone along the gap. Smooth it with a wet finger or a shaping tool, peel the tape away straight away, and leave it to cure for the time stated on the tube before using the shower. Good ventilation afterwards keeps the new seal fresh for longer.

quiz.q: Which power tool is described as the most useful for a starter kit?
quiz.e: A drill driver both drills holes and drives screws.

quiz.q: What should you do with a material you suspect contains asbestos?
o: Avoid disturbing it and get it tested
Paint over it and drill as normal
quiz.e: Asbestos cannot be identified by eye, so leave it alone and get it tested.

quiz.q: Who can legally replace a power point in Australia?
quiz.e: All electrical wiring work, including power points, needs a licensed electrician.

quiz.q: Where are cables commonly found inside a wall?
o: Running straight up or down from switches and power points
quiz.e: Avoid drilling directly above or below switches and power points.

quiz.q: What is a quick fix for a hinge screw that just spins?
o: Pack the hole with matchsticks and glue
quiz.e: Filling the stripped hole gives the screw something to bite into.

LESSONS.title: Gardening basics for Australian conditions
LESSONS.hook: Australian gardens face old soils, fierce sun, sudden downpours and long dry spells. Work with these conditions and even a beginner can grow something wonderful.

sections.key: Australia spans many climate zones, so local conditions decide what grows when.
sections.b: A planting guide written for Melbourne will lead a Darwin gardener badly astray. Australia's gardens range from tropical to subtropical, temperate, arid and cool highland climates, and what to plant and when depends on which one you live in. Seed packets and gardening guides often include zone maps, and a local nursery is a goldmine of practical advice. Then study your own patch. In the southern hemisphere, north facing areas get the most sun, while south facing spots stay shadier and cooler. Watch where sun falls in the morning and afternoon, which areas stay soggy after rain, and where wind whips through. Most fruiting vegetables need at least six hours of direct sun a day. Matching plants to the spot is half the battle won.

sections.key: Test your soil's texture and pH before you plant.
sections.b: Grab a handful of moist soil and squeeze it. Sandy soil feels gritty and falls apart: it drains fast but holds few nutrients. Clay soil feels sticky and forms a ribbon between your fingers: it holds nutrients but can become waterlogged and rock hard. Loam, the gardener's dream, sits in between. Many Australian soils are ancient and naturally low in nutrients, especially phosphorus. A cheap pH test kit from a garden centre tells you whether your soil is acidic or alkaline; many plants prefer slightly acidic to neutral soil, around 6 to 7. Almost every soil improves with organic matter, such as compost and well rotted manure, which feeds soil life, helps sandy soils hold water and helps clay soils drain.

sections.key: Deep, less frequent watering grows stronger, more drought tolerant roots.
sections.b: A quick sprinkle every evening feels kind, but it trains roots to stay near the surface, where they dry out fast in hot weather. Watering deeply and less often encourages roots to grow down into cooler, moister soil. Check whether a plant needs water by pushing a finger a few centimetres into the soil; if it is still damp, wait. Water early in the morning where possible, so less is lost to evaporation and leaves dry before night, which reduces fungal disease. Aim water at the soil, not the foliage. Drip irrigation delivers water efficiently right where it is needed. Some Australian soils become water repellent when dry, so water beads and runs off; a soil wetting agent helps. Always follow your local water authority's current restrictions.

sections.key: A layer of mulch saves water, cools soil and suppresses weeds.
sections.b: On a hot summer day, bare soil can bake hard and lose moisture rapidly, while soil under a blanket of mulch stays cooler and damp. Mulch is any material spread over the soil surface, such as pea straw, sugar cane mulch, wood chips or leaf litter. A layer of roughly 5 to 7 centimetres slows evaporation, keeps soil temperatures steadier, smothers many weed seeds and, as organic mulches break down, feeds the soil. Water the soil well before mulching. Keep mulch pulled back a little from plant stems and tree trunks, because constant moisture against the bark can cause rot. Finer mulches suit vegetable beds, while coarser chunky mulches last longer under shrubs and trees. Top it up as it breaks down.

sections.key: Many Australian natives are sensitive to phosphorus, so choose fertiliser carefully.
sections.b: It is tempting to think more fertiliser means a healthier garden, but too much can burn roots, wash into waterways and even kill some plants. Many Australian natives, particularly members of the Proteaceae family such as grevilleas, banksias and waratahs, evolved in low phosphorus soils and can be harmed by ordinary high phosphorus fertilisers. Use a product labelled as suitable for natives, or skip fertiliser for these plants altogether. Vegetables, by contrast, are hungry feeders and benefit from compost and a balanced fertiliser. Slow release products feed gradually, while liquid fertilisers give a quick boost. Always follow the label rates. Homemade compost is the gentlest option of all: mix greens such as vegetable scraps and grass clippings with browns such as dry leaves, and keep it moist.

sections.key: Choose plants suited to your area, avoid weeds, and handle potting mix carefully.
sections.b: Choosing local native plants is one of the easiest ways to create a garden that copes with your climate and feeds native birds and insects. Avoid plants listed as weeds in your area: some popular garden plants have escaped into bushland and caused serious damage, so check your council or state weed lists before buying. A safety note that surprises many people: potting mix and compost can carry bacteria called Legionella, which can cause a serious lung infection. Australian potting mix bags carry a warning for this reason. Open bags carefully away from your face, dampen the mix to reduce dust, wear gloves and a mask, and wash your hands afterwards. Wear gloves when gardening generally, and keep your tetanus vaccination up to date. This is general information, not medical advice.

sections.key: Start small with easy crops and plant them in the right season.
sections.b: Few things taste better than a tomato still warm from the vine. The secret to a successful first edible garden is starting small, perhaps a single raised bed or a few large pots in a sunny spot. Herbs such as parsley, basil, mint and chives are forgiving starters, though mint spreads aggressively and is best kept in a pot. Leafy greens such as lettuce and silverbeet grow quickly, so you can pick leaves within weeks. Cherry tomatoes are generally easier than large varieties. Plant in the right season for your climate zone, using a local planting calendar, since planting tomatoes in winter in Hobart will end in disappointment. Water consistently, mulch well, and visit your garden often, because catching pests and problems early makes them far easier to fix.

quiz.q: In Australia, which direction usually gets the most sun?
quiz.e: In the southern hemisphere, north facing areas receive the most sun.

quiz.q: Why is deep, infrequent watering better than a daily sprinkle?
o: It encourages deeper, more drought tolerant roots
quiz.e: Deep watering trains roots to grow down into cooler, moister soil.

quiz.q: Why should mulch be kept away from plant stems?
o: It makes the plant grow too fast
Constant moisture against bark can cause rot
It blocks sunlight to the leaves
quiz.e: A small gap around stems and trunks prevents rot.

quiz.q: Why can ordinary fertilisers harm grevilleas and banksias?
o: These plants are sensitive to phosphorus
quiz.e: Many Proteaceae evolved in low phosphorus soils and can be harmed by high phosphorus feeds.

quiz.q: Why do Australian potting mix bags carry a health warning?
quiz.e: Potting mix can carry Legionella, so avoid breathing in dust and wash your hands.

LESSONS.title: Moving house without the chaos
LESSONS.hook: Moving house is often ranked among life's most stressful events. A plan that starts weeks ahead turns moving day from a frantic scramble into a long, tiring but manageable day.

sections.key: Book removalists early, compare quotes and start decluttering.
sections.b: The worst time to discover every removalist in town is booked is the week before you move, especially at the end of the month or around school holidays, when demand peaks. Once you know your moving date, get at least two or three written quotes. Ask whether the price is fixed or hourly, what is included, and whether they offer transit insurance, and read the fine print about stairs, long carries and heavy items like pianos. If you plan to move yourself, book the trailer or truck now and line up some strong friends. This is also the moment to start decluttering. Every item you sell, donate or recycle is one less thing to pack, carry, unpack and pay to move. Start with spare rooms, sheds and cupboards.

sections.key: Use small boxes for heavy things and label each box by room and contents.
sections.b: A large box full of books can weigh as much as a person, and boxes that heavy hurt backs and burst open. The professional rule is simple: heavy items go in small boxes, light bulky items go in large ones. Wrap fragile items individually, stand plates on their edges, and fill gaps with towels or paper so nothing shifts. Label every box on the side as well as the top, since tops are hidden once boxes are stacked, with the destination room and a few words about the contents. Colour coded tape or stickers for each room speed things up on the day. Pack room by room, starting with things you use least. Take photos of the cables behind your television and computer before unplugging them, so reconnecting is easy.

sections.key: Pack one box of essentials you can find immediately.
sections.b: Picture arriving at the new place late in the evening, exhausted, surrounded by sixty identical cardboard boxes, and realising you have no idea which one holds the toilet paper. The first night box prevents this. Pack it last and keep it with you in the car rather than on the truck. Include toilet paper, soap, a towel, phone chargers, any medication, a change of clothes, basic toiletries, bed sheets, a kettle, mugs, tea or coffee, snacks, a torch, scissors, a basic toolkit and cleaning wipes. If you have children, add a favourite toy and something to keep them busy. If you have pets, pack food, bowls, leads and bedding. Keep important documents, keys, valuables and jewellery with you too, rather than with the removalists.

sections.key: Notify government agencies, banks, insurers and services, and redirect your mail.
sections.b: Changing address involves a surprisingly long list of organisations, and missing one can mean lost mail or a missed bill. Australia Post offers a paid mail redirection service, which catches anything you forget. Update your details with the Australian Electoral Commission, the ATO, Medicare and Centrelink, much of which can be done through myGov. Your state transport authority needs your new address for your driver's licence and car registration, usually within a set number of days, so check the rule in your state. Then work through your bank, superannuation fund, insurers, employer, doctor, dentist, schools, gym and subscriptions. Update your car insurance and home or contents insurance, since premiums and cover can change with your suburb. Keep a running list as you go, ticking each one off.

sections.key: Arrange connections at the new place and disconnections at the old one in advance.
sections.b: Arriving at a new home with no power, no hot water and no internet is a miserable way to start. About two weeks before moving, contact your electricity and gas retailers to arrange connection at the new address and disconnection at the old one from the right dates. It is also a good moment to compare plans, since you are switching anyway. Water is usually handled differently: owners deal with their local water authority, while renters generally have water usage arrangements set out in their lease. Internet can take the longest, so book it early, and check which connection types are available at the new address. On moving day, photograph the meter readings at both properties, so you have evidence if a final bill looks wrong.

sections.key: Clean thoroughly and compare against the entry condition report to protect your bond.
sections.b: For renters, the bond is often the biggest sum of money tied up in a move, and the condition report is the key to getting it back. Before you leave, read the entry condition report you completed when you moved in, and use it as a checklist. Clean thoroughly, including the oven, rangehood filters, windows, skirting boards and bathroom grout, and remove all rubbish. Fix any damage you caused, beyond fair wear and tear, which is the normal deterioration expected from everyday living. Take dated photos and videos of every room after cleaning. Attend the final inspection if you can, and return all keys and remotes on time. If you and the landlord disagree about the bond, your state's tenancy authority or tribunal can help. This is general information; check your state's rules.

sections.key: Supervise loading, check the new place, and do the safety basics first.
sections.b: On moving day, be at the old property early to guide the removalists, pointing out fragile items and anything that is not coming. Do a final walk through every room, cupboard and the garden shed before you leave. At the new place, direct boxes to the right rooms using your labels, and check furniture for damage before signing anything. Then do the safety basics before unpacking: find the water main, the switchboard and the gas meter, test the smoke alarms, and make sure doors and windows lock. Assemble beds first, so that whatever else happens, everyone has somewhere to sleep. Unpack the kitchen and bathroom next. Do not expect to finish everything in a weekend. Unpack a few boxes a day, and introduce yourself to the neighbours.

quiz.q: When is demand for removalists usually highest?
o: At the end of the month and around school holidays
In the middle of the month
quiz.e: End of month and holiday periods are peak moving times, so book early.

quiz.q: Which kind of box should heavy items like books go in?
quiz.e: Heavy items in small boxes keeps each box liftable and less likely to burst.

quiz.q: Where should the first night box travel?
o: At the back of the removal truck
quiz.e: Keeping it with you means essentials are on hand the moment you arrive.

quiz.q: Why photograph meter readings on moving day?
o: The utility company requires a photo to connect
It is needed to claim your bond
It gives you evidence if a final bill looks wrong
quiz.e: Dated photos of readings help you dispute an incorrect final bill.

quiz.q: What should you do at the new home before unpacking?
o: Locate the water main and switchboard and test smoke alarms
quiz.e: Safety basics come first, before the boxes.

LESSONS.title: Keeping pests out of your home
LESSONS.hook: Cockroaches, mice and termites are not signs of a dirty house so much as an inviting one. Take away what they need, and most pests simply go elsewhere.

sections.key: Pests move in for the same three things, so remove them first.
sections.b: Every pest that invades a home is looking for the same three things: food, water and a sheltered place to live. Think of your house from a cockroach's point of view, and the attractions become obvious. Crumbs under the toaster, an open packet of cereal, pet food left out overnight and a dripping tap under the sink add up to a five star resort. The most effective pest control is therefore unglamorous. Store food in sealed containers, wipe benches and sweep floors regularly, empty bins often, and rinse recyclables. Fix leaking taps and pipes, and do not leave water sitting in sinks. Reduce clutter, especially piles of cardboard and paper, which give pests shelter. Chemicals are a second line of defence, not the first.

sections.key: Block gaps, cracks and openings that pests use to enter.
sections.b: A house mouse can squeeze through a gap roughly the width of a pencil, and cockroaches can flatten themselves to slip under a door. So the next step is to make your home harder to enter. On a sunny day, look for light showing under external doors and fit door seals or brush strips. Check where pipes and cables enter walls and seal gaps around them. Steel wool or metal mesh works well for rodent holes, because mice chew through softer materials. Keep flyscreens on windows and doors in good repair. Trim tree branches and shrubs so they do not touch the roof or walls, since they act as bridges for rats and insects. Store firewood away from the house and off the ground.

sections.key: Baits that insects carry home usually work better than surface sprays.
sections.b: If you switch on the kitchen light at night and see small brown cockroaches scatter, you may be dealing with German cockroaches, a common indoor species that breeds quickly in warm kitchens. Surface sprays kill the insects you can see, but most of the population is hidden in cracks and behind appliances. Gel baits and bait stations usually work better, because cockroaches eat the bait and spread it to others in their hiding places. Place baits where they shelter, such as behind the fridge and under the sink, and keep cleaning so the bait is the most tempting food around. Ants are similar: follow the trail to find where they enter, wipe the trail away with soapy water, and use ant baits rather than sprays, which can scatter the colony.

sections.key: Snap traps are effective, while poison baits can harm pets and wildlife.
sections.b: Droppings in the pantry, gnawed packets and scratching in the ceiling at night are the classic signs of rodents. Once you have removed food and sealed entry points, traps are an effective way to deal with those already inside. Snap traps set along walls, where rodents prefer to run, are cheap and work quickly. Bait them with a small amount of peanut butter and check them daily, wearing gloves to handle dead rodents. Poison baits are widely sold but come with downsides: poisoned rodents may die inside walls and smell, and pets, owls and other wildlife that eat poisoned rodents can be poisoned themselves. If you use baits, use lockable bait stations and follow the label exactly. Clean up droppings by wetting them with disinfectant first, rather than sweeping or vacuuming dry.

sections.key: Termite damage can be costly and is often not covered by home insurance.
sections.b: Termites, often called white ants, can hollow out the timber in a house for months before anyone notices. In much of Australia they are a serious threat, and termite damage is often excluded from home insurance policies, so check yours. Warning signs include mud tunnels, called leads, running up walls or foundations, timber that sounds hollow when tapped, and paint that bubbles or cracks. If you find termites, do not disturb them or spray them, because they may simply move elsewhere in the house; call a licensed pest manager. To lower your risk, keep garden beds, mulch and stored timber away from the house's edges, do not let soil cover weep holes in brick walls, fix leaks, and keep any subfloor well ventilated. Regular professional inspections, commonly recommended at least yearly, catch problems early.

sections.key: Remove standing water weekly and keep flyscreens in good condition.
sections.b: In warm weather, mosquitoes can go from egg to biting adult in as little as a week or so, and they only need a small amount of still water to breed. A forgotten bucket, a blocked gutter, a saucer under a pot plant or an old tyre can produce hundreds of them. Once a week, tip out or refresh any standing water around your yard, including pet water bowls and birdbaths. Clean out gutters, and cover rainwater tanks with mesh screens on inlets and overflows. Flies breed in rotting food and animal waste, so keep bins sealed and clean, and pick up after pets promptly. Good flyscreens remain the best defence indoors. Mosquitoes can spread diseases in parts of Australia, so check health advice for your state when travelling or camping.

sections.key: Read the label every time, and know when to call a professional.
sections.b: Pest control products are designed to kill living things, so they need respect. The label on every registered product is your guide: it tells you where the product can be used, how much to use and what protective equipment to wear, and following it is a legal requirement as well as a safety one. Store chemicals in their original containers, locked away from children and pets, and never decant them into drink bottles. Keep people and animals away from treated areas for as long as the label says. For termites, large infestations or anything in a roof cavity, call a licensed pest manager. And remember that some visitors are protected: possums are native animals, so if one moves into your roof, contact a licensed wildlife remover rather than trying to deal with it yourself.

quiz.q: What are the three things pests are looking for in a home?
quiz.e: Removing food, water and shelter is the foundation of pest control.

quiz.q: Why is steel wool good for blocking rodent holes?
o: Mice cannot chew through it easily
It makes a noise that scares them
quiz.e: Rodents chew through softer materials but struggle with metal.

quiz.q: Why do gel baits often beat sprays for cockroaches?
o: Cockroaches carry the bait back to hidden ones
quiz.e: Baits reach the hidden population, not just the insects you can see.

quiz.q: What should you do if you find active termites?
o: Leave them undisturbed and call a licensed pest manager
quiz.e: Disturbing termites can make them move elsewhere and harder to treat.

quiz.q: How often should you tip out standing water to stop mosquitoes breeding?
quiz.e: Mosquitoes can develop from egg to adult in about a week in warm weather.

LESSONS.title: Declutter and organise your home
LESSONS.hook: Most of us use a small fraction of what we own, while the rest quietly costs us space, time and calm. Here is a practical way to clear it out and keep it clear.

sections.key: Our brains overvalue what we already own, which makes letting go hard.
sections.b: Hold up a mug you never use and ask yourself if you would buy it today. Often the answer is no, yet the mug stays. Psychologists have a name for part of this pull: the endowment effect, our tendency to value things more simply because we own them. Add 'just in case' thinking, guilt over money spent, gifts from loved ones and plain busyness, and clutter grows quietly year after year. Understanding this helps, because it means clutter is not a character flaw. It is the natural result of things coming into a home faster than they leave. Decluttering is simply the process of deliberately letting more things out, and then setting up habits so the flow stays balanced in future.

sections.key: Begin with one drawer or shelf, not a whole house.
sections.b: Deciding to declutter the whole house this weekend is a recipe for a lounge room buried under piles and a strong urge to give up. Instead, pick one small, specific space you can finish in 15 to 30 minutes: the cutlery drawer, the bathroom cabinet, the shelf by the front door. Finishing quickly gives you a visible win and builds momentum. Start with areas that hold few emotions, such as the linen cupboard or the pantry, where decisions are easy and practice sharpens your judgement. Leave photos, letters and inherited items until later, once the decision making muscle is stronger. Set a timer if it helps you stay focused. A little every day often achieves more than one exhausting marathon that you dread repeating.

sections.key: Sort each item into keep, donate, sell, or rubbish and recycling.
sections.b: Clear out your chosen space completely, so you can see everything at once, then sort each item into one of four groups: keep, donate, sell, and rubbish or recycling. Ask simple questions. Have I used this in the past year? Would I buy it again? Do I have another that does the same job? Is it in good condition? Wipe the empty space clean, then return only the keep items. Here is the vital part: deal with the other boxes promptly. Put the rubbish out that day, list sale items within the week, and put donations in your car boot so they leave the house. A box of donations sitting in the hallway for three months is not decluttering, it is just moving clutter from room to room.

sections.key: Only donate usable items, and dispose of e-waste and chemicals properly.
