sections.b: Charity shops are grateful for good quality goods, but they spend a lot of money each year disposing of donations they cannot sell, such as broken, dirty or unsafe items. Before donating, ask whether a friend would happily buy it in its current state. Check what your local charity accepts, and never leave goods outside closed shops or beside overflowing donation bins, where they are often treated as illegal dumping. Old electronics, batteries, paint and chemicals should not go in household rubbish bins: many councils run e-waste drop off points and household chemical collection days, and some retailers take back batteries. Wipe your personal data from old phones and computers first. Usable furniture and appliances can be given away through local buy nothing groups, or sold online.

sections.key: Keep the best few, and let photos hold the memories of the rest.
sections.b: A box of your children's drawings, your grandmother's tea set or decades of birthday cards can feel impossible to sort, because they are not really about the objects. They are about people and moments. A few strategies help. Rather than keeping everything, choose the very best examples and display or store them properly, so they are honoured rather than buried in a cupboard. Photograph items you want to remember but do not need to keep, such as artwork or bulky souvenirs. Remind yourself that the memory lives in you, not in the object, and that letting go of an item is not letting go of a person. And give yourself permission to come back later: you do not need to make every sentimental decision in one sitting.

sections.key: Give everything a home, store by how often you use it, and label it.
sections.b: Once you have cleared the excess, organising becomes far easier, since you are arranging fewer things. The golden rule is that everything needs a home: a specific place it lives and returns to. Store things where you use them, and by how often you use them. Daily items belong at waist to eye height and close at hand, while the Christmas decorations can live on the highest shelf. Group similar items together so you can see what you have and avoid buying duplicates. Clear containers and labels help everyone in the household find things and put them back. Use vertical space with shelves and hooks. And resist buying storage before decluttering: new containers often just let you keep more clutter, more neatly hidden.

sections.key: Simple daily habits stop clutter creeping back.
sections.b: A tidy home is not a one off project, it is a set of small habits. Try a ten minute reset each evening, putting things back in their homes so you wake to a clear kitchen and lounge. Use a one in, one out rule for categories that tend to grow, such as clothes, shoes, mugs and toys: when something new arrives, something old leaves. Deal with paper as soon as it arrives, recycling junk mail straight away and keeping a single spot for bills and letters that need action. Pause before buying, perhaps waiting a day or two for non essential purchases, and ask where the item will live. Keep a donation bag in a wardrobe so letting go is easy. Revisit problem areas every few months.

quiz.q: What is the endowment effect?
o: Valuing things more because we own them
Preferring new things to old ones
quiz.e: Ownership makes us overvalue items, which makes letting go harder.

quiz.q: What is the best place to begin decluttering?
o: One small, low emotion space like a drawer
quiz.e: Small, quick wins build momentum and decision making skill.

quiz.q: What is the most important step after sorting with the four box method?
o: Storing the boxes in the hallway
Dealing with the donate, sell and rubbish boxes promptly
quiz.e: Items need to actually leave the house for decluttering to work.

quiz.q: How should old phones and batteries be disposed of?
o: Through e-waste or battery collection points
quiz.e: Electronics and batteries need proper recycling, not landfill.

quiz.q: What does the one in, one out rule mean?
o: Only one person can tidy at a time
When something new arrives, something old leaves
Buy one storage box for each room
quiz.e: Balancing what comes in with what goes out stops clutter returning.

LESSONS.title: Doing your own tax return, step by step
LESSONS.hook: Every year millions of Australians lodge a tax return from their couch in under an hour. Here is how to do it calmly, claim what you are entitled to, and keep the records that protect you if the ATO comes asking.

sections.key: The financial year runs 1 July to 30 June, and a self-lodged return is generally due by 31 October.
sections.b: Picture July in an Australian office: someone always announces they have already lodged, and someone else always forgets until Halloween. The Australian financial year runs from 1 July to 30 June, and if you lodge yourself, your return is generally due by 31 October. If you use a registered tax agent and get on their books before that date, you usually get extra time. Rushing in on 1 July is rarely a good idea, because your employer, bank and health fund are still sending their information to the ATO. Waiting until late July or August means most of it will be ready and waiting for you. This lesson is general information, not tax advice, so check the details for your situation at ato.gov.au.

sections.key: Linking the ATO to your myGov account gives you free access to myTax, the ATO's online lodgement tool.
sections.b: The simplest way to lodge is myTax, the ATO's free online return. To reach it, create a myGov account at my.gov.au, then link the Australian Taxation Office as a service. The first time you link, you will need to prove who you are, usually by answering questions about a past notice of assessment, your bank account or a payment summary, or by using a digital ID. Once linked, the ATO section shows your tax returns, your income statements, any debts, and your super accounts in one place. Turn on two-step sign-in and never share your login, because scammers prize myGov access. If you would rather talk to a human, the ATO's Tax Help program offers free help from trained volunteers for people on modest incomes.

sections.h: Let prefill do the heavy lifting
sections.key: Wait until your income statement says 'tax ready', then check every prefilled figure rather than trusting it blindly.
sections.b: When you start a return in myTax, much of it fills itself in. Salary and tax withheld come from your employer's income statement, interest comes from your bank, and private health insurance details arrive from your fund. The key signal is your income statement in myGov being marked 'tax ready'. Until then, your employer may still be finalising figures. Prefill is a starting point, not a guarantee. Compare it with your own payslips and bank records, and add anything missing: a second job, foreign income, a side hustle, dividends, or interest from an account at a different bank. Income you leave out is still taxable, and the ATO matches data from many sources, so omissions are often picked up later with interest and penalties added.

sections.h: The three golden rules for deductions
sections.key: You can claim a work expense only if you paid for it, it relates directly to earning your income, and you have a record.
sections.b: Deductions reduce your taxable income, so it is tempting to be generous with them. The ATO boils the rules down to three tests. First, you must have spent the money yourself and not been reimbursed. Second, the expense must be directly related to earning your income, not private. Third, you need a record to prove it. If something is partly for work and partly personal, like a phone or a laptop, you can only claim the work share. Ordinary commuting between home and work, normal clothes you could wear anywhere, and childcare are generally not deductible. The ATO publishes occupation guides for many jobs, from nurses to tradies, which spell out what people in that line of work can and cannot usually claim.

sections.key: Store receipts digitally as you go and keep them for five years from when you lodge.
sections.b: The best time to organise tax records is the moment you buy something, not the following October. Take a photo of each work-related receipt and keep it in one folder, or use the free myDeductions tool in the ATO app, which lets you snap receipts and log car trips and expenses through the year, then upload them to myTax. Generally you need to keep records for five years from the date you lodge your return. For working from home, the ATO expects evidence of the hours you actually worked at home, such as a timesheet, roster or diary, not a rough estimate made up at the end of the year. Check the ATO's current working from home rules, because the methods and rates are reviewed from time to time.

sections.h: Lodge, then read your notice of assessment
sections.key: After lodging, your notice of assessment shows what the ATO calculated, and it is worth checking line by line.
sections.b: When you press submit, myTax gives you an estimate of your refund or the amount you owe. The ATO then processes the return and issues a notice of assessment, which appears in your myGov inbox. Read it rather than just checking the bottom line. It shows your taxable income, the tax worked out on it, any Medicare levy or surcharge, study loan repayments and credits for tax already withheld. If the figure differs from the estimate, the notice usually explains why. Refunds normally go to the bank account you nominated, so make sure the details are right. If you owe money and cannot pay it all by the due date, contact the ATO early, because they can often set up a payment plan.

sections.key: If you realise you made an error, you can amend your return in myTax, and a registered agent can help with complex situations.
sections.b: Discovered a forgotten bank account or a receipt you missed? You can amend a return through myTax, usually within two years of your notice of assessment for most individuals. Correcting an honest mistake yourself is far better than waiting for the ATO to find it. If your affairs are more complicated, such as owning a rental property, selling shares or running a business, a registered tax agent can be worth the fee, and that fee is itself generally deductible the following year. Always check that an agent is registered on the Tax Practitioners Board register at tpb.gov.au. Be wary of anyone promising unusually big refunds, because you, not the agent, are legally responsible for what your return says.

quiz.q: If you lodge your own tax return, when is it generally due?
quiz.e: Self-lodged returns are generally due by 31 October; registered tax agents can often lodge later.

quiz.q: What should you look for before relying on prefilled employment income?
o: A text message from the ATO with a link
Your first payslip of the new year
quiz.e: Employers finalise income statements, and the 'tax ready' label signals the figures are complete.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the ATO's three golden rules for work deductions?
o: You spent the money and were not reimbursed
The expense is directly related to earning your income
You have a record to prove it
The item cost more than a set minimum amount
quiz.e: The three rules are about who paid, the link to earning income, and having records, not a minimum cost.

quiz.q: Generally, how long should you keep tax records?
o: Five years from when you lodge
quiz.e: The ATO generally expects records to be kept for five years from the date you lodge.

quiz.q: Where can you check that a tax agent is registered?
quiz.e: Registered tax agents appear on the Tax Practitioners Board's public register at tpb.gov.au.

LESSONS.title: Super housekeeping: find, combine and check your fund
LESSONS.hook: Many Australians have super scattered across funds they barely remember, each quietly charging fees. A once-a-year check-up can tidy it up, but there are traps to look out for before you hit 'combine'.

sections.key: Changing jobs used to create a new super account each time, so many people have duplicate accounts eating fees.
sections.b: Think of someone who worked at a café during uni, then a retail chain, then an office job. Before the rules changed, each employer may have opened a new default super account for them. Every one of those accounts can charge administration and investment fees, and some carry insurance premiums too, all nibbling at balances that might be small to begin with. Since late 2021, a system called stapling means your existing fund generally follows you to a new job unless you choose otherwise, which has slowed the creation of new duplicates. But old accounts do not vanish by themselves. This lesson explains how to find and review them. It is general information, not financial advice; consider your own circumstances or speak to a licensed adviser.

sections.key: The ATO section of myGov lists all your super accounts, including lost and unclaimed super.
sections.b: The quickest way to see all your super is through myGov, once you have linked the ATO. Under the super section you will find a list of every account reported in your name, with balances, plus any lost super held by funds and any unclaimed super that has been transferred to the ATO. Unclaimed super can end up with the ATO when an account has been inactive or the fund could not contact you. You can usually ask for ATO-held money to be paid into your chosen fund online. Have your tax file number registered with each fund, because without it a fund cannot easily match accounts to you. Make sure each fund has your current address and email so you do not drift into the lost pile again.

sections.key: Closing an account can cancel the life, disability or income protection cover attached to it, so check first.
sections.b: This is the trap that catches people. Many super accounts include default insurance: cover if you die, become totally and permanently disabled, and sometimes income protection if you cannot work for a while. When you roll an account into another fund, the cover in the old account normally ends. If you have developed a health condition since joining, you may struggle to get equivalent cover elsewhere. So before consolidating, download the insurance details for each account and compare the type of cover, the amounts and the cost. Also note that cover in an account that has stopped receiving contributions can be switched off after a period of inactivity unless you ask to keep it. Decide deliberately, rather than letting a rollover decide for you.

sections.h: Other reasons not to roll over
sections.key: Defined benefit funds, employer arrangements and exit fees are worth checking before moving money.
sections.b: Some super accounts are worth keeping. Defined benefit funds, common among older public sector and some corporate schemes, calculate your benefit using a formula rather than just your account balance, and leaving can mean giving up valuable entitlements. Some employers pay into a particular fund with special arrangements, such as cheaper fees or tailored insurance, so check what your current employer contributes to before redirecting anything. Funds can no longer charge exit fees on super accounts, but selling and buying investments as money moves can still have small costs, and your money may be out of the market for a few days during the transfer. Finally, make sure your employer has the details of the fund you are keeping, so future contributions do not reopen a forgotten account.

sections.key: Once you have chosen a fund, you can usually request rollovers from myGov or through the receiving fund.
sections.b: When you have decided which fund to keep, consolidating is usually simple. In the ATO section of myGov you can select the accounts you want to transfer and the fund to receive them, and the request is sent electronically. Many funds also offer to find and combine your other accounts for you if you give consent. Transfers generally take a few days to a few weeks. Afterwards, check that the old accounts show a zero balance and that the money arrived in full. Keep the confirmation emails. If a transfer stalls, contact the receiving fund first, since they can see whether the request is in progress. Avoid any third party who charges a fee to 'find your lost super', because the official tools are free.

sections.key: The ATO's YourSuper comparison tool shows fees and long-term returns for MySuper products and flags poor performers.
sections.b: Having one account is good; having one good account is better. The ATO's YourSuper comparison tool, at ato.gov.au, ranks MySuper products, the default options most people are in, by fees and net returns over several years. Under the annual performance test, products that underperform a benchmark must write to their members to say so, and repeat failures can be closed to new members. If you receive one of those letters, take it seriously. When comparing, look at long-term net returns after fees rather than one good year, and consider whether the investment mix matches how long you have until retirement. Fees that look small as a percentage can add up to a large sum over decades, thanks to the same compounding that grows your balance.

sections.key: Check who will receive your super if you die, because super is not automatically covered by your will.
sections.b: One more item belongs on your super checklist: your beneficiary nomination. Super is generally held in trust, so it does not automatically follow your will. Most funds let you nominate who should receive your balance and any insurance payout if you die. A binding nomination, if valid, generally directs the trustee to pay the people you name, while a non-binding nomination is only a guide. Some binding nominations lapse after a set period unless renewed, and life events like marriage, separation or a new child can make an old nomination wrong. Put a reminder in your calendar once a year to log in, check contributions, fees, insurance, investment option and beneficiaries. Moneysmart.gov.au has plain-language guides to every step if you want more detail.

quiz.q: What does 'stapling' mean in Australian super?
o: Your existing fund generally follows you to a new job
All funds are merged by the government
You must change funds every job
Your employer chooses a new fund each year
quiz.e: Since late 2021, stapling means your existing fund generally follows you unless you choose otherwise.

quiz.q: What is a key risk of rolling an old super account into another fund?
o: Your tax file number is cancelled
Insurance attached to the old account normally ends
quiz.e: Cover held in the closed account usually ends, which can matter if your health has changed.

quiz.q: Why might someone keep a defined benefit fund rather than roll it over?
o: It always has the lowest fees
The benefit uses a formula that can be valuable
It cannot be found in myGov
It pays the highest interest rate
quiz.e: Defined benefit schemes calculate benefits by formula, and leaving can mean giving up valuable entitlements.

quiz.q: What happens to a MySuper product that fails the annual performance test?
o: The fund must write to members to tell them
quiz.e: Failing funds must notify members, and repeat failures can be closed to new members.

quiz.q: Why is a beneficiary nomination important?
o: Super does not automatically follow your will
It is needed to make contributions
quiz.e: Super is held in trust, so a nomination guides or directs who receives it.

LESSONS.title: Switching providers: beating the loyalty tax
LESSONS.hook: Staying with the same provider for years can quietly cost you. A little comparison, a phone call and a calendar reminder can trim your household bills without changing how you live.

sections.key: Customers who never switch often end up on older, pricier plans while new customers get the best deals.
sections.b: Picture two neighbours with identical houses and identical habits. One signed up with an energy retailer a decade ago and never looked again; the other compares plans each year. It is common for the first to pay noticeably more, simply because their discount expired or their plan was replaced by cheaper offers they never moved to. This pattern, sometimes called the loyalty tax, shows up across energy, phone, internet and insurance. Providers rely on inertia. The fix is not to switch constantly, but to check once a year whether you are on a competitive deal. A useful habit is to choose one month, perhaps around tax time, and review every regular bill in a single sitting with a cuppa.

sections.key: Your usage and tariff details are the raw material for any useful comparison.
sections.b: Before comparing anything, dig out your latest bills. For electricity and gas, find your total usage over the billing period, your daily supply charge and your usage rates, and check whether you have a single rate or time-of-use pricing, where rates vary through the day. If you have solar, note your feed-in tariff. For phone and internet, check how much data you actually use each month and what speed tier your home internet is on. Many people pay for far more mobile data than they use, or for an internet speed their household does not need. Energy bills also show your account and meter details, which you will need if you switch. Having the facts in front of you stops a salesperson's patter from steering the conversation.

sections.h: Compare energy plans the official way
sections.key: Government comparison sites show plans without commissions, and retailers must compare offers with a reference price.
sections.b: For electricity and gas, use the free government comparison sites rather than commercial ones that may be paid by retailers. In New South Wales, Queensland, South Australia, Tasmania and the ACT, the Australian Energy Regulator runs Energy Made Easy at energymadeeasy.gov.au. In Victoria, use Victorian Energy Compare. Western Australia and the Northern Territory have different market arrangements, with fewer retail choices in many areas. You can enter your usage or upload a bill to see plans available at your address. Retailers in many states must show how their offers compare with a government reference price, which makes it easier to spot genuinely cheaper deals. Look past headline discounts: conditional discounts that vanish if you pay late can make a plan dearer than it looks.

sections.key: Switching energy or telco providers is usually simple, and the new provider handles most of the work.
sections.b: Many people stay put because they imagine switching means disconnection or tradespeople. In practice, changing energy retailers usually involves no physical work at all: the same poles, wires and meter keep supplying you, and only the company billing you changes. You sign up with the new retailer, and they arrange the transfer. Check whether your current plan has exit fees and when any contract term ends. For mobile phones, you can usually keep your number when you move provider. Month-to-month plans give you freedom to leave if a better deal appears. For internet, check whether you are tied into a contract or modem repayments. Sometimes just calling your current provider and saying you are thinking of leaving gets you onto a better plan.

sections.h: Phone and internet: pay for what you use
sections.key: Match your mobile data and home internet speed to your real needs rather than the biggest plan on offer.
sections.b: Telco plans are often sold on bigger numbers: more gigabytes, faster speeds. But if your phone usually connects to home and work Wi-Fi, you may need far less mobile data than you pay for. Your provider's app shows your typical monthly use, so choose a plan that comfortably covers it with a bit of buffer. For home internet on the NBN, the right speed tier depends on how many people use it at once and what they do. A couple who browse and stream may not need the same speed as a household of gamers working from home. Providers publish typical evening speeds, which matter more than maximums. Also check for streaming services and subscriptions you no longer use, as they add up surprisingly fast.

sections.key: If you are struggling, energy retailers must offer hardship support, and many concessions are available.
sections.b: If paying bills is becoming hard, act early rather than waiting for disconnection notices. Energy retailers are required to have hardship programs, which can include payment plans, advice on cutting usage and protection from disconnection while you are participating. Telcos also have financial hardship policies. Ask for the hardship team specifically. State and territory governments offer energy concessions and rebates to eligible people, such as pensioners, healthcare card holders and some low-income households, and they are not always applied automatically, so check your state government's website. Services Australia can tell you which cards and payments you are eligible for. The free National Debt Helpline, on 1800 007 007, can connect you with a financial counsellor who can negotiate with providers for you.

sections.key: Complain to the provider first, then go to the free ombudsman if it is not resolved.
sections.b: Billing errors, surprise fees and botched transfers do happen. Start by contacting the provider, explaining the problem clearly and asking for a complaint reference number. Keep notes of every call, including the date and the name of the person you spoke with. If the problem is not fixed, you can take it to an independent ombudsman for free. For phone and internet, that is the Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman. For energy and water, most states have their own energy and water ombudsman scheme, while in the ACT complaints go to the ACT Civil and Administrative Tribunal. Ombudsmen can investigate and, in many cases, require providers to fix the problem or pay compensation. This lesson is general information only; check moneysmart.gov.au and your state's consumer affairs website for the rules that apply where you live.

quiz.q: What does the 'loyalty tax' refer to?
o: A government tax on long-term customers
Long-term customers often paying more than new customers
A discount for staying with one provider
quiz.e: Customers who never review their plans often end up on pricier deals than new customers get.

quiz.q: Which site does the Australian Energy Regulator run for comparing energy plans in several states?
quiz.e: Energy Made Easy covers NSW, Queensland, SA, Tasmania and the ACT; Victoria has its own site.

quiz.q: What usually happens physically when you switch electricity retailer?
o: A new meter must be installed
Your power is cut for a day
Nothing; only the company billing you changes
quiz.e: The same network and meter keep supplying you; only the retailer changes.

quiz.q: If you are struggling to pay an energy bill, what should you ask for?
o: A higher discount on late payments
quiz.e: Energy retailers must have hardship programs with payment plans and other support.

quiz.q: Where can you take an unresolved phone or internet complaint for free?
quiz.e: The Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman handles unresolved phone and internet complaints.

LESSONS.title: Making an insurance claim that sticks
LESSONS.hook: You pay premiums for years hoping you never need them. When something finally goes wrong, how you handle the first days of a claim can make a real difference to the outcome.

sections.key: Knowing your policy, your sum insured and your excess before disaster strikes makes claiming far easier.
sections.b: The best time to prepare for a claim is on a quiet weekday, long before a storm or a break-in. Download your product disclosure statement, the long document that sets out what your policy covers, and read the sections on what is excluded and how claims work. Check your sum insured for home and contents, because underinsurance is common: people often guess the value of their belongings and fall well short. Many insurers offer online calculators to help estimate rebuilding or replacement costs. Walk through your home filming each room and storing the video in the cloud, along with receipts for expensive items. Note your excess, the amount you pay towards each claim. This is general information, not advice; read your own policy for the details.

sections.key: Prevent further damage if you safely can, and photograph everything before cleaning up.
sections.b: Imagine coming home to water pouring through the ceiling after a burst pipe. The first priority is safety: turn off water or power if it is safe to do so, and call emergency services if anyone is in danger. Policies generally expect you to take reasonable steps to prevent further damage, such as placing a tarp or calling an emergency plumber, and the cost of reasonable emergency repairs is often covered. Before you throw anything away, take photos and video of the damage from several angles, including close-ups of serial numbers and brand labels. Keep damaged items if you can until the insurer says you may dispose of them, because an assessor may want to inspect them. For theft, report it to police and record the event number.

sections.h: Lodge promptly and keep a log
sections.key: Notify your insurer as soon as possible and keep a written record of every contact.
sections.b: Contact your insurer as soon as practical, usually through their app, website or claims line. Delays can complicate a claim, especially when damage gets worse over time. You will be given a claim number; write it on every document and email from then on. Start a simple claim log, on paper or in a notes app, recording the date and time of every call, who you spoke to and what was agreed. Follow up important phone calls with a short email confirming what was said. Be honest and accurate in everything you tell the insurer. Exaggerating a claim, even slightly, can give the insurer grounds to refuse it or cancel your policy, and it can have serious legal consequences.

sections.key: After a crash, exchange details, take photos and avoid admitting fault at the scene.
sections.b: Car accidents are stressful, and adrenaline makes it easy to forget things. Once everyone is safe, exchange names, addresses, phone numbers, registration numbers and insurer details with the other driver. If they refuse, or you suspect a crime such as drink driving, contact police. Photograph the vehicles, number plates, the road, any skid marks and the surrounding scene. Get names and phone numbers of any witnesses. Most policies ask you not to admit fault or promise to pay, because that is for the insurers to work out. Note the time, location, weather and lighting. Some states require crashes to be reported to police in particular circumstances, such as injuries or when a vehicle is towed, so check your state's rules.

sections.key: You can ask questions, get your own quotes and choose whether to accept repairs or a cash settlement.
sections.b: For larger claims, the insurer may send an assessor to inspect the damage, or ask for quotes from builders or repairers. You can generally provide your own quotes as well, and it is reasonable to ask for a copy of the assessor's report. Insurers may offer to manage repairs through their own builders, or offer a cash settlement instead. A cash settlement can seem attractive, but check carefully that it would cover the real cost of fixing the damage with a licensed tradesperson, because once you accept it the insurer usually has no further responsibility for the repairs. Ask how the figure was calculated. Keep receipts for any temporary accommodation or emergency costs, as some policies cover these up to a limit.

sections.key: Ask for decisions and their reasons in writing, and check the insurer is meeting its obligations.
sections.b: Insurers that subscribe to the General Insurance Code of Practice commit to standards for how they handle claims, including keeping you updated and making decisions within set timeframes, and to explaining their reasons. If your claim is accepted, confirm what will happen next and when. If it is denied, ask for the decision and the reasons in writing, along with the specific policy wording they relied on and any reports or information used. You are entitled to ask for this information. Read the reasons carefully and compare them with your policy. Sometimes a refusal rests on a misunderstanding that extra evidence can fix, such as a receipt, photo or tradesperson's report showing the cause of the damage.

sections.key: Lodge an internal complaint first, then take it to the Australian Financial Complaints Authority for free.
sections.b: If you disagree with a claim decision, start by making a formal complaint to the insurer. Use the word 'complaint', put it in writing, and explain what outcome you want. Insurers must have an internal dispute resolution process and generally need to respond within a set period, which for most complaints is around 30 calendar days. If you are unhappy with the response, or do not get one in time, you can lodge a complaint with the Australian Financial Complaints Authority, known as AFCA, at afca.org.au. AFCA is free for consumers and independent of insurers, and its decisions can bind the insurer. Moneysmart.gov.au has guides on claims and complaints, and a free financial counsellor can help if the stress is mounting.

quiz.q: Why is it worth checking your sum insured before anything goes wrong?
o: Underinsurance is common and can leave you short
It is required to lodge a tax return
quiz.e: Many people underestimate the value of their home or belongings and are underinsured.

quiz.q: What should you do before throwing away damaged items?
o: Photograph them and keep them until the insurer says otherwise
quiz.e: Photos and the items themselves can be important evidence for an assessor.

quiz.q: What do most policies ask you not to do at the scene of a car accident?
o: Admit fault or promise to pay
quiz.e: Fault is for the insurers to work out, so policies usually ask you not to admit it.

quiz.q: What is a risk of accepting a cash settlement?
o: The insurer usually has no further responsibility for the repairs
You must pay tax on it immediately
It cancels all your other policies
quiz.e: Once you accept cash, you generally bear the risk if repairs cost more than expected.

quiz.q: Where can you take an insurance dispute after the insurer's internal process?
quiz.e: AFCA is the free, independent external dispute body for insurance and other financial complaints.

LESSONS.title: Comparing loans: the real cost of borrowing
LESSONS.hook: The interest rate in the ad is only part of the story. Fees, terms, balloon payments and add-ons can turn a cheap-looking loan into an expensive one. Here is how to read the numbers like a lender.

sections.key: The headline rate ignores fees, so focus on the total amount you will repay over the life of the loan.
sections.b: Two car loans are advertised side by side. One has a lower interest rate; the other has no upfront fee. Which is cheaper? You cannot tell from the rates alone. The true cost of borrowing includes interest plus every fee: establishment fees, monthly account fees, early repayment fees and late fees. The most useful single number is the total amount you will repay over the life of the loan if you make every repayment on time. Lenders must give you key facts before you sign, and you can ask them directly for the total cost. Moneysmart.gov.au has a free personal loan calculator to compare options. This lesson is general information, not credit advice; consider your own situation before borrowing.

sections.h: What the comparison rate does, and doesn't, do
sections.key: A comparison rate rolls most fees into one rate, but it is based on a standard example loan that may not match yours.
sections.b: Australian law requires lenders who advertise an interest rate for many consumer loans to show a comparison rate as well. The comparison rate combines the interest rate with most upfront and ongoing fees into a single percentage, so a low rate with high fees no longer looks artificially cheap. But it is calculated on a standard example loan amount and term set out in the rules, and there is usually a warning saying the rate is true only for that example. If your loan is smaller or shorter than the example, fixed fees weigh more heavily and your real cost can be higher than the comparison rate suggests. It also excludes some costs, such as late fees and certain optional charges. Treat it as a guide, not the whole answer.

sections.key: Secured loans usually cost less but put an asset at risk, and fixed rates trade flexibility for certainty.
sections.b: A secured loan uses an asset, often the car you are buying, as security, so the lender can repossess it if you default. Because the lender's risk is lower, secured loans generally have lower rates than unsecured ones. A fixed rate stays the same for the term, which makes budgeting easy, but fixed loans often charge break costs or restrict extra repayments. A variable rate can rise or fall, but variable loans frequently allow extra repayments without penalty, which can save significant interest if you plan to pay the loan off early. Ask each lender three questions: can I make extra repayments, can I pay out the loan early, and what will each of those cost? The answers can matter as much as the rate itself.

sections.key: Lower repayments from longer terms or balloon payments usually mean paying more interest overall.
sections.b: Lenders and car dealers often advertise the weekly repayment, because it is the number that feels affordable. Two common ways to shrink that figure are a longer term and a balloon payment. A balloon, also called a residual, is a large lump sum due at the end of the loan. Because part of the debt is pushed to the end, you pay interest on a bigger balance for longer, so the total cost rises. And when the balloon falls due, you need the cash, or must refinance, or sell the car, which may by then be worth less than you owe. Longer terms work the same way: smaller repayments, more total interest. Always compare loans on the total cost, not the weekly repayment.

sections.key: Finance arranged at a car yard can be convenient, but compare it with your own quote and question any add-on insurance.
sections.b: Car yards and big retailers often offer finance on the spot. It is convenient, but it is easy to focus on the car and accept the loan without comparing. Getting pre-approval or a quote from your own bank or credit union before you shop gives you a benchmark and strengthens your hand. Watch for add-on products bundled into the loan, such as gap insurance, extended warranties or loan protection insurance. Sold this way, they have historically been poor value for many buyers, and when financed you pay interest on them too. Rules introduced in recent years restrict how some add-on insurance can be sold, including a deferred sales period, but you can still simply say no. Ask for the price of the car and the loan separately.

sections.h: Responsible lending and your credit file
sections.key: Lenders must check a loan is not unsuitable for you, and every formal application can appear on your credit report.
sections.b: Under Australia's responsible lending laws, licensed lenders must make reasonable inquiries about your income, expenses and needs, and must not offer a loan that is unsuitable, for example one you could only repay with substantial hardship. That is a protection, so be truthful in your application. Each formal application for credit is usually recorded on your credit report. Several applications in a short time can make lenders more cautious. Many lenders now offer eligibility checks or quotes that do not leave a full credit enquiry, so ask before applying. For small, short-term needs, avoid payday lenders where possible; the costs can be very high relative to the amount borrowed. People on low incomes may be eligible for no interest loans through the No Interest Loan Scheme.

sections.key: Line up each offer's total repayments, fees, flexibility and conditions before deciding.
sections.b: Here is a method that works for almost any loan. For each offer, write down the amount borrowed, the term, the interest rate, the comparison rate, every fee, whether extra repayments are allowed and at what cost, and any balloon. Then calculate or ask for the total amount repayable. Put the offers side by side. Next, ask whether you could still make repayments if your income dropped or rates rose. Finally, sleep on it: high-pressure 'today only' finance offers are a warning sign. If you already have a loan, it can be worth comparing it every year or two, because refinancing to a cheaper lender may save money even after fees. Moneysmart.gov.au has calculators and checklists to help with each step.

quiz.q: What is the most useful single figure for comparing the true cost of two loans?
o: The total amount repayable over the loan
quiz.e: Total repayments capture interest and fees together, which rates alone do not.

quiz.q: When might your real cost be higher than the comparison rate suggests?
o: When your loan is smaller or shorter than the standard example
When you make every repayment on time
When the loan has no fees
quiz.e: Fixed fees weigh more heavily on smaller or shorter loans than on the example used.

quiz.q: What is a balloon payment?
o: A refund at the end of the loan
A large lump sum due at the end of the loan
quiz.e: A balloon defers part of the debt to the end, lowering repayments but increasing total interest.

quiz.q: What is a smart step before accepting car yard finance?
o: Get your own quote or pre-approval to compare
Focus only on the weekly repayment
Sign the same day to lock in the deal
quiz.e: An independent quote gives you a benchmark and bargaining power.

quiz.q: Under responsible lending laws, what must licensed lenders do?
o: Offer the lowest rate in the market
Make reasonable inquiries and not offer unsuitable loans
quiz.e: Lenders must assess your situation and not offer a loan that is unsuitable.

LESSONS.title: Getting out of debt: a practical plan
LESSONS.hook: Debt can feel like a fog where every bill blurs into one. The way out starts with turning that fog into a list, then using free help that many people never know exists.

sections.h: Turn the fog into a list
sections.key: Write down every debt with its balance, interest rate, minimum repayment and due date.
sections.b: People in debt often avoid opening envelopes, and that is completely human. But you cannot make a plan for numbers you have not seen. Set aside an hour, gather statements and log in to every account. For each debt, write down who you owe, the balance, the interest rate, the minimum repayment and when it is due. Include credit cards, personal and car loans, buy now pay later accounts, overdue bills, money owed to friends or family, and any debt to the ATO or Centrelink. Seeing everything on one page can be confronting, but it usually feels better than the vague dread. This lesson is general information, not financial advice, and free, confidential help is available, as later sections explain.

sections.key: Prioritise housing, utilities and anything with serious consequences before unsecured debts.
sections.b: Not all debts are equal. Financial counsellors often talk about priority debts: the ones where falling behind has the most serious consequences. These usually include rent or mortgage repayments, because you could lose your home; energy and water bills, because of disconnection; and a car loan if you need the car to get to work. Fines and tax debts can also escalate. Unsecured debts such as credit cards and personal loans are important, but missing them does not immediately put a roof over your head at risk. So if money is tight, make sure the essentials are covered first, then deal with the rest. Never take out a new high-cost loan just to keep up repayments on another debt.

sections.key: Lenders and providers must consider hardship requests, and asking early gives you more options.
sections.b: If you cannot meet repayments, contact the lender before you fall far behind. Under the National Credit Code, you have the right to ask a lender for a hardship variation if you are having trouble paying because of things like illness, job loss or other changed circumstances. Options can include a pause, reduced repayments for a period or a longer loan term. Lenders must consider the request and give you a response. Energy, water and phone companies have hardship programs too. Ask for the hardship team, explain what happened and what you can realistically afford, and get any agreement in writing. Hardship arrangements can be noted on your credit report, but that is generally far less damaging than missed payments and defaults.

sections.key: Pay minimums on everything, then throw spare money at either the highest-interest debt or the smallest balance.
sections.b: Once essentials are covered and minimum repayments are being made, any extra money should go to one debt at a time. There are two popular methods. The avalanche method targets the debt with the highest interest rate first, which usually saves the most money overall. The snowball method targets the smallest balance first, regardless of rate, giving you a quick win that can build momentum. When one debt is paid off, you roll its repayment into the next one, so the amount you are throwing at debt keeps growing. Mathematically the avalanche usually wins, but the snowball can be better for people who need motivation to keep going. The best method is the one you will actually stick with.

sections.h: Careful with consolidation and balance transfers
sections.key: Combining debts can help, but only if the new loan is cheaper and you stop adding new debt.
sections.b: A consolidation loan rolls several debts into one, ideally at a lower rate with a single repayment. A balance transfer moves credit card debt to a new card with a low or zero rate for a promotional period. Both can work, but there are traps. Promotional rates end, and the balance often reverts to a high rate. New purchases on a balance transfer card may attract full interest. Consolidating into a longer loan can lower repayments but increase the total cost. And if you keep using the old cards, you can end up with the new loan plus fresh debts. If you consolidate, consider cancelling or reducing the limits on the old cards, and set a plan to clear the balance before any promotional period ends.

sections.key: Financial counsellors are free and independent; be wary of companies charging to 'fix' your debt.
sections.b: Many people do not know that free, independent financial counselling exists in Australia. The National Debt Helpline, on 1800 007 007 or at ndh.org.au, connects you with counsellors who can review your situation, explain your options and negotiate with creditors on your behalf. In contrast, some private debt management and credit repair businesses charge large fees for things you can often do yourself for free, like requesting hardship or correcting errors on your credit report. Some steer people into formal debt agreements without fully explaining the consequences. Before signing anything, speak with a free financial counsellor. For problems with a lender, you can complain to the lender first and then to the Australian Financial Complaints Authority, also free.

sections.key: Debt agreements and bankruptcy are serious, last-resort options; afterwards, a buffer helps keep debt away.
sections.b: When debts are truly unmanageable, there are formal options under federal law, including debt agreements and bankruptcy, administered through the Australian Financial Security Authority, AFSA, at afsa.gov.au. These can stop collection action, but they have serious and lasting consequences: they are recorded on public registers and your credit report, can affect your ability to borrow, and in bankruptcy some assets may be sold. Get independent advice from a financial counsellor before choosing either. Once you are on top of things, build a small emergency fund so the next car repair does not go on a credit card. Celebrate each debt you clear. Moneysmart.gov.au has a free budget planner and debt tools to help you keep going.

quiz.q: Which is usually considered a priority debt?
o: A credit card with a low limit
Money owed to a streaming service
quiz.e: Falling behind on housing costs can put your home at risk, so it is usually a priority.

quiz.q: Under the National Credit Code, what can you ask a lender for if you are struggling?
quiz.e: Borrowers can request hardship variations, which lenders must consider.

quiz.q: What does the avalanche method target first?
o: The debt with the highest interest rate
quiz.e: The avalanche method prioritises the highest-rate debt, usually saving the most interest.

quiz.q: What is the National Debt Helpline?
o: A free service connecting you with financial counsellors
quiz.e: It offers free, independent financial counselling on 1800 007 007.

quiz.q: Which body administers bankruptcy and debt agreements in Australia?
quiz.e: The Australian Financial Security Authority administers personal insolvency.

LESSONS.title: Buying big things without the debt trap
LESSONS.hook: A new fridge, a laptop, a couch: big purchases often come with a tempting offer to pay later. Here is how buy now pay later, interest-free deals and rent-to-own really work, and a better way to buy.

sections.key: Pay-later offers make big prices feel small, which is exactly why they work so well.
sections.b: You are at the checkout online, and next to the price is a friendly line: four easy payments, no interest. A thousand-dollar purchase suddenly looks like a few hundred. That shift in how a price feels is the whole point. Breaking a cost into instalments makes it easier to say yes, and research on payment methods suggests people tend to spend more when paying feels less painful. None of this makes these products evil, and used carefully they can be fine. But it means a big purchase deserves a pause, because the moment of buying is when the seller's design is working hardest on you. This lesson is general information, not financial advice; moneysmart.gov.au has more on every option here.

sections.h: How buy now pay later works
sections.key: BNPL splits a purchase into instalments, usually without interest, but late fees and multiple accounts can bite.
sections.b: Buy now pay later services typically let you pay for a purchase in several instalments, often four payments spread over about six weeks, with the first paid upfront. Many charge no interest; instead they earn money from fees charged to retailers and from late or account fees charged to customers. Since mid-2025, BNPL in Australia has been regulated as a form of credit, so providers need a credit licence and must check that their product is not unsuitable for you. The risks are mostly about how people use it. It is easy to have several plans running across different providers, making it hard to see your true commitments. Missed payments can bring fees, and repeated problems can affect your credit report.

sections.h: The fine print on interest-free deals
sections.key: Long interest-free periods on store finance can end with high interest and ongoing account fees.
sections.b: Furniture and electronics stores often advertise long interest-free periods, perhaps a year or more, through a store card or finance partner. These can be useful if you pay the full amount off within the period. The trap is what happens if you don't. After the interest-free period, any remaining balance usually starts attracting a high interest rate, often similar to a credit card. Many of these products also charge a monthly account fee, and some have an establishment fee, so the deal is not truly free. The finance account may stay open afterwards and be used for future purchases. Before signing, ask: what is the rate after the interest-free period, what are the fees, and what is the minimum repayment?

sections.key: Leasing household goods can cost far more than buying them outright, even if weekly payments look small.
sections.b: Some businesses offer appliances, furniture or electronics on a weekly lease, sometimes promoted to people on Centrelink payments with deductions taken straight from their payment. These consumer leases can end up costing much more than the retail price of the item, and at the end of the lease you may not even own it. ASIC has repeatedly warned about the high cost of some leases. If you need an essential item like a fridge or washing machine and cannot afford it, look first at alternatives: the No Interest Loan Scheme, run by Good Shepherd with community partners, offers loans for essential goods to eligible people on low incomes with no interest or fees. Services Australia may also be able to offer an advance payment if you receive certain payments.

sections.key: Wait before buying, and always ask what the purchase will cost in total, including any credit.
sections.b: A simple habit can stop most regretful purchases: wait. For anything over an amount you choose, perhaps a few hundred dollars, give yourself 48 hours, or a week for bigger items. If you still want it after the wait, it is probably a considered decision rather than an impulse. Next, work out the total cost, not the instalment. Add up every payment and fee if you are using credit. Ask yourself a blunt question: if I had to pay the full price today from my own money, would I still buy it? If the answer is no, the payment plan is making the decision for you. Check whether your existing repayments plus this one would still leave room for rent, bills and food.

sections.h: Save first with a sinking fund
sections.key: Setting aside a small amount regularly for planned purchases lets you buy outright and often negotiate a better price.
sections.b: The cheapest way to buy something big is usually to save for it first. A sinking fund is simply money set aside regularly for a known future cost: a new laptop, car registration, a holiday or replacing an ageing fridge. Divide the expected price by the number of pay cycles until you need it, and set up an automatic transfer into a separate savings account on payday. Many banks let you create several labelled savings buckets for free. Saving first means you earn a little interest instead of paying it, and having the cash can give you bargaining power. Retailers sometimes offer a better price for paying upfront, especially on big-ticket items, but you only find out if you ask politely.

sections.key: Compare prices, consider quality secondhand options, and know your consumer guarantee rights.
sections.b: Before buying, compare prices across several retailers, and check price history if you can, because 'sale' prices are not always real bargains. Ask about price matching. Consider quality secondhand or refurbished goods, which can save a lot on items like furniture, tools and electronics, but inspect them carefully and buy from reputable sellers. Lay-by is an older option where the store holds the item while you pay it off, and you take it home only when it is fully paid; check the store's fees and cancellation terms. Whatever you buy new from a business in Australia comes with automatic consumer guarantees under the Australian Consumer Law, which can matter more than an extended warranty the salesperson offers.

quiz.q: Since mid-2025, how is buy now pay later regulated in Australia?
o: As a form of credit requiring a licence
quiz.e: BNPL providers now need a credit licence and must check suitability.

quiz.q: What usually happens to a store finance balance left after the interest-free period?
o: It is converted into a gift card
It starts attracting a high interest rate
It is paid by the retailer
quiz.e: Remaining balances generally attract interest similar to a credit card rate.

quiz.q: What is a cheaper alternative to rent-to-own for essential goods on a low income?
quiz.e: No Interest Loans offer eligible people loans for essentials without interest or fees.

quiz.q: Which question helps test whether a payment plan is driving a decision?
o: Would I buy it if I had to pay the full price today?
How small is the weekly payment?
Does the product come in another colour?
quiz.e: If you would not pay the full price today, the instalments may be doing the deciding.

quiz.q: What is a sinking fund?
o: Money set aside regularly for a known future cost
A type of buy now pay later account
quiz.e: A sinking fund saves steadily toward planned expenses so you can buy outright.

LESSONS.title: Building an emergency fund from scratch
LESSONS.hook: A blown tyre, a vet bill, a sudden gap between jobs: life sends invoices without warning. An emergency fund turns those moments from a crisis into an inconvenience, and you can start with very little.

sections.key: An emergency fund stops surprise costs from turning into high-interest debt.
sections.b: Picture two people whose car needs the same expensive repair. One pays from savings, feels annoyed, and moves on. The other puts it on a credit card, then pays interest on it for months, and when the next surprise hits, the debt grows again. The difference is not income or intelligence; it is a buffer. An emergency fund is money set aside only for genuine, unplanned needs, such as urgent repairs, medical or dental costs, or a drop in income. It is one of the most effective ways to stay out of debt, and it brings a less measurable benefit too: a sense of calm. This lesson is general information, not financial advice; moneysmart.gov.au has free tools to help.

sections.key: A common target is three months of essential expenses, but any amount is a good start.
sections.b: A widely used rule of thumb is to aim for about three months of essential living expenses, meaning rent or mortgage, bills, groceries, transport and minimum debt repayments, not your full lifestyle spending. People with irregular income, such as casual workers, freelancers or those in a single-income household, may want more. But a three-month target can feel impossible when you are starting from zero, so break it down. A first milestone might be enough to cover one surprise bill, such as a car repair or a new phone. Then aim for one month of essentials, then two, then three. To work out your number, add up your essential costs from a few months of bank statements, or use Moneysmart's budget planner.

sections.key: Keep the fund separate, easy to reach within a day or so, and earning some interest.
sections.b: An emergency fund needs to be accessible quickly but not so close that you dip into it for takeaway. A separate high-interest savings account, ideally not linked to a card, is a common choice. Many such accounts pay bonus interest only if you meet conditions, like depositing a set amount and making no withdrawals in a month, so read the terms; you might lose the bonus in a month you use the fund, which is fine. If you have a home loan with an offset account, money held there reduces the interest you pay. Deposits in authorised banks, building societies and credit unions are protected by the government's Financial Claims Scheme up to a limit; check the current limit at fcs.gov.au.

sections.key: Automate a small transfer on payday, then add windfalls and money from cut costs.
sections.b: The most reliable way to build savings is to make it automatic. Set up a regular transfer to your emergency account that happens on payday, before you have a chance to spend the money. Start with an amount that does not hurt, even a small sum each pay, and increase it when you can. Add windfalls such as a tax refund, a bonus or money from selling things you no longer use. When you cut a cost, like cancelling an unused subscription or switching to a cheaper phone plan, redirect that saving straight into the fund so it does not quietly disappear into everyday spending. Some banks offer round-up features that move small change from each purchase into savings, which can help build the habit.

sections.key: Decide your rules in advance so the fund is there when you really need it.
sections.b: An emergency fund only works if it survives until an emergency. Decide in advance what counts. Good candidates are unexpected, necessary and urgent: the hot water system failing, an urgent dental bill, a car repair you need to get to work, or covering essentials after losing your job. Things that are not emergencies, however tempting the sale, include holidays, gifts and planned annual bills like car registration or insurance premiums. Those predictable costs belong in a separate savings bucket, sometimes called a sinking fund, so they do not drain your buffer. If you find yourself raiding the fund for non-emergencies, it may be a sign your everyday budget needs adjusting rather than a failure of willpower.

sections.h: After you use it, refill it
sections.key: Using the fund is a success, and rebuilding it promptly keeps you protected.
sections.b: The first time you use your emergency fund, it can feel like failure, watching the balance you worked hard for shrink. It is actually the opposite: the fund did its job, and you avoided debt. The important step is what comes next. Restart or increase your automatic transfers until the balance is rebuilt. If a large expense wiped out most of the fund, set a realistic timeframe to refill it and consider trimming discretionary spending for a few months. It also helps to check your target occasionally. As your rent, family or job situation changes, your essential costs change too, so the right size of the fund can change. A quick review once a year is usually enough.

sections.h: If you have nothing saved yet
sections.key: If an emergency strikes before your fund is ready, there is help that is cheaper than high-cost credit.
sections.b: Sometimes the emergency arrives before the fund does. If that happens, avoid the most expensive options first, such as payday loans and some consumer leases. Ask the business you owe whether they offer a payment plan; many tradespeople, vets, utilities and hospitals will. If you receive certain Centrelink payments, Services Australia may be able to give you an advance payment, which you repay from future payments, and there are crisis payments for specific severe situations; check eligibility at servicesaustralia.gov.au. The No Interest Loan Scheme can help eligible people with essential costs. And the National Debt Helpline, on 1800 007 007, offers free financial counselling. Once the immediate problem is handled, start your fund, even with a tiny first deposit.

quiz.q: What is the main job of an emergency fund?
o: To stop surprise costs becoming high-interest debt
quiz.e: A buffer lets you pay unexpected costs without turning to expensive credit.

quiz.q: What is a common rule of thumb for an emergency fund target?
o: About three months of essential expenses
quiz.e: Three months of essentials is a common target, with smaller milestones on the way.

quiz.q: What protects deposits in authorised Australian banks up to a limit?
quiz.e: The government's Financial Claims Scheme protects deposits in authorised institutions up to a limit.

quiz.q: Which of these is best paid from a sinking fund rather than an emergency fund?
quiz.e: Predictable costs like registration belong in a separate sinking fund.

quiz.q: If you receive certain Centrelink payments, what might Services Australia offer in a pinch?
o: An advance payment repaid from future payments
quiz.e: Eligible recipients may get an advance on their payments, repaid over time.

LESSONS.title: Income protection: insuring your pay
LESSONS.hook: Your ability to earn may be worth more than your house or car, yet many people insure those and not their income. Here is how income protection works, and the questions to ask before you buy or keep it.

sections.key: For most working people, future earnings are worth far more than anything they own.
sections.b: Ask someone what their most valuable asset is and they will usually name their home or car. But for a working adult, the stream of pay they expect to earn over the coming decades is often worth far more. Illness or injury that stops you working for months can drain savings quickly, while rent, loan repayments and bills keep arriving. Income protection insurance is designed to replace part of your income if you cannot work because of illness or injury. It is different from life insurance, which pays when you die, and from total and permanent disability cover, which pays a lump sum if you are unlikely to work again. This lesson is general information, not financial advice; consider your situation or speak to a licensed adviser.

sections.key: Income protection usually pays a monthly benefit covering a portion of your income, not all of it.
sections.b: Income protection typically pays a regular monthly benefit while you are unable to work because of a covered illness or injury. It replaces only part of your income, commonly up to around 70 percent of your pre-disability earnings in many current policies, though the exact amount and how it is calculated vary. The idea is to cover essentials while leaving an incentive to return to work when you are able. Policies differ in how they define being unable to work, for example whether you must be unable to do your own job or any job suited to your skills. Some include partial benefits if you can return to work part-time. These definitions matter enormously at claim time, so read the product disclosure statement carefully.

sections.key: The waiting period sets when payments start, and the benefit period sets how long they can last.
sections.b: Two choices shape both the cost and the usefulness of a policy. The waiting period is how long you must be unable to work before benefits start, often options like 30, 60 or 90 days, or longer. A longer waiting period usually means a cheaper premium, which can make sense if you have sick leave or an emergency fund to bridge the gap. The benefit period is how long payments can continue once they start, such as two years, five years or until a set age. Longer benefit periods cost more but protect against long-term illness, which is exactly the scenario that does the most financial damage. Think about how long your savings and leave could realistically carry you, then choose combinations to compare.

sections.key: Many super funds include income protection, which is convenient but often more limited than a standalone policy.
sections.b: Many people already have some income protection through their super fund without realising it. Check your fund's website or annual statement. Cover inside super is paid for from your super balance, which spares your weekly budget but reduces your retirement savings, and it often has shorter benefit periods and stricter definitions than standalone policies. Default cover can be switched off if your account has been inactive for a period, or for some younger members and low balances, unless you opt in. A standalone policy, bought directly or through an adviser, can usually be tailored more closely. You can also hold both, although benefits may be offset against each other so you cannot claim more than the policy limits allow. Compare before you add or cancel anything.

sections.key: Premiums for income protection held outside super are generally tax-deductible, and benefits are generally taxable.
sections.b: The tax treatment surprises some people. If you pay premiums for income protection held outside super, the ATO generally allows you to claim them as a deduction in your tax return, because the policy replaces taxable income. The flip side is that benefit payments are generally taxable income too. Premiums paid from within super are not claimed in your personal return. If a policy bundles income protection with other cover, such as life insurance, only the income protection part is usually deductible, and your insurer should show the split. Premiums can be stepped, rising with age, or level, starting higher but rising more slowly, and both generally increase over time. Check the ATO website for the current rules that apply to you.

sections.key: Answer health and lifestyle questions honestly, because non-disclosure can lead to a claim being refused.
sections.b: When applying for standalone cover, you will be asked about your health, job, income and lifestyle, sometimes including hobbies. Answer fully and honestly. Under Australian law, you have a duty to take reasonable care not to make a misrepresentation, and inaccurate answers can give the insurer grounds to reduce a payout, refuse a claim or cancel the policy. Insurers may exclude particular pre-existing conditions or charge more for risky occupations. Get quotes from more than one insurer or speak to a licensed adviser, and ask how premiums are expected to change over time. Keep copies of your application. When comparing, look closely at the definition of disability, the benefit amount, waiting and benefit periods, and exclusions, not just the price.

sections.key: Sick leave, workers compensation and government payments can also help, but each has limits.
sections.b: Income protection is one layer among several. Employees generally accrue paid personal leave, which covers short absences. If you are injured at work or develop a work-related illness, your state or territory workers compensation scheme may pay part of your wages and medical costs, whether or not you have private insurance. If you have a car accident, some states have compulsory third party or no-fault schemes that may help. Services Australia offers income support for people who cannot work for a time, but payments are means-tested and usually much lower than a working wage. Understanding where these safety nets end helps you decide how much private cover makes sense. Moneysmart.gov.au has a plain-language guide to income protection and life insurance in super.

quiz.q: How does income protection differ from life insurance?
o: It pays only if you die
It replaces part of your income if illness or injury stops you working
It covers damage to your home
It pays your super contributions only
quiz.e: Income protection pays a regular benefit while you cannot work; life insurance pays on death.

quiz.q: What usually happens to premiums if you choose a longer waiting period?
quiz.e: A longer wait before benefits start generally lowers the premium.

quiz.q: How are premiums for income protection inside super usually paid?
o: By your employer on top of super
quiz.e: Cover inside super is funded from your super account, reducing retirement savings.

quiz.q: What is the general tax treatment of income protection held outside super?
o: Premiums and benefits are both tax-free
Premiums are taxed and benefits deductible
Premiums are generally deductible and benefits generally taxable
quiz.e: Because it replaces taxable income, premiums are generally deductible and benefits taxable.

quiz.q: Why must you answer application questions honestly?
o: Misrepresentation can lead to a claim being reduced or refused
quiz.e: Inaccurate answers can give the insurer grounds to reduce or refuse a claim.

LESSONS.title: Writing a resume that gets read
LESSONS.hook: A recruiter might give your resume less than a minute on the first pass. Here is how to make those seconds count, step by step.

sections.key: Your resume is first skimmed, not read, so make the top third do the heavy lifting.
sections.b: Picture a hiring manager with sixty applications, a cold coffee and a meeting in twenty minutes. They are not reading every line. They glance at the top of page one, scan your most recent job title, look for a few words that match the ad and decide whether to keep going. That means your resume has two audiences: the busy human skimming it and, at many larger employers, software that sorts applications before a person sees them. The good news is that both reward the same things: a clear layout, plain headings, relevant words near the top and evidence that you can do the job. Before you write anything, print the job ad and highlight every skill, tool and duty it mentions. That highlighted list is your brief.

sections.key: Use a simple, predictable order: contact details, summary, experience, skills, education.
sections.b: Australian resumes tend to follow a familiar pattern, and familiar is good because readers know where to look. Start with your name, phone, email, suburb and state, and a LinkedIn link if you keep it current. You do not need your full street address, a photo, your date of birth or your marital status, and leaving them out also helps protect you from unconscious bias. Next comes a short summary of two or three sentences, then your work history in reverse order, most recent first. After that, list key skills, then education and any licences or tickets, such as a white card, RSA or driver's licence. Two to three pages is common for experienced workers; one or two is fine early in your career. Use a clean font, generous margins and consistent dates.

sections.key: Show what changed because you were there, using numbers where you honestly can.
sections.b: Most resumes read like job descriptions: 'responsible for customer service', 'duties included stock control'. That tells the reader what the role was, not how well you did it. Swap duties for achievements. A useful pattern is action, task and result. Instead of 'handled customer complaints', try 'resolved escalated complaints for a busy retail store, helping lift our customer survey score over six months'. Numbers make claims concrete: how many customers, how big a budget, how much time saved, how many people trained. Only use figures you can explain in an interview, because good interviewers will ask. If you cannot measure something, describe the scale or the outcome instead. Start each line with a strong verb such as led, built, reduced, organised, trained or launched, and cut filler words wherever you find them.

sections.key: A tailored resume beats a generic one, and tailoring takes less time than you think.
sections.b: Sending the same resume to fifty jobs feels efficient but usually is not. Keep a master document with everything you have ever done, then make a copy for each application. Go back to your highlighted job ad and make sure the most relevant experience appears near the top and uses the same language. If the ad says 'stakeholder engagement' and you wrote 'working with other teams', use their phrase, as long as it is honest. Reorder your skills so the ones they asked for come first. Trim older or unrelated roles to a single line. Many employers use applicant tracking systems that search for keywords, so matching terms can matter, but stuffing in words you cannot back up will backfire with the human who reads it next. Twenty focused minutes per application is a sensible target.

sections.h: The summary and the cover letter
sections.key: A sharp summary and a short, specific cover letter tell the reader why you, why this job.
sections.b: Your summary sits at the top and answers one question: who are you, professionally, and what do you offer? Something like 'Hospitality supervisor with six years in busy venues, strong at rostering, training new staff and keeping service calm on big nights' works far better than 'hard-working team player seeking new challenges'. If the ad asks for a cover letter, keep it to about a page. Open by naming the role and one genuine reason you want it. In the middle, pick two or three requirements from the ad and give a brief example of how you meet each. Close by saying you would welcome the chance to talk. Address it to a real person if the ad names one. Never send a letter with another company's name left in, a classic and costly mistake.

sections.key: Small errors and vague claims sink more applications than missing experience does.
sections.b: Recruiters often say the fastest way to the 'no' pile is a typo in the first few lines. Read your resume aloud, slowly, then ask someone else to read it too. Watch for inconsistent dates, mixed tenses and an unprofessional email address. Avoid long blocks of text; short lines with clear headings are easier to scan. Leave out reasons for leaving each job, salary history and personal details that do not relate to the work. Do not exaggerate titles or qualifications: employers can and do check, and a stretched claim can cost you the job later. Gaps in your work history are normal and do not need long explanations; a brief line such as 'career break, caring for family' or 'travel and study' is enough. Save and send the file as a PDF unless the employer asks otherwise.

sections.key: Line up referees before you apply and give them a heads up about each role.
sections.b: Most Australian employers check references before making an offer, usually by phone. Choose two or three people who have supervised your work recently, such as a manager or team leader, rather than friends or family. Always ask permission first, confirm their current phone number and email, and tell them which jobs you are going for so they can speak to what matters. Many people write 'referees available on request', which is perfectly acceptable and keeps their details private until needed. Before you hit send, run one final checklist: the file name includes your name, the contact details are correct, the job title in your cover letter matches the ad and the most relevant achievements sit on page one. Then keep a simple spreadsheet of where you applied, when and what happened, so you can follow up.

quiz.q: Which of these is generally best left off an Australian resume?
quiz.e: Personal details such as date of birth are not needed and leaving them out helps reduce bias.

quiz.q: What turns a duty into an achievement?
quiz.e: Achievements show what changed because of your work, ideally with honest numbers.

quiz.q: Why mirror the job ad's language when it is honest to do so?
o: It helps both keyword software and skimming humans spot the match
Recruiters only read the last page
quiz.e: Many employers use tracking systems that search for keywords, and humans skim for the same terms.

quiz.q: How should you handle a gap in your work history?
o: Write a full page explaining it
Leave the whole job history off
quiz.e: Gaps are common, and a short honest line is enough.

quiz.q: What should you do before listing someone as a referee?
o: Ask permission and tell them about the role
Give their details only to the recruiter's competitor
quiz.e: Referees should agree in advance and know what job you are going for.

LESSONS.title: Reading your payslip
LESSONS.hook: That little document on payday tells you whether you are being paid correctly. Most people never really read it. Here is how.

sections.key: Your payslip is your best everyday check that you are being paid what you are owed.
sections.b: Imagine working the same Saturday shifts for a year, only to discover your weekend penalty rate was never applied. Underpayment in Australia is more common than many people realise, and it is not always deliberate: payroll errors, wrong award classifications and outdated rates all happen. Your payslip is where these mistakes show up first. In Australia, employers generally must give employees a payslip within one working day of payday, either on paper or electronically, and it must include certain details. Reading it each pay takes two minutes and can save you hundreds or even thousands of dollars over time.
