This lesson is general information, not legal or financial advice, and the Fair Work Ombudsman at fairwork.gov.au is the official place to check your specific situation.

sections.key: The law sets out the information a payslip has to show, so you know what to look for.
sections.b: A compliant payslip should name your employer, including their ABN, and name you. It should show the pay period and the date you were paid. It must show your gross pay, which is the total before tax, and your net pay, which is what lands in your bank account. It should list any deductions, such as tax or salary sacrifice, and any bonuses, loadings, allowances or penalty rates. If you are paid by the hour, it should show your hourly rate and how many hours were paid at that rate. It should also show the superannuation your employer is paying for you and the fund it is going to. If any of these are missing, it is worth politely asking your payroll team why.

sections.key: The gap between gross and net pay is mostly tax withheld and sent to the ATO for you.
sections.b: Under the pay as you go system, your employer withholds tax from each pay and sends it to the Australian Taxation Office. How much they withhold depends on how much you earn, how often you are paid and what you told them on your tax file number declaration when you started. One key choice on that form is whether to claim the tax-free threshold. Most people claim it from one employer only, usually their main job. If you claim it from two jobs at once, too little tax may be withheld and you could face a bill at tax time. The ATO website has calculators that estimate how much tax should come out of a given pay, which is a handy cross check if something looks off.

sections.key: Check that super is being paid, at the right rate, into the fund you chose.
sections.b: Superannuation is money your employer pays on top of your wages into a retirement fund. The super guarantee is a set percentage of your ordinary time earnings, and the rate has risen in steps over the years, so check the current figure on the ATO website. Your payslip should show how much super has been calculated for the period. But a payslip only shows what your employer says it will pay, not what actually arrived. Every few months, log in to your super fund's app or website, or check through myGov, and confirm the contributions are landing. Unpaid super is a common problem and can be hard to spot without checking. If money is missing, raise it with your employer first, and if that does not fix it, the ATO has a process for reporting unpaid super.

sections.key: Your base rate and any penalty rates usually come from an award or agreement, and you can look them up.
sections.b: Many Australian workers are covered by a modern award, a legal document that sets minimum pay and conditions for an industry or occupation. Others are covered by an enterprise agreement negotiated at their workplace. These set your minimum base rate and extras such as casual loading, overtime and penalty rates for evenings, weekends and public holidays. To check yours, use the Fair Work Ombudsman's pay calculator or download the pay guide for your award. You will need to know your award, your classification level and whether you are full time, part time or casual. Minimum rates are usually reviewed each year, with changes commonly starting from the first full pay period on or after 1 July, so a rate that was right last year might be wrong now.

sections.key: Spend two minutes each payday comparing your hours, rate and super against what you expect.
sections.b: Build a simple habit. Keep a note of your hours each week, in your phone or a diary, including start and finish times and breaks. When your payslip arrives, compare the hours paid with your record. Check that each type of hour, such as ordinary time, overtime or Sunday work, is paid at the right rate. Glance at the year to date totals, which add up your earnings, tax and super since 1 July and should grow steadily. Make sure your leave balances look sensible if you are permanent, and check that any leave you took was paid. Keep every payslip, ideally saved as a PDF in one folder, because records are your best evidence if anything ever needs to be fixed. Old payslips can also help at tax time.

sections.key: Raise errors calmly and in writing first, then know where to get help.
sections.b: Most pay problems are fixed with a polite conversation. Start by checking your own numbers, then write a short message to your manager or payroll: say what you noticed, what you believe the correct amount is and how you worked it out, and ask them to look into it. Keep a copy. Give them a reasonable chance to respond. If the problem is not fixed, the Fair Work Ombudsman offers free information, templates for raising issues and, in some cases, help resolving disputes. For unpaid super, contact the ATO. If you are a union member, your union can also help. Be aware that there are time limits for recovering unpaid wages, so do not let a problem sit for years. Raising a genuine pay concern is a workplace right, and employers must not punish you for it.

quiz.q: How soon after payday must an employer generally provide a payslip?
o: Only at the end of the financial year
quiz.e: Employers generally must provide a payslip within one working day of payday.

quiz.q: What is the main reason net pay is lower than gross pay?
o: Super is taken out of your wages
Tax is withheld and sent to the ATO
quiz.e: Under PAYG, employers withhold tax from each pay and send it to the ATO.

quiz.q: Why check your super fund as well as your payslip?
o: Super is optional for most employers
The payslip shows what is owed, not proof it arrived
quiz.e: A payslip shows what the employer says it will pay, so confirm contributions are actually landing.

quiz.q: Which official tool helps you check minimum award rates?
o: The Australian Bureau of Statistics census
The Fair Work Ombudsman's pay calculator
quiz.e: The FWO pay calculator and pay guides show minimum rates for each award.

quiz.q: What is a good first step if your pay seems wrong?
o: Post about it on social media
Raise it calmly in writing with payroll or your manager
quiz.e: Most errors are fixed with a clear written query, and help is available if that fails.

LESSONS.title: Asking for a pay rise
LESSONS.hook: Many people wait years to be offered more money. Here is how to prepare for, start and handle the pay rise conversation yourself.

sections.key: Silence rarely gets you paid more, and most managers expect the question at some point.
sections.b: Sam has been in the same role for three years. She has trained two new starters, taken on the rostering and quietly fixed the ordering system. Her pay has only moved when the award minimum went up. Sam is not alone: plenty of people never ask, because it feels awkward, greedy or risky. Yet from a manager's point of view, a well prepared request from a valued employee is a normal part of running a team, and far better than that person resigning without warning. Asking does not guarantee a yes. But a clear, evidence based conversation usually leads somewhere useful: a rise now, a plan for one later or honest feedback about what is standing in the way. Each of those is better than wondering.

sections.key: Start by checking the legal minimum for your role, because you might already be owed money.
sections.b: Before you ask for more, make sure you are getting at least what you are legally entitled to. If you are covered by an award or enterprise agreement, it sets minimum rates for your classification. Use the Fair Work Ombudsman's pay calculator or pay guides to check, and look closely at your classification level, since duties often grow faster than job titles. If your responsibilities now match a higher level, that is a strong, concrete point to raise. If you are paid below the minimum, that is not a pay rise conversation, it is an underpayment to be fixed, and the Fair Work Ombudsman can help. This lesson offers general information, not legal or financial advice. Once you know your floor, you can think about what you are actually worth in the market.

sections.key: Research what similar roles pay so your number is grounded in evidence, not hope.
sections.b: Your market value is roughly what another employer would pay someone with your skills, in your location, for similar work. Several job sites publish salary ranges, and many job ads now list pay, so spend an evening collecting examples for roles like yours. Industry surveys and professional associations can also help. In Australia, you are also legally free to talk about your own pay with colleagues if you choose to, and employers cannot stop you, which can give you useful real world information. Look for a range, not a single figure, and be honest about where you sit within it given your experience. Then decide on a specific amount to request, near the upper end of what you can justify, along with the lowest outcome you would be genuinely happy with.

sections.key: Make your request about the value you add, not about your personal expenses.
sections.b: The strongest case focuses on what you contribute. Gather evidence: projects you delivered, problems you solved, money or time you saved, new responsibilities you took on, positive feedback from customers or colleagues. Write these down in a short document, one or two pages at most. Be specific: 'took over weekly rostering for a team of twelve' is better than 'helped out with admin'. Avoid leading with personal reasons such as rent or the cost of living. They are real pressures, but they are not reasons your employer should pay you more than someone else in the same role. If you have been given a bigger job without a bigger title or pay, say so plainly. Show how your role has changed since your pay was last set.

sections.key: Timing matters: ask when your value is visible and the budget is still open.
sections.b: Good moments include your annual performance review, soon after a clear win, when you take on new responsibilities, or a few months before budgets are set for the next financial year, which for many Australian organisations starts on 1 July. Bad moments include the middle of a crisis, straight after a round of redundancies or late on a Friday afternoon. Do not ambush your manager in a corridor. Instead, ask for a meeting: 'I would like to book half an hour to talk about my role and pay. Would next week work?' That gives them time to prepare and signals you are serious. If your workplace has a formal review cycle, find out when decisions are made, because by the time the review meeting happens the money may already be allocated.

sections.key: State your request clearly, back it with evidence, then stop talking and listen.
sections.b: Open simply and warmly: say you enjoy the role and want to talk about your pay given how your work has grown. Then walk through two or three of your strongest examples. Make a specific request, such as an amount or a percentage, and briefly explain how you arrived at it. Then pause. Silence feels uncomfortable, but it gives your manager space to respond. Listen carefully to their answer and ask questions if anything is unclear. Stay calm and professional, even if the first response is disappointing. Avoid ultimatums unless you are truly prepared to leave, because a threat can damage trust even when it works. Close by agreeing on next steps and when you will hear back, then send a short email afterwards summarising what was discussed.

sections.key: A no today can become a yes later if you turn it into a clear plan.
sections.b: Sometimes the budget genuinely is not there, or your manager does not yet see the case. Ask what would need to change for a rise to happen, and try to get specific, measurable goals and a date to revisit it, perhaps in three or six months. Put that agreement in writing. You can also ask about other things that matter to you: extra training, a study allowance, more flexible hours, a better title or additional leave. These can be easier to approve and still improve your working life. Then follow through, track your progress and bring it back at the agreed time. If promises are repeatedly broken, that is useful information too. Sometimes the best pay rise is a new job, and the case you prepared will help in those interviews.

quiz.q: Why check your award or agreement before asking for a rise?
o: You might already be underpaid or at the wrong level
It is required before any meeting
quiz.e: If you are below the legal minimum, that is an underpayment to fix, not a pay rise request.

quiz.q: In Australia, can an employer stop you discussing your own pay with colleagues?
o: No, employees can choose to share it
quiz.e: Employees have a legal right to disclose their own pay if they choose.

quiz.q: Which is the strongest basis for a pay rise request?
o: Evidence of the value you add and how your role has grown
How long since your last holiday
quiz.e: Requests built on contribution and responsibility are more persuasive than personal costs.

quiz.q: Why might asking well before a review meeting help?
o: Budgets may already be set by the time of the review
quiz.e: Pay decisions are often made before the formal review, so early timing can matter.

quiz.q: What is a constructive response to a no?
o: Agree on specific goals and a date to revisit
quiz.e: Turning a no into a measurable plan gives you a clear path to a future yes.

LESSONS.title: Running a meeting worth attending
LESSONS.hook: Most of us have sat through a meeting that should have been an email. Here is how to run one people are glad they came to.

sections.h: The cost of a bad meeting
sections.key: A meeting uses everyone's time at once, so its cost is multiplied by the number of people in the room.
sections.b: Picture eight people in a one hour meeting. That is not one hour of work, it is eight hours, nearly a full working day, gone. If the meeting drifts, ends without a decision and needs a follow up, the cost doubles. Bad meetings also drain energy, interrupt focused work and teach people that their time does not matter. Yet good meetings are powerful. They can settle in thirty minutes a question that would take two weeks of emails, help a team feel connected and get everyone moving in the same direction. The difference is rarely luck. Good meetings are designed, and the person running them makes a handful of simple choices before, during and after. Anyone can learn them, whether you lead a team or are organising your first catch up.

sections.key: Before booking anything, check that a meeting is the best tool for the job.
sections.b: Start by asking what you want to achieve. If the goal is simply to share information that needs no discussion, an email, a short document or a recorded update is often better, because people can read it when it suits them. Meetings are best for things that need live conversation: making a decision, solving a tricky problem, building agreement on a plan, brainstorming or handling a sensitive issue. If you cannot write the purpose in one sentence, you are not ready to book the meeting. Try finishing this line: 'By the end of this meeting, we will have...'. For example, 'chosen a supplier for the new uniforms' or 'agreed who covers the December roster'. That sentence becomes your north star, and it goes right at the top of the invitation.

sections.key: Fewer, better chosen attendees make for faster and more honest discussions.
sections.b: Every extra person adds opinions, side conversations and scheduling headaches. Invite only those who need to make the decision, have information you cannot get elsewhere or must carry out what is agreed. People who just need to know the outcome can get a summary afterwards. Think about who will be affected by the decision, too, because leaving out a key person often means redoing the meeting later. Be thoughtful about timing. Respect different working hours and flexible arrangements, and avoid booking meetings at times when part time staff or parents on school runs cannot attend. Choose a length that fits the task: many meetings that default to an hour could be done in twenty five or fifty minutes, leaving a buffer between back to back calls so people can stretch, refill and arrive ready.

sections.key: A useful agenda lists questions to answer, not just topics to talk about.
sections.b: An agenda that says 'budget, rosters, other business' tells nobody what to prepare. A better agenda turns each item into a question and gives it a time. For example: 'Which of the two venue quotes do we accept? Ten minutes. Read the attached comparison first.' Put the most important item first, while energy is high, and send the agenda with any reading at least a day ahead. Ask attendees to come having read it, and say so plainly. Some teams start with a few quiet minutes for everyone to read the key document together, which levels the playing field and means nobody bluffs. If someone wants to add an item, ask them to tell you before the meeting so you can plan the time. An agenda is a promise about how you will use people's time.

sections.key: Start on time, keep the discussion on track and make sure every voice is heard.
sections.b: Begin on time, even if someone is late, and restate the purpose in a sentence. Your job as chair is to guide, not to dominate. Keep an eye on the clock and gently steer drifting conversations: 'That is a good point, let us park it and come back if we have time.' Keep a visible parking lot list for those side issues so people know they have not been ignored. Draw out quieter people by asking them directly, and politely rein in those who speak at length. In hybrid meetings, where some people are in the room and others are online, make sure remote attendees can hear, see shared material and get a fair turn, perhaps by calling on them first. If the discussion is going in circles, summarise where things stand and ask what is needed to decide.

sections.key: Every meeting should end with clear decisions, named owners and due dates.
sections.b: The last five minutes are the most important, yet they are often squeezed out. Leave time to wrap up properly. Read back what was decided, in plain words, so everyone hears the same thing. Then list the actions: what will be done, who will do it and by when. An action without a name next to it usually does not happen. If something could not be decided, agree on what is needed to decide it and when. Check whether anyone disagrees with the summary before you close. Finishing a few minutes early is a gift people remember. A simple test of a good meeting is whether every attendee could tell a colleague afterwards, in one or two sentences, what was decided and what they personally need to do next.

sections.key: A short written summary sent the same day turns talk into action.
sections.b: Within a few hours, send a brief note to everyone who attended and anyone else who needs to know. Keep it short: the decisions made, the actions with owners and dates, and any open questions. Share it where your team can find it later, such as a shared folder or channel, so new people can catch up without another meeting. Then check in on the actions when they are due. Over time, review your regular meetings. Ask the team whether the weekly catch up still earns its place, and be willing to shorten it, change it or cancel it. Teams that regularly prune their meeting calendars often find they get more done. And when you attend someone else's meeting, you can quietly help by asking, 'What do we want to decide today?'

quiz.q: Why is an eight person, one hour meeting costly?
o: It uses about eight hours of combined working time
quiz.e: Everyone's time is used at once, so the cost multiplies with each attendee.

quiz.q: When is a meeting usually better than an email?
o: To share a document nobody needs to discuss
To make a decision that needs live discussion
quiz.e: Meetings suit decisions, problem solving and sensitive issues that need conversation.

quiz.q: What makes an agenda item more useful?
o: Making it a single vague word
Framing it as a question with a time and any pre reading
Adding it at the last minute
quiz.e: Question based items with times and reading tell people exactly how to prepare.

quiz.q: What is a 'parking lot' in a meeting?
o: A list of off topic issues to return to later
A list of people not invited
quiz.e: Parking side issues keeps the meeting on track without dismissing them.

quiz.q: What should every action agreed in a meeting have?
o: A vote by the whole company
A named owner and a due date
quiz.e: Actions without an owner and a date usually do not happen.

LESSONS.title: Giving and receiving feedback at work
LESSONS.hook: Feedback can lift a team or wreck a week. A few practical techniques make it clearer, kinder and far more useful.

sections.key: Most feedback fails because it is vague, late or delivered in a way that triggers defence.
sections.b: Think of the last time someone said 'Can I give you some feedback?' Your heart probably sped up a little. Feedback feels personal because work is tied to our sense of competence and belonging. When it is delivered badly, people stop listening and start defending. Common problems are easy to spot. Feedback that is vague, such as 'you need to be more professional', gives nothing to act on. Feedback saved up for an annual review arrives months too late to be useful. Feedback mixed with frustration sounds like an attack. And praise that is generic, like 'great job', feels hollow. The good news is that both giving and receiving feedback are skills. A few simple structures can make conversations shorter, clearer and much less painful for everyone.

sections.key: Describe when it happened, what the person did and the effect it had.
sections.b: One widely used structure, developed by the Center for Creative Leadership, is called situation, behaviour, impact. First, name the situation: 'In Tuesday's client meeting'. Second, describe the specific behaviour you saw or heard, without guessing at motives: 'you interrupted the client twice while they were explaining the problem'. Third, explain the impact: 'they seemed frustrated and we did not get the full picture'. This keeps the conversation anchored in facts rather than character judgements like 'you are rude'. Then pause and invite their view: 'How did it look from your side?' There may be context you missed. The same structure works brilliantly for praise: 'When you stayed calm with that upset customer this morning, the whole queue relaxed, and she thanked us on the way out.'

sections.key: Give feedback soon, in private for criticism, and when both of you can actually listen.
sections.b: Feedback is most useful close to the event, while memories are fresh, ideally within a day or two. But soon does not mean straight away in the heat of the moment. If you are angry, wait until you can speak calmly. Give constructive criticism in private, never in front of colleagues or customers. Praise can be public, though some people prefer it quietly, so learn what your team members like. Ask before diving in: 'Have you got ten minutes? I would like to talk about the handover yesterday.' That small courtesy gives the other person a moment to prepare. Avoid delivering important feedback by text or chat, where tone is easily misread; a conversation, in person or by video, usually works better, followed up in writing if needed.

sections.key: Good feedback ends with what to do next, agreed together.
sections.b: Once you have described what happened and heard the other person's view, shift the conversation forward. Ask questions such as 'What could we try next time?' or 'What would help?' People are far more committed to solutions they helped shape. If you have a specific request, say it clearly: 'In client meetings, please let them finish before you jump in. Jot notes and raise points at the end.' Agree on one or two changes, not ten. Then follow up. Notice when things improve and say so, because recognising progress makes change stick. Some people find it helpful to think of feedback as coaching rather than judgement: the goal is not to win an argument about the past but to make the next week go better for both of you.

sections.key: Listen, ask questions and thank the person, even when it stings.
sections.b: Being on the receiving end is often harder. When feedback lands, your instinct may be to explain, justify or counter attack. Try to resist that, at least at first. Breathe, listen to the whole message and ask clarifying questions: 'Can you give me an example?' or 'What would good look like?' Summarise what you heard to check you understood. Then thank them, even if you disagree, because giving feedback takes effort and some courage. You do not have to accept every point on the spot. It is fine to say, 'I want to think about that and come back to you.' Later, when you are calmer, sort what you heard into three piles: useful and true, partly true and simply not right. Act on the first pile.

sections.key: Asking for specific feedback regularly makes it easier to hear and much more useful.
sections.b: Waiting for feedback to arrive means you get it on someone else's schedule, often when something has gone wrong. Instead, ask for it. Make your request specific, because 'Any feedback?' usually produces 'No, all good'. Try 'What is one thing I could do to make my reports more useful for you?' or 'In that presentation, what part landed and what part lost people?' Ask a mix of people: your manager, peers and, if you lead a team, the people who report to you, who may need extra reassurance that honesty is safe. When someone gives you honest input, thank them and show that you acted on it. People who see their feedback used are much more likely to offer more, and over time the conversations get easier for everyone.

sections.key: If you lead others, how you handle feedback sets the tone for the whole team.
sections.b: Leaders shape a team's feedback culture more than any policy does. If you get defensive when challenged, people learn to stay quiet, and you lose early warnings about problems. If you thank people for raising concerns, even uncomfortable ones, they learn it is safe to speak. Make feedback routine rather than rare, with regular one to one catch ups that include a few minutes on what is going well and what could improve. Keep a light record of praise and concerns through the year so reviews contain no surprises. Be careful to separate feedback on behaviour from formal performance or disciplinary processes, which have their own rules and fairness requirements. For guidance on handling performance issues in Australian workplaces, the Fair Work Ombudsman publishes free guides for managers and employees.

quiz.q: In the situation, behaviour, impact model, what should the behaviour part describe?
o: What you specifically saw or heard
How long they have worked there
quiz.e: Describing observable behaviour keeps feedback factual and less personal.

quiz.q: Where is constructive criticism best given?
quiz.e: Criticism given privately is less likely to cause embarrassment and defensiveness.

quiz.q: Why involve the other person in deciding what to do next?
o: It shortens the meeting to one minute
People commit more to solutions they helped shape
quiz.e: Shared solutions tend to stick better than instructions handed down.

quiz.q: What is a good first response when receiving tough feedback?
quiz.e: Listening fully and asking for examples helps you understand before reacting.

quiz.q: Which request is most likely to produce useful feedback?
o: 'What is one thing that would make my reports more useful?'
'Let me know if there are problems.'
quiz.e: Specific questions invite specific, actionable answers.

LESSONS.title: Burnout and the right to disconnect
LESSONS.hook: Burnout is more than a bad week. Learn the warning signs, what you can change and what Australian workplace rules say about switching off.

sections.key: Burnout is a work related pattern of exhaustion, cynicism and a sense of not getting anywhere.
sections.b: Jess used to love her job. Now Sunday nights bring a knot in her stomach, she snaps at colleagues and tasks that once took an hour drag on all afternoon. She is not lazy and she is not simply tired: she may be burning out. The World Health Organization describes burnout as an occupational phenomenon, not a medical condition, resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed. It has three features: feelings of energy depletion or exhaustion, increased mental distance from your job or feelings of negativity or cynicism about it, and reduced professional effectiveness. Burnout is about work specifically, which matters, because the solutions often involve how work is organised, not just personal resilience. This lesson is general information, not medical, legal or professional advice.

sections.key: Burnout builds slowly, so learn to notice the early signals in yourself and others.
sections.b: Burnout rarely arrives overnight. Early signs can include trouble switching off in the evening, poor sleep, constant tiredness that rest does not fix, irritability, dreading work, getting sick more often and making uncharacteristic mistakes. You might notice you have stopped caring about things that used to matter, or that you feel numb about work. Others may notice before you do, so take it seriously if a partner or friend says you seem different. These signs can also overlap with other health issues, including depression and anxiety, so it is important not to self diagnose. If you are struggling, speak with your GP, who can check what is going on and connect you with support. Healthdirect and Beyond Blue also offer free, reliable information and phone support around the clock.

sections.key: Burnout is driven mostly by working conditions, not personal weakness.
sections.b: Researchers who study burnout often point to a mismatch between people and their work in several areas. These include workload that is too heavy for too long, a lack of control over how you do your job, too little recognition or reward, a breakdown of community such as conflict or isolation, a sense that things are unfair, and a clash between your values and what you are asked to do. Long hours alone do not always cause burnout; people can work hard on things they care about and feel energised. The danger zone is high demands combined with low control and little support. Understanding this helps in two ways. It reduces self blame, and it points you towards practical changes, some of which are within your control and some of which are your employer's responsibility.

sections.key: Australian work health and safety laws cover psychological health, not just physical safety.
sections.b: Under work health and safety laws, employers must, so far as is reasonably practicable, ensure the health and safety of workers, and health includes psychological health. In recent years, most Australian jurisdictions have introduced regulations that spell out how employers should manage psychosocial hazards, which are aspects of work that can cause psychological harm. Examples include excessive job demands, poor support, low role clarity, bullying, harassment and poor workplace relationships. This means a sustained, unmanageable workload is not just your personal problem; it is a workplace risk your employer should be identifying and controlling. Safe Work Australia and your state or territory regulator publish guidance on this. Many employers also offer an Employee Assistance Program, which typically provides free, confidential short term counselling, so it is worth asking whether yours does.

sections.key: Many Australian employees can now refuse unreasonable contact outside working hours.
sections.b: In 2024, Australia added a right to disconnect to the Fair Work Act. It began applying to employees of non small business employers in August 2024 and was extended to small business employees in August 2025. In broad terms, it means an employee can refuse to monitor, read or respond to contact, or attempted contact, from their employer or a third party such as a client outside their working hours, unless that refusal is unreasonable. Whether a refusal is unreasonable depends on factors such as the reason for the contact, how it is made, whether you are paid to be available, your role and your personal circumstances. Emergencies and genuine on call arrangements are treated differently. For details on how this applies to you, check the Fair Work Ombudsman website.

sections.key: Small, consistent habits help protect your time and energy.
sections.b: Rules help, but daily habits matter just as much. Set a clear end to your workday, and mark it with a small ritual such as closing the laptop, writing tomorrow's top three tasks or going for a walk. Turn off work notifications on your phone outside hours, or use focus modes that only let urgent contacts through. If you manage others, avoid sending late night emails, or schedule them to arrive in the morning, because a message from the boss at ten pm can feel like an instruction. Protect your leave and actually take it, including switching off fully while away. During the day, take your breaks away from the desk. Keep up sleep, movement and time with people you enjoy. None of these fix a broken workload, but they help you recover.

sections.key: Raise workload early, with specifics and options, rather than waiting until you break.
sections.b: Many people wait until they are close to collapse before saying anything. It is far easier to fix things earlier. Book a private conversation with your manager and describe the situation concretely: what is on your plate, how many hours it is taking and what is slipping. Avoid framing it as a confession of weakness. Instead, frame it as a resourcing problem you want to solve together. Bring options: which tasks could be paused, delegated, delayed or done more simply. Ask your manager to help you prioritise: 'If I can only do three of these well this month, which three matter most?' Follow up the conversation in writing. If nothing changes, consider talking to HR, a union, your health and safety representative or the Fair Work Ombudsman for information about your options.

quiz.q: How does the World Health Organization describe burnout?
o: As an occupational phenomenon, not a medical condition
quiz.e: The WHO classes burnout as an occupational phenomenon resulting from unmanaged chronic workplace stress.

quiz.q: Which combination is most strongly linked to burnout?
o: High demands, low control and little support
quiz.e: Heavy demands with little control or support form the classic danger zone.

quiz.q: What does Australian work health and safety law say about psychological health?
o: Employers must manage psychosocial risks as far as reasonably practicable
It is entirely the worker's responsibility
It applies only to the public service
quiz.e: WHS duties cover psychological as well as physical health.

quiz.q: Under the right to disconnect, when can an employee's refusal of after hours contact be unacceptable?
o: When the refusal is unreasonable in the circumstances
quiz.e: The right applies unless the refusal is unreasonable, judged on factors such as role, pay and the reason for contact.

quiz.q: What is a constructive way to raise an unmanageable workload?
o: Describe it specifically and bring options to prioritise
quiz.e: Specific details and options make it easier for a manager to help fix the problem.

LESSONS.title: Working on an ABN: contractor or employee?
LESSONS.hook: More Australians are picking up work as contractors. Here is how to tell if it is genuine, and what to sort out if you go it alone.

sections.key: Contracting can offer freedom, but it shifts many responsibilities from the business to you.
sections.b: Liam is offered a job building websites: good money, but they ask him to get an ABN and send invoices instead of going on the payroll. It sounds simple. Yet the difference between being an employee and an independent contractor changes almost everything: who pays your tax, who pays your super, whether you get paid leave, whether you are covered by an award and what happens if the work dries up. Plenty of people contract happily, from tradies and consultants to designers and side hustlers, and enjoy the flexibility. But the label is not just paperwork. This lesson explains how the distinction works and what to set up if you are genuinely contracting. It is general information, not legal, tax or financial advice, so check your own situation with official sources.

sections.key: The real nature of the working relationship matters more than what the contract calls it.
sections.b: There is no single test. Courts and tribunals look at the whole working relationship, including how it works in practice, not just what the paperwork says. Following changes to the Fair Work Act in 2024, the law makes clear that the real substance of the arrangement counts. Factors that tend to suggest you are an employee include the business controlling how, when and where you work, being paid for your time rather than a result, using the business's equipment, working only for them, being part of their team and being unable to send someone else to do the work. Factors suggesting genuine contracting include running your own business, choosing how to do the job, taking on financial risk, using your own tools, working for several clients and being able to delegate.

sections.key: Calling an employee a contractor to avoid obligations is illegal.
sections.b: Sham contracting is when a business falsely presents what is really employment as an independent contracting arrangement. This can happen deliberately, to avoid paying super, leave and award rates, or through genuine misunderstanding. It is against the law for an employer to misrepresent employment as contracting, to dismiss an employee in order to re engage them as a contractor doing much the same work, or to pressure someone into becoming a contractor with a false statement. If you are really an employee, you may be entitled to back pay, super and leave even if you signed a contractor agreement and held an ABN. If you are unsure, the Fair Work Ombudsman has information on the difference, and the ATO offers an employee or contractor decision tool on its website.

sections.key: An Australian Business Number is free to apply for, but you must actually be running a business.
sections.b: If you are genuinely carrying on a business, you can apply for an Australian Business Number through the Australian Business Register at abr.gov.au. It is free, and you do not need to pay anyone to do it for you, though many websites offer to for a fee. You will need your tax file number and some details about your business activity. Not everyone is entitled to an ABN: you need to be carrying on an enterprise, not simply working as an employee or pursuing a hobby. Once you have one, quote it on your invoices, because businesses may be required to withhold tax from payments to suppliers who do not provide one. Business.gov.au is a good starting point for registrations, business names and choosing a structure such as sole trader.

sections.h: Tax, GST and setting money aside
sections.key: As a contractor, no one withholds tax for you, so you need your own system.
sections.b: When you are paid as a contractor, usually the full invoice amount lands in your account with no tax taken out. That money is not all yours. You will need to include it in your tax return, and if your business income grows you may be placed into the ATO's pay as you go instalments system, which collects tax in advance through the year. Many contractors open a separate savings account and move a set share of every payment into it for tax. You must register for GST once your turnover reaches the threshold, and some industries, such as ride sourcing, must register regardless. Check current thresholds and rules on the ATO website. Keep good records of income and business expenses, and consider getting a registered tax agent to help.

sections.key: Contractors usually have to build their own safety net.
sections.b: Employees get paid leave, employer super and workers compensation cover. Genuine contractors often get none of these automatically, so your rates should cover them. Many contractors make voluntary super contributions themselves; check the ATO website and your fund for rules and caps. Note that under super law, some contractors who are paid mainly for their labour can still be entitled to super guarantee payments from the business that engages them, even with an ABN, so it is worth checking the ATO's guidance. Think about insurance as well: public liability and professional indemnity cover may be required by clients, and income protection can replace earnings if illness or injury stops you working. Without paid sick days or holidays, build time off into your plans, or you may find you have accidentally created a job with no breaks.

sections.key: Set rates that cover your real costs, and put agreements in writing.
sections.b: A common mistake is setting your rate by dividing an employee salary by working hours. As a contractor, you also need to cover super, leave you will not be paid for, insurance, equipment, software, accounting fees and quiet periods between jobs. That is why contract rates are often noticeably higher than the equivalent wage. Before starting, agree in writing on the scope of work, the price, payment terms, who owns the work you produce and how either side can end the arrangement. Send clear invoices with your ABN and payment details, and follow up late payments promptly. Some contractors and small businesses have protections against unfair contract terms under Australian law, and business.gov.au explains these. If a deal feels unclear or lopsided, getting independent legal advice before you sign can save trouble.

quiz.q: What matters most in deciding whether someone is an employee?
o: The real substance of the working relationship
quiz.e: Courts look at the whole relationship and how it works in practice, not just the label.

quiz.q: What is sham contracting?
o: Falsely presenting employment as a contracting arrangement
quiz.e: Misrepresenting employment as contracting to avoid obligations is illegal.

quiz.q: Who is entitled to an ABN?
o: Any employee who asks their employer
Someone genuinely carrying on a business or enterprise
Only people whose turnover is above the GST threshold
quiz.e: You need to be carrying on an enterprise, not simply working as an employee or pursuing a hobby.

quiz.q: Why do many contractors move part of every payment into a separate account?
o: Because no tax has been withheld and it will be due later
quiz.e: Contractors are usually paid in full and must cover their own tax.

quiz.q: Why are contract rates often higher than the equivalent hourly wage?
o: They must cover super, unpaid leave, insurance and quiet periods
quiz.e: Rates need to cover costs and entitlements an employer would otherwise provide.

LESSONS.title: Leaving a job the right way
LESSONS.hook: How you leave a job can shape your references, your final pay and your reputation for years. Here is how to resign well.

sections.key: People often remember how you left more clearly than how you worked.
sections.b: Industries are smaller than they look. The manager you leave behind may one day interview you, become your client or be called as your referee. The colleague who covered your workload after a messy exit may end up at your next workplace. That is why how you leave matters. A good exit protects your references, makes sure you receive everything you are owed and leaves the door open for future opportunities. A bad exit, such as walking out mid shift, posting complaints online or vanishing without a handover, can follow you for years. Leaving well does not mean pretending everything was perfect. It means being clear, professional and fair, even if you are glad to be going. This lesson is general information, not legal advice; the Fair Work Ombudsman has details for your situation.

sections.key: Your award, agreement or contract usually says how much notice you must give.
sections.b: Before you resign, find out how much notice you need to give. For many employees, this is set by their award, enterprise agreement or employment contract, so check all three. Notice periods of one to four weeks are common, often depending on how long you have worked there, while senior roles may require longer. Casual employees often have different rules, and in many cases need not give notice, but check your award. If you do not give the required notice, some awards and agreements allow your employer to deduct an amount from your final pay, so it is worth getting this right. Your employer may also choose to pay you instead of having you work out the notice period. Read the clauses carefully, and ask HR if anything is unclear.

sections.key: Tell your manager in person or by video, then confirm it in writing.
sections.b: Your manager should hear the news from you, not from the grapevine or an email that lands without warning. Ask for a short private meeting. Keep it simple and positive: say you have decided to leave, give your planned last day and thank them for the opportunity. You do not have to explain where you are going or why, and you should avoid using the meeting to air every grievance. If there are real problems worth raising, an exit interview or a separate conversation may be better. Then follow up with a short resignation letter or email. Include the date, your role, a clear statement that you are resigning, your intended last day and a brief thank you. Keep a copy for your records, since the date matters for your notice period.

sections.key: Think carefully before accepting a counter offer, and stay calm if the reaction is tough.
sections.b: Sometimes an employer responds to a resignation with a counter offer: more money, a new title or a promise that things will change. It can be flattering and occasionally it is exactly what you wanted. But pause and ask yourself why you started looking in the first place. If the reasons were about pay alone, a counter offer might solve the problem. If they were about culture, management, workload or growth, money rarely fixes those for long. Also consider why it took a resignation to get the offer. On the other side, some managers react badly, with anger or guilt. Stay polite, firm and brief. Your decision is yours to make. You must not be threatened or punished for exercising workplace rights, and the Fair Work Ombudsman can give information if things go wrong.

sections.key: A clear handover is the best way to protect your reputation on the way out.
sections.b: Use your notice period to make life easy for whoever takes over your work. Write a handover document covering current projects, where key files and passwords are stored through approved channels, upcoming deadlines, regular tasks and important contacts. Note anything that is half finished and what needs to happen next. Offer to train a colleague or your replacement if there is time. Finish what you reasonably can and be honest about what you cannot. Keep turning up and working properly until your last day; coasting is noticed. Return equipment such as laptops, phones, keys and uniforms, and do not take confidential information, client lists or company files with you, which could breach your contract or the law. Say goodbye to colleagues and swap personal contact details with those you want to stay in touch with.

sections.key: Make sure your final pay includes everything you are owed, and keep your records.
sections.b: When you leave, your final pay should include your wages up to your last day and any other outstanding amounts. Under the National Employment Standards, unused annual leave is paid out when employment ends, including any leave loading if your award, agreement or contract provides for it. Unused personal or carer's leave is generally not paid out. Long service leave rules depend mostly on your state or territory and sometimes your award, so check whether you have an entitlement. Check your final payslip carefully against your last ordinary payslip and your leave balance. Make sure your final super contribution is paid, and download copies of your payslips before your access to work systems ends. If something is missing, raise it in writing, and contact the Fair Work Ombudsman if it is not resolved.

sections.key: End on good terms, ask for references and keep your network warm.
sections.b: Before your last day, ask your manager or a senior colleague whether they would be willing to act as a referee, and confirm their preferred contact details. If you have an exit interview, give honest but constructive feedback; focus on what would help the organisation improve rather than personal attacks. Update your LinkedIn profile after you have finished, not before you have told your manager. Send a short farewell message to colleagues thanking them and sharing how they can reach you. Avoid criticising your old employer publicly, in interviews or online, even if they deserve it. Many people end up returning to a former employer years later, or working with old colleagues in new places. A graceful exit costs you very little and keeps those possibilities alive.

quiz.q: Where should you look to find your notice period?
quiz.e: Notice periods are usually set by your award, enterprise agreement or employment contract.

quiz.q: What is the best way to tell your manager you are leaving?
o: Ask a colleague to pass it on
Leave a note on their desk
Talk to them privately, then confirm in writing
quiz.e: A private conversation followed by a written resignation is clear and respectful.

quiz.q: When might a counter offer fail to solve the problem?
o: When you left only because of pay
When the real issues are culture, management or growth
quiz.e: Money rarely fixes non financial reasons for leaving for long.

quiz.q: Under the National Employment Standards, which leave is paid out when you leave?
quiz.e: Unused annual leave is paid out on termination, while personal leave generally is not.

quiz.q: When should you update your LinkedIn to show you are leaving?
o: After you have told your manager and finished up
quiz.e: Your manager should hear first, so update your profile afterwards.

LESSONS.title: The people who wrote the dictionary
LESSONS.hook: Somebody had to decide what every word means. Meet the stubborn, eccentric and occasionally imprisoned people who built the English dictionary.

sections.key: For most of its history, English had no dictionary at all.
sections.b: Picture Shakespeare writing his plays without a single dictionary on his desk. That was normal. For centuries, English speakers simply used words and argued about them. The first English dictionaries appeared around 1600 and were modest things. Robert Cawdrey's A Table Alphabeticall, published in 1604, listed only about 2,500 'hard words', mostly borrowed from Latin, French and Greek, with brief explanations for readers who found them puzzling. Nobody thought ordinary words like 'dog' or 'run' needed defining, because everyone already knew them. These early books were more like glossaries for the newly educated than records of the whole language. The idea that a dictionary should capture every word, common or rare, and show how each one was really used took another century and a half to arrive.

sections.h: Samuel Johnson takes on the job
sections.key: Johnson produced a landmark dictionary almost single-handedly in about nine years.
sections.b: In 1746 a group of London booksellers hired Samuel Johnson, a brilliant but often broke writer, to produce a proper dictionary of English. The French Academy had taken decades to make its national dictionary with dozens of scholars. Johnson, working with a handful of copying assistants in a house off Fleet Street, took about nine years. His Dictionary of the English Language appeared in 1755 with roughly 42,000 entries. Its real innovation was evidence. Johnson read widely through English writers and marked passages that showed words in action, then used more than 100,000 quotations to illustrate meanings. That method, defining words by how good writers actually used them, became the foundation of serious dictionary making in English for centuries afterwards.

sections.key: A few famous entries reveal Johnson's wit and his personality.
sections.b: Johnson's dictionary is mostly sober and careful, but a few entries let his personality peek through. He defined 'lexicographer' as 'a writer of dictionaries; a harmless drudge', poking fun at himself. His definition of 'oats' is the most quoted of all: 'a grain, which in England is generally given to horses, but in Scotland supports the people.' Johnson enjoyed teasing the Scots, even though his close friend and biographer James Boswell was one. These jokes are rare, and modern readers sometimes overrate them, but they help explain why the book became so loved. It was the work of a real person with opinions, not an anonymous committee. That human voice is part of why Johnson is still one of the most quoted figures in English.

sections.key: Webster used his dictionary to give the United States its own spelling.
sections.b: Across the Atlantic, the schoolteacher Noah Webster believed the new United States deserved its own version of English. He published An American Dictionary of the English Language in 1828, and he used it to push spelling changes he thought were simpler and more logical. That is why Americans write 'color', 'center' and 'defense' while Australians, following British habits, write 'colour', 'centre' and 'defence'. Webster wanted even bigger reforms, but most of his more radical ideas never caught on. Still, his choices stuck where it mattered most: in schools, newspapers and printing houses. A single determined dictionary maker helped split English spelling into two traditions, and every spellchecker that asks whether you want Australian or American English is living with his legacy.

sections.key: The OED set out to trace the history of every English word, and it took about 70 years.
sections.b: In 1857 members of the Philological Society in London called for a new kind of dictionary, one that would record every English word since around the 12th century and show how its meaning had changed over time. The project grew far beyond anyone's expectations. A Scottish schoolmaster named James Murray became editor in 1879 and worked in a corrugated iron shed he called the Scriptorium, lined with pigeonholes for slips of paper. The first part appeared in 1884, covering only 'A' to 'Ant'. Murray died in 1915, long before the end. The complete dictionary was finally finished in 1928, in ten large volumes, roughly 70 years after it was first proposed.

sections.key: Ordinary readers, including one remarkable prisoner, sent in millions of quotations.
sections.b: The OED could never have been written by its editors alone. Murray issued public appeals asking readers to search books for examples of words and post them in on slips of paper. Thousands of volunteers in Britain, America, Australia and elsewhere responded, and millions of slips arrived over the years. One of the most productive contributors was William Chester Minor, an American former army surgeon who was confined to Broadmoor, a hospital for the criminally insane in England, after killing a man in London in 1872. From his room, surrounded by books, Minor sent thousands of carefully chosen quotations. His story was later told in a popular book and film. It is a striking reminder that dictionaries are built by communities of readers, not only by scholars.

sections.key: Modern dictionaries describe how people really speak rather than lay down the law.
sections.b: Australia got its own major dictionary, the Macquarie, in 1981, recording words like 'arvo', 'doona' and 'ute' alongside Australian meanings and pronunciations. That shift reflects a bigger change in thinking. Early dictionary makers often wanted to fix the language and decide what was correct. Most modern lexicographers are descriptive instead: they observe how people actually use words and record it, including slang and new coinages. When a dictionary adds a word, it is not approving it, only noting that enough people use it. Today editors search huge digital collections of text to spot new words and shifting meanings, and online dictionaries are updated several times a year. The job Johnson did with paper slips and quill pens now runs on databases, but the goal is much the same.

quiz.q: What did early English dictionaries like Cawdrey's mainly list?
o: Hard words borrowed from other languages
quiz.e: Early dictionaries were glossaries of difficult, mostly borrowed words.

quiz.q: What was the key innovation in Johnson's 1755 dictionary?
quiz.e: Johnson used more than 100,000 quotations from writers to illustrate meanings.

quiz.q: Why do Americans write 'color' instead of 'colour'?
quiz.e: Webster's 1828 dictionary promoted simplified American spellings that stuck.

quiz.q: Roughly how long did the Oxford English Dictionary take to complete?
quiz.e: Proposed in 1857, it was finished in 1928.

quiz.q: What does it mean that modern dictionaries are 'descriptive'?
o: They tell you which words are wrong
They record how people actually use language
quiz.e: Descriptive dictionaries observe and record real usage rather than dictate it.

LESSONS.title: How Australian English was born
LESSONS.hook: Within a generation of 1788, visitors noticed that children in the colony sounded different. Here is how a new way of speaking English took shape.

sections.h: A new accent in a new place
sections.key: The Australian accent formed surprisingly quickly among the first colonial children.
sections.b: The First Fleet that arrived in 1788 carried people from all over Britain and Ireland: Londoners, people from rural England, Irish convicts, Scots and more. Their parents spoke a jumble of regional dialects. But children growing up together in Sydney did what children everywhere do: they copied each other more than their parents. By the 1820s, visitors were already remarking that native born children, sometimes called currency lads and lasses, had a distinct way of speaking. Linguists call this dialect levelling. When many accents are mixed together, the strongest regional quirks tend to drop out, and a new shared accent emerges. That is a big part of why Australian English came out fairly uniform across a huge continent from very early on.

sections.key: Many everyday Australian words were borrowed from Aboriginal languages.
sections.b: When Captain Cook's expedition was stranded near what is now Cooktown in 1770, his crew recorded a word that sounded like 'kangaroo' from the local Guugu Yimithirr people. It became one of the most famous loanwords in the world. After 1788, settlers in Sydney borrowed many more words from the Dharug language, including 'dingo', 'wombat' and 'koala'. 'Boomerang' also came from a Sydney area language, and 'billabong' is thought to come from Wiradjuri. Hundreds of Australian place names, from Wagga Wagga to Kakadu, have Aboriginal origins too. Before colonisation there were around 250 Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages, many with several dialects. Many are now endangered, and communities around the country are working hard to revive and teach them.

sections.key: Australians love shortening words and adding an 'o' or 'ie' to the end.
sections.b: Ask an Aussie what they did this arvo and you might hear that they stopped at the servo, grabbed a sanga and caught up with a rello. Australian English is famous for its diminutives: shortened words with an ending added. The two big endings are 'ie' or 'y', as in 'brekkie', 'barbie' and 'sunnies', and 'o', as in 'arvo', 'ambo', 'smoko' and 'bottle-o'. Linguists have counted thousands of these forms. Despite the stereotype, they are not about laziness. Research suggests they often signal friendliness, informality and shared identity, a way of saying 'we are relaxed with each other'. Notice how 'ambo' sounds warmer than 'paramedic'. Several of these words, like 'barbie', have travelled overseas, partly thanks to Australian films and television.

sections.key: Many classic Australian expressions have murky or surprising origins.
sections.b: Some of the most Australian sounding phrases turn out to have roots in British dialects. 'Dinkum', for example, appears in English regional speech in the 1800s, where it seems to have meant work or a fair share of work. In Australia it took on the sense of genuine or honest, and 'fair dinkum' became a national catchphrase. A popular story claims it comes from Chinese miners on the goldfields saying 'ding kum' for real gold, but there is no good evidence for this, and the British dialect origin is more likely. 'Cobber', meaning mate, may come from a British dialect word too. Etymology is full of tempting stories like these, and the less exciting explanation is usually the correct one.

sections.key: Australian accents vary along a spectrum more than by region.
sections.b: In the 1960s, the linguists Alexander Mitchell and Arthur Delbridge recorded thousands of school students and described three broad types of Australian accent. 'Broad' is the stereotypical outback sound, heard in the voice of Steve Irwin. 'Cultivated' is closer to British pronunciation and was once common among radio announcers. 'General', in between, is what most Australians speak. These are points on a scale rather than separate boxes, and the same person may slide along it depending on the situation. Over recent decades, the cultivated accent has become much rarer, and Australians have grown more comfortable sounding Australian on the national broadcaster and in parliament. Regional differences exist, but they are small compared with Britain or the United States.

sections.key: Small regional word differences reveal where an Australian grew up.
sections.b: Australian accents may be fairly uniform, but vocabulary is a different story. What you wear to the beach depends on your state: 'bathers' is common in Victoria, South Australia and Western Australia, 'togs' in Queensland, and 'swimmers' or 'cossie' in New South Wales. A slice of fried potato in batter is a 'potato cake' in Melbourne and a 'potato scallop' in Sydney. The processed meat in school sandwiches has gone by names like 'devon', 'fritz', 'polony' and 'Belgium sausage', depending on where you lived. A 'port' is a school bag in parts of Queensland. These words travel less than accents do, so they work like little badges of home, and they make a fun conversation starter with anyone from interstate.

sections.h: Not mumbling to keep out the flies
sections.key: The Australian accent is a normal accent with a normal history, not a lazy one.
sections.b: An old myth says Australians speak with half closed mouths to keep out the flies, or that the accent comes from convicts being drunk or lazy. Linguists reject these ideas. Every accent is simply the result of how a community's speech has drifted over time, and Australian English follows the same rules of sound change as any other variety. In 1965, a humorous book called Let Stalk Strine, by the pen name Afferbeck Lauder, played with how Australian speech sounds to the ear, and 'Strine' became a jokey name for the accent. Today Australian English sits alongside British, American, Indian and other Englishes as one of the major national varieties, with its own dictionaries, its own spelling habits and a growing cultural influence.

quiz.q: What process helped create a fairly uniform Australian accent?
quiz.e: Mixing many regional accents caused strong quirks to drop out, forming a new shared accent.

quiz.q: Which Aboriginal language gave English the word 'kangaroo'?
quiz.e: Cook's crew recorded it from Guugu Yimithirr speakers near Cooktown in 1770.

quiz.q: According to research, what do diminutives like 'ambo' often signal?
quiz.e: Diminutives often signal warmth, informality and shared identity.

quiz.q: What is the most likely origin of 'dinkum'?
quiz.e: It appears in British regional dialects, and the goldfields story lacks evidence.

quiz.q: In Queensland, what are swimwear most commonly called?
quiz.e: 'Togs' is the usual Queensland word.

LESSONS.title: The secret history of punctuation
LESSONS.hook: Ancient Romans wrote without spaces, commas or full stops. The marks we now take for granted were invented one by one, often by monks and printers.

sections.key: Ancient Greek and Latin texts were usually written as one unbroken stream of letters.
sections.b: Imagine reading a book where every line looked like THISISHOWMOSTANCIENTTEXTSLOOKED. Much ancient Greek and Latin was written in this style, which scholars call scriptio continua, meaning continuous script. There were no spaces between words, no lower case letters and very little punctuation. It worked because reading was usually done aloud, often by trained readers who prepared a text in advance, much as an actor studies a script. The reader worked out where words and sentences broke by sounding them out. To us it seems maddening, but to a skilled Roman reader it was simply normal. Punctuation, as we know it, began as a set of helpful notes for performers, telling them where to pause and breathe.

sections.key: An ancient librarian invented dots at different heights to mark pauses.
sections.b: Around 200 BCE, a scholar named Aristophanes of Byzantium, who worked at the great library in Alexandria, is credited with a simple system to help readers. He placed dots at different heights beside the text. A low dot marked a short pause, a middle dot a slightly longer one, and a high dot the end of a complete thought. These pauses had names that still echo today. The short section was a 'komma', Greek for a piece cut off, and the complete thought was a 'periodos', a full circuit. Those words became our comma and period. His system was used patchily for centuries, and many writers ignored punctuation entirely, leaving it to readers to add their own marks.

sections.h: Monks and the gift of spaces
sections.key: Irish and English scribes began separating words to help readers of Latin.
sections.b: The humble space between words may be the most important punctuation mark of all, and we owe it largely to early medieval monks. From around the 7th century, Irish and Anglo-Saxon scribes copying Latin texts began leaving gaps between words. Latin was a foreign language to them, so they could not rely on knowing it by ear, and spaces made it far easier to read. The practice spread across Europe over the following centuries. Word spacing also helped make silent reading more common, because readers no longer needed to sound out text to find where words began and ended. In monasteries, scribes also experimented with marks to show questions and sentence endings, slowly building the toolkit we use today.

sections.key: Venetian printers gave us the semicolon and helped standardise punctuation.
sections.b: When printing spread across Europe in the late 1400s, punctuation became more consistent, because thousands of copies now came from the same set of type. One of the most influential printers was Aldus Manutius in Venice. In the 1490s his press printed a work by the scholar Pietro Bembo that used the semicolon, a mark that became popular across Europe. Aldus is also associated with italic type and with the elegant small books that were the paperbacks of their day. Printers needed rules so that compositors setting type would make the same choices, and over time they settled on many of the conventions we still follow. Much of what we call correct punctuation began as a printing house's house style.

sections.key: The apostrophe arrived in English in the 1500s and has caused confusion ever since.
sections.b: The apostrophe came into English in the 16th century, borrowed from French and Italian printing, where it marked missing letters, as in 'don't' for 'do not'. Its use for possession, as in 'the dog's bone', developed gradually and was not fully settled until around the 1700s and 1800s. Even then, there were awkward exceptions, such as 'its' for possession and 'it's' for 'it is', which still trip up careful writers. The so called greengrocer's apostrophe, as in 'banana's $3 a kilo', is a much mocked error, but it shows how slippery the rules really are. Some place names have dropped the apostrophe altogether, and Australian naming authorities generally prefer place names without it, as in Kings Cross.

sections.key: Some new punctuation marks were proposed and never caught on.
sections.b: Not every new mark succeeds. In 1962, an American advertising executive named Martin Speckter proposed the interrobang, a question mark and exclamation mark merged into one symbol, for sentences like 'You did what?!' It had a brief burst of fame and even appeared on some typewriters, but it never entered everyday writing. Over the centuries others have suggested an irony mark, a backwards question mark to show a statement should not be taken literally, but none has stuck. The lesson is that punctuation spreads only when large numbers of writers, printers and readers adopt it at once. That is hard to arrange, which is why the core set of marks has changed surprisingly little in the past few hundred years.

sections.h: Punctuation in the age of texting
sections.key: Online messaging is giving old marks new meanings.
sections.b: Send a friend a text that simply says 'Fine.' and they may worry you are upset. In casual messaging, the full stop at the end of a short message has picked up an extra meaning. Because chat often leaves sentences unpunctuated, adding a full stop can look deliberate, and some research suggests readers find such messages less sincere or a little cold. Exclamation marks, by contrast, often signal warmth rather than shouting. Ellipses can read as hesitant or passive aggressive, depending on who is reading. Emoji now do some of the work that tone of voice does in speech. This is not a decline in standards. It is punctuation doing what it has always done: adapting to help people make their meaning clear.

quiz.q: What was 'scriptio continua'?
o: A style of handwriting with joined letters
Writing with no spaces between words
quiz.e: Many ancient texts ran all the words together without spaces.

quiz.q: The words 'comma' and 'period' come from which language?
quiz.e: They come from the Greek 'komma' and 'periodos'.

quiz.q: Who began routinely putting spaces between words?
quiz.e: Early medieval scribes in Ireland and England added spaces to help read Latin.

quiz.q: Which printer's press helped popularise the semicolon?
quiz.e: Aldus Manutius in Venice printed a 1490s work by Pietro Bembo using the semicolon.

quiz.q: What is an interrobang?
o: A question mark and exclamation mark combined
An early form of the apostrophe
quiz.e: Martin Speckter proposed it in 1962 for excited questions.

LESSONS.title: How the detective story was invented
LESSONS.hook: From a murder in a Paris apartment to Sherlock Holmes and Agatha Christie, the whodunnit has a surprisingly short and lively history.

sections.key: Edgar Allan Poe is usually credited with inventing the modern detective story in 1841.
sections.b: In 1841, the American writer Edgar Allan Poe published 'The Murders in the Rue Morgue'. Two women are found brutally killed in a Paris apartment that seems impossible to enter or leave. The police are baffled. Then an eccentric amateur named C. Auguste Dupin solves the mystery through pure reasoning, noticing clues everyone else missed. The answer is famously bizarre, and involves an escaped orangutan. Poe wrote only three Dupin stories, but they established the basic pattern of the genre: a brilliant, slightly odd detective, a less clever friend who narrates, a puzzling crime and a final explanation that makes everything click. Almost every fictional detective since owes something to Dupin.

sections.key: Detective fiction emerged alongside modern police forces and growing cities.
sections.b: It is no accident that detective stories appeared in the 1800s. London's Metropolitan Police was founded in 1829, and in 1842 it set up a small detective branch. Big, crowded cities were full of strangers, and crime became something to be investigated with evidence rather than simply punished. Newspapers fed public fascination with real murder cases. At the same time, science was transforming how people thought about the world, and the idea that careful observation could reveal hidden truths was exciting. The fictional detective captured that spirit. He, and later she, was a kind of scientist of crime, bringing order and reason to the chaos of the modern city. Readers found that deeply reassuring, and many still do.

sections.key: Arthur Conan Doyle's Holmes became the most famous detective in the world.
sections.b: In 1887, a young doctor named Arthur Conan Doyle published A Study in Scarlet, introducing Sherlock Holmes and his companion Dr Watson. Doyle modelled Holmes partly on Joseph Bell, a teacher at the Edinburgh medical school who could deduce a patient's job and history from small details. Holmes became a sensation when short stories appeared in The Strand Magazine from 1891. Doyle grew tired of him and in 1893 killed him off at the Reichenbach Falls in Switzerland. Readers were outraged, and many cancelled their magazine subscriptions. Doyle eventually gave in. Holmes returned, first in The Hound of the Baskervilles, set before his death, and then properly in 1903, when Doyle revealed he had survived the fall.

sections.key: One of the 19th century's biggest crime novels was set in Melbourne.
sections.b: A year before Holmes first appeared, a young New Zealand raised lawyer named Fergus Hume published The Mystery of a Hansom Cab in Melbourne in 1886. It begins with a man found dead in a horse drawn cab travelling through the city at night, and it moves between the wealthy homes of Melbourne and the slums of Little Bourke Street. The book was a huge success in Australia and then in Britain, selling far more copies than Doyle's first Holmes novel and becoming one of the bestselling crime novels of its century. Hume reportedly sold the rights cheaply and saw little of the profit. Australia has kept up the tradition, from Arthur Upfield to Kerry Greenwood and Jane Harper.

sections.key: Between the world wars, the puzzle mystery reached its peak.
sections.b: The years between the First and Second World Wars are often called the Golden Age of detective fiction. Agatha Christie published her first novel, The Mysterious Affair at Styles, in 1920, introducing the Belgian detective Hercule Poirot. She went on to become one of the bestselling novelists in history. Dorothy L. Sayers, Margery Allingham and New Zealand's Ngaio Marsh were among the other leading writers. These books were often set in country houses or villages, with a closed group of suspects and a body in the library. The fun was the puzzle itself. In 1930 many of these writers formed the Detection Club in London, a social club whose members promised to play fair with their readers.

sections.key: Golden Age writers believed readers deserved a fair chance to solve the crime.
sections.b: The central idea of the Golden Age was fair play. Every clue the detective used had to be shown to the reader too, so that a sharp enough reader could, in theory, solve the case first. In 1929 the writer and priest Ronald Knox published a tongue in cheek list of rules for detective fiction. They included that the criminal must be mentioned early in the story, that no supernatural forces should be involved, and that no undiscovered poisons should be used. Writers loved to test these rules. Christie broke expectations so cleverly in some books that readers felt cheated and delighted at the same time. The genre became a game between author and reader, with misdirection as the main weapon.

sections.key: American hardboiled writers took the detective out of the drawing room.
sections.b: Not everyone loved tidy country house puzzles. In 1920s and 1930s America, writers like Dashiell Hammett and Raymond Chandler created hardboiled detectives: tough, weary private investigators working in corrupt cities like San Francisco and Los Angeles. Their stories were less about clever clues and more about violence, money and moral compromise, told in sharp, wisecracking prose. Chandler's Philip Marlowe became the model for countless film noir heroes. Since then, crime fiction has split into many branches: police procedurals, psychological thrillers, Scandinavian noir and rural Australian crime, among others. Yet the basic appeal Poe discovered remains. A crime throws the world out of balance, and the detective, by thinking hard and noticing what others miss, puts it right again.

quiz.q: Who created the detective C. Auguste Dupin?
quiz.e: Poe introduced Dupin in 'The Murders in the Rue Morgue' in 1841.

quiz.q: Who was a real life model for Sherlock Holmes?
quiz.e: Doyle based Holmes partly on Joseph Bell, an Edinburgh medical teacher.

quiz.q: The Mystery of a Hansom Cab was set in which city?
quiz.e: Fergus Hume's 1886 bestseller was set in Melbourne.

quiz.q: Which detective was introduced in Christie's first novel?
quiz.e: The Mysterious Affair at Styles (1920) introduced Poirot.

quiz.q: What was the main principle of Golden Age 'fair play'?
o: The detective must be a police officer
Readers must be shown every clue
The murderer must be a stranger
Every story must be set in London
quiz.e: Readers were meant to have the same clues as the detective.

LESSONS.title: The dark origins of fairy tales
LESSONS.hook: Before Disney, Cinderella's stepsisters cut off parts of their feet to fit the slipper. Fairy tales have a long, strange and sometimes gruesome history.

sections.key: Fairy tales began as spoken folk tales passed down for generations.
sections.b: Long before anyone wrote them down, fairy tales were told aloud: by grandparents at the fire, by workers passing the time, by nurses to children. They were not originally just for kids. Adults told stories of clever peasants, cruel stepmothers, talking animals and magical helpers to entertain each other and pass on lessons about the world. Because they lived in memory, they changed with each teller and travelled across borders. That is why very similar stories pop up in many countries. Folklorists have catalogued thousands of these tale types in a system now called the Aarne Thompson Uther index, which gives each story pattern a number. Cinderella type stories, for example, are found across Europe, Asia and Africa.

sections.key: Versions of the Cinderella story have been recorded for well over a thousand years.
sections.b: The Greek geographer Strabo, writing around 2,000 years ago, recorded a tale about a woman named Rhodopis whose sandal was snatched by an eagle and dropped in the lap of an Egyptian king, who then searched for its owner. In China, a story written down in the 9th century tells of Ye Xian, a kind girl mistreated by her stepmother, who loses a golden shoe at a festival and is found by a king. Her magical helper is not a fairy godmother but the bones of a fish. These versions differ in detail, but they share a core: a mistreated young woman, a magical helper, a lost shoe and a royal search. The pattern clearly appealed to people everywhere.
