sections.b: Pitcher plants use a passive but very effective trap: a deep cup of leaf tissue holding a pool of digestive fluid. Nectar and colour lure insects to the rim, which in many species becomes extremely slippery when wet. Visitors lose their footing, tumble in and cannot climb the waxy inner walls. The tropical pitcher plants of the genus Nepenthes, found mostly in Southeast Asia, include giants whose pitchers can hold a litre or more of fluid. Some large species in Borneo have an unusual relationship with tree shrews, which lick sweet secretions from the pitcher lid and leave their droppings behind, giving the plant a useful dose of nitrogen. Australia has native Nepenthes too, growing in the far north of Queensland on Cape York Peninsula.

sections.key: Sundews trap insects with glistening droplets of glue, and Australia has a large share of the world's species.
sections.b: Sundews look as if they are covered in morning dew. Each leaf bristles with tentacles tipped with a glistening droplet, but the droplets are a sticky glue. An insect that lands is held fast, and in many species the tentacles slowly bend inward to press it against the leaf, where enzymes digest it. Sundews belong to the genus Drosera, and Australia is one of the world's great centres of sundew diversity, especially the south-west of Western Australia. Some Australian species are tiny 'pygmy sundews' no bigger than a coin, while others climb through shrubs on long stems. Many survive dry summers as underground tubers, sprouting again with winter rain. If you walk through heathland in Western Australia in winter or spring, look closely at the ground and you may spot them.

sections.h: Underwater traps and an Australian original
sections.key: Bladderworts suck in prey in a split second, and the Albany pitcher plant grows nowhere else on Earth.
sections.b: Some of the most impressive carnivorous plants are almost invisible. Bladderworts live in water or wet soil and carry tiny bladders that pump out water to create low pressure inside. When a small creature such as a water flea brushes a trigger hair, a trapdoor swings open and the bladder sucks it in, all in a tiny fraction of a second. It is one of the fastest movements known in the plant kingdom. Australia also has a true original: the Albany pitcher plant, which grows wild only in a small coastal region of south-west Western Australia. It is so distinctive that it is the only species in its plant family. Its small, hairy pitchers sit at ground level, catching mostly ants and other crawling insects.

sections.key: Habitat loss and illegal collecting threaten many carnivorous plants in the wild.
sections.b: Because carnivorous plants are specialists of nutrient-poor wetlands and heaths, they are vulnerable when those places change. Draining swamps, clearing land, adding fertiliser and suppressing the natural fires that keep competing plants in check can all push them out. Their striking looks also attract collectors. In the wild, the Venus flytrap's small range has made poaching a serious problem, and in North Carolina, taking the plants from the wild without permission has been treated as a felony since 2014. Several Nepenthes species in Southeast Asia are listed as threatened, partly because of illegal collecting. If you want to grow carnivorous plants, buy them from reputable nurseries that propagate their own stock, rather than plants that may have been taken from the wild. Never dig them up from bushland yourself.

sections.key: Carnivorous plants need rainwater, poor soil and plenty of light, and they do not need feeding with meat.
sections.b: Carnivorous plants can make fascinating pets, but they break most of the usual gardening rules. Because they evolved in nutrient-poor soils, ordinary potting mix and fertiliser can burn their roots. Most are grown in a mix of peat moss or a peat substitute with sand or perlite. Tap water often contains enough dissolved minerals to harm them over time, so use rainwater or distilled water, and many types like to sit in a shallow tray of it. Most need plenty of bright light. Resist the urge to feed them pieces of meat, which can rot in the trap, and avoid setting off flytrap traps for fun, since every closure uses energy. Outdoors, the plants will usually catch all the insects they need on their own.

quiz.q: Why do carnivorous plants catch animals?
o: To protect their flowers from pests
To get nutrients missing from poor soils
quiz.e: They still make food from sunlight; prey mainly supplies nutrients like nitrogen and phosphorus.

quiz.q: What makes a Venus flytrap snap shut?
o: Any single touch on the leaf
Its trigger hairs being touched twice in quick succession
Warm air from an animal's breath
quiz.e: Two touches within about 20 seconds trigger the trap, which helps it ignore raindrops and debris.

quiz.q: Which part of Australia is a major centre of sundew diversity?
quiz.e: South-west Western Australia is one of the world's great centres of sundew diversity.

quiz.q: What is special about the Albany pitcher plant?
o: It grows wild only in south-west Western Australia
It is the largest pitcher plant in the world
quiz.e: It grows wild only in a small part of south-west WA and is the only species in its family.

quiz.q: What water is best for most carnivorous plants?
quiz.e: They are sensitive to dissolved minerals, so rainwater or distilled water is best.

LESSONS.title: Masters of disguise: how animals hide
LESSONS.hook: A bird that becomes a broken branch, a fish that looks like seaweed, a cuttlefish that changes its skin in a blink: inside nature's art of hiding.

sections.h: The bird that is a branch
sections.key: Camouflage is about not being noticed, and it can rely on behaviour as much as colour.
sections.b: At dusk in an Australian park, you might walk right past a tawny frogmouth without seeing it. By day this bird sits motionless on a branch, its mottled grey and brown feathers matching the bark. If it senses danger, it stretches its body, points its beak upward, narrows its eyes to slits and freezes, so that it looks just like a broken stump. The disguise works because of the whole package: colour, shape and stillness. That is the heart of camouflage. It is not just about being the right colour. It is about defeating the eyes and brain of whoever is looking, whether that is a hungry predator or prey that needs to be ambushed. Over millions of years, animals have evolved many different ways to do it.

sections.key: Many animals match their background and use countershading to flatten out the shadows that reveal their shape.
sections.b: The simplest strategy is background matching: being the same colour and pattern as your surroundings. A grasshopper on dry grass or a sand flathead on the seabed both use it. But there is a problem. Light usually comes from above, so the top of a body is brightly lit and the belly is in shadow, and that shading makes an object look solid and easy to pick out. Many animals counter this by being darker on top and paler underneath. This is called countershading, and it cancels out the shadow so the body looks flatter and fades into the background. Many fish, sharks and dolphins use it. Seen from above, their dark backs blend with the deep water below. Seen from beneath, their pale bellies blend with the bright surface.

sections.key: Bold, contrasting patches can break up an animal's outline so that the eye does not recognise its shape.
sections.b: Our brains are very good at spotting outlines, so another strategy is to destroy them. This is disruptive colouration: bold patches of contrasting colour that cut across the edges of the body. The eye picks up the patches as separate shapes rather than one animal. Many moths, frogs and snakes use it, and stripes running across an eye can help hide one of the most recognisable features of all. Humans borrowed the idea. During the First World War, many ships were painted in striking stripes and zigzags known as dazzle camouflage. It was not meant to make them invisible at sea, which is almost impossible. Instead, the idea was to confuse enemy submarine crews trying to judge a ship's shape, speed and direction, so that their torpedoes would miss.

sections.key: Some animals do not hide at all but look like an object a predator would ignore, such as a stick, leaf or seaweed.
sections.b: Some animals are perfectly visible but go unnoticed because they look like something boring or inedible. This is called masquerade. Stick insects look like twigs, and many sway gently as if moved by the wind. Leaf insects look like leaves, complete with fake veins and even nibbled edges. Some caterpillars and spiders look like bird droppings, which few predators want to eat. One of the most beautiful examples lives in southern Australia's cool waters. The leafy seadragon, a relative of seahorses, is covered in leaf-like flaps of skin and drifts slowly through kelp and seagrass, looking just like a piece of floating seaweed. It is the marine emblem of South Australia, and divers can spend a long time staring at weed before realising it is looking back at them.

sections.key: Harmless animals can gain protection by copying the warning colours of dangerous ones.
sections.b: Not all disguises are about hiding. Many dangerous animals advertise themselves with bold warning colours, such as the yellow and black of wasps. Predators learn to avoid them. That opens a door for harmless species to cheat. Many hoverflies, which cannot sting, are striped yellow and black and look a lot like wasps or bees. This is called Batesian mimicry, after the naturalist Henry Walter Bates, who studied it among butterflies in the Amazon in the 1800s. Sometimes several genuinely dangerous species share the same warning pattern, which helps predators learn the lesson faster; this is called Mullerian mimicry. One of the most extraordinary mimics is the mimic octopus of Southeast Asia, which can change its shape and movement to resemble a flatfish, a venomous lionfish or a sea snake.

sections.key: Cuttlefish change colour in moments using thousands of tiny pigment sacs controlled by their nervous system.
sections.b: Cuttlefish, octopuses and squid have some of the most advanced camouflage on Earth. Their skin contains thousands of tiny elastic sacs of pigment called chromatophores, each surrounded by muscles controlled directly by nerves. By stretching or squeezing these sacs, a cuttlefish can change its colour and pattern in well under a second, and it can even raise bumps on its skin to match rough rock or weed. Strangely, most of these animals appear to be colour-blind, and scientists are still working out how they match colours so well. Each winter, around Point Lowly near Whyalla in South Australia, huge numbers of giant cuttlefish gather to breed. Some small males have been seen disguising themselves as females to slip past larger rival males and reach a mate, a trick right out of a spy story.

sections.key: Camouflage evolves through natural selection, as predators and prey keep driving each other to improve.
sections.b: Camouflage is a product of natural selection. Individuals that are slightly harder to spot are more likely to survive and pass on their genes, while predators with sharper eyes catch more food. The result is an ongoing arms race. A classic example is the peppered moth in England. During the Industrial Revolution, soot darkened tree trunks, and a dark form of the moth, which was once rare, became common in industrial areas because birds found the pale moths easier to spot. After clean air laws reduced pollution in the twentieth century, the pale form became common again. Today camouflage faces new challenges, as climate change shifts the timing of seasons. In some places, animals that turn white for winter are now sometimes stranded in white coats on brown, snowless ground.

quiz.q: How does the tawny frogmouth hide when it senses danger?
o: It changes the colour of its feathers
It freezes in a pose that resembles a broken branch
quiz.e: It stretches upward, narrows its eyes and freezes, looking just like a broken stump.

quiz.q: What is countershading?
o: Being darker on top and paler underneath
Having stripes that cross the eyes
quiz.e: Dark backs and pale bellies cancel out the shading that would make a body look solid.

quiz.q: What was dazzle camouflage on First World War ships meant to do?
o: Confuse judgements of a ship's speed and direction
quiz.e: Dazzle patterns aimed to confuse submarine crews trying to judge a ship's course and speed.

quiz.q: Which animal masquerades as floating seaweed in southern Australian waters?
quiz.e: The leafy seadragon's leaf-like flaps make it look like drifting seaweed.

quiz.q: What lets cuttlefish change colour so quickly?
o: Pigment sacs controlled by nerves and muscles
quiz.e: Chromatophores are stretched or squeezed by muscles under direct nervous control.

LESSONS.title: The hidden kingdom of fungi
LESSONS.hook: The mushroom you see is just the tip of the iceberg. Below ground, fungi feed forests, recycle the dead and sometimes grow into some of the largest living things on Earth.

sections.key: Fungi are a kingdom of their own, more closely related to animals than to plants.
sections.b: After autumn rain, mushrooms seem to appear overnight on lawns and in bushland. It is tempting to think of them as odd little plants, but fungi are something else entirely. They cannot make food from sunlight. Instead, they feed by releasing digestive enzymes into their surroundings and absorbing the nutrients that are broken down. Their cell walls are made of chitin, the same tough material found in insect shells, not the cellulose of plants. Genetic studies show that fungi are actually more closely related to animals than to plants. The kingdom is vast and varied, including yeasts, moulds, mushrooms, rusts and lichen partners. Scientists have named around 150,000 species, but estimates of the true total run into the millions, and in Australia most fungi are thought to be still undescribed.

sections.key: A mushroom is only a fruiting body; the main fungus is a network of fine threads called mycelium.
sections.b: A mushroom is to a fungus roughly what an apple is to an apple tree: a temporary structure for spreading spores. The main body of most fungi is the mycelium, a web of microscopic threads called hyphae that spread through soil, wood or leaf litter. A teaspoon of healthy soil can contain a startling length of these threads. Mycelium can also grow enormous. In a forest in Oregon in the United States, a single individual of a honey fungus has been found spreading through the soil across nearly ten square kilometres, and it is thought to be thousands of years old. It is often described as one of the largest living organisms on Earth. Above ground, all you would notice is the occasional clump of honey-coloured mushrooms and some unhealthy trees.

sections.key: Most land plants rely on mycorrhizal fungi, which trade water and nutrients for sugars.
sections.b: Dig up almost any healthy plant and look closely at its roots, and you will probably find fungi wrapped around them or growing inside them. These partnerships are called mycorrhizas, from Greek words meaning 'fungus root', and the large majority of land plants form them. The deal is a trade. The fungus's fine threads reach far further through the soil than roots can, gathering water and nutrients such as phosphorus and nitrogen and passing them to the plant. In return, the plant feeds the fungus sugars made by photosynthesis. Many scientists think this partnership helped the first plants colonise dry land hundreds of millions of years ago. In Australia, many native plants have important fungal partners, and some orchids cannot even germinate from seed without the right fungus.

sections.h: The 'wood wide web': what we know
sections.key: Fungal networks do connect plants, but popular claims about trees sharing and communicating go beyond the evidence.
sections.b: In 1997 the Canadian ecologist Suzanne Simard and colleagues published research suggesting that carbon could move between trees through shared fungal networks. A journal cover nicknamed it the 'wood wide web', and the idea took off. Books and documentaries now describe 'mother trees' feeding their seedlings and forests that warn each other of danger through underground networks. It is a beautiful story, and fungal networks linking the roots of different plants are real. However, how much material they move between trees, and whether this significantly helps them, is still debated. A 2023 review by a group of forest scientists argued that the evidence for some popular claims was weaker than often suggested. The careful view is that underground networks matter, but we are still learning how they really work.

sections.key: Fungi break down dead wood and leaves, releasing nutrients that keep ecosystems running.
sections.b: Without fungi, forests would be buried in their own dead wood. Wood is tough to digest because it contains lignin, a complex material that stiffens plant cell walls. Few organisms can break lignin down efficiently, and some fungi, particularly the so-called white rot fungi, are among the best at it. As fungi, bacteria and small animals break down fallen logs, leaves and dead animals, they release nitrogen, phosphorus and other nutrients back into the soil for living plants to use. A rotting log in Australian bushland may look like waste, but it is a busy recycling plant and a home for beetles, frogs, lizards and small mammals. That is one reason many land managers now leave fallen timber on the ground rather than tidying it away.

sections.key: Fungi give us bread, cheese, soy sauce and life-saving medicines like penicillin.
sections.b: You probably ate something made with fungi today. Baker's yeast is a single-celled fungus that releases carbon dioxide to make bread rise, and related yeasts ferment sugars into the alcohol in beer and wine. The blue veins in some cheeses are moulds from the genus Penicillium, and a mould called koji is used to make soy sauce, miso and sake. Mushrooms themselves are a valuable food. Fungi have also changed medicine. In 1928 Alexander Fleming noticed that a Penicillium mould was killing the bacteria on one of his laboratory dishes, which eventually led to penicillin, one of the first antibiotics. A drug that helps prevent organ rejection after transplants, cyclosporine, also came from a fungus. Researchers continue to search fungi for new medicines and enzymes.

sections.h: The darker side, and staying safe
sections.key: Some fungi are deadly to eat or devastating to wildlife, so never eat wild mushrooms you cannot identify with certainty.
sections.b: Fungi have a darker side. Certain fungi infect insects and alter their behaviour; in some tropical forests, infected ants climb up a plant and clamp on before the fungus kills them and sprouts from their bodies. The chytrid fungus has caused declines in hundreds of frog species worldwide, including in Australia, and is linked to several frog extinctions here. Some fungi are deadly to people. The death cap mushroom, an introduced species found around Canberra and Melbourne, has caused deaths in Australia, and its toxins can destroy the liver. Many poisonous mushrooms look similar to edible ones, and cooking does not make them safe. This is general information, not advice: never eat wild mushrooms unless an expert has identified them, and if you suspect poisoning, call the Poisons Information Centre on 13 11 26.

quiz.q: Fungi are more closely related to which group?
quiz.e: Genetic studies show fungi are more closely related to animals than to plants.

quiz.q: What is mycelium?
o: The spore-producing cap of a mushroom
A network of fine threads that forms the main body of a fungus
A chemical that helps plants photosynthesise
quiz.e: Mycelium is the web of hyphae; the mushroom is just a temporary fruiting body.

quiz.q: What does a plant usually give its mycorrhizal fungus in return for water and nutrients?
quiz.e: The plant supplies sugars, while the fungus gathers water and nutrients like phosphorus.

quiz.q: What is the fairest summary of the 'wood wide web' idea?
o: Trees are proven to talk to each other like people
Fungal networks are real, but some popular claims go beyond the evidence
It only applies to tropical rainforests
quiz.e: Networks linking roots exist, but how much they help trees is still debated.

quiz.q: If you suspect mushroom poisoning in Australia, who should you call?
quiz.e: Call the Poisons Information Centre on 13 11 26; cooking does not make poisonous mushrooms safe.

LESSONS.title: Ants: the superorganism
LESSONS.hook: There may be around 20 quadrillion ants on Earth. Individually simple, together they farm, build, wage war and solve problems no single ant could.

sections.key: Scientists estimate around 20 quadrillion ants live on Earth, outweighing all wild birds and mammals combined.
sections.b: Sit on almost any patch of Australian ground for a few minutes and an ant will find you. That is not surprising when you look at the numbers. In 2022, researchers combined hundreds of studies from around the world and estimated that there are about 20 quadrillion ants on Earth, roughly two and a half million for every person. Together, they estimated, ants weigh more than all wild birds and wild mammals combined. More than 14,000 species have been named, and many more await description. Australia is especially rich in ants, with well over a thousand known species and probably many more. They live almost everywhere except the coldest places, from rainforest canopies to the hottest deserts, and they shape their environments by moving soil, spreading seeds and eating other insects.

sections.key: An ant colony works like a single organism, with a queen that reproduces and sterile workers doing everything else.
sections.b: To understand ants, it helps to stop thinking about individual ants. A typical colony is a family. At its heart is one or more queens, whose main job is laying eggs. Almost all the ants you see are workers, which are female and usually do not reproduce. Males appear only at certain times, mostly to fly off and mate, and they die soon after. Workers divide up the jobs: caring for young, building and defending the nest, and gathering food. In many species, an ant's job changes as it ages, with younger workers staying inside and older ones heading out to forage. Because the colony survives and reproduces as a unit, biologists often call it a superorganism, with workers acting a little like the cells of a body.

sections.key: Ants coordinate using chemical signals, and simple rules followed by many ants can produce clever group behaviour.
sections.b: No ant is in charge. The queen does not give orders, and no worker sees the big picture. Instead, ants communicate mainly with chemicals called pheromones. A forager that finds food lays a scent trail on the way home, and others follow it, adding their own scent if they also find food. Shorter routes get reinforced faster, because ants complete round trips more quickly, so the colony tends to settle on efficient paths without anyone planning them. This is an example of emergent behaviour, where intelligent-looking results arise from many individuals following simple rules. It has inspired computer scientists, who developed 'ant colony optimisation' methods for problems such as finding efficient routes. Ants also use touch, sound and alarm chemicals to warn nestmates of danger.

sections.key: Some ants grow fungus gardens and others tend insects for their sugary honeydew, long before humans farmed.
sections.b: Humans began farming roughly 12,000 years ago, but some ants have been doing it for tens of millions of years. The leafcutter ants of Central and South America do not eat the leaves they carry. Instead, they chew them into a pulp to feed a fungus that grows in underground gardens, and the fungus becomes their food. Their nests can contain millions of ants and cover large areas. Other ants are herders. They protect sap-sucking insects such as aphids and scale insects from predators and in return collect honeydew, a sugary liquid the insects excrete. Gardeners sometimes notice ants running up and down plants covered in scale insects, which is exactly this partnership in action. Some ants even carry their insect 'livestock' to fresh plants to feed.

sections.key: Honeypot ants store nectar in their swollen bodies, and green tree ants sew leaves together with silk.
sections.b: Australia has some of the world's most remarkable ants. In the arid centre, honeypot ants have workers called repletes that are fed so much nectar and honeydew that their abdomens swell into round, amber-coloured balls the size of a small grape. They hang from the ceilings of underground chambers as living food stores for the colony in lean times. Aboriginal people have long dug them up as a sweet food. In the tropical north, green tree ants, also called weaver ants, build nests by pulling leaves together. Some workers hold the leaves in place while others carry larvae, which produce silk that is used to glue the leaves together. Green tree ants are also a traditional bush food, and many people describe their bodies as having a sharp, lemony taste.

sections.key: Most ants are harmless to people, but bull ants and jack jumpers can cause serious allergic reactions.
sections.b: Most ants are a nuisance at worst, but Australia's bull ants and jack jumpers are worth respecting. These large, long-jawed ants have excellent eyesight, can be aggressive near their nests and deliver a painful sting. For most people the sting causes pain, swelling and redness that settles down. For a minority who are allergic, particularly to jack jumper venom, a sting can cause anaphylaxis, a severe whole-body reaction that can be life-threatening. Jack jumper allergy is especially well known in Tasmania. This is general information, not medical advice. Signs such as difficulty breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or collapse need urgent help, so call 000. People with a known allergy should follow their doctor's plan, and healthdirect has reliable information on insect stings and allergic reactions.

sections.key: Invasive ants such as red imported fire ants and yellow crazy ants can devastate wildlife, farms and lifestyles.
sections.b: Some of the world's most damaging invasive species are ants. Red imported fire ants, originally from South America, were found in Brisbane in 2001 and have been the target of a major eradication effort ever since. They deliver painful stings, can harm people, pets, livestock and wildlife, and could cost Australia's economy and environment heavily if they spread widely. On Christmas Island, introduced yellow crazy ants formed huge 'supercolonies' and killed millions of the island's famous red crabs, prompting long-running control programs. Invasive ants often succeed because many colonies cooperate rather than fight, and because they arrive without their natural enemies. If you live in an affected area, learn what fire ants and their nests look like, and report suspected sightings to the national fire ant program or your state biosecurity agency.

quiz.q: According to a 2022 estimate, how do ants compare with wild birds and mammals by weight?
o: Ants weigh about the same as wild birds alone
Ants weigh more than wild birds and mammals combined
Nobody has tried to estimate it
quiz.e: The study estimated about 20 quadrillion ants, outweighing all wild birds and mammals combined.

quiz.q: Which ants make up almost all of the ants you see in a colony?
quiz.e: Workers are female and usually do not reproduce; males appear mainly to mate.

quiz.q: How do ant colonies tend to find efficient routes to food?
o: Shorter trails get reinforced with pheromones faster
Scouts draw maps in the soil
They follow the sun's position only
quiz.e: Ants on shorter routes return sooner, reinforcing those scent trails more quickly.

quiz.q: What do honeypot ant repletes do?
o: Store nectar and honeydew in swollen abdomens
quiz.e: Repletes hang in underground chambers as living food stores for the colony.

quiz.q: What should you do if you suspect red imported fire ants?
o: Dig up the nest to check
Report it to the fire ant program or state biosecurity agency
quiz.e: Suspected sightings should be reported so the eradication program can respond.

LESSONS.title: Eucalypts: trees built for fire
LESSONS.hook: Gum trees define the Australian landscape. Their oils, bark and hidden buds tell the story of a continent shaped by fire.

sections.key: Eucalypts dominate most of Australia's forests and woodlands, with hundreds of species.
sections.b: Step out into the bush after rain and you may catch it: the sharp, clean scent of eucalyptus oil rising from the leaves. Gum trees are so familiar that it is easy to forget how remarkable they are. Botanists group the eucalypts into three closely related genera: Eucalyptus, Corymbia, which includes many bloodwoods and the spotted gums, and Angophora. Together they include more than 800 species, almost all native to Australia, with a few in New Guinea and nearby islands. They dominate roughly three-quarters of Australia's native forests, and they grow in almost every environment, from snowy mountains to the dry inland. Over millions of years, as the continent dried out and fire became more common, eucalypts became extraordinarily good at living with both drought and flame.

sections.key: Eucalypts range from shrubby mallees to mountain ash, the tallest flowering plants on Earth.
sections.b: Eucalypts come in a dazzling range of forms. In semi-arid southern Australia, mallees grow as clumps of slender stems from a single swollen base, often only a few metres tall. At the other extreme is the mountain ash of Victoria and Tasmania, the world's tallest flowering plant. A mountain ash in southern Tasmania known as Centurion has been measured at about 100 metres tall, taller than a 25-storey building. Their bark varies just as much. Stringybarks have thick, fibrous bark, ironbarks have hard, deeply furrowed black bark, and smooth-barked gums shed their outer layer each year to reveal fresh, colourful trunks underneath. The famous scribbly gums carry winding tracks on their bark, made by the larvae of tiny moths tunnelling between the old and new layers.

sections.key: Eucalyptus leaves are full of aromatic oils that deter many animals and are highly flammable.
sections.b: Hold a eucalyptus leaf up to the light and you may see tiny translucent dots. These are oil glands. The oils are a mix of aromatic compounds that help protect the leaves from many insects and animals that would otherwise eat them. Only specialists, such as koalas, some possums and certain insects, can cope with large amounts. People have used eucalyptus oil for generations in cleaning products and remedies for colds. The oils are also flammable, and on hot days some of these compounds evaporate from the leaves. Along with other natural chemicals released by the trees, they are thought to contribute to the blue haze that gives the Blue Mountains near Sydney their name. That same volatility helps explain why eucalypt forests can burn so fiercely in extreme weather.

sections.key: Many eucalypts survive fire by resprouting from buds protected under their bark or from woody lumps at their base.
sections.b: A few months after a bushfire, the blackened trunks of many eucalypt forests become covered in soft green and red shoots. This is one of the most striking sights in Australian nature. Many eucalypts have epicormic buds, dormant buds hidden beneath their thick bark along the trunk and branches. Fire may kill the leaves, but the insulated buds survive and sprout once the danger has passed, rebuilding the canopy far faster than a seedling could. Many species also have a lignotuber, a woody swelling at the base of the trunk, partly underground, packed with buds and food reserves. If the whole tree above ground is destroyed, it can resprout from this lump. Mallees are a classic example, regrowing from their lignotubers again and again after fire.

sections.h: The trees that must burn and wait
sections.key: Some eucalypts, such as mountain ash, are killed by intense fire and rely on seed to regenerate.
sections.b: Not all eucalypts resprout. Mountain ash and its close relative alpine ash are usually killed by intense fire. Instead, they bet on their seeds. Their capsules, the gumnuts, hold seeds that are released in huge numbers after the heat of a fire. The seeds fall onto a bed of nutrient-rich ash in full sunlight, and a dense new forest springs up, with all the trees roughly the same age. This strategy works well when big fires come at long intervals. The danger comes when fires return too often. Young mountain ash take many years, often around two decades, to produce plenty of seed. If a young forest burns again before then, there may be no seed left, and the forest can be replaced by shrubs or other species.

sections.key: Aboriginal people have shaped Australian landscapes with fire for tens of thousands of years.
sections.b: Fire in Australia is not only a natural force. Aboriginal people have used it as a land management tool for tens of thousands of years. Traditional burning, often called cultural burning, typically involves cooler, smaller fires lit at chosen times of year to create a patchwork of burnt and unburnt country. This can reduce fuel, encourage fresh growth that attracts animals and keep paths through the land open. Many of these practices were disrupted after colonisation. Today, a growing number of land managers work with Aboriginal rangers and communities to bring cultural burning back. The Black Summer fires of 2019 and 2020, which burned millions of hectares, highlighted how hotter, drier conditions linked to climate change are making fire seasons more dangerous, and how much we still need to learn.

sections.h: Gum trees at home and abroad
sections.key: Eucalypts are planted worldwide, and some can drop large branches without warning.
sections.b: Eucalypts have spread far beyond Australia. Fast-growing species have been planted in many countries, including California, Portugal, Brazil, India and parts of Africa, for timber, paper pulp and fuel. In some places they are valued plantation trees; in others they are criticised for using a lot of water or for adding to fire risk where they have spread. At home, it is worth knowing that some gums, particularly river red gums and other large eucalypts, can shed big limbs suddenly, sometimes on calm, hot days with no warning. That has earned them the grim nickname 'widowmaker'. When camping, parking or picnicking, avoid setting up directly under large overhanging branches. For bushfire preparation, follow your state fire service's advice, which explains how to manage trees and vegetation around your home.

quiz.q: Roughly what share of Australia's native forests are dominated by eucalypts?
quiz.e: Eucalypts dominate roughly three-quarters of Australia's native forests.

quiz.q: What is special about mountain ash?
o: It is the world's tallest flowering plant
It is the only eucalypt found outside Australia
quiz.e: Mountain ash is the tallest flowering plant, with one Tasmanian tree measured at about 100 metres.

quiz.q: What are epicormic buds?
o: Flowers that open only after rain
Dormant buds under the bark that sprout after fire
quiz.e: Protected under thick bark, they sprout after fire and rebuild the canopy quickly.

quiz.q: Why can frequent fires threaten mountain ash forests?
o: Young trees may be burned before they produce enough seed
Fire makes their seeds too heavy to spread
They resprout too slowly from lignotubers
quiz.e: Mountain ash rely on seed and take many years to produce plenty of it.

quiz.q: Why do some large gums carry the nickname 'widowmaker'?
o: They can drop large branches suddenly
quiz.e: Some large gums, like river red gums, can shed big limbs without warning.

LESSONS.title: Animals that cheat ageing
LESSONS.hook: A shark born before Captain Cook sailed, a rodent that barely seems to age, a jellyfish that turns back its own clock: what nature's longest lives reveal about growing old.

sections.key: Some animals live for centuries, and their ages can be read from growth layers in shells and bodies.
sections.b: In 2006, scientists dredging the seabed off Iceland pulled up an ordinary-looking clam. Like the rest of the haul, it was frozen on board as routine, so it was already dead when, back in the lab, scientists counted the growth rings in its shell, much as you would count the rings of a tree, and realised it was extraordinary. The clam, an ocean quahog later nicknamed Ming, turned out to be about 507 years old. It had been alive since around the start of the 1500s. Ming is one of the oldest individual animals whose age has been reliably measured. Its story raises a big question that has puzzled biologists for generations. If some animals can live for centuries, why do others, including us, age and die on a much shorter schedule? Nature offers some surprising clues.

sections.h: Why do we age at all?
sections.key: Evolutionary theory suggests ageing happens because natural selection weakens later in life.
sections.b: From an evolutionary point of view, ageing is a puzzle. Why would natural selection allow bodies to wear out? Biologists such as Peter Medawar and George Williams developed an influential answer in the mid twentieth century. In the wild, most animals die young from predators, disease, accidents or starvation. Genes that cause problems late in life are rarely 'seen' by natural selection, because few individuals live long enough for them to matter. Some genes that help early in life, for example by boosting reproduction, might even cause harm later. A related idea, the 'disposable soma' theory, suggests bodies invest in reproduction rather than perfect long-term repair. The theory makes a prediction: animals that face less danger from the outside world should evolve to age more slowly. Many long-lived species fit that pattern.

sections.key: Greenland sharks and bowhead whales may live for centuries in cold Arctic waters.
sections.b: In the cold, dark waters of the North Atlantic and Arctic lives the Greenland shark, a predator that can grow to several metres long. Its age is hard to measure, because sharks lack the bony growth rings of many fish. In 2016, researchers used radiocarbon dating on the lenses of the sharks' eyes, which form before birth and do not change. They estimated that the largest shark in their study was around 400 years old, although with a wide margin of uncertainty. That would make it the longest-lived vertebrate known. The bowhead whale, another Arctic giant, may live for more than 200 years. Old harpoon tips from the 1800s have been found embedded in whales caught in modern times. Cold temperatures, slow growth and large bodies seem to go together with very long lives.

sections.key: Naked mole-rats can live for over 30 years, rarely get cancer and do not seem to become more likely to die as they age.
sections.b: The naked mole-rat of East Africa is pink, wrinkled and almost hairless, and it may be one of the most intriguing animals in ageing research. A mouse of similar size usually lives two or three years. Naked mole-rats have lived for more than 30 years in captivity. Even more surprising, a study of thousands of animals found that their risk of dying did not seem to rise as they got older, unlike almost every other mammal, including humans, whose risk of death climbs steadily with age. They also rarely develop cancer. Naked mole-rats live in large underground colonies, protected from many predators, which fits the evolutionary theory of ageing. Scientists are studying their cells, proteins and metabolism closely to work out which of their traits might explain their resilience.

sections.key: Some simple animals, like the 'immortal jellyfish' and hydra, show little or no sign of ageing.
sections.b: Some of the most dramatic examples come from simple animals. A tiny jellyfish called Turritopsis dohrnii has been nicknamed the immortal jellyfish. When it is injured, stressed or old, it can transform back into an earlier life stage, a polyp attached to the seabed, and then grow into a new jellyfish again. In principle, it could repeat this cycle many times. In practice, individuals still die from predators and disease, so it is not truly immortal. The freshwater hydra, a small relative of jellyfish, also appears to show little or no ageing. Its body is constantly renewed by stem cells, and in laboratory studies hydra did not show the usual increase in death rate over time. These animals suggest that ageing is not an unbreakable law of biology.

sections.key: Big, long-lived animals have far more cells but do not get more cancer, a mystery called Peto's paradox.
sections.b: Cancer starts when a cell picks up harmful mutations and begins dividing out of control. So you might expect animals with more cells, living longer, to get more cancer. An elephant has vastly more cells than a mouse, and a blue whale more still. Yet large animals do not seem to have higher cancer rates than small ones. This puzzle is known as Peto's paradox, after the English epidemiologist Richard Peto. Some answers are emerging. Elephants have around 20 copies of a gene called TP53, which helps detect damaged DNA and trigger the death of faulty cells, while humans have just one pair. Bowhead whales appear to be unusually good at repairing damaged DNA. Large animals seem to have evolved extra defences that let them grow big and live long.

sections.key: Long-lived animals inspire ageing research, but there is no proven shortcut to a much longer human life.
sections.b: Long-lived animals are giving researchers real leads, from DNA repair to how cells manage damaged proteins. Bats are another useful example: some small bats live for several decades, far longer than mammals their size usually do. Even a fish from Queensland made the record books. An Australian lungfish nicknamed Granddad lived at an aquarium in Chicago for more than 80 years and was thought to be over 90 when he died. It is important to be realistic, though. These discoveries do not yet translate into treatments that extend human life, and many products marketed as anti-ageing are not backed by good evidence. This is general information, not health advice. For now, the well-tested basics, such as not smoking, staying active, sleeping well and eating well, remain the best supported.

quiz.q: How was the age of Ming the clam worked out?
o: Counting growth rings in its shell
quiz.e: Like tree rings, the growth layers in its shell revealed an age of about 507 years.

quiz.q: According to evolutionary theory, which animals should evolve to age more slowly?
o: Those facing more danger from predators
Those facing less danger from the outside world
quiz.e: When fewer individuals die young, selection favours better long-term maintenance.

quiz.q: How did scientists estimate the age of Greenland sharks?
o: Radiocarbon dating of their eye lenses
quiz.e: Eye lenses form before birth and do not change, so radiocarbon dating them gave age estimates.

quiz.q: What is unusual about the naked mole-rat's risk of dying?
o: It drops sharply after age two
It does not seem to rise as the animal ages
It is higher than any other rodent
quiz.e: A large study found their risk of death did not climb with age, unlike most mammals.

quiz.q: What is Peto's paradox?
o: Large animals do not get more cancer despite having more cells
Small animals live longer than large ones
Jellyfish can reverse their life cycle
quiz.e: Elephants and whales have far more cells than mice but not higher cancer rates.

LESSONS.title: The trolley problem: would you pull the lever?
LESSONS.hook: A runaway tram, five people on the track and one lever in your hand. This simple puzzle has become one of the most argued-about scenarios in moral philosophy, and it now shapes how we think about self-driving cars.

sections.key: The trolley problem asks whether it is right to divert a runaway tram so it kills one person instead of five.
sections.b: Picture yourself beside a railway line. A tram with failed brakes is hurtling towards five workers who cannot get out of the way. You are standing next to a lever. Pull it, and the tram swings onto a side track, where it will kill one worker instead. Do nothing, and five people die. Most people, when asked, say they would pull the lever. Five lives seem to outweigh one. But the puzzle is not really about trams. It is a carefully built thought experiment, a stripped-down scenario that isolates one question so we can look at our moral instincts under a bright light. The question here is whether the numbers are all that matter, or whether how a death comes about matters too.

sections.key: The British philosopher Philippa Foot introduced the scenario in 1967, and Judith Jarvis Thomson named and extended it.
sections.b: The puzzle began in a 1967 paper by the British philosopher Philippa Foot, who was writing about a much older idea called the doctrine of double effect. Her original version involved a driver steering a runaway tram, and she used it alongside other cases to probe the difference between killing someone and letting them die. In the 1970s and 1980s the American philosopher Judith Jarvis Thomson took up the example, gave it the name 'the trolley problem' and invented many of its famous variations. Since then it has escaped the seminar room. It appears in psychology experiments, television comedies, internet memes and engineering ethics courses. Few thought experiments have travelled so far, partly because anyone can grasp it in thirty seconds, yet it remains genuinely hard to answer.

sections.key: When saving five means pushing one person to their death, most people's answer flips.
sections.b: Thomson's most famous variation moves you onto a footbridge above the track. There is no lever this time. The only way to stop the tram is to push a very large stranger off the bridge into its path. His body would halt it, saving the five, but he would die. The arithmetic is identical: one life for five. Yet in surveys, most people who would pull the lever say they would not push the man. Many find the idea of pushing him deeply wrong, even if they struggle to explain why. That gap is what makes the puzzle so productive. If the numbers are the same, something else must be driving our judgement, and philosophers have spent decades trying to work out what it is, and whether it should count.

sections.key: Consequentialists judge actions by their outcomes, so they tend to see saving five as the right choice in both versions.
sections.b: One family of answers comes from consequentialism, the view that the rightness of an action depends on its results. The best known version, utilitarianism, associated with Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill, says we should aim for the greatest overall wellbeing. From this angle, the lever case is straightforward: five deaths are worse than one, so you should pull. A consistent consequentialist may say the same about the footbridge, arguing that our reluctance to push is a gut reaction, not a moral insight. Defenders point out that this approach is impartial and takes every life equally seriously. Critics reply that if outcomes are all that matter, it could justify terrible things, such as harvesting one healthy patient's organs to save five others, which almost everyone rejects.

sections.key: Other thinkers argue some things must not be done to a person, even to produce a better outcome.
sections.b: A rival tradition, often linked to the German philosopher Immanuel Kant, holds that people must never be treated merely as a means to an end. Pushing the man off the bridge uses his body as a tool to stop the tram, which looks like exactly that kind of treatment. Pulling the lever is different: the one worker dies as a side effect of redirecting the threat, not as the means of stopping it. This is the heart of the doctrine of double effect, which traces back to the medieval thinker Thomas Aquinas. It says that causing harm as a foreseen side effect can sometimes be permissible when causing the same harm intentionally would not be. Critics question whether that distinction can really carry so much moral weight.

sections.key: Psychologists have used the trolley problem to study how emotion and reasoning interact in moral choices.
sections.b: Around the start of this century, the psychologist and philosopher Joshua Greene and colleagues began scanning people's brains while they considered trolley dilemmas. Their work suggested that up close, personal harms like pushing someone tend to trigger stronger emotional responses, while impersonal cases like the lever invite more calculating reasoning. Greene proposed a 'dual process' account in which both systems compete. The findings have been debated, and some later studies have questioned how well the original results hold up. Philosophers also argue about what the science shows. Even if our reluctance to push comes from emotion, that does not settle whether the emotion is tracking something real, such as respect for persons, or merely reflecting an evolved discomfort with violence.

sections.key: Self-driving cars have turned an old thought experiment into a practical design question.
sections.b: For decades critics complained that trolley problems were too artificial to matter. Then came autonomous vehicles. If a car's software must choose between swerving into one pedestrian or hitting several, someone has to decide in advance what it should do. A large online project from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, called the Moral Machine, collected millions of responses from people around the world to such scenarios and was published in 2018. It found broad agreement on sparing more lives and sparing humans over animals, but notable differences between regions on other questions. Many engineers stress that real crashes rarely look like neat dilemmas and that avoiding collisions altogether is the real goal. Still, the old puzzle now prompts serious discussion about who should set the rules for machines.

quiz.q: Who first introduced the scenario now known as the trolley problem?
quiz.e: Philippa Foot described it in a 1967 paper, and Judith Jarvis Thomson later named and extended it.

quiz.q: In the footbridge version, how do most people respond compared with the lever version?
o: They are more willing to act
They are less willing to act
quiz.e: Although the numbers are identical, most people who would pull the lever say they would not push the man.

quiz.q: What does a consequentialist mainly use to judge whether an action is right?
quiz.e: Consequentialism judges actions by their results, such as how much overall wellbeing they produce.

quiz.q: What does the doctrine of double effect say?
o: Every action has two equal effects
Harm caused as a foreseen side effect can sometimes be allowed when intended harm would not
Two wrongs can make a right
Only the second effect of an action counts
quiz.e: The doctrine distinguishes harm used as a means from harm that is a side effect of pursuing a good aim.

quiz.q: What was the Moral Machine?
o: An online project collecting people's choices in self-driving car dilemmas
quiz.e: The MIT project gathered millions of responses to car crash scenarios from people around the world.

LESSONS.title: The ship of Theseus: what makes you the same person?
LESSONS.hook: Replace every plank of a ship, one by one, and is it still the same ship? This ancient puzzle leads straight to one of the most personal questions in philosophy: what makes you, you, over a lifetime of change?

sections.key: The ancient puzzle asks whether an object stays the same after all its parts are gradually replaced.
sections.b: The Greek writer Plutarch, around the turn of the second century, told of the ship in which the hero Theseus was said to have sailed home from Crete. The Athenians kept it for generations, he wrote, removing old timbers as they decayed and fitting new ones in their place. Philosophers, Plutarch said, used the ship as an example in arguments about growth: some said it remained the same ship, others that it did not. Imagine the process carried to the end, with not one original plank left. Is it still Theseus's ship? If you say yes, what makes it so? If you say no, at which plank did it stop being the original? Neither answer is as comfortable as it first seems.

sections.key: Thomas Hobbes asked what happens if someone rebuilds the ship from all the discarded planks.
sections.b: In the 1600s the English philosopher Thomas Hobbes added a mischievous complication. Suppose someone collected every old plank as it was removed and later reassembled them, in the same order, into a ship. Now there are two ships. One sits in the harbour, continuously maintained, with no original material. The other is built entirely of the original timbers. Which one is the ship of Theseus? Both have a strong claim. One has continuity of history and use, the other has continuity of material. You might say both, or neither, or that the question has no single right answer. Hobbes's version shows that our everyday idea of 'the same thing' bundles together several different features that usually travel together but can come apart.

sections.key: Your body constantly replaces material, which turns the puzzle into a question about personal identity.
sections.b: The puzzle becomes personal when you notice that you are a bit like that ship. Many of your body's cells are replaced over time, from skin to blood to the lining of your gut, although some, including most neurons in the brain, can last a lifetime. Your beliefs, tastes and memories change even more. The child in your earliest photos shares little with you in material, knowledge or personality. Yet you probably feel certain that child was you. Philosophers call this the problem of personal identity: what makes a person at one time the same person as someone at another time? The answer matters for everyday things, like holding someone responsible for a promise or a crime, and for deeper ones, like what it would mean to survive.

sections.key: John Locke argued that personal identity depends on consciousness and memory, not on the body.
sections.b: The English philosopher John Locke, writing in the late 1600s, offered an influential answer. A person, he suggested, is a thinking being who can consider itself as itself at different times and places. What makes you the same person as someone in the past is that you can remember, from the inside, that person's experiences. Locke illustrated this with a story in which the consciousness of a prince enters the body of a cobbler. The result, he said, would be the prince in a cobbler's body, not the cobbler. Locke's view captures something many people feel: that what matters is the continuing stream of mind, not the particular atoms. It also explains why memory loss can seem so frightening, because it threatens the self.

sections.key: Critics pointed out that memory-based identity leads to contradictions and leaves gaps.
sections.b: Locke's theory met objections. Nearly a century later, the Scottish philosopher Thomas Reid offered a famous one, often called the brave officer. A boy is flogged for stealing; as a young officer he remembers the flogging; as an old general he remembers being the officer but has forgotten the flogging. On Locke's view the general is the officer and the officer is the boy, yet the general is not the boy. That seems to break the basic logic of 'same as'. Others noted that we forget most of our lives, including much of early childhood, yet we do not think we were someone else as babies. Later philosophers repaired the theory by appealing to overlapping chains of memory and psychological connection, rather than direct recall of every moment.

sections.key: Some Buddhist thinkers argued there is no fixed self at all, only a changing collection of parts.
sections.b: Long before Locke, Buddhist thinkers had approached the puzzle from another direction. A well-known text, the Questions of King Milinda, records a dialogue between a Greek-descended king and a monk named Nagasena. Nagasena asks the king whether his chariot is the axle, the wheels, the frame or the reins. None of them alone is the chariot, the king agrees, nor is the chariot something separate from them. 'Chariot' is a convenient name for parts working together. In the same way, Nagasena argues, 'Nagasena' is a name for a changing combination of body, feelings, perceptions and mental activity, with no unchanging core self underneath. This idea, called anatta or non-self, is central to many Buddhist traditions, which see letting go of attachment to a fixed self as a path away from suffering.

sections.key: Derek Parfit used thought experiments about teleportation to argue that identity may matter less than we think.
sections.b: The British philosopher Derek Parfit, in his 1984 book Reasons and Persons, sharpened these puzzles with science fiction. Imagine a teleporter that scans your body, destroys it and builds an exact copy on Mars, with all your memories and character. Is the person on Mars you, or a new person who merely thinks they are you? Now suppose the machine malfunctions and the original is not destroyed. Which one is you? Parfit concluded that there may sometimes be no fact of the matter, and that what really matters is psychological continuity and connection, not identity itself. He found this freeing, saying it made him care less about his own death. Many philosophers disagree with him, and the debate remains open, but his questions are hard to forget.

quiz.q: According to Plutarch, what did the Athenians do with Theseus's ship?
o: Kept it, replacing timbers as they decayed
quiz.e: Plutarch wrote that the ship was preserved by replacing old planks with new ones.

quiz.q: What complication did Thomas Hobbes add to the puzzle?
o: The old planks are reassembled into a second ship
The ship is painted a new colour
quiz.e: Hobbes imagined the discarded planks rebuilt into a ship, leaving two rivals for the title.

quiz.q: What did John Locke think personal identity depends on?
quiz.e: Locke argued that being the same person depends on consciousness, especially memory of past experiences.

quiz.q: What point does Nagasena make with the chariot?
o: The self is located in the heart
There is no fixed self, only a changing combination of parts
quiz.e: Like 'chariot', the self is a label for working parts, not an unchanging core.

quiz.q: What did Derek Parfit conclude from teleporter thought experiments?
o: The soul always stays with the original body
Psychological continuity may matter more than identity itself
Memory has nothing to do with the self
quiz.e: Parfit argued that what matters is psychological continuity and connection, not identity as such.

LESSONS.title: Descartes: I think, therefore I am
LESSONS.hook: What if everything you believe is a dream, or a trick? René Descartes set out to doubt everything he possibly could, and what was left became one of the most famous sentences ever written.

sections.h: A man in a warm room
sections.key: René Descartes decided to tear down his beliefs and rebuild knowledge on a foundation that could not be doubted.
sections.b: In the winter of 1619, a young Frenchman named René Descartes was stuck in Germany, serving with an army. By his own account, he spent a day alone in a room heated by a stove, thinking. He had been educated at one of the best schools in Europe, yet he felt that much of what he had learned was uncertain. Scholars disagreed about nearly everything. Descartes, who was also a brilliant mathematician, admired the certainty of geometry, where proofs build step by step from secure starting points. He resolved to do something similar with all knowledge: to clear away every belief that could be doubted and see whether anything solid remained to build on. Years later he set out this project in his most famous works.

sections.key: Descartes began by noting that the senses sometimes deceive us, so they cannot be the foundation of certain knowledge.
sections.b: In his Meditations on First Philosophy, published in 1641, Descartes started with the senses. We trust them constantly, yet they sometimes mislead us. A tower looks round from far away and square up close. A straight stick looks bent in water. If a source of information has fooled you even once, he reasoned, it is not wise to trust it completely. This was not a claim that we should stop using our senses in daily life. Descartes was clear that his doubt was a tool for a special purpose, to be used once in a lifetime in a quiet hour of reflection. The aim was not to live as a sceptic but to find out what, if anything, could survive the strongest possible doubt.

sections.key: Descartes asked how we could know we are not dreaming, or being fooled by a powerful deceiver.
sections.b: Descartes then raised a stronger worry. He had often dreamed he was sitting by the fire in his dressing gown when he was actually asleep in bed. Is there any sure sign that tells waking life from a vivid dream? If not, even the scene in front of him might be unreal. Finally, he imagined the most extreme possibility: an evil demon, supremely powerful and cunning, devoting all its energy to deceiving him about everything, perhaps even about simple sums. Modern philosophers have updated the demon into a brain in a vat, kept alive and fed false experiences by scientists, an idea that inspired films such as The Matrix. The question is the same: can you prove this is not happening to you right now?

sections.key: Descartes concluded that even if he is deceived about everything else, he must exist in order to be deceived.
sections.b: Here Descartes found his foothold. Suppose the demon is deceiving him about everything. Still, to be deceived, he must exist. To doubt, he must be thinking. However far the doubt is pushed, it cannot reach the fact that there is a doubter. In the Meditations he put it as 'I am, I exist', which must be true whenever he thinks it. In his earlier Discourse on the Method of 1637, written in French, he expressed it in the form that became famous, usually rendered in Latin as cogito, ergo sum: I think, therefore I am. Interestingly, the early Christian thinker Augustine had made a similar point more than a thousand years earlier, arguing that if he was mistaken, he must exist to be mistaken.

sections.key: From the cogito, Descartes tried to prove God's existence and then restore trust in clear reasoning and the outside world.
sections.b: Knowing only that you exist is a lonely position. Descartes tried to climb out of it. He argued that he had an idea of a perfect being, and that such an idea could only have come from a being that really was perfect, namely God. A perfect God would not be a deceiver, he reasoned, so the things he perceived very clearly and distinctly could be trusted, and the physical world was real after all. Many readers have found this the weakest part of his project. Critics in his own time pointed to the so-called Cartesian circle: he seems to rely on clear and distinct ideas to prove God exists, then rely on God to guarantee clear and distinct ideas. Defenders have offered various replies, and scholars still debate them.

sections.key: Descartes argued that mind and body are two different kinds of thing, which raised the question of how they interact.
sections.b: Descartes's method led him to a view called dualism. He could doubt that he had a body, he reasoned, but not that he was thinking, so the mind must be a different kind of thing from the body: a thinking substance rather than an extended, physical one. This raised an obvious problem, which was put to him sharply by Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia in letters beginning in 1643. If the mind is not physical, how can it move the arm, or feel the burn of a flame? Descartes suggested the two met in the pineal gland in the brain, an answer few found satisfying. Most philosophers and scientists today reject his form of dualism, though questions about how mind relates to brain remain lively.

sections.key: Descartes is often called the father of modern philosophy because he made the question of how we know things central.
sections.b: Descartes died in Stockholm in 1650, not long after moving there at the invitation of Queen Christina of Sweden. His influence was enormous. By starting from the individual mind and asking what it can know for certain, he pushed questions about knowledge, called epistemology, to the centre of philosophy for centuries. Later thinkers such as John Locke and David Hume answered him by stressing experience rather than pure reason. He also helped shape modern science and gave us coordinate geometry, the familiar x and y axes, which is why they are called Cartesian coordinates. Even people who reject his conclusions still use his method: when in doubt, slow down, question your assumptions and ask what you really have good reason to believe.

quiz.q: Why did Descartes think the senses could not be the foundation of certain knowledge?
quiz.e: Since the senses have misled us before, Descartes reasoned they cannot be trusted completely.

quiz.q: What is the modern update of Descartes's evil demon?
quiz.e: The brain in a vat imagines scientists feeding a brain false experiences, much like the demon.

quiz.q: What can Descartes be certain of, even if a demon deceives him?
o: That he exists, because he is thinking
quiz.e: To be deceived or to doubt, he must exist and be thinking.

quiz.q: What is the 'Cartesian circle' criticism?
o: Descartes drew circles to prove theorems
He used God to guarantee clear ideas and clear ideas to prove God
He argued in circles about geometry
He travelled in a circle around Europe
quiz.e: Critics argued his reasoning was circular, relying on what it was meant to prove.

quiz.q: Who challenged Descartes on how an immaterial mind could move the body?
quiz.e: Elisabeth pressed Descartes on this question in letters beginning in 1643.

LESSONS.title: Epicurus: the surprising philosophy of pleasure
LESSONS.hook: Today 'epicurean' suggests fine wine and rich food. But Epicurus, the philosopher behind the word, lived simply in a garden, ate bread and water, and taught that the secret of happiness was needing less.

sections.key: Around 306 BC Epicurus founded a school in a garden outside Athens, open to women and enslaved people as well as citizens.
sections.b: Epicurus was born on the Greek island of Samos in 341 BC. After years of study and teaching elsewhere, he bought a house with a garden near Athens, and his followers became known as the Garden. It was an unusual community for its time. Ancient sources say it welcomed women and enslaved people, who were usually excluded from philosophical schools. Members lived simply and placed great value on friendship. The ancient biographer Diogenes Laertius reports that Epicurus lived mainly on bread and water, and once asked a friend to send a little pot of cheese so that he could have a feast whenever he liked. The man whose name now suggests luxury apparently thought a piece of cheese was a treat.

sections.key: Epicurus taught that pleasure is the goal of life, but he meant mainly the absence of pain and worry.
sections.b: Epicurus held that pleasure is the beginning and end of a happy life. That sounds like an invitation to indulge, and his enemies, ancient and modern, often presented it that way. But Epicurus defined pleasure in a particular way. The highest pleasure, for him, was a calm state of body and mind: freedom from physical pain, which he called aponia, and freedom from mental disturbance, called ataraxia. A banquet might bring a burst of enjoyment, followed by a hangover, debt or jealousy. A simple meal with friends, eaten without anxiety, could bring deeper and more lasting contentment. In his surviving Letter to Menoeceus, he explicitly says that by pleasure he does not mean the pleasures of the profligate.

sections.key: Epicurus divided desires into natural and necessary, natural but unnecessary, and empty ones that can never be satisfied.
sections.b: A practical tool at the heart of Epicureanism is a way of sorting desires. Some are natural and necessary, like the need for food, shelter and friendship. These are easy to satisfy and bring real peace. Some are natural but not necessary, like the desire for fancy food: fine to enjoy when they come along, but not worth chasing. A third kind he regarded as empty or vain, like the desire for fame, power or limitless wealth. These are dangerous because they have no natural limit. However much you get, there is always more to want, so they generate endless anxiety. The lesson sounds strikingly modern. Advertising and social media often work by turning unnecessary desires into what feel like needs.

sections.key: Epicurus believed everything is made of atoms moving in empty space, and that the gods do not interfere in human life.
sections.b: Epicurus built his ethics on a view of nature borrowed and adapted from the earlier philosopher Democritus. Everything, he taught, is made of tiny indivisible particles called atoms moving through empty space. The universe was not designed and is not steered by divine purpose. He did not deny that gods existed, but he argued that perfectly happy beings would have no interest in punishing or rewarding humans. Thunderstorms, earthquakes and disease have natural causes. This mattered for happiness, because he believed fear of angry gods was a major source of misery. Later writers, such as the Roman poet Lucretius in his long poem On the Nature of Things, carried these ideas forward, and the poem's rediscovery in 1417 influenced Renaissance and early scientific thinking.

sections.key: Epicurus argued that death is nothing to us, because when death is present we no longer exist to experience it.
sections.b: Epicurus's most famous argument is about death. In the Letter to Menoeceus he says that death is nothing to us, since all good and bad lie in sensation, and death is the end of sensation. When we exist, death is not present; when death is present, we do not exist. So there is no moment at which death can harm the one who has died. The Roman Lucretius added the symmetry argument: we do not feel distress about the endless time before we were born, so why fear the endless time after? Many people find these arguments comforting; others say they miss the point, because what we dread is losing the good things life would have held. Philosophers still debate whether death can harm the one who dies.

sections.key: Later Epicureans summed up the teaching in a 'fourfold remedy' for anxiety.
sections.b: Later followers condensed Epicurus's teaching into a short formula, known as the tetrapharmakos or fourfold remedy, found in the writings of the Epicurean philosopher Philodemus. In a common translation it runs: don't fear god, don't worry about death, what is good is easy to get, and what is terrible is easy to endure. The last line reflects Epicurus's view that intense pain tends to be brief, while long-lasting pain is usually bearable. Modern readers may find that too optimistic, especially about chronic illness. But the overall approach, treating philosophy as medicine for the mind, has parallels in modern therapy, which also encourages people to question the beliefs that feed their worries. A gravestone formula popular in the Roman world captured the mood: I was not, I was, I am not, I do not care.

sections.key: Epicurus prized friendship and advised withdrawing from politics, a view that drew both admiration and criticism.
sections.b: Of all the things wisdom provides for a happy life, Epicurus is reported to have said, the greatest is friendship. The Garden was built around shared meals and conversation. He also recommended 'living unnoticed', keeping away from politics and public competition, which he saw as breeding fear and rivalry. Critics, including the Stoics and later the Roman statesman Cicero, accused the Epicureans of selfishness and of neglecting civic duty. Christian writers often attacked their denial of an afterlife. Yet the philosophy never quite disappeared. The American founder Thomas Jefferson called himself an Epicurean in a letter late in life. Today, in an age of burnout and endless wanting, its central question feels fresh: what do you actually need to be content?

quiz.q: What was unusual about Epicurus's Garden for its time?
o: It welcomed women and enslaved people
quiz.e: Ancient sources say the Garden admitted women and enslaved people, who were usually excluded.

quiz.q: What did Epicurus mean by the highest pleasure?
o: Freedom from pain and mental disturbance
quiz.e: He valued aponia and ataraxia: freedom from bodily pain and mental disturbance.

quiz.q: Which desire would Epicurus class as empty or vain?
quiz.e: Desires like fame and limitless wealth have no natural limit, so they breed anxiety.

quiz.q: What is Epicurus's argument about death?
o: Death leads to reward or punishment
Death should be feared above all
Death is only for the unwise
When death is present we no longer exist to experience it
quiz.e: Since death is the end of sensation, it cannot harm the one who has died.

quiz.q: What was the tetrapharmakos?
o: A Greek medicine made from herbs
A fourfold remedy summarising Epicurean teaching
quiz.e: It condensed the teaching into four lines about gods, death, good and suffering.

LESSONS.title: Ubuntu: I am because we are
LESSONS.hook: A person is a person through other people. This idea from southern Africa helped guide a nation through its transition from apartheid, and it offers a challenge to the way many Western philosophies picture the self.

sections.h: A greeting that says a lot
sections.key: Ubuntu is an idea from southern Africa holding that we become fully human through our relationships with others.
sections.b: In many parts of southern Africa, a common way of greeting someone translates roughly as 'I see you', and the reply as 'I am here'. The exchange hints at a philosophy in which existence is affirmed through recognition by others. That philosophy is often summed up in the word ubuntu, found in Nguni languages such as isiZulu and isiXhosa, with related words across many Bantu languages. Ubuntu is usually translated as 'humanness' or 'humanity towards others'. It is captured in the isiZulu saying umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu, commonly translated as 'a person is a person through other persons'. Ubuntu is not one written theory by one founding philosopher. It is a living ethical outlook, carried in proverbs, customs and everyday expectations, that thinkers have more recently set out in systematic form.

sections.key: Ubuntu sees personhood as something achieved through relationships, not simply possessed by an isolated individual.
sections.b: Many influential Western philosophies start with the individual. Descartes began with a single mind doubting everything; social contract theorists imagined separate individuals agreeing to form a society. Ubuntu starts somewhere else. It treats people as fundamentally bound up with one another. On many accounts, personhood is not just a biological fact but something you grow into by how you treat others. In everyday speech in some communities, a person who behaves cruelly or selfishly may be said to lack ubuntu, or even to be 'not a person', meaning not living up to what a human being should be. The Kenyan-born philosopher John Mbiti, writing in 1969, put a related African communal outlook memorably: 'I am, because we are; and since we are, therefore I am.'

sections.key: Ubuntu emphasises values such as generosity, hospitality, compassion, respect and the pursuit of harmony.
sections.b: In practice, ubuntu is associated with a cluster of values: sharing with those in need, welcoming strangers, showing respect to elders, and repairing damaged relationships rather than simply punishing. A frequently told illustration is of a traveller passing through a village, who would expect to be offered food and water without having to ask. The American-born philosopher Thaddeus Metz, who works in South Africa, has tried to state the core of ubuntu precisely. He suggests that, on an ubuntu view, right actions are those that respect and promote harmonious relationships, where people identify with one another and act for each other's good. Wrong actions are those that are unfriendly or divisive. That makes ubuntu different from both rule-based and outcome-based ethics: the focus is on the quality of relationships.

sections.key: Ubuntu played a prominent role in South Africa's transition from apartheid, especially through the Truth and Reconciliation Commission.
sections.b: Ubuntu became internationally known during South Africa's transition to democracy in the 1990s. The country's interim Constitution of 1993 ended with a passage saying there was 'a need for ubuntu but not for victimisation'. Archbishop Desmond Tutu, who chaired the Truth and Reconciliation Commission set up after apartheid, often explained his approach in terms of ubuntu. Rather than relying only on trials and punishment, the commission offered amnesty to some perpetrators who fully disclosed politically motivated crimes, and gave victims a public platform to tell their stories. Tutu argued that because humanity is shared, the dehumanising of others also diminishes the oppressor, and healing requires restoring relationships. The commission remains controversial: some victims felt justice was sacrificed, while others saw it as a remarkable alternative to cycles of revenge.

sections.key: South African courts have drawn on ubuntu in landmark rulings, including the 1995 decision to abolish the death penalty.
sections.b: Ubuntu has also shaped South African law. In 1995, in the case known as S v Makwanyane, the new Constitutional Court ruled the death penalty unconstitutional. Several judges referred to ubuntu, arguing that it values life and human dignity and favours rehabilitation and reconciliation over retribution. Courts have since invoked ubuntu in other areas, from evictions to defamation, often to encourage dialogue and apology rather than purely financial penalties. Legal scholars debate how useful this is. Supporters say ubuntu grounds the constitution in local values rather than borrowed ones. Critics worry that the concept is too broad to give judges clear guidance and that it can be used to justify almost any conclusion. Both sides agree it has given the idea new public weight.

sections.key: Critics argue ubuntu can be vague, romanticised or used to pressure people into conformity.
sections.b: Like any philosophy, ubuntu has thoughtful critics, including African philosophers. Some argue the term has become a slogan, used in corporate training and marketing until it means little more than 'teamwork'. Others warn against romanticising a single 'African' worldview across a vast continent with hundreds of cultures and long traditions of debate. A deeper philosophical worry concerns individual rights. If personhood depends on community, what protects people who dissent, or who are marginalised by their own communities, such as women in some traditional settings?
