Defenders reply that ubuntu, properly understood, condemns treating anyone as less than human, and that respecting individuals is part of maintaining genuine harmony. The Ghanaian philosopher Kwame Gyekye proposed a 'moderate communitarianism' that tries to give both community and individual rights their due.

sections.key: Ubuntu is part of a rich tradition of African philosophy that is increasingly studied around the world.
sections.b: Ubuntu is one strand in a broad field of African philosophy. The Ghanaian philosopher Kwasi Wiredu urged what he called conceptual decolonisation: examining ideas inherited from colonial languages and asking whether African languages carve up concepts like truth or mind differently. The Kenyan philosopher Henry Odera Oruka recorded the reasoning of respected local sages, arguing that critical philosophy existed in oral cultures, not only in written ones. These thinkers challenge the old assumption that philosophy is a mainly European story. Ubuntu also invites comparison with other relational outlooks, such as the Confucian idea that we are defined by our roles and relationships. Whatever you conclude, it poses a question worth asking: how much of who you are was made by other people?

quiz.q: What does the saying umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu commonly mean?
o: A person is a person through other persons
quiz.e: This isiZulu saying is the classic summary of ubuntu.

quiz.q: Who wrote 'I am, because we are; and since we are, therefore I am'?
quiz.e: John Mbiti expressed this communal outlook in a 1969 book.

quiz.q: According to Thaddeus Metz's interpretation, what makes an action right on an ubuntu view?
o: It respects and promotes harmonious relationships
quiz.e: Metz suggests ubuntu judges actions by whether they promote harmonious relationships.

quiz.q: In S v Makwanyane in 1995, what did South Africa's Constitutional Court decide?
o: To adopt ubuntu as the national motto
quiz.e: Several judges cited ubuntu when ruling the death penalty unconstitutional.

quiz.q: What concern do some critics raise about ubuntu?
o: It is too focused on individual rights
It has no connection to Africa
It can be vague or pressure people into conformity
quiz.e: Critics worry it can become a slogan or be used to override dissenting individuals.

LESSONS.title: Philosophy's golden age in the Islamic world
LESSONS.hook: Between Ancient Greece and the European Renaissance, some of the boldest philosophy on Earth was written in Arabic. Meet the thinkers who preserved Aristotle, argued about cause and effect, and imagined a man floating in the air.

sections.key: From the 8th century, scholars in the Abbasid world translated huge amounts of Greek philosophy and science into Arabic.
sections.b: In the late 700s and 800s, under the Abbasid caliphs based in Baghdad, a remarkable translation movement got under way. Scholars, many of them Christians fluent in Greek and Syriac, translated the works of Aristotle, Plato's ideas as passed down by later writers, and Greek medicine, astronomy and mathematics into Arabic. Wealthy patrons paid well for this work. Baghdad's House of Wisdom is often associated with the movement, although historians debate how far it was a formal academy rather than a palace library. The result was that a great deal of Greek learning, much of it scarcely read in Western Europe at the time, became part of a lively intellectual culture stretching from Central Asia to Spain. Thinkers did not just preserve these texts; they argued with them.

sections.key: Al-Kindi and al-Farabi set out to show how Greek philosophy related to Islamic belief and to politics.
sections.b: Al-Kindi, who worked in Baghdad in the 800s, is often called 'the philosopher of the Arabs'. He argued that truth should be welcomed whatever its source, even if it came from foreign peoples, and tried to show that philosophy and revelation pointed in the same direction. A generation or two later, al-Farabi, who probably came from Central Asia, became so respected as an interpreter of Aristotle that he was known as 'the Second Teacher', Aristotle being the first. Al-Farabi wrote on logic, music and especially politics. Inspired partly by Plato's Republic, he described a 'virtuous city' led by a wise ruler who would guide citizens towards true happiness. His work shaped how later thinkers connected philosophy, religion and the good society.

sections.key: Ibn Sina, known in Europe as Avicenna, was one of history's most influential philosophers and physicians.
sections.b: Ibn Sina was born around 980 near Bukhara, in what is now Uzbekistan. He was famously precocious: in his autobiography he says he had mastered most of the sciences by eighteen, and that he read Aristotle's Metaphysics many times without understanding it until a commentary by al-Farabi made it click. His Canon of Medicine was used as a medical textbook in Europe for centuries. In philosophy he built a vast system of his own. One influential idea was a distinction between what a thing is, its essence, and the fact that it exists. You can understand what a unicorn is without knowing whether any exist. From this he argued for a necessary being, whose essence includes existence, which he identified with God.

sections.key: Avicenna imagined a person created in mid-air with no sensations, to argue that we know our own existence directly.
sections.b: Avicenna's most famous thought experiment asks you to imagine a person created suddenly and fully formed, but suspended in the air, blindfolded, with limbs spread so that they do not touch each other, and with no sensations of any kind. Would this person know that they exist? Avicenna argued yes. Even with no awareness of a body or the outside world, they would be aware of their own self. He took this to show that the self is something distinct from the body. Readers often notice the similarity to Descartes's argument six centuries later. Whether Descartes knew of it is debated. Critics of both arguments question whether being able to imagine yourself without a body really shows that you could exist without one.

sections.key: Al-Ghazali argued that the philosophers had gone too far, and questioned whether we ever see true cause and effect.
sections.b: Not everyone welcomed the philosophers' confidence. Abu Hamid al-Ghazali, a celebrated scholar of the late 1000s, wrote The Incoherence of the Philosophers, attacking Avicenna and others on several points, including their claim that the world had always existed. His most striking argument concerned causation. When cotton touches fire, it burns. But what do we actually observe? Only that burning follows contact. We never see a necessary connection forcing it. Al-Ghazali concluded that God directly creates each event, usually in regular patterns, so that miracles are possible. Centuries later the Scottish philosopher David Hume made a similar observation about cause and effect, though for very different reasons. Al-Ghazali also wrote movingly about a personal crisis of doubt that led him to leave a prestigious teaching post and seek certainty through mysticism.

sections.key: Ibn Rushd, known as Averroes, defended philosophy and wrote commentaries on Aristotle that shaped medieval Europe.
sections.b: In Córdoba, in Muslim Spain, the judge and physician Ibn Rushd, known in Latin as Averroes, answered al-Ghazali in the 1100s with a book whose title is usually translated The Incoherence of the Incoherence. He argued that al-Ghazali had misrepresented the philosophers, and that religious law itself encouraged people capable of it to study nature through reason. If scripture seemed to conflict with sound demonstration, he said, it should be read allegorically. His greatest legacy was his detailed commentaries on Aristotle. Translated into Latin, they became so influential in European universities that Thomas Aquinas referred to him simply as 'the Commentator'. Some of his ideas, as interpreted by European followers, caused fierce controversy in Paris in the 1200s. Dante placed him among the great thinkers of the past in the Divine Comedy.

sections.key: The Arabic philosophical tradition linked Greek, Jewish, Christian and Muslim thinkers and continued long after the 12th century.
sections.b: This was not only a Muslim story. The Jewish philosopher Moses Maimonides, born in Córdoba and later working in Egypt, wrote his Guide for the Perplexed in Arabic, engaging closely with Aristotle and Islamic philosophy. Christian scholars in Spain translated Arabic works into Latin, feeding the rise of medieval European universities. Ibn Tufayl wrote a philosophical novel about a boy raised alone on an island who reasons his way to deep truths; it is often thought to have been known in Europe by the time of Robinson Crusoe. It is also a myth that Islamic philosophy ended in the 1100s. It continued to flourish, especially in Persia, with thinkers such as Mulla Sadra in the 1600s. These debates on reason, faith and the self belong to everyone's intellectual history.

quiz.q: In which city were the Abbasid caliphs based during the great translation movement?
quiz.e: The Abbasid caliphs ruled from Baghdad, where much translation from Greek into Arabic took place.

quiz.q: Why was al-Farabi called 'the Second Teacher'?
o: He was a highly respected interpreter of Aristotle, the first teacher
He taught for only two years
quiz.e: Aristotle was regarded as the First Teacher, and al-Farabi as his great successor.

quiz.q: What did Avicenna's floating man thought experiment aim to show?
o: That the senses are perfectly reliable
That we know our own existence without bodily sensation
That God created the world in time
quiz.e: Avicenna argued the floating person would still be aware of their own self.

quiz.q: What example did al-Ghazali use when discussing cause and effect?
quiz.e: He argued we only see burning follow contact, not a necessary connection between them.

quiz.q: What did Thomas Aquinas call Averroes?
quiz.e: His commentaries on Aristotle were so influential that Aquinas called him simply 'the Commentator'.

LESSONS.title: Hume's problem: why trust that the sun will rise?
LESSONS.hook: You are sure the sun will rise tomorrow. But can you prove it? David Hume's simple question about learning from experience has troubled philosophers and scientists for nearly three centuries, and a black swan from Western Australia became its mascot.

sections.key: David Hume asked what justifies our expectation that the future will resemble the past.
sections.b: In 1739 a young Scottish philosopher named David Hume published A Treatise of Human Nature, which he later said 'fell dead-born from the press'. In it, and in a shorter book in 1748, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, he raised a question that seems almost silly at first. Why do we believe the sun will rise tomorrow? Because it always has, you might say. But that is exactly the problem. We have only observed the past. Our confidence about tomorrow rests on an assumption that nature will continue to behave as it has. Hume asked what justifies that assumption. His answer, that reason alone cannot, is now known as the problem of induction, and it remains one of philosophy's most famous unsolved puzzles.

sections.key: Deduction guarantees its conclusions, while induction moves from observed cases to general claims that could turn out false.
sections.b: To see the puzzle, it helps to separate two kinds of reasoning. In deduction, if the premises are true, the conclusion must be true. All humans are mortal; Socrates is human; so Socrates is mortal. There is no way around it. Induction is different. It moves from observed cases to general rules or predictions: every piece of copper I have heated has expanded, so copper expands when heated. However many cases you observe, the conclusion could still be false. Science, medicine, cooking and crossing the road all depend on induction. We could not survive without it. Hume did not suggest we stop using it. He asked a narrower question: can we give a good argument that inductive reasoning is reliable, one that does not simply assume what it is trying to prove?

sections.key: Any argument that induction works seems to rely on induction itself, which is circular.
sections.b: Hume's argument runs roughly like this. Any justification for induction must be either a deductive proof or an argument from experience. It cannot be deductive, because there is no contradiction in imagining the future being different: you can coherently picture the sun failing to rise, or bread suddenly ceasing to nourish. So it must come from experience. But an argument from experience would go: induction has worked well in the past, so it will work in the future. That is itself an inductive argument, so it assumes the very thing in question. Hume concluded that our expectations come not from reason but from custom or habit. After seeing one event follow another many times, the mind simply comes to expect it. This, he thought, is how human nature works.

sections.key: Bertrand Russell's chicken and the discovery of black swans in Australia show how expectations built on past experience can fail.
sections.b: The British philosopher Bertrand Russell gave a grim illustration in 1912. A chicken is fed every day by the farmer, and comes to expect food whenever he appears. One day, the farmer wrings its neck instead. Its past experience was real, but it misled the chicken completely. A more cheerful example comes from Australia. For centuries Europeans used 'black swan' as a phrase for something impossible, because every swan they had seen was white. In 1697 the Dutch explorer Willem de Vlamingh's expedition recorded black swans on a river in Western Australia, which they named the Swan River. A rule supported by countless observations was overturned by one. The black swan is now a common emblem of the limits of induction.

sections.key: Karl Popper argued that science does not rely on induction, but advances by trying to falsify bold theories.
sections.b: The Austrian-born philosopher Karl Popper, in work first published in 1934, offered a radical response. He agreed with Hume that induction cannot be justified. But science, he argued, does not actually need it. Scientists do not prove theories by piling up confirming cases. They propose bold conjectures and then try hard to refute them. A single genuine black swan can falsify 'all swans are white', and that falsification is a matter of deduction. Theories that survive tough tests are not proven true; they are simply the best we have so far. Popper also used falsifiability to separate science from what he called pseudo-science. Critics reply that in practice we still rely on theories that have survived testing to predict the future, which seems to bring induction back in.

sections.key: Nelson Goodman showed that even deciding which patterns to project into the future is a deep puzzle.
sections.b: In 1955 the American philosopher Nelson Goodman deepened the problem. Define a made-up word, 'grue', to mean green if first observed before some future date, and blue otherwise. Every emerald ever observed has been green. But every emerald ever observed has also been grue, since all were observed before that date. So the same evidence seems to support 'emeralds are green' and 'emeralds are grue', which make opposite predictions about emeralds first seen after the date. Obviously we should project green, not grue. But why? Saying grue is an artificial word does not settle it, because from a different starting vocabulary green could look artificial too. Goodman's new riddle shows that the hard part is not only trusting patterns but knowing which patterns count.

sections.key: Philosophers still debate responses, from probability theory to pragmatism, but Hume's lesson about humility endures.
sections.b: Many responses to Hume have been attempted. Some philosophers argue that induction can be justified in terms of probability, using tools such as Bayesian reasoning to show how evidence should raise or lower our confidence, though critics say these methods still need assumptions about the world. Others take a pragmatic line: if any method can predict the future, induction will, so it is our best bet. Some argue that the demand for a non-circular justification is unreasonable, since the most basic forms of reasoning cannot all be proved without using themselves. Immanuel Kant said that reading Hume woke him from his 'dogmatic slumber'. Whatever view you take, Hume's lesson is practical: hold general beliefs with confidence proportional to the evidence, and stay open to the black swan.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between deduction and induction?
o: Deduction is used only in maths
True premises guarantee a deductive conclusion, but not an inductive one
quiz.e: Deduction guarantees its conclusion; induction moves to conclusions that could still be false.

quiz.q: According to Hume, where do our expectations about the future really come from?
quiz.e: Hume argued that repeated experience creates a habit of expectation, not a rational proof.

quiz.q: Where did a Dutch expedition record black swans in 1697?
quiz.e: Willem de Vlamingh's expedition recorded black swans on what became the Swan River.

quiz.q: How did Karl Popper respond to the problem of induction?
o: He argued science advances by trying to falsify bold theories
He said habit is a form of proof
quiz.e: Popper held that science works by conjecture and attempted refutation, not by proving theories inductively.

quiz.q: What does Goodman's word 'grue' show?
o: Choosing which patterns to project is itself a puzzle
quiz.e: The same evidence supports 'green' and 'grue', so we need a reason to project one pattern over another.

LESSONS.title: The veil of ignorance: designing a fair society
LESSONS.hook: Imagine designing the rules of society without knowing whether you would be born rich or poor, healthy or sick. John Rawls's thought experiment reshaped debates about justice, and drew powerful critics who saw things very differently.

sections.key: John Rawls asked what rules people would choose for society if they did not know their own place in it.
sections.b: Imagine you are about to be born into a society, but you do not yet know who you will be. You might be born into wealth or poverty, with great talents or a serious disability, into a majority group or a minority. Before you find out, you get to help choose the basic rules of that society: how wealth is shared, which freedoms are protected, how opportunities are distributed. What rules would you pick? This is the heart of the most famous thought experiment in modern political philosophy, set out by the American philosopher John Rawls in his 1971 book A Theory of Justice. Rawls argued that the rules people would agree to in that situation of uncertainty are the rules of a just society.

sections.key: Rawls called this imagined situation the original position, where a veil of ignorance hides each person's particular circumstances.
sections.b: Rawls drew on a long tradition of social contract thinking. Earlier philosophers such as Thomas Hobbes, John Locke and Jean-Jacques Rousseau imagined people agreeing to form a society. Hobbes famously described life without government as 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short'. Rawls's twist was to make the agreement fair by design. In what he called the original position, people choose principles from behind a 'veil of ignorance'. They know general facts about economics and human psychology, but not their own sex, class, abilities, religion or idea of a good life. The point is to strip away bias. If you do not know whether you will be rich, you cannot rig the rules to favour the rich. Whatever principles emerge should then be acceptable from every position.

sections.key: Rawls argued people would choose equal basic liberties for all, and allow inequalities only under strict conditions.
sections.b: Rawls argued that people behind the veil would choose two principles. First, everyone should have an equal right to the most extensive basic liberties compatible with the same liberties for others, such as freedom of speech, conscience and political participation. Second, social and economic inequalities are acceptable only if two conditions are met. Positions must be open to all under fair equality of opportunity, meaning people with similar talent and effort should have similar chances regardless of the family they are born into. And inequalities must work to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged members of society. This last condition is the famous difference principle. Rawls ranked the first principle above the second, so that basic liberties could not be traded away for economic gain.

sections.key: The difference principle permits inequality only when it makes the worst-off better off than they would otherwise be.
sections.b: The difference principle is often misunderstood as demanding equal incomes. It does not. Rawls accepted that paying some people more, for example to encourage training or hard work, could make the whole economy more productive. If those gains lift up the worst-off, the inequality is justified. What it rules out is inequality that benefits those at the top without benefiting those at the bottom. Rawls thought people behind the veil would reason cautiously, focusing on how bad the worst outcome could be, because the stakes are a whole life and they have no basis for estimating the odds. Economists call this a 'maximin' strategy: maximise the minimum. Critics, such as the economist John Harsanyi, argued that rational people would instead choose to maximise average wellbeing.

sections.key: Robert Nozick argued that justice depends on how holdings came about, not on matching a pattern of distribution.
sections.b: Rawls's most famous critic was his Harvard colleague Robert Nozick, whose 1974 book Anarchy, State, and Utopia defended a libertarian view. Nozick argued that a distribution of wealth is just if people acquired their holdings fairly and transferred them voluntarily, whatever pattern results. He illustrated this with a basketball star of the day, Wilt Chamberlain. Suppose society begins with a distribution you consider perfectly fair, and then a million fans each happily pay a small sum to watch Chamberlain play. He becomes rich, and the pattern is upset. Yet every step was voluntary. Nozick asked how the result could be unjust. He concluded that maintaining any fixed pattern would require continual interference in people's free choices, and that redistributive taxation risks treating people's labour as a resource others may claim.

sections.key: Communitarians, feminists and capability theorists challenged Rawls from different directions.
sections.b: Criticism also came from other angles. Communitarian philosophers, such as Michael Sandel in a 1982 book, argued that the people behind the veil are 'unencumbered selves', stripped of the loyalties, traditions and communities that actually make us who we are, and that a theory built on them misunderstands human life. The feminist philosopher Susan Moller Okin argued that Rawls had not taken justice within the family seriously enough, even though families shape children's opportunities so profoundly. The economist and philosopher Amartya Sen, with the philosopher Martha Nussbaum, developed the capabilities approach, arguing that justice should focus less on resources and more on what people are actually able to do and be, since people with different needs convert the same income into very different lives.

sections.key: Whatever its flaws, the veil of ignorance remains a practical tool for testing whether rules are fair.
sections.b: Rawls refined his views over the following decades, notably in Political Liberalism in 1993, where he asked how people with deeply different religious and moral beliefs can share a stable, fair society. His work and the responses to it frame much of today's argument about tax, welfare, health care and opportunity, across the political spectrum. Even people who reject his conclusions often find the veil of ignorance a useful thinking tool. When debating a policy, from school funding to disability support, you can ask: would I accept this rule if I did not know which side of it I would end up on? That question does not settle every disagreement, and reasonable people still reach different answers. But it pushes us to see a society from more than our own seat.

quiz.q: In which book did John Rawls set out the veil of ignorance?
quiz.e: Rawls presented the original position and veil of ignorance in A Theory of Justice in 1971.

quiz.q: What does the veil of ignorance hide from people choosing principles?
o: Their own particular circumstances, such as class and abilities
quiz.e: People know general facts but not their own place in society, which removes bias.

quiz.q: What does the difference principle allow?
o: Inequalities that benefit the least advantaged
Inequalities that benefit the most talented only
quiz.e: Inequality is acceptable only if it works to the greatest benefit of the worst-off.

quiz.q: What point did Robert Nozick make with the Wilt Chamberlain example?
o: Voluntary transfers can upset any pattern without seeming unjust
quiz.e: Nozick argued that free exchanges from a fair start produce a just result, whatever the pattern.

quiz.q: What does the capabilities approach of Sen and Nussbaum focus on?
o: What people are actually able to do and be
quiz.e: It shifts attention from resources to people's real capabilities to live lives they value.

LESSONS.title: The invisible gorilla: why we miss what's in front of us
LESSONS.hook: Half the people in a famous experiment failed to notice a gorilla walking through a basketball game. They weren't careless. They were human, and so are you.

sections.key: When we focus hard on one thing, we can miss something huge and obvious.
sections.b: In 1999, psychologists Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris made a short video of students passing basketballs. Viewers were asked to count the passes made by the team in white shirts. Partway through, a person in a full gorilla suit strolls into the middle of the game, faces the camera, thumps their chest and walks off. It is on screen for several seconds. Roughly half the viewers never saw it. When told afterwards, many refused to believe it until they watched the video again, and some accused the researchers of swapping the tape. The study became one of the best known in psychology, and it has been repeated many times with similar results. The lesson is unsettling: we do not see everything our eyes are pointed at.

sections.h: Attention is a spotlight, not a floodlight
sections.key: Your brain processes only a small slice of what reaches your eyes in detail.
sections.b: It feels as though we take in the whole scene in front of us in rich detail, like a camera. We do not. Your eyes send the brain far more information than it can fully process, so attention acts like a spotlight, picking out what seems relevant and leaving the rest dim. Psychologists call the failure to notice an unexpected object while focused on something else inattentional blindness. The term was popularised by Arien Mack and Irvin Rock, who wrote a book with that title in 1998. Crucially, the missed object is not hidden. It is in plain view, often right in the centre of your vision. What is missing is not light hitting your eyes but attention turning that light into conscious experience.

sections.key: We often fail to spot big changes, even to the person we are talking to.
sections.b: A close cousin of inattentional blindness is change blindness: failing to notice that something has changed. In a well known 1998 study, Daniel Simons and Daniel Levin had a researcher stop pedestrians on a university campus to ask for directions. Mid conversation, two workers carrying a door walked rudely between them. Behind the door, the original researcher was swapped for a different person, who carried on the chat. Around half the pedestrians did not notice they were now talking to someone else, despite differences in height, clothing and voice. Film continuity errors work the same way. Drinks change level, shirts change colour and props jump between hands from shot to shot, and most audiences never notice. Our brains assume the world is stable unless something demands attention.

sections.key: Expertise sharpens what you look for, which can blind you to what you don't expect.
sections.b: You might think trained professionals would be immune. In a 2013 study, Trafton Drew, Melissa Vo and Jeremy Wolfe asked radiologists to search lung scans for small nodules that can signal cancer. In the final case, the researchers had inserted a small image of a gorilla, many times larger than a typical nodule. About four in five radiologists did not report it, even though eye tracking showed most of them had looked directly at the spot where it sat. This is not a sign that radiologists are bad at their job. They were brilliantly tuned to find nodules, and that is exactly the point. Expertise tells you where to look and what to look for, and anything outside that search template can slip by unseen.

sections.key: On the road, inattentional blindness can be deadly.
sections.b: Road safety researchers have a name for a common type of crash: 'looked but failed to see'. A driver pulls out of a side street and hits a motorcyclist or cyclist, then insists they checked and the road was clear. Often they are telling the truth as they experienced it. They looked, but their attention was tuned to cars, the most common and dangerous thing on the road, so a smaller, less expected vehicle did not register. Research by David Strayer and colleagues has found that phone conversations make this worse, and that hands free calls are still distracting, because the problem is divided attention, not just your hands. Australian road rules on phones vary by state, so check your state transport authority, but the psychology is the same everywhere.

sections.h: Why your brain works this way
sections.key: Selective attention is a feature, not a bug.
sections.b: It is tempting to see the invisible gorilla as a flaw, but selective attention is what lets you function at all. Imagine trying to read this sentence while consciously processing every sound in the room, the feeling of your clothes, the hum of a fridge and every object in your peripheral vision. Filtering lets you hold a conversation in a noisy cafe or concentrate on a recipe while the radio plays. The cost is that the filter sometimes throws out something important. Interestingly, people who are told about the gorilla in advance nearly always see it, and in a later variation by Simons, people who knew about the original gorilla were no better at spotting other unexpected changes in the scene. Knowing about the effect does not switch it off.

sections.key: You can't remove blind spots, but you can design around them.
sections.b: The most useful takeaway is humility about your own perception. If you are certain you would have noticed something, remember that confidence is not evidence. In everyday life this suggests a few habits. When driving, make a deliberate second look for bikes, motorbikes and pedestrians, especially at intersections. When checking important work, use checklists or a second pair of eyes, because a fresh person with a different focus may see what you cannot. In arguments about what 'really happened', allow that two honest people can genuinely have seen different things. And when you are deeply focused, accept that the world beyond your task is partly invisible to you. The gorilla is always there somewhere. The trick is building systems that catch it when you don't.

quiz.q: In the original gorilla study, roughly what share of viewers failed to notice the gorilla?
quiz.e: Roughly half the viewers counting passes never saw the gorilla walk through the game.

quiz.q: In the 1998 'door study', what happened behind the door?
o: The pedestrian was given a reward
The researcher asking for directions was swapped for someone else
quiz.e: About half the pedestrians did not notice they were suddenly talking to a different person.

quiz.q: Why did most radiologists miss the gorilla in the lung scans?
o: Their search was tuned to nodules, not unexpected shapes
The gorilla was too small to see
They did not look at that part of the scan
quiz.e: Eye tracking showed many looked right at it, but their attention was set to find nodules.

quiz.q: What does 'looked but failed to see' describe?
o: A type of optical illusion in art
Crashes where a driver looked but did not register a hazard
quiz.e: Drivers often genuinely look but fail to register smaller, unexpected road users.

quiz.q: What happened when people already knew about the gorilla?
o: They became immune to all blindness
They saw the gorilla but were no better at spotting other unexpected changes
quiz.e: Knowing about one gorilla did not help them notice other surprises in the scene.

LESSONS.title: Cognitive dissonance: why we twist the facts to feel better
LESSONS.hook: When reality clashes with what we believe or what we've done, something has to give. Surprisingly often, it isn't the belief.

sections.h: The night the world didn't end
sections.key: A doomsday group gave psychologists a front row seat to a mind under pressure.
sections.b: In 1954, a small group in the American Midwest believed a flood would destroy much of the world on 21 December, and that a flying saucer would rescue the faithful beforehand. Some members quit jobs and gave away possessions. Unknown to the group, several of its new members were researchers working with psychologist Leon Festinger. They watched as midnight passed with no spaceship and no flood. Rather than abandon the belief, the leader announced that the group's faith had saved the world, and some members began actively seeking publicity and recruits for the first time. Festinger and his colleagues described the episode in the 1956 book When Prophecy Fails. It became a vivid illustration of an idea Festinger would soon make famous.

sections.key: Holding two clashing thoughts creates discomfort we are driven to reduce.
sections.b: In 1957, Festinger published A Theory of Cognitive Dissonance. His core idea was simple. When we hold two beliefs, or a belief and an action, that conflict with each other, we feel an uncomfortable tension. A smoker who knows smoking kills experiences dissonance every time they light up. That discomfort motivates us to restore consistency, and there are only a few ways to do it. We can change our behaviour, by quitting. We can change our belief, by deciding the risks are exaggerated. Or we can add new thoughts that soften the clash, such as 'my grandfather smoked and lived to ninety' or 'everyone dies of something'. Changing behaviour is often the hardest option, so the mind quietly reaches for the others.

sections.key: The most famous dissonance study is a classic that has recently been challenged.
sections.b: In a 1959 experiment by Festinger and James Carlsmith, students spent an hour on mind numbingly dull tasks, such as turning pegs on a board. Afterwards, they were paid either one dollar or twenty dollars to tell the next participant that the tasks were fun. Later, they rated how enjoyable the tasks really were. The surprise was that the one dollar group rated the task as more enjoyable. The explanation offered was that twenty dollars was a good enough reason to lie, but one dollar was not, so those students resolved their dissonance by deciding the task wasn't so bad. However, a large multi lab replication published in 2024, testing a closely related setup in which people write essays arguing against their own views, did not find the expected effect, so this family of findings deserves more caution than textbooks usually give it.

sections.h: After you choose, you love your choice
sections.key: Once we commit to a decision, we tend to talk ourselves into it.
sections.b: Dissonance is thought to be especially strong after a hard decision. If you agonised between two similar cars and bought one, you might suddenly notice how good your choice is and how flawed the other was. In a 1956 study, Jack Brehm had people rate household appliances, choose between two they liked similarly, then rate them again. The chosen item tended to rise and the rejected one fall. Later researchers pointed out a statistical problem with this design that could create the pattern by itself, and newer studies that correct for it still often find a smaller effect. A related finding comes from a 1968 study at a racetrack: punters who had just placed a bet were more confident their horse would win than those still waiting in line.

sections.h: Effort makes us value things more
sections.key: We tend to justify our suffering by valuing what it bought us.
sections.b: If you have ever been through a gruelling initiation, a tough course or a painful renovation, you may have noticed you valued the result more because of what it cost you. Researchers call this effort justification. A classic 1959 study by Elliot Aronson and Judson Mills found that people who went through an embarrassing initiation to join a dull discussion group later rated the group more positively than those who had an easy entry. This helps explain why hazing rituals, harsh boot camps and some high pressure groups can generate fierce loyalty. Admitting that you suffered for something worthless creates dissonance, so the mind upgrades the prize instead. It is also one reason people stay committed to failing projects long after they should have walked away.

sections.key: The theory remains influential, but psychologists still argue about how it works.
sections.b: Dissonance theory has been hugely influential, yet it has always had critics. In the 1960s, Daryl Bem argued that many results could be explained more simply: we infer our attitudes by watching our own behaviour, just as we would judge a stranger's. Others suggested the real driver is protecting our self image as a good, sensible person, rather than inconsistency as such. The doomsday study has also been questioned, partly because the researchers' presence may have influenced the group, and not every member doubled down. Today, most psychologists accept that people often rationalise their choices and beliefs, but specific classic experiments are treated more cautiously. That is itself a healthy example of science updating its beliefs, rather than explaining away awkward evidence.

sections.key: Noticing your own discomfort can help you think more honestly.
sections.b: The practical value of dissonance theory is self awareness. When you feel defensive, irritated or eager to explain something away, that may be a sign that a cherished belief has met an inconvenient fact. Pausing to ask 'what would change my mind?' can help. Separating your identity from your opinions makes it easier too: being wrong about a decision does not make you a foolish person. In relationships, it helps to remember that others feel dissonance as well, so cornering someone with evidence often makes them dig in. Offering a face saving way to change their mind works better. There is even a famous anecdote from Benjamin Franklin, who said he won over a rival by asking to borrow a rare book. Helping you, perhaps, made the rival like you more.

quiz.q: What did the doomsday group's leader say after the prophecy failed?
o: That the date had been miscalculated by a year
That the group's faith had saved the world
That the researchers had sabotaged it
quiz.e: Rather than abandon the belief, the group reinterpreted the failure and some began recruiting.

quiz.q: Which is an example of reducing dissonance by adding a new thought?
o: A smoker saying 'my grandfather smoked and lived to ninety'
quiz.e: Adding a softening thought reduces the clash without changing behaviour.

quiz.q: What happened when a large 2024 multi lab study retested a closely related dissonance experiment?
o: It did not find the expected effect
It has been replicated perfectly every time
It was proven to be fraud
quiz.e: The failed replication means this family of classic findings is now treated with more caution.

quiz.q: What is 'effort justification'?
o: Working harder to get paid more
Valuing something more because it was hard to get
Avoiding effort to protect self esteem
quiz.e: People who suffer to obtain something tend to rate it more highly.

quiz.q: What alternative explanation did Daryl Bem propose?
o: That dissonance is caused by hunger
That we infer our attitudes by observing our own behaviour
quiz.e: Bem's self perception theory said we read our attitudes from our actions, like an outside observer.

LESSONS.title: Impostor feelings: when success feels like a fluke
LESSONS.hook: You got the job, passed the exam or won the award, and you're quietly waiting to be found out. You are in very good company.

sections.key: Many capable people secretly believe they don't deserve their success.
sections.b: Picture a doctor who has just finished years of training, a manager freshly promoted, or a student who topped the class. From the outside they look confident. Inside, a different story runs on repeat: 'I got lucky. They overestimated me. Any day now, someone will realise I don't really know what I'm doing.' This feeling of being a fraud, despite clear evidence of competence, is widely known as impostor syndrome. It is one of the most commonly recognised experiences in modern working life, and talking about it openly often brings relief, because people discover that colleagues they admire feel exactly the same. Understanding where the feeling comes from, and what it is and isn't, makes it much easier to manage.

sections.key: Two psychologists named it in 1978 while studying high achieving women.
sections.b: The concept was introduced in 1978 by American psychologists Pauline Rose Clance and Suzanne Imes. Working with high achieving women, including academics and students with impressive records, they noticed many believed their success was due to luck, charm or an error in judgement by others, rather than ability. They called it the 'impostor phenomenon'. Note the word phenomenon, not syndrome. It is not a mental illness or a diagnosis, and it does not appear in psychiatric diagnostic manuals. It describes a pattern of thoughts and feelings that many ordinary, healthy people experience at times. Later research found it in men as well as women, and across many professions and cultures, although how it shows up can vary with a person's background and workplace.

sections.key: Estimates vary enormously, but it is clearly widespread.
sections.b: You may have seen claims that 70 per cent of people experience impostor feelings at some point. That figure is repeated often, but its origins are murky. A 2020 systematic review led by Dena Bravata looked at dozens of studies and found reported rates ranging from under ten per cent to over eighty per cent, depending on who was studied and how it was measured. The honest conclusion is that nobody knows the exact figure, but impostor feelings are very common, particularly during transitions such as starting university, a new job or a promotion. They seem especially frequent among people who are among the first in their family or community to reach a particular position, and in competitive fields where everyone around you seems brilliant.

sections.key: Overpreparing or procrastinating can both keep the feeling alive.
sections.b: Clance described a self sustaining loop sometimes called the impostor cycle. Faced with a task, a person feels anxious and doubtful. They respond in one of two ways: by overpreparing, working far longer than necessary, or by procrastinating, then working frantically at the last minute. The task goes well. But instead of concluding 'I'm good at this', they explain the success away. If they overprepared, it was only the extra effort. If they procrastinated, it was luck. Either way, the success does not count as evidence of ability, so the doubt is ready and waiting for the next task. Breaking the cycle often starts with noticing how you explain your wins, and whether you would accept that explanation from a friend.

sections.h: Not the same as Dunning and Kruger
sections.key: Impostor feelings are about how you interpret success, not a lack of skill.
sections.b: Impostor feelings are sometimes described as the opposite of the Dunning Kruger effect, the idea that people with low skill overestimate themselves. The comparison is catchy but loose. People with impostor feelings are usually genuinely competent, and the problem is how they interpret their success. Interestingly, expertise itself can feed the feeling. The more you learn about a field, the more you see how much you don't know, while beginners may be blissfully unaware of the gaps. So an experienced surgeon might feel less certain than a first year student in some situations. That is not a sign of fraudulence. It is often a sign of a realistic understanding of how complex the work actually is.

sections.h: When it's the environment, not you
sections.key: Sometimes feeling like an outsider reflects real signals from the people around you.
sections.b: Some writers and researchers have criticised the impostor syndrome label for putting all the focus on individuals. If you are the only person like you in a room, hear subtle comments questioning whether you belong, or never see anyone with your background in senior roles, feeling out of place may be a reasonable response to real signals, not a distorted thought. Seen this way, fixing the problem is partly a job for workplaces and institutions, through fair processes, mentoring and clear feedback. This doesn't mean individual strategies are useless. It means that if impostor feelings are widespread in a team, leaders should ask what the environment is communicating, rather than simply telling people to be more confident.

sections.key: Practical habits can help you see your achievements more accurately.
sections.b: Several simple habits can loosen the grip of impostor feelings. Talk about it: hearing that respected colleagues feel the same is powerfully reassuring. Keep a record of positive feedback, results and things you have learned, and reread it when doubts flare. Separate feelings from facts by asking, 'What evidence would convince me I'm competent?' and then checking whether it already exists. Accept that not knowing everything is normal at every level of expertise. Mentors are valuable because they can tell you what 'good' looks like in your field. If self doubt is persistent, affecting your sleep or mood, or stopping you from going for opportunities, it is worth speaking to your GP. This is general information, not personal advice, and healthdirect and Beyond Blue have useful resources.

quiz.q: Who first described the 'impostor phenomenon' in 1978?
o: Pauline Rose Clance and Suzanne Imes
quiz.e: Clance and Imes named it after studying high achieving women.

quiz.q: What did a 2020 systematic review find about how common impostor feelings are?
o: Exactly 70 per cent of people have them
Reported rates varied hugely between studies
quiz.e: Rates ranged from under ten to over eighty per cent depending on the study.

quiz.q: In the impostor cycle, how does someone who procrastinated explain their success?
quiz.e: Success is explained away, so it never counts as evidence of ability.

quiz.q: Why might expertise sometimes increase impostor feelings?
o: Experts are less skilled than beginners
Experts see more clearly how much they don't know
quiz.e: Knowing a field well reveals its complexity and your remaining gaps.

quiz.q: What is a key criticism of the 'impostor syndrome' label?
o: It is too medical and should be a diagnosis
It can put all the focus on individuals rather than their environment
It was invented by a company
quiz.e: Feeling out of place can be a reasonable response to real signals in a workplace.

LESSONS.title: The spotlight effect: nobody's watching as closely as you think
LESSONS.hook: That embarrassing stumble, the stain on your shirt, the awkward thing you said: you're replaying it all night. Everyone else has already forgotten.

sections.key: People hugely overestimate how much others notice them.
sections.b: In a study published in 2000, psychologist Thomas Gilovich and colleagues at Cornell University asked students to put on a T-shirt with a large picture of singer Barry Manilow, chosen because it was considered deeply uncool among students at the time. Each student then walked into a room of peers already filling in questionnaires, stayed briefly, and left. Afterwards, the wearers were asked to estimate how many people in the room had noticed the shirt. They guessed about half. In reality, only about a quarter could say who was on it. The researchers named this the spotlight effect: the tendency to believe we are far more noticed, by both good and bad, than we really are.

sections.key: We start from our own intense view of ourselves and don't adjust enough.
sections.b: Why does this happen? You are the one person you can never escape from. You feel every flush of embarrassment, notice every bad hair day and replay every clumsy sentence in high definition. When you guess what others see, you naturally start from that intense inner experience and then try to adjust for the fact that other people are less focused on you. Researchers argue we usually don't adjust nearly enough. Psychologists call this pattern anchoring and adjustment. Meanwhile, everyone else is busy with their own spotlight, worrying about their own shirt, their own words and their own impression. In a sense, a room full of people is a room full of individuals each convinced they are being watched, while mostly watching themselves.

sections.h: Mistakes fade faster than you fear
sections.key: Others judge our slip ups less harshly than we expect.
sections.b: The spotlight effect is not just about being noticed, but about being judged. In related studies, Kenneth Savitsky, Nicholas Epley and Gilovich asked people to imagine or experience embarrassing moments, such as setting off a library security alarm or blanking on a quiz answer. People consistently predicted observers would judge them more harshly than observers actually did. One reason is that the person who stumbled focuses on the mistake itself, while observers see it in a wider context, take situational factors into account and recognise it could happen to anyone. Observers also remember that they have made similar mistakes. So while you are mentally rerunning your blunder at two in the morning, the witnesses have most likely moved on, if they noticed at all.

sections.key: We think our nerves and feelings are written on our faces. Mostly they aren't.
sections.b: A close cousin of the spotlight effect is the illusion of transparency: the belief that our inner states are more visible to others than they really are. In experiments by Gilovich, Savitsky and Victoria Medvec in the late 1990s, people who told lies overestimated how many observers would catch them, and people tasting an unpleasant drink while trying to keep a straight face overestimated how obvious their disgust was. Public speaking is the classic example. A speaker may feel their heart pounding and voice wobbling and assume the audience can see their terror. Usually the audience sees someone who looks a little nervous at most. Your internal alarm bells are loud to you, but largely silent to everyone else.

sections.key: Simply learning about the illusion can make you calmer and better.
sections.b: There is good news hidden in the research. In a 2003 study, Savitsky and Gilovich asked students to give short speeches. Some were told about the illusion of transparency: that their nervousness would be much less visible than they feared. Those students felt less anxious and their speeches were rated as better by observers, compared with students who were simply reassured or given no information. Understanding the illusion seems to break a vicious circle. Normally, worrying that people can see your nerves makes you more nervous, which you then assume is even more visible. Knowing that the audience can't see inside your head helps calm the loop. It is one of the rare cases where knowing about a bias genuinely helps.

sections.key: After chatting with strangers, we underestimate how much they liked us.
sections.b: A more recent finding extends the theme to friendships. In 2018, Erica Boothby, Gus Cooney and colleagues paired strangers for conversations, then asked each person how much they liked their partner and how much they thought their partner liked them. Consistently, people underestimated how much they were liked. The researchers called this the liking gap. After a conversation, we tend to pick over our own awkward moments and missteps, while our partner was busy worrying about theirs. The gap appeared in lab studies, among university students getting to know their housemates and in a workshop setting. It suggests many of us leave conversations more pessimistic than we should be, which might make us hesitate to follow up and build new friendships.

sections.key: Remembering that others are mostly thinking about themselves can be freeing.
sections.b: The spotlight effect can make us cautious, stop us speaking up in meetings, trying a new dance class or wearing something different. Knowing about it offers practical freedom. Before turning down an opportunity because you fear looking foolish, remember the Barry Manilow shirt: far fewer people will notice than you imagine, and fewer still will care tomorrow. When you replay a mistake, ask how much you remember of someone else's similar slip last week. Probably very little. After meeting someone new, assume they liked you more than your inner critic suggests, and consider sending that follow up message. The people around you are not your audience. They are the stars of their own shows, mostly too busy to study yours.

quiz.q: In the Barry Manilow T-shirt study, what did wearers predict compared with reality?
o: They predicted a quarter would notice; about half did
They predicted nobody would notice; everyone did
They predicted about half would notice; about a quarter could name the singer
quiz.e: Wearers roughly doubled the true number of people who noticed.

quiz.q: Why do we tend to overestimate how much others notice us?
o: We start from our intense inner experience and don't adjust enough
quiz.e: We anchor on our own vivid view and under adjust for others' lack of focus on us.

quiz.q: What is the illusion of transparency?
o: Believing others can read our inner feelings more than they can
quiz.e: Our nerves and emotions are usually far less visible than we assume.

quiz.q: What happened when speakers were told about the illusion of transparency?
o: They felt calmer and their speeches were rated better
quiz.e: Understanding the illusion helped break the cycle of nerves feeding on themselves.

quiz.q: What is the 'liking gap'?
o: People underestimate how much new conversation partners liked them
People like friends more than family
Couples like each other less over time
Strangers dislike each other at first
quiz.e: After conversations, people consistently think they were liked less than they were.

LESSONS.title: Deja vu and other glitches of memory
LESSONS.hook: That eerie sense that you've lived this exact moment before. Is it a glimpse of the future, a past life, or something stranger and more ordinary?

sections.key: Deja vu is a feeling of familiarity that you know is false.
sections.b: You walk into a cafe you have never visited, and suddenly everything feels oddly known: the light through the window, the clatter of cups, the conversation at the next table. For a few seconds you feel certain you have lived this moment before, while also knowing that you can't have. Then it fades. The French phrase deja vu means 'already seen', and the term is usually credited to French researcher Emile Boirac in the late nineteenth century. Surveys suggest roughly two thirds of people have experienced it at least once. It is most common in teenagers and young adults and tends to happen less as we get older. It has also been linked with tiredness and stress.

sections.h: The key ingredient: knowing it's false
sections.key: What makes deja vu strange is the clash between feeling and knowledge.
sections.b: Plenty of things feel familiar, so what makes deja vu special? Researchers stress that it involves two things at once: a strong sense of familiarity and the awareness that this familiarity is wrong. If you simply believed you had been somewhere before, that would just be a false memory. With deja vu, part of your mind says 'I know this' while another part says 'no, you don't'. Psychologist Chris Moulin and colleagues have argued this clash is the heart of the experience. It suggests that deja vu is not a malfunction of memory so much as a moment when your brain's checking system notices something odd and flags it, giving you a brief glimpse behind the scenes of how memory works.

sections.key: A new place can feel known if its layout echoes somewhere you've forgotten.
sections.b: One of the leading explanations comes from psychologist Anne Cleary at Colorado State University. Her idea is that deja vu can occur when a new scene resembles something from your past that you can't consciously recall. In experiments, people explored scenes in virtual reality. Later they were shown new scenes that had a similar spatial layout to earlier ones, but different objects. When people could not recall the earlier scene, the matching layouts were more likely to trigger a sense of deja vu. So that unfamiliar cafe might share an arrangement of tables, windows and counter with a room you visited years ago and have long since forgotten. The familiarity is real. You just can't find where it comes from.

sections.key: Deja vu often comes with a sense you know what will happen next, but you don't.
sections.b: Many people say deja vu brings an eerie sense that they know what is about to happen. Cleary and her colleagues tested this in a 2018 study. During moments of deja vu in their virtual reality scenes, participants often felt strongly that they could predict which way to turn next. But when the researchers checked, their predictions were no better than chance. The feeling of premonition was an illusion layered on top of the familiarity. This may help explain why deja vu has long been linked to psychic powers or past lives. The sensation of knowing the future is real as a feeling, but there is no evidence it gives any genuine insight into what comes next.

sections.h: The brain checking its own memory
sections.key: Brain scans suggest deja vu may involve your mind fact checking itself.
sections.b: Researchers have found ways to trigger something like deja vu in the lab. In one method, people hear a list of related words such as bed, pillow, night and dream, but never the word sleep. Later, when asked whether they heard any words starting with 's', they know they did not, yet 'sleep' feels oddly familiar. In a study presented in 2016, Akira O'Connor and colleagues scanned brains during these moments. Activity showed up mainly in frontal areas involved in decision making and conflict, rather than in the memory hubs of the brain. One interpretation is that deja vu reflects the brain checking its memories for errors. If so, it may be a sign of a healthy memory system doing its job.

sections.h: When deja vu is a medical clue
sections.key: Very frequent or unusual deja vu can occasionally signal a seizure.
sections.b: For most people, deja vu is harmless and occasional. However, it has a known link with temporal lobe epilepsy. Some people with this form of epilepsy experience intense deja vu as an aura, a warning sensation at the start of a seizure. Brain surgeons stimulating parts of the temporal lobe during operations have also been able to trigger deja vu like feelings, which helped researchers pin down where the sensation arises. Clues that deja vu might need checking include it happening very often, lasting a long time, or coming with other symptoms such as blank spells, strange smells or tastes, or confusion. This is general information rather than medical advice. If you are concerned, talk to your GP, and healthdirect has more information.

sections.h: Jamais vu and tip of the tongue
sections.key: Memory has other glitches, including its eerie opposite.
sections.b: Deja vu has a stranger opposite called jamais vu, 'never seen'. It is the sense that something you know well, such as a familiar word or face, suddenly seems foreign. You can trigger a version yourself by writing a common word like 'door' over and over until it starts to look wrong. In 2023, Chris Moulin, Akira O'Connor and colleagues won an Ig Nobel Prize, the award for research that first makes people laugh and then think, for studying this. Another familiar glitch is the tip of the tongue state, when you are sure you know a name but can't retrieve it, often recalling its first letter or number of syllables. Together, these quirks reveal memory as a busy, self monitoring process, not a simple recording.

quiz.q: What makes deja vu different from an ordinary false memory?
o: You feel familiarity while also knowing it is false
It happens only once in life
quiz.e: Deja vu combines a sense of familiarity with awareness that the familiarity is wrong.

quiz.q: According to Anne Cleary's research, what can trigger deja vu?
o: A new scene with a similar layout to a forgotten one
quiz.e: Matching spatial layouts made people more likely to report deja vu when they could not recall the earlier scene.

quiz.q: During deja vu, how good were people at predicting what came next?
quiz.e: The feeling of premonition was strong, but predictions were at chance level.

quiz.q: Which condition has a known link with intense deja vu?
quiz.e: Some people with temporal lobe epilepsy experience deja vu as an aura before a seizure.

quiz.q: What is jamais vu?
o: A familiar thing suddenly feeling unfamiliar
quiz.e: Jamais vu is the eerie opposite of deja vu: the familiar seems strange.

LESSONS.title: Boredom: the feeling we'll do almost anything to escape
LESSONS.hook: Given the choice between sitting quietly with their thoughts and giving themselves an electric shock, many people chose the shock. What is boredom trying to tell us?

sections.key: Many people find being alone with their thoughts surprisingly unpleasant.
sections.b: In a series of studies published in 2014, psychologist Timothy Wilson and colleagues at the University of Virginia asked people to sit alone in a plain room for about six to fifteen minutes with nothing to do but think. No phone, no book, no pen. Many found it unpleasant. In one version, participants had earlier been given a mild electric shock and many said they would pay money to avoid feeling it again. Yet when left alone with a button that would deliver the same shock, about two thirds of men and a quarter of women chose to shock themselves at least once. One participant pressed it 190 times. The study made headlines, and it raised an intriguing question: what exactly is boredom?

sections.key: Boredom is wanting to be engaged but being unable to.
sections.b: Boredom is not the same as having nothing to do. You can relax happily on a beach with nothing to do, and you can be bored stiff in a meeting while technically busy. In 2012, psychologist John Eastwood and colleagues defined boredom as 'the aversive experience of wanting, but being unable, to engage in satisfying activity'. The key is a mismatch: your mind is ready and wanting to be used, but the situation offers nothing that captures it. That can happen because a task is too easy, too hard, lacks meaning or is out of your control. Boredom often feels restless and sluggish at the same time, and it tends to make time drag, which is why a bored afternoon can feel endless.

sections.key: Boredom may exist to push us towards something better.
sections.b: Many researchers now see boredom as a useful emotion, much like hunger or pain. Hunger tells you to eat. Boredom, the argument goes, tells you that what you are doing is not worth your attention and that you should change course. Philosophers and psychologists such as Andreas Elpidorou have described it as a regulatory signal that keeps us moving towards goals that matter. Seen this way, boredom is not laziness or a moral failing. It is a nudge that can help us leave unfulfilling situations, seek new challenges and learn new things. The trouble starts when we can't or don't respond well to the signal, either because we are stuck, or because we reach for the quickest escape rather than a meaningful one.

sections.key: Some studies suggest a bored mind wanders in creative directions, but evidence is mixed.
sections.b: There is a popular idea that boredom makes us more creative. In a 2014 study, Sandi Mann and Rebekah Cadman had some participants do a deliberately dull task, copying numbers from a phone book. Afterwards, these participants came up with more ideas when asked to think of uses for a pair of plastic cups than people who had not been bored. The theory is that when the outside world is dull, the mind wanders and makes unexpected connections. It is an appealing finding, but the studies have been small, and results across different experiments have been mixed. It is reasonable to say that some mind wandering time may help creativity, but treating boredom as a guaranteed creativity booster goes beyond the evidence.

sections.key: Some people get bored much more easily, and it matters.
sections.b: We all get bored sometimes, but people differ in how often. In 1986, Richard Farmer and Norman Sundberg developed a Boredom Proneness Scale, and since then researchers have found that people who are easily bored tend to report more problems with attention, impulsive behaviour and low mood. Boredom proneness has also been linked with risky behaviours such as gambling, overeating and substance use, possibly because these offer quick stimulation. Researchers are careful to note that these are associations rather than proof that boredom causes the problems. Still, they suggest that how we handle boredom matters. Being able to tolerate a little dullness, or turn it into curiosity, may be a quietly important life skill.

sections.key: Smartphones make it easy never to feel bored, which may have a cost.
sections.b: Think of the last time you waited in a queue, sat at a red light or stood on a train platform without reaching for your phone. For many people, those moments have almost disappeared. Smartphones offer an instant escape from even a few seconds of boredom. That is convenient, but some researchers worry it trains us to avoid the feeling entirely. If boredom is a signal to seek something more meaningful, endlessly scrolling may silence the signal without satisfying it, leaving us restless and still bored, just more distracted. Studies on whether phones actually make us more bored overall are still developing, so the case is not settled. But many people notice that a mindless scroll rarely leaves them feeling refreshed.

sections.key: Treat boredom as a question: what would be worth my attention?
sections.b: If boredom is a signal, the trick is to listen to it. When you feel bored, ask what is missing: challenge, meaning, novelty or control. A task that is too easy can sometimes be made into a game, such as beating your previous time. A task that is too hard may need breaking into smaller steps. If something feels pointless, connecting it to a goal you care about can help. It is also worth occasionally letting yourself be bored without escaping, such as going for a walk without headphones or sitting with a cup of tea and no screen. Many people find that ideas, plans and solutions surface in those quiet gaps. Boredom, used well, can be the start of something interesting.

quiz.q: In the 2014 'just think' studies, what did many participants do when left alone?
quiz.e: About two thirds of men and a quarter of women shocked themselves at least once.

quiz.q: How did John Eastwood and colleagues define boredom?
o: Wanting but being unable to engage in satisfying activity
quiz.e: Boredom is a mismatch between a mind ready to engage and a situation that offers nothing.

quiz.q: How do many researchers now view boredom?
o: As a signal pushing us to change course
As a sign of low intelligence
quiz.e: Like hunger, boredom may tell us our current activity is not worth our attention.

quiz.q: What is the best summary of the evidence on boredom and creativity?
o: Boredom always makes people more creative
There is no research at all
Some small studies suggest a link, but results are mixed
quiz.e: The idea is appealing, but the evidence is limited and inconsistent.

quiz.q: What has boredom proneness been associated with?
o: Problems with attention and risky behaviours
quiz.e: Researchers found associations with attention problems, impulsivity and risky behaviours, not proof of cause.

LESSONS.title: The paradox of choice: can more options make us less happy?
LESSONS.hook: Twenty four jams, hundreds of streaming shows, dozens of super funds. More choice sounds like freedom, so why does it sometimes leave us stuck?

sections.key: A famous supermarket experiment suggested more choice can mean fewer sales.
sections.b: In a supermarket in California, psychologists Sheena Iyengar and Mark Lepper set up a tasting booth for gourmet jams. On some days the booth offered 24 flavours, and on others just six. The big display attracted more passing shoppers to stop and look. But when it came to buying, the result flipped. Of the shoppers who stopped at the large display, about three per cent bought a jar. At the small display, about thirty per cent did. Published in 2000, the study became one of the most quoted findings in popular psychology, cited in business books, TED talks and marketing meetings. Its message seemed clear and surprising: too much choice can leave people overwhelmed and walking away with nothing.

sections.key: Barry Schwartz argued abundant options can bring stress and regret.
sections.b: In 2004, psychologist Barry Schwartz built on findings like the jam study in his bestselling book The Paradox of Choice. He argued that while some choice is clearly good, beyond a certain point more options can make us less satisfied. Every option we turn down becomes a possible regret. With more alternatives, it is easier to imagine that one of them would have been better, so even a good choice can feel disappointing. Expectations also rise: with hundreds of jeans to choose from, surely one should fit perfectly. And when a decision goes badly, we tend to blame ourselves, because with so many options, a perfect one surely existed. These ideas struck a chord in a world of endless online shopping and streaming menus.

sections.key: Large reviews found the effect is far less reliable than the jam study suggested.
sections.b: As researchers tried to repeat choice overload experiments, the picture grew messier. In 2010, Benjamin Scheibehenne, Rainer Greifeneder and Peter Todd pooled the results of about fifty experiments. On average, they found that the effect of the number of options on satisfaction or buying was close to zero. Some studies found choice overload, some found the opposite, with more options leading to more buying, and many found no difference. This doesn't mean the jam study was wrong for that situation, but it does mean 'more choice is bad' is not a general law. The story is a good reminder that one striking study, however famous, is a starting point for science, not the final word.

sections.h: When too much really is too much
sections.key: Choice overload seems most likely under certain conditions.
sections.b: So when does choice overload actually happen? In 2015, Alexander Chernev, Ulf Bockenholt and Joseph Goodman analysed the research and found that the effect depended on several factors. Overload was more likely when the options were complex and hard to compare, when the decision itself was difficult or time pressured, when people did not have clear preferences and when they wanted to get the decision over with quickly. In contrast, if you already know you love apricot jam, a huge range poses no problem: you simply find apricot. Experts are generally less troubled by large selections than novices, because they know what matters. In other words, choice overload is less about the number of options and more about how hard they are to navigate.

sections.key: Some people search for the best; others settle for good enough.
sections.b: How you choose also matters. Economist Herbert Simon coined the term satisficing for choosing the first option that meets your standards, rather than searching for the absolute best. Schwartz and colleagues later contrasted satisficers with maximisers, people who feel they must examine every option to find the optimal one. In a 2002 study, people who scored high on maximising tended to report more regret and less happiness and life satisfaction. A later study of university graduates found maximisers tended to land jobs with higher starting salaries, but felt less satisfied with them. Being a satisficer does not mean having low standards. It means knowing what is good enough for you, then stopping, rather than chasing a perfect option that may not exist.

sections.key: When choices feel overwhelming, many people stick with the default.
sections.b: Choice overload matters most for big, complex decisions such as insurance, energy plans and retirement savings. Research by Iyengar and colleagues on American retirement plans found that, as the number of investment funds offered increased, participation tended to dip slightly. When people feel overwhelmed, they often delay or simply accept the default option. In Australia, many workers never actively choose a super fund, and their contributions go into a default fund, which is part of why rules about default products matter. This is general information, not financial advice. If you want to compare super funds, energy plans or insurance, government tools such as Moneysmart and the ATO's YourSuper comparison tool can narrow the field and make the options easier to compare.

sections.h: Choosing well in a world of options
sections.key: A few simple strategies can make big menus manageable.
sections.b: You can protect yourself from the downsides of abundant choice. First, decide what matters before you start looking: write down two or three must haves, then ignore options that fail them. Second, limit your search, perhaps by comparing only three options or setting a time limit. Third, for decisions that don't matter much, such as which brand of toothpaste or which show to watch tonight, deliberately satisfice: pick something good enough and move on. Fourth, once you have chosen, stop shopping around. Constantly checking alternatives keeps regret alive. Finally, use trusted recommendations and comparison tools to do some of the sorting for you. Choice is a privilege, but you don't have to experience every option to enjoy it.

quiz.q: In the jam study, which display led to a higher percentage of purchases?
quiz.e: About thirty per cent bought from the small display, compared with about three per cent from the large one.

quiz.q: What did a 2010 analysis of about fifty choice overload experiments find?
o: The average effect was close to zero
quiz.e: Results varied widely, and on average the effect of more options was near zero.

quiz.q: When is choice overload most likely to occur?
o: When people know exactly what they want
When options are complex and preferences are unclear
quiz.e: Complexity, difficulty and unclear preferences make overload more likely.

quiz.q: What is a 'satisficer'?
o: Someone who always buys the most expensive option
Someone who picks the first option that meets their standards
Someone who returns everything they buy
quiz.e: Satisficers choose what is good enough, rather than searching exhaustively for the best.

quiz.q: When people feel overwhelmed by complex choices, what do they often do?
o: Accept the default or delay deciding
quiz.e: Overwhelming choices often lead people to stick with defaults or put off the decision.

LESSONS.title: Willpower: what the marshmallow test really tells us
LESSONS.hook: A child, a marshmallow and a promise of two if they can wait. It became psychology's most famous test of self control, and the real story is more interesting than the legend.

sections.h: One treat now, or two later
sections.key: A simple test in the 1960s became a legend about self control.
sections.b: In the late 1960s and early 1970s, psychologist Walter Mischel and colleagues ran a series of experiments at a nursery school at Stanford University in California. A young child sat at a table with a treat, such as a marshmallow, a pretzel or a biscuit. The researcher explained they had to leave the room. If the child waited until they returned, they would get two treats. If they couldn't wait, they could ring a bell and eat the single treat straight away. Some children gobbled it immediately. Others squirmed, sang, covered their eyes, or even licked the treat without eating it. Mischel's original aim was to understand what strategies helped children delay gratification, not to predict their futures. That came later.

sections.key: Later studies linked waiting longer with better outcomes, and the legend grew.
sections.b: Years after the original experiments, Mischel and colleagues tracked down some of the children, by then teenagers. In a 1990 study, they reported that children who had waited longer tended to have higher scores on the SAT, the American university entrance test, and were rated by parents as more competent. Later follow ups linked waiting time with other outcomes in adulthood. The story spread widely through books, articles and talks: a few minutes with a marshmallow at age four seemed to predict success in life. Self control looked like a powerful, almost fixed trait that could be measured in childhood. But the original follow up samples were small and drawn from children of families connected to a wealthy, highly educated university.

sections.key: A larger, more diverse study found a much weaker link.
sections.b: In 2018, Tyler Watts, Greg Duncan and Haonan Quan revisited the idea using a much larger and more diverse sample of several hundred children from a long running American study. They found that waiting longer at age four was linked with better academic achievement at age fifteen, but the association was only about half the size of the original. More importantly, once the researchers accounted for factors such as family background, home environment and early cognitive skills, the link shrank substantially, and much of it disappeared. This suggested that a lot of what the marshmallow test seemed to measure might reflect a child's circumstances, rather than a stable inner trait of willpower. The test still told us something, but far less than the legend implied.

sections.key: Sometimes eating the marshmallow is the rational choice.
sections.b: A 2013 study by Celeste Kidd and colleagues at the University of Rochester added an important twist. Before the marshmallow test, children were promised better art supplies.
