For one group, the researcher returned with the supplies as promised. For the other, the researcher came back empty handed with an apology. Children who had experienced a reliable adult waited, on average, around four times longer than those who had been let down. The lesson is striking. If you grow up in an environment where promises are often broken and resources can disappear, grabbing what you can now may be a perfectly sensible strategy, not a lack of self control. Decisions about waiting depend on trust and circumstance, not only on character.

sections.h: Ego depletion and the willpower battery
sections.key: The idea that willpower runs out like a battery has not held up well.
sections.b: Another hugely influential idea was ego depletion. In a 1998 study, Roy Baumeister and colleagues asked hungry participants to resist freshly baked cookies and eat radishes instead. Afterwards, the radish eaters gave up sooner on an unsolvable puzzle than people who had eaten the cookies. The conclusion was that willpower is a limited resource, like a muscle that tires. Hundreds of studies followed. Then in 2016, a coordinated replication involving more than twenty labs and over two thousand participants found an effect close to zero. A later large multi lab project led by Kathleen Vohs, one of the original proponents, also found at most a very small effect. Today, the strong 'willpower battery' version of ego depletion is widely doubted.

sections.key: People who seem disciplined often just avoid temptation in the first place.
sections.b: If willpower isn't a heroic battle, what does work? Interestingly, Mischel's original research was about strategies. Children who distracted themselves, looked away or imagined the marshmallow as a fluffy cloud waited longer than those who stared at it. Later research on adults points the same way. A 2012 study by Wilhelm Hofmann and colleagues, which pinged people throughout the day to ask about desires, found that those with high self control reported fewer temptations overall. They seemed to arrange their lives so they rarely had to resist. Psychologists such as Angela Duckworth emphasise situational strategies: removing temptations, changing your environment and making good choices easier. In practice, self control is often less about strength and more about smart design.

sections.key: Simple if then plans and routines beat gritted teeth.
sections.b: One well supported technique is the implementation intention, developed by Peter Gollwitzer. Instead of a vague goal such as 'eat healthier', you make a specific plan: 'If I feel like a snack after dinner, then I will have a piece of fruit.' Many studies suggest these if then plans make people more likely to follow through. Habits help too, because a behaviour repeated in the same context eventually needs little conscious effort. It is also worth treating lapses with kindness rather than harsh self criticism, which can make people give up entirely. The marshmallow story still has value, but its real lesson is not that some children are born winners. It is that self control depends on strategies, environments and trust, all of which can change.

quiz.q: What was Walter Mischel's original aim with the marshmallow experiments?
o: To predict which children would go to university
To understand strategies that help children delay gratification
quiz.e: The predictive follow ups came later; the original focus was on strategies.

quiz.q: What did the 2018 replication by Watts, Duncan and Quan find?
o: The link was weaker and shrank once family background was considered
The link was twice as strong as before
quiz.e: The association was about half as large and largely disappeared after accounting for background factors.

quiz.q: In Celeste Kidd's study, which children waited much longer?
o: Children who had experienced an unreliable adult
Children who had experienced a reliable adult
quiz.e: Trust in the researcher made waiting a more sensible strategy.

quiz.q: What did a 2016 replication of ego depletion involving over twenty labs find?
quiz.e: The coordinated replication found little evidence for the classic ego depletion effect.

quiz.q: According to Hofmann's 2012 study, what distinguished people with high self control?
o: They resisted temptations through sheer effort
quiz.e: They seemed to arrange their lives to avoid temptation, so they had less to resist.

LESSONS.title: Floods: if it's flooded, forget it
LESSONS.hook: Floodwater that looks shallow and calm can sweep a car off the road in seconds. Here is how floods catch people out, and how to stay on the right side of the water.

sections.key: Floodwater is deceptive: it hides its depth, its speed and what lies underneath.
sections.b: Picture a country road after a night of heavy rain. Ahead, brown water covers a dip for twenty metres or so. You know this road, and it looks barely ankle deep. This is exactly the moment emergency services worry about. Floodwater is murky, so you cannot see how deep it is, whether the road beneath has washed away, or whether a branch or a fence is hidden under the surface. The current is often far stronger than it looks from a driver's seat. Driving into floodwater is one of the most common ways people die in Australian floods, which is why state emergency services repeat one short message: if it's flooded, forget it. Turning around costs you a few minutes. Pressing on can cost you your life.

sections.key: It takes surprisingly little moving water to lift a car and carry it away.
sections.b: A car feels heavy and solid, but it is really a sealed box full of air. Once water gets a few tens of centimetres deep, that box starts to become buoyant, and the tyres lose their grip on the road. Add a current pushing sideways and a small car can be lifted and swept off a causeway into a creek. Larger four wheel drives are not immune: they are taller, but they also present a bigger side for the water to push against. Walking is no safer. Fast flowing water only around knee height can knock an adult off their feet, and once you are down, debris and the current make it very hard to stand again. Emergency services often say the same thing: never drive, walk, ride or swim through floodwater.

sections.key: Many Australians live in flood prone areas without realising it.
sections.b: Australia's rivers can rise slowly over days or explode in minutes. Riverine floods build as rain upstream drains into big catchments, giving towns hours or days of warning. Flash floods follow intense downpours, often in hilly or built up areas, where drains overflow and creeks rise almost instantly. Storm surge from cyclones can flood low lying coastal land. A good first step is to find out whether your home, work or regular routes are at risk. Many local councils publish flood maps, and state emergency service websites explain local risks. It also pays to notice the small clues: a street name like Creek Road, a low dip on the way to school, or a causeway with depth markers. Those markers are there for a reason, and it is worth trusting them.

sections.h: Warnings and where to find them
sections.key: Australia uses a shared warning system, and the Bureau of Meteorology issues flood watches and warnings.
sections.b: Australia now uses a national Australian Warning System with three levels, each with a colour and a clear action. Advice means an incident has started and you should stay up to date. Watch and Act means conditions are changing and you need to take action now to protect yourself. Emergency Warning is the highest level: you are in danger and must act immediately. Alongside this, the Bureau of Meteorology issues flood watches and flood warnings for river systems. Good places to check include your state emergency service website and app, the Bureau's website, and local ABC radio, which acts as an emergency broadcaster. Do not wait for an official warning before acting if water is rising around you. Warnings help, but your own eyes on a rising creek matter too.

sections.key: Preparation done in dry weather makes the stressful part far easier.
sections.b: The best time to prepare for a flood is on a sunny day. Write a simple household plan that covers where you would go if you had to leave, such as friends or family on higher ground, and how you would get there without crossing flooded roads. Put together an emergency kit with a torch, a battery radio, medicines, copies of important documents, chargers and water. Think about pets and livestock early, because moving animals takes time. Around the house, store valuables and chemicals up high and know how to turn off electricity and gas. Check what your insurance actually covers, because flood cover is not automatic in every policy. If you need help with a flood or storm emergency that is not life threatening, the SES can be reached on 132 500.

sections.key: Leave early, take the safest route and call Triple Zero (000) if life is at risk.
sections.b: If authorities tell you to evacuate, go, and go early. Roads can be cut long before water reaches your door, and leaving late often means trying to cross rising water in the dark. If you are trapped by floodwater and your life is in danger, call Triple Zero (000). Move to the highest safe point of the building, take a phone, a torch and warm clothes, and wait for rescue rather than trying to swim out. Never let children play in floodwater or stormwater drains, which can suck people in. Floodwater can also carry sewage, chemicals, sharp debris and displaced snakes and spiders. Avoid touching it where you can, and wash well if you do. This lesson is general information only; follow the advice of your state emergency service.

sections.key: The danger does not end when the water drops.
sections.b: When floodwater recedes, it leaves a new set of hazards. Only return home when authorities say it is safe. Power lines may be down, and any electrical appliance or wiring that has been underwater should be checked by a licensed electrician before it is used. Gas leaks are possible, so if you smell gas, leave and call for help. Walls and floors may be weakened, and mud can hide broken glass, nails and animals. Wear gloves, sturdy boots and long sleeves while cleaning, and wash your hands often. Throw out any food that has touched floodwater, and check with your local council or water authority before drinking tap water. Floods are also emotionally exhausting, so check on neighbours and do not be shy about asking for help yourself.

quiz.q: What is the core message state emergency services use about floodwater on roads?
o: Only cross in a four wheel drive
Check the depth by walking in first
quiz.e: The safest choice is never to enter floodwater at all.

quiz.q: Why can a car be swept away in fairly shallow moving water?
o: Water makes the brakes fail instantly
It is full of air, so it becomes buoyant and the tyres lose grip
quiz.e: A car is a sealed box of air, so even modest depths can lift it and let the current push it.

quiz.q: What usually makes a flash flood different from a riverine flood?
o: It rises very quickly after intense rain
It always gives days of warning
It is caused only by cyclones
quiz.e: Flash floods follow intense downpours and can rise in minutes.

quiz.q: In the Australian Warning System, what does an Emergency Warning mean?
o: Conditions are changing, prepare to act
You are in danger and must act immediately
quiz.e: Emergency Warning is the highest level and calls for immediate action.

quiz.q: If you are trapped by rising floodwater and your life is in danger, what should you do?
o: Call Triple Zero (000) and move to the highest safe point
Wait until morning before calling anyone
quiz.e: Call 000 and move to higher ground in the building rather than trying to swim out.

LESSONS.title: Surviving a heatwave
LESSONS.hook: Heatwaves do not burn houses or wash away roads, yet they are one of Australia's deadliest natural hazards. Here is how heat harms the body, and how to stay safe when the mercury soars.

sections.key: Heatwaves are often described as Australia's deadliest natural hazard, largely because their danger is easy to underestimate.
sections.b: When a bushfire or cyclone strikes, the danger is obvious: smoke, flames, roaring wind. A heatwave is different. The sky is blue, the streets look normal, and most people simply feel uncomfortable. Yet heatwaves are often described by Australian emergency and health agencies as having caused more deaths than any other natural hazard in the country's recorded history. Much of the harm happens quietly, indoors, to older people living alone or to people with health conditions whose bodies cannot cope with days of relentless heat. Hot nights make it worse, because the body never gets a chance to recover. The Bureau of Meteorology publishes heatwave forecasts that rate events as low intensity, severe or extreme. When a severe or extreme heatwave is forecast, it is time to plan, not just to complain.

sections.key: Your body cools itself mainly by sweating, and that system has limits.
sections.b: Your body works best at a core temperature of around 37 degrees. When it heats up, blood vessels near the skin widen to shed heat, and you sweat. As sweat evaporates, it carries heat away. This is a clever system, but it depends on two things: enough water in your body to make sweat, and air dry enough for sweat to evaporate. In humid conditions, sweat just drips off without cooling you much. If you lose lots of fluid without replacing it, you become dehydrated and the system starts to falter. Your heart works harder, pushing blood to the skin and to working muscles at the same time. For people with heart conditions, or for the very old and very young, that extra strain can be dangerous.

sections.key: Anyone can be harmed by heat, but some people are far more vulnerable.
sections.b: Heat can affect anyone, including fit young people working or exercising hard outdoors. Some groups, though, need special care. Older people, especially those over about 75 or living alone, may not feel thirst as strongly and may not notice they are overheating. Babies and young children heat up quickly and depend on adults to keep them cool and hydrated. Pregnant women, people with heart, kidney or lung conditions, people with diabetes and people taking certain medicines can all be more sensitive to heat. Outdoor workers, people experiencing homelessness and people without air conditioning or with high power bills may struggle to escape the heat at all. During a heatwave, one of the most useful things you can do is check on vulnerable neighbours, friends and relatives, ideally at least once a day.

sections.key: Stay hydrated, stay out of the hottest part of the day and keep your home as cool as possible.
sections.b: The basics are simple but they work. Drink water regularly through the day, even before you feel thirsty, and go easy on alcohol and very sugary drinks. If your doctor has told you to limit fluids, ask them what to do in hot weather. Plan errands and exercise for the cooler early morning or evening, and rest during the middle of the day. Wear light, loose clothing and a hat outdoors. At home, close curtains and blinds on sunny windows early, and open windows when it cools down outside. Fans help, but in very high temperatures they may not cool you enough on their own. A cool shower, a damp cloth on the neck, or a few hours in an air conditioned library or shopping centre can all make a real difference.

sections.h: Never leave anyone in a car
sections.key: A parked car can become dangerously hot within minutes, even with the windows down a little.
sections.b: On a warm day, the inside of a closed car can quickly become far hotter than the air outside, often by tens of degrees. Much of the rise happens in the first few minutes, and leaving a window slightly open does very little to help. Children are especially vulnerable because their bodies heat up faster than adults' and they cannot get themselves out. Pets are at serious risk too. The rule is simple: never leave children, vulnerable adults or animals in a parked car, not even for a quick dash into a shop. If you see a child or animal locked in a hot car and they appear distressed, call Triple Zero (000) straight away. Make a habit of checking the back seat every time.

sections.key: Heatstroke is a medical emergency: call Triple Zero (000) and start cooling the person.
sections.b: Heat illness often starts with heat cramps or heat exhaustion. Signs of heat exhaustion include heavy sweating, pale skin, weakness, dizziness, headache, nausea and fainting. Move the person somewhere cool, have them lie down, loosen clothing, cool them with water and fans, and give small sips of water if they are fully alert. If they do not improve quickly, seek medical help. Heatstroke is more serious and can be fatal. The body's cooling has failed. The person may become confused, slur their words, collapse, have a seizure or lose consciousness, and their skin may be hot and either dry or sweaty. Call Triple Zero (000) immediately. While you wait, cool them with water, wet sheets, fans and cold packs in the armpits, groin and neck. Do not give drinks to someone who is not fully conscious.

sections.key: A simple heat plan, made in advance, protects you and the people around you.
sections.b: Heatwaves are becoming more common and more intense in Australia, so it makes sense to plan for them the way you might plan for a storm. Before summer, check that fans and air conditioners work, and think about where you could go to cool off if the power fails. Keep a supply of water and easy food that does not need cooking. Store medicines as the label directs, since some are damaged by heat. Make a list of people you will check on, and ask someone to check on you if you live alone. Watch the Bureau of Meteorology heatwave forecasts and your state health department's heat advice. This lesson is general information, not medical advice: healthdirect (1800 022 222) can help, and doing a first aid course is a great idea.

quiz.q: Why are heatwaves especially dangerous compared with more dramatic disasters?
o: They only affect people in the desert
Their danger is easy to underestimate, and much harm happens quietly indoors
They always cause power lines to fall
quiz.e: Heatwaves look ordinary, so people underestimate them while vulnerable people suffer out of sight.

quiz.q: Why does humid weather make heat harder to cope with?
o: Humidity stops you sweating at all
Humid air raises your heart rate directly
Sweat evaporates less, so it cools you less
quiz.e: Cooling depends on sweat evaporating, which happens less in humid air.

quiz.q: What does leaving a car window slightly open do on a hot day?
o: Very little to stop the temperature rising
Makes the car cooler than outside
Is enough for pets but not children
quiz.e: A slightly open window barely slows the dangerous rise in temperature inside a parked car.

quiz.q: Someone in the heat becomes confused and collapses. What is the right first action?
o: Give them a large drink of water
Call Triple Zero (000) and start cooling them
quiz.e: These are signs of heatstroke, a medical emergency needing 000 and rapid cooling.

quiz.q: When is the best time to exercise or run errands during a heatwave?
quiz.e: The cooler parts of the day put less strain on your body.

LESSONS.title: Home fires: alarms, escape plans and kitchen fires
LESSONS.hook: A house fire can make a home deadly in a matter of minutes. A working smoke alarm and a practised escape plan are the two things most likely to get everyone out alive.

sections.key: A house fire can become unsurvivable very quickly, so early warning and a fast exit matter most.
sections.b: In films, people stroll through burning houses calmly. Real house fires are nothing like that. Modern homes are full of synthetic materials such as foam couches, plastics and carpets that burn hot and fast and release thick, toxic smoke. Fire services warn that a room can become deadly within a few minutes. The smoke, not the flames, is usually what kills, because it fills the air with poisonous gases like carbon monoxide and makes it impossible to see. Many fatal house fires happen at night, when people are asleep. Smoke does not wake you up; it can make you sleep more deeply. That is why fire services focus on two simple things: hearing the warning early, and getting out fast without stopping to collect belongings.

sections.key: Working smoke alarms are required by law in Australian homes, and they need regular care.
sections.b: Every Australian state and territory requires smoke alarms in homes, but the exact rules differ. Queensland, for example, has been moving to interconnected photoelectric alarms in every bedroom, hallway and level of a home, so when one sounds they all sound. Fire services generally recommend photoelectric alarms, because they are good at detecting the smouldering fires that often start at night. An alarm only helps if it works. A common guideline is to test each alarm monthly by pressing the test button, to clean dust from the vents regularly, and to replace alarms that are about ten years old. If your alarm uses a replaceable battery, change it as the manufacturer recommends. Check your state fire service website for the current rules where you live, especially if you rent or are selling.

sections.key: Know two ways out of every room and agree on a meeting place outside.
sections.b: When an alarm sounds at 2am, you will not have time to think things through. That is why fire services encourage every household to draw a simple floor plan and mark two ways out of each room, usually a door and a window. Make sure security screens and deadlocks can be opened quickly from inside, and keep keys in the lock or nearby when you are home. Choose a safe meeting place outside, such as the letterbox or a neighbour's driveway, so you can count heads. Practise the plan with everyone in the home, including children, at least once or twice a year. Children sometimes hide from fire under beds or in cupboards, so teach them that the right thing to do is get out and stay out.

sections.key: Get down low, close doors behind you and never go back inside.
sections.b: If there is smoke, get down low, where the air is cleaner and cooler, and crawl to the nearest safe exit. Before opening a closed door, feel it with the back of your hand. If it is hot, use your other way out. Close doors behind you as you leave, because a closed door can slow the spread of fire and smoke. Once you are out, call Triple Zero (000) and stay out. Never go back inside for pets, phones or valuables, as many people have died doing exactly that; tell firefighters if anyone is missing. If you cannot get out, close the door, block gaps with towels or clothing, open a window if safe, and call 000. If your clothes catch fire, stop, drop to the ground, cover your face and roll.

sections.key: Keep looking while cooking, and never put water on burning oil.
sections.b: The kitchen is where many house fires start, often when someone leaves food cooking and gets distracted. Fire services sum it up neatly: keep looking while cooking. If a pan of oil or fat catches fire, never throw water on it. Water sinks under the hot oil, flashes into steam and can blast burning oil across the kitchen in a fireball. Instead, if it is safe, turn off the heat and smother the flames by sliding a lid or a fire blanket over the pan, then leave it covered until it has completely cooled. Do not try to carry the burning pan outside. A fire blanket mounted near the kitchen exit is cheap and easy to use. If the fire is spreading or you are unsure, get everyone out, close the door and call Triple Zero (000).

sections.key: Many fires start from heaters, overloaded power points and damaged lithium batteries.
sections.b: Winter brings a rise in house fires as heaters, electric blankets and clothes dryers work harder. Keep heaters at least a metre away from curtains, bedding, clothes and furniture, and turn them off when you leave the room or go to bed. Check electric blankets for frayed cords or worn spots before winter. Clean the lint filter of your clothes dryer every time you use it. Avoid overloading power boards, and never cover them with rugs. A newer worry is lithium ion batteries in e-bikes, e-scooters and power tools. Damaged or poor quality batteries can overheat and burn fiercely. Use the charger that came with the device, avoid charging bulky batteries overnight or near your exit path, and stop using any battery that is swollen, hot or damaged.

sections.key: Cool a burn under running water for 20 minutes, and call Triple Zero (000) for serious burns.
sections.b: If someone is burned, the first aid advice in Australia is clear: cool the burn under cool running water for 20 minutes. This helps even if a little time has passed. Remove jewellery and clothing from the area unless it is stuck to the skin. Do not use ice, butter, toothpaste or creams. After cooling, cover the burn loosely with plastic cling wrap or a clean, non stick dressing, and keep the person warm. Call Triple Zero (000) for burns that are large, deep, on the face, hands, feet, groin or airway, caused by chemicals or electricity, or on a child or older person. This lesson is general information only. A proper first aid course teaches these skills hands on, and it is one of the best investments a household can make.

quiz.q: What usually kills people in house fires?
quiz.e: Toxic smoke, not flames, is the main killer in house fires.

quiz.q: What type of smoke alarm do fire services generally recommend?
quiz.e: Photoelectric alarms are good at detecting smouldering fires that often start at night.

quiz.q: Why should you close doors behind you as you escape a fire?
o: To slow the spread of fire and smoke
So firefighters know the room is empty
quiz.e: A closed door can hold back fire and smoke, buying precious time.

quiz.q: A pan of oil catches fire on the stove. What should you NOT do?
o: Turn off the heat if safe
Slide a lid over the pan
quiz.e: Water on burning oil can cause a violent fireball.

quiz.q: How long should a burn be cooled under running water?
o: Until it stops hurting, then apply butter
quiz.e: Australian first aid advice is 20 minutes of cool running water.

LESSONS.title: Get ready: your emergency kit and household plan
LESSONS.hook: When disaster strikes, the decisions you make in the first hour matter most. A little planning on a quiet weekend can make those decisions almost automatic.

sections.key: People who plan ahead cope better in emergencies and recover faster afterwards.
sections.b: Imagine your phone buzzes at midnight with an emergency warning. Water is rising, or a fire is moving toward town, and you have perhaps half an hour. Where are the car keys? Who is picking up the kids from their other parent's house? What about the dog, the medicines and the passports? In the middle of a crisis, stress makes clear thinking hard, and people waste time or make risky choices. Emergency organisations such as the Australian Red Cross and state emergency services encourage every household to plan ahead for exactly this reason. Being prepared does not mean expecting the worst every day. It means doing the thinking once, in calm conditions, so that in a real emergency you can act quickly and spend your energy on staying safe.

sections.key: Different places face different hazards, so start by learning which ones apply to you.
sections.b: Australia's hazards vary enormously by region. Northern coasts face cyclones and storm surge. River towns face floods. Bushland edges face fire. Cities face heatwaves, severe storms and the occasional power or water outage. Almost everyone could face a house fire. Start your plan by finding out which hazards are most likely where you live, work and travel. Your local council and state emergency service websites usually explain local risks, and many publish flood or bushfire maps. Talk to neighbours who have lived in the area for years, because they often remember events that newer residents have never seen. Once you know your risks, your plan can focus on the things that matter most for you, rather than trying to prepare for every possible disaster at once.

sections.key: A good plan answers where you will go, how you will get there and how you will stay in touch.
sections.b: A household emergency plan does not need to be complicated. It should answer a few key questions. When will you leave, and what will trigger that decision? Where will you go: a friend or relative's place in a safer area, or an evacuation centre? How will you get there, and what is your back up route if roads are closed? How will family members contact each other if phones are down or you are split up? Many families choose one contact person who lives in another area. Write down important numbers on paper too, in case your phone battery dies. The Australian Red Cross offers free planning tools, including its Get Prepared app. Share the plan with everyone in the household and review it each year.

sections.key: An emergency kit holds the basics to get through the first few days without help.
sections.b: An emergency kit is a collection of supplies stored together, ready to grab or to use at home. Common recommendations include drinking water, with a common guideline of around three litres per person per day for at least three days, and food that does not need cooking or refrigeration. Add a torch, a battery powered radio and spare batteries, a first aid kit, a power bank and charging cables, and some cash in case card machines are down. Include medicines and prescriptions, glasses, toiletries, and anything needed for babies, older family members or people with a disability. Keep copies of important documents, such as identification and insurance papers, in a waterproof bag or saved securely online. Check the kit every six months or so and replace anything out of date.

sections.key: Animals are part of the family, so include them in your plan from the start.
sections.b: People have sometimes delayed evacuating, or gone back into danger, because they could not take their pets. Planning ahead can prevent this. Make sure pets are microchipped and that your contact details are up to date, and keep a recent photo of each animal on your phone. Pack food, water, leads, medicines and a carrier or crate in your kit. Find out in advance which friends, boarding kennels or evacuation centres can take animals, since not every centre can. For horses and livestock, plans take much longer to carry out, so owners often need to move animals early, well before any official warning. Some agriculture departments and animal welfare groups provide guides for large animals. The key idea is simple: decide early, so you never have to choose between your animals and your safety.

sections.key: Know where official warnings come from, and have a way to receive them if the power goes out.
sections.b: During an emergency, reliable information can be the difference between leaving in time and being trapped. Australia uses a national warning system with three levels: Advice, Watch and Act, and Emergency Warning. Each state and territory has its own emergency websites and apps, so find the ones for your area before you need them. The Bureau of Meteorology provides weather and flood warnings, and ABC local radio is an official emergency broadcaster that often keeps broadcasting when other services fail. A battery or wind up radio is useful if power and mobile networks go down. Be careful with social media. It can spread useful local news quickly, but rumours and old photos also circulate. Check official sources before acting, and if your life is in danger, call Triple Zero (000).

sections.key: Neighbours are often the first helpers in a disaster, so get to know them now.
sections.b: In many Australian disasters, the first people to help were not police or firefighters but neighbours. They checked on older residents, shared generators, moved livestock and offered spare rooms. Strong local connections are one of the best predictors of how well a community copes and recovers. You can build them in simple ways: swap phone numbers with neighbours, find out who might need help to evacuate, and join a local community group or volunteer organisation. If you have a medical condition or disability, consider letting trusted neighbours know what support you may need. After a disaster, recovery can take months or years, and stress and grief are normal. Organisations such as the Australian Red Cross, local councils and recovery centres can help. This lesson is general information, so follow official advice for your area.

quiz.q: Why is it useful to choose one contact person who lives in another area?
o: They can drive you to safety
Family members can all check in with one person if they are separated
quiz.e: A single out of area contact helps a scattered family stay connected.

quiz.q: What is a common guideline for emergency drinking water?
o: One glass per person per day
Around three litres per person per day for at least three days
Ten litres per household in total
No water is needed if you have food
quiz.e: A common guideline is around three litres per person per day for at least three days.

quiz.q: Why is a battery or wind up radio useful in an emergency?
o: It still works if power and mobile networks fail
quiz.e: Radio, including ABC local radio, can keep you informed when other services are down.

quiz.q: Why do owners of horses and livestock often need to act early?
o: Moving large animals takes a long time
Animals are not allowed in cars
quiz.e: Moving large animals is slow, so plans need to start well before warnings escalate.

quiz.q: Who are often the first helpers in a disaster?
quiz.e: Neighbours are frequently first on the scene, which is why local connections matter.

LESSONS.title: Severe storms and cyclones
LESSONS.hook: Every year, wild storms and tropical cyclones tear roofs off, drop trees on cars and cut power to thousands of homes. Knowing what to do before and during one can keep your family safe.

sections.key: Severe storms can strike almost anywhere in Australia, and cyclones threaten the north.
sections.b: On a hot spring afternoon in south east Queensland or western Sydney, towering clouds can build into a storm that drops giant hail, flattens fences and floods streets in less than an hour. Severe thunderstorms happen across most of Australia, bringing damaging winds, large hail, heavy rain, flash flooding and lightning. In the tropical north, the bigger threat is the tropical cyclone, a vast spinning storm system that forms over warm ocean water. The official cyclone season in Australia runs from November to April, and cyclones affect coasts from Western Australia across the Northern Territory to Queensland, and sometimes travel further south. The Bureau of Meteorology issues severe thunderstorm and cyclone warnings, and state emergency services, reachable on 132 500, help with storm damage in non life threatening situations.

sections.key: Australia rates cyclones from Category 1 to Category 5 based on their strongest wind gusts.
sections.b: The Bureau of Meteorology uses a five step scale for tropical cyclones. A Category 1 cyclone has damaging gales that can damage trees, caravans and crops. As the categories climb, wind gusts become far stronger, and Category 5 cyclones can bring extremely destructive winds capable of causing widespread devastation. Category 3 and above are described as severe tropical cyclones. However, the category only describes wind. A weaker cyclone can still be deadly through flooding rain, which can spread hundreds of kilometres inland, or through storm surge. Cyclones are also unpredictable, sometimes strengthening rapidly or changing direction. So it is wise not to relax because a cyclone is 'only' a low category. Follow the Bureau's track maps and warnings closely, and act on advice from your local emergency services.

sections.key: Storm surge can push the sea far inland and is one of a cyclone's deadliest effects.
sections.b: When a strong cyclone approaches a coast, its powerful winds push ocean water toward the shore, and the low air pressure at its centre lets the sea bulge upward. The result is a storm surge: a rise in sea level well above the normal high tide, topped with large waves. If it arrives at high tide, the effect can be devastating, flooding low lying coastal suburbs, roads and caravan parks. Around the world, storm surge has caused many of the deadliest cyclone disasters in history. In Australia, authorities may order people in storm surge zones to evacuate even if their homes are well built, because the threat is from water rather than wind. If you live near the coast in cyclone country, find out whether you are in a storm surge zone.

sections.key: Simple jobs before storm season can stop much of the damage.
sections.b: Many storm injuries and much property damage come from flying debris and falling trees. Before the season, clean gutters and downpipes so heavy rain can drain away. Trim overhanging branches, ideally using a qualified arborist for large trees. Check that your roof is in good repair. Make a list of loose outdoor items, such as trampolines, outdoor furniture, bins and pot plants, that you would secure or bring inside when a storm or cyclone is forecast. In cyclone areas, residents often prepare by fitting shutters or protecting windows, and by knowing whether their home was built to modern cyclone standards. Keep your emergency kit stocked, fill vehicles with fuel, and charge phones and power banks when a warning is issued. Park cars under cover or away from trees if hail is forecast.

sections.key: Shelter in the strongest part of the building, away from windows, and stay inside until it is truly over.
sections.b: When a severe storm or cyclone hits, the safest place is usually indoors in the strongest part of the building. This is often a small internal room such as a bathroom, laundry or hallway, away from windows and glass doors. If the building starts to break up, protect yourself under a sturdy table or mattress. Unplug electrical appliances and avoid using landline phones during lightning. In a cyclone, be very careful of the calm eye. When the centre passes over, the wind can drop suddenly and the sky may even clear, tempting people outside. Then the winds return, often from the opposite direction and just as strongly. Stay inside until authorities say the cyclone has passed. If you are in danger at any time, call Triple Zero (000).

sections.key: If you can hear thunder, you are close enough to be struck by lightning.
sections.b: Lightning can strike many kilometres away from the heaviest rain, which is why safety agencies say that if you can hear thunder, you are within range. A good habit is to head indoors or into a hard topped car as soon as you hear it, and to wait a good while after the last rumble before going back outside. Avoid open fields, beaches, water, hilltops, isolated trees and metal fences. Swimmers, golfers, campers and people working outdoors are particularly exposed. Indoors, stay off corded phones and away from plumbing and electrical appliances during the storm. If someone is struck by lightning, it is safe to touch them, because people do not hold an electrical charge. Call Triple Zero (000) straight away, and begin CPR if they are not breathing normally.

sections.key: Fallen power lines, damaged buildings and floodwater remain serious hazards.
sections.b: Once the wind dies down, the clean up brings its own risks. Always assume fallen power lines are live. Stay well clear of them, at least 8 metres according to many electricity networks, and remember that water, fences and wet ground near a fallen line can be electrified too. Report them to your electricity distributor, or call Triple Zero (000) if there is immediate danger. Do not enter badly damaged buildings, and watch out for broken glass, exposed nails and asbestos in older homes. Avoid driving through floodwater or under damaged trees. Chainsaw and ladder injuries are common after storms, so be cautious or leave big jobs to professionals and the SES. Photograph damage before clearing it for insurance. This lesson is general information; always follow official advice for your area.

quiz.q: When does Australia's official tropical cyclone season run?
quiz.e: The official season runs from November to April.

quiz.q: Why should you not relax just because a cyclone is a low category?
o: Low categories always strengthen to Category 5
Category only measures wind, and rain or storm surge can still be deadly
Low categories are only rated at night
quiz.e: The category describes wind, but flooding rain and storm surge can still kill.

quiz.q: Why might people in a storm surge zone be told to evacuate even if their homes are strong?
o: The threat comes from rising sea water rather than wind
quiz.e: Storm surge floods low lying land, so even sturdy homes can be dangerous.

quiz.q: What is dangerous about the eye of a cyclone?
o: The calm can tempt people outside before winds return
quiz.e: Winds return after the eye passes, often from the opposite direction.

quiz.q: How should you treat a fallen power line?
o: Move it with a dry stick
Assume it is live and stay well clear
quiz.e: Always assume fallen lines are live and keep well away.

LESSONS.title: Staying alive on long drives
LESSONS.hook: Australia's long, empty roads are beautiful, but fatigue, wildlife and remote breakdowns catch out even experienced drivers. Here is how to make every road trip end safely.

sections.key: Country roads carry a disproportionate share of Australia's road deaths.
sections.b: There is something hypnotic about a long Australian highway: straight bitumen, red dirt, a horizon that never seems to get closer. That hypnotic quality is part of the danger. Although most Australians live in cities, a large share of road deaths happen on rural and regional roads, often in single vehicle crashes where a car leaves the road or hits a tree. Speeds are higher, roads may be narrow or unsealed, help can be hours away, and the scenery can lull drivers into lapses of attention. Road safety campaigns often talk about the 'fatal five': speeding, drink and drug driving, not wearing a seatbelt, fatigue and distraction. On long drives, fatigue and distraction become especially important, because they creep up on people who feel perfectly fine when they set out.

sections.key: Tired driving can be as dangerous as drink driving, and you cannot will yourself to stay awake.
sections.b: Fatigue is one of the biggest killers on Australian roads. Being awake for a long time impairs your reactions and judgement in a way research has compared to having alcohol in your blood. The most frightening part is the microsleep: a few seconds when your brain simply switches off, often without you realising. At 100 kilometres per hour, a car travels close to 28 metres every second, so a four second microsleep can carry you well over 100 metres with nobody in control. Warning signs include yawning, sore or heavy eyes, drifting in your lane, missing signs and not remembering the last few kilometres. Opening the window or turning up the music does not fix tiredness. The only real cure is sleep, so pull over somewhere safe and have a rest or a power nap.

sections.key: Get a good night's sleep, plan breaks every two hours and share the driving.
sections.b: Fatigue is much easier to prevent than to fight. Start a long drive well rested, and avoid setting out after a full day of work or in the hours when your body normally sleeps, such as late at night and in the mid afternoon slump. Road safety agencies commonly recommend a break of at least 15 minutes every two hours. Get out, walk around and have a drink and a snack. Look out for Driver Reviver sites, which often operate on major highways during holiday periods and offer free tea, coffee and a friendly chat. If you can, share the driving with another licensed driver. Be honest about how far you can go. An extra night in a motel is a small price compared with the cost of a crash.

sections.key: Brake firmly in a straight line rather than swerving hard to avoid an animal.
sections.b: Kangaroos, wallabies, wombats, emus and livestock are a real hazard on country roads, especially around dawn and dusk, when many native animals are most active, and at night. Slow down in areas with wildlife warning signs and scan the roadside verges, where animal eyes may reflect your headlights. If an animal jumps out in front of you, the general advice is to brake firmly in a straight line and avoid swerving violently. Many serious crashes happen when drivers swerve, lose control and hit a tree or oncoming vehicle, when hitting the animal itself might have caused only damage to the car. Kangaroos are notoriously unpredictable and can change direction suddenly, and where there is one there are often more. If you hit an animal, only stop when it is safe to do so.

sections.key: Give big vehicles plenty of room, and slow right down on gravel.
sections.b: In outback Australia you may meet road trains, trucks pulling two, three or even more trailers, which can stretch more than 50 metres long. Overtaking one takes a long stretch of clear road and plenty of patience, so only pass when you can see well ahead and be sure it is safe. When a road train is coming the other way on a narrow road, slow down and move left, as it may not be able to move over. Unsealed roads bring their own dangers: loose gravel, corrugations, bulldust holes and sharp edges can all make a car slide. Drive slower than you would on bitumen, avoid harsh braking and steering, and keep your headlights on to be visible in dust. Check road conditions before you go, as roads may close after rain.

sections.h: If you break down in remote areas
sections.key: In remote areas, stay with your vehicle: it is much easier to find than a person.
sections.b: Before heading into remote country, tell someone your route and when you expect to arrive, and check in when you do. Carry far more water than you think you will need, along with food, a first aid kit, a spare tyre and tools. Mobile coverage disappears across large parts of Australia, so many remote travellers carry a satellite communication device or a personal locator beacon. If you break down or get stuck, the standard advice is to stay with your vehicle. A car is far easier for searchers to spot than a person walking, and it provides shade and shelter. People have died walking away from a vehicle in search of help, often in extreme heat. Rest in the shade during the hottest part of the day and conserve your water and energy.

sections.key: Know how to call Triple Zero (000) and share your exact location.
sections.b: If there is a crash, first make sure you are safe from other traffic: switch on hazard lights and, if you can, get yourself and passengers away from the road. Call Triple Zero (000) for any crash where someone is injured or trapped, a vehicle is on fire, or the road is dangerously blocked. On a mobile phone, emergency calls can usually connect through any available network, even if it is not your provider's. The free Emergency+ app, developed by Australian emergency services, can show your GPS location so you can read it to the operator, which is vital on long, featureless roads. Do not move injured people unless they are in immediate danger. This lesson is general information, and a first aid course will prepare you to help at a crash.

quiz.q: What is a microsleep?
o: A few seconds when the brain switches off without warning
A long sleep at a rest stop
A sleep disorder only in truck drivers
quiz.e: A microsleep is a brief, often unnoticed lapse into sleep, deadly at highway speed.

quiz.q: How often do road safety agencies commonly recommend a break on long drives?
quiz.e: A break of at least 15 minutes every two hours is commonly recommended.

quiz.q: A kangaroo jumps in front of your car. What is the general advice?
o: Brake firmly in a straight line
quiz.e: Swerving violently often causes worse crashes than hitting the animal.

quiz.q: If you break down in a remote area, what is the standard advice?
o: Split up to search for help
quiz.e: A vehicle is easier to spot and provides shelter.

quiz.q: What can the Emergency+ app help you do?
o: Share your GPS location with the 000 operator
quiz.e: Emergency+ shows your location so you can tell the operator exactly where you are.

LESSONS.title: Heart attack and stroke: spotting the signs
LESSONS.hook: Heart attacks and strokes are medical emergencies where every minute counts. Recognising the warning signs, and calling for help fast, can save a life or prevent lifelong disability.

sections.h: Time is muscle, time is brain
sections.key: In heart attacks and strokes, delay causes damage, so acting fast is everything.
sections.b: A man in his fifties feels a heavy pressure in his chest while mowing the lawn. He tells himself it is indigestion and sits down for a while. A woman notices her husband's speech has become slurred at dinner, but he says he is just tired. Scenes like these happen in Australian homes every day, and the delay can be devastating. In a heart attack, part of the heart muscle is starved of blood. In most strokes, part of the brain is. The longer the blockage lasts, the more tissue dies. Doctors say 'time is muscle' for the heart and 'time is brain' for strokes. Modern hospital treatments can open blocked vessels, but many work best when given early, which only happens if someone calls for help quickly.

sections.h: What happens in a heart attack
sections.key: A heart attack happens when a blocked artery stops blood reaching part of the heart.
sections.b: Your heart muscle is fed by its own blood vessels, the coronary arteries. Over years, fatty plaque can build up inside them. If a plaque cracks, a blood clot can form on top and block the artery. The heart muscle beyond the blockage is then starved of oxygen and begins to die. This is a heart attack, which doctors call a myocardial infarction. It is different from a cardiac arrest, though the two are often confused. In a cardiac arrest, the heart's electrical rhythm goes haywire and it stops pumping effectively, so the person collapses, stops breathing normally and becomes unresponsive. A heart attack can trigger a cardiac arrest, which is one reason a heart attack must never be ignored or treated as something to wait out.

sections.key: Chest discomfort is common, but symptoms vary and are not always dramatic.
sections.b: Many people imagine a heart attack as a sudden, crushing collapse. In reality, the signs can be subtle and can come on slowly. The Heart Foundation describes warning signs such as pain, pressure, heaviness or tightness in the chest, which may spread to the arm, shoulder, neck, jaw or back. Other signs include shortness of breath, nausea, a cold sweat, dizziness or feeling light headed. Some people, including many women, older people and people with diabetes, may have less typical symptoms, such as unusual tiredness, breathlessness or discomfort in the back or jaw rather than obvious chest pain. Symptoms can come and go. Because the signs vary so much, it is worth taking any unusual chest discomfort seriously rather than waiting to see whether it passes on its own.

sections.h: What to do for a suspected heart attack
sections.key: If symptoms are severe, getting worse or lasting more than 10 minutes, call Triple Zero (000).
sections.b: The Heart Foundation's warning signs action plan is straightforward. If you have warning signs, stop what you are doing and rest. If symptoms are severe, get worse quickly or last longer than 10 minutes, call Triple Zero (000) and ask for an ambulance. Do not drive yourself to hospital, and do not let someone else drive you unless there is truly no alternative, because paramedics can begin treatment straight away and handle a cardiac arrest if it happens. The operator may give advice about medicines such as aspirin, so follow their instructions. If the person collapses and is not breathing normally, start CPR and ask someone to bring a defibrillator. Many public places now have one, and they are designed to be used by untrained bystanders by following the spoken instructions.

sections.key: A stroke is a sudden interruption of blood supply to part of the brain.
sections.b: There are two main types of stroke. Most are ischaemic strokes, caused when a blood clot or plaque blocks an artery supplying the brain. Others are haemorrhagic strokes, where a blood vessel in or around the brain bursts and bleeds. Either way, brain cells in the affected area are cut off from oxygen and begin to die. Researchers estimate that in a typical large stroke, the brain can lose close to two million nerve cells for every minute it goes untreated. Which abilities are affected depends on which part of the brain is damaged: movement, speech, vision, balance or understanding. Hospitals can now treat many ischaemic strokes with clot dissolving drugs or by physically removing the clot, but these treatments are time sensitive, so getting to hospital fast is crucial.

sections.key: Check the Face, Arms and Speech, and if any are affected, it is Time to call Triple Zero (000).
sections.b: The Stroke Foundation's F.A.S.T. test is a simple way to recognise the most common signs of stroke. Face: check their face. Has their mouth drooped? Arms: can they lift both arms? Speech: is their speech slurred, and do they understand you? Time is critical: if you see any of these signs, call Triple Zero (000) straight away. Other possible signs of stroke include sudden numbness or weakness, especially on one side of the body, sudden loss of vision, dizziness or loss of balance, a sudden severe headache, or trouble swallowing. Note the time the symptoms started, because doctors will ask, and it helps them choose treatment. Do not give the person anything to eat or drink, and stay with them, reassuring them, until the ambulance arrives.

sections.key: Symptoms that vanish quickly still need urgent attention, and many risks can be reduced.
sections.b: Sometimes stroke symptoms appear and then disappear within minutes or hours. This is often a transient ischaemic attack, or TIA, sometimes called a mini stroke. It can be a warning that a major stroke may follow, so it still needs urgent medical attention, even if the person feels fine. For both heart attack and stroke, many risk factors can be reduced: high blood pressure, high cholesterol, smoking, diabetes, physical inactivity, excess weight and heavy drinking. Regular health checks with a GP help find problems early. This lesson is general information, not medical advice. For more, see the Heart Foundation, the Stroke Foundation and healthdirect. In an emergency, always call Triple Zero (000), and consider doing a first aid course, which teaches CPR and defibrillator use hands on.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a heart attack and a cardiac arrest?
o: A heart attack is a blocked artery; a cardiac arrest is when the heart stops pumping effectively
A cardiac arrest only affects children
A heart attack always happens in the brain
quiz.e: A heart attack is a blockage, while cardiac arrest is a rhythm failure where the heart stops pumping properly.

quiz.q: Which of these can be a warning sign of a heart attack?
o: Pain spreading to the jaw or back
An itchy rash on the legs
quiz.e: Chest discomfort can spread to the arm, shoulder, neck, jaw or back.

quiz.q: Why should a person having a heart attack not drive themselves to hospital?
o: Paramedics can start treatment and manage a cardiac arrest
It is illegal to drive after dark
Ambulances are always faster than cars
quiz.e: Paramedics can treat immediately and handle a collapse on the way.

quiz.q: In the F.A.S.T. test, what does the A stand for?
quiz.e: A is for Arms: can the person lift both arms?

quiz.q: Stroke symptoms disappear after 15 minutes. What should happen?
o: Seek urgent medical attention, as it may be a TIA
quiz.e: A TIA can warn of a coming major stroke, so it still needs urgent care.

LESSONS.title: Lost in the bush: how to be found
LESSONS.hook: Every year in Australia, bushwalkers, campers and tourists get lost, and most are found alive. The ones who do best usually prepared before they left and stayed calm once things went wrong.

sections.key: Getting lost usually starts with small, ordinary mistakes rather than a dramatic event.
sections.b: Few people set out to have an adventure that ends in a police search. More often, it begins with something small. A walker follows a faint side trail that looks like a shortcut. A day hike runs late and the light fades. Mist rolls in on a ridge, and every gum tree suddenly looks the same. A tired walker takes a wrong turn at an unmarked junction and keeps going, hoping the track will reconnect. Search and rescue teams know these patterns well. People rarely realise they are lost straight away, and the urge to keep moving, to fix the problem quickly, often carries them further from where searchers will look. Understanding how it happens is the first step to avoiding it, and to responding well if it happens to you.

sections.key: Leave a trip plan, check conditions and carry the right gear, including a way to call for help.
sections.b: The single most important safety step happens before you leave home. Tell a reliable person where you are going, your route, who is with you, and when you expect to be back, along with a time when they should raise the alarm. Some national parks also have walker registration or trip intention forms. Check the weather forecast, fire danger ratings and park alerts. Carry more water than you expect to need, extra food, warm and waterproof layers, a torch, a first aid kit, and a map with a compass or a GPS device, and know how to use them. Do not rely on a phone alone, since coverage is patchy and batteries die. Many experienced walkers carry a personal locator beacon, and in some areas you can borrow one free.

sections.key: A PLB can send a distress signal with your location to rescuers via satellite, even with no phone coverage.
sections.b: A personal locator beacon, or PLB, is a small device that, when activated, sends a distress signal via satellite to search and rescue authorities. In Australia, these signals are received by the Australian Maritime Safety Authority, which coordinates with police and other agencies. Most modern beacons include GPS, so rescuers receive your location accurately, often within minutes. PLBs work almost anywhere outdoors with a clear view of the sky, far beyond mobile coverage, and do not need a subscription. You should register your beacon with AMSA, which is free, so rescuers know who you are and who to contact. Only activate it in a genuine life threatening emergency. Some newer smartphones and satellite messengers offer emergency satellite messaging too, but check exactly how your device works before relying on it.

sections.key: If you realise you are lost, stop moving, stay calm and make a plan.
sections.b: The moment you realise you do not know where you are, the most useful thing you can do is stop. Many outdoor organisations teach the idea of STOP: Stop, Think, Observe, Plan. Sit down, have a drink of water and let the first rush of panic pass. Think about when you last knew for certain where you were. Observe your surroundings, the time of day, the weather and how much water, food and battery you have. Then make a plan. If you can confidently retrace your steps to a known point, that may be sensible. If not, the best plan is usually to stay where you are, especially if someone knows your trip plan. Wandering further makes you harder to find, burns energy and water, and can lead into steep or dangerous country.

sections.key: Protecting yourself from the weather is often more urgent than finding food.
sections.b: Survival instructors often use a rough rule of threes as a reminder of priorities: a person can survive around three hours in harsh conditions without shelter, around three days without water and around three weeks without food. The numbers vary greatly, but the order is useful. In hot conditions, find shade, rest during the heat of the day and ration your effort rather than your water, drinking what you need. In cold, wet or windy conditions, which occur in alpine areas and Tasmania even in summer, hypothermia is a serious danger. Put on all your layers, get out of the wind, and insulate yourself from the cold ground with leaves, a pack or anything dry. Food matters least. Most people can go several days without eating and still be found in reasonable health.

sections.key: Make yourself big, bright and noisy, and stay close to open ground.
sections.b: Searchers on foot, in vehicles and in helicopters will be looking for you, so make yourself easy to spot. Choose a spot near a clearing, track or open ridge if you can reach one safely, as people under thick canopy are very hard to see from the air. Lay out bright clothing, a space blanket or other colourful gear. Three of anything, such as three whistle blasts, three flashes of light or three piles of rocks, is widely recognised as a distress signal. A whistle carries much further than a voice and uses far less energy. A small mirror, or even a phone screen, can flash sunlight toward aircraft. If you have a phone, turn it off or into low power mode between checks, so it lasts long enough to be useful.

sections.key: If you have any signal, call Triple Zero (000), and keep your phone charged for searchers.
sections.b: If you have mobile reception, call Triple Zero (000) and ask for police, who coordinate land searches in Australia. In many cases, an emergency call from a mobile can connect through another carrier's network if yours has no coverage. The Emergency+ app can show your GPS coordinates to read to the operator. Once you have reported your situation, stay where you are unless told otherwise, and follow instructions carefully. If you cannot get a call through, a text message to family may sometimes slip through when a call will not. Remember too that being found is not the end of the story: rescuers may need to treat dehydration, hypothermia or injuries. This lesson is general information, not a substitute for proper training, so consider a first aid and outdoor navigation course.

quiz.q: What often makes lost walkers harder to find?
o: The urge to keep moving to fix the problem quickly
quiz.e: Moving on takes people further from where searchers will look.

quiz.q: In Australia, which agency receives signals from personal locator beacons?
quiz.e: AMSA receives beacon signals and coordinates with police and rescue agencies.

quiz.q: What does the STOP approach stand for?
quiz.e: Stop, Think, Observe, Plan helps you avoid panicked decisions.

quiz.q: According to the rough rule of threes, which priority comes before water?
quiz.e: Protection from harsh weather is usually the most urgent need.

quiz.q: Which is widely recognised as a distress signal?
o: Three of anything, such as three whistle blasts
quiz.e: Three signals in a row is a widely recognised call for help.

LESSONS.title: Magnetism: the invisible pull
LESSONS.hook: A fridge magnet, a compass needle and the southern lights are all showing you the same hidden force at work.

sections.key: People knew magnetic rocks for thousands of years before anyone could explain them.
sections.b: Long before anyone understood it, people noticed that certain dark rocks could pull iron towards them. These rocks, called lodestones, are made of a mineral called magnetite that has become naturally magnetised, possibly by lightning strikes. Ancient Greek and Chinese writers both described them. In China, lodestones were shaped into spoons that swung round to point in a fixed direction, and by around the eleventh century Chinese sailors were using magnetised needles to steer at sea. The compass later spread to the Arab world and Europe, where it helped make the great ocean voyages possible. For centuries, though, nobody could say why a sliver of iron should care which way north was. The answer turned out to lie deep inside atoms, and deep inside the Earth itself.

sections.key: Every electron behaves like a tiny magnet, and magnetism appears when those tiny magnets line up.
sections.b: Every atom contains electrons, and each electron behaves like a minuscule bar magnet with its own north and south pole. This comes from a quantum property physicists call spin, along with the way electrons move around the nucleus. In most materials, electrons pair up so that their magnetic effects point in opposite directions and cancel out. Wood, plastic, water and your own body are mostly like this, which is why a fridge magnet ignores them. In a few materials, however, some electrons are left unpaired, and their little magnetic fields can add together instead of cancelling. When enough of them point the same way, the whole object becomes magnetic. So a magnet is not doing anything mysterious: it is simply what happens when billions upon billions of tiny magnets agree on a direction.

sections.key: Iron, nickel and cobalt contain magnetic domains that can be lined up, and heat can scramble them again.
sections.b: Try sticking a magnet to a soft drink can and it will slide off, because aluminium is barely magnetic. A steel food tin is a different story. Iron, nickel and cobalt are the classic magnetic metals, a behaviour called ferromagnetism. Inside them, atoms group into tiny regions called domains, each one already magnetised in its own direction. In an ordinary nail, the domains point every which way and cancel out. Bring a strong magnet near and the domains swing into line, so the nail itself becomes a magnet for a while. Permanent magnets are materials whose domains stay aligned. Heat works against all this order. Above a certain temperature, called the Curie point, which is about 770 degrees Celsius for iron, the jiggling of atoms scrambles the domains and the magnetism disappears.

sections.h: Electricity and magnetism are one force
sections.key: In the 1800s scientists discovered that moving electric charges make magnetism, and moving magnets make electricity.
sections.b: In 1820, the Danish physicist Hans Christian Oersted noticed something odd during a lecture demonstration: a compass needle twitched whenever he switched on an electric current in a nearby wire. Electricity, it seemed, could create magnetism. About a decade later, in 1831, Michael Faraday in London showed the reverse. Moving a magnet near a coil of wire made a current flow, an effect called electromagnetic induction. In the 1860s, the Scottish physicist James Clerk Maxwell wrote down a set of equations showing that electricity and magnetism are two faces of a single force, electromagnetism. His equations also predicted waves of electric and magnetic fields travelling at the speed of light. The conclusion was startling: light itself is an electromagnetic wave, and so are radio waves, microwaves and X-rays.

sections.h: Magnets that run the modern world
sections.key: Generators, motors, speakers and medical scanners all rely on the link between magnets and electricity.
sections.b: Faraday's discovery quietly powers your life. Nearly every power station, whether it burns coal, uses falling water or harnesses wind, makes electricity the same basic way: something spins a magnet and a coil of wire relative to each other, and induction pushes a current through the coil. Electric motors run the trick backwards, using current and magnets to create a spinning force. There are motors in your fridge, washing machine, car windows and phone's vibrating buzzer. Speakers and headphones use a magnet and a coil to push a thin cone back and forth, turning an electrical signal into sound. Hospitals use enormously powerful magnets in MRI machines, which line up the hydrogen atoms in your body and then listen to the faint radio signals they give off, producing detailed images without X-rays.

sections.key: Swirling molten iron deep underground makes Earth a giant magnet that protects us from the solar wind.
sections.b: The Earth behaves like a huge magnet, which is why compasses work. Its field is generated about 3,000 kilometres below your feet, in the outer core, where molten iron churns and flows. That moving, electrically conducting metal acts as a natural dynamo, keeping the field going. The field reaches far out into space and deflects most of the solar wind, a stream of charged particles pouring off the Sun. Some of those particles are funnelled towards the poles, where they collide with gases in the upper atmosphere and make them glow: in the Southern Hemisphere, that glow is the aurora australis, sometimes seen from Tasmania. The field is restless. The magnetic poles wander, and every so often the whole field flips. The last full reversal happened roughly 780,000 years ago.

sections.key: Many animals sense Earth's magnetic field, although exactly how they do it is still being worked out.
sections.b: Humans need a compass, but many animals seem to carry one inside them. Experiments have shown that migratory birds, sea turtles, salmon and even some insects use Earth's magnetic field to find their way. Young loggerhead turtles, for example, appear to read the field's strength and angle to stay on course across thousands of kilometres of open ocean. How they actually sense it is one of biology's lingering puzzles. One leading idea is that light-sensitive proteins in birds' eyes react to magnetism, perhaps letting them 'see' the field as a faint pattern laid over their vision. Another is that tiny grains of magnetite in some animals' bodies act like compass needles. Both may be true in different species. Either way, the force holding a shopping list to your fridge steers animals around the planet.

quiz.q: What are naturally magnetic rocks called?
quiz.e: Lodestones are pieces of the mineral magnetite that have become naturally magnetised.

quiz.q: What happens to iron above its Curie point?
o: It loses its magnetism as heat scrambles its domains
quiz.e: Above about 770 degrees Celsius, atomic jiggling scrambles iron's magnetic domains.

quiz.q: What did Maxwell's equations reveal about light?
o: It is made of tiny magnets
quiz.e: Maxwell showed that waves of electric and magnetic fields travel at the speed of light, so light is electromagnetic.

quiz.q: What causes the aurora australis?
o: Charged particles from the Sun, funnelled towards the poles, making upper-atmosphere gases glow
quiz.e: Earth's magnetic field steers some solar wind particles towards the poles, where they make gases in the upper atmosphere glow.

quiz.q: Which statement about animal magnetic sense is accurate?
o: Scientists are still working out exactly how animals sense the field
quiz.e: Many animals use the field, but the mechanism is still an open research question.

LESSONS.title: How sound travels
LESSONS.hook: Every voice, song and thunderclap is just air being squeezed and stretched, and the physics explains everything from echoes to sonic booms.

sections.key: Sound is a travelling ripple of pressure, not a stream of air rushing from the source to your ear.
sections.b: Clap your hands and you shove the air between them outwards. Those air molecules bump into their neighbours, which bump into theirs, and a ripple of squashed and stretched air spreads out in every direction. That travelling ripple is sound. It is a pressure wave, and the air itself barely moves: each molecule just nudges back and forth and passes the push along, a bit like a ripple running down a slinky. When the wave reaches you, it pushes and pulls on your eardrum, which vibrates in step. Tiny bones in your middle ear pass that vibration to the fluid filled cochlea, where thousands of hair cells turn it into nerve signals. Your brain then does the remarkable work of turning those signals into a friend's laugh or a favourite song.

sections.key: Sound travels about 343 metres per second in air, and much faster through water and solids.
sections.b: In air at around 20 degrees Celsius, sound travels about 343 metres every second, roughly a kilometre in three seconds. Light is almost a million times faster, which is why you see lightning before you hear the thunder. You can use this to estimate how far away a storm is: count the seconds between the flash and the rumble, then divide by three to get the distance in kilometres. Sound moves faster in warm air than cold air, and much faster through liquids and solids, where particles are packed closely and pass the push along more quickly. In seawater it travels at roughly 1,500 metres per second, and in steel several times faster again. That is why you can hear an approaching train through the rails before you hear it through the air.

sections.key: How high or low a sound seems depends on how many times per second the wave vibrates.
sections.b: The number of pressure waves that pass each second is called the frequency, measured in hertz. A deep note vibrates slowly and a high note vibrates quickly. The A above middle C, which orchestras often tune to, is usually set at 440 hertz, meaning 440 vibrations every second. Young people can typically hear from about 20 hertz up to about 20,000 hertz. The top of that range shrinks with age, which is why some teenagers can hear a high pitched whine from electronics that their parents cannot. Below our range lies infrasound, used by elephants to communicate over long distances. Above it lies ultrasound, which dogs, bats and dolphins can hear. Musical instruments sound different even on the same note because each adds its own mix of higher frequencies, called overtones.

sections.key: The decibel scale is logarithmic, so small increases in the number mean big jumps in sound energy.
sections.b: Loudness depends on how strongly the wave squeezes the air, and we measure it in decibels. The scale is logarithmic: every increase of 10 decibels means ten times more sound energy, and our ears hear it as roughly twice as loud. A quiet library might sit around 30 to 40 decibels, normal conversation around 60, and a loud concert can reach well over 100. That means a concert carries many millions of times more sound energy than a whisper. Your hearing is precious and hard to repair. Long or repeated exposure to sounds above roughly 85 decibels can permanently damage the delicate hair cells in your inner ear. This is general information rather than medical advice, so if you notice ringing or muffled hearing, healthdirect is a good place to start.

sections.key: Bats, dolphins, ships and hospital scanners all use returning echoes to build a picture of the world.
sections.b: Shout across a valley and the sound bounces off the far side and returns as an echo. Some animals have turned this into a superpower. Many bats send out rapid, high pitched calls and listen to the echoes, judging the distance, size and even texture of insects in total darkness. Dolphins and toothed whales do something similar underwater with clicks. This skill is called echolocation. Humans copied the idea with sonar, which ships and submarines use to map the seafloor and detect objects beneath the waves. Medical ultrasound works on the same principle. A probe sends very high frequency sound into the body and listens for echoes bouncing off organs and tissues, which a computer turns into an image. It is how many parents first see their baby on a screen.

sections.key: A sound's pitch rises as its source approaches you and falls as it moves away.
sections.b: Stand beside a road as an ambulance races past and you will hear its siren drop in pitch the moment it passes. The siren itself has not changed. As the ambulance comes towards you, each new sound wave is sent out from a little closer than the last, so the waves bunch up and arrive more often, giving a higher pitch. As it moves away, the waves are stretched out and the pitch falls. This is called the Doppler effect, after the Austrian physicist Christian Doppler, who described it in 1842. It works for any kind of wave. Police radar uses it with radio waves to measure a car's speed, weather radar uses it to track wind inside storms, and astronomers use it with light to tell how fast distant galaxies are moving away.

sections.h: Silence in space and the sound barrier
sections.key: Sound needs something to travel through, and anything that outruns it creates a sonic boom.
sections.b: Science fiction films are full of roaring explosions in space, but real space would be silent. Sound is a vibration passed from particle to particle, and the near vacuum between planets has almost no particles to carry it. Astronauts on a spacewalk talk to each other by radio, which uses electromagnetic waves that need no medium. Back on Earth, something interesting happens when an object travels faster than sound. A jet flying at supersonic speed outruns its own pressure waves, which pile up into a cone shaped shock wave. When that shock wave sweeps over you, you hear a sudden sonic boom. The first officially confirmed supersonic flight in level flight was made by American pilot Chuck Yeager in the Bell X-1 rocket plane in 1947. A cracking whip makes a tiny sonic boom too.

quiz.q: What actually travels from a sound source to your ear?
o: A stream of air rushing towards you
A pressure wave passed between molecules
quiz.e: Air molecules only nudge back and forth, passing along a wave of pressure.

quiz.q: Roughly how far away is a storm if thunder arrives six seconds after the lightning?
quiz.e: Sound travels roughly a kilometre every three seconds, so six seconds means about two kilometres.

quiz.q: An increase of 10 decibels means about how much more sound energy?
quiz.e: The decibel scale is logarithmic: each 10 decibel step is ten times more energy.

quiz.q: What do bats use echolocation for?
o: Finding and judging objects in the dark
quiz.e: Bats listen to the echoes of their calls to locate insects and obstacles in darkness.

quiz.q: Why does an ambulance siren drop in pitch as it passes?
o: The driver changes the siren setting
Sound slows down after passing you
The waves are stretched out as it moves away
quiz.e: This is the Doppler effect: moving away stretches the waves, lowering the pitch.

LESSONS.title: Photosynthesis: how plants eat sunlight
LESSONS.hook: A towering gum tree is built mostly from thin air, and the process that does it also made the oxygen you are breathing.

sections.h: Where a tree's weight comes from
sections.key: A tree's mass comes mostly from carbon dioxide in the air, not from the soil.
sections.b: In the 1600s, the Flemish scientist Jan Baptist van Helmont ran a famous experiment. He planted a small willow in a pot of carefully weighed, dried soil and gave it nothing but water for five years. The willow gained a great deal of weight, yet when he dried and weighed the soil again, it had barely changed. Van Helmont concluded that the tree was made from water. He was partly right, but he missed the most surprising ingredient. Most of the dry mass of a plant is carbon, and that carbon comes from carbon dioxide drawn out of the air. A huge gum tree is, in a very real sense, built from thin air, stitched together with water and powered by sunlight. The process that does this is called photosynthesis.
