sections.key: Plants use light energy to turn carbon dioxide and water into sugar, releasing oxygen as a by-product.
sections.b: Photosynthesis takes three simple ingredients and makes something far more valuable. A plant draws water up from its roots and takes in carbon dioxide through tiny pores in its leaves called stomata. Using the energy in sunlight, it rearranges these molecules into glucose, a sugar, and releases oxygen into the air. In chemical shorthand, six molecules of carbon dioxide plus six of water become one molecule of glucose and six of oxygen. The glucose is the plant's food and building material. It can be burned for energy, stored as starch, or linked into long chains of cellulose to make tough cell walls and wood. Almost every food you eat traces back to this reaction, whether you eat the plant directly or eat an animal that did.

sections.key: Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light and reflects green, which is the colour we see.
sections.b: The green colour of leaves comes from a pigment called chlorophyll, packed inside tiny structures called chloroplasts. Chlorophyll is very good at absorbing red and blue light, which it uses to power photosynthesis. It is poor at absorbing green light, so much of that green bounces back towards our eyes. Leaves also contain yellow and orange pigments called carotenoids. In many deciduous trees, autumn reveals them. As days shorten, the tree stops making chlorophyll and breaks down what it has, and the hidden yellows and oranges show through. Red autumn colours are different: they often come from new pigments made in the leaf at that time of year. Most Australian native trees, including eucalypts, are evergreen, so the famous autumn displays here usually come from introduced species.

sections.key: Plants split water molecules, and the oxygen they release comes from that water, not from carbon dioxide.
sections.b: It seems natural to assume that the oxygen plants breathe out comes from the carbon dioxide they take in. After all, carbon dioxide contains oxygen. But experiments in the 1940s using a heavier, traceable form of oxygen showed something different. When scientists labelled the oxygen in water, the labelled oxygen appeared in the gas the plants released. When they labelled the carbon dioxide instead, it did not. The oxygen we breathe comes from water molecules that plants rip apart using the energy of light. This splitting of water is one of the hardest tricks in chemistry, and plants do it at ordinary temperatures, powered only by sunshine. Researchers are still trying to copy it efficiently in the lab, in the hope of making clean fuels such as hydrogen from sunlight and water.

sections.key: Light reactions capture energy, and a second set of reactions uses it to build sugar from carbon dioxide.
sections.b: Photosynthesis happens in two linked stages inside the chloroplast. In the first, called the light dependent reactions, chlorophyll absorbs light and uses its energy to split water, release oxygen and charge up two energy carrying molecules, known as ATP and NADPH. Think of them as freshly charged batteries. In the second stage, often called the Calvin cycle after the American chemist Melvin Calvin, those batteries power the construction of sugar. Carbon dioxide from the air is grabbed by an enzyme called RuBisCO and fixed into an organic molecule, which is then reshaped step by step into sugar. RuBisCO is slow and sometimes grabs oxygen by mistake, so plants make vast amounts of it. It is often described as probably the most abundant protein on Earth.

sections.h: Plants built for heat and drought
sections.key: Some plants, such as sugarcane and cacti, use clever variations of photosynthesis to cope with heat and dryness.
sections.b: Every time a plant opens its stomata to take in carbon dioxide, precious water escapes. In hot, dry places, that is a real problem. Some plants have evolved ways around it. Sugarcane, maize and many tropical grasses use a method called C4 photosynthesis. They first capture carbon dioxide into a small four carbon molecule, then concentrate it around RuBisCO, which makes the process more efficient in heat and strong light. Australia's spinifex grasses, which cover huge areas of the arid inland, also use this approach. Cacti, pineapples and many succulents go further with a method called CAM. They open their stomata only at night, when it is cooler and less water is lost, store the carbon dioxide as an acid, and then use it for photosynthesis during the day with their pores shut tight.

sections.key: Tiny microbes that learned to photosynthesise filled the air with oxygen and transformed Earth.
sections.b: Photosynthesis is far older than plants. It was first developed by microbes, and one group, the cyanobacteria, worked out how to split water and release oxygen. Over hundreds of millions of years, their oxygen built up, and around 2.4 billion years ago the atmosphere changed dramatically in what geologists call the Great Oxidation Event. Some of that early oxygen reacted with iron dissolved in the oceans, helping to form banded iron formations. Western Australia's Pilbara region holds spectacular examples, and they supply much of the iron ore the country exports. Today, tiny ocean plankton are thought to produce around half of the world's oxygen, with land plants providing much of the rest. Even the coal, oil and gas we burn are stored sunlight, captured by photosynthesis millions of years ago.

quiz.q: Where does most of a tree's dry mass come from?
quiz.e: Most of a plant's dry mass is carbon taken from carbon dioxide in the air.

quiz.q: Why do most leaves look green?
o: Chlorophyll reflects green light rather than absorbing it
Green light is the strongest in sunlight
quiz.e: Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light well but reflects much of the green.

quiz.q: Where does the oxygen released by plants come from?
o: Water molecules split using light energy
quiz.e: Labelling experiments showed the oxygen comes from water, not carbon dioxide.

quiz.q: What is special about CAM plants such as cacti?
o: They take in oxygen instead of carbon dioxide
They open their pores at night to save water
quiz.e: CAM plants collect carbon dioxide at night, when less water is lost, and keep their pores shut by day.

quiz.q: What was the Great Oxidation Event?
o: The build up of oxygen in the atmosphere about 2.4 billion years ago
quiz.e: Oxygen released by cyanobacteria built up in the air around 2.4 billion years ago.

LESSONS.title: The cell: life's building block
LESSONS.hook: You are a walking city of tens of trillions of cells, each one a busy factory with its own power stations, post office and instruction library.

sections.h: A look through a slice of cork
sections.key: Cells were first seen in the 1600s, when early microscopes opened up a hidden world.
sections.b: In 1665, the English scientist Robert Hooke published a book called Micrographia, full of detailed drawings of what he saw through his microscope. Looking at a thin slice of cork, he saw rows of tiny empty boxes. They reminded him of the small rooms monks lived in, so he called them cells. What he was actually seeing were the walls of dead plant cells. A few years later, the Dutch draper Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, who ground his own remarkably powerful lenses, looked at pond water and scrapings from his own teeth. He was astonished to find them swarming with tiny moving creatures he called animalcules. These were bacteria and other single celled organisms, and no human had ever seen them before. A whole living world had been invisible all along.

sections.key: All living things are made of cells, and every cell comes from an existing cell.
sections.b: It took nearly two centuries for scientists to grasp how important cells are. In the late 1830s, the German scientists Matthias Schleiden and Theodor Schwann argued that all plants and all animals are built from cells. In the 1850s, the physician Rudolf Virchow popularised a crucial addition: every cell comes from another cell. Together, these ideas became cell theory, one of the foundations of biology. It sounds simple, but it overturned the old belief that life could spring spontaneously from mud or rotting meat. It also changed medicine. If the body is a community of cells, then disease can be understood as something going wrong in those cells. Virchow used this thinking to study conditions such as cancer, and modern medicine still works at this cellular level.

sections.key: An adult human body contains roughly 30 trillion cells, most of them red blood cells.
sections.b: Counting the cells in a human body is surprisingly hard, but recent scientific estimates suggest an average adult has somewhere around 30 trillion of them. That is thousands of times more than the number of people on Earth. By far the most numerous are red blood cells, which make up most of the total by count. They are tiny discs with no nucleus, built to carry oxygen. Cells come in a dazzling range of shapes and sizes. Some nerve cells send fibres that can run from the base of your spine down to your foot, about a metre long. A human egg cell is one of the largest and can just about be seen with the naked eye. You also carry a similar number of bacteria, mostly in your gut.

sections.key: Every cell is wrapped in a thin, oily membrane that controls what gets in and out.
sections.b: Every cell is surrounded by a membrane, a flexible skin only a few billionths of a metre thick. It is made of two layers of fatty molecules called phospholipids. Each has a head that likes water and a tail that avoids it, so in a watery environment they naturally line up tail to tail, forming a double layer that keeps the inside in and the outside out. But a cell cannot be sealed shut, because it needs to take in food and get rid of waste. So the membrane is studded with proteins that act as gates, pumps and messengers. Some let only certain substances through, such as sugar or particular salts. Others act like doorbells, receiving signals from hormones or other cells and passing the message inside, so the cell knows how to respond.

sections.key: Cells contain specialised parts that store instructions, build proteins and supply energy.
sections.b: A typical animal or plant cell is crowded with specialised parts called organelles. The nucleus is the control centre, holding the DNA that contains instructions for building proteins. Those instructions are copied and sent out into the cell, where ribosomes, tiny molecular machines, read them and assemble proteins one building block at a time. A folded network called the endoplasmic reticulum helps make and transport many proteins, and the Golgi apparatus packages and labels them for delivery, a bit like a post office. Mitochondria release energy from food, producing a molecule called ATP that powers almost everything the cell does. Plant cells also contain chloroplasts for photosynthesis and a stiff wall for support. Bacteria are simpler cells with no nucleus at all; their DNA simply floats inside them.

sections.key: The power stations in your cells are descended from free living bacteria swallowed long ago.
sections.b: One of the most surprising ideas in biology is that parts of your cells were once separate living things. The theory, championed by the American biologist Lynn Margulis from the late 1960s, says that mitochondria began as free living bacteria. Long ago, more than a billion years back, one cell engulfed another but did not digest it. Instead the two formed a partnership: the guest supplied energy and the host supplied shelter and food. Over time, the guest became a permanent part of the cell. The evidence is strong. Mitochondria have their own small loop of DNA, similar to bacterial DNA, and they divide on their own, much as bacteria do. Chloroplasts in plants appear to have the same kind of origin, from captured cyanobacteria. You inherit your mitochondria from your mother.

sections.key: Cells constantly divide to grow and repair the body, and cancer happens when that control breaks down.
sections.b: You began as a single fertilised egg, and every one of your trillions of cells came from that first cell dividing again and again. Before a cell divides, it copies its DNA, then splits so each new cell gets a full set. This process continues throughout life. The lining of your gut is renewed every few days, and red blood cells last only about four months before being replaced. Most nerve cells in your brain, however, are thought to last most of your life. Division is tightly controlled by signals telling a cell when to grow, stop or die. Cancer is what happens when mutations break those controls, so cells keep dividing when they should not. Understanding the cell is why modern cancer treatments can target specific faults.

quiz.q: Why did Robert Hooke choose the word 'cell'?
o: The boxes looked like small rooms monks lived in
quiz.e: The cork's tiny boxes reminded Hooke of monks' small rooms, called cells.

quiz.q: Which idea is part of cell theory?
o: Life can arise from rotting meat
Only animals are made of cells
Every cell comes from another cell
Cells are made of atoms of life
quiz.e: Cell theory says all living things are made of cells and every cell comes from an existing cell.

quiz.q: Which cells are the most numerous in the human body by count?
quiz.e: Red blood cells make up most of the body's cells by number.

quiz.q: What do ribosomes do?
quiz.e: Ribosomes read copied instructions and assemble proteins.

quiz.q: What is a key piece of evidence that mitochondria were once bacteria?
o: They are found only in plants
They have their own DNA, similar to bacterial DNA
They can live outside the body
quiz.e: Mitochondria carry their own bacterial style DNA and divide independently.

LESSONS.title: Radioactivity: the restless atom
LESSONS.hook: Some atoms are quietly falling apart all around you, and learning to understand them gave us carbon dating, cancer treatment and nuclear power.

sections.key: Radioactivity was discovered by accident in 1896 when uranium fogged a photographic plate.
sections.b: In 1896, the French physicist Henri Becquerel was investigating whether uranium salts, after soaking up sunlight, gave off the newly discovered X-rays. His plan was to put the salts in the sun on top of photographic plates wrapped in black paper, then see if the plates darkened. A spell of cloudy Paris weather interrupted the experiment, so he tucked everything away in a drawer. When he developed the plates anyway, he found clear images of the uranium salts. No sunlight had been needed. The uranium was giving off some kind of invisible, penetrating radiation all on its own, all the time. Becquerel had stumbled on a property of matter nobody had imagined: some atoms are not stable at all, but are slowly and spontaneously breaking down.

sections.h: Marie Curie and the new elements
sections.key: Marie Curie named radioactivity, discovered two new elements and became the first person to win two Nobel Prizes.
sections.b: Becquerel's discovery caught the attention of a young Polish born scientist in Paris, Marie Sklodowska Curie. Working with her husband Pierre, she measured the mysterious rays and found that their strength depended on the amount of uranium, not its chemical form, suggesting the effect came from inside the atom itself. She coined the term radioactivity. Processing tonnes of uranium ore by hand in a leaky shed, the Curies discovered two new, intensely radioactive elements in 1898: polonium, named after her homeland, and radium. Marie Curie shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics and won the 1911 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, making her the first person to win two. The dangers were not understood then. She died in 1934 of an illness linked to radiation exposure, and her notebooks are still radioactive.

sections.key: Unstable atoms release three main kinds of radiation, each with very different penetrating power.
sections.b: An atom is radioactive when its nucleus has an unstable mix of protons and neutrons. To settle down, it throws off energy or particles, a process called decay. In the early 1900s, the New Zealand born physicist Ernest Rutherford and others identified three main types. Alpha particles are clumps of two protons and two neutrons. They are heavy and slow, and a sheet of paper or the outer layer of your skin stops them, though they are harmful if breathed in or swallowed. Beta particles are fast electrons, stopped by a thin sheet of aluminium. Gamma rays are high energy electromagnetic waves, like extremely powerful X-rays, and need thick lead or concrete to block them. When an atom gives off an alpha or beta particle, it actually turns into a different element.

sections.key: No one can predict when a single atom will decay, but a large group decays at a perfectly regular rate.
sections.b: Radioactive decay is truly random. There is no way to predict when any particular unstable atom will break down. Yet in a large collection of atoms, the overall pattern is beautifully regular. The half-life is the time it takes for half of the atoms in a sample to decay. After one half-life, half remain; after two, a quarter; after three, an eighth. Half-lives range wildly, from tiny fractions of a second to billions of years. Uranium-238 has a half-life of about 4.5 billion years, roughly the age of the Earth. Carbon-14, which is constantly made in the atmosphere and absorbed by living things, has a half-life of about 5,730 years. Measuring how much is left in old bones, wood or charcoal lets scientists date them back roughly 50,000 years.

sections.key: We are exposed to low levels of natural background radiation every day, from rocks, space and even food.
sections.b: Radiation is not only found in power plants and laboratories. Everyone is exposed to a low level of natural background radiation all the time. Some comes from rocks and soil, which contain traces of uranium, thorium and potassium. Some comes from radon, a radioactive gas that seeps out of the ground. More arrives from space as cosmic rays, which is why you receive a little extra on a long haul flight. Even your food is slightly radioactive. Bananas, for example, contain potassium, a tiny fraction of which is radioactive, and so does your own body. None of this means you should worry about bananas: the doses are extremely small. In Australia, radiation safety is overseen by ARPANSA, the Australian Radiation Protection and Nuclear Safety Agency, which publishes clear information online.

sections.key: Splitting heavy atoms releases enormous energy, which can power cities or, in weapons, destroy them.
sections.b: In late 1938, the German chemists Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann found that bombarding uranium with neutrons produced barium, a much lighter element. Their former colleague Lise Meitner and her nephew Otto Frisch worked out the startling explanation: the uranium nucleus had split in two. They called it fission. The pieces weigh slightly less than the original atom, and the missing mass becomes a huge amount of energy, as Einstein's famous E equals mc squared predicts. Each split also frees more neutrons, which can split more atoms in a chain reaction. Controlled, that heat can boil water to drive turbines in a nuclear power station. Uncontrolled, it is the basis of the atomic bomb. Australia holds some of the world's largest known uranium resources, and whether it should have nuclear power remains a lively debate.

sections.key: Carefully controlled radiation is one of medicine's most valuable tools for diagnosis and treatment.
sections.b: The same property that makes radiation dangerous also makes it useful. Because it can damage cells, carefully aimed beams of radiation are used in radiotherapy to destroy cancer cells while sparing as much healthy tissue as possible. Radioactive substances can also act as tracers. A patient might receive a tiny dose of a short lived radioactive substance, and special cameras then track where it goes, revealing how organs such as the heart, bones or thyroid are working. One of the most widely used is technetium-99m, which has a half-life of about six hours. In Australia, it is produced from materials made in the OPAL research reactor at Lucas Heights in Sydney. This is general information only, so talk to your doctor about any specific scan or treatment.

quiz.q: How was radioactivity discovered?
o: Uranium fogged photographic plates kept in a drawer
A lightning strike hit a lab
Marie Curie saw radium glowing at night
quiz.e: Becquerel found that uranium darkened wrapped photographic plates without any sunlight.

quiz.q: What distinction did Marie Curie achieve?
o: First woman to fly solo across an ocean
First person to win two Nobel Prizes
First person to split the atom
quiz.e: She won Nobel Prizes in Physics in 1903 and Chemistry in 1911.

quiz.q: Which type of radiation can be stopped by a sheet of paper?
quiz.e: Alpha particles are heavy and slow, so paper or the outer layer of skin stops them.

quiz.q: A sample has a half-life of 10 years. How much remains after 20 years?
quiz.e: Two half-lives leave half of a half, which is a quarter.

quiz.q: Who explained that Hahn and Strassmann had split the uranium nucleus?
quiz.e: Meitner and Frisch worked out that the uranium nucleus had split, and named the process fission.

LESSONS.title: Heat and temperature: what 'hot' really means
LESSONS.hook: Why does a tiled floor feel colder than carpet in the same room? The answer reveals what heat and temperature really are.

sections.key: Two objects at the same temperature can feel different because they move heat away from your skin at different rates.
sections.b: On a winter morning, step barefoot from the carpet onto the bathroom tiles and the tiles feel icy. Yet if both have been sitting in the same room overnight, a thermometer would show they are at the same temperature. So why the difference? Your skin does not actually sense temperature directly. It senses how quickly heat is flowing into or out of it. Tiles are good conductors of heat, so they pull warmth away from your feet quickly, and your nerves report cold. Carpet is full of trapped air, a poor conductor, so heat leaves your feet slowly and it feels warmer. The same trick explains why metal playground equipment can burn on a summer afternoon while a wooden bench in the same sun feels merely warm to the touch.

sections.key: Temperature measures how fast particles are moving, while heat is energy flowing from hotter to colder things.
sections.b: Everything is made of atoms and molecules, and they are never still. In a gas they fly about and collide; in a liquid they slide past one another; in a solid they vibrate in place. Temperature is a measure of how vigorously they are moving, on average. Heat is something slightly different. It is energy that flows from a hotter object to a cooler one because of that temperature difference. When you warm your hands on a mug of tea, the fast moving molecules in the mug knock into the slower ones in your skin and pass on some of their energy. A bathtub of warm water holds far more thermal energy than a cup of boiling water, because it has vastly more molecules, even though the cup is at a higher temperature.

sections.key: There is a lowest possible temperature, minus 273.15 degrees Celsius, where particle motion is at its minimum.
sections.b: If temperature is the jiggling of particles, then there must be a point where the jiggling is as small as it can possibly be. That point is called absolute zero: minus 273.15 degrees Celsius. Nothing can be colder. Scientists often use the Kelvin scale, named after the Belfast born physicist William Thomson, Lord Kelvin, which starts at absolute zero. One kelvin is the same size as one degree Celsius, so water freezes at about 273 kelvin and boils at about 373. Absolute zero can never quite be reached, but researchers have cooled atoms to within billionths of a degree of it. At such extreme cold, matter behaves strangely. Some metals lose all electrical resistance, becoming superconductors, and some liquids flow without any friction at all, even creeping up the walls of their containers.

sections.key: Heat travels by conduction through materials, by convection in moving fluids and by radiation through space.
sections.b: Heat gets from place to place in three ways. Conduction is heat passing directly through a material, particle bumping particle, like the handle of a metal spoon warming up in hot soup. Convection happens in liquids and gases, which can flow. Warm fluid is less dense and rises, cooler fluid sinks, and the circulation carries heat around, which is how a heater warms a room and why a pot of water heated from below warms all the way through. Radiation needs no material at all. Every warm object gives off infrared light, and that is how the Sun's warmth crosses 150 million kilometres of empty space to reach your face. A vacuum flask blocks all three: a vacuum between its walls stops conduction and convection, and shiny surfaces reflect radiation back where it came from.

sections.h: Why water is slow to heat
sections.key: Water needs a lot of energy to warm up, which shapes coastal weather and keeps your body cool.
sections.b: Put a metal saucepan and the water inside it on the stove, and the pan gets hot long before the water does. Water has an unusually high heat capacity, meaning it takes a lot of energy to raise its temperature, and it releases that energy slowly as it cools. This has huge effects on weather. Oceans warm up and cool down far more slowly than land, so coastal cities such as Perth and Sydney tend to have milder swings in temperature than inland towns such as Alice Springs. On a hot afternoon, land heats faster than the sea, warm air rises over the land, and cooler air flows in from the ocean as a sea breeze. Water's thirst for energy also cools you: as sweat evaporates, it carries heat away from your skin.

sections.key: The Fahrenheit and Celsius scales both date from the 1700s, and Australia switched to Celsius in the early 1970s.
sections.b: The first reliable thermometers appeared in the early 1700s. The German born instrument maker Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit built accurate mercury thermometers and created the scale that still bears his name, on which water freezes at 32 degrees and boils at 212. A few decades later, the Swedish astronomer Anders Celsius proposed a scale with 100 degrees between freezing and boiling. His original version ran upside down, with water boiling at 0. The scale was flipped soon after his death into the form we use today. Most countries now use Celsius, while the United States still uses Fahrenheit for everyday purposes. Australia switched from Fahrenheit to Celsius in the early 1970s as part of its move to the metric system, which is why older Australians sometimes still talk about a 'century' for a 100 degree day.

sections.key: A fridge does not make cold: it pumps heat from inside to outside using a fluid that evaporates and condenses.
sections.b: Heat naturally flows from hot to cold, never the other way on its own. A fridge pushes it uphill, from the cold inside to the warmer kitchen, and it pays for this with electricity. The trick is a special fluid called a refrigerant, circulating in a closed loop of pipes. Inside the fridge, the refrigerant evaporates at low pressure, and evaporating soaks up heat, just as sweat cools your skin. A compressor then squeezes the vapour, making it hot, and it releases that heat through coils at the back or sides of the fridge, which is why they feel warm. The fluid condenses back to a liquid and the cycle repeats. Reverse cycle air conditioners and heat pumps use the same principle, often moving several units of heat for each unit of electricity used.

quiz.q: Why do tiles feel colder than carpet at the same temperature?
o: Tiles conduct heat away from your skin faster
Tiles absorb moisture from your feet
quiz.e: Your skin senses heat flow, and tiles draw heat away much faster than air filled carpet.

quiz.q: What is absolute zero in degrees Celsius?
quiz.e: Absolute zero is minus 273.15 degrees Celsius, or 0 kelvin.

quiz.q: How does the Sun's heat reach Earth?
quiz.e: Radiation needs no material, so infrared and visible light carry the Sun's energy across space.

quiz.q: Why do coastal cities usually have milder temperature swings than inland towns?
o: Water warms and cools much more slowly than land
Sea breezes only happen at night
quiz.e: Water's high heat capacity means oceans change temperature slowly, moderating nearby climates.

quiz.q: What does a refrigerator actually do?
o: Creates cold and pumps it in
Pumps heat from inside to outside
quiz.e: A fridge uses an evaporating and condensing fluid to move heat out of the cabinet.

LESSONS.title: Enzymes: life's tiny machines
LESSONS.hook: Reactions that would take millions of years on their own happen in your cells in a split second, thanks to molecules called enzymes.

sections.key: Most of the chemical reactions life depends on are far too slow to keep anything alive without help.
sections.b: Your body runs on chemistry. Every second, your cells break down sugars, copy DNA, build proteins and clear away waste. The trouble is that most of these reactions, left to themselves at body temperature, would crawl along at a hopeless pace. Some would take years, and a few would take longer than the age of the Earth. A chemist in a lab might speed things up with strong acids, high pressure or fierce heat, but none of those are options inside a living cell. Life solved the problem with enzymes: large molecules, nearly all of them proteins, that make specific reactions happen enormously faster without being used up themselves. Molecules that speed up reactions in this way are called catalysts, and enzymes are among the most impressive catalysts known.

sections.key: Enzymes were first studied through fermentation, and in 1926 one was shown to be a protein.
sections.b: People used enzymes for thousands of years before anyone knew they existed, in brewing beer, baking bread and making cheese. In the 1800s, scientists argued about fermentation. Louis Pasteur believed it needed living yeast cells. In 1897, the German chemist Eduard Buchner showed that juice squeezed from ground up yeast, with no living cells left, could still turn sugar into alcohol. Something in the juice was doing the work, and he won a Nobel Prize for the finding. The word enzyme, coined in 1877, comes from Greek words meaning 'in yeast'. But what were enzymes made of? In 1926, the American chemist James Sumner crystallised an enzyme called urease from jack beans and showed it was a protein. Many doubted him at first, but he too eventually shared a Nobel Prize.

sections.key: Enzymes lower the energy hurdle a reaction must clear, so many more molecules make it over.
sections.b: Picture a reaction as a ball that must be pushed over a hill before it can roll down the other side. That hill is called the activation energy. Even if the end products are more stable than the starting materials, few molecules have enough energy to get over the top, so the reaction is slow. An enzyme provides an easier route, effectively lowering the hill. It does this in several ways. It can hold reacting molecules close together in exactly the right orientation, stretch or strain chemical bonds so they break more easily, and position charged parts of itself to stabilise the fleeting, awkward arrangement at the top of the hill. An enzyme does not change where the reaction ends up, only how quickly it gets there, and it emerges unchanged, ready to work again.

sections.h: Lock, key and a better fit
sections.key: Each enzyme has an active site shaped to grab particular molecules, and it often changes shape as it does.
sections.b: Enzymes are remarkably choosy. Most work on only one molecule, or a small family of similar ones, called their substrates. The reason is shape. An enzyme is a long chain of amino acids folded into a precise three dimensional form, and somewhere on its surface is a pocket or groove called the active site. In 1894, the German chemist Emil Fischer suggested that a substrate fits its enzyme like a key in a lock. That idea was later refined. In 1958, the American biochemist Daniel Koshland proposed the induced fit model: the active site is somewhat flexible and moulds itself around the substrate as it binds, a bit like a glove tightening around a hand. This shape change can help squeeze the substrate into the form needed for the reaction to happen.

sections.h: Heat, acid and the fragile fold
sections.key: Enzymes work best within narrow ranges of temperature and acidity, and too much heat destroys their shape.
sections.b: Because an enzyme's power depends on its precise folded shape, anything that disturbs that shape can stop it working. Warming an enzyme usually speeds it up at first, as molecules move faster and collide more often. Beyond a certain point, though, the heat shakes the fold apart, a process called denaturation, and activity collapses. You see denaturation every time you cook an egg: the clear egg white turns solid and white as its proteins unravel and tangle, and it never turns back. Most human enzymes work best around body temperature. Acidity matters too. Pepsin, which starts digesting protein in your stomach, thrives in strong acid, while enzymes in your small intestine prefer much milder conditions. Some microbes living in hot springs carry enzymes that keep working close to the boiling point of water.

sections.key: Cells control their enzymes with switches and inhibitors, and many medicines work by blocking enzymes.
sections.b: A cell cannot simply leave all its enzymes running at full speed, or it would waste resources and make too much of some products. So enzymes are regulated. Often the end product of a chain of reactions binds to an enzyme near the start of the chain and slows it down, a neat form of feedback that keeps supplies in balance. Other molecules act as inhibitors, either jamming the active site directly or binding elsewhere and changing the enzyme's shape. Medicine makes heavy use of this. Aspirin works partly by blocking enzymes involved in making substances that cause pain and inflammation. Penicillin blocks enzymes bacteria need to build their cell walls. Many other drugs target specific enzymes too. This is general information only, so ask a doctor or pharmacist about any particular medicine.

sections.h: Enzymes at work in everyday life
sections.key: Enzymes are used in washing powders, food production and research, and scientists now design new ones.
sections.b: Enzymes are quietly at work in many products you use. Biological laundry powders contain enzymes that break down protein, fat and starch stains, letting them work well in cooler water. Cheesemakers have long used rennet, which contains an enzyme that curdles milk. Enzymes help clarify fruit juice, make sweet syrups from starch and tenderise meat; papaya and pineapple contain enzymes that do this, which is why fresh pineapple can stop jelly from setting. In research, an enzyme from a hot spring bacterium, able to survive repeated heating, made possible the PCR technique used to copy DNA. Scientists are now improving enzymes and even designing new ones. The American chemical engineer Frances Arnold shared the 2018 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for using directed evolution to breed better enzymes in the lab.

quiz.q: What is a catalyst?
o: A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up
A product formed at the end of a reaction
quiz.e: Catalysts, including enzymes, speed reactions and come out unchanged.

quiz.q: What did Eduard Buchner show in 1897?
o: Yeast must be alive to ferment sugar
Juice from ground up yeast, with no living cells, could still ferment sugar
quiz.e: Buchner showed the active ingredient worked without living cells.

quiz.q: How does an enzyme speed up a reaction?
o: By adding heat to the cell
By being consumed in the reaction
quiz.e: Enzymes provide an easier route over the energy hill without changing where the reaction ends up.

quiz.q: What happens when an enzyme is denatured?
o: It turns into a different enzyme
Its folded shape unravels and it stops working
quiz.e: Too much heat or the wrong acidity unravels the enzyme's precise fold.

quiz.q: How does penicillin work?
o: It blocks enzymes bacteria need to build their cell walls
It provides energy to immune cells
quiz.e: Penicillin inhibits bacterial enzymes involved in cell wall construction.

LESSONS.title: The secret life of soil
LESSONS.hook: The ground beneath your feet is not dirt: it is a living, breathing system that took thousands of years to build and feeds almost everything on land.

sections.key: Healthy soil is packed with living things, from bacteria and fungi to worms and insects.
sections.b: Scoop up a handful of rich garden soil and you are holding one of the most crowded habitats on Earth. Soil scientists often point out that a single teaspoon of healthy soil can contain more microorganisms than there are people on the planet. Many are bacteria, along with fungi, single celled protists and microscopic worms called nematodes. Add mites, springtails, beetle larvae, ants and earthworms, and soil turns out to be teeming with life. Most of these organisms have never been studied, and many have not even been named. That earthy smell after rain comes partly from a compound called geosmin, made by certain soil bacteria. People are remarkably sensitive to it. Far from being lifeless dirt, soil is a busy underground city where the business of recycling life goes on day and night.

sections.key: Soil forms slowly as rock breaks down and mixes with decaying plants and animals.
sections.b: Soil begins with rock. Over long periods, rock is broken apart by heat and cold, by water freezing in cracks, by plant roots and by chemical reactions with rainwater. Lichens and mosses colonise the surface, and as they live and die they add organic material. Microbes and small animals then break that material down, mixing it with the mineral grains. Gradually, layers form. Near the top is usually a darker layer rich in decomposed organic matter called humus, with paler, more mineral layers below, and the parent rock beneath them all. This process is extremely slow. Depending on climate and rock type, forming just a few centimetres of new soil can take hundreds of years or more. That is why soil lost to erosion is, on any human timescale, effectively lost for good.

sections.key: The size of mineral particles in soil controls how it holds water, air and nutrients.
sections.b: The mineral part of soil is made of particles of three main sizes. Sand grains are the largest and feel gritty between your fingers. Silt is finer and feels smooth, a bit like flour. Clay particles are tiny, far too small to see, and feel sticky when wet. The balance of these three gives a soil its texture, and texture matters enormously. Sandy soil drains quickly and warms up fast but struggles to hold water and nutrients. Clay holds plenty of water and nutrients but can become waterlogged, and sets hard when it dries out. Gardeners prize loam, a mix of all three, which holds moisture while still letting air reach the roots. A simple test is to roll a moist pinch between your fingers: clay forms a ribbon, sand falls apart.

sections.key: Most plants partner with soil fungi, trading sugar for water and nutrients.
sections.b: Dig up the roots of most plants and look closely, and you will often find them wrapped in fine threads of fungus. These partnerships are called mycorrhizae, from Greek words meaning 'fungus' and 'root', and they are thought to involve the large majority of land plant species. The deal is a trade. The plant supplies the fungus with sugars made by photosynthesis. In return, the fungus spreads a vast web of thread-like hyphae through the soil, reaching far beyond the roots and bringing back water and nutrients, especially phosphorus. Fossil evidence suggests these partnerships are ancient and may have helped the first plants colonise land. Popular claims that forests share food and warnings through a fungal 'wood wide web' are debated by scientists, so treat them with caution.

sections.key: Earthworms and decomposers turn dead material back into nutrients that plants can use again.
sections.b: Charles Darwin was fascinated by earthworms. His last book, published in 1881, was devoted entirely to them and argued that worms had a huge influence on the landscape by constantly churning and enriching the soil. He was right. Earthworms swallow soil and decaying plant matter, then leave behind castings that are rich in nutrients. Their tunnels let air and water reach deep into the ground. Alongside them, bacteria and fungi do the bulk of decomposition, breaking down fallen leaves, dead animals and droppings into simpler substances that plants can absorb again. Without these recyclers, the world would be buried under dead material and nutrients would stay locked away. Australia has its own remarkable worms, including the giant Gippsland earthworm of Victoria, which is commonly around a metre long and lives deep in moist soils.

sections.key: Many Australian soils are old, weathered and low in nutrients, and native plants have adapted in clever ways.
sections.b: Compared with many other continents, Australia's soils are often very old and very poor. Much of the land has been geologically stable for a long time, without recent glaciers grinding up fresh rock or widespread volcanoes spreading new mineral rich ash. Over millions of years, rain has leached many nutrients away, and phosphorus in particular is often scarce. Native plants have adapted remarkably. Banksias, grevilleas and their relatives grow dense mats of fine roots, called cluster roots, that release chemicals to free up tightly bound phosphorus. Some native plants are actually harmed by the high phosphorus levels in ordinary garden fertilisers. Australian farmers have long worked with these soils, adding fertilisers such as superphosphate, and scientists continue to study how to farm them sustainably without degrading them further or causing salinity problems.

sections.key: Soil stores huge amounts of carbon, and losing it to erosion has caused some of history's worst disasters.
sections.b: Soil is one of the planet's great carbon stores. Worldwide, it is estimated to hold more carbon than the atmosphere and all living plants combined, mostly in the form of decaying organic matter. Farming practices that protect and build that organic matter can help keep carbon in the ground and make soil more fertile and better at holding water. When soil is mistreated, the results can be devastating. In the 1930s, drought and poor farming practices on the American Great Plains led to the Dust Bowl, when enormous dust storms stripped away topsoil and forced many families to abandon their farms. Australia has had its own serious erosion and dust storms. The community Landcare movement began in Victoria in the late 1980s and has grown into thousands of local groups working to repair land.

quiz.q: Which compound, made by soil bacteria, helps create the smell after rain?
quiz.e: Geosmin, produced by certain soil bacteria, is a key part of that earthy smell.

quiz.q: Roughly how long can it take to form a few centimetres of new soil?
quiz.e: Soil forms extremely slowly, so a few centimetres can take hundreds of years or more.

quiz.q: Which soil type drains quickly but struggles to hold water and nutrients?
quiz.e: Sand has large particles with big gaps, so water drains through fast.

quiz.q: What do plants give mycorrhizal fungi in exchange for water and nutrients?
quiz.e: Plants supply sugars from photosynthesis, and the fungi bring back water and nutrients.

quiz.q: How have banksias adapted to phosphorus poor soils?
o: They grow cluster roots that free up bound phosphorus
They get phosphorus from the air
quiz.e: Cluster roots release chemicals that help unlock scarce phosphorus from the soil.

LESSONS.title: Hammurabi's Code: law carved in stone
LESSONS.hook: Nearly 4,000 years ago a Babylonian king had his laws carved into a towering black stone for everyone to see. It is one of the oldest legal texts we can still read, and it is far stranger and more human than 'an eye for an eye' suggests.

sections.key: The best-known copy of Hammurabi's laws was found in 1901, far from where it was made.
sections.b: In the winter of 1901 to 1902, French archaeologists digging at Susa, an ancient city in what is now south-western Iran, unearthed three large pieces of polished black stone. Fitted together, they formed a pillar more than two metres tall, covered from top to bottom in tiny wedge-shaped writing. It was a law code issued by Hammurabi, king of Babylon, who ruled from about 1792 to 1750 BCE. But Susa is not in Babylon. Scholars think an Elamite king carried the stone off as war plunder in the 12th century BCE, centuries after it was made. Today it stands in the Louvre in Paris, one of the most visited objects in the museum's collection of ancient Near Eastern art.

sections.key: Hammurabi turned a modest city-state into the centre of a large Mesopotamian kingdom.
sections.b: When Hammurabi came to the throne, Babylon was one of several competing cities in Mesopotamia, the land between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers. Over roughly four decades he used diplomacy, alliances and war to bring much of southern and central Mesopotamia under his control. Running a kingdom that size meant managing canals, taxes, trade and disputes between people who had lived under different local customs. Letters from his reign show a hands-on ruler, writing to officials about everything from flood repairs to a single stolen field. His law collection, written in the Akkadian language using cuneiform script, was probably set up late in his reign. It was meant to show the gods and his subjects that he had brought order and fairness to the land.

sections.key: The carving above the text links the king's laws to divine justice.
sections.b: Before you read a single law, the stone makes a statement. At its top is a carved scene of Hammurabi standing respectfully before a seated god, usually identified as Shamash, the sun god and god of justice. The sun saw everything, so it made sense that the god of the sun watched over honest dealing. Below the picture comes a long prologue in which Hammurabi lists his achievements and the cities he cared for, then the laws themselves, then an epilogue. In the epilogue he says he set up the laws so that the strong would not oppress the weak, and invites any wronged person to come and have the stone read to them. The message is clear: this king's power was meant to be just power.

sections.key: The roughly 282 laws cover ordinary life, from farming and trade to marriage and medicine.
sections.b: Modern scholars have divided the text into about 282 laws, though a section near the end of the stone was deliberately rubbed away in antiquity and has been partly recovered from other copies. Most laws follow a simple pattern: if someone does this, then this happens. They deal with surprisingly everyday matters. There are rules on renting fields and boats, on interest for loans, on wages for workers and fees for doctors, on inheritance, divorce and the care of children. A builder whose badly built house collapsed and killed the owner could be put to death. A tavern keeper who overcharged for beer could be punished. Reading them is like opening a window onto the worries of ordinary Babylonians: debts, floods, unpaid bills and family quarrels.

sections.h: An eye for an eye, but not for everyone
sections.key: Punishments depended heavily on the social rank of the victim and the offender.
sections.b: The most famous line of the code is the principle of retaliation: if a man destroys the eye of another man, his own eye will be destroyed. That sounds brutally simple, but it applied mainly between people of the same high status. Babylonian society had roughly three ranks: free citizens, a middle group of commoners or dependants, and enslaved people. If a free man blinded a commoner, he paid a fine in silver instead. If he injured an enslaved person, he paid compensation to the owner. Women's rights depended on their family position, and some laws protected wives and widows. To a modern reader the code is both fair-minded and deeply unequal, which is a good reminder that every legal system reflects the values of its time.

sections.h: Not the first, and maybe not a rulebook
sections.key: Older law codes existed, and historians debate how Hammurabi's laws were used in court.
sections.b: Hammurabi is often called the first lawgiver, but he was not. Fragments of older collections survive, including one linked to Ur-Nammu, a king of Ur who ruled roughly three centuries earlier. What makes Hammurabi's stone special is how complete and well preserved it is. Historians also debate what the code was for. Thousands of Babylonian legal documents survive, such as contracts and court records, yet they rarely cite the code directly. Many scholars think it worked less like a modern statute book and more like a royal showcase of wise judgments, a model of justice for judges and scribes to learn from. Scribes certainly copied it for centuries after Hammurabi's death, which shows how highly it was respected as a piece of learning.

sections.key: The big idea that lasted was writing laws down where people could see them.
sections.b: Few people today would want to live under Hammurabi's rules, with their harsh punishments and fixed social ranks. Yet the stone captured ideas that still shape how we think about law. Rules should be written down, not just held in a ruler's head. They should be public, so people can know them in advance. Punishment should be proportionate rather than unlimited revenge. Judges should not simply change their minds once a decision is made, and false accusations should themselves be punished. These ideas resurface again and again in later legal history, from Roman law to the courts of modern Australia. Nearly four thousand years on, the stone remains a vivid reminder of one of humanity's earliest attempts to make power answer to rules.

quiz.q: Where is the best-known copy of Hammurabi's law stone today?
quiz.e: It was found at Susa in 1901 to 1902 and taken to the Louvre in Paris.

quiz.q: Which god is usually identified in the carving at the top of the stone?
o: Shamash, the sun god and god of justice
quiz.e: Shamash, the all-seeing sun god, was associated with justice and fairness.

quiz.q: What kind of matters do most of Hammurabi's laws deal with?
o: Everyday matters like trade, wages, debts and family
quiz.e: The laws are full of ordinary concerns such as loans, fees, inheritance and building.

quiz.q: What usually happened if a free man injured a commoner rather than another free man?
o: He paid a fine in silver
quiz.e: Exact retaliation applied mainly between equals; injuring a lower-ranked person usually meant a payment.

quiz.q: Why do many historians doubt the code was used like a modern statute book?
o: It was written in a secret language
It was destroyed soon after it was made
Surviving court records rarely cite it directly
quiz.e: Babylonian legal documents seldom refer to it, so it may have been a model of royal justice instead.

LESSONS.title: Trial by jury: twelve ordinary people
LESSONS.hook: Somewhere in Australia today, twelve strangers are sitting in a small room deciding whether someone is guilty of a serious crime. Why do we hand such power to ordinary citizens, and what actually happens if your name is drawn?

sections.key: Jury service starts with an official letter, because jurors are drawn at random from the electoral roll.
sections.b: Picture an ordinary Tuesday. Among the bills and junk mail is an envelope from the sheriff's office or the court, telling you that you have been selected for possible jury service. For many Australians it comes as a surprise, but it is a normal part of being enrolled to vote. In every state and territory, potential jurors are chosen at random from the electoral roll. Not everyone summoned ends up on a jury. Some people are ineligible, such as many lawyers, police officers and politicians, and others can ask to be excused for good reasons, like caring duties or serious hardship. The details differ between states, so the letter itself and your local court's website are the best guides to what you need to do.

sections.key: Juries became central to English justice after trial by ordeal was abandoned in the 13th century.
sections.b: For much of the early Middle Ages, guilt in England could be tested by ordeal. An accused person might carry a red-hot iron or be lowered into water, and the outcome was believed to reveal God's judgment. In 1215 the Church's Fourth Lateran Council banned priests from taking part in ordeals, which quickly made them unworkable. English courts needed another method, and they turned to a body that already existed: groups of local men who were asked about crimes in their area. Over time these groups changed from witnesses who knew the facts into neutral judges of evidence presented in court. By the end of the Middle Ages, the idea of being judged by a group of one's peers was firmly rooted in English law.

sections.h: The jurors who would not budge
sections.key: A 1670 case established that jurors cannot be punished for their verdict.
sections.b: In 1670 two Quakers, William Penn and William Mead, were tried in London for preaching to an unlawful gathering. The jury refused to convict them, even after the judge locked the jurors up without food, water or heat and fined them. One juror, Edward Bushel, refused to pay and challenged his imprisonment. In what became known as Bushel's Case, the senior judge Sir John Vaughan ruled that jurors could not be punished simply for reaching a verdict the judge disliked. It was a turning point. From then on, a jury's verdict was its own, free from official pressure. William Penn later founded the American colony of Pennsylvania, and the principle of an independent jury travelled with English law around the world, including to Australia.

sections.key: Most jury trials in Australia are for serious criminal charges heard in state courts.
sections.b: Juries are not used for most legal matters in Australia. Minor offences and most civil disputes, such as contract claims, are decided by a magistrate or judge alone. Juries mainly decide serious criminal cases, such as murder, sexual offences, serious assault and large-scale fraud. Criminal juries usually have twelve members. Section 80 of the Australian Constitution says that a trial on indictment for an offence against a Commonwealth law must be by jury, though the High Court has read that protection fairly narrowly. In some states an accused person can choose to be tried by a judge alone in certain circumstances. Civil juries are rare, but some states still allow them in particular kinds of cases, such as some defamation claims.

sections.key: Jurors decide the facts, while the judge explains the law they must apply.
sections.b: In a jury trial, the work is divided. The judge controls the courtroom, rules on what evidence can be heard and explains the law. The jury decides what actually happened. In a criminal case, jurors must be satisfied of guilt beyond reasonable doubt, a high standard designed to protect innocent people from wrongful conviction. Jurors are told to decide only on the evidence presented in court. Doing your own research, searching online about the case or visiting the scene can be a criminal offence, because it can lead to an unfair trial. Discussions in the jury room are strictly confidential, even after the case ends. Traditionally verdicts had to be unanimous, but most states now allow majority verdicts in some circumstances after long deliberation.

sections.key: Supporters value juries as a democratic check, while critics question their consistency.
sections.b: Supporters say juries bring community values into the courtroom and act as a check on the power of the state, since a government cannot imprison someone for a serious crime without convincing ordinary citizens. Juries also spread responsibility for grave decisions across many people rather than one official, and they give citizens a direct role in justice. Critics raise real concerns too. Complex fraud or scientific evidence can be hard for non-experts to follow, trials with juries take longer and cost more, and jurors may be swayed by media coverage or personal impressions. Some countries, such as Japan, use mixed panels of judges and citizens instead. Most Australian legal experts accept that the system is imperfect, and debates about how to improve it continue.

sections.key: Jury service is a legal duty, and courts provide practical support to jurors.
sections.b: If you are summoned, read the letter carefully and respond by the deadline, because ignoring a summons can lead to a fine. Employers generally cannot penalise you for doing jury service, and jurors are paid an allowance, though the amount and whether your employer tops up your wages vary, so check the current rules for your state. Many people find the experience absorbing and meaningful, and a little nerve-racking. Some trials involve distressing evidence, and courts in most states offer free, confidential counselling for jurors afterwards. This lesson is general information, not legal advice, and the official juror information pages run by your state or territory courts are the place to check what applies to you. Whatever the verdict, you will have taken part in a tradition many centuries old.

quiz.q: Where are potential jurors in Australia drawn from?
quiz.e: Jurors are chosen at random from people enrolled to vote.

quiz.q: What event in 1215 helped push English courts towards using juries?
o: The Church banning priests from taking part in ordeals
quiz.e: The Fourth Lateran Council made trial by ordeal unworkable, so courts needed another method.

quiz.q: What did Bushel's Case in 1670 establish?
o: Jurors cannot be punished for their verdict
quiz.e: Sir John Vaughan ruled jurors could not be punished simply for a verdict the judge disliked.

quiz.q: Why is it risky for a juror to research the case online?
o: It can be a criminal offence and lead to an unfair trial
It is allowed but frowned upon
It only matters in civil cases
quiz.e: Jurors must decide only on evidence presented in court.

quiz.q: What is one common criticism of jury trials?
o: Complex technical evidence can be hard for non-experts to follow
quiz.e: Critics worry about complex cases, cost, delays and outside influence.

LESSONS.title: Separation of powers: why no one holds all the keys
LESSONS.hook: Who makes the laws, who carries them out, and who decides what they mean? Keeping those three jobs apart is one of the oldest safeguards against tyranny, and Australia does it in its own distinctive way.

sections.key: Government power can be divided into three jobs: making, carrying out and judging laws.
sections.b: Imagine a bank vault that needs three keys turned at once, held by three different people. No single person can empty it alone. That is the basic idea behind the separation of powers. Government does three broad kinds of work. The legislature makes laws; in Australia that is Parliament. The executive puts laws into action and runs the country day to day; that includes the Prime Minister, ministers and the public service. The judiciary interprets laws and settles disputes about them; that is the courts. If one person or group controlled all three, they could write any rule they liked, enforce it however they chose and then judge their own case. Splitting the keys makes that much harder.

sections.key: A French writer in 1748 argued that liberty depends on keeping these powers apart.
sections.b: The idea has ancient roots, but its most influential statement came from the French aristocrat and thinker Montesquieu. In 1748 he published The Spirit of the Laws, a sprawling study of governments around the world. Montesquieu admired what he saw as the English system, where Parliament, the Crown and the courts each held part of the power. He argued that when the same body both makes and enforces laws, liberty is at risk, and that there can be no real freedom if judges are not separate from lawmakers and rulers. His analysis of England was not entirely accurate, but his argument travelled far. It was read closely by the people who designed the United States Constitution, and through them it shaped modern democracies everywhere.

sections.key: The United States separates its three branches strictly and builds in checks and balances.
sections.b: The framers of the United States Constitution in 1787 took Montesquieu seriously. They put Congress, the President and the Supreme Court in separate articles of the Constitution and kept their members apart: the President does not sit in Congress, and members of Congress cannot serve in the President's cabinet at the same time. They also added checks and balances, so each branch can restrain the others. The President can veto bills, Congress can override a veto with a large enough majority, the Senate must approve many appointments and the courts can strike down laws that breach the Constitution. Supporters say this makes power hard to abuse. Critics say it can also make government slow and prone to deadlock when the branches are controlled by rival parties.

sections.key: Australia's Constitution separates the courts firmly but deliberately fuses Parliament and the executive.
sections.b: Australia's founders borrowed from two traditions. From the United States they took a written Constitution with separate chapters: Chapter I covers Parliament, Chapter II the executive government and Chapter III the courts. From Britain they took the Westminster system of responsible government, where ministers must be members of Parliament and answer to it. Section 64 of the Constitution says a minister must become a senator or member of the House within three months. So in Australia, the legislature and the executive overlap heavily: the government is formed by whoever holds the confidence of the House of Representatives. What keeps this in check is that ministers can be questioned in Parliament every sitting day, can lose the confidence of the House and must face voters at regular elections.

sections.key: The High Court has insisted that federal judicial power stays with real courts.
sections.b: Where Australia is strict is the judiciary. In a landmark 1956 decision known as the Boilermakers' Case, the High Court ruled that a federal body could not combine judicial power, such as deciding legal guilt and punishment, with non-judicial functions like setting wages through arbitration. Judicial power under Chapter III must be exercised by courts, and courts should not be handed tasks that compromise their independence. Later cases extended some protection to state courts too, because they can exercise federal power. Judges are also protected in other ways. Federal judges can only be removed by the Governor-General after both houses of Parliament ask for it on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity, and their pay cannot be cut while they hold office.

sections.key: Many familiar parts of Australian politics are really checks on power.
sections.b: Once you know what to look for, checks and balances appear everywhere. When the Senate rejects or amends a government bill, that is one house checking another. Senate estimates hearings, where officials are grilled about how money is spent, are Parliament checking the executive. When a court rules that a government decision was unlawful, that is the judiciary checking the executive. Independent bodies such as the Auditor-General, ombudsmen and anti-corruption commissions add further checks. A free press and the right to vote sit outside government entirely but act as checks too. None of these work perfectly, and people argue about whether particular checks are too weak or too strong, but together they make it harder for any one group to act without scrutiny.

sections.key: Every democracy strikes its own balance between effective government and limited power.
sections.b: There is no perfect way to divide power. Separate it too strictly and government can grind to a halt, unable to respond to emergencies or pass a budget. Concentrate it too much and those in charge may slip free of accountability. Different democracies have landed in different places. Britain has no single written constitution and relies heavily on convention. The United States has rigid separation. Australia sits in between, with fused law-making and executive power but strongly independent courts. Arguments about the right balance never end, and they often cut across party lines, since people tend to value checks more when their side is out of power. Understanding the idea helps you judge those debates on their merits rather than on who happens to be winning.

quiz.q: Which branch of government interprets laws and settles disputes about them?
quiz.e: The courts form the judiciary, which interprets and applies the law.

quiz.q: Which thinker set out the separation of powers in The Spirit of the Laws in 1748?
quiz.e: Montesquieu argued that liberty depends on keeping these powers apart.

quiz.q: What does section 64 of the Australian Constitution require of ministers?
o: They must never sit in Parliament
They must be approved by the High Court
They must become a member of Parliament within three months
quiz.e: This is a key part of Australia's Westminster-style responsible government.

quiz.q: What did the High Court decide in the 1956 Boilermakers' Case?
o: Federal judicial power must stay with real courts and not be mixed with non-judicial roles
Parliament can overrule any court decision
States cannot have their own courts
quiz.e: The case set a strict separation of federal judicial power.

quiz.q: Which of these is an example of Parliament checking the executive?
o: A court hearing a criminal trial
quiz.e: Estimates hearings let senators scrutinise how government departments spend money.

LESSONS.title: The Dismissal: Australia's 1975 constitutional crisis
LESSONS.hook: On 11 November 1975 the Governor-General removed an elected Prime Minister from office. Half a century later, Australians still argue about whether it was a constitutional necessity or a step too far.

sections.key: On 11 November 1975, Prime Minister Gough Whitlam was dismissed by the Governor-General.
sections.b: Just after one o'clock on 11 November 1975, Prime Minister Gough Whitlam arrived at Government House in Canberra expecting a routine meeting. Instead, Governor-General Sir John Kerr handed him a letter terminating his commission as Prime Minister. Within hours, Kerr had appointed Opposition Leader Malcolm Fraser as caretaker Prime Minister. Later that afternoon, on the steps of Parliament House, Kerr's official secretary read out the proclamation dissolving both houses of Parliament. Whitlam, standing behind him, told the crowd: 'Well may we say God save the Queen, because nothing will save the Governor-General.' It was the only time a Governor-General has dismissed a federal Prime Minister. To understand why it happened, you need to go back several weeks to a fight over money.

sections.key: The crisis began when the Opposition-controlled Senate refused to pass the government's budget bills.
sections.b: Every government needs Parliament to approve its spending through appropriation bills, often called supply. Without supply, the money to pay public servants and run services eventually runs out. Whitlam's Labor government, elected in 1972 and re-elected in 1974, controlled the House of Representatives but not the Senate. In 1975 it faced a run of controversies, the most damaging being the Loans Affair, in which ministers had sought to raise a very large overseas loan through unconventional channels. In October 1975 the Coalition Opposition, led by Fraser, used its Senate numbers to defer the supply bills, saying it would pass them only if Whitlam called an election. Whitlam refused, arguing that a government's survival should depend on the House, not the Senate. Neither side backed down.

sections.key: Two Senate vacancies filled by non-Labor appointees helped give the Opposition its leverage.
sections.b: The Opposition's control of the Senate was itself controversial. Under the Constitution at the time, when a senator died or resigned, the state parliament chose a replacement and was not required to pick someone from the same party. By long convention, it usually did. In 1975, however, two Labor Senate vacancies, one in New South Wales and one in Queensland, were filled by people who were not Labor nominees. Without those changes, the Opposition would have found it far harder to block supply. Labor supporters saw this as a breach of fair play. Coalition supporters pointed out that the state parliaments had acted within their legal powers. Either way, it shows how unwritten conventions, not just written laws, hold a system together, and what happens when they are tested.

sections.key: Kerr used the Crown's reserve powers, arguing a government without supply must go to an election.
sections.b: Section 64 of the Constitution says ministers hold office during the Governor-General's pleasure, and section 61 gives the Governor-General executive power. Normally these powers are used only on the Prime Minister's advice. But the Governor-General also has so-called reserve powers that can be used in rare cases without advice. Kerr concluded that a government unable to obtain supply should either advise an election or be dismissed. He sought the view of the Chief Justice of the High Court, Sir Garfield Barwick, who advised in writing that dismissal was within his power. Kerr did not warn Whitlam beforehand, because he feared Whitlam would ask the Queen to remove him first. Fraser was commissioned on condition he obtain supply and advise a double dissolution, which happened that same afternoon.

sections.key: At the December 1975 election, the Coalition won in a landslide.
sections.b: The dismissal unleashed fierce emotion. Protesters gathered outside Parliament House, and supporters on both sides felt their democracy was under threat, though for opposite reasons. Labor's slogan became a call to maintain the rage. That afternoon the House of Representatives passed a motion of no confidence in Fraser, but Parliament was dissolved before the Speaker could present it to the Governor-General. The question went to voters at a double dissolution election on 13 December 1975. The result was decisive: the Fraser-led Coalition won a large majority in both houses. Supporters of the dismissal saw this as the people endorsing the outcome. Critics replied that an election victory could not settle whether the method used to force the election had been proper in the first place.

sections.key: The debate turns on the Senate's power over money and the limits of the Crown's reserve powers.
sections.b: Supporters of Kerr's action argue that the Constitution gives the Senate the power to reject money bills, that a government which cannot pay its bills cannot govern, and that sending the dispute to the voters was the most democratic outcome available. Critics argue that the Senate should not use that power to bring down a government elected by the House, that Kerr should have warned Whitlam or given him more time, and that an unelected official should not remove an elected Prime Minister. Some also question whether Barwick, as Chief Justice, should have given advice at all. Both views are held by serious constitutional scholars, and many people's opinions still line up with their political sympathies. Weighing each side's strongest argument is the best way to form your own view.

sections.key: The crisis led to constitutional change, new conventions and decades of historical research.
sections.b: The dismissal changed Australian politics. In 1977 voters approved a referendum requiring a replacement senator to come from the same party as the senator who left, closing the loophole exposed in 1975. No Opposition since has blocked supply in the same way, and many observers think a new convention has formed against it. The episode also fed into later debates about whether Australia should become a republic and how a president might be chosen. Historians kept digging. In 2020, after a High Court case brought by historian Jenny Hocking, the National Archives released Kerr's correspondence with the Queen's private secretary, known as the Palace Letters. They showed Kerr had discussed the reserve powers with the Palace beforehand, but did not tell the Queen in advance of his decision.

quiz.q: Who did Sir John Kerr appoint as caretaker Prime Minister on 11 November 1975?
quiz.e: Fraser was commissioned on condition he obtain supply and advise an election.

quiz.q: What triggered the 1975 crisis?
o: The Senate deferring the government's supply bills
quiz.e: Without supply, the government's money would eventually run out.

quiz.q: Whose advice did Kerr seek before dismissing Whitlam?
quiz.e: Barwick advised in writing that dismissal was within the Governor-General's power.

quiz.q: What happened at the election on 13 December 1975?
o: The Coalition won a large majority
The result was a hung parliament
quiz.e: The Fraser-led Coalition won decisively in both houses.

quiz.q: What did the 1977 referendum change?
o: It required replacement senators to come from the same party
It abolished the Senate's power over money
quiz.e: This closed the casual vacancy loophole exposed in 1975.

LESSONS.title: Mabo and the end of terra nullius
LESSONS.hook: In 1992 a man from a tiny island in the Torres Strait changed the foundations of Australian land law. The Mabo decision overturned a legal fiction that had stood since 1788 and reshaped the national conversation about who owns the country.

sections.key: Eddie Mabo's case began with his deep connection to family land on Murray Island.
sections.b: Mer, also called Murray Island, is a small volcanic island at the eastern edge of the Torres Strait, closer to Papua New Guinea than to Cairns. For generations the Meriam people have tended gardens there, with plots passed down through families according to their own laws. Eddie Koiki Mabo grew up on Mer and later worked on the mainland, including as a gardener at James Cook University in Townsville. There, in the 1970s, he was shocked to learn from academics that under Australian law his family's land on Mer was legally owned by the Crown, not by his people. To Mabo this made no sense. His family had always known exactly which land was theirs. That conversation set him on a path to the High Court.

sections.key: Australian law had long treated the continent as if no one had owned the land before 1788.
sections.b: When Britain claimed eastern Australia, its law treated the continent as if it had been settled peacefully rather than conquered. The courts later explained this using the idea that the land was legally empty of any recognisable system of ownership, an idea often summed up as terra nullius, Latin for land belonging to no one. The practical result was that, under Australian law, the Crown owned all land and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples had no legal title to their country. A 1971 case, Milirrpum v Nabalco, brought by Yolngu people on the Gove Peninsula, had tried to challenge this. The judge accepted that the Yolngu had a sophisticated system of law, but ruled that it did not give them property rights recognised by Australian law.

sections.key: The Mabo case took a decade and included an earlier High Court win over Queensland.
sections.b: In 1982 Eddie Mabo and four other Meriam people, including David Passi and James Rice, began a case in the High Court claiming their traditional rights to land on Mer. The Queensland Government responded in 1985 by passing a law declaring that any such rights had been wiped out when the islands were annexed in 1879. In 1988, in what is now called Mabo No 1, the High Court struck that law down because it was inconsistent with the federal Racial Discrimination Act. The main case then went back to fact-finding, with weeks of evidence about Meriam customs and land holding. It was gruelling, expensive and slow. Eddie Mabo died of cancer in January 1992, just months before the High Court gave its final decision.

sections.key: On 3 June 1992 the High Court recognised native title by a majority of six to one.
sections.b: On 3 June 1992, in Mabo v Queensland No 2, the High Court ruled by six judges to one that the Meriam people held native title to most of the land on Mer. More broadly, the court held that the common law of Australia recognises a form of native title, reflecting the rights of Indigenous peoples under their traditional laws and customs. The judges rejected the idea that the land had belonged to no one as a basis for denying those rights, describing that view as out of step with history and with modern values. But the decision also set limits. Native title could be extinguished by valid government acts, such as granting freehold land, and it survives only where a group has kept up its connection with the land.

sections.key: Parliament passed the Native Title Act in 1993 to create a system for claims.
sections.b: The decision raised urgent questions. Which other lands might be subject to native title? Were existing titles safe? How would claims be made? After months of intense negotiation with Indigenous leaders, industry groups and state governments, the federal Parliament passed the Native Title Act 1993 under the Keating Labor government. It confirmed the validity of existing titles, set up a process for making and deciding claims and created the National Native Title Tribunal to help mediate. Claims are now decided or approved by the Federal Court. In 1996 the High Court's Wik decision found that pastoral leases did not necessarily extinguish native title, prompting the Howard Coalition government to pass significant amendments in 1998. Both stages were fiercely debated.

sections.h: What native title is and is not
sections.key: Native title varies from place to place and usually sits alongside other people's rights.
sections.b: Native title is often misunderstood. It is not a single type of ownership, and it does not let anyone take away people's suburban backyards: freehold land generally extinguishes native title. What native title includes depends on the traditional laws and customs of the group and on what other rights already exist over the land. In some places it can amount to exclusive possession. More often it is a set of shared rights, such as to camp, hunt, fish, hold ceremonies or be consulted about development, existing alongside the rights of pastoralists, miners or the public. Proving a claim can be very hard. Groups must show a continuing connection under traditional law, which can be difficult for peoples who were forcibly moved off their country during colonisation.

sections.key: Mabo changed Australian law and remains a landmark in debates about history and reconciliation.
sections.b: Reactions to the decision were sharply divided in the 1990s.
