Some business groups and politicians warned of uncertainty for mining and farming, while many Indigenous advocates felt the system that followed gave them too little. Over time, native title has been recognised over a large share of the Australian continent, often through negotiated agreements rather than courtroom battles, though the rights involved vary greatly. The anniversary of the judgment, 3 June, is now marked as Mabo Day and closes National Reconciliation Week, which begins on 27 May, the date of the 1967 referendum. Eddie Mabo did not live to see his victory, but his name has become shorthand for a turning point: the moment Australian law formally recognised that the land had owners long before 1788.

quiz.q: Where did Eddie Mabo's family land lie?
quiz.e: Mer is a small island at the eastern edge of the Torres Strait.

quiz.q: Why did the High Court strike down Queensland's 1985 law in Mabo No 1?
o: It conflicted with the federal Racial Discrimination Act
It had not been signed by the Governor
It breached the right to vote
It applied only to mining land
quiz.e: The 1988 decision cleared the way for the main case to continue.

quiz.q: What was the majority in the 1992 Mabo decision?
quiz.e: Six of the seven High Court judges recognised native title.

quiz.q: Which 1996 High Court case dealt with native title on pastoral leases?
quiz.e: Wik found pastoral leases did not necessarily extinguish native title.

quiz.q: What generally happens to native title on freehold land?
o: It is converted into a lease
quiz.e: Freehold grants generally extinguish native title.

LESSONS.title: The Nuremberg trials and the birth of international criminal law
LESSONS.hook: In 1945 the leaders of a defeated regime were put on trial before the world for crimes so vast there were barely words for them. The Nuremberg trials invented much of modern international law, and their critics raised questions we are still answering.

sections.key: In November 1945, surviving Nazi leaders went on trial in the bombed city of Nuremberg.
sections.b: On 20 November 1945, in a courtroom in the Bavarian city of Nuremberg, twenty-one men sat in two rows of a wooden dock. Among them were Hermann Göring, once Hitler's designated successor, the former deputy leader Rudolf Hess and the foreign minister Joachim von Ribbentrop. Much of the city around them lay in ruins. Nuremberg was chosen partly because its Palace of Justice had survived the bombing with a prison attached, and partly for its symbolism: it was where the Nazi Party had held its huge rallies. For the first time, the leaders of a modern state were being tried before an international tribunal for crimes committed in waging war and against civilians. Interpreters wearing headsets translated proceedings simultaneously into four languages, a novelty at the time.

sections.key: The Allies chose a trial over summary execution, partly to create a lasting record.
sections.b: As the war ended, Allied leaders debated what to do with captured Nazi leaders. Some, including at times Winston Churchill, favoured simply shooting the most senior figures once identified. Others, especially in the United States, argued for a trial. A courtroom would test the evidence, give the accused a chance to defend themselves and build a public record that could not easily be denied later. In August 1945 the United States, Britain, France and the Soviet Union signed the London Charter, creating the International Military Tribunal and defining the crimes it would judge. The American chief prosecutor, Supreme Court Justice Robert H. Jackson, said in his opening address that it was a great tribute to reason that the victors stayed their hand and submitted their enemies to the judgment of the law.

sections.key: The tribunal judged conspiracy, crimes against peace, war crimes and crimes against humanity.
sections.b: The London Charter listed the charges. Crimes against peace covered planning and waging wars of aggression. War crimes covered breaches of the laws of war, such as murdering prisoners or civilians in occupied territory. Crimes against humanity covered murder, extermination, enslavement, deportation and persecution of civilian populations. A further count of conspiracy tied these together. The idea of crimes against humanity was especially important, because it reached acts a government committed against its own people, which traditional international law had largely ignored. A related word was also entering use. In 1944 the Polish-Jewish lawyer Raphael Lemkin had coined the term genocide to describe the deliberate destruction of a people. It was mentioned at Nuremberg, and in 1948 the United Nations adopted a convention against it.

sections.key: Most defendants were convicted, but three were acquitted.
sections.b: The prosecution relied heavily on the Nazis' own documents, including orders, minutes and reports, as well as film shot by Allied troops in liberated concentration camps. Survivors and former officials testified. The trial lasted almost a year. On 1 October 1946 the judges delivered their verdicts. Twelve defendants were sentenced to death, including Martin Bormann, who was tried in his absence. Seven received prison terms, from ten years to life. Three were acquitted, which surprised many observers and showed the judges were not simply rubber-stamping the prosecution. The tribunal also rejected the defence of superior orders: following orders could reduce a sentence but did not excuse a crime. Göring took his own life the night before the executions, which were carried out on 16 October 1946.

sections.key: Critics argued the trials were victors' justice and applied some laws retrospectively.
sections.b: Even at the time, serious people had doubts. The most common criticism was victors' justice: only the defeated were tried, while Allied actions, such as the area bombing of German cities, were never examined. The Soviet Union's presence was particularly awkward, since it had invaded Poland in 1939 alongside Germany, and the Soviet prosecutors tried to blame the Katyn massacre of Polish officers on the Germans, though the Soviets were responsible. The tribunal did not convict on that charge. Others argued that crimes against peace had not clearly been crimes when the acts were committed, breaching the principle that no one should be punished under a law made after the fact. Defenders replied that aggression had already been outlawed by treaty and that the atrocities were crimes under any civilised legal system.

sections.key: The trials laid the groundwork for later international courts, including the International Criminal Court.
sections.b: Nuremberg was followed by other trials. The International Military Tribunal for the Far East tried Japanese leaders in Tokyo, with the Australian judge Sir William Webb as its president. American military courts at Nuremberg held twelve further trials of doctors, judges, industrialists and others. The doctors' trial produced the Nuremberg Code, a set of principles for ethical medical research. In 1950 the United Nations' International Law Commission summarised the Nuremberg Principles. Then the Cold War largely froze the project for decades. It revived in the 1990s, when the United Nations created tribunals for the former Yugoslavia and Rwanda. In 1998 countries adopted the Rome Statute, and in 2002 the permanent International Criminal Court began work in The Hague. Australia ratified the Rome Statute in 2002.

sections.key: Nuremberg established that individuals can answer for state crimes, but enforcement is still uneven.
sections.b: Nuremberg's most lasting principle is simple to state: individuals, even heads of state, can be held personally responsible for the gravest crimes, and acting on behalf of a government is no shield. That idea is now part of international law. Yet putting it into practice remains difficult. International courts depend on countries to arrest suspects and hand them over, and several major powers, including the United States, China and Russia, are not members of the International Criminal Court. Supporters argue that imperfect justice is far better than none and that the threat of prosecution can deter atrocities. Sceptics worry about selective enforcement and political influence. Both sides tend to agree, though, that the questions first asked in that Nuremberg courtroom are far from settled.

quiz.q: Which four powers signed the London Charter creating the Nuremberg tribunal?
o: The US, Britain, Canada and Australia
The US, Britain, France and the Soviet Union
Britain, France, China and the US
The US, the Soviet Union, Poland and Britain
quiz.e: These four Allied powers set up the International Military Tribunal in August 1945.

quiz.q: What made the charge of crimes against humanity especially significant?
o: It replaced the laws of war
It could reach acts a government committed against its own people
quiz.e: Traditional international law had largely ignored how states treated their own citizens.

quiz.q: How did the tribunal treat the defence of following superior orders?
o: As not excusing a crime, though it could reduce a sentence
quiz.e: Following orders could mitigate punishment but did not remove guilt.

quiz.q: What is the criticism known as victors' justice?
o: Only the defeated side's actions were put on trial
The trials were held in secret
quiz.e: Allied conduct, such as area bombing, was never examined.

quiz.q: Which Australian judge presided over the Tokyo war crimes tribunal?
quiz.e: Webb was president of the International Military Tribunal for the Far East.

LESSONS.title: Votes for women: how Australia led the world
LESSONS.hook: In the 1890s, a colony on the edge of the British Empire did something almost no government on Earth had done: it let women vote and stand for parliament. The story of how Australian women won the vote is full of determined campaigners, giant petitions and some uncomfortable exceptions.

sections.key: Campaigners gathered tens of thousands of signatures on enormous petitions.
sections.b: In 1891 Victorian campaigners presented their parliament with a petition so long it was rolled up like a carpet. Known as the Monster Petition, it carried around 30,000 signatures, gathered door to door by women across the colony asking for the right to vote. It did not succeed straight away, but it showed something politicians could not ignore: huge numbers of ordinary women wanted a say. Similar petitions were organised across the Australian colonies in the 1880s and 1890s. Campaigners held public meetings, wrote to newspapers and lobbied members of parliament one by one. Many were involved in other social causes too, especially the Woman's Christian Temperance Union, which campaigned against alcohol abuse and saw the vote as a way for women to protect their families and communities.

sections.key: In 1894 South Australia gave women both the vote and the right to stand for parliament.
sections.b: New Zealand became the first self-governing country to give women the vote in national elections, in 1893. South Australia followed in December 1894 and went one step further: its law let women both vote and stand as candidates for parliament, a first anywhere in the world. Campaigners such as Mary Lee, an Irish-born widow who threw herself into the cause, had worked for years to get there. A petition with more than 11,000 signatures was presented to the South Australian parliament in 1894. Opponents had hoped that adding the right to stand for parliament would make the bill too radical to pass. The tactic backfired, and the bill passed with that right included. South Australian women voted for the first time in 1896.

sections.key: Supporters and opponents argued about women's nature, family and fairness.
sections.b: It helps to understand the arguments people actually made. Opponents claimed that politics was too rough for women, that women's influence belonged in the home, that wives would simply copy their husbands' votes or, oddly, that they would cause conflict in marriages by voting differently. Some worried that women would vote as a single bloc on issues like alcohol. Supporters answered that women paid taxes and obeyed the laws, so they deserved a say in making them. Others argued that women would bring a moral and caring perspective to public life, while some simply insisted that equal citizenship was a matter of basic justice. These debates were not neatly divided along modern party lines, and supporters and opponents came from across the political spectrum.

sections.h: A nation is born, with a catch
sections.key: The Commonwealth Franchise Act 1902 gave most women the federal vote but excluded most Aboriginal people.
sections.b: When the colonies federated in 1901, the new national Parliament had to decide who could vote in federal elections. The Commonwealth Franchise Act 1902 gave women the right to vote and stand for federal Parliament on the same terms as men, making Australia one of the first nations in the world to do so. But the same Act excluded most Aboriginal people, as well as people from Asia, Africa and the Pacific Islands other than New Zealand, unless they were already entitled to vote in their state. In practice, many Aboriginal people were denied the vote for decades. Aboriginal people gained the clear right to enrol for federal elections in 1962, and enrolment and voting became compulsory for them, as for everyone else, in 1984.

sections.key: Four women stood for federal Parliament in 1903, but none were elected.
sections.b: At the 1903 federal election, four women nominated as candidates, the first women anywhere in the British Empire to stand for a national parliament. The best known was Vida Goldstein, a Melbourne campaigner who ran for the Senate in Victoria and won tens of thousands of votes, though not enough to be elected. The others were Selina Anderson, Nellie Martel and Mary Moore-Bentley. Goldstein stood several more times without success. Catherine Helen Spence, a writer and reformer from South Australia, had already made history in 1897 when she stood for the convention that drafted the Constitution, becoming Australia's first female political candidate. Their campaigns showed women could take part fully in politics, even if voters were slow to elect them.

sections.key: Winning the vote came long before women were elected in significant numbers.
sections.b: The states gave women the vote at different times. Western Australia followed South Australia in 1899, and Victoria was the last state, in 1908. Being allowed to stand was one thing; being elected was another. The first woman elected to any Australian parliament was Edith Cowan, who won a seat in the Western Australian Legislative Assembly in 1921. Federally, it took until 1943 for the first women to be elected: Enid Lyons in the House of Representatives and Dorothy Tangney in the Senate. They came from opposite sides of politics, Lyons from the conservative United Australia Party and Tangney from Labor. For decades afterward, women remained a small minority in Australian parliaments, and their numbers grew significantly only from the late 20th century.

sections.key: Australia's early start is a point of pride, and a reminder that rights can be partial.
sections.b: Australia's suffrage story is often told as a simple triumph, and there is real reason for pride. A young democracy on the far side of the world helped lead a global change that took many countries, including Britain and the United States, decades longer. Yet the full story is more complicated. The same laws that welcomed many women into political life shut out most Aboriginal women and men. Recognising both parts lets us see that rights are rarely won all at once. Today, voting is compulsory for all adult citizens, and you can check your enrolment on the Australian Electoral Commission's website. Every time you cast a ballot, you are using a right that people campaigned for, petition by petition, for decades.

quiz.q: What was the 1891 Victorian Monster Petition?
o: A petition of around 30,000 signatures for women's right to vote
quiz.e: It was gathered door to door and presented to the Victorian parliament.

quiz.q: What did South Australia's 1894 law achieve that was a world first?
o: Allowing women to stand as candidates for parliament
quiz.e: New Zealand had given women the vote in 1893, but South Australia also let them stand.

quiz.q: Who was largely excluded by the Commonwealth Franchise Act 1902?
quiz.e: Most Aboriginal people were denied the federal vote unless already enrolled in their state.

quiz.q: Which campaigner stood for the Senate in Victoria in 1903?
quiz.e: Goldstein was one of four women who stood for federal Parliament in 1903.

quiz.q: Who was the first woman elected to any Australian parliament?
quiz.e: Cowan won a seat in the Western Australian Legislative Assembly in 1921.

LESSONS.title: The social contract: why we agree to be governed
LESSONS.hook: Why should anyone obey the government? For nearly four centuries, philosophers have answered with a powerful thought experiment: imagine life with no rulers at all, then ask what deal reasonable people would strike.

sections.key: Social contract thinkers begin by imagining life without any state.
sections.b: Picture waking up tomorrow to find there are no police, no courts, no laws and no government of any kind. No one would stop a stronger neighbour from taking your food or your home. Would people cooperate peacefully, or would fear take over? This imagined situation is called the state of nature, and it is the starting point for one of the most influential ideas in political philosophy: the social contract. The idea is that governments are legitimate because, in some sense, the people they govern have agreed to them, trading some freedom for security and order. The great social contract thinkers disagreed sharply about what the state of nature would be like, and that disagreement shaped very different views about how much power governments should have.

sections.h: Hobbes and the war of all against all
sections.key: Thomas Hobbes argued that without a powerful ruler, life would be constant fear and conflict.
sections.b: The English philosopher Thomas Hobbes lived through the violence of the English Civil War, and it shows. In Leviathan, published in 1651, he argued that in a state of nature people would be roughly equal in their ability to harm one another, and constantly suspicious. The result would be a war of every person against every person. There would be no farming, no industry, no arts and no society, and, in his famous phrase, the life of man would be solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short. The only escape, Hobbes said, was for people to hand power to a single sovereign strong enough to keep the peace. He believed even a harsh ruler was better than the chaos of no rule at all.

sections.key: John Locke argued that people have rights before government exists, and governments must protect them.
sections.b: John Locke, writing a few decades later, painted a gentler picture. In his Two Treatises of Government, published around 1689, he argued that even in a state of nature people are bound by a natural law that forbids harming others in their life, health, liberty or possessions. People form governments not to escape total chaos, but to protect these rights more reliably, with impartial judges and enforcement. That changes everything. If a government is created to protect rights, it can lose its legitimacy by violating them. Locke argued that people could then resist and replace it. His ideas about consent and natural rights echoed through the American Declaration of Independence in 1776, which speaks of unalienable rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness.

sections.key: Jean-Jacques Rousseau argued that a legitimate society must express the shared will of its citizens.
sections.b: The Geneva-born thinker Jean-Jacques Rousseau took the idea in a different direction. His book The Social Contract, published in 1762, opens with the famous line usually translated as 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.' Rousseau thought existing societies had corrupted people and entrenched inequality. A legitimate society, he argued, would be one where citizens collectively make the laws they live under, guided by the general will: what is genuinely in the common interest, not just the sum of private wants. In obeying such laws, people would in effect be obeying themselves. His ideas inspired democratic and revolutionary movements, especially in France. Critics, though, worried that the notion of a general will could be twisted to justify forcing people to conform.

sections.key: Critics point out that no real person ever agreed to the social contract.
sections.b: The obvious objection is that no one ever signed anything. You were born into a country with laws already in place. The Scottish philosopher David Hume made this point sharply in the 18th century, arguing that most governments began in conquest or usurpation, not agreement. Some contract theorists reply that by staying in a country and accepting its benefits, you give tacit consent. Hume answered with a memorable comparison: saying a poor labourer has consented to the state because he could leave is like saying a man consented to a ship's captain because he could jump overboard. Later critics went further. Some feminist and other scholars argued that historical versions of the contract quietly excluded many people, including women and colonised peoples, from the agreement altogether.

sections.h: Rawls and the veil of ignorance
sections.key: John Rawls revived the social contract as a test for fairness rather than history.
sections.b: In 1971 the American philosopher John Rawls breathed new life into the idea with A Theory of Justice. Rawls did not claim anyone had made a real contract. Instead he asked what principles people would choose if they were designing a society from behind a veil of ignorance, not knowing whether they would be rich or poor, talented or not, or which gender, race or religion they would have. Rawls argued they would choose equal basic liberties for all and would accept inequalities only if they benefited the least advantaged. Not everyone agreed. His Harvard colleague Robert Nozick argued in 1974 that people's rights to what they have earned strictly limit what the state may redistribute, defending a much smaller government.

sections.key: Social contract ideas sit quietly underneath many modern political arguments.
sections.b: You may never use the phrase, but social contract thinking is everywhere. When people argue that taxes are the price of a civilised society, or that government has broken faith with its citizens, they are drawing on it. Debates about how much freedom to trade for safety, from lockdowns to surveillance, echo the argument between Hobbes and Locke. Arguments over welfare and redistribution often replay Rawls and Nozick. The theories do not settle these questions, and thinkers on many sides of politics have used contract ideas to support very different conclusions. What they offer is a useful habit of mind: when someone claims authority over you, ask what would make that authority reasonable to accept, and whether the people affected could genuinely agree to it.

quiz.q: What is the state of nature in social contract theory?
o: An imagined situation with no government at all
quiz.e: Thinkers use it as a starting point to ask why government is justified.

quiz.q: How did Hobbes describe life in the state of nature?
o: Solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short
quiz.e: Hobbes thought only a powerful sovereign could prevent constant conflict.

quiz.q: According to Locke, what can people do if a government violates their natural rights?
o: Nothing, since all rule is legitimate
quiz.e: Locke tied legitimacy to protecting rights, so violating them could forfeit it.

quiz.q: What point did David Hume make with his ship comparison?
o: Staying in a country is not real consent if leaving is not a realistic choice
quiz.e: Hume doubted that tacit consent showed genuine agreement.

quiz.q: What is Rawls's veil of ignorance designed to test?
o: Which principles of justice people would choose without knowing their place in society
How much people know about politics
quiz.e: Not knowing your position pushes you to choose principles fair to everyone.

LESSONS.title: Auroras and space weather
LESSONS.hook: The southern lights are a solar storm hitting Earth's invisible shield, and the same storms can knock out power grids and drag satellites from the sky.

sections.key: Auroras are glowing light shows high in the atmosphere, triggered by activity on the Sun.
sections.b: On the night of 10 May 2024, people across southern Australia stepped outside to find the sky glowing pink and green. Phones lit up with photos from Tasmania, Victoria, South Australia and Western Australia, and the display was seen far further north than usual. It was the aurora australis, the southern lights, during one of the strongest geomagnetic storms in about two decades. Auroras usually hang around the polar regions, shimmering in curtains, arcs and rays that ripple and pulse across the sky. They happen in the upper atmosphere, roughly 100 to several hundred kilometres up, well above where planes fly. Their northern twin is the aurora borealis. Both are caused by the same thing: our star reaching out across 150 million kilometres of space.

sections.key: The Sun constantly streams charged particles into space, a flow called the solar wind.
sections.b: The Sun's outer atmosphere, the corona, is so hot, over a million degrees, that it can't be held in by the Sun's gravity. It boils away into space as a steady stream of charged particles, mostly protons and electrons, called the solar wind. This wind blows outward in every direction at hundreds of kilometres per second, carrying the Sun's magnetic field with it and filling the whole solar system. It usually takes a few days to reach Earth. The Sun's activity rises and falls over a cycle of roughly 11 years, swinging between a quiet solar minimum with few sunspots and a stormy solar maximum with many. The most recent maximum arrived around 2024 to 2025, which is why so many Australians saw auroras then.

sections.key: Earth's magnetic field deflects most of the solar wind and funnels some particles towards the poles.
sections.b: Earth is protected by a magnetic bubble called the magnetosphere, generated by molten iron churning in the planet's outer core. On the side facing the Sun, the solar wind squashes it; on the far side it stretches out into a long tail. Most of the solar wind flows around this bubble. But the magnetic field lines dip down into the atmosphere near the magnetic poles, and energy stored in the magnetosphere can drive charged particles down along them. That is why auroras form in rings, called auroral ovals, around the north and south magnetic poles. When the solar wind is calm, the southern oval mostly sits over Antarctica and the Southern Ocean. When the Sun hits Earth hard, the ovals expand towards the equator, and that is when Tasmania and the mainland get a show.

sections.key: Different gases at different heights glow different colours when struck by incoming particles.
sections.b: An aurora is a little like a neon sign. Fast particles slam into atoms and molecules of air, giving them extra energy, which they release as light. The colour depends on which gas is hit and how high up it is. Oxygen around 100 to 250 kilometres up gives off the most common colour, a vivid green. Higher still, where the air is extremely thin, oxygen can glow a deep red, which is why great storms often paint the sky crimson at the top. Nitrogen adds blues and purples, often along the lower edges. Our eyes are poor at seeing colour in dim light, so a faint aurora can look like a pale grey cloud to the naked eye. A phone or camera, gathering light for several seconds, often reveals colours you couldn't quite see.

sections.key: Solar flares and coronal mass ejections are sudden outbursts that can trigger strong geomagnetic storms.
sections.b: Sunspots are cooler, darker patches where tangled magnetic fields poke through the Sun's surface. When those fields snap and reconnect, they can release enormous energy in two main ways. A solar flare is an intense flash of radiation that reaches Earth in about eight minutes. A coronal mass ejection, or CME, is a vast cloud of magnetised gas, billions of tonnes of it, flung into space and usually arriving one to three days later. If a CME's magnetic field is lined up the right way when it hits, it can pour energy into the magnetosphere and spark a geomagnetic storm. The biggest on record is the Carrington Event of 1859, when auroras were reported far into the tropics and telegraph systems sparked and failed.

sections.key: Strong solar storms can disrupt power grids, satellites, radio and navigation on Earth.
sections.b: Space weather is not just pretty. In March 1989 a geomagnetic storm induced powerful electrical currents in the power grid of Quebec in Canada, and millions of people lost electricity for hours. Storms also heat and puff up the upper atmosphere, increasing drag on low satellites. In February 2022, SpaceX lost dozens of newly launched Starlink satellites after a fairly modest storm dragged them down before they could climb to safer orbits. Solar activity can scramble high frequency radio, which aircraft and remote communities may rely on, and reduce the accuracy of GPS. Astronauts and airline crews on polar routes can also receive extra radiation. That is why agencies around the world, including Australia's Bureau of Meteorology, run space weather services that watch the Sun and issue warnings.

sections.key: Your best chance in Australia is a dark, clear, south-facing spot in the far south during a strong storm.
sections.b: Tasmania is Australia's aurora capital, but strong storms can bring displays to Victoria, South Australia, southern New South Wales and the south of Western Australia. Get well away from city lights, ideally somewhere with a clear, low southern horizon such as a beach or hilltop. A cloudless, moonless night helps enormously. Auroras can appear at any time of year, often around the middle of the night, and they can surge and fade within minutes, so patience pays. Many people sign up for alerts from the Bureau of Meteorology's space weather service or follow local aurora groups online. Bring warm clothes and a phone or camera you can set to night mode or a long exposure. Even when your eyes see only a faint glow, the camera may capture vivid colour.

quiz.q: What is the solar wind?
o: A stream of charged particles flowing out from the Sun
Air currents in Earth's upper atmosphere
Gas escaping from Earth into space
quiz.e: The Sun's hot corona constantly leaks charged particles that flow outward through the solar system.

quiz.q: Why do auroras mostly appear near the poles?
o: Earth's magnetic field guides charged particles down near the magnetic poles
The Sun only shines on the poles
There is more oxygen at the poles
quiz.e: Magnetic field lines dip into the atmosphere near the magnetic poles, so auroras form in ovals around them.

quiz.q: What usually produces the most common green colour in auroras?
quiz.e: Energised oxygen atoms at those heights release green light.

quiz.q: What was the Carrington Event?
o: The first photograph of an aurora
An enormous solar storm in 1859 that disrupted telegraphs
quiz.e: The 1859 storm produced auroras far into the tropics and made telegraph systems spark and fail.

quiz.q: Why did SpaceX lose dozens of Starlink satellites in February 2022?
o: They were hit by a meteor shower
A solar storm increased atmospheric drag on them
quiz.e: Storms heat and expand the upper atmosphere, dragging down satellites in very low orbits.

LESSONS.title: Shooting stars and meteorites
LESSONS.hook: Most shooting stars are specks of dust smaller than a grain of rice, yet a few space rocks survive the fall and carry chemistry older than the Sun.

sections.key: A shooting star is not a star at all, but a tiny piece of space debris burning up in the atmosphere.
sections.b: Lie on your back somewhere dark for half an hour and you will probably see a few shooting stars: brief streaks of light that flash across the sky and vanish. Despite the name, they have nothing to do with stars. Each one is a small piece of rock or dust, often no bigger than a grain of sand, hitting Earth's atmosphere at tremendous speed, somewhere between about 11 and 72 kilometres per second. At that speed it rams into the air so violently that it heats up, vaporises and makes the surrounding air glow, usually somewhere around 70 to 100 kilometres above the ground. Scientists estimate that many tonnes of this cosmic dust fall on Earth every single day, most of it settling unnoticed as fine particles.

sections.key: It's a meteoroid in space, a meteor while it glows, and a meteorite if it reaches the ground.
sections.b: Astronomers use three related words, and they are easy to mix up. A meteoroid is a small rocky or metallic body drifting through space, ranging from a dust grain to a boulder. Anything much bigger is usually called an asteroid. When a meteoroid plunges into the atmosphere and glows, the streak of light is a meteor. An unusually bright meteor, brighter than the planet Venus, is called a fireball, and one that explodes is sometimes called a bolide. If any part of the object survives the fiery trip and lands on the ground, that piece is a meteorite. Most meteors burn up completely, so meteorites are comparatively rare. Comets, by contrast, are icy bodies that grow glowing tails as they near the Sun, and they leave trails of dust behind them.

sections.key: Meteor showers happen when Earth ploughs through trails of dust shed by comets.
sections.b: On most nights you might see a handful of random meteors an hour. But on certain dates each year, the count jumps, sometimes to dozens an hour. These are meteor showers, and they happen like clockwork because Earth passes through the same streams of debris at the same point in its orbit. Most streams were shed by comets as they swung past the Sun, leaving a trail of dust along their path. Halley's Comet, for example, feeds two showers: the Eta Aquariids in May and the Orionids in October. The meteors in a shower all appear to fly out from one point in the sky, called the radiant, and the shower is named after the constellation where that point lies. It is a perspective effect, like parallel railway lines seeming to meet in the distance.

sections.key: The Geminids in December and the Eta Aquariids in May are two of the best showers to watch from Australia.
sections.b: Some famous showers favour the Northern Hemisphere. The Perseids in August, for instance, are low or invisible from much of Australia. Southern observers do better with the Eta Aquariids, peaking in early May, whose radiant rises higher in our pre-dawn sky. The Geminids, peaking around the middle of December, are among the richest showers of the year and can be seen from Australia, though the radiant sits lower than for northern viewers. Unusually, the Geminids come from an asteroid called Phaethon rather than a comet. For any shower, get away from city lights, let your eyes adjust for at least 20 minutes, and lie back to take in as much sky as possible. Counts are usually best after midnight, when your side of Earth faces forward into the debris stream.

sections.key: Meteorites are mostly stony, with rarer iron and stony-iron types, and some preserve the solar system's oldest material.
sections.b: Meteorites come in three broad families. Stony meteorites are by far the most common falls, and most of them are chondrites, containing tiny round grains that formed in the cloud of dust and gas that built the planets about 4.6 billion years ago. Iron meteorites are chunks of metal, mostly iron and nickel, thought to come from the cores of shattered early asteroids. Stony-iron meteorites are a striking mix of both. Australia holds some of the world's most important specimens. On 28 September 1969, a meteorite broke up over the town of Murchison in Victoria, scattering fragments over a wide area. The Murchison meteorite has since been found to contain amino acids, the building blocks of proteins, and microscopic grains that are older than the Sun itself.

sections.key: Large impacts are rare but powerful, as Wolfe Creek Crater and the 2013 Chelyabinsk fireball show.
sections.b: Most space rocks are slowed by the air, but very large ones barely notice it and strike at full speed, blasting out craters. In Western Australia's Kimberley lies Wolfe Creek Crater, about 880 metres wide, one of the best preserved impact craters on Earth. The Jaru people call it Kandimalal and have their own stories about its origin. Scientists think it formed tens of thousands of years ago or more, when an iron meteorite hit. A modern reminder came on 15 February 2013, when an object roughly 20 metres across exploded in the air over Chelyabinsk in Russia. The shock wave shattered windows across the city, and around 1,500 people were injured, mostly by flying glass. Nobody was killed, but it showed why agencies now track asteroids that cross Earth's path.

sections.key: Real meteorites are usually heavy, often magnetic and coated in a dark crust, but most suspected finds turn out to be Earth rocks.
sections.b: Australia's deserts are excellent meteorite hunting grounds, because dark rocks stand out on pale ground and the dry climate slows weathering. Researchers at Curtin University run the Desert Fireball Network, cameras that photograph bright fireballs so their landing spots can be calculated and fragments recovered. Its first find, in 2007, came from the Nullarbor. If you think you've found a meteorite, look for a rock that feels unusually heavy for its size, often attracts a magnet, and has a thin, dark, glassy crust from melting during its fall. Real meteorites rarely have bubbly holes. Most candidates turn out to be iron-rich Earth rocks or industrial slag, nicknamed meteorwrongs. State museums can often identify specimens, and in some states meteorites legally belong to the state, so check the rules before selling one.

quiz.q: What is a meteorite?
o: A rock that is still drifting through space
The glowing streak in the sky
A piece of a space rock that survives and reaches the ground
quiz.e: It's a meteoroid in space, a meteor while glowing, and a meteorite once it lands.

quiz.q: Why do meteor showers happen on the same dates each year?
o: Earth passes through the same debris streams at the same point in its orbit
Comets visit every year on those dates
The Moon releases dust on a fixed schedule
quiz.e: Debris trails stay along fixed paths, so Earth meets them at the same time each year.

quiz.q: What is unusual about the Geminid meteor shower?
o: Its meteors move slower than sound
It comes from an asteroid, Phaethon, not a comet
quiz.e: Most showers come from comets, but the Geminids come from the asteroid Phaethon.

quiz.q: What has the Murchison meteorite been found to contain?
o: Amino acids and grains older than the Sun
quiz.e: The 1969 Victorian meteorite contains amino acids and presolar grains formed before the Sun.

quiz.q: What is a sign that a rock might be a real meteorite?
o: It has lots of bubbly holes
It feels heavy and has a thin, dark, glassy crust
It is very light and chalky
quiz.e: Meteorites are often dense, frequently magnetic, and have a fusion crust from melting in the atmosphere.

LESSONS.title: Neutron stars and pulsars
LESSONS.hook: Imagine squeezing more than the mass of the Sun into a ball the size of a city, then spinning it hundreds of times a second.

sections.key: A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a sphere only about 20 kilometres across.
sections.b: A neutron star is what remains when a massive star's core collapses. It is typically around 1.4 times the mass of the Sun, yet only about 20 kilometres in diameter, roughly the size of a large city. That makes it one of the densest objects known. A teaspoon of its material would weigh something like a billion tonnes on Earth. Gravity at the surface is so intense that a marshmallow dropped onto it would strike with the energy of a nuclear bomb, a vivid comparison astronomers like to use. The surface is thought to be incredibly smooth, with mountains only millimetres tall. Beneath it, matter is crushed so tightly that most electrons and protons have merged into neutrons, which is how these strange objects got their name.

sections.key: When a giant star runs out of fuel, its core collapses in under a second and the outer layers explode.
sections.b: Stars much more massive than the Sun live fast. They fuse lighter elements into heavier ones in their cores until they produce iron, which cannot release energy through fusion. With no more energy pushing outward, gravity wins. The core, about the mass of the Sun, collapses in a fraction of a second from thousands of kilometres across to just a few dozen. The infalling outer layers rebound and are blasted outward in a supernova, which can briefly outshine an entire galaxy. What is left behind depends mostly on how heavy the core is. A lighter remnant becomes a neutron star; a heavier one keeps collapsing into a black hole. The Crab Nebula, the wreckage of a supernova recorded by Chinese astronomers in 1054, has a neutron star at its centre.

sections.key: Pulsars were discovered in 1967 by Jocelyn Bell Burnell, a postgraduate student in Cambridge.
sections.b: In 1967 a young postgraduate student at the University of Cambridge, Jocelyn Bell, was checking hundreds of metres of chart paper from a new radio telescope she had helped build. She noticed a tiny bit of 'scruff' that turned out to be a signal pulsing with astonishing regularity, about every 1.3 seconds. It was so precise that the team half jokingly labelled it LGM-1, for 'little green men', wondering whether it could be an artificial signal. When she found more of them in other parts of the sky, an alien explanation became very unlikely. They were soon identified as rapidly spinning neutron stars and named pulsars. The 1974 Nobel Prize in Physics went to her supervisor Antony Hewish and Martin Ryle, an omission many scientists still consider unfair. She later became Dame Jocelyn Bell Burnell.

sections.key: Pulsars sweep beams of radiation across space as they spin, so we see a pulse each time a beam passes us.
sections.b: When a star's core collapses, it keeps its spin, and shrinking makes it spin much faster, just as a figure skater speeds up by pulling in their arms. Newborn neutron stars can rotate many times a second. They also have intense magnetic fields that channel beams of radio waves and other radiation out from their magnetic poles. If those poles are tilted relative to the spin axis, the beams sweep around like a lighthouse. Each time one crosses Earth, our telescopes record a pulse. Some pulsars, called millisecond pulsars, have been spun up by pulling material from a companion star. The fastest known rotates over 700 times a second, meaning a point on its equator moves at a sizeable fraction of the speed of light.

sections.key: Magnetars are neutron stars with the strongest magnetic fields known, capable of colossal outbursts.
sections.b: Some neutron stars have magnetic fields even more extreme than usual. These magnetars have fields estimated to be up to around a thousand trillion times stronger than Earth's. A field that strong would, in theory, distort atoms and wipe every credit card on Earth from a distance of thousands of kilometres. As the crust of a magnetar shifts under these enormous magnetic stresses, it can unleash sudden bursts of X-rays and gamma rays. In December 2004 a giant flare from a magnetar called SGR 1806-20, on the far side of our galaxy, was so powerful that it measurably disturbed Earth's upper atmosphere. Astronomers now suspect that some magnetars are behind fast radio bursts, brief and extremely energetic flashes of radio waves detected from across the universe.

sections.key: When two neutron stars merge, they create heavy elements such as gold and platinum.
sections.b: Many neutron stars live in pairs, slowly spiralling towards each other as they lose energy. In 1974 Russell Hulse and Joseph Taylor discovered a binary pulsar whose orbit shrank exactly as Einstein's theory predicted it would if the pair were radiating gravitational waves, work that earned a Nobel Prize in 1993. On 17 August 2017, detectors on Earth finally caught the gravitational wave signal of two neutron stars colliding, about 130 million light-years away. Telescopes around the world, including in Australia, then watched the glowing aftermath, called a kilonova. Its light carried the signature of freshly made heavy elements. Astronomers estimate that mergers like this have produced a significant share of the universe's gold, platinum and other heavy metals, possibly including some of the gold in your jewellery.

sections.key: Pulsars are such precise clocks that astronomers use them to test physics and detect giant gravitational waves.
sections.b: Some millisecond pulsars tick with a regularity that rivals atomic clocks. Australia has played a big role in studying them, and CSIRO's Parkes radio telescope, Murriyang, has discovered a large share of all known pulsars. By timing dozens of pulsars over many years, astronomers can watch for tiny, shared shifts in when their pulses arrive. In 2023, several international teams, including the Parkes Pulsar Timing Array, reported evidence of a faint background of very long gravitational waves rippling through the galaxy, likely produced by pairs of supermassive black holes. Pulsars have even been proposed as a galactic GPS for future spacecraft. The plaques on the Pioneer probes and the Voyager records already carry a map showing the Sun's position relative to 14 pulsars, a cosmic return address.

quiz.q: Roughly how big is a typical neutron star?
o: About the size of the Sun
quiz.e: It holds more than the Sun's mass in a sphere only about the size of a city.

quiz.q: Who discovered the first pulsar in 1967?
quiz.e: Jocelyn Bell spotted the regular signal while analysing data from a new radio telescope at Cambridge.

quiz.q: Why do pulsars appear to pulse?
o: Clouds pass in front of them
Their beams sweep across Earth as they spin
quiz.e: Like a lighthouse, a rotating beam is seen as a pulse each time it points at us.

quiz.q: What did the 2017 neutron star merger show?
o: Neutron stars are made of iron
Such collisions produce heavy elements like gold
quiz.e: The kilonova's light carried the signature of freshly made heavy elements.

quiz.q: Why are millisecond pulsars useful to astronomers?
o: They are bright enough to see by eye
They tick so regularly they work as precise cosmic clocks
quiz.e: Their precise timing lets astronomers test physics and detect gravitational waves.

LESSONS.title: Gravitational waves: hearing the universe
LESSONS.hook: A century after Einstein predicted them, scientists caught a ripple in space itself that had travelled for over a billion years from two colliding black holes.

sections.key: Gravitational waves are ripples in the fabric of spacetime, created when massive objects accelerate.
sections.b: Drop a stone into a still pond and ripples spread outward. In 1916 Albert Einstein realised that his new theory of gravity, general relativity, predicted something similar in space itself. In his theory, mass and energy curve spacetime, and gravity is how objects move through those curves. When massive objects accelerate, especially when they orbit each other closely, they should send out ripples in that curvature, travelling at the speed of light. As a wave passes, it stretches space in one direction while squeezing it in the perpendicular direction, then reverses, over and over. Everything in its path, including you, is stretched and squeezed too. But the effect is fantastically small, so small that Einstein himself doubted anyone would ever be able to measure it.

sections.key: Even waves from colliding black holes change distances on Earth by far less than the width of a proton.
sections.b: Spacetime is extraordinarily stiff, which is why only the most violent events in the universe make waves we can hope to detect, and why they are so weak by the time they arrive. The first wave ever measured changed the length of a four kilometre detector arm by a tiny fraction of the width of a single proton. Measuring something that small is a bit like measuring the distance to the nearest star to within the width of a human hair. For decades the only evidence was indirect. Astronomers watched a pair of neutron stars, discovered in 1974, slowly spiral towards each other at exactly the rate expected if they were losing energy as gravitational waves. That was convincing, but nobody had yet caught a wave passing through Earth.

sections.key: LIGO uses lasers bouncing along two four kilometre arms to detect the tiny stretching of space.
sections.b: The Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory, LIGO, has two detectors in the United States, at Hanford in Washington state and Livingston in Louisiana. Each is shaped like a giant letter L, with two arms four kilometres long at right angles. A laser beam is split in two and sent down both arms in vacuum tubes, bouncing off mirrors many times before the beams are recombined. Normally they cancel out perfectly. If a gravitational wave passes, one arm stretches slightly while the other shrinks, the beams fall out of step, and a flicker of light appears. Having two widely separated detectors helps rule out local disturbances such as passing trucks or earthquakes. Europe's Virgo detector in Italy and Japan's KAGRA have since joined the hunt, helping pinpoint sources in the sky.

sections.key: On 14 September 2015 LIGO detected waves from two black holes merging about 1.3 billion light-years away.
sections.b: On 14 September 2015, just days after the upgraded detectors switched on, both LIGO sites recorded the same signal, milliseconds apart. Turned into sound, it rose in pitch and volume and ended in a sudden 'chirp'. It came from two black holes, each roughly 30 times the mass of the Sun, spiralling together and merging about 1.3 billion years ago. In the final fraction of a second, an amount of energy equal to about three Suns' worth of mass was converted into gravitational waves, briefly outpowering all the stars in the observable universe combined. The discovery was announced in February 2016, almost exactly a century after Einstein's prediction. In 2017 Rainer Weiss, Barry Barish and Kip Thorne received the Nobel Prize in Physics for their roles in making it possible.

sections.key: Australian scientists helped build LIGO's technology and analyse its data, through groups now united in OzGrav.
sections.b: Australia has been part of the gravitational wave story for decades. Researchers at the Australian National University, the University of Western Australia, the University of Adelaide and other institutions developed technologies used in LIGO, including precise laser and optics techniques and ways to reduce quantum noise in the measurements. Australians were among the authors on the discovery papers. Today many of these researchers belong to OzGrav, the ARC Centre of Excellence for Gravitational Wave Discovery, which works on detecting signals, analysing data and following up events with telescopes. Australian astronomers have also helped search the sky for the light from mergers. The country's position in the Southern Hemisphere is useful for this, since it covers parts of the sky that northern telescopes cannot see well.

sections.key: In 2017 a neutron star collision was seen in both gravitational waves and light, opening a new kind of astronomy.
sections.b: Black hole mergers produce gravitational waves but little or no light. Neutron star collisions are different. On 17 August 2017, LIGO and Virgo picked up a signal from two neutron stars merging about 130 million light-years away. About 1.7 seconds later, a space telescope recorded a short burst of gamma rays from the same region. Within hours, telescopes around the world were watching the glowing debris. This was the birth of what scientists call multi-messenger astronomy, studying a single event through different kinds of signals. The near-simultaneous arrival of light and gravitational waves, after a journey of 130 million years, confirmed that gravity travels at the speed of light to extraordinary precision, and ruled out several alternative theories of gravity in a single stroke.

sections.key: Detectors have now recorded hundreds of candidate events, and new instruments will hear different frequencies.
sections.b: Since 2015 the global network has improved steadily, and detections that once made headlines now arrive routinely, with hundreds of candidate events so far. Each tells astronomers something about how black holes and neutron stars form, how heavy they get and how often they collide. Different instruments listen for different 'notes'. Ground detectors like LIGO hear the final seconds of smaller mergers. Pulsar timing arrays, using the steady ticks of distant pulsars, have found evidence of extremely slow waves likely produced by supermassive black hole pairs. The European Space Agency is developing LISA, a planned trio of spacecraft millions of kilometres apart, to catch waves in between. There is even hope of one day detecting gravitational waves from the earliest moments of the universe itself.

quiz.q: Who first predicted gravitational waves?
quiz.e: Einstein's general relativity predicted them in 1916.

quiz.q: How does LIGO detect a gravitational wave?
o: By listening with microphones in space
By measuring tiny changes in the length of two laser arms
quiz.e: A passing wave stretches one arm and squeezes the other, putting the laser beams out of step.

quiz.q: What produced the first detected gravitational waves in 2015?
quiz.e: Two black holes, each around 30 solar masses, merged about 1.3 billion light-years away.

quiz.q: What is OzGrav?
o: An Australian gravitational wave detector in the outback
An Australian research centre for gravitational wave discovery
quiz.e: OzGrav is the ARC Centre of Excellence uniting Australian gravitational wave researchers.

quiz.q: What did the 2017 neutron star merger confirm?
o: Gravity travels at the speed of light
Gravitational waves are too weak to detect
quiz.e: Light and gravitational waves arrived almost together after 130 million years.

LESSONS.title: Ocean moons: hidden seas of the outer solar system
LESSONS.hook: Some of the best places to look for alien life may be dark oceans hidden beneath the ice of moons orbiting Jupiter and Saturn.

sections.key: Several icy moons far from the Sun appear to hide liquid water oceans beneath their frozen surfaces.
sections.b: For a long time scientists assumed the outer solar system was a deep freeze. Out past Mars, sunlight is weak, and surface temperatures on the moons of Jupiter and Saturn sit well below minus 100 degrees Celsius. Yet spacecraft have revealed something astonishing: several of these moons appear to have global oceans of liquid water hidden beneath shells of ice. Europa, a moon of Jupiter, may hold more water than all of Earth's oceans combined. Saturn's small moon Enceladus sprays its ocean into space. Others, including Ganymede and Titan, show strong signs of buried oceans too, and Callisto may have one as well. Since liquid water is essential to all life we know, these hidden seas have become some of the most exciting targets in the search for life beyond Earth.

sections.key: Tidal heating, the constant flexing caused by a giant planet's gravity, keeps these oceans from freezing.
sections.b: How can water stay liquid so far from the Sun? The main answer is tidal heating. These moons follow slightly oval orbits around enormous planets, and often tug on each other too. As a moon moves closer to and further from its planet, the changing pull of gravity squeezes and stretches it, flexing its interior. Bend a paperclip back and forth and it warms up; something similar happens inside the moon, generating heat through friction. Jupiter's moon Io shows the extreme version: it is so heavily flexed that it is the most volcanically active world in the solar system. Further out, gentler tidal heating, along with heat from radioactive elements in the rock, appears to be enough to keep oceans liquid beneath kilometres of insulating ice.

sections.key: Jupiter's moon Europa has a cracked icy crust over an ocean that may be in contact with a rocky seafloor.
sections.b: Europa is slightly smaller than our Moon, but its surface looks nothing like it. It is bright white ice, crisscrossed by long reddish brown cracks and ridges, with very few craters, a sign that the surface is young and constantly reshaped. In the late 1990s, NASA's Galileo spacecraft measured how Europa disturbed Jupiter's magnetic field, and the best explanation was a salty, electrically conducting ocean beneath the ice. The ice shell is thought to be several to a few dozen kilometres thick, with an ocean perhaps around 100 kilometres deep below it. Crucially, that ocean probably sits on a rocky seafloor, where water and rock could react chemically, as they do around hydrothermal vents in Earth's deep oceans, where life thrives without sunlight.

sections.key: Saturn's tiny moon Enceladus sprays jets of ocean water into space, which Cassini flew through and sampled.
sections.b: Enceladus is only about 500 kilometres across, small enough to fit within the width of Victoria, so scientists did not expect much from it. Then in 2005 NASA's Cassini spacecraft spotted jets of water vapour and ice grains erupting from long cracks near its south pole, nicknamed tiger stripes. These plumes feed one of Saturn's rings. Cassini later flew directly through them, essentially tasting an alien ocean. It detected water, salts, carbon dioxide, ammonia and a range of organic molecules. Tiny silica grains hinted at hot water reacting with rock on the seafloor, and later analysis found phosphorus, an essential ingredient for life on Earth. Enceladus appears to tick many of the boxes for habitability: liquid water, chemical energy and the right raw materials.

sections.key: Titan has a thick atmosphere, methane rain and lakes of liquid hydrocarbons, plus a likely water ocean below.
sections.b: Saturn's largest moon, Titan, is bigger than the planet Mercury and the only moon with a thick atmosphere, made mostly of nitrogen, like Earth's. Its surface air pressure is about one and a half times ours. At around minus 180 degrees Celsius, water is frozen as hard as rock, but methane and ethane behave as liquids. Titan has clouds, rain, rivers and large lakes and seas, all made of liquid hydrocarbons rather than water. In 2005 the European Huygens probe parachuted through the orange haze and landed on a damp plain strewn with rounded pebbles of ice. Measurements suggest Titan also hides a water ocean deep beneath its icy crust. That makes it a world with two very different liquid environments, each potentially interesting for chemistry and life.

sections.key: Ganymede, the solar system's largest moon, and several other icy worlds may also harbour buried oceans.
sections.b: Jupiter's Ganymede is the largest moon in the solar system, bigger than Mercury, and the only moon known to generate its own magnetic field. Observations with the Hubble Space Telescope of how its auroras shift back and forth suggested a salty ocean deep beneath its surface, perhaps sandwiched between layers of ice. Callisto, Jupiter's heavily cratered outer large moon, may also hold a deep ocean, though it is less certain. Scientists have raised the possibility of oceans further out too, including inside Saturn's moon Mimas, Neptune's moon Triton and even the dwarf planet Pluto. If buried oceans turn out to be common, then liquid water might be far more widespread in the universe than on rocky, sunlit planets like Earth, greatly increasing the number of places where life could arise.

sections.key: New missions are heading to these moons, and old spacecraft were deliberately destroyed to avoid contaminating them.
sections.b: Several spacecraft are now on their way. The European Space Agency's JUICE mission, launched in 2023, will study Jupiter's icy moons and eventually orbit Ganymede. NASA's Europa Clipper, launched in 2024, will make dozens of close flybys of Europa to measure its ice, ocean and chemistry. NASA's Dragonfly, a nuclear powered rotorcraft drone, is planned to fly between sites on Titan in the 2030s. Scientists take great care not to contaminate these worlds with Earth microbes, a principle called planetary protection. That is why the Galileo spacecraft was deliberately plunged into Jupiter in 2003, and Cassini into Saturn in 2017, as their fuel ran low. If we ever find life in an ocean moon, we need to be sure we didn't bring it there ourselves.

quiz.q: What mainly keeps these moons' oceans from freezing?
o: Tidal heating from the flexing caused by gravity
quiz.e: Changing gravitational pulls squeeze and stretch the moons, generating heat inside.

quiz.q: Why is Europa's ocean especially interesting for life?
o: It probably touches a rocky seafloor where chemical reactions can occur
quiz.e: Water reacting with rock could supply energy, as at hydrothermal vents on Earth.

quiz.q: What did Cassini discover at Enceladus?
o: Jets of water and ice erupting from its south pole
quiz.e: Cassini saw plumes from the tiger stripes and flew through them to sample the ocean.

quiz.q: What are Titan's lakes and seas made of?
o: Liquid hydrocarbons like methane and ethane
quiz.e: At about minus 180 degrees, methane and ethane are liquid while water is frozen solid.

quiz.q: Why was Cassini deliberately crashed into Saturn?
o: To avoid any risk of contaminating moons that might host life
Because it was struck by debris
To make room for a new mission
quiz.e: Planetary protection rules aim to keep Earth microbes away from potentially habitable moons.

LESSONS.title: Space junk: the litter problem in orbit
LESSONS.hook: Tens of thousands of dead satellites and rocket parts are racing around Earth faster than bullets, and once in 1979 a big piece landed near Esperance.

sections.key: Earth is surrounded by debris: dead satellites, spent rocket stages and countless fragments.
sections.b: Since Sputnik in 1957, people have launched thousands of objects into orbit, and much of what goes up stays there long after it stops working. Space junk, or orbital debris, includes dead satellites, used rocket stages, lost tools, flakes of paint and fragments from explosions and collisions. Space agencies track tens of thousands of pieces larger than about a softball, and estimates suggest there are around a million pieces bigger than a centimetre and many millions smaller still, too tiny to track. Most of it sits in low Earth orbit, within about 2,000 kilometres of the surface, the same busy region used by the International Space Station, Earth observation satellites and internet constellations. Some debris also lingers in the much higher geostationary belt, where many communication and weather satellites sit.

sections.key: In low orbit, debris travels at about 7 to 8 kilometres per second, so even tiny pieces can do serious damage.
sections.b: To stay in low Earth orbit, an object must travel at roughly 28,000 kilometres per hour, around ten times faster than a rifle bullet. Two objects in different orbits can meet at a combined speed of around ten kilometres per second or more. At those speeds, even a fleck of paint carries surprising energy. Space Shuttle windows were replaced many times after being chipped by tiny impacts. A marble-sized fragment could disable a satellite, and anything larger could destroy one. The International Space Station has extra shielding on vulnerable areas and regularly fires its engines to dodge tracked debris, and astronauts have occasionally sheltered in their docked return capsules when a close pass was predicted at short notice. Satellite operators receive collision warnings and perform avoidance manoeuvres too.

sections.key: In 2009 two satellites collided by accident, and experts warn collisions could trigger a chain reaction.
sections.b: On 10 February 2009, a working American communications satellite, Iridium 33, smashed into a dead Russian military satellite, Kosmos 2251, about 790 kilometres above Siberia. It was the first known accidental collision between two intact satellites, and it created well over a thousand trackable fragments, many of which are still in orbit. Back in 1978, NASA scientist Donald Kessler warned of exactly this danger. He pointed out that if debris became dense enough, collisions would create more fragments, which would cause more collisions, in a cascading chain reaction. This scenario is now known as the Kessler syndrome. In its worst form, some orbits could become so cluttered that they are too risky to use for generations, affecting services we rely on every day.

sections.key: Deliberate tests that blow up satellites with missiles have created some of the worst debris clouds.
sections.b: Some of the biggest debris clouds were created on purpose. In January 2007, China tested an anti-satellite missile by destroying one of its own old weather satellites, Fengyun-1C, about 860 kilometres up. The blast created more than 3,000 trackable fragments, the largest single debris event on record, and at that altitude much of it will remain for decades. The United States destroyed a failing satellite with a missile in 2008, though at a much lower altitude where debris fell back relatively quickly. In November 2021 Russia blew up its own defunct satellite Kosmos 1408, creating a cloud of fragments that forced the crew of the International Space Station to shelter in their spacecraft. Since 2022 a number of countries, including Australia, have pledged not to conduct destructive anti-satellite missile tests.

sections.key: Most debris eventually falls back and burns up, but large objects sometimes reach the ground, including in Australia.
sections.b: Thin traces of atmosphere slowly drag on objects in low orbit, so they gradually sink and eventually burn up on re-entry. Large, sturdy parts can survive, though. In July 1979, the American space station Skylab broke apart over the Indian Ocean and scattered debris across the region around Esperance in Western Australia. Nobody was hurt, and the local shire famously issued NASA a $400 fine for littering, which was eventually paid decades later by an American radio host. In 2022, pieces of a SpaceX capsule's trunk section landed on farms in the Snowy Mountains of New South Wales. Today, operators often steer big spacecraft down over a remote part of the South Pacific near Point Nemo, the place on Earth furthest from land, nicknamed the spacecraft cemetery.

sections.key: Thousands of new internet satellites are making orbit busier, raising collision risks and affecting astronomy.
sections.b: The number of active satellites has soared in recent years, mainly because of megaconstellations: huge fleets of small satellites providing internet from low orbit. SpaceX's Starlink alone has launched many thousands, and other companies and countries are building their own. These networks bring fast internet to remote areas, including outback Australia, and they are designed to fall out of orbit within a few years when retired. But more satellites mean more close approaches to manage, and operators must perform large numbers of avoidance manoeuvres. Astronomers have raised another concern: sunlit satellites leave bright streaks across telescope images and can interfere with radio observations. Companies have experimented with darker coatings and sunshades, but the growing traffic is changing how scientists plan observations of the night sky.

sections.key: Rules now push operators to remove satellites after use, and companies are testing ways to capture debris.
sections.b: The first fix is not to make more mess. International guidelines have long asked operators to remove satellites from busy low orbits within 25 years of the end of their mission, and in 2022 the United States regulator set a stricter five year rule for satellites it licenses. Rocket stages are increasingly designed to burn up quickly, and satellites carry fuel to lower themselves at the end. Removing existing junk is harder, because every piece is moving fast and tumbling. Japanese company Astroscale has flown missions that approached and inspected a discarded rocket stage, and European projects are developing robotic arms, nets and other ways to catch dead satellites. In Australia, the Australian Space Agency works with industry on space situational awareness, tracking objects to help keep orbits safe.

quiz.q: Roughly how fast does debris travel in low Earth orbit?
quiz.e: Objects in low orbit move at roughly 28,000 kilometres per hour.

quiz.q: What is the Kessler syndrome?
o: A chain reaction of collisions creating ever more debris
An illness astronauts get in orbit
quiz.e: Donald Kessler warned that collisions could cascade and make orbits unusable.

quiz.q: What created the largest single debris event on record in 2007?
quiz.e: China destroyed its Fengyun-1C weather satellite, creating over 3,000 trackable pieces.

quiz.q: What happened near Esperance in 1979?
o: Debris from the Skylab space station fell there
quiz.e: Skylab broke up and scattered debris over the region, and the shire fined NASA for littering.

quiz.q: Why are astronomers concerned about megaconstellations?
o: Their satellites leave bright streaks across telescope images
quiz.e: Sunlit satellites streak across images and can interfere with radio observations.

LESSONS.title: How we measure the universe
LESSONS.hook: No one has ever stretched a tape measure to a star, yet we know distances across billions of light-years. The trick is a ladder of clever steps.

sections.key: Astronomers measure cosmic distances in light-years, the distance light travels in a year.
sections.b: Light is the fastest thing there is, covering about 300,000 kilometres every second. Even so, sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach us, and light from the nearest star beyond the Sun, Proxima Centauri, takes over four years. So astronomers measure space in light-years: the distance light travels in a year, about 9.5 trillion kilometres. A light-year is a distance, not a time. Using it has a fascinating consequence: when you look at a star a thousand light-years away, you see light that left it a thousand years ago. Looking further means looking back in time. But how do we know any of these distances? No single method works for everything, so astronomers built a chain of techniques, each one checked against the last, called the cosmic distance ladder.

sections.key: Nearby distances in the solar system are measured by bouncing radar and laser beams off objects and timing the echo.
sections.b: The first rung of the ladder is our own neighbourhood. Because we know the speed of light precisely, we can measure distance by sending out a signal and timing how long the echo takes to return. Since the 1960s, astronomers have bounced radar off Venus, Mars and asteroids, pinning down the scale of the solar system with great accuracy. The average distance from Earth to the Sun, called the astronomical unit, is about 150 million kilometres. For the Moon, observatories fire powerful laser pulses at reflectors left on the surface by Apollo astronauts and Soviet rovers. Timing the round trip, which takes about two and a half seconds, reveals the Moon's distance to within millimetres, and shows it is drifting away from Earth by a few centimetres each year.

sections.key: Parallax, the apparent shift of a nearby star as Earth orbits the Sun, gives direct distances to nearby stars.
sections.b: Hold a thumb at arm's length and look at it with one eye, then the other. It seems to jump against the background. That shift is called parallax, and the closer the thumb, the bigger the jump. Astronomers do the same with stars, but instead of two eyes they use two positions of Earth, six months apart, on opposite sides of its orbit. A nearby star appears to shift very slightly against much more distant ones, and simple geometry turns that shift into a distance. The effect is tiny, and it wasn't measured until 1838, when German astronomer Friedrich Bessel managed it for a star called 61 Cygni. Today the European Space Agency's Gaia spacecraft has measured positions, and for many stars parallaxes, for more than a billion stars.

sections.key: Henrietta Leavitt found that certain pulsing stars reveal their true brightness, making them cosmic measuring sticks.
sections.b: Parallax only works for stars in our part of the galaxy. Beyond that, astronomers need standard candles: objects whose true brightness is known. If you know how bright a light really is, how dim it looks tells you how far away it is. In the early 1900s, Henrietta Swan Leavitt was working at Harvard College Observatory, one of a group of women employed to analyse photographic plates, often for low pay. Studying the Small Magellanic Cloud, which is easily seen from Australia, she noticed that stars called Cepheid variables, which brighten and dim in a regular rhythm, followed a pattern: the slower the pulse, the brighter the star. Published in 1912, her discovery meant a Cepheid's rhythm reveals its true brightness, and therefore its distance.

sections.key: Using Cepheids, Edwin Hubble showed in the 1920s that Andromeda is a separate galaxy far beyond the Milky Way.
sections.b: In the early 1920s, astronomers were divided over a big question. Were the faint spiral shapes in the sky, then called spiral nebulae, clouds within our own Milky Way, or entire separate galaxies? Edwin Hubble settled it using Leavitt's discovery. Working at Mount Wilson Observatory in California, he found Cepheid variables in the Andromeda nebula and measured their rhythms. Their faintness showed they were far beyond the edge of our galaxy. Andromeda, it turned out, was a vast galaxy in its own right, and modern measurements put it about 2.5 million light-years away. Almost overnight the known universe grew enormously, from a single galaxy to countless billions. Hubble went on to show that distant galaxies are moving away from us, the first evidence that the universe is expanding.

sections.key: Type Ia supernovae are bright enough to measure distances across billions of light-years, revealing an accelerating universe.
sections.b: Cepheids are bright, but not bright enough to see in very distant galaxies. For that, astronomers use a particular kind of exploding star called a Type Ia supernova. These are thought to occur when a white dwarf, the dense remnant of a star like the Sun, is pushed over a critical limit and blows apart. Because they explode in a fairly consistent way, their peak brightness can be worked out, making them standard candles visible across billions of light-years. In 1998 two teams used them to discover that the universe's expansion is speeding up, not slowing down. One team was led by Brian Schmidt, working at the Australian National University's Mount Stromlo Observatory near Canberra. He shared the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics with Saul Perlmutter and Adam Riess.

sections.key: For the most distant galaxies, redshift reveals distance, but two ways of measuring the expansion rate disagree.
sections.b: At the top of the ladder is redshift. As the universe expands, light travelling through it is stretched to longer, redder wavelengths. The further away a galaxy is, the faster it appears to recede and the more its light is reddened, a relationship known as Hubble's law. Once the ladder is calibrated, a galaxy's redshift tells astronomers roughly how far away it is. But there is a puzzle. Measuring today's expansion rate using the ladder of Cepheids and supernovae gives a noticeably higher answer than calculating it from the faint afterglow of the Big Bang, the cosmic microwave background. This mismatch, called the Hubble tension, has persisted as measurements have improved. It might be a subtle error somewhere, or a sign that our picture of the universe is missing something.

quiz.q: What is a light-year?
o: The distance light travels in a year
quiz.e: A light-year is a distance, about 9.5 trillion kilometres.

quiz.q: How does parallax measure the distance to a star?
o: By its apparent shift as Earth moves around its orbit
quiz.e: Viewing from opposite sides of Earth's orbit makes nearby stars appear to shift slightly.

quiz.q: What did Henrietta Leavitt discover about Cepheid variables?
o: The slower they pulse, the brighter they truly are
They are all the same distance away
They only appear in the Northern Hemisphere
quiz.e: This period and brightness link turned Cepheids into standard candles.

quiz.q: What did Edwin Hubble show about Andromeda?
o: It is a nebula inside the Milky Way
It is a cluster of comets
It is about to collide with the Sun
It is a separate galaxy far beyond the Milky Way
quiz.e: Cepheids in Andromeda showed it lay far outside our galaxy.

quiz.q: What did Type Ia supernovae reveal in 1998?
o: The expansion of the universe is speeding up
The Milky Way is the only galaxy
Light travels slower over long distances
quiz.e: Brian Schmidt's team and another found the expansion is accelerating.

LESSONS.title: First Nations astronomy
LESSONS.hook: Long before telescopes, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples read the night sky as a calendar, a map, a law book and a library of stories.

sections.key: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have observed and used the night sky for many thousands of years.
sections.b: Australia's First Peoples have lived on this continent for at least 50,000 years, and many researchers think longer. For all that time they have looked up at the same southern sky, and their knowledge of it is woven through culture, law and daily life. There is no single 'Aboriginal astronomy'. Australia has hundreds of distinct nations and language groups, each with its own stories and ways of reading the sky, though some stories are shared across vast distances. The stars were used to tell the seasons, find food, navigate, mark ceremonies and pass on rules for living. Researchers working alongside communities, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander scientists, are helping more people appreciate how sophisticated this knowledge is, while respecting that some of it is sacred and not for public sharing.

sections.key: Many groups see an emu formed by the dark dust lanes of the Milky Way, and its changing position signals emu breeding.
sections.b: Western constellations join up bright stars. Many Aboriginal traditions also look at the spaces between them. The best known example is the Emu in the Sky. Its head is the Coalsack, a dark cloud of dust beside the Southern Cross, and its neck, body and legs stretch along dark lanes in the Milky Way. On autumn evenings, after dark, the emu appears to be running across the sky. For a number of groups this coincides with the time emus are mating and laying eggs, a useful signal for when eggs could be collected.
