Later in the year, the emu's shape appears to change position, reflecting different stages of the emu's breeding cycle. Today the Emu in the Sky features in many planetarium shows and astronomy outreach programs.

sections.key: The Pleiades star cluster is the centre of Seven Sisters stories that travel thousands of kilometres across the desert.
sections.b: The Pleiades, a small, tight cluster of stars, has inspired stories in cultures all over the world, from ancient Greece to Japan. In Australia, it is the heart of the Seven Sisters, one of the most widespread and important Aboriginal stories. In many desert versions, a group of sisters is pursued across the country by a man, often linked to stars in the constellation Westerners call Orion. As they flee, their journey creates and names features of the landscape, forming songlines, routes that link sites over thousands of kilometres and carry knowledge, law and ceremony. In 2017 the National Museum of Australia staged a major exhibition, Songlines: Tracking the Seven Sisters, developed with Anangu, Martu and Ngaanyatjarra communities, sharing parts of this story through paintings, song and dance.

sections.key: In the Torres Strait, the great star figure Tagai guides fishing, planting, navigation and the seasons.
sections.b: For Torres Strait Islanders, the most important figure in the sky is Tagai, a great fisherman standing in his canoe. In common descriptions, his left hand holds a fishing spear, represented by the Southern Cross, and his right hand holds a sorbi fruit, represented by stars Westerners know as the constellation Corvus. His canoe and crew are made of other stars, including parts of Scorpius and the Pleiades. Tagai's story teaches the importance of following rules and sharing, and his position in the sky through the year guides when to plant gardens, when to fish and hunt turtle and dugong, and when winds and seasons will change. His story shows how deeply sky, sea and law are connected.

sections.key: The rising and setting of particular stars has long been used to signal seasonal events on the land.
sections.b: Across Australia, the appearance of certain stars at dawn or dusk has long been linked to events on the ground: plants flowering, animals breeding or weather changing. In the 1850s, a settler named William Stanbridge recorded the sky knowledge of the Boorong people of north-western Victoria, one of the earliest written records of Aboriginal astronomy. It describes many stars and constellations, including a star associated with the malleefowl, whose appearance in the evening sky was linked to the time malleefowl build their nesting mounds. Other groups connected the first appearance of the Pleiades at dawn with the arrival of colder weather. These star calendars are tailored to local country, since seasons in Arnhem Land are very different from those in the southern deserts or along the Murray River.

sections.key: Traditional knowledge includes links between the Moon and tides, explanations of eclipses and notice of stars that vary in brightness.
sections.b: Aboriginal sky knowledge was not only about stories; it also recorded careful observations. The Yolngu people of north-east Arnhem Land have traditional knowledge linking the tides to the Moon. They understood that high tides coincide with particular phases and that the Moon fills with water as the tides rise, a description that captures the real connection between the two. Several groups have stories explaining solar and lunar eclipses, often as the Sun woman and Moon man coming together. Researchers have also found traditions that appear to describe stars changing in brightness, such as Betelgeuse and Antares, which Western astronomy recognises as variable stars. Some scholars think stories about the Wolfe Creek Crater and other impact sites may preserve memories of real events, though that is hard to prove.

sections.key: First Nations sky knowledge belongs to specific communities, so learning about it means listening and following protocols.
sections.b: Interest in First Nations astronomy has grown rapidly, with books, planetarium shows, school lessons and guided night tours led by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander educators. Some universities run courses on the subject, and Indigenous astronomers and physicists are increasingly visible in Australian science. If you want to learn more, the best sources are those created by or with communities themselves, such as Aboriginal-run tours, museum resources and publications that credit their knowledge holders. Remember that stories differ between nations, and some knowledge is restricted, so a story you read about one group should not be assumed to apply everywhere. Next time you see the Southern Cross on a clear night, look just beside it for the dark head of the emu, a reminder that this sky has been read for a very long time.

quiz.q: What forms the Emu in the Sky?
o: The dark dust lanes of the Milky Way
quiz.e: The emu is traced in the dark lanes, with its head in the Coalsack beside the Southern Cross.

quiz.q: Which star cluster is at the heart of the Seven Sisters stories?
quiz.e: The Pleiades cluster is linked to Seven Sisters stories across much of Australia.

quiz.q: Who is Tagai in Torres Strait Islander tradition?
o: A great fisherman standing in his canoe
quiz.e: Tagai's position through the year guides fishing, planting and the seasons.

quiz.q: How did many communities use the appearance of certain stars?
o: As seasonal calendars for food and weather
To tell the time of day
quiz.e: Stars rising or setting at certain times signalled seasonal events on country.

quiz.q: What traditional knowledge do the Yolngu people hold about tides?
o: The tides are linked to the Moon
quiz.e: Yolngu tradition connects the rising tides with the Moon, capturing the real connection.

LESSONS.title: How touchscreens feel your finger
LESSONS.hook: Your phone screen has no buttons, yet it knows exactly where you tapped, swiped or pinched. The secret is that your finger is part of an electrical circuit.

sections.key: A touchscreen is a sensor layered over a display, constantly measuring where you touch.
sections.b: Pick up your phone and tap an app. The glass under your finger does not move, click or bend in any way you can feel, yet the phone responds instantly and precisely. That small miracle happens billions of times a day around the world, on phones, tablets, car dashboards, self-service checkouts and ATMs. A touchscreen is really two things stacked together: a display that shows you pictures, and a transparent sensor on top that works out where your fingers are. The display and the sensor are separate jobs. The screen lights up pixels, while the sensor quietly measures tiny electrical changes across its surface many times every second. Understanding those changes is the key to the whole trick, and it starts with an older, more mechanical approach.

sections.key: Older resistive screens work when pressure pushes two conductive layers together.
sections.b: The first touchscreens most people met were resistive. They appeared on early handheld organisers, GPS units, some ATMs and the signature pads at shop counters. A resistive screen has two thin, flexible layers coated with a conductive material, separated by a tiny gap of air or spacer dots. When you press down, the top layer bends and touches the bottom one, completing a circuit at that spot. By measuring voltages across the layers, the device calculates where the contact happened. Because they respond to pressure, resistive screens work with a fingernail, a gloved hand or a plastic stylus. The downside is that they need a firm press, feel slightly spongy, and traditionally handled only one touch at a time, which makes pinching and zooming difficult.

sections.h: Capacitive screens: your finger as a conductor
sections.key: Modern phones use capacitive screens, which detect the electrical effect of your conductive skin.
sections.b: Almost every modern smartphone uses a capacitive screen instead. Your body conducts electricity, mainly because it is full of salty water. Beneath the glass sits a fine grid of transparent electrodes, usually made from a material called indium tin oxide, which conducts electricity while letting light through. The grid holds a small electric field. When your fingertip comes close, it disturbs that field and changes the capacitance, which is the ability of nearby conductors to store electric charge, at the points nearest your finger. You do not need to press at all; a light brush is enough. That is why capacitive screens feel so responsive, and why they are covered by tough, smooth glass rather than soft, flexible plastic that has to bend.

sections.key: A controller chip scans the electrode grid many times a second to pinpoint every finger.
sections.b: The electrodes are laid out in rows and columns, like lines on graph paper. A small controller chip rapidly tests each crossing point, measuring how much its capacitance has shifted. Where a finger is resting, a little cluster of crossings shows a change, and the chip calculates the centre of that cluster to find the touch position, often more precisely than the spacing of the grid itself. Because every crossing is measured separately, the screen can track several fingers at once. This approach, called projected capacitance, is what makes multi-touch gestures such as pinch to zoom possible. Phones repeat the scan many times per second, and gaming phones advertise especially high touch sampling rates, so fast swipes feel smooth rather than jerky or delayed.

sections.h: Why gloves and raindrops cause trouble
sections.key: Gloves block your finger's electrical effect, while water can mimic a touch.
sections.b: Capacitive screens explain some everyday frustrations. Ordinary woollen or leather gloves insulate your fingertip, so the screen cannot sense it, which is why touchscreen gloves have conductive thread woven into the fingertips. A standard plastic stylus does nothing for the same reason, so styluses for phones have conductive tips. Water is the opposite problem. Droplets on the glass are conductive enough to disturb the field, so a wet screen may register phantom taps or ignore real ones. Manufacturers now use software to tell the difference between the small, steady signal of a raindrop and the moving signal of a finger, and some phones have a wet touch mode. Even so, using your phone in heavy rain or underwater remains unreliable for most people.

sections.key: Touchscreens date back to the 1960s, but the smartphone made them universal.
sections.b: Touchscreens are older than many people assume. In the mid 1960s, a British engineer named E. A. Johnson, working at the Royal Radar Establishment in Malvern, described a capacitive touchscreen intended for air traffic control displays. In the early 1970s, engineers at CERN, the European physics laboratory near Geneva, built capacitive touchscreens to control a particle accelerator. Resistive screens developed around the same era and spread through industry, kiosks and handheld gadgets in the following decades. The big leap into everyday life came in 2007, when Apple launched the first iPhone with a multi-touch capacitive screen designed for fingers rather than a stylus. Within a few years, physical keyboards on phones had largely disappeared, and swiping had become something even toddlers attempt on picture books.

sections.key: Clever software turns raw touch data into taps, swipes and pinches, and ignores accidental contact.
sections.b: The sensor only reports where your fingers are; software decides what you meant. It distinguishes a tap from a long press by timing, a swipe from a scroll by speed and direction, and a pinch by tracking two points moving apart or together. Tablets use palm rejection to ignore the side of your hand when you write with a stylus. Many phones also predict where a moving finger is heading, which helps hide the small delay between touching the glass and seeing a response. Some add haptic feedback, a tiny vibration that fools your fingertip into feeling a click. Next time you type a message on flat glass, remember the invisible grid, the rapid scanning and the software constantly guessing your intentions.

quiz.q: What makes a resistive touchscreen register a touch?
o: Pressure pushing two conductive layers together
quiz.e: Pressing bends the top layer so it contacts the bottom layer, completing a circuit.

quiz.q: Why can your finger operate a capacitive screen?
o: Your body conducts electricity and disturbs the screen's electric field
Your fingerprint ridges grip the glass
quiz.e: Conductive skin changes the capacitance of the electrodes nearest your finger.

quiz.q: What does projected capacitance make possible?
o: Screens that work through thick gloves
Charging the phone through the screen
Tracking several fingers at once for multi-touch
quiz.e: Each crossing in the grid is measured separately, so multiple touches can be tracked.

quiz.q: Why do touchscreen gloves work when normal gloves do not?
o: They have conductive thread in the fingertips
quiz.e: Conductive thread lets the finger's electrical effect reach the screen.

quiz.q: Which 2007 product made multi-touch capacitive screens mainstream?
quiz.e: The original iPhone was designed around a finger-friendly multi-touch screen.

LESSONS.title: How Wi-Fi works (and an Aussie connection)
LESSONS.hook: Every time you stream a show on the couch, your devices are holding a fast, invisible radio conversation. Part of the technology that makes it reliable came from Australian radio astronomers.

sections.key: Wi-Fi is a way for devices to exchange data using radio waves instead of cables.
sections.b: Sit in a café and you are probably surrounded by dozens of conversations you cannot hear. Phones, laptops, tablets and smart speakers are all talking to wireless routers using radio waves. Wi-Fi is simply a set of agreed rules, or standards, that let devices from different companies send and receive data through the air instead of along a cable. Those rules cover which radio frequencies to use, how to turn digital ones and zeros into radio signals, and how devices take turns so they do not drown each other out. The name itself is a brand. It was coined in 1999 for an industry group now called the Wi-Fi Alliance and, despite the popular belief, it was never officially short for 'wireless fidelity'.

sections.key: Wi-Fi mainly uses the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands, with newer gear adding 6 GHz.
sections.b: Wi-Fi is radio, the same basic physics as the FM station in your car, just at much higher frequencies. Most Wi-Fi uses two bands: around 2.4 gigahertz, meaning the wave oscillates about 2.4 billion times a second, and around 5 gigahertz. Newer equipment can also use a band near 6 gigahertz where regulators allow it. Data is carried by rapidly changing the wave's strength and timing in precise patterns that the receiver decodes back into ones and zeros. Each band is divided into channels, a bit like lanes on a motorway. The 2.4 gigahertz band travels further and passes through walls better, while the higher bands carry more data but fade faster over distance, so modern routers usually offer both.

sections.key: The router translates between radio signals in your home and the wired internet connection outside.
sections.b: The box blinking in your hallway is really several devices in one. A modem part connects to your internet service, whether that arrives through the NBN by fibre, cable, a fixed wireless dish or another technology. A router part manages your home network, giving each device a local address and directing traffic to the right place. A wireless access point part does the radio work, converting data from the wired connection into Wi-Fi signals and back again. When you open a website, your phone sends its request by radio to the access point, the router passes it out to the internet, and the reply returns the same way in reverse. All of this typically takes a small fraction of a second.

sections.h: Taking turns on a shared channel
sections.key: Devices sharing a Wi-Fi channel take turns, which is why crowded networks feel slow.
sections.b: A radio channel is shared space, like a room where only one person can speak clearly at a time. Wi-Fi devices therefore listen before they transmit. If the channel sounds busy, they wait a short, random time and try again, which helps avoid collisions. Data travels in small chunks called packets, and the receiver confirms that each one arrived; anything lost is sent again. Newer Wi-Fi generations add clever tricks, such as sending to several devices at once and splitting a channel into smaller slices, which helps in busy homes. Still, when many devices and neighbouring networks crowd the same channel, everyone spends more time waiting. That is why an apartment block in the evening can feel sluggish even when your internet plan is fast.

sections.key: Distance, walls, water and interference all weaken Wi-Fi signals.
sections.b: Radio waves spread out and weaken with distance, and they lose strength each time they pass through obstacles. Brick, concrete and metal are especially effective at blocking Wi-Fi, which is why a router in one corner of a double brick house may struggle to reach the far bedroom. Water absorbs these frequencies well too, so fish tanks, and even crowds of people, can dampen a signal. Mirrors and metal appliances reflect it. There is also interference: microwave ovens work at roughly the same frequency as 2.4 gigahertz Wi-Fi, so heating leftovers can briefly disrupt a nearby connection. Signals also bounce off walls and furniture, arriving at your device several times over with slight delays, a problem that turned out to be crucial in Wi-Fi's history.

sections.key: CSIRO scientists helped solve the indoor echo problem, and their patent earned Australia hundreds of millions of dollars.
sections.b: In the early 1990s, a team at CSIRO, Australia's national science agency, led by radio astronomer John O'Sullivan, set out to make fast wireless networking work indoors. The big obstacle was those echoes. Signals bouncing around a room smeared into each other, scrambling the data. Drawing partly on techniques used to sharpen faint signals in radio astronomy, the team developed a way of spreading data across many frequencies and correcting for the echoes. CSIRO patented the approach, and it became important to fast Wi-Fi standards. CSIRO later took legal action against major technology companies over the patent, and the settlements brought in hundreds of millions of dollars. Many Australians proudly call Wi-Fi an Aussie invention, though in truth it combined work from many people and countries.

sections.key: Router placement, newer equipment and good security make a big difference.
sections.b: A few simple habits improve most home networks. Put the router somewhere central and elevated, out in the open rather than inside a cupboard, behind the television or on the floor. Keep it away from microwaves and large metal objects. In bigger or multi-storey homes, a mesh system uses several units that talk to each other to blanket the house, which usually works better than a single powerful router. Restart and update your router occasionally, since manufacturers fix bugs and security holes. Protect your network with a strong password and the newest security option your devices support, typically WPA3 or WPA2. Finally, remember that Wi-Fi only covers the last few metres; if your internet plan itself is slow, no router can fix that.

quiz.q: What is the name 'Wi-Fi' officially?
o: A brand name coined for an industry group
An acronym for a radio standard
quiz.e: Wi-Fi was a brand name created in 1999 and was never officially short for 'wireless fidelity'.

quiz.q: Which statement about the 2.4 GHz band is true?
o: It always carries more data than 5 GHz
It is only used by microwave ovens
It travels further and through walls better than higher bands
quiz.e: Lower frequencies reach further and penetrate walls better, though they carry less data.

quiz.q: What do Wi-Fi devices do before transmitting on a shared channel?
o: Increase their power to drown out others
Listen to check whether the channel is busy
Ask the internet provider for permission
quiz.e: Devices listen first and wait a short random time if the channel is busy.

quiz.q: Why can a microwave oven interfere with Wi-Fi?
o: It operates near the 2.4 GHz frequency
It uses the same electrical circuit
It blocks all radio waves permanently
quiz.e: Microwave ovens work at roughly the same frequency as 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi.

quiz.q: What problem did the CSIRO team help solve?
quiz.e: Their work corrected for signals bouncing around rooms and smearing together.

LESSONS.title: Where the cloud really lives
LESSONS.hook: Your photos, emails and streamed shows are not floating in the sky. They live in giant, humming buildings full of computers, and those buildings are some of the most carefully guarded places on Earth.

sections.key: The cloud means storing data and running software on computers owned by someone else.
sections.b: Take a photo on your phone and, within moments, a copy may be backed up to the cloud. The word suggests something weightless and everywhere, but the reality is solid metal, cables and electricity. The cloud simply means using computers that belong to another company, reached over the internet, instead of your own device. When you check email in a browser, watch a streaming service or save a document to an online drive, the real work and storage happen in a data centre, possibly hundreds or thousands of kilometres away. Technology people often joke that 'the cloud is just someone else's computer'. That is a little simplistic, but it captures the idea: your files are on a physical machine you will probably never see.

sections.key: Data centres are warehouse-sized buildings packed with rows of servers.
sections.b: A large data centre looks a bit like a library where the shelves are full of computers. Long rows of tall metal racks hold servers, which are computers without screens or keyboards, stacked like pizza boxes. Each rack is connected by bundles of cables, and the building is linked to the wider internet by high capacity fibre optic lines, often from several providers in case one fails. The largest facilities, sometimes called hyperscale data centres, can hold tens of thousands of servers, and big cloud companies run many of them in different regions. Security is serious: fences, guards, cameras, mantraps that let one person through at a time, and biometric checks. Few people inside work directly with the machines; much of the monitoring is automated.

sections.key: Servers produce enormous heat, so cooling is one of a data centre's biggest jobs.
sections.b: Every server turns electricity into heat, and thousands of them packed together could quickly cook themselves. Cooling is therefore one of the central engineering challenges. Many data centres arrange racks in alternating hot and cold aisles: cool air is pushed through the front of the servers and hot air is captured from the back. Large chillers, fans and cooling towers then remove the heat. Some facilities use water to cool, which raises concerns in dry regions. Others pump liquid directly to the hottest chips, an approach that has become more common as artificial intelligence hardware runs hotter. Some companies build in cold climates, such as the Nordic countries, to use chilly outside air, and a few have experimented with reusing waste heat to warm nearby homes.

sections.key: Data centres use backup batteries and generators so they keep running through blackouts.
sections.b: A data centre cannot simply switch off during a storm. Most have several layers of protection against power cuts. Electricity usually arrives from the grid, sometimes through more than one connection. If the supply flickers, banks of batteries in what is called an uninterruptible power supply take over instantly, keeping servers running without a hiccup. Within seconds to minutes, large diesel or gas generators start up and carry the load for as long as their fuel lasts, and operators keep contracts for fuel deliveries during emergencies. The whole system is tested regularly. Big cloud companies have also signed deals to buy large amounts of renewable energy, though the details of how green any particular data centre really is can be complicated.

sections.key: Cloud services keep multiple copies of your data, often in different places, so one failure does not lose it.
sections.b: Hard drives fail all the time, and in a building with many thousands of them, some fail every day. Cloud services plan for this. When you upload a photo, it is typically stored as several copies, or split into pieces with extra error correcting information, across different drives and machines. Important services also copy data to separate buildings, or to another region entirely, so that a fire, flood or major outage at one site does not wipe it out. This is called redundancy, and it is why a cloud backup is generally safer than a single external drive in your desk drawer. Still, no system is perfect. Accounts get hacked and services shut down, so keeping your most precious files in more than one place is wise.

sections.key: Content delivery networks store popular content near users so it loads quickly.
sections.b: When you press play on a popular show, the video probably does not travel from a central data centre overseas. Streaming services and many websites use content delivery networks, which keep copies of popular content on servers placed close to where people live, including in Australian cities and inside some internet providers' networks. Your request is quietly directed to the nearest suitable server, so the video starts faster and the long international links are not clogged with millions of identical streams. The same trick speeds up news sites, software updates and online games. This matters a lot in Australia, which is physically far from many of the world's big data hubs, so every round trip to the United States or Europe adds a noticeable delay.

sections.key: Data centres use a growing share of the world's electricity, and where data is stored can matter legally.
sections.b: All this convenience has a footprint. Estimates from bodies such as the International Energy Agency suggest data centres use somewhere around one to two percent of the world's electricity, and demand is rising quickly as artificial intelligence grows. In Australia, Sydney and Melbourne host most of the country's data centres, and new projects are competing for grid connections and land. Location also matters legally. Data stored in another country may be subject to that country's laws, so governments, banks and health services often require sensitive information to stay onshore. As a user, you can make sensible choices: delete things you no longer need, and check where and how a service stores your data, especially for anything personal or confidential.

quiz.q: What does 'the cloud' really refer to?
o: Computers owned by another company, reached over the internet
A special part of your phone's memory
quiz.e: Cloud services run on physical servers in data centres owned by other organisations.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of hot and cold aisles in a data centre?
o: To manage airflow for cooling servers
quiz.e: Cool air is pushed through servers and hot exhaust air is captured separately.

quiz.q: What takes over instantly when grid power flickers?
o: Batteries in an uninterruptible power supply
quiz.e: Batteries bridge the gap until the generators start.

quiz.q: Why do cloud services keep multiple copies of your data?
o: So a failed drive or building does not lose it
To make files load in colour
Because the law forbids single copies
quiz.e: Redundancy protects data against hardware failures and disasters.

quiz.q: Why do streaming services use content delivery networks?
o: To store copies of popular content close to viewers
quiz.e: Nearby copies mean faster loading and less traffic on long-distance links.

LESSONS.title: Inside the battery in your pocket
LESSONS.hook: Lithium-ion batteries power your phone, laptop, cordless drill and maybe your car. Knowing how they work explains why they slowly fade, and how to make them last longer.

sections.key: A lithium-ion battery stores energy by moving lithium ions between two electrodes.
sections.b: Every time you unplug your phone in the morning, you are carrying around a small chemical machine. A lithium-ion battery has two electrodes: the anode, usually made of graphite, a form of carbon, and the cathode, made from a compound containing lithium and metals such as cobalt, nickel, manganese or iron. Between them is an electrolyte, a liquid or gel that lets lithium ions pass through, and a thin porous separator that stops the electrodes touching. When the battery powers your phone, lithium ions travel through the electrolyte from anode to cathode, while electrons travel the long way round, through the phone's circuits. That flow of electrons is the electric current doing useful work. Charging simply pushes everything back the other way.

sections.key: Lithium is very light and gives up electrons easily, so it packs a lot of energy into little weight.
sections.b: Lithium is the lightest metal, and it is very eager to give up an electron. Those two properties make it ideal for batteries that need to store a lot of energy without much weight. Compared with older rechargeable types such as nickel cadmium, lithium-ion batteries hold much more energy for their size, lose little charge sitting on a shelf, and do not suffer badly from the so-called memory effect that once made people fully drain batteries before recharging. That combination made truly portable electronics possible. Australia has a direct stake in this story: it is one of the world's largest producers of mined lithium, much of it dug from hard rock deposits in Western Australia and shipped overseas for processing.

sections.key: Three scientists shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for developing the lithium-ion battery.
sections.b: The lithium-ion battery took decades of work by many researchers. In the 1970s, during the oil crisis, British chemist M. Stanley Whittingham built an early rechargeable lithium battery, but it used pure lithium metal and could be dangerous. Around 1980, American physicist John Goodenough, working at Oxford, found a cobalt oxide cathode that delivered much higher voltage. In the mid 1980s, Japanese chemist Akira Yoshino replaced reactive lithium metal with a carbon based anode, producing a far safer design. Sony began selling lithium-ion batteries commercially in 1991, first in a video camera. In 2019, the three scientists shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Goodenough was 97 at the time, making him the oldest person ever to receive a Nobel Prize.

sections.key: Every charge cycle causes tiny chemical damage that slowly reduces capacity.
sections.b: Your phone's battery holds less charge after a couple of years, and that is chemistry, not a conspiracy. Each time lithium ions move in and out of the electrodes, the materials swell and shrink slightly, and small side reactions use up some lithium. A thin crust forms on the anode, growing gradually thicker and trapping lithium that can no longer carry charge. Heat speeds up these reactions dramatically, which is why leaving a phone on a hot car dashboard in an Australian summer is especially bad for it. Holding a battery at completely full or completely empty for long periods also adds stress. Most phones now show a battery health figure, letting you see how much capacity remains compared with when it was new.

sections.key: Fast charging slows down near full, and avoiding heat and extremes helps batteries last.
sections.b: Ever noticed your phone charges quickly to around 80 percent, then crawls the rest of the way? That is deliberate. Chargers push a high current while the battery is low, then gradually reduce it as the battery approaches full to avoid damage. To extend battery life, keep devices out of heat, avoid regularly running them flat, and do not worry about topping up often, since partial charges are fine for lithium-ion. Many people find keeping charge roughly between 20 and 80 percent helps longevity, and many phones offer optimised or limited charging settings that hold the battery below full overnight. Use reputable chargers and cables, because cheap, poorly made ones can lack safety protections. Cold weather temporarily reduces performance, but the battery usually recovers once it warms up.

sections.key: Damaged lithium-ion batteries can overheat in a chain reaction called thermal runaway.
sections.b: Lithium-ion batteries are generally very safe, but they store a lot of energy in a small space and contain a flammable electrolyte. If a battery is crushed, punctured, badly made or overcharged without protection, an internal short circuit can make it heat up. That heat can trigger further reactions that release more heat, a spiral called thermal runaway, which can lead to fire or even an explosion of burning gas. These fires are hard to put out and can reignite. Warning signs include swelling, hissing, unusual heat or a strange smell. If you notice these, stop using and charging the device, and move it somewhere safe if you can. This is general safety information; for specific risks, check your fire service's advice.

sections.key: Never put lithium-ion batteries in household bins; take them to a battery recycling drop-off.
sections.b: Australian fire services and councils regularly report fires in garbage trucks, recycling centres and landfill caused by batteries thrown into household bins. When a truck compacts rubbish, a battery can be crushed and burst into flames. The fix is simple: keep used batteries, and devices containing them, out of your kerbside bins. Instead, take them to a battery drop-off point. Australia has a national battery recycling scheme called B-cycle, and many supermarkets, hardware stores and council facilities have collection points. Before dropping off loose batteries, cover the terminals with clear sticky tape to stop them shorting against each other. Recycling also recovers valuable materials such as cobalt, nickel and lithium, which matters as demand rises for electric cars and home batteries.

quiz.q: What moves through the electrolyte when a lithium-ion battery is in use?
quiz.e: Lithium ions travel through the electrolyte while electrons flow through the device's circuit.

quiz.q: Why is lithium well suited to batteries?
o: It is light and gives up electrons easily
It is very heavy and stable
quiz.e: Its lightness and eagerness to lose electrons let it store lots of energy per kilogram.

quiz.q: Who shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for lithium-ion batteries?
quiz.e: Each made a key step in developing the modern lithium-ion battery.

quiz.q: Why does a phone charge more slowly after about 80 percent?
o: The phone stops charging at night
Charging current is reduced near full to protect the battery
quiz.e: Chargers deliberately slow down as the battery approaches full.

quiz.q: What should you do with an old lithium-ion battery in Australia?
o: Put it in the recycling bin
Take it to a battery drop-off point such as a B-cycle collection
Throw it in the general rubbish
quiz.e: Batteries in kerbside bins can cause fires, so use a dedicated drop-off point.

LESSONS.title: The internet lives under the sea
LESSONS.hook: When you video call someone overseas, your voice almost certainly travels as flashes of light through a cable lying on the ocean floor. These hidden lines carry the vast majority of the world's international data.

sections.key: Most international internet traffic travels through fibre optic cables on the seabed, not via satellites.
sections.b: Ask people how the internet crosses oceans and many will guess satellites. Satellites do play a role, especially for remote areas, ships and planes, but the overwhelming majority of data travelling between continents goes through cables laid on the sea floor. There are several hundred of these submarine cables in service worldwide, stretching well over a million kilometres in total. They link continents and islands in a web that most people never think about. When an Australian watches an overseas video that is not cached locally, sends an email to London or joins a meeting with colleagues in Singapore, the data races through these cables. They are faster, carry vastly more data and are far cheaper per bit than satellites, which is why they dominate.

sections.key: Inside each cable, hair-thin glass fibres carry data as pulses of laser light.
sections.b: At the heart of a submarine cable are a handful of optical fibres, strands of extremely pure glass about as thin as a human hair. Lasers send pulses of light down each fibre, and the light stays inside by bouncing off the boundary of the glass, an effect called total internal reflection. Each pulse represents data, and modern systems send many colours of light down the same fibre at once, each carrying its own stream. Around the fibres are layers of protection: a tube of gel, steel wires for strength, a copper layer to carry power, and plastic insulation. In the deep ocean, where few things disturb it, the whole cable may be only about as thick as a garden hose.

sections.key: Repeaters along the cable amplify the light so it can cross entire oceans.
sections.b: Even in the purest glass, light gradually fades as it travels. To cross thousands of kilometres of ocean, cables include repeaters, sealed devices spaced at intervals of very roughly 50 to 100 kilometres along the line. Inside, optical amplifiers boost the light without first converting it back into electricity. The repeaters need power, so electricity is sent along the copper layer in the cable from stations on the shore, at thousands of volts. Engineers design repeaters to work for decades without maintenance, since retrieving one from several kilometres down is expensive and slow. Thanks to this system, light entering a cable in Sydney can emerge in California with its information intact, taking only a fraction of a second to make the crossing.

sections.h: Laying a cable across an ocean
sections.key: Specialised ships carefully survey the route and lay cable across the seabed, burying it near shore.
sections.b: Before a cable is laid, surveyors map the seabed along the planned route, avoiding steep slopes, rocky ridges, undersea volcanoes and busy anchorages. Then specialised cable ships, carrying thousands of kilometres of cable coiled in huge tanks, set out. In deep water, the ship slowly pays out cable, which sinks and rests on the sea floor, sometimes more than eight kilometres down. Closer to shore, where fishing and anchors pose dangers, the cable is thicker and more heavily armoured, and a seabed plough often buries it in a trench. Finally the cable comes ashore at a landing station, where it connects to networks on land. A long cable can take many months to lay, and projects often cost hundreds of millions of dollars.

sections.key: Most cable damage comes from fishing gear and ship anchors, and repair ships are on standby.
sections.b: Cables do break, quite often. Industry groups estimate there are well over a hundred faults worldwide each year. Most are caused by people, particularly fishing trawlers dragging gear and ships dropping or dragging anchors. Earthquakes and underwater landslides cause others. Sharks have been filmed biting cables, which made memorable headlines, but they are not a significant cause of damage. When a fault occurs, traffic is usually rerouted over other cables, so users may notice only slower speeds. A repair ship then locates the break, uses a grappling hook or a remotely operated vehicle to lift the cable, splices in a new section on deck, and lowers it back. Because damage can be costly, many countries protect cable zones near their coasts.

sections.key: The first transatlantic telegraph cable in 1858 failed within weeks, but a lasting link followed in 1866.
sections.b: Undersea communication is older than you might think. In 1858, after several failed attempts, a telegraph cable was laid across the Atlantic between Ireland and Newfoundland. Queen Victoria exchanged messages with US President James Buchanan, sparking celebrations, but the cable failed within weeks, partly because operators applied too much voltage. In 1866, the enormous steamship Great Eastern laid a durable transatlantic cable, and it worked. Australia joined this network in 1872, when the Overland Telegraph Line from Adelaide to Darwin was completed and linked to an undersea cable running north toward Java. Suddenly, messages that had taken weeks or months to travel between Australia and Britain by ship could arrive within hours. The cables were made with gutta percha, a natural latex, as insulation.

sections.key: Australia depends on a modest number of submarine cables, making them strategically important.
sections.b: Because Australia is an island continent far from most of the world, almost all of its international internet traffic depends on submarine cables. They land at a small number of locations, mainly around Sydney and Perth, with others in places such as Darwin and the Sunshine Coast. The government declares protection zones around some cables near the coast, where activities like anchoring and certain types of fishing are restricted. Cables connect Australia to the United States, Asia, New Zealand and Pacific nations, and new ones are added regularly as demand grows. Increasingly, big technology companies such as Google, Meta and Amazon help fund or own new cables. Governments, meanwhile, treat cables as critical infrastructure, worrying about deliberate sabotage and about who builds and controls them.

quiz.q: How does most international internet data travel?
quiz.e: Submarine cables carry the vast majority of intercontinental data.

quiz.q: What keeps light travelling inside an optical fibre?
quiz.e: Light bounces off the boundary of the glass, staying inside the fibre.

quiz.q: Why do undersea cables include repeaters?
o: To anchor the cable to the seabed
To amplify the fading light signal
quiz.e: Repeaters boost the light so it can travel across whole oceans.

quiz.q: What causes most undersea cable damage?
quiz.e: Human activity, particularly fishing and anchoring, causes most faults.

quiz.q: What happened to the first transatlantic telegraph cable in 1858?
o: It was cut deliberately by pirates
quiz.e: It worked briefly but failed within weeks, partly due to excessive voltage.

LESSONS.title: Babbage, Lovelace and the first computer
LESSONS.hook: In the 1830s, long before electricity was in homes, a cranky English mathematician designed a programmable computer made of brass gears. A young countess saw what it could become.

sections.key: Victorian navigation, science and finance relied on printed tables calculated by hand, which were riddled with errors.
sections.b: In the early 1800s, sailors, engineers, astronomers and bankers relied on thick books of mathematical tables: logarithms, tide times, star positions and interest calculations. These were worked out by people called 'computers', a job title long before it meant a machine, and then copied and typeset by hand. Errors crept in at every stage, and a single wrong digit in a navigation table could, in principle, put a ship on the rocks. Charles Babbage, a brilliant and famously argumentative English mathematician, was frustrated by these mistakes. According to a story he told later, while checking tables with his friend John Herschel, he wished the calculations could be executed by steam. That wish became one of the most ambitious engineering projects of his century.

sections.key: Babbage's Difference Engine was designed to calculate and print tables automatically using gears.
sections.b: In the 1820s, Babbage designed a machine to produce tables mechanically. It used a mathematical technique called the method of differences, which turns the calculation of many formulas into repeated addition, something gears can do reliably. His Difference Engine would even print results, removing copying errors. The British government funded the project, and Babbage hired a skilled engineer, Joseph Clement, to build it. A small working section was completed and impressed visitors. But the project was enormously complex, needing thousands of precisely machined parts, and it was plagued by disputes over money and ownership of tools. Work stopped in the early 1830s. Babbage had, in any case, become distracted by a far more ambitious idea that would make the Difference Engine look simple.

sections.key: Babbage's Analytical Engine had the key parts of a modern computer, including memory and a processor.
sections.b: Babbage's new design, the Analytical Engine, was not limited to one type of calculation. It was a general purpose machine. It had a 'store', where numbers were held, and a 'mill', where arithmetic was performed, roughly what we now call memory and a processor. Instructions would be fed in on punched cards, an idea borrowed from the Jacquard loom, which used chains of punched cards to weave complex patterns into silk. Crucially, the machine could make decisions, choosing what to do next based on its own results, and repeat sets of instructions. Those features mean it could, in principle, follow programs, the defining trait of a computer. Babbage refined the design for decades, but the Analytical Engine was never built.

sections.key: Ada Lovelace, daughter of the poet Lord Byron, became fascinated by Babbage's engines.
sections.b: Augusta Ada Byron was born in 1815, the only legitimate child of the poet Lord Byron, who left the family when she was a baby. Her mother, Annabella Milbanke, keen to steer her away from her father's wild poetic temperament, ensured she had an unusually strong education in mathematics and science. At around seventeen, Ada met Babbage at one of his famous London gatherings and saw a demonstration of part of the Difference Engine. She was captivated. She later married and became the Countess of Lovelace, but kept up a lively correspondence with Babbage about mathematics and his machines. Babbage admired her intellect greatly, and she brought a rare mix of mathematical understanding and imagination to his ideas.

sections.key: Lovelace's 1843 notes on the Analytical Engine included what is often called the first published computer program.
sections.b: In 1842, Italian engineer Luigi Menabrea published a paper in French describing the Analytical Engine. Lovelace translated it into English and, encouraged by Babbage, added her own notes, which ended up about three times longer than the original article. Published in 1843, the notes explained how the engine would work. In the final one, Note G, she set out a detailed step by step method for the engine to calculate a sequence called the Bernoulli numbers. This is often described as the first published computer program. Historians debate how much of the underlying work was Babbage's, since he had sketched similar procedures, but Lovelace's notes were the clearest and most thoughtful account of the machine's possibilities written at the time.

sections.key: Lovelace realised a computer could work with any symbols, not just numbers, and might one day compose music.
sections.b: Lovelace's most remarkable insight was about what the engine could become. Babbage mostly thought of it as a powerful calculator. Lovelace suggested it could manipulate any symbols whose relationships could be expressed in rules, not just numbers. She speculated that, if the relationships of musical sounds could be captured that way, the engine might compose elaborate pieces of music. That is close to the modern idea of computing as general symbol processing. She also cautioned that the engine could only do what it was instructed to do and could not originate anything by itself. A century later, Alan Turing discussed this point in his famous 1950 paper on machine intelligence, calling it 'Lady Lovelace's objection'. Lovelace died in 1852, aged just 36.

sections.key: The Science Museum in London built a working Difference Engine No. 2 from Babbage's plans, finished in 1991.
sections.b: Was Babbage simply too far ahead of his time, or were his designs flawed? In the 1980s, the Science Museum in London set out to find out. Using Babbage's detailed drawings for an improved Difference Engine No. 2, designed in the late 1840s, engineers built the calculating section using materials and tolerances achievable in his era. It was completed in 1991, around the bicentenary of his birth, and it worked, producing correct results. The printer was finished some years later. The machine weighs several tonnes and has thousands of parts. Babbage died in 1871, but his ideas, and Lovelace's vision, live on: a programming language created for the US Department of Defense is named Ada in her honour.

quiz.q: Who were 'computers' in the early 1800s?
o: People who did calculations by hand
quiz.e: Before machines, 'computer' was a job title for people who calculated.

quiz.q: Where did Babbage borrow the idea of punched cards from?
quiz.e: Jacquard looms used punched cards to weave complex patterns.

quiz.q: Who was Ada Lovelace's father?
quiz.e: She was the daughter of the poet Lord Byron.

quiz.q: What did Lovelace's Note G describe?
o: A design for a steam engine
A method for the engine to calculate Bernoulli numbers
quiz.e: Note G is often called the first published computer program.

quiz.q: What happened in 1991 at the Science Museum in London?
o: The calculating section of Difference Engine No. 2 was completed and worked
The Analytical Engine was found in storage
quiz.e: Engineers built it from Babbage's plans, and it produced correct results.

LESSONS.title: How files get squeezed: the art of compression
LESSONS.hook: A whole CD's worth of music can shrink to about a tenth of its size, so thousands of songs fit on your phone. Compression works by finding patterns, and by cleverly throwing away what your eyes and ears will not miss.

sections.key: Without compression, photos, music and video would be far too big to store and stream easily.
sections.b: A single uncompressed minute of CD quality stereo audio takes about ten megabytes. An uncompressed high definition video would need hundreds of megabytes every few seconds, far more than a typical home internet connection could carry. Yet you stream films on a train and store thousands of photos on a phone. The trick is compression: representing the same information, or something close enough, using fewer bits. There are two broad families. Lossless compression shrinks a file so it can be perfectly rebuilt, bit for bit. Lossy compression goes further by discarding details people are unlikely to notice, so the rebuilt file is similar but not identical. Most of the media you enjoy every day relies on clever lossy methods, built on top of lossless ideas.

sections.key: Lossless methods replace repeated patterns with shorter references to earlier copies.
sections.b: Imagine a picture of a clear blue sky, where a row contains a thousand identical blue pixels. Rather than storing blue a thousand times, you could store 'blue, repeated 1,000 times'. That simple idea is called run length encoding. A more powerful approach, developed by Abraham Lempel and Jacob Ziv in the late 1970s, scans a file for sequences that have appeared before and replaces later copies with a short pointer saying, in effect, 'go back this far and copy this many characters'. Text is full of such repetition: common words, phrases and spaces recur constantly. Variations of these methods power ZIP files, PNG images and the compression used when web pages are sent to your browser. Unpack the file and every original bit returns exactly.

sections.key: Giving frequent symbols shorter codes, as Morse code and Huffman coding do, saves space.
sections.b: Samuel Morse's telegraph code, developed in the 1830s and 1840s, already used a key compression idea. The letter E, the most common in English, is a single dot, while rare letters like Q get longer patterns. In 1952, David Huffman, then a student at MIT, published a method for building the best possible code of this kind for any set of symbols, based on how often each appears. Frequent symbols get short codes and rare ones get long codes, and no code is the beginning of another, so a stream of bits can be read without ambiguity. Huffman coding, and related techniques, are still used inside many formats, often as the final step after other methods have found the patterns. Lossless compression cannot shrink completely random data at all.

sections.key: JPEG compression discards fine detail and colour information that human vision barely notices.
sections.b: Lossy image compression exploits quirks of human vision. JPEG, a standard released in the early 1990s, starts by separating brightness from colour. Our eyes are far more sensitive to differences in brightness than in colour, so JPEG usually stores colour at lower resolution. Next it divides the image into small blocks, typically eight by eight pixels, and uses a mathematical tool called the discrete cosine transform to describe each block as a mix of smooth patterns, from broad gradients to fine stripes. The fine, busy patterns matter least to our eyes, so they are rounded off heavily or thrown away. Lossless coding then packs what remains. Push the quality setting down and the trick shows: blurry edges, smudged colours and visible square blocks appear.

sections.key: Audio compression removes sounds that human hearing cannot pick out, such as quiet sounds masked by loud ones.
sections.b: Audio formats such as MP3, developed in Germany in the late 1980s and early 1990s, and the later AAC, are built on psychoacoustics, the science of how we perceive sound. Human hearing has limits. We cannot hear very high or very low frequencies well, and a loud sound tends to mask quieter sounds at nearby frequencies, especially at the same moment. An encoder analyses the music in short slices, works out which parts would be masked or inaudible, and spends fewer bits on them or drops them altogether. The result can be roughly a tenth the size of the original CD audio while sounding very similar to most listeners. At low bit rates, though, you may hear swirly, watery artefacts, particularly in cymbals and applause.

sections.key: Video compression stores full frames occasionally and mostly records the changes between frames.
sections.b: Video seems like a huge challenge, since it is dozens of images every second. But consecutive frames are usually very similar. In a newsreader shot, the background barely changes while the mouth and eyes move. Modern video codecs, such as H.264, H.265 and AV1, store complete keyframes only occasionally. For the frames in between, they describe how blocks of the picture have moved since an earlier frame, plus small corrections, which takes far less data. Each frame is also compressed internally using methods similar to JPEG. This is why streams sometimes break into smeared, blocky messes when data goes missing: the decoder is applying movements to the wrong picture until the next keyframe arrives. Confetti, rain and fast panning shots are notoriously hard to compress well.

sections.key: Lossy compression involves trade-offs, and repeatedly recompressing a file steadily degrades it.
sections.b: Every compression format balances size, quality and computing effort. Higher compression usually needs more processing to encode and decode, which is why newer video codecs needed dedicated chips in phones before they became common. Lossy formats also have a hidden cost: generation loss. Each time you open a JPEG, edit it and save it as a JPEG again, more detail is discarded. Share a photo through several messaging apps, each recompressing it, and it gradually grows blurrier and blockier, a familiar look on images that have circulated online for years. The practical lesson is to keep an original, high quality copy of anything important, such as wedding photos or scanned documents, and make compressed versions from that master rather than from other compressed copies.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between lossless and lossy compression?
o: Lossy discards some detail, while lossless rebuilds the file exactly
quiz.e: Lossless restores every bit, while lossy keeps only an approximation.

quiz.q: Why is the letter E a single dot in Morse code?
o: It is the most common letter in English, so a short code saves time
quiz.e: Giving common symbols short codes is a core compression idea.

quiz.q: Why does JPEG often store colour at a lower resolution than brightness?
o: Our eyes are more sensitive to brightness than colour
quiz.e: JPEG exploits the fact that human vision notices brightness detail more.

quiz.q: How do video codecs save most of their space?
o: By lowering the frame rate to one per second
By recording mainly the changes between frames
quiz.e: Most frames describe movement and corrections relative to earlier frames.

quiz.q: What is generation loss?
o: Quality degrading each time a lossy file is recompressed
quiz.e: Each re-save of a lossy file discards more detail.

LESSONS.title: From sand to silicon: how microchips are made
LESSONS.hook: The chip in your phone holds billions of switches, each smaller than most viruses. Making one is arguably the most precise manufacturing humans have ever attempted.

sections.key: A microchip is a slice of silicon carrying billions of transistors, tiny switches that process information.
sections.b: Every app you open, photo you edit and message you send is processed by transistors, microscopic switches that turn electric current on and off. Combine enough of them in the right patterns and they can add numbers, compare values, store data and run any program. The first transistor, built at Bell Labs in the United States in 1947, was about the size of a thumbnail. Today a high end phone processor packs well over ten billion transistors onto a chip roughly the size of a fingernail. Building them requires making features only tens of atoms across, layered with astonishing accuracy, across an entire disc of silicon at once. The whole process can take a few months from bare wafer to finished chip.

sections.key: Silicon is purified to extreme levels, grown into a single crystal and sliced into thin wafers.
sections.b: Silicon is the second most abundant element in Earth's crust, found in quartz sand and rock. But chips need silicon purer than almost anything else people make, with impurities at the level of roughly one atom in a billion. After quartz is refined into high purity silicon, it is melted in a crucible. A small seed crystal is dipped in and slowly drawn upward while rotating, so the silicon solidifies into one giant, perfect crystal called an ingot, a technique named after Polish scientist Jan Czochralski. Modern ingots can be as wide as a dinner plate and around two metres long. Diamond saws slice them into wafers less than a millimetre thick, which are then polished until they are flatter than almost any other surface.

sections.key: Photolithography uses light shone through a pattern to print circuit designs onto the wafer.
sections.b: The key technique is photolithography, which works a bit like old fashioned photography. The wafer is coated with a light sensitive chemical called photoresist. Light is shone through a mask, a plate carrying the circuit pattern, and focused through lenses that shrink the image onto the wafer. Wherever light hits, the photoresist changes chemically, so it can be washed away, leaving the pattern exposed. The exposed areas can then be etched away with chemicals or plasma, or have material added, or be bombarded with atoms of other elements to change how they conduct electricity, a process called doping. The machine steps across the wafer, printing the same pattern hundreds of times, once for each chip that the wafer will eventually become.

sections.h: Layer upon layer, in a cleanroom
sections.key: Chips are built from dozens of layers in ultra clean factories where a speck of dust can ruin a chip.
sections.b: A modern chip is not a single printed layer. The transistors sit at the bottom, and above them are many layers of incredibly fine metal wiring connecting them, all separated by insulating material. Building one can involve hundreds or even more than a thousand individual steps of coating, printing, etching, depositing and polishing. Because features are so small, a single particle of dust can destroy a chip. Chip factories, called fabs, therefore use cleanrooms with air thousands of times cleaner than a hospital operating theatre. Workers wear full body suits, often nicknamed bunny suits, and much of the wafer handling is done by robots in sealed containers. Even so, not every chip on a wafer works, and the percentage that does, called the yield, is closely guarded.

sections.key: The most advanced chips are printed with extreme ultraviolet light from machines made by one Dutch company.
sections.b: The smaller the wavelength of light, the finer the patterns it can print. For years, chipmakers used deep ultraviolet light and clever tricks such as exposing the same layer several times. The most advanced chips now use extreme ultraviolet, or EUV, light with a wavelength of 13.5 nanometres. Producing it is extraordinary: tiny droplets of molten tin are hit by a powerful laser, tens of thousands of times a second, creating a plasma that emits EUV light. Because EUV is absorbed by air and glass, the beam travels in a vacuum and is steered with ultra smooth mirrors rather than lenses. Only one company, ASML in the Netherlands, makes these machines. Each is roughly the size of a bus and costs hundreds of millions of dollars.

sections.key: Moore's law described transistor counts doubling regularly, and today's 'nanometre' labels are mostly marketing names.
sections.b: In 1965, Gordon Moore, who later co-founded Intel, observed that the number of components on a chip was doubling at a regular pace. In 1975 he revised his estimate to roughly every two years, and that prediction, known as Moore's law, held surprisingly well for decades, driving computers to become vastly more powerful and cheaper. The pace has slowed as features approach atomic scales and costs soar. You may see chips described as '3 nanometre' or '5 nanometre'. Those names once related to real physical dimensions, but they are now mostly labels for each new generation of technology; no single feature on the chip necessarily measures that size. Chipmakers increasingly improve performance by stacking components vertically and redesigning transistors rather than simply shrinking them.

sections.key: Chipmaking depends on a few highly specialised companies and places, making it a major geopolitical issue.
sections.b: No single country makes a modern chip from start to finish. Designs often come from companies in the United States, the most advanced manufacturing is concentrated in Taiwan, especially at the giant contract manufacturer TSMC, EUV machines come from the Netherlands, and specialised chemicals, materials and equipment come from Japan, South Korea, Europe and elsewhere. Building a leading edge fab costs tens of billions of dollars and takes years. This concentration became painfully obvious during the chip shortages after 2020, when car makers and appliance companies struggled to get parts. Governments in the United States, Europe and Asia are now spending heavily to build local chip factories, and trade restrictions on advanced chips and equipment have become a central issue in global politics.

quiz.q: What is a transistor in a microchip?
o: A microscopic switch that controls electric current
quiz.e: Billions of transistors switching on and off process information.

quiz.q: How is a single crystal silicon ingot made?
o: By stacking thin sheets of glass
By slowly drawing a rotating seed crystal out of molten silicon
quiz.e: This Czochralski method grows one large, perfect crystal.

quiz.q: Why are chips made in cleanrooms?
o: Because a single dust particle can ruin a chip
quiz.e: Features are so tiny that dust can destroy the circuits.

quiz.q: Which company makes EUV lithography machines?
quiz.e: ASML in the Netherlands is the only maker of EUV lithography machines.

quiz.q: What do labels like '3 nanometre' mostly mean today?
o: Every transistor is exactly 3 nanometres wide
A marketing name for a technology generation
quiz.e: The labels no longer match a single physical dimension on the chip.

LESSONS.title: Philosophical razors: shaving away bad explanations
LESSONS.hook: Your car won't start. Is it a flat battery, or sabotage by a jealous neighbour? A handful of simple rules called 'razors' can save you from chasing the wrong answer.

sections.key: A razor is a rule of thumb for cutting away unlikely explanations.
sections.b: Picture a detective with ten suspects and one afternoon. She can't investigate everyone equally, so she needs a way to decide where to look first. Thinkers have long used short rules for exactly this job, and they are nicknamed 'razors' because they shave away explanations that are possible but improbable. A razor never proves anything. It doesn't tell you the answer is definitely the simple one. It tells you where the smart money is, so you can spend your time and attention sensibly. Think of razors as tie breakers and starting points rather than verdicts. Used well, they stop you from getting lost in elaborate theories. Used badly, as a way to end every conversation, they can become a lazy excuse not to think at all.

sections.key: Prefer the explanation that needs the fewest extra assumptions.
sections.b: The most famous razor is named after William of Ockham, an English friar and philosopher who lived around 1287 to 1347. The popular slogan 'entities should not be multiplied beyond necessity' was written by later scholars rather than by him, but the idea runs through his work. In plain terms: when two explanations fit the facts equally well, favour the one that asks you to assume less. If your biscuits vanish from the pantry, a hungry teenager requires one assumption. A burglar who broke in, ignored your laptop and took only the Tim Tams requires several. Notice the key phrase: equally well. Occam's razor doesn't say simple explanations are always true. It says complexity has to earn its place by explaining something the simpler version can't.

sections.key: Don't assume malice when carelessness or confusion would explain it.
sections.b: A colleague leaves you off an important email chain. Your first thought might be that they are freezing you out. Hanlon's razor suggests a gentler first guess: they probably just forgot. The usual wording is 'never attribute to malice that which is adequately explained by stupidity', a line usually credited to a man named Robert Hanlon, who submitted it to a joke book about Murphy's Law around 1980. You might prefer a kinder version: don't assume bad intent when busyness, ignorance or a simple mistake would do. The razor is useful because our brains are quick to see enemies. It saves friendships, workplaces and a great deal of wasted anger. It isn't naive, though. If the 'mistakes' keep happening in one direction, the pattern itself becomes evidence worth noticing.

sections.key: The burden of proof sits with the person making the claim.
sections.b: Someone tells you a celebrity is secretly a lizard in disguise. When you ask for evidence, they reply, 'Well, prove they're not.' The writer Christopher Hitchens offered a crisp response to this move: 'What can be asserted without evidence can also be dismissed without evidence.' The point is about who has to do the work. A person making a claim should supply reasons to believe it. You are not obliged to disprove every idea that someone invents, because anyone can invent ideas faster than they can be checked. This razor is a handy shield against people who try to win arguments by exhausting you. It doesn't mean the claim is false. It means you are entitled to set it aside until someone gives you a reason not to.

sections.key: Common causes are more likely than rare ones, so check them first.
sections.b: Medical students are often taught a saying: when you hear hoofbeats, think of horses, not zebras. In other words, a patient with a headache and a runny nose most likely has a cold, not an exotic tropical disease. The saying is usually traced to an American doctor teaching in the 1940s, though its exact origin is fuzzy. The logic applies far beyond medicine. If your internet drops out, a tired router is a horse. A targeted hack is a zebra. If a friend is late, traffic is a horse. Kidnapping is a zebra. This is really about base rates, the background frequency of each explanation. Of course zebras do exist, and doctors also talk about not missing them. The trick is to rule out the horses first.

sections.h: When razors cut the wrong way
sections.key: Razors guide your first guess, but evidence always gets the final word.
sections.b: By the 1840s, astronomers had known for years that Uranus wasn't moving quite as the maths predicted. The simple response would have been to assume small measurement errors. Instead, some argued for a more complicated answer: an unseen planet tugging on it. In 1846 Neptune was found close to where the calculations said it would be. The more elaborate explanation was right because it explained something the simpler one couldn't. That is the right way to think about every razor. They set your starting odds, not your conclusion. Reality is sometimes messy, people are sometimes genuinely malicious, and zebras sometimes turn up. If the evidence starts pointing towards the complicated, sinister or unusual answer, follow it. A razor that stops you looking has stopped being a tool and become a blindfold.

sections.key: Ask a few quick questions before you settle on any explanation.
sections.b: You can carry these razors around as a short mental checklist. When something surprising happens, ask: what is the simplest explanation that fits all the facts, not just some of them? Could this be a mistake rather than a plot? Who is making the claim, and have they offered any reason to believe it? What is the most common cause of something like this? Running through those questions takes seconds and often defuses a spiral of worry or suspicion. It is especially useful online, where elaborate theories spread fast and the boring truth rarely trends. Then stay open. Treat your first answer as a working hypothesis and be ready to swap it for a better one. Good thinkers aren't people who never guess; they are people who guess sensibly and update.

quiz.q: What does Occam's razor actually recommend?
o: The simplest explanation is always true
When explanations fit equally well, prefer the one with fewer assumptions
Always choose the most detailed explanation
quiz.e: Occam's razor is a tie breaker: complexity must earn its place by explaining more.

quiz.q: Hanlon's razor warns against assuming what?
o: Malice when a mistake would explain it
quiz.e: It suggests carelessness or confusion is usually a better first guess than bad intent.

quiz.q: According to Hitchens's razor, who should provide evidence?
quiz.e: Claims made without evidence can be set aside until someone supplies reasons.

quiz.q: In the 'horses, not zebras' saying, what are the zebras?
quiz.e: Zebras stand for rare causes, which should be considered after the common ones.

quiz.q: Why was the discovery of Neptune a lesson about razors?
o: It proved simple explanations are always wrong
It was found by accident with no theory
A more complex explanation was right because it explained more
quiz.e: The unseen planet explained Uranus's odd motion, which the simpler idea could not.

LESSONS.title: Why conspiracy theories feel so convincing
LESSONS.hook: Real conspiracies happen, yet most grand theories about secret plots fall apart. Learn why they grip clever people, and how to tell a real cover-up from a story.

sections.key: Powerful people do sometimes plot in secret, which is why the idea is so believable.
sections.b: In 1972, burglars were caught inside the Democratic Party's offices in the Watergate building in Washington. Over the next two years, journalists and investigators uncovered a cover-up that reached the White House, and President Richard Nixon resigned in 1974. For decades, tobacco companies also played down what their own scientists knew about the harms of smoking. So the claim that powerful people sometimes collude and lie is simply true. That matters, because it is what makes conspiracy theories plausible. The question isn't whether conspiracies ever happen. It is how to tell the real ones, which tend to be uncovered through documents, whistleblowers and court cases, from the many theories that never produce solid evidence however long people look.

sections.key: We instinctively feel that a huge event must have an equally huge cause.
sections.b: When something shocking happens, a small, random cause can feel insulting. Psychologists call this proportionality bias: the sense that a big effect needs a big explanation. The assassination of US President John F. Kennedy in 1963 is a classic example. The idea that a lone gunman could change world history feels wrong to many people, so a grand plot seems more fitting. Similar feelings follow the deaths of famous people and major disasters. A lone individual, bad luck or ordinary incompetence just doesn't seem to match the scale of the tragedy. Recognising this bias doesn't mean big events never have hidden causes. It means you should notice when an explanation appeals to you mainly because it feels emotionally right rather than because the evidence points there.

sections.key: Our brains are built to spot patterns and intentions, even where there are none.
sections.b: Imagine our distant ancestors hearing a rustle in the grass. Assuming a predator and running away was cheap. Assuming wind and being wrong could be fatal. Many researchers think this helped shape minds that over-detect patterns and intentions. We see faces in clouds and purpose behind random events. Conspiracy theories feed this tendency by turning chaos into a story with villains and a plan. Strangely, that can be comforting. A world run by hidden plotters is frightening, but at least someone is in charge, and you are one of the few who see the truth. Research suggests people are more drawn to these theories when they feel anxious, powerless or uncertain, which helps explain why they flourish during crises such as pandemics.

sections.key: A theory that treats all evidence against it as proof of a cover-up can never be wrong.
sections.b: Here is a warning sign worth memorising. Ask a believer what evidence would change their mind. If the answer is 'nothing', or if every piece of contrary evidence is explained away as part of the plot, the theory has become self-sealing. Missing evidence proves the cover-up. Official denials prove the cover-up. Experts who disagree are in on it. This structure feels powerful because it can't be refuted, but that is exactly its weakness. A claim that survives every possible observation tells you nothing about the world. Real investigations work the other way. Journalists who exposed Watergate could point to specific money trails, tapes and witnesses. When a theory's main evidence is the absence of evidence, treat it with great caution.

sections.key: The more people a secret needs, the harder it is to keep.
sections.b: The Apollo programme that landed astronauts on the Moon employed hundreds of thousands of people across government agencies, universities and private companies. A hoax would have needed all of them, plus rival scientists in the Soviet Union who were tracking the missions, to stay silent for over fifty years. In 2016, the physicist David Grimes published a model estimating how quickly large conspiracies would be likely to leak, and his rough conclusion was that secrets involving thousands of people tend to come out within a few years. You don't need the maths to see the logic. People talk, change jobs, write memoirs, fall out with their bosses and seek fame. Real conspiracies usually involve small groups, and even those are often exposed eventually.

sections.key: Conspiracy content can be a business, so follow the money behind the messenger.
sections.b: Ask not only who benefits from the alleged plot but also who benefits from you believing in it. Some promoters sell supplements, survival gear, courses, books or paid subscriptions alongside their claims. Others earn advertising money from clicks and views, and outrage keeps people watching. Some foreign governments have been documented spreading divisive stories to weaken trust in other countries' institutions. None of this proves a particular claim is false, and sincere believers exist everywhere. But it is a useful question to ask, because the people warning you about hidden motives may have very visible motives of their own. A healthy scepticism should be applied evenly: to governments and corporations, yes, and also to the influencers and websites telling you what governments and corporations are hiding.

sections.key: Curiosity and respect work better than ridicule.
sections.b: If someone you care about has fallen down a rabbit hole, mockery almost always backfires. It confirms the story that outsiders are arrogant and closed-minded. Researchers who study persuasion suggest a gentler path. Ask genuine questions: what first made you think this, and what would change your mind? Find common ground, such as a shared distrust of corruption or a love of their kids. Share your own uncertainty honestly. Another approach, called prebunking, teaches people the common tricks of manipulation before they meet a specific claim, a bit like a vaccine for the mind. Researchers at the University of Cambridge have built short online games to do this. Most importantly, keep the relationship. People rarely leave a belief because they lost an argument, but they often return through trusted friends.

quiz.q: Why does the Watergate scandal matter when thinking about conspiracy theories?
o: It proves all conspiracy theories are true
It shows real conspiracies exist and are exposed through evidence
It was later shown to be a hoax
quiz.e: Watergate was a real conspiracy, uncovered through documents, tapes and witnesses.

quiz.q: What is proportionality bias?
o: Believing small groups are more trustworthy
Feeling that a big event must have a big cause
quiz.e: We tend to feel a shocking event needs an equally grand explanation.

quiz.q: What makes a theory 'self-sealing'?
o: It is supported by many experts
It has been tested in a laboratory
It treats evidence against it as proof of a cover-up
It is only believed by a few people
quiz.e: If nothing could ever count against a theory, it tells you nothing about the world.

quiz.q: What did David Grimes's 2016 model suggest about large conspiracies?
o: They are likely to leak within a fairly short time
They only fail because of journalists
quiz.e: His rough estimate was that secrets shared by thousands tend to come out within years.

quiz.q: What is 'prebunking'?
o: Deleting false posts before they spread
