Teaching common manipulation tricks before people encounter a claim
quiz.e: Prebunking works like a mental vaccine, building resistance in advance.

LESSONS.title: Cold reading: how psychics seem to know you
LESSONS.hook: 'You have a great deal of unused potential.' Sounds just like you, doesn't it? Discover the simple tricks that make strangers seem to read your mind.

sections.key: Vague, flattering descriptions feel personal even when they are written for anyone.
sections.b: In 1948, the psychologist Bertram Forer gave his students a personality test, then handed each of them a supposedly personal analysis. They rated how well it described them, and on average they scored it above four out of five. Then he revealed the twist: every student had received exactly the same text, assembled largely from astrology material. It included lines such as 'you have a great need for other people to like and admire you' and 'at times you are extroverted, affable, sociable, while at other times you are introverted, wary, reserved'. This tendency to accept general statements as uniquely true of ourselves is called the Forer effect, or the Barnum effect, after the showman P. T. Barnum. It has been repeated in many later studies.

sections.key: The best statements are flattering, two-sided and true of almost everyone.
sections.b: Look closely at a typical 'reading' and you will find statements that are nearly impossible to get wrong. 'You can be your own worst critic.' 'You have a secret you haven't told many people.' 'Though you seem confident, you sometimes doubt yourself.' Each one sounds insightful, but think of a single adult it doesn't describe. Some statements cover both sides at once, a trick the British mentalist Ian Rowland called the 'rainbow ruse'. 'You are generally easygoing, but when someone crosses a line, you can be fierce.' Whatever you are like, you hear yourself in it. Add a dash of flattery, such as hidden talents or a big heart, and most people happily agree. Agreement then feels like evidence the reader is gifted.

sections.key: Readers throw out guesses, watch your reactions and quietly build on the hits.
sections.b: Imagine a medium on stage. 'I'm getting an older man, a father figure, maybe a grandfather or uncle. There's a name with a J, or perhaps an M.' In a room of two hundred people, almost everyone has lost an older male relative, and many know someone named John, James, Mary or Michael. This scattershot approach is called shotgunning. When someone gasps or nods, the medium narrows in. Readers also fish by asking questions dressed up as statements, such as 'Who is the person with the heart problem?' You supply the answer, and later you may remember the medium telling you. Skilled readers watch faces, posture, clothing, jewellery and accents. Every flicker of recognition guides the next guess. It feels like a revelation, but you are doing most of the work.

sections.key: Our memories keep the striking guesses and quietly drop the misses.
sections.b: After a reading, people often say the psychic knew things no stranger could. Yet when researchers record sessions and count, they usually find plenty of wrong guesses. Most of us remember the one astonishing hit, such as the correct name of a pet, and forget the dozen misses that came before it. Misses are also rescued in the moment. 'You don't know a Margaret? Keep that name, it will make sense later.' Or the reader reinterprets the guess: perhaps the water they sensed was a bath, a beach holiday or a leaky tap. This combination of selective memory and flexible meaning, a form of confirmation bias, turns an ordinary hit rate into an apparent miracle. Recording a reading and reviewing it calmly is often eye-opening.

sections.key: Some performers simply gather information in advance.
sections.b: Not every psychic relies on clever guessing. 'Hot reading' means collecting real information beforehand and presenting it as a supernatural insight. In the past this meant chatting with audience members before a show or noting names from a guest list. Today a quick look at someone's social media can reveal their pets, their hometown, a recent bereavement and the names of their children. A famous exposure came in the 1980s, when the sceptic James Randi showed that the American faith healer Peter Popoff had been receiving details about audience members through a hidden earpiece, fed by his wife from backstage. Popoff had presented this information as messages from God. Whenever a reader knows something impossible, it is worth asking first whether that information was actually available.

sections.key: Cold reading can cost people money, time and good decisions.
sections.b: Many people enjoy a horoscope or a tarot reading as harmless fun, and that is fine. The danger comes when the same techniques are used to win trust and then money. Some scams begin with a 'psychic' who senses a curse, then offers to lift it for a fee, followed by another fee, and another. Grieving people may be especially vulnerable to someone claiming contact with a lost loved one. Personality tests used in workplaces can also lean on Barnum statements, making a weak tool feel accurate. If you think you have been targeted by a psychic scam in Australia, Scamwatch, run by the ACCC, explains how to report it. This is general information, so seek proper advice for your own situation.

sections.key: A fair test removes the cues a reader could use.
sections.b: How would you check whether someone truly has psychic powers? You would remove every ordinary source of information. The reader shouldn't see or hear the person, shouldn't know anything about them in advance, and shouldn't receive feedback during the session. Then you would compare their accuracy with chance, ideally with several people each picking out which reading was meant for them. When tests like this have been run, claimed psychic abilities have generally not stood up. For many years, James Randi's foundation offered a large cash prize to anyone who could demonstrate a paranormal ability under agreed test conditions, and the prize was never claimed. Keep that framework handy. Whenever something seems uncanny, ask: what could they have seen, heard, guessed or looked up?

quiz.q: What did Bertram Forer's students not realise about their personality descriptions?
o: They were written by an astrologer in person
The descriptions were randomly generated by computer
They were based on their handwriting
quiz.e: All the students got identical text yet rated it as highly accurate.

quiz.q: Which of these is a classic 'rainbow ruse' statement?
o: You're easygoing, but fierce when someone crosses a line
quiz.e: It covers both sides, so almost anyone can recognise themselves in it.

quiz.q: What is 'shotgunning' in cold reading?
o: Firing off many general guesses and building on the hits
Asking the audience to write down questions
Speaking very quickly to confuse listeners
quiz.e: Broad guesses across a crowd almost guarantee some hits to work with.

quiz.q: What did James Randi reveal about Peter Popoff?
o: He received audience details through a hidden earpiece
quiz.e: Popoff's 'divine' knowledge was being fed to him by his wife backstage.

quiz.q: What is the key feature of a fair test of a psychic?
o: Letting the psychic choose the conditions
Testing in front of a large audience
Removing every ordinary source of information and comparing with chance
Asking the psychic to explain their method
quiz.e: Without ordinary cues, accuracy can be compared fairly with guessing.

LESSONS.title: Why you understand less than you think
LESSONS.hook: You use a zip every day. Could you explain how it actually works? Most people are surprised by how quickly their confidence collapses.

sections.key: We often confuse familiarity with understanding.
sections.b: Try a quick experiment. On a scale of one to seven, how well do you understand how a zip works? Now explain, step by step, how the teeth lock together and why pulling the slider separates them again. Most people start confidently and stall within a sentence or two. In a well-known study published in 2002, the Yale psychologists Leonid Rozenblit and Frank Keil asked people to rate their understanding of everyday objects such as zips, flush toilets and locks. Then they asked them to write detailed explanations. After trying, people's ratings of their own understanding dropped noticeably. The researchers named this the illusion of explanatory depth. We feel we understand things deeply because we know what they look like and how to use them.

sections.key: Even objects we've used for years can be surprisingly hard to draw.
sections.b: Picture a bicycle. Now imagine drawing one accurately: frame, pedals, chain and wheels. Easy, surely. The British psychologist Rebecca Lawson tested this in the mid 2000s by asking people to draw or complete diagrams of bicycles. Many made errors that would make a real bike impossible to ride, such as attaching the chain to the front wheel or joining the frame in ways that would stop the handlebars from turning. Interestingly, regular cyclists did better, but even some of them slipped up. The point isn't that people are foolish. It's that knowing how to use something is a completely different skill from knowing how it works. Our everyday knowledge is mostly a set of useful shortcuts, not a detailed blueprint.

sections.key: Our brains store just enough to get by and borrow the rest from the world.
sections.b: Why would our minds fool us this way? One reason is efficiency. Storing the full workings of every gadget you use would be a huge waste of mental effort. You don't need to understand a toilet's valve to flush it. Instead, the mind keeps a rough outline and leans on the world itself as a reference. When you look at a bicycle, the details are right there, so it feels as if they are in your head too. Explanations also come in layers, and each layer can hide the next. You know a car burns fuel to move. But how does burning fuel turn the wheels? How does the spark happen? Most of us stop at the first layer and mistake it for the bottom.

sections.key: Much of what we 'know' really lives in other people's heads.
sections.b: The cognitive scientists Steven Sloman and Philip Fernbach describe human knowledge as a community effort. No single person understands how to make a pencil from scratch, let alone a smartphone or a vaccine. We get by because knowledge is spread across experts, books, tools and institutions, and we trust that it is there when we need it. This is one of humanity's great strengths. It lets us build skyscrapers and send probes to Mars. The catch is that knowledge held by the community can feel like knowledge held by us. Because we can look things up or ask someone, we sense that we understand them. The illusion becomes a problem when we act on that borrowed confidence as if we had done the thinking ourselves.

sections.key: Explaining how a policy works can soften extreme views.
sections.b: The illusion doesn't stop at zips and toilets. Many of us hold firm opinions on complex issues such as tax, health systems or climate policy while knowing little about how the proposals would actually work. In a 2013 study, Fernbach and colleagues asked people in the United States to rate their understanding of political policies, then explain in detail how those policies would work. Afterwards, people rated their understanding lower and their views tended to become less extreme. Interestingly, simply listing reasons for their position didn't have the same effect. Reasons let you stay on familiar ground. Mechanisms force you to confront the gaps. It's a powerful idea: asking someone to explain the how, rather than defend the why, can make a heated conversation calmer.

sections.key: Try to explain something simply, step by step, before you trust your understanding.
sections.b: You can turn the illusion into a learning tool. Before you decide you understand something, try explaining it out loud, as if teaching a curious twelve year old. This approach is often linked to the physicist Richard Feynman, who was famous for his clear explanations. Wherever you stumble or reach for jargon, you have found a gap. Go back to the source, fill it, then try again. Writing works even better, because vague ideas look obviously vague on paper. This is why teachers often say they never really understood a subject until they had to teach it. The goal isn't to understand everything deeply, which is impossible. It's to know where your real understanding ends and your borrowed confidence begins.

sections.key: Humility about your own knowledge makes you a better thinker and listener.
sections.b: None of this means you should feel embarrassed for not knowing how a zip works. Relying on the knowledge of others is perfectly sensible. The lesson is about calibration. When you notice yourself feeling very certain about something complex, ask: could I explain how it works, in detail, to a sceptical friend? If not, hold your view a little more loosely. Be curious about what experts know that you don't. Listen more closely to people who disagree, since they may understand parts of the mechanism you have skipped. And when someone confidently explains a big issue in one simple sentence, gently ask how. Often the most honest and useful thing anyone can say about a complicated topic is: 'I'm not sure; let me find out.'

quiz.q: What happened when people in Rozenblit and Keil's study tried to explain everyday objects?
o: Their ratings of their own understanding dropped
quiz.e: Attempting a detailed explanation revealed how shallow their understanding was.

quiz.q: What did Rebecca Lawson's bicycle study reveal?
o: Only children struggle to draw bikes
Many people drew bikes that couldn't work
quiz.e: Using something often is very different from knowing how it works.

quiz.q: According to Sloman and Fernbach, where does much human knowledge live?
o: Spread across a community of people and tools
quiz.e: We rely on knowledge held by others, which can feel like our own.

quiz.q: In Fernbach's 2013 study, what softened people's political views?
o: Explaining how a policy would actually work
quiz.e: Explaining mechanisms exposed knowledge gaps; listing reasons didn't.

quiz.q: What is the 'explain-it test'?
o: Asking an expert to explain for you
Explaining something simply, step by step, to find your gaps
quiz.e: Where your explanation stumbles shows where your understanding ends.

LESSONS.title: Science or pseudoscience? How to tell the difference
LESSONS.hook: Astrology, crystal healing and a revolutionary new diet can all sound scientific. A few sharp questions reveal which ideas are willing to be proven wrong.

sections.key: A young Karl Popper noticed that some theories could explain absolutely anything.
sections.b: In Vienna after the First World War, a young Karl Popper was surrounded by bold new ideas. Einstein's theory of relativity made a risky prediction: starlight passing the Sun should bend by a specific amount. In 1919, expeditions led by Arthur Eddington measured starlight during a solar eclipse, and the results supported Einstein. The theory could have failed, and it didn't. Popper compared this with some popular theories of psychology and history that seemed to explain every possible outcome. Whatever a person did, the theory had an account of it. Fans saw this as strength. Popper saw it as weakness. A theory that fits every possible result, he argued, isn't telling you anything. This puzzle of separating science from non-science is known as the demarcation problem.

sections.key: A scientific claim has to risk being wrong.
sections.b: Popper's answer was falsifiability. A claim is scientific if you can describe an observation that would show it to be false. 'All swans are white' is falsifiable: one black swan breaks it, and Europeans found plenty of black swans in Western Australia. 'Invisible fairies tend my garden but leave no trace' isn't falsifiable, because no observation could ever count against it. Falsifiable doesn't mean false. It means testable. Good science sticks its neck out and says, 'If I'm right, you will see this, and if you see that instead, I'm wrong.' Philosophers have since added nuance, noting that real scientists don't drop a theory at the first awkward result. But the core question remains a powerful filter: what would prove this idea wrong?

sections.key: Pseudoscience tends to share a recognisable set of habits.
sections.b: Pseudoscience is anything dressed up to look scientific that doesn't behave like science. It tends to show familiar warning signs. Claims are vague, so they can't easily be checked. Evidence comes mainly from testimonials and anecdotes rather than controlled studies. Scientific words are borrowed for their glamour, so 'quantum', 'energy' and 'frequency' appear without precise meaning. When a test fails, excuses appear: the sceptic's negative energy interfered, or the conditions weren't right. The idea hasn't changed much in decades or centuries, despite new evidence. Critics are dismissed as closed-minded or paid off. And there is often something to buy. No single sign proves an idea is bogus, but when several appear together, it is time to look much more carefully before you believe or spend.

sections.key: When astrology has been tested fairly, it hasn't performed better than chance.
sections.b: Astrology makes claims that can, in principle, be tested: your birth chart is supposed to reveal your personality. In a study published in the journal Nature in 1985, the physicist Shawn Carlson ran a double-blind test with astrologers who had agreed to the method in advance. They were given people's birth charts and asked to match each one to the correct personality profile from a small set of options. Their success rate was about what you would expect from guessing. Other studies have looked for links between star signs and personality or career and generally found nothing meaningful. Astrology can still be enjoyable, a prompt for reflection or a bit of fun. But as a scientific claim about how people work, it hasn't passed the test.

sections.key: Australia's peak health research body found no reliable evidence homeopathy works.
sections.b: Homeopathy was developed in Germany around 1800 by Samuel Hahnemann. Its central idea is that a substance causing symptoms can cure similar symptoms when heavily diluted, and that more dilution makes it stronger. Many remedies are diluted so far that, statistically, not one molecule of the original substance is likely to remain. In 2015, Australia's National Health and Medical Research Council published a major review of the evidence and concluded that there were no health conditions for which there was reliable evidence that homeopathy was effective. The council warned that people who choose it over proven treatments may put their health at risk. This is general information rather than medical advice: talk to a doctor, and healthdirect is a reliable starting point for health questions in Australia.

sections.key: The real mark of science is a system for catching its own mistakes.
sections.b: Science gets things wrong all the time, which surprises some people. What makes it different is that it has ways of finding and fixing those errors. Studies are checked by other experts, results are repeated by independent teams, and ideas that fail are revised or dropped. For decades, doctors thought stomach ulcers were mainly caused by stress. Then two Perth researchers, Barry Marshall and Robin Warren, showed that a bacterium, Helicobacter pylori, played a central role. Marshall even swallowed a culture of the bacteria to help prove the point. The medical world was sceptical at first, but the evidence won, and the pair received the Nobel Prize in 2005. Pseudoscience rarely has a story like this, because it rarely updates.

sections.key: Being rejected by experts doesn't make you a misunderstood genius.
sections.b: Promoters of fringe ideas often compare themselves with Galileo, who faced persecution for supporting the idea that Earth moves around the Sun. The message is: experts laughed at him too, and he was right. But the logic doesn't work. For every rejected idea later proven correct, there are vast numbers that were rejected because they were wrong. Galileo was ultimately vindicated not because he was mocked but because his observations and reasoning held up. Marshall and Warren won over doctors with evidence, not complaints about the establishment. So when someone says experts are ignoring their breakthrough, ask the useful questions. What would prove it wrong? Has it been tested fairly? Have independent researchers repeated the results? Being an outsider is fine. Avoiding tests isn't.

quiz.q: According to Karl Popper, what makes a claim scientific?
o: It is believed by most scientists
It can be tested and potentially shown to be false
quiz.e: Falsifiability means a claim risks being proven wrong by observation.

quiz.q: Which of these is a common warning sign of pseudoscience?
o: Heavy reliance on testimonials and borrowed scientific words
Willingness to change in light of evidence
quiz.e: Anecdotes and buzzwords like 'quantum' often replace real testing.

quiz.q: What did Shawn Carlson's 1985 test find about astrologers?
o: They matched charts to profiles far better than chance
Their success was about what guessing would give
They were accurate only for fire signs
quiz.e: Under fair double-blind conditions, astrologers performed at about chance level.

quiz.q: What did Australia's NHMRC conclude about homeopathy in 2015?
o: It works for most minor illnesses
No health condition had reliable evidence of its effectiveness
It needs more dilution to work
quiz.e: The review found no reliable evidence that homeopathy is effective for any condition.

quiz.q: How did Barry Marshall help prove bacteria cause stomach ulcers?
o: By swallowing a culture of the bacteria
quiz.e: His self-experiment helped support the evidence that won over sceptical doctors.

LESSONS.title: Seeing patterns in random noise
LESSONS.hook: Shuffle a playlist and the same artist plays three times in a row. Rigged? Probably not. Randomness is far lumpier than our brains expect.

sections.key: Real randomness contains streaks and clusters that feel deliberate.
sections.b: Ask a class of students to write down a made-up sequence of 100 coin tosses, and ask another group to actually toss a coin 100 times. Teachers who run this classroom trick can usually spot the fakes. Invented sequences switch between heads and tails too often and avoid long runs. Real tosses often include a streak of five or six of the same result, because over 100 tosses such runs are quite likely. Our intuition says random things should look evenly spread out, like sprinkles neatly scattered on a cake. In reality, randomness is clumpy. Rain falls unevenly, stars cluster in the sky, and buses arrive in bunches. When we see a clump, our brains shout 'pattern', even when chance alone would produce it.

sections.key: Londoners saw a targeting pattern in V-1 strikes; statistics showed chance.
sections.b: During the Second World War, German V-1 flying bombs fell on London. Many residents became convinced the strikes were targeted, since some neighbourhoods seemed to be hit repeatedly while others were spared. Some people even moved to apparently safer districts. In 1946, a British actuary named R. D. Clarke published an analysis. He divided a section of south London into hundreds of equal squares and counted the hits in each. The pattern of counts closely matched what you would expect if the bombs had landed at random. The clusters that felt so meaningful were just the natural clumping of chance. The idea of seeing clusters in random data now has a name: the clustering illusion. It still shapes how people interpret crime maps, disease outbreaks and accidents.

sections.key: Drawing the target after the shots makes any pattern look impressive.
sections.b: Imagine a cowboy firing randomly at the side of a barn. Afterwards, he paints a bullseye around the tightest group of holes and declares himself a sharpshooter. This joke gives its name to the Texas sharpshooter fallacy: finding a cluster first, then treating it as if it had been predicted. It happens whenever people look through lots of data, spot an interesting clump, and forget how many other places they looked. A town might seem to have an unusual number of a particular illness. But there are thousands of towns and many kinds of illness, so somewhere, by chance, there will be a striking cluster. Investigators do take such reports seriously, and some turn out to be real. Many, though, prove to be painted bullseyes.

sections.key: Researchers argued for decades about whether winning streaks are real.
sections.b: Basketball fans have long believed in the 'hot hand': a player who has sunk a few shots is more likely to sink the next. In 1985, Thomas Gilovich, Robert Vallone and Amos Tversky analysed shooting records and concluded that streaks were about what chance would produce. The hot hand became a textbook example of seeing patterns in noise. Then, in a paper published in 2018, the economists Joshua Miller and Adam Sanjurjo identified a subtle statistical bias in the way streaks had been measured. Correcting for it, they argued that a modest hot hand effect may exist after all. This is a wonderful twist. It shows that the clustering illusion is real, but also that 'it's just randomness' can itself be a mistake. Careful analysis matters on both sides.

sections.key: Our brains are primed to find meaningful shapes, especially faces.
sections.b: In 1976, the Viking 1 spacecraft photographed a region of Mars called Cydonia. One rocky hill, lit by a low Sun, looked startlingly like a human face. Some people claimed it was an artificial monument. Later, sharper images from other spacecraft showed an ordinary eroded mesa. The 'face' had come from shadows, low resolution and our brains. Seeing meaningful images, especially faces, in random shapes is called pareidolia. People find faces in power sockets, burnt toast and the front of cars. It probably reflects how important faces have been to human survival, since recognising friends, enemies and emotions quickly matters. Pareidolia is a lovely quirk. It becomes a problem only when we treat what our pattern detector suggests as if it were evidence.

sections.key: Truly random can feel rigged, so some designers make things less random.
sections.b: When Apple's iPod shuffle feature first appeared, some users complained it wasn't random because it played songs by the same artist close together. Steve Jobs reportedly joked that the company was making shuffle less random to make it feel more random. Whether or not that was the full story, the problem is real and widespread. Music and video apps often adjust their shuffle so that the same artist doesn't come up twice in a row, precisely because genuine randomness feels suspicious. Lottery players show the same instinct. Many avoid numbers like 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 because they look too orderly, even though that combination is exactly as likely as any other. Our sense of randomness is really a sense of what looks messy.

sections.key: Decide what you're looking for before you look, and ask how often chance would do it.
sections.b: So how do you avoid fooling yourself? First, ask how many chances there were for a pattern to appear. A one in a million coincidence is likely in a country of millions of people. Second, decide what you are testing before you look at the data, rather than searching for something interesting and then explaining it. Scientists do this by registering their plans in advance. Third, check whether the pattern holds up in fresh data. A real effect should show up again; a random clump usually won't. Finally, be humble in both directions. Some patterns are real and important, such as an actual disease cluster or a genuine hot streak. The goal isn't to dismiss every pattern but to test it before you trust it.

quiz.q: How do invented 'random' coin sequences usually differ from real ones?
o: They switch between heads and tails too often
They are identical to real sequences
quiz.e: People avoid long runs, but real randomness often produces them.

quiz.q: What did R. D. Clarke's analysis of V-1 strikes on London show?
o: The hits closely matched a random pattern
quiz.e: The apparent clusters were consistent with bombs landing at random.

quiz.q: What is the Texas sharpshooter fallacy?
o: Shooting at targets that are too far away
Drawing the target around a cluster after the fact
quiz.e: Finding a cluster first, then treating it as predicted, makes chance look meaningful.

quiz.q: What did Miller and Sanjurjo's 2018 work suggest about the hot hand?
o: A statistical bias hid a modest hot hand effect
It was invented by sports journalists
quiz.e: Correcting a subtle measurement bias suggested a small hot hand may be real.

quiz.q: What is pareidolia?
o: Seeing meaningful images, like faces, in random shapes
quiz.e: Our brains readily find faces and shapes in clouds, toast or Martian hills.

LESSONS.title: Regression to the mean: why extremes don't last
LESSONS.hook: A footballer has a dream season, then a so-so one. A new treatment seems to cure your worst week. Often the real cause is a quiet statistical force.

sections.key: Praise seemed to make pilots worse and criticism seemed to make them better.
sections.b: The psychologist Daniel Kahneman told a story from his time teaching Israeli air force flight instructors. One instructor objected to the idea that praise works better than punishment. When he praised a trainee for an excellent manoeuvre, he said, the next attempt was usually worse. When he shouted at a trainee for a bad one, the next attempt was usually better. Kahneman realised the instructor was seeing something real but drawing the wrong conclusion. An unusually good flight is partly skill and partly luck, and luck tends not to repeat. So the next attempt is likely to be closer to average, whatever the instructor says. The same goes for unusually bad flights. The praise and shouting were mostly irrelevant. This pattern is called regression to the mean.

sections.key: Any result that mixes skill and luck will drift back towards average after an extreme.
sections.b: Here is the core idea. Think of any measured performance as skill plus luck. Skill is fairly stable from one day to the next. Luck bounces around randomly. When you pick out an extreme result, the very best or very worst, you are partly selecting for skill and partly selecting for unusually good or bad luck. Next time, the skill is still there, but the luck is likely to be more ordinary. So the result moves back towards the typical level. Crucially, this happens without any cause. Nobody got lazy, discouraged or complacent. It is simply what happens when chance plays a role. The more luck matters in an activity, the stronger the pull back to the average. Pure skill wouldn't regress; pure luck would regress completely.

sections.key: The idea was first described by Francis Galton studying the heights of parents and children.
sections.b: In the 1880s, the Victorian scientist Francis Galton studied the heights of parents and their adult children. He noticed that very tall parents tended to have children who were tall, but on average not quite as tall as the parents. Very short parents tended to have children who were short, but not quite as short. Galton called this 'regression towards mediocrity', which is where the term comes from. Importantly, this doesn't mean everyone is gradually becoming average height. The spread of heights stays roughly the same from one generation to the next, because some children of average parents end up very tall or very short. Extremes keep appearing; they just aren't always in the same families. It's a reminder that regression describes groups and averages, not destiny.

sections.key: Many famous 'curses' are just regression in disguise.
sections.b: For decades, people have joked about the Sports Illustrated cover jinx: athletes who appear on the American magazine's cover often seem to slump soon after. Similar talk follows players who win big awards or sign large contracts. But think about when someone lands on a magazine cover. It is usually after a remarkable stretch of performance, often their best ever, which almost certainly involved some good luck. The following season is likely to be closer to their usual level, which looks like a slump by comparison. No curse required. The same logic applies to businesses that are praised after a record year, fund managers who topped the charts, and restaurants that have just won an award. Picking people at their peak practically guarantees an apparent decline afterwards.

sections.key: People often seek treatment at their worst and improve anyway.
sections.b: Think about when you are most likely to try a new remedy for back pain, a headache or a cold. Usually it is when symptoms are at their worst. Many conditions naturally fluctuate, so after a bad patch, things are likely to improve somewhat, whatever you do. If you took a remedy at the peak, it will seem to have worked. This is a major reason medical researchers use control groups. In a well designed trial, some patients get the treatment and others get a placebo or standard care, and both groups are chosen in the same way. Regression affects both groups equally, so only a genuine difference between them shows a real effect. This is general information, so speak to a health professional about your own situation.

sections.key: Fixes aimed at the worst spots often look more effective than they are.
sections.b: Imagine a road safety program that installs cameras at the intersections with the most crashes last year. The following year, crashes at those sites fall. Success? Partly, perhaps. But some of those sites were probably at the top of the list because of an unusually unlucky year, and would have improved even with no camera at all. Road safety researchers know about this problem and try to account for it, for example by comparing the treated sites with similar untreated ones or by looking at several years of data rather than one. The same trap appears in schools, where extra help goes to students with the lowest test scores, and in workplaces, where struggling teams get a new manager. Some improvement is real; some is just regression.

sections.key: When you select extremes, expect them to move back towards average.
sections.b: How can you put this idea to work? First, whenever something is chosen because it was extreme, expect it to look less extreme next time, and don't invent a story to explain the change. Second, when judging an intervention, ask what would have happened without it. Was there a fair comparison group, or just a before and after? Third, predict cautiously. If a new employee has a brilliant first month or a student aces one test, the best forecast for next time sits somewhere between that result and the average. Finally, be careful about lessons drawn from praise and blame. Kahneman's flight instructors were not wrong about what they saw. They were wrong about why. Remembering that luck fades is one of the most useful habits in statistics.

quiz.q: Why did the flight instructor's criticism seem to work?
o: Criticism is more effective than praise
Unusually bad flights were usually followed by more average ones anyway
Trainees were afraid of the instructor
The instructor gave better tips when angry
quiz.e: Bad luck tends not to repeat, so performance naturally drifted back towards average.

quiz.q: Which kind of activity would show the strongest regression to the mean?
o: One where luck plays a big role
quiz.e: The more luck contributes to results, the stronger the pull back towards average.

quiz.q: What did Francis Galton notice about very tall parents?
o: Their children were usually even taller
Their children were tall, but on average less tall than them
quiz.e: Children's heights tended to fall between their parents' heights and the average.

quiz.q: Why do medical trials use control groups?
o: So regression and other effects hit both groups and only a real difference shows
To test doctors rather than treatments
quiz.e: Comparing similar groups separates genuine effects from natural improvement.

quiz.q: Why might crashes fall at new camera sites even without the cameras?
o: The sites were chosen after unusually bad years that would naturally improve
quiz.e: Selecting the worst sites picks up bad luck, which tends to fade.

LESSONS.title: Berkson's paradox: when filtering creates false patterns
LESSONS.hook: Why do the best restaurants seem to be in the worst locations, and why do attractive dates seem more likely to be rude? The answer is a sneaky trick of selection.

sections.key: Looking only at hospital patients can create links between diseases that don't exist outside.
sections.b: In 1946, the American statistician Joseph Berkson pointed out a puzzle in medical research. When researchers studied patients in hospital, two unrelated conditions could appear to be linked, either more or less often found together than in the general population. The reason was the way patients got into the data. People are admitted to hospital because they have one condition or another, or both. Looking only at hospital patients means you've filtered the population according to those very conditions. That filtering alone can create a statistical relationship that wouldn't exist in the wider world. This effect is now called Berkson's paradox or Berkson's bias. It is a cousin of selection bias, and once you understand it, you start spotting it in dating, hiring, restaurants and headlines.

sections.key: If you only date people who are nice or attractive, those traits will seem to clash.
sections.b: The mathematician Jordan Ellenberg popularised a memorable example. Suppose someone will only date a person who is reasonably kind, reasonably attractive, or both. In the general population, imagine kindness and good looks have nothing to do with each other. Now look only at the people this person actually dates. Anyone who is neither kind nor attractive has been filtered out. Among those left, the attractive ones only need to clear one bar, so many of them are not especially kind. The kind ones are often not especially attractive. Within this group, looks and kindness now seem to be opposites. It feels as though attractive people are more likely to be rude. In fact, nothing about the people changed. The filter created the pattern.

sections.key: Imagine a scatter plot where one corner has been cut away.
sections.b: Picture a square scatter plot full of dots, with talent along one axis and charm along the other. If the two traits are unrelated, the dots fill the square evenly, like a random sprinkle with no tilt. Now imagine a selection rule: only people whose talent plus charm exceeds a certain total are admitted. Draw a diagonal line across the lower left corner and remove every dot beneath it. Look at the dots that remain. Suddenly they slope downwards. Among those who passed, the most talented tend to be less charming and the most charming tend to be less talented. A negative correlation has appeared from nowhere. This is the essence of Berkson's paradox: selecting on a combination of two traits manufactures a relationship between them.

sections.key: Things that survive often do so because they are strong in at least one way.
sections.b: Why does it sometimes seem that the best food is found in obscure, awkward locations? A restaurant can survive in a busy, prime spot even if the food is ordinary, because foot traffic keeps it going. A restaurant in a bad location only survives if the food is excellent. So among restaurants that are still open, location and quality can appear negatively linked. Similar logic applies to books and films. A novel can become widely known because it is brilliantly written or because it has a gripping, marketable plot. Among famous novels, you may notice that the most gripping ones aren't always the best written, and vice versa. The pattern may tell you more about how things became popular than about any real trade off.

sections.key: Controlling for the wrong thing can create a false link between a cause and an effect.
sections.b: Researchers call the variable at the heart of this problem a 'collider': something influenced by two other factors. Filtering on it, or statistically controlling for it, can create a misleading link between those factors. A well-known puzzle involves birth weight. Babies of mothers who smoke tend to be lighter at birth, and low birth weight is linked to higher risk. Yet among only low birth weight babies, some studies found those born to smokers did slightly better. Smoking wasn't protective. Low birth weight can result from smoking or from other, often more serious problems, so comparing within that group mixed very different situations. During the COVID-19 pandemic, researchers warned that some early studies, which only included tested or hospitalised patients, could be affected by similar collider bias.

sections.key: Among people who passed a selection, the criteria can seem to work against each other.
sections.b: Imagine a university that admits students based on a combination of school results and an entrance test. Among admitted students, those with lower school results must have done especially well on the test, and those with lower test scores must have had especially strong school results. So within the student body, the two measures may seem barely related or even negatively related. Someone looking only at current students might conclude that the entrance test predicts nothing. That conclusion could be quite wrong across the full population of applicants. The same trap appears in hiring, where employers sometimes notice that interview performance doesn't seem to predict job success among the people they hired. Part of that may be real, but part may be a filter hiding the relationship.

sections.key: Always ask how the people or things in a dataset got there.
sections.b: The key defence against Berkson's paradox is a simple question: how did these cases end up in front of me? If the group you're looking at was selected based on the very traits you're comparing, be suspicious of any pattern within it. Your social circle, your newsfeed, a hospital ward, a list of successful companies and the people you have dated are all filtered samples. Patterns within them may be produced by the filter rather than by the world. When possible, look at a broader, unfiltered group. When that isn't possible, be careful about drawing big conclusions. The paradox is a reminder that data never simply speaks for itself. It always arrives through some process, and understanding that process is half the work of understanding the data.

quiz.q: Why did Joseph Berkson find misleading links between diseases in hospital patients?
o: Patients were admitted because of those conditions, filtering the sample
quiz.e: Selecting patients based on the conditions themselves can create a false relationship.

quiz.q: In the dating example, why do kind and attractive traits seem opposed?
o: Attractive people really are less kind
People who were neither kind nor attractive were filtered out
quiz.e: Removing those with neither trait leaves a group where the traits look negatively linked.

quiz.q: What happens to an unrelated scatter plot when you remove the lower left corner?
o: The remaining dots show a downward slope
quiz.e: Selecting on a combined total creates a negative correlation among those who pass.

quiz.q: What is a 'collider' in research?
o: A variable influenced by two other factors
quiz.e: Filtering or controlling for a collider can create misleading links between its causes.

quiz.q: What is the best first question to guard against Berkson's paradox?
o: How did these cases end up in the data?
quiz.e: Knowing how the sample was selected reveals whether a filter created the pattern.

LESSONS.title: Your heart and blood
LESSONS.hook: Your heart beats about 100,000 times a day, pushing blood through a network of vessels that, by common estimates, could wrap around the Earth more than twice.

sections.key: The heart is a muscular pump about the size of a fist that beats around 100,000 times a day.
sections.b: Your heart sits in the middle of your chest, tilted slightly left, and is roughly the size of your clenched fist. It's made of cardiac muscle, which is built to resist fatigue in a way skeletal muscle isn't. At rest it beats about 60–100 times a minute, around 100,000 times a day and roughly 2.5 to 3 billion times in a lifetime. Each beat is triggered by an electrical signal from a natural pacemaker, the sinoatrial node, in the upper right chamber. That signal spreads through the heart in a set sequence, so the upper chambers squeeze first and the lower chambers follow a fraction of a second later.

sections.key: The right side pumps blood to the lungs; the left side pumps it to the rest of the body.
sections.b: The heart has four chambers: two upper atria that receive blood and two lower ventricles that pump it out. The right side collects oxygen-poor blood from the body and sends it on a short trip to the lungs to pick up oxygen and drop off carbon dioxide. The left side receives oxygen-rich blood from the lungs and pumps it to the whole body, from your brain to your toes. The left ventricle has the thickest wall because it pushes hardest. Four one-way valves keep blood flowing in the right direction, and their closing makes the familiar 'lub-dub' sound a doctor hears through a stethoscope.

sections.key: Arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins carry it back, and capillaries connect them.
sections.b: Arteries have thick, elastic walls to handle high pressure from each heartbeat; the pulse you feel in your wrist or neck is an artery stretching. The biggest, the aorta, is roughly as wide as a garden hose. Arteries branch into tiny capillaries, so narrow that red blood cells pass in single file, where oxygen and nutrients move into tissues and waste moves out. Veins carry blood back to the heart under much lower pressure, relying on one-way valves and squeezing leg muscles to push it along. Laid end to end, an adult's blood vessels would stretch for tens of thousands of kilometres, most of it capillaries.

sections.key: Blood contains red cells, white cells, platelets and plasma.
sections.b: An adult has about five litres of blood. Just over half is plasma, a yellowish liquid carrying nutrients, hormones, salts and proteins. Red blood cells, made in bone marrow, carry oxygen using haemoglobin, an iron-rich protein that makes blood red. They're shaped like flattened discs, which gives them more surface area and lets them squeeze through tight capillaries. White blood cells, far fewer in number, fight infection. Platelets are cell fragments that clump together to plug wounds and start clotting. Red blood cells live about 120 days, and your body replaces them at a rate of roughly two million every second.

sections.key: Blood groups depend on markers on red cells, and matching them makes transfusions safe.
sections.b: Red blood cells carry markers called antigens. The ABO system sorts blood into groups A, B, AB and O, and the Rh factor adds positive or negative. Giving someone blood with markers their immune system doesn't recognise can trigger a dangerous reaction, which is why blood is carefully matched. O negative can be given to almost anyone in an emergency, so it's in constant demand. AB positive people can usually receive red cells from any group. In Australia, donations are collected by Australian Red Cross Lifeblood. One donation is split into parts, such as red cells, plasma and platelets, so it can help several patients.

sections.key: Blood pressure measures the force of blood on artery walls; high pressure damages the heart and vessels.
sections.b: Blood pressure is written as two numbers in millimetres of mercury, like 120/80. The top number, systolic, is the pressure when the heart beats; the bottom, diastolic, is the pressure between beats. It naturally rises and falls through the day with activity, stress and sleep. Persistently high blood pressure, hypertension, often has no symptoms but strains the heart and damages arteries, raising the risk of heart attack, stroke and kidney disease. That's why it's called a silent killer, and why regular checks matter, especially from middle age. Checks are quick, painless and available from GPs and many pharmacies.

sections.key: Coronary arteries feed the heart muscle; a blockage in one causes a heart attack.
sections.b: The heart pumps blood to every organ, but it can't feed itself from the blood inside its chambers. Instead, its muscle is supplied by coronary arteries that wrap around its surface like a crown, which is where the name comes from. Over decades, fatty plaque can build up inside these arteries, a process called atherosclerosis, narrowing them. If a plaque ruptures, a clot can form and block the artery. The heart muscle beyond it is starved of oxygen and starts to die: that's a heart attack. Fast treatment to reopen the artery saves muscle, which is why every minute counts.

sections.key: Exercise, not smoking, healthy eating and managing blood pressure protect your heart.
sections.b: Heart disease is one of the leading causes of death in Australia. The main risk factors are smoking, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes, physical inactivity, obesity and too much alcohol. Many are modifiable. Regular exercise strengthens the heart; eating more vegetables, whole grains, legumes and fish and less salt helps too. Adults aged 45 and over (30 and over for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people) can ask their GP for a Heart Health Check. Know the signs of a heart attack, like chest pain or pressure, pain spreading to the arm, jaw or back, and breathlessness, and call 000 immediately.

quiz.q: About how many times does the heart beat each day?
quiz.e: Around 60–100 times a minute at rest.

quiz.q: Where does the right side of the heart send blood?
quiz.e: To pick up oxygen.

quiz.q: What do capillaries do?
o: Connect arteries and veins, exchanging oxygen and waste with tissues
quiz.e: Red cells pass in single file.

quiz.q: What makes blood red?
quiz.e: It carries oxygen.

quiz.q: Why is high blood pressure called a silent killer?
o: It often has no symptoms but causes serious damage
quiz.e: Regular checks matter.

LESSONS.title: How digestion works
LESSONS.hook: From first bite to final exit, your food travels through several metres of tubing and takes a day or more. Here's what happens along the way.

sections.key: Digestion starts in the mouth, where teeth and saliva begin breaking down food.
sections.b: The digestive tract is a long tube running from mouth to anus, often quoted as around nine metres in an adult, though it's shorter in a living body with its muscles toned. Chewing breaks food into smaller pieces, and saliva contains an enzyme, amylase, that starts breaking starch into sugar. That's why bread tastes slightly sweet if you chew it for a long time. You make roughly half a litre to one and a half litres of saliva a day. Swallowing pushes food into the oesophagus, where waves of muscle contraction, called peristalsis, move it down to the stomach, even if you're upside down.

sections.key: The stomach churns food with acid and enzymes into a thick liquid called chyme.
sections.b: The stomach is a stretchy muscular bag that can hold about a litre or more after a big meal. Its muscular walls churn food and mix it with strong hydrochloric acid, which kills many microbes, and the enzyme pepsin, which starts digesting protein. A layer of mucus protects the stomach lining from its own acid, and the lining itself is renewed every few days. Some things are absorbed here, including alcohol. After a few hours, food becomes a thick liquid called chyme, and a ring of muscle, the pyloric sphincter, releases it gradually into the small intestine.

sections.key: Most digestion and nutrient absorption happens in the small intestine.
sections.b: Despite its name, the small intestine is the longest part of the tract, several metres long and only a few centimetres wide. Here, bile from the liver breaks fat into small droplets, and enzymes from the pancreas break down carbohydrates, proteins and fats into small molecules like sugars, amino acids and fatty acids. The intestine's wall is covered in millions of tiny finger-like villi, themselves covered in even smaller microvilli, which give it a huge surface area to absorb nutrients into the blood. Food typically spends several hours here, and most of digestion's real work happens along this stretch.

sections.key: The liver processes nutrients and makes bile; the pancreas makes enzymes and insulin.
sections.b: Blood from the intestines goes first to the liver, which processes nutrients, stores energy as glycogen, and removes toxins, including alcohol. It's the largest internal organ and can regenerate remarkably after damage. It also makes bile, which is stored and concentrated in the gall bladder. The pancreas, tucked behind the stomach, produces digestive enzymes and hormones, including insulin, which helps cells absorb sugar from the blood. Diabetes involves problems with insulin: in type 1, the body makes little or none because the cells that produce it are destroyed; in type 2, cells stop responding to it well.

sections.key: The large intestine absorbs water and hosts trillions of gut bacteria.
sections.b: What's left, mostly fibre, water and bacteria, passes into the large intestine, or colon, about 1.5 metres long. Here water and salts are absorbed, turning liquid waste into solid stool, which can take a day or more. The colon is home to trillions of bacteria, the gut microbiome, which ferment fibre, produce some vitamins such as vitamin K, and help train the immune system. When they ferment fibre, they make short-chain fatty acids that help nourish the colon lining. Researchers are actively studying links between the microbiome and health, though many popular claims go beyond current evidence.

sections.key: Hormones and nerves between gut and brain tell you when to eat and when to stop.
sections.b: Your gut and brain talk constantly, through hormones and through the vagus nerve. When your stomach is empty, it releases ghrelin, a hormone that increases hunger. As you eat, the stomach stretches and the intestine releases hormones that signal fullness. Fat tissue releases leptin, which helps regulate appetite over the longer term. These signals take time to register, which is one reason eating quickly makes it easier to overeat. Sleep, stress and habits also influence appetite: short sleep, for example, is linked to stronger hunger. The gut even has its own vast network of nerves, sometimes called the second brain.

sections.key: Reflux, food intolerances, coeliac disease and irritable bowel are common gut problems.
sections.b: Reflux happens when stomach acid flows back into the oesophagus, causing heartburn; large meals, lying down after eating and alcohol can make it worse. Many adults produce less lactase, the enzyme that digests milk sugar, after childhood, so dairy may cause bloating. Coeliac disease is an immune reaction to gluten that damages the small intestine; it affects roughly 1 in 70 Australians, and most don't know they have it. Irritable bowel syndrome causes pain and changed bowel habits without visible damage. Because symptoms overlap, it's worth seeing a GP for a proper diagnosis rather than cutting out foods on your own.

sections.key: Fibre, water, plants and movement support healthy digestion.
sections.b: Most Australians eat less fibre than recommended. Fibre from vegetables, fruit, legumes and whole grains keeps bowel movements regular and feeds healthy gut bacteria. Eating a wide variety of plant foods may support a more diverse microbiome. Drinking water, staying active and not rushing meals help too. Probiotics may help in some specific situations, but they're not a cure-all. See a doctor about persistent changes in bowel habits, blood in stool, or unexplained weight loss. Australia's National Bowel Cancer Screening Program offers free home test kits from age 45, and they're mailed out automatically every two years from 50 to 74.

quiz.q: What is peristalsis?
o: Waves of muscle contraction that move food along
quiz.e: It works even upside down.

quiz.q: What protects the stomach from its own acid?
quiz.e: Hydrochloric acid is strong.

quiz.q: Where does most nutrient absorption happen?
quiz.e: Villi give it a huge surface area.

quiz.q: Which organ makes insulin?
quiz.e: It helps cells absorb sugar.

quiz.q: What lives in the large intestine?
o: Trillions of bacteria, the gut microbiome
quiz.e: They ferment fibre.

LESSONS.title: Muscles and bones
LESSONS.hook: Your skeleton is living tissue that rebuilds itself constantly, and your muscles are the engines that move it.

sections.key: An adult skeleton has 206 bones, supporting and protecting the body.
sections.b: Babies are born with around 270 to 300 bones or bony pieces, many of which fuse as they grow, leaving about 206 in adults. The soft spots on a baby's skull, called fontanelles, are gaps that close as the skull bones join. The skeleton supports your body, protects organs (the skull guards the brain; the ribs protect the heart and lungs), and anchors muscles. More than half your bones are in your hands and feet. The largest bone is the femur, in the thigh; the smallest is the stapes, in the middle ear, about the size of a grain of rice.

sections.key: Bones are living tissue that constantly break down and rebuild.
sections.b: Bone isn't dead and dry. It's living tissue with blood vessels and nerves, made of a flexible protein framework, mostly collagen, hardened with calcium and phosphate minerals. That mix makes it both strong and slightly springy. Cells called osteoclasts break down old bone, and osteoblasts build new bone, so your skeleton is gradually renewed over years. Inside many bones is marrow, which produces blood cells. Bones store calcium and release it when the body needs it. They also respond to stress: weight-bearing exercise makes bones denser and stronger, while long bed rest or spaceflight makes them lose mass.

sections.key: Joints connect bones, with cartilage and fluid allowing smooth movement.
sections.b: Where bones meet, joints allow movement. Hinge joints, like the knee and elbow, bend mainly one way; ball-and-socket joints, like the hip and shoulder, rotate in many directions. The shoulder is the most mobile joint in the body, which is also why it dislocates more easily. Smooth cartilage covers bone ends, and synovial fluid lubricates them. Cartilage has no blood supply, so it heals poorly, and its wear is part of osteoarthritis. Ligaments connect bone to bone, and tendons connect muscle to bone. The Achilles tendon, at the back of the ankle, is the body's strongest.

sections.key: Muscles can only pull, not push, so they work in opposing pairs.
sections.b: The body has over 600 skeletal muscles. Muscle fibres contain protein filaments, actin and myosin, that slide past each other when a nerve signal arrives, making the muscle shorten and pull on a bone. Muscles can only pull, so they work in pairs: to bend your elbow, the biceps contracts while the triceps relaxes; to straighten it, the reverse. There are also smooth muscles, in organs like the gut and blood vessels, which work without conscious control, and cardiac muscle in the heart. Working muscles also produce a lot of heat, which is why shivering warms you up.

sections.key: Slow-twitch fibres suit endurance, while fast-twitch fibres deliver speed and power.
sections.b: Skeletal muscles contain a mix of fibre types. Slow-twitch fibres contract relatively gently but resist fatigue, using oxygen efficiently; they power posture, walking and long-distance running. Fast-twitch fibres contract quickly and powerfully but tire sooner; they're recruited for sprinting, jumping and heavy lifting. The mix varies between muscles and between people, partly because of genes, which helps explain why some people are naturally drawn to endurance or power sports. Training can't completely change your fibre mix, but it can make both types work much better. Endurance training improves stamina, while strength training makes fibres thicker and stronger.

sections.key: Broken bones heal in stages, first with a soft callus and then new hard bone.
sections.b: When a bone breaks, bleeding forms a clot around the break. Within days, cells lay down a soft callus of cartilage and fibrous tissue that bridges the gap. Over the following weeks, osteoblasts replace it with a harder bony callus, and over months the bone is remodelled back towards its original shape. Many simple fractures in adults take roughly six to eight weeks to heal enough for normal use, though full remodelling takes longer, and children heal faster. Casts and splints hold the pieces in line so they knit correctly. Smoking slows bone healing noticeably.

sections.key: Muscle and bone strength decline with age and inactivity but respond to exercise at any age.
sections.b: From around your 30s or 40s, muscle mass slowly declines, and in older age this loss of muscle and strength is called sarcopenia. Bone density also falls, especially in women after menopause, raising the risk of osteoporosis, where bones become fragile and break easily, often at the hip, spine or wrist. Weak muscles also make falls more likely, and falls are a major cause of injury in older Australians. The good news: strength training and weight-bearing exercise, like walking or stair climbing, build muscle and bone at any age, even in people in their 80s and 90s.

sections.key: Calcium, vitamin D, protein and regular exercise keep muscles and bones strong.
sections.b: Bones need calcium, found in dairy foods, some leafy greens, canned fish with bones and fortified foods, and vitamin D, which your skin makes from sunlight, to absorb it. In Australia, balance sun protection with enough exposure, as advised for your skin type and region. Muscles need enough protein spread across the day, and regular activity. Australian guidelines suggest adults do muscle-strengthening activities on at least two days a week. Avoiding smoking and excess alcohol helps both. Good technique when lifting reduces injury risk. If you're concerned about bone health, a GP can check your risk and arrange a bone density scan.

quiz.q: How many bones does an adult skeleton have?
quiz.e: Babies have more, which fuse.

quiz.q: What do osteoblasts do?
quiz.e: Bone is constantly renewed.

quiz.q: What connects muscle to bone?
quiz.e: Ligaments connect bone to bone.

quiz.q: Why do muscles work in pairs?
o: They can only pull, not push
quiz.e: Biceps and triceps, for example.

quiz.q: What builds muscle and bone at any age?
quiz.e: Even in people in their 90s.

LESSONS.title: How your senses work
LESSONS.hook: You have far more than five senses. And every one of them is your brain's interpretation, not a direct window on the world.

sections.key: Beyond sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch, we sense balance, body position, temperature, pain and more.
sections.b: The idea of five senses goes back to Aristotle. Scientists now count many more, depending on how you define a sense. Proprioception tells you where your limbs are without looking, which is how you can touch your nose with your eyes closed. The vestibular system in your inner ear senses balance and motion. Separate receptors detect temperature and pain. Interoception tells you about your body's internal state, like hunger, thirst, a full bladder or a racing heart. All of them work the same basic way: specialised receptor cells convert physical signals into nerve impulses the brain interprets.

sections.key: The eye focuses light onto the retina, where rods and cones convert it into nerve signals.
sections.b: Light enters through the cornea and lens, which focus it onto the retina at the back of the eye. The iris adjusts the pupil's size to control how much light gets in. The retina contains about 120 million rods, which work in dim light but don't see colour, and about 6 million cones, which detect colour in three types, roughly sensitive to red, green and blue. Cones are packed into a small central spot, the fovea, which gives your sharpest vision. The image on the retina is upside down; the brain flips it. Each eye also has a blind spot where the optic nerve leaves, which your brain fills in.

sections.key: Sound waves vibrate the eardrum and tiny bones; hair cells in the cochlea turn vibrations into signals.
sections.b: Sound waves travel into the ear canal and vibrate the eardrum. Three tiny bones, the hammer, anvil and stirrup, amplify the vibrations and pass them to the cochlea, a fluid-filled spiral about the size of a pea. Inside, thousands of hair cells bend with the vibrations, with different parts responding to different pitches. Young people can typically hear from about 20 to 20,000 vibrations per second, and the upper limit drops with age. Loud noise can permanently damage these hair cells, which don't regrow in humans. That's why hearing protection matters.

sections.key: The inner ear's vestibular system senses head movement and gravity to keep you balanced.
sections.b: Next to the cochlea sit three fluid-filled semicircular canals, arranged at roughly right angles to each other. When you turn your head, the fluid lags behind and bends tiny hair cells, signalling rotation in any direction. Two small organs nearby contain tiny crystals that shift with gravity and straight-line movement, telling you which way is up and when you speed up in a car or lift. The brain combines these signals with vision and proprioception. When they disagree, as when reading in a moving car, the result can be motion sickness. Spinning makes you dizzy because the fluid keeps moving after you stop.

sections.key: Smell wires almost directly into the brain's emotion and memory centres, and taste and smell cells are constantly replaced.
sections.b: Taste and smell are chemical senses: they detect molecules rather than light or sound. You have several thousand taste buds, mostly on the tongue, and their receptor cells wear out and are replaced roughly every week or two, which is why a burnt tongue recovers. Smell is the richer sense. Humans have around 400 types of smell receptor, and combinations of them let us tell apart a very large number of odours, far more than once believed. Smell signals travel almost directly to brain areas for emotion and memory, which is why a scent can instantly bring back a place. Smell cells are renewed too, but loss of smell becomes more common with age, and a sudden loss is worth mentioning to a doctor.

sections.key: The skin has several types of receptors for pressure, vibration, temperature and pain.
sections.b: Your skin, the body's largest organ, contains different receptors for light touch, pressure, vibration, stretch, heat, cold and pain. They're not evenly spread: fingertips and lips are packed with them, while your back has far fewer. That's why a map of the brain's touch areas, the 'homunculus', has huge hands and lips. Many touch receptors also adapt quickly, which is why you stop noticing your clothes soon after dressing. Pain receptors warn of damage, and people born unable to feel pain, a rare genetic condition, often suffer serious injuries without realising it.

sections.key: Senses provide data, but the brain combines and interprets it to build our experience.
sections.b: Your brain combines information from different senses, fills gaps, and makes predictions. What you see changes what you hear, as in the McGurk effect, where watching lips say one sound makes you hear a different one. Expectations change how things taste, which is why the same wine can taste better when people are told it's expensive. Optical illusions reveal the shortcuts your visual system takes. Some people experience synaesthesia, where senses blend, such as seeing colours when hearing music. Perception, in short, is an active construction, not a camera recording.

sections.key: Protect your eyes and ears, get regular checks and notice changes early.
sections.b: Many sensory losses are gradual and preventable. Australia's strong sunlight makes good sunglasses and hats worthwhile, as UV exposure contributes to cataracts and other eye problems. Regular eye tests can pick up conditions like glaucoma before you notice any vision loss. For hearing, a common workplace guide is that noise averaging 85 decibels over eight hours is the limit before protection is needed, and louder sounds are safe for much less time; earbuds at high volume count. Sudden loss of smell, hearing or vision, or new dizziness, is worth seeing a doctor about promptly.

quiz.q: What is proprioception?
o: Sensing where your limbs are without looking
quiz.e: One of many senses beyond five.

quiz.q: What do cones in the retina detect?
quiz.e: Rods work in dim light.

quiz.q: Why is loud noise so dangerous for hearing?
o: It damages hair cells that don't regrow
quiz.e: Protect your hearing.

quiz.q: Why can a smell instantly bring back a memory?
o: Smell signals travel almost directly to brain areas for emotion and memory
Smells are processed by the eyes
quiz.e: Smell is closely wired to memory and emotion.

quiz.q: Why does the brain's 'homunculus' have huge hands and lips?
quiz.e: Touch receptors aren't evenly spread.

LESSONS.title: How neurons talk
LESSONS.hook: Every thought, memory and movement comes down to cells sending electrical and chemical messages. Here's how they do it.

sections.key: Neurons are cells specialised to send signals, with dendrites, a cell body and an axon.
sections.b: A neuron has three main parts. Branching dendrites receive signals from other neurons. The cell body, containing the nucleus, combines those inputs. A long, thin axon carries the output signal away, sometimes over a metre, like those running from your lower spine to your toes. Many axons are wrapped in myelin, a fatty insulating layer that speeds signals up enormously; the signal jumps between small gaps in the myelin rather than creeping along. The brain has around 86 billion neurons, a figure from careful cell-counting studies, plus a similar number of supporting glial cells.

sections.key: Neurons fire an all-or-nothing electrical pulse called an action potential.
sections.b: A neuron at rest keeps a small voltage across its membrane, about minus 70 millivolts, by pumping charged particles, ions, in and out. When enough input arrives to push it past a threshold, channels open, sodium ions rush in, and a spike of voltage, the action potential, races down the axon. Potassium then flows out to reset it. It's all-or-nothing: a neuron either fires or it doesn't. Stronger stimuli make neurons fire more often, not more strongly. Signals in thin, unmyelinated fibres crawl at about a metre per second, while in myelinated axons they can travel over 100 metres per second.

sections.key: At synapses, neurons pass signals using chemical messengers called neurotransmitters.
sections.b: Most neurons don't quite touch. Between them is a tiny gap, the synapse, far narrower than a human hair. When an action potential reaches the end of an axon, it releases neurotransmitter molecules from little packets called vesicles. These cross the gap in a fraction of a millisecond and bind to receptors on the next neuron, making it more or less likely to fire. Then the neurotransmitters are broken down or recycled back into the sending cell. Each neuron may connect to thousands of others, creating an estimated 100 trillion or more synapses in the human brain.

sections.key: Some signals push neurons to fire, others hold them back; balance is essential.
sections.b: Glutamate is the brain's main excitatory neurotransmitter, encouraging neurons to fire. GABA is the main inhibitory one, calming activity down. Each neuron is constantly adding up excitatory and inhibitory inputs to decide whether to fire. The brain depends on balancing the two. Too much excitation can cause seizures, which is why many epilepsy drugs boost inhibition or dampen excitation. Alcohol and some sedative medicines enhance GABA's effects, which is part of why they slow reactions and cause drowsiness. Other neurotransmitters, like dopamine and serotonin, act more like volume controls, tuning whole networks.

sections.key: Connections between neurons strengthen with use, the basis of learning.
sections.b: In 1949, psychologist Donald Hebb proposed that when one neuron repeatedly helps another fire, the connection between them strengthens. This is often summarised as 'neurons that fire together, wire together'. In 1973, researchers reported a mechanism called long-term potentiation in the hippocampus, a memory hub, where repeated stimulation made synapses stronger for hours or longer. Practice physically strengthens pathways, adding receptors and even new connections, while unused connections can weaken and be pruned. This is how skills and memories are built, and why regular practice and review work better than a single long session.

sections.key: Glial cells insulate, feed, protect and clean up after neurons.
sections.b: Neurons get the attention, but glial cells are just as numerous and essential. Oligodendrocytes wrap axons in the brain and spinal cord with myelin; Schwann cells do the same in the rest of the body. Astrocytes, star-shaped cells, help supply energy to neurons, regulate chemicals around synapses and help maintain the barrier between blood and brain. Microglia are the brain's immune cells, clearing debris and damaged cells and helping prune unused synapses during development. Once seen as mere glue, which is what 'glia' means in Greek, these cells are now known to take an active part in how the brain works.

sections.key: Many brain conditions involve problems with neurons, myelin or neurotransmitters.
sections.b: In multiple sclerosis, the immune system attacks myelin, slowing or blocking signals and causing symptoms like numbness, weakness or vision problems. Parkinson's disease involves the loss of dopamine-producing neurons, affecting movement. Alzheimer's disease damages synapses and neurons, especially in memory areas, and involves build-ups of abnormal proteins. Many medicines work at synapses: some antidepressants, for example, affect how serotonin is recycled, and some anaesthetics and pain relievers act on specific receptors. Understanding how neurons talk remains one of the most important frontiers in medicine.

sections.key: Brain-computer interfaces decode neurons' electrical activity, letting some paralysed people control computers by thought.
sections.b: Because neurons communicate electrically, their activity can be recorded and decoded. Brain-computer interfaces place sensors on or near the motor cortex, the strip of brain that plans movement, and use software to translate patterns of firing into commands. In trials in the early 2000s, people with paralysis learned to move a computer cursor simply by imagining moving their hand. An Australian-developed approach, the Stentrode from Melbourne company Synchron, avoids open brain surgery: it's threaded up through the jugular vein into a blood vessel beside the motor cortex. From 2019, its first recipients, people with motor neurone disease, used it to text, shop and bank online. The technology is still experimental, but it's advancing quickly.

quiz.q: What does the axon do?
o: Carries the output signal away from the cell body
quiz.e: Dendrites receive signals.

quiz.q: What is special about an action potential?
quiz.e: Stronger stimuli mean more frequent firing.

quiz.q: What happens to neurotransmitters after they've passed on their signal?
o: They stay in the gap permanently
They're broken down or recycled back into the sending cell
They travel on to the next synapse
quiz.e: Clearing them quickly lets the synapse send its next message.

quiz.q: What is GABA?
quiz.e: It calms activity.

quiz.q: What does 'neurons that fire together, wire together' describe?
quiz.e: Proposed by Donald Hebb in 1949.

LESSONS.title: Dopamine, serotonin and friends
LESSONS.hook: Pop culture calls dopamine the 'pleasure chemical' and serotonin the 'happy chemical'. The truth is more interesting.

sections.key: Neurotransmitters and hormones carry messages that shape mood, motivation and behaviour.
sections.b: Neurotransmitters carry signals between neurons across tiny gaps; hormones travel through the blood to affect distant organs, working over seconds to days. Some, like adrenaline, act as both. Each chemical affects many systems, and its effects depend on which receptors and brain regions are involved. Dopamine alone has five main receptor types. So simple labels like 'the happy chemical' are misleading. You also can't measure your brain's levels with a blood test. Still, knowing a few key players helps make sense of motivation, mood, stress and how many medicines and drugs work.

sections.key: Dopamine drives motivation and learning from rewards more than pleasure itself.
sections.b: Dopamine is often called the pleasure chemical, but research by Kent Berridge and others suggests it's more about wanting than liking: motivation, anticipation and learning which actions lead to rewards. Dopamine neurons fire strongly when a reward is better than expected, and dip when it's worse, teaching the brain to repeat what worked. Unpredictable rewards, like slot machines or social media notifications, tap into this system powerfully. Dopamine is also essential for movement, which is why its loss in Parkinson's disease affects motor control, and why treatment often involves a drug the brain converts into dopamine.

sections.key: Serotonin influences mood, sleep, appetite and digestion; most of it is in the gut.
sections.b: Serotonin affects mood, sleep, appetite and impulse control. Surprisingly, around 90% of the body's serotonin is found in the gut, where it helps regulate digestion, and it can't easily cross from the blood into the brain. The popular idea that depression is simply caused by low serotonin is now considered too simple; a widely publicised 2022 review found no consistent evidence for it, though some researchers disputed how it was reported. Antidepressants that affect serotonin help many people, but probably through more complex effects, such as on brain plasticity. Decisions about medication should always be made with a doctor.

sections.key: Oxytocin supports bonding, trust and childbirth, but it's no simple 'love hormone'.
sections.b: Oxytocin is made in the hypothalamus and released by the pituitary gland. It triggers contractions during childbirth and milk release during breastfeeding, and it's involved in bonding between parents and babies, and between partners. It's often called the love or cuddle hormone. But research shows its effects depend on context: some studies found it can increase trust and closeness towards one's own group while increasing defensiveness towards outsiders. Some well-known early findings, like oxytocin nasal sprays increasing trust, haven't reliably replicated, a reminder to be cautious about headline-friendly science.

sections.key: Stress hormones prepare the body for action, but chronic stress causes harm.
