sections.b: In a threat, adrenaline (also called epinephrine) rapidly raises heart rate and breathing, sends blood to muscles and sharpens alertness, the fight-or-flight response. Cortisol, released more slowly by the adrenal glands, raises blood sugar and helps the body cope with stress over hours. Cortisol also follows a daily rhythm, normally peaking soon after waking. These responses are life-saving in short bursts. But chronic stress, with cortisol elevated for weeks or months, is linked to poor sleep, weakened immunity, weight gain and higher risk of heart disease and depression.

sections.key: Endorphins are the body's natural painkillers, released during exercise, laughter and pain.
sections.b: Endorphins are the body's own opioids, reducing pain and producing feelings of wellbeing. They're released during injury, intense or prolonged exercise, and laughter, and they help explain why people sometimes feel little pain right after a serious injury. The 'runner's high' was long credited to endorphins, though research suggests endocannabinoids, the body's cannabis-like chemicals, also play a big role. Opioid drugs like morphine and oxycodone act on the same receptors, which is why they relieve pain so powerfully, and also why they can be addictive and dangerous in overdose.

sections.key: Melatonin rises in darkness and signals to the body that it's night.
sections.b: Melatonin is a hormone made by the pineal gland, a small structure deep in the brain. Its release is controlled by a master clock in the hypothalamus that responds to light entering the eyes. Levels rise in the evening as it gets dark, stay high overnight and fall in the morning. Bright light at night, especially blue-rich light from screens and LEDs, can suppress it and delay sleepiness. Melatonin is less a knockout sleeping pill than a timing signal, which is why it's mainly used for jet lag and certain sleep timing problems. In Australia, melatonin is available only from a pharmacist or on prescription.

sections.key: Brain chemicals work as systems, so be sceptical of quick fixes that promise to 'hack' them.
sections.b: Popular advice often promises to boost or reset one chemical, from 'dopamine detox' to foods that raise serotonin. Brain chemistry doesn't work that simply, and there's little evidence for most such claims. The principles behind them can still be sensible: cutting back on constant notifications can make everyday activities feel more rewarding, and regular exercise, daylight, good sleep and time with people you care about all support mood and stress resilience. If low mood, anxiety or stress persists for weeks, talk to a GP, who can discuss options including therapy and medication.

quiz.q: What does research suggest dopamine is mostly about?
o: Wanting, motivation and learning from rewards
quiz.e: Unpredictable rewards tap into it.

quiz.q: Where is most of the body's serotonin found?
quiz.e: Around 90%.

quiz.q: What did a 2022 review find about serotonin and depression?
o: No consistent evidence that low serotonin is the simple cause
quiz.e: Antidepressants still help many people.

quiz.q: When do cortisol levels normally peak each day?
o: In the middle of the night
quiz.e: Cortisol follows a daily rhythm, normally peaking soon after you wake.

quiz.q: What are endorphins?
quiz.e: Released during exercise and laughter.

LESSONS.title: Why we dream
LESSONS.hook: You spend about six years of your life dreaming. Scientists still debate why, but they've learned a lot about how.

sections.key: REM sleep was discovered in the early 1950s, when a student noticed sleepers' eyes darting beneath their lids.
sections.b: In the early 1950s Eugene Aserinsky, a graduate student in Nathaniel Kleitman's sleep lab at the University of Chicago, wired sleepers to an old brainwave machine, starting with his eight-year-old son, Armond. Several times a night the pens traced bursts of rapid, jerky eye movements, while the brain's activity looked almost awake. At first he suspected the machine was faulty. In 1953 he and Kleitman published their discovery of rapid eye movement, or REM, sleep. A few years later William Dement, in the same lab, woke volunteers at different moments. Roused from REM, most described vivid dreams; roused at other times, far fewer did. Dreams do happen outside REM, but they tend to be shorter and less story-like.

sections.key: Most dreams are forgotten within minutes of waking.
sections.b: Most people dream several times a night but remember few dreams, and some people rarely recall any. Brain chemistry during sleep, including low levels of noradrenaline, seems to make it hard to store dreams in long-term memory. If you wake during or just after a dream, you're more likely to remember it, which is why an alarm during REM can leave you with a vivid fragment. Keeping a notebook by the bed and writing dreams down immediately on waking improves recall, as does simply intending to remember. Lying still with your eyes closed for a moment before moving can help too.

sections.key: Dreams mostly feature familiar people, places and worries, often with strong emotions.
sections.b: Researchers have collected tens of thousands of dream reports. Psychologist Calvin Hall began systematically cataloguing them in the mid-20th century, and his coding system is still used. Most dreams are less bizarre than we assume: they often feature familiar people and settings, and the recent concerns of waking life. Negative emotions such as fear, anxiety and frustration are common. Some themes appear across many cultures, including being chased, falling, flying, and being late or unprepared for an exam. Dreams rarely involve reading, writing or using a phone, perhaps because the brain regions for those tasks are less active during REM.

sections.key: Theories range from Freud's wish fulfilment to memory processing and threat simulation.
sections.b: Sigmund Freud, in his book The Interpretation of Dreams, published in late 1899 though dated 1900, argued dreams disguise hidden wishes, a theory few scientists accept today. In 1977, the activation-synthesis hypothesis proposed dreams are the brain's attempt to make sense of random activity from the brainstem. Other theories suggest dreams help process emotions, consolidate memories, or rehearse responses to threats, an idea put forward by Finnish researcher Antti Revonsuo in 2000. Many researchers think dreaming may serve several functions, or be partly a by-product of what sleep does for the brain.

sections.key: REM sleep may help process emotional experiences, taking the sting out of them.
sections.b: Sleep researcher Matthew Walker and others have suggested REM sleep acts as 'overnight therapy', helping the brain process emotional memories while stress chemicals like noradrenaline are low. Some studies suggest people react less intensely to emotional images after a night's sleep, though findings are mixed. In post-traumatic stress disorder, nightmares can replay trauma, and this process may break down. Therapies such as imagery rehearsal, rewriting a nightmare's ending while awake and rehearsing the new version, can reduce nightmares. Poor sleep also makes people more emotionally reactive the next day.

sections.key: In lucid dreams, people know they're dreaming, and sometimes control the dream.
sections.b: In a lucid dream, you become aware that you're dreaming while still asleep. In the 1970s and 80s, researchers including Keith Hearne and Stephen LaBerge showed lucid dreaming was real: sleepers in labs signalled with pre-agreed eye movements while brain recordings confirmed they were in REM sleep. Around half of people report having had at least one lucid dream, though frequent lucid dreaming is much rarer. Techniques to increase them include reality checks during the day, like asking 'am I dreaming?', and setting a clear intention to recognise dreams before falling asleep.

sections.key: Many animals have REM-like sleep, and rats appear to replay their day while sleeping.
sections.b: REM-like sleep has been found in mammals and birds, and signs of similar sleep states have been reported in some reptiles and even octopuses. We can't ask animals what they experience, but there are clues. In a well-known 2001 study, researchers recorded neurons in rats' hippocampus as they ran a maze, then found similar firing patterns replayed during the rats' REM sleep. Pet owners often see dogs twitch, paddle their legs or whimper in sleep. Whether animals experience anything like human dreams is unknown, but the replay findings support the idea that sleep helps process memories.

sections.key: Occasional nightmares are normal; frequent ones can be treated.
sections.b: Nightmares are common, especially in children and during stressful times. Frequent, distressing nightmares may be linked to anxiety, trauma, some medications, alcohol or sleep disorders. Sleepwalking and sleep talking usually happen in non-REM sleep, not during dreams. REM sleep behaviour disorder, where people act out dreams because muscle paralysis fails, is uncommon but important to diagnose, as it can be an early sign of Parkinson's disease and related conditions. Regular sleep hours and a calm wind-down routine help sleep overall. If nightmares or sleep problems are affecting your life, a GP can help or refer you to a sleep specialist.

quiz.q: Who first described REM sleep, in 1953?
quiz.e: Their discovery opened up the modern science of sleep and dreaming.

quiz.q: How can you remember dreams better?
o: Write them down immediately on waking
quiz.e: Intention helps too.

quiz.q: What did Freud argue dreams were?
quiz.e: Few scientists accept this today.

quiz.q: What might REM sleep do for emotional memories?
o: Help process them, taking the sting out
quiz.e: 'Overnight therapy'.

quiz.q: How did researchers show lucid dreaming was real?
o: Sleepers signalled with pre-agreed eye movements
quiz.e: In the 1970s and 80s.

LESSONS.title: The mystery of consciousness
LESSONS.hook: Why does it feel like something to be you? Science can map the brain in astonishing detail, yet this question remains unsolved.

sections.key: Consciousness is subjective experience: what it feels like to be you.
sections.b: Right now, you're experiencing colours, sounds, thoughts and feelings. Philosopher Thomas Nagel captured this in a famous 1974 essay, 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?': a creature is conscious if there is something it is like to be that creature. A bat navigating by echolocation presumably has experiences, but ones we may never be able to imagine. Scientists can study which brain processes accompany experiences, but explaining why there's any experience at all, rather than just information processing in the dark, is extraordinarily hard.

sections.key: Philosopher David Chalmers called explaining subjective experience 'the hard problem'.
sections.b: In the mid-1990s, Australian philosopher David Chalmers distinguished 'easy problems', explaining how the brain processes information, directs attention or controls behaviour, from 'the hard problem': why any of this is accompanied by subjective experience. The easy problems aren't actually easy, but they're the kind science knows how to tackle. The hard problem seems different in kind. Chalmers illustrated it with the idea of a philosophical zombie, a being physically identical to you but with no inner experience. Some philosophers think the problem will dissolve with more knowledge; others think it reveals a deep gap in our understanding.

sections.key: Scientists look for brain activity that reliably matches conscious experience.
sections.b: Many neuroscientists study the neural correlates of consciousness: the minimal brain activity needed for a specific experience. In experiments like binocular rivalry, each eye sees a different image, but people consciously see only one at a time, switching back and forth. Researchers compare brain activity when the same image is seen or not seen. Such studies show much brain processing happens unconsciously, and only some reaches awareness. In blindsight, people with damage to the visual cortex can point to objects they insist they can't see, showing vision without conscious experience.

sections.key: Leading theories include Global Workspace Theory and Integrated Information Theory.
sections.b: Global Workspace Theory, developed by Bernard Baars and extended by Stanislas Dehaene, proposes that information becomes conscious when it's broadcast widely across the brain, like being put on a stage for all systems to use. Integrated Information Theory, from Giulio Tononi, proposes consciousness corresponds to how much a system integrates information, measured as a quantity called phi. In 2023, a large 'adversarial collaboration' tested predictions of both, with mixed results. The debate grew heated, with some researchers publicly questioning whether Integrated Information Theory counts as science at all.

sections.key: Some thinkers argue experience is an illusion; others think it's everywhere.
sections.b: Not everyone accepts the hard problem as usually framed. Illusionists, influenced by philosopher Daniel Dennett, argue that the sense of an inner, private experience is itself a kind of trick the brain plays, and that explaining why we believe we have it is the real task. At the other extreme, panpsychists, such as philosopher Philip Goff, suggest consciousness may be a basic feature of matter, present in simple forms everywhere. Most scientists sit somewhere in between, assuming consciousness arises from brain activity but unsure how. None of these views has decisive evidence, and each has serious critics.

sections.key: Sleep, anaesthesia, meditation and psychedelics show consciousness can change dramatically.
sections.b: Consciousness isn't simply on or off. It fades in deep sleep, transforms in dreams, and vanishes under general anaesthesia, which doctors use safely every day but still don't fully understand. Patients in comas or vegetative states raise hard questions: in a landmark 2006 study, brain scans showed an apparently unresponsive patient following instructions, like imagining playing tennis, with the same brain activity as healthy volunteers. Later studies found similar hidden awareness in a minority of such patients. Meditation and psychedelic drugs also alter consciousness in ways researchers are now studying for clues.

sections.key: Which animals, and whether future AI, might be conscious, are open questions.
sections.b: In 2012, a group of scientists signed the Cambridge Declaration on Consciousness, stating that many animals, including mammals, birds and octopuses, possess the brain structures needed for consciousness. A 2024 New York declaration went further, suggesting there's at least a realistic possibility of consciousness in reptiles, fish and some invertebrates. The question grows more urgent with artificial intelligence. Current AI systems can produce convincingly human-like language, but whether anything like experience accompanies that remains deeply uncertain, and without a theory of consciousness, it's hard to know how we'd ever tell.

sections.key: How we understand consciousness shapes medicine, animal welfare and how we treat AI.
sections.b: This isn't just an armchair puzzle. Doctors need to judge whether an unresponsive patient might be aware, which affects care and end-of-life decisions. Anaesthetists work to prevent the rare but distressing experience of awareness during surgery. Laws on animal welfare increasingly depend on which creatures can feel pain; the UK, for example, recognised octopuses, crabs and lobsters as sentient in a 2022 law. And as AI becomes more capable, societies will face questions about whether machines could ever deserve moral consideration. Staying curious, and humble about what we don't know, is the honest position.

quiz.q: What was Thomas Nagel's famous essay called?
o: What Is It Like to Be a Bat?
quiz.e: Published in 1974.

quiz.q: What is 'the hard problem' of consciousness?
o: Explaining why brain processing is accompanied by subjective experience
quiz.e: Named by David Chalmers in the mid-1990s.

quiz.q: What does binocular rivalry show?
o: We see two images at once
quiz.e: Much processing is unconscious.

quiz.q: What does Global Workspace Theory propose?
o: Information becomes conscious when broadcast widely across the brain
quiz.e: Like being put on a stage.

quiz.q: What did the Cambridge Declaration on Consciousness state?
o: Many animals possess the brain structures for consciousness
quiz.e: Signed in 2012.

LESSONS.title: What atoms are made of
LESSONS.hook: Everything you can touch is made of atoms, and atoms are almost entirely empty space.

sections.key: The idea of atoms dates to ancient Greece, but solid evidence came only in the last two centuries.
sections.b: The Greek thinker Democritus proposed around 400 BC that matter is made of tiny, uncuttable particles; atomos means 'uncuttable'. For two thousand years it stayed a philosophical guess, and Aristotle's view that matter is continuous won out. Around 1808, English chemist John Dalton revived the idea with evidence: elements combine in fixed proportions by weight, which made sense if they came in discrete units. Even then, many scientists treated atoms as a handy bookkeeping device rather than real objects. In 1905, Albert Einstein's explanation of Brownian motion, the jittery dance of tiny particles suspended in water, gave strong evidence atoms really exist, and Jean Perrin's experiments soon confirmed it.

sections.key: Atoms are roughly 0.1 to 0.5 nanometres across, far too small to see with a light microscope.
sections.b: Atoms are almost unimaginably small, roughly 0.1 to 0.5 nanometres across, where a nanometre is a millionth of a millimetre. Several hundred thousand carbon atoms lined up side by side would only just span the width of a human hair. A single grain of table salt contains around a billion billion atoms. Ordinary light microscopes can never show them, because atoms are far smaller than the wavelength of visible light. Individual atoms were first imaged in the 1950s, and scanning tunnelling microscopes, invented in the 1980s, later let scientists move them too. In 1989, IBM researchers famously spelled out the company's logo using 35 xenon atoms, nudged into place one at a time.

sections.key: Atoms have a tiny nucleus of protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons.
sections.b: In 1897, J.J. Thomson discovered the electron, a tiny negatively charged particle about 1,800 times lighter than a hydrogen atom. Around 1909, Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden, working under New Zealand-born Ernest Rutherford, fired alpha particles at thin gold foil. Most passed straight through, but a few bounced almost straight back. In 1911 Rutherford concluded that an atom has a tiny, dense, positive nucleus with electrons around it. The nucleus holds positive protons and, as James Chadwick showed in 1932, neutral neutrons. If an atom were the size of a football stadium, the nucleus would be about the size of a pea.

sections.key: Atoms are more than 99.9999% empty space, yet solid objects feel solid.
sections.b: More than 99.9% of an atom's mass is packed into the nucleus, while nearly all its volume is space where electrons might be found. Electrons are not tiny planets on neat orbits; quantum physics describes them as fuzzy clouds of probability. So why can't your hand pass through a table? Electrons repel other electrons, and a quantum rule called the Pauli exclusion principle stops them crowding into the same state. Together these effects make matter feel solid and stiff. When you 'touch' something, your atoms never actually touch the object's atoms; what you feel is electromagnetic repulsion across a tiny gap.

sections.key: The number of protons defines an element; neutrons create isotopes.
sections.b: Every atom with one proton is hydrogen; six protons, carbon; eight, oxygen; 79, gold. That count is the atomic number, and it fixes the element's identity. Atoms of the same element can carry different numbers of neutrons; these versions are called isotopes. They behave almost identically in chemical reactions but differ in mass and stability. Carbon-12 has six neutrons and makes up about 99% of natural carbon. Carbon-14 has eight and is radioactive, decaying at a known rate, which lets scientists date once-living material up to about 50,000 years old, a technique called radiocarbon dating. Heavy water contains the hydrogen isotope deuterium.

sections.key: Unstable nuclei decay at a steady rate, measured by a half-life.
sections.b: In 1896, French physicist Henri Becquerel found that uranium salts fogged photographic plates kept in the dark. In 1898, Marie and Pierre Curie discovered two new radioactive elements, polonium and radium. Radioactivity happens when an unstable nucleus breaks down, releasing alpha particles, beta particles or gamma rays. Each radioactive isotope has a half-life, the time it takes for half of a sample to decay. Carbon-14's half-life is about 5,730 years; uranium-238's is about 4.5 billion years, which helps geologists date rocks and the Earth itself. Radioactivity has everyday uses too: many household smoke alarms contain a tiny amount of americium-241.

sections.key: Electrons, especially the outermost ones, determine how atoms bond and react.
sections.b: Chemistry is mostly about electrons. They occupy energy levels, or shells, around the nucleus, and atoms tend to be most stable when their outer shell is full. To get there, atoms share, give away or take electrons, forming chemical bonds. Sodium readily gives away its single outer electron and chlorine readily takes one, so together they form sodium chloride, table salt. Carbon, with four outer electrons, shares them in long chains and rings, which is why it forms the backbone of millions of compounds, including every living thing. Helium's shell is already full, so it barely reacts at all, making it safe for party balloons.

sections.key: Protons and neutrons are made of quarks; electrons appear to be fundamental.
sections.b: In the 1960s and 70s, physicists found that protons and neutrons are themselves made of smaller particles called quarks, bound by the strong force, the most powerful of nature's four fundamental forces. A proton contains two 'up' quarks and one 'down' quark; a neutron has one up and two down. Quarks are never seen alone, because trying to pull them apart creates new quarks. Electrons, as far as we know, aren't made of anything smaller. The Standard Model of particle physics describes these particles and three of the four forces, with gravity the missing one. The Higgs boson, detected at CERN in 2012, completed the model.

quiz.q: What does 'atomos' mean?
quiz.e: From Democritus, around 400 BC.

quiz.q: What did Rutherford's gold foil experiment reveal?
o: Atoms have a tiny, dense nucleus
quiz.e: Most particles passed straight through.

quiz.q: Why do solid objects feel solid?
quiz.e: Atoms are mostly empty space.

quiz.q: What defines which element an atom is?
quiz.e: Neutrons create isotopes.

quiz.q: What mainly determines how atoms react?
quiz.e: Atoms seek full outer shells.

LESSONS.title: The periodic table
LESSONS.hook: One chart organises every element in the universe, and when it was invented, it predicted elements nobody had found yet.

sections.key: In 1869, Dmitri Mendeleev arranged elements by weight and properties into a table.
sections.b: By the 1860s, chemists knew of about 60 elements but had no agreed pattern linking them. Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev, a professor in St Petersburg writing a chemistry textbook, wrote each element's properties on cards and arranged them by atomic weight, grouping those with similar behaviour in columns. Legend says the final arrangement came to him in a dream, though the story may be embellished. Others, including Germany's Lothar Meyer, were working on similar schemes at the same time. Mendeleev's crucial move was boldness: he left gaps where the pattern suggested undiscovered elements should be, and swapped a few elements whose weights seemed out of place.

sections.key: Mendeleev predicted unknown elements' properties, and they were later discovered.
sections.b: Mendeleev predicted elements he called eka-aluminium, eka-silicon and eka-boron, describing their likely atomic weight, density and behaviour. Gallium was discovered in 1875, scandium in 1879 and germanium in 1886, each matching his predictions closely. When gallium's first measured density disagreed with his forecast, Mendeleev suggested the sample was impure, and a remeasurement proved him right. This was powerful evidence that the table reflected something real about nature. Today's table is ordered by atomic number, the number of protons, rather than weight. English physicist Henry Moseley established this in 1913 using X-rays, which explained why a few elements had seemed out of order.

sections.key: Rows are periods; columns are groups of elements with similar properties.
sections.b: Each row, or period, corresponds to a new shell of electrons being filled, and the table has seven periods. Each column, or group, contains elements with the same number of outer electrons, which is why they behave similarly. Group 1, the alkali metals like sodium and potassium, are so reactive they're stored under oil, and they fizz or even explode in water. Group 17, the halogens like fluorine and chlorine, are highly reactive non-metals; chlorine compounds disinfect swimming pools. Group 18, the noble gases like helium, neon and argon, barely react at all. Argon makes up almost 1% of the air you breathe.

sections.key: Most elements are metals; non-metals cluster on the right side.
sections.b: More than three-quarters of the elements are metals: usually shiny, good conductors of heat and electricity, and able to be hammered into sheets or drawn into wires. They sit on the left and centre of the table. Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature. Non-metals, including carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, sulfur and the halogens, cluster on the right, with hydrogen an odd one out at the top left. A staircase-shaped zone between them holds the metalloids, like silicon and germanium, with mixed properties. Silicon's in-between electrical behaviour, which can be finely controlled, makes it the foundation of computer chips.

sections.key: The central block holds the transition metals; the rows below hold the rare earths and actinides.
sections.b: The wide central block holds the transition metals, including iron, copper, nickel, gold and platinum. Many form brightly coloured compounds and make excellent catalysts, and they're the workhorses of industry. The two rows usually printed below the main table are the lanthanides and actinides. The lanthanides, together with scandium and yttrium, are known as rare earth elements, though most aren't especially rare, just hard to find in concentrated, easily mined deposits. Neodymium makes powerful magnets for wind turbines and electric car motors. Australia is one of the world's larger producers of rare earths, with a major mine at Mount Weld in Western Australia.

sections.key: Element symbols often come from Latin names, places or famous scientists.
sections.b: Each element has a one- or two-letter symbol, and some reveal old Latin names. Sodium is Na from natrium, potassium is K from kalium, iron is Fe from ferrum, gold is Au from aurum, silver is Ag from argentum, and lead is Pb from plumbum, which also gives us the word 'plumber'. Other names honour places: the Swedish village of Ytterby lent its name to four elements, yttrium, ytterbium, terbium and erbium. Some honour scientists, such as curium, einsteinium and mendelevium, named after Mendeleev himself. New names are approved by IUPAC, the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry.

sections.key: There are 118 known elements; the heaviest are made in labs and exist for fractions of a second.
sections.b: Almost all elements up to uranium, atomic number 92, occur naturally; technetium and promethium are exceptions, found only in tiny traces. Heavier ones have been created in nuclear reactors and particle accelerators by smashing atoms together. The seventh row was completed with element 118, oganesson, officially named in 2016 along with nihonium, moscovium and tennessine. Many superheavy elements have been made only a few atoms at a time, and they last milliseconds or less before decaying. Physicists predict a possible 'island of stability' where some heavier nuclei might survive longer, and labs are still trying to make elements 119 and 120.

sections.key: Light elements came from the Big Bang; heavier ones were forged in stars and stellar explosions.
sections.b: Hydrogen, helium and a little lithium formed in the first few minutes after the Big Bang, about 13.8 billion years ago. Stars then fuse lighter elements into heavier ones, building carbon, oxygen and others up to iron, where fusion stops releasing energy. Elements heavier than iron form mainly in extreme events, like supernova explosions and collisions between neutron stars. A neutron star merger observed in 2017 was seen producing heavy elements, probably including gold and platinum. The calcium in your bones and the iron in your blood were made inside stars that died before the Sun was born. As Carl Sagan put it, we are made of star stuff.

quiz.q: Who created the periodic table in 1869?
quiz.e: He arranged elements on cards.

quiz.q: Why were Mendeleev's gaps so important?
o: They predicted undiscovered elements that were later found
quiz.e: Gallium and germanium matched.

quiz.q: Which group barely reacts at all?
quiz.e: Helium, neon, argon.

quiz.q: Why is silicon used in computer chips?
quiz.e: It's a metalloid.

quiz.q: Where were elements heavier than iron made?
o: In extreme events like supernovae and neutron star collisions
quiz.e: We are made of star stuff.

LESSONS.title: Chemical reactions
LESSONS.hook: Cooking, rusting, burning, breathing. Chemical reactions rearrange atoms into new substances, and they're happening in you right now.

sections.key: In a chemical reaction, atoms rearrange to form new substances; no atoms are created or destroyed.
sections.b: In a chemical reaction, the bonds holding atoms together break and new bonds form, producing substances with different properties. Hydrogen and oxygen are both gases, yet when hydrogen burns in oxygen it becomes water. Sodium is a violently reactive metal and chlorine a poisonous gas, but together they make table salt. In the 1770s and 1780s, French chemist Antoine Lavoisier used careful weighing to show that mass is conserved in reactions: atoms are rearranged, never created or destroyed. A burning log seems to vanish, but most of its atoms have gone into the air as carbon dioxide and water vapour, leaving only a little ash.

sections.key: Chemical equations must balance, with the same atoms on both sides.
sections.b: Chemists describe reactions with equations. Burning hydrogen is written 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O: two hydrogen molecules react with one oxygen molecule to make two water molecules. The number written after a symbol counts the atoms of that element in a molecule, and the number in front counts molecules. Because atoms are never created or destroyed, an equation must balance, with the same number of each kind of atom on both sides. Here there are four hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms on each side. Balanced equations let chemists calculate exactly how much of each ingredient is needed, whether making medicines, plastics or fertiliser.

sections.key: Physical changes alter form; chemical changes create new substances.
sections.b: Melting ice, boiling water or dissolving sugar are physical changes: the substance stays the same, just in a different form, and the change is often easily reversed. Chemical changes create something new, as in burning, rusting, cooking an egg or baking a cake. Signs of a chemical change include a new colour, gas bubbles that aren't just boiling, light or heat being produced, a new smell, or a solid forming when two liquids are mixed. The distinction isn't always obvious: dissolving salt in water might look like a reaction, but evaporating the water gives the salt back, so it's physical. You can't un-bake a cake.

sections.key: Some reactions release energy (exothermic); others absorb it (endothermic).
sections.b: Breaking bonds takes energy; forming new bonds releases it. If more energy is released than absorbed, the reaction is exothermic and gives off heat, like burning fuel, setting concrete, or the iron powder oxidising inside disposable hand warmers. If it absorbs more than it releases, it's endothermic and draws heat from its surroundings. Instant cold packs work this way, as dissolving ammonium nitrate in water pulls heat in, although strictly that's dissolving rather than a reaction. Photosynthesis is endothermic on a grand scale, storing the Sun's energy in sugar. Even exothermic reactions often need a spark or flame to start them, called activation energy.

sections.key: Heat, concentration, surface area and catalysts speed reactions.
sections.b: Reactions happen when particles collide with enough energy and the right orientation. Heating makes particles move faster and collide harder; as a rough rule, many reactions go about twice as fast for every 10°C rise, one reason refrigeration slows food spoiling. Higher concentration or pressure means more frequent collisions. Smaller pieces offer more surface area, which is why fine flour or coal dust can explode while a sack of flour won't. Catalysts speed reactions without being used up, by offering an easier pathway. Your car's catalytic converter turns toxic exhaust gases into less harmful ones, and enzymes are the biological catalysts running your body.

sections.key: Oxidation reactions, like burning and rusting, involve losing electrons, often to oxygen.
sections.b: Oxidation originally meant combining with oxygen and now more broadly means losing electrons; its partner, reduction, means gaining them, and the two always happen together. Rusting is slow oxidation of iron into iron oxide, needing both oxygen and water; salt speeds it up, which is why cars in coastal towns rust faster. Galvanising coats steel in zinc, which corrodes first and protects the iron beneath. Burning is fast oxidation, releasing heat and light. Even your cells run on controlled oxidation: cellular respiration combines glucose with oxygen to release energy step by step, producing the carbon dioxide you breathe out.

sections.key: Many reactions are reversible and settle into a balance called equilibrium.
sections.b: Many reactions can run both ways. In a closed container they reach equilibrium, a balance where the forward and reverse reactions happen at the same rate, so the amounts stop changing even though molecules keep reacting. In 1884, French chemist Henri Le Chatelier described how such a system responds to change: it shifts to partly counteract the disturbance. Add more of an ingredient and more product forms; keep removing the product and the reaction keeps going. The principle matters in industry and biology alike. It helps explain how haemoglobin picks up oxygen in your lungs, where oxygen is plentiful, and releases it in tissues where it's scarce.

sections.key: Some reactions, like making ammonia for fertiliser, transformed civilisation.
sections.b: In the early 1900s, German chemists Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch developed a way to combine nitrogen from the air with hydrogen to make ammonia. The reaction is reversible, so the process uses high pressure, high temperature and an iron catalyst to push the equilibrium towards ammonia quickly enough to be practical. The Haber-Bosch process made synthetic fertiliser possible and is estimated to help feed around half the world's population today. It also consumes a notable share of the world's energy, mostly from natural gas. Haber also developed chemical weapons in World War I, a sobering reminder that chemistry's power can be used for good or harm.

quiz.q: What happens to atoms in a chemical reaction?
quiz.e: Mass is conserved.

quiz.q: Which is a chemical change?
quiz.e: It creates new substances.

quiz.q: What is an endothermic reaction?
quiz.e: Like instant cold packs.

quiz.q: What does a catalyst do?
o: Speeds reactions without being used up
quiz.e: Enzymes are biological catalysts.

quiz.q: What did the Haber-Bosch process make possible?
quiz.e: It helps feed around half the world.

LESSONS.title: Acids and bases
LESSONS.hook: From lemon juice to stomach acid to drain cleaner, acids and bases are everywhere, and the pH scale measures them.

sections.key: Acids release hydrogen ions in water; bases accept them or release hydroxide ions.
sections.b: When acids dissolve in water, they release hydrogen ions (H+), which quickly attach to water molecules. Acids taste sour, like lemons, vinegar and yoghurt, and strong ones can corrode metals and burn skin. Bases remove hydrogen ions or release hydroxide ions (OH−); bases that dissolve in water are called alkalis. They often feel slippery and taste bitter, like soap or baking soda. This definition comes largely from Swedish chemist Svante Arrhenius in the 1880s, and was later broadened to cover reactions without water. Never taste unknown chemicals, though: strong bases like drain cleaner are just as dangerous as strong acids.

sections.key: The pH scale runs from 0 to 14: below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral, above 7 is basic.
sections.b: The pH scale measures how acidic or basic a solution is, usually running from 0 to 14. Pure water is neutral at pH 7. Lemon juice is around pH 2; stomach acid is typically around 1.5–3.5; coffee is around 5; blood is slightly basic at about 7.4; seawater is about 8.1; bleach is around 12–13. The scale is logarithmic: each step is ten times more acidic or basic, so pH 3 is ten times more acidic than pH 4 and a hundred times more than pH 5. The idea was introduced in 1909 by Danish chemist Søren Sørensen, working at the Carlsberg brewery's laboratory.

sections.key: Strong acids split completely into ions; weak acids only partly. That's different from concentration.
sections.b: Strong and weak don't mean the same as concentrated and dilute. A strong acid, like hydrochloric acid, splits almost completely into ions in water. A weak acid, like the acetic acid in vinegar or the citric acid in lemons, releases only a small fraction of its hydrogen ions. Concentration is about how much acid is dissolved in a given amount of water. So a very dilute strong acid can be less harsh than a concentrated weak one. The same applies to bases: sodium hydroxide, found in some drain cleaners, is strong, while ammonia is weak. Weak acids are why a salad dressing can taste tangy without being dangerous.

sections.key: Acids and bases neutralise each other, producing water and a salt.
sections.b: When an acid and a base react, they neutralise each other, forming water and a salt. Chemists use 'salt' for any compound made this way; table salt, sodium chloride, is just one example, formed from hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide. Antacid tablets contain bases like calcium carbonate that neutralise excess stomach acid, easing heartburn. Farmers spread lime on acidic soils, which are common in parts of Australia, so crops can take up nutrients. Baking soda reacts with acidic ingredients like buttermilk or vinegar to release carbon dioxide bubbles, which makes cakes rise and school volcanoes erupt. Chemists measure neutralisation precisely using a technique called titration.

sections.key: Your body tightly controls pH; stomach acid is strong, but blood stays near 7.4.
sections.b: Your stomach produces hydrochloric acid to help digest proteins and kill microbes, and a layer of mucus stops it digesting the stomach itself. Your blood, however, must stay between about 7.35 and 7.45; shifts outside that range can be life-threatening, so your lungs and kidneys constantly adjust it, partly by changing how much carbon dioxide you breathe out. Hard exercise produces acidic conditions in working muscles. Tooth enamel starts to dissolve below about pH 5.5, which is why frequent sugary drinks, which mouth bacteria turn into acid, and acidic drinks like soft drink and juice can harm teeth. Saliva helps by neutralising acid between meals.

sections.key: Indicators change colour depending on pH, like red cabbage juice.
sections.b: Some substances change colour depending on pH, which makes them useful indicators. Litmus, a dye extracted from lichens, turns red in acid and blue in base. Red cabbage juice is a natural indicator: it's red-pink in acids, purple around neutral, and green or yellow in strong bases, making it a classic kitchen experiment. Universal indicator mixes several dyes to show a rainbow of colours across the whole scale, and digital pH meters give precise readings. Hydrangeas act like living indicators: in acidic soil they tend to grow blue flowers and in alkaline soil pink, because acidity makes aluminium in the soil available to the plant.

sections.key: Oceans absorbing carbon dioxide are becoming more acidic, threatening shell-building sea life.
sections.b: The oceans absorb roughly a quarter of the carbon dioxide humans emit, which slows climate change but comes at a cost. When CO2 dissolves in seawater, it forms carbonic acid, lowering pH. Average surface ocean pH has fallen from about 8.2 to about 8.1 since the industrial revolution. Because the scale is logarithmic, that small-looking change means roughly 30% more hydrogen ions. The oceans aren't acidic yet; they're becoming less alkaline. That makes it harder for corals, oysters and some plankton to build shells and skeletons from calcium carbonate, adding pressure on reefs like the Great Barrier Reef, already stressed by marine heatwaves.

sections.key: Many cleaners are strong acids or bases, and some become dangerous when mixed.
sections.b: Many household cleaners are acids or bases. Descalers and some toilet cleaners are acidic; oven cleaners, drain cleaners and ammonia-based sprays are alkaline; household bleach is alkaline and contains sodium hypochlorite. Never mix cleaning products. Bleach mixed with acidic cleaners can release chlorine gas, and bleach mixed with ammonia releases toxic chloramine gases; both can badly damage the lungs. Store chemicals in their original, labelled containers, out of reach of children, and wear gloves with strong products. If a chemical is swallowed or splashed in the eyes, rinse with water and call the Poisons Information Centre on 13 11 26, or 000 in an emergency.

quiz.q: What do acids release in water?
quiz.e: Bases accept them.

quiz.q: What pH is neutral?
quiz.e: Pure water is pH 7.

quiz.q: How much more acidic is pH 3 than pH 5?
quiz.e: The scale is logarithmic.

quiz.q: What do antacid tablets do?
quiz.e: They contain bases.

quiz.q: What happens as oceans absorb CO2?
quiz.e: Harder for corals and shellfish to build shells.

LESSONS.title: The chemistry of cooking
LESSONS.hook: Every time you cook, you're running chemistry experiments. Understanding them makes you a better cook.

sections.key: Browning of meat, bread and coffee comes from the Maillard reaction between sugars and proteins.
sections.b: When food containing proteins and sugars is heated, a cascade of reactions called the Maillard reaction creates hundreds of flavour compounds and a brown colour. It runs quickly above about 140°C, which is why it happens in a hot pan or oven but not in boiling water, which stays near 100°C. It's why seared steak, toast, roasted coffee, fried onions and bread crusts taste so rich. It's named after French chemist Louis-Camille Maillard, who described it in 1912. Tip: pat meat dry and don't crowd the pan, since surface water and trapped steam keep the surface too cool to brown.

sections.key: Heating sugar alone breaks it down into caramel's rich flavours.
sections.b: Caramelisation is different from Maillard: it happens when sugar alone is heated, with no protein involved. For table sugar it gets going around 160°C. Sugar molecules break apart and recombine into hundreds of new compounds, producing caramel's amber colour and complex, slightly bitter flavour, with notes like butterscotch. Fructose, the sugar in fruit and honey, caramelises at a lower temperature than table sugar. Slowly cooked onions get their deep sweetness from both caramelisation and Maillard reactions. Watch closely: caramel moves from golden to burnt within seconds, turning bitter and black. A wet caramel, started with a little water, heats more evenly and suits beginners.

sections.key: Heat unfolds and links proteins, turning runny egg white firm.
sections.b: Egg white is mostly water plus proteins folded into tight shapes. Heat makes the proteins unfold, a process called denaturation, and then tangle together into a solid network, turning clear liquid into opaque white solid. Egg whites begin to set at around 62–65°C, while yolks thicken at roughly 65–70°C, which is how chefs make eggs with firm whites and runny yolks. Overcook them and the network tightens, squeezing out water and turning rubbery; the grey-green ring around an overboiled yolk is iron sulfide. Acid and salt can also denature proteins: ceviche 'cooks' fish in citrus juice without heat.

sections.key: Cut apples, bananas and avocados brown when an enzyme meets oxygen; acid, cold and keeping air out slow it.
sections.b: Slicing an apple, banana or avocado breaks open cells and lets an enzyme called polyphenol oxidase meet oxygen from the air. It turns natural compounds called polyphenols into brown pigments, the same kind of chemistry that darkens tea leaves as they are processed. The browning is harmless, just unappealing, and you can slow it by denying the enzyme what it needs. Lemon or lime juice lowers the pH, which the enzyme dislikes, and its vitamin C undoes the first step of the reaction. Chilling slows it, blanching in boiling water destroys the enzyme, and pressing cling wrap directly onto guacamole keeps air away. Leaving the avocado stone in only protects the flesh it touches.

sections.key: Cutting an onion releases a sulfur gas that irritates your eyes; chilling it and using a sharp knife help.
sections.b: A whole onion is fairly calm. Cutting it breaks cells and mixes enzymes with sulfur-containing compounds, and one of the products is a volatile gas called syn-propanethial-S-oxide. It drifts up and irritates nerves in the surface of your eyes, and tears flow to wash it away. The same broken-cell chemistry gives raw onion its sharp bite; cooking tames it, turning the sulfur compounds sweet and savoury. To cry less, chill the onion first so less gas escapes, and use a sharp knife, which crushes fewer cells than a blunt one. Garlic works similarly: its pungent compound, allicin, forms only once a clove is cut or crushed.

sections.key: Emulsions like mayonnaise combine oil and water with help from an emulsifier.
sections.b: Oil and water don't mix, because water molecules cling to each other and push oil away. An emulsion suspends tiny droplets of one liquid in the other. Mayonnaise is oil droplets suspended in egg yolk and lemon juice or vinegar, held stable by lecithin in the yolk, an emulsifier with one end that attracts water and one that attracts oil. Milk and butter are natural emulsions too. Vinaigrettes separate because they lack a strong emulsifier; a spoonful of mustard helps hold them together. If mayo 'breaks', whisking it slowly, a little at a time, into a fresh yolk can usually rescue it.

sections.key: Starch swells to thicken sauces, then slowly recrystallises, which makes bread go stale.
sections.b: Starch, found in flour, rice, potatoes and cornflour, is made of long chains of glucose packed into tiny granules. Heated in water, the granules absorb liquid and swell, a process called gelatinisation, which is how cornflour thickens gravy and custard. Cooling partly reverses this: the starch chains realign and squeeze out water, called retrogradation. That's the main reason bread goes stale, and it happens fastest at fridge temperatures, so bread keeps better at room temperature or in the freezer. Briefly reheating stale bread partly reverses the process. Cooked and cooled rice or potatoes also form some resistant starch, which is digested more slowly.

sections.key: Salt enhances flavour and changes texture; acid brightens food.
sections.b: Salt does more than make food salty: it suppresses bitterness, enhances other flavours, draws moisture out of vegetables such as eggplant and cabbage, and in brines helps meat hold onto its juices by changing how its proteins behave. Salting pasta water seasons the pasta from within. Acid, from lemon, vinegar, wine or tomatoes, brightens flavours and balances richness. Fat carries many flavour compounds, which is why low-fat versions can taste flat. Understanding the chemistry helps you fix dishes: if food tastes flat, it may need salt; if it's heavy or dull, a squeeze of lemon often helps; if it's too sour, a pinch of sugar can balance it.

quiz.q: Why doesn't meat brown when it's boiled?
o: Boiling water stays near 100°C, too cool for fast Maillard browning
quiz.e: Browning runs quickly only above about 140°C.

quiz.q: How does caramelisation differ from Maillard?
quiz.e: Starting around 160°C for table sugar.

quiz.q: What happens to egg proteins when heated?
o: They unfold and link into a solid network
quiz.e: Called denaturation.

quiz.q: Why does lemon juice stop cut apple going brown?
o: Its acid and vitamin C slow the browning reaction
It seals the surface with oil
quiz.e: Browning happens when an enzyme meets oxygen.

quiz.q: What emulsifier holds mayonnaise together?
quiz.e: One end likes water, the other oil.

LESSONS.title: Newton's laws of motion
LESSONS.hook: Three simple rules explain why seatbelts save lives, rockets fly, and a heavy trolley is hard to stop.

sections.key: In 1687, Isaac Newton published three laws of motion that explained how objects move.
sections.b: Newton's great book began with a question. In 1684, the astronomer Edmond Halley visited him in Cambridge and asked what path a planet would follow if the Sun's pull weakened with the square of the distance. Newton answered at once: an ellipse. He had worked it out years earlier but couldn't find his calculations, so he redid them, and the work grew into the Principia, written in Latin in about 18 months and published in 1687. It set out three laws describing how forces change motion. Halley, not the Royal Society, paid for the printing. The laws are still used to design cars, bridges, rollercoasters and spacecraft, and for everyday life they work superbly.

sections.key: Objects keep doing what they're doing unless a force acts on them.
sections.b: The first law says an object at rest stays at rest, and a moving object keeps moving in a straight line at the same speed, unless an outside force acts on it. This resistance to changes in motion is called inertia, and the more mass something has, the more inertia it has. On Earth, friction and air resistance usually slow things down, which is why people believed for centuries, following Aristotle, that motion needs a constant push. Galileo saw through this first. In a car crash, the car stops suddenly but your body keeps moving forward: that's why seatbelts and airbags save lives.

sections.key: Force equals mass times acceleration: more force or less mass means more acceleration.
sections.b: The second law says acceleration depends on force and mass: force equals mass times acceleration, or F = ma. Push an empty shopping trolley and it speeds up easily; push a full one with the same force and it barely moves. It works for stopping too: a loaded truck needs far more braking force than a car, and more distance at the same speed. Force is measured in newtons, named after Newton himself: one newton accelerates one kilogram by one metre per second, every second. That's roughly the weight of a small apple, a fitting coincidence. Acceleration only happens when forces are unbalanced.

sections.key: For every action there's an equal and opposite reaction.
sections.b: When you push on something, it pushes back on you just as hard, in the opposite direction. When you jump, you push down on the Earth and the Earth pushes you up; the Earth moves too, but by an immeasurably tiny amount because its mass is so huge. A rocket pushes exhaust gases backwards at high speed, and the gases push the rocket forwards. It doesn't need air to push against, which is why rockets work in space. The two forces act on different objects, so they don't cancel out. The recoil of a gun, or the kick of a fire hose, is the third law in action.

sections.key: Momentum is mass times velocity; in collisions, total momentum is conserved.
sections.b: Momentum is mass times velocity: a heavy truck crawling along can carry as much momentum as a much lighter car travelling fast. In a collision, the total momentum of all the objects stays the same, it's just shared differently, which is why Newton's cradle keeps clicking and a cue ball can stop dead while the ball it hits rolls on. Changing momentum requires a force applied over time, so stretching out the time reduces the force. Crumple zones in cars lengthen the time a collision takes, reducing the force on passengers. Bending your knees when landing from a jump, or a cricketer drawing their hands back when catching, does the same.

sections.key: Friction and air resistance oppose motion; without them you couldn't walk or brake.
sections.b: Friction is the force that resists surfaces sliding over each other. It can be a nuisance, wasting energy as heat in engines and machinery, but it's also essential: without it, tyres couldn't grip the road and you couldn't walk. Wet or icy roads reduce friction, so braking distances grow. Air resistance, or drag, increases rapidly with speed, which is why driving faster uses more fuel. A falling skydiver speeds up until drag balances their weight, reaching a terminal velocity of roughly 200 km/h in a belly-down position. Opening the parachute adds enormous drag, slowing them to a speed safe enough for landing.

sections.key: Anything moving in a circle needs a force pulling it towards the centre.
sections.b: Newton's first law says moving objects travel in straight lines, so anything moving in a circle must be constantly pulled towards the centre. This inward force is called centripetal force. For a car turning a corner, it comes from friction between tyres and road; for the Moon, from Earth's gravity; for clothes in a spinning washing machine, from the drum wall pushing on them, while water escapes through the holes. The outward 'fling' you feel in a turning car isn't a real force pushing you out: it's your inertia trying to carry you straight on while the car turns beneath you.

sections.key: Newton's laws explain sport, transport, and space travel.
sections.b: A footballer's kick applies a force that accelerates the ball (second law). A swimmer pushes water backwards to move forwards (third law). A bowled cricket ball slows because of air resistance and friction with the pitch; without them it would keep going (first law). Engineers apply the same rules to design safer car seats, bike helmets and sports equipment. NASA and other space agencies still use Newton's laws to calculate most spacecraft trajectories. In a letter written in the 1670s, Newton said that if he had seen further, it was by standing on the shoulders of giants; Galileo and Kepler were among those his work built on.

quiz.q: What is inertia?
o: An object's tendency to keep doing what it's doing
quiz.e: Why seatbelts matter.

quiz.q: What does F = ma mean?
quiz.e: Newton's second law.

quiz.q: Why can rockets work in space?
o: They push exhaust backwards, which pushes them forwards
quiz.e: Action and reaction.

quiz.q: What do car crumple zones do?
o: Lengthen collision time to reduce force on passengers
quiz.e: Like bending knees when landing.

quiz.q: When did Newton publish his laws?
quiz.e: In the Principia.

LESSONS.title: Gravity
LESSONS.hook: It holds you to the ground, keeps the Moon in orbit and shapes galaxies. It's also the weakest force in nature.

sections.key: Every mass attracts every other mass; the force grows with mass and falls with distance.
sections.b: Newton realised the force pulling an apple down is the same one holding the Moon in orbit. His law of universal gravitation, published in 1687, says every object attracts every other object with a force that increases with their masses and decreases with the square of the distance between them. Double the distance, and gravity drops to a quarter; triple it, and it drops to a ninth. In 1798, Henry Cavendish measured the tiny pull between lead balls in his laboratory, which allowed Earth's density and mass to be calculated. You're gravitationally attracting the device in your hand right now, just very, very weakly.

sections.key: Without air resistance, all objects fall at the same rate regardless of mass.
sections.b: Aristotle taught that heavy objects fall faster than light ones, and for almost 2,000 years few people checked. Galileo showed otherwise around 1600, most likely by rolling balls down ramps rather than, as legend says, dropping them from the Leaning Tower of Pisa. Heavier objects feel a stronger pull but also resist acceleration more, so the effects cancel exactly. In 1971, Apollo 15 astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a falcon feather on the airless Moon, and they hit the ground together. On Earth, air resistance makes a feather drift, but in a vacuum chamber a feather and a bowling ball fall side by side.

sections.key: Mass is how much matter you have; weight is the force of gravity on that mass.
sections.b: Your mass, how much matter you contain, is the same everywhere. Your weight, the force of gravity on that mass, depends on where you are. On the Moon, with about one-sixth of Earth's gravity, a 70 kg person would register about 12 kg on bathroom scales designed for Earth. On Mars they'd register roughly 26 kg, and near Jupiter's cloud tops they'd feel over twice as heavy. Strictly, weight is a force measured in newtons, but everyday scales convert it to kilograms. Near Earth's surface, falling objects speed up by about 9.8 metres per second every second, written as 9.8 m/s², ignoring air resistance.

sections.key: An orbit is falling around a planet while moving sideways fast enough to keep missing it.
sections.b: Newton imagined a cannon on a mountaintop firing balls faster and faster. Each would land further away, until one travelled so fast that it curved down exactly as quickly as Earth's surface curved away beneath it. That ball would fall forever without hitting the ground: an orbit. The International Space Station orbits about 400 km up at roughly 28,000 km/h, circling Earth about every 90 minutes. Astronauts float not because there's no gravity up there, since it's about 90% as strong as on the ground, but because they and the station are falling together. Geostationary satellites orbit about 36,000 km up, keeping pace with Earth's rotation.

sections.key: Because gravity weakens with distance, big bodies stretch each other, flexing moons and even tearing some apart.
sections.b: Because gravity weakens with distance, a planet pulls harder on the near side of a moon than on its far side, stretching it slightly. These tidal forces do far more than move oceans. Even Earth's solid ground rises and falls by tens of centimetres twice a day as the Moon passes overhead, without anyone noticing. Jupiter's moon Io is squeezed and flexed so strongly by Jupiter's gravity that its interior melts, making it the most volcanically active world in the solar system. Get too close and tidal stretching can pull an object apart: in 1992 Jupiter tore Comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 into more than 20 fragments, which crashed into the planet in 1994.

sections.key: Gravity is by far the weakest fundamental force, but it always attracts and adds up.
sections.b: Gravity is by far the weakest of nature's four fundamental forces. A small fridge magnet holds itself up against the gravitational pull of the entire Earth. Between two protons, the electric repulsion is roughly 10 to the power of 36 times stronger than their gravitational attraction. So why does gravity rule the cosmos? Electric charges come in positive and negative, which usually cancel out in bulk matter, while gravity only ever attracts and keeps adding up. Its reach is unlimited, so across huge masses and distances it wins, pulling planets into spheres, holding galaxies together and shaping the large-scale structure of the universe.

sections.key: Einstein described gravity as the curving of space and time by mass.
sections.b: Newton's law worked brilliantly, but he admitted he couldn't explain how gravity acted across empty space, and refused to guess. In 1915, Einstein's general relativity answered that massive objects curve space and time around them, and other objects simply follow those curves. A common picture is a bowling ball on a trampoline with marbles rolling around the dip, though the real curving involves time as well as space. One consequence is that gravity isn't instant: if the Sun vanished, Earth would keep circling its empty position for about eight minutes. In 2017, gravitational waves and light from a neutron star collision arrived within two seconds of each other after a 130-million-year journey, confirming gravity travels at light speed.

sections.key: Gravity shapes your body, and it isn't quite the same everywhere on Earth.
sections.b: Gravity shapes your body more than you might notice. In orbit, without the constant load of weight, astronauts can lose around 1% of bone density in weight-bearing bones each month, so they exercise about two hours a day to limit muscle and bone loss. Their spines also lengthen, making them temporarily a few centimetres taller, and fluids shift towards the head, giving a puffy face. On Earth, gravity squeezes your spinal discs through the day, so you're slightly taller in the morning. Gravity isn't quite uniform either: because of Earth's spin and bulging equator, you weigh about 0.5% less at the equator than at the poles.

quiz.q: What happens to gravity if distance doubles?
quiz.e: The inverse square law.

quiz.q: What did the hammer-and-feather drop on the Moon show?
o: Without air, all objects fall at the same rate
There's no gravity on the Moon
quiz.e: Done by David Scott in 1971.

quiz.q: What changes on the Moon: mass or weight?
quiz.e: Moon gravity is about one-sixth of Earth's.

quiz.q: Why do astronauts float on the ISS?
o: They and the station are falling together
quiz.e: Gravity there is about 90% as strong.

quiz.q: How did Einstein describe gravity?
quiz.e: General relativity, 1915.

LESSONS.title: Energy: what it is and where it goes
LESSONS.hook: Energy can't be created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another. Almost all of it on Earth started in the Sun.

sections.key: Energy is the ability to do work or cause change.
sections.b: Energy is what makes things happen: moving, heating, lighting up, growing. Physicists define it as the capacity to do work, meaning to apply a force over a distance. It comes in many forms. Kinetic energy is the energy of motion. Potential energy is stored, like water behind a dam, a book on a high shelf or a stretched rubber band. Chemical energy is stored in the bonds of food and fuel. There's also thermal, electrical, light, sound and nuclear energy. Energy is measured in joules, named after English brewer and physicist James Joule; food energy is labelled in kilojoules in Australia.

sections.key: The law of conservation of energy says energy changes form but the total stays the same.
sections.b: One of physics' deepest rules is that energy is never created or destroyed; it only changes form. In the 1840s, James Joule showed that a set amount of mechanical work always produces the same amount of heat, helping to establish this law. When you ride a bike downhill, potential energy becomes kinetic energy. When you brake, kinetic energy becomes heat in the brake pads. A car engine turns chemical energy in fuel into motion, plus a lot of heat. The total always adds up. When we say we 'use' or 'waste' energy, we really mean we convert it into forms that are less useful to us.

sections.key: Kinetic energy grows with the square of speed, so doubling speed quadruples it.
sections.b: Kinetic energy depends on mass and, even more, on speed: it equals half the mass times the speed squared. Double your speed and your kinetic energy quadruples. That has real consequences on the road. A car at 60 km/h carries four times the energy of the same car at 30 km/h, and all of it must be absorbed by the brakes or, in a crash, by the vehicle and the people inside. It's a key reason braking distances grow so quickly with speed, and why lower limits in busy areas, like 40 km/h school zones, save lives. Small increases in speed matter more than they feel.

sections.key: Every energy conversion wastes some energy as heat, which spreads out and becomes less useful.
sections.b: No machine converts energy perfectly. Old incandescent light bulbs turned only about 5% of electricity into light and the rest into heat; LEDs use roughly 75–80% less electricity for the same light. Petrol car engines turn roughly 20–30% of fuel energy into motion, while electric motors manage around 90%. Heat pumps, including reverse-cycle air conditioners, seem to beat the rules by moving heat rather than making it, delivering three or more units of heat per unit of electricity. The underlying principle is the second law of thermodynamics: energy tends to spread out and become less concentrated, which is why perpetual motion machines are impossible.

sections.key: Most energy on Earth ultimately comes from the Sun.
sections.b: Plants capture sunlight through photosynthesis, storing it as chemical energy that feeds almost every food chain, including yours. Coal, oil and gas are the remains of ancient plants and marine organisms buried for millions of years, so they're effectively stored ancient sunlight. Wind is driven by the Sun heating Earth unevenly. Hydro power relies on rain, which depends on the Sun evaporating water. Solar panels tap sunlight directly, and the sunlight striking Earth in an hour or two carries about as much energy as humanity uses in a whole year. The exceptions are nuclear energy, from elements forged in long-dead stars, geothermal heat from Earth's interior, and tidal energy, which comes mainly from the Moon's gravity.

sections.key: Your body converts food energy, measured in kilojoules, into movement, heat and life.
sections.b: Your body is an energy converter too. Food energy is measured in kilojoules; one food calorie is about 4.2 kilojoules. Australian food labels use 8,700 kilojoules a day as a reference for an average adult, although individual needs vary with body size, age and activity. Your body turns that chemical energy into movement, heat and the constant work of keeping cells alive. Even at rest, your brain uses about a fifth of your energy. Like engines, muscles are far from perfectly efficient, converting only around a quarter of the energy they use into movement and the rest into heat, which is why exercise warms you up.

sections.key: Power is how fast energy is used, measured in watts.
sections.b: Power is how fast energy is transferred, measured in watts: one watt is one joule per second. An electric kettle might draw around 2,000 watts or more, a laptop around 50 watts and a phone charger about 5–20 watts. Electricity bills charge in kilowatt-hours: one kilowatt-hour is 1,000 watts for an hour, like running a small heater for an hour. The biggest users in most homes are heating and cooling, hot water, and appliances like clothes dryers and pool pumps. Standby power adds up too. Checking Energy Rating Label stars when buying appliances, and running dishwashers and washing machines full, helps cut bills.

sections.key: Einstein showed mass and energy are equivalent; a tiny mass holds enormous energy.
sections.b: In 1905, Einstein showed that mass itself is a form of energy: E = mc², energy equals mass times the speed of light squared. Because the speed of light is huge, about 300,000 km per second, a tiny amount of mass holds enormous energy. One gram of matter, fully converted, would release roughly as much energy as 20,000 tonnes of TNT. The Sun converts about four million tonnes of mass into energy every second through nuclear fusion, and will keep shining for billions of years yet. Nuclear power plants and nuclear weapons both release energy by converting a small fraction of their fuel's mass.

quiz.q: What is potential energy?
o: Stored energy, like water behind a dam
quiz.e: Kinetic energy is motion.

quiz.q: What does the law of conservation of energy say?
o: Energy changes form but the total stays the same
Energy only comes from the Sun
quiz.e: It's never created or destroyed.

quiz.q: Why are perpetual motion machines impossible?
o: Every conversion wastes some energy as heat
quiz.e: The second law of thermodynamics.

quiz.q: Where does the energy in coal originally come from?
quiz.e: Fossil fuels are stored sunlight.

quiz.q: What does E = mc² mean?
quiz.e: A tiny mass holds vast energy.

LESSONS.title: How electricity works
LESSONS.hook: Flick a switch and the lights come on. Behind that is a flow of electrons, a power station, and a grid spanning a continent.

sections.key: Electric current is the flow of electric charge, usually electrons moving through a wire.
sections.b: Atoms contain negatively charged electrons. In metals like copper, some outer electrons are free to wander between atoms. When a battery or power supply pushes them, they drift through the wire, forming an electric current. Surprisingly, individual electrons move very slowly, often less than a millimetre per second, but the push travels through the wire at a large fraction of light speed. It's like a pipe already full of water: push at one end and water comes out the other immediately. Copper is used for most wiring because it conducts well and costs far less than silver, the best conductor of all.

sections.key: Static electricity is built-up charge; lightning is the same effect on a colossal scale.
sections.b: Static electricity is charge that builds up rather than flows. Rub a balloon on your hair and electrons transfer from hair to balloon, leaving both charged, so the balloon clings to walls and your hair stands on end. The zap from a car door or a synthetic carpet on a dry day is stored charge suddenly jumping to or from you. Lightning is the same thing on a colossal scale: collisions between ice particles in storm clouds separate charge until a discharge, typically tens of thousands of amps, leaps between cloud and ground. It heats the air to around 30,000 degrees, and the explosive expansion is thunder.

sections.key: Voltage is the push, current is the flow, and resistance opposes it.
sections.b: Voltage, measured in volts, is the electrical 'pressure' pushing charge around a circuit. Current, measured in amps, is how much charge flows per second. Resistance, measured in ohms, is how strongly a material opposes the flow. They're linked by Ohm's law, published by German physicist Georg Ohm in 1827: voltage equals current times resistance. Multiply voltage by current and you get power in watts. Australian household power is 230 volts, compared with about 120 volts in North America. It's not voltage alone that makes shocks dangerous but the current through the body; wet skin has much lower resistance, letting far more current flow.

sections.key: Electricity needs a complete loop, a circuit, to flow.
sections.b: Current only flows around a complete path from the power source and back. A switch simply breaks or connects the loop. In a series circuit, components share one path, so if one fails, they all stop, like some old strings of Christmas lights. In a parallel circuit, each component has its own path, which is how house wiring works, so one broken appliance doesn't cut power to the rest. Fuses and circuit breakers cut the power if too much current flows, preventing overheated wires and fires. Safety switches, or RCDs, detect current leaking to earth, perhaps through a person, and cut the power in a fraction of a second.

sections.key: Most electricity is generated by spinning magnets near coils of wire.
sections.b: In 1831, English scientist Michael Faraday discovered that moving a magnet near a coil of wire produces a current, a process called electromagnetic induction. Almost all power stations use it: something spins a turbine connected to a generator, where magnets and coils rotate past each other. Coal and nuclear plants boil water to make high-pressure steam that spins turbines; gas plants mostly spin them with hot combustion gases; wind and hydro spin them directly. Car alternators and bicycle dynamos use the same idea on a small scale. Solar panels are the big exception: they turn light directly into electricity through the photovoltaic effect in silicon, with no moving parts.

sections.key: Grids use alternating current (AC); batteries provide direct current (DC).
sections.b: Direct current flows one way, like from a battery. Alternating current rapidly reverses direction, 50 times a second in Australia. In the 1880s, Thomas Edison championed DC while Nikola Tesla and George Westinghouse promoted AC, a rivalry called the 'war of the currents'. AC won for grids because transformers can easily raise its voltage for efficient long-distance transmission, then lower it for homes. High voltage means lower current, and lower current wastes less energy as heat in the wires. Your phone charger converts AC back to DC. Today, high-voltage DC links serve some very long or undersea cables, like Basslink between Victoria and Tasmania.

sections.key: Australia's east-coast grid is one of the longest in the world, and supply must match demand every second.
sections.b: Australia's main grid, the National Electricity Market, links Queensland, New South Wales, the ACT, Victoria, South Australia and Tasmania, stretching around 5,000 km, one of the longest interconnected systems in the world. Western Australia and the Northern Territory run separate systems. Because electricity is hard to store at scale, supply must match demand every moment, and operators balance it around the clock. Big batteries, pumped hydro schemes like the Snowy 2.0 project, and rooftop solar are changing how the grid works. In South Australia, rooftop solar has at times supplied most of the state's demand, while evenings, when solar fades and households cook and run heaters, remain the peak.

sections.key: Water, damaged cords and overloaded power boards are key electrical hazards.
sections.b: Water conducts electricity well, so keep appliances away from baths, sinks and pools. Never use damaged cords, and don't overload power boards or plug power boards into each other. In Australia, it's illegal to do your own fixed electrical wiring unless you're a licensed electrician. Make sure your home has working safety switches, and test them with their test button regularly; many authorities suggest every three months. If someone is being electrocuted, don't touch them: switch off the power at the switchboard or wall if it's safe, then call 000. Stay at least eight metres from fallen power lines and always treat them as live.

quiz.q: What is electric current?
quiz.e: Usually electrons moving through a wire.

quiz.q: What does voltage measure?
quiz.e: Australian homes use 230 volts.

quiz.q: Why is house wiring done in parallel?
o: So one broken appliance doesn't cut power to the rest
quiz.e: Each has its own path.

quiz.q: Who discovered electromagnetic induction?
Why did AC win for power grids?
o: Its voltage can be easily changed with transformers
quiz.e: The 'war of the currents'.

LESSONS.title: Light and colour
LESSONS.hook: Light is the fastest thing in the universe, it's both a wave and a particle, and colour doesn't exist without a brain to see it.

sections.key: Light travels at about 300,000 kilometres per second, the universe's ultimate speed limit.
sections.b: Light travels at about 299,792 kilometres per second in a vacuum, usually rounded to 300,000. It could circle the Earth about seven and a half times in one second. Light from the Moon takes about 1.3 seconds to reach us; from the Sun, about 8 minutes and 20 seconds. Light from Proxima Centauri, the nearest star beyond the Sun, takes over four years. When you look at distant stars, you're seeing light that left them years, centuries or millennia ago: you're looking into the past. Light slows down in glass and water, but nothing with mass can ever reach its speed in a vacuum.

sections.key: Visible light is a small part of the electromagnetic spectrum.
sections.b: Light is electromagnetic radiation, a travelling wave of electric and magnetic fields, as Scottish physicist James Clerk Maxwell showed in the 1860s. Visible light is just a narrow band, with wavelengths from about 400 to 700 nanometres. Longer wavelengths include infrared, which you feel as heat, then microwaves and radio waves. Shorter ones include ultraviolet, which causes sunburn, then X-rays and gamma rays. They're all the same kind of thing, differing only in wavelength and energy. Some animals sense beyond our range: bees see ultraviolet patterns on flowers that are invisible to us, and some snakes detect the infrared glow of warm-blooded prey.

sections.key: Light bounces off surfaces and bends when it passes from one material to another.
sections.b: When light hits a surface it can bounce off, pass through or be absorbed. Smooth surfaces like mirrors and still water reflect it at the same angle it arrives, which is why you see clear images in them. When light passes from one material into another, like air into water, it changes speed and bends, which is called refraction. That's why a straw looks broken in a glass of water and a pool looks shallower than it really is. Lenses in glasses, cameras and your own eyes use refraction to focus light. Optical fibres trap light by total internal reflection, carrying internet data across oceans.

sections.key: White light is a mix of all colours, which a prism or raindrops can separate.
sections.b: In the 1660s, Isaac Newton passed sunlight through a glass prism and split it into a spectrum of colours, then used a second prism to recombine them into white light, showing that white light is a mixture rather than pure. Different colours bend by slightly different amounts when entering glass or water, violet the most and red the least. Rainbows form when sunlight enters raindrops, bends, reflects off the back of each drop and bends again on the way out, spreading into colours. You always see a rainbow with the Sun behind you, and in a double rainbow the fainter outer bow has its colours reversed.

sections.key: Objects look coloured because they absorb some wavelengths and reflect others.
sections.b: A banana looks yellow because it reflects mostly yellowish wavelengths and absorbs the rest. A black T-shirt absorbs most visible light, which is why it heats up in the sun, while a white one reflects most of it.
