The sky is blue because air molecules scatter shorter blue wavelengths much more strongly than red, a process called Rayleigh scattering, after British physicist Lord Rayleigh. At sunrise and sunset, light travels through far more air, so much of the blue is scattered away, leaving reds and oranges. Clouds look white because their much larger water droplets scatter all colours roughly equally.

sections.key: Light behaves both as a wave and as particles called photons.
sections.b: In the early 1800s, Thomas Young shone light through two narrow slits and saw a pattern of light and dark bands on a screen, just as overlapping water waves reinforce and cancel each other. This was strong evidence that light is a wave. But in 1905, Einstein explained the photoelectric effect, where light knocks electrons out of metal, by treating light as a stream of particles, later called photons. He won the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics for this, not for relativity. Light behaves as both, depending on how it's measured, a puzzle at the heart of quantum physics. Solar panels rely on a close cousin, the photovoltaic effect.

sections.key: Colour is created by the brain from signals of three types of cone cells.
sections.b: Wavelengths are physical, but colour is an experience created by your brain. Your eyes have three types of cone cells, most sensitive to long, medium and short wavelengths, and your brain compares their signals. That's why screens can make almost any colour from tiny red, green and blue dots, and why magenta, which matches no single wavelength, still looks like a real colour. About 8% of men and 0.5% of women of Northern European descent have some form of colour vision deficiency, usually difficulty telling red and green apart. Research suggests a small number of women may have a fourth cone type.

sections.key: Lasers make intense light of a single colour in a tight beam, and they're hidden in everyday technology.
sections.b: A laser produces light in which the waves all have the same wavelength and march in step, forming a narrow beam that barely spreads. The name stands for Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation, a process Einstein predicted in 1917. American physicist Theodore Maiman built the first working laser in 1960, using a ruby crystal, and it was jokingly called a solution looking for a problem. Today lasers read barcodes at supermarket checkouts, send data down optical fibres, cut steel, reshape corneas in eye surgery and guide surveyors. Even weak laser pointers can damage eyes, and in Australia powerful ones are banned or tightly restricted.

quiz.q: How long does sunlight take to reach Earth?
quiz.e: Light travels about 300,000 km/s.

quiz.q: Which kind of radiation do you feel as heat?
quiz.e: Infrared has longer wavelengths than visible red light.

quiz.q: What did Newton show with a prism?
o: White light is a mix of colours
quiz.e: In the 1660s.

quiz.q: Why is the sky blue?
o: Air scatters blue light more than red
quiz.e: Rayleigh scattering.

quiz.q: What did Young's double-slit experiment show?
quiz.e: Einstein later showed particle behaviour too.

LESSONS.title: Einstein's relativity, simply
LESSONS.hook: Moving clocks run slow, space bends, and your head ages faster than your feet. Relativity is strange, and it's been confirmed again and again.

sections.key: Light's speed is the same for every observer, no matter how they're moving.
sections.b: If you're on a train going 100 km/h and throw a ball forward at 20 km/h, someone on the platform sees it move at 120 km/h. Light doesn't work that way. In 1887, Albert Michelson and Edward Morley tried to detect Earth's motion through a supposed 'ether' that carried light waves, and found nothing: light's speed came out the same in every direction. Light always travels at about 300,000 km per second, whether you're moving towards it or away. In 1905, Albert Einstein, then a 26-year-old clerk at the Swiss patent office in Bern, took this as a basic law and followed it to astonishing conclusions.

sections.key: Moving clocks run slow compared to stationary ones: time dilation.
sections.b: If light's speed is fixed for everyone, something else must give, and that something is time. Special relativity says a clock moving relative to you runs slower from your point of view, an effect called time dilation. At everyday speeds it's tiny, but it's real and measurable. In 1971, physicists flew atomic clocks around the world on airliners and found they differed from ground clocks by billionths of a second, as relativity predicted. Tiny particles called muons, created when cosmic rays hit the upper atmosphere, should mostly decay long before reaching the ground, yet many arrive, because from our point of view their clocks run slow.

sections.key: A twin who travels near light speed and returns will be younger than the one who stayed home.
sections.b: Imagine twins: one stays on Earth while the other flies to a distant star and back at close to light speed. When the traveller returns, they'll be younger than the twin who stayed home, perhaps by years. This seems paradoxical, since each twin sees the other moving. The resolution is that the situations aren't symmetrical: the travelling twin has to accelerate, turn around and come back, changing reference frames, while the Earth twin doesn't. The effect is real on small scales. Astronauts on the International Space Station, moving at about 28,000 km/h, age a few thousandths of a second less than people on Earth over a six-month mission.

sections.h: Lengths shrink, speed has a limit
sections.key: Moving objects shrink in length along their direction of travel, and nothing with mass reaches light speed.
sections.b: Special relativity also predicts that fast-moving objects contract in length along their direction of motion, as measured by a stationary observer, though the travellers themselves notice nothing unusual. As an object approaches light speed, each extra increase in speed takes more and more energy, and reaching light speed would take infinite energy, which is why nothing with mass can get there. Particle accelerators such as CERN's Large Hadron Collider push protons to over 99.999999% of light speed, but never beyond. Pouring in more energy mostly makes them more energetic rather than noticeably faster. Einstein's famous E = mc² emerged from the same 1905 theory.

sections.key: Space and time are woven together into 'spacetime'.
sections.b: Einstein's former university teacher Hermann Minkowski showed in 1908 that relativity treats space and time as a single four-dimensional fabric: spacetime. He declared that space and time on their own were doomed to fade into mere shadows. Different observers slice spacetime into 'space' and 'time' differently depending on their motion, which is why they can disagree about whether two distant events happened at the same moment, and neither is wrong. There's no universal 'now' across the universe, a deeply unsettling idea. What all observers do agree on is the spacetime interval between events, a combination of distance and time that is the same for everyone.

sections.key: In 1915 Einstein explained gravity as mass curving spacetime.
sections.b: General relativity, completed in 1915, extended the theory to gravity and acceleration. Einstein's key insight was that falling freely feels exactly like floating with no gravity at all, which he later called the happiest thought of his life. In his theory, mass and energy curve spacetime, and objects move along those curves, which we experience as gravity. Physicist John Wheeler summarised it: spacetime tells matter how to move; matter tells spacetime how to curve. It explained a puzzling drift in Mercury's orbit and predicted that light bends around massive objects, confirmed by Arthur Eddington's expeditions during a 1919 solar eclipse, making Einstein world famous overnight.

sections.key: General relativity predicted gravitational lensing and frame dragging, both since observed.
sections.b: Because mass bends spacetime, a massive galaxy or cluster of galaxies can act like a giant lens, bending and magnifying the light of objects far behind it. Einstein worked this out in 1936 but thought it would never be seen. The first lensed quasar was spotted in 1979, and today lensing lets telescopes like James Webb study galaxies too faint to see otherwise. When the alignment is perfect, the background object is smeared into a circle called an Einstein ring. Relativity also predicts that a spinning mass drags spacetime around with it, like a ball twisting in honey. NASA's Gravity Probe B satellite measured this tiny effect around Earth, reporting its results in 2011.

sections.key: Gravity slows time too, and GPS must correct for both relativity effects every day.
sections.b: Gravity affects time as well as speed does: clocks run faster where gravity is weaker. A clock on a mountaintop ticks slightly faster than one at sea level, and in principle your head ages a tiny bit faster than your feet; modern atomic clocks can detect the difference over a height change of less than a metre. GPS satellites combine both effects. Their speed slows their clocks, while the weaker gravity at their altitude speeds them up more, for a net gain of about 38 microseconds a day. Without relativity corrections, positions would drift by around 10 kilometres a day. Every map app on your phone quietly depends on Einstein.

quiz.q: What's special about the speed of light?
o: It's the same for every observer
quiz.e: Einstein followed this in 1905.

quiz.q: What is time dilation?
o: Moving clocks running slow relative to stationary ones
quiz.e: Muons reaching the ground confirm it.

quiz.q: Why can't anything with mass reach light speed?
o: It takes more and more energy to accelerate
quiz.e: Particle accelerators get very close.

quiz.q: What confirmed general relativity in 1919?
o: Starlight bending around the Sun during an eclipse
quiz.e: It made Einstein famous.

quiz.q: What would happen to GPS without relativity corrections?
o: Positions would drift by around 10 km a day
quiz.e: Clocks tick differently in orbit.

LESSONS.title: Polynesian navigators
LESSONS.hook: Without compasses or charts, Polynesian voyagers settled the vast Pacific, reading stars, swells and birds to find specks of land in an ocean.

sections.key: Polynesians settled a vast triangle of islands spanning much of the Pacific Ocean.
sections.b: The Polynesian triangle stretches from Hawai'i in the north to Aotearoa New Zealand in the south-west and Rapa Nui (Easter Island) in the south-east. Its sides are each several thousand kilometres long, and most of what lies inside is open ocean dotted with tiny islands. Finding them meant aiming for targets a few kilometres wide across distances greater than the width of Australia. Hawai'i, Rapa Nui and New Zealand were among the last to be reached, and New Zealand was one of the last major places on Earth settled by humans, around 1250–1300 AD.

sections.key: The ancestors of Polynesians, the Lapita people, reached Fiji, Tonga and Samoa about 3,000 years ago.
sections.b: The story begins with the Lapita culture, named after a site in New Caledonia and recognised by its distinctive stamped pottery. Lapita people, whose ancestors came from Island South-East Asia, spread rapidly into the western Pacific about 3,000 years ago, reaching Fiji, Tonga and Samoa. Here Polynesian culture and languages took shape. Then came a long pause of well over a thousand years. Roughly 1,000 years ago, a burst of voyaging carried people east to the Society Islands and, within a few centuries, to the far corners of the triangle.

sections.key: Double-hulled canoes carried families, plants and animals across thousands of kilometres.
sections.b: Polynesians sailed in large double-hulled canoes, two hulls joined by a deck, with sails woven from pandanus leaves. Hulls were shaped with stone adzes and lashed together with coconut-fibre cord, with no metal at all. They were stable, fast and could carry dozens of people along with everything needed to start a new life: taro, breadfruit, coconuts, pigs, dogs and chickens. These weren't accidental drifts; genetic, linguistic and archaeological evidence shows deliberate, planned voyages of settlement, often sailing into the prevailing winds so that returning home downwind stayed possible.

sections.key: Navigators memorised where hundreds of stars rose and set to hold their course.
sections.b: A master navigator memorised a 'star compass': the points on the horizon where many stars rise and set. As one star climbed too high to be useful, the next along the same path took its place through the night. Stars passing directly overhead also told navigators their latitude, so they could sail to the right latitude and then run along it to find an island. By day they used the Sun and the steady direction of the swells. This knowledge was passed down orally over many years of apprenticeship, often within families, and guarded carefully.

sections.key: Navigators used ocean swells, birds, clouds and even the colour of the water to find land.
sections.b: Swells travel long distances in consistent directions; skilled navigators could feel them through the hull, even lying down, and detect how islands bent and reflected them. Certain seabirds, such as terns and noddies, fly out to sea to fish in the morning and back to land at dusk, pointing the way. Because these birds range only a few dozen kilometres, they effectively widen each island into a much bigger target. Clouds pile up over islands, and a greenish tinge under clouds can reveal a lagoon. Floating plants and changes in water colour offered more clues.

sections.key: The Ra'iatean navigator Tupaia sailed with James Cook and drew a chart of dozens of Pacific islands.
sections.b: When James Cook's Endeavour visited Tahiti in 1769, Tupaia, a high-ranking priest and navigator from nearby Ra'iatea, joined the voyage. He guided the ship through the surrounding islands and, working with the Europeans, produced a chart showing more than 70 islands spread across thousands of kilometres of ocean. Scholars still debate exactly how to read it, because it seems to combine Polynesian and European ideas of direction. Tupaia also helped Cook communicate with Māori in New Zealand, whose language was related to his own. He died of illness in Batavia in 1770.

sections.key: In 1976 the replica canoe Hōkūle'a sailed from Hawai'i to Tahiti using traditional navigation.
sections.b: For much of the twentieth century, some Western scholars doubted Polynesians could have navigated deliberately, suggesting they drifted by accident. In 1976, the Polynesian Voyaging Society's double-hulled canoe Hōkūle'a, about 19 metres long, sailed about 4,000 kilometres from Hawai'i to Tahiti in roughly a month. It was guided by Mau Piailug, a master navigator from the island of Satawal in Micronesia, one of the few people still holding these skills, using no instruments. The voyage proved the methods worked and sparked a revival of traditional navigation across the Pacific.

sections.key: Traditional wayfinding is being taught again, and Polynesians probably reached South America.
sections.b: Mau Piailug went on to train Hawaiian navigators such as Nainoa Thompson, breaking with tradition to share knowledge beyond his own people so it would survive. Hōkūle'a later sailed around the world between 2014 and 2017, and voyaging canoes now sail from Aotearoa, Tahiti, the Cook Islands and elsewhere. Evidence suggests Polynesians also reached South America. The sweet potato, a South American plant, was growing across Polynesia long before Europeans arrived, and a 2020 genetic study found signs of contact between Polynesians and Native Americans around 1150–1230. The Pacific wasn't a barrier; it was a highway.

quiz.q: Which place was among the last major places settled by humans?
quiz.e: Around 1250–1300 AD.

quiz.q: What did voyaging canoes carry?
o: Families, plants and animals to start new lives
quiz.e: Voyages were deliberate settlement.

quiz.q: What is a 'star compass'?
o: Memorised points where stars rise and set on the horizon
quiz.e: Passed down orally.

quiz.q: How could birds help navigators?
o: Some fly out to sea in the morning and back to land at dusk
quiz.e: Pointing the way to land.

quiz.q: Who navigated Hōkūle'a to Tahiti in 1976?
quiz.e: Using no instruments.

LESSONS.title: Marco Polo and the Silk Road
LESSONS.hook: A young Venetian travelled to the court of Kublai Khan and wrote the book that made Europe dream of the East.

sections.key: The Silk Road was a network of trade routes linking China to the Mediterranean.
sections.b: The Silk Road wasn't one road but a web of land and sea routes across Central Asia, the Middle East and India, active from around the 100s BC. The name itself is modern, coined by the German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen in 1877. Silk, spices, porcelain, horses, glass and paper travelled along it, usually passing through many traders' hands, so few people ever travelled the whole length. Ideas travelled too: Buddhism spread from India to China, and technologies like papermaking moved west. Diseases travelled as well, including, eventually, the Black Death in the 1300s.

sections.key: The Mongol Empire made travel across Asia safer than ever before.
sections.b: In the 1200s, Genghis Khan and his successors built the largest contiguous land empire in history, stretching from Korea to Eastern Europe. The conquests were brutal, and cities that resisted were often destroyed. But once established, the Mongols protected trade routes and travellers, ran a network of relay stations for messengers, and tolerated many religions, a period sometimes called the Pax Mongolica. This made it possible for European merchants and missionaries to travel all the way to China, which was now ruled by Genghis's grandson, Kublai Khan.

sections.key: Marco Polo left Venice in 1271 with his father and uncle, reaching China around 1275.
sections.b: Marco's father Niccolò and uncle Maffeo, Venetian merchants, had already visited Kublai Khan's court in the 1260s, and the Khan had asked them to return with Christian scholars and holy oil from Jerusalem. In 1271, they set out again, taking 17-year-old Marco. The journey across Persia, Central Asia and the Gobi Desert took about three and a half years. Venice at the time was a wealthy trading republic whose merchants dealt with the East every day, so the Polos were adventurous but not unusual in their ambitions.

sections.key: Marco described a China far richer and more advanced than Europe, with paper money and huge cities.
sections.b: According to Marco's account, Kublai Khan took a liking to him and sent him on missions across China. Kublai had founded the Yuan dynasty in 1271, ruling from his capital Khanbaliq, on the site of modern Beijing, and a summer palace at Shangdu, the 'Xanadu' of later English poetry. Marco described things that astonished Europeans: paper money accepted across the empire, black stones burned for heat (coal), a postal relay system with thousands of horses, and cities like Hangzhou that dwarfed Venice. Some of his claims about his own importance were probably exaggerated.

sections.key: The Polos returned by sea in the early 1290s, escorting a Mongol princess to Persia.
sections.b: After about 17 years in China, the Polos were keen to go home, but Kublai was reluctant to let them leave. Their chance came when a Mongol princess, Kököchin, needed an escort to Persia to marry its Mongol ruler. According to Marco, they sailed from southern China around 1291 with a fleet of ships, travelling via Sumatra, Sri Lanka and India. The voyage took about two years and many passengers died. By the time they arrived, her intended husband had died, and she married his son instead. The Polos reached Venice in 1295.

sections.key: Marco's stories, written down in prison, became one of the most famous travel books ever.
sections.b: Back in Venice, Marco was captured during a war with Genoa, probably around 1298. In prison, he told his stories to Rustichello da Pisa, a writer of romances, who wrote them down in French with an Italian flavour. The book, known in English as The Travels of Marco Polo, was copied by hand in many versions, with details added or lost along the way, so no single original survives. Many Europeans thought it was exaggerated; in Italy it became known as 'Il Milione', perhaps for his 'million' tall tales. Marco lived in Venice until his death in 1324.

sections.key: Some question whether Marco went to China, but most historians think he did.
sections.b: Sceptics point out that the book doesn't mention the Great Wall, tea or foot binding, and that Chinese records don't name him. Supporters reply that the Great Wall most people picture was built later, under the Ming dynasty, that he mixed mainly with Mongol rather than Chinese society, and that his book contains accurate details, such as about salt production, paper money and the princess's voyage, that he'd have struggled to know otherwise. A Persian source records the princess's journey, matching his account. Most historians today accept that he went, even if some stories were embellished.

sections.key: Marco Polo's book inspired later explorers, including Christopher Columbus.
sections.b: The Travels spread across Europe in many languages, shaping European images of Asia for centuries. Mapmakers used its place names, and the 1375 Catalan Atlas drew on it. Christopher Columbus owned a printed Latin copy, heavily annotated with notes, which survives in Seville, and hoped to reach the riches it described by sailing west. When the Mongol Empire fragmented and the Ottomans rose, overland trade became harder, which helped push Europeans to seek sea routes to Asia, leading to the Age of Discovery. Today Venice's airport is named after him.

quiz.q: What was the Silk Road?
o: A network of trade routes linking China and the Mediterranean
quiz.e: Ideas and diseases travelled too.

quiz.q: Why could Europeans travel to China in the 1200s?
o: The Mongol Empire protected trade routes
quiz.e: The Pax Mongolica.

quiz.q: Whose court did Marco Polo visit?
quiz.e: Genghis's grandson.

quiz.q: How was Marco Polo's book written?
o: He told his stories to a writer while in prison
quiz.e: Rustichello da Pisa wrote them down.

quiz.q: Which explorer owned an annotated copy of Marco Polo's book?
quiz.e: He hoped to reach Asia by sailing west.

LESSONS.title: Columbus, da Gama and the Age of Discovery
LESSONS.hook: In a few decades, European sailors reached India by sea and crossed the Atlantic, connecting the world, with enormous and often devastating consequences.

sections.key: Europeans sought sea routes to Asia's spices, gold and trade.
sections.b: Spices like pepper, cinnamon, nutmeg and cloves were hugely valuable in Europe, used to flavour food, make medicines and display wealth. They came overland through Middle Eastern and Venetian middlemen, who raised prices at each step. After the Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453, the eastern Mediterranean trade was even more firmly in others' hands. Portugal and Spain, on the Atlantic edge of Europe, wanted direct sea routes to Asia. Religious motives, spreading Christianity, and rivalry with Muslim powers also drove exploration, alongside the simple hope of personal fortune and fame.

sections.key: The caravel, compass and astrolabe made long ocean voyages possible.
sections.b: Long voyages needed better tools. The caravel, developed by the Portuguese, was small, light and could sail closer to the wind than older ships, thanks partly to triangular lateen sails; larger carracks carried more cargo and supplies. The magnetic compass, first used for navigation in China and appearing in Europe by around 1200, showed direction even under cloud. The astrolabe and quadrant measured the height of the Sun or the Pole Star, giving latitude. Longitude, however, could only be estimated from speed and time, a problem not truly solved until marine chronometers arrived in the 1700s.

sections.key: Portugal systematically explored the African coast in the 1400s.
sections.b: Portuguese Prince Henry, known as 'the Navigator', sponsored voyages down the west coast of Africa from the 1420s, though he didn't sail himself. Each expedition pushed a little further, mapping the coast and learning the Atlantic's wind patterns, including the trick of swinging far out to sea to catch favourable winds home. Portuguese ships traded in gold, ivory and, tragically, enslaved Africans. In 1488, Bartolomeu Dias rounded the southern end of Africa, passing the Cape of Good Hope, proving a sea route to the Indian Ocean was possible. His exhausted crew forced him to turn back.

sections.key: In 1492, Christopher Columbus crossed the Atlantic and reached the Caribbean.
sections.b: Christopher Columbus, a Genoese sailor, believed he could reach Asia by sailing west. He badly underestimated Earth's size (educated Europeans already knew it was round), and experts rejected his plan for years. Sponsored by Spain's Queen Isabella and King Ferdinand, he sailed in 1492 with three ships, the Santa María, Pinta and Niña, and reached the Bahamas on 12 October, landing on an island home to the Taíno people. He believed he'd reached Asia, calling the inhabitants 'Indians'. He made four voyages, and his governorship of Hispaniola was notoriously brutal, even by the standards of his time.

sections.key: In 1494 Spain and Portugal agreed to split newly found lands between them in the Treaty of Tordesillas.
sections.b: Columbus's return sparked a dispute between Spain and Portugal over who owned new lands. In 1494 they signed the Treaty of Tordesillas, drawing a north-south line through the Atlantic: lands to the west went to Spain, those to the east to Portugal. The line later gave Portugal a claim to Brazil, reached by Pedro Álvares Cabral in 1500, which is why Brazilians speak Portuguese today. The people who already lived in these lands were not consulted. Meanwhile, the voyages of Amerigo Vespucci convinced many that a 'New World' had been found, and a 1507 map named it America.

sections.key: In 1498, Vasco da Gama became the first European to reach India by sea.
sections.b: Following Dias's route, Portuguese captain Vasco da Gama left Lisbon in 1497, sailed around Africa and, guided by a local pilot from East Africa, crossed the Indian Ocean to Calicut in India in 1498. The return journey was grim, and scurvy killed many of his crew, but the spices he brought back were worth many times the voyage's cost. Portugal soon built a trading empire of forts and ports from East Africa to Indonesia, including Goa and Malacca, often using violence to control trade that Arab, Indian and Chinese merchants had run for centuries.

sections.key: Contact between the hemispheres transferred crops, animals and diseases, changing the whole world.
sections.b: In 1972, historian Alfred Crosby named the Columbian Exchange: the transfer of plants, animals, people and diseases between the Americas and the rest of the world. Potatoes, maize, tomatoes, chillies and cacao went east, transforming diets from Ireland to China; it's hard to imagine Italian food without tomatoes or Thai food without chillies. Horses, cattle, wheat, sugar cane and coffee went west. Diseases like smallpox and measles, to which Indigenous Americans had no prior exposure, devastated their communities, and populations collapsed by perhaps 90% in some regions within about a century.

sections.key: The Age of Discovery created global trade, but also colonialism and the Atlantic slave trade.
sections.b: For the first time, all inhabited continents became linked by regular trade. Silver from mines like Potosí, in modern Bolivia, flowed to Europe and China, and from 1565 Spanish galleons sailed across the Pacific between Mexico and Manila. European powers built empires that lasted centuries. The demand for labour on plantations drove the Atlantic slave trade, which carried about 12 million Africans across the ocean in brutal conditions. Historians now often prefer terms like 'contact' or 'encounter' to 'discovery', since the lands Europeans 'discovered' were already home to millions of people.

quiz.q: Why did Europeans want sea routes to Asia?
o: To trade directly for valuable spices
quiz.e: Middlemen raised prices.

quiz.q: Who first rounded the Cape of Good Hope in 1488?
quiz.e: Proving a sea route was possible.

quiz.q: What did Columbus get wrong?
quiz.e: Educated Europeans knew Earth was round.

quiz.q: Who reached India by sea in 1498?
quiz.e: Guided by a local pilot.

quiz.q: What was the Columbian Exchange?
o: The transfer of crops, animals and diseases between hemispheres
quiz.e: Named by Alfred Crosby.

LESSONS.title: Magellan: the first voyage around the world
LESSONS.hook: Five ships and about 270 men set out in 1519. Three years later, one battered ship and 18 survivors limped home. They had sailed around the planet.

sections.key: Ferdinand Magellan set out in 1519 to reach the Spice Islands by sailing west.
sections.b: Ferdinand Magellan, Fernão de Magalhães in Portuguese, was an experienced sailor who had fought for Portugal in India and South-East Asia. After falling out with Portugal's king, he offered his services to Spain. He proposed reaching the valuable Spice Islands, the Moluccas in modern Indonesia, by sailing west around South America. Under the Treaty of Tordesillas, the world was split between Spain and Portugal, and Magellan argued that the Spice Islands might fall on Spain's side of the line. The young King Charles I, later Emperor Charles V, agreed to back him.

sections.key: Five ships and a crew of many nationalities left Spain in September 1519.
sections.b: In September 1519, the fleet left Sanlúcar de Barrameda in southern Spain: the Trinidad, San Antonio, Concepción, Victoria and Santiago, carrying around 270 men. The crew included Spaniards, Portuguese, Italians, Greeks, French, Africans and others. Among them was Antonio Pigafetta, a scholar from Vicenza, whose detailed journal is our main source for the voyage. Magellan's Spanish captains resented taking orders from a Portuguese commander, and Portugal sent ships to try to intercept him. No one knew how far away Asia was, or how big the ocean on the other side of South America would be.

sections.key: Magellan put down a mutiny, then found a passage around South America.
sections.b: The fleet sailed down the coast of South America, searching for a way through. Over the harsh winter at Port San Julián in Patagonia, in April 1520, several captains mutinied; Magellan crushed the revolt and executed or marooned the leaders. The Santiago was wrecked while scouting. In late 1520, the fleet found and navigated a treacherous passage at the continent's southern tip, now called the Strait of Magellan, a winding channel about 570 kilometres long. During the passage, the San Antonio deserted and sailed home. To the south, the crew saw fires on shore, and named the land Tierra del Fuego.

sections.key: The crossing of the Pacific took over three months, and many sailors died of starvation and scurvy.
sections.b: Emerging into calm waters in late November 1520, Magellan named the ocean the Pacific, meaning peaceful. It was far larger than anyone imagined, covering about a third of Earth's surface. The crossing took over three months without fresh food, and by chance the fleet missed almost every inhabited island. According to Pigafetta, sailors ate rat-infested biscuit crumbs, sawdust and leather strips softened in seawater, and rats were sold for half a ducat each. Many died of scurvy, a disease caused by lack of vitamin C, which bleeds the gums and weakens the body. They finally reached Guam in March 1521.

sections.key: Magellan was killed in the Philippines in 1521, in a battle with Lapulapu's warriors.
sections.b: Reaching the Philippines in March 1521, Magellan allied with Rajah Humabon of Cebu, converted him and many of his people to Christianity, and became involved in local rivalries. He attacked the island of Mactan, whose chief, Lapulapu, refused to submit. Magellan landed with around 50 men, too few against a much larger force, and his ships couldn't get close enough over the shallow reef to help. He was killed in the battle on 27 April 1521. Lapulapu is celebrated today in the Philippines as a national hero, the first to resist European colonisation.

sections.key: After Magellan's death, the survivors burned one ship and finally reached the Moluccas.
sections.b: Magellan's death shattered the alliance with Cebu. Days later, several of the expedition's leaders were killed at a feast hosted by Humabon. With too few men to sail three ships, the survivors burned the Concepción and wandered through the islands for months before reaching Tidore, in the Moluccas, in November 1521. There they loaded cloves, among the most valuable spices in the world. The Trinidad, leaking badly, tried to sail back east across the Pacific to Spanish-held Mexico but was driven back and captured by the Portuguese. Only the Victoria was left to try for home.

sections.key: Juan Sebastián Elcano led the last ship, the Victoria, home in 1522.
sections.b: The Victoria, captained by Basque navigator Juan Sebastián Elcano, continued west across the Indian Ocean and around Africa, avoiding Portuguese ships and ports. Men kept dying of scurvy and hunger, and at the Portuguese-held Cape Verde Islands 13 crew were detained when they went ashore for supplies. In September 1522, three years after leaving, the Victoria arrived in Spain with 18 of the original crew. They had completed the first circumnavigation of the globe. The cloves in its hold were enough to cover much of the expedition's cost, and Elcano received a coat of arms showing a globe.

sections.key: The voyage proved the world's oceans are connected, and that Earth is far larger than believed.
sections.b: The voyage confirmed that the world's oceans are connected, that the Americas were a separate landmass from Asia, and that the Earth was much bigger than Columbus had thought. The human cost was enormous: most of the roughly 270 men who set out never returned. It also revealed a curious puzzle: the crew's log was one day behind the calendar in Spain, because they'd travelled west with the Sun and experienced one fewer sunrise. It was an early hint of what we now handle with the International Date Line. Spain's claim to the Moluccas was later sold to Portugal in 1529.

quiz.q: What was Magellan trying to reach?
quiz.e: The Moluccas in modern Indonesia.

quiz.q: Why did Magellan name it the Pacific Ocean?
quiz.e: Pacific means peaceful.

quiz.q: What caused scurvy among sailors?
quiz.e: It bleeds the gums and weakens the body.

quiz.q: Who is Lapulapu?
o: A chief who defeated Magellan, now a Philippine national hero
quiz.e: Magellan died at Mactan in 1521.

quiz.q: Who led the Victoria home to complete the circumnavigation?
quiz.e: 18 of the original crew returned.

LESSONS.title: James Cook's voyages
LESSONS.hook: A farm labourer's son became the Pacific's greatest mapmaker. His voyages changed science, and the fate of the peoples he met.

sections.key: James Cook rose from humble origins to become a brilliant navigator and surveyor.
sections.b: James Cook was born in Yorkshire in 1728, the son of a farm labourer. He learned seamanship on coal ships sailing out of Whitby in the North Sea, joined the Royal Navy in 1755 and rose quickly. During the Seven Years' War he helped chart the St Lawrence River in Canada, then made his name mapping the coast of Newfoundland with remarkable precision. He was a skilled mathematician and astronomer, largely self-taught, rare for someone without a privileged education. In 1768, he was chosen to command a scientific voyage to the Pacific aboard the Endeavour, a converted Whitby coal ship.

sections.key: Cook's first voyage observed the transit of Venus from Tahiti to help measure the solar system.
sections.b: The official purpose of Cook's first voyage (1768–1771) was to observe Venus passing across the face of the Sun from Tahiti on 3 June 1769. Transits of Venus come in pairs about eight years apart, more than a century between pairs, so it was a rare chance. Astronomers hoped measurements from around the world would help calculate the distance from Earth to the Sun. Cook also carried secret orders to search for a rumoured great southern continent, Terra Australis. On board was the wealthy young botanist Joseph Banks, who collected thousands of plant specimens with his colleague Daniel Solander.

sections.h: New Zealand and the east coast
sections.key: Cook charted New Zealand and the east coast of Australia in 1769–70.
sections.b: Cook circumnavigated and mapped both islands of New Zealand, whose coastline had been partly seen by Dutch explorer Abel Tasman in 1642. His first encounters with Māori, at Tūranganui-a-Kiwa (Gisborne), ended in bloodshed. Then, in April 1770, he reached the east coast of Australia, landing at Kamay (Botany Bay), named for the abundance of new plants Banks found. Local Gweagal men opposed the landing, and shots were fired. Cook charted the coast northward and, on Possession Island in the Torres Strait in August 1770, claimed the east coast for Britain as New South Wales, without the consent of its peoples.

sections.key: The Endeavour struck the Great Barrier Reef and was repaired at the Endeavour River.
sections.b: In June 1770, the Endeavour ran aground on the Great Barrier Reef. The crew threw cannons, ballast and supplies overboard to lighten it and, after refloating the ship, slowed the leak by drawing a sail packed with oakum and wool under the hull, a technique called fothering. They limped to the mouth of what's now the Endeavour River, near Cooktown, Queensland. Repairs took about seven weeks. There, the crew had extended contact with the local Guugu Yimithirr people, and recorded the word 'kangaroo', from the Guugu Yimithirr word gangurru.

sections.key: Cook's voyages carried scientists and artists, and his second voyage tested a new marine chronometer.
sections.b: Cook's voyages were floating laboratories. Banks and Solander brought back many plant species then unknown to European science, and artist Sydney Parkinson made hundreds of drawings before dying on the voyage home. On the second voyage, Cook carried a copy of John Harrison's marine chronometer, a clock accurate enough to calculate longitude at sea, and praised its reliability. He also fought scurvy with fresh food, sauerkraut and strict cleanliness, and lost very few men to it. The first voyage was still deadly, though: more than a third of the crew died, most from disease caught at Batavia (Jakarta).

sections.key: Cook disproved the great southern continent and died in Hawai'i in 1779.
sections.b: On his second voyage (1772–1775), Cook crossed the Antarctic Circle, showing that any southern continent must lie in the icy far south, not in the temperate latitudes Europeans had imagined. On his third voyage (1776–1780), searching for a Northwest Passage above North America, he became the first European known to reach Hawai'i, in 1778, then sailed north through the Bering Strait until ice blocked the way. Returning to Hawai'i, amid rising tensions over a stolen boat, he was killed in a confrontation at Kealakekua Bay on 14 February 1779. His crew completed the voyage without him.

sections.key: Cook's reports led Britain to establish a penal colony in New South Wales in 1788.
sections.b: Cook's charts and Banks's enthusiasm for Botany Bay influenced Britain's decision to send convicts to New South Wales after losing its American colonies. The First Fleet arrived in January 1788, but Captain Arthur Phillip found Botany Bay unsuitable, with poor soil and little fresh water, and moved about 12 kilometres north to Sydney Cove in Port Jackson, a harbour Cook had noted but not entered. The colony's founding, on 26 January, is now marked as Australia Day, a date many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people mourn as the beginning of invasion.

sections.key: Cook is celebrated as a navigator and scientist, but his voyages opened the way to colonisation.
sections.b: Cook's maps were so accurate some were used for over a century, and his voyages advanced botany, astronomy and knowledge of the Pacific. Places across Australia, New Zealand and the Pacific bear his name. But for many Aboriginal Australians, Māori and Pacific peoples, his arrival marks the beginning of invasion, dispossession and disease. Statues of Cook have become sites of protest, particularly around Australia Day. Both views reflect real history: a remarkable navigator whose voyages had devastating consequences for others. Holding both at once is part of understanding Australia's past honestly.

quiz.q: What was Cook's background?
quiz.e: He rose through skill.

quiz.q: What was the official purpose of Cook's first voyage?
o: To observe the transit of Venus
quiz.e: From Tahiti in 1769.

quiz.q: What was Botany Bay named for?
o: The abundance of new plants Banks found
quiz.e: Known to locals as Kamay.

quiz.q: How did Cook's crew slow the leak after the Endeavour struck the reef?
o: They poured hot tar into the hold
They drew a sail packed with oakum and wool under the hull
They nailed empty barrels over the hole
They filled the hold with sand
quiz.e: The technique, called fothering, let them limp to the Endeavour River for repairs.

quiz.q: Where did Cook die?
quiz.e: At Kealakekua Bay in 1779.

LESSONS.title: The race to the poles
LESSONS.hook: Frostbite, starvation and extraordinary endurance. The early 1900s 'heroic age' of polar exploration produced triumph and tragedy.

sections.key: From about 1897 to 1922, explorers raced to reach the poles and chart Antarctica.
sections.b: By 1900, the North and South Poles were among the last great unreached places on Earth. The period known as the Heroic Age of Antarctic Exploration, usually dated from about 1897 to Shackleton's death in 1922, saw expeditions from Britain, Norway, Australia, Japan, Germany and elsewhere. Explorers faced temperatures below minus 40 degrees, blizzards, hidden crevasses and months of darkness, equipped with wool and fur clothing, sledges, and little or no radio contact with the outside world. Expeditions often lasted two or three years. Many men didn't return.

sections.key: Norway's Roald Amundsen reached the South Pole first, on 14 December 1911.
sections.b: Roald Amundsen had already sailed the Northwest Passage and had learned polar techniques from Inuit people in the Arctic: fur clothing, dog sledging and careful pacing. He secretly switched his plans from the North Pole to the South, only announcing it once at sea. From his base at the Bay of Whales, he planned meticulously, laying supply depots and using sled dogs, some of which were killed to feed the others and the men as the journey went on. His five-man team, on skis, reached the South Pole on 14 December 1911 and returned safely.

sections.key: Robert Falcon Scott's team reached the pole weeks later and died on the return journey.
sections.b: Britain's Robert Falcon Scott relied partly on ponies and motor sledges, which failed, and then on man-hauling heavy sledges. His five-man team reached the pole on 17 January 1912, only to find Amundsen's tent and Norwegian flag. On the return, weakened by hunger, cold and exhaustion, they all died. Lawrence Oates, crippled by frostbite, walked out into a blizzard to avoid slowing the others, reportedly saying, 'I am just going outside and may be some time.' Scott and his last two companions died in their tent about 18 kilometres from a large supply depot.

sections.key: Dogs, skis, experience and careful planning gave Amundsen a decisive edge.
sections.b: Historians still debate Scott's choices, but some differences are clear. Amundsen's dogs could travel fast over snow and ice, and could be eaten along the way; Scott's ponies suffered in the cold and his men exhausted themselves hauling sledges. Amundsen's team were expert skiers and dog drivers, and he marked his depots so they could be found in poor visibility. Scott also faced unusually cold weather on his return, and his team hauled about 16 kilograms of rock samples to the end, reflecting the expedition's scientific aims. Amundsen later wrote that victory awaits the one who has everything in order.

sections.key: Australian Douglas Mawson survived alone after both companions died in Antarctica.
sections.b: Adelaide geologist Douglas Mawson led the Australasian Antarctic Expedition (1911–1914), based at Cape Denison, one of the windiest places on Earth at sea level. In December 1912, his companion Belgrave Ninnis fell into a crevasse with the sledge carrying most of their food. Mawson and Xavier Mertz turned back, eating their dogs to survive. Mertz grew sick and died, probably partly from vitamin A poisoning from eating dog liver. Mawson struggled on alone for about a month, falling into a crevasse himself, and reached base just after his ship had left. He survived another winter there.

sections.key: Ernest Shackleton's whole crew survived for months after their ship was crushed by ice.
sections.b: In 1915, Ernest Shackleton's ship Endurance was trapped and crushed by sea ice in the Weddell Sea. The 28 men camped on drifting ice for months, then sailed lifeboats to remote Elephant Island. Shackleton and five others, including New Zealand navigator Frank Worsley, sailed the small boat James Caird about 1,300 kilometres across stormy seas to South Georgia, then crossed its unmapped mountains to reach a whaling station. After several attempts, every one of the Endurance's crew was rescued. The wreck of Endurance was found in 2022, about 3,000 metres down and remarkably preserved.

sections.key: Early claims to reach the North Pole are disputed, and the first verified sighting came by airship in 1926.
sections.b: The North Pole sits on drifting sea ice, not land, which makes it hard to reach and even harder to prove you've reached. American Robert Peary claimed to have got there in 1909 with Matthew Henson and four Inuit men, Ootah, Egingwah, Seegloo and Ooqueah, while Frederick Cook claimed 1908. Both claims have been widely doubted, as their reported speeds and navigation records are hard to believe. In 1926, Amundsen, American Lincoln Ellsworth and Italian Umberto Nobile flew over the pole in the airship Norge, generally regarded as the first verified visit.

sections.key: Antarctica is now protected by an international treaty for peace and science.
sections.b: The 1959 Antarctic Treaty set aside Antarctica for peaceful scientific research, banning military activity and, under a later protocol, mining. Australia claims about 42% of the continent, the largest share, though claims are held in abeyance under the treaty, and runs research stations like Mawson, Davis and Casey, supplied from Hobart. Scientists there study climate history through ice cores, which hold air bubbles hundreds of thousands of years old. The Arctic, by contrast, is an ocean surrounded by nations, and its shrinking summer sea ice is one of the clearest signs of a warming climate.

quiz.q: What was the Heroic Age of Antarctic Exploration?
o: A period of expeditions to the poles around 1897–1922
quiz.e: Many explorers didn't return.

quiz.q: Who reached the South Pole first?
quiz.e: On 14 December 1911.

quiz.q: What happened to Scott's team?
o: They reached the pole second and died on the return
quiz.e: Oates walked out into a blizzard.

quiz.q: How did Mawson survive?
o: He struggled on alone after both companions died
quiz.e: He reached base just after his ship left.

quiz.q: What happened to Shackleton's men?
quiz.e: After Endurance was crushed by ice.

LESSONS.title: Mesopotamia: where civilisation began
LESSONS.hook: Between two rivers in modern Iraq, people built the first cities, the first written laws and some of the first empires. You still use their ideas every time you check the time.

sections.key: Mesopotamia means 'land between rivers', the Tigris and Euphrates in modern Iraq.
sections.b: Mesopotamia sat in the Fertile Crescent, an arc of good farmland curving from the eastern Mediterranean coast down to the Persian Gulf. Farming began in this wider region more than 10,000 years ago, with wheat, barley, sheep and goats. The southern plain was hot and dry, and the rivers flooded unpredictably, sometimes too early, sometimes too violently. So people dug canals, dykes and irrigation ditches to control the water and grow surplus food. A surplus meant not everyone had to farm: some could become priests, craftspeople, soldiers and rulers. That shift, from everyone feeding themselves to specialised jobs, is the seed of civilisation.

sections.key: Sumerian cities like Uruk, around 3500–3000 BC, are among the world's first true cities.
sections.b: In southern Mesopotamia, the Sumerians built cities such as Uruk, Ur and Lagash. Uruk may have held tens of thousands of people by around 3000 BC, enormous for its time, inside walls about 9 kilometres long. Each city had its own ruler and patron god, worshipped in a temple on a stepped mud-brick platform called a ziggurat. The ziggurat of Ur, partly rebuilt in modern times, still stands in southern Iraq. Cities traded grain and woollen textiles for timber, metals and stone, which the river plain lacked. They also fought each other, often for generations, over land, borders and water rights.

sections.key: Temples and palaces organised work, paying labourers in rations of barley, bread and beer.
sections.b: Much of a Sumerian city's economy ran through its temple and palace. They owned land and herds, employed weavers, brewers and farm workers, and paid them in rations of barley, bread, oil and beer. Beer was a daily staple, thick and nutritious, and a goddess named Ninkasi was linked with brewing. Society was layered: rulers and priests at the top, then free farmers, merchants and craftspeople, with enslaved people at the bottom, often war captives or debtors. Most people lived in mud-brick houses around small courtyards. Boys from wealthier families could train for years in scribal schools, copying signs onto clay.

sections.key: The Sumerians are credited with early writing, the wheel and the 60-based counting we use for time.
sections.b: Sumerians developed cuneiform, one of the first writing systems, around 3200 BC. They were among the first to use the wheel, first for making pottery and then for carts. They counted in base 60, a handy number because it divides evenly by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20 and 30. Their Babylonian successors carried the system on, which is why we still have 60 seconds in a minute, 60 minutes in an hour and 360 degrees in a circle. Sumerians recorded the movements of the sky, and their poems about the hero-king Gilgamesh became the basis of the Epic of Gilgamesh, one of the oldest surviving works of literature.

sections.key: Sargon of Akkad united Mesopotamia around 2300 BC, often called the first empire.
sections.b: Around 2334 BC by the traditional dating, Sargon rose to power. Legend says he was found as a baby floating in a reed basket on the river and raised by a water-drawer. He conquered the Sumerian cities and built the Akkadian Empire, ruling from a capital called Akkad whose ruins have never been found. The empire stretched across Mesopotamia and beyond, governing many peoples and languages from one centre, which is why it's often called the world's first empire. Akkadian, a Semitic language, became the region's main written language for centuries. The empire lasted under two centuries before breaking apart.

sections.key: King Hammurabi of Babylon wrote one of the earliest known law codes, around 1754 BC.
sections.b: Hammurabi ruled Babylon for about 40 years and united much of Mesopotamia. He had 282 laws carved onto a tall black stone pillar, topped with an image of him receiving authority from the sun god Shamash. The pillar is now in the Louvre in Paris. The laws covered trade, wages, loans, marriage, property, medical fees and crime. Many followed the principle of 'an eye for an eye', but punishments varied depending on whether the victim was a noble, a commoner or enslaved. What made the code important was the idea that laws should be written down and publicly displayed, so rules applied predictably rather than at a ruler's whim.

sections.key: Later empires, Assyria and Babylon, dominated the region until the Persians conquered it in 539 BC.
sections.b: In the first millennium BC, the Assyrians of northern Mesopotamia built a powerful and feared military empire. From their capital Nineveh, near modern Mosul, King Ashurbanipal gathered a great library of clay tablets, many of which survive in the British Museum. Nineveh fell in 612 BC, and Babylon rose again under Nebuchadnezzar II, who rebuilt the city with huge walls and the blue-glazed Ishtar Gate, now reconstructed in a Berlin museum. The famous Hanging Gardens of Babylon are described by later Greek writers, but no clear trace has been found, so whether they existed there is debated. In 539 BC, Cyrus the Great of Persia took Babylon.

sections.key: Mesopotamia gave the world cities, writing, law codes, and our system of hours and minutes.
sections.b: Mesopotamian ideas travelled far beyond the region. Its astronomy and mathematics influenced Greek scholars, who inherited Babylonian records of eclipses and planetary movements. Its stories influenced neighbouring cultures, including the writers of the Hebrew Bible: the flood story in Gilgamesh has striking parallels with the story of Noah. The seven-day week may also draw partly on Mesopotamian traditions. Much of this was forgotten until the 1800s, when archaeologists dug up tablets and scholars deciphered cuneiform. Today, looting and conflict threaten many Iraqi sites. When you check your watch, measure an angle or read a written law, you're using ideas first worked out here.

quiz.q: What does 'Mesopotamia' mean?
quiz.e: The Tigris and Euphrates rivers.

quiz.q: What was a ziggurat?
quiz.e: Each city had its patron god's temple.

quiz.q: Why do we have 60 minutes in an hour?
quiz.e: Also why a circle has 360 degrees.

quiz.q: Who created what's often called the first empire?
quiz.e: Around 2300 BC.

quiz.q: Why was Hammurabi's code important?
o: Laws were written down and publicly displayed
It was the first religious text
quiz.e: Rules applied predictably.

LESSONS.title: The invention of writing
LESSONS.hook: Writing was invented from scratch only a handful of times in history. It began with accountants, not poets.

sections.key: Before writing, knowledge lived only in memory, speech and simple symbols.
sections.b: For most of human history, knowledge passed from person to person through speech, song and memory. People used tally marks, knotted cords and pictures, but these couldn't record language itself. Oral cultures developed powerful memory techniques, and many kept vast bodies of knowledge this way. Aboriginal Australian songlines, for example, carry knowledge of country, law, navigation and seasons across many generations through song, story and dance. Oral knowledge isn't inferior, but it depends on living people to carry it. As farming villages grew into cities, with taxes, trade, rations and debts to track across thousands of people, administrators needed a record that didn't rely on anyone's memory.

sections.key: Writing in Mesopotamia likely grew from clay tokens and marks used to record goods.
sections.b: In Mesopotamia, people used small clay tokens, shaped like cones, spheres and discs, to stand for goods such as sheep or jars of oil. A leading theory holds that these tokens were sealed inside clay envelopes and marked on the outside, and that people eventually realised the marks alone would do. By around 3200 BC in Uruk, scribes were drawing signs for objects and numbers on clay tablets to record grain, livestock and labour. Most of the earliest tablets are accounts and receipts. Writing began as bookkeeping. Poems, letters, laws and stories came later, as people found signs could represent spoken words.

sections.key: Cuneiform, written with a reed pressed into wet clay, was used for about 3,000 years.
sections.b: Sumerian scribes wrote by pressing a cut reed into damp clay, making wedge-shaped marks. That's where the name comes from: cuneus is Latin for wedge. Over centuries, pictures became abstract symbols, some standing for whole words and others for syllables. Learning the hundreds of signs took years of schooling. Cuneiform was adapted for many languages, including Akkadian, Hittite and, in a simplified form, Old Persian. Hundreds of thousands of clay tablets survive, because clay lasts, especially when fires baked it hard, as happened when Nineveh was sacked. Scholars in the 1800s deciphered it partly using a trilingual inscription carved on a cliff at Behistun in Iran.

sections.key: Egyptian hieroglyphs appeared around 3200 BC and were decoded in 1822 using the Rosetta Stone.
sections.b: Egyptian hieroglyphs appear around 3200 BC, about the same time as Mesopotamian writing, and may have developed independently. The system mixed signs for sounds with signs for whole ideas. Carved hieroglyphs decorated temples and tombs, while scribes used faster, simplified scripts called hieratic and later demotic for everyday business, written in ink on papyrus. After the last known hieroglyphic inscription in AD 394, the knowledge was lost. The breakthrough came from the Rosetta Stone, found in 1799, which carries the same decree in hieroglyphs, demotic and Greek. Using it, the French scholar Jean-François Champollion announced his decipherment in 1822.

sections.key: Writing was independently invented in Mesopotamia, China and Mesoamerica, and probably Egypt.
sections.b: In China, writing carved on animal bones and turtle shells, used to ask questions of ancestors and spirits, dates to around 1200 BC, and modern Chinese characters descend directly from it. That makes Chinese the oldest writing system still in continuous use. In Mesoamerica, several peoples developed writing, and the Maya created a full system of several hundred signs that could record anything they could say. Each of these systems started with pictures and then developed signs for sounds. Scholars generally accept only these few independent inventions: nearly every other writing system in the world was borrowed or adapted from one of them, or inspired by the idea.

sections.key: The alphabet, with signs for individual sounds, began among Semitic-speaking peoples around 1800 BC.
sections.b: Early systems needed hundreds or thousands of signs, so only trained scribes could write. Around 1800 BC, Semitic-speaking workers in Egypt and Sinai borrowed some hieroglyph shapes to make a small set of signs for consonant sounds. The Phoenicians, a seafaring trading people from modern Lebanon, spread their version around the Mediterranean. It also gave rise to scripts such as Hebrew and Arabic. The Greeks added vowels, and the Romans adapted a Greek-derived alphabet, partly via the Etruscans, into the Latin alphabet used for English today. With only a couple of dozen letters, far more people could learn to read. The word alphabet comes from alpha and beta.

sections.key: Writing materials shaped who could write, from clay and papyrus to Chinese paper and the printing press.
sections.b: What people wrote on mattered almost as much as the script. Mesopotamians used clay, which was cheap and durable but heavy. Egyptians made papyrus from reeds growing along the Nile. Europeans later used parchment, made from animal skin, while early Chinese scribes wrote on strips of bamboo and silk. Paper was developed in China during the Han dynasty, around 2,000 years ago, and slowly spread west through the Islamic world to Europe. The Chinese also pioneered printing, with woodblocks and later movable type. In Europe, Johannes Gutenberg's printing press, around 1450, made books far cheaper and helped spread reading across society.

sections.key: Writing made history, law, science and literature possible on a new scale.
sections.b: Writing let people record events, so history became possible, which is why historians distinguish prehistory from history. It let laws be fixed and shared, contracts be enforced, and knowledge build up over generations instead of being lost when someone died. It also changed thinking itself: lists, tables and long arguments are much easier on a page than in the head. Writing concentrated power too, because for thousands of years only a small elite could read. The spread of literacy, especially after the printing press and mass schooling, changed who could learn and question. Every message you type today stands on that 5,000-year-old invention.

quiz.q: What were the earliest Mesopotamian texts mostly about?
quiz.e: Writing began as bookkeeping.

quiz.q: Why is it called 'cuneiform'?
o: From the Latin for wedge, after its wedge-shaped marks
quiz.e: Made by pressing a reed into wet clay.

quiz.q: Which is the oldest writing system still in continuous use?
quiz.e: Modern Chinese characters descend directly from writing on oracle bones from around 1200 BC.

quiz.q: Who added vowels to the alphabet?
quiz.e: They adapted the Phoenician consonant alphabet.

quiz.q: What distinguishes history from prehistory?
quiz.e: Writing made history possible.

LESSONS.title: The Indus Valley civilisation
LESSONS.hook: Five thousand years ago, cities in modern Pakistan and India had grid streets and covered drains. We still can't read their writing.

sections.key: The Indus Valley or Harappan civilisation flourished around 2600–1900 BC.
sections.b: Along the Indus River and its neighbours, in today's Pakistan and north-west India, a major civilisation arose around the same time as Egypt's pyramids. It is also called the Harappan civilisation, after Harappa, the first site excavated. It was forgotten for thousands of years until archaeologists recognised it in the 1920s at sites like Harappa and Mohenjo-daro. At its height it covered a larger area than Egypt or Mesopotamia, with more than a thousand known settlements, from small villages to big cities such as Dholavira and Rakhigarhi. Population estimates vary widely, but some scholars suggest several million people at its peak.

sections.key: Indus cities were carefully planned, with grid-like streets and standardised bricks.
sections.b: Mohenjo-daro and Harappa had streets laid out in a rough grid, with wide main roads and smaller lanes, and houses facing inward onto courtyards. Buildings used baked or sun-dried bricks made in consistent proportions, roughly 1:2:4 for thickness, width and length, across hundreds of kilometres. That suggests shared rules or organisation. Many cities had a raised area, often called a citadel, with large public buildings, and a lower residential town. Mohenjo-daro's Great Bath, a pool about 12 metres long, lined with fitted bricks and sealed with bitumen to make it watertight, may have been used for ritual bathing.

sections.key: Many homes had private bathrooms and connected to covered street drains.
sections.b: The civilisation's water engineering was remarkable. Mohenjo-daro alone may have had hundreds of brick-lined wells. Many houses had bathing areas with sloping floors and toilets that drained into covered brick sewers along the streets, with removable covers and inspection holes for cleaning. Dholavira, in a drier area, built large reservoirs to store rainwater. Few places in the world had anything comparable for thousands of years. This suggests a strong concern with cleanliness and some form of city-wide coordination to build and maintain the drains, although we don't know exactly who ran these cities or how.

sections.key: Indus people farmed wheat and barley, grew cotton and made fine beads, pottery and figurines.
sections.b: Most Indus people were farmers and herders, growing wheat, barley, peas and sesame and keeping cattle, sheep and goats. They were among the earliest people known to grow cotton and weave it into cloth. Craftspeople drilled long, polished beads from red carnelian, a skill so specialised that similar beads turn up in Mesopotamian royal tombs. They made painted pottery, copper and bronze tools, and small clay toys such as carts and animals. A famous bronze figurine from Mohenjo-daro, nicknamed the 'Dancing Girl', shows skilled metal casting. The port of Lothal, in Gujarat, had a large brick basin that many think was a dockyard.

sections.key: Indus people traded widely, including with Mesopotamia, and left thousands of carved stone seals.
sections.b: Indus merchants traded cotton, beads, gems and timber, travelling overland and by sea along the Arabian coast. Mesopotamian texts mention a land called Meluhha, probably the Indus region, and Indus seals have been found in Mesopotamia. Archaeologists have found standardised cube-shaped stone weights, following a consistent system, which suggests organised trade. Thousands of small square seals, often showing animals like a one-horned beast, bulls or elephants, with short inscriptions, were probably pressed into clay to seal and identify goods and their owners. The one-horned animal, sometimes called a unicorn, is the most common image, and its meaning is unknown.

sections.key: The Indus script has never been deciphered, so we can't read their words.
sections.b: Several thousand inscribed objects survive, using around 400 different signs, but most inscriptions are only about five signs long. There's no long text and no bilingual inscription to act as a key, as the Rosetta Stone did for Egyptian. Many decipherment attempts have been published, but none is accepted by scholars. Some researchers even debate whether the signs fully recorded language, although most think they did. Scholars do agree it was usually written from right to left. Until it is read, we don't know the civilisation's language, the names of any people, or what their inscriptions actually say.

sections.key: Indus cities show little clear evidence of palaces, royal tombs or large-scale warfare.
sections.b: Unlike Egypt and Mesopotamia, Indus sites have revealed no obvious palaces, grand royal tombs or monuments glorifying rulers. A small stone bust from Mohenjo-daro was nicknamed the 'Priest-King' by archaeologists, but nobody knows who it shows. Houses vary in size, yet the gap between rich and poor seems smaller than in other early civilisations. There are few signs of large-scale warfare. This has led some scholars to suggest power was shared among councils, merchants or religious leaders. Others caution that absence of evidence isn't evidence of absence. How these cities were governed remains one of archaeology's great open questions.

sections.key: The cities declined after about 1900 BC, probably due to climate and river changes.
sections.b: Over a few centuries, the big cities were gradually abandoned as people moved to smaller villages, especially eastward toward the Ganges plain. The leading explanations involve a weakening monsoon, rivers shifting course or drying up, and a decline in trade with Mesopotamia. Older ideas about a sudden invasion that destroyed the cities are no longer widely accepted. The culture didn't vanish entirely: some farming practices, crafts, weights and possibly religious ideas may have continued into later South Asian traditions. Today, Mohenjo-daro is a UNESCO World Heritage site, threatened by salt and erosion, and new finds keep reshaping what we know.

quiz.q: Why is it also called the Harappan civilisation?
o: After Harappa, the first of its sites to be excavated
After the river it grew along
After the language its people spoke
quiz.e: Harappa was excavated in the 1920s, followed soon after by Mohenjo-daro.

quiz.q: What suggests Indus cities were carefully organised?
quiz.e: Standard bricks were used over hundreds of kilometres.

quiz.q: What was unusual about Indus homes?
o: Many had bathrooms connected to covered drains
quiz.e: Sanitation was remarkably advanced.

quiz.q: Why can't we read the Indus script?
o: It's never been deciphered, with no bilingual key
quiz.e: Most inscriptions are very short.

quiz.q: What probably caused the decline of Indus cities?
quiz.e: Rivers shifted and monsoons weakened.

LESSONS.title: Ancient China and the first emperor
LESSONS.hook: One ruler united China, standardised its writing, linked its first great walls and was buried with an army of clay soldiers.

sections.key: Chinese history is traditionally told as a series of ruling families called dynasties.
sections.b: Chinese civilisation grew along the Yellow and Yangtze rivers, where people farmed millet and rice. The Shang dynasty (about 1600–1046 BC) left the earliest known Chinese writing, on oracle bones: priests carved questions to ancestors onto bones and shells, heated them and read the cracks. The Shang were also masters of bronze casting. The Zhou dynasty that overthrew them introduced the Mandate of Heaven: the idea that heaven granted the right to rule to a just ruler, and withdrew it from a bad one. Floods, famines and revolts could be read as signs a dynasty had lost the mandate, which justified rebellion.

sections.key: From about 475 to 221 BC, rival states fought for control of China.
sections.b: As Zhou power faded, China split into competing states, and by the end seven major powers were fighting for survival. Constant war drove new ideas, in what is often called the age of the Hundred Schools of Thought. Confucius (who lived slightly earlier) taught respect, duty, family loyalty and government by virtuous example. Daoism, traditionally traced to the possibly legendary Laozi, emphasised harmony with nature. Legalists argued that strict laws, rewards and harsh punishments made a state strong. Military thinking flourished too, including The Art of War, traditionally credited to Sun Tzu. Iron tools and crossbows also changed farming and warfare.

sections.key: In 221 BC the state of Qin conquered its rivals and its king became China's first emperor.
sections.b: King Ying Zheng of Qin, using Legalist ideas and a ruthless, well-organised army, conquered the other states and declared himself Qin Shi Huang, 'First Emperor of Qin'. The name China likely comes from Qin. He replaced hereditary local lords with officials appointed and paid by the centre, a system later dynasties kept. He was also brutal: according to the historian Sima Qian, writing about a century later, he ordered many books burned and had scholars executed, though some details may be exaggerated. Obsessed with immortality, he sought elixirs of life. He died in 210 BC, and his dynasty collapsed within four years.

sections.key: The first emperor standardised writing, money, weights, measures and even cart axles.
sections.b: To bind his empire together, Qin Shi Huang imposed one writing script, one currency and standard weights and measures. The new coins were round with a square hole in the middle, a design used in China for about 2,000 years. He even fixed the width of cart axles so wagons could travel the same ruts on roads. The standard script mattered hugely: people speaking different languages could read the same characters, and that remains true of Chinese writing today. He also built a network of roads and canals, allowing troops, officials and goods to move quickly between distant provinces.

sections.key: Qin Shi Huang linked earlier walls, but most of the Great Wall seen today was built much later, under the Ming.
sections.b: Several Warring States had built walls against rivals and northern nomads. Qin Shi Huang joined and extended the northern ones into a long barrier, built largely of rammed earth by soldiers, convicts and forced labourers, many of whom died. Later dynasties, especially the Han, built their own walls. Most of the stone and brick wall that tourists visit today dates from the Ming dynasty, mainly the 1400s–1600s, over 1,500 years after Qin. Counting all its branches, the walls stretch more than 20,000 kilometres. A popular myth says the wall is visible from the Moon with the naked eye; astronauts say it isn't.

sections.key: The emperor was buried with around 8,000 life-size clay soldiers.
sections.b: In 1974, farmers digging a well near Xi'an discovered part of an astonishing tomb complex. The Terracotta Army is estimated at around 8,000 life-size soldiers, plus horses and chariots, arranged in battle formation to guard the emperor in the afterlife. Many of the figures have still not been excavated. Each face appears individual, and they were once brightly painted, though most paint flaked off on contact with air. They carried real bronze weapons. The emperor's own burial mound has never been opened. Sima Qian described rivers of mercury inside, and soil tests have found unusually high mercury levels there. Archaeologists are waiting for better preservation techniques.

sections.h: The Han and the Silk Road
sections.key: The Han dynasty (206 BC–AD 220) opened the Silk Road trade routes to the West.
sections.b: The Han dynasty kept Qin's centralised system but softened it, adopting Confucian ideas and choosing officials partly by recommendation and examination rather than birth alone. Around 138 BC, the envoy Zhang Qian travelled deep into Central Asia, and his reports helped open trade routes later called the Silk Road, and Han armies soon secured the Hexi Corridor leading west. Along these routes, silk, spices, horses, glass, ideas and religions moved between China, Central Asia, Persia and India, with Chinese silk eventually reaching Rome. Buddhism reached China from India this way. The Han mattered so much that China's majority ethnic group still calls itself the Han people.

sections.key: Ancient China gave the world paper, early compasses and a merit-based civil service.
sections.b: Han China developed paper, which an official named Cai Lun improved around AD 105, a technology that eventually transformed learning worldwide. Han scholars built early magnetic direction-finders, spoon-shaped lodestones used at first for divination, the ancestors of the compass. The astronomer Zhang Heng designed an instrument around AD 132 to detect distant earthquakes. The idea of choosing officials by exams grew into China's imperial civil service examinations, used for more than a thousand years and admired by European thinkers. The emperor system itself lasted until 1912. Much of modern China's language, philosophy and sense of unity traces back to the Qin and Han.

quiz.q: What was the Mandate of Heaven?
o: The idea that heaven grants the right to rule to a just ruler
quiz.e: Disasters could signal a dynasty had lost it.

quiz.q: Which thinker taught respect, duty and good government?
quiz.e: Confucian ideas shaped China for centuries.

quiz.q: The name 'China' likely comes from which dynasty?
quiz.e: Qin Shi Huang was the first emperor.

quiz.q: Why did a standard script matter so much?
o: People speaking different languages could read the same characters
quiz.e: It helped bind the empire together.

quiz.q: How was the Terracotta Army discovered?
o: By farmers digging a well in 1974
quiz.e: Near Xi'an.

LESSONS.title: The Maya, Aztecs and Inca
LESSONS.hook: Pyramids, floating gardens and a road network across the Andes. The Americas produced great civilisations with no contact with Europe or Asia.

sections.key: Great civilisations developed independently in Mesoamerica and the Andes.
sections.b: People reached the Americas at least 15,000 years ago, most likely from Asia. Without any contact with Eurasia, they domesticated crops that now feed the world: maize, potatoes, tomatoes, cacao for chocolate, chillies, squash and many beans. In Mesoamerica (modern Mexico and Central America) and the Andes mountains of South America, complex societies arose with cities, monumental architecture and states. The Olmecs, from around 1200 BC, are often called Mesoamerica's first civilisation, famous for colossal carved stone heads. In the Andes, Caral in Peru was building large ceremonial mounds nearly 5,000 years ago, around the time of Egypt's early pyramids.

sections.key: The Maya built cities of stone pyramids and developed writing, astronomy and a sophisticated calendar.
sections.b: The Maya flourished especially between about AD 250 and 900, in city-states such as Tikal, Palenque and Copán in modern Mexico, Guatemala, Belize and Honduras. They were never one empire: rival kingdoms formed alliances and fought wars. Kings recorded their deeds on carved stone monuments called stelae. The Maya developed the most complete writing system in the ancient Americas, using several hundred glyphs, which scholars have largely deciphered since the 1970s and 1980s. Many southern lowland cities were abandoned around 800–900, probably due to drought, warfare and environmental strain. But Maya cities in the north, like Chichén Itzá, continued, and millions of Maya people live in the region today.

sections.key: The Maya used a base-20 number system with zero and interlocking calendars.
sections.b: Maya mathematics counted in base 20 using just three symbols: a dot for one, a bar for five and a shell for zero. They were among the few ancient peoples to develop zero independently. Priests tracked the Sun, Moon and Venus with impressive precision and could predict eclipses. The Maya ran several calendars at once, including a 260-day ritual cycle, a 365-day solar year and the Long Count, which tallied days from a starting date in 3114 BC. The idea that the Maya predicted the world would end in 2012 is a modern myth: a Long Count cycle simply rolled over, like an odometer.

sections.key: The Aztecs built the island city of Tenochtitlan and ruled a tribute empire in central Mexico.
sections.b: The Mexica, or Aztecs, founded Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco around 1325. It grew into one of the world's largest cities, with perhaps 200,000 people, connected to the shore by causeways and fed partly by chinampas, farm plots built up from the lake bed with mud and plants. From 1428 the Aztecs led an alliance of three cities that conquered much of central Mexico, demanding regular tribute of maize, cloth, cacao, feathers and gold. They practised human sacrifice on a large scale, believing it helped keep the Sun moving and the world in balance. Modern Mexico City stands on the ruins.

sections.key: The Inca ruled the largest empire in the Americas along the Andes, linked by roads and runners.
sections.b: In the 1400s, especially under the ruler Pachacuti, the Inca expanded from their capital, Cusco, to control an empire stretching about 4,000 kilometres, from modern Ecuador to Chile. They called it Tawantinsuyu, 'the four parts together'. They built a network of roughly 40,000 kilometres of roads, with rope bridges across deep gorges, and relay runners called chasquis carried messages hundreds of kilometres in a day or two. Their stonework, as at Machu Picchu and Cusco, fits so tightly that you can't slide a knife blade between some blocks, and many walls have survived major earthquakes that toppled later Spanish buildings.

sections.key: The Inca organised labour, food stores and records using khipu, knotted cords.
sections.b: The Inca had no written script as we know it, yet they ran an empire of millions. Officials recorded numbers, and possibly other information, on knotted cords called khipu, where the type and position of knots showed values in a base-10 system.
