Instead of money, people paid tax through labour, called mit'a: farming state fields, building roads or serving in the army. In return, the state stored food, cloth and weapons in thousands of storehouses. Farmers built steep terraces to grow crops in the mountains and freeze-dried potatoes into long-lasting chuño. The Inca also spread Quechua as a common language across the empire.

sections.key: Spanish invaders conquered the Aztec and Inca empires in the 1500s, helped by disease and local allies.
sections.b: Hernán Cortés arrived in Mexico in 1519 with a few hundred Spaniards. Allied with tens of thousands of Indigenous people, especially the Tlaxcalans, who resented Aztec rule, he conquered Tenochtitlan in 1521 after a long siege. Francisco Pizarro captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa in 1532, arriving as the empire was split by a civil war between Atahualpa and his brother. Atahualpa paid a huge ransom in gold and silver but was executed anyway. The biggest killer was disease: smallpox and other illnesses, to which Indigenous Americans had no immunity, killed a huge proportion of the population, in some regions the great majority.

sections.key: Indigenous cultures, languages and foods from these civilisations continue today.
sections.b: Millions of people still speak Mayan languages, Nahuatl (the Aztec language) and Quechua (the Inca language). English words like chocolate, tomato, avocado and chilli come from Nahuatl. Potatoes from the Andes transformed European diets and populations, and maize is now among the world's most-grown crops. Only a handful of pre-conquest Maya books survive, because Spanish officials burned many as idolatry. Historians today stress that these weren't vanished 'lost' civilisations but ancestors of living peoples, whose histories were long told mostly by their conquerors. Many Indigenous communities now lead efforts to protect their languages, sites and traditions, and to tell those histories themselves.

quiz.q: Which crop was first domesticated in the Americas?
quiz.e: Along with maize, tomatoes, chocolate and more.

quiz.q: What did the Maya develop that was unusual in the ancient Americas?
quiz.e: Largely deciphered since the 1970s.

quiz.q: What were chinampas?
o: Farm plots built up from the lake bed
quiz.e: They helped feed Tenochtitlan.

quiz.q: What were khipu?
o: Knotted cords used to record numbers
quiz.e: The Inca had no conventional script.

quiz.q: What killed the most people during the Spanish conquest?
quiz.e: Indigenous Americans had no immunity.

LESSONS.title: Athens and Sparta: the Greek city-states
LESSONS.hook: Ancient Greece was never one country. It was hundreds of fiercely independent cities, and two of them couldn't have been more different.

sections.key: Ancient Greece was a patchwork of hundreds of independent city-states, each called a polis.
sections.b: Greece's mountains and islands split people into small, separate communities. From around 800 BC, these grew into city-states, each called a polis (the root of words like politics and police). A polis was a city plus the farmland around it, with its own government, laws, army, coins and gods it especially honoured. Modern scholars have counted roughly a thousand of them, most with only a few thousand people. Greeks shared a language, religion, the oracle at Delphi and the Olympic Games, and called non-Greek speakers 'barbarians'. Yet they fought each other constantly, over borders, trade and pride.

sections.key: Greek city-states planted colonies right around the Mediterranean and Black Sea.
sections.b: Farmland was scarce, so from the 700s BC many cities sent groups of settlers abroad to found new, independent colonies. They spread from Spain to the Black Sea. Marseille in France began as the Greek colony of Massalia, Naples as Neapolis ('new city'), and Istanbul as Byzantium. Syracuse in Sicily became one of the largest and richest Greek cities of all. Colonies usually kept religious and emotional ties to their mother city but governed themselves. The Greeks, as Plato put it, lived around the sea 'like frogs around a pond', linked by ships, trade and ideas.

sections.key: Athens became a centre of democracy, philosophy, drama and art.
sections.b: Athens, built around the rocky hill of the Acropolis, grew rich from trade, the silver mines at Laurion and its powerful navy. In the 400s BC it became the cultural capital of the Greek world. Athenian citizens governed themselves in an early democracy, debating in the Assembly and trading in the agora, the bustling marketplace and meeting ground. The city produced philosophers like Socrates and Plato, playwrights like Sophocles, and the historian Thucydides. Its most famous building, the Parthenon, a marble temple to the goddess Athena, was completed in 432 BC and still stands above the modern city.

sections.key: Sparta organised its whole society around producing elite soldiers.
sections.b: Sparta, in the southern Peloponnese, took a very different path. At about age seven, Spartan boys left home for the agoge, a harsh state-run training system that taught endurance, discipline and fighting. Adult men lived and ate with their army messes and were banned from trade, so their full-time job was war. Spartan women had unusual freedom for the ancient world: they exercised outdoors, owned land and ran estates. All this rested on the helots, a huge enslaved population who did the farming and outnumbered Spartan citizens many times over. Fear of a helot revolt shaped Spartan life.

sections.key: 'Laconic', meaning brief in speech, comes from Laconia, Sparta's home region.
sections.b: Spartans were famous for saying a lot in few words. According to ancient writers, when Philip II of Macedon threatened, 'If I invade Laconia, I will destroy you', the Spartans replied with one word: 'If.' That's where laconic comes from. Spartans also went without city walls for centuries, claiming their soldiers were the walls. Mothers supposedly told sons heading to war to come back 'with your shield or on it'. Their reputation made them legendary, but historians note that most of what we know comes from outsiders, such as Athenians, who admired or feared them, so some of it is myth.

sections.key: Sparta had two kings at once, plus elected officials and a council of elders.
sections.b: Sparta's government was unusual even by Greek standards. It had two kings at the same time, drawn from two royal families, who led the army and performed religious duties. Real day-to-day power was shared with others. A council of elders, the gerousia, had 28 men aged over 60 plus the two kings, and prepared laws. Five officials called ephors were elected every year and could supervise, and even put on trial, the kings. An assembly of adult Spartan men approved major decisions, famously voting by shouting. Greeks admired this mix as a stable, balanced system.

sections.key: Athens and Sparta fought a long, destructive war from 431 to 404 BC, which Sparta won.
sections.b: As Athens built an empire of allied cities, Sparta and its allies grew alarmed. War broke out in 431 BC and lasted, on and off, 27 years. Athens had the stronger navy, Sparta the stronger army, so each struggled to land a knockout blow. A plague struck crowded Athens in 430 BC, killing perhaps a quarter of the population, and its leader Pericles died the following year. A disastrous Athenian invasion of Sicily in 415–413 BC cost thousands of lives. With Persian money, Sparta built a fleet, and in 404 BC a starving Athens surrendered.

sections.key: Weakened by war, the Greek city-states were eventually conquered by Macedon.
sections.b: After the war, city-states kept fighting each other: Sparta, then Thebes, took turns on top. Thebes shattered Sparta's army at Leuctra in 371 BC and freed many of its helots, and Sparta never recovered. Meanwhile, the kingdom of Macedon to the north grew strong under Philip II, who defeated Athens and Thebes at the Battle of Chaeronea in 338 BC. His son, Alexander the Great, would carry Greek culture as far as India. The age of independent city-states was over, but their ideas about citizenship, law and debate have outlived them by thousands of years.

quiz.q: What was a polis?
quiz.e: Each polis had its own government, laws and army.

quiz.q: Which temple stands on the Acropolis in Athens?
quiz.e: The Parthenon, a temple to Athena, was completed in 432 BC.

quiz.q: Who did most of the farming in Sparta?
quiz.e: The helots made Sparta's military lifestyle possible.

quiz.q: What one-word reply did the Spartans reportedly send to Philip II's threat?
quiz.e: He had warned, 'If I invade Laconia, I will destroy you.'

quiz.q: Who won the Peloponnesian War?
quiz.e: Athens surrendered in 404 BC.

LESSONS.title: The birth of democracy
LESSONS.hook: Around 2,500 years ago, the citizens of Athens tried something radical: letting ordinary people make the decisions.

sections.key: Democracy comes from Greek words meaning 'rule by the people'.
sections.b: Demokratia combines demos, the people, and kratos, power or rule. Before democracy, Athens was ruled by aristocrats and, at times, by tyrants: strongmen who seized power. Around 594 BC the lawmaker Solon eased debt slavery and gave poorer citizens a voice, laying groundwork. Then in 508 BC a reformer named Cleisthenes reorganised Athenian society into ten new tribes that mixed people from the city, coast and countryside, so power flowed from citizens across the whole region rather than a few noble families. This is usually counted as the birth of Athenian democracy, though it kept developing over the following decades.

sections.key: In Athens, citizens voted directly on laws and decisions in the Assembly.
sections.b: Athens had a direct democracy: citizens didn't elect representatives to decide for them, they decided themselves. The Assembly, or ekklesia, met about 40 times a year on a hillside called the Pnyx, overlooking the city. Any citizen could attend, speak and vote, usually by a show of hands. A herald opened debate with the question, 'Who wishes to speak?' A quorum of 6,000 was needed for some special decisions. Citizens voted on war and peace, laws, taxes, treaties and building projects. Imagine Australians gathering in person to vote on every new law.

sections.key: Most Athenian officials were picked by random lottery, not elections.
sections.b: Athenians thought elections favoured the rich, famous and persuasive. So most public jobs were filled by lot. A council of 500 citizens, 50 from each tribe, was chosen randomly each year to prepare business for the Assembly. Most people could serve only twice in a lifetime, so many citizens took a turn. They even had a machine, the kleroterion, a stone slab with rows of slots for citizens' name tokens and a tube that released black and white balls to decide who was picked. Only a few jobs needing expertise, like the ten military generals, were elected.

sections.key: Athenian cases were decided by huge citizen juries, with no professional judges or lawyers.
sections.b: Athens had no police force, public prosecutors or professional judges. Ordinary citizens brought cases themselves, and each side had to speak in person, although they could pay a speechwriter. Speeches were timed with a water clock, the klepsydra, which let water run from one pot to another. Juries were enormous, often 201, 501 or more citizens aged over 30, chosen by lot on the day to make bribery hard. They voted by secret ballot using bronze discs and gave no reasons. Socrates was tried by a jury of about 500. Modern juries echo the same idea of ordinary citizens judging cases.

sections.key: Athens paid citizens for jury and Assembly service so poorer people could participate.
sections.b: Democracy only works if ordinary people can afford to show up. A labourer who spent a day on a jury lost a day's wages. So in the mid-400s BC, the statesman Pericles introduced pay for jurors, and around 400 BC Athens began paying citizens to attend the Assembly as well. The amounts were modest, roughly enough to live on for a day. Critics grumbled that it encouraged idle crowds, but it meant farmers, craftsmen and rowers could genuinely take part. Paying politicians and public servants today follows the same logic: public office shouldn't be only for the wealthy.

sections.key: Only free adult men with Athenian parents could take part, perhaps 10–20% of the population.
sections.b: Athenian democracy had big limits. Women couldn't vote, speak in the Assembly or hold office, though they had important religious roles. Enslaved people, who may have made up a large share of the population, had no political rights at all. Foreign residents, called metics, couldn't vote even if their families had lived in Athens for generations, and they paid a special tax. From 451 BC, citizenship required both parents to be Athenian. So 'rule by the people' really meant rule by a minority of free men, a reminder of how much ideas about who counts have changed.

sections.key: Athenians could vote to exile a citizen for ten years, a practice called ostracism.
sections.b: Once a year, Athenians could choose to hold a vote to banish someone they feared was becoming too powerful. Citizens scratched a name on a piece of broken pottery called an ostrakon. If enough votes were cast, probably at least 6,000, the person named most often was exiled for ten years, though they kept their property and citizenship. There was no trial and no crime needed. Famous victims included the general Themistocles, hero of the Persian Wars. Archaeologists have found thousands of these shards, some written in identical handwriting, hinting at organised campaigns. It gave us the word ostracise.

sections.key: Athenian democracy inspired modern democracies, though most today are representative, not direct.
sections.b: Many Greeks criticised democracy. Plato thought it let ignorant crowds and smooth talkers rule, and it was a democratic jury that sentenced his teacher Socrates to death in 399 BC. Athens' democracy lasted, with interruptions, until the Macedonians curbed it in 322 BC. Still, the idea that ordinary citizens should govern themselves proved powerful. When modern democracies emerged in the 1700s and 1800s, their founders studied Athens. Most chose representative democracy, electing people to decide for them, but juries, referendums and citizens' assemblies chosen by lot all echo the Athenian model.

quiz.q: What does 'democracy' literally mean?
quiz.e: From demos (people) and kratos (rule).

quiz.q: In Athens' direct democracy, who voted on laws?
quiz.e: Any citizen could attend, speak and vote.

quiz.q: How were most Athenian officials chosen?
quiz.e: Athenians thought elections favoured the rich and persuasive.

quiz.q: From 451 BC, what did Athenian citizenship require?
quiz.e: Even long-settled foreign residents, called metics, were excluded.

quiz.q: What word comes from the Athenian practice of exiling people by vote?
quiz.e: Voters wrote names on pottery shards called ostraka.

LESSONS.title: Marathon, Thermopylae and Salamis
LESSONS.hook: In the 400s BC the mighty Persian Empire invaded Greece twice. Three battles decided whether Greek civilisation would survive.

sections.key: The Persian Empire was the largest the world had yet seen, stretching from Egypt to India.
sections.b: By 500 BC, the Achaemenid Persian Empire ruled millions of people across three continents, linked by royal roads and governed through provinces called satrapies. Greek cities on the coast of Ionia, in modern Turkey, were under Persian control. When they rebelled in 499 BC, Athens and Eretria sent ships to help, and rebels burned the provincial capital of Sardis. The Persian king Darius I crushed the revolt and resolved to punish Athens. The wars that followed pitted a vast, well-organised empire against a handful of quarrelsome Greek city-states, and the outcome shaped the history of Europe.

sections.key: Greeks fought as heavily armoured hoplites on land and in oared warships called triremes at sea.
sections.b: A Greek hoplite was a citizen-soldier who bought his own armour: a bronze helmet, a large round shield and a long thrusting spear. Hoplites fought shoulder to shoulder in a phalanx, each man's shield partly protecting his neighbour, so discipline mattered more than individual heroics. At sea, the key weapon was the trireme, a sleek warship rowed by about 170 oarsmen on three levels, with a bronze ram at the bow for smashing enemy hulls. Rowers were often poorer citizens, and their importance to the navy later strengthened their political voice in Athens.

sections.key: At Marathon, a smaller Athenian army defeated the Persian invasion force.
sections.b: In 490 BC a Persian fleet landed at Marathon, about 40 kilometres from Athens. The Athenians, joined by the small city of Plataea, were outnumbered but charged across the plain and won a decisive victory. Herodotus says about 6,400 Persians died against 192 Athenians, figures that may be inflated. He also tells of a runner, Pheidippides, who ran roughly 240 kilometres to Sparta to ask for help before the battle. The more famous story, of a messenger running from Marathon to Athens and dying after announcing victory, appears in later writers. It inspired the marathon race at the 1896 Olympics.

sections.key: Xerxes invaded in 480 BC with a huge army, bridging the Hellespont to cross from Asia.
sections.b: Darius died before he could strike again, so his son Xerxes planned a far bigger invasion. His engineers built bridges of boats across the Hellespont, the strait dividing Asia from Europe, and dug a canal through the Athos peninsula so his fleet could avoid a dangerous headland. In 480 BC a vast army and navy moved into Greece. Many Greek cities submitted. Others, led by Sparta and Athens, formed an alliance. When the Athenians consulted the oracle at Delphi, they were told to trust a 'wooden wall', which Themistocles argued meant their ships.

sections.key: At Thermopylae, a small Greek force led by 300 Spartans held a narrow pass for three days.
sections.b: A Greek force of several thousand, including King Leonidas and 300 Spartans, blocked the narrow coastal pass of Thermopylae while the Greek fleet fought nearby at Artemisium. For three days they held off the Persians, including Xerxes' elite troops, the Immortals. Then a local Greek, Ephialtes, showed the Persians a mountain path around the pass. Leonidas sent most of the army away and stayed with a rearguard, including his Spartans and several hundred Thespians, who were killed. It was a defeat, but it bought time and became one of history's great legends of courage.

sections.key: The Greek navy crushed the Persian fleet in the narrow straits of Salamis.
sections.b: After Thermopylae, the Persians burned Athens, whose people had evacuated to nearby islands and towns. A few years earlier, Themistocles had persuaded the city to spend a rich silver strike on a fleet of around 200 triremes. Now he lured the bigger Persian fleet into the narrow straits near the island of Salamis, reportedly by sending a false message that the Greeks were about to flee. Crowded together, the Persian ships couldn't manoeuvre. The Greek triremes rammed and sank many of them while Xerxes watched from a throne on the shore. It was one of history's most important naval battles.

sections.key: In 479 BC, Greek forces defeated the remaining Persian army at Plataea, ending the invasion.
sections.b: Xerxes went home but left a large army in Greece under his general Mardonius. In 479 BC, the largest Greek army yet assembled, commanded by the Spartan Pausanias, defeated it at Plataea, and Mardonius was killed. Around the same time, the Greeks won another battle at Mycale on the coast of modern Turkey, destroying what remained of the Persian fleet there. The invasions were over. Many Greek cities under Persian rule gained their freedom, and Athens became leader of a new alliance, the Delian League, which gradually turned into an Athenian empire.

sections.key: Victory gave Greek culture room to flourish; Herodotus recorded it, becoming the 'father of history'.
sections.b: Had Persia won, Athens' democracy and the golden age of Greek art and philosophy that followed might never have happened. The historian Herodotus, writing a generation later, set out to record the wars and explain why they happened. His Histories are often considered the first real work of history, which is why he's called the father of history. Historians today note he also included myths, rumours and good stories, so his numbers, such as Xerxes' army of millions, are almost certainly exaggerated. Modern estimates for the invading army range much lower, perhaps a few hundred thousand at most.

quiz.q: Why did Persia first attack Athens?
o: Athens had helped Greek cities rebel against Persia
quiz.e: Athens sent ships to support the revolt of 499 BC.

quiz.q: What modern event was inspired by the Battle of Marathon?
quiz.e: Legend says a messenger ran to Athens with the news.

quiz.q: What happened at Thermopylae?
o: A small force held a pass for three days before being defeated
quiz.e: It was a defeat that became a legend of courage.

quiz.q: Why did the Greeks win at Salamis?
o: They lured the Persian fleet into narrow straits
Persia's ships sank in a storm
quiz.e: The large Persian fleet couldn't manoeuvre.

quiz.q: Why is Herodotus called the 'father of history'?
o: He was the first king of Greece
His Histories are considered the first real work of history
quiz.e: He set out to explain the Persian Wars and their causes.

LESSONS.title: Socrates, Plato and Aristotle
LESSONS.hook: Three thinkers, teacher to student to student, laid the foundations of Western philosophy, science and politics.

sections.key: Earlier Greek thinkers began explaining the world through reason rather than myth.
sections.b: Around 600 BC, thinkers in Greek cities began asking what the world was made of, without appealing to gods. Thales of Miletus thought everything came from water, and is said to have predicted a solar eclipse. Pythagoras and his followers found mathematical patterns in music and the cosmos. Heraclitus said everything is always changing: you can't step into the same river twice. Democritus, building on his teacher Leucippus, proposed that all matter is made of tiny indivisible particles, which he called atoms. They were often wrong in the details, but the method mattered: seeking natural explanations and arguing about them openly.

sections.key: Socrates taught by asking questions, exposing what people didn't really know.
sections.b: Socrates (about 470–399 BC) wrote nothing down. We know him through his students, mainly Plato and the soldier-writer Xenophon. A stonemason's son who served as a hoplite, he wandered Athens barefoot, questioning people who claimed to know about justice, courage or goodness, until their confident definitions fell apart. He said he was wise only because he knew how little he knew. In 399 BC, a jury convicted him of corrupting the youth and disrespecting the city's gods, and he was sentenced to death by drinking hemlock. He refused his friends' offer to help him escape.

sections.key: The Socratic method tests ideas through a chain of probing questions rather than lectures.
sections.b: Socrates' technique, often called the Socratic method, starts with a claim, such as 'courage is standing firm in battle', then asks questions that reveal exceptions and contradictions, forcing a better definition. Many dialogues end without a final answer, but everyone understands the problem more clearly. At his trial, as Plato records it, Socrates declared that 'the unexamined life is not worth living'. The method lives on in tutorials, law school classes where students are questioned on cases, and coaching and therapy that help people examine their own assumptions. Its core habit, asking 'how do you know?', is useful anywhere.

sections.key: Plato argued that behind the changing world lie perfect, unchanging 'Forms'.
sections.b: Plato (about 428–348 BC) wrote around 35 dialogues, most starring Socrates, and founded the Academy in Athens, one of the first institutions of higher learning, around 387 BC. He argued that the things we see are imperfect copies of perfect, eternal Forms: every circle you draw is slightly flawed, but the Form of a circle is perfect, and we grasp it with the mind, not the eyes. In his famous allegory of the cave, prisoners chained in the dark mistake shadows on a wall for reality. Philosophy, he said, is the difficult journey out of the cave into the light.

sections.key: In The Republic, Plato imagined an ideal state ruled by philosopher-kings.
sections.b: Plato's most famous work asks: what is justice? His answer imagined a city divided into three classes, workers, guardians and rulers, each doing what it does best, ruled by philosopher-kings trained for decades to know the Good. Guardians would own no private property, and Plato argued that suitable women could be guardians too, a radical idea at the time. He distrusted democracy, partly because it had executed Socrates. Critics, from Aristotle to Karl Popper, have argued his ideal state would be authoritarian. Still, The Republic remains one of the most influential books ever written about politics and ethics.

sections.key: Aristotle studied nearly everything and grounded knowledge in observation.
sections.b: Aristotle (384–322 BC) studied at Plato's Academy for about 20 years, tutored the young Alexander the Great, then founded his own school in Athens, the Lyceum. Unlike Plato, he believed knowledge starts with careful observation of the real world. He wrote on logic, biology, physics, ethics, politics, poetry and more. He dissected animals and described hundreds of species, correctly noting that dolphins breathe air and give birth to live young. He developed the first formal system of logic, the study of valid reasoning. Some of his science was wrong, like the idea that heavier objects fall faster, but his method endured.

sections.key: Aristotle taught that happiness comes from living virtuously, and virtue lies between extremes.
sections.b: Aristotle asked what makes a human life go well. His answer was eudaimonia, often translated as happiness or flourishing: living well by using reason and practising virtues over a whole lifetime, not just feeling good. He argued each virtue is a balance, a 'mean', between two extremes. Truthfulness about yourself sits between boastfulness and false modesty; wit between buffoonery and boorishness. We become virtuous by practice, the way we become builders by building. He also stressed friendship and community as essential to a good life. These ideas, in the Nicomachean Ethics, still shape modern ethics and psychology.

sections.key: Their works passed through Roman, Byzantine and Islamic scholars before shaping medieval and modern Europe.
sections.b: After antiquity, much Greek learning was lost in western Europe but preserved in the Greek-speaking Byzantine Empire and in the Islamic world. In Baghdad from the 800s, scholars translated Aristotle into Arabic, and thinkers such as Avicenna (Ibn Sina) and Averroes (Ibn Rushd) wrote major commentaries. These reached Europe through Latin translations, and in the 1200s Thomas Aquinas blended Aristotle with Christian theology. Plato's dialogues returned to western Europe in full during the Renaissance. The philosopher Alfred North Whitehead later wrote that European philosophy consists of 'a series of footnotes to Plato'.

quiz.q: What did Democritus propose everything was made of?
quiz.e: He was remarkably close to later science.

quiz.q: Why was Socrates sentenced to death?
o: For corrupting the youth and disrespecting the gods
quiz.e: A jury convicted him in 399 BC.

quiz.q: What does Plato's allegory of the cave describe?
quiz.e: Philosophy is the journey out into the light.

quiz.q: How did Aristotle's approach differ from Plato's?
o: He grounded knowledge in observation of the real world
quiz.e: He dissected animals and classified species.

quiz.q: What did Aristotle mean by eudaimonia?
o: Flourishing: living well by practising virtue over a whole life
quiz.e: It describes how a whole life goes, not a passing feeling.

LESSONS.title: Alexander the Great
LESSONS.hook: Before he turned 33, he built one of the largest empires in history. Then it fell apart almost overnight.

sections.key: Alexander was born in 356 BC, son of King Philip II of Macedon, and was tutored by Aristotle.
sections.b: Macedon, north of Greece, was seen by many Greeks as half-barbarian. Philip II turned it into a military power, reorganising its army around the phalanx: dense blocks of soldiers with pikes called sarissas, around five to six metres long. His son Alexander was educated by Aristotle, who taught him philosophy, medicine and literature. Alexander reportedly slept with a copy of Homer's Iliad under his pillow and saw himself as a new Achilles. At 18 he commanded cavalry at Chaeronea. When Philip was assassinated in 336 BC, Alexander became king at 20 and quickly crushed rivals and rebellious Greek cities.

sections.key: Alexander defeated the Persian Empire in a series of battles between 334 and 331 BC.
sections.b: In 334 BC Alexander crossed into Asia with around 40,000 soldiers. He defeated Persian forces at the Granicus River, then beat King Darius III himself at Issus in 333 BC, capturing Darius's mother, wife and daughters. After a seven-month siege of the island city of Tyre, he took Egypt, where he founded the city of Alexandria and was welcomed as pharaoh. In 331 BC he crushed Darius again at Gaugamela, in modern Iraq, and marched into Babylon and the Persian capitals. Darius fled and was killed by his own nobles in 330 BC. Alexander now ruled the old Persian Empire.

sections.key: Stories like the taming of Bucephalus and the cutting of the Gordian knot built Alexander's legend.
sections.b: According to Plutarch, a young Alexander tamed a wild horse no one else could ride by noticing it was frightened of its own shadow and turning it towards the sun. That horse, Bucephalus, carried him for years, and when it died in India Alexander named a city Bucephala after it. At Gordium, in modern Turkey, in 333 BC, he faced a famously tangled knot that legend said only the future ruler of Asia could undo. Ancient accounts differ, but the popular version says he simply sliced it with his sword. 'Cutting the Gordian knot' now means solving a hard problem boldly.

sections.h: To the edge of the world
sections.key: His campaigns reached India before his exhausted army refused to go further.
sections.b: Alexander kept marching east through modern Afghanistan, Uzbekistan and Pakistan, fighting difficult guerrilla campaigns in the mountains. In 326 BC he defeated King Porus at the Hydaspes River, in modern Pakistan, in a hard-fought battle that included war elephants. Impressed by Porus, he let him keep ruling as an ally. Alexander wanted to push on to what he believed was the edge of the world, but at the Hyphasis River his soldiers, who had marched thousands of kilometres over eight years, refused. He turned back, leading part of the army through the Gedrosian desert, a brutal crossing that cost many lives.

sections.key: Alexander was a brilliant tactician who led from the front, but he could also be ruthless.
sections.b: Alexander never lost a major battle. He combined infantry, cavalry and siege engineering skilfully and often charged at the head of his Companion cavalry, suffering many wounds. He tried to blend Greek and Persian rule, adopting Persian dress and court customs and marrying the Bactrian noblewoman Roxana and, later, Persian princesses. At Susa in 324 BC he held a mass wedding of his officers to Persian noblewomen, which angered some Macedonians. He could be brutal: he razed the city of Thebes, killed or enslaved thousands at Tyre, and killed his friend Cleitus in a drunken rage.

sections.key: Alexander died in Babylon in 323 BC, aged 32, and his generals split the empire.
sections.b: In 323 BC, planning new campaigns, possibly into Arabia, Alexander fell ill in Babylon after a banquet and died after about two weeks, aged 32. The cause is still debated: fever, typhoid, malaria, heavy drinking and poison have all been suggested. Asked on his deathbed who should inherit his empire, he supposedly said, 'To the strongest.' His infant son and half-brother were only figureheads, and his generals, the Successors, fought each other for decades. The empire broke into kingdoms, including Ptolemaic Egypt, whose last ruler was Cleopatra, and the Seleucid Empire in Asia.

sections.key: His conquests spread Greek language and culture across the Middle East, starting the Hellenistic Age.
sections.b: The three centuries after Alexander are called the Hellenistic period, from Hellas, the Greek name for Greece. A common form of Greek, koine, became a shared language from Egypt to Afghanistan. Alexandria in Egypt grew into the intellectual capital of the ancient world, with its famous Library and scholars like Euclid, the father of geometry. Its lighthouse, the Pharos, became one of the Seven Wonders. Greek art mixed with local traditions, producing, for example, Greek-influenced Buddhist statues in Gandhara. The New Testament was later written in Greek partly because of this spread.

sections.key: Most surviving accounts of Alexander were written centuries after his death, so historians read them carefully.
sections.b: Several people who marched with Alexander wrote about him, including his general Ptolemy, but those works are lost. The main surviving histories, by Arrian, Plutarch, Diodorus, Quintus Curtius and Justin, were written between about 300 and 500 years later, drawing on those earlier accounts. Some writers portrayed him as a hero, others as a tyrant ruined by power and drink. Coins, inscriptions and the cities he founded add evidence. So when you meet a vivid Alexander story, it's worth asking who told it, when, and why. That habit is the heart of good history.

quiz.q: Who tutored the young Alexander?
quiz.e: Aristotle taught him philosophy, medicine and literature.

quiz.q: Which famous city did Alexander found in Egypt?
quiz.e: It became the intellectual capital of the ancient world.

quiz.q: Why did Alexander turn back from India?
o: His exhausted army refused to go further
quiz.e: They had marched for eight years.

quiz.q: How old was Alexander when he died?
quiz.e: He died in Babylon in 323 BC.

quiz.q: What is the Hellenistic period?
o: The era when Greek culture spread across the Middle East after Alexander
quiz.e: Hellas is the Greek name for Greece.

LESSONS.title: What the Greeks gave us
LESSONS.hook: Theatre, the Olympics, geometry, medicine and thousands of everyday words. You use Ancient Greece every day without noticing.

sections.key: The ancient Olympics began at Olympia, traditionally in 776 BC, and ran for over a thousand years.
sections.b: Every four years, athletes from across the Greek world gathered at Olympia to honour Zeus, whose giant gold-and-ivory statue there was one of the Seven Wonders. A sacred truce allowed safe travel. The earliest event was a sprint of about 190 metres, the stadion, which gave us the word stadium. Later came wrestling, boxing, chariot racing and the pentathlon. Winners received an olive wreath, though their home cities often showered them with rewards. Athletes competed naked, and married women were generally barred from watching. The games ended around AD 393 and were revived in Athens in 1896.

sections.key: The Greeks invented tragedy and comedy as forms of theatre.
sections.b: In Athens, plays were performed at festivals for the god Dionysus in huge open-air theatres; the one at Epidaurus seated around 14,000 and its acoustics still impress visitors. Tragedies, by playwrights like Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides, explored fate, pride and suffering: Sophocles' Oedipus the King is still performed today. Comedies, especially by Aristophanes, mocked politicians, philosophers and celebrities of the day. Actors, all men, wore masks and played several roles, while a chorus sang and commented on the action. Words like drama, scene, chorus, tragedy, comedy and theatre are all Greek.

sections.key: Homer's Iliad and Odyssey, and the Greek myths, remain some of the most retold stories on Earth.
sections.b: The Iliad and the Odyssey, epic poems credited to Homer, were probably written down in the 700s BC after generations of oral performance. The Iliad tells of the rage of Achilles during the Trojan War; the Odyssey follows Odysseus' ten-year struggle to get home. Greeks memorised and quoted them as we might quote Shakespeare. Greek myths of gods and heroes, from Zeus and Athena to Heracles and Medusa, still fill films, novels and games. Phrases like Achilles' heel, a Trojan horse, Pandora's box and a herculean task all come from these stories.

sections.key: Greek thinkers like Euclid, Pythagoras and Archimedes laid foundations of maths and science.
sections.b: Euclid's Elements, written in Alexandria around 300 BC, organised geometry into proofs built from a few simple starting assumptions. It was used as a textbook for over 2,000 years. Archimedes showed that pi lies between 3 10/71 and 3 1/7 and worked out the principle of buoyancy, which explains why ships float. Eratosthenes estimated the circumference of the Earth by comparing noon shadows in two Egyptian cities, getting surprisingly close. Aristarchus even suggested the Earth orbits the Sun. The Greek approach of proving things step by step from clear principles still underpins mathematics.

sections.key: Hippocrates argued disease has natural causes, and the Hippocratic Oath still echoes in medicine.
sections.b: Hippocrates of Kos, born around 460 BC, is called the father of medicine. He and his followers taught that illnesses have natural causes rather than being punishments from the gods, and that doctors should carefully observe and record symptoms, diet and environment. Their theory of four bodily fluids, or humours, turned out to be wrong, yet it dominated Western medicine for about 2,000 years. Their emphasis on observation and ethics lasted too. The Hippocratic Oath, promising to help patients, avoid harm and keep confidences, inspired modern medical pledges, such as the World Medical Association's Declaration of Geneva.

sections.key: Greek columns and temple designs still shape public buildings around the world.
sections.b: Greek temples followed strict proportions and used three main column styles, called orders. Doric columns are plain and sturdy, Ionic columns have scroll-shaped tops, and Corinthian columns are topped with carved acanthus leaves. Builders even used subtle tricks: the Parthenon's columns swell slightly and lean inwards so the building looks perfectly straight from a distance. The Romans copied these styles, and they spread again during the Renaissance and the Greek Revival of the 1700s and 1800s. Look at courthouses, banks and museums, including many in Australian cities, and you'll often see Greek-style columns and triangular pediments.

sections.key: The Greeks added vowels to a Phoenician script, creating an alphabet that led to the one you're reading now.
sections.b: Around the 800s BC, Greeks adapted the alphabet of the Phoenicians, seafaring traders from the coast of modern Lebanon. Phoenician writing recorded only consonants, so the Greeks turned some unneeded letters into vowels, creating one of the first alphabets to represent vowels fully. The Greek alphabet then passed to the Etruscans and Romans in Italy, becoming the Latin alphabet used for English today, and later inspired the Cyrillic script used for Russian. Greek letters are still everywhere in maths and science: pi for circles, delta for change, and alpha, beta and gamma for types of radiation.

sections.key: Thousands of English words come from Greek, especially in science and medicine.
sections.b: English is packed with Greek: democracy, philosophy, biology, geography, telephone, photograph, microscope, psychology and alphabet, from alpha and beta. Medical terms are often Greek: cardiology comes from kardia, heart, and the suffix -itis means inflammation, as in tonsillitis. Many everyday ideas carry Greek names too: an odyssey is a long journey, after Homer's Odysseus; a marathon is a long race; and a narcissist is named after Narcissus, who fell in love with his own reflection. Learning a few Greek roots, like tele (far), graph (write) and bio (life), helps you decode unfamiliar words.

quiz.q: What did ancient Olympic winners receive?
quiz.e: Their home cities often added other rewards.

quiz.q: Which two forms of theatre did the Greeks invent?
quiz.e: Performed at festivals for Dionysus.

quiz.q: What did Eratosthenes estimate?
quiz.e: He used shadows in two cities.

quiz.q: What did Hippocrates teach about disease?
o: It was punishment from the gods
quiz.e: He's called the father of medicine.

quiz.q: Which column style has scroll-shaped tops?
quiz.e: Ionic tops curl into scrolls; Corinthian columns have carved leaves.

LESSONS.title: What actually makes people happy
LESSONS.hook: Money, success, relationships, genes? Decades of research give some surprising and reassuring answers.

sections.key: Researchers measure happiness through life satisfaction and day-to-day emotions.
sections.b: Psychologists usually split happiness, or subjective wellbeing, into two parts: how satisfied you are with your life as a whole, and how you feel from moment to moment. Life satisfaction is often measured with the Cantril ladder, which asks people to rate their life from 0, the worst possible, to 10, the best possible. Daily emotions are tracked with diaries and phone apps that ping people at random times. The World Happiness Report, published since 2012 using Gallup World Poll data, ranks countries each year. Finland has topped it every year from 2018 to 2026, Nordic neighbours like Denmark sit close behind, and Australia regularly places in the top 20.

sections.key: The quality of close relationships is one of the strongest predictors of happiness.
sections.b: The Harvard Study of Adult Development began in 1938, following Harvard students alongside young men from poor Boston neighbourhoods, and was later extended to their children. It's one of the longest-running studies of adult life ever conducted. Its fourth director, psychiatrist Robert Waldinger, summarised the findings: good relationships are the clearest predictor of long, healthy, happy lives, more than wealth, fame or social class. People who were most satisfied in their relationships at 50 were the healthiest at 80, as if warm connections buffered the knocks of ageing. Loneliness, by contrast, is linked to poorer health, faster decline and shorter lives. Quality mattered more than the number of relationships.

sections.h: Money matters, up to a point
sections.key: More money is linked to more happiness, but the gains shrink as income rises.
sections.b: Money does affect happiness, especially when it lifts people out of poverty and constant financial stress. A well-known 2010 study by Daniel Kahneman and Angus Deaton suggested day-to-day emotional wellbeing stopped rising above about US$75,000 a year, while life satisfaction kept climbing. In 2023, Kahneman teamed up with Matthew Killingsworth, whose own data disagreed, and together they found happiness keeps rising with income for most people, but for the least happy fifth or so it levels off. How you spend matters too. Research by Elizabeth Dunn and Michael Norton found spending on others lifts mood more than spending on yourself, and experiences tend to outlast possessions.

sections.key: Genes explain part of happiness, but choices and circumstances matter a lot.
sections.b: Twin studies, comparing identical and non-identical twins, suggest roughly a third to a half of the differences in wellbeing between people is linked to genes, which shape temperament, such as how easily you worry or bounce back. Circumstances matter too: health, income, safety, work and the society you live in. A popular 2005 claim that 50% of happiness is genetic, 10% is circumstances and 40% is under our deliberate control has since been criticised as too neat, including by some of its own authors. Genes set tendencies, not a fixed destiny. Research shows activities like exercise, kindness and connection reliably boost wellbeing, whatever your starting point.

sections.key: Exercise, sleep, kindness, time in nature and absorbing activities reliably improve mood.
sections.b: Regular physical activity is one of the most reliable mood boosters, and even a brisk walk helps. Sleep matters enormously: after a poor night, people rate their mood and patience noticeably lower. Acts of kindness increase happiness in the giver, a finding repeated in studies across many countries. Time outdoors in green spaces and near water is linked to better mood and lower stress. And psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi found people are often happiest in 'flow', fully absorbed in an activity that stretches their skills, like playing music, surfing, gardening or engaging work. Flow tends to happen when the challenge sits just a little beyond what feels comfortable.

sections.key: Many studies find a dip in life satisfaction in middle age, though the pattern is debated.
sections.b: Economists David Blanchflower and Andrew Oswald, analysing surveys from dozens of countries, reported that life satisfaction tends to follow a gentle U-shape: fairly high in early adulthood, dipping to a low somewhere around the mid-40s to early 50s, then rising again into the 60s and 70s. Suggested reasons include the squeeze of work, mortgages and caring for children and parents at the same time, and older people's tendency to focus on what matters most to them. The size of the dip is contested, and some long-term studies following the same people find it small or absent. Either way, the stereotype of a gloomy old age isn't supported.

sections.key: Constantly pursuing happiness can make people less happy.
sections.b: Studies by psychologist Iris Mauss and colleagues found that people who place great value on happiness, and constantly check whether they're happy enough, can end up less happy and, in one study, lonelier. Setting a high bar turns ordinary moments into disappointments. Happiness tends to arrive as a by-product of living well: connecting with people, doing meaningful things and getting absorbed in activities. Accepting negative emotions as a normal part of life, rather than a sign of failure, is associated with better wellbeing over time. Philosopher John Stuart Mill made a similar point in 1873: those who aim at something other than their own happiness often find it along the way.

sections.key: Invest in people, protect sleep and movement, and spend on experiences and others.
sections.b: The research points to a few practical habits rather than a secret formula. Protect time for the people who matter, and treat catch-ups as seriously as work meetings. Move your body most days and guard your sleep. When you have spare money, consider spending it on shared experiences, on buying back time from chores you dislike, or on other people. Look for activities that absorb you, and do small kindnesses without keeping score. Don't treat happiness as a test you're failing. And if low mood persists for weeks, that's worth raising with a GP, since depression is common and treatable.

quiz.q: What did the Harvard Study of Adult Development find best predicts happy, healthy lives?
quiz.e: It has run since 1938.

quiz.q: What kind of spending tends to bring more happiness?
quiz.e: How you spend matters.

quiz.q: Roughly how much of the difference in wellbeing is linked to genes?
o: About a third to a half
quiz.e: Circumstances and choices matter too.

quiz.q: What is 'flow'?
o: Being fully absorbed in a challenging activity
quiz.e: Described by Csikszentmihalyi.

quiz.q: What happens when people constantly chase happiness?
o: They can end up less happy
quiz.e: Happiness is often a by-product.

LESSONS.title: Why new things stop making us happy
LESSONS.hook: The new car, the pay rise, the bigger house. The thrill fades fast. Understanding the 'hedonic treadmill' can save you money and disappointment.

sections.key: People adapt to good and bad changes, returning towards their usual level of happiness.
sections.b: Psychologists Philip Brickman and Donald Campbell described the 'hedonic treadmill' in 1971: as circumstances improve, expectations and desires rise with them, and we end up feeling roughly as we did before. Like a runner on a treadmill, we move without getting anywhere. It's why a pay rise feels wonderful for a few months, then simply becomes the new normal, and the next rise is what we want. Later researchers refined the idea: people don't always return exactly to where they started, and the speed of adaptation varies. Adaptation also works in hard times, helping people recover from setbacks, which is the upside of the same system.

sections.key: A famous 1978 study found lottery winners weren't much happier than others after a while.
sections.b: In 1978, Brickman, Dan Coates and Ronnie Janoff-Bulman compared lottery winners in Illinois with similar people who hadn't won, and with people recently paralysed in accidents. The winners weren't significantly happier than the comparison group, and they took less pleasure in ordinary things like chatting with a friend or hearing a joke. Those with serious injuries were less happy, but less unhappy than most people would predict. The study was small, with only 22 winners, and later research shows some changes, like disability or long-term unemployment, can have lasting effects. Larger recent studies of big lottery wins find modest, lasting gains in life satisfaction. Still, it captured a real pattern.

sections.key: People overestimate how long good and bad events will affect them.
sections.b: Psychologists Daniel Gilbert and Timothy Wilson study 'affective forecasting', how well we predict our future feelings. We're surprisingly poor at it. People overestimate how happy a new job, house or partner will make them, and how devastated they'd be by a breakup, a rejection or a lost election, a mistake called the impact bias. One reason is focalism: we zoom in on the change and forget all the ordinary things that will still fill our days, like commuting, cooking and chatting. Another is that we underestimate our 'psychological immune system', the natural ways we make sense of setbacks and cope with them.

sections.key: Our brains respond most to change, so constant good things fade into the background.
sections.b: Our nervous systems are built to notice change more than steady states. Walk into a room with a strong smell and within minutes you barely notice it; the same happens with a humming fridge, a new sofa or a view you once found stunning. Something always present stops grabbing attention because it no longer carries new information. From an evolutionary angle this makes sense: permanent satisfaction wouldn't have pushed our ancestors to seek food, safety, status or better shelter. Adaptation keeps us striving and learning. The catch is that, in a world full of things to buy, it can leave people endlessly chasing the next upgrade.

sections.key: We judge what we have against others, so rising incomes all round don't always raise happiness.
sections.b: Adaptation has a partner: comparison. We often judge our situation not in absolute terms but against the people around us. Economist Richard Easterlin noted in 1974 that while richer people within a country were happier, average happiness in the United States hadn't risen much as the nation grew richer, a finding now called the Easterlin paradox and still debated. Other research found people report lower wellbeing when their neighbours earn more. Social media makes the comparison group enormous, and mostly shows highlight reels. Noticing whose life you're measuring yours against is a useful first step towards stepping off the treadmill.

sections.key: Variety, gratitude and savouring help good things keep giving.
sections.b: Research suggests several ways to slow adaptation. Add variety: change how, where or with whom you enjoy something. Savour deliberately by pausing to notice pleasant moments, and share them with others, which tends to amplify them. Practise gratitude by naming what you already have. Imagine not having something, a technique the Stoics used, often called negative visualisation. Spacing pleasures out helps too: a 2009 study by Leif Nelson and colleagues found people enjoyed TV shows more when they were interrupted by ad breaks, because the interruptions reset adaptation. Ending a good thing slightly early can leave you wanting more rather than bored.

sections.key: We adapt less to experiences, relationships, and some ongoing stresses like long commutes.
sections.b: Some things resist adaptation. Experiences often keep giving through anticipation, memories and the stories we tell about them, and they're harder to compare with other people's. Close relationships renew themselves through change and shared growth. On the negative side, research suggests people don't fully adapt to some ongoing stresses. Swiss economists Alois Stutzer and Bruno Frey found people with long commutes reported lower life satisfaction, and that higher pay or cheaper housing didn't seem to fully make up for it, a finding they called the commuting paradox. Persistent noise and chronic pain are also hard to get used to, because they keep demanding attention.

sections.key: Weigh daily, ongoing factors more heavily than one-off features when making big decisions.
sections.b: Knowing about adaptation is a practical tool for big choices. When comparing houses, a bigger kitchen or an extra bedroom will soon feel normal, but a 90-minute daily commute will be felt every working day. When weighing jobs, the people you'll spend your days with and how much control you'll have may matter more over time than a modest salary bump. Before a big purchase, ask how you'll feel about it in six months, not six days. Try imagining an ordinary Tuesday in the new situation. And remember that adaptation cuts both ways: you'll likely cope with disappointments better than you fear.

quiz.q: What is the hedonic treadmill?
o: Adapting to changes and returning to our usual happiness
quiz.e: We run to stay in the same place.

quiz.q: What did the 1978 lottery study find?
o: Winners weren't much happier after a while
quiz.e: The study was small but influential.

quiz.q: What is affective forecasting?
o: Predicting how we'll feel in future
quiz.e: We're usually bad at it.

quiz.q: Which helps slow adaptation?
quiz.e: Even ad breaks helped enjoyment.

quiz.q: Which do people adapt to less well?
quiz.e: Weigh daily factors heavily.

LESSONS.title: Gratitude
LESSONS.hook: One of the simplest, most researched ways to feel better. And it takes about five minutes.

sections.key: Gratitude is noticing and appreciating the good things in life and where they come from.
sections.b: Gratitude includes appreciating what you have and recognising that good things often come from other people, or from luck, rather than being owed to you. Psychologist Robert Emmons, a leading gratitude researcher at the University of California, Davis, describes it in two steps: affirming that there is goodness in your life, and recognising that its sources lie at least partly outside yourself. It can be a passing emotion, like the warm feeling when a stranger hands back your lost wallet, or a lasting trait. It's valued in nearly every philosophy and religion, from Stoicism and Buddhism to Christianity, Islam and Judaism, which hints at something useful.

sections.key: People who wrote weekly about things they were grateful for felt better about their lives.
sections.b: In a 2003 study, Emmons and Michael McCullough asked university students to write down, once a week for ten weeks, either five things they were grateful for, five hassles or five neutral events. Entries in the gratitude group ranged from 'waking up this morning' to 'the generosity of friends'. By the end, that group felt more optimistic about the coming week and more positive about their lives overall, and reported fewer physical complaints and more time exercising than the hassles group. Many later studies found similar benefits, though usually modest ones. It was a simple, cheap exercise, which is partly why it caught on so widely.

sections.key: Writing and delivering a letter of thanks produces a strong boost in happiness.
sections.b: In a 2005 study led by Martin Seligman, often called the founder of positive psychology, participants wrote a letter to someone who had been kind to them but whom they'd never properly thanked, then delivered and read it in person. This 'gratitude visit' produced the largest short-term boost in happiness of the exercises tested, with effects lasting about a month. Recipients are usually more moved than writers expect. In 2018, Amit Kumar and Nicholas Epley found letter writers consistently underestimated how surprised and happy their recipients would feel, and overestimated how awkward it would be. That miscalculation is one reason people send far fewer thank-yous than they could.

sections.key: Gratitude counteracts adaptation and the brain's bias towards negatives.
sections.b: Our brains have a negativity bias: criticism, threats and losses grab attention more than praise, safety and gains. That was useful for ancestors scanning for danger, but it can skew how we see an ordinary good day. Gratitude deliberately redirects attention to what's going well, balancing the scales. It also fights hedonic adaptation: noticing a warm home, clean water or a reliable friend makes them feel fresh again instead of invisible. And because gratitude focuses on what others have given, it draws attention outward, away from rumination about ourselves. Grateful people also tend to report better sleep, though that research is mostly correlational.

sections.key: Expressing thanks helps people find, remind and bind to good relationships.
sections.b: Gratitude seems to have evolved partly to strengthen relationships. Psychologist Sara Algoe's 'find, remind and bind' theory proposes that feeling grateful helps us find people who would make good partners and friends, reminds us of existing good relationships, and binds us more closely to them. In studies of couples, partners who felt more appreciated by each other felt more satisfied and were more likely to stay together. Thanking a colleague, a teammate or a partner signals that you noticed their effort, which encourages them to keep helping. Research by Adam Grant and Francesca Gino found being thanked made people more willing to help others too, not just the person who thanked them.

sections.key: Be specific, vary it, and focus on people rather than things.
sections.b: Research suggests quality beats quantity. In one study by Sonja Lyubomirsky and colleagues, people who counted their blessings once a week became happier, while those who did it three times a week didn't, perhaps because it stayed fresh rather than becoming a chore. Be specific: not 'my family', but 'my sister calling to check on me when I was sick'. Focus on people more than possessions. Try imagining life without something good, like your health or a friendship. Link the habit to a routine, like the drive home or brushing your teeth. And say thanks out loud: a text to someone who helped you costs little and means more than you'd guess.

sections.key: Gratitude exercises have real but modest benefits, and aren't a treatment for depression on their own.
sections.b: Gratitude research is popular, and some claims have been oversold. Reviews that pool dozens of studies generally find that gratitude exercises produce small but genuine improvements in wellbeing and mood. However, they often perform only slightly better than comparison activities, like writing about the events of the day, and effects on anxiety and depression are small. Many studies use university students and short follow-up periods. None of that makes gratitude useless: it's free, quick and low risk. But it's one helpful habit among several, not a cure. Anyone dealing with persistent low mood or anxiety should talk to a GP or mental health professional.

sections.key: Gratitude shouldn't mean ignoring real problems or pretending everything's fine.
sections.b: Gratitude isn't toxic positivity. It doesn't mean ignoring injustice, pretending pain isn't real, or being told to 'just be grateful' when something is genuinely wrong, like unsafe working conditions or an unfair relationship. Used that way, it becomes a tool for silencing people. Research suggests gratitude works best alongside acknowledging difficulties, not as a replacement for dealing with them. You can be grieving, struggling or angry about something and still notice a kind neighbour or a good cup of tea. Both can be true at once. Many therapists describe this as holding the hard parts and the good parts together, rather than choosing one story.

quiz.q: In Emmons and McCullough's study, how did the gratitude group feel?
o: More optimistic and positive about their lives
quiz.e: They also reported exercising more.

quiz.q: What did the gratitude letter exercise produce?
o: One of the biggest short-term happiness boosts tested
quiz.e: Recipients are more moved than writers expect.

quiz.q: What is negativity bias?
o: The brain's tendency to focus on bad things more than good
quiz.e: Gratitude helps balance it.

quiz.q: What's a good tip for gratitude lists?
o: Be specific and focus on people
quiz.e: Quality beats quantity.

quiz.q: Does gratitude mean ignoring real problems?
o: No, it works alongside acknowledging difficulties
quiz.e: Both can be true.

LESSONS.title: Friendship and loneliness
LESSONS.hook: Researchers compare the health risks of chronic loneliness to smoking. Friendship might be the most underrated health habit there is.

sections.key: Humans evolved in small groups; social connection is a basic need.
sections.b: For most of human history, being cut off from the group meant danger: fewer people to share food, spot predators or care for you when sick. In 1995, psychologists Roy Baumeister and Mark Leary argued that the need to belong is a fundamental human motivation, comparable to hunger or thirst. People everywhere form bonds easily and resist breaking them. Brain imaging studies suggest social rejection activates some of the same regions involved in the distress of physical pain, though how closely the two overlap is debated. That's one reason exclusion stings so sharply, even when it comes from strangers in a lab game, and why connection feels so good.

sections.key: Chronic loneliness is linked to higher risks of heart disease, dementia and early death.
sections.b: A 2010 review of 148 studies by psychologist Julianne Holt-Lunstad, covering more than 300,000 people, found that those with stronger social relationships had about a 50% greater likelihood of survival over the study periods, which averaged around seven and a half years. The size of the effect was compared with well-known risks like smoking and physical inactivity. Loneliness and isolation are also linked to higher risks of heart disease, stroke, depression and dementia. In 2023, US Surgeon General Vivek Murthy issued an advisory on an 'epidemic of loneliness and isolation', and Australian surveys also suggest a substantial share of adults often feel lonely.

sections.key: Chronic loneliness keeps the body on alert, which may explain some of its health effects.
sections.b: Neuroscientist John Cacioppo spent decades studying how loneliness gets under the skin. He argued it works like a warning signal that we're socially unsafe, putting the brain on alert for threats. Lonely people in his studies tended to sleep less restfully, with more brief awakenings, and showed signs of higher stress and inflammation. Being on alert also changes perception: lonely people are quicker to notice rejection and may read neutral faces as unfriendly, which can make them withdraw further. Cacioppo saw this as a self-reinforcing loop. Understanding it helps: the wariness is a normal response to isolation, not proof that others dislike you.

sections.key: Loneliness is the gap between the connection you want and the connection you have.
sections.b: Being alone isn't the same as being lonely. Some people enjoy plenty of solitude and still feel well connected; others feel lonely in a crowded office, a share house or a marriage. Researchers define loneliness as the painful feeling that your relationships don't meet your needs, either in number or in depth. Social isolation, by contrast, is an objective measure, like living alone or rarely seeing people. The two often overlap, but not always. Young adults report high rates of loneliness, not just older people. Recognising loneliness as a common signal, like hunger, rather than a personal failing, makes it easier to act on.

sections.key: Friendships grow through repeated time together, often more than people expect.
sections.b: Communication researcher Jeffrey Hall, at the University of Kansas, estimated in 2018 that it takes roughly 50 hours together to move from acquaintance to casual friend, about 90 hours to become a friend, and more than 200 hours to become close friends. What you do together matters too: joking around, catching up and meaningful conversation built closeness faster than small talk. Friendship grows from proximity and repetition, seeing the same people regularly at school, work, a club or a sports team. That's why adult friendships can take more effort, and why regular shared activities matter so much. Time together is the raw ingredient.

sections.key: A few close relationships matter more than many shallow ones; small interactions help too.
sections.b: Anthropologist Robin Dunbar suggested humans can maintain roughly five very close relationships, around 15 good friends and about 150 meaningful relationships, the last figure known as Dunbar's number. The figures are rough and debated, but the inner circle matters most for wellbeing. Lighter contact counts too. In studies by Nicholas Epley and Juliana Schroeder, Chicago commuters asked to chat with a stranger on the train enjoyed the ride more than those told to sit quietly, even though most had predicted the opposite. Researchers Gillian Sandstrom and Elizabeth Dunn found that on days when people had more brief chats with 'weak ties', like baristas, classmates and neighbours, they felt happier and more connected.

sections.key: Using technology to actively connect tends to help; passive scrolling rarely replaces real contact.
sections.b: Research on technology and loneliness is mixed and still developing. Video calls, group chats and messages can keep relationships alive across distance, which matters in a country where families are often spread between cities or overseas. Some studies suggest active use, like messaging friends or commenting thoughtfully, is linked to feeling more connected, while passively scrolling through other people's lives is linked to feeling worse, though not all research agrees. A useful test is whether an app leads to real contact or replaces it. Using online groups to find people who share your interests, then meeting in person, often works best.

sections.key: Reaching out is appreciated far more than people expect.
sections.b: Studies show people underestimate how much others appreciate being contacted, especially out of the blue by someone they haven't heard from in a while. So send the message to the old friend. Invite someone for a coffee or a walk. Join something that meets regularly, like a community garden, sporting club, men's shed or choir. Show up consistently, since reliability builds trust. Offering help, through volunteering or checking on a neighbour, is a good way in too. If loneliness feels overwhelming or persistent, talking to a GP or counsellor can help, and in Australia, Lifeline (13 11 14) is available 24 hours a day.

quiz.q: What did Baumeister and Leary argue about belonging?
o: It's a fundamental human need, like hunger
quiz.e: Rejection can feel like pain.

quiz.q: What did Holt-Lunstad's review find?
o: Strong relationships linked to about 50% higher likelihood of survival
quiz.e: Compared to risks like smoking.

quiz.q: What is loneliness?
o: The gap between the connection you want and have
quiz.e: You can be lonely in a crowd.

quiz.q: Roughly how many hours together does it take to become close friends?
quiz.e: About 50 hours for casual friends.

quiz.q: What happened when Chicago commuters were asked to chat with a stranger on the train?
o: They found it awkward and unpleasant
They enjoyed the ride more than those who sat quietly
quiz.e: Most had predicted the opposite.

LESSONS.title: Meaning and purpose
LESSONS.hook: A happy life and a meaningful life aren't quite the same thing. Research suggests you need both.

sections.key: Happiness is about feeling good now; meaning is about connecting to something bigger over time.
sections.b: A 2013 study by Roy Baumeister and colleagues surveyed about 400 Americans and found that happiness and meaningfulness overlap a lot but also differ in revealing ways. Happiness was linked to getting what you want, feeling healthy and feeling good in the present. Meaning was linked to thinking about the past and future, contributing to others, and expressing who you are, and it sometimes came with stress, worry and struggle. Being a taker was linked to happiness; being a giver was linked to meaning. Raising children is the classic example: it can lower moment-to-moment happiness while bringing some of the deepest meaning people report.

sections.h: Frankl and the will to meaning
sections.key: Viktor Frankl argued the search for meaning is the deepest human motivation.
sections.b: Austrian psychiatrist Viktor Frankl was deported by the Nazis in 1942 and survived several camps, including Auschwitz. His wife, parents and brother died in the Holocaust. In Man's Search for Meaning, first published in 1946, he argued that people can endure almost anything if they find meaning in it, and that even in terrible circumstances, we keep the freedom to choose our attitude. He saw meaning coming from three sources: creating something or doing a deed, experiencing love or beauty, and the way we face unavoidable suffering. His approach, which he had begun developing before the war, is a school of therapy called logotherapy, from the Greek logos, meaning 'reason' or 'meaning'.

sections.key: A sense of purpose is linked to better health and longer life.
sections.b: Studies have linked a strong sense of purpose to lower risks of heart disease, stroke, dementia and early death, even after accounting for factors like income, education and existing illness. A 2019 analysis of about 7,000 Americans over 50, for example, found those with the lowest purpose scores were more likely to die during the study period. People with purpose tend to exercise more, use preventive health services and cope better with stress. Researchers can't be certain purpose causes these benefits, since healthier people may simply find it easier to feel purposeful. But the association is consistent across many countries and age groups.

sections.key: Researchers often break meaning into coherence, purpose and significance.
sections.b: Psychologists Frank Martela and Michael Steger proposed in 2016 that meaning in life has three parts. Coherence is the sense that your life makes sense and hangs together, rather than feeling random or chaotic. Purpose is having goals and direction, something you're working towards. Significance, sometimes called mattering, is the feeling that your life has value and makes a difference to someone. People can be strong in one area and weak in another: a new retiree may have a coherent life story but lose the daily purpose work provided. Thinking in these three parts can help you pinpoint what feels missing when life seems flat.

sections.key: Many cultures have concepts for a purposeful life, like the Japanese idea of ikigai.
sections.b: Ikigai is a Japanese word roughly meaning 'reason for being' or 'what makes life worth living'. In Japan it often refers to everyday sources of purpose, like a hobby, a role in the family, looking forward to seeing grandchildren, or community work, not necessarily a grand life mission. It became widely known overseas partly through interest in long-lived communities in Okinawa. The popular four-circle diagram combining what you love, what you're good at, what the world needs and what you can be paid for is a Western addition, not the traditional meaning. Many traditions echo the idea, including Aristotle's eudaimonia, flourishing through living well.

sections.key: Meaning often comes from relationships, contribution, growth and something beyond yourself.
sections.b: Research points to a few common sources of meaning. Close relationships come first for most people. Contributing to others matters, through paid work, volunteering, parenting or caring for someone. Growth and mastery help too: getting better at something that matters to you, whether it's carpentry, coaching or a language. And many people find meaning in connection to something larger, like a community, a cause, nature, faith or cultural tradition. Meaning is usually found in doing rather than discovered by thinking. People rarely stumble on a sense of purpose while waiting for it; it tends to grow from commitments they've already made.

sections.key: The same job can feel like a job, a career or a calling, and people can reshape it to feel more meaningful.
sections.b: Psychologist Amy Wrzesniewski found people tend to see their work in one of three ways: as a job, done mainly for pay; a career, focused on advancement; or a calling, seen as worthwhile in itself. Surprisingly, all three views appeared among people doing the same role, such as administrative assistants. In a study of hospital cleaners, some saw their work purely as cleaning, while others emphasised comforting patients and helping nurses, and found it far more meaningful. Researchers call this job crafting: reshaping your tasks, relationships or how you think about work, to connect it with what you value.

sections.key: Small daily acts of contribution and connection build a meaningful life.
sections.b: You don't need a grand mission. Try asking at the end of each day: what did I do that mattered to someone? Look for ways to use your strengths to help others, even in small ways. Reflect on your values and check whether your calendar matches them. Tell your story: psychologist Dan McAdams found that people who see their lives as stories of growth or redemption, where hard times led to something good, tend to report more meaning and wellbeing. And remember that meaning can grow from difficulty, not just despite it, a point Frankl made from painful experience.

quiz.q: How do happiness and meaning differ, according to Baumeister's study?
o: Happiness is feeling good now; meaning connects past, future and others
quiz.e: Raising children can bring meaning with stress.

quiz.q: What did Viktor Frankl argue?
o: People can endure almost anything if they find meaning
quiz.e: He survived Nazi camps.

quiz.q: What is purpose linked to?
quiz.e: The association is consistent across countries.

quiz.q: What does ikigai roughly mean?
quiz.e: The four-circle diagram is a Western addition.

quiz.q: Where does meaning often come from?
o: Relationships, contribution, growth and something larger
quiz.e: Often found in doing.

LESSONS.title: Mindfulness and meditation
LESSONS.hook: Ancient practice, modern science. What mindfulness is, what the evidence says, and how to start in two minutes.

sections.key: Mindfulness is paying attention to the present moment, on purpose, without judgement.
sections.b: The best-known definition comes from Jon Kabat-Zinn, a molecular biologist who founded the Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction program at the University of Massachusetts Medical School in 1979: paying attention in a particular way, on purpose, in the present moment, and non-judgementally. The idea has deep roots in Buddhist meditation, where the Pali word sati is often translated as mindfulness, but modern programs teach it as a secular skill. You can be mindful while eating, walking or washing the dishes, simply by noticing what you're doing instead of drifting into plans and worries. It's less about emptying the mind and more about noticing what's in it.

sections.key: People's minds wander nearly half the time, and wandering is linked to lower mood.
sections.b: In a 2010 study, Harvard researchers Matthew Killingsworth and Daniel Gilbert used an iPhone app to contact about 2,250 adults at random moments and ask what they were doing, what they were thinking about and how they felt. Minds were wandering about 47% of the time, and at least 30% of the time during every activity except sex. People were less happy when their minds wandered, even to pleasant topics, and mind-wandering seemed to come before low mood more than follow it. The title of their paper summed it up: 'A wandering mind is an unhappy mind'. Mindfulness trains attention to notice the drift and come back.

sections.key: Mindfulness programs modestly help stress, anxiety and depression, but they're not a cure-all.
sections.b: Hundreds of trials suggest mindfulness programs produce small-to-moderate benefits for stress, anxiety and depression, roughly comparable to other active approaches like exercise or relaxation training, rather than clearly better. Mindfulness-based cognitive therapy, an eight-week group program, reduces the risk of relapse in people who have had repeated episodes of depression, and is recommended for that purpose in some national clinical guidelines. But much early research was small or poorly controlled, and some benefits were hyped. Mindfulness doesn't suit everyone. For some people, especially those with a history of trauma, intensive meditation can occasionally bring up distressing experiences, so guidance from a trained teacher matters.

sections.key: Some early brain-change findings haven't reliably replicated, so be sceptical of big claims.
sections.b: Headlines often say meditation 'rewires' or 'grows' the brain. Some small early studies reported changes in grey matter after eight-week courses, but larger and better-controlled studies have often failed to find the same effects. A 2022 study from the University of Wisconsin, combining two randomised trials, found no clear structural brain changes from an eight-week mindfulness course compared with control groups. Brain imaging does suggest meditation affects activity in networks involved in attention and mind-wandering, and very experienced meditators may differ from beginners. But the neuroscience is younger and messier than the marketing. Judge mindfulness by whether it helps you, not by brain-scan claims.

sections.key: Focus on the breath, notice when your mind wanders, and gently return.
sections.b: Sit comfortably, with your back upright but not stiff. Close your eyes or lower your gaze. Notice the physical feeling of breathing, perhaps the cool air at the nostrils or the rise and fall of your belly. Before long your mind will wander to plans, memories or an itch; that's normal and expected, not a failure.
