If studying feels a little like hard work, that's often a good sign.

sections.key: Sleep, short focused sessions and genuine curiosity support all learning.
sections.b: No technique beats the basics. Sleep consolidates memories, and all-nighters before exams harm recall. Short, focused sessions with breaks beat long, distracted ones, so put the phone away while you study. Regular physical exercise supports brain health and mood. Curiosity helps: research suggests that when you're curious about a question, you remember not only the answer but other things around it. Finally, the popular 'learning styles' idea, that people learn best only visually or aurally, isn't supported by evidence; a 2008 review found no good studies backing it. Match the method to the material instead.

quiz.q: Which popular study habit was rated low in usefulness?
quiz.e: It creates familiarity, not knowledge.

quiz.q: What is interleaving?
o: Mixing different types of problems in practice
quiz.e: It feels messier but works better later.

quiz.q: What is elaborative interrogation?
o: Asking why and how to connect ideas
quiz.e: Connections make memories easier to find.

quiz.q: What does the Feynman technique involve?
o: Explaining a concept simply to find gaps
quiz.e: If you can't explain it simply, you don't fully get it.

quiz.q: What does evidence say about 'learning styles'?
o: The idea isn't supported by evidence
quiz.e: Basics like sleep matter more.

LESSONS.title: Focus and deep work
LESSONS.hook: Your attention is your most valuable resource, and your phone is designed to take it. How to get it back.

sections.key: Many apps are designed to capture as much of your attention as possible.
sections.b: Social media, news and many games make money from your attention, mostly through advertising, so they're designed to keep you scrolling. Infinite feeds, notifications, likes and autoplay all use principles from behavioural psychology. Unpredictable rewards are especially compelling: like a poker machine, you never know whether the next refresh will bring something good, so you keep checking. Former tech designers, such as Tristan Harris, have spoken publicly about how these features are engineered. Knowing this helps you see distraction as partly a design problem, not just a personal weakness, and that makes it easier to fix.

sections.key: Switching between tasks costs time and leaves 'attention residue'.
sections.b: Every time you switch from a task to a notification and back, you pay a cost. Researcher Sophie Leroy described 'attention residue': part of your mind stays on the previous task, reducing performance on the new one, especially if the first task was left unfinished. Studies of office workers have found frequent interruptions and long times to get back to deep engagement. Even a phone that's silenced and face down on the desk has been linked in some studies to slightly lower performance on demanding tasks, though results are mixed. Out of sight tends to mean more out of mind.

sections.key: On dull watching tasks, attention fades within about half an hour, a pattern called the vigilance decrement.
sections.b: During World War II, Britain's Royal Air Force wanted to know why radar operators hunting for submarines missed more signals as their watch wore on. Psychologist Norman Mackworth built a 'clock test': a pointer ticked around a dial in small steps and occasionally made a double jump, which observers had to report. Accuracy fell noticeably within the first half-hour and kept sliding. This vigilance decrement has since been found in lifeguards, security screeners and long-distance drivers. Watching for rare events is surprisingly tiring, even though it feels like doing nothing. That's why screening jobs rotate staff regularly, and why road-safety campaigns urge drivers to take a break at least every two hours.

sections.key: Deep work is focused, distraction-free effort on demanding tasks, and it's increasingly rare and valuable.
sections.b: Computer scientist Cal Newport, in his 2016 book Deep Work, coined the term for professional activities done in distraction-free concentration that push your abilities to their limit: writing, coding, analysis, learning hard skills. 'Shallow work' is logistical, easily interrupted tasks like email and scheduling. Newport argues deep work is becoming rarer just as it becomes more valuable, because it produces the results that are hard to copy. Most people can manage only a few hours of truly deep work a day, often less at first, so protecting those hours, ideally when you're freshest, matters most.

sections.key: Alertness rises and falls through the day, so save demanding work for your sharpest hours.
sections.b: Attention isn't constant across the day. For most people, alertness climbs through the morning, dips in the early afternoon, the so-called post-lunch dip, and often recovers somewhat later, though natural night owls peak later than early birds. Timing matters in real life. A 2016 Danish study of around two million national test results found that children scored lower the later in the day they sat a test, and that a 20 to 30 minute break beforehand more than made up for an hour's decline. The practical lesson: notice when your own mind is sharpest, guard that time for your hardest thinking, and push email, admin and routine meetings into the slump.

sections.key: Unfinished tasks nag at your attention, but a specific plan for finishing them quietens the noise.
sections.b: Unfinished business has a way of intruding. Incomplete tasks keep popping into mind, which may help us remember to return to them but pulls attention away from whatever we're doing now. In 2011, psychologists E.J. Masicampo and Roy Baumeister found that reminding people of an unfinished goal made their minds wander more and hurt their performance on an unrelated task. But when people wrote down a specific plan for when, where and how they would finish it, the interference largely disappeared, even though the task itself was still undone. Cal Newport builds on this with an end-of-day 'shutdown ritual': review what's unfinished, note the next step for each, then genuinely stop thinking about work.

sections.key: Flow is deep absorption that happens when challenge matches skill.
sections.b: Psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi studied moments when people become so absorbed that time seems to vanish, from rock climbers to surgeons and painters. He called this state flow. It tends to arise when a task has clear goals, gives immediate feedback, and offers a challenge just a little beyond your current skill. Too easy and you get bored; too hard and you get anxious. Flow is fragile, so a single notification can break it. People often describe flow periods as among the most satisfying of their lives, which makes protecting focus about enjoyment as well as productivity.

sections.key: Breaks, boredom, sleep and nature help restore attention.
sections.b: Attention gets tired. Real breaks, like walking, stretching or looking out a window, restore it better than switching to your phone, which keeps the brain busy with new information. Some research suggests time in nature, even a short walk through a park, helps restore attention. Letting yourself be bored occasionally, without reaching for a screen, gives the mind space to wander, which is linked to creativity and problem-solving. And sleep is non-negotiable: sleep deprivation seriously impairs concentration, memory and judgement. Focus isn't about grinding longer; it's about alternating real effort with real rest.

quiz.q: Why are many apps so hard to put down?
o: They're designed to capture attention, often for advertising
quiz.e: Unpredictable rewards are especially compelling.

quiz.q: What is 'attention residue'?
o: Part of your mind staying on the previous task
quiz.e: Switching has a real cost.

quiz.q: What is 'deep work'?
o: Focused, distraction-free effort on demanding tasks
quiz.e: Coined by Cal Newport.

quiz.q: According to a 2011 study, what stopped unfinished tasks from nagging at people?
o: Writing a specific plan for when and how to finish them
Trying hard not to think about them
quiz.e: A concrete plan quietened the mental noise, even before the task was done.

quiz.q: Which is the best break for restoring attention?
o: A short walk or looking outside
quiz.e: Your phone keeps the brain busy.

LESSONS.title: Mindset: can you get smarter?
LESSONS.hook: Believing you can improve does matter, but the famous research is more modest than the posters suggest.

sections.key: Carol Dweck distinguished a 'fixed mindset' from a 'growth mindset' about ability.
sections.b: Stanford psychologist Carol Dweck proposed that people hold different beliefs about ability. With a fixed mindset, you believe intelligence and talent are set at birth; a failure means you're simply not smart, so it's safer to avoid hard challenges. With a growth mindset, you believe abilities can be developed through effort, good strategies and help from others; a failure is information about what to work on next. Most people hold a mix, and it can vary by area, such as maths versus sport. Her 2006 book, Mindset, became hugely popular in schools and workplaces worldwide.

sections.key: Children praised for effort tackled harder problems than children praised for intelligence.
sections.b: In a 1998 study with Claudia Mueller, school children solved a set of problems and were praised either for being smart or for working hard. Those praised for intelligence then tended to choose easier tasks, avoiding risk to their 'smart' label, enjoyed the work less and did worse after a setback. Some even overstated their scores when reporting them to others. Those praised for effort chose harder tasks and persisted. The takeaway many teachers adopted: praise the process, such as effort, strategy and improvement, rather than fixed traits like being clever or gifted.

sections.key: The brain physically adapts with learning, which supports a growth view of ability.
sections.b: Neuroscience supports the basic idea that abilities can grow. Practice strengthens connections between neurons, and new skills reshape the brain. In a 2004 study, adults who spent three months learning to juggle showed increased grey matter in brain areas that process visual motion, and the gains partly faded once they stopped practising. Other studies have found similar changes in musicians and people learning new languages. Intelligence test scores are fairly stable in adults, and genes play a real role, but skills, knowledge and expertise can be built substantially. You can get much better at almost anything you practise well.

sections.key: Deliberate practice, focused on weaknesses with feedback, builds skill better than repetition.
sections.b: Psychologist Anders Ericsson studied how experts get so good. His answer was deliberate practice: working on specific weaknesses, just beyond your comfort zone, with clear goals and quick feedback, often from a coach. Playing a song you already know is not the same as drilling the bar you keep fumbling. Malcolm Gladwell's book Outliers popularised a '10,000-hour rule', which Ericsson said oversimplified his work. Later reviews found practice matters a great deal but explains less of the difference between people than once claimed, with talent, starting age and opportunity also playing roles.

sections.key: Large studies find mindset interventions have small effects, mainly for struggling students.
sections.b: As mindset became a global phenomenon, researchers tested it at scale. A large 2019 study of over 12,000 US high school students found a short online growth-mindset lesson had a small positive effect on grades, mainly for lower-achieving students, and mostly in schools whose culture supported the message. Some meta-analyses found overall effects near zero, while others argued well-designed programs help specific groups. The honest summary: mindset matters somewhat, but it's not a magic fix, and simply putting up posters or telling people to 'have a growth mindset' does little on its own.

sections.key: Praising effort alone isn't enough; strategy and seeking help matter too.
sections.b: Dweck herself warned about a 'false growth mindset': praising effort even when it's not working, or claiming a growth mindset without changing behaviour. Trying hard with the wrong approach just leads to frustration and, eventually, to the fixed belief that you can't do it. A genuine growth approach means effort plus effective strategies plus seeking feedback and help from people who know more. 'You worked hard' is less useful than 'That approach didn't work; what could you try next?' Effort is the fuel, but strategy is the steering, and you need both to get anywhere.

sections.key: How parents and leaders respond to mistakes may shape mindset more than what they say.
sections.b: Children and employees watch what adults do, not just what they say. A 2016 study by Kyla Haimovitz and Carol Dweck suggested that parents' beliefs about intelligence didn't pass on to their children very directly. What seemed to matter more was how parents reacted to failure: treating a bad mark as a disaster, or as a chance to learn and plan. Workplaces show similar patterns. Teams that treat mistakes as information, and review them without blame, tend to learn faster. If you lead or parent, your reaction to the next setback is the lesson people will remember.

sections.key: Treat abilities as improvable, focus on strategies, and add the word 'yet'.
sections.b: Practical takeaways that fit the evidence: notice when you think 'I'm just not a maths person' and replace it with 'I'm not good at this yet'. See mistakes as feedback, and ask what specifically went wrong. Compare yourself to your past self, not to others. Choose challenges slightly beyond your level, and look for good teachers, coaches or resources rather than relying on effort alone. And be kind to yourself: believing you can improve isn't the same as expecting to be instantly good, and progress in anything real, from guitar to a new job, takes time.

quiz.q: What is a growth mindset?
quiz.e: Proposed by Carol Dweck.

quiz.q: What happened to children praised for being smart?
o: They chose easier tasks and did worse after setbacks
quiz.e: They avoided risking their label.

quiz.q: What did large-scale studies find about mindset interventions?
o: Small effects, mainly for struggling students
quiz.e: Mindset matters, but it's not magic.

quiz.q: What is a 'false growth mindset'?
o: Praising effort even when the approach isn't working
quiz.e: Strategy and help matter too.

quiz.q: Which phrase reflects a growth mindset?
o: I'm just not a maths person
I'm not good at this yet
quiz.e: The power of 'yet'.

LESSONS.title: What emotions actually are
LESSONS.hook: Emotions aren't the opposite of thinking. They're fast, ancient information systems, and understanding them is the first step to handling them.

sections.key: Emotions are rapid responses that prepare us to act on things that matter.
sections.b: An emotion is a coordinated response of body and mind to something significant. Fear raises your heart rate and sharpens attention to threats; disgust makes you pull away from potential contamination, like spoiled food; anger mobilises energy to overcome obstacles; sadness slows us down and can draw support from others. Charles Darwin argued in his 1872 book The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals that emotions evolved because they helped our ancestors survive. They're not irrational noise. They're fast signals about what matters to you, often arriving before you've consciously worked it out.

sections.key: Some facial expressions seem widely recognised, though culture shapes emotion more than once thought.
sections.b: In the 1960s and 70s, Paul Ekman studied people in many cultures, including the Fore people of Papua New Guinea, who had little contact with Western media. He argued that six basic emotions, happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise and disgust, have universally recognised facial expressions. More recent research, including work by Lisa Feldman Barrett, challenges this, showing people often don't make or read these 'classic' faces consistently, and that culture and context shape emotions heavily. Some languages have emotion words with no neat English equivalent. The debate continues, with most researchers now accepting a mix of shared biology and cultural learning.

sections.key: Emotions involve the body: heart, gut, muscles and hormones, not just the mind.
sections.b: Emotions are deeply physical. A racing heart, tight chest, butterflies in the stomach, flushed face or tense shoulders are all part of the emotional response, not side effects of it. Brain regions like the amygdala help detect threats quickly, sometimes before you're aware of them, while areas of the prefrontal cortex help interpret and regulate responses. Hormones like adrenaline and cortisol prepare the body for action. Because the loop runs both ways, the body influences feelings too. That's why physical approaches, like slow breathing, a walk or loosening your shoulders, can genuinely calm emotions.

sections.key: Emotions are brief and aimed at something; moods are longer and more diffuse.
sections.b: Psychologists separate a few related ideas. An emotion is usually brief, lasting seconds to minutes, and triggered by something specific: you're angry at a rude driver. A mood lasts longer, hours or days, and often has no clear cause: you're just irritable today. A 'feeling' usually means the conscious experience of either. Many researchers map feelings along two dimensions: pleasant to unpleasant, and calm to activated. Excitement and anxiety are both high-energy, for example, which partly explains why one can tip into the other. Noticing whether you're dealing with an emotion or a mood helps you respond sensibly.

sections.key: Being able to name emotions precisely helps people manage them better.
sections.b: Researchers call it emotional granularity: the ability to distinguish between similar feelings, like frustrated, disappointed, resentful or embarrassed, rather than just 'bad' or 'stressed'. People with higher granularity tend to cope better with stress and, in some studies, are less likely to turn to unhealthy coping like binge drinking. A precise name suggests a precise response: disappointment calls for something different from anxiety, and loneliness calls for something different from boredom. Some languages offer extra precision: German's Schadenfreude names the pleasure felt at someone else's misfortune. Building a richer emotional vocabulary is a skill anyone can practise.

sections.key: Emotions are essential for good decisions, not just obstacles to them.
sections.b: Neuroscientist Antonio Damasio studied patients with damage to parts of the prefrontal cortex that link emotion and reasoning. They scored normally on intelligence tests and could reason logically about options, yet struggled terribly with everyday decisions, sometimes deliberating endlessly over when to book an appointment. In his 1994 book Descartes' Error, Damasio concluded that emotions tag options as good or bad, guiding choices before we reason them through. Emotions can mislead too, as when anger drives rash decisions or fear makes us overestimate rare risks, but decision-making without emotion doesn't work well at all.

sections.key: Emotional intelligence is the ability to perceive, understand and manage emotions in yourself and others.
sections.b: Psychologists Peter Salovey and John Mayer introduced the idea of emotional intelligence in 1990, and journalist Daniel Goleman popularised it in his 1995 bestseller. It includes noticing emotions, understanding their causes, managing your own, and responding well to others'. Some popular claims, such as that it matters more than IQ for success, are overstated and not well supported. Measuring it is also tricky, since many tests rely on people rating themselves. But the underlying skills are real, teachable, and linked to better relationships, teamwork and wellbeing, which is why they now feature in many school and workplace programs.

sections.key: Treat emotions as information: notice, name, then choose what to do.
sections.b: A useful habit is to treat emotions as messages rather than commands. First, notice what's happening in your body. Then name the feeling as precisely as you can. Ask what it might be telling you: anger often signals that something feels unfair, anxiety that something matters and feels uncertain. Then decide what, if anything, to do. Check the basics too, since being hungry, tired or run-down amplifies everything. Avoid big decisions at an emotional peak. And if strong emotions regularly feel unmanageable, talking to a GP or psychologist is a sensible, practical step.

quiz.q: What's a good description of emotions?
o: Fast responses that prepare us to act on what matters
quiz.e: Darwin argued they evolved for survival.

quiz.q: Who argued six basic emotions have universal facial expressions?
quiz.e: Recent research challenges this.

quiz.q: What is emotional granularity?
quiz.e: Linked to better coping.

quiz.q: What did Damasio find about patients unable to link emotion and reasoning?
o: They struggled to make everyday decisions
quiz.e: Emotions guide choices.

quiz.q: Who introduced the idea of emotional intelligence in 1990?
quiz.e: Goleman popularised it in 1995.

LESSONS.title: Managing big emotions
LESSONS.hook: You can't stop feeling things. But you can change what happens next. Evidence-based ways to handle anger, anxiety and overwhelm.

sections.key: Emotional regulation means influencing emotions, not bottling them up.
sections.b: Emotional regulation is how we influence which emotions we have, when we have them, and how we express them. It isn't the same as suppression, pushing feelings down and hiding them behind a neutral face. Research by Stanford psychologist James Gross and others found habitual suppression tends to backfire: it doesn't reduce the inner experience much, raises physical signs of stress and can make relationships feel less close, because others sense something is being held back. Healthy regulation changes the emotion itself or how we respond to it, rather than just covering it up.

sections.key: You can shape an emotion at several stages, from choosing situations to changing your response.
sections.b: Gross's widely used 'process model' describes five points where we can influence emotions. Situation selection: choosing whether to go into a situation at all, like skipping a party where an ex will be. Situation modification: changing it, like moving a tense chat to a walk. Attentional deployment: shifting focus, such as distracting yourself during a painful injection. Cognitive change: rethinking what the situation means. Response modulation: changing how you act once the emotion is here, for instance by breathing slowly. Earlier strategies are often easier, because the emotion hasn't built up steam yet.

sections.key: Creating a pause between feeling and acting is the foundation of regulation.
sections.b: Strong emotions push us to act immediately: shout, send the angry email, storm out. A short pause lets the thinking parts of the brain catch up with the fast, reactive ones. Techniques include counting to ten, stepping away, or saying 'let me get back to you on that'. Some therapists teach the acronym STOP: Stop, Take a breath, Observe what you're feeling, Proceed deliberately. For written messages, a simple rule helps: draft it, but don't send it until tomorrow. The Stoics had a similar idea: the gap between event and reaction is where our freedom lies.

sections.key: Trusted people help regulate our emotions, even through simple touch.
sections.b: We don't regulate emotions only on our own. Humans evolved to lean on each other, a process psychologists call co-regulation. In a well-known 2006 study, psychologist James Coan and colleagues scanned the brains of married women while they waited for a possible mild electric shock. Holding their husband's hand reduced activity in threat-related brain regions, holding a stranger's hand helped less, and the calming effect was strongest in the happiest marriages. Babies learn to settle through a carer's soothing voice and touch, and adults keep using the same system. Talking a problem through with a calm friend or getting a hug can take the edge off distress. Choose carefully, though: anxious people can also wind each other up.

sections.key: Reframing how you interpret a situation is one of the most effective regulation strategies.
sections.b: Cognitive reappraisal means changing the meaning you give a situation. A friend didn't reply: instead of 'they're ignoring me', consider 'they're probably busy'. Someone cuts you off in traffic: perhaps they're rushing to a hospital. A racing heart before a speech can be relabelled as excitement, and studies suggest that reframing nerves this way can improve performance. The aim isn't fake positivity but a more accurate, balanced view. Research consistently finds reappraisal reduces negative emotion without the costs of suppression. It's a core skill in cognitive behavioural therapy, one of the best-supported psychological treatments.

sections.key: Putting feelings into words reduces their intensity.
sections.b: Psychiatrist Dan Siegel coined the phrase 'name it to tame it'. Brain imaging research by Matthew Lieberman at UCLA found that labelling an emotion, simply thinking or saying 'I feel anxious', reduces activity in the amygdala and increases activity in parts of the prefrontal cortex. Writing about feelings works too: psychologist James Pennebaker found that people who wrote about difficult experiences for 15–20 minutes a day over a few days often showed benefits to mood and even to physical health. Journalling, or talking things through with someone you trust, can be a powerful form of regulation.

sections.key: Emotions rise, peak and pass, so you can often wait out an urge without acting on it.
sections.b: Even intense emotions tend to peak and fade within minutes if we don't keep feeding them with fresh thoughts. Psychologist Alan Marlatt, who worked on addiction, described 'urge surfing': observing a craving or impulse like a wave, noticing where you feel it in the body, and letting it crest and subside without acting on it. Dialectical behaviour therapy, developed by Marsha Linehan, adds 'opposite action': when an emotion pushes you towards something unhelpful, gently do the opposite, such as approaching when fear says avoid. Acceptance and action work together here.

sections.key: Sleep, food, exercise and connection make emotions much easier to manage.
sections.b: Everything is harder when you're exhausted, hungry or isolated. Research suggests sleep deprivation makes the amygdala more reactive, so minor frustrations feel huge. 'Hangry' has some basis too: being hungry can make people more irritable. Regular exercise reduces anxiety and improves mood, and time with trusted people helps us process feelings. Alcohol may take the edge off briefly but tends to worsen mood and sleep afterwards. If emotions regularly feel overwhelming, a GP or psychologist can help, and in Australia a GP can refer you for Medicare-subsidised sessions. Lifeline (13 11 14) offers 24-hour support.

quiz.q: Why does habitual suppression tend to backfire?
o: It barely reduces inner feelings and raises stress
quiz.e: Healthy regulation changes the emotion or response.

quiz.q: What does STOP stand for?
o: Stop, Take a breath, Observe, Proceed
quiz.e: A pause before acting.

quiz.q: In James Coan's hand-holding study, when was the brain's threat response calmed most?
o: Holding their spouse's hand, especially in happy marriages
quiz.e: Trusted people help regulate our emotions.

quiz.q: What is cognitive reappraisal?
o: Changing how you interpret a situation
quiz.e: A core CBT skill.

quiz.q: What does 'name it to tame it' mean?
o: Labelling an emotion reduces its intensity
quiz.e: Labelling calms the amygdala.

LESSONS.title: Empathy
LESSONS.hook: Feeling with someone isn't the same as understanding them, and both are different from caring enough to help.

sections.key: Empathy includes feeling others' emotions, understanding their perspective, and caring about them.
sections.b: Psychologists often split empathy into parts. Emotional empathy is feeling what another person feels: wincing when someone stubs their toe, or tearing up at a friend's sad news. Cognitive empathy is understanding what someone thinks and feels, seeing the situation from their perspective. Empathic concern, or compassion, is caring about their wellbeing and wanting to help. These can come apart. A con artist may have excellent cognitive empathy with no compassion at all, while someone overwhelmed by emotional empathy may feel so distressed that they struggle to help. Good empathy usually blends all three.

sections.key: Seeing others in pain activates some of the same brain regions as feeling pain ourselves.
sections.b: Brain imaging studies show that watching someone else in pain activates some regions involved in our own pain experience, especially areas tied to its emotional unpleasantness rather than the physical sensation. In the 1990s, researchers in Parma, Italy, discovered 'mirror neurons' in monkeys, cells that fire both when the monkey performs an action and when it watches another do the same. They were once hyped as the key to empathy and even to civilisation; the reality is more complicated and still debated. But we are clearly wired to resonate with others, from contagious yawns to shared laughter.

sections.key: Empathy develops in stages through childhood, from shared distress to understanding other minds.
sections.b: Newborns often cry when they hear another baby cry, an early form of emotional contagion. By around 18 months to two years, many toddlers try to comfort someone who is upset, though they may offer their own teddy, assuming others want what they want. Around age four, most children pass 'false-belief' tests: they grasp that another person can believe something the child knows is wrong. Psychologists call this theory of mind. Understanding others keeps developing through adolescence and beyond, shaped by relationships, conversation and experience, and parents who talk about feelings seem to help it along.

sections.key: Empathy is biased towards people who are similar, close or identifiable.
sections.b: Empathy has blind spots. We feel more for people who look like us, belong to our group, or are close by. We feel more for one named child in trouble than for thousands in a statistic, a pattern called the identifiable victim effect, which charities know well. Psychologist Paul Bloom, in his 2016 book Against Empathy, argued that emotional empathy acts like a spotlight, narrowly focused and easily manipulated, and can distort moral decisions. He suggested compassion and reason are better guides. Others argue empathy is still vital for kindness and connection, but works best balanced with fairness.

sections.key: Constantly feeling others' pain can lead to burnout; compassion is more sustainable.
sections.b: Nurses, carers, counsellors, paramedics and other frontline workers can experience compassion fatigue from absorbing others' suffering day after day. Research by German neuroscientist Tania Singer and colleagues suggests a useful distinction. Empathic distress, feeling others' pain as if it were your own, is draining and activates pain-related networks. Compassion, warm concern with a wish to help, activates reward and connection networks and is more sustainable. In their studies, short compassion training helped people feel more positive when seeing others suffer. Caring well may mean feeling for people, not feeling exactly as they do.

sections.key: Empathic listening means seeking to understand before responding.
sections.b: The most practical empathy skill is listening. Give full attention, which means putting the phone away. Don't rush to fix the problem or compare ('That happened to me too…'), which moves the spotlight onto you. Reflect back what you hear: 'That sounds really frustrating.' Ask open questions like 'What was that like?' and be comfortable with pauses. Validating someone's feelings doesn't mean agreeing with everything they say; it means acknowledging that their experience makes sense from where they stand. People who feel understood calm down faster and are more open to other views.

sections.key: Understanding the other side's perspective helps resolve disagreements and negotiations.
sections.b: Empathy is especially useful, and especially hard, when we disagree with someone. Research by social psychologist Adam Galinsky and colleagues found that in negotiations, actively considering what the other side thinks and wants tended to help people reach better deals for both sides, sometimes more than simply feeling for them. In an argument, try stating the other person's view so well that they'd agree with your summary before you give your own. Understanding someone's reasons is not the same as accepting them, but it makes a real solution far more likely.

sections.key: Empathy can be developed through curiosity, reading fiction and meeting different people.
sections.b: Empathy isn't fixed. Getting to know people from different backgrounds, through work, sport, volunteering or travel, widens the circle of people we naturally empathise with. Some studies suggest reading literary fiction can improve people's ability to understand others' minds, though results are mixed and effects may be small. Curiosity helps most: asking people about their lives and genuinely listening to the answers. Imagining yourself in someone's specific situation, rather than just thinking about them from the outside, makes perspective-taking stronger. And looking after yourself matters, since stress and exhaustion shrink our capacity to care.

quiz.q: What is cognitive empathy?
quiz.e: It can exist without compassion.

quiz.q: What did psychologist Paul Bloom argue in Against Empathy?
o: Emotional empathy is a narrow spotlight that can distort moral decisions
Empathy always leads to fair decisions
quiz.e: He suggested compassion and reason are better guides.

quiz.q: What does research suggest is more sustainable than empathic distress?
o: Compassion, warm concern with a wish to help
quiz.e: It activates reward and connection networks.

quiz.q: What should empathic listening avoid?
o: Rushing to fix or compare experiences
quiz.e: Seek to understand first.

quiz.q: Which may help grow empathy?
o: Meeting different people and reading fiction
quiz.e: Curiosity widens empathy.

LESSONS.title: Resilience: bouncing back
LESSONS.hook: Most people are more resilient than they expect. Resilience isn't a rare trait; it's a set of resources you can build.

sections.key: After hardship, most people recover well, a pattern researchers call 'ordinary magic'.
sections.b: Psychologist George Bonanno studied people after bereavement, disasters and other potentially traumatic events, and found that the most common response is resilience: a period of distress, then a return to fairly normal functioning within months. Psychologist Ann Masten called resilience 'ordinary magic': it comes not from rare personal qualities but from ordinary resources like supportive relationships, problem-solving skills and hope. That doesn't mean hardship doesn't hurt, or that people who struggle longer are weak. It means that, given support, people usually find their way through, often more capably than they expected.

sections.key: Supportive relationships are the strongest predictor of resilience.
sections.b: Across studies of children facing adversity and adults after trauma, one factor stands out: connection. For children, having at least one stable, caring relationship with an adult is one of the most powerful protective factors known. Support helps practically, with meals, lifts, money and information, and emotionally, by reducing loneliness and stress. Asking for and accepting help is a resilience skill, not a weakness. Giving support to others helps the giver too, adding purpose and perspective. Even brief contact counts: a phone call, a coffee or a message checking in can make a real difference.

sections.key: Seeing setbacks as temporary, specific and changeable supports recovery.
sections.b: Psychologist Martin Seligman studied how people explain bad events to themselves. Pessimistic explanations see setbacks as permanent ('it'll always be like this'), pervasive ('everything's ruined') and personal ('it's all my fault'). More resilient explanations see them as temporary, limited to one area of life, and influenced by circumstances as well as your own choices. Losing a job might become 'this is a hard period in my career' rather than 'I'm a failure'. Learning to question catastrophic thoughts, as taught in cognitive behavioural therapy, can shift these patterns over time.

sections.key: Focusing effort on what you can influence reduces helplessness.
sections.b: In a crisis, much is outside your control: the economy, the weather, other people's choices, a diagnosis. Resilient people tend to identify what they can influence, even small things like daily routines, sleep, exercise and one concrete next step, and focus their energy there. This echoes the ancient Stoic idea of separating what's up to us from what isn't. A useful exercise is to draw two circles, listing worries in one and actions in the other. Taking small actions restores a sense of agency, which counteracts the helplessness that fuels despair.

sections.key: Moderate, manageable challenges can build the capacity to cope with later ones.
sections.b: A life with no difficulty at all may not be ideal preparation for hard times. A 2010 US study by Mark Seery and colleagues found that people who had experienced some adversity in their lives reported better mental health and wellbeing than both those with a great deal of adversity and those with none. The idea, sometimes called stress inoculation, is that coping with manageable challenges builds skills and confidence. This doesn't mean hardship is good or should be sought out, and severe or ongoing stress is clearly harmful. But past struggles you got through can be evidence you'll cope again.

sections.key: Some people experience 'post-traumatic growth', finding new meaning after hardship.
sections.b: Psychologists Richard Tedeschi and Lawrence Calhoun described post-traumatic growth: after struggling with major adversity, some people report deeper relationships, greater appreciation of life, new priorities or a stronger sense of personal strength. Viktor Frankl, an Austrian psychiatrist who survived Nazi concentration camps, wrote in his 1946 book Man's Search for Meaning that having a purpose, someone to return to or work to finish, helped people endure. Growth isn't guaranteed or required, suffering isn't good in itself, and pain and growth often exist side by side. But meaning can emerge, sometimes long after the event.

sections.key: Resilience is shared: strong local connections help whole communities recover.
sections.b: Resilience isn't only individual. After disasters such as bushfires, floods and cyclones, communities with strong social ties, local groups and trusted leaders tend to recover better. Research following Victoria's 2009 Black Saturday bushfires, including the long-term Beyond Bushfires study, found that social connection was linked to better mental health in affected towns. Practical help from neighbours, volunteers and organisations like the SES and Red Cross matters, and so does simply gathering and grieving together. Joining a local club, volunteering or knowing your neighbours builds resilience for everyone before it's needed.

sections.key: Sleep, movement, connection, purpose and self-compassion build resilience before you need it.
sections.b: Resilience is easier to build in calm times. Keep up sleep, exercise and good food, the foundations for coping with anything. Invest in friendships and community. Practise small discomforts, like learning a new skill or trying something unfamiliar, so setbacks feel less foreign. Treat yourself with the kindness you'd show a friend, known as self-compassion, which research links to better recovery than harsh self-criticism. And know when to seek help: support from a GP, a psychologist, or Lifeline on 13 11 14 isn't the opposite of resilience. It's part of being resilient.

quiz.q: What's the most common response to hardship, according to Bonanno?
quiz.e: Masten called it 'ordinary magic'.

quiz.q: What is the strongest predictor of resilience?
quiz.e: Asking for help is a resilience skill.

quiz.q: Which explanation style supports resilience?
o: Setbacks are permanent and all my fault
Setbacks are temporary, specific and changeable
quiz.e: From Seligman's research.

quiz.q: Who wrote Man's Search for Meaning?
quiz.e: A psychiatrist who survived the camps.

quiz.q: What does research say about self-compassion?
o: It's linked to better recovery than harsh self-criticism
quiz.e: Treat yourself like a friend.

LESSONS.title: The Great Depression
LESSONS.hook: In 1929 the world economy began to collapse. By the early 1930s, a quarter or more of workers in countries like the US and Australia had no job, and the politics of the decade turned dark.

sections.key: The 1920s boom in the US was fuelled partly by borrowing and stock speculation.
sections.b: After World War I, the United States boomed. Cars, radios, refrigerators and other electric appliances spread into ordinary homes, often bought on new instalment plans, and share prices soared. Many people bought shares 'on margin', paying a small deposit and borrowing the rest, betting prices would keep rising. That works while prices climb, but a modest fall can wipe out the buyer's whole stake. Farmers, meanwhile, struggled with falling prices after the wartime demand for food ended. The boom rested on shaky foundations: easy credit, unequal wealth, and a widespread belief that prices could only go up.

sections.key: The Wall Street Crash of October 1929 wiped out huge amounts of wealth.
sections.b: In late October 1929, panic selling hit the New York Stock Exchange. On 'Black Tuesday', 29 October, a record number of shares changed hands as prices collapsed, and brokers demanded that margin borrowers repay loans they could not cover. After a brief rally in 1930, the slide continued: by mid-1932 the market had lost about 89% of its peak value, and it did not regain that 1929 peak until 1954. People who had borrowed to buy shares were ruined. But the crash alone didn't cause the Depression; it was the start of a broader collapse in spending, lending and confidence.

sections.key: Thousands of US banks failed, and unemployment reached about 25%.
sections.b: As frightened depositors rushed to withdraw savings, thousands of American banks failed, around 9,000 between 1930 and 1933, with no deposit insurance to protect savers. When a bank collapsed, families simply lost their money. Businesses cut production and workers, so people had less to spend, which led to more cuts: a vicious circle economists call a deflationary spiral. Prices fell, which made existing debts harder to repay. By 1933 about a quarter of American workers were unemployed. Shanty towns of the homeless, nicknamed 'Hoovervilles' after President Herbert Hoover, appeared on the edges of cities.

sections.key: Drought and over-farming turned parts of the US Great Plains into a dust bowl.
sections.b: Nature added to the misery. In the 1920s, farmers on the southern Great Plains had ploughed up millions of hectares of native grassland to grow wheat. When severe drought struck in the early 1930s, the exposed topsoil dried and blew away in enormous dust storms. On 'Black Sunday', 14 April 1935, a wall of dust darkened skies across Oklahoma and Texas. Hundreds of thousands of people left the region, many heading west to California in search of farm work, a story told in John Steinbeck's novel The Grapes of Wrath. The disaster led to new soil conservation programs.

sections.key: The Depression spread worldwide; Australia's unemployment peaked near 30%.
sections.b: The collapse spread through trade and finance. American lenders called in loans made to Europe, and countries raised tariffs to protect their own industries, like the US Smoot-Hawley tariff of 1930. Others retaliated, and world trade shrank by around two-thirds in value between 1929 and 1934. Germany, already burdened by war reparations and foreign debt, was hit especially hard. Australia, dependent on exporting wool and wheat and on borrowing from London, suffered badly as export prices fell and credit dried up. Unemployment peaked at around 30% in 1932, among the highest in the developed world.

sections.key: Australian governments argued fiercely over whether to cut spending or repay debts, and many families relied on 'the susso'.
sections.b: In 1930 Sir Otto Niemeyer of the Bank of England visited and urged Australian governments to cut spending to keep repaying their London loans. The 1931 Premiers' Plan did that, reducing wages, pensions and public spending. NSW Premier Jack Lang refused to pay interest to British bondholders, and in 1932 the NSW Governor, Sir Philip Game, dismissed him, a rare and still-debated event. Unemployed people received food relief known as 'the susso', short for sustenance, often in return for work. Many men went 'on the track', carrying a swag from town to town looking for jobs, and evictions sparked protests.

sections.key: Governments experimented with new policies, including Roosevelt's New Deal.
sections.b: At first, many governments cut spending to balance budgets, which most economists now believe made things worse. In 1933, US President Franklin D. Roosevelt launched the New Deal: public works programs that built roads, dams and schools, bank reforms, federal deposit insurance and, in 1935, social security for older people. Britain's economist John Maynard Keynes argued, most famously in his 1936 General Theory, that governments should spend more during downturns to boost demand. Leaving the gold standard also helped countries recover by freeing them to lower interest rates. Recovery was slow, and full employment returned in many countries only with rearmament for World War II.

sections.key: The Depression fuelled extremism, and shaped modern economic policy.
sections.b: Mass unemployment and despair helped extremist movements, most catastrophically in Germany, where the Nazi Party's vote surged from under 3% in 1928 to about 37% in July 1932 as the economy collapsed. The Depression also shaped economics for generations. Deposit insurance, unemployment benefits, central banks acting as lenders of last resort, and government stimulus during recessions all grew from its lessons. They were used again in the 2008 global financial crisis, when Australia paid cash stimulus to households, and in the 2020 pandemic, with JobKeeper wage subsidies. The period is a reminder that economic hardship can reshape politics, not just household budgets.

quiz.q: What was buying shares 'on margin'?
o: Paying a small deposit and borrowing the rest
quiz.e: It magnified losses when prices fell.

quiz.q: What was Black Tuesday?
o: 29 October 1929, a day of collapsing share prices
quiz.e: The market lost about 89% by 1932.

quiz.q: What were 'Hoovervilles'?
quiz.e: Named after President Hoover.

quiz.q: Roughly how high did Australian unemployment go?
quiz.e: Among the highest in the developed world.

quiz.q: What was the New Deal?
o: Roosevelt's programs of public works and reforms
quiz.e: Launched in 1933.

LESSONS.title: The Holocaust
LESSONS.hook: The systematic, state-sponsored murder of six million Jews by Nazi Germany. Understanding how it happened is essential to preventing it again.

sections.key: The Holocaust was the Nazi regime's murder of about six million European Jews between 1941 and 1945.
sections.b: The Holocaust, also called the Shoah, meaning 'catastrophe' in Hebrew, was the deliberate, organised persecution and murder of European Jews by Nazi Germany and its collaborators. About six million Jews were killed, around two-thirds of Europe's Jewish population, including roughly 1.5 million children. Whole communities that had existed for centuries, in places like Poland, Lithuania and Hungary, were destroyed. The Nazis also murdered Roma and Sinti people, disabled people, Polish and Soviet civilians, Soviet prisoners of war, political opponents, gay men and others. Nazi ideology treated Jews as a 'race' to be eliminated entirely, which made their persecution uniquely total.

sections.key: Persecution escalated gradually from discrimination to murder.
sections.b: The Holocaust didn't begin with killing. After Adolf Hitler came to power in 1933, Jewish businesses were boycotted and Jews were fired from government jobs, universities and the professions. The 1935 Nuremberg Laws stripped Jews of citizenship and banned marriage with non-Jews. In the Kristallnacht pogrom of November 1938, synagogues and Jewish shops were destroyed across Germany and around 30,000 Jewish men were sent to concentration camps. Many Jews tried to emigrate, but most countries, including Australia at the 1938 Evian Conference, accepted few refugees. Each step was tested against public reaction; too few objected. This gradual escalation is one of the Holocaust's most important lessons.

sections.key: Jews were forced into ghettos, and mobile killing units shot over a million people.
sections.b: After invading Poland in 1939, the Nazis forced Jews into overcrowded, sealed ghettos. In Warsaw's ghetto, over 400,000 people were crammed into a small area of the city, and tens of thousands died of starvation and disease. When Germany invaded the Soviet Union in June 1941, mobile killing units called Einsatzgruppen followed the army, helped by police battalions and local collaborators, shooting Jews in mass executions at pits outside towns and villages. At Babi Yar near Kyiv, over 33,000 Jews were murdered in two days in September 1941. Historians sometimes call this phase 'the Holocaust by bullets'.

sections.key: The Nazis built extermination camps where millions were murdered in gas chambers.
sections.b: In January 1942, senior Nazi officials met at the Wannsee Conference to coordinate the 'Final Solution', the plan to murder all European Jews. Extermination camps, including Auschwitz-Birkenau, Treblinka, Sobibor, Belzec, Chelmno and Majdanek, were built in occupied Poland. Victims arrived in packed freight trains from across Europe, from France and the Netherlands to Greece. Most were murdered in gas chambers on arrival; others were selected for slave labour, where many were worked to death. About 1.1 million people were killed at Auschwitz alone, around a million of them Jews. At Treblinka, around 800,000 or more were murdered in little over a year.

sections.key: Some Jews resisted, and some non-Jews risked their lives to rescue them.
sections.b: Despite overwhelming odds, Jews resisted: the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising of April 1943 held out for about a month against German troops, and prisoners revolted at Treblinka and Sobibor that year. Jewish partisans fought in forests across eastern Europe. Many resisted by preserving culture, education and records, like the hidden Oneg Shabbat archive, buried in milk cans and boxes in Warsaw and partly recovered after the war. Some non-Jews hid or rescued Jews at great risk; in 1943 Danes ferried most of Denmark's Jews to safety in Sweden. Israel's Yad Vashem memorial honours rescuers as Righteous Among the Nations. Most people, though, remained bystanders.

sections.key: Allied troops liberated the camps in 1944–45, but survivors faced loss, displacement and often nowhere to return.
sections.b: As Allied armies advanced, the SS forced prisoners on brutal 'death marches' away from the front, and many thousands died. Soviet troops reached Auschwitz on 27 January 1945, now marked as International Holocaust Remembrance Day. British soldiers entering Bergen-Belsen in April 1945 found thousands of unburied bodies; Anne Frank had died there of typhus only weeks earlier. Liberation did not end the suffering. Survivors were often sick and starving, their families murdered and their homes taken. Hundreds of thousands lived for years in displaced persons camps before emigrating to Israel, the United States, Australia and elsewhere.

sections.key: The Nuremberg trials and the new crime of genocide aimed to make such atrocities punishable under international law.
sections.b: From 1945 to 1946, surviving Nazi leaders were tried before an international military tribunal at Nuremberg for crimes including crimes against humanity; twelve were sentenced to death. Further trials followed for doctors, judges, industrialists and camp staff, though many perpetrators were never punished. In 1961 Israel tried Adolf Eichmann, a key organiser of the deportations, in a televised trial that brought survivors' testimony to the world. The word genocide was coined in 1944 by Polish-Jewish lawyer Raphael Lemkin, who had lost much of his family. The United Nations adopted the Genocide Convention in 1948, making genocide a crime under international law.

sections.key: The Holocaust shaped international law and remains a warning about hatred and indifference.
sections.b: Survivors, including many who rebuilt their lives in Australia, told their stories. Melbourne became home to one of the largest communities of Holocaust survivors per head of population outside Israel, and the Jewish Holocaust Centre there was founded by survivors in 1984. Holocaust denial persists, despite overwhelming evidence, including the Nazis' own records, photographs and thousands of testimonies. Remembering matters because the Holocaust was carried out by a modern, educated society, step by step, with laws, bureaucracy and ordinary officials, while many looked away. Its lessons point to noticing early warning signs: dehumanising language, scapegoating and the quiet removal of rights.

quiz.q: About how many Jews were murdered in the Holocaust?
quiz.e: About two-thirds of Europe's Jews.

quiz.q: What did the 1935 Nuremberg Laws do?
quiz.e: Persecution escalated step by step.

quiz.q: What was the Wannsee Conference?
o: A 1942 meeting to coordinate the murder of European Jews
quiz.e: The 'Final Solution'.

quiz.q: Whom does Yad Vashem honour as 'Righteous Among the Nations'?
o: Non-Jews who risked their lives to rescue Jews
quiz.e: Most people remained bystanders.

quiz.q: Who coined the word 'genocide'?

LESSONS.title: The end of empires
LESSONS.hook: In 1945, European empires ruled a large share of the world's people. Within about three decades, most colonies had become independent nations.

sections.key: After WWII, European empires still controlled large parts of Africa, Asia and the Pacific.
sections.b: In the early 20th century, Britain's empire covered about a quarter of the world's land, and after World War I it grew larger still. France, the Netherlands, Belgium and Portugal also held vast colonies. World War II weakened the European powers economically and militarily, and damaged their prestige: Japan had defeated European forces across Asia, capturing Singapore from Britain in 1942. Colonised peoples who had fought for the Allies asked why freedom should apply to Europe but not to them. The 1941 Atlantic Charter had promised people the right to choose their own government, and the new United States and Soviet superpowers both opposed old-style empires.

sections.key: India won independence in 1947, but partition caused mass violence and displacement.
sections.b: India's independence movement, led by figures like Mahatma Gandhi and Jawaharlal Nehru through the Indian National Congress, used mass nonviolent protest against British rule, such as Gandhi's 1930 Salt March to the sea. After the war, a weakened Britain decided to leave quickly. In August 1947 it partitioned the subcontinent into mostly Hindu India and mostly Muslim Pakistan, which then included today's Bangladesh. The borders were drawn hastily. Partition triggered one of history's largest migrations: around 15 million people moved, and between hundreds of thousands and two million died in violence. Gandhi was assassinated in January 1948.

sections.key: Some colonies won freedom only after bloody wars.
sections.b: Where colonial powers resisted, wars followed. Indonesia declared independence in 1945 and fought the Netherlands until 1949; Australian waterside workers supported it by refusing to load Dutch ships. Vietnam defeated France at Dien Bien Phu in 1954, before a long war involving the United States and Australia. Algeria's war against France (1954–1962) killed hundreds of thousands and brought down a French government. In Kenya, Britain brutally suppressed the Mau Mau uprising in the 1950s, detaining tens of thousands in camps. Portugal held on to Angola, Mozambique and Guinea-Bissau until a 1974 revolution in Lisbon, leaving them all by 1975.

sections.key: In 1960 alone, 17 African countries gained independence.
sections.b: Ghana, led by Kwame Nkrumah, became the first sub-Saharan African colony to gain independence from Britain in 1957. In 1960, often called the Year of Africa, 17 nations became independent, including Nigeria, Somalia, the Congo and most of France's colonies. That year British Prime Minister Harold Macmillan told South Africa's parliament that a 'wind of change' was blowing through the continent. Belgium's hasty exit from the Congo was followed by years of crisis. By the late 1970s, most of Africa was independent, though white-minority rule lasted in Zimbabwe until 1980 and apartheid South Africa until 1994.

sections.key: New nations inherited artificial borders, weak institutions and economies built for export.
sections.b: Many colonial borders, drawn up by European powers in treaties during the 'Scramble for Africa' that followed the 1884–85 Berlin Conference, grouped rival groups together or split peoples apart. Colonial economies were often designed to export raw materials like cotton, cocoa, copper or rubber rather than develop local industry. Some colonies reached independence with very few university graduates to run a government. Some new nations built lasting democracies, like India and Botswana; others fell into civil wars, military coups or dictatorships, sometimes backed by Cold War superpowers. Historians continue to debate how much later problems stemmed from colonial legacies versus post-independence choices.

sections.key: Many new nations tried to stay out of the Cold War through the Non-Aligned Movement.
sections.b: Independence arrived as the United States and the Soviet Union competed for influence, and both courted new nations with aid and weapons. In 1955, leaders from 29 Asian and African countries met at Bandung in Indonesia to promote cooperation and oppose colonialism. In 1961 the Non-Aligned Movement was founded in Belgrade, led by figures such as India's Nehru, Egypt's Gamal Abdel Nasser, Indonesia's Sukarno and Yugoslavia's Josip Broz Tito. The 1956 Suez Crisis, when Britain and France failed to retake the Suez Canal from Egypt under American pressure, showed how far the old imperial powers had declined.

sections.key: Papua New Guinea became independent from Australia in 1975.
sections.b: Australia administered Papua from 1906 and took over German New Guinea during World War I, later governing it under League of Nations and then United Nations mandates. The combined territory gained self-government in 1973 and became independent as Papua New Guinea on 16 September 1975, under its first prime minister, Michael Somare. Many Pacific nations gained independence in the same era, including Samoa (1962, from New Zealand), Nauru (1968, from Australian-led administration) and Fiji (1970, from Britain). Today the United Nations has 193 member states, up from 51 founding members in 1945.

sections.key: The end of empire still shapes languages, borders, migration and politics around the world.
sections.b: Imperial history is still visible everywhere. English, French, Spanish and Portuguese are spoken across continents because of it. The Commonwealth of Nations, a voluntary association of mostly former British territories, has over 50 members, including Australia. Britain returned Hong Kong to China in 1997, and Timor-Leste, abandoned by Portugal in 1975 and then occupied by Indonesia, became independent in 2002. The UN still lists around 17 'non-self-governing territories'. New Caledonia, a French territory near Australia, voted against independence in referendums in 2018, 2020 and 2021. Debates continue about apologies, reparations and returning museum artefacts.

quiz.q: How did WWII affect European empires?
o: Weakened them economically, militarily and in prestige
quiz.e: Japan's victories damaged European prestige.

quiz.q: What happened at India's independence in 1947?
o: It was partitioned into India and Pakistan
quiz.e: Around 15 million people moved.

quiz.q: Where did France fight a long war against an independence movement from 1954 to 1962?
quiz.e: Hundreds of thousands were killed.

quiz.q: Why is 1960 called the Year of Africa?
quiz.e: Macmillan spoke of a 'wind of change'.

quiz.q: When did Papua New Guinea gain independence from Australia?
quiz.e: 16 September 1975.

LESSONS.title: The civil rights movement
LESSONS.hook: Bus boycotts, sit-ins and marches. How ordinary people used nonviolent protest to dismantle legal segregation in America, and inspired Australians too.

sections.key: After slavery ended, southern US states imposed segregation laws known as Jim Crow.
sections.b: After the Civil War ended slavery in 1865, southern states passed laws segregating Black and white Americans in schools, transport, restaurants, hospitals and even cemeteries, and used poll taxes, literacy tests and intimidation to stop Black citizens voting. In Plessy v. Ferguson (1896), the Supreme Court approved 'separate but equal' facilities, though in practice Black facilities were far worse. Lynchings, public murders by white mobs, terrorised Black communities; thousands were killed. Millions of Black southerners moved to northern and western cities in the Great Migration, but met discrimination there too. This system of laws and customs was known as Jim Crow.

sections.key: In 1954 the Supreme Court ruled segregated public schools unconstitutional.
sections.b: Lawyers from the NAACP, the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, led by Thurgood Marshall, spent years building legal challenges to school segregation. In Brown v. Board of Education (1954), the Supreme Court unanimously ruled that separate schools were inherently unequal, overturning the reasoning of Plessy for public education. Many southern states resisted fiercely, a campaign politicians called 'massive resistance', and some closed schools rather than integrate. In 1957, nine Black students, the Little Rock Nine, needed federal troops to escort them into a high school in Arkansas. Marshall later became the first Black Supreme Court justice, in 1967.

sections.key: Rosa Parks's arrest in 1955 sparked a year-long bus boycott led by Martin Luther King Jr.
sections.b: In December 1955, Rosa Parks, an experienced activist and secretary of the local NAACP branch, refused to give up her bus seat to a white passenger in Montgomery, Alabama, and was arrested. Black residents, who made up most of the bus company's riders, boycotted the city's buses for 381 days, walking long distances or sharing organised carpools. A 26-year-old minister, Martin Luther King Jr., emerged as a leader, and his house was bombed. The boycott ended in December 1956 after the Supreme Court ruled bus segregation unconstitutional. It showed the power of organised, disciplined, nonviolent mass action.

sections.key: Nonviolent protests drew national attention, culminating in the 1963 March on Washington.
sections.b: In February 1960, four Black students sat at a whites-only lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina, and refused to leave; sit-ins spread across the South. In 1961, Freedom Riders rode buses through the South to challenge segregated terminals and were violently attacked, one bus firebombed. In 1963, police in Birmingham, Alabama, turned fire hoses and dogs on young protesters, shocking the nation on television. That August, around 250,000 people joined the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom, where King gave his 'I Have a Dream' speech. Television coverage helped turn local struggles into a national issue.

sections.key: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 and Voting Rights Act of 1965 outlawed segregation and discrimination in voting.
sections.b: After President John F. Kennedy's assassination in November 1963, President Lyndon B. Johnson pushed Congress to pass the Civil Rights Act of 1964, banning segregation in public places and discrimination in employment. In March 1965, state troopers attacked peaceful marchers on the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma, Alabama, on 'Bloody Sunday'. Months later the Voting Rights Act outlawed literacy tests and other discriminatory voting practices and sent federal officials to register voters. Black voter registration in the South rose dramatically; in Mississippi it jumped from under 10% to around 60% within a few years. The legal foundations of Jim Crow were gone.

sections.key: By the late 1960s, some activists rejected nonviolence, and King's assassination in 1968 shook the movement.
sections.b: Not everyone shared King's strategy. Malcolm X, for years a powerful speaker for the Nation of Islam, argued Black Americans had a right to self-defence and criticised integration as a goal; he broke with the Nation in 1964 and was assassinated in 1965. From 1966, the slogan 'Black Power' called for pride, self-reliance and political power, and the Black Panther Party organised armed patrols and community breakfast programs. Riots erupted in many cities, often triggered by police incidents. King broadened his focus to poverty and the Vietnam War before he was assassinated in Memphis on 4 April 1968. A week later, Congress passed the Fair Housing Act.

sections.key: In 1965, Charles Perkins led a Freedom Ride through NSW to expose discrimination against Aboriginal people.
sections.b: Inspired by the American movement, University of Sydney students led by Charles Perkins, an Arrernte and Kalkadoon man who in 1966 became one of the first Aboriginal university graduates, toured country towns in NSW by bus in February 1965. They surveyed living conditions and exposed segregation at swimming pools, clubs, cinemas and shops. In Moree, where Aboriginal children were barred from the town pool, and in Walgett, the students faced angry crowds. The publicity helped build support for the 1967 referendum, in which about 90.8% of Australians voted to count Aboriginal people in the census and let the federal government make laws for them.

sections.key: The movement ended legal segregation, but debates about equality, voting and policing continue.
sections.b: The civil rights movement transformed American law and politics. Black elected officials, rare in the South in 1965, now number in the thousands, and in 2008 Barack Obama was elected the first Black president. Yet gaps in wealth, health, schooling and incarceration rates remain large, and arguments continue. In 2013 the Supreme Court struck down a key part of the Voting Rights Act, and later protests, such as those after George Floyd's murder by a police officer in 2020, echoed earlier struggles. The movement's methods, patient organising, boycotts, legal challenges and disciplined nonviolent protest, are still studied by campaigners worldwide.

quiz.q: What were Jim Crow laws?
o: Laws enforcing segregation in the US South
quiz.e: Plus barriers to voting.

quiz.q: What did Brown v. Board of Education rule?
quiz.e: Unanimously, in 1954.

quiz.q: What sparked the Montgomery bus boycott?
o: Rosa Parks's arrest for refusing to give up her seat
quiz.e: It lasted over a year.

quiz.q: What did the Voting Rights Act of 1965 do?
quiz.e: Passed after Selma.

quiz.q: Who led Australia's 1965 Freedom Ride?
quiz.e: Exposing discrimination in NSW towns.

LESSONS.title: The First Fleet and colonisation
LESSONS.hook: In 1788, eleven ships arrived in Sydney Cove. For Britain it was a new colony; for the land's Aboriginal owners, it was an invasion.

sections.key: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples had lived in Australia for more than 50,000 years, possibly 65,000 or more.
sections.b: When Europeans arrived, Australia was home to hundreds of distinct Aboriginal nations and more than 250 languages, with Torres Strait Islander peoples to the north. Archaeologists agree people have lived here for more than 50,000 years, and excavations at Madjedbebe in Arnhem Land suggest about 65,000, though that date is still debated. Aboriginal peoples managed the land with fire, fish traps and trade networks, and lived by complex systems of law, kinship and knowledge. Dutch sailors had mapped parts of the coast from 1606, and James Cook charted the east coast in 1770, claiming it for Britain despite its people.

sections.key: Britain sent convicts to Australia after losing its American colonies.
sections.b: Britain had shipped around 50,000 convicts to its American colonies until the American Revolution ended that option in the 1770s. Harsh laws made many minor thefts serious crimes, and prisons and old ships used as floating prisons, called hulks, overflowed. In 1786 the government chose Botany Bay, which Cook's expedition had visited and botanist Joseph Banks had recommended, as a new penal colony. Strategic interests, like a base in the Pacific and access to timber and flax for the navy, may also have played a role; historians still debate how much. Captain Arthur Phillip, a naval officer, was appointed commander and first governor.

sections.key: The First Fleet of 11 ships carried around 1,400 people, about half of them convicts.
sections.b: The First Fleet left Portsmouth on 13 May 1787 and sailed for over eight months, via Tenerife, Rio de Janeiro and Cape Town, where it loaded livestock and seeds. Its eleven ships, two navy vessels, six convict transports and three store ships, carried roughly 1,400 people, including about 750 convicts, marines, officers, sailors and some families. Most convicts had been sentenced for theft; the oldest was in her eighties and the youngest was a child. Botany Bay proved unsuitable, with poor soil and little fresh water, so Phillip moved to Port Jackson, and on 26 January 1788 raised the British flag at Sydney Cove.

sections.key: The colony nearly starved in its first years.
sections.b: Few convicts had farming skills. Crops failed in poor, sandy soils, cattle strayed into the bush, and supply ships were delayed; the store ship Guardian was wrecked in 1789. Rations were cut severely, and Phillip sent people to Norfolk Island to ease the pressure. The Second Fleet arrived in 1790 with hundreds of convicts dead or dying from neglect by the private contractors who carried them. A smallpox epidemic in 1789 devastated Aboriginal communities around Sydney, killing a large share of the local population; how it began is still debated by historians. Only in the mid-1790s did farms along the Hawkesbury River ease food shortages.

sections.key: Early relations with the Eora people mixed curiosity, kidnapping, negotiation and violence.
sections.b: Relations with the Eora and neighbouring peoples began with some curiosity but quickly deteriorated as colonists took fish, land and water. Hoping to learn the local language and customs, Phillip had Aboriginal men captured. Arabanoo, seized at Manly in late 1788, died of smallpox in 1789. Bennelong, a Wangal man, was captured with Colebee later that year, escaped, then chose to return. In 1790 Phillip was speared in the shoulder at Manly Cove, but did not retaliate. Bennelong travelled to England with Phillip in 1792 and returned in 1795. His wife Barangaroo is now remembered in the name of a Sydney precinct.

sections.key: As settlement spread, frontier wars and dispossession devastated Aboriginal communities.
sections.b: Britain treated Australia as terra nullius in practice, land belonging to no one, and made no treaties, apart from John Batman's unrecognised 1835 attempt near Melbourne. As colonists took land for farming and grazing, Aboriginal people resisted, and violent frontier conflicts continued for over a century, into the 1920s. Warriors like Pemulwuy, a Bidjigal man, led resistance around Sydney until he was killed in 1802. Massacres of Aboriginal people occurred across the country; after the Myall Creek massacre in 1838, seven colonists were hanged, a rare case of punishment. Disease, violence and loss of land caused catastrophic population decline.

sections.key: Transportation continued until 1868, and many convicts built new lives as free settlers.
sections.b: Between 1788 and 1868, about 162,000 convicts were transported to the Australian colonies, to New South Wales, Van Diemen's Land (now Tasmania), Moreton Bay and, last of all, Western Australia. Well-behaved convicts could earn a 'ticket of leave' to work for themselves, and many who finished their sentences, known as emancipists, became farmers, merchants and builders. Governor Lachlan Macquarie (1810–1821) championed them, appointing emancipists to official posts and commissioning convict architect Francis Greenway. Free settlers arrived in growing numbers from the 1820s, and opposition to transportation grew. Many Australians today have convict ancestors, once a source of shame, now often of pride.

sections.key: 26 January is Australia Day, but many Aboriginal people mark it as Invasion Day or Survival Day.
sections.b: The anniversary of the First Fleet's landing gradually became a national holiday, observed on 26 January by all states and territories only from 1994. For many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, it marks the beginning of dispossession. On 26 January 1938, the 150th anniversary, Aboriginal activists including William Cooper, Jack Patten and William Ferguson held a Day of Mourning in Sydney, and the date has been a day of protest ever since. Today Australians hold a range of views: some celebrate, some mourn, some want the date changed. Understanding these perspectives is part of understanding Australian history.

quiz.q: When did Dutch sailors begin mapping parts of Australia's coast?
quiz.e: Dutch ships charted parts of the coast from 1606, more than 160 years before James Cook reached the east coast.

quiz.q: Why did Britain start a penal colony in Australia?
o: It could no longer send convicts to America
quiz.e: Prisons were overflowing.

quiz.q: Where did Phillip establish the colony on 26 January 1788?
quiz.e: Botany Bay proved unsuitable.

quiz.q: What was the Myall Creek massacre?
o: A massacre of Aboriginal people in 1838
quiz.e: Frontier violence spread across the country.

quiz.q: What did Aboriginal activists hold on 26 January 1938?
quiz.e: The date remains contested.

LESSONS.title: The gold rushes
LESSONS.hook: In the 1850s, gold transformed Australia almost overnight, nearly tripling its population and sparking its most famous rebellion.

sections.key: In 1851 gold was discovered in NSW and then Victoria, triggering massive gold rushes.
sections.b: In February 1851, Edward Hargraves, freshly back from the California gold rush, found gold near Bathurst in New South Wales and publicised it widely. Within months, even richer finds were made in the new colony of Victoria, at Ballarat, Bendigo and Mount Alexander near Castlemaine. Victoria became one of the richest goldfields in the world, producing a large share of the world's gold during the 1850s. Shepherds, clerks, sailors, shopkeepers and servants abandoned their jobs to head to the diggings. Some ships in Melbourne's harbour were left stranded when their crews deserted for the goldfields.

sections.key: Australia's non-Indigenous population nearly tripled in the 1850s.
sections.b: News of gold spread around the world, and people poured in from Britain, Ireland, Europe, the United States and China. Australia's non-Indigenous population grew from about 430,000 in 1851 to over 1.1 million by 1861, and Victoria's grew roughly sevenfold. Many newcomers were young, educated and skilled, and brought ideas about democracy with them. Gold wealth paid for grand public buildings, railways and banks, and Melbourne grew rapidly into one of the world's richest cities, earning the nickname 'Marvellous Melbourne' by the 1880s. The rushes changed Australia from a collection of convict and pastoral colonies into a diverse, wealthy society.

sections.key: Life on the goldfields was hard, crowded and unpredictable.
sections.b: Diggers lived in tents and bark huts, working claims with picks, shovels, pans and wooden cradles to wash gold from dirt. As surface gold ran out, they sank deep shafts, and later companies used machinery to crush quartz rock. Water, food and supplies were expensive, and diseases like dysentery spread in crowded camps. A few struck it rich, finding huge nuggets like the 'Welcome Stranger', found near Moliagul in Victoria in 1869 and weighing around 72 kilograms. Most found little. Many made their fortunes not from digging but by selling supplies, food, transport and services to the diggers.

sections.key: Tens of thousands of Chinese miners came, facing heavy discrimination.
sections.b: By the late 1850s, around 40,000 Chinese people were in Victoria, mostly men from southern China seeking gold. They often worked in organised groups, patiently reworking claims others had abandoned. Resentment grew, leading to violent attacks, like the Buckland River riot in Victoria in 1857 and the Lambing Flat riots in NSW in 1860–61. Colonies imposed special taxes on Chinese arrivals, so many ships landed at Robe in South Australia instead, and passengers walked hundreds of kilometres to the Victorian fields. This hostility fed into the later White Australia policy. Chinese communities also left lasting legacies, from market gardens to Chinatowns.

sections.key: In 1854, miners at Ballarat rebelled against licence fees and harsh policing at the Eureka Stockade.
sections.b: Miners had to pay for an expensive monthly licence to dig, 30 shillings at first, whether they found gold or not, and police conducted brutal 'licence hunts'. Diggers had no vote. Anger boiled over at Ballarat in 1854 after a hotel keeper was acquitted of killing a miner, and the hotel was burned. Miners formed the Ballarat Reform League, then, led by Peter Lalor, swore allegiance to the blue-and-white Southern Cross flag and built a rough stockade. Early on 3 December 1854, soldiers and police attacked; the fight lasted about 15 minutes, and around 30 people died, mostly miners.

sections.key: Eureka helped win voting rights and became a symbol of Australian democracy.
sections.b: Public sympathy swung behind the miners. In 1855, Melbourne juries refused to convict 13 men charged with treason. The licence was replaced with a cheaper miner's right costing one pound a year, which came with a vote.
