The feeling of choosing is real, but it's produced by brain processes we don't control. In 1814 the French mathematician Pierre-Simon Laplace imagined an intellect that knew the position of every particle and could therefore predict the entire future. Some modern thinkers, like the neuroscientist Robert Sapolsky in his 2023 book Determined, argue this should make us rethink blame and punishment, focusing on prevention, treatment and rehabilitation rather than retribution.

sections.key: Libertarians argue we have genuine free will that isn't fully determined by prior causes.
sections.b: In philosophy, 'libertarian' free will, which has nothing to do with the political kind, holds that some of our choices aren't fully determined: we are the true originators of our actions. Defenders often point to the vivid experience of deliberating between real options. Some point to quantum physics, which suggests that at the smallest scales events may be genuinely random, as showing the universe isn't fully determined. Critics reply that randomness doesn't give us control either: a choice caused by a random event in your neurons isn't more 'yours' than one caused by earlier events. Explaining how uncaused choices would work remains difficult.

sections.key: Compatibilists argue free will is compatible with determinism, defined as acting on your own reasons without coercion.
sections.b: Most professional philosophers are compatibilists: in the large PhilPapers survey of 2020, a clear majority leaned that way. They argue free will doesn't require escaping cause and effect. Instead, you act freely when you act according to your own desires, reasons and values, without being forced, manipulated or compelled. If you choose coffee because you want coffee, that's free, even if your wanting was caused. If someone holds a gun to your head, it isn't. Philosophers such as David Hume in the 1700s and, more recently, the late Daniel Dennett defended versions of this view.

sections.key: Harry Frankfurt argued we can be responsible even when we couldn't have done otherwise.
sections.b: In 1969 the American philosopher Harry Frankfurt challenged a common assumption: that you're only responsible if you could have done otherwise. Imagine a scientist has secretly placed a device in Jones's brain. If Jones is about to decide not to vote for a certain candidate, the device will make him vote for them anyway. But Jones decides to vote for them entirely on his own, and the device never activates. Jones couldn't have done otherwise, yet he seems fully responsible, because the choice came from his own reasons. Frankfurt's cases gave compatibilists a powerful new argument, though debate continues.

sections.key: Brain activity before conscious decisions sparked debate, but doesn't settle the question.
sections.b: In the early 1980s, the neuroscientist Benjamin Libet asked people to flex a wrist whenever they felt like it and to note, using a special clock, when they felt the urge. A build-up of brain activity called the readiness potential began several hundred milliseconds before people reported deciding. Some concluded the brain decides before 'we' do. Later research questioned this interpretation. A 2012 study led by Aaron Schurger suggested the readiness potential may partly reflect random background fluctuations rather than a decision. Libet himself argued people could still 'veto' an action at the last moment. The experiments are debated, not decisive.

sections.key: The Stoics were early compatibilists, while the Epicureans proposed a random 'swerve' of atoms.
sections.b: The debate is ancient. The Stoics believed everything happens according to fate, a chain of causes, yet insisted we are responsible for our actions. Chrysippus used the image of a cylinder: if you push it, it rolls, but it rolls because of its own shape. The push is an outside cause, yet how things respond depends on their own nature. Likewise, events prompt us, but our response comes from our own character and judgement. The rival Epicureans, worried that pure determinism would destroy freedom, proposed that atoms occasionally make a tiny, unpredictable 'swerve'.

sections.key: Views on free will shape how we think about responsibility, punishment and self-improvement.
sections.b: The free will debate isn't just abstract. It affects how we think about criminal responsibility, addiction, poverty and success. Courts already consider factors like age, mental impairment and duress when judging blame. If people's choices are shaped by circumstances they didn't choose, perhaps we should be more compassionate and less quick to condemn, and take pride in our own success more humbly. Yet most people, including most philosophers, think it still makes sense to hold ourselves responsible and try to become better. Whatever the metaphysics, the practical advice is similar: build habits and surroundings that make good choices easier.

quiz.q: What is the problem of free will?
o: If everything is caused, how can choices be free?
quiz.e: Free will versus determinism.

quiz.q: What do hard determinists believe?
o: Free will is real and uncaused
quiz.e: Sapolsky is a modern example.

quiz.q: What do compatibilists argue?
o: Free will and determinism can't coexist
Free will means acting on your own reasons without coercion, even if caused
quiz.e: Most philosophers are compatibilists.

quiz.q: What did Libet's experiments measure?
quiz.e: The interpretation is debated.

quiz.q: Which ancient school were early compatibilists?
quiz.e: They combined fate with responsibility.

LESSONS.title: Existentialism
LESSONS.hook: No script, no predetermined purpose. Existentialists argued we're free to create meaning, and responsible for what we make of ourselves.

sections.key: Existentialists argued humans exist first, then define themselves through choices.
sections.b: In a famous 1945 lecture in Paris, Jean-Paul Sartre summed up existentialism in the phrase 'existence precedes essence'. He used the example of a paper knife: a craftsman has its purpose in mind before making it, so its essence comes first. Humans, Sartre argued, have no pre-set purpose. We exist first, then create who we are through our choices and actions. There's no fixed human nature or divine plan telling us what to be. For Sartre, an atheist, this followed from the absence of a creator. It's both frightening and liberating: you are what you make of yourself.

sections.key: Sartre said we are 'condemned to be free' and fully responsible for our choices.
sections.b: Because there's no script, Sartre argued, we're 'condemned to be free': we can't escape choosing, and even refusing to choose is a choice. With freedom comes total responsibility. This can produce anxiety, what existentialists called angst or anguish. Many people flee it through 'bad faith': pretending they have no choice, blaming their job, upbringing or society rather than owning their decisions. In Being and Nothingness (1943), Sartre described a café waiter whose movements are a little too perfect, as if he were playing at being a waiter, hiding his freedom behind the role.

sections.key: Kierkegaard and Nietzsche, in the 1800s, laid the foundations of existentialism.
sections.b: The Danish philosopher Søren Kierkegaard (1813–1855) focused on the individual facing anxiety and choice. He argued each person must make a passionate personal commitment that reason alone can't justify, which for him meant Christian faith; this is often summarised as a 'leap of faith'. The German philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche (1844–1900) declared in 1882 that 'God is dead', meaning belief in God was fading in Europe, leaving a crisis of values. He feared nihilism, the sense that nothing matters, and challenged people to create their own values and to affirm life fully, even its suffering.

sections.key: After the Second World War, existentialism became a cultural movement centred on Paris.
sections.b: Existentialism was shaped by the Second World War and the German occupation of France, when ordinary people faced stark choices about resistance and collaboration. After liberation, it became a sensation. Sartre, Simone de Beauvoir and their circle wrote and argued in Left Bank cafés such as the Café de Flore, founded the journal Les Temps modernes in 1945, and were followed by newspapers. Existentialist ideas flowed into novels, plays and even fashion, with black clothes and jazz clubs. Sartre was offered the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1964 and declined it, saying a writer shouldn't become an institution.

sections.key: Albert Camus argued life is absurd, but we can rebel by living fully anyway.
sections.b: Albert Camus, a French writer born in Algeria in 1913, rejected the existentialist label but is closely linked to it. He described the absurd: the clash between our longing for meaning and a silent, indifferent universe. His novel The Stranger (1942) follows a man who refuses to pretend to feelings he doesn't have. In The Myth of Sisyphus, published the same year, he retold the Greek myth of a man condemned to push a boulder uphill forever. Camus concluded: 'One must imagine Sisyphus happy.' Embracing life in full awareness of the absurd is a kind of rebellion. He won the Nobel Prize in 1957.

sections.key: De Beauvoir applied existentialism to women's lives: 'One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman.'
sections.b: Simone de Beauvoir, a philosopher, novelist and Sartre's lifelong partner, wrote The Second Sex (1949), one of the founding texts of modern feminism. She argued that women had been defined as 'the Other' in relation to men, treated as secondary rather than as free subjects, and that ideas of femininity are shaped by society rather than fixed by nature. Her famous line, 'One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman', applied the existentialist idea that we're not bound by a fixed essence. She also wrote The Ethics of Ambiguity (1947), arguing that true freedom requires willing freedom for others too.

sections.key: Existentialism was criticised as bleak and individualistic, and its leaders fell out over politics.
sections.b: Existentialism had plenty of critics. Religious thinkers objected to Sartre's atheism, while Marxists called it too focused on the individual and not enough on society and class. Others found it gloomy, obsessed with anxiety, death and absurdity. Its leaders quarrelled too. Sartre and Camus were friends until 1952, when a harsh review of Camus's book The Rebel in Sartre's journal led to a bitter public split. Camus had condemned political violence and Soviet labour camps, while Sartre, for a time, defended the Soviet Union. The two never reconciled before Camus died in a car accident in 1960.

sections.key: Existentialism encourages authenticity, owning choices and creating meaning through action.
sections.b: Existentialism's practical message is demanding but empowering. Live authentically, according to values you've chosen rather than simply what others expect. Take responsibility instead of hiding behind excuses like 'I had no choice' or 'that's just how I am'. Accept that some anxiety comes with freedom, especially at big decision points like choosing a career or ending a relationship. Create meaning through commitments to people, work and causes. The psychiatrist Viktor Frankl's logotherapy and modern existential psychotherapy both draw on these ideas to help people facing big questions about purpose, loss and death.

o: We're born with a fixed purpose
We exist first, then define ourselves through choices
quiz.e: Sartre's summary of existentialism.

quiz.q: What is 'bad faith' in Sartre's sense?
o: Pretending you have no choice to avoid responsibility
quiz.e: Blaming job, upbringing or society.

quiz.q: Who declared 'God is dead'?
quiz.e: He meant belief in God was fading.

quiz.q: What did Camus conclude about Sisyphus?
quiz.e: Living fully is a rebellion against the absurd.

quiz.q: Who wrote The Second Sex?
quiz.e: A founding text of modern feminism.

LESSONS.title: A short history of AI
LESSONS.hook: AI did not arrive overnight. It is a 70-year story of bold promises, bitter winters and a few moments that stunned the world.

sections.key: In 1950 Alan Turing asked 'Can machines think?' and proposed a test based on conversation.
sections.b: In 1950 the British mathematician Alan Turing, famous for his wartime code-breaking work, published a paper called 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence'. It opened with a bold question: can machines think? Because 'thinking' is so hard to define, Turing suggested a practical substitute he called the imitation game, now known as the Turing test. If a judge chatting through text could not reliably tell a machine from a person, he argued, we should take the machine's intelligence seriously. Turing also predicted that machines might one day learn, rather than be programmed step by step. That idea would take decades to pay off.

sections.key: The field was named at a 1956 summer workshop at Dartmouth College in the United States.
sections.b: The term 'artificial intelligence' was coined by the computer scientist John McCarthy in a proposal for a summer workshop held at Dartmouth College, in New Hampshire, in 1956. Organised with Marvin Minsky, Claude Shannon and Nathaniel Rochester, the workshop was built on a confident claim: that every aspect of learning or intelligence could in principle be described so precisely that a machine could simulate it. The meeting produced no single breakthrough, but it gave the field a name, a community and an ambitious agenda. Many of its attendees went on to lead AI research for the next several decades.

sections.key: Early AI used hand-written rules and logic, and its pioneers made predictions that proved far too optimistic.
sections.b: The first decades of AI were dominated by symbolic AI: programs built from hand-written rules and logic. Researchers created programs that proved maths theorems, played draughts and solved puzzles. In 1966 Joseph Weizenbaum's ELIZA mimicked a therapist using simple pattern matching, and some users became emotionally attached to it, which alarmed its creator. Confidence ran high. In 1965 Herbert Simon predicted that within twenty years machines would be capable of doing any work a person can do. Meanwhile, Frank Rosenblatt's 1958 perceptron, an early learning machine loosely inspired by brain cells, hinted at a different path that was largely sidelined for years.

sections.key: Twice, overhyped promises led to funding cuts and slumps known as 'AI winters'.
sections.b: Real-world problems turned out to be far messier than puzzles. Programs that worked in tidy demonstrations failed when faced with the complexity of everyday language and vision, and computers were too slow and data too scarce. In the early 1970s, critical reviews such as Britain's 1973 Lighthill report led governments to cut funding, beginning the first 'AI winter'. The 1980s brought a boom in expert systems, rule-based programs that captured specialist knowledge for businesses. They proved expensive and brittle, and by the late 1980s and early 1990s the market collapsed into a second winter. The lesson: hype can outrun what the technology can actually do.

sections.key: In 1997 IBM's Deep Blue became the first computer to beat a reigning world chess champion in a match.
sections.b: In May 1997 IBM's Deep Blue defeated world chess champion Garry Kasparov in a six-game match in New York, winning 3.5 to 2.5. Kasparov had beaten an earlier version the year before. It was a landmark moment, widely reported as machine overtaking human. Yet Deep Blue did not learn the way people do. It relied on specialised hardware that could evaluate around 200 million positions per second, combined with chess knowledge programmed by experts. It was superb at chess and could do nothing else. That narrowness was typical of AI at the time: impressive in one domain, helpless outside it.

sections.key: Around 2012, neural networks trained on big data with powerful chips began to dominate AI.
sections.b: The idea of learning machines never died. Researchers such as Geoffrey Hinton, Yann LeCun and Yoshua Bengio kept refining artificial neural networks through the lean years. By the 2010s three ingredients had arrived: huge datasets from the internet, fast graphics chips called GPUs, and better training methods. In 2012 a network called AlexNet, from Hinton's group in Toronto, won the ImageNet image-recognition competition by a striking margin. Within a few years, 'deep learning', meaning networks with many layers, transformed speech recognition, translation and image analysis. Hinton, LeCun and Bengio later shared the 2018 Turing Award, often called the Nobel Prize of computing.

sections.key: In 2016 DeepMind's AlphaGo beat Go champion Lee Sedol, a feat many experts thought was a decade away.
sections.b: Go, an ancient board game, has vastly more possible positions than chess, so brute-force search alone could not master it. In March 2016, AlphaGo, built by the London-based company DeepMind, beat the top professional Lee Sedol four games to one in Seoul. It combined deep neural networks with a search method and reinforcement learning, improving partly by playing against itself. In game two it played Move 37, a move human experts first thought was a mistake but which later looked brilliant. Many experts had expected this milestone to be years away. A later version, AlphaGo Zero, learned purely through self-play, with no human games at all.

sections.h: The rise of large language models
sections.key: The transformer design of 2017 led to large language models, which reached the public with ChatGPT in 2022.
sections.b: In 2017 Google researchers introduced the transformer, a neural network design that made it practical to train on enormous amounts of text. This led to large language models, which learn to predict text and can then write, summarise, translate and answer questions. When OpenAI released ChatGPT in November 2022, it became one of the fastest-growing consumer apps in history, and many rival assistants followed. The story is still unfolding. History offers a useful lens: past predictions were often wildly optimistic, yet the deep learning era has repeatedly surprised the sceptics too. Treat confident forecasts in either direction with healthy caution.

o: The imitation game, a conversation-based test of machine intelligence
quiz.e: Now known as the Turing test.

quiz.q: Where was the term 'artificial intelligence' launched in 1956?
o: A summer workshop at Dartmouth College
quiz.e: John McCarthy coined the term in the proposal.

quiz.q: What caused the 'AI winters'?
o: Overhyped promises that weren't met, leading to funding cuts
quiz.e: Hype outran what the technology could do.

quiz.q: How did Deep Blue mainly beat Kasparov in 1997?
o: Fast search of millions of positions plus programmed chess knowledge
quiz.e: It evaluated around 200 million positions per second.

quiz.q: What made AlphaGo's 2016 win so notable?
o: Many experts thought beating a top Go player was years away
quiz.e: It beat Lee Sedol four games to one.

LESSONS.title: How machines learn
LESSONS.hook: Nobody wrote the rules that let your phone recognise your face. The machine worked them out from examples. Here's how.

sections.key: Machine learning means a computer finds patterns in data instead of following rules a programmer wrote.
sections.b: Traditional software follows rules that a programmer writes by hand: if this, then that. That works well for payroll or calculators, but try writing rules to recognise a cat in a photo, or to tell spam from a real email. There are too many exceptions. Machine learning takes a different approach. Instead of writing the rules, you give the computer many examples and let it find the patterns itself. Show a spam filter millions of emails marked 'spam' or 'not spam', and it learns which features, such as certain phrases, links or senders, tend to signal junk. The result is called a model.

sections.key: Training is when a model learns from data; inference is when the finished model is used to make predictions.
sections.b: Machine learning has two distinct stages. Training is the learning phase: the model is shown data, makes predictions, measures how wrong they are and adjusts itself, over and over. For large models this can take weeks on thousands of specialised chips and cost a great deal of money and energy. Inference is what happens afterwards, when the trained model is put to work on new inputs: your banking app flagging an unusual transaction, or your phone turning speech into text. Inference is usually quick and cheap per use. Importantly, most models do not keep learning while you use them; they only change when retrained.

sections.key: In supervised learning, a model learns from examples that come with the correct answers, called labels.
sections.b: The most common kind of machine learning is supervised learning. The training data comes with labels, the right answers. To predict house prices, you might feed a model thousands of past sales with details like suburb, land size and bedrooms, along with what each sold for. The model learns how those features relate to price, then estimates prices for homes it has never seen. The same approach powers medical image tools trained on scans labelled by specialists, and banks' fraud detectors trained on past transactions marked as genuine or fraudulent. The catch: good labels are often slow and expensive to create, and the model can only be as good as they are.

sections.key: Unsupervised learning finds structure in data that has no labels, such as natural groupings.
sections.b: Sometimes you have plenty of data but no labels. Unsupervised learning looks for structure on its own. A common task is clustering: grouping similar items together. A supermarket might analyse loyalty card data and discover distinct groups of shoppers, such as busy families, bargain hunters and weekend entertainers, without anyone defining those groups in advance. Another use is anomaly detection, spotting things that don't fit the usual pattern, like an odd reading from a machine that may be about to fail. Unsupervised methods are powerful for exploration, but people still have to interpret the results, because the model doesn't know what its groups actually mean.

sections.key: In reinforcement learning, a system learns by trial and error, guided by rewards and penalties.
sections.b: Reinforcement learning works a bit like training a dog with treats. An agent, the learning system, takes actions in an environment and receives rewards for good outcomes and penalties for bad ones. Over many attempts it learns which strategies earn the most reward. This is how DeepMind's AlphaGo improved by playing millions of games against itself, and how systems have learned to play video games from raw screen pixels. It is also used in robotics and in controlling complex systems such as data centre cooling. A version of it, using feedback from human raters, helps make AI chatbots more helpful. Designing the right reward is tricky: systems can find unexpected shortcuts.

sections.key: Neural networks are layers of simple connected units whose connection strengths are adjusted during training.
sections.b: Many modern models are artificial neural networks, loosely inspired by the brain. A network is made of layers of simple units, sometimes called neurons. Each unit takes in numbers, weights them, adds them up and passes a result to the next layer. The weights, the strength of each connection, are what the network learns. During training, a method called backpropagation works out how each weight contributed to an error and nudges it slightly in a better direction. Repeat that billions of times and useful patterns emerge. 'Deep' learning simply means networks with many layers. Despite the name, they work very differently from real brains.

sections.key: Overfitting is when a model memorises its training data instead of learning patterns that generalise.
sections.b: Imagine a student who memorises last year's exam answers word for word. They ace the practice paper but fail when the questions change. Machine learning models can do the same thing, called overfitting. A model that fits its training data too closely, including its noise and quirks, performs brilliantly on familiar examples and poorly on new ones. To catch this, developers hold back a portion of data the model never sees during training, called a test set, and judge performance on that. Using more varied data, simpler models and techniques that discourage memorising all help. The goal is always generalisation: working well on the real world.

sections.key: Models learn whatever patterns are in their data, including unfair ones, so data quality matters enormously.
sections.b: A model learns what its data shows, including society's past biases. In 2018 Reuters reported that Amazon had scrapped an experimental recruiting tool after finding it penalised CVs that mentioned women's activities. It had learned from a decade of mostly male applicants. Studies have also found some facial analysis systems made more errors on darker-skinned faces, largely because they were trained on unrepresentative photos. None of this requires anyone to intend harm. For you, the practical takeaway is simple: when an automated system judges a loan, a job application or a medical image, it's reasonable to ask what data it learned from and how it was tested.

quiz.q: What is the key idea of machine learning?
o: Programmers write every rule by hand
The computer finds patterns from examples
Data is stored and never used
quiz.e: The result of the learning is called a model.

quiz.q: What is 'inference' in machine learning?
o: Using a trained model to make predictions on new inputs
quiz.e: Training is learning; inference is using.

quiz.q: Predicting house prices from past sales with known prices is an example of...
quiz.e: The past sale prices are the labels.

quiz.q: How does reinforcement learning work?
o: By trial and error guided by rewards and penalties
quiz.e: AlphaGo improved by playing itself.

quiz.q: What is overfitting?
o: When a model memorises training data and fails on new data
When a model is too small to run
quiz.e: Test sets help catch it.

LESSONS.title: AI images and deepfakes
LESSONS.hook: Type a sentence, get a photo that never existed. Understanding how image generators work is the first step to not being fooled by them.

sections.key: AI image generators learn from vast numbers of image and caption pairs, then create new images from text prompts.
sections.b: AI image generators turn a text description, called a prompt, into a new picture. Type 'a kookaburra in a raincoat, watercolour style' and seconds later you get an image no one has ever painted. To learn this, these systems are trained on enormous collections of images paired with captions, often billions of pairs gathered from the internet. From them, the model learns statistical links between words and visual features: what 'watercolour' tends to look like, what shape a kookaburra has, how light falls on wet fabric. It doesn't paste together pieces of stored photos. It generates new pixels based on the patterns it has learned.

sections.key: Diffusion models learn to remove noise from images, then create pictures by gradually turning random static into an image.
sections.b: Many leading image generators use a technique called diffusion. The training idea is surprisingly simple. Take a real image and add random noise, a little at a time, until it becomes pure static, like an old TV with no signal. Then train a neural network to reverse each small step: given a noisy image, predict what it looked like with slightly less noise. After enough practice, the model can start from pure random static and remove noise step by step until a clear image emerges. Because it starts from different random noise each time, the same prompt can produce many different pictures.

sections.key: The text prompt guides each denoising step, pushing the image towards what the words describe.
sections.b: Without guidance, a diffusion model would produce random but plausible images. The prompt steers it. The text is converted into numbers that capture its meaning, using a model trained to link words and pictures. At every denoising step, those numbers nudge the image towards something that matches the description. That is why wording matters: adding style, lighting or camera details changes the result. It also explains some weaknesses. The model has learned associations, not rules about the world, so it has historically struggled with things like correct numbers of fingers or legible text on signs. Newer systems handle these much better, but mistakes still slip through.

sections.key: Deepfakes are AI-made or AI-altered images, video or audio that convincingly show real people doing or saying things they didn't.
sections.b: A deepfake is synthetic media that makes a real person appear to do or say something they never did. The term emerged around 2017 from face-swapping videos shared online. Today, tools can clone a voice from a short recording and generate realistic video. There are harmless uses, such as film effects or satire that is clearly labelled, but the harms are serious. They include non-consensual sexual images, political fakes and scams. In a widely reported 2024 case in Hong Kong, an employee at an engineering firm transferred roughly US$25 million after a video call in which the 'executives' were deepfakes. Criminals also use cloned voices to impersonate family members.

sections.key: Visual clues help but are fading, so check the source and context before believing or sharing an image.
sections.b: Older fakes often gave themselves away with warped hands, mismatched earrings, garbled text, odd shadows or skin that looked too smooth. Those clues are still worth checking, but they are becoming less reliable as the technology improves, so don't depend on them. Better habits focus on context. Who posted this first, and are they credible? Is any reputable news outlet reporting it? Look for the same moment from other angles: a real event is usually captured by many people, while a fake often exists as a single striking image. Some companies now add invisible watermarks or 'content credentials' to AI images, but these aren't universal. If a clip provokes strong emotion, that is a signal to slow down.

sections.key: In 2024 Australia made sharing non-consensual sexually explicit deepfakes a federal criminal offence.
sections.b: Laws are catching up. In 2024 Australia passed federal legislation making it a criminal offence to share sexually explicit deepfakes of adults without their consent, with serious penalties. Other existing laws, covering defamation, fraud, harassment and misleading conduct, can also apply to fakes. Australia's eSafety Commissioner can help remove image-based abuse, including AI-generated images, and you can report it at esafety.gov.au. Many other countries are introducing their own rules, and major platforms have policies against deceptive synthetic media, though enforcement is uneven. If you or someone you know is targeted, keep evidence such as screenshots and links, report it, and consider getting legal advice.

sections.key: Whether training on copyrighted images is fair, and who owns AI-generated art, are unresolved legal questions.
sections.b: Image generators were largely trained on images collected from the web, often without the permission of the artists and photographers who made them. Many creators argue this is unfair copying that lets AI compete with them using their own work. Developers generally argue that learning patterns from public images is lawful, similar to how human artists learn by looking. Several court cases have been launched, including by Getty Images and groups of artists, and results may differ between countries. A second question is ownership. Copyright law in Australia generally requires a human author, so images made purely by AI may not be protected. These issues are still being settled.

sections.key: Use AI images openly, avoid depicting real people without consent, and pause before sharing striking pictures.
sections.b: Image generators can be genuinely useful: mocking up a room renovation, illustrating a presentation, sketching a logo idea or just having fun. A few habits keep you on solid ground. Be open when an image is AI-made, especially if it could be mistaken for a real photo. Don't create images of real people, particularly private individuals, without their consent. Check the terms of the tool you use before using its output commercially, and consider paying human artists for work that matters. Most importantly, build a reflex of scepticism: before sharing a shocking or perfect-looking image, take ten seconds to check where it came from.

quiz.q: How does a diffusion model create an image?
o: It gradually removes noise from random static
It searches the web for a matching photo
It draws outlines then colours them in
quiz.e: It learned to reverse the process of adding noise.

quiz.q: Why have image generators struggled with things like fingers or text?
o: They learn statistical associations, not rules about the world
quiz.e: Newer systems are better, but errors still happen.

quiz.q: What is a deepfake?
o: Synthetic media showing a real person doing or saying something they didn't
quiz.e: Voices can be cloned too.

quiz.q: Why are clues like warped hands becoming a weak test for AI fakes?
o: AI images no longer show people
Newer generators make far fewer of these mistakes
quiz.e: Check the source and context instead.

quiz.q: What does Australian copyright law generally require for protection?
quiz.e: Purely AI-made images may not be protected.

LESSONS.title: Using AI well
LESSONS.hook: AI assistants can save you hours or quietly lead you astray. The difference usually comes down to how you use them.

sections.key: Treat an AI assistant like a fast, well-read helper whose work you still need to check.
sections.b: The most useful way to think about an AI chatbot is as a very fast, widely read assistant who is eager to please and sometimes confidently wrong. It can draft an email in seconds, explain a tricky concept five different ways and summarise a long document. But it doesn't know your situation unless you tell it, it can misunderstand what you want, and it can produce errors that sound completely convincing. People who get the most out of AI tend to stay in charge: they give clear direction, review everything important and treat the output as a draft rather than a final answer. You remain responsible for what you do with it.

sections.key: Better prompts include the goal, the audience, the format you want and any key details.
sections.b: AI can't read your mind, and vague requests get generic answers. Compare 'Write a letter to my landlord' with 'Write a polite but firm email to my landlord in Brisbane asking for a leaking tap to be repaired. I reported it three weeks ago. Keep it under 150 words.' The second gives the goal, the situation, the tone and the length. A useful checklist: what you want, who it's for, what format you'd like, and any constraints or facts it must include. You can also ask it to take on a role, such as 'explain this like a patient maths tutor', or show an example of the style you want.

sections.key: Refine results by giving feedback, asking for alternatives and letting the AI ask you questions.
sections.b: Your first prompt rarely produces the perfect result, and that's fine. Treat it as a conversation. Say what you liked and what to change: 'shorter', 'less formal', 'more Australian examples', 'turn this into dot points'. Ask for several options, then choose or combine them. For bigger tasks, break the work into steps rather than asking for everything at once. A powerful trick is to ask the AI to interview you first: 'Before you write my CV summary, ask me five questions about my experience.' This surfaces details you might forget and produces something far more personal than a one-shot request.

sections.key: Chatbots can 'hallucinate', producing confident, plausible-sounding information that is simply false.
sections.b: Language models generate text that sounds right based on patterns, which is not the same as checking whether it is right. When they lack reliable information, they can fill the gap with fluent inventions: a fake statistic, a book that doesn't exist, a made-up quote or a misremembered date. This is called hallucination. A famous example came in 2023, when lawyers in New York were fined after filing a court document citing legal cases that a chatbot had invented. Similar incidents have occurred in courts elsewhere, including Australia. Tools that search the web and cite sources reduce the problem, but they don't eliminate it.

sections.key: Verify important facts, figures and sources yourself, especially for health, money and legal questions.
sections.b: The more a mistake would cost you, the more checking an answer deserves. For a birthday poem, errors hardly matter. For medication doses, tax rules or a contract, they matter a lot. Good habits include clicking through to any cited sources and confirming they exist and actually say what the AI claims; cross-checking key facts with trusted sites such as government agencies or well-known organisations; and redoing important calculations yourself or with a calculator. Asking 'How confident are you, and what might be wrong here?' can surface weak points, but a model's confidence isn't a guarantee. Rules also vary between countries, so check that advice applies in Australia.

sections.key: Don't paste passwords, financial details or other people's private information into AI tools.
sections.b: What you type into an online AI tool is sent to the company that runs it. Depending on the service and your settings, conversations may be stored, reviewed by staff or used to improve future models. So treat a chatbot like any online service. Never share passwords, full card or bank details, or identity documents. Think twice before pasting in medical records, legal disputes or anything about other people, such as a client's details or a friend's private message. Check the privacy settings, which often let you limit how your data is used. At work, follow your employer's AI policy, because putting confidential information into public tools can breach privacy obligations.

sections.key: AI shines at first drafts, explaining, organising and rehearsing, where you can judge the result.
sections.b: AI assistants earn their keep on tasks where a good first draft saves time and you can judge the result. Some less obvious uses: pasting in a confusing letter from an insurer or government agency, with personal details removed, and asking what it means and what you need to do; turning a messy brain dump into a to-do list; rehearsing a tough conversation, such as asking for a pay rise, with the AI playing the other person; or adapting a recipe to what's in your fridge. They also make patient study partners: ask one to quiz you on a topic, or to find the gaps in your explanation of it. A good rule of thumb is to use AI to get started or unstuck, then add your own judgement and knowledge.

sections.key: Be cautious using AI for high-stakes decisions, very recent events, or as a replacement for people.
sections.b: AI is weaker, or riskier, in some areas. It may not know about very recent events unless it can search the web. It shouldn't be your only source for decisions about your health, finances or legal rights; use it to prepare questions, then talk to a doctor, licensed financial adviser or lawyer. If you're learning a skill, leaning on AI too heavily can mean you never build it yourself. And while chatbots can be comforting to talk to, they are not a substitute for friends, family or professional support. If you are struggling, Lifeline is available on 13 11 14. Used thoughtfully, AI is a tool that amplifies your judgement, not a replacement for it.

quiz.q: Which prompt is likely to get the most useful result?
o: A request that states the goal, audience, tone and length
quiz.e: Context beats vague requests.

quiz.q: What is a useful trick for bigger or personal tasks?
o: Ask the AI to interview you with questions first
Use as few words as possible
Ask the same question in capitals
quiz.e: It surfaces details you might forget.

quiz.q: What happened to New York lawyers in 2023 who relied on a chatbot for a court filing?
o: They were fined for citing cases the chatbot had invented
quiz.e: Fluent, confident inventions like these are called hallucinations.

quiz.q: Which of these should you avoid pasting into a public AI tool?
quiz.e: Conversations may be stored or reviewed.

quiz.q: How should you use AI for a serious health or money decision?
o: Use it to prepare questions, then talk to a qualified professional
Ask it to decide for you
quiz.e: It shouldn't be your only source.

LESSONS.title: AI's risks and debates
LESSONS.hook: Some experts call AI the most important technology in history. Some think the fears are overblown. Here's what they actually disagree about.

sections.key: AI risks range from present-day harms to long-term concerns, and informed experts disagree about their size.
sections.b: Debates about AI can sound like shouting matches between boosters and doomsayers, but the real picture is more interesting. Serious researchers, economists and policymakers disagree about how quickly AI will improve, how much it will change society and which risks matter most. Some focus on harms happening now, such as bias, scams and privacy breaches. Others worry most about future systems that could be far more capable than today's. Many care about both. These views aren't necessarily in conflict, but they compete for attention and funding. A good way to navigate the debate is to ask of any claim: what's the evidence, and what timeframe is being discussed?

sections.key: Automated systems can repeat unfair patterns in data, and flawed automation can harm many people quickly.
sections.b: When AI helps decide who gets a loan, a job interview or extra scrutiny from a government agency, errors and biases can affect huge numbers of people at once. Models trained on historical data can absorb past discrimination, as when a 2016 ProPublica investigation reported that a US tool used to predict reoffending wrongly flagged Black defendants as high risk far more often than white defendants. Australia has its own cautionary tale about automation, even though it didn't involve modern AI: Robodebt, an automated scheme that used averaged income data to raise welfare debts, many of them wrong. A 2023 Royal Commission called it crude and cruel. The broad lesson is that automated decisions need human oversight, transparency and a clear way for people to challenge them.

sections.key: AI makes convincing fake text, images and audio cheap to produce, and makes it easier to dismiss real evidence as fake.
sections.b: Generative AI makes it cheap and fast to produce persuasive fake content: realistic images, cloned voices, fake news sites and armies of automated social media accounts. Scammers already use these tools. There are concerns about elections too, although researchers still debate how much AI fakes have actually changed voters' minds so far. A subtler risk is sometimes called the liar's dividend: once people know anything could be faked, it becomes easier for someone caught on a genuine recording to claim it's fake. In response, researchers and companies are developing watermarking and content-verification tools, while many experts stress that media literacy matters just as much.

sections.key: Economists broadly agree AI will change many jobs, but disagree about how fast and whether net employment will suffer.
sections.b: Earlier automation mostly affected routine physical work. Today's AI can also do tasks once thought safely human, such as drafting text, writing code, analysing documents and producing images, so it touches office and creative jobs too. What happens next is genuinely contested. Optimists point out that past technologies, from tractors to computers, eliminated some jobs but created new ones and raised living standards over time. Others argue AI could change work faster and more broadly than before, leaving some people worse off even if the economy grows. Most economists agree that tasks within jobs will change, that transitions can be painful, and that skills and retraining will matter.

sections.key: AI makes it easier to identify, track and profile people, raising serious privacy concerns.
sections.b: AI is very good at finding patterns in personal data, which is useful for recommendations and fraud detection but also enables surveillance. Facial recognition can identify people in crowds, and data from phones, purchases and social media can be combined to build detailed profiles. In Australia, the Privacy Commissioner found in 2021 that Clearview AI breached Australians' privacy by scraping online photos to build a facial recognition database, and in 2024 found that Bunnings breached privacy law with its in-store facial recognition, a finding a tribunal partly overturned in 2026. Supporters say such tools can help fight crime; critics warn of mass surveillance and errors. Where to draw the line remains a live debate.

sections.key: Alignment means making AI systems reliably do what people intend; how serious the long-term risks are is hotly debated.
sections.b: The alignment problem is the challenge of making AI systems reliably pursue the goals people actually intend, rather than a flawed version of them. Today this shows up as chatbots that can be tricked into harmful answers, or systems that find loopholes in their instructions. Experts also worry about misuse, such as help with cyberattacks. Some prominent researchers, including Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio, have warned that future systems could pose extreme risks if they become more capable than humans, and in 2023 hundreds of experts signed a statement calling extinction risk from AI a global priority. Others, such as Yann LeCun, argue these fears are overblown and distract from present harms.

sections.key: Governments are experimenting with different approaches, from the EU's risk-based AI Act to voluntary guidelines.
sections.b: Governments are still working out how to regulate AI without stifling useful innovation. The European Union adopted its AI Act in 2024, taking a risk-based approach: a few uses, such as certain kinds of social scoring, are banned, high-risk uses face strict requirements, and lower-risk uses face lighter rules. Other countries have leaned more on existing laws and voluntary commitments from companies. International cooperation is growing, including a series of global AI summits that began at Bletchley Park in the UK in 2023. In its 2025 National AI Plan, Australia chose to rely mainly on existing laws, such as privacy and consumer law, plus voluntary guidance and a new AI Safety Institute, rather than a dedicated AI act.

sections.key: Stay informed, be sceptical of hype in both directions, and focus on the risks you can act on.
sections.b: With so much noise, it helps to have a few principles. Be wary of confident predictions from any side, and notice who benefits from a particular story: companies may overstate their products, while headlines reward alarm. Distinguish between what AI can do now and speculation about the future; both matter, but they call for different responses. Focus on what you can control: protect your personal data, verify surprising content before sharing it, watch for voice and video scams, and keep building skills that complement AI. Finally, remember that these are choices, not destiny. How AI develops will be shaped by laws, businesses and the public, including you.

quiz.q: What lesson did Australia's Robodebt scheme offer about automation?
o: Automated decisions need human oversight and ways to challenge them
quiz.e: A 2023 Royal Commission called it crude and cruel.

quiz.q: What is the 'liar's dividend'?
o: The ease of dismissing real evidence as fake once fakes are common
quiz.e: Knowing anything could be faked cuts both ways.

quiz.q: What do most economists agree about AI and jobs?
o: All jobs will disappear within five years
Tasks within many jobs will change, and transitions can be painful
quiz.e: The scale and speed are contested.

quiz.q: What is the 'alignment problem'?
o: Making AI reliably pursue the goals people actually intend
quiz.e: Experts disagree about how serious long-term risks are.

quiz.q: What approach does the EU's AI Act take?
o: It is a risk-based approach with stricter rules for higher-risk uses
It relies only on voluntary promises
quiz.e: Adopted in 2024.

LESSONS.title: Marsupials: life in the pouch
LESSONS.hook: Born the size of a jellybean, finished in a pouch. Australia's marsupials took a very different path to the rest of the mammal world.

sections.key: Marsupials give birth to tiny, underdeveloped young that finish growing attached to a teat, usually in a pouch.
sections.b: Marsupials are mammals that give birth very early. Instead of a long pregnancy nourished by a complex placenta, a marsupial mother has a short pregnancy and delivers a tiny, barely formed baby that completes its development attached to a teat. In many species that teat sits inside a pouch, but not all marsupials have one; some small species simply carry young clinging underneath. There are roughly 330 marsupial species worldwide. Around two-thirds live in Australia and New Guinea, and most of the rest are opossums in the Americas. Australia has more than 150 species, from tiny planigales to the red kangaroo.

sections.key: A newborn kangaroo weighs under a gram and crawls unaided to the pouch.
sections.b: A red kangaroo's pregnancy lasts only about 33 days. The newborn joey is pink, hairless and weighs less than a gram, about the size of a jellybean. Using its relatively strong front legs, it crawls through its mother's fur to the pouch, latches onto a teat and stays there for months. Kangaroos have more tricks. A mother can pause the development of a new embryo, known as embryonic diapause, until conditions improve or the pouch is free. She can also feed a young joey at foot and a newborn in the pouch at the same time, producing two different kinds of milk from two different teats.

sections.key: Kangaroos hop using springy tendons, which makes fast travel remarkably energy-efficient.
sections.b: Kangaroos and wallabies belong to the macropods, meaning 'big feet', a family of around 60 species. The red kangaroo is the largest living marsupial; big males standing upright can be as tall as a person. Hopping looks tiring, but it isn't: long tendons in the legs store and release energy like springs, so once a kangaroo is moving, going faster costs surprisingly little extra effort. Red kangaroos can briefly reach around 50 kilometres per hour. When moving slowly, kangaroos use their strong tail as a fifth leg. For drivers, the practical lesson is that kangaroos are most active around dawn and dusk, when collisions are most common.

sections.key: Koalas live on eucalyptus leaves, a poor diet that explains their long hours of rest.
sections.b: Koalas are not bears, despite the old name 'koala bear'. They feed almost entirely on eucalyptus leaves, which are low in nutrients, high in fibre and laced with compounds toxic to most animals. A long gut, including a caecum up to about two metres long, and specialised microbes help them cope. The diet provides so little energy that koalas rest or sleep for around 18 to 22 hours a day. Young koalas eat a special soft faeces from their mother, called pap, which passes on the gut microbes they need. In 2022, koalas in Queensland, New South Wales and the ACT were listed as endangered, mainly because of habitat loss, disease, dogs and cars.

sections.key: Wombats produce cube-shaped droppings, formed by uneven elasticity in their intestine walls.
sections.b: Wombats are the only animals known to produce cube-shaped poo, depositing dozens of neat cubes each night, often on rocks and logs where they act as territory markers. How they did it was a mystery until a 2018 study by researchers from the United States and the University of Tasmania found that the final stretch of the wombat intestine has regions of differing stiffness, which shape the drying droppings into cubes. The work won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2019. Wombats are powerful diggers, with a backward-facing pouch that stops soil getting in, and a tough rump they use to block their burrow entrance.

sections.key: Tasmanian devils, the largest surviving carnivorous marsupials, are threatened by a contagious cancer.
sections.b: The Tasmanian devil is the largest carnivorous marsupial still alive, with one of the most powerful bites for its size of any mammal. Devils disappeared from mainland Australia roughly 3,000 years ago and survived in the wild only in Tasmania. Their famous screeching usually happens around shared carcasses. Since the mid-1990s, devils have been hit by devil facial tumour disease, a rare cancer that spreads between animals through biting. It has caused severe declines across much of Tasmania. Insurance populations have been bred in captivity and on disease-free sites, and since 2020 a small number of devils have been released into a fenced sanctuary in New South Wales.

sections.key: The last known thylacine died in a Hobart zoo in 1936; bounties had helped drive it to extinction.
sections.b: The thylacine, or Tasmanian tiger, was the largest carnivorous marsupial of modern times: a dog-like hunter with dark stripes across its lower back. It vanished from the mainland around the same time as the devil, then survived only in Tasmania. Seen as a threat to sheep, it was targeted by a government bounty from 1888 to 1909, with more than 2,000 bounties paid. The last known thylacine died at Beaumaris Zoo in Hobart on 7 September 1936, a date now marked as National Threatened Species Day. Unconfirmed sightings continue, and proposals to 'de-extinct' the species with gene technology are ambitious and scientifically debated.

sections.key: Isolation let marsupials evolve into roles filled elsewhere by placental mammals.
sections.b: Australia's marsupial richness is a story of isolation. After Australia separated from Antarctica tens of millions of years ago and drifted north, its marsupials evolved in relative isolation, filling roles that placental mammals fill elsewhere. The results show striking convergent evolution: sugar gliders resemble flying squirrels, the marsupial mole resembles golden moles, and the thylacine looked remarkably like a wolf. For you, the practical side is simple. Drive slowly at dawn and dusk in the bush, and if you find an injured animal or a dead kangaroo or wombat by the road, call a local wildlife rescue service, because a living joey may still be in the pouch.

quiz.q: Roughly how much does a newborn red kangaroo weigh?
quiz.e: It's about the size of a jellybean.

quiz.q: What makes fast hopping efficient for kangaroos?
o: Springy tendons that store and release energy
quiz.e: Tendons act like springs.

quiz.q: Why do koalas rest for up to 22 hours a day?
o: Eucalyptus leaves provide very little energy
quiz.e: A low-energy diet means a low-energy lifestyle.

quiz.q: What gives wombat poo its cube shape?
o: Regions of different stiffness in the intestine wall
Wombats press it with their paws
quiz.e: Shown by a 2018 study.

quiz.q: When did the last known thylacine die?
quiz.e: At Beaumaris Zoo, Hobart, on 7 September 1936.

LESSONS.title: Platypus and echidnas: the egg-laying mammals
LESSONS.hook: When the first platypus reached Britain, scientists checked it for stitches. It was real, and it was even stranger than it looked.

sections.key: Monotremes, the platypus and echidnas, are the only living mammals that lay eggs.
sections.b: Only five living mammal species lay eggs: the platypus and four species of echidna. Together they form the monotremes, a group that split from the ancestors of all other mammals more than 160 million years ago. The name means 'single opening', because, like birds and reptiles, they have one opening, the cloaca, for waste and reproduction. The platypus lives only in eastern Australia, including Tasmania. The short-beaked echidna lives across Australia and New Guinea, while the three long-beaked echidnas live only in New Guinea. They are not 'primitive' leftovers but highly specialised animals with a very long, separate evolutionary history.

sections.key: Monotremes have fur and make milk, but they have no nipples; milk seeps from patches of skin.
sections.b: Monotremes are unmistakably mammals. They have fur, a single lower jawbone, the three tiny middle ear bones typical of mammals, and they feed their young on milk. But there's a twist: they have no nipples. Milk seeps out through pores on patches of skin on the mother's belly, and the young lick or suck it up from there. Monotremes are warm-blooded, but they run cooler than most mammals, with a body temperature of around 32 degrees Celsius compared with our 37. Adult platypuses have no teeth; they grind food with hard pads, while echidnas never have teeth at all.

sections.key: Platypuses incubate eggs in a burrow; echidnas carry a single egg in a temporary pouch.
sections.b: A female platypus digs a long burrow in a riverbank, seals herself inside and lays usually one to three small, soft, leathery eggs. She incubates them curled around them for roughly ten days. The hatchlings feed on milk for several months before they first venture into the water. An echidna lays a single egg directly into a temporary pouch that forms on her belly. The egg hatches after about ten days, and the tiny baby, known as a puggle, stays in the pouch until its spines begin to grow, when the mother leaves it in a burrow and returns to feed it.

sections.key: A platypus finds food with its eyes shut, sensing tiny electrical signals through its bill.
sections.b: The platypus bill is not hard like a duck's. It is soft, rubbery and packed with sensors. When a platypus dives, it closes its eyes, ears and nostrils, so it hunts almost blind. Instead, its bill carries tens of thousands of electroreceptors that detect the faint electric fields produced by the muscles of prey, plus many touch receptors. Sweeping its head from side to side, it locates insect larvae, worms and yabbies in the mud of the riverbed. It stores the food in cheek pouches and chews it at the surface. A platypus eats a large share of its body weight every day.

sections.key: Male platypuses have a venomous ankle spur; a sting is agonising but not fatal to people.
sections.b: Male platypuses carry a sharp spur on the inside of each hind ankle, connected to a venom gland. The platypus is one of very few venomous mammals. Venom production increases in the breeding season, which suggests it is mainly used in fights between rival males. For humans, a spur injury is not known to be fatal, but it causes severe, long-lasting pain and swelling that ordinary painkillers barely touch, sometimes for weeks. The simple rule: don't handle a wild platypus. Male echidnas also have ankle spurs, but they don't deliver venom; a gland on the spur appears to produce a secretion during the breeding season, possibly for communication.

sections.key: The short-beaked echidna is Australia's most widespread native mammal, found from deserts to snowfields.
sections.b: The short-beaked echidna lives in almost every habitat in Australia, from deserts and forests to the snowy high country, making it the most widespread native mammal on the continent. Its spines are modified hairs. It uses a long, sticky tongue to lap up ants and termites, and its snout carries electroreceptors too, though far fewer than a platypus bill. When threatened, an echidna digs straight down or curls into a spiky ball. In winter, several males sometimes follow a female in a line known as an 'echidna train'. Echidnas are also long-lived for their size, surviving for decades in the wild and even longer in captivity.

sections.key: British scientists first suspected the platypus was a hoax; egg-laying wasn't confirmed until 1884.
sections.b: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples had known these animals for tens of thousands of years, but European naturalists were baffled. When a preserved platypus reached Britain in the late 1790s, the zoologist George Shaw, who described it in 1799, openly wondered whether it was a fake, with a duck's bill stitched onto a mammal's body. For decades scientists argued over whether monotremes truly laid eggs, as Aboriginal informants had said. In 1884, Scottish zoologist William Caldwell, working in Queensland, found an echidna egg and a platypus that had laid one, and sent a famous telegram announcing that monotremes were 'oviparous', meaning egg-laying.

sections.key: Platypuses face threats from dams, drought and yabby traps; you can help by using platypus-safe gear.
sections.b: The platypus is listed as Near Threatened globally, and some local populations have declined or disappeared. Threats include dams and altered river flows, drought, land clearing, pollution, foxes and dogs, and drowning in enclosed 'opera house' style yabby traps, which have been banned in several states. Its genome, sequenced in 2008, revealed a mix of features seen in reptiles, birds and mammals. If you want to see one in the wild, go at dawn or dusk to a quiet creek or river known for platypuses, stay still and watch for rings of ripples. Pick up rubbish near waterways, since fishing line and hair ties can entangle them.

quiz.q: How many living mammal species lay eggs?
quiz.e: The platypus and four species of echidna.

quiz.q: How do monotreme babies get milk?
o: From milk seeping through patches of skin
quiz.e: Monotremes have no nipples.

quiz.q: How does a platypus find prey underwater?
o: By sensing electric fields with its bill
quiz.e: Its eyes, ears and nostrils are closed.

quiz.q: What is true of the male platypus spur?
o: It is used to dig burrows
It delivers venom that causes severe pain
quiz.e: Painful for weeks, but not known to kill people.

quiz.q: When was monotreme egg-laying confirmed by European science?
quiz.e: William Caldwell's telegram announced it in 1884.

LESSONS.title: Australia's remarkable birds
LESSONS.hook: Nearly half the world's bird species descend from ancestors that sang in ancient Australia. The birds here are older, louder and cleverer than you might think.

sections.key: Genetic evidence shows songbirds, now almost half of all bird species, originated in the Australian region.
sections.b: Songbirds, the group that includes robins, finches, crows and sparrows, make up roughly 5,000 species, close to half of all the birds on Earth. For a long time, scientists assumed they originated in the Northern Hemisphere. DNA studies from the early 2000s changed that picture: the oldest songbird lineages, including lyrebirds, scrub-birds, bowerbirds and treecreepers, are found in Australia and New Guinea. The strong current consensus is that songbirds first evolved in this region tens of millions of years ago, and later spread across the globe. So when a European blackbird sings in a garden in London, it is carrying an Australian inheritance.

sections.key: Male lyrebirds are master mimics, copying dozens of other species in their songs.
sections.b: The superb lyrebird of south-eastern forests is one of the world's greatest vocal mimics. Much of a male's song is made up of near-perfect copies of other birds, such as kookaburras, whipbirds and rosellas, woven together with his own calls while he displays his spectacular lacy tail. Some lyrebirds, especially captive ones, have also copied human sounds like camera shutters and machinery. Lyrebirds are also serious gardeners of the forest floor: raking for insects, they turn over enormous quantities of leaf litter and soil each year, which affects decomposition and even fire behaviour. A lyrebird features on the Australian ten-cent coin.

sections.key: Sydney's sulphur-crested cockatoos learned to open wheelie bins, and the skill spread by copying.
sections.b: Australia is a parrot heartland, with more than 50 species, including cockatoos, galahs, lorikeets and the budgerigar. Cockatoos are exceptionally intelligent and long-lived; a Major Mitchell's cockatoo named Cookie lived to about 83 in a zoo in the United States. In Sydney, sulphur-crested cockatoos learned to lift the lids of wheelie bins to raid the rubbish. A study published in 2021 tracked how the skill spread from a few suburbs to many others as birds learned by watching, a rare example of animal culture spreading across a city. Residents responded with bricks and gadgets, and the cockatoos keep testing them.

sections.key: Emus are Australia's tallest birds, and the fathers do all the incubating.
sections.b: The emu is the world's second-tallest bird after the ostrich, standing up to about 1.9 metres. It can't fly, but it can run at around 50 kilometres per hour and swim well. Emus roam widely across the mainland, following rain and food. Their breeding arrangement is unusual: the female lays large, dark green eggs, then often leaves, and the male incubates them for about eight weeks. During that time he barely eats or drinks, losing a lot of weight. He then guards the striped chicks for months. The emu and the kangaroo appear together on Australia's coat of arms.

sections.key: The southern cassowary is a vital rainforest seed-spreader and can be dangerous if provoked.
sections.b: The southern cassowary lives in the tropical rainforests of far north Queensland, as well as New Guinea. It is Australia's heaviest bird, with a tall helmet-like casque, bright blue and red skin on the neck and a dagger-like inner claw on each foot. Cassowaries swallow fruit whole and pass the seeds intact, often far away, making them crucial gardeners of the rainforest; some plants rely heavily on them. The Australian population is listed as endangered, threatened by habitat loss, cars and dogs. They are usually shy, but can kick hard when cornered or fed. Never feed a cassowary, and give them plenty of space.

sections.key: Australian magpies are not true magpies; they sing complex songs and live in cooperative groups.
sections.b: The Australian magpie is not related to European magpies; it is closer to butcherbirds and currawongs. Its rich, warbling carol is one of the best-known sounds in the country, and groups often sing together to announce their territory. Magpies live in family groups and can be remarkably cooperative. In a study published in 2022, researchers fitting magpies with small tracking harnesses watched other magpies help remove them, apparently working together. Swooping happens in spring, roughly August to October, when some males defend nests. Most magpies never swoop at all. If one does, calmly walk away from the area, and consider taking a different route for a few weeks.

sections.key: In 1932, soldiers with machine guns were sent against emus in Western Australia, with little success.
sections.b: In late 1932, after a large number of emus, often estimated at around 20,000, moved onto wheat farms in Western Australia's Campion district, farmers, many of them former soldiers, asked the federal government for help. The Minister for Defence, George Pearce, sent Major G.P.W. Meredith with a small group of soldiers, two Lewis machine guns and 10,000 rounds of ammunition. The emus scattered into small groups, ran fast and proved very hard to hit. After two attempts, the military withdrew; Meredith claimed 986 kills for 9,860 rounds fired, a figure historians treat cautiously. Later bounty schemes and better fencing did more to protect crops. The 'war' became a famous piece of Australian folklore.

sections.key: Australia has more than 800 bird species, and simple habits help the ones near you.
sections.b: More than 800 bird species have been recorded in Australia, and a large share are found nowhere else. You don't need to travel to enjoy them: a local park, wetland or backyard can host dozens. Taking part in citizen science, such as BirdLife Australia's Aussie Backyard Bird Count each October, turns your observations into useful data. To help birds, plant local native shrubs that provide food and shelter, offer a shallow bird bath with clean water and keep cats indoors, especially at night. Avoid feeding wild birds bread or mince, which can make them sick and create dependence. A pair of binoculars and a field guide app go a long way.

quiz.q: Where did songbirds originally evolve?
quiz.e: The oldest songbird lineages are found here.

quiz.q: What are male lyrebirds best known for?
quiz.e: They copy many other birds' calls.

quiz.q: Which emu parent incubates the eggs?
quiz.e: He sits for about eight weeks, barely eating.

quiz.q: Why are cassowaries so important to rainforests?
o: They spread seeds by swallowing fruit whole
quiz.e: They are gardeners of the rainforest.

quiz.q: What did the military bring to the 1932 Emu War?
quiz.e: The emus proved very hard to hit.

LESSONS.title: Australia's reptiles, up close
LESSONS.hook: Australia is a reptile superpower, home to giant crocodiles, dinosaur-like lizards and some of the world's most venomous snakes. Here's how to appreciate them safely.

sections.key: Australia has more than 1,000 reptile species, most found nowhere else.
sections.b: Australia has more than 1,000 described reptile species, one of the richest reptile faunas of any country, and new ones are still being named every year. The vast majority are found nowhere else on Earth. Lizards dominate: skinks alone make up several hundred species, joined by geckos, dragons, legless lizards and monitors. The dry interior is especially rich, because warm, sunny conditions suit animals that rely on outside heat to regulate their body temperature. Reptiles also cope well with scarce food and water, since they need far less energy than mammals or birds of the same size. Many are small, shy and active at night.

sections.key: Australia has many highly venomous snakes, but deaths average only about two a year.
sections.b: Most Australian land snakes belong to the elapid family, which includes the highly venomous taipans, brown snakes, tiger snakes and death adders. The inland taipan has the most toxic venom of any land snake in laboratory tests, yet it lives in remote inland Australia, is shy, and has no recorded human deaths. Brown snakes cause the most deaths, largely because they are common near farms and towns. Even so, Australia averages only around two snakebite deaths a year. Some bites are 'dry', delivering little or no venom, and effective antivenoms, fast ambulance services and good first aid mean nearly everyone who is bitten survives.

sections.key: Saltwater crocodiles are the largest living reptiles and have recovered strongly since protection.
sections.b: The saltwater crocodile is the world's largest living reptile. Big males commonly reach about five metres and can weigh around a tonne, while females are much smaller. Despite the name, 'salties' live in rivers, billabongs, estuaries and coastal waters across northern Australia, and can travel long distances by sea. By the 1970s, hunting for skins had reduced them to a fraction of their former numbers. After protection began in the early 1970s, populations recovered dramatically, and the Northern Territory now has around 100,000 wild saltwater crocodiles. The smaller freshwater crocodile is far less dangerous, but still deserves respect. As in many reptiles, nest temperature helps determine whether hatchlings are male or female.

sections.key: Australia has more monitor lizard species than any other continent, including the perentie.
sections.b: Goannas are monitor lizards, members of the genus Varanus. Australia has around 30 species, more than any other continent, ranging from pygmy monitors shorter than a ruler to the perentie, Australia's largest lizard, which can exceed two metres. Goannas are active hunters and scavengers, tasting the air with a forked tongue to track food. Research suggests many monitors have venom glands, though how important the venom is for hunting is still debated. The lace monitor is a familiar sight in eastern forests and campsites, where it climbs trees and raids bins. A giant relative, often called Megalania, roamed Australia until tens of thousands of years ago.

sections.key: Frill-necked lizards flare a large skin frill as a bluff, then flee on their hind legs.
sections.b: The frill-necked lizard lives in the tropical woodlands of northern Australia and southern New Guinea, spending much of its time in trees. Normally its frill lies folded like a cape around its neck. When threatened, the lizard opens its mouth wide, hisses and flares the frill into a startling disc, making itself look far bigger than it is. If the bluff fails, it turns and sprints away upright on its hind legs, often to the nearest tree. It eats mainly insects and other small animals. The frill-necked lizard appeared on the Australian two-cent coin and became a national icon.

sections.key: Thorny devils drink through their skin, and blue-tongues flash their tongues as a warning.
sections.b: Australia's reptiles are full of surprises. The thorny devil, a small spiky desert lizard, has tiny grooves between its scales that draw water from damp sand or dew by capillary action towards its mouth, so it can drink through its skin. The blue-tongue lizard, a common garden visitor, opens its mouth to flash a bright blue tongue when threatened. The shingleback, a close relative, often returns to the same partner year after year. Six of the world's seven species of sea turtle occur in Australian waters, and dozens of sea snake species live in tropical seas. Many harmless lizards, like blue-tongues, are great for gardens because they eat snails.

sections.key: Most snakebites happen when people try to catch or kill snakes; leave them alone.
sections.b: Snakes generally avoid people and bite in self-defence. Many bites happen when someone tries to catch, move or kill a snake, so the safest approach is to keep still, then back away slowly and let it move on. Around the home, keep grass short, clear rubbish piles and control mice, which attract snakes. In the bush, wear boots and long pants, watch where you step and use a torch at night. If a snake is inside, keep people and pets away and call a licensed snake catcher. In most states, native reptiles are protected, and killing one can be an offence as well as risky.

sections.key: For a bite, use a pressure immobilisation bandage and call 000; in croc country, obey warning signs.
sections.b: For any suspected snakebite in Australia, call 000, keep the person still and calm, and apply a pressure immobilisation bandage over the bite and up the whole limb, then splint it. Don't wash, cut or suck the bite, and don't use a tourniquet. A first aid course is worth doing. In crocodile country, obey warning signs, never swim where crocodiles may live, stand well back from the water's edge, don't clean fish or leave food scraps near water, and camp well away from riverbanks; Queensland advises at least 50 metres. Treated with respect, Australia's reptiles are fascinating neighbours rather than threats.

quiz.q: About how many reptile species does Australia have?
quiz.e: One of the richest reptile faunas in the world.

quiz.q: Which snake has the most toxic venom of any land snake, but no recorded human deaths?
quiz.e: It is shy and lives in remote areas.

quiz.q: What happened to saltwater crocodile numbers after protection in the 1970s?
o: They became extinct in the NT
quiz.e: The NT now has around 100,000.

quiz.q: What does a frill-necked lizard do when threatened?
quiz.e: Then it runs away on its hind legs.

quiz.q: In Queensland croc country, how far from the water's edge are campers advised to set up?
o: Distance doesn't matter in a tent
quiz.e: Also stand well back from the edge and never leave fish scraps near the water.

LESSONS.title: How clever are animals?
LESSONS.hook: Crows that craft tools, dolphins with names, elephants that cooperate. Animal minds are far richer than we once assumed, and harder to measure.

sections.key: Each species is clever in ways suited to its life, so there's no single ladder of intelligence.
sections.b: Comparing intelligence across species is surprisingly hard. Each animal evolved to solve the problems of its own world: a squirrel remembers thousands of buried nuts, a bat navigates by echoes, a bee learns which flowers pay off. Tests designed around human strengths can make other species look dull. Scientists also learned caution from Clever Hans, a German horse in the early 1900s that seemed to do arithmetic. In 1907, psychologist Oskar Pfungst showed Hans was actually reading tiny, unconscious cues from his questioner. Today researchers use careful controls and look at abilities like problem-solving, memory, learning from others and understanding what other individuals know.

sections.key: New Caledonian crows make and shape tools, and crows can remember human faces for years.
sections.b: Crows, ravens and their relatives are among the cleverest animals known. New Caledonian crows, from a Pacific island east of Australia, make tools in the wild, shaping hooked sticks and cutting stepped strips from pandanus leaves to extract grubs. In a famous 2002 Oxford experiment, a crow named Betty bent a straight piece of wire into a hook to lift a food basket from a tube. In other tests, crows drop stones into water to raise the level and reach floating food. American researchers who wore a particular mask while trapping crows found that the birds scolded that mask for years afterwards, and taught other crows to do the same.

sections.key: Jane Goodall's 1960 discovery of chimpanzee tool use changed how we define humans.
sections.b: In 1960, Jane Goodall saw chimpanzees in Gombe, Tanzania, strip leaves from twigs and poke them into termite mounds to fish out termites. Tool-making had been seen as uniquely human, and her mentor Louis Leakey famously responded that we would now have to redefine 'tool', redefine 'man', or accept chimpanzees as humans. Since then, researchers have found that chimpanzee communities have different traditions, such as cracking nuts with stone hammers in West Africa, which young animals learn over years. Orangutans and bonobos also use tools. Claims about apes learning human language are more contested: some learned many signs or symbols, but whether that amounts to language is debated.

sections.key: Dolphins use sponges as tools and have signature whistles that work much like names.
sections.b: Bottlenose dolphins have large brains and complex social lives. In Shark Bay, Western Australia, some dolphins tear off marine sponges and wear them over their beaks while probing the sandy seafloor for fish, protecting themselves from scrapes. This 'sponging' is passed down mainly from mothers to their calves, especially daughters, which makes it a form of culture. Each dolphin also develops its own signature whistle early in life. Other dolphins copy these whistles to call specific individuals, and dolphins respond when they hear their own, so the whistles work much like names. Dolphins also cooperate when hunting and form long-term alliances.
