sections.key: Elephants rely on the memories of older females and can cooperate to solve problems.
sections.b: The idea that elephants never forget has some truth. Elephant family groups are led by an older female, the matriarch, whose knowledge of water sources, dangers and routes can be vital in droughts. Research in Kenya found that families with older matriarchs were better at telling apart the calls of familiar and unfamiliar elephants, and at reacting appropriately to the roars of male lions, the more dangerous threat. In cooperation experiments, pairs of elephants learned to pull two ends of a rope at the same time to bring food within reach, and would wait for a partner before pulling. Elephants also pay close attention to the bones of dead elephants.

sections.key: The mirror test checks if an animal uses a mirror to inspect a mark on its own body.
sections.b: In 1970, psychologist Gordon Gallup Jr developed the mirror test. An animal is given time with a mirror, then a coloured mark is placed on its body somewhere it can only see in the mirror. If it uses the reflection to touch or inspect the mark, that suggests it recognises the image as itself. Chimpanzees passed, and later so did other great apes, some bottlenose dolphins, an Asian elephant at the Bronx Zoo, and Eurasian magpies. Humans usually pass at around 18 months to two years. Most animals, including monkeys and many birds, treat their reflection as another individual, or simply lose interest in it.

sections.key: Failing the mirror test doesn't prove an animal lacks self-awareness.
sections.b: The mirror test is useful but narrow. It relies on vision, so it may be unfair to animals that experience the world mainly through smell or sound. Dogs usually fail it, but a 2017 study found dogs spent longer sniffing their own urine when it had been altered with an added scent, suggesting a kind of self-recognition by smell. Many gorillas fail, possibly because they avoid direct eye contact. Animals may also simply not care about a mark. And in 2019, a small reef fish, the cleaner wrasse, appeared to pass, sparking fierce debate about what the test actually measures. Passing suggests something interesting; failing proves little.

sections.key: Intelligence evolved many times in different forms, a good reason for humility and care.
sections.b: The big lesson is that complex minds have evolved many times, in very different bodies. Birds' brains are wired differently from ours but can pack in large numbers of neurons, and octopuses, bees, parrots, rats and pigs all show impressive learning. In 2012, a group of scientists signed the Cambridge Declaration on Consciousness, stating that many animals possess the brain systems that support conscious experience. You can see animal smarts yourself: watch local magpies, crows or cockatoos solve problems, or try puzzle feeders with a dog. Recognising animal minds has practical weight too, informing debates about farming, zoos, research and wildlife protection.

quiz.q: What did Clever Hans actually do?
o: Read tiny cues from his questioner
quiz.e: A classic warning for animal researchers.

quiz.q: What did Betty the crow famously do in 2002?
o: Bent wire into a hook to retrieve food
quiz.e: She made a new tool from a straight wire.

quiz.q: What did Jane Goodall observe chimpanzees doing in 1960?
o: Using twigs to fish for termites
quiz.e: It challenged the idea that only humans make tools.

quiz.q: What is 'sponging' in Shark Bay dolphins?
o: Wearing sponges on their beaks while foraging
quiz.e: Passed mainly from mothers to calves.

quiz.q: Why can failing the mirror test be misleading?
o: It relies on vision and the animal may not care about the mark
quiz.e: Dogs may recognise themselves by smell instead.

LESSONS.title: Senses beyond our own
LESSONS.hook: Bats see with sound, turtles read the Earth's magnetism and sharks feel your heartbeat's electricity. Every animal lives in a different sensory world.

sections.key: Every species perceives a different slice of reality, called its umwelt.
sections.b: In the early 1900s, the German biologist Jakob von Uexküll used the word umwelt, meaning 'surrounding world', for the particular slice of reality each animal can sense. A tick responds to warmth and the smell of butyric acid in mammal sweat; a bee lives in a world of ultraviolet patterns; a dog in a world of scent trails. Our own umwelt is narrow. We can't hear the ultrasonic calls of bats, see ultraviolet light or feel electric fields. Understanding other animals' senses helps explain their behaviour, and has inspired technologies from sonar to medical ultrasound. It is also a useful reminder that our view of reality is just one of many.

sections.key: Many bats and toothed whales find their way by listening to the echoes of their own calls.
sections.b: Bats that hunt insects at night produce rapid, high-pitched calls, mostly above the range of human hearing, and listen to the returning echoes. From these they can judge the distance, size, direction and texture of objects, precisely enough to snatch flying insects in total darkness. American scientist Donald Griffin coined the term echolocation in the 1940s. Dolphins and other toothed whales echolocate with clicks, and some blind people have learned to navigate using tongue clicks. Bats are not blind, by the way. Australia's large flying foxes mostly don't echolocate at all; they find fruit and nectar with good eyesight and a keen sense of smell.

sections.key: Many migratory animals sense Earth's magnetic field, though exactly how is still debated.
sections.b: Many animals can detect Earth's magnetic field and use it to navigate, including migratory birds, sea turtles, salmon and some insects. Experiments with European robins from the 1960s showed caged birds oriented themselves in the migratory direction, and changed direction when the magnetic field around them was altered. Young sea turtles appear to learn the magnetic 'signature' of their home coastline and use it years later to return to nest. How animals sense magnetism is still debated. One leading idea involves light-sensitive proteins called cryptochromes in birds' eyes; another involves tiny magnetic iron particles in the body. Some animals may use both.

sections.key: Many insects, birds and fish see ultraviolet light, revealing patterns invisible to us.
sections.b: Human eyes detect three primary colours, and our lens blocks most ultraviolet light. Many other animals see into the ultraviolet, including bees, butterflies, many birds, fish and reptiles. To a bee, many flowers that look plain to us carry bold UV patterns, often called nectar guides, that point towards the pollen and nectar. Many birds have four types of colour receptor rather than our three, and in many species males and females that look identical to us have distinct UV markings. Reindeer can also see some ultraviolet light, which may help them spot lichen and predators against the bright snow of the Arctic.

sections.key: Dogs have hundreds of millions of scent receptors, making them superb detectors.
sections.b: A dog's nose is a remarkable instrument. Dogs have an estimated 200 to 300 million scent receptors, compared with roughly five or six million in humans, and a large part of their brain is devoted to analysing smells. When a dog sniffs, air is diverted to a special region for smelling, and exhaled air leaves through side slits so it doesn't blow away incoming scent. Estimates of how much better dogs smell than we do vary widely, but it is many thousands of times. Australia's biosecurity detector dogs sniff out undeclared food and plant material at airports and mail centres, and dogs are trained to find explosives, drugs and missing people.

sections.key: Sharks detect the faint electric fields of prey using jelly-filled pores called ampullae of Lorenzini.
sections.b: Sharks and rays have hundreds to thousands of tiny jelly-filled pores on their snouts called ampullae of Lorenzini. These detect extremely weak electric fields, such as those produced by the muscles and heartbeat of a fish buried in sand. The wide head of a hammerhead shark spreads these sensors out, helping it sweep the seabed for hidden rays. This sense inspired electrical shark deterrents, some of which have been shown in testing to reduce, but not eliminate, the chance of a shark approaching. Popular claims that sharks can smell one drop of blood from kilometres away are exaggerated; their sense of smell is good, but comparable to many other fish.

sections.key: Mantis shrimp have up to 16 types of photoreceptor, yet are worse than us at telling similar colours apart.
sections.b: Mantis shrimp are often described as seeing a rainbow of colours we can't imagine, because they have up to 16 types of photoreceptor, including around 12 for colour, compared with our three. But a 2014 study led by researchers at the University of Queensland found that mantis shrimp are actually worse than humans at telling apart similar colours. They seem to use a different system: rather than comparing signals from receptors, they may recognise colours quickly and directly, like a barcode scanner. They can also see polarised light, including circular polarisation, which is extremely rare. And some species strike prey with one of the fastest punches in the animal kingdom.

sections.key: Goldfish have good memories, bulls aren't angered by red, and human senses are just one slice of reality.
sections.b: Some familiar ideas about animal senses are wrong. Goldfish don't have three-second memories; they can learn and remember tasks for months. Bulls don't charge at red; they are colour-blind to red and react to the movement of the matador's cape. Other senses are real but under-appreciated: pythons and pit vipers detect body heat with infrared-sensing pits, and many birds can hear infrasound far below our range. For you, the lesson is practical: when an animal's behaviour seems strange, ask what it might be sensing. Your dog may be reading a scent story, and a bird may be seeing colours on a flower you can't.

quiz.q: What does the word 'umwelt' describe?
o: The slice of reality an animal can sense
quiz.e: Each species has its own sensory world.

quiz.q: Which statement about Australian flying foxes is true?
o: They mostly don't echolocate and rely on sight and smell
They use echolocation to find fruit
They sense magnetic fields to find food
quiz.e: Bats are not blind.

quiz.q: What are nectar guides?
o: Ultraviolet patterns on flowers visible to bees
quiz.e: Invisible to us, obvious to a bee.

quiz.q: How does a hammerhead's wide head help it hunt?
o: It spreads its electric sensors out to sweep the seabed
quiz.e: It helps it find rays hidden in the sand.

quiz.q: What did a 2014 study find about mantis shrimp colour vision?
o: They see millions more colours than us
They are worse than humans at telling similar colours apart
quiz.e: They seem to use a quick, different system.

LESSONS.title: The great animal migrations
LESSONS.hook: A young bird flies from Alaska to Tasmania without landing. Moths navigate by the stars. Migration is one of nature's most astonishing feats.

sections.key: Migration is a regular round trip to use seasonal food and safe breeding places.
sections.b: Migration is a regular, usually seasonal, movement between places, often a round trip repeated every year. Animals migrate to take advantage of resources that come and go: summer insects in the Arctic, fresh grass after rain, safe breeding beaches or warmer winter refuges. It is a gamble, because the journey is costly and dangerous, but the reward is access to abundant food or safer places to raise young. The record-holder for distance is the Arctic tern, which flies from the Arctic to the Antarctic and back each year, tracked covering roughly 70,000 kilometres or more, and seeing more daylight than any other animal.

sections.key: In 2022, a young bar-tailed godwit flew about 13,500 kilometres nonstop from Alaska to Tasmania.
sections.b: The bar-tailed godwit, a long-billed shorebird, holds the record for the longest nonstop flight by a bird. In October 2022, a five-month-old godwit fitted with a satellite tag in Alaska flew about 13,500 kilometres to Tasmania in around 11 days, without landing to feed, drink or rest. It was making the journey for the first time. Before departure, godwits eat intensively until fat makes up a large share of their body weight, while organs they won't need in flight, such as parts of the gut, shrink. Many godwits spend the southern summer on the coasts of Australia and New Zealand.

sections.key: Millions of shorebirds use the East Asian–Australasian Flyway, but many species are declining.
sections.b: Each year, millions of migratory shorebirds travel along the East Asian–Australasian Flyway, breeding in Siberia and Alaska during the northern summer and spending the rest of the year on Australian and New Zealand coasts. Sites like Roebuck Bay near Broome and Moreton Bay in Queensland are internationally important. On the way, the birds refuel on the tidal mudflats of the Yellow Sea, between China and Korea, where large areas have been lost to land reclamation. Several species have declined sharply. The far eastern curlew, the world's largest shorebird, was listed as critically endangered in Australia in 2015. Protecting their feeding and roosting sites matters at every stop.

sections.key: Tens of millions of red crabs migrate to the sea to breed, timed to rain and the moon.
sections.b: Christmas Island, an Australian territory in the Indian Ocean, is home to tens of millions of red land crabs that live in the forest. With the first heavy rains of the wet season, usually around October to December, they march to the coast to breed, covering roads, rocks and even houses in red. Males dig burrows near the shore, and mating follows. Females then release their eggs into the sea at the turn of the high tide, before dawn, around the last quarter of the moon. Park rangers close roads and have built crab bridges and underpasses. Invasive yellow crazy ants are a serious threat.

sections.key: Bogong moths fly up to about 1,000 kilometres to the Australian Alps, navigating partly by the stars.
sections.b: Each spring, billions of bogong moths leave the plains of southern Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria and fly up to about 1,000 kilometres to cool caves and rock crevices in the Australian Alps, where they rest through summer before returning in autumn. Research published in 2025 showed that bogong moths can use the starry night sky, including the Milky Way, as a compass, alongside Earth's magnetic field. For thousands of years, the moths were an important food for Aboriginal peoples, who gathered in the high country during the moth season. Moth numbers crashed during severe drought around 2017 to 2019, and the species is now listed as endangered internationally.

sections.key: Eastern monarchs travel thousands of kilometres to Mexico, a journey spread across several generations.
sections.b: In North America, eastern monarch butterflies fly up to around 4,000 kilometres from Canada and the United States to overwinter in fir forests in the mountains of central Mexico, where millions cluster on the trees. No single butterfly makes the whole round trip. The migrating 'super generation' lives for many months, while the summer generations that carry the return journey northwards live only a few weeks each. Monarchs navigate using a sun compass, correcting for the sun's movement with an internal clock in their antennae. Monarchs also reached Australia in the 1870s, where they are sometimes called wanderers, and some cluster together over winter.

sections.key: More than a million wildebeest follow the rains in a vast loop through the Serengeti and Masai Mara.
sections.b: In East Africa, more than a million wildebeest, joined by hundreds of thousands of zebras and gazelles, move in a great loop through Tanzania's Serengeti and Kenya's Masai Mara, following the rains and fresh grass. Early in the year, in the southern Serengeti, hundreds of thousands of calves are born within a few weeks, a timing that overwhelms predators. Later, the herds head north, where dramatic crossings of the Mara River, lined with crocodiles, usually happen from around July to October. The migration shapes the whole ecosystem, feeding lions, hyenas and crocodiles, and fertilising the grasslands with the herds' dung.

sections.key: Animals navigate using the sun, stars, magnetism, landmarks and smell, often in combination.
sections.b: Migrating animals use a toolkit of cues. Many birds use a sun compass by day and star patterns by night; in the 1960s, experiments in a planetarium showed that indigo buntings learn to orient using the stars around the pole. Magnetic sensing, landmarks such as coastlines and mountains, and smell also play roles; salmon return to their home streams partly by scent. Many young birds make their first migration alone, guided by inherited directions. Today, migrating animals face habitat loss, climate change and artificial light at night, which disorients birds and moths. Turning off unneeded outdoor lights and protecting wetlands genuinely helps.

quiz.q: Which bird has the longest annual migration?
quiz.e: Roughly 70,000 kilometres a year or more.

quiz.q: What record did a bar-tailed godwit set in 2022?
o: Longest nonstop bird flight, Alaska to Tasmania
quiz.e: About 13,500 km in around 11 days.

quiz.q: What triggers the Christmas Island red crab migration?
o: The first heavy rains of the wet season
quiz.e: Spawning is then timed to the moon and tides.

quiz.q: What did 2025 research show bogong moths use to navigate?
o: The starry sky, including the Milky Way
quiz.e: Alongside Earth's magnetic field.

quiz.q: How do monarch butterflies complete their migration?
quiz.e: No single butterfly makes the round trip.

LESSONS.title: The first artists
LESSONS.hook: Tens of thousands of years before writing, people crawled into dark caves and painted animals so well they still take your breath away.

sections.key: Figurative art is at least 50,000 years old, many times older than writing, which appeared only about 5,000 years ago.
sections.b: Writing was invented only about 5,000 years ago, but people were making pictures long before that. Painted and engraved images of animals, people and hands have been found on every inhabited continent. The oldest dated figurative painting is more than 51,000 years old, and a hand stencil found on the Indonesian island of Muna, dated in 2026, is at least 67,800 years old, the oldest known rock art. Art is not a late luxury of civilisation. It appears to be one of the oldest and most widespread things our species does, as basic to being human as language or cooking.

sections.key: Lascaux in France, painted about 17,000 years ago, holds around 600 paintings and was found by teenagers in 1940.
sections.b: In September 1940, four teenagers in south-western France followed a hole near the village of Montignac and found a cave covered in paintings. Lascaux, as it became known, holds around 600 paintings and about 1,500 engravings, made roughly 17,000 years ago. Its Hall of the Bulls shows horses, deer and huge aurochs, an extinct wild cattle, some more than five metres long. So many visitors came after the war that their breath and body heat damaged the walls, and the cave was closed to the public in 1963. Today people visit detailed replicas instead.

sections.key: Chauvet Cave, discovered in 1994, contains paintings over 30,000 years old, including lions, rhinos and mammoths.
sections.b: In 1994, three cave explorers in the Ardèche region of southern France discovered Chauvet Cave. Its paintings shocked experts: they are more than 30,000 years old, roughly twice the age of Lascaux, yet just as skilful. The artists used shading, scraped the rock to make it paler, and drew overlapping outlines that seem to suggest movement, like frames of animation. Unusually, many of the animals are dangerous ones: cave lions, woolly rhinoceroses, mammoths and bears. Chauvet has never been opened to the public. A full-scale replica opened nearby in 2015.

sections.key: Cave paintings on the Indonesian island of Sulawesi are among the oldest known, dated to at least 45,000 to 51,000 years ago.
sections.b: For a long time, Europe was thought to be the birthplace of cave art. Discoveries on Sulawesi, in Indonesia, to Australia's north, overturned that idea. In 2014, researchers dated hand stencils there to about 40,000 years old. In 2021 a painting of a warty pig in the cave of Leang Tedongnge was dated to at least 45,500 years, and in 2024 a scene of human-like figures with a pig was dated to at least 51,200 years. These dates come from mineral crusts that formed over the paint, so they are minimum ages.

sections.key: Australia has one of the richest rock art records on Earth, in places like the Kimberley, Arnhem Land and Murujuga.
sections.b: Australia has one of the largest and longest rock art traditions in the world, created by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples. In the Kimberley, Gwion Gwion paintings show elegant human figures with tassels and headdresses, and a painted kangaroo has been dated to about 17,000 years old. In western Arnhem Land and neighbouring Kakadu, sites such as Ubirr show fish and animals in 'x-ray' style, with backbones and organs visible. Murujuga, on the Burrup Peninsula in Western Australia, holds more than a million engravings, and was added to the World Heritage List in 2025.

sections.key: Unlike the European caves, much Australian rock art belongs to cultures that still care for it and know its meaning.
sections.b: European cave art was made by cultures that vanished long ago, so its meaning is guesswork. Much Australian rock art is different: Traditional Owners still care for the sites, know the stories connected to them, and in some places have repainted or added to them within living memory. Some Arnhem Land paintings record the arrival of outsiders, showing Macassan fishing boats from Sulawesi, European ships, horses and rifles. Many sites are sacred, and some are not meant to be visited or photographed. Where sites are open, go with a guide or follow posted guidance, and never touch the paintings.

sections.key: Nobody knows for sure why the ancient cave art was made; ideas include ritual, storytelling, teaching and marking place.
sections.b: For the ancient European caves, we can only infer purpose, and every theory is debated. Early scholars suggested 'hunting magic', painting animals to help catch them, but the animals shown often don't match what people mostly ate. Others argue the deep, hard-to-reach chambers point to ritual or spiritual experience. Art may also have passed on knowledge about animals and seasons, told stories, or marked who belonged to a place. Handprints feel like a signature: 'I was here.' It is likely there was no single reason, just as there isn't for art today.

sections.key: Cave art shows that the urge to make images is ancient, universal and deeply human.
sections.b: Cave art is a reminder that people tens of thousands of years ago were not simple or primitive. They had the same brains we do, and the same urge to observe carefully, remember and share. When you look at a Chauvet lion or a Kimberley figure, you are seeing the work of someone who studied the world closely and wanted it to last. You can explore online virtual tours of Lascaux and Chauvet, visit rock art sites in Kakadu or near Sydney with a guide, and read about the Traditional Owners who care for them.

quiz.q: Why was Lascaux closed to the public in 1963?
o: It was declared unsafe after an earthquake
Visitors' breath and body heat were damaging the paintings
The paintings were found to be fakes
quiz.e: Crowds changed the cave's air and moisture, and mould and damage followed, so visitors now see replicas.

quiz.q: Roughly how old are the paintings in Chauvet Cave?
quiz.e: Chauvet's paintings are more than 30,000 years old, around twice the age of Lascaux.

quiz.q: What did discoveries on Sulawesi show about cave art?
o: Some of the oldest known figurative paintings are in Indonesia, not Europe
Cave art was invented in the Middle Ages
All cave art was copied from Lascaux
quiz.e: Paintings on Sulawesi dated to at least 45,000 to 51,000 years overturned the idea that figurative art began in Europe.

quiz.q: Which site on the Burrup Peninsula holds more than a million rock engravings?
quiz.e: Murujuga in Western Australia has one of the largest concentrations of rock engravings in the world.

quiz.q: What is the most honest answer to why ancient people painted caves?
o: Nobody knows for sure, and there were probably several reasons
It was a way of writing words
quiz.e: Theories include ritual, storytelling, teaching and marking place, but for the ancient European caves the purpose is debated.

LESSONS.title: Aboriginal art
LESSONS.hook: The world's oldest continuous art tradition is also one of its most exciting contemporary art movements, and it has never been just one style.

sections.key: Aboriginal art is not a single style: it varies hugely between hundreds of cultures and regions.
sections.b: At the time of British colonisation, Australia was home to more than 250 distinct Aboriginal languages, each belonging to its own peoples with their own Country, law and stories. Art reflects that diversity. Dot painting from the Central and Western Desert is famous, but it is only one tradition. Arnhem Land is known for bark painting and fine cross-hatching called rarrk. The Tiwi Islands have bold ochre designs and carved poles. South-eastern peoples carved trees and made possum-skin cloaks. Torres Strait Islanders, a distinct culture, are renowned for masks, headdresses and linocut prints.

sections.key: Much Aboriginal art records law, Country and ancestral stories, not just decoration.
sections.b: In many Aboriginal cultures, art is not separate from law, religion and knowledge of the land. Designs can record ancestral beings and their journeys, show waterholes and landmarks, or identify the family groups responsible for a place. The English word 'Dreaming' is often used for this body of law and story, though each language has its own term, such as Tjukurrpa in parts of the Western Desert. Many people prefer 'Dreaming' to the older 'Dreamtime', because it is ongoing, not only in the past. The same design can carry public and restricted layers of meaning.

sections.key: Rock art and bark painting are among the oldest forms, and bark paintings played a key role in land rights.
sections.b: Rock art across Australia stretches back tens of thousands of years, from Kimberley figures to engravings in the Sydney sandstone. Bark painting, done with natural ochres on flattened sheets of stringybark, is strongly associated with Arnhem Land. It became politically powerful too. In 1963, Yolŋu people at Yirrkala sent the federal parliament petitions typed on paper and framed by bark paintings, protesting a bauxite mine on their land. The Yirrkala Bark Petitions are recognised as foundational documents in the land rights movement, and they are still displayed at Parliament House in Canberra.

sections.key: The contemporary dot painting movement began at Papunya in 1971 and led to the Papunya Tula Artists company.
sections.b: In 1971, at Papunya, a settlement west of Alice Springs, schoolteacher Geoffrey Bardon encouraged a group of senior men to paint a mural on the school wall. The Honey Ant Dreaming mural sparked something remarkable. Men began painting ancestral designs, previously made in sand, on body or on objects, using acrylic paint on board and later canvas. In 1972 they formed Papunya Tula Artists, a company owned by the artists. Painters such as Clifford Possum Tjapaltjarri and Kaapa Tjampitjinpa became internationally known, and the movement spread across the desert.

sections.key: Dots and symbols translate ceremonial designs into paint, and were partly used to veil sacred details.
sections.b: Desert paintings often use a shared visual language: concentric circles can mean a waterhole or campsite, U shapes can mean people seated, and lines show travel between places. These echo designs made in sand and body paint for ceremony. Early Papunya paintings showed some sacred designs openly, which caused distress when they were seen by people not entitled to see them. Artists responded partly by covering or surrounding those elements with dots and infill. The result is a style that can share a story publicly while keeping its deepest meanings for those with the right to know.

sections.key: Albert Namatjira and Emily Kame Kngwarreye are two of Australia's most celebrated artists.
sections.b: Albert Namatjira, a Western Arrernte man from Hermannsburg (Ntaria), learned watercolour in the 1930s and painted the MacDonnell Ranges in glowing colour. He became a national celebrity, and in 1957 he and his wife Rubina were among the first Aboriginal people granted full citizenship rights. Emily Kame Kngwarreye, an Anmatyerre woman from Utopia, began painting on canvas in her late 70s, around 1988. In roughly eight years she produced thousands of works, from dense dots to sweeping lines. She has since had major retrospectives in Canberra and London. Her name is now often spelt Kngwarray.

sections.key: Stories and designs belong to particular people, and copying them without permission causes real harm.
sections.b: In Aboriginal law, the right to paint a particular story or design is usually inherited and held by specific people, often with responsibilities to Country and kin. Using those designs without permission is not flattery; it can be a serious breach. Australian courts have recognised this in copyright cases, such as the 1994 'carpets case', where imported rugs copied artists' designs. Fake 'Aboriginal-style' souvenirs have also led to penalties. Namatjira's family lost control of his copyright after his death and regained it only in 2017, a long campaign that highlights why ownership matters.

sections.key: Buy from Aboriginal-owned art centres, use respectful language, and listen to how communities describe their art.
sections.b: If you buy Aboriginal art, look for Aboriginal-owned community art centres or dealers who sign the Indigenous Art Code, so artists are paid fairly and work is authentic. Say 'Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples' or, better, the specific nation, such as Warlpiri or Yolŋu, rather than lumping everyone together. Avoid words like 'primitive', and don't treat the art as only ancient: it is a living, contemporary practice. Some communities avoid images or names of people who have died, so heed warnings. Most of all, let artists and communities explain their work in their own words.

quiz.q: What is 'rarrk'?
o: A type of Western Desert dot painting
Fine cross-hatching associated with Arnhem Land art
A watercolour technique used by Namatjira
quiz.e: Rarrk is the fine cross-hatching found in bark paintings and other art from Arnhem Land.

quiz.q: What were the Yirrkala Bark Petitions of 1963?
o: Petitions to federal parliament, framed by bark paintings, protesting a mine
quiz.e: Yolŋu people sent the petitions to protest bauxite mining on their land; they are key documents in the land rights movement.

quiz.q: Where did the contemporary dot painting movement begin in 1971?
quiz.e: At Papunya, men painted the Honey Ant Dreaming mural and then formed Papunya Tula Artists in 1972.

quiz.q: What is remarkable about Emily Kame Kngwarreye's painting career?
o: She began painting on canvas in her late 70s and made thousands of works in about eight years
quiz.e: Kngwarreye started on canvas around 1988 and became one of Australia's most celebrated artists.

quiz.q: In many Aboriginal cultures, who has the right to paint a particular story or design?
o: Specific people who inherit that right
quiz.e: Rights to stories and designs are usually inherited and held by particular people, so copying without permission can be a serious breach.

LESSONS.title: Impressionism
LESSONS.hook: Rejected by the art establishment and mocked by critics, a group of painters in 1870s Paris changed how the world sees light.

sections.key: In 19th-century France, the official Salon decided which art was seen and valued.
sections.b: In 19th-century Paris, an artist's career depended on the Salon, the official exhibition run by the state-backed Académie des Beaux-Arts. Its juries favoured large, highly finished paintings of history, myth and religion, with smooth surfaces that hid the brushwork. Thousands of works were rejected each year. In 1863 so many were turned away that Emperor Napoleon III allowed a Salon des Refusés, an exhibition of the rejected. Crowds came partly to laugh, especially at Édouard Manet's Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe, which showed a naked woman picnicking with clothed men in modern dress.

sections.key: In 1874 a group of artists held their own exhibition, and a critic's insult gave them their name.
sections.b: Frustrated with the Salon, a group including Claude Monet, Pierre-Auguste Renoir, Edgar Degas, Camille Pissarro and Berthe Morisot organised their own show in 1874, in the former studio of the photographer Nadar. One of Monet's works was titled Impression, Sunrise, a hazy view of the port of Le Havre. The critic Louis Leroy seized on it and mockingly called the group 'Impressionists', meaning their pictures looked like unfinished sketches. The artists eventually adopted the name. They held eight group exhibitions between 1874 and 1886.

sections.key: Impressionists often painted en plein air, outdoors, helped by new paint tubes and railways.
sections.b: Traditional painters sketched outside but finished their pictures in the studio. The Impressionists wanted to capture a real moment of light and weather, so many worked en plein air, French for 'in the open air'. New technology helped. Paint in collapsible metal tubes, invented in 1841, made colours portable, and new railway lines carried Parisians to riverside towns and the coast for the day. Working fast before the light changed, painters used quick, visible brushstrokes and put bright colours side by side, letting the viewer's eye blend them.

sections.key: Monet painted the same subjects again and again to show how light changes them.
sections.b: Claude Monet (1840–1926) became the movement's most devoted student of light. He painted series of the same subject at different times of day and year: haystacks in 1890 and 1891, the front of Rouen Cathedral, and poplars along a river. The subject almost became secondary; the real topic was light, air and colour. In later life at Giverny, outside Paris, he built a water garden and painted it about 250 times in his Water Lilies works. Some of these late canvases are enormous and so loose they point toward abstract art.

sections.key: Renoir painted joyful social life, Degas dancers and modern Paris, and Morisot intimate domestic scenes.
sections.b: The Impressionists were not all alike. Renoir loved people enjoying themselves, as in Bal du moulin de la Galette (1876), with dappled sunlight falling on Parisians dancing outdoors. Degas disliked the Impressionist label and preferred working indoors; he is known for ballet dancers, racecourses and cafés, often seen from odd angles like snapshots. Berthe Morisot showed in seven of the eight exhibitions, painting women and children at home with feathery brushwork. As a woman she could not freely roam cafés and streets the way male colleagues did, which shaped her subjects. Mary Cassatt, an American, also joined.

sections.key: Impressionism shocked because it showed ordinary modern life with visible brushwork and no moral story.
sections.b: Today Impressionism is among the most loved art in the world, so it is hard to imagine it as radical. But it broke several rules at once. The paintings looked unfinished, with brushstrokes left visible. Their subjects were ordinary modern life: train stations, boating parties and suburban gardens, not gods or battles. They told no moral story. Shadows were painted in blues and purples rather than brown and black. Influences came from new places too, including Japanese woodblock prints, with their flat colour and cropped compositions, and photography, with its frozen moments.

sections.key: Australia's Heidelberg School, including Roberts, Streeton and McCubbin, painted the bush in the open air in the 1880s and 1890s.
sections.b: In the late 1880s, a group of Melbourne painters including Tom Roberts, Arthur Streeton, Frederick McCubbin, Charles Conder and Jane Sutherland set up artists' camps at Box Hill and Heidelberg, then on the city's rural edge. Painting outdoors, they tried to capture the harsh, bright Australian light. In 1889 they held the 9 by 5 Impression Exhibition, with many works painted on cigar-box lids about 9 by 5 inches. Later works such as Roberts's Shearing the Rams (1890) and Streeton's Fire's On (1891) became national icons. Historians debate how closely they followed French Impressionism.

sections.key: Step back from an Impressionist painting to let the colours blend, then step close to see the brushwork.
sections.b: Impressionist paintings reward a simple trick: look from two distances. Up close, you see separate dabs of colour, rough and energetic. Step back a few metres and they merge into shimmering water or sunlight. Notice what time of day it seems to be, and where the light comes from. Look at the colours in the shadows. Australian galleries hold fine examples: the National Gallery of Australia, the Art Gallery of New South Wales and the National Gallery of Victoria have French Impressionist works, and state galleries hold major Heidelberg School paintings.

quiz.q: Where did the name 'Impressionism' come from?
o: The artists chose it in a manifesto
A critic mocked Monet's painting Impression, Sunrise
It was the name of a Paris café
Napoleon III gave it to them
quiz.e: Critic Louis Leroy used the title of Monet's painting to mock the group in 1874.

quiz.q: Which invention helped artists paint outdoors?
quiz.e: Paint in portable tubes, invented in 1841, made it practical to work en plein air.

quiz.q: Why did Monet paint the same haystacks and cathedral many times?
o: To study how light and atmosphere changed the scene
Because he ran out of subjects
quiz.e: Monet's series show one subject under different light, weather and seasons.

quiz.q: Which Impressionist is best known for ballet dancers and disliked the Impressionist label?
quiz.e: Degas preferred to call himself a realist or independent and painted dancers, racecourses and cafés.

quiz.q: What was the 9 by 5 Impression Exhibition?
o: A Paris exhibition of rejected works
A Melbourne exhibition of small works, many on cigar-box lids
A series of Monet water lily paintings
quiz.e: Held in Melbourne in 1889, it featured Heidelberg School artists' small oil sketches.

LESSONS.title: Modern art, explained
LESSONS.hook: Melting clocks, soup cans and paint dripped on the floor: the ideas behind a century of art that people love to argue about.

sections.key: Post-Impressionists like Cézanne, Van Gogh, Gauguin and Seurat pushed beyond capturing light.
sections.b: By the 1880s, some artists felt Impressionism was too focused on fleeting light. The critic Roger Fry later grouped them as 'Post-Impressionists'. Paul Cézanne rebuilt nature from simple shapes and planes, aiming for solidity. Vincent van Gogh used swirling brushwork and intense colour to express emotion, as in The Starry Night (1889); he sold very few paintings in his lifetime. Paul Gauguin used flat, symbolic colour. Georges Seurat built pictures from tiny dots of pure colour, a method called pointillism. Each moved away from copying what the eye sees toward expressing ideas and feelings.

sections.key: Picasso and Braque's Cubism showed objects from several viewpoints at once, breaking with centuries of perspective.
sections.b: Since the Renaissance, European painting had used perspective to show a scene from one fixed viewpoint, like a window. Around 1907 to 1914, Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque, working closely in Paris, broke that rule. Inspired partly by Cézanne, they broke objects into facets and showed several sides at once, as if walking around a guitar or a face and combining the views. Picasso's Les Demoiselles d'Avignon (1907) startled even his friends. Cubists also invented collage, gluing newspaper and wallpaper onto canvas. The idea that a painting is a flat object, not a window, changed everything after.

sections.key: In the 1910s, artists like Kandinsky, Malevich and Mondrian made art with no recognisable subject at all.
sections.b: If a painting need not copy the world, could it show nothing recognisable at all? In the 1910s, several artists said yes. Wassily Kandinsky compared colour and form to music, which moves us without depicting anything. Kazimir Malevich painted Black Square (1915), a stark black square on white. Piet Mondrian reduced his paintings to straight lines and primary colours. The Swedish painter Hilma af Klint made large abstract works even earlier, from 1906, but kept them largely private. Meanwhile Marcel Duchamp, in 1917, submitted a factory-made urinal titled Fountain, asking a provocative question: what makes something art?

sections.key: Surrealists, inspired by Freud, painted dreams and the unconscious mind.
sections.b: After the horror of World War I, many artists distrusted reason itself. In 1924, the French writer André Breton published the Surrealist Manifesto, inspired by Sigmund Freud's ideas about dreams and the unconscious. Surrealists tried to unlock the irrational through dream imagery, chance and automatic drawing. Salvador Dalí's The Persistence of Memory (1931), with its melting clocks, is the most famous example. René Magritte painted a pipe with the words 'This is not a pipe' underneath, a witty reminder that a picture of a thing is not the thing. Surrealism spread into film, photography and advertising.

sections.key: In post-war New York, Pollock and Rothko made huge abstract paintings about action and emotion.
sections.b: After World War II, the centre of the art world shifted from Paris to New York. The Abstract Expressionists made huge, abstract canvases meant to carry intense feeling. Jackson Pollock laid canvas on the floor and dripped, poured and flung paint across it, so the painting recorded his movement. Mark Rothko painted soft rectangles of glowing colour, hoping viewers would stand close and feel something profound. In 1973, the Australian government bought Pollock's Blue Poles for $1.3 million for the new national gallery, causing a public uproar. It is now one of the most valuable works in Australia.

sections.key: Pop Art turned advertising, celebrities and mass-produced goods into subjects for fine art.
sections.b: By the late 1950s and 1960s, some artists reacted against the seriousness of Abstract Expressionism. Pop Art took its imagery from consumer culture: advertising, comics, packaging and celebrities. In Britain, Richard Hamilton made collages of the modern home. In the United States, Andy Warhol painted Campbell's Soup Cans (1962) and used screen printing to repeat images of Marilyn Monroe like products on a shelf. Roy Lichtenstein enlarged comic-book panels, dots and all. Pop Art asked whether the line between high art and everyday commercial images was real, and it made art fun, bright and accessible.

sections.key: Modern art is usually about ideas and choices, not just technical difficulty, and experts can often tell it apart from children's work.
sections.b: The complaint that a child could paint a Rothko or a Pollock misses what these artists were doing. Many were highly trained: Picasso painted in a skilled academic style as a teenager, then chose to abandon it. The point was often the idea, the risk of doing something first, and hundreds of deliberate choices about scale, colour and balance. A 2011 study found that people, including non-experts, more often preferred and rated as better works by abstract artists than similar-looking pictures by children or animals, even when some were mislabelled. The difference is subtle, but real.

sections.key: Ask what the artist was reacting to, what choices they made, and how the work makes you feel.
sections.b: Modern art makes more sense when you know what each movement was reacting against: the Salon, perspective, reason, or the seriousness of the art that came before. When you meet a puzzling work, ask three questions. What is this artist rejecting or testing? What deliberate choices can I see, in size, colour, material or placement? How does it feel to stand in front of it? You are allowed not to like it. But try to understand it before deciding. The National Gallery of Australia in Canberra, home to Blue Poles, is a great place to start.

quiz.q: What is pointillism?
o: Building a picture from small dots of pure colour
quiz.e: Georges Seurat developed pointillism, placing dots of colour for the eye to blend.

quiz.q: What was the key innovation of Cubism?
o: Showing objects from several viewpoints at once
quiz.e: Picasso and Braque broke objects into facets, combining multiple viewpoints in one image.

quiz.q: Surrealism was strongly influenced by whose ideas about the unconscious?
quiz.e: André Breton's 1924 manifesto drew on Freud's ideas about dreams and the unconscious.

quiz.q: Which famous painting did the Australian government buy in 1973, sparking controversy?
quiz.e: Blue Poles by Jackson Pollock cost $1.3 million, a huge sum at the time; it is now worth far more.

quiz.q: What is the best response to 'my kid could do that'?
o: Modern art is always about technical difficulty
It is usually about ideas and deliberate choices, and people can often tell the difference
quiz.e: Many modern artists were highly trained and made deliberate choices; studies suggest viewers can often distinguish their work from children's.

LESSONS.title: How to look at a painting
LESSONS.hook: Most gallery visitors spend less than half a minute in front of a painting. Here is how to see far more in the same wall.

sections.key: Studies suggest gallery visitors often spend less than 30 seconds looking at each artwork.
sections.b: Researchers who have quietly timed visitors in major museums, such as the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, have found that people often spend less than 30 seconds in front of a work, and part of that time is spent reading the label. It is not surprising. Galleries are big, walls are crowded, and we are used to scrolling. But paintings were usually made over weeks or months, and they were designed to be looked at slowly. A few simple habits can turn a quick glance into a real encounter.

sections.key: Begin by noticing your gut reaction and what grabs your eye first.
sections.b: Before analysing anything, notice your first reaction. Are you drawn in, bored, uneasy or delighted? Where did your eye land first? That first point is rarely an accident: artists use contrast, colour, light and placement to pull attention to a focal point. Then describe what you actually see, as if to someone on the phone. It sounds basic, but naming things forces you to notice them. A useful set of questions, from an approach called Visual Thinking Strategies, is: What is going on here? What do I see that makes me say that? What more can I find?

sections.key: Composition is how an artist arranges shapes, lines and space to guide your eye.
sections.b: Composition is the arrangement of everything in the picture. Look for the big shapes first: many Renaissance paintings arrange figures in a stable triangle or pyramid. Notice lines, such as roads, arms, gazes or the edge of a table, that lead your eye around the picture. Check where the horizon sits: low makes the sky dominate, high makes the ground feel close. Look at empty space too, which can create calm or loneliness. Try squinting: details disappear and the underlying structure of light and dark shapes becomes much easier to see.

sections.key: Colour sets mood, through warm and cool tones, contrast and how bright or muted colours are.
sections.b: Colour carries emotion before you have worked out the subject. Warm colours, like reds, oranges and yellows, tend to feel energetic or advance toward you; cool blues and greens feel calmer and seem to recede. Complementary colours, opposite each other on the colour wheel, such as blue and orange or red and green, make each other look more intense when placed side by side. Van Gogh used this deliberately. Also notice whether colours are bright and saturated or muted and earthy. Ask yourself: if the colours changed, how would the mood change?

sections.key: Where light falls, and how strong the shadows are, shapes drama and meaning.
sections.b: Find the light source. Is it a window, a candle, the sun or nowhere in particular? Strong contrasts between light and dark, called chiaroscuro, create drama and a sense of solid form. The Italian painter Caravaggio, around 1600, used spotlights of light against deep darkness, like a stage. Rembrandt used light to reveal emotion in faces. Johannes Vermeer's soft window light makes quiet domestic moments feel almost sacred. Light can also carry meaning: in religious art, it often signals the divine, and in Impressionism, it becomes the subject itself.

sections.key: Knowing who made a work, when, for whom and what its symbols meant deepens what you see.
sections.b: Once you have looked closely, context adds layers. Who made this, when and where? Who paid for it, and where was it meant to hang: a church, a palace, a home, a gallery? What did its symbols mean to people at the time? In old European paintings, a skull or a snuffed candle reminds viewers of death, and a dog often suggests loyalty. For Aboriginal art, meaning may be tied to Country and law, and some of it is not public. Read the label and wall text after your first look, not before, so your own eyes do the work first.

sections.key: Spending several minutes with one artwork reveals details and feelings a quick glance misses.
sections.b: Slow looking simply means spending a long time with one work. Harvard art historian Jennifer Roberts famously asks her students to look at a single artwork for three hours, and they report noticing things they would never have seen at first glance. You don't need three hours. Try five or ten minutes with one painting. Sit down if there is a bench. Look at the edges and corners, which people ignore. Notice small details, then step back for the whole. Many galleries now run slow-looking sessions, and some people take part in an annual Slow Art Day.

sections.key: See a few works well rather than everything badly, and use free entry, tours and quiet times.
sections.b: You don't have to see everything. 'Museum fatigue' is real: attention drops fast after an hour or so. Pick one room or a handful of works and look properly, then leave while you are still enjoying it. General admission to many major Australian galleries, including the National Gallery of Australia, the National Gallery of Victoria, the Art Gallery of New South Wales and QAGOMA in Brisbane, is free, so short repeat visits cost nothing. Go early or on a weekday, join a free guided tour, or try a quick sketch, which makes you look harder than a photo ever will.

quiz.q: Roughly how long do studies suggest visitors often spend looking at a single artwork?
quiz.e: Timed studies in major museums found many people spend under half a minute per work, including reading the label.

quiz.q: Why might you squint at a painting?
o: To see the colours more brightly
To reveal the underlying structure of light and dark shapes
To make the painting look older
quiz.e: Squinting blurs detail so the big shapes and composition stand out.

quiz.q: Which pair are complementary colours?
quiz.e: Complementary colours sit opposite each other on the colour wheel and intensify each other.

quiz.q: What is chiaroscuro?
o: Strong contrast between light and dark
quiz.e: Chiaroscuro uses light and shadow to create drama and a sense of solid form, as in Caravaggio's work.

quiz.q: When is it usually best to read the label?
o: Only if the work is famous
quiz.e: Looking first lets your own eyes do the work; the label then adds context.

LESSONS.title: The great epics
LESSONS.hook: Long before novels or films, people gathered to hear poems about heroes, gods and monsters. Some of those poems are still read, performed and argued over thousands of years later.

sections.key: An epic is a long narrative poem about heroic deeds, often involving gods, fate and the story of a people.
sections.b: An epic is a long story told in verse, centred on a hero whose deeds matter to a whole community or nation. Epics usually feature gods or supernatural forces, great journeys or wars, and big questions about fate, honour and death. Many began as oral poetry, performed from memory by professional singers long before anyone wrote them down. Repeated phrases, like Homer's 'rosy-fingered Dawn', helped performers keep track of thousands of lines. Scholars distinguish these traditional epics from later 'literary' epics, written by a single known author who deliberately imitated the old style.

sections.key: The Epic of Gilgamesh, from ancient Mesopotamia, is one of the oldest surviving works of literature.
sections.b: The Epic of Gilgamesh comes from Mesopotamia, in modern Iraq. Poems about Gilgamesh, a king of the city of Uruk, were written in Sumerian around 4,000 years ago, and a longer Babylonian version was assembled later, probably by about 1200 BC. Gilgamesh is arrogant and powerful until he befriends the wild man Enkidu. When Enkidu dies, Gilgamesh sets out in terror to find the secret of eternal life, and fails. Its clay tablets were rediscovered at Nineveh in the 1850s, and in 1872 George Smith caused a sensation by translating a flood story strikingly similar to Noah's.

sections.key: Homer's Iliad tells of a few weeks in the tenth year of the Trojan War, focused on the rage of Achilles.
sections.b: The Iliad is traditionally credited to Homer, a Greek poet who probably lived around the 700s BC, though whether he was one person, and whether he could write, is still debated. Its roughly 15,700 lines don't tell the whole Trojan War. Instead they cover a few weeks in its tenth year, beginning with a quarrel between the Greek commander Agamemnon and his greatest warrior, Achilles. The poem is brutal about war's cost, yet deeply humane. It ends not with Troy's fall but with the funeral of the Trojan prince Hector, after his father begs Achilles for his body.

sections.key: The Odyssey follows Odysseus on his ten-year journey home from Troy to Ithaca and his wife Penelope.
sections.b: The Odyssey, also credited to Homer, follows the clever hero Odysseus on his ten-year struggle to return home to the island of Ithaca after the Trojan War. Along the way he outwits the one-eyed Cyclops Polyphemus by telling him his name is 'Nobody', resists the deadly song of the Sirens and is held for years by the nymph Calypso. Meanwhile, his wife Penelope holds off a crowd of suitors at home. The poem gave English the word 'odyssey', meaning any long, eventful journey. Emily Wilson's 2017 translation made it newly popular with modern readers.

sections.key: Virgil's Aeneid gave Rome a founding epic, tracing its origins to the Trojan refugee Aeneas.
sections.b: The Roman poet Virgil wrote the Aeneid between about 29 and 19 BC, during the rule of Augustus, Rome's first emperor. Deliberately echoing Homer, it follows Aeneas, a Trojan prince who escapes burning Troy and, after a tragic love affair with Queen Dido of Carthage, reaches Italy, where his descendants will found Rome. The poem celebrates Rome's destiny but is haunted by the suffering that destiny demands. Virgil died in 19 BC before finishing it and reportedly asked for the manuscript to be burned. Augustus refused, and the Aeneid became a cornerstone of Western education for nearly 2,000 years.

sections.key: India's Mahabharata is among the longest poems ever composed and contains the Bhagavad Gita.
sections.b: The Mahabharata, written in Sanskrit, is often called the longest poem in the world, with around 100,000 verses in its longest versions, many times the length of the Iliad and Odyssey combined. Traditionally attributed to the sage Vyasa, it grew over many centuries, roughly between 400 BC and AD 400. Its core story is a bitter conflict between two branches of a royal family, the Pandavas and Kauravas, ending in a devastating war at Kurukshetra. Within it sits the Bhagavad Gita, a dialogue between the warrior Arjuna and Krishna about duty and action, which is sacred to hundreds of millions of Hindus.

sections.key: Beowulf, the great Old English epic, survives in a single manuscript that narrowly escaped a fire in 1731.
sections.b: Beowulf is the most famous poem in Old English, the language of the Anglo-Saxons. Its date is debated, with estimates ranging from about AD 700 to 1000. Though written in England, it is set in Scandinavia. The hero Beowulf kills the monster Grendel, then Grendel's vengeful mother, and in old age dies fighting a dragon. The poem survives in just one manuscript, which was scorched in a 1731 fire at a library in London. In 1936, J.R.R. Tolkien gave an influential lecture arguing that its monsters deserved to be taken seriously, and its echoes run through The Hobbit.

sections.key: Epics endure because they tackle universal questions and their story patterns still shape films and novels.
sections.b: Epics survive because their questions never date: how to face death, what we owe our families and communities, whether glory is worth the cost. Their story patterns are everywhere. The scholar Joseph Campbell argued in 1949 that many myths share a 'hero's journey', an idea that influenced Star Wars, though scholars dispute how universal the pattern really is. Oral storytelling is also a living tradition in Australia, where Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have passed down stories over many generations. To try an epic yourself, start with a modern translation or an audiobook: these poems were made to be heard.

quiz.q: Where does the Epic of Gilgamesh come from?
quiz.e: Gilgamesh was a king of Uruk, in modern Iraq.

quiz.q: The Iliad covers which part of the Trojan War?
o: A few weeks in its tenth year
quiz.e: It ends with Hector's funeral, not Troy's fall.

quiz.q: What did Virgil reportedly want done with the unfinished Aeneid?
quiz.e: Augustus refused, and the poem survived.

quiz.q: Which famous text is contained within the Mahabharata?
quiz.e: It is a dialogue between Arjuna and Krishna.

quiz.q: What does Beowulf fight at the end of his life?
quiz.e: He dies fighting a dragon in old age.

LESSONS.title: Shakespeare
LESSONS.hook: A glove-maker's son from a small market town wrote plays that are still performed somewhere in the world every day, and he put words in your mouth you didn't know were his.

sections.key: Shakespeare was born in Stratford-upon-Avon in 1564 and married Anne Hathaway at 18.
sections.b: William Shakespeare was baptised in Stratford-upon-Avon, a market town in England, on 26 April 1564. His father John was a glove-maker who became a local official. William probably attended the town's grammar school, where boys studied Latin and classical authors such as Ovid. At 18 he married Anne Hathaway, who was 26. They had three children: Susanna, then twins Hamnet and Judith. Hamnet died in 1596, aged 11. Surprisingly little is known about Shakespeare's personal life, and there is a gap in the records from about 1585 to 1592 that scholars call 'the lost years'.

sections.h: A working man of the theatre
sections.key: Shakespeare was an actor, playwright and shareholder in a leading company that built the Globe in 1599.
sections.b: By 1592 Shakespeare was working in London, where rival playwright Robert Greene mocked him as an 'upstart crow'. He became a leading member of the Lord Chamberlain's Men, an acting company that became the King's Men after James I took the throne in 1603. Unusually, he was actor, writer and part-owner, which made him fairly wealthy. In 1599 the company built the Globe Theatre on the south bank of the Thames. It burned down in 1613 when a cannon fired during a performance set the thatched roof alight. A reconstruction opened near the original site in 1997.

sections.key: He wrote about 37 plays and 154 sonnets; the 1623 First Folio saved around half the plays from being lost.
sections.b: Shakespeare is credited with about 37 plays, some co-written, plus 154 sonnets and several longer poems. Plays were working scripts, not literature, and many of his were never printed in his lifetime. In 1623, seven years after his death, two fellow actors, John Heminges and Henry Condell, published 36 of his plays in one volume now called the First Folio. About 18 of those, including Macbeth, The Tempest and Twelfth Night, had never been printed before and might otherwise have vanished. Roughly 750 copies were printed and about 235 are known to survive, including one in Sydney's State Library of NSW.

sections.key: His tragedies, such as Hamlet, Macbeth, Othello and King Lear, trace how a flaw or choice leads to ruin.
sections.b: Shakespeare's tragedies follow powerful people destroyed by their own choices, flaws or circumstances. Hamlet, a prince who learns his uncle murdered his father, agonises over revenge. Macbeth, spurred by a prophecy and his wife's ambition, kills his king and spirals into tyranny and paranoia. Othello, a respected general, is manipulated by the scheming Iago into jealousy and murder. King Lear divides his kingdom between his daughters and is betrayed. Romeo and Juliet, an early tragedy, shows young love crushed by a family feud. The tragedies are admired for their psychological depth: characters think aloud in soliloquies, letting us overhear their minds.

sections.key: His comedies end in marriages, his histories dramatise English kings, and late romances mix loss with reconciliation.
sections.b: Shakespeare's comedies, such as A Midsummer Night's Dream, Twelfth Night and Much Ado About Nothing, feature mistaken identities, disguises, witty lovers and happy endings, usually weddings. Because women were not allowed on the English stage, female roles were played by boys, which made plots with women disguised as men especially playful. His history plays, including Richard III and Henry V, dramatise English kings and civil wars, and shaped popular ideas of those rulers far more than historians would like. Late plays such as The Tempest and The Winter's Tale are often called romances: stories of loss, magic and forgiveness.

sections.key: Shakespeare is the earliest recorded source of many English words and phrases, like 'wild-goose chase' and 'green-eyed monster'.
sections.b: The Oxford English Dictionary lists Shakespeare as the earliest known source for many words, with popular counts in the high hundreds or more. Examples include 'eyeball', 'bedroom' and 'swagger'. Scholars caution that some of these were probably already in speech and he was simply the first to be recorded, but he clearly played with language boldly. Phrases first found in his plays include 'wild-goose chase' (Romeo and Juliet), 'green-eyed monster' for jealousy and 'a foregone conclusion' (both Othello), and 'more sinned against than sinning' (King Lear). Hamlet's 'To be, or not to be' is probably the most quoted line in English.

sections.key: Much of Shakespeare is written in blank verse: unrhymed lines of iambic pentameter, close to natural speech.
sections.b: Shakespeare's plays mix prose with verse, mostly blank verse: unrhymed lines of iambic pentameter. That means ten syllables per line in an alternating unstressed-stressed beat, da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM, a rhythm close to natural English speech. Kings and lovers tend to speak in verse, while servants and comic characters often speak prose, and a character switching between them can signal a change in mood or status. Rhyming couplets often close a scene, like a musical full stop. Reading the lines aloud usually makes them easier to follow, because the rhythm guides where the emphasis falls.

sections.key: Shakespeare lasts because his themes are universal and his plays adapt to any setting, from film to Australian stages.
sections.b: Shakespeare's plays survive because they deal with things that never go away: ambition, jealousy, love, grief, power and family conflict. They are also endlessly adaptable. West Side Story reworks Romeo and Juliet, 10 Things I Hate About You updates The Taming of the Shrew, and The Lion King borrows from Hamlet. Australian director Baz Luhrmann's Romeo + Juliet (1996) kept the original language in a modern setting. Bell Shakespeare, founded by John Bell in 1990, tours his plays around Australia. The best way in is to watch a performance first: these were scripts for actors, not texts for exams.

quiz.q: Where was Shakespeare born?
quiz.e: He was baptised there in April 1564.

quiz.q: What happened to the original Globe Theatre in 1613?
o: It burned down after a cannon set the roof alight
It was closed by the king
quiz.e: A reconstruction opened in 1997.

quiz.q: Why is the 1623 First Folio so important?
o: About 18 of its plays had never been printed before
It was written by Shakespeare himself
It was the first English book
quiz.e: Without it, plays like Macbeth might be lost.

quiz.q: Which phrase first appears in Othello?
o: To be, or not to be
quiz.e: It describes jealousy.

quiz.q: What is blank verse?
quiz.e: Ten syllables, da-DUM rhythm, no rhyme.

LESSONS.title: The rise of the novel
LESSONS.hook: The novel is the youngest of the great literary forms, yet it became the way billions of people explore other lives. Here's how it began, and the Australian books worth knowing.

sections.key: A novel is a long work of prose fiction; one early landmark is Japan's Tale of Genji, from around AD 1000.
sections.b: A novel is a long, invented story told in prose rather than verse, usually focused on the inner lives of characters. The word comes from the Italian 'novella', meaning a new story or piece of news. Long prose fiction has several claimed starting points. Ancient Greek and Roman writers produced prose romances, and in Japan, around AD 1000, the court lady Murasaki Shikibu wrote The Tale of Genji, a long, subtle story of love and life at the imperial court. It is often called the world's first novel, though what counts as 'first' depends on how strictly you define the form.

sections.key: Cervantes' Don Quixote (1605 and 1615) is often called the first modern novel.
sections.b: In Europe, the book most often called the first modern novel is Don Quixote by the Spanish writer Miguel de Cervantes, published in two parts in 1605 and 1615. It follows a country gentleman who reads so many tales of chivalry that he decides to become a knight, riding out with his down-to-earth squire Sancho Panza. He famously attacks windmills, believing them to be giants. The book is comic, but also clever and moving about how stories shape the way we see the world. It gave English the word 'quixotic', meaning idealistic to the point of being impractical, and the phrase 'tilting at windmills'.

sections.key: Daniel Defoe's Robinson Crusoe (1719) is often called the first English novel, praised for its realistic detail.
sections.b: In 1719, Daniel Defoe published Robinson Crusoe, often called the first English novel. It presented itself as the true account of a sailor shipwrecked for 28 years on a remote island, and its power came from ordinary, practical detail: how Crusoe salvages tools, builds shelter, grows grain and keeps a journal. Defoe was probably partly inspired by the real Scottish sailor Alexander Selkirk, marooned on an island off Chile from 1704 to 1709. Other early English novels soon followed, including Samuel Richardson's Pamela (1740), told through letters, and Henry Fielding's sprawling comic novel Tom Jones (1749).

sections.key: The novel boomed in the 1700s and 1800s thanks to rising literacy, cheaper printing, lending libraries and a growing middle class.
sections.b: The novel spread quickly through the 1700s and 1800s because several changes arrived together. Printing became cheaper, literacy rose, and a growing middle class had money and leisure time. Circulating libraries let readers borrow books for a subscription fee, and many readers and writers were women, which critics of the time often sneered at. Unlike epics about kings and heroes, novels focused on ordinary people: marriages, money, work and inner feelings. The form proved endlessly flexible, producing Mary Shelley's Frankenstein (1818), one of the first works of science fiction, as well as mysteries, social satire and the love story.

sections.key: Jane Austen's six novels, including Pride and Prejudice (1813), pioneered sharp irony and deep insight into characters' minds.
sections.b: Jane Austen (1775–1817) published four novels in her lifetime, all anonymously, the first credited only to 'a Lady': Sense and Sensibility, Pride and Prejudice, Mansfield Park and Emma. Northanger Abbey and Persuasion appeared after her death at 41. Pride and Prejudice (1813) opens with one of fiction's most famous lines: 'It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.' Austen wrote about courtship, class and money among the English gentry, with sharp irony. She refined a technique of slipping in and out of a character's thoughts that shaped novels ever since.

sections.key: Dickens published his novels in serial instalments and used them to expose poverty and injustice in Victorian England.
sections.b: Charles Dickens (1812–1870) was the superstar novelist of Victorian England. When he was 12, his father was jailed for debt and young Charles worked in a factory pasting labels on pots of boot polish, an experience that fuelled his anger at poverty and cruelty. Most of his novels were published in weekly or monthly instalments, so readers waited eagerly for each episode, much like a TV series. His works include Oliver Twist, A Christmas Carol (1843), David Copperfield, Bleak House and Great Expectations, in which a key character is a convict transported to New South Wales. 'Dickensian' now describes grim, overcrowded poverty.

sections.key: Classic Australian novels include For the Term of His Natural Life, My Brilliant Career and Patrick White's Voss.
sections.b: Australian novels grew out of the colonial experience. Marcus Clarke's For the Term of His Natural Life, first serialised in the early 1870s, told a harrowing story of the convict system. Miles Franklin's My Brilliant Career (1901), about a spirited young woman in the bush, was published when she was in her early twenties, and her bequest later funded the Miles Franklin Literary Award. Henry Handel Richardson was the pen name of Ethel Richardson, author of The Getting of Wisdom. Patrick White, author of Voss and The Tree of Man, won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1973, still the only writer to win it as an Australian.

sections.key: Tim Winton, Kate Grenville, Kim Scott and Alexis Wright are among Australia's most celebrated modern novelists.
sections.b: Tim Winton has won the Miles Franklin Award four times; his novel Cloudstreet (1991), about two working-class families sharing a big old house in Perth, is often voted a favourite Australian book. Kate Grenville's The Secret River (2005) follows a convict settler on the Hawkesbury River and confronts the violence of colonisation. Kim Scott, a Noongar writer, became the first Aboriginal author to win the Miles Franklin, for Benang in 2000, and Waanyi writer Alexis Wright won it for Carpentaria in 2007. To start reading, pick one classic and one modern novel, and try a local library's free audiobook and ebook apps.

quiz.q: The Tale of Genji, often called the first novel, came from which country?
quiz.e: Murasaki Shikibu wrote it around AD 1000.

quiz.q: In Don Quixote, what does the hero attack believing they are giants?
quiz.e: Hence 'tilting at windmills'.

quiz.q: Which real sailor probably helped inspire Robinson Crusoe?
quiz.e: Selkirk was marooned off Chile from 1704 to 1709.

quiz.q: How were most of Dickens' novels first published?
quiz.e: Readers waited for each episode, like a TV series.

quiz.q: Which Australian novelist won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1973?
quiz.e: Born in London to Australian parents, he grew up in Sydney.

LESSONS.title: How poetry works
LESSONS.hook: Poetry is the oldest way humans have made words memorable. Learn a few of its tools and you'll hear them everywhere, from song lyrics to advertising slogans.

sections.key: Poetry compresses language, using sound, rhythm and imagery to make words memorable and meaningful.
sections.b: Poetry is language shaped with extra care for sound, rhythm and image, so that a few words carry a lot of meaning and feeling. It is probably the oldest form of literature. Before writing was widespread, rhythm and repetition helped people memorise long stories, laws and genealogies, which is why the earliest epics are poems. Poetry also works differently from prose: it uses line breaks, compression and ambiguity on purpose, inviting you to slow down and read again. Song lyrics, nursery rhymes, advertising jingles and football chants all use the same tools, so almost everyone already knows more poetry than they think.

sections.key: Metre is a regular pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables; the most common in English is iambic pentameter.
sections.b: English words have stressed and unstressed syllables: we say 'to-DAY' and 'MOTH-er'. When a poem arranges these into a regular pattern, it has metre. The basic unit is the foot. An iamb is an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed one, da-DUM. Five iambs make iambic pentameter, the most common metre in English poetry, used by Shakespeare and many others. Read aloud his line 'Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?' and you'll hear the beat. Poets often break the pattern deliberately, because a surprise in the rhythm draws attention to a word.

sections.key: Other feet include the trochee (DUM-da), anapest (da-da-DUM) and dactyl (DUM-da-da), each with a different feel.
sections.b: Iambs aren't the only option. A trochee flips the iamb to DUM-da, giving a strong, chanting feel; the witches in Macbeth speak in trochees ('Double, double toil and trouble'). An anapest, da-da-DUM, creates a galloping rhythm, heard in the 1823 poem 'Twas the night before Christmas'. A dactyl, DUM-da-da, is the metre of Homer's epics in Greek. Many ballads and hymns use 'common metre', alternating lines of four and three beats, which is why so many poems can be sung to the same tunes. Tapping a poem's beat on a table is a quick way to find its metre.

sections.key: Rhyme links lines through matching sounds; half-rhyme and internal rhyme create subtler effects.
sections.b: Rhyme is the repetition of matching sounds, usually at the ends of lines. Poets describe patterns with letters: ABAB means the first and third lines rhyme, and the second and fourth. Full rhyme matches exactly (night and light), while half or slant rhyme only nearly matches (bone and moon), giving a subtler, unsettled effect that Emily Dickinson used brilliantly. Internal rhyme falls within a line. Rhyme makes words stick in memory, which is why advertisers love it, and one 2000 study found that people rated rhyming sayings as more truthful than the same ideas phrased without rhyme.

sections.key: A sonnet is a 14-line poem, usually in iambic pentameter, with a turn in thought called the volta.
sections.b: The sonnet is a 14-line poem that began in Italy, where Petrarch made it famous in the 1300s with love poems to a woman named Laura. The Italian or Petrarchan sonnet divides into eight lines setting up a problem and six answering it. Shakespeare's sonnets use three four-line stanzas and a closing rhyming couplet, rhymed ABAB CDCD EFEF GG. Almost all sonnets contain a 'volta', or turn, where the argument or mood shifts. The strict limits are the point: squeezing a big feeling into 14 lines forces poets to be precise, and sonnets are still written today on every subject imaginable.

sections.key: Haiku is a short Japanese form, traditionally 17 sound units in a 5-7-5 pattern, often with a seasonal reference.
sections.b: Haiku is a Japanese form made famous by Matsuo Basho in the 1600s. A traditional haiku has 17 sound units, called 'on', in a pattern of 5, 7 and 5, and usually includes a seasonal word and a 'cut' that sets two images side by side. Basho's best-known haiku describes an old pond and the sound of a frog jumping in: a tiny moment that opens into stillness. Japanese sound units are shorter than English syllables, so many English-language haiku poets use fewer than 17 syllables. The aim is not cleverness but sharp, clear attention to a single moment.

sections.key: Free verse abandons regular metre and rhyme, relying instead on natural speech rhythms, line breaks and imagery.
sections.b: Free verse is poetry without a regular metre or rhyme scheme. It is not formless: the poet still chooses exactly where each line breaks, which words sit together and what images build the effect. The American poet Walt Whitman pioneered it in Leaves of Grass (1855), with long, rolling lines celebrating ordinary people and the body. In the early 1900s, modernist poets such as T.S. Eliot and Ezra Pound made free verse central to poetry in English. Today most published poetry is free verse, and line breaks do much of the work that rhyme once did, creating pauses, surprises and emphasis.

sections.key: Banjo Paterson, Oodgeroo Noonuccal and Judith Wright are three of Australia's most important poets.
sections.b: Andrew 'Banjo' Paterson (1864–1941) wrote rollicking bush ballads such as 'The Man from Snowy River' (1890), which opens 'There was movement at the station', and the words of 'Waltzing Matilda' (1895). Oodgeroo Noonuccal (1920–1993), a Noonuccal woman from Minjerribah (North Stradbroke Island), published We Are Going in 1964, widely recognised as the first book of poetry by an Aboriginal Australian; she was also a leading campaigner for the 1967 referendum. Judith Wright (1915–2000) wrote vividly about the land and campaigned for the environment and Aboriginal land rights. To start, read one poem aloud, twice, before deciding what it means.

quiz.q: What is an iamb?
quiz.e: Da-DUM, as in 'to-DAY'.

quiz.q: What is slant or half rhyme?
quiz.e: Such as bone and moon.

quiz.q: How many lines does a sonnet have?
quiz.e: Usually with a turn called the volta.

quiz.q: Which poet pioneered free verse in Leaves of Grass?
quiz.e: It appeared in 1855.

quiz.q: Oodgeroo Noonuccal's We Are Going (1964) is widely recognised as what?
o: The first book of poetry by an Aboriginal Australian
quiz.e: She was also a campaigner for the 1967 referendum.

LESSONS.title: Dystopian classics
LESSONS.hook: Surveillance, censorship, engineered happiness, stripped rights: the great dystopian novels imagined them decades ago. Here's why these warnings still feel so current.

sections.key: A dystopia is an imagined society gone badly wrong, the dark mirror of a utopia.
