sections.b: In 1516, the English statesman Thomas More published Utopia, describing an ideal island society. He built a pun into the name: in Greek it can mean both 'no place' and 'good place'. A dystopia is the opposite, an imagined society where things have gone terribly wrong, often in the name of making them better. The philosopher John Stuart Mill is credited with one of the earliest recorded uses of 'dystopian', in an 1868 speech to the British Parliament. Dystopian fiction takes a trend in the present, such as surveillance, propaganda or technology, and pushes it to a frightening extreme.

sections.key: H.G. Wells and Yevgeny Zamyatin laid the groundwork for the great 20th-century dystopias.
sections.b: Dystopian fiction gathered pace as industry, science and mass politics transformed the world. H.G. Wells' The Time Machine (1895) imagined humanity split into two degraded species, a dark joke about class division. The most important forerunner, though, was We by the Russian writer Yevgeny Zamyatin, written around 1920–21 in the early years of the Soviet state. It depicts a society where people have numbers instead of names, live in glass apartments and follow a strict timetable. Banned in the Soviet Union, it was first published in English in 1924, and George Orwell reviewed it in 1946 before writing his own dystopia.

sections.key: Aldous Huxley's Brave New World (1932) imagines a society controlled not by fear but by pleasure and conditioning.
sections.b: Aldous Huxley's Brave New World (1932) is set in a future World State where babies are grown in hatcheries and conditioned into fixed castes, from clever Alphas to deliberately limited Epsilons. Everyone is kept content with easy pleasures, constant entertainment and a mood-lifting drug called soma. Family, deep love, art and religion have been abolished as sources of instability. The novel's disturbing twist is that most citizens are happy. Its central question is whether comfort and stability are worth the loss of freedom, truth and genuine feeling. The title comes from a line in Shakespeare's The Tempest, spoken with unintended irony.

sections.key: Orwell's 1984 (1949) depicts a totalitarian state of surveillance, propaganda and rewritten history.
sections.b: George Orwell, the pen name of Eric Blair, published Nineteen Eighty-Four in 1949, a few months before he died. Set in Oceania, a superstate ruled by the Party and its figurehead Big Brother, it follows Winston Smith, a clerk whose job is rewriting old newspaper records so the past always matches the Party's latest claims. Two-way screens watch citizens at home, the Thought Police punish forbidden ideas, and a shrinking official language called Newspeak aims to make rebellion unthinkable. The book gave English words like 'Big Brother', 'doublethink' and 'Orwellian', now used for any government that manipulates truth or watches its citizens.

sections.key: Orwell feared control through pain and censorship; Huxley feared control through pleasure and distraction.
sections.b: Readers have long compared the two books. Orwell imagined people controlled by fear, surveillance and censorship. Huxley imagined people who didn't need controlling, because they had been conditioned to love their servitude and were too distracted to care. In a 1949 letter to Orwell, his former teacher at Eton, Huxley praised Nineteen Eighty-Four but predicted that rulers would find gentler methods more efficient. In 1985 the American critic Neil Postman argued in Amusing Ourselves to Death that television culture made Huxley the better prophet. Many people now see elements of both in the modern world, which is part of their lasting power.

sections.key: Ray Bradbury's Fahrenheit 451 (1953) imagines firemen who burn books in a society numbed by screens.
sections.b: In Ray Bradbury's Fahrenheit 451 (1953), firemen don't put out fires: they start them, burning any books they find. The title refers to the temperature at which Bradbury believed paper catches fire, about 233 degrees Celsius. The hero, fireman Guy Montag, begins secretly reading the books he is meant to destroy. Although the novel is often read as a story about censorship, Bradbury later said it was just as much about people choosing wall-sized screens and shallow entertainment over reading and thinking. He wrote the first draft on a coin-operated typewriter in a university library basement, paying ten cents per half hour.

sections.key: Margaret Atwood's The Handmaid's Tale (1985) imagines a regime that strips women of their rights.
sections.b: Canadian author Margaret Atwood published The Handmaid's Tale in 1985. In the near future, a theocratic regime called Gilead has overthrown the US government. With birth rates falling, fertile women are forced to become 'handmaids', bearing children for powerful families, and women are forbidden to read, work or own property. The story is told by a handmaid called Offred. Atwood has said she included nothing that had not already happened somewhere in human history, which gives the book its chill. A 2017 TV series brought it to a new audience, and its red-cloaked costume has been worn at protests in many countries.

sections.key: Dystopias are warnings, not predictions: they sharpen our attention to trends in the present.
sections.b: Dystopias are best read as warnings rather than forecasts. By exaggerating something already present, they help readers notice it: how much we share with tech companies, how language can be bent, how rights can quietly erode. They also ask what makes us human when systems try to flatten individuality. The genre remains hugely popular, from Suzanne Collins' The Hunger Games (2008) to Nevil Shute's On the Beach (1957), a post-apocalyptic novel set in Melbourne. When you read one, ask two questions: what present-day fear is this story built on, and which warning signs, if any, can you see around you?

quiz.q: Who wrote Utopia in 1516?
quiz.e: The name puns on 'no place' and 'good place'.

quiz.q: In Brave New World, how are citizens mainly kept in line?
o: Pleasure, conditioning and the drug soma
quiz.e: Most citizens are genuinely content.

quiz.q: What is Winston Smith's job in Nineteen Eighty-Four?
o: Rewriting old records to match the Party's claims
quiz.e: The past is edited to fit the present.

quiz.q: What do firemen do in Fahrenheit 451?
quiz.e: Paper burns at about 451 degrees Fahrenheit, Bradbury believed.

quiz.q: What guiding rule did Atwood describe for The Handmaid's Tale?
o: Nothing included that hadn't happened somewhere in history
quiz.e: That is why it feels so plausible.

LESSONS.title: Finding an idea worth building
LESSONS.hook: Most new products fail not because they were built badly, but because nobody wanted them. The fix starts long before you build anything.

sections.key: Good business ideas usually start with a painful, frequent problem, not a clever solution.
sections.b: The strongest business ideas rarely begin with 'wouldn't it be cool if'. They begin with a problem that real people have, often, and that costs them time, money or stress. A useful test is to ask three questions: how painful is this problem, how often does it happen, and what are people doing about it now? If people already cobble together spreadsheets, workarounds or paid help to deal with it, that's a strong signal. If nobody has ever tried to solve it, it may not hurt enough to pay for.

sections.key: Your own work, frustrations and skills are often the richest source of business ideas.
sections.b: Many successful businesses come from founders scratching their own itch. Tradespeople build quoting software because they hated doing quotes at night. Parents start products after struggling to find something for their kids. Look for moments at work or at home when you think 'there must be a better way'. Also look at changes in the world: new technology, new regulations, an ageing population or shifts in how people shop. Change creates new problems, and new problems create openings that established businesses are often slow to notice.

sections.key: Before building, identify the one belief that, if wrong, sinks the whole idea, and test it first.
sections.b: Every idea rests on assumptions: that people have this problem, that they'll pay, that you can reach them, that you can deliver at a profit. Write them down and ask which one, if false, would kill the business. That's your riskiest assumption, and it's the one to test first and most cheaply. Founders often do the opposite, spending months perfecting a logo, website or app while the basic question, does anyone actually want this, goes unanswered until launch day.

sections.key: Ask people about their past behaviour and real problems, not whether they like your idea.
sections.b: Customer conversations are the cheapest research there is, but most people do them badly. If you describe your idea and ask 'would you use this?', friendly people will say yes to be polite. Rob Fitzpatrick's book The Mom Test suggests a better approach: talk about their life, not your idea. Ask about specifics in the past. When did this last happen? What did you do? What did it cost you? Have you looked for a solution? Past behaviour is far more reliable than predictions about the future.

sections.key: Compliments are cheap; commitments of time, money or reputation are real evidence of demand.
sections.b: Not all positive feedback is equal. 'Great idea!' costs nothing and predicts almost nothing. Stronger signals involve a commitment: someone agrees to a second meeting, introduces you to their boss, joins a waitlist with their details, pays a deposit or pre-orders. The more a person gives up, the more you can trust their interest. A handful of people willing to pay before the product is finished is worth more than hundreds of people saying they love the concept in a survey.

sections.key: A minimum viable product is the smallest thing that tests whether people want what you offer.
sections.b: A minimum viable product, or MVP, is the simplest version of your offer that lets you learn whether people want it. It doesn't have to be software. Dropbox co-founder Drew Houston famously made a short demo video before the product was ready, and the sign-up waitlist reportedly jumped from about 5,000 to 75,000 people overnight. Zappos began with its founder photographing shoes in local stores and buying them at full price when orders came in. Both proved demand before heavy investment.

sections.h: Competition is not a bad sign
sections.key: Existing competitors usually prove a market exists; the question is how you'll be meaningfully different.
sections.b: New founders often panic when they find a competitor, or claim they have none. But competition usually proves that people will pay to solve the problem. No competitors at all can mean no market. The real question is what you'll do better or differently for a specific group of customers: cheaper, faster, simpler, more local, better service, or built for a niche the big players ignore. Look at competitors' reviews, especially the one- and two-star ones, which are a free list of unmet needs.

sections.key: Pick a specific customer, talk to at least ten of them, and test demand cheaply before spending big.
sections.b: Before quitting your job or spending your savings, try this. Write down who exactly your customer is, as narrowly as you can. Find at least ten of them and have real conversations about the problem, not your solution. Identify your riskiest assumption and design a cheap test, such as a landing page, a pre-sale or a manual version of the service. Set a clear bar for success in advance. If the evidence is weak, adjust the idea. It's far cheaper to change course now than after launch.

quiz.q: Which is usually the strongest starting point for a business idea?
o: A painful, frequent problem people already try to solve
A clever technology looking for a use
A market with no competitors at all
quiz.e: Ideas grounded in real, frequent problems that people already spend time or money on tend to have genuine demand.

quiz.q: According to The Mom Test approach, what should you ask potential customers about?
o: What they would pay in the future
Specific things they did in the past
quiz.e: Past behaviour is a more reliable guide than polite opinions or predictions about the future.

quiz.q: Which is the strongest evidence of real demand?
o: A friend saying it's a great idea
A survey where people say they'd probably buy
Customers paying a deposit before launch
quiz.e: Commitments of money, time or reputation are much stronger signals than compliments.

quiz.q: What did Dropbox famously use to test demand before the product was ready?
quiz.e: Drew Houston's demo video drove a huge jump in waitlist sign-ups, showing demand before launch.

quiz.q: Why can competitors be a good sign?
o: They mean you can copy their prices
They show people already pay to solve the problem
They guarantee your business will succeed
quiz.e: Competition usually confirms a market exists; your job is to be meaningfully different for some customers.

LESSONS.title: How businesses make money
LESSONS.hook: A great product isn't a business until you know who pays, how much, and whether what's left over covers the costs.

sections.key: A business model explains how a business creates value for customers and captures some of it as profit.
sections.b: A business model is the logic of how a business works: who it serves, what it offers them, how it reaches them, and how the money flows. Two businesses can sell almost the same thing with very different models. One cafe sells coffee by the cup; another sells beans by subscription; a third runs a coffee-making course. Each has different customers, costs and risks. Getting the model right often matters as much as the product itself, because a loved product can still lose money on every sale.

sections.key: Your value proposition is the specific reason a customer chooses you over the alternatives, including doing nothing.
sections.b: A value proposition answers a simple question: why would a particular customer choose this? It usually does one of three things: relieves a pain (saves time, reduces risk, removes hassle), creates a gain (better results, status, enjoyment) or does a job the customer needs done. A strong proposition is specific. 'Quality accounting services' is vague. 'Fixed-fee bookkeeping for tradies, done by Friday, no surprise bills' tells the right customer exactly why to call. Remember that your real competitor is often the customer's current workaround, or simply putting up with the problem.

sections.key: Common revenue models include one-off sales, subscriptions, usage fees, commissions, advertising and licensing.
sections.b: There are many ways to charge. One-off sales are the classic model: a product or job for a price. Subscriptions, like streaming services or software, bring recurring revenue that's easier to predict. Usage-based pricing charges by amount used, like electricity or cloud storage. Marketplaces such as Airtasker or Airbnb take a commission for connecting buyers and sellers. Media businesses often sell advertising and give content away. Freemium offers a free basic version and charges for more. The 'razor and blades' model sells a cheap device and profits on refills.

sections.key: Fixed costs stay the same as sales change; variable costs rise with every unit you sell.
sections.b: Costs come in two broad types. Fixed costs, like rent, insurance, software subscriptions and salaried staff, stay roughly the same whether you sell ten items or a thousand. Variable costs rise with each sale: ingredients, packaging, shipping, payment fees and sales commissions. This distinction matters. A business with high fixed costs needs a lot of sales just to break even, but once it does, extra sales can be very profitable. A business with high variable costs is less risky to start but may struggle to grow its margins.

sections.key: Break-even is the point where sales cover all costs: fixed costs divided by the margin on each sale.
sections.b: The break-even point is where total revenue equals total costs, so you're making neither profit nor loss. A simple way to calculate it is to divide your monthly fixed costs by the contribution margin, which is the price of one sale minus its variable costs. Imagine a candle maker with $2,000 of fixed costs a month who sells candles for $30 that cost $10 each to make and ship. Each candle contributes $20, so she needs to sell 100 candles a month just to break even.

sections.key: Unit economics compares what it costs to win a customer with the profit that customer brings over time.
sections.b: Unit economics looks at the profit or loss on a single sale or customer. Two numbers are especially useful. Customer acquisition cost, or CAC, is what you spend on marketing and sales to win one new customer. Customer lifetime value, or LTV, is the total profit a typical customer brings over the whole relationship. If it costs $200 to win a customer who only brings $150 in profit, growing faster just loses money faster. A commonly quoted rule of thumb, especially for subscription businesses, is an LTV at least three times CAC.

sections.key: The Business Model Canvas maps a business on one page across nine building blocks.
sections.b: In 2010, Alexander Osterwalder and Yves Pigneur published Business Model Generation, which popularised the Business Model Canvas. It fits a whole business onto one page using nine blocks: customer segments, value propositions, channels, customer relationships, revenue streams, key resources, key activities, key partners and cost structure. The right side covers customers and revenue; the left covers how you deliver and what it costs. Its strength is speed: you can sketch several versions of a business in an afternoon and spot weak links before investing real money.

sections.key: Write your model on one page, run the numbers honestly, and treat every figure as an assumption to test.
sections.b: To pressure-test your own idea, sketch a canvas and fill in each block in a few words. Then run rough numbers: your price, variable cost per sale, monthly fixed costs, break-even point and a realistic estimate of what it will cost to win each customer. Be conservative: founders almost always overestimate sales and underestimate costs and time. Treat every number as a guess to be tested with real customers. For decisions involving significant money or tax, a qualified accountant can help you check the figures.

quiz.q: What does a value proposition describe?
o: The legal structure of a business
Why a specific customer would choose you over the alternatives
The total value of a company's shares
How much tax a business pays
quiz.e: A value proposition is the specific reason a customer chooses your offer, including over doing nothing.

quiz.q: Which of these is typically a variable cost?
quiz.e: Variable costs rise with each sale; packaging is used up with every unit sold.

quiz.q: Fixed costs are $2,000 a month; each product sells for $30 and costs $10. What is the monthly break-even?
quiz.e: Each sale contributes $20, and $2,000 divided by $20 is 100 units.

quiz.q: What does customer acquisition cost (CAC) measure?
o: What it costs to win one new customer
The profit from a customer over time
The cost of making one unit
quiz.e: CAC is your marketing and sales spend divided by the number of new customers won.

quiz.q: How many building blocks does the Business Model Canvas have?
quiz.e: The canvas has nine blocks, from customer segments to cost structure.

LESSONS.title: Marketing basics
LESSONS.hook: Marketing isn't shouting louder than everyone else. It's knowing exactly who you serve and making it easy for them to find and choose you.

sections.key: Marketing is everything that shapes whether the right people know about, want and choose your offer.
sections.b: Many people think marketing means advertising. Advertising is only one part. Marketing covers deciding who your customers are, what you offer them, how you price it, where they can buy it and how they hear about it. A plumber who answers the phone promptly, turns up on time and leaves a tidy job is marketing just as much as one who buys billboard space. At its best, marketing starts before the product is made, by understanding what customers need, and continues long after the sale.

sections.key: The more precisely you can describe your customer, the easier every other marketing decision becomes.
sections.b: 'Everyone' is not a customer. Trying to appeal to everybody usually means your message excites nobody. Start by describing your ideal customer in concrete terms: who they are, what problem they have, what they've already tried, where they spend time, what words they use to describe their frustration and what makes them trust a business. Some businesses write this up as a customer profile or persona. The best source is real conversations and reviews, not guesswork. Using your customers' own language in your marketing makes it feel instantly relevant.

sections.key: Positioning is the specific place you want to hold in a customer's mind compared with alternatives.
sections.b: Positioning, an idea popularised by Al Ries and Jack Trout from the 1970s, is about the place your business occupies in the customer's mind. Customers mentally file businesses: the cheap one, the fast one, the premium one, the one for beginners. If you don't choose a position, customers will choose one for you, or forget you entirely. A clear position often means deliberately not serving some people. A gym for over-50s, or a bakery known only for sourdough, is easier to remember and recommend than a business trying to be everything.

sections.key: The marketing mix is often summarised as Product, Price, Place and Promotion.
sections.b: In 1960, American marketing professor E. Jerome McCarthy summarised the marketing mix as the 4 Ps. Product is what you offer, including quality, features and service. Price is what you charge, and it sends a signal: too cheap can suggest poor quality. Place is where and how customers buy, such as online, in stores or through resellers. Promotion is how you communicate, including advertising, social media, PR and sales. The Ps work together; a premium product sold at a discount price in the wrong place sends a confusing message.

sections.key: Pick a small number of channels where your specific customers already are, and do them well.
sections.b: A channel is any route to reach customers: search engines, social media, email, local newspapers, trade shows, partnerships, letterbox flyers or direct sales. New businesses often spread themselves thin trying to be everywhere. It's usually better to find one or two channels where your customers already spend time and learn to use them well. A wedding photographer might focus on Instagram and venue referrals; an accountant might focus on search results and local business networks. Track where customers actually come from so you can stop wasting money.

sections.h: The power of word of mouth
sections.key: Recommendations from people customers trust are among the most persuasive and cheapest forms of marketing.
sections.b: People trust recommendations from friends, family and colleagues far more than advertising. For many small businesses, word of mouth is the main source of new customers. You can't fully control it, but you can encourage it: deliver an experience worth talking about, make it easy to share, and ask happy customers for reviews or referrals. Online reviews act as word of mouth at scale. Respond to negative reviews calmly and helpfully; potential customers often judge a business as much by its replies as by the complaint.

sections.key: Research on brand growth suggests reaching many light buyers and being easy to remember matters a great deal.
sections.b: Research from the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute at the University of South Australia, summarised in Byron Sharp's 2010 book How Brands Grow, challenged some marketing assumptions. It argued that brands grow mainly by reaching lots of occasional buyers, not just by deepening loyalty among existing fans. It stressed being easy to think of when buying moments arise and easy to buy. Consistent, distinctive colours, logos and slogans help. The findings are influential but still debated, and small local businesses face different conditions from supermarket brands.

sections.key: Define your customer, sharpen your position, pick one or two channels and measure what works.
sections.b: A simple starting plan: write one sentence describing exactly who you serve and why they should choose you. Check that your product, price, place and promotion all tell the same story. Choose one or two channels where your customers already are, and commit to them for long enough to learn. Make word of mouth easy by asking for reviews at the moment customers are happiest. Finally, measure. Ask every new customer how they found you, and shift time and money towards what actually brings people in.

quiz.q: Why is 'everyone' a poor answer to 'who is your customer?'
o: It is illegal to market to everyone
A message aimed at everyone tends to excite nobody
quiz.e: Precise customer definitions make messages more relevant and marketing decisions easier.

quiz.q: What is positioning?
o: Where your shop is located on the street
The place your business holds in customers' minds compared with alternatives
The order of products on a shelf
quiz.e: Positioning is how customers mentally file your business relative to competitors.

quiz.q: What are the 4 Ps of the marketing mix?
quiz.e: E. Jerome McCarthy's 1960 model lists Product, Price, Place and Promotion.

quiz.q: What is usually the smarter approach to marketing channels for a new business?
o: Be on every platform at once
Avoid tracking results to save time
Focus on one or two channels where customers already are
quiz.e: Doing a few channels well, and tracking results, beats spreading effort thinly.

quiz.q: Which Australian research institute is known for the work summarised in How Brands Grow?
quiz.e: The Ehrenberg-Bass Institute at the University of South Australia produced the research Byron Sharp summarised.

LESSONS.title: Cash flow: the lifeblood of business
LESSONS.hook: A business can be profitable on paper and still run out of money. Understanding why is one of the most important lessons in business.

sections.key: Profit measures earnings over a period; cash flow tracks when money actually moves in and out.
sections.b: Profit and cash are related but different. Profit is revenue minus expenses over a period, and under standard accounting it's recorded when a sale is made, not when the money arrives. Cash flow is the actual timing of money entering and leaving your bank account. You can make a $10,000 sale in March, book the profit, and not see the money until June. In the meantime you still have to pay rent, wages, suppliers and tax. Profit keeps score; cash keeps the lights on.

sections.key: Many businesses close not because they're unprofitable but because they run out of cash to pay bills.
sections.b: A business can fail while its sales are growing. Imagine a manufacturer that wins a big order. It must buy materials, pay staff and cover overheads for months, while the customer pays 60 days after delivery. If the cash runs out in between, the business may be unable to pay its debts on time, even though the order is profitable. Rapid growth that outpaces available cash is sometimes called overtrading. Many small business advisers cite cash flow problems as one of the most common reasons small businesses struggle or close.

sections.key: The longer money is tied up in stock and unpaid invoices, the more cash a business needs to operate.
sections.b: Think of cash as flowing in a loop. You spend cash on stock or labour, turn it into a product or service, sell it, wait to be paid, and finally get cash back. The time this loop takes is called the cash conversion cycle. The longer it is, the more cash is tied up. A cafe paid instantly at the counter has a short cycle. A builder who buys materials, works for weeks and invoices at the end has a long one, and needs much more cash to keep going.

sections.key: Clear invoices, sensible payment terms and prompt follow-up are the simplest ways to improve cash flow.
sections.b: Late payments are a common cash drain for small businesses. Small habits help a lot. Invoice immediately when work is done, not at the end of the month. Make invoices clear, with what was delivered, the amount, the due date and easy payment options. If you're registered for GST, your invoices need to meet tax invoice requirements, which the ATO explains on its website. Consider shorter payment terms, deposits for large jobs, or progress payments on long ones. Follow up politely but promptly when payments are late.

sections.key: Timing your own payments, controlling stock and setting aside tax helps keep cash in the business.
sections.b: Cash flow is also about outflows. Pay suppliers on time to protect relationships, but there's usually no need to pay weeks early. Avoid tying up cash in excess stock that sits on shelves. Lease or finance big equipment where that suits your situation, rather than draining your cash reserve. One of the most common traps is tax: GST collected from customers isn't your money, and neither is income tax you'll owe later. Many owners move a set percentage of each payment into a separate account so tax bills don't come as a shock.

sections.key: Runway is how many months your cash will last at the current rate of spending.
sections.b: Runway is a simple but vital number, especially for new businesses not yet making a profit. Divide the cash you have by your monthly net cash outflow, often called burn rate. If you have $60,000 in the bank and you're spending $10,000 more than you bring in each month, you have about six months of runway. Knowing this number early gives you time to act: cut costs, raise prices, chase sales or find funding. Discovering it when only a few weeks remain leaves very few good options.

sections.key: A rolling cash flow forecast shows upcoming shortfalls before they happen, so you can plan for them.
sections.b: A cash flow forecast doesn't need to be fancy. A spreadsheet with weeks or months across the top works well. List expected cash coming in, based on when customers will realistically pay, not when you'll invoice. List expected cash going out: wages, rent, suppliers, loan repayments, super, GST and tax. Subtract one from the other to get a running bank balance. Many businesses keep a rolling 13-week forecast and update it weekly. The goal isn't perfect prediction; it's spotting the dips early enough to do something about them.

sections.key: Check your cash position weekly, keep a buffer and get professional advice early when things look tight.
sections.b: A few habits make a big difference. Look at your bank balance and unpaid invoices every week. Build a cash buffer, with many advisers suggesting enough to cover at least a few months of fixed costs. Keep business and personal money in separate accounts. Use accounting software to track who owes you and what you owe. If cash is getting tight, act early: talk to your accountant, your bank and, if needed, the ATO about payment arrangements. This is general information only; a registered tax agent or accountant can advise on your situation.

quiz.q: Why can a business show a profit but have little cash?
o: Profit is recorded when sales are made, not when money arrives
Cash is only counted once a year
quiz.e: Under standard accounting, profit is booked at the time of sale, even if the customer pays months later.

quiz.q: What is overtrading?
o: Growing faster than the cash available to fund that growth
Charging prices that are too high
quiz.e: Rapid growth ties up cash in stock, wages and unpaid invoices, which can cause a cash crisis.

quiz.q: Which habit most directly improves the timing of cash coming in?
o: Invoicing as soon as work is done
Waiting until year end to send invoices
quiz.e: Prompt, clear invoices and follow-up shorten the time you wait to be paid.

quiz.q: You have $60,000 in cash and spend $10,000 more than you earn each month. What's your runway?
quiz.e: Runway is cash divided by monthly net outflow: $60,000 divided by $10,000 is six months.

quiz.q: Why do many owners set aside GST in a separate account?
o: GST collected isn't theirs; it must be paid to the ATO
quiz.e: GST collected from customers is owed to the ATO, so spending it can leave a painful bill later.

LESSONS.title: Starting a business in Australia
LESSONS.hook: ABN, ASIC, GST, sole trader or company: the paperwork sounds daunting, but the basic steps are simpler than most people think.

sections.key: The ATO looks at factors like intention to profit, regularity and business-like behaviour to decide if you're in business.
sections.b: Not every side activity is a business. The ATO considers factors such as whether you intend to make a profit, whether the activity is repeated and regular, whether it's organised in a business-like way, and its size. Selling a few of your own paintings each year may be a hobby; producing them regularly for sale, marketing them and keeping records looks like a business. The distinction matters for tax: business income is generally taxable and business expenses may be deductible. The ATO and business.gov.au both have guidance to help you decide.

sections.key: The main structures are sole trader, partnership, company and trust, each with different tax and liability rules.
sections.b: Your business structure affects your tax, your legal responsibilities and your personal risk. A sole trader is the simplest and cheapest: you and the business are legally the same, you use your own tax file number, and business profit is taxed at your personal rates. A partnership is two or more people running a business together and sharing profits. A company is a separate legal entity with its own obligations. Trusts are another option, often used for family businesses. You can change structure later, though it can involve costs.

sections.key: Sole traders and partners are generally personally liable for debts; companies offer more protection but more obligations.
sections.b: The biggest difference between structures is liability. As a sole trader, you are personally responsible for all business debts, so your house and savings could be at risk. In a partnership, partners are generally liable for debts of the whole partnership, including ones another partner caused. A company offers limited liability, which can protect personal assets, though directors can still be personally liable in some situations, such as trading while insolvent. Companies cost more to set up and run, need an ASIC registration and require directors to meet legal duties.

sections.key: An Australian Business Number is a free 11-digit identifier for your business, applied for through the Australian Business Register.
sections.b: Most people starting a business apply for an Australian Business Number, or ABN, an 11-digit number that identifies your business to government and other businesses. Applying is free through the Australian Business Register, which you can reach via business.gov.au. Beware of third-party websites that charge fees for the same thing. You need an ABN to register a business name and for GST. Without one, businesses that pay you may be required to withhold tax from their payments at the top marginal rate, which hurts cash flow.

sections.key: If you trade under any name other than your own personal name, you generally must register it with ASIC.
sections.b: If you're a sole trader called Sarah Nguyen trading as Sarah Nguyen, you don't need to register a business name. But if you trade as 'Northside Dog Walking', you generally must register that name with ASIC, the Australian Securities and Investments Commission, which charges a fee for one or three years. Registering a business name does not give you exclusive ownership of it. To protect a brand, you'd look at a trade mark through IP Australia. Check that the name and a matching website domain are available before committing.

sections.key: You must register for GST once your GST turnover reaches $75,000 a year; many choose to register earlier.
sections.b: Goods and services tax is a 10% tax on most goods and services in Australia. You must register for GST when your annual GST turnover reaches $75,000, or $150,000 for non-profit organisations. Taxi and ride-sourcing drivers must register regardless of turnover. Once registered, you generally add GST to your prices, lodge a business activity statement, or BAS, and pass the GST you collect to the ATO, minus GST credits on your business purchases. You can register voluntarily below the threshold; whether that's worthwhile depends on your customers and costs.

sections.key: Check which licences and insurance you need, and keep business records, generally for five years.
sections.b: Depending on your industry and location, you may need licences or permits, from food handling to building work. The Australian Business Licence and Information Service, ABLIS, on business.gov.au can help you find them. If you employ staff, workers' compensation insurance is compulsory, and you'll have obligations such as paying super. Public liability and professional indemnity insurance aren't always legally required but are common, and some clients or industries insist on them. The ATO generally requires you to keep business records for five years, so set up a good system early.

sections.key: Use business.gov.au, keep business finances separate, and get advice from an accountant or lawyer on key decisions.
sections.b: A sensible order: check whether you're really in business, choose a structure, apply for an ABN, register a business name if needed, and consider GST. Open a separate business bank account from day one. Set up simple accounting software and a system for receipts. Check licences, insurance and any council rules. Business.gov.au, run by the Australian Government, is a free and reliable starting point, and many states offer small business advice services. This is general information only: rules change, so talk to a registered tax agent, accountant or lawyer about your situation.

quiz.q: Under which structure are you and the business legally the same entity?
quiz.e: A sole trader is legally the same as the business and uses their own tax file number.

quiz.q: What is a key advantage of a company structure?
o: No need to register with anyone
Limited liability that can help protect personal assets
quiz.e: Companies are separate legal entities, which can limit owners' personal liability, though directors still have duties.

quiz.q: How much does it cost to apply for an ABN through the Australian Business Register?
quiz.e: Applying for an ABN through the official register is free; beware of sites that charge.

quiz.q: Does registering a business name with ASIC give you exclusive ownership of it?
o: Yes, but only in your state
No, a trade mark is needed to protect a brand
quiz.e: Business name registration doesn't grant exclusive rights; trade marks through IP Australia do.

quiz.q: At what annual GST turnover must most businesses register for GST?
quiz.e: Most businesses must register at $75,000; the threshold for non-profits is $150,000.

LESSONS.title: Lessons from startup wins and flops
LESSONS.hook: Canva was rejected by investors again and again. Juicero raised over $100 million and vanished. What separates them is rarely luck alone.

sections.key: Canva grew from a Perth yearbook business into a global design platform after many investor rejections.
sections.b: In 2007, Melanie Perkins, then a university student in Perth, noticed how hard design software was to learn. With Cliff Obrecht she started Fusion Books, an online tool for designing school yearbooks, run from her mother's lounge room. It proved the idea of simple online design. Pitching a broader platform, Perkins has said she was rejected by more than 100 investors. With co-founder Cameron Adams, Canva launched in 2013. It has since grown into one of the world's most valuable private tech companies, used by millions.

sections.key: Atlassian started in Sydney in 2002 with a credit card, and grew by letting good products sell themselves.
sections.b: Mike Cannon-Brookes and Scott Farquhar met at the University of New South Wales and founded Atlassian in Sydney in 2002, reportedly funded with about $10,000 on a credit card. Their best-known early product, Jira, helped software teams track bugs and tasks. Unusually, they grew for years without a traditional sales team, selling online at transparent, affordable prices and relying on word of mouth among developers. Atlassian listed on the US Nasdaq exchange in 2015, becoming one of Australia's biggest tech success stories.

sections.key: Product-market fit means being in a good market with a product that market strongly wants.
sections.b: Investor Marc Andreessen popularised the term product-market fit in a 2007 essay, describing it as being in a good market with a product that can satisfy that market. You can often feel it: customers use the product eagerly, tell others and complain loudly when it breaks. Growth marketer Sean Ellis proposed a simple test: ask users how they'd feel if they could no longer use your product. If around 40% or more say 'very disappointed', you may be close. Before fit, focus on learning; after it, on growing.

sections.h: Juicero: solving a problem nobody had
sections.key: Juicero's expensive juicer failed partly because a cheaper alternative, squeezing by hand, worked just as well.
sections.b: Juicero launched in 2016 with a Wi-Fi-connected juice press that initially sold for about US$700, later cut to about US$400, and used proprietary juice packs. It raised roughly US$120 million from investors. Then in 2017, Bloomberg reporters showed the packs could be squeezed by hand to produce much the same juice. The company shut down later that year. The lesson isn't that hardware is doomed; it's that a sophisticated solution must deliver real value beyond the simplest alternative, and customers will notice when it doesn't.

sections.h: Quibi and the limits of money
sections.key: Quibi raised well over a billion dollars but shut down within about six months of launch.
sections.b: Quibi, a short-form streaming service for phones founded by Hollywood veteran Jeffrey Katzenberg, raised about US$1.75 billion before launching in April 2020. It shut down about six months later. Observers pointed to several problems: it launched during COVID-19 lockdowns when people weren't commuting, it made sharing clips hard, and it competed with free platforms like YouTube and TikTok. The takeaway many drew was that money and famous names can't substitute for testing whether customers truly want the product in the form offered.

sections.key: Failed startups often cite no market need and running out of cash among the top reasons.
sections.b: Research firm CB Insights has analysed post-mortems written by founders of failed startups. In its widely cited reports, 'no market need' and 'ran out of cash' have ranked among the most common reasons, alongside being outcompeted, pricing problems and team issues. These reasons are self-reported, so they're not perfect data, but the pattern is consistent with experience: building something people don't need is the most common and most avoidable mistake. Running out of money is often the final symptom rather than the root cause.

sections.key: A pivot is a deliberate change of direction based on evidence; famous examples include Slack, Instagram and YouTube.
sections.b: A pivot is a structured change in strategy while keeping what you've learned. Slack emerged from a company building an online game called Glitch; the game failed, but the team's internal chat tool became the product. Instagram began as Burbn, a check-in app, before its founders focused on the photo-sharing feature people actually used. YouTube's founders have said it was first pitched as a video dating site. The hard judgement is when to persist and when to pivot. Evidence from customer behaviour, not pride or sunk costs, should decide.

sections.key: Test demand early, watch your cash, listen to customer behaviour and be willing to change your mind.
sections.b: The patterns repeat. Canva and Atlassian solved real, widespread problems and built products people wanted to share. Juicero and Quibi spent heavily before proving demand. So talk to customers early and keep talking. Launch something small and learn from how people actually use it. Watch your runway closely, because cash buys time to learn. Stay stubborn about the problem you're solving but flexible about the solution. And remember survivorship bias: for every famous success, many similar companies failed, so success stories show what's possible, not what's guaranteed.

quiz.q: Canva's founders first proved their idea with which business?
o: An online school yearbook design tool
quiz.e: Fusion Books let schools design yearbooks online, showing simple design tools could work.

quiz.q: What was unusual about Atlassian's early growth?
o: It was funded by the government
It grew for years without a traditional sales team
It only sold to Australian customers
It started as a hardware company
quiz.e: Atlassian sold online at transparent prices and relied on word of mouth rather than salespeople.

quiz.q: In Sean Ellis's test, what share of users saying 'very disappointed' suggests product-market fit?
quiz.e: Ellis suggested that around 40% or more being very disappointed without the product is a good sign.

quiz.q: What undermined Juicero's product?
o: Its juice packs could be squeezed by hand
quiz.e: Reporters showed the packs could be squeezed by hand, undercutting the value of the expensive press.

quiz.q: Slack emerged as a pivot from what?
quiz.e: The team's internal chat tool, built while making the game Glitch, became Slack.

LESSONS.title: What code really is
LESSONS.hook: Every app on your phone is just a very long, very precise recipe. Once you see the five ingredients, software stops being magic.

sections.key: Code is a set of precise instructions that a computer follows exactly, step by step.
sections.b: At its heart, code is a list of instructions written for a computer. Think of a recipe: preheat the oven, mix the flour and eggs, bake for 30 minutes. A computer follows instructions the same way, one step at a time, in order. The difference is that a computer has no common sense. A human cook will notice if the recipe forgets to say 'crack the eggs first'. A computer will happily throw the eggs in whole. Programming is the craft of writing instructions so clear that something with zero judgement can still get them right.

sections.key: Ada Lovelace published what is often called the first computer program in 1843.
sections.b: The idea is older than electronic computers. In 1843 the English mathematician Ada Lovelace published notes on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine, a mechanical computer that was designed but never completed. Her notes included a step-by-step method for the machine to calculate a sequence called the Bernoulli numbers, often described as the first published computer program. She also saw that such a machine might one day work with music or symbols, not just numbers. Today a modern car runs on tens of millions of lines of code, but each line is still an instruction in the spirit of hers.

sections.key: A variable is a named container that holds a value the program can read and change.
sections.b: Programs need to remember things, and they do it with variables. Picture a row of jars in a pantry, each with a label: 'sugar', 'flour', 'eggs left'. A variable is a labelled jar holding a value, such as a number, a word or a list. A banking app might keep a variable called balance holding 250. When you buy a coffee, the program takes the value out, subtracts 5, and puts 245 back in the same jar. The label stays the same while the contents change, which is exactly why it is called a variable.

sections.key: Conditions let a program choose what to do, using 'if this, then that, otherwise something else'.
sections.b: Recipes contain decisions: if the cake is still wet in the middle, bake it for another five minutes. Code does the same with conditions, usually written with the word 'if'. A thermostat program might say, in effect: if the temperature is above 24 degrees, turn on the cooling; otherwise, leave it off. Conditions can be combined, such as if it is a weekday and before 7am, sound the alarm. Every time an app reacts differently to different situations, like rejecting a wrong password, a condition is doing the work behind the scenes.

sections.key: A loop repeats a set of instructions, either a set number of times or until something changes.
sections.b: Imagine a recipe that says 'stir, stir, stir' 200 times. Nobody writes it like that; they write 'stir until smooth'. That is a loop. Instead of repeating the same instruction over and over, a programmer tells the computer to repeat a block of steps a certain number of times, or until a condition is met. A music app uses a loop to go through every song in a playlist. An email program loops through thousands of messages to find the ones containing a search word. Loops are where computers shine, because they never get bored or tired.

sections.key: A function is a named, reusable block of instructions that can be called whenever it's needed.
sections.b: Many recipe books have a basic white sauce on one page, and other recipes simply say 'make one quantity of white sauce'. That saves rewriting the same steps in every lasagne and moussaka. In code, this is a function: a named bundle of instructions you can call on whenever you need it. A function might take ingredients in, called inputs, and hand a result back. A shopping app could have a function that takes a price and a postcode and returns the delivery cost. Write it once, test it once, and use it everywhere.

sections.key: Real programs are built by combining variables, conditions, loops and functions in layers.
sections.b: These few building blocks combine into everything from calculators to video games. Consider a simple step counter. A variable stores today's steps. A loop keeps checking the motion sensor. A condition asks whether the phone moved in a walking pattern, and if so, adds one to the count. A function turns steps into kilometres, and another condition checks whether you've hit your goal and sends a congratulations message. Large programs work the same way, just with many more pieces, organised into layers so that teams of people can each work on one part.

sections.key: Free visual tools like Scratch let anyone experiment with the building blocks of code.
sections.b: You don't need to become a programmer to benefit from understanding code, but trying it helps the ideas stick. Scratch, a free tool from MIT, lets you snap together coloured blocks labelled 'repeat', 'if' and 'set variable', and watch a cartoon character follow your instructions. Many adults start there alongside their kids. When you next use an app, try spotting the building blocks: where does it remember something, make a decision or repeat a task? That habit makes technology less mysterious and helps you ask better questions about the software you rely on.

quiz.q: Why must code be written so precisely?
o: Computers follow instructions exactly and have no common sense
Code is checked by a human before it runs
quiz.e: A computer does exactly what it is told, so any gap or ambiguity in the instructions leads to mistakes.

quiz.q: In the pantry analogy, what is a variable?
o: A labelled jar whose contents can change
A shopping list that never changes
quiz.e: A variable is a named container holding a value the program can read and update.

quiz.q: Which building block would a program use to reject a wrong password?
quiz.e: Conditions let a program choose different actions, such as allowing or refusing entry.

quiz.q: A music app playing every song in a playlist, one after another, is an example of what?
quiz.e: A loop repeats a block of instructions, here once for each song.

quiz.q: Who published what is often called the first computer program, in 1843?
quiz.e: Ada Lovelace's notes on Babbage's Analytical Engine included a method for calculating Bernoulli numbers.

LESSONS.title: Algorithms, explained
LESSONS.hook: The word sounds futuristic, but it comes from a scholar in 9th-century Baghdad, and you use algorithms every time you look up a word or take the fastest route home.

sections.key: An algorithm is a clear, step-by-step method for solving a problem or completing a task.
sections.b: An algorithm is simply a precise method for getting something done. Long division, as taught in school, is an algorithm: follow the steps and you get the answer every time. So is the method you use to find a name in a phone book. Code is how an algorithm is written down for a computer, but the algorithm itself is the idea behind it. A good algorithm must be unambiguous, must finish at some point, and must produce the right result. The same algorithm can be written in many different programming languages.

sections.key: The word comes from al-Khwarizmi, and Euclid's algorithm from around 300 BC is still used today.
sections.b: The word 'algorithm' comes from the name of Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi, a Persian mathematician who worked in Baghdad in the 9th century. His books explained step-by-step methods for calculation, and Latin translations spread them through Europe. His work also gave us the word 'algebra'. But algorithms are older still. Around 300 BC, the Greek mathematician Euclid described a method for finding the largest number that divides evenly into two others. Euclid's algorithm is still taught today and is used inside some of the encryption that protects online banking.

sections.key: Binary search halves the possibilities each step, finding one item in a million in about 20 steps.
sections.b: Imagine guessing a number between 1 and 100, and being told 'higher' or 'lower' after each guess. Guessing 1, 2, 3 in order could take 100 tries. A smarter approach is to guess 50, then 25 or 75, halving the possibilities each time. This is called binary search, and it will always find the number within seven guesses. The power grows with size: among a million sorted items, binary search needs only about 20 steps. It only works if the items are in order, which is one big reason computers spend so much effort sorting.

sections.key: Different sorting algorithms reach the same result, but some are vastly faster on large lists.
sections.b: Sorting, putting things in order, is one of the most studied problems in computing. One simple method, bubble sort, walks through a list swapping neighbouring items that are in the wrong order, and repeats until nothing needs swapping. It works, but it is painfully slow on big lists. Merge sort takes a different approach: split the list in half, sort each half, then merge the two sorted halves together, much like combining two sorted piles of exam papers. On a list of a million items, a method like merge sort can be tens of thousands of times faster.

sections.key: Efficiency describes how an algorithm's work grows as the amount of data grows.
sections.b: Computer scientists care less about how fast an algorithm is on ten items and more about how its work grows as the data grows. Some algorithms double their work when the data doubles. Others quadruple it, and some grow so explosively that even the fastest supercomputer could not finish before the sun burns out. This is why choosing the right algorithm often matters more than buying a faster computer. A clever method on an old laptop can beat a clumsy method on a data centre. Programmers describe this growth with a notation called 'Big O'.

sections.key: Map apps use shortest-path algorithms, descended from Dijkstra's 1956 method, plus live traffic data.
sections.b: When a map app plots the fastest drive from Parramatta to Bondi, it is solving a shortest-path problem. Roads become a network of points and connections, each with a travel time. In 1956 the Dutch computer scientist Edsger Dijkstra devised a method for finding the shortest route through such a network, reportedly in about 20 minutes while sitting at a cafe in Amsterdam. Modern map apps use faster descendants of his idea, combined with live traffic reports from other phones, to recalculate your route when a crash blocks the motorway ahead.

sections.h: What shows up in your feed
sections.key: Social media feeds use ranking algorithms that predict what will keep you engaged.
sections.b: When people say 'the algorithm' in everyday talk, they usually mean the ranking systems behind social media, video and shopping sites. These systems look at signals such as what you have watched, liked, shared or lingered on, and predict which posts you are most likely to engage with. Early Google search relied on an algorithm called PageRank, which treated links from other pages as votes of importance. Modern feed algorithms are far more complex and often use machine learning. Because they optimise for engagement, they can favour content that provokes strong emotions, which is a real and debated concern.

sections.key: You can shape feed algorithms with your choices, and use algorithmic thinking for everyday problems.
sections.b: Knowing how algorithms work gives you some control. Feed algorithms learn from your behaviour, so deliberately following, muting and choosing 'not interested' changes what you see. Pausing on outrage teaches the system to show more of it. Algorithmic thinking also helps offline. Looking for a lost item? Search systematically, room by room, rather than randomly. Packing a car boot? Big items first is a simple algorithm that usually works well. Breaking a messy task into clear, repeatable steps is exactly what programmers do, and it works just as well in a kitchen or an office.

quiz.q: What is an algorithm?
o: A clear, step-by-step method for solving a problem
quiz.e: An algorithm is the method itself; code is one way of writing it down for a computer.

quiz.q: What does Euclid's algorithm, described around 300 BC, find?
o: The largest number that divides evenly into two numbers
The shortest route between two cities
quiz.e: It is still taught today and is used inside some of the encryption that protects online banking.

quiz.q: Roughly how many steps does binary search need to find one item among a million sorted items?
quiz.e: Halving a million possibilities about 20 times narrows them down to one.

quiz.q: Which computer scientist devised a famous shortest-path algorithm in 1956?
quiz.e: Dijkstra's method underpins the route-finding ideas used in modern map apps.

quiz.q: What do social media feed algorithms mainly try to predict?
o: Which posts are most factually accurate
Which posts you are most likely to engage with
quiz.e: Feeds rank posts by predicted engagement, based on signals like what you watch, like and share.

LESSONS.title: Why there are so many programming languages
LESSONS.hook: There are thousands of programming languages, from Python to COBOL. Here's why, and which ones actually run your world.

sections.key: Programming languages let humans write instructions that are translated into the machine code a processor runs.
sections.b: A computer's processor only understands machine code: long strings of ones and zeros representing very basic operations, such as add these two numbers or move this value. Writing that by hand is slow and error-prone. Programming languages sit in the middle. They let people write instructions using words and symbols that are closer to human thinking, which are then translated into machine code. The earliest programmers in the 1940s often worked almost directly with machine instructions. Every language since has been an attempt to make that translation easier, safer or better suited to a particular job.

sections.key: FORTRAN (1957) and COBOL (1959) were early high-level languages, and COBOL still runs many banking systems.
sections.b: FORTRAN, released by IBM in 1957 and led by John Backus, was one of the first widely used high-level languages, built for scientists and engineers doing heavy maths. COBOL followed in 1959, designed for business record-keeping and strongly influenced by the work of computing pioneer Grace Hopper. Remarkably, COBOL is still running in many banks, insurers and government agencies worldwide, because rewriting decades of reliable code is risky and expensive. Since then, thousands of languages have been created, though only a few dozen are in wide everyday use.

sections.key: Languages differ because they make different trade-offs between speed, safety, ease and purpose.
sections.b: Why not one language for everything? For the same reason there isn't one tool in a shed. A hammer and a screwdriver both help you build, but each suits different jobs. Some languages are designed for raw speed, giving the programmer close control over memory and hardware. Others prioritise safety, catching mistakes before the program runs. Some are designed to be easy to read and quick to write. Others are specialised for one domain, such as databases or statistics. Every design choice involves a trade-off, and new languages appear when people want a different balance.

sections.key: Compiled languages are translated ahead of time; interpreted languages are translated as the program runs.
sections.b: There are two broad ways to translate code into something a computer can run. A compiled language, such as C, C++, Rust or Go, is translated in full before it runs, a bit like translating an entire book before publishing it. The result usually runs very fast. An interpreted language, like Python, is translated while the program runs, more like a live interpreter at a meeting. That makes it easier to experiment, but it often runs more slowly. In practice the line has blurred, and many modern languages, including JavaScript in web browsers, use clever mixtures of both.

sections.key: Python is popular for data, science and AI; JavaScript is the language of web browsers.
sections.b: Python, created by Dutch programmer Guido van Rossum and first released in 1991, is named after the comedy group Monty Python, not the snake. It is known for clean, readable code and is widely used in data analysis, science, automation and artificial intelligence. JavaScript was created by Brendan Eich at Netscape in 1995, famously in about ten days. Despite the name, it has little to do with the older language Java; the name was largely a marketing decision. JavaScript runs in every major web browser, making it one of the most used languages on Earth.

sections.key: Swift and Kotlin build phone apps, SQL talks to databases, and C underpins operating systems.
sections.b: Many other languages have clear homes. Swift, introduced by Apple in 2014, is used to build iPhone and Mac apps. Kotlin is Google's preferred language for Android apps, alongside the older and still very widespread Java, which is also common in large business systems. SQL, usually pronounced 'sequel' or spelled out, is used to ask questions of databases, such as 'show all customers in Victoria'. C, created in the early 1970s at Bell Labs, remains the foundation of operating systems like Linux. C# is popular for business software and for games made with the Unity engine.

sections.key: Most languages share the same core concepts, so learning one makes learning the next much easier.
sections.b: The good news for learners is that languages are more alike than they look. Nearly all of them have variables, conditions, loops and functions. Once you understand those ideas in one language, a second language is mostly new spelling and grammar for familiar concepts, a bit like learning Spanish after Italian. Experienced programmers often switch between several languages in one week. Employers generally care more about problem-solving skill than about any single language. The hard part of programming is not memorising commands but learning to break problems into small, precise steps.

sections.key: Pick one beginner-friendly language, such as Python, and build small projects you actually care about.
sections.b: If you want to try coding, pick one language and stick with it for a while. Python is a common first choice because its code reads almost like English. If websites interest you more, start with HTML, CSS and JavaScript. There are many free, reputable courses online, and public libraries in Australia often run coding sessions. The biggest predictor of progress is building small things you care about, like a budget calculator or a quiz for your kids. Expect to feel stuck often. Being confused and then working it out is not failure; it is what programming actually feels like.

quiz.q: What is the only kind of code a computer's processor directly understands?
quiz.e: Processors run machine code; programming languages are translated into it.

quiz.q: Which early language, influenced by Grace Hopper, still runs many banking systems today?
quiz.e: COBOL (1959) was designed for business records and remains in use in banks and government systems.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between compiled and interpreted languages?
o: Compiled languages can only run on phones
Compiled code is translated before running; interpreted code is translated as it runs
quiz.e: Compiling is like translating a whole book first; interpreting is like live translation.

quiz.q: Python is named after what?
quiz.e: Guido van Rossum named it after Monty Python, not the reptile.

quiz.q: Which language was introduced by Apple in 2014 for building iPhone apps?
quiz.e: Swift is Apple's language for iOS and Mac apps; Kotlin is Google's preferred language for Android.

LESSONS.title: How websites work
LESSONS.hook: Type a web address and a page appears in under a second. Behind that blink is a relay race across the planet.

sections.key: A browser on your device requests files from a server, a computer that stores and sends out the website.
sections.b: Every website visit is a conversation between two computers. Your browser, such as Safari, Chrome, Firefox or Edge, is the client: it asks for things. A server is a computer, usually sitting in a data centre, that stores a website's files and sends them out when asked. Servers are not special machines at heart; they are computers built to run all day and answer many requests at once. Big sites run on thousands of servers spread around the world. When you load a page, your browser asks, the server answers, and the browser turns the answer into what you see.

sections.key: The first website, info.cern.ch, went live in 1991, and a 1993 browser called Mosaic helped take the web to the public.
sections.b: The web's first server was a NeXT computer in Tim Berners-Lee's office at CERN, with a handwritten label warning colleagues not to switch it off. The first website, at info.cern.ch, went live in 1991 and simply explained what the web was and how to set up a server of your own. It was plain text. In 1993 a browser called Mosaic, from the University of Illinois, displayed pictures alongside text and was easy to install, and public interest exploded. That April, CERN released the web's software into the public domain. CERN restored the first website in 2013, and you can still visit it today.

sections.key: Domain names read from right to left, from a top-level ending like .au down to the name its owner registered.
sections.b: Behind the scenes, computers find each other with numeric IP addresses, but people use domain names, and those names have a structure. Read abc.net.au from right to left: .au is Australia's country-code ending, .net.au is a category within it, and abc is the name its owner registered. Australian names are overseen by auDA, a not-for-profit body that sets the rules. Since 2022, anyone with an Australian connection can register a name directly under .au, such as example.au, without a .com in the middle. Domain names are rented, not owned outright: you pay a registrar for one to five years at a time, and if you forget to renew, someone else can grab the name.

sections.key: HTML describes a page's structure and content: headings, paragraphs, images and links.
sections.b: Web pages are built from three main languages, each with its own job. The first is HTML, short for HyperText Markup Language. HTML describes what is on the page and how it is organised: this is a heading, this is a paragraph, here is an image, this text is a link to another page. It is like the frame and rooms of a house. HTML is written using tags that wrap around content, marking where each element begins and ends. Links, the feature that makes the web a web, are part of HTML.

sections.key: CSS controls how a page looks; JavaScript makes it interactive and responsive.
sections.b: If HTML is the frame of the house, CSS, short for Cascading Style Sheets, is the paint, furniture and interior design. CSS controls colours, fonts, spacing and layout, and can rearrange a page to fit a phone or a big monitor. JavaScript is the wiring and plumbing: it makes things happen. When a menu slides open, a form warns that you've missed your postcode, or new posts appear as you scroll, JavaScript is at work. Keeping structure, style and behaviour separate makes websites easier to build, maintain and redesign.

sections.key: Loading a page involves a DNS lookup, a secure connection, a request, a response and rendering.
sections.b: Here is roughly what happens when you type a web address and press enter. First, your browser uses DNS to find the server's numeric address. Next, it opens a connection to that server and, for secure sites, agrees on encryption, shown by the padlock icon. Then it sends a request, using a set of rules called HTTP, for the page. The server responds with the HTML. The browser reads it, discovers it also needs images, fonts, CSS and JavaScript files, and requests those too. Finally it assembles everything into the page, often all within a second.

sections.key: The front end runs in your browser; the back end runs on servers, handling data, accounts and logic.
sections.b: Web developers often talk about the front end and the back end. The front end is everything that runs in your browser: the layout, buttons and animations you interact with. The back end runs on the servers and handles the things you don't see, such as checking your password, storing your order in a database, or working out which products to show you. When you check out from an online shop, the front end collects your details and the back end processes the payment, updates stock levels and triggers a confirmation email.

sections.key: Check the address carefully, understand that HTTPS protects the connection but not honesty, and manage cookies.
sections.b: Knowing how the web works helps you stay safe. HTTPS and the padlock mean your connection to a site is encrypted, so others on the network can't read it. They do not mean the site is honest; scam sites use HTTPS too. Always check the domain name carefully, since scammers register look-alike addresses, such as an extra letter or a different ending. Cookies are small files sites store in your browser to remember logins and preferences, and sometimes to track you across sites. Your browser settings let you view and clear them.

quiz.q: In a website visit, what is the role of a server?
o: It displays the page on your screen
It stores the website's files and sends them when requested
It is another name for a browser
quiz.e: The browser requests; the server stores and sends the website's files.

quiz.q: Which 1993 browser helped make the web popular by showing pictures alongside text?
quiz.e: Mosaic, from the University of Illinois, was easy to install and use, and public interest in the web took off.

quiz.q: What became possible for Australian domain names in 2022?
o: Registering a name directly under .au, like example.au
quiz.e: Since 2022, people with an Australian connection can register names directly under .au, without .com or .net in the middle.

quiz.q: Which language controls the colours, fonts and layout of a web page?
quiz.e: HTML gives structure, CSS gives style, and JavaScript adds behaviour.

quiz.q: What does the padlock and HTTPS on a website guarantee?
o: The site is run by a trustworthy business
Your connection to the site is encrypted
quiz.e: HTTPS protects the connection, but scam sites can use it too, so still check the domain name.

LESSONS.title: Bugs and debugging
LESSONS.hook: A moth in a relay, a rocket lost in under a minute, and a rubber duck on a desk: the surprising story of how software goes wrong and gets fixed.

sections.key: A bug is a mistake in software that makes it behave in ways its creators didn't intend.
sections.b: A bug is an error in a program that causes it to do something unintended: crash, freeze, show the wrong number or open a security hole. Most bugs are not the computer's fault. The computer did exactly what it was told; the instructions were wrong or incomplete. Bugs are unavoidable in any large program, because software is enormously complex and people make mistakes. Professional programmers expect to spend a large share of their time finding and fixing bugs. Debugging, the process of tracking them down, is one of the most important skills in all of programming.

sections.key: In 1947 Harvard operators taped a moth into a logbook as the 'first actual case of bug being found'.
sections.b: On 9 September 1947, operators of the Harvard Mark II computer traced a fault to a moth trapped in one of its relays. They removed it and taped it into the logbook with the note 'First actual case of bug being found.' The joke was that engineers already called faults 'bugs'; Thomas Edison used the word in the 1870s. The story is often credited to computing pioneer Grace Hopper, who worked on the Harvard team and loved to tell it, though she was not necessarily the person who found the moth. The logbook page is held by the Smithsonian.

sections.key: Bugs include syntax errors, logic errors and edge cases the programmer didn't anticipate.
sections.b: Bugs come in several flavours. Syntax errors are like spelling or grammar mistakes, such as a missing bracket, and the computer usually refuses to run the program until they're fixed. Logic errors are sneakier: the program runs happily but gives the wrong answer, like a discount calculation that subtracts 10 dollars instead of 10 percent. Then there are edge cases, unusual situations the programmer didn't think of. What happens if someone's surname has an apostrophe, a customer orders zero items, or a date falls on 29 February? Many real-world bugs live at these edges.

sections.key: Good debugging means reproducing the bug, narrowing down where it happens, forming a theory and testing it.
sections.b: Effective debugging is closer to detective work than guesswork. The first step is to reproduce the bug reliably: exactly what actions make it happen? Next, narrow down where it occurs, often by checking the program's values at different points to see where things first go wrong. A handy trick is halving: if the problem is somewhere in 1,000 lines, check the middle, then keep halving. Then form a theory about the cause, change one thing, and test again. Changing many things at once may make the bug disappear without revealing why, and it may come back.

sections.key: In 1996 an Ariane 5 rocket was destroyed about 40 seconds after launch because of a number conversion error.
sections.b: On 4 June 1996, the European Space Agency's first Ariane 5 rocket veered off course and was destroyed about 40 seconds after launch, taking four scientific satellites with it. The cause was a software error. Guidance code reused from the older Ariane 4 tried to squeeze a large number, related to the rocket's horizontal speed, into a space too small to hold it. Ariane 5 was faster than Ariane 4, so the number overflowed and the system shut down. The backup ran identical software and failed the same way. The loss is often estimated at several hundred million US dollars.

sections.key: The Y2K problem came from storing years as two digits; massive fixing work meant few serious failures.
sections.b: For decades, to save expensive memory, many programs stored years as two digits, so 1999 was just 99. The worry was that on 1 January 2000, the year 00 would be read as 1900, confusing calculations for interest, ages, bookings and schedules. Governments and businesses worldwide, including in Australia, spent enormous sums, estimated in the hundreds of billions of US dollars globally, checking and fixing code. When the date arrived, problems were mostly minor. Some argue the threat was exaggerated, but many experts credit the huge repair effort for the smooth changeover.

sections.key: Explaining your code line by line, even to a rubber duck, often reveals the mistake.
sections.b: One of programming's most loved techniques involves a bath toy. The 1999 book The Pragmatic Programmer, by Andrew Hunt and David Thomas, tells of a programmer who kept a rubber duck on the desk and explained code to it, line by line, when stuck. The trick works surprisingly often. Explaining forces you to slow down and state what each step actually does, rather than what you assume it does, and the gap between the two is often where the bug hides. Many programmers find that halfway through asking a colleague for help, they suddenly see the answer themselves.

sections.key: Update your software, report bugs clearly, and use debugging habits to solve everyday problems.
sections.b: Bugs affect everyone, not just programmers. Software updates often fix bugs, including security flaws, so installing them promptly is one of the simplest ways to stay safe. When reporting a problem to a company or IT help desk, describe it like a debugger would: what you did, what you expected, what actually happened, and whether you can make it happen again. The same mindset works for a car that won't start or a recipe that failed. Reproduce the problem, change one thing at a time, and explain it out loud. Sometimes the duck knows best.

quiz.q: What was found in the Harvard Mark II computer in 1947?
o: A moth trapped in a relay
quiz.e: Operators taped the moth into the logbook, noting the 'first actual case of bug being found'.

quiz.q: Was 1947 the first time engineers used the word 'bug' for a fault?
o: Yes, the moth gave us the word
No, Grace Hopper invented it in 1950
No, engineers such as Thomas Edison used it decades earlier
Yes, it was coined by NASA
quiz.e: The logbook note was a joke precisely because 'bug' was already engineering slang, used by Edison in the 1870s.

quiz.q: A discount program runs without crashing but subtracts 10 dollars instead of 10 percent. What kind of bug is this?
quiz.e: The program runs, but its logic produces the wrong answer.

quiz.q: What caused the Ariane 5 rocket failure in 1996?
o: A number too large for the space the software tried to store it in
quiz.e: Code reused from Ariane 4 overflowed when converting a large speed-related value, and the backup failed identically.

quiz.q: Why does the rubber duck method work?
o: Ducks are good luck in programming
Explaining code step by step exposes gaps between what you assume and what it does
