quiz.e: Slowing down to explain each line often reveals the mistake.

LESSONS.title: Mental models: a toolkit for thinking
LESSONS.hook: The best thinkers don't know everything. They carry a handful of reliable ways of seeing, and reach for the right one at the right moment.

sections.key: A mental model is a simplified way of understanding how something works; having several beats relying on one.
sections.b: A mental model is a simplified picture of how something works, like supply and demand, or compound interest. Everyone uses them, mostly without noticing. The investor Charlie Munger, Warren Buffett's long-time partner, argued in a well-known 1994 talk that you need a 'latticework' of models drawn from many fields: economics, psychology, physics, biology and more. His warning was the saying 'to a man with a hammer, everything looks like a nail'. If you only know one way of seeing, you'll force every problem into it. A few broadly useful models, practised until they become habits, can sharpen almost any decision.

sections.key: First-principles thinking breaks a problem down to basic truths and rebuilds from there, instead of copying what's usual.
sections.b: Most of the time we reason by analogy: we do what others do, with small changes. First-principles thinking, an idea going back to Aristotle, means stripping a problem back to what you know is fundamentally true, then reasoning up from there. Ask: what are we sure of, and what is merely assumed? Suppose a quote to renovate a bathroom seems huge. Instead of accepting that 'bathrooms just cost that much', list the parts: materials, labour hours, waterproofing, plumbing, permits. You may find where the real cost sits, and which parts are negotiable. It's slower than copying, so save it for problems that matter.

sections.key: Inversion means flipping a problem: ask what would guarantee failure, then avoid those things.
sections.b: The mathematician Carl Jacobi is often credited with the advice 'invert, always invert', and Munger made it famous in business. Instead of asking 'how do I succeed?', ask 'what would make this fail for certain?', then avoid those things. Want a happy marriage? Listing what reliably wrecks one, such as contempt, secrecy and never listening, is often clearer than defining perfection. Planning a big project? Imagine it's a year later and it failed badly, then ask why. Psychologist Gary Klein calls this a 'pre-mortem'. Inversion works because avoiding obvious mistakes is often easier, and more valuable, than finding brilliant moves.

sections.key: Second-order thinking asks 'and then what?', tracing consequences beyond the immediate effect.
sections.b: First-order thinking stops at the immediate result: this medicine relieves pain, this price cut wins customers. Second-order thinking keeps asking 'and then what?' A price cut may win customers, but then competitors cut too, and everyone earns less. A widely told story, possibly exaggerated, describes a colonial bounty on cobras in Delhi that led people to breed cobras for the reward. Whether or not it happened exactly that way, the 'cobra effect' names a real pattern: well-meant rules that create the opposite of what was intended. Before acting, sketch the likely reactions of the people and systems affected, over months, not just days.

sections.key: Build in a buffer for error, because estimates of time, money and risk are usually too optimistic.
sections.b: Engineers don't design a bridge to carry exactly the heaviest truck they expect; they build it to carry several times that load. The investor Benjamin Graham, Warren Buffett's teacher, borrowed the idea for finance and called it a 'margin of safety': only buy when the price is well below your estimate of value, so you're protected if you're wrong. It works in everyday life too. Leave 20 minutes spare for the airport run. Add a contingency of 10 to 20% to a renovation budget. Borrow less than the bank says you can. We're reliably over-optimistic about how long things take and what they cost, so a buffer isn't pessimism; it's realism. The less reversible the decision, the bigger the margin you want.

sections.key: Know the boundaries of what you genuinely understand, and be most careful outside them.
sections.b: Buffett and Munger describe a 'circle of competence': the areas where you truly understand how things work, based on real experience. Inside it, your judgement is reasonably reliable. Outside it, confidence can be dangerous, because you don't know what you don't know. The size of the circle matters less than knowing where its edge is. A skilled electrician may make excellent calls about wiring and poor ones about cryptocurrency. This connects to the Dunning-Kruger effect, where limited knowledge can come with overconfidence. When you're outside your circle, slow down, seek people with genuine expertise, and prefer small, reversible bets over big ones.

sections.h: The map is not the territory
sections.key: Every model, plan or number is a simplification of reality, useful but never complete.
sections.b: The phrase 'the map is not the territory' comes from Polish-American scholar Alfred Korzybski in the early 1930s. A map leaves things out on purpose; that's what makes it useful. But when the map and the ground disagree, trust the ground. Budgets, spreadsheets, forecasts, performance reviews and even this lesson are maps. A company can hit every target on its dashboard while customers quietly leave. A GPS can direct you onto a flooded road. Related is 'Chesterton's fence', from writer G.K. Chesterton: before removing a rule or fence that seems pointless, find out why it was put there.

sections.key: Pick a few models, practise them on small decisions, and use them as questions, not answers.
sections.b: Mental models are tools, not formulas. They work best as questions you routinely ask. For a significant decision, try a quick checklist. First principles: what's actually true here? Inversion: what would guarantee a bad outcome? Second order: and then what? Margin of safety: what if I'm wrong? Circle of competence: do I really understand this? Map and territory: what is my information leaving out? Practise on low-stakes choices, like a phone plan or a weekend plan, so the questions become automatic for big ones. And remember Munger's point: no single model is enough. Use several, and notice where they disagree.

quiz.q: What does first-principles thinking involve?
o: Breaking a problem down to basic truths and reasoning up from them
Following the first idea that comes to mind
Asking an expert for the principle to apply
quiz.e: First principles means stripping away assumptions to what is fundamentally true, then rebuilding.

quiz.q: Inversion asks you to:
o: Do the opposite of what others do
Reverse your decision if it feels uncomfortable
Consider what would guarantee failure, then avoid it
Start a project from the end and work backwards in time
quiz.e: Inversion flips the question to 'how could this fail?' so you can avoid the obvious mistakes.

quiz.q: The 'cobra effect' is an example of neglecting:
quiz.e: A policy can trigger reactions that produce the opposite of what was intended.

quiz.q: Why do engineers and investors build in a 'margin of safety'?
o: To protect against errors and over-optimistic estimates
Because the law requires exactly double
quiz.e: A buffer protects you when your estimates turn out wrong, as they often do.

quiz.q: 'The map is not the territory' means:
o: Models and plans simplify reality and always leave things out
You should never rely on plans
quiz.e: Every model is a useful simplification; when it clashes with reality, trust reality.

LESSONS.title: Understanding risk
LESSONS.hook: People fear sharks and plane crashes, then drive home tired without a second thought. Our risk radar is badly calibrated, and it can be fixed.

sections.key: We judge risk by how vivid and emotional it feels, not by how likely it is.
sections.b: Humans didn't evolve to read statistics. We judge danger with fast, emotional shortcuts. Psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman described the 'availability heuristic': we rate things as more likely when examples spring easily to mind. A shark attack or plane crash gets saturation news coverage, so it feels common. Heart disease, falls at home and car crashes rarely make headlines because they happen every day, so they feel ordinary. Research by psychologist Paul Slovic and others found we also fear risks that feel uncontrollable, unfamiliar or imposed on us far more than those we choose, even when the numbers point the other way.

sections.key: Rare, dramatic events that kill many at once trigger outsized fear and can push people into riskier choices.
sections.b: A 'dread risk' is a rare event that kills many people at once, like a terrorist attack or plane crash. These trigger fear far beyond their statistical danger. Psychologist Gerd Gigerenzer studied what happened after the September 11 attacks in 2001. Many Americans avoided flying and drove instead. He estimated that the extra driving led to roughly 1,500 additional road deaths in the following year, more than the number of passengers killed on the four hijacked planes. The lesson is uncomfortable but important: fear of a vivid risk can lead us straight into a larger, quieter one.

sections.key: Per trip and per kilometre, commercial flying is far safer than driving.
sections.b: Australia's road toll has been roughly 1,100 to 1,300 deaths a year in recent years, plus tens of thousands of serious injuries. Deaths on Australian commercial airline flights, by contrast, are extremely rare; Qantas is famous for never having had a fatal jet accident. Globally, large commercial aviation has become dramatically safer over the decades, with fatal accidents now rare relative to the tens of millions of flights each year. Per kilometre travelled, flying on a major airline is many times safer than driving. The most dangerous part of many trips is the drive to the airport, especially if you're tired or rushing.

sections.key: 'Doubles your risk' can mean going from 1 in a million to 2 in a million; always ask for the absolute numbers.
sections.b: Headlines love relative risk: 'X doubles your risk of Y'. But doubling a tiny risk still leaves a tiny risk. In 1995, UK authorities warned that newer contraceptive pills doubled the risk of a type of blood clot. That sounded terrifying, but the absolute increase was roughly from 1 in 7,000 women to 2 in 7,000. Many women stopped taking the pill, and researchers later linked the scare to a rise in unplanned pregnancies and abortions, which carry their own risks. Whenever you hear 'increases risk by 50%', ask: 50% of what? How many people out of 1,000 or 10,000 are actually affected?

sections.key: The base rate is how common something is to begin with; ignoring it leads to wildly wrong conclusions.
sections.b: The base rate is how often something happens in the first place, and we routinely ignore it when a good story comes along. Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky described 'Steve': shy, tidy and helpful, with a need for order and a passion for detail. Is he more likely a librarian or a farmer? Most people say librarian, because he fits the stereotype. But in the United States there were more than 20 male farmers for every male librarian, so even a bookish-sounding man is far more likely to farm. The same trap catches us with a 'sure thing' share tip, a start-up that looks like the next big success, or a stranger who 'looks suspicious'. Before judging by how well something fits a story, ask how common it is to begin with.

sections.key: Common, familiar risks like driving, falls, drowning and inactivity cause far more harm than headline risks.
sections.b: Australia records a handful of fatal shark bites in a typical year, which is tragic but rare. Roughly 300 or more people drown in Australian waterways each year, according to Royal Life Saving, many in rivers, lakes and backyard pools rather than at patrolled beaches. Falls are a leading cause of injury death, especially for older Australians. And the biggest killers overall are slow and familiar: heart disease, dementia, cancers, and lifestyle factors like smoking and physical inactivity. None of this means ignoring rare dangers, but if you want to be safer, focus your worry and effort where the numbers are.

sections.key: Useful risk questions: how likely, how bad, compared with what, and can I reduce it?
sections.b: Good risk thinking asks four questions. How likely is it, in absolute terms? How bad would it be, and is it reversible? Compared with what, including the risks of the alternative? And can I cheaply reduce it? Some researchers use the 'micromort', a one-in-a-million chance of death, to compare activities on a single scale. Also watch for 'risk compensation', a debated idea that people sometimes take more risks when they feel safer, such as driving faster with better brakes. Evidence for it is mixed, but it's a reminder that safety gear works best when paired with good behaviour, not instead of it.

sections.key: Ask for absolute numbers, check base rates, compare alternatives, and focus on the big, common risks.
sections.b: Some habits that help. Translate percentages into natural frequencies: '3 in 1,000' is clearer than '0.3%'. Ask for absolute risk whenever you hear a relative figure. Compare every risk with the risk of the alternative, as with flying versus driving. Notice when a vivid story is doing the work that data should be doing. Put your effort into common, controllable risks: seatbelts, not driving tired, pool fences, sun protection, regular health checks. And accept that zero risk doesn't exist; every choice, including doing nothing, carries some. For medical decisions, ask your doctor to explain the numbers in plain terms.

quiz.q: The availability heuristic means we judge risks as more likely when:
quiz.e: Vivid, memorable examples make a risk feel more common than it is.

quiz.q: After 9/11, Gerd Gigerenzer estimated that extra driving by people avoiding planes led to:
o: Roughly 1,500 extra road deaths in the following year
A fall in airline ticket prices only
quiz.e: Fear of a dread risk pushed people into a larger, quieter one.

quiz.q: What followed the 1995 UK warning that newer contraceptive pills 'doubled' a clot risk?
o: Many women stopped the pill, and unplanned pregnancies and abortions rose
quiz.e: The absolute risk rose only from about 1 in 7,000 to 2 in 7,000, but the scary relative figure changed behaviour.

quiz.q: In Kahneman and Tversky's 'Steve' example, why is a shy, tidy man more likely to be a farmer than a librarian?
o: There are far more male farmers than male librarians, so the base rate outweighs the stereotype
Surveys show shy people prefer farming
quiz.e: How well someone fits a stereotype shouldn't override how common each group is.

quiz.q: Per kilometre travelled, flying on a major airline compared with driving is:
quiz.e: Commercial aviation is far safer than road travel per kilometre.

LESSONS.title: Game theory for everyday life
LESSONS.hook: Why rivals end up in price wars, why cooperation survives among strangers, and what a 1950s puzzle reveals about neighbours, workmates and nations.

sections.key: Game theory studies strategic situations, where your best move depends on what others do.
sections.b: Game theory is the study of strategic decisions: situations where the outcome for you depends not only on your own choice but also on the choices of others. The 'games' can be anything from chess and poker to business competition, wage negotiations, elections and arms races. Modern game theory was launched by mathematician John von Neumann and economist Oskar Morgenstern in their 1944 book 'Theory of Games and Economic Behavior'. It's now used across economics, politics, biology and computer science. You don't need the maths to benefit. The core habit is simple: before acting, think about how others will respond, and they're doing the same.

sections.key: In the prisoner's dilemma, each player's self-interest leads both to a worse result than cooperating would.
sections.b: The most famous game was developed at the RAND Corporation around 1950 and given its prison story by mathematician Albert Tucker. Two suspects are questioned separately. If both stay silent, each gets one year. If one betrays the other, the betrayer walks free and the silent one gets ten years. If both betray, each gets five. Whatever your partner does, betraying looks better for you. So two rational players both betray and get five years each, when silence would have given them one. The dilemma captures a painful truth: individually sensible choices can add up to a collectively bad outcome.

sections.key: A Nash equilibrium is a situation where no player can do better by changing only their own choice.
sections.b: Mathematician John Nash, whose life was portrayed in the film 'A Beautiful Mind', described a key idea in 1950. A Nash equilibrium is a set of choices where no player can improve their result by changing their own choice alone, given what the others are doing. In the prisoner's dilemma, both betraying is the equilibrium, even though it's worse for both. Nash shared the 1994 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for this work. The concept explains why bad situations can be stable: everyone may want change, but no one gains by moving first on their own.

sections.key: Price wars, doping in sport and overwork cultures often have the structure of a prisoner's dilemma.
sections.b: Once you recognise the pattern, you see it everywhere. Two petrol stations on the same corner would both profit if prices stayed high, but each is tempted to undercut, and they can slide into a price war. In sport, athletes may feel pressure to dope because they fear rivals are doing so. In workplaces, if everyone stays back late to look committed, no one gains an edge, yet everyone loses their evenings. Nations face the same logic in arms races. Seeing the structure matters, because it shows the problem often isn't bad people. It's a bad set of incentives.

sections.key: In repeated games, the simple strategy of cooperating first then copying the other player often does very well.
sections.b: Real life is rarely a one-off. Around 1980, political scientist Robert Axelrod ran computer tournaments where strategies played the prisoner's dilemma against each other many times. The winner was the simplest entry, 'tit-for-tat', submitted by Anatol Rapoport: cooperate on the first move, then copy whatever the other player did last time. Axelrod concluded that successful strategies were nice (never betray first), retaliatory (respond to betrayal), forgiving (return to cooperation quickly) and clear (easy to read). Later research found that slightly more forgiving variants can do better when mistakes happen. Repetition and reputation make cooperation rational.

sections.key: When a shared resource is open to all, individual overuse can destroy it, unless people build rules to manage it.
sections.b: In 1968, ecologist Garrett Hardin popularised the 'tragedy of the commons'. Imagine a pasture open to all herders. Each gains by adding one more cow, while the cost of overgrazing is shared by everyone, so the pasture is eventually ruined. Overfishing, traffic congestion and pollution follow similar logic. But political economist Elinor Ostrom, who in 2009 became the first woman to win the economics Nobel, showed that communities around the world often manage shared resources successfully for centuries, using local rules, monitoring and fair penalties. The tragedy is a risk, not a certainty.

sections.key: Some games are about coordinating on the same choice; credible commitments can change how others act.
sections.b: Not every game is a conflict. In coordination games, everyone wins if they choose the same option. Which side of the road to drive on doesn't matter much, as long as everyone agrees; Australians drive on the left and it works. Economist Thomas Schelling, a 2005 Nobel laureate, showed how people often coordinate on obvious 'focal points' without talking. He also studied credible commitment: limiting your own options can strengthen your position. A union that publicly commits to a strike, or a seller with a firm 'no discounts' policy, changes what others expect. A threat only works if people believe you'll follow through.

sections.key: Think about others' incentives, play the long game, build reputation, and look for ways to change the rules.
sections.b: A few practical lessons. First, map the incentives: what does each person gain or lose from each choice? Second, remember that most relationships, at work, with neighbours or with a co-parent, are repeated games, so reputation and trust are worth more than a one-off win. Start cooperative, respond firmly to bad behaviour, and forgive quickly. Third, when you're stuck in a dilemma, look for ways to change the game itself: agreements, contracts, shared rules or clear communication. Fourth, look for positive-sum options, where both sides can gain. Many negotiations are less about splitting a pie than making it bigger.

quiz.q: In the prisoner's dilemma, what happens when both players act in narrow self-interest?
o: Both end up worse off than if they had cooperated
quiz.e: Betrayal is individually tempting, but mutual betrayal leaves both worse off.

quiz.q: A Nash equilibrium is a situation where:
o: Everyone gets the best possible outcome
No player can do better by changing only their own choice
The game ends in a draw
quiz.e: An equilibrium can be stable even when it's bad for everyone.

quiz.q: Which strategy won Robert Axelrod's famous computer tournaments?
quiz.e: Cooperating first, then copying the other player, proved simple and very effective.

quiz.q: Elinor Ostrom's research on shared resources showed that:
o: Communities can often manage commons successfully with local rules
The tragedy of the commons is inevitable
Governments must control all shared resources
quiz.e: Ostrom found many long-lasting examples of communities governing commons well.

quiz.q: Deciding which side of the road to drive on is an example of:
quiz.e: Everyone wins as long as everyone chooses the same option.

LESSONS.title: Insurance without the confusion
LESSONS.hook: Most of us pay for insurance for years without reading a word of the policy. Here's how it actually works, and how to avoid a nasty surprise at claim time.

sections.key: Insurance pools many people's premiums to pay the large losses of the few.
sections.b: Insurance is a way of sharing risk. Thousands of people each pay a relatively small, predictable amount, the premium, into a pool. In any year, only a few of them suffer a big loss, like a house fire or serious car crash, and the pool pays for it. Insurers use statistics on how often losses happen to set premiums, and add their costs and profit on top. That means, on average, customers pay more in premiums than they get back. That's fine: you're not buying an investment, you're buying protection from a loss you couldn't comfortably afford to cover yourself.

sections.key: Insure against losses that would seriously hurt you; consider self-insuring small ones.
sections.b: The golden rule: insure the things you can't afford to lose, not the things you can. Losing your house, your income for a year, or being liable for injuring someone could wreck your finances, so insurance makes sense. Replacing a cheap phone, by contrast, is annoying but affordable, and extended warranties or small-item covers are often poor value. Australian Consumer Law already gives you rights to a repair, replacement or refund when products have a major fault, whether or not you buy an extended warranty. An emergency fund lets you 'self-insure' small losses, and lets you choose cheaper policies with higher excesses.

sections.key: Medicare covers public hospital care; private hospital cover adds choice, and the Lifetime Health Cover loading rewards joining by 31.
sections.b: Medicare gives Australians free treatment as a public patient in public hospitals. Private health insurance comes as hospital cover, which lets you be a private patient and choose your doctor, and extras cover for things like dental and physio. Since 2019, hospital policies are grouped into Gold, Silver, Bronze and Basic tiers to make comparison easier. Two government rules matter. The Medicare Levy Surcharge adds tax for higher earners without appropriate hospital cover. And the Lifetime Health Cover loading adds 2% to your premium for each year you're over 30 when you first take out hospital cover, up to 70%, removed after ten continuous years.

sections.key: Building, contents and car covers protect big assets; CTP covers injuries to people, not damage to cars.
sections.b: Home building insurance covers the structure; contents insurance covers your belongings, and renters usually need only contents. Check whether flood, storm and bushfire are covered, as these matter hugely in Australia. For cars, Compulsory Third Party (CTP) insurance, generally tied to your registration, covers injuries you cause to other people, but not damage to cars or property. Third-party property cover pays for damage you do to other people's cars and property. Adding fire and theft covers your own car for those events. Comprehensive cover also pays for damage to your own car. Crashing into a luxury car without property cover can be very costly.

sections.key: Life, TPD, trauma and income protection insurance protect your family and your ability to earn.
sections.b: Your ability to earn an income is often your biggest financial asset. Income protection insurance typically pays a monthly benefit, commonly up to around 70% of your income, if illness or injury stops you working, after a waiting period. Life insurance pays a lump sum to your beneficiaries if you die. Total and Permanent Disability (TPD) cover pays if you can never work again, and trauma cover pays on diagnosis of specified serious illnesses. Many Australians have some of these through their super fund by default, which is convenient and can be cheaper, but premiums reduce your balance, so check what you have and whether it suits you.

sections.key: The excess is what you pay towards a claim; a higher excess usually means a lower premium.
sections.b: The excess is the amount you pay out of your own pocket when you make a claim. If your car repair costs $4,000 and your excess is $800, the insurer pays $3,200. Choosing a higher excess usually lowers your premium, which can make sense if you have savings to cover it and rarely claim. Some policies have different excesses for different situations, such as young or unlisted drivers. Premiums also depend on your address, claims history and what's being insured. Don't just auto-renew; premiums often rise each year, so compare at renewal and ask your current insurer for a better price.

sections.key: The PDS explains what's covered and excluded; check exclusions, limits and definitions before you need to claim.
sections.b: Every policy comes with a Product Disclosure Statement (PDS), and home insurance also has a shorter Key Facts Sheet. Yes, they're long, but a few minutes on the right sections can save thousands. Look at what's covered, what's excluded, and the limits, such as caps on jewellery or laptops in contents cover. Check key definitions, like what counts as 'flood' or 'accidental damage'. When applying, answer questions honestly and carefully, because misleading information can reduce or void a claim. If a claim goes badly and the insurer's internal complaint process doesn't fix it, the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA) offers a free dispute service.

sections.key: Many people are underinsured; check sums insured and update them as costs and circumstances change.
sections.b: Being underinsured means your cover isn't enough to replace what you lose. After major bushfires and floods, many Australian households have discovered their sum insured couldn't cover a rebuild, because building costs had risen, or demolition, debris removal and upgrades to current building codes weren't factored in. Use a building cost calculator rather than guessing, and review your cover every year. Do a room-by-room tally for contents; most people underestimate. Revisit life and income cover when you have children, buy a home or change jobs. This is general information only; for advice on your situation, talk to a licensed financial adviser or insurance broker.

quiz.q: Insurance works mainly by:
o: Investing your premiums for a high return
Pooling many premiums to pay the losses of the few
Guaranteeing you get your money back
quiz.e: Many people pay premiums so the unlucky few can be paid for large losses.

quiz.q: The Lifetime Health Cover loading adds what to hospital premiums?
o: 2% for each year over 30 when you first take out cover
quiz.e: The loading is 2% per year over 30, capped at 70%, and removed after ten continuous years.

quiz.q: What does Compulsory Third Party (CTP) insurance cover?
o: Injuries you cause to other people
quiz.e: CTP covers injuries to people, not damage to vehicles or property.

quiz.q: Choosing a higher excess usually:
quiz.e: Taking on more of each claim yourself generally reduces what you pay the insurer.

quiz.q: Being underinsured means:
o: Your cover isn't enough to replace what you lose
quiz.e: Rising rebuild costs and extra expenses often leave people short when disaster strikes.

LESSONS.title: Planning for retirement in Australia
LESSONS.hook: Retirement could last 25 years or more. How super, the Age Pension and your own savings fit together, and how to work out what 'enough' looks like.

sections.key: Many Australians will spend 20 to 30 years in retirement, so planning early matters.
sections.b: Australians are living longer than ever. A 65-year-old today can expect, on average, to live roughly another 20 years or more, and many will reach their 90s. That means retirement may last a quarter or even a third of your adult life. Planning for it early gives compound growth decades to work, and gives you choices later, like when to stop work and whether to wind down gradually. Australia's retirement system rests on three pillars: compulsory superannuation paid by employers, the means-tested Age Pension as a safety net, and voluntary savings, including your home, extra super contributions and other investments.

sections.key: Recently retired Australians stopped work at about 64 on average, but many leave earlier than planned, often because of health.
sections.b: When to stop work is one of the biggest retirement choices, and it doesn't always go to plan. In its 2024–25 survey, the Australian Bureau of Statistics found that recent retirees stopped at an average age of about 64, while workers aged 45 and over planned to retire at around 65 or 66. The most common reason retirees gave for leaving their last job was reaching retirement age or qualifying for super, but their own illness, injury or disability came second, and those who retired for health reasons stopped at about 57 on average. So build a buffer for finishing earlier than you expect. Many people now ease out gradually, cutting back hours rather than stopping all at once.

sections.key: At retirement, super can be taken as a lump sum or an account-based pension; withdrawals are generally tax-free from 60.
sections.b: When you retire, you can take super as a lump sum, turn it into a regular income, or combine both. A common choice is an account-based pension: your money stays invested, and you draw regular payments, with a minimum percentage you must withdraw each year that rises with age. For most people, payments from a taxed super fund are tax-free from age 60, and investment earnings inside a retirement pension account are generally untaxed too, within limits. Some people also buy an annuity or lifetime income product, which trades flexibility for guaranteed payments. The right mix depends on your health, needs and other income.

sections.key: The Age Pension is a means-tested government payment, currently available from age 67, for those who meet residency rules.
sections.b: The Age Pension is a government payment for older Australians, paid through Services Australia. Pension age rose gradually and has been 67 since July 2023. You generally need to have been an Australian resident for at least ten years. It's not based on how much tax you paid. Instead, it's means-tested, so the amount depends on your income and assets. Around 60% of Australians of pension age receive a full or part pension, according to government figures, often alongside their super. Rates and thresholds are adjusted regularly, usually in March, July and September, so check Services Australia's website for current figures rather than relying on old articles.

sections.key: The pension applies both an income test and an assets test, and pays whichever gives the lower amount.
sections.b: Services Australia applies two tests. The income test looks at earnings, including 'deemed' income from financial assets: rather than tracking actual returns on your savings, shares and account-based pensions, it assumes they earn a set rate. The assets test counts things like investments, super in retirement phase, cars, caravans and investment property. Your family home is exempt, which is why non-homeowners are allowed higher asset thresholds. Whichever test produces the lower pension is the one that applies. Couples are assessed together. Even a small part pension can be valuable, because it usually brings a Pensioner Concession Card with cheaper medicines and other discounts.

sections.key: ASFA's Retirement Standard sets 'modest' and 'comfortable' budgets; your own spending plan matters more.
sections.b: The most quoted benchmark is the ASFA Retirement Standard, from the Association of Superannuation Funds of Australia. It estimates yearly budgets for a 'modest' and a 'comfortable' lifestyle for singles and couples, and the super balance needed at retirement to fund them, assuming you own your home and receive a part Age Pension. The figures are updated regularly, so look up the current edition. Treat them as a starting point, not a verdict. Renters generally need considerably more, because rent is a big ongoing cost. The best estimate is your own: sketch what you expect to spend in retirement, including travel, health and home repairs.

sections.key: Many retirees spend too cautiously, and super funds must now have a strategy to help members turn savings into income.
sections.b: Saving is only half the job; spending well is the other half. The federal government's Retirement Income Review, published in 2020, found that many retirees draw only the legal minimum from their super and die with most of the wealth they retired with still intact, often having lived more frugally than they needed to. Fear of running out is understandable, but it can mean missing travel and comforts while you're healthy enough to enjoy them. Spending also tends to be highest in the active early years and eases later, though health and aged care costs can rise near the end. Since July 2022, super funds have had to have a retirement income strategy for their members, so ask yours what help it offers.

sections.key: Check your balance, use a retirement calculator, and get licensed advice for big decisions.
sections.b: A few practical steps. Log in to your super fund and check your balance, fees, investment option and insurance. Use Moneysmart's free retirement planner to project your income from super and the Age Pension. If you're getting close, Services Australia's Financial Information Service offers free general education about retirement and payments. Think about the non-financial side too: purpose, health, social connection and how you'll spend your time. Rules change regularly, so check official sources for current settings. This lesson is general information only, not personal financial advice. For decisions about your own situation, talk to a licensed financial adviser.

quiz.q: According to ABS data for 2024–25, at roughly what age did recently retired Australians stop work, on average?
quiz.e: Recent retirees averaged about 64, though health problems push many people out earlier than they planned.

quiz.q: The Age Pension age in Australia has been 67 since:
quiz.e: Pension age rose gradually from 65 and reached 67 in July 2023.

quiz.q: How is the Age Pension means-tested?
o: Only on the value of your home
On how much tax you paid while working
An income test and assets test are applied, and the lower result is paid
quiz.e: Both tests are applied, and whichever gives the lower pension is used.

quiz.q: What does the ASFA Retirement Standard provide?
o: The maximum pension you can receive
quiz.e: ASFA estimates yearly budgets and the lump sums needed to fund them.

quiz.q: For most people, payments from a taxed super fund from age 60 are:
quiz.e: Super income from a taxed fund is generally tax-free from 60.

LESSONS.title: Inside the Earth
LESSONS.hook: Nobody has ever drilled even halfway through the crust, yet we know the Earth has a solid metal heart as hot as the surface of the Sun. Here's how.

sections.key: Earth is layered like a peach: a thin crust, a thick rocky mantle and a metal core.
sections.b: The Earth has a radius of about 6,371 kilometres, and it is built in layers. On the outside is the crust, a thin rocky skin. Below that is the mantle, a vast layer of hot rock that makes up roughly 84% of the planet's volume. At the centre is the core, made mostly of iron and nickel, split into a liquid outer core and a solid inner core. A useful picture is a peach: the skin is the crust, the flesh is the mantle and the stone is the core. The layers formed early in Earth's history, when heavy metals sank towards the centre and lighter rock floated to the top.

sections.key: Oceanic crust is thin and dense; continental crust is thicker, lighter and much older.
sections.b: There are two kinds of crust. Oceanic crust, under the sea floor, is usually only 5 to 10 kilometres thick and made of dense, dark basalt. It is constantly created at mid-ocean ridges and destroyed where it sinks back into the mantle, so almost none of it is older than about 200 million years. Continental crust is thicker, typically 30 to 50 kilometres and up to about 70 kilometres under big mountain ranges like the Himalayas. It is lighter, so it floats higher and rarely sinks. That is why continents hold the oldest rocks on Earth, including zircon crystals from the Jack Hills in Western Australia dated to about 4.4 billion years old.

sections.key: The mantle is solid rock that flows very slowly, carrying heat up from the core.
sections.b: The mantle reaches down to about 2,900 kilometres. It is often drawn as a sea of molten lava, but it is almost entirely solid. Under enormous heat and pressure, though, this solid rock can creep and flow very slowly, a few centimetres a year, rather like a glacier or very stiff toffee. Hotter rock rises and cooler rock sinks in slow convection currents that carry heat out of the planet. The top of the mantle and the crust together form the rigid lithosphere, which is broken into tectonic plates. These plates ride on a softer layer beneath, called the asthenosphere, and the mantle's motion helps drive them.

sections.key: The outer core is liquid iron and nickel; the inner core is solid, at around 5,000 to 6,000 degrees.
sections.b: The core begins about 2,900 kilometres down. The outer core, roughly 2,200 kilometres thick, is liquid metal, mostly iron with some nickel and lighter elements. The inner core is a solid ball about 1,220 kilometres in radius, roughly two-thirds the size of the Moon. Its temperature is estimated at around 5,000 to 6,000 degrees Celsius, similar to the surface of the Sun. It stays solid despite that heat because the pressure at the centre, millions of times the air pressure at the surface, squeezes the atoms together. The inner core is slowly growing as the planet cools and the liquid metal around it freezes onto it.

sections.key: Earthquake waves bend, speed up and vanish as they pass through different layers, revealing the interior.
sections.b: The deepest hole ever drilled, the Kola Superdeep Borehole in Russia, stopped at about 12 kilometres, a tiny scratch. Almost everything we know about the deep Earth comes from earthquakes. Quakes send seismic waves through the planet. P-waves are push-pull waves that travel through solids and liquids. S-waves are side-to-side waves that cannot pass through liquid. Seismometers around the world record when and where each type arrives. Waves speed up, slow down and bend at boundaries between layers. In 1909 Andrija Mohorovičić found the base of the crust, now called the Moho, and in the early 1900s others located the core and measured its depth.

sections.h: The shadow zone and Inge Lehmann
sections.key: S-waves never cross the core, proving it is liquid; Inge Lehmann discovered the solid inner core in 1936.
sections.b: After a large earthquake, there is a broad region on the far side of the planet where S-waves never arrive, called the shadow zone. Since S-waves cannot travel through liquid, this showed that the outer core must be molten. But faint P-waves were turning up in places that a simple liquid core could not explain. In 1936 Danish seismologist Inge Lehmann studied these puzzling signals and proposed that a solid inner core was reflecting them. Her idea was confirmed as instruments improved. Other clues fit too: Earth's average density is about 5.5 times that of water, far denser than surface rocks, so heavy metal must lie deep inside.

sections.key: Churning liquid iron in the outer core generates Earth's magnetic field, which shields us from the solar wind.
sections.b: The swirling liquid iron in the outer core acts like a giant dynamo. As the electrically conducting metal moves, driven by heat and Earth's rotation, it generates electric currents, which in turn produce a magnetic field. This field is why a compass points roughly north. It also extends far into space, deflecting most of the solar wind, a stream of charged particles from the Sun, so most of it never reaches the lower atmosphere. Some particles are funnelled towards the poles, where they make the upper atmosphere glow. In the south this is the aurora australis, sometimes visible from Tasmania and southern Victoria.

sections.key: The magnetic poles drift constantly, and the whole field has reversed many times; the last full flip was about 780,000 years ago.
sections.b: Earth's magnetic field is not fixed. The magnetic poles wander, and the north magnetic pole has moved hundreds of kilometres over the past century, which is why navigation charts and phone compasses need regular updates. Over geological time, the whole field has flipped many times, so a compass would once have pointed south. We know because volcanic rock records the field's direction as it cools. The last full reversal happened about 780,000 years ago. Reversals are irregular and take thousands of years, and there is no good evidence they caused mass extinctions. Next time you use a compass, remember that it is responding to molten metal nearly 3,000 kilometres beneath your feet.

quiz.q: Why does the inner core stay solid despite temperatures similar to the Sun's surface?
o: Immense pressure squeezes the atoms together
It is made of rock, not metal
It is cooled by the oceans
quiz.e: The pressure at the centre is so great that the iron stays solid even at around 5,000 to 6,000 degrees.

quiz.q: What showed scientists that Earth's outer core is liquid?
o: S-waves cannot pass through it, creating a shadow zone
quiz.e: S-waves cannot travel through liquid, so the S-wave shadow zone revealed a molten outer core.

quiz.q: Why do continents hold the oldest rocks on Earth?
o: Continental crust is lighter, so it rarely sinks back into the mantle
quiz.e: Oceanic crust is recycled within about 200 million years, but buoyant continental crust survives for billions of years.

quiz.q: What generates Earth's magnetic field?
o: The solid inner core acting as a bar magnet
The solar wind hitting the atmosphere
Moving liquid iron in the outer core
quiz.e: The churning, electrically conducting liquid iron of the outer core works like a dynamo.

quiz.q: Which best describes the mantle?
o: Solid rock that flows very slowly
quiz.e: The mantle is almost entirely solid, but under heat and pressure it creeps a few centimetres a year.

LESSONS.title: Volcanoes, earthquakes and tsunamis
LESSONS.hook: Australia feels rock-solid, yet in 1989 an earthquake killed 13 people in Newcastle. Here's what makes the ground shake and mountains explode.

sections.key: Runny magma makes gentle, flowing eruptions; thick, gassy magma makes explosive ones.
sections.b: Whether a volcano oozes or explodes depends mostly on its magma. Runny, low-silica basalt lets gas escape easily, so it tends to pour out as lava flows that build broad, gently sloping shield volcanoes, like those of Hawaii. Thicker, silica-rich magma traps gas like a shaken soft drink, until the pressure blasts it apart into ash and rock. That builds the steep, layered cones called stratovolcanoes, such as Mount Fuji and Indonesia's many peaks. Australia has volcanoes too. The Newer Volcanics Province of western Victoria and south-east South Australia includes Mount Gambier, whose crater holds the Blue Lake. It last erupted roughly 5,000 to 6,000 years ago and is thought to be dormant rather than extinct.

sections.key: The Ring of Fire around the Pacific hosts most of the world's active volcanoes and big earthquakes.
sections.b: The Pacific Ocean is ringed by a horseshoe of subduction zones about 40,000 kilometres long, running from New Zealand up through Indonesia, the Philippines and Japan, across to Alaska, and down the Americas to Chile. This is the Ring of Fire. It contains roughly three-quarters of the world's active volcanoes and produces most of its earthquakes, including nearly all of the very largest. Our near neighbours sit right on it: Indonesia has more active volcanoes than any other country, and New Zealand, Papua New Guinea and Vanuatu all experience frequent earthquakes and eruptions. Australia, by contrast, sits near the middle of its plate, far from the edges.

sections.key: Each whole step on the magnitude scale means about 32 times more energy.
sections.b: In 1935 seismologist Charles Richter created a scale to compare earthquakes in California. Today scientists mainly use the moment magnitude scale, which works better for very large quakes, though news reports often still say 'Richter'. The scale is logarithmic: each whole number up means about ten times more ground shaking and roughly 32 times more energy released. So a magnitude 7 releases about 1,000 times the energy of a magnitude 5. Magnitude measures the size of the quake itself. Intensity is different: it describes how strongly shaking was felt in a particular place, which depends on distance, depth and local soil. A moderate quake directly under a city can do more damage than a huge one far offshore.

sections.key: Tambora in 1815 caused a 'year without a summer'; Krakatoa in 1883 was heard thousands of kilometres away.
sections.b: In 79 AD Mount Vesuvius buried the Roman towns of Pompeii and Herculaneum under ash and scorching gas flows, preserving a snapshot of daily life. In 1815 Mount Tambora in Indonesia produced the largest eruption in recorded history. Its ash and sulfur haze cooled global climate, and 1816 became known in Europe and North America as the 'year without a summer', with crop failures and famine. In 1883 Krakatoa, between Java and Sumatra, exploded with a sound heard across the Indian Ocean, including in parts of Western Australia. Its tsunamis killed tens of thousands of people, and fine dust in the upper atmosphere produced vivid red sunsets around the world.

sections.key: The largest earthquake recorded was magnitude 9.5 in Chile in 1960.
sections.b: The most powerful earthquake ever recorded struck Chile in 1960, at magnitude 9.5. The 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake off Sumatra, about magnitude 9.1, generated tsunamis that killed roughly 230,000 people in 14 countries, making it one of the deadliest natural disasters in modern history. In 2011 a magnitude 9.0 to 9.1 earthquake off north-east Japan triggered a tsunami that killed around 18,000 people and caused the Fukushima nuclear accident. All three struck at subduction zones, where huge areas of plate can lock together for centuries and then slip all at once. Despite decades of research, scientists still cannot predict the exact time and place of an earthquake, only estimate the long-term risk.

sections.key: Australia's largest quakes struck the sparsely populated interior; the smaller 1989 Newcastle quake was deadlier because it hit a city.
sections.b: Australia is not immune. Stress transmitted through the plate still cracks its interior. On 14 October 1968, a quake of about magnitude 6.5 wrecked much of the Wheatbelt town of Meckering in Western Australia and ripped open a fault scarp tens of kilometres long. On 22 January 1988, three quakes, the largest about magnitude 6.6, struck near Tennant Creek in the Northern Territory within 12 hours, the biggest recorded on the mainland. Because both hit sparsely populated areas, no one died. The magnitude 5.6 Newcastle quake of 28 December 1989 was far smaller, yet it killed 13 people, nine of them in the collapse of the Newcastle Workers Club, because it struck a city partly built on soft ground. It led to tougher building standards.

sections.key: Tsunamis are fast, long waves set off when the sea floor moves; they grow as they reach shallow water.
sections.b: A tsunami is usually caused when an undersea earthquake suddenly lifts or drops the sea floor, moving the entire column of water above it. Landslides and volcanic eruptions can also cause them. In the deep ocean a tsunami can travel at around 800 kilometres an hour, as fast as a jet, yet be less than a metre high, so ships barely notice it. As it reaches shallow water it slows and piles up, sometimes into a wall of water many metres high. Unlike a normal wave, it can keep surging inland for many minutes. Often the first sign is the sea dramatically drawing back from the shore, exposing the sea floor.

sections.key: If you feel strong shaking: drop, cover and hold on. Near the coast, get to high ground if the sea suddenly retreats.
sections.b: In an earthquake, the standard advice is to drop to the ground, take cover under a sturdy table and hold on until the shaking stops. Most injuries come from falling objects and debris, not the ground itself, so stay away from windows and don't run outside past falling masonry. Near the coast, a strong or long earthquake, or the sea suddenly retreating, is a natural warning to move to high ground straight away without waiting for an official alert. Australia's Joint Australian Tsunami Warning Centre, run by the Bureau of Meteorology and Geoscience Australia, monitors the region around the clock. When travelling in Bali, Japan or New Zealand, check local warning signs and evacuation routes.

quiz.q: Roughly how much more energy does a magnitude 7 earthquake release than a magnitude 6?
quiz.e: Each whole step on the magnitude scale means roughly 32 times more energy.

quiz.q: Roughly how long is the Pacific Ring of Fire?
quiz.e: The horseshoe of subduction zones runs about 40,000 kilometres around the Pacific.

quiz.q: Why did the 1989 Newcastle quake kill 13 people when larger Australian quakes at Meckering and Tennant Creek killed no one?
o: It struck close to a city
quiz.e: Meckering and Tennant Creek hit sparsely populated areas; Newcastle hit a city partly built on soft ground.

quiz.q: Why do ships in the deep ocean barely notice a passing tsunami?
o: Tsunamis only form near the coast
In deep water it is less than a metre high, though very fast
Tsunamis are too slow to feel
quiz.e: In deep water a tsunami is fast but low, only growing tall when it slows in shallow water.

quiz.q: Which eruption led to the 'year without a summer' in 1816?
quiz.e: Tambora's 1815 eruption, the largest in recorded history, cooled the global climate the following year.

LESSONS.title: How weather works
LESSONS.hook: Every forecast you check is the result of sunlight, spinning air and some of the most powerful computers on the planet.

sections.key: Weather is driven by the Sun heating the Earth unevenly, and the atmosphere moving heat around.
sections.b: All weather begins with sunlight. The Sun heats the tropics far more strongly than the poles, because near the equator its rays hit the ground almost head-on, while at high latitudes the same energy is spread over a larger area. Land also heats and cools faster than water. The atmosphere and oceans are constantly trying to even out these differences, moving warm air towards the poles and cold air towards the equator. That restless movement of air, heat and moisture is what we call weather. Weather is the day-to-day state of the atmosphere; climate is the long-term average, usually measured over 30 years or more.

sections.key: High pressure usually brings settled, dry weather; low pressure brings cloud, wind and rain.
sections.b: Air has weight. At sea level it presses down with an average pressure of about 1013 hectopascals, the unit you see on weather maps. Where air is sinking, pressure rises, forming a high. Sinking air warms and dries, so highs usually bring clear skies, light winds and, in winter, cold frosty nights. Where air is rising, pressure falls, forming a low. Rising air cools, its moisture condenses into cloud, and lows bring wind and rain. Air flows from high to low pressure, but Earth's spin deflects it. In the Southern Hemisphere, winds circle anticlockwise around highs and clockwise around lows, the reverse of the north.

sections.key: A front is the boundary between air masses; cold fronts bring the southern 'cool change'.
sections.b: Large bodies of air, called air masses, take on the temperature and moisture of where they formed, such as the hot interior of Australia or the cold Southern Ocean. The boundary between two air masses is a front. In southern Australia, cold fronts sweep in from the west every few days, especially in winter. They are marked on weather maps as lines with triangles. Ahead of a front, hot, dry northerly winds can blow, raising fire danger in summer. When the front passes, the wind swings to the south-west, the temperature can drop ten degrees or more within an hour, and showers often follow. Melburnians know this well as the 'cool change'.

sections.key: Clouds form when rising air cools and its water vapour condenses onto tiny particles.
sections.b: Air always contains invisible water vapour. When air rises, it expands and cools, and cool air can hold less vapour. Eventually the vapour condenses into tiny droplets or ice crystals, each forming around a speck of dust, salt or smoke. Billions of these make a cloud. Air can be forced to rise by heating from the ground, by mountains, or by fronts. The main cloud families are named in Latin: cumulus (heap), puffy fair-weather clouds; stratus (layer), flat grey sheets; and cirrus (curl of hair), wispy high ice clouds. Cumulonimbus are towering storm clouds that can reach over 12 kilometres high and bring lightning, hail and heavy rain.

sections.key: Cloud droplets must grow roughly a million times in volume to fall as raindrops.
sections.b: Cloud droplets are so small that rising air easily holds them up. To fall as rain, they must grow enormously; a typical raindrop contains the water of around a million cloud droplets. In warm clouds, droplets collide and merge as they are tossed around. In colder clouds, ice crystals grow at the expense of nearby supercooled water droplets, then fall and melt into rain on the way down. Hail forms when strong updrafts in thunderstorms carry ice up and down repeatedly, adding layers like an onion. Despite cartoons, raindrops are not teardrop-shaped; small ones are nearly round, and larger ones flatten into something like a hamburger bun as they fall.

sections.key: Modern forecasts come from supercomputers solving the physics of the atmosphere, fed by millions of observations.
sections.b: Modern forecasting is called numerical weather prediction. Observations from weather stations, balloons, ships, aircraft, radar and satellites, including Japan's Himawari satellites that watch our region, are fed into supercomputers. These divide the atmosphere into a three-dimensional grid and use the laws of physics to calculate how it will change, step by step. Because tiny errors grow over time, forecasters run the model many times with slightly different starting conditions, called an ensemble, to estimate the range of possibilities. Forecasts have improved steadily, by roughly a day of useful accuracy per decade. Even so, the chaotic nature of the atmosphere means detailed forecasts beyond about 10 days remain unreliable.

sections.key: Tropical cyclones form over seas warmer than about 26.5°C and, in the Southern Hemisphere, spin clockwise.
sections.b: Tropical cyclones, called hurricanes or typhoons elsewhere, form over tropical oceans where the water is warmer than about 26.5 degrees Celsius. Warm, moist air rises, its vapour condenses and releases heat, and that heat powers a spiralling storm that can be hundreds of kilometres across. Like other lows in the Southern Hemisphere, they spin clockwise. Australia's cyclone season runs from November to April, with around ten forming in our region in a typical season. The Bureau of Meteorology rates them from category 1 to 5; a category 5 brings gusts above 280 kilometres an hour. Storm surge and flooding rain often do more harm than wind. Cyclone Tracy flattened much of Darwin on Christmas Day 1974, leading to far stronger building codes across the north.

sections.key: A 70% chance of rain means a 70% chance of at least 0.2 millimetres falling at that location.
sections.b: A few tips make forecasts more useful. In BOM forecasts, 'chance of rain' means the chance of at least 0.2 millimetres falling at that location during the period, not the share of the area or the day that will be wet. Check the expected rainfall amounts too: a 90% chance of 1 millimetre is very different from a 40% chance of 30 millimetres. Watch for fronts and wind changes on the synoptic chart if you're planning outdoor activities, especially on hot, windy days when fire danger is high. For severe weather, rely on official warnings from the BOM and your state emergency services, and check the radar before heading out.

quiz.q: What kind of weather does a high-pressure system usually bring?
o: Settled, dry weather with light winds
quiz.e: Sinking air in a high warms and dries, so highs usually bring clear, settled weather.

quiz.q: What typically happens when a cold front passes through southern Australia in summer?
o: The wind swings north and temperatures rise
The wind swings south-west and temperatures drop sharply
Humidity stays the same and skies clear
quiz.e: After a cold front, winds turn south-westerly and temperatures can fall ten degrees or more: the 'cool change'.

quiz.q: Roughly how warm must the sea be for a tropical cyclone to form?
quiz.e: Warm seas supply the heat and moisture that power the storm.

quiz.q: In a BOM forecast, what does a 70% chance of rain mean?
o: It will rain on 70% of the area
It will rain for 70% of the day
A 70% chance of at least 0.2 mm at that location
quiz.e: BOM's chance of rain is the probability of at least 0.2 millimetres falling at the location.

quiz.q: What is the main reason clouds form?
o: Rising air cools and its water vapour condenses
The Sun heats water droplets in the sky
quiz.e: As air rises it cools, and its vapour condenses onto tiny particles to form cloud droplets.

LESSONS.title: Ice ages
LESSONS.hook: Twenty thousand years ago you could have walked from Melbourne to Hobart, and on to New Guinea. The reason lies in a slow wobble in Earth's orbit.

sections.h: We're still in an ice age
sections.key: Technically we live in an ice age, in a warm interglacial period that began about 11,700 years ago.
sections.b: To geologists, an ice age is any long period when large ice sheets exist on Earth. By that definition we are living in one right now, because Antarctica and Greenland are covered in ice. The current ice age began about 2.6 million years ago. Within it, the climate has swung back and forth between cold glacial periods, when ice sheets spread across North America and northern Europe, and shorter warm interglacial periods like today's. Our current interglacial, called the Holocene, began about 11,700 years ago. When people say 'the Ice Age', they usually mean the most recent glacial period, which peaked around 20,000 years ago.

sections.key: Slow, regular changes in Earth's orbit and tilt, called Milankovitch cycles, pace the ice ages.
sections.b: In the early 20th century, Serbian scientist Milutin Milanković calculated how small changes in Earth's orbit alter the sunlight reaching different latitudes. There are three main cycles. Eccentricity is the shape of Earth's orbit, which stretches from nearly circular to slightly oval over about 100,000 years. Obliquity is the tilt of Earth's axis, which varies between about 22 and 24.5 degrees over about 41,000 years. Precession is the slow wobble of the axis, like a spinning top, over roughly 23,000 years. Together they change how strong the seasons are, especially how much summer sunshine reaches the far north, where the great ice sheets grow and melt.

sections.key: Deep-sea sediments confirmed Milankovitch's theory in 1976; feedbacks like carbon dioxide amplify the small orbital nudge.
sections.b: Milanković's idea was debated for decades. In 1976 scientists James Hays, John Imbrie and Nicholas Shackleton analysed deep-sea sediment cores and found climate cycles matching his predicted rhythms, a landmark confirmation. But the orbital changes alone are fairly small nudges. They are amplified by feedbacks. As ice spreads, its bright white surface reflects more sunlight, cooling things further. Colder oceans absorb more carbon dioxide, lowering greenhouse warming. Antarctic ice cores, containing tiny bubbles of ancient air stretching back about 800,000 years, show carbon dioxide at roughly 180 parts per million in glacial periods and about 280 in warm periods, rising and falling closely with temperature.

sections.key: Around 20,000 years ago, ice sheets up to 3 kilometres thick covered much of North America and Europe.
sections.b: The coldest part of the last glacial period, called the Last Glacial Maximum, was roughly 26,000 to 19,000 years ago. Ice sheets up to about 3 kilometres thick covered Canada and the northern United States as far south as present-day New York and Chicago, and much of northern Europe, including most of Britain and Scandinavia. Estimates suggest global average temperatures were around 6 degrees Celsius colder than before the industrial era, though figures vary. The world was also drier and dustier. Woolly mammoths, woolly rhinoceroses and cave lions roamed the cold grassy steppes of Europe and Asia, and humans survived in the milder regions further south.

sections.key: Ice-age Australia was colder, drier and windier, with small glaciers in Tasmania and the Snowy Mountains.
sections.b: Australia was never covered by large ice sheets, but it was very different. Much of the continent was colder, drier and windier, and desert dune fields expanded. Glaciers carved the highlands of Tasmania, leaving features such as Cradle Mountain's lakes and valleys, and small glaciers formed around Mount Kosciuszko, where glacial lakes like Blue Lake remain today. Many inland lakes, such as those of the Willandra Lakes region including Lake Mungo, held water at various times and later dried out. Aboriginal people had already lived in Australia for tens of thousands of years, and they adapted to these harsh conditions and to the great changes that followed.

sections.key: With so much water locked in ice, sea levels were about 120 metres lower, joining Australia, New Guinea and Tasmania.
sections.b: Ice sheets hold water that would otherwise be in the oceans. At the Last Glacial Maximum, so much water was locked up on land that global sea levels were roughly 120 metres lower than today. Coastlines moved far out, and shallow seas became dry plains. Australia, New Guinea and Tasmania formed a single landmass that scientists call Sahul. The Bass Strait region was a broad plain, dotted with lakes and low hills, that could be walked across. To the north, the land bridge across what is now Torres Strait and the Gulf of Carpentaria connected Cape York to New Guinea. Around Asia, a similar exposed landmass called Sunda joined many Indonesian islands to the mainland.

sections.key: Rising seas cut off Tasmania roughly 12,000 years ago and New Guinea roughly 8,000 years ago.
sections.b: As the ice sheets melted, sea levels rose rapidly, at times by more than a metre per century. Rising water flooded the Bass Strait plain and cut Tasmania off from the mainland roughly 12,000 years ago, though estimates vary by a few thousand years. The land bridge to New Guinea was drowned later, around 8,000 years ago. Sea levels reached roughly their present height about 7,000 years ago. Communities living on these coasts would have watched the shoreline creep inland over generations. Some researchers suggest certain Aboriginal oral traditions may preserve memories of these rising seas, an idea that is taken seriously but still debated.

sections.key: Ice ages show how sensitive climate is: small nudges, amplified by feedbacks, changed sea levels by over 100 metres.
sections.b: Ice ages carry an important lesson. A modest change in sunlight, amplified by ice and carbon dioxide feedbacks, was enough to shift global temperatures by several degrees and sea levels by over 100 metres. Today, carbon dioxide has risen from about 280 parts per million before industry to well over 400, higher than at any time in the ice-core record, and far faster than natural glacial cycles. On orbital grounds alone, scientists expect the next glacial period is many tens of thousands of years away, and human emissions may delay it further. The coastlines we know, and the Aboriginal history written into them, are a reminder that the map is never permanent.

quiz.q: What are Milankovitch cycles?
o: Slow changes in Earth's orbit, tilt and wobble
quiz.e: Milankovitch cycles are regular changes in eccentricity, axial tilt and precession that alter the sunlight Earth receives.

quiz.q: About how much lower were sea levels at the Last Glacial Maximum?
quiz.e: So much water was locked in ice sheets that seas were roughly 120 metres lower.

quiz.q: What was the ice-age landmass joining Australia, New Guinea and Tasmania called?
quiz.e: Sahul was the single landmass of Australia, New Guinea and Tasmania; Sunda was its Asian counterpart.

quiz.q: Why do geologists say we are still in an ice age?
o: The last glacial period never ended
Large ice sheets still cover Antarctica and Greenland
quiz.e: An ice age is any period with large ice sheets; we are in a warm interglacial within one.

quiz.q: How do feedbacks strengthen the effect of Milankovitch cycles?
o: Spreading ice reflects sunlight and colder oceans absorb carbon dioxide
Volcanoes erupt more often during glacials
The Moon moves closer to Earth
quiz.e: Bright ice reflects sunlight and lower carbon dioxide reduces greenhouse warming, amplifying the orbital nudge.

LESSONS.title: Renewable energy
LESSONS.hook: Australia has more rooftop solar per person than almost anywhere on Earth. Here's how renewables work, and what makes the switch hard.

sections.key: Renewable energy comes from sources that are naturally replenished, like sunlight, wind and flowing water.
sections.b: Renewable energy comes from sources that are constantly replenished: sunlight, wind, flowing water, and heat from the Earth. Fossil fuels like coal and gas release carbon dioxide stored over millions of years when burned, and electricity generation has long been one of Australia's largest sources of greenhouse emissions. Renewables produce almost no emissions while running, although making and installing them does have a footprint. Across their whole lifetime, solar, wind and hydro emit only a small fraction of the carbon of coal per unit of electricity. They also use free fuel, which is a big reason the cost of renewable electricity has fallen so sharply over the past two decades.

sections.key: Solar panels turn sunlight directly into electricity using silicon cells, with key advances made in Australia.
sections.b: Solar photovoltaic panels, or PV, convert sunlight directly into electricity. Each panel contains cells made from specially treated silicon. When light hits the cell, it knocks electrons loose, and the cell's structure pushes them in one direction, creating a direct current. An inverter then converts this into the alternating current used in homes. Australian researchers have played a major role. A team at the University of New South Wales, led by Martin Green, developed the PERC cell design in the 1980s, which became the world's dominant solar cell technology for years. The price of solar panels fell by around 90% during the 2010s, as mass production scaled up, largely in China.

sections.key: Australia has one of the highest rates of rooftop solar in the world, with over a third of houses fitted.
sections.b: Australia has embraced rooftop solar like few other countries. Sunshine, government rebates and falling prices helped more than a third of Australian houses install panels, around four million systems by the mid-2020s, one of the highest rates per person in the world. On sunny days, rooftop panels can supply most of South Australia's electricity demand at times. This success brings new challenges. Around the middle of the day, so much solar floods the grid that demand from power stations drops very low, which can make the system harder to manage. Wholesale prices sometimes go negative. That is one reason for the growing interest in batteries and time-of-use tariffs.

sections.key: Wind turbines turn moving air into electricity and complement solar because wind often blows at night.
sections.b: Wind turbines capture the energy of moving air. The wind turns large blades, which spin a generator, usually through a gearbox. Modern turbines are huge: towers can exceed 100 metres, with blades longer than an Olympic swimming pool. Because wind speeds increase with height and power rises steeply with wind speed, taller turbines produce much more electricity. Australia's best wind resources are along the southern coastline and in elevated areas, and South Australia has become a leader, getting well over half its electricity from wind and solar combined in recent years. Wind is a useful partner for solar because it often blows at night and in winter, when solar output is low.

sections.key: Hydroelectricity uses falling water and can start quickly; Snowy 2.0 will store energy by pumping water uphill between reservoirs.
sections.b: Hydroelectric power uses water flowing downhill through turbines. It is Australia's oldest large-scale renewable energy source, and a hydro station can ramp up within minutes, which makes it a valuable backup when solar and wind dip. Tasmania gets most of its electricity from hydro, and the Snowy Mountains Scheme remains the mainland's biggest. The newer Snowy 2.0 project is pumped hydro: it links two existing reservoirs, Tantangara and Talbingo, through about 27 kilometres of tunnels, pumping water uphill when electricity is cheap and releasing it through turbines when needed, like a giant battery. Its estimated cost has blown out from about $2 billion when announced in 2017 to more than $12 billion, with full operation now expected around 2028.

sections.key: Batteries store surplus renewable energy and respond to grid problems in fractions of a second.
sections.b: The sun sets and the wind drops, so storage is essential. In 2017, after a statewide blackout in South Australia the previous year, the Hornsdale Power Reserve was built near Jamestown. At 100 megawatts, it was then the world's largest lithium-ion battery, and it was built in under 100 days. It proved especially good at stabilising the grid, responding to faults in fractions of a second, faster than traditional power stations, and it has since been expanded. Many large batteries have followed. At home, batteries let households store daytime solar for the evening. Pumped hydro, like Snowy 2.0, provides longer-duration storage, lasting days rather than hours.

sections.key: Renewables need backup, storage, new transmission lines, land and mined minerals, and each raises hard questions.
sections.b: Renewables are not without costs. Solar and wind are variable, so the grid needs storage, backup generation such as gas, and smarter demand management to keep the lights on. Good renewable sites are often far from cities, so thousands of kilometres of new transmission lines are needed, which can face strong opposition from landholders and communities. Wind and solar farms use large areas of land, and turbines can affect birds and landscapes. Panels, turbines and batteries require mining of materials such as lithium, copper and rare earths, and recycling them at scale is still developing. Honest debate about renewables means weighing these trade-offs against the costs of continuing with fossil fuels.

sections.key: Renewables supply a rising share of Australia's electricity, and a federal target aims for 82% by 2030.
sections.b: Australia's electricity system is changing quickly. In the main eastern and southern grid, renewables supplied roughly 40% of electricity by the mid-2020s, up from under 10% in the early 2000s, while ageing coal-fired power stations are scheduled to close over the coming decades. In 2022 the federal government set a target of 82% renewable electricity by 2030, though progress towards it is debated. For households, the practical questions are usually whether rooftop solar or a battery suits your roof, usage and budget. Get several quotes from accredited installers, check government rebates, and consider independent advice before committing to a large purchase.

quiz.q: What does an inverter do in a solar system?
o: Converts direct current into alternating current
Tracks the Sun across the sky
quiz.e: Panels produce direct current; the inverter converts it to the alternating current used in homes.

quiz.q: What makes Snowy 2.0 different from a regular hydro power station?
o: It pumps water uphill to store energy for later
It burns gas when water is low
quiz.e: Pumped hydro stores energy by pumping water uphill when power is cheap and releasing it when needed.

quiz.q: What was the Hornsdale Power Reserve especially good at?
o: Stabilising the grid by responding in fractions of a second
Replacing all coal power in South Australia
quiz.e: The battery responded to grid faults faster than traditional power stations.

quiz.q: Why is wind a useful partner for solar?
o: Wind often blows at night and in winter
quiz.e: Wind often picks up when solar output is low, smoothing total renewable supply.

quiz.q: Which is a genuine challenge of expanding renewables?
o: They produce large emissions while running
They need new transmission lines, storage and mined minerals
They cannot work in Australia's climate
quiz.e: Renewables have free fuel and low emissions, but need transmission, storage, land and materials.

LESSONS.title: GDP: measuring an economy
LESSONS.hook: One number gets quoted every quarter as the scorecard for an entire nation. Here's what it actually counts, and what it quietly leaves out.

sections.key: GDP, gross domestic product, is the total value of final goods and services produced in a country over a period.
sections.b: Gross domestic product is the market value of all the final goods and services produced within a country's borders over a set period, usually a quarter or a year. 'Final' matters: a loaf of bread counts, but the flour the baker bought is not counted again separately, or it would be double counted. 'Domestic' means inside the country, whoever owns the business. In Australia the Australian Bureau of Statistics publishes GDP every three months. In the mid-2020s the Australian economy produced roughly $2.5–2.7 trillion of output a year, placing it among the world's larger economies despite a modest population.

sections.h: Three ways to add it up
sections.key: GDP can be measured by production, spending or income, and in theory all three give the same total.
sections.b: Every dollar spent on a final product is a dollar of someone's output and a dollar of someone's income, so GDP can be measured three ways. The production approach adds up the value each industry adds. The income approach adds up wages, profits and similar earnings. The expenditure approach, the most quoted, adds household consumption, business investment, government spending and exports, then subtracts imports, often written C + I + G + (X − M). In practice the three measures never match perfectly, because the data come from different surveys, so statisticians reconcile them. Revisions to past quarters are normal as better data arrive.

sections.key: Real GDP strips out price rises, so it shows whether an economy is actually producing more.
sections.b: If prices rise 4% and output stays flat, the dollar value of GDP still rises about 4%. That dollar figure is nominal GDP. To see whether the economy is genuinely producing more, economists use real GDP, which adjusts for inflation by valuing output at constant prices. When news reports say 'the economy grew 0.5% last quarter', they almost always mean real GDP. Over the long run, Australia's real GDP has typically grown somewhere around 2–3% a year, though growth varies a lot from year to year. Small annual differences compound: 3% growth doubles an economy in roughly 24 years.

sections.key: GDP per capita divides output by population and is a better guide to average living standards.
sections.b: A country can grow its GDP simply by adding people. Australia's population has grown quickly for decades, largely through immigration, so total GDP can rise even when output per person is flat or falling. That is why economists watch GDP per capita, total output divided by population. Australia's is high by world standards, in the order of $100,000 per person in the mid-2020s. In 2023 and 2024 Australia recorded several quarters where total GDP grew but GDP per person fell, which some commentators called a 'per capita recession'. Per capita figures are averages, though, and say nothing about how income is shared.

sections.key: GDP leaves out unpaid work like caring and volunteering, and counts some harmful activity as growth.
sections.b: GDP only counts activity with a market price. Cooking dinner at home, raising children, caring for an ageing parent and volunteering with the local fire brigade add nothing to GDP, even though the ABS has estimated that unpaid work would be worth a very large sum if it were paid. Meanwhile some bad events raise GDP. Rebuilding after a bushfire or flood adds output, but the community is not better off than if the disaster had never happened.
