Running down a forest or a mineral deposit counts as income, with no deduction for what has been used up. GDP measures activity, not whether that activity is wise.

sections.key: Even GDP's creator warned it doesn't measure welfare; other indicators try to fill the gap.
sections.b: Modern national accounts grew out of work in the 1930s by economists including Simon Kuznets, who himself warned that a nation's welfare can hardly be inferred from a measure of national income. In 1968 US senator Robert Kennedy said gross national product, GDP's close cousin, measures everything 'except that which makes life worthwhile'. GDP ignores leisure time, health, pollution, inequality and how safe people feel. Alternatives include the United Nations' Human Development Index, which adds life expectancy and education, and the OECD's Better Life Index. In 2023 the Australian Government released 'Measuring What Matters', a framework tracking around 50 indicators of wellbeing alongside traditional economic figures.

sections.key: Services dominate Australia's economy, while mining punches far above its share of jobs.
sections.b: Like most rich countries, Australia is mainly a services economy. Health care, education, finance, retail, construction, professional services and public administration together produce most of the nation's output and employ the large majority of workers. Mining is the famous exception: it contributes roughly a tenth of GDP in many years, and a much bigger share of exports, but employs only around 2% of workers because it is so capital intensive. Manufacturing has shrunk as a share of the economy since the mid-20th century, and agriculture is now only a few per cent of GDP, though both remain important exporters. On the spending side, household consumption makes up around half of GDP.

sections.key: Treat GDP as one useful dashboard light, not a verdict on how people are doing.
sections.b: When quarterly GDP figures come out, a few questions help you read them. Is the figure real or nominal? Is it quarterly growth or annual? What happened per person? Which parts drove the change, households, government, mining or exports? One weak quarter is not a crisis, and first estimates are often revised. Pair GDP with other signals such as unemployment, wages growth, inflation and household disposable income to get a fuller picture. And remember the limits: a rising GDP can sit alongside falling wellbeing for many people, while some of the most valuable things in your own life will never appear in the national accounts.

quiz.q: Why isn't the flour a baker buys counted separately in GDP?
o: It would be double counted, since its value is already in the bread
quiz.e: GDP counts final goods and services only.

quiz.q: What does real GDP adjust for?
quiz.e: Real GDP values output at constant prices.

quiz.q: How could total GDP rise while living standards per person fall?
o: If population grows faster than output
quiz.e: That's why economists watch GDP per capita.

quiz.q: Which of these adds nothing to GDP?
o: Caring for an ageing parent unpaid
quiz.e: GDP only counts activity with a market price.

quiz.q: Which sector produces most of Australia's output and jobs?
quiz.e: Mining is big in exports but employs only about 2% of workers.

LESSONS.title: Interest rates and the RBA
LESSONS.hook: A decision made in a Sydney boardroom can change your mortgage repayment within weeks. Here's how the cash rate works and why it moves.

sections.key: The cash rate is the interest rate banks charge each other for overnight loans, and the RBA sets a target for it.
sections.b: Every day, banks lend money to each other overnight to settle payments. The interest rate on those loans is the cash rate, and the Reserve Bank of Australia, the RBA, sets a target for it. The RBA doesn't dictate the rates on your mortgage or savings account, but because the cash rate is the base cost of short-term money for banks, most other rates in the economy move with it. The RBA holds the rate near its target by adjusting the interest it pays and charges banks on the money they hold with it. Decisions are announced after scheduled meetings, currently eight a year, at 2:30 pm Sydney time.

sections.key: The RBA aims to keep inflation between 2 and 3% while supporting full employment.
sections.b: The Reserve Bank is Australia's central bank, independent of the government of the day in setting interest rates. Since 1993 it has targeted consumer price inflation of 2–3% on average over time, and in recent years it has focused on getting inflation back to the middle of that band. It must also consider full employment and the economic welfare of Australians. Since 2025, rate decisions have been made by a dedicated Monetary Policy Board, following a 2023 independent review of the RBA. Central bank independence is designed to keep short-term politics, such as the temptation to cut rates before an election, out of rate setting.

sections.key: Higher rates cool spending and borrowing, which helps bring inflation down.
sections.b: When the economy runs too hot, with strong demand pushing prices up faster than the target, the RBA raises the cash rate. Borrowing becomes more expensive, so households with mortgages have less to spend and businesses think twice about expanding. Saving becomes a little more attractive. Demand slows, and over time price rises ease. The catch is that slower demand can also mean fewer jobs. After inflation surged following the pandemic, the RBA lifted the cash rate from a record low of 0.1% in May 2022 to 4.35% by November 2023, one of the fastest rises in its history. It cut rates in 2025, then began raising them again in 2026 as inflation picked up, taking the cash rate to 4.60% by September 2026.

sections.key: Lower rates encourage borrowing and spending to support a weak economy.
sections.b: When the economy is sluggish, unemployment is rising or inflation is falling below target, the RBA cuts rates. Cheaper loans encourage households to spend and businesses to invest, and lower returns on savings nudge people to spend or invest rather than hoard cash. During the 2008 global financial crisis the RBA cut rates sharply, and in 2020 it took the cash rate to 0.1%, the lowest ever, and bought government bonds to push longer-term rates down too. Cutting has limits: rates can't go far below zero, and very cheap money can inflate house prices and encourage risky borrowing.

sections.key: Most Australian home loans are variable, so rate changes flow to repayments quickly.
sections.b: Most Australian mortgages are on variable rates, which lenders usually adjust soon after an RBA decision, though they are free to move by more or less than the cash rate. That makes Australian households more sensitive to rate changes than, say, Americans, who mostly have 30-year fixed loans. The numbers add up fast. On a $500,000, 30-year loan, a rise of 0.25 percentage points lifts monthly repayments by roughly $80. The 2022–23 rises added well over $1,000 a month to many such loans. Borrowers on fixed rates are shielded until their fixed term ends, when they face the new rates all at once.

sections.key: Rate rises usually help savers and tend to lift the Australian dollar; cuts do the opposite.
sections.b: Rate changes cut both ways. When rates rise, banks generally lift what they pay on savings accounts and term deposits, though often more slowly and by less than they raise loan rates, so it pays to compare accounts. Retirees living off deposits welcome higher rates; borrowers don't. Rates also affect the exchange rate. Higher Australian rates, relative to other countries, can attract foreign money and lift the Australian dollar, making imports and overseas holidays cheaper and exporters less competitive. Rates influence share and property prices as well, because they change what investors can earn elsewhere and how much buyers can borrow.

sections.key: Rate changes take a year or more to have their full effect, which makes central banking hard.
sections.b: Economists often say monetary policy works with 'long and variable lags', a phrase from American economist Milton Friedman. A rate rise today may take a year or two to have its full effect on spending, jobs and inflation. So the RBA must act on forecasts, steering by where it thinks the economy is heading rather than where it is now. Move too slowly and inflation can become entrenched as people come to expect it; move too hard and the economy can tip into recession. Australia learnt the first danger in the 1970s, when inflation topped 15% and took more than a decade to bring back down.

sections.key: Build a buffer against rate rises and review your loan and savings rates regularly.
sections.b: No one reliably predicts interest rates, including the experts, so plan for a range of outcomes. If you borrow, lenders in Australia generally test whether you could still afford repayments if rates rose around 3 percentage points, and it's wise to apply a similar buffer to your own budget. Extra repayments or an offset account made while rates are low give breathing room later. Check your rate against what new customers are offered, since banks often reward switching, and ask your lender for a better deal. Savers should shop around too. For decisions about your own loans or investments, talk to a licensed financial adviser or broker.

quiz.q: How does the RBA keep the cash rate near its target?
o: By setting every bank's mortgage rate
By adjusting the interest it pays and charges banks on money they hold with it
quiz.e: Most other rates in the economy then move with the cash rate.

quiz.q: What inflation target does the RBA aim for?
quiz.e: It has targeted 2–3% on average since 1993.

quiz.q: Why would the RBA raise rates?
o: To cool demand and bring inflation down
quiz.e: Higher borrowing costs slow spending.

quiz.q: Why do RBA decisions affect Australian households quickly?
o: Most loans are fixed for 30 years
Banks must match the cash rate exactly
quiz.e: Lenders usually adjust variable rates soon after a decision.

quiz.q: What does 'long and variable lags' mean?
o: Rate changes take a year or more to have full effect
quiz.e: So the RBA has to act on forecasts.

LESSONS.title: Why countries trade
LESSONS.hook: Australia digs, ships and teaches its way to prosperity. The idea behind it, comparative advantage, is one of economics' most surprising insights.

sections.key: Trade lets people and countries specialise in what they do best and swap for the rest.
sections.b: Imagine having to grow your own food, sew your own clothes and build your own phone. You would be poor, busy and badly dressed. Instead, you specialise in your job and trade your earnings for things others make better or cheaper. Countries do the same. Australia has vast iron ore deposits and good farmland but a small population and high wages, so it makes sense to export resources and farm products and import cars, electronics and clothing. Specialisation lets workers get very good at a few things, and trade lets everyone enjoy a far wider range of goods than they could produce alone.

sections.key: Even a country that is better at everything gains by focusing on what it gives up least to produce.
sections.b: In 1817 British economist David Ricardo showed something counterintuitive. Suppose Portugal can make both wine and cloth more efficiently than England. Trade still benefits both, as long as each specialises in what it is relatively best at, the good with the lowest opportunity cost. A simple example: a top lawyer may type faster than her assistant, but her time is worth far more doing legal work, so she hires the assistant to type. Both are better off. This is comparative advantage, as opposed to absolute advantage, and it explains why even highly productive countries import things they could make themselves.

sections.key: Exports are sold to other countries; imports are bought from them. Both can make a country better off.
sections.b: Exports are goods and services sold to foreigners, bringing money into the country. Imports are goods and services bought from abroad. Politicians often treat exports as wins and imports as losses, but most economists see imports as the point of trade: they are what we get in return. Services count too. When an overseas tourist visits the Great Barrier Reef, or a foreign student studies in Melbourne, that's an Australian export, because a foreigner is paying for something Australia provides. The difference between exports and imports is the trade balance. A deficit isn't automatically bad, and Australia ran trade deficits for much of its history while growing rich.

sections.key: Iron ore, coal and natural gas dominate Australia's exports, with education the biggest services export.
sections.b: Australia is one of the world's great resource exporters. Iron ore, mostly from Western Australia's Pilbara and used to make steel, is usually the single largest export, often worth over $100 billion a year. Coal and liquefied natural gas typically follow, with gold, beef, wheat and other farm products also significant. International education is the largest services export and usually ranks among the top handful of exports overall, because students' fees and living costs count as export earnings. Tourism is another big services export. China is Australia's largest trading partner by far, buying around a third of its goods exports, followed by partners such as Japan, South Korea, the US and India.

sections.key: Tariffs are taxes on imports; they protect some local jobs but raise prices for everyone else.
sections.b: A tariff is a tax on imported goods. It makes imports dearer, which can protect local producers from competition. The costs are spread widely: consumers pay higher prices and businesses pay more for inputs. For much of the 20th century Australia sheltered its manufacturers behind high tariffs. From the 1970s onward, starting with a 25% across-the-board cut in 1973, governments dismantled most of that protection. Some industries shrank, and local car manufacturing ended in 2017, but prices fell and more efficient industries grew. History also offers a warning: the US Smoot-Hawley tariffs of 1930 triggered retaliation that helped world trade collapse during the Great Depression.

sections.key: FTAs cut tariffs and other barriers between partner countries, under rules overseen globally by the WTO.
sections.b: Since 1995 the World Trade Organization, which replaced the earlier GATT system, has set global trade rules and settled disputes. On top of that, countries sign free trade agreements with particular partners. Australia's first was with New Zealand in 1965, replaced by the Closer Economic Relations agreement of 1983. Others include deals with the United States (2005), China (2015) and the United Kingdom (2023), plus large regional pacts such as the CPTPP, in force from 2018, and RCEP, from 2022. FTAs typically lower tariffs, open up services and investment and set rules on standards. Critics note they can be complex and that benefits are often smaller than governments promise.

sections.key: Trade makes nations richer overall, but gains are uneven and dependence on one buyer is a risk.
sections.b: Economists broadly agree that trade raises national income, but not everyone wins. Workers in industries facing new import competition can lose jobs, and those losses are often concentrated in particular towns. Good policy helps with retraining and support rather than blocking trade. Dependence is another risk. From 2020 China imposed restrictions or tariffs on a range of Australian goods, including barley, wine, coal and lobster, during a diplomatic dispute. Exporters were hit hard, though many found other markets, and most restrictions were lifted by 2024. The episode prompted talk of diversifying trade, while shocks like the pandemic highlighted the fragility of long supply chains.

sections.key: Much of what you use daily is imported, and many Australian jobs depend on exports.
sections.b: Look around: your phone, laptop, car, clothes and much of your furniture were probably made overseas, often from parts sourced across several countries. Trade makes these things cheaper and more varied than they would otherwise be. In turn, many Australian jobs depend on exports, not only in mines and farms but in ports, transport, universities, tourism and professional services. When you hear debates about tariffs or trade deals, useful questions include: who gains, who pays, and by how much? Protection tends to have visible winners and hidden costs spread thinly across millions of consumers, so the costs are easy to overlook.

quiz.q: What does comparative advantage say?
o: Only the most efficient country should produce anything
Countries gain by specialising in what has the lowest opportunity cost for them
quiz.e: Ricardo showed this in 1817.

quiz.q: Why is a foreign student studying in Melbourne counted as an Australian export?
o: Because a foreigner is paying for a service Australia provides
quiz.e: Education is the largest services export.

quiz.q: What is usually Australia's single largest export?
quiz.e: Mostly mined in WA's Pilbara.

quiz.q: What is a tariff?
quiz.e: It makes imports dearer.

quiz.q: Which goods did China restrict from Australia from 2020?
quiz.e: Most restrictions were lifted by 2024.

LESSONS.title: Recessions: when economies shrink
LESSONS.hook: Australia once went almost 30 years without one, a record for a rich country at the time. What exactly is a recession, and what can governments do about it?

sections.key: A common rule of thumb is two consecutive quarters of falling real GDP, but economists use broader definitions.
sections.b: A recession is a significant, widespread decline in economic activity lasting more than a few months. In Australia and many other countries, the media usually applies a simple rule of thumb: two consecutive quarters of falling real GDP, known as a 'technical recession'. Economists prefer a broader view. In the United States, a committee of the National Bureau of Economic Research dates recessions by looking at employment, incomes, spending and production together. An economy can have a mild dip without a technical recession, and a sharp rise in unemployment can hurt more than the GDP figures suggest. A very deep, long recession is called a depression.

sections.key: Recessions are triggered by shocks that cut spending, such as financial crises, high interest rates or pandemics.
sections.b: Recessions usually start when spending drops sharply across the economy. Common triggers include financial crises, when banks stop lending; central banks raising rates hard to fight inflation; sudden supply shocks, like the oil price spikes of the 1970s; the bursting of asset bubbles in shares or property; and events such as wars or pandemics. Once spending falls, a vicious circle can take hold. Businesses sell less, so they cut staff and investment. Newly unemployed people spend less, which hurts other businesses. Fear itself spreads: worried households save rather than spend, even if their own jobs are safe, deepening the downturn.

sections.key: The Great Depression of the 1930s was the worst downturn of the modern era; Australian unemployment peaked at around 30% or more.
sections.b: The Great Depression began around 1929, marked by the Wall Street crash in October that year, and lasted much of the 1930s. World trade collapsed, thousands of US banks failed and prices fell. Australia, heavily dependent on wool and wheat exports and on overseas borrowing, was hit especially hard. Unemployment peaked at around 30% in 1932 by trade union estimates. One thing that helped was the exchange rate: in 1931 the Australian pound was devalued, ending up about 20% below sterling, which made exports cheaper for foreign buyers and gave farmers and miners some relief. Recovery was still slow, and unemployment stayed high for most of the decade.

sections.key: Australia's 1990–91 recession pushed unemployment to about 11% and followed interest rates near 17%.
sections.b: Australia's last major recession before the pandemic came in 1990–91. In the late 1980s, a boom in borrowing, property and share prices pushed inflation up, and the Reserve Bank lifted interest rates sharply, with mortgage rates reaching about 17% in 1989. The economy contracted, several banks and building societies ran into serious trouble, and unemployment rose to about 11% in 1992. Treasurer Paul Keating famously called it 'the recession we had to have'. It took years for unemployment to recover. The pain was real, but the period also locked in lower inflation, and the RBA formally adopted its inflation target soon after, in 1993.

sections.key: From 1991 to 2020 Australia went almost 29 years without a recession, a record among advanced economies at the time.
sections.b: After 1991, Australia went nearly three decades without a technical recession, the longest such run by any advanced economy at the time. Several factors helped: earlier reforms such as floating the dollar in 1983 and cutting tariffs, a flexible exchange rate that absorbed shocks, an independent central bank, strong population growth, and huge demand for minerals from a rapidly growing China. Luck and policy both mattered. Critics point out that population growth flattered the figures, since GDP per person fell in some periods, and that there were difficult slowdowns along the way. Still, the run was widely admired around the world.

sections.key: The 2008 global financial crisis caused deep recessions abroad, but Australia avoided a technical recession.
sections.b: The global financial crisis grew out of risky US home lending and complex financial products built on it. When US house prices fell, losses spread through the global banking system, and investment bank Lehman Brothers collapsed in September 2008. Much of the world fell into its worst recession since the 1930s. Australia recorded one quarter of negative growth but avoided a technical recession. Reasons included a well-regulated banking system, fast and large RBA rate cuts, a government guarantee of bank deposits, big stimulus spending including cash payments of up to $900 and school building programs, and China's own massive stimulus, which kept demand for Australian resources strong.

sections.key: Lockdowns in 2020 caused Australia's first recession in almost 30 years, followed by a rapid rebound.
sections.b: The pandemic ended Australia's long run. As borders closed and lockdowns began in 2020, real GDP fell about 7% in the June quarter, the largest quarterly fall since records began, after a smaller fall in the March quarter. Unlike most recessions, this one was caused deliberately by health measures, not by a financial crash or high rates. The response was enormous. The JobKeeper program paid employers $1,500 a fortnight per eligible worker to keep staff on, JobSeeker payments were temporarily doubled, and the RBA cut rates to 0.1%. The economy rebounded quickly, though the stimulus is widely thought to have contributed to the inflation that followed.

sections.key: Governments fight recessions with lower interest rates, extra spending and tax cuts; households can build buffers.
sections.b: Governments have two main tools. Monetary policy, run by the Reserve Bank, cuts interest rates to encourage borrowing and spending. Fiscal policy, run by the government, uses extra spending, tax cuts and payments to support demand. Some support happens automatically: when unemployment rises, welfare payments rise and tax revenue falls, cushioning the blow. These are called automatic stabilisers. Economists still debate how big stimulus should be and how quickly to withdraw it. For households, sensible preparation includes an emergency fund of a few months' expenses, keeping debt manageable and maintaining your skills. For personal financial decisions, talk to a licensed financial adviser.

quiz.q: What is a 'technical recession'?
o: Any fall in the share market
Two consecutive quarters of falling real GDP
quiz.e: Economists also use broader definitions.

quiz.q: What helped Australian exporters recover during the Great Depression?
o: A 1931 devaluation of the Australian pound
quiz.e: A cheaper currency made Australian exports more competitive.

quiz.q: Who called 1990–91 'the recession we had to have'?
quiz.e: He was Treasurer at the time.

quiz.q: Which of these helped Australia avoid a technical recession during the GFC?
o: Stimulus spending and strong Chinese demand
quiz.e: RBA rate cuts and a deposit guarantee also helped.

quiz.q: What are automatic stabilisers?
o: Welfare and tax changes that cushion downturns without new decisions
quiz.e: Payments rise and tax revenue falls when unemployment rises.

LESSONS.title: Writing work emails people read
LESSONS.hook: Most work emails get skimmed in seconds. A few simple habits make yours the ones that get read, understood and acted on.

sections.key: Assume your reader is busy and will skim, so make the point impossible to miss.
sections.b: Your reader is probably reading on a phone, between meetings, with dozens of other messages waiting. Many emails get a glance at the subject line and the first couple of lines before a decision is made: act now, deal with later or ignore. Good work emails are designed for that reality. Before you write, ask yourself two questions: what do I want this person to know, and what do I want them to do? If you can't answer both in a sentence, you're not ready to write yet. Clear emails save time twice: once for your reader, and again for you when fewer confused replies come back.

sections.key: A good subject line tells the reader what the email is about and what's needed.
sections.b: The subject line is your headline. 'Quick question' or 'Update' tells the reader nothing and is hard to find later. Be specific: 'Approval needed: Q3 marketing budget by Friday' or 'Moved: Tuesday team meeting now 2 pm'. Some workplaces use prefixes such as 'Action:', 'FYI:' or 'Decision needed:' so people can triage at a glance. If a conversation changes topic, update the subject line rather than burying a new issue in an old thread. For a very short message, some people put the whole thing in the subject line followed by 'EOM', end of message, so the reader never needs to open it.

sections.key: Put your main point or request in the first sentence or two, then the detail.
sections.b: Many of us were taught to write chronologically: background, then reasoning, then the point. At work, flip it. Put the bottom line up front, a habit known as BLUF, borrowed from military writing. Start with the conclusion, decision or request, then add the context for anyone who wants it. Compare 'Following our discussion last week, and after reviewing the supplier quotes, I've looked at our options...' with 'I recommend we go with Supplier B; it's $4,000 cheaper and can deliver two weeks sooner. Details below.' The second version can be understood and acted on even if the reader stops after one sentence.

sections.key: Keep emails brief, one topic each, with short paragraphs and lists for multiple points.
sections.b: Aim for an email that fits on a phone screen without much scrolling. Cut warm-up sentences, repeated context and phrases like 'I just wanted to reach out to touch base regarding'. Stick to one topic per email where you can; mixing a budget question with a holiday roster request means one of them gets forgotten. Use short paragraphs of two or three sentences. If you have several questions or items, number them, so the reader can reply 'Yes to 1, no to 2'. Put key dates and figures where the eye lands. If it truly needs pages of explanation, attach a document or book a meeting instead.

sections.key: Say exactly what you need, from whom and by when, and make it easy to say yes.
sections.b: Vague requests produce vague results, or none at all. 'Thoughts?' invites delay. 'Can you confirm by Thursday 5 pm whether the venue booking for 40 people is okay?' gets an answer. Name the person when an email goes to several people, because a request addressed to everyone is often done by no one. Give a deadline, and a reason if it helps. Make responding easy: offer options ('Does 10 am or 2 pm Wednesday suit?') rather than open questions, and include any links, files or numbers they will need. If you need nothing back, say so ('No reply needed'), which busy colleagues appreciate.

sections.key: Email strips out voice and facial expression, so write a little warmer and clearer than feels necessary.
sections.b: In person, tone of voice and facial expression soften our words. In email they vanish, and readers tend to read neutral messages as more negative than intended. A clipped 'Fine.' or 'Per my last email' can land as irritation. A friendly greeting and sign-off cost nothing: in Australian workplaces 'Hi Sam' and 'Thanks' or 'Kind regards' are standard. Avoid sarcasm and jokes that rely on tone, excessive exclamation marks and ALL CAPS, which reads as shouting. Match the formality of your workplace and the person you're writing to. Before sending anything sensitive, read it aloud and imagine how it sounds to someone having a bad day.

sections.key: Pick up the phone or talk in person for anything urgent, emotional, complex or likely to go back and forth.
sections.b: Email is great for information, requests and records. It's poor for some things. If something is truly urgent, call. If it's emotionally charged, such as feedback, a conflict or bad news, talk in person or by video where you can read reactions and respond. If an email chain has gone back and forth three or four times without resolution, stop and have a quick conversation, then send a short summary of what was agreed. Never send an email while angry: write it if you must, save it as a draft and reread it later. And remember that work emails can be forwarded, and may be retrieved in legal disputes.

sections.key: Run a quick final check: recipients, attachments, the ask and the tone.
sections.b: A thirty-second check prevents most email embarrassments. Are the right people in To (who must act) and Cc (who just need to know)? Should that person really be included? Use Reply All only when everyone genuinely needs your reply. Did you actually attach the file you mentioned? Is your key point in the first lines, and is any request clear, with a deadline? Are names spelt correctly? Many email programs let you delay sending by a minute or schedule messages, which gives you a window to catch mistakes and avoids sending late-night emails that pressure colleagues to respond outside hours. Then send, and move on.

quiz.q: Which subject line is most effective?
o: Approval needed: Q3 budget by Friday
quiz.e: Specific subject lines help readers triage and find emails later.

quiz.q: What does 'BLUF' stand for?
quiz.e: Put the main point or request first.

quiz.q: Why should you name a specific person when making a request to a group?
o: A request to everyone is often done by no one
quiz.e: Clear ownership gets things done.

quiz.q: Why can neutral emails come across badly?
o: Readers tend to read them as more negative than intended
quiz.e: Email strips out voice and facial expression.

quiz.q: When is email usually the wrong tool?
quiz.e: Talk in person or by video for sensitive matters.

LESSONS.title: Acing a job interview
LESSONS.hook: Interviews reward preparation far more than charisma. Here's how to research, structure your stories and follow up like a pro.

sections.key: Interviews reward preparation: know the role, your own stories and the logistics.
sections.b: Most interviewers aren't looking for perfect people. They want to know three things: can you do the job, will you want to do it, and will you work well with the team? Your task is to give clear evidence for all three. Start with the job ad or position description and highlight the key skills and selection criteria. For each one, think of a real example from your work, study or life that shows it. Then sort out the practical details: the time, the location or video link, who you're meeting, and what to wear. Aim to arrive about ten minutes early, or test your technology beforehand for online interviews.

sections.key: Learn what the organisation does, its recent news and its values, and connect them to your experience.
sections.b: Few things impress an interviewer like a candidate who clearly understands the organisation. Read its website, especially the 'about', 'careers' and news pages. For larger companies, skim the latest annual report or its highlights. Check recent news coverage, the organisation's social media and the LinkedIn profiles of the people interviewing you, if they're listed. Find out who its customers and competitors are and what challenges the industry faces. The goal isn't to recite facts but to connect them to yourself: 'I saw you're expanding into Queensland; I managed a similar regional rollout in my last role.' That shows genuine interest and relevant thinking.

sections.key: Answer behavioural questions with STAR: Situation, Task, Action, Result.
sections.b: Many interviews use behavioural questions, which ask how you handled real situations: 'Tell me about a time you dealt with a difficult customer.' The idea is that past behaviour is a reasonable guide to future behaviour. The STAR method gives your answer a clear shape. Situation: briefly set the scene. Task: what you needed to achieve. Action: what you did, the heart of the answer, so use 'I' rather than 'we'. Result: what happened, ideally with a number, and what you learnt. Aim for one to two minutes per answer. Prepare six to eight STAR stories in advance; each can usually be adapted to several different questions.

sections.key: Prepare for the classic questions, especially 'tell me about yourself' and 'why this role'.
sections.b: Some questions come up again and again. 'Tell me about yourself' is an invitation for a brief professional summary, around a minute or two, covering your current role, relevant experience and why you're interested in this job, not your life story. 'Why do you want this role?' tests your research and motivation. 'What are your strengths?' should be backed by examples. 'What's a weakness?' calls for a genuine but manageable weakness and what you're doing about it, rather than a disguised boast like 'I'm a perfectionist'. You may also be asked why you're leaving your current job. Stay positive and never criticise a former employer.

sections.key: Pause, ask for clarification if needed, and be honest when you don't know something.
sections.b: Nerves are normal, and interviewers expect them. If a question stumps you, it's fine to pause and say, 'That's a good question, let me think for a moment.' If you're unsure what they're asking, ask them to clarify. When you don't know something, say so honestly and explain how you'd find out, rather than bluffing. For questions about salary expectations, research typical pay for the role beforehand and give a sensible range. In Australia, anti-discrimination laws generally prohibit employers from basing hiring decisions on attributes such as age, pregnancy, race or disability, so you can politely steer back to your ability to do the job.

sections.key: Always have two or three thoughtful questions ready; it shows interest and helps you decide.
sections.b: Near the end, you'll almost always be asked, 'Do you have any questions for us?' Saying 'No, I think you've covered everything' is a missed opportunity. Prepare a few questions that show you're thinking seriously about the role. Good options include: 'What would success look like in the first six months?', 'What are the biggest challenges facing the team right now?', 'How would you describe the team culture?' and 'What are the next steps in the process?' Remember an interview is two-way. The answers help you judge whether you actually want this job. Leave detailed questions about leave and pay for later, usually once an offer is likely.

sections.key: Send a brief thank-you, prepare your referees, and reflect on what to improve.
sections.b: Within a day, consider sending a short email thanking the interviewer for their time and briefly restating your interest. It won't rescue a poor interview, but it's courteous and keeps you front of mind. In Australia, reference checks with previous managers are common, so give your referees a heads-up and tell them about the role. Then write down the questions you were asked and how you answered while it's fresh; it's valuable practice for next time. If you haven't heard back by the date they mentioned, a polite follow-up email is fine. If you miss out, it's reasonable to ask for feedback, though not every employer will provide it.

sections.key: Practise out loud, be on time, and let warmth and enthusiasm show.
sections.b: Interviewers form early impressions, so small things matter: arriving on time, a friendly greeting, dressing slightly more formally than the everyday dress of the workplace, and being polite to everyone you meet, including the receptionist. For video interviews, check your lighting, framing, sound and background, and look at the camera when speaking. The most useful single habit is practising answers out loud, ideally with a friend playing interviewer or by recording yourself. Things that sound fine in your head often come out rambling the first time. Finally, let genuine enthusiasm show. Employers often choose the capable candidate who clearly wants the job over a slightly stronger but indifferent one.

quiz.q: What three things are most interviewers trying to find out?
o: Whether you can do the job, want to do it and will fit with the team
quiz.e: Your job is to give evidence for all three.

quiz.q: What does STAR stand for?
quiz.e: It gives behavioural answers a clear shape.

quiz.q: What's the best approach to 'Tell me about yourself'?
o: A brief professional summary linked to the role
Asking them to read your CV
quiz.e: Keep it to a minute or two.

quiz.q: Why should you prepare questions to ask the interviewer?
o: It shows interest and helps you judge the job
quiz.e: An interview is a two-way conversation.

quiz.q: What's a sensible step after the interview?
o: Call them daily for an update
Send a brief thank-you and brief your referees
quiz.e: Also note the questions you were asked.

LESSONS.title: Genes and inheritance
LESSONS.hook: Why do you have your mother's eyes but your grandfather's chin, and why can two siblings look like strangers?

sections.key: A gene is a stretch of DNA carrying instructions for a protein, and you inherit two copies of most genes.
sections.b: A gene is a section of DNA that holds instructions, usually for building a particular protein. Proteins do most of the work in your body, from carrying oxygen to colouring your eyes. Humans have about 20,000 protein-coding genes, packed into 23 pairs of chromosomes inside almost every cell. One chromosome in each pair came from your mother and one from your father, so you carry two copies of most genes. Different versions of the same gene are called alleles. One allele might produce more pigment, another less, and the combination you inherit shapes the result.

sections.key: Gregor Mendel discovered the basic rules of inheritance in the 1860s by breeding pea plants.
sections.b: The rules of inheritance were first worked out by Gregor Mendel, a monk in what is now the Czech Republic. Between about 1856 and 1863 he grew and crossed thousands of pea plants in his monastery garden, carefully tracking traits like flower colour, seed shape and plant height. He noticed that traits didn't blend: crossing tall and short plants gave tall offspring, not medium ones. Mendel published his results in 1866, but they were largely ignored. Around 1900, three scientists independently rediscovered his work, and he became known as the father of genetics.

sections.key: A dominant allele shows its effect with one copy; a recessive allele needs two copies to show.
sections.b: Mendel's key insight was that some versions of a trait mask others. A dominant allele shows its effect even if you have only one copy. A recessive allele only shows if you have two copies, one from each parent. When Mendel crossed purple-flowered and white-flowered peas, the first generation was all purple. But when those plants bred with each other, white flowers reappeared in about one in four offspring, a ratio of roughly three to one. The white allele hadn't vanished; it had been hidden, carried silently until two copies met.

sections.key: People can carry a recessive allele without knowing; two carrier parents have a 1 in 4 chance per child of passing on two copies.
sections.b: Because recessive alleles can hide, many people carry one copy of a gene variant linked to a genetic condition without any sign of it. Cystic fibrosis is a well-known example: roughly 1 in 25 Australians carries a copy of a cystic fibrosis variant. If two carriers have a child, each pregnancy has a 1 in 4 chance of the child inheriting two copies, a 1 in 2 chance of being a carrier, and a 1 in 4 chance of inheriting neither. This is why reproductive carrier screening is offered in Australia; a GP or genetic counsellor can explain the options.

sections.key: Most traits, like height and eye colour, are shaped by many genes plus environment, not a single gene.
sections.b: Mendel chose his pea traits well, because each was controlled mainly by one gene. Most human traits are far messier. Height is influenced by thousands of genetic variants, each with a tiny effect, plus nutrition and health in childhood. Eye colour is often taught as a simple dominant-recessive trait, but it involves several genes, which is why two blue-eyed parents can, occasionally, have a brown-eyed child. Traits shaped by many genes are called polygenic. Environment matters too: genes load the dice, but diet, experience and chance also help decide how they roll.

sections.key: Each parent passes on a random half of their DNA, so siblings share about 50% of their variable DNA on average.
sections.b: Each egg or sperm cell carries only one chromosome from each pair, and which one goes in is random. With 23 pairs, that alone allows over 8 million possible combinations from each parent. On top of that, chromosomes swap segments before being passed on, a process called crossing over, which shuffles genes into fresh combinations. The result is that each child gets a unique mix. Full siblings share, on average, about half of the DNA that varies between people, which is why brothers and sisters can look strikingly alike or surprisingly different. Identical twins are the exception, sharing almost all of it.

sections.key: Genes on the X chromosome explain why conditions like red-green colour blindness are far more common in men.
sections.b: One chromosome pair works differently. Most females have two X chromosomes, while most males have one X and one much smaller Y. Genes carried on the X chromosome therefore behave unusually. If a male inherits a recessive variant on his single X, there is no second copy to mask it. That is why red-green colour blindness affects roughly 1 in 12 men of northern European ancestry but only about 1 in 200 women. Haemophilia, a blood-clotting disorder, follows the same pattern. Such X-linked conditions usually pass from mothers, who are often unaffected carriers, to sons.

sections.key: Family history and genetic testing can help, but genes are influences, not destiny.
sections.b: Knowing how inheritance works helps you read your own family history. If a condition appears in several relatives, it's worth mentioning to your GP, who may suggest screening or referral to a genetic counsellor. Be wary of assuming too much, though. Having a gene variant linked to a disease often raises risk rather than guaranteeing illness, and lifestyle can matter a great deal for conditions like heart disease and type 2 diabetes. Consumer DNA tests can be fun for ancestry but vary in accuracy for health claims. For anything medical, talk to a doctor or genetic counsellor.

quiz.q: What did Gregor Mendel use to discover the rules of inheritance?
quiz.e: Mendel crossed thousands of pea plants in his monastery garden in the 1850s and 1860s.

quiz.q: When Mendel bred his first-generation purple peas together, what ratio of purple to white appeared?
quiz.e: White flowers reappeared in about one in four offspring, a 3:1 ratio, because the recessive allele had been hidden.

quiz.q: If two parents are both carriers of a recessive condition, what is the chance each child inherits two copies?
quiz.e: Each parent has a 1 in 2 chance of passing on the variant, so the chance of both doing so is 1 in 4.

quiz.q: Why can full siblings look quite different?
o: They have different numbers of chromosomes
Each receives a random shuffle of each parent's DNA
Only one sibling inherits the father's genes
DNA changes after birth to match environment
quiz.e: Random chromosome assortment and crossing over give each child a unique mix, sharing about half their variable DNA.

quiz.q: Why is red-green colour blindness more common in men?
o: Men have more genes for colour
It is caused by the Y chromosome
Men have only one X chromosome, so a recessive variant isn't masked
quiz.e: With one X chromosome, a male has no second copy to mask a recessive variant on it.

LESSONS.title: The human story
LESSONS.hook: For most of the last few hundred thousand years, we weren't alone: several kinds of human shared the planet, and some of them are in your DNA.

sections.key: Humans didn't evolve from chimpanzees; we share a common ancestor that lived roughly 6 to 7 million years ago.
sections.b: A common misunderstanding is that humans evolved from chimpanzees. In fact, humans and chimps are cousins: both descend from a shared ancestral ape that lived in Africa roughly 6 to 7 million years ago, though estimates vary. Since then, both lineages have kept evolving. The species on the human side of the split are called hominins. Rather than a neat ladder from ape to human, the hominin family tree is more like a bushy shrub, with many branches, several living at the same time, and most ending in extinction. We are the only surviving twig.

sections.key: Lucy, a 3.2-million-year-old Australopithecus found in Ethiopia in 1974, showed that walking upright came before big brains.
sections.b: In 1974, in Ethiopia's Afar region, a team led by Donald Johanson found about 40% of a skeleton of a small female hominin. They named her Lucy, after the Beatles song playing in their camp. Lucy belonged to the species Australopithecus afarensis and lived about 3.2 million years ago. She stood around a metre tall and had a brain roughly the size of a chimpanzee's, yet her hips and legs show she walked upright. Fossilised footprints at Laetoli, Tanzania, about 3.6 million years old, confirm it. Walking on two legs came long before big brains.

sections.key: Stone tools appear over 3 million years ago, and early Homo species had steadily larger brains.
sections.b: The oldest known stone tools, from Lomekwi in Kenya, are about 3.3 million years old, older than our own genus, Homo. From around 2.5 million years ago, simple sharp flakes struck from stones become common across East Africa. Early members of the genus Homo, such as Homo habilis, appear in the fossil record around this time, though exactly which species belong where is debated. Over the next two million years, hominin brains grew substantially. Better tools gave access to meat and marrow, and richer food probably helped fuel those energy-hungry brains.

sections.key: Homo erectus had near-modern body proportions and was the first hominin known to spread beyond Africa.
sections.b: Homo erectus appeared in Africa roughly 2 million years ago and was a hominin success story. It had long legs and a body shaped much like ours, suited to walking and running long distances. It made carefully shaped stone hand axes, and at some point hominins learned to control fire, though exactly when is debated. Homo erectus was the first hominin known to leave Africa: fossils around 1.8 million years old have been found in Georgia, and the species reached China and Java. On Java it may have survived until around 110,000 years ago, an astonishing run of nearly two million years.

sections.key: The oldest known Homo sapiens fossils, from Morocco, are about 300,000 years old.
sections.b: Our own species, Homo sapiens, evolved in Africa. The oldest fossils generally assigned to it come from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco and are about 300,000 years old. Those early people had faces much like ours, though their skulls were longer and lower. Many researchers now think modern humans emerged across Africa, with populations in different regions exchanging genes, rather than in one small cradle. Signs of symbolic thinking, like shell beads and engraved ochre, appear in Africa over 70,000 years ago. Small groups made early trips into the Middle East, but the major dispersal came later.

sections.key: Neanderthals and Denisovans were close human relatives, and most people today carry some of their DNA.
sections.b: When modern humans spread out of Africa, they met other humans. Neanderthals lived across Europe and western Asia from roughly 400,000 until about 40,000 years ago. They were strong, skilled toolmakers who buried some of their dead and made pigments. Denisovans are known mainly from DNA, first read in 2010 from a finger bone in Denisova Cave, Siberia. Both groups interbred with our ancestors. People with ancestry from outside Africa typically carry around 1 to 2% Neanderthal DNA, and people in Papua New Guinea and many Aboriginal Australians carry several per cent Denisovan DNA. Other species, like the small Homo floresiensis of Indonesia, also survived until relatively recently.

sections.key: Modern humans spread across the world from about 60,000 to 70,000 years ago and reached Australia at least 50,000 and possibly 65,000 years ago.
sections.b: The main dispersal of modern humans out of Africa happened roughly 60,000 to 70,000 years ago. People moved along coasts and across Asia with remarkable speed, and reaching Australia required sea crossings even when sea levels were low. Excavations at Madjedbebe rock shelter in Arnhem Land have produced dates of about 65,000 years, though some researchers argue for closer to 50,000; the range is still debated. At Lake Mungo in New South Wales, the burials of Mungo Lady and Mungo Man are around 40,000 years old. Many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples also hold that they have always been on this land.

sections.key: Every living person belongs to one species that is young, closely related and remarkably mobile.
sections.b: The human story has a few big lessons. First, all living people belong to one young species, and genetically we are very similar; there is more genetic variation within Africa than between Africa and the rest of the world. Second, being the only human species is unusual. For most of hominin history, several kinds of human lived at once. Third, the story keeps changing as new fossils and ancient DNA emerge, so treat any date as a best current estimate. When you read a headline about a 'missing link', remember the family tree is a bush, not a chain.

quiz.q: What are hominins?
o: Species on the human side of the split from chimpanzees
quiz.e: The hominin family tree is a bushy shrub with many extinct branches, and we are the only surviving twig.

quiz.q: What did Lucy's skeleton show?
o: Big brains came before walking upright
Walking upright came before big brains
quiz.e: Lucy had a chimp-sized brain but walked upright, about 3.2 million years ago.

quiz.q: Which hominin was the first known to spread beyond Africa?
quiz.e: Homo erectus fossils around 1.8 million years old have been found in Georgia, and the species reached China and Java.

quiz.q: How much Neanderthal DNA do people with ancestry from outside Africa typically carry?
quiz.e: Interbreeding left most non-African populations with around 1 to 2% Neanderthal DNA.

quiz.q: Which site in Arnhem Land has produced dates of about 65,000 years for human presence?
quiz.e: Madjedbebe has produced dates of about 65,000 years, though some researchers argue for a younger age.

LESSONS.title: Extinction
LESSONS.hook: Over 99% of all species that have ever lived are gone. What wiped them out, and are we living through the next great loss?

sections.key: More than 99% of all species that have ever lived are now extinct.
sections.b: Extinction is the permanent loss of a species, and it is a normal part of life's history. Scientists estimate that more than 99% of all species that have ever existed are now extinct. Species naturally come and go as environments change, competitors arrive and new species evolve. A typical species lasts somewhere around one to ten million years in the fossil record, though some survive far longer. So extinction itself is not unusual. What matters is the rate: how many species are disappearing, and how fast, compared with the usual background pace.

sections.key: Background extinction is the slow, steady loss of species; a mass extinction wipes out most species in a geologically short time.
sections.b: Most of the time, species disappear slowly, a process called background extinction. Estimates vary, but one widely used figure is roughly one extinction per million species per year, meaning if there were a million species, about one would vanish each year. Occasionally, though, something far more dramatic happens. A mass extinction is when a large share of Earth's species, often defined as at least three-quarters, disappears in a geologically short time, perhaps thousands to a few million years. These events reshape life entirely, clearing space for new groups to rise.

sections.key: Five mass extinctions stand out, from the end-Ordovician 445 million years ago to the end-Cretaceous 66 million years ago.
sections.b: Scientists recognise five great mass extinctions. The end-Ordovician, about 445 million years ago, struck when ice ages dropped sea levels. The Late Devonian, around 372 million years ago, was a drawn-out crisis for reefs and marine life. The end-Permian, about 252 million years ago, was the worst of all, wiping out roughly 90% of marine species. The end-Triassic, about 201 million years ago, cleared the way for dinosaurs. The end-Cretaceous, 66 million years ago, killed off the non-bird dinosaurs, along with around three-quarters of all species.

sections.key: Mass extinctions are usually driven by rapid environmental change, especially massive volcanism, climate shifts and, once, an asteroid.
sections.b: Each mass extinction had its own trigger, but a common thread is rapid environmental change. The end-Permian and end-Triassic events coincide with enormous volcanic eruptions that released vast amounts of carbon dioxide, driving global warming, ocean acidification and oxygen-starved seas. The end-Cretaceous event is linked to an asteroid about 10 kilometres wide that struck near Chicxulub in Mexico, though huge eruptions in India were also underway. The lesson is not that any single force is deadly, but that fast change, faster than species can adapt or move, is what kills.

sections.key: Human activity is driving extinctions far above the background rate, with around a million species threatened.
sections.b: Today, extinctions are running far above the background rate. A major 2019 global assessment by the scientific body IPBES estimated that around one million animal and plant species are threatened with extinction, many within decades. The main drivers are habitat destruction, especially clearing land for farming, overhunting and overfishing, invasive species, pollution and climate change. Whether this already counts as a 'sixth mass extinction' is debated: the losses so far are well short of three-quarters of species. But many scientists warn that, at current rates, we could be heading that way.

sections.key: Australia has lost more than 30 native mammal species since 1788, one of the worst records in the world.
sections.b: Australia has one of the worst records for mammal extinctions of any country. Since European colonisation in 1788, more than 30 native mammal species have been lost, including the lesser bilby, the pig-footed bandicoot and several hopping-mice and rat-kangaroos. The main culprits are introduced predators, especially feral cats and foxes, along with land clearing and changed fire patterns. Small and medium-sized ground-dwelling mammals, from about the size of a mouse to a small wallaby, were hit hardest. Many survivors now cling on in small pockets or on offshore islands.

sections.key: The Christmas Island pipistrelle vanished in 2009 as a rescue came too late; the Bramble Cay melomys is considered the first mammal lost to human-driven climate change.
sections.b: Some extinctions happen in plain sight. The Christmas Island pipistrelle, a tiny bat weighing only a few grams, declined steeply through the 2000s, and by early 2009 only around 20 were thought to remain. A captive-breeding rescue was approved that July, but by then searchers could find just one bat, and they failed to catch it. Its last echolocation call was recorded on 26 August 2009. A more recent loss is the Bramble Cay melomys, a small rodent found only on a tiny coral cay in the Torres Strait. Rising seas and storm surges repeatedly flooded its island, and it was officially declared extinct in 2019, widely described as the first mammal lost to human-driven climate change.

sections.key: Controlling feral predators, protecting habitat and safe havens have already brought Australian species back from the brink.
sections.b: The news isn't all bad. Conservation works when it tackles the real causes. In Australia, fenced predator-free sanctuaries and islands cleared of cats, foxes and rats have allowed species like bilbies, bettongs and numbats to recover in places. Lord Howe Island's rodent eradication, carried out in 2019, has helped native birds and insects rebound. Individuals can help too: keep cats indoors or contained, choose native plants, support habitat protection, and report sightings of threatened species to citizen science programs. Every species kept alive keeps options open for the future.

quiz.q: Roughly what share of all species that have ever lived are now extinct?
quiz.e: Extinction is normal over deep time; more than 99% of all species ever to exist are gone.

quiz.q: Which was the worst mass extinction, wiping out roughly 90% of marine species?
quiz.e: The end-Permian extinction, about 252 million years ago, is known as the Great Dying.

quiz.q: What is the most common thread behind mass extinctions?
o: Gradual cooling over hundreds of millions of years
quiz.e: Fast change, such as massive volcanism or an asteroid impact, outpaces species' ability to adapt.

quiz.q: What are the main causes of Australia's mammal extinctions since 1788?
o: Feral cats and foxes, land clearing and changed fire patterns
quiz.e: Introduced predators, habitat loss and altered fire regimes hit small and medium ground-dwelling mammals hardest.

quiz.q: Why is the Bramble Cay melomys significant?
o: It is widely described as the first mammal lost to human-driven climate change
It was the last thylacine relative
quiz.e: Rising seas and storm surges repeatedly flooded its tiny Torres Strait island.

LESSONS.title: Gene editing and CRISPR
LESSONS.hook: A tool borrowed from bacteria now lets scientists rewrite DNA letter by letter. It has already cured patients, and caused a scandal.

sections.key: CRISPR began as a bacterial immune system that stores snippets of virus DNA and uses them to cut invaders.
sections.b: CRISPR started life not in a lab but in bacteria. Bacteria are constantly attacked by viruses, and many defend themselves by storing short snippets of viral DNA in a region of their own genome called CRISPR. If the same virus attacks again, the bacterium makes RNA copies of those snippets, which guide cutting proteins, such as Cas9, to the matching viral DNA and slice it apart. It is a kind of genetic memory. Scientists studying this system in the 2000s realised that if they could reprogram the guide, they could direct the cut to almost any DNA sequence they chose.

sections.key: In 2012 Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier showed CRISPR-Cas9 could be programmed to cut chosen DNA, winning the 2020 Nobel Prize.
sections.b: In 2012, Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier published a landmark paper showing that CRISPR-Cas9 could be programmed to cut a chosen DNA sequence in a test tube. Within months, several teams, including Feng Zhang's, showed it worked in human and other cells. Earlier gene-editing tools, such as zinc finger nucleases and TALENs, existed, but they were slow and expensive to redesign for each new target. CRISPR was cheap, fast and flexible, and it spread through laboratories worldwide. Doudna and Charpentier received the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the discovery.

sections.key: A guide RNA leads Cas9 to a matching DNA sequence, where it cuts, and the cell's repair either disables the gene or inserts a new sequence.
sections.b: The system has two main parts. A short guide RNA, designed to match about 20 letters of target DNA, leads the Cas9 protein to the right spot in the genome. Cas9 then cuts both strands of the DNA. The cell rushes to repair the break. Often the repair is sloppy, adding or deleting a few letters, which usually disables the gene. If scientists also supply a template, the cell can sometimes copy it in, inserting a corrected sequence. Newer versions, called base editing and prime editing, can change individual letters without fully cutting the DNA, making edits more precise.

sections.key: Casgevy, approved in 2023, uses CRISPR on patients' own stem cells to treat sickle cell disease and beta thalassaemia.
sections.b: The first approved CRISPR medicine is Casgevy, which was approved in the United Kingdom in November 2023 and in the United States soon after. It treats sickle cell disease and beta thalassaemia, inherited blood disorders caused by faulty haemoglobin. Doctors collect a patient's blood stem cells and edit them to switch back on a form of haemoglobin normally made only before birth. After chemotherapy clears the old bone marrow, the edited cells are returned. Many patients in trials became free of severe pain crises or regular transfusions. The treatment is gruelling and extremely expensive, costing millions of dollars per patient.

sections.key: Genetically modified crops have been grown for decades; in Australia, most cotton is GM and GM canola is grown in several states.
sections.b: Genetic modification of crops long predates CRISPR. The first GM food, a slow-softening tomato, went on sale in the United States in 1994. In Australia, nearly all the cotton crop is genetically modified to resist insect pests and tolerate herbicides, and GM canola has been grown in several states since 2008. Tasmania still maintains a moratorium. GM crops are regulated by the federal Gene Technology Regulator, and food labelling by Food Standards Australia New Zealand. Since 2019, Australia has not treated simple CRISPR edits that add no new DNA as GMOs, since they resemble natural mutations.

sections.key: Somatic edits affect only one patient; germline edits to embryos, eggs or sperm would be passed to future generations.
sections.b: A crucial distinction in gene editing is where the change is made. Somatic editing changes cells in a patient's body, such as blood or liver cells. The effects stay with that person and are not passed on to children, much like any other medical treatment. Germline editing changes embryos, eggs or sperm, so the edit would appear in every cell of the resulting person and could pass to all their descendants. That raises much deeper questions about safety, consent and unintended effects. Many countries, including Australia, prohibit making heritable changes to the human genome.

sections.key: In 2018 He Jiankui announced the birth of gene-edited twins, provoking global condemnation and a prison sentence.
sections.b: In November 2018, Chinese scientist He Jiankui announced that twin girls had been born from embryos he had edited to disable a gene called CCR5, aiming to make them resistant to HIV. A third edited child was later born. The announcement shocked scientists worldwide. The edits were medically unnecessary, the risk of the father passing on HIV could already be managed by other means, the editing was imprecise, and there were serious concerns about the parents' informed consent. A Chinese court sentenced He to three years in prison in 2019. The case prompted calls for stronger international oversight of germline editing.

sections.key: Gene editing offers real hope for inherited diseases, but raises questions of safety, cost, fairness and where to draw the line.
sections.b: Gene editing is moving fast. Trials are testing treatments for inherited blindness, high cholesterol and rare liver diseases, and scientists are exploring gene drives, which could spread edits through wild populations of pests like malaria-carrying mosquitoes. Each raises questions worth thinking about. How do we check for unintended edits? Who can afford treatments costing millions? Where is the line between treating disease and enhancement? When you read about a new 'breakthrough', look for whether it's in cells, animals or human trials, and whether the results have been peer reviewed. Most advances take years to reach patients.

quiz.q: Where did the CRISPR system originally come from?
o: It was invented from scratch by chemists
A bacterial immune defence against viruses
quiz.e: Bacteria store snippets of viral DNA in CRISPR regions and use them to guide proteins that cut invaders.

quiz.q: What role does the guide RNA play in CRISPR-Cas9?
o: It leads Cas9 to a matching DNA sequence
quiz.e: The guide RNA matches about 20 letters of target DNA, directing Cas9 to cut at that spot.

quiz.q: What does the approved CRISPR therapy Casgevy treat?
o: Sickle cell disease and beta thalassaemia
quiz.e: Casgevy edits patients' blood stem cells to switch on a form of haemoglobin normally made before birth.

quiz.q: What makes germline editing especially controversial?
o: It is cheaper than somatic editing
The changes can be passed on to future generations
quiz.e: Edits to embryos, eggs or sperm appear in every cell and can be inherited by descendants.

quiz.q: What did He Jiankui announce in 2018?
o: A cure for sickle cell disease
quiz.e: He edited embryos to disable the CCR5 gene, was widely condemned, and was sentenced to three years in prison.

LESSONS.title: The first life on Earth
LESSONS.hook: Some of the oldest evidence of life on Earth is in Western Australia, and you can still see its living relatives at Shark Bay.

sections.key: Earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago; Australian zircon crystals suggest water existed within a few hundred million years.
sections.b: Earth formed about 4.54 billion years ago from dust and rock orbiting the young Sun. Early on, a Mars-sized body is thought to have smashed into it, flinging out the debris that became the Moon. The surface was bombarded by space rocks and there was no oxygen in the air. Yet it may have cooled faster than once thought. Tiny zircon crystals from the Jack Hills in Western Australia, about 4.4 billion years old, are the oldest known pieces of Earth, and their chemistry suggests liquid water, perhaps even oceans, existed remarkably early.

sections.key: No one knows exactly how life began; leading ideas include hydrothermal vents, shallow ponds and an early 'RNA world'.
sections.b: How non-living chemistry became life is one of science's great open questions. In 1952, Stanley Miller and Harold Urey passed sparks through a mix of gases and water and produced amino acids, the building blocks of proteins, showing that life's ingredients can form naturally. Today, leading ideas include deep-sea hydrothermal vents, where mineral-rich water provides energy, and shallow ponds that repeatedly dry out and refill, concentrating chemicals, an echo of Darwin's 'warm little pond'. Many researchers think early life used RNA, which can both store information and speed up reactions, before DNA and proteins took over.

sections.key: The oldest widely accepted evidence of life, about 3.5 billion years old, comes from the Pilbara in Western Australia.
sections.b: Some of the oldest widely accepted evidence of life on Earth comes from the Pilbara region of Western Australia. Rocks there, about 3.5 billion years old, contain stromatolites: layered structures built by communities of microbes. Around 3.4 billion-year-old reef-like stromatolites at Strelley Pool are among the best-studied examples. Older claims exist, including possible stromatolites about 3.7 billion years old in Greenland and chemical traces of carbon in even older rocks, but these are contested, because non-living processes can sometimes mimic signs of life. Either way, life appears to have started surprisingly soon after Earth became habitable.

sections.key: Living stromatolites at Hamelin Pool in Shark Bay, WA, show what the earliest life may have built.
sections.b: You can see living stromatolites today at Hamelin Pool in Shark Bay, Western Australia, part of a World Heritage Area. The water there is about twice as salty as normal seawater, which keeps away many snails and other grazers that would eat the microbial mats. The mats trap sediment and bind it together, building up dome-shaped structures very slowly, often a fraction of a millimetre a year. Some of the Hamelin Pool stromatolites are thought to be a few thousand years old. They offer a rare glimpse of what shallow coastlines may have looked like for much of Earth's history.

sections.key: LUCA, the last universal common ancestor, is the population from which all living things today descend.
sections.b: Every living thing today, from bacteria to blue whales, shares the same basic genetic code, the same way of making proteins and many identical genes. That points to a single shared ancestor, known as LUCA, the last universal common ancestor. LUCA was not the first life, but the most recent population from which all surviving life descends. By comparing genes across living species, scientists infer that LUCA was a single-celled microbe that probably lived in a warm, oxygen-free environment. One 2024 study estimated it lived about 4.2 billion years ago, although its timing is still debated.

sections.key: Around 2.4 billion years ago, oxygen from photosynthesising cyanobacteria began to build up in the air, transforming the planet.
sections.b: For its first two billion years, Earth's air had almost no oxygen. That changed when cyanobacteria began photosynthesising, using sunlight to split water and releasing oxygen as waste. At first the oxygen was absorbed by iron dissolved in the oceans, which rusted and settled to form banded iron formations. The Pilbara's huge iron-ore deposits in the Hamersley Range formed in this era, so Australia's iron exports partly owe their existence to ancient microbes. Around 2.4 billion years ago, oxygen began building up in the atmosphere, an event called the Great Oxidation Event. It was toxic to many microbes but opened the way for complex life.

sections.key: Complex cells arose when one cell engulfed another, whose descendants became mitochondria.
sections.b: The next great step was the complex cell, called a eukaryote, which has a nucleus and internal compartments. Plants, animals and fungi are all made of these cells. A key event was when one microbe engulfed another but did not digest it. Instead, the two lived together, and the swallowed partner became the mitochondrion, the cell's power station. Plants gained chloroplasts in a similar way, by absorbing cyanobacteria. This idea, called endosymbiosis, was championed by biologist Lynn Margulis in the 1960s and is now widely accepted. Complex cells appear in the fossil record at least 1.6 billion years ago.

sections.key: Around 538 million years ago, most major animal groups appeared relatively rapidly in the fossil record.
sections.b: For most of Earth's history, life was microscopic. Soft-bodied multicellular organisms appeared in the Ediacaran Period, from about 635 million years ago. Then, from around 538 million years ago, most major groups of animals appear in the fossil record over a relatively short span of perhaps 20 million years, an event called the Cambrian explosion. Animals developed eyes, shells, legs and jaws, and predators and prey began an evolutionary arms race. Famous Cambrian fossil sites include the Burgess Shale in Canada, Chengjiang in China, and the Emu Bay Shale on Kangaroo Island in South Australia.

quiz.q: What are the Jack Hills zircons in Western Australia famous for?
o: Being the oldest known pieces of Earth
quiz.e: At about 4.4 billion years old, they are the oldest known Earth material and hint at early liquid water.

quiz.q: What are stromatolites?
o: Layered structures built by microbial communities
quiz.e: Microbial mats trap and bind sediment, building layered structures over time.

quiz.q: Why do stromatolites survive at Hamelin Pool in Shark Bay?
o: The very salty water keeps away many grazing animals
quiz.e: Water about twice as salty as normal seawater keeps away many grazers that would eat the mats.

quiz.q: What caused the Great Oxidation Event around 2.4 billion years ago?
quiz.e: Cyanobacteria released oxygen as a waste product, which eventually built up in the atmosphere.

quiz.q: What was the Cambrian explosion?
o: The asteroid that killed the dinosaurs
The relatively rapid appearance of most major animal groups
quiz.e: From about 538 million years ago, most major animal groups appeared over a geologically short span.

LESSONS.title: Fossils
LESSONS.hook: Almost nothing that dies becomes a fossil. The few that do are messages from deep time, and Australia holds some of the most important.

sections.key: Fossilisation is rare: an organism usually has to be buried quickly, before scavengers and decay destroy it.
sections.b: Most living things vanish after death. Scavengers eat them, bacteria break them down, and weather scatters what's left. To become a fossil, an organism usually needs to be buried quickly, by mud, sand, volcanic ash or sediment at the bottom of a lake or sea, cutting off oxygen and scavengers. Hard parts like bones, teeth and shells have the best chance of surviving. That's why the fossil record is dominated by shelled sea creatures and why a complete dinosaur skeleton is a rare prize. Remains are generally only called fossils once they are more than about 10,000 years old.

sections.key: In many fossils, minerals from groundwater fill or replace the original material, turning it into rock.
sections.b: Once buried, remains can be preserved in several ways. In permineralisation, groundwater seeps into tiny spaces in bone or wood and deposits minerals such as silica or calcite, gradually turning it to stone while keeping fine detail. Sometimes the original material dissolves completely, leaving a hollow mould that may later fill with minerals to form a cast. Occasionally, soft tissue survives: insects trapped in amber, mammoths frozen in Siberian permafrost, or animals preserved in tar pits. In some exceptional sites, fine sediment preserves skin, feathers or even internal organs.

sections.key: Trace fossils, like footprints, burrows and fossilised dung, record behaviour rather than bodies.
sections.b: Not all fossils are bodies. Trace fossils record what living things did: footprints, trackways, burrows, bite marks, nests and coprolites, which is the polite name for fossilised dung. Trace fossils can reveal things that bones can't, such as how fast an animal moved, whether it travelled in groups, or what it ate. At Lark Quarry near Winton in Queensland, thousands of dinosaur footprints were once interpreted as a stampede; some researchers now argue they were made by dinosaurs wading or swimming. Either way, they capture a moment of behaviour about 95 million years ago.

sections.key: Fossils are dated using rock layers and radiometric dating of nearby volcanic rock; carbon dating only works to about 50,000 years.
sections.b: Scientists date fossils in two main ways. Relative dating uses the principle of superposition: in undisturbed layers, deeper rocks are older. Certain widespread fossils, called index fossils, help match layers across regions. For actual ages, scientists use radiometric dating, measuring the steady decay of radioactive elements such as uranium or potassium in volcanic ash layers above and below a fossil. A common myth is that dinosaurs are carbon dated. In fact, radiocarbon dating only works back to about 50,000 years, so it's useful for mammoths or early human sites, not dinosaurs.

sections.key: Mary Anning's marine reptiles and the first named dinosaurs, Megalosaurus and Iguanodon, changed how we understood the history of life.
sections.b: Some fossil finds changed science. In the early 1800s, Mary Anning, a working-class woman from Lyme Regis in England, found the first ichthyosaur skeleton to be recognised scientifically and one of the first plesiosaurs, helping prove that extinction was real. She was largely denied credit in her lifetime. In 1824, William Buckland described Megalosaurus from bones found near Oxford, the first dinosaur to be scientifically named. A year later Gideon Mantell named Iguanodon from teeth that resembled giant iguana teeth. Early reconstructions got a lot wrong: Iguanodon's thumb spike was first placed on its nose like a rhino's horn. Each new find forced a rethink.

sections.key: The Ediacara fossils of the Flinders Ranges are among the oldest complex life, and gave their name to a geological period.
sections.b: In 1946, geologist Reg Sprigg noticed strange impressions in rocks in the Ediacara Hills of South Australia's Flinders Ranges. They turned out to be some of the oldest large, complex organisms known, soft-bodied creatures living on the sea floor over 550 million years ago, before the Cambrian explosion. Some, like the oval, ribbed Dickinsonia, are now thought to be early animals. In 2004, a new geological time period, the Ediacaran, was named after the site, the first new period added to the geological timescale in over a century, with its official boundary marker in the Flinders Ranges.

sections.key: Only a tiny fraction of species ever fossilised, and the record favours hard parts, seas and certain environments.
sections.b: The fossil record is a hugely incomplete library. Only a tiny fraction of all species that have ever lived are thought to have been preserved, and fewer still have been found. It is biased toward animals with hard parts, living in or near water where sediment builds up. Soft-bodied creatures, and those in forests or mountains, rarely fossilise. Much fossil-bearing rock has been eroded, buried deep or recycled by plate tectonics. Gaps are expected, not suspicious. Yet predictions still work: in 2004, researchers searched rocks of the right age and found Tiktaalik, a transitional fish with limb-like fins.

sections.key: Fossil collecting is restricted in parks and many sites; check the rules and report significant finds to a museum.
sections.b: Fossil hunting can be a rewarding hobby, but rules matter.
