Collecting is generally banned in national parks and many protected sites, and important fossils, such as those at Ediacara, are protected by law. Rules vary between states, so check before you dig, and always get landholder permission on private land. If you find something that looks significant, photograph it where it lies, note the location, and contact your state museum. Many major Australian finds, including dinosaurs around Winton, were first spotted by farmers and members of the public. Museum fossil days and guided digs are a great way to start.

quiz.q: What usually has to happen for an organism to become a fossil?
o: It must die in a desert
It must be eaten by a predator
quiz.e: Rapid burial protects remains from scavengers and decay, giving fossilisation a chance.

quiz.q: Which of these is a trace fossil?
quiz.e: Trace fossils record behaviour, like footprints, burrows and coprolites, rather than body parts.

quiz.q: Why aren't dinosaur fossils dated with radiocarbon?
o: It only works back to about 50,000 years
quiz.e: Radiocarbon decays too quickly; dinosaurs are dated using radiometric methods on nearby volcanic layers.

quiz.q: Which was the first dinosaur to be scientifically named, in 1824?
quiz.e: William Buckland described Megalosaurus from bones found near Oxford; Iguanodon followed in 1825.

quiz.q: What is special about the Ediacara fossils of the Flinders Ranges?
o: They are among the oldest complex life and named a geological period
quiz.e: The Ediacaran Period, named in 2004, was the first new geological period in over a century.

LESSONS.title: Cardio fitness
LESSONS.hook: Your heart is a muscle that answers to training. How fit it is may say more about your future health than almost any other number.

sections.key: Cardio trains your heart, lungs, blood vessels and muscles to deliver and use oxygen more efficiently.
sections.b: Cardiovascular exercise is any sustained activity that raises your heart rate and breathing: brisk walking, cycling, swimming, running, rowing, even vigorous gardening. It trains a whole delivery system. With regular training, the heart pumps more blood with each beat, so it can beat less often. Muscles grow more tiny blood vessels, called capillaries, and more mitochondria, the structures inside cells that turn oxygen and fuel into energy. That's why a trained person's resting heart rate is often lower. A typical adult resting rate sits somewhere between 60 and 100 beats per minute, and many endurance athletes rest in the 40s or 50s.

sections.key: Regular cardio lowers the risk of heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes and several cancers.
sections.b: Heart disease is one of the leading causes of death in Australia, and regular aerobic exercise is one of the most reliable ways to reduce the risk. It helps lower blood pressure, improves cholesterol levels, makes the body more sensitive to insulin and helps with weight management. People who stay active also have lower rates of stroke, type 2 diabetes, depression and some cancers, including bowel and breast cancer. The benefits start quickly: even a week or two of regular activity improves how your body handles blood sugar. You don't need to become an athlete; the biggest gains come when an inactive person starts moving.

sections.key: Heart rate zones are rough bands of effort, based on a percentage of your maximum heart rate.
sections.b: Many fitness trackers divide effort into zones based on your maximum heart rate. A common rough estimate of maximum is 220 minus your age, so about 180 beats per minute for a 40-year-old, though real maximums vary by 10 or more beats either way. Easy, conversational effort, often called zone 2, sits at roughly 60 to 70% of maximum. That overlaps the lower end of moderate intensity, which runs up to about 76% of maximum; vigorous work sits above that. Wrist-based heart rate readings can lag or jump during intervals, so many coaches also use a simple 0 to 10 effort scale alongside them, where easy zone 2 work feels like about a 3 or 4.

sections.key: Most training can be easy, with a smaller amount of harder intervals to push fitness up.
sections.b: Many endurance coaches follow a pattern often called polarised training: roughly 80% of sessions at an easy, comfortable pace and about 20% at hard effort. Easy sessions build the aerobic base with little strain, so you can do more of them. Hard intervals, such as four bouts of four minutes at high effort with recovery in between, push the heart and lungs close to their limit and are an efficient way to raise fitness. High-intensity interval training, or HIIT, suits people short on time. The exact best ratio is still debated, but mixing mostly easy work with some hard work is well supported.

sections.key: VO2 max, the most oxygen your body can use, is strongly linked with longer life.
sections.b: VO2 max measures the maximum amount of oxygen your body can take in and use during hard exercise, usually expressed in millilitres per kilogram of body weight per minute. It's the gold-standard measure of aerobic fitness, measured precisely in a lab with a mask, though many smartwatches now give an estimate. Large observational studies have found that people with higher cardiorespiratory fitness tend to live longer, and low fitness is associated with a mortality risk comparable to well-known risk factors like smoking. VO2 max naturally declines with age, but training slows that decline, and people who start at any age can improve it.

sections.key: Australia's 2026 guidelines ask adults for 30 minutes or more of moderate to vigorous activity on most days, and 7,000 or more steps a day.
sections.b: In March 2026, Australia replaced its physical activity guidelines with 24-hour movement guidelines that cover the whole day: activity, sitting and sleep. For cardio, the message is now simpler. Adults of all ages should do 30 minutes or more of moderate to vigorous activity on most days, adding up to about two and a half hours a week, plus several hours of light activity, such as pottering around the house or garden. Australia also became the first country to put a daily step target in its official advice: 7,000 or more steps for adults aged 18 to 64 who track them. Muscle strengthening on two or more days, and balance and mobility work on three or more, round out the week.

sections.key: Start gently, build gradually and see a doctor first if you have symptoms or a heart condition.
sections.b: For most people, moderate activity like walking is very safe, and the risks of staying inactive are far greater. But if you have a heart condition, chest pain, dizziness, unexplained shortness of breath, or other chronic health issues, speak with your GP before starting something new. Exercise & Sports Science Australia publishes a short pre-exercise screening questionnaire that helps flag when to get checked first. Stop and seek medical help if you feel chest pain or pressure, severe breathlessness or faintness during exercise. Begin with sessions you can finish comfortably, and increase time or intensity a little each week rather than all at once.

sections.key: Consistency beats intensity: pick something you enjoy and make it easy to repeat.
sections.b: The best cardio is the kind you'll keep doing. Walking is underrated: it's free, low-impact and counts as moderate activity if it's brisk. Try pairing movement with things you already do, like walking part of your commute or taking phone calls on foot. Swimming and cycling are kind to sore joints. Parkrun, the free weekly 5 km event held in hundreds of Australian locations, welcomes walkers as well as runners. Tracking minutes rather than distance helps beginners stay patient. Remember this is general information, not personal advice; a GP or accredited exercise physiologist can tailor a plan to your health.

quiz.q: Why does a trained person often have a lower resting heart rate?
o: Their heart pumps more blood with each beat
Their muscles need no oxygen at rest
quiz.e: Training increases the amount of blood pumped per beat, so the heart can beat less often.

quiz.q: Roughly what effort is 'zone 2'?
o: Easy, conversational effort around 60–70% of maximum
quiz.e: Zone 2 is easy, conversational effort at roughly 60 to 70% of maximum heart rate.

quiz.q: What does VO2 max measure?
o: The maximum oxygen your body can use during hard exercise
How many steps you take a day
quiz.e: VO2 max is the maximum rate at which you can take in and use oxygen, a key marker of aerobic fitness.

quiz.q: What daily step target do Australia's 2026 movement guidelines set for adults who track their steps?
quiz.e: The 2026 guidelines recommend 7,000 or more steps a day, a level that captures most of the health benefits of walking.

quiz.q: Which symptom during exercise means you should stop and seek medical help?
quiz.e: Chest pain or pressure, severe breathlessness or faintness during exercise needs prompt medical attention.

LESSONS.title: Strength training
LESSONS.hook: Muscle is not vanity. It is what lets you climb stairs, carry shopping and get up off the floor at 85.

sections.h: Why strength matters at every age
sections.key: Strength training protects muscle, bone and independence, and benefits people of every age.
sections.b: From around your 30s, you gradually lose muscle mass and strength unless you do something about it, and the loss speeds up after about 60. Severe age-related muscle loss has a name: sarcopenia. It raises the risk of falls, fractures and losing independence. Strength training is the most effective way to slow or reverse this. It also improves blood sugar control, supports healthy bones and joints, and helps with everyday tasks. Studies show that people in their 80s and 90s can still build meaningful strength with supervised training. Grip strength, a simple measure of overall strength, is linked with longer life in large studies.

sections.key: Loading muscles and bones makes them adapt; muscle also helps the body manage blood sugar.
sections.b: Muscle and bone both respond to load. When you lift something challenging, muscle fibres are stressed and then rebuild stronger. Bones also adapt to the forces placed on them, which is why resistance and impact exercise matter for preventing osteoporosis. An Australian trial at Griffith University, called LIFTMOR, found that carefully supervised heavy resistance and impact training improved bone density in postmenopausal women with low bone mass. Muscle is also the body's biggest store for glucose from food, so more muscle helps keep blood sugar steady. Each kilogram of muscle burns only slightly more energy at rest than fat, so the metabolism boost is often overstated.

sections.key: To keep getting stronger, gradually increase the challenge: more weight, reps or sets over time.
sections.b: The core principle of strength training is progressive overload. Your body adapts to the demands you place on it, then stops adapting once a load feels easy. To keep improving, you gradually increase the challenge: add a little weight, do an extra repetition, add a set, slow the movement down or reduce rest. For example, if you can do 10 good squats with a 10 kg dumbbell, you might aim for 12 next week, then move to 12 kg. Research shows muscles can grow across a wide range of loads, from about 6 to 30 repetitions, as long as sets are taken close to fatigue.

sections.key: Compound lifts like squats, deadlifts, presses and rows work many muscles at once.
sections.b: Compound exercises use several joints and muscle groups at once, so they give you the most return for your time. The classic big movements are the squat, the deadlift or hip hinge, the bench or push-up, the overhead press, and the row or pull-up. Together they train your legs, hips, back, chest, shoulders and arms, and they mirror real life: squatting to sit, hinging to lift a box, pushing a door and pulling a heavy bag. Machines, dumbbells, resistance bands and bodyweight all work. Learning good technique with lighter weights first, ideally with a qualified coach, reduces injury risk.

sections.key: Australian guidelines recommend muscle-strengthening activity on at least two days a week.
sections.b: Australia's 24-hour movement guidelines, updated in 2026, recommend muscle-strengthening activities on at least two days each week for adults, alongside aerobic exercise. Two full-body sessions of 30 to 45 minutes are enough for most beginners to make steady gains. A simple starting point is one exercise for each major movement pattern, two or three sets each, stopping with one to three repetitions still 'in the tank'. All adults are now encouraged to do balance and mobility activities on three or more days a week, which matters most later in life for preventing falls. More experienced lifters may train three to five days a week, often splitting upper and lower body, but beginners improve well on much less.

sections.key: Protein supports muscle repair; many lifters aim for about 1.2–1.6 g per kilogram of body weight daily.
sections.b: Muscles are built from protein, so eating enough supports your training. Australia's nutrient reference values set a baseline of about 0.84 grams per kilogram of body weight a day for men and 0.75 for women, rising for people over 70. Research on people who lift suggests benefits for muscle growth tend to level off at around 1.6 grams per kilogram. Spreading intake across the day, with a decent serve of about 20 to 40 grams at each meal, seems helpful. Eggs, meat, fish, dairy, tofu, legumes and nuts all count. Most people can meet their needs from food; protein powder is convenient, not essential.

sections.key: Muscles get stronger during rest, so sleep, food and recovery days are part of training.
sections.b: Training is the stimulus; recovery is when you actually get stronger. After a hard session, muscles need time to repair, and many programs give each muscle group around 48 hours before training it hard again. Sleep matters a great deal, because growth and repair processes are active overnight. Muscle soreness a day or two after a new workout, called delayed onset muscle soreness, is normal and fades as you adapt; it isn't a measure of how good a session was. Sharp pain, pain in a joint, or pain that doesn't settle is different, and worth getting checked by a physiotherapist or doctor.

sections.key: Women won't get 'bulky' by accident, you can't spot-reduce fat, and supervised lifting is safe for teens.
sections.b: Several myths keep people out of the weights room. Women worry about getting bulky, but building large muscles takes years of deliberate training and eating; most women simply get stronger and more toned. You can't burn fat from one spot by exercising it, so endless crunches won't flatten a stomach on their own. Properly supervised strength training is considered safe for children and teenagers and doesn't stunt growth. And it's never too late: older beginners often see the biggest improvements. This is general information, not personal advice; if you have a health condition, talk to your doctor or an accredited exercise physiologist first.

quiz.q: What is sarcopenia?
o: Age-related loss of muscle mass and strength
quiz.e: Sarcopenia is severe age-related loss of muscle, which raises the risk of falls and frailty.

quiz.q: What is progressive overload?
o: Gradually increasing the challenge over time
Only lifting until you feel sore
quiz.e: Progressive overload means steadily increasing weight, reps, sets or difficulty so your body keeps adapting.

quiz.q: Which of these is a compound exercise?
quiz.e: A squat works the hips, knees and ankles and many muscles at once, making it a compound movement.

quiz.q: Around what daily protein intake do benefits for muscle growth tend to level off?
o: 0.2 g per kg of body weight
5 g per kg of body weight
10 g per kg of body weight
About 1.6 g per kg of body weight
quiz.e: Research on people who lift suggests gains tend to plateau at around 1.6 grams per kilogram per day.

quiz.q: Can you burn fat from your stomach by doing lots of crunches?
o: Yes, fat burns where the muscle works
Only if you do them daily
quiz.e: Fat loss happens across the body; exercising one area doesn't burn fat from that spot.

LESSONS.title: Alcohol and your body
LESSONS.hook: It's Australia's favourite social drug. Here's what actually happens after that first sip, and what 'a standard drink' really means.

sections.key: Alcohol is absorbed mostly through the small intestine and reaches every organ within minutes.
sections.b: The alcohol in drinks is ethanol, a small molecule that dissolves in both water and fat, so it spreads easily through the body. A little is absorbed through the stomach, but most passes into the blood from the small intestine. Food in the stomach slows this, which is why drinking on an empty stomach hits harder. Within minutes it reaches the brain and every other organ. People with less body water, often smaller people and women on average, reach a higher blood alcohol concentration from the same drink. Alcohol also carries energy: about 29 kilojoules per gram, nearly as much as fat, with no nutritional value.

sections.key: The liver clears roughly one standard drink an hour, and nothing speeds that up.
sections.b: Your liver does most of the work of clearing alcohol. Enzymes first convert ethanol into acetaldehyde, a toxic compound that damages cells and DNA, then convert that into acetate, which the body can use or break down. The liver works at a fairly fixed pace, roughly one standard drink an hour for many people, though it varies. Coffee, cold showers, food after the fact or exercise don't speed it up; they may make you feel more alert, but your blood alcohol level only falls with time. That's why you can still be over the limit the morning after a big night.

sections.key: In Australia, a standard drink contains 10 grams of pure alcohol, and most serves hold more than one.
sections.b: In Australia, one standard drink contains 10 grams of pure alcohol, whatever the drink. Serves rarely line up neatly. A 375 mL can of full-strength beer is about 1.4 standard drinks, while mid-strength is about one. A 150 mL glass of wine, a common restaurant pour, is about 1.5, and a 750 mL bottle of wine is around 7 to 8. A 30 mL nip of spirits is about one, but pre-mixed cans are often 1.5 to 2 or more. Australian labels must state the number of standard drinks, so checking the label is the easiest way to keep count.

sections.key: To reduce health risks, healthy adults should drink no more than 10 standard drinks a week and no more than 4 on any one day.
sections.b: Australia's National Health and Medical Research Council updated its alcohol guidelines in 2020. To reduce the risk of harm from alcohol-related disease or injury, healthy adults should drink no more than 10 standard drinks a week and no more than 4 standard drinks on any one day. The guidelines also say the less you drink, the lower your risk. People under 18 should not drink alcohol, and women who are pregnant, planning a pregnancy or breastfeeding are advised not to drink. The guidelines describe a level of risk, not a safe threshold: no amount of drinking is completely risk-free.

sections.key: In the short term, alcohol slows reaction time, impairs judgement and disrupts sleep.
sections.b: Alcohol is a depressant: it slows communication in the brain. A drink or two can bring relaxation and lower inhibitions, but also slower reactions and poorer judgement, which is why the blood alcohol limit for fully licensed drivers across Australia is 0.05. At higher levels come slurred speech, poor coordination, vomiting and memory blackouts, and very high levels can suppress breathing. Alcohol may help you fall asleep, but it disrupts sleep later in the night, especially REM sleep. Hangovers come from a mix of dehydration, poor sleep, inflammation and the effects of acetaldehyde. Alcohol is also a factor in many injuries, falls and assaults.

sections.key: Regular drinking raises the risk of at least seven cancers, liver disease, heart problems and dependence.
sections.b: The International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies alcohol as a Group 1 carcinogen, its highest category of evidence. Alcohol is linked with at least seven cancers: mouth, throat, voice box, oesophagus, liver, bowel and breast. Risk rises with the amount you drink over time. Long-term heavy drinking can cause fatty liver, hepatitis and cirrhosis, high blood pressure, irregular heart rhythms and a weakened heart muscle. It can also affect mood, memory and sleep, and lead to dependence. The older idea that a daily drink protects the heart is now contested, as newer research suggests earlier studies overstated the benefit.

sections.key: Drinking is deeply woven into Australian social life, and understanding your own pattern matters more than labels.
sections.b: Alcohol is part of many Australian celebrations, sports and workplaces, and most people who drink do so for ordinary reasons: to relax, to celebrate or to fit in socially. There's no need for shame in looking at your habits honestly. It can help to notice patterns rather than labels. Do you drink mostly when stressed, bored or with certain people? Do weekend sessions go well past four drinks? Do you find it hard to stop once you start? Signs worth taking seriously include drinking more than you meant to, needing more to feel the effect, or feeling unwell when you don't drink.

sections.key: Alcohol-free days, counting drinks and choosing low or no-alcohol options all help reduce intake.
sections.b: If you want to drink less, small practical steps work well. Plan several alcohol-free days each week. Count your standard drinks using the labels or a tracking app. Alternate alcoholic drinks with water, eat before and while drinking, and try mid-strength beer or the growing range of zero-alcohol options. Having a ready answer, such as 'I'm driving', makes it easier to say no. Many people try a month off to see how they sleep and feel. If you're worried about your drinking, talk to your GP, or contact the National Alcohol and Other Drug Hotline on 1800 250 015. Heavy drinkers should not stop suddenly without medical advice, as withdrawal can be dangerous.

quiz.q: What speeds up how quickly your liver clears alcohol?
o: Nothing: only time lowers blood alcohol
quiz.e: The liver clears alcohol at a fairly fixed rate; coffee or showers may make you feel alert but don't lower blood alcohol.

quiz.q: How much pure alcohol is in one Australian standard drink?
quiz.e: An Australian standard drink contains 10 grams of pure alcohol.

quiz.q: What does the NHMRC guideline recommend for healthy adults?
o: No more than 14 drinks a week and 6 a day
No more than 10 drinks a week and 4 on any one day
No more than 2 drinks a week
No more than 20 drinks a week
quiz.e: The 2020 guideline is no more than 10 standard drinks a week and no more than 4 on any one day.

quiz.q: How does the International Agency for Research on Cancer classify alcohol?
quiz.e: Alcohol is in Group 1, the category with the strongest evidence that it causes cancer in humans.

quiz.q: Why shouldn't a heavy drinker stop suddenly without medical advice?
o: It lowers blood pressure too far
quiz.e: Alcohol withdrawal in heavy drinkers can be serious, so medical supervision is advised.

LESSONS.title: Knife skills
LESSONS.hook: One good knife, used well, makes cooking faster, safer and far more enjoyable.

sections.key: A chef's knife, a paring knife and a serrated bread knife cover almost everything.
sections.b: You don't need a block of 15 knives. Most cooking needs three. A chef's knife, usually 20 to 25 centimetres long, does the bulk of chopping, slicing and dicing. A small paring knife, around 8 to 10 centimetres, handles fiddly jobs like peeling, trimming and hulling strawberries. A serrated bread knife saws through crusty bread and ripe tomatoes without squashing them. When choosing a chef's knife, hold it if you can: it should feel balanced and comfortable, with enough knuckle clearance above the board. A mid-priced knife that's kept sharp will outperform an expensive one that's neglected.

sections.key: Western knives are usually tougher and thicker; Japanese knives are usually harder, thinner and sharper.
sections.b: Most knives fall into two broad styles. Western, especially German-style, knives tend to use slightly softer, tougher steel and a thicker blade with a curved edge suited to rocking. They're forgiving and easy to maintain. Japanese-style knives, such as the gyuto and santoku, usually use harder steel, which holds a finer, sharper edge, often sharpened to around 15 degrees per side versus roughly 20 for many Western knives. The trade-off is that hard, thin edges can chip if twisted or used on bones or frozen food. Neither style is better overall; it depends on how you cook and how much care you'll give them.

sections.key: Use a pinch grip: thumb and forefinger pinch the blade just in front of the handle.
sections.b: How you hold the knife matters as much as the knife. Most chefs use a pinch grip: the thumb and the side of the index finger pinch the flat of the blade just in front of the handle, with the other three fingers wrapped around the handle. This gives far more control than holding the handle alone with a pointing finger on top. Stand square to the board with the knife in line with your forearm. Let the knife do the work, using a smooth forward or rocking motion rather than pushing straight down, which crushes food instead of slicing it.

sections.key: Curl your guiding hand's fingertips under, and let your knuckles guide the side of the blade.
sections.b: Your other hand, the guiding hand, holds the food using the claw grip. Curl your fingertips under so they're tucked behind your knuckles, with your thumb tucked behind your fingers. The flat side of the blade rests lightly against your knuckles, which act as a guide. As you cut, walk your claw back gradually, and the blade can never reach your fingertips because they're tucked out of the way. It feels awkward at first, so practise slowly on something easy, like a cucumber or carrot. Speed comes naturally with repetition; professional chefs are fast because the motion is automatic, not because they rush.

sections.key: Learn to slice, dice, mince, julienne and chiffonade; even pieces cook evenly.
sections.b: Uniform pieces cook at the same rate, which is the main reason cuts matter. Slicing means cutting across into even pieces. Dicing means cutting into cubes: large, medium or small. Mincing is chopping very finely, used for garlic, ginger and herbs. Julienne is thin matchsticks, around 3 millimetres wide, and brunoise is tiny cubes cut from those matchsticks. Chiffonade is for leafy herbs like basil: stack the leaves, roll them tightly and slice across to make fine ribbons. To dice an onion, halve it through the root, peel, make horizontal and vertical cuts toward the root without cutting through it, then slice across.

sections.key: Stop the board slipping, cut food flat side down, and use wood or plastic boards.
sections.b: Most knife injuries happen when something moves unexpectedly. Put a damp tea towel or a non-slip mat under your chopping board so it can't slide. Before cutting something round, like a potato or onion, slice a thin piece off one side so it sits flat and stable. Use wooden or plastic boards; glass, marble and stone boards blunt knives quickly and are slippery. Keep a separate board for raw meat, or wash it thoroughly after use. Clear clutter and scraps from the board as you go, and give yourself enough space to work.

sections.key: Honing realigns the edge; sharpening removes metal to create a new edge.
sections.b: Honing and sharpening are different jobs. A honing steel, the rod that often comes with knife sets, doesn't really sharpen; it realigns an edge that has bent slightly with use, and a few light strokes before cooking keep a knife performing well. Sharpening grinds away a little metal to form a fresh edge. Whetstones give the best results: a medium grit around 1,000 for regular sharpening, and a finer stone of 3,000 or more for polishing. Pull-through sharpeners are easier but can remove more metal. Many kitchen shops offer sharpening services. A simple test: a sharp knife slices a tomato skin cleanly without pressing.

sections.key: A sharp knife is safer; hand-wash it, store it properly and never catch a falling knife.
sections.b: A sharp knife is safer than a blunt one, because a blunt blade needs more force and is more likely to slip. Wash knives by hand and dry them straight away; dishwashers dull edges and can damage handles. Never leave a knife in a sink of soapy water where someone might reach in. Store knives in a block, on a magnetic strip or with blade guards, not loose in a drawer. Carry a knife point down by your side, and tell people nearby when you're walking behind them with it. If you drop a knife, step back and let it fall; never try to catch it.

quiz.q: Which knife handles the bulk of everyday chopping and slicing?
quiz.e: A chef's knife, usually 20 to 25 cm, does most kitchen cutting.

quiz.q: In the claw grip, what guides the side of the blade?
quiz.e: Fingertips tuck under and the knuckles rest against the flat of the blade as a guide.

quiz.q: What is chiffonade?
o: Fine ribbons of rolled leafy herbs
quiz.e: Chiffonade means stacking and rolling leaves like basil, then slicing across into ribbons.

quiz.q: What does a honing steel mainly do?
o: Removes metal to make a new edge
Realigns an edge that has bent with use
quiz.e: Honing realigns the existing edge; sharpening removes metal to create a new one.

quiz.q: What should you do if you drop a knife?
o: Step back and let it fall
quiz.e: Never try to catch a falling knife; step back and let it land.

LESSONS.title: The science of flavour
LESSONS.hook: Taste happens on your tongue, but flavour happens mostly in your nose. Knowing the difference turns good cooks into great ones.

sections.key: Taste comes from the tongue; flavour combines taste, smell, texture, temperature and more.
sections.b: In everyday speech we use taste and flavour interchangeably, but scientists separate them. Taste is what taste receptors on the tongue and mouth detect: a small set of basic qualities. Flavour is the much bigger experience that combines taste with aroma, texture, temperature, and sensations like the burn of chilli or the fizz of bubbles. Even sound and appearance play a part: people often rate crisps as fresher when the crunch is louder. When you understand which sense each element hits, you can work out what a dish is missing, rather than simply adding more of everything.

sections.key: The five basic tastes are sweet, salty, sour, bitter and umami, detected all over the tongue.
sections.b: Humans detect five well-established basic tastes. Sweet signals energy from sugars. Salty signals sodium, an essential mineral. Sour signals acidity, found in citrus, vinegar and fermented foods. Bitter may have evolved as a warning, since many toxic plants are bitter, though we learn to love bitterness in coffee, dark chocolate and beer. Umami is the savoury taste of glutamate. The old 'tongue map', showing each taste in a separate zone, is a myth: every area with taste buds can detect all five. Researchers are investigating other possible tastes, such as fat, but these remain under debate.

sections.key: Most of what we call flavour comes from smell, including aroma travelling up from the back of the mouth.
sections.b: Your tongue can only report a handful of tastes, but your nose can distinguish a vast range of aromas. When you chew, aroma molecules travel from the back of your mouth up into your nasal cavity, called retronasal smell. That's why food tastes bland with a blocked nose. Try it: pinch your nose, eat a jellybean, and you'll notice only sweetness; let go and the fruit flavour arrives. The often-quoted figure that 80% of flavour is smell isn't precise, but smell clearly contributes most of the variety. Fresh herbs, toasted spices and citrus zest are powerful because they are packed with aromas.

sections.key: Umami is the savoury taste of glutamate, identified in 1908 by Japanese chemist Kikunae Ikeda.
sections.b: In 1908, Japanese chemist Kikunae Ikeda identified glutamate as the source of the deep savoury taste of kombu seaweed broth and named it umami, roughly 'pleasant savoury taste'. It was accepted internationally as a basic taste after receptors for it were found around 2000. Glutamate is abundant in parmesan, ripe tomatoes, mushrooms, soy sauce, fish sauce, anchovies and Vegemite. Umami gets a big boost from synergy: combining glutamate with compounds found in meat, fish and dried shiitake intensifies it far more than either alone. MSG is purified glutamate; food regulators including FSANZ consider it safe, and controlled studies haven't confirmed 'Chinese restaurant syndrome'.

sections.key: Western cooking tends to pair ingredients that share aroma compounds, while East Asian cooking often does the opposite.
sections.b: Why do tomato and basil, or strawberries and cream, feel so right together? One idea, the food pairing hypothesis, says ingredients that share key aroma compounds tend to go well together. It gained fame after British chef Heston Blumenthal found that white chocolate and caviar made a surprisingly good match. In 2011, researchers analysed about 56,000 recipes and found that North American and Western European cuisines do tend to combine ingredients with shared flavour compounds, while East Asian cuisines, such as Korean, tend to avoid them and rely more on contrast. So there's no single rule. Shared aromas create harmony; clashing ones create excitement. Trying both is how cooks discover new favourites.

sections.key: Chilli burn is a pain signal from heat-sensing nerves, not a taste, and fat soothes it better than water.
sections.b: Chilli heat comes from capsaicin, which switches on a receptor in our nerves, called TRPV1, whose normal job is detecting painful heat. So the burn is a pain signal rather than a taste, and your body reacts as if your mouth were genuinely hot, with sweating, flushing and watering eyes. American physiologist David Julius used capsaicin to track down that receptor, work that earned a share of the 2021 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Menthol plays a similar trick on cold-sensing nerves, which is why mint feels cool. Capsaicin dissolves in fat, so milk, yoghurt or coconut milk soothe a burning mouth better than water. Birds barely feel capsaicin, so they eat chillies happily and spread the seeds.

sections.key: Temperature changes how we perceive taste, and contrast in texture and flavour keeps food interesting.
sections.b: Temperature shapes flavour. Cold dulls our perception of sweetness and aroma, which is why ice cream mix tastes cloyingly sweet when warm, and why chilled dishes like gazpacho or potato salad usually need more seasoning than hot ones. Warm food releases more aroma. Contrast also matters: our senses adapt quickly to constant sensations, so a dish that is all one texture or flavour becomes boring. Crunchy toppings on soft food, a sharp pickle beside rich meat, or a sprinkle of salt flakes on caramel keep each mouthful interesting. Many great dishes, from tacos to a bowl of pho with fresh herbs and lime, rely on contrast.

sections.key: Taste as you cook and fix problems: flat needs salt or acid, too salty needs dilution or acid.
sections.b: 'Season to taste' means taste, adjust and taste again. Try a spoonful at each stage, not just at the end. If a dish tastes flat, add salt first, then acid. If it's too salty, dilute it with more unsalted base, or balance it with acid, fat or a little sweetness; the idea that a potato draws out salt is largely a myth, as it mostly just dilutes. Too sour? Add a little sweetness or fat. Too sweet? Add acid or salt. Too bitter? Salt, sweetness and fat all help. Too hot? Add dairy, more base or a touch of sugar. Adjust in small amounts.

quiz.q: Which of these is a myth?
o: Different tongue zones each detect only one taste
Salt is detected by taste buds
quiz.e: Every area with taste buds can detect all five tastes; the tongue map is a myth.

quiz.q: Why does food taste bland when you have a blocked nose?
o: Retronasal smell, which provides most flavour variety, is blocked
quiz.e: Aroma travels from the mouth up to the nose; a blocked nose cuts off most of the flavour.

quiz.q: Who identified umami in 1908?
quiz.e: Japanese chemist Kikunae Ikeda identified glutamate as the source of umami in kombu broth.

quiz.q: What is chilli burn, according to the science of flavour?
o: A pain signal from heat-sensing nerves
An aroma detected by the nose
quiz.e: Capsaicin switches on TRPV1, a receptor that normally detects painful heat, so the burn is pain rather than a taste.

quiz.q: Why do chilled dishes often need more seasoning?
o: Cold dulls our perception of taste and aroma
quiz.e: Cold temperatures reduce how strongly we perceive sweetness, aroma and other flavours.

LESSONS.title: Food safety at home
LESSONS.hook: Australians get food poisoning millions of times a year, and much of it starts in home kitchens. A few habits prevent most of it.

sections.key: Australia has an estimated 4 to 5 million cases of food poisoning each year.
sections.b: Food poisoning is far more common than most people realise. Food Standards Australia New Zealand estimates Australians experience around 4 to 5 million cases each year, leading to tens of thousands of hospitalisations. Many cases are never diagnosed, dismissed as a '24-hour bug'. Common causes include bacteria such as Campylobacter, Salmonella, Listeria and toxin-producing E. coli, and viruses such as norovirus. Some people face a higher risk of serious illness: pregnant women, babies and young children, older people, and anyone with a weakened immune system. For them, extra care matters most, particularly with high-risk foods like soft cheeses, deli meats and raw eggs.

sections.key: Bacteria grow fastest between 5°C and 60°C, so keep cold food cold and hot food hot.
sections.b: Most food poisoning bacteria multiply fastest between 5°C and 60°C, known as the temperature danger zone. In ideal conditions, some can double in number every 20 minutes or so. Below 5°C, growth slows right down; above 60°C, most stop growing and start to die. So keep your fridge at 5°C or below, ideally around 3 to 4°C, and your freezer at about minus 18°C. Hot food that is being held for serving should stay above 60°C. Cooking kills most bacteria, but some produce toxins that heat doesn't destroy, which is why prevention matters more than reheating.

sections.key: Under 2 hours in the danger zone: use or refrigerate. 2–4 hours: use now. Over 4 hours: throw out.
sections.b: The 2-hour/4-hour rule, used by Australian food safety authorities, is a simple guide for ready-to-eat food that's been left out. It counts the total time food has spent between 5°C and 60°C. Under 2 hours, it can be used or put back in the fridge. Between 2 and 4 hours, it should be used straight away and not refrigerated again. Over 4 hours, throw it out. It's especially useful for picnics, barbecues and buffets. On a hot Australian summer day, food warms quickly, so bring an esky with ice bricks and put food away promptly.

sections.key: Keep raw meat away from ready-to-eat food, and wash hands, boards and knives in between.
sections.b: Cross-contamination happens when bacteria spread from raw food, usually meat, poultry or seafood, to food that won't be cooked again. Store raw meat in sealed containers on the bottom shelf of the fridge so juices can't drip onto other food. Use separate chopping boards for raw meat and for salads, or wash boards and knives in hot soapy water between uses. Wash your hands with soap for about 20 seconds after handling raw meat. Don't wash raw chicken: splashing water can spread Campylobacter around the sink and benches, and proper cooking kills the bacteria anyway.

sections.key: Cook chicken, mince and sausages to 75°C in the centre, and take special care with raw-egg dishes.
sections.b: Some foods need to be cooked all the way through. Chicken, minced meat, sausages, rolled or stuffed meats, and burgers should reach 75°C in the thickest part, because mincing or rolling mixes surface bacteria through the middle. A cheap digital meat thermometer takes the guesswork out: push it into the thickest part, away from bone. Eggs deserve special care. In Australia, dishes made with raw or lightly cooked eggs, such as homemade mayonnaise, aioli, eggnog and some desserts, are a leading cause of Salmonella outbreaks. Use pasteurised egg products for anything served raw, keep raw-egg sauces in the fridge and use them within a day.

sections.key: Cool leftovers quickly, refrigerate them promptly, eat within 2–3 days and reheat to steaming hot.
sections.b: Leftovers are safe if handled well. Put cooked food in the fridge as soon as it stops steaming, rather than letting it cool on the bench for hours. Divide large batches into smaller, shallow containers so they cool faster. Eat refrigerated leftovers within about 2 to 3 days, or freeze them. When reheating, make sure food is steaming hot all the way through, ideally 75°C, and only reheat it once. Cooked rice needs extra care: spores of the bacterium Bacillus cereus can survive cooking and produce toxins if rice sits at room temperature, so cool and refrigerate it quickly.

sections.h: Symptoms and when to get help
sections.key: Symptoms include nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, cramps and fever; see a doctor if they're severe or persistent.
sections.b: Food poisoning symptoms usually include nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, stomach cramps, and sometimes fever, headache or aches. They can start within a few hours of eating or take several days, depending on the cause; Listeria can take weeks. That means the last meal you ate isn't always the culprit. Most cases pass within a few days. The main priority is fluids: sip water or oral rehydration solution from a pharmacy. See a doctor if you have blood in your stool, signs of dehydration such as dizziness or very little urine, a high fever, or symptoms lasting more than a few days, and seek help early if you're in a high-risk group.

sections.key: Clean, chill, separate and cook: four habits prevent most home food poisoning.
sections.b: Most home food poisoning can be prevented with four habits. Clean: wash hands before cooking and after handling raw meat, and keep benches, boards and tea towels clean. Chill: refrigerate food promptly and check your fridge temperature with a cheap thermometer. Separate: keep raw and ready-to-eat foods apart. Cook: cook high-risk foods thoroughly. Also avoid cooking for others while you're sick with vomiting or diarrhoea, and for at least 48 hours after symptoms stop. Don't use cracked or dirty eggs. When in doubt, throw it out; a smell test can't detect many harmful bacteria. This is general information, not medical advice.

quiz.q: In ideal conditions, how quickly can some food poisoning bacteria double in number?
quiz.e: That's why food left in the 5°C to 60°C danger zone becomes risky surprisingly quickly.

quiz.q: Ready-to-eat food has been out of the fridge for 3 hours. What does the 2-hour/4-hour rule say?
o: Use it straight away, don't refrigerate
quiz.e: Between 2 and 4 hours, food should be used immediately and not put back in the fridge.

quiz.q: Why shouldn't you wash raw chicken?
o: Splashing water spreads bacteria around the kitchen
quiz.e: Washing splashes bacteria like Campylobacter onto sinks and benches; cooking kills them anyway.

quiz.q: Which homemade foods are a leading cause of Salmonella outbreaks in Australia?
o: Raw-egg dishes like mayonnaise and aioli
quiz.e: Raw or lightly cooked eggs can carry Salmonella, so use pasteurised egg products for dishes served raw.

quiz.q: Why does cooked rice need extra care?
o: Bacillus cereus spores can survive cooking and produce toxins
quiz.e: Bacillus cereus spores survive cooking and can produce toxins if rice is left at room temperature.

LESSONS.title: The science of baking
LESSONS.hook: A cake is a chemistry experiment you get to eat. Understand the reactions and your baking stops being luck.

sections.key: Baking is less forgiving than cooking because the ingredients are reacting chemically, not just heating up.
sections.b: A stir-fry forgives a heavy hand with the garlic. A cake is less generous, because once batter goes into the oven you can't taste and adjust. Flour, water, fat, sugar, eggs and raising agents are all reacting with each other: proteins bond, gases expand, starches swell and set, sugars brown. Each ingredient does a specific job, and changing one quantity changes the whole structure. That is why swapping butter for oil, halving the sugar or skipping an egg can turn a good recipe into a dense, dry or collapsed one. Knowing what each ingredient does lets you troubleshoot instead of guess.

sections.key: You control gluten through flour choice, mixing, resting and fat: more makes a bake chewy, less keeps it tender.
sections.b: Gluten is the stretchy protein network that forms when wheat flour is wetted and worked. It traps gas and gives baked goods their structure, and how much you want depends on what you're making. You control it in four ways. Flour choice: bread flour typically has around 12% protein or more, while plain flour usually has around 10%, so bread flour builds a stronger, chewier network. Mixing: overmixed muffin batter comes out tough, with long tunnels inside. Resting: time lets gluten relax, which is why pastry and pizza dough roll out more easily after a rest in the fridge. Fat: it coats the proteins and limits gluten, which is why pastry fat is called 'shortening': it keeps gluten strands short.

sections.key: Yeast ferments sugars into carbon dioxide and alcohol, raising dough slowly and adding flavour.
sections.b: Baker's yeast is a single-celled fungus, Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Given warmth, moisture and food, it ferments sugars from the flour into carbon dioxide gas and a little alcohol. The gluten network traps the gas and the dough rises. Fermentation also builds flavour, which is why slow, cool rises, even overnight in the fridge, often make tastier bread. Yeast likes lukewarm conditions; very hot water can kill it, and it dies in the oven as the loaf heats through. Salt slows yeast down, so it helps control the rise, but don't dump salt directly onto yeast. Sourdough uses wild yeasts and bacteria instead.

sections.key: Bicarb soda is roughly three to four times stronger than baking powder, and both lose power with age.
sections.b: Chemical raising agents work much faster than yeast, but they are easy to get wrong. Bicarb soda is roughly three to four times as powerful as baking powder, so swapping one for the other spoon for spoon can ruin a bake. Baking powder also loses strength once the tin is opened, especially in a humid kitchen. To test it, stir half a teaspoon into a little hot water: lively fizzing means it's still good. Test bicarb with a splash of vinegar instead. Out of self-raising flour? A common substitute is two teaspoons of baking powder sifted into each cup of plain flour. Cocoa matters too: Dutch-processed cocoa has been alkalised, so it won't react with bicarb the way natural cocoa does.

sections.key: Beaten air and steam also raise baked goods, while eggs add structure, richness and emulsifying power.
sections.b: Not all rise comes from yeast or powders. Creaming butter and sugar beats in thousands of tiny air bubbles that expand in the oven. Whisked egg whites trap air too, which is how a sponge or pavlova rises with little or no raising agent. Steam matters as well: choux pastry and Yorkshire puddings puff up almost entirely from water turning to steam. Eggs do several jobs at once. Their proteins set when heated, holding the structure in place; the yolks add fat and richness; and the lecithin in yolks is an emulsifier, helping fat and water blend into a smooth batter.

sections.key: Crust colour depends on sugar, protein, moisture and heat, and glazes or rack position let you control it.
sections.b: Crust colour comes mainly from browning reactions between sugars and proteins, which need a dry surface and temperatures well above boiling point, so the moist crumb inside stays pale. Bakers can steer it. An egg wash adds shine and colour: yolk alone gives a deep golden finish, whole egg a golden gloss, and milk a softer, less shiny brown. Doughs rich in sugar, milk or eggs brown faster, which is why brioche darkens quickly. Alkaline conditions speed browning, so traditional pretzels are dipped in an alkaline bath before baking to get their glossy mahogany crust. If tops darken before the middle is cooked, lay a loose sheet of foil over them. A lower oven rack gives a browner base; a higher one browns the top.

sections.key: Weighing ingredients is far more accurate than cups, and Australian cup and spoon sizes differ from overseas ones.
sections.b: A cup of flour can vary by 20% or more depending on whether you scoop it straight from the bag or spoon it in lightly. That is enough to turn a moist cake into a dry one. Most professional bakers weigh everything, including liquids, using digital scales. Australian measures also differ from others: an Australian cup is 250 millilitres and an Australian tablespoon is 20 millilitres, while the US cup is about 240 millilitres and most other countries use a 15 millilitre tablespoon. Check where a recipe comes from, especially for bicarb soda and salt, where an extra five millilitres really matters.

sections.key: Know your oven, follow the recipe first time, and change one thing at a time when fixing a problem.
sections.b: Ovens often run hotter or cooler than the dial says, so an inexpensive oven thermometer is one of the best baking tools you can own. Fan-forced ovens cook faster; many recipes suggest lowering the temperature by about 20°C. Opening the door early can make cakes sink as the structure hasn't set yet. Common fixes: a peaked, cracked cake usually means the oven was too hot; a dense one may mean old raising agent or overmixing; a pale crust suggests the oven was too cool. Bake a new recipe exactly as written first, then change only one variable at a time so you can see what worked.

quiz.q: Why do muffin recipes tell you to mix only until just combined?
o: To avoid developing too much gluten, which makes them tough
To stop the yeast from dying
To prevent the Maillard reaction starting early
To keep the sugar from dissolving
quiz.e: Extra mixing strengthens the gluten network, giving tough muffins with tunnels inside.

quiz.q: How can you check whether an opened tin of baking powder still works?
o: Stir a little into hot water and look for lively fizzing
Check that it has gone lumpy
Mix it with flour and leave it overnight
quiz.e: Baking powder loses strength over time; strong fizzing in hot water shows it's still active.

quiz.q: Why are traditional pretzels dipped in an alkaline solution before baking?
o: To speed browning and give a deep, glossy crust
quiz.e: Alkaline conditions speed up browning reactions, giving pretzels their dark, shiny crust.

quiz.q: How big is a standard Australian tablespoon?
quiz.e: The Australian tablespoon is 20 mL, larger than the 15 mL tablespoon used in most other countries.

quiz.q: What effect does salt have on yeast in bread dough?
o: It feeds the yeast so the dough rises faster
It slows the yeast down, helping control the rise
It has no effect on yeast
It turns the yeast's gas into steam
quiz.e: Salt slows fermentation, which helps control the rise; just don't dump it directly onto the yeast.

LESSONS.title: Meal planning that works
LESSONS.hook: Twenty minutes of planning on the weekend can save you money, waste and the nightly 'what's for dinner?' dread.

sections.key: Planning meals ahead saves money, cuts food waste and removes daily decision fatigue.
sections.b: Australian households throw away a surprising amount of food. National estimates put household food waste at around 2.5 million tonnes a year, commonly estimated at over $2,000 per household. Much of it is fresh produce bought with good intentions and forgotten in the crisper. Meal planning attacks that directly: you buy what you will actually cook. It also removes the nightly scramble that leads to expensive takeaway, and it makes healthy eating easier because the decision is made while you're calm and not hungry. A plan doesn't have to be rigid. Even three or four planned dinners a week makes a real difference.

sections.key: Check your calendar and what's already in the fridge, freezer and pantry before choosing any meals.
sections.b: Good plans begin with reality, not recipes. Look at the week ahead: which nights are busy with sport, late shifts or visitors, and which nights have time to cook? Match meals to the night: a 15-minute stir-fry for Tuesday training, a slow roast for Sunday. Next, check what you already have. Look in the fridge, freezer and pantry, and note anything that needs using soon, like half a pumpkin or chicken thighs in the freezer. Build your first meals around those. This 'shop your kitchen first' habit is one of the simplest ways to cut both waste and your grocery bill.

sections.key: Choose meals that share ingredients, plan for leftovers, and use theme nights to make choosing easy.
sections.b: When choosing meals, look for overlap. A bunch of coriander can go into Monday's tacos and Wednesday's curry; a roast chicken on Sunday becomes Monday's wraps and Tuesday's soup. This 'cook once, eat twice' approach saves time and uses everything up. Theme nights can remove decision fatigue: pasta Monday, stir-fry Wednesday, fish Friday, with the specific dish changing each week. Keep a list of ten or so reliable family favourites to rotate through, and add one new recipe a week if you enjoy variety. Leave a gap night for leftovers or unexpected plans, because real weeks rarely go exactly as written.

sections.key: Write a list from your plan, grouped by supermarket section, and stick to it.
sections.b: Once meals are chosen, go through each recipe and write down every ingredient you don't already have, with quantities. Group the list by store section, such as produce, meat, dairy and pantry, so you move through the shop once without doubling back. Keep a running list on the fridge or in a phone app for staples as they run low, so you're not caught without oil or rice. A shared digital list helps households avoid buying three jars of the same thing. Then stick to it. Supermarkets are designed to encourage impulse buys, and a list is your best defence against them.

sections.key: Compare unit prices, buy in season, use frozen and tinned staples, and lean on cheaper proteins.
sections.b: Larger Australian supermarkets must display unit prices, such as the price per kilogram or per 100 grams, on shelf labels. Use them: the larger pack isn't always cheaper, and specials sometimes aren't special. Fruit and vegetables in season are usually cheaper and tastier. Frozen vegetables are picked and frozen quickly, keeping their nutrients, and never go limp in the fridge. Tinned tomatoes, beans, lentils and chickpeas are cheap, nutritious and last for ages. Stretch meat with legumes, or use eggs and cheaper cuts like chuck steak or chicken thighs, which suit slow cooking. Home brands are often made to similar standards. And never shop hungry.

sections.key: Cook in bulk, cool food quickly, refrigerate within two hours and freeze portions labelled with the date.
sections.b: Batch cooking means making a big pot of bolognese, curry or soup and portioning it for later meals. It turns one hour of cooking into several dinners. Food safety matters here. Cool cooked food quickly by dividing it into shallow containers, and get it into the fridge within about two hours; you don't need to wait until it is cold. Keep the fridge at 5°C or below and the freezer at about minus 18°C. Label everything with the contents and date. Eat refrigerated leftovers within two to three days, and reheat until steaming hot throughout. Frozen meals keep safely for months, though quality slowly declines.

sections.key: Use-by dates are about safety, best-before dates are about quality; store food well and eat older items first.
sections.b: Date labels confuse many people. A use-by date is about safety: food shouldn't be eaten after it. A best-before date is about quality: food is usually still safe afterwards if stored properly, though it may have lost some freshness. Plenty of good food is binned because of that mix-up. Store food well: leafy greens in a container with a paper towel, bread in the freezer if you won't finish it, herbs in water like flowers. Put older items at the front of the fridge, and try an 'eat me first' shelf for anything close to its date. Wilting vegetables can go into soups, fried rice or frittatas.

sections.key: Start small: plan four dinners, shop from a list, cook once for two meals, and review what worked.
sections.b: Don't try to plan every meal perfectly on day one. Pick one planning time, such as Sunday morning, and plan four dinners. Include one batch-cook meal for leftovers and one quick meal for your busiest night. Check the fridge first, write the list, shop once. At the end of the week, notice what got eaten, what got wasted and what felt like too much effort, then adjust. Keep your plans; after a month you'll have a rotation you can reuse. The Australian Dietary Guidelines recommend plenty of vegetables, and a handy rule of thumb is to fill about half your dinner plate with vegetables or salad.

quiz.q: What is the best way to organise a shopping list?
o: By supermarket section, such as produce, dairy and pantry
By which meal needs it first
quiz.e: Grouping by section gets you through the shop once, without doubling back or forgetting items.

quiz.q: What does a best-before date tell you?
o: The food is unsafe after that date
The food must be frozen by that date
The food is at its best quality until then, but usually still safe after if stored well
The shop must throw it away that day
quiz.e: Best-before is about quality. Use-by is the date that matters for safety.

quiz.q: How soon should cooked food for batch cooking go into the fridge?
o: Only once it is completely cold, however long that takes
quiz.e: Cool food quickly in shallow containers and refrigerate within about two hours.

quiz.q: What do unit prices on Australian supermarket shelf labels show?
o: The price per item in the pack
The discount compared with last week
The price per standard amount, like per kilogram or 100 grams
quiz.e: Unit prices let you compare the true cost of different pack sizes and brands.

quiz.q: What does 'cook once, eat twice' mean?
o: Reheating the same meal twice in one night
Planning a meal so it also becomes another meal later in the week
Cooking everything at double the temperature
Only cooking on two nights a week
quiz.e: A Sunday roast chicken can become Monday's wraps, saving time and using everything up.

LESSONS.title: CPR: how to save a life
LESSONS.hook: When someone's heart stops, the next few minutes decide everything. Anyone can help, and doing something is always better than doing nothing.

sections.key: In cardiac arrest the heart stops pumping effectively; without CPR, the chance of survival drops with every minute.
sections.b: A heart attack is a blocked blood supply to the heart muscle; the person is usually awake and in pain. Cardiac arrest is different: the heart's electrical rhythm fails and it stops pumping blood. The person collapses, becomes unresponsive and stops breathing normally. A heart attack can trigger cardiac arrest, but so can drowning, electric shock and other causes. Without blood flow, the brain starts to be damaged within minutes, and survival falls with every minute that passes without CPR. In Australia only around one in ten people survive a cardiac arrest outside hospital, but prompt CPR and defibrillation by bystanders greatly improve those odds.

sections.key: DRSABCD is the Australian first aid action plan: Danger, Response, Send for help, Airway, Breathing, CPR, Defibrillation.
sections.b: Australian first aid follows the ANZCOR action plan DRSABCD. Check for Danger to yourself, bystanders and the casualty. Check Response: talk loudly and squeeze their shoulders. If there is no response, Send for help: call Triple Zero (000), put the phone on speaker, and send someone to find a defibrillator. Open the Airway, turning them onto their side to clear it only if there is something in the mouth. Check Breathing: look, listen and feel for up to 10 seconds. If they are unresponsive and not breathing normally, start CPR. Attach a Defibrillator as soon as one arrives. The Triple Zero operator can talk you through it.

sections.key: If someone is unresponsive and not breathing normally, including occasional gasps, start CPR.
sections.b: One of the biggest reasons bystanders hesitate is uncertainty about breathing. In the first minutes after cardiac arrest, many people make slow, irregular gasping or snoring sounds, called agonal breathing. It can look like breathing, but it isn't effective, and it is actually a sign of cardiac arrest. ANZCOR guidance is clear: if the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally, start CPR. Don't waste time searching for a pulse; that is unreliable even for trained people. If you start CPR on someone who turns out not to need it, the risk of harm is low. The risk of waiting is far higher.

sections.key: Push hard and fast in the centre of the chest: about a third of the chest depth, at 100 to 120 compressions a minute.
sections.b: Kneel beside the person, who should be on their back on a firm surface. Place the heel of one hand on the lower half of the breastbone, in the centre of the chest, with your other hand on top. Keep your arms straight and shoulders over your hands. Press down about one third of the depth of the chest, then let it fully rise again. Aim for 100 to 120 compressions per minute; the beat of the Bee Gees' 'Stayin' Alive' is about right. It is hard physical work. You may hear or feel ribs crack. Keep going: a broken rib heals, but a stopped heart doesn't restart on its own.

sections.key: Give 30 compressions then 2 breaths; if you can't or won't give breaths, continuous compressions alone are fine.
sections.b: The standard ratio in Australia is 30 compressions followed by 2 rescue breaths, for adults, children and infants. To give a breath to an adult, tilt the head back with one hand on the forehead, lift the chin, pinch the nose, seal your mouth over theirs and blow for about one second, watching for the chest to rise. For an infant, keep the head in a neutral position and cover the nose and mouth with your mouth. If you are untrained, unable or unwilling to give breaths, ANZCOR advises doing continuous chest compressions alone. Hands-only CPR still moves oxygen that is already in the blood.

sections.key: An AED can restart a heart in a shockable rhythm; anyone can use one by following its voice prompts.
sections.b: An automated external defibrillator, or AED, analyses the heart's rhythm and delivers an electric shock if it detects a rhythm that can be corrected. You don't need training: turn it on and follow the spoken instructions. Expose the chest, dry it if wet, and stick the pads where the pictures show. Stand clear when told, so no one touches the person while it analyses or shocks. Resume CPR immediately afterwards unless the machine says otherwise. AEDs are designed not to shock someone who doesn't need it. They are found in shopping centres, gyms, sporting clubs and workplaces. Using one within minutes can dramatically increase survival.

sections.key: For children use one or two hands, for infants two fingers; swap rescuers about every two minutes to stay effective.
sections.b: CPR on children follows the same plan and ratio, adjusted for size. For a child, use the heel of one or two hands on the lower half of the breastbone, pressing about one third of the chest depth. For an infant under one year, use two fingers on the lower half of the breastbone. If an AED arrives, use paediatric pads or settings if available; if not, adult pads can be used. Compressions quickly tire you, and tired rescuers push too shallowly. If others are there, swap every two minutes or so with minimal pause. Keep going until the person responds, paramedics take over, or you physically can't continue.

sections.key: Doing CPR is always better than doing nothing; the Triple Zero operator will guide you, and a course builds confidence.
sections.b: Many people worry they will do it wrong or be sued. In reality, a person in cardiac arrest is already clinically dead, and your CPR can only improve their chances. Good Samaritan laws in every Australian state and territory protect people who help in good faith. If you are unsure, call Triple Zero (000): the operator will talk you through each step. Once the person starts breathing normally, place them in the recovery position and watch them closely. This lesson is general information, not a substitute for training. A first aid course, ideally refreshed every year for CPR, gives you hands-on practice and the confidence to act.

quiz.q: What is the recommended rate of chest compressions?
o: As slowly as needed to be accurate
quiz.e: ANZCOR recommends 100 to 120 compressions per minute, about the tempo of 'Stayin' Alive'.

quiz.q: When giving a rescue breath to an adult, about how long should each breath last?
o: About five seconds, as hard as you can
A quick puff lasting a fraction of a second
About one second, watching for the chest to rise
quiz.e: Blow for about one second and watch for the chest to rise.

quiz.q: An unresponsive person makes occasional slow, gasping breaths. What should you do?
o: Start CPR, because gasping is not normal breathing
Check their pulse for a full minute first
quiz.e: Agonal gasping is a sign of cardiac arrest, so start CPR.

quiz.q: You are untrained and not willing to give rescue breaths. What does ANZCOR advise?
o: Shake the person to wake them
quiz.e: Hands-only CPR is far better than no CPR.

quiz.q: Who can use an AED?
o: Anyone, by following its voice prompts
Only people with a current first aid certificate
quiz.e: AEDs are designed for untrained bystanders and only shock rhythms that need it.

LESSONS.title: Bites and stings in Australia
LESSONS.hook: Australia has some of the world's most venomous animals, yet deaths are rare. Good first aid is a big part of why.

sections.key: Australian snakebite deaths are rare; call Triple Zero, keep the person still and never wash, cut or suck the bite.
sections.b: Australia is home to many of the world's most venomous snakes, including brown snakes, tiger snakes and taipans, yet snakebite deaths average only a few per year. Fast first aid and antivenom are the reasons. Many bites are painless and leave little to see, so treat any suspected bite seriously. Call Triple Zero (000). Keep the person lying down and as still as possible, because venom mostly travels through the lymphatic system, which is driven by muscle movement. Don't wash the bite, as venom on the skin can help hospitals identify the snake. Never cut, suck or apply a tourniquet, and don't try to catch or kill the snake.

sections.key: Apply a firm elastic bandage over the bite and then up the whole limb, splint it and keep the person still.
sections.b: The pressure immobilisation technique, developed in Australia, slows the spread of venom. Use a broad elastic bandage if possible, about 10 to 15 centimetres wide. Apply it firmly over the bite first, then start again at the fingers or toes and bandage up to cover the entire limb, as tightly as you would for a sprain. You should just be able to slide a finger under it. Mark the bite site on the bandage with a pen if you can. Then splint the limb to stop it moving, and keep the person completely still until the ambulance arrives. Don't remove the bandage once it is on.

sections.key: Funnel-web spider, blue-ringed octopus and cone shell bites or stings are also treated with a pressure immobilisation bandage.
sections.b: Funnel-web spiders, found mainly along the east coast including Sydney, have venom that can be life-threatening, especially from the males. Since antivenom was introduced in 1981 there have been no recorded deaths, but it depends on good first aid and fast hospital care. Treat any bite from a large black spider in these areas as a funnel-web: call Triple Zero (000), apply a pressure immobilisation bandage and keep the person still, just as for a snake. The same bandage treatment is used for blue-ringed octopus bites and cone shell stings. Blue-ringed octopus venom can stop breathing, so be ready to give rescue breaths or CPR.

sections.key: For redback and most other spider bites, use a cold pack, not a pressure bandage, and seek help if pain is severe.
sections.b: Redback spiders are common around homes, sheds and outdoor furniture. Their bite can cause intense local pain that spreads, along with sweating, nausea and feeling unwell, but no deaths have been recorded since antivenom arrived in the 1950s. Do not apply a pressure bandage: redback venom acts slowly, and pressure makes the pain worse. Instead, wash the area, apply an ice pack or cold compress for pain relief, and seek medical advice, especially if pain is severe or symptoms spread. For most other Australian spiders, such as huntsmen or white-tails, use a cold pack. Call Triple Zero (000) if the person becomes very unwell.

sections.key: For bluebottle stings, pick off tentacles, rinse with seawater, then soak in hot water for 20 minutes; don't use vinegar.
sections.b: Bluebottles, also called Pacific man o' war, wash up on beaches around much of Australia, especially after onshore winds. Their stings are very painful but rarely dangerous. Current ANZCOR guidance is to keep the person still, pick off any remaining tentacles with your fingers, and rinse the area with seawater, not fresh water. Then place the stung area in hot water, as hot as the person can comfortably tolerate without scalding, for about 20 minutes. If hot water isn't available, a cold pack can help ease the pain. Vinegar is not recommended for bluebottle stings; save it for tropical jellyfish. Watch for signs of an allergic reaction.

sections.key: For box jellyfish and other tropical stings, call Triple Zero, douse with vinegar for at least 30 seconds and be ready to start CPR.
sections.b: Box jellyfish stings are among the most dangerous in the world and can stop the heart within minutes. The tiny Irukandji jellyfish, some about the size of a fingernail, cause Irukandji syndrome: the sting may feel mild at first, but often around half an hour later severe back and muscle pain, vomiting, sweating and dangerously high blood pressure can follow. For any sting in tropical waters, get the person out of the water, call Triple Zero (000) and be ready to start CPR. Pour vinegar liberally over the sting for at least 30 seconds to deactivate stinging cells that haven't yet fired, then carefully remove any tentacles. Don't rub the area or use fresh water. Many northern beaches keep vinegar stations for exactly this.

sections.key: Remove a bee sting fast, use a cold pack for most insect stings, and freeze ticks rather than pulling them off.
sections.b: A honeybee leaves its barbed sting in the skin, still pumping venom. Remove it as quickly as possible; speed matters more than technique, so scrape it sideways with a fingernail or pull it out. Then apply a cold pack. Wasps and ants such as jack jumpers don't leave stings behind; wash the area and use a cold pack. For ticks, Australian allergy experts advise 'freeze it, don't squeeze it': kill the tick where it is with a freezing spray such as one containing ether, let it drop off or remove it carefully, rather than squeezing or pulling a live tick, which can inject more allergen.

sections.key: Signs include difficulty breathing, throat or tongue swelling and collapse; lay the person flat, give adrenaline and call Triple Zero.
sections.b: Anaphylaxis is a severe, rapid allergic reaction and can be fatal. In Australia, insect stings, especially from bees and jack jumper ants, are a common cause. Warning signs include difficult or noisy breathing, swelling of the tongue, swelling or tightness in the throat, a hoarse voice, wheezing or persistent coughing, dizziness or collapse, and, in young children, looking pale and floppy. Lay the person flat; don't let them stand or walk, though they can sit if breathing is hard. Give an adrenaline autoinjector into the outer mid-thigh and call Triple Zero (000). If in doubt, give adrenaline. This is general information; a first aid course is strongly recommended.

quiz.q: How should a pressure immobilisation bandage be applied for a snakebite?
o: Only a tight tourniquet above the bite
A small plaster over the bite only
Firmly over the bite, then up the whole limb, then splint it
Loosely around the bite after washing it
quiz.e: Bandage over the bite, then cover the entire limb as tightly as for a sprain, and splint it.

quiz.q: What is the recommended first aid for a redback spider bite?
o: Apply a cold pack and seek medical advice
quiz.e: Redback venom acts slowly and pressure increases the pain, so a cold pack is used instead.

quiz.q: After removing tentacles and rinsing with seawater, how should a bluebottle sting be treated?
o: Soak it in hot water for about 20 minutes
quiz.e: Hot water, as hot as can be comfortably tolerated, for about 20 minutes is recommended.

quiz.q: Which of these should you avoid doing to a box jellyfish sting?
o: Rubbing it or rinsing it with fresh water
quiz.e: Rubbing or fresh water can make unfired stinging cells discharge. Use vinegar, call Triple Zero and be ready for CPR.

quiz.q: Someone stung by a bee has a swollen tongue and noisy breathing. What should you do?
o: Walk them to the car and drive to a GP
Give them a cold drink and wait
Lay them flat, give an adrenaline autoinjector and call Triple Zero
Remove the sting and watch for an hour
quiz.e: These are signs of anaphylaxis, a medical emergency. Adrenaline and Triple Zero (000) come first.

LESSONS.title: Water safety
LESSONS.hook: Drowning rarely looks like the movies: no splashing, no shouting. Knowing what it really looks like could save someone you love.

sections.key: Several hundred people drown in Australia each year, mostly men, and more in rivers than at beaches.
sections.b: Australia's love of water comes at a cost. Royal Life Saving Australia's annual reports typically record several hundred drowning deaths each year, and many more non-fatal drownings that can leave lasting brain injury. Around four in five people who drown are male. Many people assume beaches are the biggest danger, but rivers, creeks and lakes are often the leading location, particularly in regional areas, where there are no lifeguards and hazards like snags, cold water and strong currents are hidden. Children under five are most at risk in and around home swimming pools. Most drownings are preventable with the right knowledge, supervision and choices.

sections.key: Red and yellow flags mark the area lifesavers are actively watching; always swim between them.
sections.b: The red and yellow flags on Australian beaches mark the safest area to swim, chosen by lifesavers or lifeguards that day, and the part of the water they are actively watching. Swimming outside them, or at unpatrolled beaches, greatly increases the risk of drowning. Before you swim, read the safety signs, check conditions and ask a lifesaver if unsure. Patrol times and seasons vary, so check before you go; apps and websites such as Beachsafe list patrolled beaches. If you get into trouble anywhere, stay calm, raise one arm in the air and wave for help. That is the signal lifesavers look for.

sections.key: Rips often look like calm, deeper, darker gaps with fewer breaking waves, which is why they fool swimmers.
sections.b: Rip currents are strong channels of water flowing away from shore. They are the leading hazard on Australian beaches and have been linked to more deaths than sharks, floods and bushfires combined. The dangerous part is that rips often look like the calmest spot. Look for deeper, darker water; a gap where waves aren't breaking; a rippled surface surrounded by smoother water; sandy or foamy water flowing out past the waves; or debris moving seaward. Spend a few minutes watching from high on the beach before you go in. If you can't tell, swim between the flags, where lifesavers have already chosen a spot away from rips.

sections.key: Stay calm and float; raise an arm to signal for help; swim parallel to shore or towards breaking waves if you can.
sections.b: If you are caught in a rip, the most important thing is not to panic or exhaust yourself swimming straight back against the current. Relax and float to conserve energy; many rips circulate and may bring you back towards shallow water. Raise an arm and wave to signal for help. If you are a capable swimmer, swim parallel to the beach or towards the breaking waves, which usually push back towards shore. If you see someone else caught in a rip, call Triple Zero (000) and alert a lifesaver. Don't go in yourself unless trained; throw them something that floats, such as a boogie board or esky.

sections.key: People who are drowning usually can't shout or wave; they are upright, head low, mouth at water level.
sections.b: Real drowning rarely involves splashing and shouting. A person who is drowning is focused on getting air, so they often can't call out or wave for help. Warning signs include a head low in the water, mouth at water level, tilted back, glassy or unfocused eyes, an upright position with little leg movement, and arms pressing down on the water or making ineffective climbing movements. Children can slip under silently in seconds, sometimes within metres of adults who don't notice. If someone isn't answering when you call out, act immediately. Once they are out of the water, call Triple Zero (000) and follow DRSABCD, starting CPR if needed.

sections.key: Actively watch young children within arm's reach, fence pools properly and never rely on older kids or floaties.
sections.b: Royal Life Saving's Keep Watch program has four simple messages: supervise, restrict access, water awareness and resuscitate. Young children should be within arm's reach of an adult who is actively watching, not on their phone, cooking or chatting. Older children and inflatable toys are not a substitute. Pools must be fenced under state and territory laws, with gates that self-close and self-latch; never prop a gate open, and keep chairs and climbable items away from the fence. Empty buckets, baths and paddling pools after use, since toddlers can drown in just a few centimetres of water. Swimming lessons help, and parents who learn CPR are better prepared.

sections.key: Wear a lifejacket, never fish alone, study the conditions first and never turn your back on the ocean.
sections.b: Rock fishing is one of Australia's most dangerous recreational activities, because large 'king waves' can sweep people off rocks with little warning. Wear a lifejacket; in some high-risk areas of New South Wales it is compulsory. Never fish alone, and tell someone where you are going.
