Check the weather, swell and tide before you go, and watch the spot for at least 20 minutes before setting up. Wear light clothing and non-slip footwear, and never turn your back on the ocean. If you are washed in, swim away from the rocks and float until help arrives. On boats, kayaks and paddleboards, wear a lifejacket too.

sections.key: Alcohol and drugs contribute to many adult drownings; don't drink around water and know your own limits.
sections.b: Alcohol is a factor in a significant share of adult drowning deaths in Australia. It impairs judgement, balance and coordination, lowers body temperature, and encourages risky decisions like swimming at night, jumping into rivers or going out on a boat without a lifejacket. Avoid alcohol and drugs before and during swimming, boating or fishing, and don't swim alone. Be honest about your swimming ability, especially as you age or if you have heart conditions; cold water and fatigue affect everyone. Check conditions and never jump or dive into water you haven't checked for depth. In any emergency, call Triple Zero (000). A first aid and CPR course is a valuable investment.

quiz.q: What do the red and yellow flags on an Australian beach mark?
o: The area patrolled and watched by lifesavers
quiz.e: Swim between the flags, the area lifesavers have chosen and are actively watching.

quiz.q: Which of these can be a sign of a rip current?
o: A calm-looking, darker gap where waves aren't breaking
Lots of seagulls on the beach
quiz.e: Rips often look deceptively calm, deeper and darker, with fewer breaking waves.

quiz.q: What is the first thing to do if you are caught in a rip?
o: Stay calm, float and raise an arm to signal for help
Swim as hard as you can straight back to shore
Dive to the bottom and push off
Take off your clothes to swim faster
quiz.e: Floating conserves energy; signalling brings help. Swim parallel to shore if you can.

quiz.q: What does drowning usually look like?
o: Waving both arms above the head
Quiet, with the head low and mouth at water level
quiz.e: People who are drowning usually can't call out or wave, which is why it is easy to miss.

quiz.q: Which of these is recommended for rock fishing?
o: Fishing alone so you can concentrate
Wearing a lifejacket and never turning your back on the ocean
Fishing at high tide in big swell for better catches
quiz.e: Lifejackets save lives in rock fishing, and waves can arrive without warning.

LESSONS.title: Bushfire safety
LESSONS.hook: Bushfires are part of the Australian landscape. The people who survive them are usually the ones who planned before the smoke appeared.

sections.key: You are at risk if you live, work or travel near bush or grassland, not just deep in the forest.
sections.b: Bushfires can start anywhere there is dry vegetation, including grasslands, farmland and the edges of suburbs. If you live near bush or grass, or travel through it, you are at risk. In southern Australia the main fire season is usually summer and autumn, while in northern Australia it is typically winter and spring, during the dry season. Fires are driven by heat, low humidity, strong wind and dry fuel, and can travel fast; grass fires in particular can outrun a person. Fires can also start without warning, so don't wait for an official message before acting. Your state fire service website can help you understand your area's risk.

sections.key: The Australian Fire Danger Rating System has four levels: Moderate, High, Extreme and Catastrophic.
sections.b: Since September 2022, all states and territories use the Australian Fire Danger Rating System. It tells you how dangerous a fire would be if one started. There are four levels. Moderate, shown in green, means plan and prepare. High, in yellow, means prepare to act. Extreme, in orange, means take action now to protect life and property. Catastrophic, in dark red, means for your survival, leave bush fire risk areas. On days with minimal risk, no rating may be issued. Ratings are forecast for each fire weather district, so check yours daily during the fire season through your state fire service, apps or local news.

sections.key: Bushfire warnings use three levels: Advice, Watch and Act, and Emergency Warning.
sections.b: Once a fire starts, warnings follow the Australian Warning System, which uses three levels. Advice, shown in yellow, means a fire has started but there is no immediate danger; stay up to date. Watch and Act, in orange, means conditions are changing and you need to start taking action to protect yourself and your family. Emergency Warning, in red, means you are in danger and need to take action immediately; any delay puts your life at risk. You may not receive a warning at all, and conditions can change faster than warnings can be issued. If you see or smell smoke and feel threatened, act on your plan straight away.

sections.key: A written plan sets out when you will leave, where you will go, how you'll get there and what you'll take.
sections.b: Every household in a bushfire risk area should have a written bushfire survival plan, and state fire services provide free templates and apps to help. The plan should answer key questions: What will trigger you to leave, such as a certain fire danger rating or warning level? Where will you go, perhaps a friend's house in town or a shopping centre away from the bush? Which routes will you take, and what's the backup? What will you do with pets and livestock? Who needs to be contacted, and who might need help, such as elderly neighbours? Pack an emergency kit with medications, documents, water and chargers. Practise the plan together.

sections.key: Leaving early, well before a fire threatens, is always the safest option; late evacuation is very dangerous.
sections.b: Fire services are clear that leaving early is the safest choice. 'Early' means before a fire starts or at least well before it reaches your area, not when you can already see flames. Late evacuation is extremely dangerous: roads can be blocked by fallen trees, crashes or fire, and heavy smoke makes driving nearly impossible. In the 2009 Black Saturday fires in Victoria, 173 people died, and the Royal Commission found many had left late or sheltered in homes that couldn't protect them. On Catastrophic days, leave high-risk areas. Staying to defend should only be considered by well-prepared, physically fit people with suitable homes and equipment.

sections.key: Clear gutters, cut grass, remove flammable material near the house and block gaps where embers can enter.
sections.b: Most homes lost in bushfires are ignited by embers, which can travel kilometres ahead of the fire front, rather than by the flames themselves. Preparation reduces that risk. Before the season, clean leaves out of gutters, mow grass short, trim branches overhanging the roof, and move firewood, doormats, mulch and gas bottles away from the house. Seal gaps under roofing, eaves and doors, and fit metal mesh screens to windows and vents. Keep hoses long enough to reach all around the house. A well-prepared home is also safer for neighbours and firefighters, even if you plan to leave. Your state fire service can advise on what suits your property.

sections.key: Use your state fire service website or app, ABC local radio and the Emergency Alert system, and never rely on one source.
sections.b: Each state and territory fire service publishes fire danger ratings and live warnings on its website and app, such as Hazards Near Me in New South Wales and VicEmergency in Victoria. ABC local radio is an official emergency broadcaster and will interrupt programs with warnings; keep a battery-powered radio in case power and mobile networks fail. Emergency Alert can send voice messages to landlines and text messages to mobiles in affected areas. Local social media pages can help but may be out of date or wrong, so check official sources. Never rely on a single source, and don't wait to be told to leave.

sections.key: If trapped, seek shelter from radiant heat; in a car, park in a clear area, stay inside and get low under a woollen blanket.
sections.b: Radiant heat is the biggest killer in a bushfire, so shelter from it. Wear long clothing made of natural fibres like wool or cotton, sturdy boots, and cover your nose and mouth. If you are trapped in a car, park away from trees and long grass, ideally in a clear area, with headlights and hazard lights on. Close the windows and vents, stay in the car, get down below window level and cover yourself with a woollen blanket until the front passes, drinking water if you can. Some areas have designated Neighbourhood Safer Places as a last resort. In any emergency, call Triple Zero (000).

quiz.q: What does a Catastrophic fire danger rating tell you to do?
o: Stay home and defend your property
For your survival, leave bush fire risk areas
quiz.e: Catastrophic is the highest rating, and the advice is to leave high-risk areas.

quiz.q: What does a 'Watch and Act' warning mean?
o: Conditions are changing and you need to start taking action
There is no fire in your area
You are in immediate danger and it may be too late to leave
quiz.e: Watch and Act, in orange, is the middle warning level. Emergency Warning is the highest.

quiz.q: According to fire services, what is the safest option in a bushfire?
o: Waiting until you see flames before leaving
Leaving early, well before the fire arrives
Driving towards the fire to check it
quiz.e: Late evacuation is very dangerous due to smoke, blocked roads and fire.

quiz.q: What causes most homes to catch fire in bushfires?
o: Direct flame contact from the fire front only
Embers carried ahead of the fire
quiz.e: Embers can travel kilometres ahead of the fire and ignite gutters, gaps and flammable material.

quiz.q: If you are trapped in a car during a bushfire, what should you do?
o: Get out and run through the smoke
Park in a clear area, stay in the car, get low and cover yourself with a woollen blanket
Open the windows to let smoke out
Keep driving towards the flames to get through quickly
quiz.e: The car body offers shelter from radiant heat while the fire front passes.

LESSONS.title: The continents
LESSONS.hook: Ask how many continents there are and the answer depends on where you went to school. Even the shape of the world on your wall is a compromise.

sections.key: A continent is a large landmass, but where one ends and another begins is partly a human convention.
sections.b: A continent is one of Earth's great landmasses, usually defined by a mix of geology and tradition. Geologists think about continental crust: thick, relatively light rock that floats higher than the dense crust under the oceans, including the shallow continental shelves around the coasts. Everyday maps, though, lean on history and culture. Continents are not neatly separated by oceans. Africa is joined to Asia at the Isthmus of Suez, and North and South America meet at Panama. So the list of continents is less a law of nature than an agreed way of dividing up the land, and different traditions have divided it differently.

sections.key: Australian schools teach seven continents, but six-, five- and four-continent models are also common.
sections.b: In Australia, as in much of the English-speaking world, children learn seven continents: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America and South America. In much of Latin America and parts of Europe, the Americas are taught as a single continent, making six. Some geographers join Europe and Asia into Eurasia, because no ocean divides them. The five Olympic rings stand for the five inhabited continents, leaving out Antarctica. Push the logic further and Afro-Eurasia, the connected landmass of Africa, Europe and Asia, can be treated as one, giving four. None of these is wrong; each reflects a different choice about what counts as separate.

sections.key: Asia is the largest and most populous continent; Australia is the smallest.
sections.b: Asia is the giant, covering about 44 million square kilometres, roughly 30% of Earth's land, and home to around 4.8 billion people, close to 60% of humanity (2024). Africa comes second in area, about 30 million square kilometres, and has the fastest-growing population, around 1.5 billion people (2024). Antarctica, at about 14 million square kilometres, is larger than Europe or Australia but has no permanent residents, only a few thousand researchers in summer. Australia is the smallest continent at about 7.7 million square kilometres. It is also the flattest, with an average elevation of only about 330 metres, while ice-covered Antarctica has the highest average elevation.

sections.key: The Europe–Asia boundary is a historical convention, commonly drawn along the Urals, the Caucasus and the Bosphorus.
sections.b: The split between Europe and Asia is the clearest example of continents as a cultural idea. Ancient Greek geographers divided the world they knew into Europe, Asia and Libya, meaning Africa, and the names stuck. Today the boundary is conventionally drawn along the Ural Mountains and Ural River in Russia, the Caspian Sea, the Caucasus Mountains, the Black Sea and the narrow Bosphorus strait. That line runs through countries: Russia, Turkey, Kazakhstan and Georgia all have territory on both sides. Istanbul famously straddles the Bosphorus, with suburbs in Europe and Asia connected by bridges and tunnels. Geologically, though, Europe sits on the same plate as most of Asia.

sections.key: The Australian continent includes New Guinea and Tasmania; Oceania is a wider region taking in the Pacific islands.
sections.b: Two different ideas often get blurred. The continent of Australia, sometimes called Sahul by scientists, is the landmass on the Australian continental shelf: the mainland, Tasmania and New Guinea. During the last ice age, when sea levels were far lower, these were joined by dry land, and people walked between them. Oceania is a broader region used by geographers, sporting bodies and the United Nations. It covers Australia plus the thousands of Pacific islands usually grouped as Melanesia, Micronesia and Polynesia. New Zealand belongs to Oceania but not to the Australian continent. Australia is also the only country that occupies an entire continental mainland on its own.

sections.key: Zealandia is a mostly drowned continent of about 5 million square kilometres, with New Zealand and New Caledonia as its peaks.
sections.b: In 2017, a team of geologists made a formal case that a mostly submerged landmass in the south-west Pacific qualifies as a continent. They named it Zealandia, or Te Riu-a-Māui in Māori. It covers about 5 million square kilometres, more than half the size of Australia, but roughly 94% of it lies under the sea. New Zealand and New Caledonia are its highest parts. Zealandia is made of continental crust that broke away from the supercontinent Gondwana, which also included Australia and Antarctica, beginning around 85 million years ago. The crust then stretched and thinned, and most of it sank. Not every geographer lists it, but many now accept it.

sections.key: The continents move a few centimetres a year and have joined and split apart many times.
sections.b: The continents are not fixed in place. They ride on tectonic plates that move a few centimetres a year, about as fast as fingernails grow. Around 300 million years ago most land was joined in the supercontinent Pangaea, which later broke apart. Australia was part of its southern half, Gondwana, alongside Antarctica, Africa, South America and India. Australia finally separated from Antarctica in the last 50 million years or so and has been drifting north ever since, currently at about 7 centimetres a year. That movement adds up: Australia's official coordinate system was updated in 2017, shifting positions by about 1.8 metres, so that maps line up with GPS.

sections.key: Flat maps must distort the round Earth; the Mercator projection keeps shapes but hugely inflates areas near the poles.
sections.b: You cannot flatten a sphere without stretching it, so every world map distorts something. The most familiar, the Mercator projection, was designed in 1569 by the Flemish mapmaker Gerardus Mercator for sailors: a constant compass bearing appears as a straight line. The price is that areas balloon towards the poles. Greenland looks about as big as Africa, yet Africa is roughly 14 times larger. Australia looks smaller than it is next to Europe. Equal-area maps, such as the Gall-Peters projection, show true sizes but squash shapes. Compromise projections like the Winkel tripel balance the errors. For true proportions, look at a globe, or compare countries with an online true-size tool.

quiz.q: Why do different countries teach different numbers of continents?
o: Continents are defined partly by convention, not only by nature
Some continents have sunk in recent centuries
The United Nations changes the list every decade
Only seven landmasses sit on continental crust
quiz.e: Whether the Americas or Europe and Asia count as one or two continents is a matter of tradition.

quiz.q: Which of these is part of the Australian continent but not the country of Australia?
quiz.e: New Guinea sits on the same continental shelf and was joined to the mainland by land during the last ice age.

quiz.q: About how much of Zealandia lies under the sea?
quiz.e: Only New Zealand, New Caledonia and a few small islands rise above the waves.

quiz.q: What is the main drawback of the Mercator projection?
o: It greatly exaggerates the size of land near the poles
It cannot show the Southern Hemisphere
It squashes the shapes of all countries
quiz.e: Mercator keeps local shapes and straight bearings but inflates areas towards the poles, so Greenland looks as big as Africa.

quiz.q: Which continent is the smallest?
quiz.e: At about 7.7 million square kilometres, Australia is the smallest continent, and also the flattest.

LESSONS.title: Rivers and mountains
LESSONS.hook: The world's highest peak has seashells at its summit, and nobody can quite agree which river is the longest. Welcome to the restless shape of the land.

sections.h: The longest river: a real debate
sections.key: The Nile is usually listed as longest at about 6,650 km, but some measurements put the Amazon ahead.
sections.b: Most reference books list the Nile as the world's longest river, at about 6,650 kilometres, flowing north to the Mediterranean from a basin shared by eleven countries. The Amazon is usually given as about 6,400 kilometres, but some researchers, including Brazilian scientists in 2007, have argued it is longer, up to around 7,000 kilometres, depending on which remote Andean stream is taken as its source and where its huge estuary is judged to end. The question is genuinely unsettled. On volume there is no contest: the Amazon carries around a fifth of all the fresh water that rivers deliver to the oceans, more than the next several largest rivers combined.

sections.h: Why rivers are hard to measure
sections.key: A river's length depends on choices about its source, its mouth and how finely its bends are traced.
sections.b: Measuring a river sounds simple, but every step involves a judgement. Which of many headwater streams is the true source: the longest, the one carrying the most water, or the one tradition names? Where does the river end in a wide estuary or a delta with many channels? Rivers also meander, and the more detail your map shows, the more bends you trace and the longer the river becomes. Channels shift over time too, as floods cut off old loops. That is why published lengths vary by hundreds of kilometres. After the Nile and Amazon, the Yangtze in China, about 6,300 kilometres, is usually ranked third and is Asia's longest.

sections.key: The Murray is Australia's longest river, and the Murray–Darling Basin covers about one-seventh of the continent.
sections.b: The Murray River, about 2,500 kilometres long, is Australia's longest. It rises in the Australian Alps, forms much of the border between New South Wales and Victoria, and reaches the sea in South Australia. With the Darling, Murrumbidgee and other tributaries it drains the Murray–Darling Basin, about a million square kilometres across four states and the ACT, roughly one-seventh of Australia. The basin is the heart of the nation's irrigated farming. It is also a fragile system: Australia's rivers are highly variable, and heavy water use plus drought left the Murray mouth needing regular dredging from the early 2000s. The 2012 Basin Plan aims to share water between farms, towns and the environment.

sections.key: Most great ranges form where tectonic plates collide; others come from volcanoes or blocks of crust lifted along faults.
sections.b: Mountains are built mainly by plate tectonics. Where two continents collide, neither sinks easily, so the crust crumples and thickens into fold mountains like the Himalayas and the Alps. Where an ocean plate dives under a continent, the rock melts and feeds chains of volcanoes such as the Andes. Some mountains are single volcanoes built over hot spots or rifts, like Kilimanjaro. Others form when blocks of crust are pushed up along faults. Building is only half the story. From the moment rock rises, rain, ice, wind and gravity start wearing it down, which is why young ranges are tall and jagged and old ones are low and rounded.

sections.key: Everest stands about 8,849 metres above sea level and is still rising as India pushes into Asia.
sections.b: Mount Everest, on the border of Nepal and China, is Earth's highest point above sea level. A joint survey announced in 2020 measured it at 8,848.86 metres. It is known as Sagarmatha in Nepal and Chomolungma in Tibet. The Himalayas began rising roughly 50 million years ago when the Indian plate crashed into Asia, and India is still pushing north, so the range is still rising by a few millimetres a year. Limestone near the summit contains fossils of sea creatures, lifted from an ancient ocean floor. Edmund Hillary of New Zealand and Tenzing Norgay, a Sherpa mountaineer, made the first confirmed ascent on 29 May 1953.

sections.h: Highest depends on how you measure
sections.key: Mauna Kea is tallest from base to peak, and Chimborazo's summit is farthest from Earth's centre.
sections.b: Everest is highest above sea level, but there are other ways to rank mountains. Mauna Kea, a volcano in Hawai'i, rises only about 4,200 metres above the sea, yet measured from its base on the ocean floor it stands over 10,000 metres, taller than Everest. Because Earth bulges at the equator, the summit of Chimborazo in Ecuador, about 6,260 metres high, is actually the point on the surface farthest from Earth's centre, about 2 kilometres farther out than Everest's peak. Meanwhile Everest's neighbour K2, at about 8,600 metres, is the second highest and is widely regarded as a much deadlier climb.

sections.key: Kosciuszko, 2,228 m, is the mainland's highest peak, but Mawson Peak on Heard Island is higher.
sections.b: Australia's highest mainland peak, Mount Kosciuszko in New South Wales, is 2,228 metres, modest by world standards. The Polish explorer Paweł Strzelecki climbed in the area in 1840 and named it after the Polish patriot Tadeusz Kościuszko. It is an easy walk from the Thredbo chairlift in summer. Australia's continent is low because it is old and tectonically quiet, and its mountains have been eroding for hundreds of millions of years. Outside the Australian Antarctic Territory, Australia's highest mountain is not on the mainland: Mawson Peak, an active volcano on remote Heard Island in the Southern Ocean, an Australian external territory, rises to about 2,745 metres.

sections.key: The Great Dividing Range runs more than 3,500 km down the east and splits short coastal rivers from long inland ones.
sections.b: The Great Dividing Range is Australia's longest mountain system and one of the longest in the world, stretching more than 3,500 kilometres from Cape York in Queensland to the Grampians in western Victoria. It is not a single ridge but a chain of ranges, plateaus and tablelands, including the Blue Mountains and the Australian Alps. It shapes much of eastern Australia. Rain falls on its seaward side, feeding short, fast rivers to the Pacific. On the inland side, rivers flow slowly west into the Murray–Darling system or towards Kati Thanda–Lake Eyre. It also forms a rain shadow, which is one reason inland Australia is so much drier than the coast.

quiz.q: Why is it disputed whether the Nile or the Amazon is longer?
o: The Nile has dried up in places
Results depend on where the source and mouth are judged to be
Nobody has travelled the whole Amazon
The Amazon is measured in miles and the Nile in kilometres
quiz.e: Choosing different headwater streams and estuary end points changes the result by hundreds of kilometres.

quiz.q: What is Australia's longest river?
quiz.e: At about 2,500 kilometres, the Murray is Australia's longest river.

quiz.q: Why are there marine fossils near the top of Everest?
o: Birds carried shells up the mountain
Early climbers left them as offerings
Sea levels were once 8 kilometres higher
The rock formed on an ancient sea floor and was pushed up by colliding plates
quiz.e: India's collision with Asia lifted old ocean-floor limestone into the Himalayas.

quiz.q: What is the highest mountain on Australian territory outside Antarctica?
quiz.e: Mawson Peak, about 2,745 metres, is higher than Kosciuszko's 2,228 metres.

quiz.q: Which best describes the Great Dividing Range?
o: A chain of ranges and plateaus that splits east-flowing from inland rivers
A mountain range along Western Australia's coast
The highest range in the Southern Hemisphere
quiz.e: The range runs more than 3,500 km down the east and divides coastal from inland drainage.

LESSONS.title: Deserts
LESSONS.hook: The biggest desert on Earth is covered in ice. Deserts are defined by thirst, not heat, and they are far more alive than they look.

sections.key: A desert is defined by very low rainfall, often under about 250 mm a year, not by temperature.
sections.b: Most people picture a desert as hot sand, but geographers define deserts by dryness. A common rule of thumb is less than about 250 millimetres of rain or snow a year, though a better measure compares rainfall with how much water could evaporate. Where evaporation far outstrips rainfall, the land is arid. Areas a little wetter, often around 250 to 500 millimetres, are called semi-arid. By these standards, arid and semi-arid lands together cover roughly a third of Earth's land. Dry air also explains the famous temperature swings: with little moisture or cloud to trap heat, desert nights can be cold even after scorching days.

sections.key: Antarctica is the world's largest desert, with much of its interior receiving less than 50 mm of snow a year in water terms.
sections.b: By the dryness definition, the world's largest desert is Antarctica, about 14 million square kilometres. Cold air holds very little moisture, so much of its high interior receives less than 50 millimetres of precipitation a year, measured as melted water. The ice sheet is kilometres thick not because a lot of snow falls, but because what does fall almost never melts and has built up over hundreds of thousands of years. The Arctic is usually ranked the second-largest desert. Antarctica's McMurdo Dry Valleys, largely free of ice, are among the driest places on the planet and have been used by NASA to study conditions resembling Mars.

sections.key: The Sahara is the largest hot desert, about 9 million km², mostly rock and gravel, and was green a few thousand years ago.
sections.b: The Sahara, across northern Africa, is the largest hot desert, about 9 million square kilometres, bigger than Australia. Only around a quarter of it is sand dunes; most is rocky plateau and gravel plain. It is a dramatic example of changing climate. Between roughly 11,000 and 5,000 years ago, shifts in Earth's orbit strengthened the African monsoon and the 'Green Sahara' had lakes, grasslands, hippos and crocodiles. Rock art from that time shows herds of cattle and what appear to be people swimming. On the southern edge lies the Sahel, a semi-arid belt where drought and overuse of land have caused serious desertification, prompting projects like Africa's Great Green Wall.

sections.h: Why deserts form where they do
sections.key: Most deserts form under sinking subtropical air, in rain shadows, far from the sea or beside cold ocean currents.
sections.b: Several forces make deserts. The biggest is global air circulation: warm, moist air rises near the equator, drops its rain, then sinks as dry air around 30 degrees north and south. That belt holds the Sahara, the Arabian, the Kalahari and much of inland Australia. Rain shadows form where mountains wring moisture from the air on one side, leaving the far side dry, as in Patagonia. Some deserts, like the Gobi, are simply too far from the sea for moist air to reach. Others, like the Atacama in Chile and the Namib in southern Africa, sit beside cold ocean currents that chill the air and stop rain clouds forming.

sections.key: Australia has ten named deserts covering about 18% of the mainland, and about 70% of the continent is arid or semi-arid.
sections.b: Australia is the driest inhabited continent. Geoscience Australia lists ten named deserts covering about 18% of the mainland, and around 70% of the continent is arid or semi-arid. The largest is the Great Victoria Desert, spanning Western Australia and South Australia. Others include the Great Sandy, Tanami, Gibson and Simpson. The Simpson Desert is known for its long, parallel red sand dunes, some running for well over 100 kilometres. Much of the interior drains towards Kati Thanda–Lake Eyre, Australia's lowest point at about 15 metres below sea level. The lake is usually a salt crust, filling completely only a few times a century, when it attracts huge numbers of breeding waterbirds.

sections.key: Desert plants and animals survive by storing water, avoiding heat and responding fast to rare rain.
sections.b: Deserts are full of clever survival strategies. Cacti in the Americas and many succulents store water in thick stems or leaves. Australia's spinifex grass forms tough hummocks that shelter small animals. After rare heavy rain, dormant seeds burst into flower and complete their lives in weeks. The thorny devil, a small Australian lizard, has grooves between its scales that draw water by capillary action to the corners of its mouth, so it can drink from damp sand or dew. Many desert animals are active only at night. Camels do not store water in their humps, which hold fat; instead they tolerate dehydration and conserve water extremely well.

sections.key: Aboriginal peoples have lived in Australia's deserts for tens of thousands of years, guided by deep knowledge of country and water.
sections.b: Humans have lived in deserts for a very long time. In Australia, Aboriginal peoples, including the many language groups of the Western Desert, have lived in arid country for tens of thousands of years. Survival depended on detailed knowledge of rock holes, soaks and seasonal plants, passed down through song, story and ceremony, and many of these places remain culturally significant today. Elsewhere, nomadic herders such as the Tuareg of the Sahara and the Bedouin of Arabia developed ways of life built around mobility. Modern desert cities like Dubai, Phoenix and Alice Springs depend on engineering: deep bores, pipelines, desalination and air conditioning.

sections.key: In outback Australia, carry far more water than you think, tell someone your plans and stay with your vehicle if stranded.
sections.b: Australia's deserts are beautiful and increasingly visited, but they punish poor preparation. Distances between fuel and water can be hundreds of kilometres, phone coverage disappears quickly and summer temperatures can pass 45 degrees. Carry far more water than you expect to need, commonly several litres per person per day plus extras for emergencies. Check road conditions, since dirt roads close after rain, and some remote tracks need permits, including to cross Aboriginal land. Tell someone your route and expected arrival. Carry a personal locator beacon or satellite device. If you break down, stay with your vehicle: it provides shade and is far easier for searchers to spot than a person walking.

quiz.q: What mainly defines a desert?
o: Very low precipitation compared with evaporation
Sand dunes covering most of the ground
quiz.e: Deserts are defined by dryness. A common rule of thumb is under about 250 mm of precipitation a year.

quiz.q: What is the world's largest desert?
quiz.e: Antarctica, about 14 million square kilometres, receives very little precipitation, making it a desert.

quiz.q: Why is the Atacama Desert so dry?
o: A cold ocean current and mountains block rain
It sits exactly on the equator
It is at the centre of a large continent
It is covered by ice all year
quiz.e: Cold currents off Chile chill the air and stop rain clouds forming, while the Andes add a rain shadow.

quiz.q: How does the thorny devil get water?
o: It stores water in a hump
It digs wells with its claws
Grooves in its skin draw water to its mouth
quiz.e: Capillary grooves between its scales channel moisture from damp sand or dew to its mouth.

quiz.q: If your car breaks down in remote desert, what is the standard advice?
o: Walk to the nearest town at night
Leave a note and follow the road
Split up to search for help faster
quiz.e: A vehicle gives shade and is far easier for searchers to see than a person on foot.

LESSONS.title: Borders
LESSONS.hook: There is an island that changes countries every six months and a town where the border runs through people's living rooms. Borders are human inventions, and it shows.

sections.key: Borders are human agreements, often following rivers or mountains, straight survey lines, or old colonial deals.
sections.b: No border exists in nature. Every one is a human agreement, or a disagreement, drawn onto the land. Some follow physical features: the Pyrenees between France and Spain, or the Rio Grande between the United States and Mexico. Rivers make obvious lines but can shift course, causing arguments. Other borders are geometric, following lines of latitude or longitude, such as much of the long border between Canada and the United States, the world's longest shared border at almost 9,000 kilometres. Still others follow language, religion or the limits of old kingdoms, or reflect whatever a peace treaty happened to say when a war ended.

sections.key: Many borders in Africa and the Middle East were drawn by European powers with little regard for the people living there.
sections.b: Some of the world's most consequential borders were drawn far away. In the late 19th century, European powers competed to claim Africa, and the Berlin Conference of 1884–85 set rules for how they did it. The resulting borders, many of them straight lines on maps, often cut across ethnic groups or bundled rivals together. After the First World War, Britain and France divided much of the former Ottoman Empire in the Middle East. When colonies became independent, most new countries kept these borders, partly because redrawing them risked endless conflict. Historians still debate how much these lines contribute to later tensions, but their origins are not in doubt.

sections.key: Australian state borders mostly follow survey lines, and a surveying error still shapes the South Australia–Victoria border.
sections.b: Australia's internal borders were drawn mostly by colonial officials using lines of longitude and latitude. Western Australia's eastern border follows the 129th meridian, which is why it runs dead straight through the desert. The South Australia–Victoria border was meant to follow the 141st meridian, but the surveyed line of the 1840s ended up a few kilometres too far west. South Australia sued, and in 1914 the Privy Council in London ruled that the marked line stood, so the error remains. Borders that normally go unnoticed can suddenly matter: during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 and 2021, several states closed their borders to travellers from other states.

sections.key: Enclaves, exclaves and shared islands show how strange borders can get.
sections.b: Borders produce some delightful oddities. In the town of Baarle-Hertog and Baarle-Nassau, dozens of small Belgian and Dutch enclaves are scattered through each other, and the line runs through some houses and shops. Pheasant Island, in a river between France and Spain, switches rule every six months under a treaty from 1659. Three countries, Lesotho, San Marino and Vatican City, are entirely surrounded by a single other country. In the Bering Strait, Big Diomede (Russia) and Little Diomede (United States) are only a few kilometres apart but sit on opposite sides of the International Date Line, so their clocks differ by almost a full day.

sections.key: Many territories are claimed by more than one country; describing them fairly means noting who controls them and who disputes it.
sections.b: Around the world, dozens of places are claimed by more than one government. Kashmir, in the Himalayas, is divided between areas administered by India, Pakistan and China, and has been contested since 1947. Most of Western Sahara is controlled by Morocco, while a movement called the Polisario Front seeks independence, and its final status remains unresolved at the UN. Maps themselves become part of these disputes: many countries require their official maps to show their own claims, so the same border can look different depending on where a map was printed. A fair description usually states who controls an area, who claims it and what international bodies have said.

sections.key: Under the UN law of the sea, countries control a 12-nautical-mile territorial sea and a 200-nautical-mile exclusive economic zone.
sections.b: Borders also extend offshore. The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, agreed in 1982, sets out the main zones. A country's territorial sea reaches 12 nautical miles from its coast, about 22 kilometres, and is treated much like its land. Beyond that, its exclusive economic zone, or EEZ, stretches to 200 nautical miles, about 370 kilometres, giving it rights over fishing, oil, gas and minerals, though other ships may pass freely. Where coasts are closer than 400 nautical miles apart, neighbours must negotiate a line. Overlapping claims create tension in places like the South China Sea, where several countries claim the same reefs and waters.

sections.key: Australia's EEZ is one of the world's largest, and it has negotiated sea boundaries with neighbours including Indonesia, PNG and Timor-Leste.
sections.b: Thanks to its long coastline and remote islands, Australia has one of the largest exclusive economic zones in the world, around 8 million square kilometres, bigger than the mainland itself. Setting its edges has taken decades of diplomacy. The 1978 Torres Strait Treaty with Papua New Guinea deals with islands such as Saibai, only a few kilometres from the PNG coast, and lets traditional inhabitants on both sides move within a protected zone for customary activities. In 2018, after the first ever conciliation under the law of the sea convention, Australia and Timor-Leste signed a treaty setting a permanent maritime boundary in the Timor Sea, rich in oil and gas.

sections.key: Seven countries claim parts of Antarctica, including Australia's claim to about 42%, but the Antarctic Treaty sets these claims aside.
sections.b: Antarctica is the one continent without agreed borders. Seven countries have claimed slices of it: Argentina, Australia, Chile, France, New Zealand, Norway and the United Kingdom. Australia's claim, the Australian Antarctic Territory, covers about 42% of the continent, the largest of all. Some claims overlap, and most countries do not recognise any of them. The Antarctic Treaty of 1959 put the issue on ice: it neither accepts nor rejects the claims, bans military activity, and, through a later protocol, mining, and reserves the continent for peaceful science. It is a rare example of rival nations agreeing to share a whole continent, and it has held for more than 60 years.

quiz.q: Which is the world's longest border between two countries?
quiz.e: The Canada–US border, including Alaska's, runs for almost 9,000 kilometres.

quiz.q: Why is the South Australia–Victoria border not exactly on the 141st meridian?
o: A surveying error in the 1840s was upheld by the Privy Council
quiz.e: The surveyed line ended up a few kilometres west, and in 1914 the Privy Council ruled that it stood.

quiz.q: Which country is entirely surrounded by South Africa?
quiz.e: Lesotho, San Marino and Vatican City are each completely surrounded by a single other country.

quiz.q: How far does a country's exclusive economic zone extend?
quiz.e: The EEZ reaches 200 nautical miles, about 370 kilometres, giving rights over resources like fish and gas.

quiz.q: What does the Antarctic Treaty do about territorial claims?
o: Sets the claims aside without accepting or rejecting them
Gives all of Antarctica to the United Nations
quiz.e: The 1959 treaty freezes the claims and reserves Antarctica for peaceful science.

LESSONS.title: Cities
LESSONS.hook: For almost all of human history most people lived in the countryside. That changed only within the last couple of decades, and Australia got there long before most.

sections.key: More than half of humanity now lives in urban areas, a milestone reached only around 2007.
sections.b: The first cities appeared in Mesopotamia, in today's Iraq, more than 5,000 years ago; Uruk may have held tens of thousands of people. Yet for most of history cities were small islands in a rural world. As late as 1800, only a small minority of people, commonly estimated at under 10%, lived in towns and cities. Industrialisation changed that, pulling workers from farms to factories. The United Nations estimates that around 2007 the world became majority urban for the first time, and it projects that about two-thirds of people will live in urban areas by 2050. Most of that future growth is expected in Asia and Africa.

sections.key: Countries define 'urban' very differently, so city sizes and rankings depend on where the boundary is drawn.
sections.b: Comparing cities is surprisingly tricky, because there is no single definition. Some countries count any settlement over a few thousand people as urban; others set the bar much higher. A city can also be measured three ways: the core municipality, the built-up urban area, or the wider metropolitan region of people who commute into it. The City of Sydney council area has only about 200,000 residents, while Greater Sydney has more than 5 million. To make fairer comparisons, the UN and other agencies have developed a standard method based on population density measured on satellite-derived grids, which can produce quite different rankings from national statistics.

sections.key: Megacities have 10 million or more people; Tokyo long topped UN lists, and newer methods put Jakarta and Dhaka at the top.
sections.b: A megacity is an urban area of 10 million or more. In 1950 only New York and Tokyo qualified; today there are more than 30, from Delhi, Shanghai and Cairo to São Paulo, Lagos and Mexico City. For decades the UN ranked greater Tokyo first, at around 37 million people. A 2025 UN report using the newer standardised definition instead placed Jakarta first, with Dhaka and Tokyo close behind, and noted that Tokyo's population has begun to shrink. The exact order matters less than the trend: most of the world's biggest and fastest-growing cities are now in Asia and Africa, not Europe or North America.

sections.h: Why cities grow where they do
sections.key: Cities grow at harbours, river crossings, trade routes and resources, and then attract more people simply by being big.
sections.b: Look at almost any major city and geography explains its location. Water comes first: rivers and harbours provide drinking water, transport and trade, which is why so many great cities sit on coasts or rivers. London grew at the lowest point where the Thames could easily be bridged. Crossroads of trade routes, mountain passes and defensible hills also attracted settlement. Resources matter too: Australia's gold rushes built Ballarat, Bendigo and later Kalgoorlie. Once a city is established, it tends to keep growing because businesses, workers and customers benefit from being close together. Economists call this agglomeration, and it helps explain why big cities are often the most productive.

sections.key: Some cities are founded by decision: Canberra was chosen as a compromise between Sydney and Melbourne.
sections.b: Not every city grows organically. Some are created by governments. When the Australian colonies federated in 1901, Sydney and Melbourne were rivals, so the Constitution required the national capital to be in New South Wales but at least 100 miles from Sydney. The Canberra site was chosen in 1908, and an international design competition was won by the American architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin. The city was named in 1913 and Parliament moved there from Melbourne in 1927. Other planned capitals include Washington DC, Brasília, opened in 1960 to draw development inland, and Abuja, which replaced Lagos as Nigeria's capital in 1991.

sections.h: Australia: a nation of city dwellers
sections.key: About 86% of Australians live in urban areas and around two-thirds live in the capital cities.
sections.b: Despite the outback image, Australia is one of the most urbanised countries on Earth. About 86% of people live in urban areas, and roughly two-thirds live in the eight capital cities, according to recent ABS figures. Sydney and Melbourne each have more than 5 million people (2023), while Brisbane and Perth have over 2 million. Most Australians also live near the sea, with commonly cited estimates of around 85% within 50 kilometres of the coast. This pattern reflects history and climate: colonial settlement began at ports, and the dry interior supports few people. Few other countries concentrate so much of their population in so few big cities.

sections.key: Cities bring congestion, housing pressure, heat islands and, in poorer countries, large informal settlements.
sections.b: Rapid urban growth brings real problems. Housing costs rise as more people compete for land near jobs, a familiar story in Sydney and Melbourne. Sprawl lengthens commutes and makes public transport harder to provide. Cities also trap heat: dark roads and roofs absorb sunlight and release it at night, so urban areas can be several degrees warmer than surrounding countryside, a pattern called the urban heat island effect that is especially noticeable in Western Sydney. In many lower-income countries, cities grow faster than housing and services can be built, and UN-Habitat estimates that around a billion people live in slums or informal settlements.

sections.key: Cities concentrate jobs, ideas and services, and well-planned density can be efficient and greener per person.
sections.b: People keep moving to cities because, on balance, they offer more: jobs, higher wages, universities, hospitals, culture and a wider choice of friends and partners. Density also has environmental upsides. Apartments share walls and heat, public transport is viable, and residents of compact cities often drive less than people in sprawling suburbs. The challenge for planners is to get the benefits without the costs, through good public transport, trees and shade to cool streets, and enough housing near jobs. When you compare cities or choose where to live, look past headline rankings to the things that shape daily life: commute times, housing costs, green space and access to services.

quiz.q: Roughly when did more than half of the world's people first live in urban areas?
quiz.e: The UN estimates the world became majority urban around 2007.

quiz.q: Why do lists of the world's biggest cities often disagree?
o: Some cities refuse to hold censuses
Countries and agencies draw city boundaries in different ways
quiz.e: Whether you count the core, the built-up area or the wider metro region changes the numbers dramatically.

quiz.q: What is agglomeration?
o: The benefit businesses and workers gain from clustering together
The merging of two local councils
The spread of suburbs into farmland
A type of city planning law
quiz.e: Being close to customers, suppliers and workers makes firms more productive, so big cities tend to keep growing.

quiz.q: Why was Canberra built as Australia's capital?
o: It was the oldest colonial settlement
It was a compromise between rivals Sydney and Melbourne
quiz.e: The Constitution required the capital to be in NSW but at least 100 miles from Sydney.

quiz.q: What is the urban heat island effect?
o: Cities being warmer than surrounding countryside
A cooling breeze from the coast
quiz.e: Roads, roofs and buildings absorb heat and release it at night, keeping cities warmer.

LESSONS.title: World population
LESSONS.hook: It took all of human history to reach one billion people, and just over a decade to go from seven billion to eight. Now the world is quietly changing direction.

sections.key: The world's population passed 8 billion in 2022, after taking until about 1804 to reach its first billion.
sections.b: The United Nations marked 15 November 2022 as the day the world's population reached 8 billion, an estimate rather than an exact count. The first billion took until about 1804. The second arrived around 1927, the third in 1960, and after that a billion was added roughly every 12 to 14 years: 4 billion in 1974, 5 billion in 1987, 6 billion in 1999 and 7 billion in 2011. This explosion was not mainly caused by people having more children. It happened because far fewer people died young, thanks to clean water, sanitation, vaccines, antibiotics and more reliable food supplies, while birth rates took time to catch up.

sections.key: Global growth peaked at over 2% a year in the 1960s and has since fallen below 1%; the UN projects a peak in the 2080s.
sections.b: Even as numbers climb, growth is slowing. The world's population growth rate peaked at a little over 2% a year in the 1960s and fell below 1% around 2020. The UN's 2024 projections expect the population to peak at around 10.3 billion in the mid-2080s and then decline slightly by 2100. These are projections, not certainties; they depend on assumptions about future birth and death rates, and other research groups expect an earlier, lower peak. Growth is also uneven. Much of Europe and East Asia is already shrinking or close to it, while more than half of expected growth to 2050 is in sub-Saharan Africa.

sections.key: Replacement fertility is about 2.1 children per woman; the world average is now around 2.3, and most countries are below replacement.
sections.b: The key number in demography is the total fertility rate: roughly, the average number of children a woman has over her lifetime. In rich countries, about 2.1 keeps a population stable in the long run, a level called replacement; it is a little higher where child mortality is higher. In the 1960s the global average was around 5. Today it is about 2.3, and most people live in countries below replacement. Australia's rate was about 1.5 in 2023, a record low. South Korea's fell to a record 0.72 in 2023 and was still only about 0.8 in 2025, the lowest in the world. The highest rates, around six, are in parts of the Sahel, such as Niger.

sections.key: As death rates fall, birth rates follow, driven by child survival, education, urbanisation and access to contraception.
sections.b: Demographers describe a common pattern called the demographic transition. In traditional societies, both birth and death rates are high, so population grows slowly. Then death rates fall as health and food improve, while birth rates stay high for a generation or two, and the population surges. Eventually birth rates fall too. The main drivers are well established: when most children survive, parents have fewer; education, especially for girls, and paid work give women more choices; city living makes children more expensive; and contraception makes smaller families possible. Europe went through this over more than a century. Countries such as South Korea and Iran went through it in a few decades.

sections.h: India, China and the shifting map
sections.key: India overtook China as the most populous country in 2023; China's population has been falling since 2022.
sections.b: The world's population map is shifting. In 2023, UN estimates showed India overtaking China as the most populous country, each with about 1.4 billion people. China's population began falling in 2022, a result of decades of low fertility, including the one-child policy from 1980 to 2015. Japan's population has been shrinking since around 2010, and Italy and South Korea are also declining. Meanwhile Nigeria, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Ethiopia are growing fast, and Africa is projected to hold around a quarter of humanity by 2050. Shifts like these will reshape economies, workforces and politics this century.

sections.key: People are living longer and having fewer children, so the share of older people is rising almost everywhere.
sections.b: Longer lives and fewer births mean the world is getting older. Global life expectancy is now around 73 years, up from about 46 in 1950. Japan is the oldest major country, with nearly 30% of its people aged 65 or over, and a median age near 49. Niger, by contrast, has a median age of about 15. Australia is in between, with roughly 17% of people aged 65 or over. Ageing is a success story, but it brings challenges: fewer workers per retiree, higher health and aged care costs, and pressure on pension systems. That is one reason Australia built compulsory superannuation and why governments encourage people to work longer.

sections.key: Around 300 million people live outside their country of birth; in Australia, about 30% of residents were born overseas.
sections.b: Migration is the third driver of population change, alongside births and deaths. The United Nations estimated about 304 million international migrants in 2024, around 3.7% of the world's people. Most move for work, family or study; tens of millions more have been forced from their homes by conflict or disaster. Australia is one of the most migration-shaped countries on Earth. About 30% of residents were born overseas (2023), with England, India, China and New Zealand the most common birthplaces, and around half of Australians were born overseas or have a parent who was. In most recent years, net overseas migration has added more people than natural increase.

sections.key: Treat projections as scenarios, check the year and source, and be wary of both 'overpopulation' and 'population collapse' alarm.
sections.b: Population debates attract bold predictions. In 1798 Thomas Malthus argued that population would always outrun food; in 1968 Paul Ehrlich's The Population Bomb forecast mass famines in the 1970s. Farming productivity rose faster than either expected, though hunger has not disappeared. Today, some warn instead of population collapse. A few habits help you judge such claims. Check the year and source of any figure, since estimates are revised regularly. Treat projections as scenarios. Remember that impact depends on consumption as well as headcount: a person in a rich country typically uses far more resources than one in a poor country. And watch the slow trends, like ageing, that shape budgets for decades.

quiz.q: What mainly caused the rapid rise in world population over the past two centuries?
o: People having many more children than before
quiz.e: Clean water, sanitation, vaccines and better food cut death rates while birth rates took time to fall.

quiz.q: What is the approximate replacement fertility rate in rich countries?
quiz.e: About 2.1 children per woman keeps a population stable in the long run where child mortality is low.

quiz.q: Which of these is a well-established driver of falling birth rates?
quiz.e: When most children survive, parents tend to have fewer, especially as education and city living spread.

quiz.q: Which country became the world's most populous in 2023, according to UN estimates?
quiz.e: India overtook China, each having about 1.4 billion people, while China's population began to fall.

quiz.q: About what share of Australia's residents were born overseas (2023)?
quiz.e: Roughly 30% of Australians were born overseas, one of the highest shares among large countries.

LESSONS.title: How democracy works
LESSONS.hook: Rule by the people sounds simple. For most of history it was rare, fragile and limited. Here's how it grew, and what actually keeps it alive.

sections.key: Democracy means the people hold ultimate power, either deciding directly or choosing representatives.
sections.b: The word democracy comes from the Greek demos, the people, and kratos, power or rule. The core idea is that political authority comes from the citizens rather than from a monarch, a priesthood or a military. There are two broad ways to put this into practice. In a direct democracy, citizens vote on laws and decisions themselves. In a representative democracy, citizens elect people to make those decisions on their behalf, and can remove them at the next election. Almost every democracy today is mainly representative, with some direct elements mixed in.

sections.key: Athens is the famous example, but assemblies also ran early republics in ancient India and Iceland's Althing, founded in 930.
sections.b: Athens is the best-known early democracy, but it wasn't the only place where ordinary people shared power. Ancient Indian texts describe republics called ganas or sanghas, such as the Vajji confederacy around Vaishali, where councils of clan leaders debated and voted around the 500s BC, although only an elite took part. In Iceland, Norse settlers founded the Althing in 930. Free men gathered each summer at Thingvellir to settle disputes and make laws, and it is often called one of the world's oldest surviving parliaments. In two small Swiss cantons, citizens still meet in the town square once a year and vote on laws by raising their hands.

sections.key: Representative government developed through the Roman Republic, medieval parliaments and English constitutional struggles.
sections.b: After Athens, rule by the people largely disappeared for centuries, but pieces of the idea survived. The Roman Republic elected magistrates and had a Senate, though wealthy families dominated it. In medieval England, Magna Carta in 1215 established that even the king was bound by law, and parliaments of nobles, clergy and later commoners gradually won control over taxation. Conflicts in the 1600s, including a civil war and the Glorious Revolution of 1688, left Parliament stronger than the monarch. This parliamentary model, developed at Westminster in London, later shaped Australia, Canada, New Zealand and many others.

sections.key: The American and French revolutions spread the idea of popular sovereignty; the vote then widened slowly.
sections.b: Enlightenment thinkers such as John Locke argued that governments get their legitimacy from the consent of the governed. The American Revolution of 1776 and the French Revolution of 1789 put this idea at the centre of new political systems. Yet early electorates were small, often limited to men who owned property. Over the next century and a half, the vote was extended to working men, then to women, and later to groups that had been excluded by race. The idea that every adult citizen should have an equal vote, called universal suffrage, is surprisingly recent.

sections.key: Australian colonies were early adopters of paid MPs and proportional representation, and produced the world's first Labour government.
sections.b: The Australian colonies were busy laboratories of democracy. In 1870 Victoria began paying members of parliament, so that working men, not just the wealthy, could afford to serve. In 1899 Queensland's Anderson Dawson became premier of what is usually described as the world's first Labour government, although it lasted only about a week. Tasmania trialled the Hare-Clark system of proportional representation in Hobart and Launceston in the 1890s and adopted it statewide in 1909; it is still used there and in the ACT. And in 1921 Edith Cowan won a seat in Western Australia, becoming the first woman elected to an Australian parliament.

sections.key: Referendums and citizen initiatives let voters decide some questions directly, as in Switzerland and Australia.
sections.b: Pure direct democracy is impractical for a nation of millions, but elements of it survive. Switzerland is the best-known example: citizens vote on national questions several times a year, and can force a vote on a new law by gathering enough signatures. Many US states let citizens put proposals on the ballot. In Australia, the main direct element is the constitutional referendum: the Constitution can only be changed if voters approve. Supporters say direct votes give people real ownership of big decisions. Critics warn that complex issues can be reduced to slogans and that turnout and information vary.

sections.key: Free and fair elections alone aren't enough; democracy also needs rule of law, a free press and peaceful handovers.
sections.b: Holding elections doesn't guarantee a working democracy. Political scientists usually point to several supporting pillars. Elections must be free and fair, run by an independent body, with secret ballots and a real choice of candidates. The rule of law means everyone, including leaders, is subject to the same laws, enforced by independent courts. A free press and free speech let citizens learn what the government is doing and criticise it without fear. Protection of minorities stops the majority from simply overriding others' basic rights. And losers must accept the result, allowing a peaceful transfer of power.

sections.key: Democracy depends on informed citizens who vote, check sources and engage beyond election day.
sections.b: Winston Churchill famously told the British Parliament in 1947 that democracy had been called the worst form of government except for all the others that had been tried. Democracies can be slow, argumentative and frustrating, but they allow mistakes to be corrected and leaders to be replaced without violence. They also depend on everyday citizens. You can help by enrolling and voting thoughtfully, checking where political claims come from, contacting your local member about issues you care about, and respecting people who vote differently. Democracy isn't only something governments do; it's something citizens practise.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between direct and representative democracy?
o: Direct democracy has no elections at all
In direct democracy citizens vote on decisions themselves; in representative democracy they elect others to decide
Direct democracy is run by a monarch
quiz.e: Most modern democracies are mainly representative with some direct elements.

quiz.q: Where did Norse settlers found the Althing, one of the world's oldest parliaments, in 930?
quiz.e: Free men met each summer at Thingvellir to make laws and settle disputes.

quiz.q: Which colony produced what is usually called the world's first Labour government, in 1899?
quiz.e: Anderson Dawson's Labour government held office for only about a week.

quiz.q: What is the main direct-democracy element in Australia's national system?
quiz.e: The Constitution can only be changed if voters approve at a referendum.

quiz.q: Which of these is a pillar of a working democracy beyond elections?
quiz.e: A free press lets citizens learn what government is doing and criticise it.

LESSONS.title: Left, right and the big political ideas
LESSONS.hook: Why do we say 'left' and 'right'? The answer involves a French assembly hall in 1789, and the ideas that grew from it still shape every election.

sections.key: The terms come from the French National Assembly of 1789, where radicals sat on the left and supporters of the king on the right.
sections.b: The labels left and right began in France in 1789, in the early months of the French Revolution. In the National Assembly, members who wanted to keep strong powers for the king, such as a royal veto over laws, tended to sit to the right of the presiding officer. Those who wanted more radical change sat to the left. The seating habit stuck, and the words spread. Over time, left came to mean favouring change and greater equality, and right came to mean favouring tradition, order and established institutions. The meanings have shifted many times since.

sections.key: Left and right usually describe views on equality, the role of government in the economy, and the pace of social change.
sections.b: Today the left-right spectrum is a rough shorthand for several different questions bundled together. On economics, the left generally favours more government action to reduce inequality, through taxes, welfare and public services, while the right generally favours lower taxes, freer markets and more reliance on individual effort and private enterprise. On social questions, the left is often associated with faster change and the right with preserving tradition. But the bundles don't always hold together, and the labels mean different things in different countries and eras. Most people hold a mix of views that don't sit neatly on one line.

sections.key: Liberalism puts individual freedom, rights and consent of the governed at the centre of politics.
sections.b: Liberalism grew from Enlightenment thinkers such as John Locke, who argued that people have natural rights to life, liberty and property, and that government rests on consent. Classical liberals emphasised free markets, free speech, religious tolerance and limited government. Later, social liberals argued that real freedom also needs education, health care and a safety net, so government has a bigger role. Supporters credit liberalism with modern democracy and individual rights. Critics on different sides say it can neglect community and tradition, or tolerate too much inequality. Confusingly, 'liberal' signals the centre-left in the United States, while Australia's Liberal Party sits on the centre-right.

sections.key: Conservatism values tradition, stability and gradual change, trusting institutions tested by experience.
sections.b: Modern conservatism is often traced to the Irish-born politician Edmund Burke, whose 1790 book Reflections on the Revolution in France warned against tearing down institutions in the name of abstract theory. Conservatives generally believe that customs, families, religion and long-standing institutions carry accumulated wisdom, and that change should be careful and gradual. Many also support free markets, strong national defence and law and order. Supporters argue that conservatism protects what works and guards against reckless experiments. Critics argue that it can defend unfair arrangements simply because they are old, and can be slow to respond to new problems.

sections.key: Socialism aims for greater equality through collective or public ownership and control of key parts of the economy.
sections.b: Socialism emerged in the 1800s as a response to the harsh conditions of the Industrial Revolution. Socialists argue that wealth is produced collectively, so key industries and resources should be owned or controlled by the public, workers or the state, and shared more equally. It takes many forms. Karl Marx predicted revolution; communist states later built one-party systems with centrally planned economies. Democratic socialists and social democrats instead pursue change through elections, favouring strong unions, public services and welfare within a market economy. Supporters see socialism as the path to fairness. Critics point to the economic failures and repression of communist states and argue that it weakens incentives.

sections.key: Libertarianism seeks to maximise individual liberty in both economic and personal life, with a minimal state.
sections.b: Libertarians believe individuals should be free to live as they choose, so long as they don't harm others, and that the state should be as small as possible. That typically means low taxes, free markets and minimal regulation, which sounds right-wing, combined with personal freedoms on issues like speech and private behaviour, which can sound left-wing. The philosopher Robert Nozick made an influential case in his 1974 book Anarchy, State, and Utopia. Supporters argue that freedom and voluntary exchange produce both prosperity and dignity. Critics argue that a minimal state would leave the vulnerable unprotected and struggle with shared problems like pollution.

sections.h: Beyond a single line: the political compass
sections.key: Two-axis models add an authoritarian-versus-libertarian dimension to economic left and right.
sections.b: Because one line mixes up too many questions, some people use two axes instead. The horizontal axis measures economic views, from more state control on the left to more free market on the right. The vertical axis measures personal freedom, from authoritarian, favouring strong state control of behaviour, to libertarian, favouring minimal control. The American libertarian David Nolan drew an early version, and a popular online quiz called the Political Compass made the idea widely known. Even two axes simplify reality: environmentalism, nationalism and populism, for example, cut across these lines in different ways, and political scientists debate how best to map beliefs.

sections.key: Each tradition has thoughtful supporters and serious critics; understanding the best version of other views improves your own thinking.
sections.b: Every major political tradition contains serious thinkers responding to real problems: liberty, fairness, stability and security all matter, and people weigh them differently. A useful habit is to describe an opposing view so well that its supporters would agree with your summary, sometimes called steelmanning. Be wary of labels used as insults, and check whether a claim about 'the other side' describes its mainstream or its fringe. Most people's views are a mix and change over their lives. Understanding the ideas, rather than just the teams, makes political debate more useful and far less exhausting.

quiz.q: On economic questions, what does the left generally favour?
o: More government action to reduce inequality, through taxes, welfare and public services
Relying mainly on private enterprise and individual effort
Restoring the powers of a monarch
quiz.e: The right generally favours lower taxes and freer markets, though the labels vary between countries and eras.

quiz.q: Which writer is often seen as a founder of modern conservatism?
quiz.e: Burke's 1790 Reflections on the Revolution in France warned against sweeping change.

quiz.q: Which idea is most central to liberalism?
o: Individual rights and government by consent
quiz.e: Liberalism grew from Enlightenment ideas about natural rights and consent.

quiz.q: Which combination best describes libertarianism?
o: High taxes and strict social rules
Free markets and broad personal freedoms with a minimal state
Central planning and a single party
quiz.e: Libertarians favour minimal government in both economic and personal life.

quiz.q: What does the vertical axis of the political compass measure?
o: Authoritarian versus libertarian views on personal freedom
quiz.e: The horizontal axis measures economic views; the vertical measures state control over behaviour.

LESSONS.title: How Australia's Parliament works
LESSONS.hook: Two chambers, a Prime Minister who isn't mentioned in the Constitution, and a Governor-General with rarely used powers. Here's how laws really get made in Canberra.

sections.key: Australia uses a Westminster-style system: the government is formed from, and answerable to, Parliament.
sections.b: Australia's system of government is based on the Westminster model, named after the British Parliament in London. Its defining feature is responsible government: ministers are members of Parliament, and the government stays in office only as long as it keeps the confidence of the lower house. Ministers must answer questions in Parliament, including in the daily Question Time. Australia's founders also borrowed from the United States, creating a federation with a strong elected Senate representing the states. Because of this blend, the system is sometimes nicknamed the 'Washminster' system, combining Westminster traditions with American federal features.

sections.key: The House has about 150 members, each representing one electorate; the party with majority support forms government.
sections.b: The House of Representatives, the lower house, has about 150 members, each elected to represent a single electorate, or seat, which on average has more than 100,000 voters. Seats are distributed among the states roughly by population, so New South Wales and Victoria have the most. Members serve terms of up to three years. The party or coalition that can win the support of a majority in the House forms government, and its leader becomes Prime Minister. The largest group outside government forms the Opposition, whose leader heads a shadow ministry that scrutinises the government and offers an alternative.

sections.key: The Senate has 76 senators, 12 per state and 2 per territory, and acts as a house of review.
sections.b: The Senate, the upper house, has 76 senators: 12 from each of the six states, regardless of population, and 2 each from the ACT and the Northern Territory. This equal representation was a condition of the smaller colonies joining federation. State senators serve six-year terms, with half elected every three years, while territory senators' terms follow House elections. Because senators are elected by proportional representation, minor parties and independents often hold the balance of power. The Senate is a house of review: it examines and amends bills, and its committees investigate government activity. It cannot introduce tax bills or amend certain tax and spending bills, but it can reject them.

sections.key: A bill passes three readings in each house, then receives Royal Assent from the Governor-General.
sections.b: A proposed law is called a bill. Most are introduced by ministers, though any member or senator can introduce one. At the first reading the bill is formally introduced. At the second reading its main purpose is debated and voted on, and it may be sent to a committee for closer study. Next it can be examined and amended clause by clause. At the third reading the house votes on the final version. The bill then goes through the same process in the other house, and both houses must pass it in identical form. Finally, the Governor-General gives Royal Assent, and it becomes an Act.

sections.key: If the Senate repeatedly blocks a bill, a double dissolution election can break the deadlock.
sections.b: Governments often lack a Senate majority, so they negotiate with crossbenchers to pass legislation. If the Senate twice rejects or fails to pass a bill from the House, with a gap of at least three months, section 57 of the Constitution allows the government to seek a double dissolution: both houses are dissolved and every seat in Parliament is contested. If the new Parliament still disagrees, the bill can be put to a joint sitting of both houses. Double dissolutions are rare. The most recent was in 2016, and the 1974 election produced the only joint sitting so far.

sections.key: The PM and cabinet run the government by convention; neither is mentioned in the Constitution.
sections.b: Surprisingly, the Constitution doesn't mention the Prime Minister or the cabinet. Both rest on conventions, unwritten rules inherited from British practice. The Prime Minister is the leader of the party or coalition with majority support in the House, and is chosen by that party, not directly by voters. The PM selects ministers to run departments such as health, defence and treasury. The most senior form the cabinet, which makes the government's key decisions in confidential meetings. Under cabinet solidarity, ministers must publicly support cabinet decisions or resign. A PM can be replaced mid-term if the party changes leader.

sections.key: The Governor-General represents the monarch and usually acts on ministers' advice, with rarely used reserve powers.
sections.b: Australia is a constitutional monarchy. The King of Australia is represented by the Governor-General, appointed by the monarch on the Prime Minister's advice. The Governor-General's formal powers look huge on paper: summoning and dissolving Parliament, assenting to laws, and commanding the defence force. By convention, though, they almost always act on the advice of ministers. A small set of reserve powers can be used independently in a crisis. The most famous use came in 1975, when Governor-General Sir John Kerr dismissed Prime Minister Gough Whitlam during a budget deadlock, a decision still debated today. Each state also has its own governor.

sections.key: States and territories have their own parliaments; local councils are created by state law.
sections.b: Australia has three tiers of government. Each state has its own parliament, led by a Premier, and handles areas like schools, hospitals, police and roads. All state parliaments have two houses except Queensland's, which abolished its upper house in 1922. The ACT and Northern Territory have single-house assemblies led by Chief Ministers. The third tier is local government: more than 500 councils run services such as rubbish collection, local roads, libraries and planning approvals. Councils aren't recognised in the federal Constitution; they're created by state laws. Knowing which level handles what tells you whether to contact your councillor, your state MP or your federal member.

quiz.q: What is the defining feature of responsible government in the Westminster system?
o: The government must keep the confidence of the lower house
The head of state is directly elected
quiz.e: Ministers sit in Parliament and govern only while they have majority support in the House.

quiz.q: How many senators does each state elect?
quiz.e: Each state has 12 senators; each territory has 2, making 76.

quiz.q: What is the final step before a bill becomes an Act?
o: A third reading in the Senate only
quiz.e: Both houses must pass the bill in identical form, then the Governor-General assents.

quiz.q: Where does the role of Prime Minister come from?
o: An Act of the British Parliament in 1986
quiz.e: The Prime Minister and cabinet rest on conventions inherited from British practice.

quiz.q: Which state has only one house of parliament?
quiz.e: Queensland abolished its Legislative Council in 1922.

LESSONS.title: How voting works in Australia
LESSONS.hook: Australia gave the world the secret ballot, makes voting compulsory, and counts your vote more than once. Here's what happens to your ballot after it drops in the box.

sections.key: Voting in federal elections has been compulsory since 1924, and turnout is usually around 90%.
sections.b: Australia is one of a small number of democracies where voting is compulsory.
