Enrolment for federal elections became compulsory in 1911, and voting followed in 1924, first applying at the 1925 election. Before the change, turnout at the 1922 federal election had fallen below 60%. Since then it has usually been around 90% or more. Strictly, the legal duty is to attend a polling place, have your name marked off, and mark your ballot paper and put it in the box; because the ballot is secret, nobody checks how, or whether, you filled it in. People who don't vote without a valid reason receive a modest fine. Supporters say compulsion gives governments a mandate from everyone; critics argue that voting should be a free choice.

sections.key: Citizens must enrol from 18, can enrol at 16 or 17, and can vote early, by post or on election day.
sections.b: Australian citizens aged 18 and over must enrol, and 16 and 17 year olds can enrol early so they're ready to vote once they turn 18. You enrol or update your address with the Australian Electoral Commission, usually online. Federal elections are held on a Saturday, and on election day you can vote at any polling place in your state or territory. If you can't make it, you can vote early at a pre-polling centre or apply for a postal vote. Polling places are often schools and community halls, where fundraising sausage sizzles have become a well-loved tradition.

sections.key: In the House, you number every candidate in order of preference, and a winner needs more than 50% of votes.
sections.b: For the House of Representatives, Australia uses full preferential voting, introduced federally in 1918. Instead of ticking one name, you number every box in order of preference: 1 for your favourite, 2 for your next choice, and so on. To win a seat, a candidate needs an absolute majority, more than 50% of the formal votes. Preferential voting means you can support a minor party or independent without 'wasting' your vote, because if that candidate can't win, your vote passes to your next choice. Ballots that aren't filled in correctly are called informal and don't count.

sections.key: If no one has a majority, the lowest candidate is excluded and their votes pass to the next preference.
sections.b: Counting starts with first preferences, the number 1 votes. If a candidate has more than half, they win. If not, the candidate with the fewest votes is excluded, and each of their ballots is passed to whichever remaining candidate is marked next on that ballot. This repeats until someone crosses 50%. Imagine candidates A with 44%, B with 41% and C with 15%. C is excluded; if two-thirds of C's voters put B second, B gains 10% to finish on 51% and wins, even though A led on first preferences. Results are often summarised as a 'two-party-preferred' figure.

sections.key: Senators are elected by proportional representation, where candidates need a quota of votes.
sections.b: The Senate ballot paper is large, divided by a thick black line. Above the line, you number at least six party or group boxes; below the line, you number at least twelve individual candidates. These rules have applied since 2016. Senators are elected by proportional representation using the single transferable vote. At a normal half-Senate election, six senators are elected per state, and each needs a quota of about 14.3% of the votes. Candidates who pass the quota have their surplus votes passed on at reduced value, and low candidates are excluded. This system helps smaller parties win seats in proportion to their support.

sections.key: The AEC is an independent body that runs federal elections, keeps the roll and draws electoral boundaries.
sections.b: Federal elections are run by the Australian Electoral Commission, an independent statutory authority established in 1984. It maintains the electoral roll, conducts elections and referendums, counts the votes and publishes results. It also oversees redistributions, redrawing electorate boundaries as populations change, so that seats within a state have roughly equal numbers of voters. Independent committees draw the boundaries, not politicians. The AEC also regulates political donations disclosure and works to counter false claims about the voting process. States and territories have their own electoral commissions for state and local elections, which follow broadly similar principles but different rules.

sections.key: Victoria and South Australia introduced the secret ballot in 1856; it spread worldwide as the 'Australian ballot'.
sections.b: Before the 1850s, voting in Britain and its colonies was often public: people declared their choice aloud, which made bribery and intimidation easy. In 1856, Victoria and South Australia introduced the secret ballot, with official ballot papers printed by the government, listing all candidates, and marked privately. The idea spread quickly. Britain adopted it in 1872, and when American states took it up from the late 1880s it was known there as the 'Australian ballot'. Today the secret ballot is regarded as a basic requirement of a free election, protecting voters from pressure by employers, landlords, officials or anyone else.

sections.key: Keep your enrolment current, follow the ballot instructions exactly, and remember every preference can matter.
sections.b: A few habits make sure your vote counts as you intend. Check your enrolment whenever you move house. Before election day, read about the candidates, not just the parties, and look up who holds your seat. Read the instructions on each ballot paper carefully, because a missing or repeated number can make a House vote informal. Remember that preferences matter: where you put the major parties relative to each other can decide a close seat. How-to-vote cards handed out by parties are only suggestions; you can number the boxes however you choose. Your vote is secret, and nobody can require you to reveal it.

quiz.q: Since when has voting been compulsory in Australian federal elections?
quiz.e: The law passed in 1924 and was first applied at the 1925 election.

quiz.q: What does a House of Representatives candidate need to win a seat?
o: The most first preferences, however few
More than 50% of formal votes after preferences
quiz.e: Preferences are distributed until someone has an absolute majority.

quiz.q: When no candidate has a majority, what happens first?
o: The lowest candidate is excluded and their votes go to next preferences
The two leading candidates share the seat
quiz.e: This repeats until one candidate passes 50%.

quiz.q: Above the line on the Senate ballot, how many boxes should you number at minimum?
quiz.e: Since 2016 the instruction is at least six above the line or twelve below.

quiz.q: Besides letting people vote in private, what did the 1856 secret ballot introduce?
o: Voting by a show of hands
Official ballot papers printed by the government, listing all candidates
quiz.e: Every voter received the same official paper and marked it privately, which made bribery and intimidation much harder.

LESSONS.title: Human rights: where they come from
LESSONS.hook: In 1948, after the horrors of the Second World War, the world's nations agreed on a list of rights belonging to every person. Here's what's in it, and how Australia protects rights without a bill of rights.

sections.key: Human rights are the basic freedoms and protections held by every person simply because they are human.
sections.b: Human rights are the basic rights and freedoms that belong to every person, regardless of nationality, sex, race, religion or any other status. The idea has deep roots: religious and philosophical traditions across many cultures taught the dignity of the person, Magna Carta limited a king's power in 1215, and Enlightenment thinkers wrote of natural rights. Documents such as the US Bill of Rights of 1791 and France's Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen of 1789 put rights into law. But the idea that rights apply to all humanity, and are an international concern, took shape mainly after 1945.

sections.key: The UN General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights on 10 December 1948.
sections.b: The Second World War and the Holocaust showed what could happen when states treated human beings as disposable. The new United Nations set up a commission, chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt, to draft a common standard. Australia was one of eight countries on the drafting committee, and the Australian H.V. Evatt was President of the General Assembly when the Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted in Paris on 10 December 1948. There were 48 votes in favour, none against and eight abstentions. Its 30 articles begin: 'All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.' The date is now marked each year as Human Rights Day.

sections.key: The Declaration isn't a binding treaty, but it led to binding covenants adopted in 1966.
sections.b: The Universal Declaration was not a treaty, so it didn't directly bind countries in law. It was a statement of shared aims, though it has become enormously influential and has shaped many constitutions and laws. To turn its principles into binding obligations, the UN adopted two major treaties in 1966: the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights. Together with the Declaration, they are often called the International Bill of Human Rights. Other treaties followed on specific issues, including racial discrimination, discrimination against women, torture, children's rights and disability.

sections.key: Civil and political rights protect freedom from abuse of power and the right to take part in public life.
sections.b: Civil and political rights are sometimes called 'first-generation' rights. They mainly protect people from the misuse of state power and guarantee participation in public life. They include the right to life, freedom from torture and slavery, freedom from arbitrary arrest, the right to a fair trial, freedom of thought, religion, expression and assembly, the right to privacy, and the right to vote and take part in government. Many of these rights can be limited in certain circumstances, for example to protect public safety or the rights of others, but some, such as the ban on torture, are treated as absolute.

sections.key: These rights cover work, education, health, housing and social security, and are usually realised progressively.
sections.b: Economic, social and cultural rights include the right to work in fair conditions, to form and join trade unions, to social security, to an adequate standard of living including food and housing, to the highest attainable standard of health, and to education. Because these depend on resources, the treaty asks countries to achieve them progressively, using the maximum resources available. People disagree about their status. Some argue they are just as fundamental as civil rights, and that freedom means little without food or schooling. Others argue they are better seen as policy goals for elected governments than as rights for courts to enforce.

sections.key: Australia has no national bill of rights; rights are protected by the Constitution, common law, statutes and scrutiny processes.
sections.b: Australia is often described as the only Western democracy without a national bill or charter of rights. Instead, rights are protected in several ways. The Constitution contains a few express rights and an implied freedom of political communication. The common law presumes Parliament doesn't intend to override basic freedoms unless it says so clearly. Federal laws ban discrimination on grounds including race (1975), sex (1984), disability (1992) and age (2004), and the Australian Human Rights Commission handles complaints. Since 2012, new federal bills must come with a statement on their compatibility with human rights, reviewed by a parliamentary committee. The ACT, Victoria and Queensland have their own human rights Acts.

sections.key: Supporters say a bill of rights would strengthen protections; critics say it would shift power from Parliament to judges.
sections.b: Whether Australia should adopt a national bill of rights is a long-running debate. Supporters argue that the current protections have gaps, that ordinary laws can be changed by any Parliament, and that a clear list of rights would help vulnerable people and educate citizens. Critics argue that elected Parliaments, answerable to voters, should make hard choices about balancing rights, not unelected judges, and that Australia already protects rights well by international standards. Some propose a middle path like the Victorian model, where courts can declare laws inconsistent with rights but Parliament keeps the final say. Reasonable people across politics disagree.

sections.key: If you face discrimination, you can complain to the Australian Human Rights Commission or a state body.
sections.b: Human rights aren't only for courts and diplomats. If you believe you've been discriminated against at work, in housing, in education or when receiving services, you can complain to the Australian Human Rights Commission or your state or territory anti-discrimination body, which usually try to resolve complaints through conciliation first. Australians can also, after exhausting local options, complain to UN committees. In a well-known 1994 case, Toonen v Australia, the UN Human Rights Committee found Tasmanian laws criminalising homosexual acts breached the right to privacy, and federal law changed soon after. This is general information; a lawyer or community legal centre can advise on your situation.

quiz.q: When was the Universal Declaration of Human Rights adopted?
quiz.e: It was adopted in Paris; 10 December is now Human Rights Day.

quiz.q: Why were the 1966 covenants important?
o: They turned the Declaration's principles into binding treaties
quiz.e: The Declaration itself was not a binding treaty.

quiz.q: Which is an example of a civil and political right?
o: The right to a fair trial
quiz.e: Civil and political rights protect against abuse of power and guarantee participation.

quiz.q: Which statement about Australia is correct?
o: It has a national bill of rights from 1901
It has no national bill of rights but protects rights through several laws and processes
It has never signed a human rights treaty
Human rights are only protected by the states
quiz.e: Protection comes from the Constitution, common law, statutes and parliamentary scrutiny.

quiz.q: What is a common criticism of a national bill of rights?
o: It would shift power from elected Parliament to judges
It would end the common law
quiz.e: Critics prefer elected, accountable Parliaments to make these trade-offs.

LESSONS.title: The United Nations
LESSONS.hook: Born from the ashes of the Second World War, the UN has 193 members, a veto that can freeze it, and agencies that helped wipe out smallpox. Here's how it works and why it divides opinion.

sections.key: The UN Charter was signed in San Francisco in June 1945 and came into force on 24 October 1945.
sections.b: The United Nations was created as the Second World War ended, with the aim of preventing another global war. Its predecessor, the League of Nations, founded in 1920, had failed to stop aggression in the 1930s, partly because major powers were absent or left. Delegates from 50 countries met in San Francisco and signed the UN Charter on 26 June 1945, and Poland soon became the 51st founding member. The Charter came into force on 24 October 1945, now marked as United Nations Day. Australia was a founding member. Membership has grown to 193 countries, with headquarters in New York.

sections.key: The UN has six principal organs, including the General Assembly, Security Council, Secretariat and International Court of Justice.
sections.b: The Charter created six principal organs. The General Assembly includes every member state. The Security Council handles threats to peace. The Economic and Social Council coordinates economic and social work. The Trusteeship Council oversaw territories moving to independence, and suspended its work in 1994 after the last one, Palau, became independent. The International Court of Justice, based in The Hague, settles legal disputes between states. The Secretariat is the UN's staff, led by the Secretary-General, who is appointed for a five-year term by the General Assembly on the Security Council's recommendation and acts as the organisation's chief administrator and public voice.

sections.key: Every member state has one vote in the General Assembly, but its resolutions are usually recommendations, not binding law.
sections.b: The General Assembly is the UN's most representative body: all 193 members sit in it, and each has one vote, whether it's China or a tiny Pacific nation like Tuvalu. It meets each year from September in New York, when leaders give speeches during a high-level week. It debates global issues, approves the UN budget, admits new members on the Security Council's recommendation and elects the Council's non-permanent members. Important questions need a two-thirds majority. But most of its resolutions are recommendations rather than binding law, so they carry moral and political weight rather than direct legal force.

sections.h: The Security Council and the veto
sections.key: The Security Council has five permanent members with a veto: China, France, Russia, the UK and the US.
sections.b: The Security Council is the UN's most powerful body. It has 15 members: five permanent members, China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States, and ten members elected for two-year terms. Its decisions on threats to peace can be binding on all members, and it can impose sanctions or authorise military force. Each permanent member has a veto: a single 'no' vote blocks any substantive resolution. The veto was the price of getting the great powers to join. It has been used many times, most often by the Soviet Union or Russia and by the United States, and has often left the Council deadlocked.

sections.key: UN agencies like WHO, UNICEF, UNHCR and UNESCO work on health, children, refugees and culture.
sections.b: Much of the UN's work happens through specialised agencies, funds and programmes. The World Health Organization, founded in 1948, coordinated the campaign that eradicated smallpox, declared in 1980, and sets international health standards. UNICEF, created in 1946, supports children's health, nutrition and education. The UN refugee agency, UNHCR, protects and assists people forced from their homes. The World Food Programme, which won the 2020 Nobel Peace Prize, delivers food aid in crises. UNESCO runs the World Heritage list, which includes Australian places such as the Great Barrier Reef, Uluru-Kata Tjuta and the Sydney Opera House.

sections.key: UN peacekeepers, the 'blue helmets', monitor ceasefires and protect civilians, with mixed results.
sections.b: The Charter doesn't mention peacekeeping; it developed through practice. Early observer missions began in the late 1940s, and Australians were among the first UN military observers, in Indonesia in 1947. The first armed peacekeeping force was sent to the Middle East after the 1956 Suez Crisis. Peacekeepers, known as blue helmets, are troops and police lent by member states to monitor ceasefires, protect civilians and support elections. UN peacekeeping received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1988. There have been successes, but also grave failures, notably in Rwanda in 1994 and at Srebrenica in Bosnia in 1995, where peacekeepers failed to prevent mass killings.

sections.key: Supporters value the UN as a global forum and aid provider; critics point to deadlock, bureaucracy and outdated power structures.
sections.b: Supporters argue the UN has helped avoid a third world war, given every nation a voice, delivered aid to millions, set shared standards on everything from human rights to aviation and postal services, and provided a place where rivals keep talking. Critics raise several points: the veto lets any permanent member block action, even when atrocities are occurring; the Council's membership reflects the power of 1945, not today; the organisation can be slow and bureaucratic; and one-country-one-vote gives tiny and huge nations equal weight. Some critics also worry about UN bodies overriding national decisions. Many reform proposals exist, but changing the Charter requires the permanent members' agreement.

sections.key: Australia helped shape the UN in 1945 and has served on the Security Council and in many peacekeeping missions.
sections.b: Australia was an active founder. At San Francisco, its delegation led by H.V. Evatt pushed for a stronger voice for smaller and middle powers and argued against the full scope of the veto, without success. Australia held the Security Council's first presidency in 1946 and has since served several terms as an elected member. Tens of thousands of Australian military and police personnel have served in UN and UN-authorised missions, including in Cyprus, Cambodia and East Timor. Whatever your view of the UN, it shapes Australian life through treaties, trade rules, health standards and heritage listings, so understanding it helps make sense of world news.

quiz.q: When did the UN Charter come into force?
quiz.e: It's now marked each year as United Nations Day.

quiz.q: How many votes does each member state have in the General Assembly?
quiz.e: Every member state, large or small, has one vote.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a permanent member of the Security Council?
quiz.e: The five are China, France, Russia, the UK and the US.

quiz.q: Which UN agency coordinated the eradication of smallpox?
quiz.e: Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980.

quiz.q: What is a common criticism of the Security Council?
o: It has no power to impose sanctions
Its permanent membership reflects the world of 1945
It meets only once a decade
quiz.e: Critics also note that any permanent member can block action with its veto.

LESSONS.title: Engines: turning fire into motion
LESSONS.hook: For most of history, all power came from muscle, wind and water. Then people learned to turn fire into motion, and the world sped up.

sections.key: Before engines, work was powered by muscle, wind and flowing water.
sections.b: For most of human history, almost all work was done by the muscles of people and animals, helped by wind and flowing water. Waterwheels ground grain and sails drove ships, but both depended on where rivers ran and which way the wind blew. The idea of steam power is ancient: in the first century AD, Hero of Alexandria described the aeolipile, a ball spun by jets of steam. It was a curiosity, not a machine that did useful work. Turning heat into reliable motion took another 1,600 years, and the push came from an unglamorous problem: flooded mines.

sections.key: Thomas Newcomen's 1712 engine was the first practical steam engine, used to pump water from mines.
sections.b: As English coal and tin mines went deeper, they filled with water. In 1698 Thomas Savery patented a steam-powered pump, but it was limited and prone to failure. The breakthrough came in 1712, when Thomas Newcomen, an ironmonger from Devon, built a working engine near Dudley in the English Midlands. Steam filled a cylinder, then a spray of cold water condensed it, creating a partial vacuum. Air pressure pushed the piston down, rocking a great wooden beam that worked the pump. Newcomen engines were slow and burned huge amounts of coal, but they worked, and hundreds were built over the following decades.

sections.key: Watt didn't invent the steam engine; his separate condenser made it far more efficient.
sections.b: James Watt is often called the inventor of the steam engine, but he improved an existing one. In 1765, after repairing a model Newcomen engine at the University of Glasgow, he realised it wasted most of its fuel reheating a cylinder that was cooled on every stroke. His fix was a separate condenser, so the cylinder could stay hot. Watt and his partner Matthew Boulton sold engines that used roughly a quarter of the coal of a Newcomen engine. Watt later adapted engines to turn wheels and coined 'horsepower' to market them. The popular tale of a boiling kettle inspiring him is a legend.

sections.key: Steam power drove the Industrial Revolution's factories, railways and steamships.
sections.b: Steam power became a driving force of the Industrial Revolution, which began in Britain around the 1760s. Factories no longer had to sit beside rivers, so they grew in towns near coal and workers. In 1804 Richard Trevithick ran the first steam locomotive on rails, in Wales, and in 1830 the Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened, the first intercity line worked entirely by steam locomotives. Steamships soon crossed oceans regardless of the wind. Australia's first steam railway opened in Melbourne in 1854, running from Flinders Street to Sandridge, now Port Melbourne. Journeys that once took days shrank to hours.

sections.key: Internal combustion engines burn fuel inside the cylinder; Otto's four-stroke cycle of 1876 became the standard.
sections.b: A steam engine burns fuel outside the cylinder to boil water. An internal combustion engine burns fuel inside the cylinder itself, so it can be much smaller and lighter for the same power. Belgian-born engineer Etienne Lenoir built a working gas-fuelled version in France around 1860. In 1876 Nicolaus Otto in Germany built a successful four-stroke engine: intake, compression, power, exhaust, a cycle most car engines still use. In the 1890s Rudolf Diesel developed an engine that ignites its fuel simply by squeezing air until it is very hot. Diesel engines now power most trucks and ships, and many trains and generators.

sections.key: Karl Benz built the first practical petrol car in 1885–86; Henry Ford made cars affordable rather than inventing them.
sections.b: Karl Benz is widely credited with the first practical motor car, a three-wheeled vehicle with a petrol engine that he built in 1885 and patented in 1886. In 1888 his wife, Bertha Benz, drove it about 100 kilometres to visit her mother, without telling him, proving it was usable on real roads. Gottlieb Daimler and Wilhelm Maybach were building petrol vehicles in Germany at the same time. A common myth is that Henry Ford invented the car. His real contribution was making it cheap: the Model T arrived in 1908, and his moving assembly line, from 1913, slashed the time needed to build one.

sections.key: Electric motors grew from Faraday's 1821 experiments and are far more efficient than fuel engines.
sections.b: Electric motors turn electricity into motion using magnetism. In 1821 Michael Faraday showed that a wire carrying a current could be made to rotate around a magnet, the basic principle behind every motor. Many inventors turned the idea into practical machines over the following decades. In the late 1880s Nikola Tesla and, independently, Italian physicist Galileo Ferraris developed the alternating current induction motor, still the workhorse of industry. Electric cars are not new either: they were fairly common around 1900 before cheap petrol won out. Electric motors typically turn around 90% of their energy into motion, while petrol engines manage roughly 20 to 35%.

sections.key: Engines were built step by step by many people; the lone-genius story is usually a myth.
sections.b: The history of engines shows that big inventions are rarely one person's flash of genius. Newcomen built on Savery, Watt improved Newcomen, and Benz, Daimler and Diesel all built on Lenoir and Otto. Names tend to stick to whoever made an idea practical or profitable, which is why Watt and Ford get credit for things they didn't originate. Engines also brought heavy costs: burning coal and oil caused air pollution and drove the rise in carbon dioxide behind climate change. Today the story is turning again, as electric motors running on renewable energy take over jobs once done by fuel engines.

quiz.q: What was Thomas Newcomen's 1712 steam engine mainly used for?
quiz.e: Newcomen's engine was built to pump water from deep mines, the first practical job for steam power.

quiz.q: What word did James Watt coin to help sell his engines?
quiz.e: Watt compared his engines' output with the work of horses, and the unit is still used for car engines today.

quiz.q: Where did Australia's first steam railway run, in 1854?
quiz.e: The line ran from Flinders Street to Sandridge, now Port Melbourne. Sydney and Adelaide followed within about two years.

quiz.q: What was Henry Ford's main contribution to motoring?
o: Making cars affordable through mass production
quiz.e: Ford didn't invent the car. The Model T and his moving assembly line made cars cheap enough for ordinary families.

quiz.q: Roughly how much of their energy do electric motors turn into motion?
quiz.e: Electric motors are around 90% efficient, far better than petrol engines, which waste most of their energy as heat.

LESSONS.title: Electric light
LESSONS.hook: Before electric light, nights were dim, smoky and a real fire risk. The story of the light bulb involves many hands, not one lone genius.

sections.key: Before electric light, people relied on candles, oil lamps, kerosene and, later, gas.
sections.b: For thousands of years, light after sunset came from flames: wood fires, animal-fat candles, beeswax and oil lamps. It was dim, smoky and costly, and house fires were a constant danger. Whale oil lit many homes in the early 1800s, and kerosene lamps spread from the 1850s. Gas made from coal lit city streets from the early 1800s, and Sydney's streets were first lit by gas in 1841, supplied by the Australian Gas Light Company, whose name survives today as AGL. Even so, most households spent their evenings in a gloom that would feel startling now.

sections.key: Dozens of inventors worked on electric lamps before Edison, starting with the arc light.
sections.b: Electric light began with the arc lamp. In the early 1800s English chemist Humphry Davy showed that electricity leaping between two carbon rods produced a brilliant glow. Arc lamps later lit streets, lighthouses and factories, but they were far too harsh, hot and fumy for a living room. The alternative was incandescence: heating a thin filament until it glows. Many inventors tried this through the 1800s, but their filaments burned out quickly, because oxygen left in the bulb destroyed them. The challenge was a filament that would last, sealed in a good vacuum, and cheap enough to make in large numbers.

sections.key: Joseph Swan in England and Thomas Edison in the US developed practical bulbs around 1879; credit is shared.
sections.b: The popular story says Thomas Edison invented the light bulb in 1879. The fuller truth is that he and English chemist Joseph Swan reached practical carbon-filament bulbs at about the same time. Swan publicly demonstrated his lamp in Newcastle upon Tyne in early 1879, and Edison's team achieved long-lasting filaments late that year, soon switching to carbonised bamboo. Both built on decades of earlier work by others. After a patent dispute in Britain, the two joined forces in 1883, forming the Edison and Swan United Electric Light Company, known as 'Ediswan'. Historians generally credit both men with the practical bulb.

sections.key: Edison's biggest contribution was a whole electrical system: generation, wiring, meters and fuses.
sections.b: Edison's greatest contribution was less the bulb than the system around it. A bulb is useless without a supply of electricity, so his team designed generators, underground cables, switches, fuses and meters to bill customers. In September 1882 his Pearl Street Station in New York began supplying paying customers in the surrounding district. Edison also ran an early industrial research laboratory at Menlo Park, New Jersey, where teams of staff tested thousands of materials systematically. That approach, organised invention by a team rather than a lone tinkerer, became a model for modern corporate research and development.

sections.key: Edison backed direct current (DC); Westinghouse and Tesla backed alternating current (AC), which won.
sections.b: Edison's system used direct current (DC), which flows one way and, at the low voltages of the day, could not travel much more than a kilometre or two without heavy losses. Alternating current (AC), which rapidly reverses direction, can be stepped up to high voltage with transformers for long-distance transmission, then stepped down for homes. Businessman George Westinghouse championed AC, licensing Nikola Tesla's AC motor patents in 1888. In the late 1880s the two camps fought a bitter public battle, and Edison's side stressed the dangers of high-voltage AC, including grim public demonstrations that electrocuted animals. AC won because it was cheaper to distribute.

sections.h: Tesla and Edison, minus the myths
sections.key: Tesla was a brilliant inventor, but neither he nor Edison is the simple hero or villain of popular legend.
sections.b: The rivalry between Tesla and Edison has become an internet legend, often told as genius hero versus greedy villain. The record is more mixed. Tesla, a Serbian-American engineer, worked briefly for Edison's company in 1884 and made major contributions to AC motors. But AC power drew on many people, including the transformer work of Lucien Gaulard, John Gibbs and William Stanley. Tesla's story of being cheated out of a $50,000 bonus comes from his own later account and can't be confirmed. And Edison did not personally kill Topsy the elephant in 1903; a film company bearing his name recorded it, years after the current wars ended.

sections.key: AC grids spread worldwide; in 1888 Tamworth became the first Australian town with electric street lighting.
sections.b: AC's victory was sealed in the 1890s, when a Westinghouse AC system lit the 1893 Chicago World's Fair and, from 1896, carried power from Niagara Falls to the city of Buffalo. In Australia, Tamworth in New South Wales became the first town to light its streets with electricity, in 1888, earning the nickname 'City of Light'. Over the following decades, local power stations were joined into larger grids, and today the east coast grid is one of the longest interconnected power systems in the world. DC has made a comeback for special jobs: the Basslink cable under Bass Strait uses high-voltage DC.

sections.key: LEDs, made possible by the bright blue LED of the early 1990s, use far less energy than old bulbs.
sections.b: Old incandescent bulbs wasted most of their energy, around 90%, as heat. Australia began phasing most of them out in 2009, one of the first countries to do so. The next leap was the light-emitting diode. Nick Holonyak built the first visible, red LED in 1962, but white light needed a bright blue LED, which Isamu Akasaki, Hiroshi Amano and Shuji Nakamura achieved in the early 1990s, earning the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics. LED bulbs use roughly 75 to 80% less energy than incandescent ones and last many times longer, so replacing any remaining old bulbs is an easy way to trim a power bill.

quiz.q: Who developed a practical carbon-filament bulb at about the same time as Edison?
quiz.e: Joseph Swan demonstrated his bulb in England in early 1879. The two later formed a joint company, 'Ediswan'.

quiz.q: What was Edison's biggest contribution to electric lighting?
o: A complete system to generate, distribute and meter electricity
quiz.e: Edison's team built the whole system, from generators and cables to fuses and meters, with Pearl Street Station opening in 1882.

quiz.q: Why did alternating current (AC) win out over direct current (DC)?
o: It was safer at any voltage
It worked better with gas lighting
Transformers let it travel long distances cheaply at high voltage
quiz.e: Transformers could step AC up for efficient long-distance transmission and down again for homes, making it cheaper to distribute.

quiz.q: Which was the first Australian town to light its streets with electricity, in 1888?
quiz.e: Tamworth switched on electric street lights in 1888 and still calls itself the 'City of Light'.

quiz.q: Which breakthrough made white LED lighting possible?
o: The bright blue LED of the early 1990s
quiz.e: White LEDs need a bright blue LED, achieved by Akasaki, Amano and Nakamura, who shared the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics.

LESSONS.title: Telephone and radio
LESSONS.hook: In 1850 news from London took months to reach Australia. Within one lifetime, voices crossed the world in a fraction of a second.

sections.key: The electric telegraph, developed in the 1830s and 1840s, sent coded messages along wires almost instantly.
sections.b: The first electrical communication system was the telegraph. In Britain, William Cooke and Charles Wheatstone patented a practical system in 1837, and railways soon used it for signalling. In the US, Samuel Morse, working with Alfred Vail, developed a simpler system and the dot-and-dash Morse code. In 1844 Morse sent the message 'What hath God wrought' from Washington to Baltimore. For the first time, information could travel faster than a horse, train or ship. A lasting telegraph cable across the Atlantic followed in 1866, after an 1858 cable failed within weeks.

sections.key: The Overland Telegraph Line, completed in 1872, connected Australia to Britain by cable.
sections.b: Australia's isolation made the telegraph revolutionary. News from Britain once came by ship and could take two months or more. In 1872 the Overland Telegraph Line was completed, running about 3,200 kilometres from Adelaide to Darwin through the centre of the continent. Built under South Australia's Charles Todd, it linked to an undersea cable from Java, connecting Australia to London. Messages that once took weeks now arrived within hours. The line crossed the Country of many Aboriginal nations, and its construction and repeater stations had lasting effects on the people there. Alice Springs grew around one of those stations.

sections.key: Bell patented the telephone in 1876, but Elisha Gray and Antonio Meucci also have serious claims.
sections.b: Alexander Graham Bell, a Scottish-born teacher of deaf students, received a US patent for the telephone in March 1876, and days later spoke the famous words to his assistant: 'Mr Watson, come here, I want to see you.' Credit remains disputed. Elisha Gray filed papers on a similar design at the patent office on the same day as Bell's application. Italian-American Antonio Meucci had built voice-transmitting devices years earlier but could not afford to keep up his patent notice. In 2002 the US House of Representatives passed a resolution honouring Meucci's work. Many people contributed; Bell won the legal battles.

sections.key: Telephones spread through exchanges, where operators were later replaced by automatic switching.
sections.b: A telephone is only useful if it connects to others, so networks grew around exchanges. At first, human operators, very often women, connected each call by hand, using plugs and cords on a switchboard. Automatic exchanges, which connected calls using the numbers dialled, appeared in the 1890s and spread through the 20th century. Australia's first telephone exchange opened in Melbourne in 1880. Long-distance and overseas calls remained expensive for decades and often had to be booked in advance. By the late 20th century, nearly every Australian home had a landline, and the phone was an ordinary part of daily life.

sections.key: Radio built on Maxwell and Hertz; Marconi made wireless telegraphy practical, but credit is shared.
sections.b: Radio rests on science from the 1860s, when James Clerk Maxwell predicted invisible electromagnetic waves, and the late 1880s, when Heinrich Hertz proved they existed. From 1895, young Italian Guglielmo Marconi turned this into practical wireless telegraphy, sending Morse code without wires over ever greater distances. In 1901 he claimed a signal across the Atlantic, though some historians doubt it was truly heard. Others made key contributions, including Oliver Lodge, Jagadish Chandra Bose, Alexander Popov, Karl Ferdinand Braun and Nikola Tesla. Marconi shared the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physics with Braun. A 1943 US Supreme Court ruling struck down some of Marconi's patent claims, but named no single inventor of radio.

sections.key: On 22 September 1918, Ernest Fisk received the first direct radio messages from Britain in Sydney.
sections.b: On 22 September 1918, Australia received the first direct wireless messages from Britain. Prime Minister Billy Hughes, visiting Wales, sent a message from Marconi's station there, and it was picked up roughly 17,000 kilometres away by Ernest Fisk at his home in Wahroonga, Sydney. Fisk went on to lead the company AWA, Amalgamated Wireless (Australasia). Regular broadcasting began in 1923, and radio soon became the nation's shared living room, bringing news, sport and serials. In the outback, Alfred Traeger's pedal-powered radio, from 1929, let remote stations call the Flying Doctor, and later made the School of the Air possible.

sections.key: The first handheld mobile call was made in 1973; Australia's first mobile network launched in 1987.
sections.b: Radio and telephone finally merged in the mobile phone. On 3 April 1973, Motorola engineer Martin Cooper made the first call from a handheld mobile phone on a New York street. His prototype weighed around a kilogram and offered only about half an hour of talk time. Australia's first mobile network, an analogue service run by Telecom Australia, launched in 1987. Digital networks followed in the 1990s, bringing text messaging, and smartphones from 2007 put the internet in our pockets. Today mobiles carry far more data than voice calls, and many households have dropped the landline altogether.

sections.key: Communication inventions were collective efforts, and each one reshaped how people live.
sections.b: The story of communication is a story of shared credit. Morse, Bell and Marconi are famous because they made ideas practical, won patents and built companies, not because they worked alone. When you hear a single name attached to an invention, it's worth asking who else was working on the same problem at the time. Each leap also changed society: the telegraph cut news times from months to hours, radio created mass audiences, and mobile phones made people reachable almost anywhere. The next time a call drops out in the bush, remember that a clear voice across Australia was once close to a miracle.

quiz.q: What did the Overland Telegraph Line, completed in 1872, connect?
o: Adelaide and Darwin, linking Australia to Britain by cable
quiz.e: The line ran about 3,200 km from Adelaide to Darwin, where an undersea cable carried messages on towards London.

quiz.q: Why is credit for the telephone disputed?
o: It was first developed in Australia
Elisha Gray and Antonio Meucci worked on similar devices
quiz.e: Gray filed papers the same day as Bell, and Meucci had built voice devices years earlier. Bell won the patent battles.

quiz.q: Which statement about Marconi is most accurate?
o: He made wireless telegraphy practical, building on others' work
A court declared him the sole inventor of radio
quiz.e: Hertz proved radio waves existed; Marconi made wireless practical, while Lodge, Bose, Popov, Braun, Tesla and others also contributed.

quiz.q: Who received the first direct wireless messages from Britain, in Sydney in 1918?
quiz.e: Ernest Fisk picked up the messages at his Wahroonga home. Billy Hughes sent one of them from Wales.

quiz.q: When did Australia's first mobile phone network launch?
quiz.e: Telecom Australia launched an analogue mobile network in 1987. The first handheld mobile call, in New York, was in 1973.

LESSONS.title: The story of flight
LESSONS.hook: People dreamed of flying for thousands of years. Then, in just 25 years, they went from a 12-second hop to crossing the Pacific.

sections.key: Humans first flew in hot-air balloons in 1783; George Cayley later worked out the forces of flight.
sections.b: People have long imagined flying, from the Greek myth of Icarus to Leonardo da Vinci's sketches of flapping machines. The first humans actually to fly went up in 1783, in a hot-air balloon built by the Montgolfier brothers in France. Balloons, though, go wherever the wind takes them. The scientific foundation for aeroplanes came from English engineer George Cayley, who around 1800 identified the four forces involved: lift, drag, thrust and weight. He realised a fixed wing could provide lift while something else provided thrust, and in 1853 one of his gliders carried a man across a small valley.

sections.key: Lilienthal's gliders and Australian Lawrence Hargrave's box kite helped pave the way for powered flight.
sections.b: In the 1890s German engineer Otto Lilienthal made around 2,000 glider flights, gathering data and inspiring others worldwide, before dying after a crash in 1896. In Sydney, Lawrence Hargrave was experimenting with flying machines. His most important invention, the box kite of 1893, was remarkably stable and strong for its weight. In 1894 at Stanwell Park, south of Sydney, he was lifted about five metres off the ground by a string of four box kites. Hargrave chose not to patent his work, sharing it freely, and box-kite-style structures influenced several early European aeroplanes. He featured on Australia's old paper $20 note.

sections.key: On 17 December 1903 the Wright brothers made the first controlled, sustained powered aeroplane flights.
sections.b: On 17 December 1903, near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, Orville Wright flew about 37 metres in 12 seconds. Later that day Wilbur flew about 260 metres in 59 seconds. Their key insight was control. The brothers, bicycle makers from Ohio, realised a flying machine had to be steered in three dimensions, so they twisted, or warped, the wings to roll the aircraft, alongside a rudder and elevator. They built their own wind tunnel to test wing shapes, and with mechanic Charlie Taylor built a light petrol engine. Rival claims exist, notably for Brazil's Alberto Santos-Dumont, who flew publicly in Paris in 1906, but most historians credit the Wrights.

sections.key: Wings turn air downward, creating lower pressure above and higher pressure below; the equal-transit-time story is wrong.
sections.b: A common explanation says air over the curved top of a wing must travel further, so it speeds up to 'meet' the air underneath at the back. This equal-transit-time idea is a myth: nothing forces the air to meet up, and in fact air over the top arrives well before the air underneath. What really happens is that the wing, tilted slightly into the airflow, turns a large mass of air downward. Pushing air down pushes the wing up, as Newton's third law describes. The same flow creates lower pressure above the wing and higher pressure below. Both descriptions are true at once, which is why planes can even fly upside down.

sections.key: Ross and Keith Smith flew England to Australia in 1919; Kingsford Smith crossed the Pacific in 1928.
sections.b: Early aviation had strong Australian threads. In 1919 brothers Ross and Keith Smith, with mechanics Wally Shiers and Jim Bennett, flew a Vickers Vimy from England to Darwin in about 28 days, winning a government prize of 10,000 pounds. In 1928 Charles Kingsford Smith and Charles Ulm, with American crew members Harry Lyon and James Warner, made the first flight across the Pacific, from California to Brisbane in the Southern Cross, stopping in Hawaii and Fiji. Later that year Kingsford Smith also made the first flight across the Tasman to New Zealand. He disappeared over the Andaman Sea in 1935.

sections.key: Qantas was founded in outback Queensland in 1920 and is one of the world's oldest airlines.
sections.b: In November 1920, Hudson Fysh, Paul McGinness and grazier Fergus McMaster founded Queensland and Northern Territory Aerial Services, now Qantas, at Winton in western Queensland. Its base soon moved to Longreach, and in 1922 it began regular airmail flights between Charleville and Cloncurry. For isolated outback communities, aircraft cut journeys of days to hours. In 1928 the first Flying Doctor flight, from Cloncurry, used an aircraft leased from Qantas. Qantas grew into Australia's international airline and is one of the oldest airlines in the world still flying. Its name began as an acronym, which is why there is no 'u' after the 'Q'.

sections.key: Jet engines, pioneered by Whittle and von Ohain, made fast long-distance passenger flight routine.
sections.b: Propeller aircraft have limits on speed and altitude. In the 1930s Frank Whittle in Britain and Hans von Ohain in Germany independently developed the jet engine, which sucks in air, compresses it, burns fuel in it and blasts the exhaust out the back. The first jet aircraft flew in Germany in 1939. The first jet airliner, Britain's de Havilland Comet, entered service in 1952, but fatal crashes caused by metal fatigue around openings in the cabin taught hard lessons in aircraft design. Boeing's 707 from 1958 and 747 from 1970 made long-haul flying ordinary, and in 2018 Qantas launched non-stop flights between Perth and London.

sections.key: Flying is extremely safe today because every accident is investigated and its lessons shared.
sections.b: In little more than a century, flight went from 12 seconds over a sand dune to hundreds of passengers crossing the planet overnight. Commercial air travel is now one of the safest ways to travel, largely because the industry investigates accidents in detail and shares the lessons worldwide, helped by inventions such as the cockpit flight recorder developed in Australia. Flight has also shrunk Australia's distances: a trip to Europe that once took weeks by ship now takes about a day. The cost is significant greenhouse gas emissions, and cleaner aviation fuels and more efficient aircraft are active areas of research.

quiz.q: What did Lawrence Hargrave invent in 1893?
quiz.e: Hargrave's stable box kite lifted him off the ground in 1894 and influenced early aeroplane designs.

quiz.q: What was the Wright brothers' key insight?
o: Controlling the aircraft in three dimensions
quiz.e: The Wrights focused on control, using wing warping, a rudder and an elevator to steer in three dimensions.

quiz.q: Why is the 'equal transit time' explanation of lift wrong?
o: Air over the top has no reason to meet the air below, and actually arrives earlier
Wings don't involve air pressure at all
Air under the wing always travels faster
Lift comes only from the engine
quiz.e: Nothing forces the airflows to meet up. Wings create lift by turning air downward, producing a pressure difference.

quiz.q: Who made the first flight across the Pacific, in 1928?
o: Charles Kingsford Smith and his crew
quiz.e: Kingsford Smith, Charles Ulm, Harry Lyon and James Warner flew the Southern Cross from California to Brisbane.

quiz.q: Where was Qantas founded in 1920?
quiz.e: Qantas was founded at Winton in western Queensland and soon moved its base to Longreach.

LESSONS.title: Genuinely Australian inventions
LESSONS.hook: From flight recorders to the tech inside Wi-Fi, some of the world's most useful ideas have Australian fingerprints. Here is what is truly ours, and what is shared.

sections.key: David Warren in Melbourne developed a flight recorder that captured cockpit voices as well as instrument data.
sections.b: In 1953 and 1954, a series of de Havilland Comet jet crashes left investigators puzzled. David Warren, a scientist at the Aeronautical Research Laboratories in Melbourne, realised that a recording of the crew's voices and instrument readings would help explain future crashes. By 1958 he had a working prototype that stored hours of cockpit sound and flight data. Simpler instrument-only recorders were being developed elsewhere, but Warren's combination of voices and data was new. Australia became one of the first countries to require cockpit voice recorders, in the 1960s. Despite the name, these 'black boxes' are painted bright orange so they are easier to find.

sections.key: Australian scientists led by George Kossoff in Sydney helped pioneer grey-scale ultrasound imaging.
sections.b: Medical ultrasound, which builds pictures from high-frequency sound echoes, was not invented in Australia; Scottish doctor Ian Donald pioneered its use in pregnancy in the 1950s. But Australian researchers made a major contribution. At the Ultrasonics Institute in Sydney, part of the Commonwealth Acoustic Laboratories, a team led by George Kossoff and David Robinson developed grey-scale imaging in the early 1970s. Earlier scans showed mostly stark outlines; grey-scale revealed shades of soft tissue, making images far easier to interpret. Their work was commercialised by the Australian company Ausonics, and grey-scale imaging became standard in ultrasound machines worldwide.

sections.key: Graeme Clark's team developed the multi-channel cochlear implant, first implanted in Melbourne in 1978.
sections.b: Professor Graeme Clark, whose father had lived with hearing loss, set out to help people with severe deafness. A cochlear implant bypasses damaged parts of the inner ear and stimulates the hearing nerve directly with electrical signals. Single-channel implants had already been tried in France and the United States, so Clark didn't invent the idea. His University of Melbourne team's achievement was a multi-channel implant able to convey speech far more clearly. The first patient, Rod Saunders, received one in 1978. The Sydney company Cochlear Limited commercialised the device in the 1980s, and it has become one of the world's leading hearing implant makers.

sections.key: CSIRO patented a key technique that made fast indoor wireless networking work; Wi-Fi itself had many contributors.
sections.b: You'll often hear that Australia invented Wi-Fi. The accurate version is narrower, but still impressive. In the early 1990s a CSIRO team including radio astronomer John O'Sullivan tackled a stubborn problem: indoors, radio signals bounce off walls and furniture, and the echoes smear fast data together. Drawing on mathematical techniques from radio astronomy, they developed a way around it and patented it, with the US patent granted in 1996. Their method became part of widely used Wi-Fi standards, starting with 802.11a and 802.11g. Wi-Fi as a whole grew from the work of many companies and engineers, but CSIRO's patent earned it hundreds of millions of dollars in licensing settlements.

sections.key: Dr Fiona Wood and scientist Marie Stoner in Perth developed a way to spray a patient's own skin cells onto burns.
sections.b: Severe burns heal slowly, and large skin grafts can leave heavy scarring. In the 1990s in Perth, plastic surgeon Dr Fiona Wood and scientist Marie Stoner developed a way to spray a patient's own skin cells onto a wound to help new skin grow. Early versions grew the cells in a laboratory first; the later ReCell device processes a small sample of healthy skin into a cell suspension during the operation itself. Wood led the burns team at Royal Perth Hospital that treated many survivors of the 2002 Bali bombings, and she was named Australian of the Year in 2005.

sections.key: Lance Hill's 1945 Hills Hoist improved on earlier rotary clotheslines and became a backyard icon.
sections.b: The rotary clothesline is a symbol of the Australian backyard, and its story shows how credit really works. In 1945 Lance Hill, in Adelaide, built a rotary clothesline with a winding crank to raise and lower it, reportedly to free up space in the family's small backyard. Demand from neighbours led him to start a business, Hills Hoist, with his brother-in-law Harold Ling. Hill did not invent the rotary clothesline: earlier designs had been patented in Australia, including by Adelaide inventor Gilbert Toyne decades before. Hill's success came from a sturdy, adjustable design and mass production in the post-war housing boom.

sections.key: Australia issued the world's first polymer banknote in 1988, developed by the Reserve Bank and CSIRO.
sections.b: Soon after decimal currency arrived in 1966, forgers produced convincing fake $10 notes. The Reserve Bank of Australia turned to CSIRO, and over about two decades they developed banknotes printed on polymer, a plastic film, rather than paper. The first, a commemorative $10 note, was issued for the 1988 Bicentenary, and by 1996 Australia had become the first country with a complete set of polymer notes. They include a clear window that is very hard to copy and last several times longer than paper notes. Dozens of countries now use polymer notes, and Australia's newest series adds a tactile feature for people with low vision.

sections.key: Google Maps began as Where 2 Technologies, a Sydney start-up, and was largely developed in Sydney.
sections.b: Google Maps began with a small Sydney start-up called Where 2 Technologies, founded by Danish-born brothers Lars and Jens Rasmussen with Noel Gordon and Stephen Ma. Google bought the company in 2004, and Google Maps launched in 2005, with much of its early development done in Google's Sydney office. It wasn't the first online map, but its smooth, draggable maps changed what people expected a website could do. Like the other stories here, it shows that Australian invention usually means solving a key part of a problem brilliantly. When you read that something was 'invented in Australia', it's worth asking which part, and who else helped.

quiz.q: What was new about David Warren's flight recorder?
o: It was the first device painted orange
It recorded cockpit voices as well as instrument data
It could fly the plane automatically
quiz.e: Instrument-only recorders existed, but Warren's design captured crew voices alongside flight data.

quiz.q: What did Graeme Clark's team develop?
quiz.e: Single-channel implants came first overseas; Clark's multi-channel implant conveyed speech far more clearly.

quiz.q: Which best describes CSIRO's role in Wi-Fi?
o: It patented a key technique for fast indoor wireless networking
It invented all of Wi-Fi alone
It had no role at all
quiz.e: CSIRO solved the indoor echo problem and patented the method, which became part of Wi-Fi standards; many others built Wi-Fi as a whole.

quiz.q: Which statement about the Hills Hoist is accurate?
o: It was the world's first rotary clothesline
It was invented in Sydney in 1888
It improved on earlier rotary clothesline designs
quiz.e: Rotary clotheslines had been patented earlier, including by Gilbert Toyne; Lance Hill's 1945 design became the famous one.

quiz.q: When did Australia issue the world's first polymer banknote?
quiz.e: A commemorative $10 polymer note was issued for the 1988 Bicentenary; the full polymer series was complete by 1996.

LESSONS.title: Risk and return
LESSONS.hook: There is no such thing as a high return with no risk. Understanding why is the first real lesson of investing.

sections.key: Investments that can earn higher returns usually come with a higher chance of losses along the way.
sections.b: The risk–return trade-off is the closest thing investing has to a law of nature. Money in a government-guaranteed bank account is very unlikely to lose value in dollar terms, so it pays a modest interest rate. Shares in companies can fall sharply, so investors demand the prospect of a higher long-run return to hold them. If an asset offered high returns with no risk, everyone would buy it until its price rose and its future return shrank. That is why any offer of 'high returns, no risk' should immediately set off alarm bells.

sections.key: In investing, risk means uncertainty: the chance that results differ from what you expected, including losing money.
sections.b: Most people think of risk as simply losing money, and that matters. But professionals use a broader meaning: uncertainty about outcomes. A term deposit paying 4% has little uncertainty; you know roughly what you will get. A share fund might return 25% one year and lose 15% the next. Other risks are quieter. Inflation risk means your money grows more slowly than prices, so you lose buying power even while your balance rises. Liquidity risk means you can't sell quickly without accepting a lower price. Every investment carries some mix of these.

sections.key: Volatility is how much an investment's value swings up and down; shares are far more volatile than cash.
sections.b: Volatility measures how widely and how often an investment's price moves. It is often expressed as standard deviation, a statistic describing how spread out returns are around the average. Cash barely moves. Shares can move dramatically: during the global financial crisis, the main Australian share index fell roughly half its value between late 2007 and early 2009, and in early 2020 it dropped by more than a third in about a month as COVID-19 spread. Both times it later recovered, but anyone forced to sell near the bottom locked in heavy losses.

sections.key: The main asset classes, from lower to higher expected risk and return, are cash, bonds, property and shares.
sections.b: Investments are grouped into asset classes that behave in broadly similar ways. Cash, such as savings accounts and term deposits, is the most stable but usually earns the least. Fixed interest, mainly bonds, pays regular interest and tends to be steadier than shares. Property can deliver rent and capital growth but is lumpy, costly to buy and sell, and can fall in value. Shares, Australian and international, have historically delivered the highest long-run returns of the main classes, with the biggest swings. Cash and bonds are often called defensive assets; property and shares are called growth assets.

sections.key: The longer you can leave money invested, the more short-term volatility you can usually ride out.
sections.b: Your time horizon is how long until you need the money. It matters because volatility tends to even out over long periods. In any single year, shares have a meaningful chance of falling. Over ten or twenty years, diversified share portfolios have historically been far more likely to end up ahead, although that is a pattern from the past, not a guarantee. Money for a house deposit in two years usually belongs somewhere stable. Money you won't touch for decades, like much of your superannuation, can generally afford more growth assets.

sections.key: Risk tolerance is how much volatility you can stomach; risk capacity is how much loss you can actually afford.
sections.b: Two different questions shape how much risk suits you. Risk tolerance is emotional: can you watch your balance drop 30% without panicking and selling? Risk capacity is financial: could you survive that drop without it wrecking your plans? A young worker with a stable job and decades until retirement has high capacity, even if they feel nervous. A retiree drawing income from savings has lower capacity, even if they feel brave. The right level of risk sits within both limits, and honest self-knowledge is worth more than bravado.

sections.key: What matters is your real return: what you earn after inflation has eroded your money's buying power.
sections.b: A return of 5% sounds decent, but if prices rise 4% that year, your real return is only about 1%. After tax, it may be close to zero. This is why keeping everything in cash is not truly risk-free over long periods: its buying power can shrink slowly, year after year. Australia's Reserve Bank targets inflation of 2–3% on average. Over decades, even that modest rate roughly halves the value of a dollar every 25 to 35 years. Growth assets carry more short-term risk but have historically been better at outpacing inflation over the long run.

sections.key: Match each pot of money to its purpose and timeframe, and be wary of anyone promising returns without risk.
sections.b: A practical approach is to think in buckets. An emergency fund belongs in cash, where it is stable and easy to reach. Short-term goals suit cash or conservative options. Long-term money, like super, can usually lean towards growth assets. Check what investment option your super fund has you in; many people never look. Remember that past returns never guarantee future ones. This lesson is general information, not personal financial advice. For advice about your situation, speak to a licensed financial adviser, and see ASIC's Moneysmart website for free, independent guidance.

quiz.q: Why don't low-risk investments usually offer high returns?
o: Because investors would buy them until prices rose and returns shrank
Because banks are required by law to cap all returns
Because low-risk investments are taxed at a higher rate
Because governments set the return on every investment
quiz.e: If an asset offered high returns with no risk, demand would push its price up and its future return down.

quiz.q: What is inflation risk?
o: The risk a company goes bankrupt
The risk that your money grows more slowly than prices, reducing buying power
The risk that you can't sell an asset quickly
The risk that interest rates are cut to zero
quiz.e: Even a rising balance can lose buying power if inflation outpaces it.

quiz.q: Which of these is usually classed as a defensive asset?
quiz.e: Cash and bonds are defensive assets; shares and property are growth assets.

quiz.q: Why does time horizon matter when choosing investments?
o: Longer periods guarantee that shares will rise
Short-term money should always go into shares
Longer horizons give more time to ride out volatility
Time horizon only affects tax, not risk
quiz.e: Volatility has tended to even out over long periods, though past patterns are no guarantee.

quiz.q: What is the difference between risk tolerance and risk capacity?
o: They mean exactly the same thing
Tolerance is emotional comfort with swings; capacity is how much loss you can afford
Tolerance applies to shares; capacity applies to property
Capacity is set by your bank; tolerance by the government
quiz.e: You need to consider both how you'll feel and what you can actually afford to lose.

LESSONS.title: Bonds explained
LESSONS.hook: Governments and companies borrow trillions of dollars from investors. Bonds are how, and they quietly shape your super and your mortgage.

sections.key: A bond is a loan to a government or company that pays you interest and returns your money at a set date.
sections.b: When you buy a bond, you are lending money. The borrower, called the issuer, promises to pay regular interest, known as the coupon, and to repay the original amount, called the face value, on a set maturity date. A five-year bond with a $100 face value and a 4% coupon pays $4 a year, usually in instalments, then returns the $100 at the end. Shares make you a part-owner of a company; bonds make you a lender. Lenders get paid before shareholders, which is part of why bonds are generally less risky.

sections.key: Government bonds are backed by the government's ability to tax, making them among the safest investments available.
sections.b: The Australian Government borrows by issuing Treasury bonds through the Australian Office of Financial Management. States borrow too, through agencies such as the NSW Treasury Corporation. Because a national government that borrows in its own currency can tax and has a central bank, the chance it fails to repay is considered very low. Australia has held the top AAA credit rating from all three major rating agencies for many years. Ordinary investors can buy some Commonwealth bonds on the ASX as exchange-traded Treasury bonds, though most people hold them through super or managed funds.

sections.key: Corporate bonds pay more than government bonds because there is a greater risk the company can't repay.
sections.b: Companies issue bonds too, from big banks to energy and property businesses. Because a company can fail, investors want extra interest to compensate for credit risk, the chance of default. Rating agencies like S&P, Moody's and Fitch grade issuers from AAA down. Bonds rated BBB- or above are called investment grade. Lower-rated bonds, known as high-yield or, less politely, junk bonds, pay more because the risk of losing money is genuinely higher. A higher interest rate on a bond is usually a price for extra risk, not a free bonus.

sections.key: When interest rates rise, existing bond prices fall; when rates fall, existing bond prices rise.
sections.b: Bonds can be bought and sold before maturity, and their prices change. Imagine you hold a bond paying 3% a year. Then interest rates rise and new bonds pay 5%. Nobody will pay full price for your 3% bond when they can get 5% elsewhere, so its market price falls until its effective return, called its yield, matches the new rate. The reverse happens when rates fall. This see-saw is the most important idea in bond investing. The longer a bond has left until maturity, the more its price moves when rates change.

sections.key: Bonds are not risk-free: in 2022, rapidly rising interest rates caused one of the worst years for bonds in decades.
sections.b: Bonds are called defensive, but they can lose value. In 2022, central banks around the world raised interest rates quickly to fight high inflation. Because bond prices fall when rates rise, many bond funds lost money, and in some markets it was among the worst years for bonds in generations. Unusually, shares fell at the same time, so holders of balanced portfolios had few places to hide. Inflation is another danger: a fixed 3% coupon buys less each year if prices rise 6%. If you hold a high-quality bond to maturity, though, you still receive the face value back.

sections.h: The role of bonds in a portfolio
sections.key: Bonds are mainly held for stability, income and to cushion falls in the share market.
sections.b: Most diversified portfolios, including many super fund options, hold a mix of shares and bonds. Bonds provide predictable income and usually swing far less than shares. Historically, high-quality government bonds have often held their value or risen during share market crashes, as investors rushed to safety and interest rates were cut. That pattern is not guaranteed, as 2022 showed, but bonds still tend to smooth the ride. Older investors, and anyone who needs money within a few years, typically hold a larger share of bonds and cash than younger investors.

sections.key: Term deposits lock money away at a fixed rate; bonds can be sold before maturity but their price may have changed.
sections.b: Term deposits and bonds both pay fixed interest, but they differ. A term deposit with an Australian bank is covered by the government's Financial Claims Scheme up to $250,000 per person per institution, and its value doesn't fluctuate, though breaking it early usually costs you interest. A bond can be sold at any time on the market, but you receive whatever price it fetches that day, which could be more or less than you paid. Bond funds, which hold many bonds, never mature at all, so their value always moves with interest rates.

sections.key: Check how much of your super sits in fixed interest, and remember that bond returns depend on interest rate moves.
sections.b: You probably already own bonds through superannuation. Look at your fund's investment option to see its split between growth assets and defensive assets like fixed interest. When you read that interest rates are rising, you'll now know why the bond portion of a balanced fund may dip, and why higher rates also mean better yields for new bonds. Be cautious with unlisted or high-yield offers promising well above market rates; that extra return reflects extra risk. This is general information only. For personal advice, speak with a licensed financial adviser, and visit Moneysmart for independent guides.

quiz.q: What are you doing when you buy a bond?
o: Lending money to the issuer in return for interest
Buying a share of a property trust
quiz.e: Bondholders are lenders; shareholders are owners.

quiz.q: Why do corporate bonds usually pay more than government bonds?
o: Companies are required to pay more by law
Investors want compensation for the higher risk of default
quiz.e: The extra interest compensates for credit risk.

quiz.q: If interest rates rise, what typically happens to the price of an existing bond?
quiz.e: Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

quiz.q: Why was 2022 a bad year for many bond investors?
o: Bonds were banned in several countries
Interest rates rose quickly, pushing bond prices down
quiz.e: Rapid rate rises to fight inflation caused large falls in bond prices.

quiz.q: What is the main role of bonds in a diversified portfolio?
o: To deliver the highest possible long-run returns
To provide stability and income and cushion share market falls
To guarantee a profit every year
quiz.e: Bonds usually swing less than shares and provide income, though they are not risk-free.

LESSONS.title: Diversification
LESSONS.hook: It's sometimes called the only free lunch in investing: a way to reduce risk without necessarily giving up return.

sections.key: Diversification means spreading your money across many investments so no single failure can sink you.
sections.b: The old saying 'don't put all your eggs in one basket' is the heart of diversification. If you invest everything in one company and it collapses, you can lose everything. Spread the same money across 200 companies, and one collapse costs you only a small slice. Companies fail more often than people think; even household names can go bust or shrink dramatically. Diversification doesn't prevent losses when the whole market falls, but it greatly reduces the damage from any one bad bet, which is the kind of loss that is hardest to recover from.

sections.key: Different investments rise and fall at different times, so their ups and downs partly cancel each other out.
sections.b: Diversification works because investments don't all move together. If one company is hit by a scandal, another may be having a great year. When some sectors struggle, others may thrive. Combine many different assets and their individual ups and downs partly offset each other, so the whole portfolio swings less than its individual parts. The economist Harry Markowitz formalised this idea in 1952 in what became modern portfolio theory, later earning a Nobel Prize. The line that diversification is 'the only free lunch in finance' is often attributed to him.

sections.key: Correlation measures how closely two investments move together; combining lowly correlated assets gives the best diversification.
sections.b: Correlation is measured on a scale from +1 to -1. A correlation of +1 means two investments move in perfect lockstep, so holding both adds no diversification. Zero means their movements are unrelated. A negative correlation means one tends to rise when the other falls. Owning shares in four big Australian banks gives little diversification, because they tend to move together. Adding assets that respond to different forces, such as bonds, international shares or different industries, does far more. One catch: in severe crises, correlations between risky assets often rise, just when you want them low.

sections.key: Mixing asset classes, such as shares, bonds, property and cash, is the broadest level of diversification.
sections.b: The biggest decision in most portfolios is the mix of asset classes, often called asset allocation. Shares offer growth but can fall sharply. Bonds and cash are steadier and have often held up better when shares slump. Property behaves differently again. A 'balanced' super option might hold roughly two-thirds in growth assets and the rest in defensive assets, although definitions vary between funds. Many researchers argue that asset allocation explains most of the ups and downs in a diversified portfolio's value over time, more than which individual shares are picked.

sections.key: The Australian share market is dominated by banks and miners, so owning only local shares leaves you concentrated in a few industries.
sections.b: Diversifying within shares means spreading across industries, or sectors. This matters in Australia because our share market is unusually lopsided. Financials, especially the big banks, and materials, especially mining companies, make up a large share of the main index. Sectors such as technology and healthcare are much smaller here than in global markets. An investor who owns only Australian shares is therefore heavily exposed to the fortunes of banks, iron ore and the local housing market. Adding global shares brings in industries that are barely represented on the ASX.

sections.key: Australia makes up only about 2% of the world's share market, yet many Australians hold mostly local shares.
sections.b: Home bias is the tendency to invest mainly in your own country. It is common everywhere, partly because familiar companies feel safer, and in Australia partly because franking credits make local dividends tax-effective for many investors. But Australia is only around 2% of the value of global share markets. Investing globally spreads your money across different economies, currencies and industries. International shares bring currency risk too: when the Australian dollar rises, overseas investments are worth less in local terms, and when it falls, they are worth more. Some funds 'hedge' to reduce this effect.

sections.key: Concentration can be hidden: owning your employer's shares, or holding many funds with the same investments, reduces diversification.
sections.b: A famous warning comes from Enron, the US energy company that collapsed in 2001. Many employees had much of their retirement savings in Enron shares, so they lost their jobs and their savings at once. Another hidden trap is 'diworsification': owning ten funds that all hold the same large companies looks diversified but isn't. Your job, your home and your super may also all depend on the same local economy. Genuine diversification means checking what you actually own underneath the labels, not just counting how many investments you have.

sections.key: Broad index funds and diversified super options are simple ways to hold hundreds or thousands of investments at low cost.
sections.b: Most people don't need to pick dozens of individual shares. A single broad index fund or exchange-traded fund can hold hundreds or thousands of companies for a low fee. Many super funds' diversified options already spread money across asset classes and countries. Check your own portfolio for concentration: one company, one sector, one country or one property making up most of your wealth. Remember that diversification reduces risk but cannot eliminate it. This is general information only. For advice on your circumstances, see a licensed financial adviser, and use ASIC's Moneysmart website for independent tools.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of diversification?
o: To reduce the damage any single bad investment can cause
To avoid paying tax on investments
To make returns as high as possible regardless of risk
quiz.e: Spreading money widely limits the impact of any one failure.

quiz.q: Which correlation between two investments provides the least diversification benefit?
quiz.e: A correlation of +1 means they move in lockstep, so holding both adds no diversification.

quiz.q: Which two sectors dominate the Australian share market?
quiz.e: Banks and miners make up a large share of the main Australian index.

quiz.q: All else being equal, what happens to the Australian-dollar value of your overseas shares if the Australian dollar rises?
