quiz.e: A stronger dollar means foreign assets convert into fewer Australian dollars; some funds hedge to reduce this effect.

quiz.q: What lesson does the Enron collapse teach?
o: Energy companies should always be avoided
Holding lots of your employer's shares concentrates your risk
quiz.e: Employees lost both jobs and savings because their money was concentrated in the same company.

LESSONS.title: Property investing in Australia
LESSONS.hook: Australians love bricks and mortar. Here is how investment property actually makes, and loses, money.

sections.key: Residential property is the biggest store of household wealth in Australia, and investment property is widely held.
sections.b: Property holds a special place in Australian finances. Residential real estate is the largest single component of household wealth, worth far more in total than the Australian share market. Around two million Australians own at least one investment property, according to tax statistics, and most own just one. Its appeal is easy to see: it is tangible, familiar and can be bought largely with borrowed money. But an investment property is a business decision, not a home, and it should be judged on its numbers, costs and risks like any other investment.

sections.key: Property investors earn money in two ways: rental income (yield) and a rise in the property's value (capital growth).
sections.b: An investment property can return money in two ways. The first is rent, measured as rental yield. Gross yield is the annual rent divided by the price: a $750,000 unit rented for $600 a week earns about $31,200 a year, a gross yield of roughly 4.2%. Net yield subtracts costs and is always lower. The second source is capital growth, the rise in the property's value over time. In many Australian cities, rental yields have been modest, so investors have relied heavily on capital growth, which is never guaranteed and varies greatly by location and period.

sections.key: Stamp duty, loan interest, rates, insurance, maintenance, agent fees and vacancies can eat much of the rent.
sections.b: Buying property is expensive before you even start. Stamp duty, a state tax on purchases, can run to tens of thousands of dollars on a typical home, and rates differ by state. Legal and inspection costs add more. Ongoing costs include loan interest, council and water rates, landlord insurance, strata fees for units, repairs, property management fees and, in some states, land tax. There will be weeks without tenants. When you sell, you pay agent fees and possibly capital gains tax. A property can rise in value and still deliver a disappointing return once every cost is counted.

sections.key: Borrowing to invest, called gearing, magnifies both gains and losses on the money you put in.
sections.b: Most property investors borrow, often most of the purchase price. This is gearing, or leverage. Suppose you buy a $600,000 property with a $120,000 deposit and a loan for the rest. If the property rises 10%, it gains $60,000, which is 50% of your own money. But if it falls 10%, you lose $60,000, half your deposit, and still owe the full loan. Leverage magnifies outcomes in both directions. It also means you must keep making repayments whether or not the property is tenanted, and if interest rates rise, those repayments can climb quickly.

sections.key: A property is negatively geared when its costs exceed its rental income; the loss has generally been deductible against other income, though this is being restricted from July 2027.
sections.b: A property is positively geared when rent exceeds costs, including interest, and negatively geared when costs exceed rent. Under Australian tax law, that net rental loss has generally been deductible against other income, such as wages, reducing the tax you pay. Legislation passed in June 2026 narrows this: from 1 July 2027, losses on established homes bought after 7:30 pm AEST on 12 May 2026 can only be offset against residential property income and gains, with any excess carried forward. Properties bought before then, and new builds, keep the old treatment. Either way, you are still losing money each year, and a tax deduction only recovers part of it. Negative gearing makes sense for an investor only if capital growth eventually outweighs those losses. Its effect on housing affordability and the budget remains a contested policy debate.

sections.key: When you sell an investment property for a profit, capital gains tax applies; the long-standing 50% discount is being replaced from 1 July 2027.
sections.b: Unlike your own home, an investment property is subject to capital gains tax when sold. The gain, roughly the sale price minus the purchase price and certain costs, is added to your taxable income. For individuals who hold the asset for more than 12 months, only half the gain has generally been taxed, under the capital gains tax discount. Under legislation passed in June 2026, from 1 July 2027 that discount is replaced by indexing the cost base for inflation, with a 30% minimum tax on gains; gains built up before that date keep the 50% discount, and new homes can use either method. Depreciation claimed on the building and fittings can affect the calculation. The rules are detailed and depend on your circumstances, so the Australian Taxation Office's guidance and a registered tax agent are essential companions for any property investor.

sections.key: A single property is a large, concentrated, illiquid bet, often on one suburb, funded with debt.
sections.b: Property prices can fall, and have done so at times in various Australian cities and regional areas, including mining towns after resource booms faded. One investment property often represents a huge share of an investor's wealth, all in one asset, one suburb and one market. It is illiquid: selling takes weeks or months and costs a lot, and you can't sell off one bedroom when you need cash. Interest rate rises, a long vacancy, a bad tenant or a major repair such as structural defects can strain your budget. Compare this with the easy diversification available in shares.

sections.key: Run the numbers with realistic costs and interest rates, stress-test for vacancies and rate rises, and get independent advice.
sections.b: Before buying, calculate the net yield using realistic costs, not the optimistic figures in a sales brochure. Stress-test your budget: could you cope with interest rates two or three percentage points higher, or three months without rent? Be wary of spruikers, seminars and 'free' property packages that earn commissions from developers; ASIC has repeatedly warned about them. Consider how the property fits your overall wealth and diversification. This lesson is general information only, not financial or tax advice. Speak with a licensed financial adviser and a registered tax agent, and see Moneysmart's property investing guides.

quiz.q: A property costs $500,000 and earns $20,000 a year in rent. What is its gross rental yield?
quiz.e: Gross yield is annual rent divided by price: $20,000 / $500,000 = 4%.

quiz.q: Which of these is a one-off purchase cost that can run to tens of thousands of dollars?
quiz.e: Stamp duty is a state tax paid when you buy; the others are ongoing costs.

quiz.q: What does gearing do to an investor's returns?
o: Magnifies both gains and losses on the investor's own money
Removes the need to repay the loan
quiz.e: Borrowing amplifies outcomes in both directions.

quiz.q: When is a property negatively geared?
o: When its costs, including interest, exceed its rental income
When it is sold at a loss
quiz.e: Costs, including interest, exceed the rent. The loss has generally been deductible against other income, though this is restricted from July 2027 for established homes bought after 12 May 2026, and it is still a loss.

quiz.q: Why is a single investment property considered a concentrated investment?
o: Because it is guaranteed to rise in value
Because it can be sold instantly
Because a large share of wealth sits in one illiquid asset in one location
quiz.e: One property ties much of your wealth to a single asset and local market.

LESSONS.title: Costly investing mistakes
LESSONS.hook: The biggest threat to most investors isn't the market. It's their own behaviour, and the people who exploit it.

sections.key: Many investing losses come from predictable behaviour: fear, greed, overconfidence and following the crowd.
sections.b: Investing is simple in principle but hard in practice, because human instincts work against it. We feel the pain of losses more strongly than the pleasure of equal gains, a pattern psychologists call loss aversion. We are overconfident in our own judgement, and we copy what others are doing. Behavioural finance, a field shaped by researchers such as Daniel Kahneman, Amos Tversky and Richard Thaler, studies how these biases lead people to buy high, sell low and trade too often. Knowing the traps in advance is the best defence against falling into them.

sections.key: A wonderful business can still be a disappointing investment if you pay too much for its shares.
sections.b: It's natural to assume that buying shares in brilliant, fast-growing companies guarantees good returns. But a share price already reflects what investors expect. If expectations are sky-high, even a company that keeps succeeding can disappoint the people who bought at the top. Microsoft is a famous example. Its business kept growing strongly after the dot-com boom, yet its share price didn't regain its December 1999 peak until late 2016, almost 17 years later. Buyers at the top had paid in advance for years of success. The reverse happens too: dull, unloved companies sometimes reward investors because so little was expected of them. Before buying, ask not only 'Is this a good company?' but 'What am I paying for it?'

sections.key: Selling in a crash turns a temporary paper loss into a permanent real one.
sections.b: When markets fall sharply, the urge to sell and stop the pain is powerful. In March 2020, as COVID-19 spread, share markets plunged, and some Australians switched their super from growth options to cash near the bottom. Markets recovered strongly within months, but those who switched had locked in their losses and missed much of the rebound. A fall in value is a paper loss until you sell. That doesn't mean you should never sell, but decisions made in fear are rarely good ones. Having a written plan before a crash makes it easier to stay calm.

sections.key: Buying whatever has recently soared, out of fear of missing out, often means buying near the peak.
sections.b: Fear of missing out, or FOMO, pushes people into investments after they have already risen dramatically. A friend made a fortune on a stock, social media is buzzing, and it feels like everyone is getting rich but you. By the time something is famous for its gains, much of the rise may be over. The dot-com boom is a classic example: the tech-heavy US Nasdaq index fell by roughly three-quarters from its 2000 peak to its 2002 low. Tips from friends, forums and influencers rarely come with any accountability when they go wrong.

sections.key: Cryptocurrencies have been extremely volatile, with repeated falls of 70% or more, and several major platforms have collapsed.
sections.b: Cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin have made some early buyers very rich, and that is exactly what fuels the hype. But their prices have been extraordinarily volatile. Bitcoin has fallen more than 70% from its peak several times, including in 2022. That same year, the major exchange FTX collapsed, and customers around the world had their funds frozen. Many smaller coins have gone to near zero. Whatever you believe about crypto's future, it is a speculative asset with no earnings or rent behind it. Only invest money you could afford to lose entirely, and be sceptical of anyone promising certainty.

sections.key: Margin loans can force you to sell at the worst possible time, as Storm Financial's clients learned in 2008.
sections.b: A margin loan lets you borrow to buy shares, using those shares as security. It feels clever in a rising market. But if prices fall far enough, the lender issues a margin call: you must add cash quickly, or it sells your shares for you, usually close to the bottom. Australians learned this painfully in the global financial crisis. Townsville-based Storm Financial had encouraged many clients, often near retirement, to borrow against their homes and then take margin loans on top. When markets crashed in 2008, margin calls wiped out savings, some clients lost their homes, and the firm collapsed in early 2009. If you ever borrow to invest, make sure you could survive a severe fall without being forced to sell.

sections.key: Any investment promising high, steady returns with little risk is almost certainly a scam, often a Ponzi scheme.
sections.b: Real investments go up and down. A classic scam sign is the opposite: returns that are high and suspiciously smooth. A Ponzi scheme, named after Charles Ponzi, who promised Boston investors 50% returns in 45 days in 1920, pays earlier investors with money from newer ones. There is no real profit, so it collapses once new money dries up. Bernie Madoff reported steady gains of around 1% a month for decades before his scheme collapsed in 2008, with paper losses of about US$65 billion. Before investing, search ASIC Moneysmart's investor alert list for the company's name, and report anything suspicious to Scamwatch.

sections.key: Invest with a plan, diversify, keep costs low, ignore the noise and seek licensed, independent advice.
sections.b: Good investing is often boring. Set clear goals and a time horizon, choose a diversified mix that matches your risk capacity, and keep costs low. Automate regular contributions so you invest through good times and bad, rather than guessing. Check your portfolio occasionally, not daily, since constant checking tends to trigger emotional decisions. Before any big move, pause and ask whether fear or greed is driving it. This lesson is general information only, not personal advice. For guidance on your situation, see a licensed financial adviser, and visit ASIC's Moneysmart website for free, independent tools.

quiz.q: What is loss aversion?
o: Feeling losses more strongly than equal gains
Refusing to ever invest in shares
A tax rule for capital losses
A type of insurance for investments
quiz.e: Loss aversion means the pain of a loss outweighs the pleasure of an equal gain, which can drive poor decisions.

quiz.q: Microsoft's business kept growing after 1999. Why did its shares take until 2016 to regain their 1999 peak?
o: Investors had paid a very high price for expected future success
Its shares stopped trading for years
quiz.e: A great company can be a poor investment if you pay too much for it.

quiz.q: What does panic selling during a crash typically do?
o: Turns a temporary paper loss into a permanent one
Has no effect on long-term outcomes
quiz.e: Selling locks in the loss and can mean missing the recovery.

quiz.q: What is a margin call?
o: A reminder to pay your broker's annual fee
A lender's demand for more cash, or it sells your shares, after prices fall
A phone call offering a hot share tip
A tax bill on share profits
quiz.e: Margin calls often force investors to sell near the bottom of a fall.

quiz.q: Which is a major warning sign of an investment scam?
o: Guaranteed high returns with little risk
Returns that vary from year to year
quiz.e: Legitimate investments can't guarantee high returns without risk.

LESSONS.title: Where language came from
LESSONS.hook: Every human society ever found has had a full, complex language. How that ability began is one of the hardest puzzles in science, and the clues are hiding in the words we still use.

sections.key: Spoken language leaves no fossils, so its origins must be pieced together from indirect clues.
sections.b: Speech vanishes the moment it is spoken, and writing was only invented around 5,000 years ago, in Mesopotamia and Egypt. By then, humans had almost certainly been talking for tens of thousands of years or more. So scientists have to reason from indirect evidence: skeletons, genes, tools, art and the languages alive today. The question attracted so much wild speculation that in 1866 the Linguistic Society of Paris banned papers on the subject. It returned as serious science only in recent decades, drawing on biology, archaeology and linguistics together.

sections.key: Estimates for when full language appeared range from about 50,000 to several hundred thousand years ago, and remain debated.
sections.b: Anatomically modern humans appeared in Africa roughly 300,000 years ago. Some researchers argue that full language arrived late, perhaps 50,000 to 100,000 years ago, pointing to a flowering of art, ornaments and symbolic objects around that time. Others think it developed much earlier and more gradually, possibly in stages, with simpler forms of communication used by earlier human species. There is no consensus. What we can say is that every living human population has language of equal complexity, which suggests the capacity was in place before our ancestors spread out of Africa.

sections.key: Anatomy and genes like FOXP2 offer hints, but there is no single 'language gene'.
sections.b: Human speech relies on fine control of breathing, the tongue and the larynx. A Neanderthal hyoid bone found at Kebara Cave in Israel in 1983 looks very like ours, hinting that Neanderthals may have had some capacity for speech, though this is still argued over. Genetics adds clues too. A gene called FOXP2 was found in 2001 to affect speech and language when damaged in one British family. It was briefly hyped as 'the language gene', but it is one of many genes involved, and Neanderthals shared our version.

sections.key: Nicaraguan Sign Language and creoles show children building full grammar from limited input.
sections.b: One of the best windows into language origins opened in Nicaragua in the late 1970s and 1980s. Deaf children brought together in new schools, most with no shared sign language, began creating their own. Younger children who joined later made it richer and more regular, and it grew into a full language with its own grammar, now called Nicaraguan Sign Language. Something similar happens with creoles, which grow when children turn a rough trading 'pidgin' into a complete native language. These cases suggest humans are strongly primed to build grammar.

sections.key: Languages descended from a common ancestor form a family; there are well over a hundred families worldwide.
sections.b: Languages change constantly, and when groups of speakers separate, their speech drifts apart until they become separate languages. Latin, for example, split into Italian, Spanish, French, Portuguese and Romanian over roughly 1,500 years. Languages that share an ancestor form a family. Linguists recognise well over a hundred families, plus 'isolates' like Basque, with no known relatives. Big families include Sino-Tibetan, which includes Chinese; Niger-Congo, with over 1,500 languages; Austronesian, stretching from Madagascar to Easter Island; and Pama-Nyungan, covering most of mainland Australia.

sections.key: Proto-Indo-European is the reconstructed ancestor of languages from English and Hindi to Russian and Persian.
sections.b: In 1786, Sir William Jones, a British judge in Calcutta, noted that Sanskrit, Greek and Latin were so alike they must share a common source. That source, now called Proto-Indo-European, was never written down, yet its descendants are spoken as a first language by nearly half the world's population, including English, Spanish, Hindi, Bengali, Russian, Persian and Greek. Many scholars think it was spoken around 6,000 years ago on the steppes north of the Black Sea. A rival theory places it earlier, in Anatolia, in modern Turkey. The debate continues.

sections.key: Regular sound changes, like Grimm's law, let linguists reconstruct words no one ever wrote down.
sections.b: Linguists rebuild lost languages using the comparative method: lining up related words and working out the regular sound changes between them. Jacob Grimm, one of the fairy-tale brothers, described a famous set of changes in Germanic languages. Where Latin kept a 'p', English shifted to 'f': pater and father, pes and foot. Latin 't' matches English 'th': tres and three. Latin 'c' (a 'k' sound) matches English 'h': centum and hundred, cornu and horn. From patterns like these, scholars can reconstruct Proto-Indo-European words for mother, father, daughter, snow and wolf.

sections.key: Every language is a living record of its speakers' history, and all are equally complex.
sections.b: Studying language origins changes how you hear speech. There are no 'primitive' languages: every known language can express abstract ideas, and many small languages have grammar more intricate than English. The words you use every day are layered history. 'Father' links you to people speaking on the Eurasian steppes thousands of years ago, and to speakers of Hindi and Persian today. Keep a healthy scepticism towards confident claims about exactly when or how language began. The honest answer is that we have strong clues, competing theories and much still to learn.

quiz.q: Why is the origin of language so hard to study?
o: Speech leaves no fossils and writing is only about 5,000 years old
Early languages were all written in lost scripts
quiz.e: Speech vanishes instantly, so researchers rely on indirect clues from bones, genes, archaeology and living languages.

quiz.q: What is the best description of the FOXP2 gene?
o: The single gene responsible for language
A gene found only in modern humans
One of many genes involved in speech and language
quiz.e: FOXP2 affects speech when damaged, but it is one of many genes involved, and Neanderthals shared our version.

quiz.q: What happened with deaf children in Nicaragua from the late 1970s?
o: They created a new sign language with its own grammar
quiz.e: Brought together in schools, they built Nicaraguan Sign Language, a full language, largely from scratch.

quiz.q: Who noticed in 1786 that Sanskrit, Greek and Latin must share a common source?
quiz.e: Jones, a British judge in Calcutta, made the observation that led to the idea of Proto-Indo-European.

quiz.q: Grimm's law explains why Latin 'pater' corresponds to which English word?
quiz.e: In Germanic languages, an ancestral 'p' regularly became 'f', giving father, foot and fish.

LESSONS.title: Where words come from
LESSONS.hook: 'Nice' once meant foolish, 'silly' once meant blessed, and 'muscle' means little mouse. Every word has a backstory, and the true ones are often stranger than the myths.

sections.key: Etymology is the study of where words come from and how their forms and meanings have changed.
sections.b: Etymology, from Greek words meaning 'the study of true meaning', traces words back through time. Etymologists compare old manuscripts, dictionaries and related languages to see how a word's sound, spelling and meaning have shifted. The Oxford English Dictionary, begun in 1857 and completed in 1928, pioneered this by printing dated quotations showing each word's earliest known uses. A word's origin doesn't fix its meaning today, but it often explains odd spellings, hidden connections between words and why we say things the way we do.

sections.key: Word meanings shift over centuries, sometimes flipping from negative to positive or back again.
sections.b: Meanings rarely stay still. 'Nice' comes from Latin nescius, meaning ignorant, and in Middle English it meant foolish or silly before drifting through 'fussy' and 'precise' to 'pleasant'. 'Silly' went the other way: Old English sælig meant happy or blessed, then innocent, then pitiable, then foolish. 'Awful' once meant inspiring awe, and 'girl' in Middle English could mean a young person of either sex. Linguists call these shifts amelioration and pejoration. They are normal, and they explain why old texts can mislead modern readers.

sections.key: Many words contain forgotten images, like 'muscle' (little mouse) and 'disaster' (bad star).
sections.b: Plenty of words hide little pictures. 'Muscle' comes from Latin musculus, 'little mouse', perhaps because a flexing muscle looked like a mouse moving under the skin. 'Disaster' comes via Italian from 'bad star', reflecting an old belief that the planets shaped events. 'Daisy' comes from Old English dæges ēage, 'day's eye', because the flower opens at dawn and closes at dusk. 'Clue' was once 'clew', a ball of thread, like the one Theseus used to find his way out of the labyrinth. 'Robot' comes from Czech robota, forced labour, popularised by Karel Čapek's 1920 play R.U.R.

sections.key: Some words changed shape because speakers misheard where one word ended and the next began.
sections.b: Sometimes words change because of how we split up speech. In Middle English, 'a napron' was heard as 'an apron', and the 'n' slid across; the old form survives in 'napkin'. The same thing happened with 'a nadder', which became 'an adder', and 'a noumpere', which became 'an umpire'. It can go the other way too: 'an ewt' became 'a newt', and 'an ekename', meaning an additional name, became 'a nickname'. Linguists call this rebracketing. It's a reminder that language lives in the ear first and on the page second.

sections.key: Neat origin stories like 'posh' meaning 'port out, starboard home' are often invented after the fact.
sections.b: Catchy word origins spread fast, and many are false. 'Posh' supposedly stands for 'port out, starboard home', the shady cabins on voyages to India, but no tickets stamped this way have ever been found. There's no evidence that 'rule of thumb' came from a law about beating wives, and 'sincere' doesn't come from sine cera, 'without wax'. Most words older than the 20th century didn't begin as acronyms. The claim that Roman soldiers were paid in salt, giving us 'salary', is also unproven, though the word is linked to Latin sal, salt. Good dictionaries flag uncertain origins.

sections.key: Australian English has borrowed hundreds of words from Aboriginal languages, such as kangaroo, koala and galah.
sections.b: Australian English has borrowed several hundred words from Aboriginal languages, mostly names for animals, plants and places. Many early loans came from the Sydney language, often called Dharug, because that's where the colony began: dingo, wallaby, wombat and koala, from a word usually recorded as gula. Others came from further afield. 'Galah' comes from Yuwaalaraay and Gamilaraay in northern New South Wales, and 'yabby' from Wemba Wemba in Victoria. Thousands of place names, from Parramatta to Wagga Wagga, also come from Aboriginal languages, though the meanings given for some are uncertain or disputed.

sections.key: 'Kangaroo' does not mean 'I don't understand'; it comes from the Guugu Yimithirr word gangurru.
sections.b: A popular story claims that when Captain Cook's crew asked what the strange animal was, locals replied 'kangaroo', meaning 'I don't understand'. It's a myth. In 1770, while the Endeavour was being repaired near present-day Cooktown in Queensland, the crew recorded the word from Guugu Yimithirr speakers. In the 1970s, the linguist John Haviland confirmed that gangurru is the Guugu Yimithirr name for a large grey or black kangaroo. Ironically, when the word was later used in Sydney, the local people didn't recognise it, and seem to have assumed it was English.

sections.key: Check a good dictionary's etymology notes, and be sceptical of origin stories that seem too neat.
sections.b: You can check word origins yourself. Most major dictionaries, including the Macquarie Dictionary for Australian English, include etymology notes, and the free Online Etymology Dictionary is a useful starting point. Look for dates of earliest recorded use and notice when a source says 'origin uncertain'; that honesty is a good sign. Be wary of stories that are too tidy, especially acronyms and tales of kings, sailors or court cases. And remember, a word's history is fascinating, but its meaning is decided by how people use it now.

quiz.q: What did 'silly' originally mean in Old English?
quiz.e: Old English sælig meant happy or blessed; the meaning slid towards foolish over centuries.

quiz.q: What does 'muscle' literally mean in Latin?
quiz.e: Musculus means little mouse, perhaps from the look of a muscle moving under the skin.

quiz.q: How did 'a napron' become 'an apron'?
o: Speakers misheard where one word ended and the next began
quiz.e: This is rebracketing: the 'n' moved from the noun to the article, as with adder and umpire.

quiz.q: What is true about the claim that 'posh' stands for 'port out, starboard home'?
o: It is confirmed by old tickets
It was coined by Queen Victoria
It's a folk etymology with no supporting evidence
It comes from an Aboriginal word
quiz.e: No tickets stamped 'POSH' have been found; the acronym story is almost certainly invented.

quiz.q: Which Aboriginal language gave Australian English the word 'koala'?
o: The Sydney language, often called Dharug
quiz.e: Many early loans, like dingo, wallaby, wombat and koala (from gula), came from the Sydney language, where the colony began.

LESSONS.title: The world's languages
LESSONS.hook: Humans speak around 7,000 languages, yet half of us speak one of just a couple of dozen. Many of the rest, including most of Australia's own, are at risk of falling silent.

sections.key: There are roughly 7,000 living languages, but half the world's people speak one of about two dozen.
sections.b: Linguists count roughly 7,000 living languages today, including a few hundred sign languages. The exact figure depends on where you draw the line between a language and a dialect, which is often as much about politics and identity as linguistics; as a famous quip puts it, 'a language is a dialect with an army and navy'. Languages are very unevenly shared. More than half the world's population speaks one of only about two dozen languages, while thousands of languages have fewer than 10,000 speakers each, and many have far fewer.

sections.key: English has the most total speakers; Mandarin Chinese has the most native speakers.
sections.b: Counting everyone who speaks a language, including as a second language, English leads with roughly 1.5 billion speakers, followed by Mandarin Chinese at over a billion, then Hindi and Spanish. Counting only native speakers, Mandarin is far ahead, with about 900 million or more, followed by Spanish and then English. Arabic, Bengali, Portuguese, Russian, French and Urdu are also among the most widely spoken. These rankings shift a little depending on how varieties are grouped, so treat any single list as approximate rather than exact.

sections.key: Papua New Guinea has about 840 languages, the most of any country.
sections.b: Language diversity is concentrated in surprising places. Papua New Guinea, with a relatively small population, has around 840 languages, more than any other country and over a tenth of the world's total. Indonesia and Nigeria each have several hundred. Rugged mountains, islands, rainforest and a long history of small, independent communities all help languages multiply. By contrast, much of Europe has relatively few. Some languages have features English speakers find astonishing, such as tones that change meaning, or words that pack a whole sentence into one.

sections.key: Around 40% of the world's languages are considered endangered.
sections.b: Around 40% of the world's languages are considered endangered, usually because children are no longer learning them at home. Pressure comes from bigger languages used in schools, jobs, government and media, and in many places from past policies that punished people for speaking their own language. When the last speakers die, a language becomes 'sleeping' or extinct, and with it can go knowledge of local plants, animals, history, law and ways of seeing the world. Estimates of how fast languages are being lost vary, but the trend is clear.

sections.key: At the time of colonisation, more than 250 Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages were spoken, with many dialects.
sections.b: When the British arrived in 1788, Australia was one of the most linguistically diverse places on Earth. More than 250 distinct Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages were spoken, with many more dialects, and most people spoke several. Most mainland languages belong to the large Pama-Nyungan family. In the Torres Strait, Meriam Mir and Kala Lagaw Ya are traditional languages, and Yumplatok, a creole, is widely spoken. Across northern Australia, Kriol, another creole, is now the first language of thousands of Aboriginal people.

sections.h: What happened, and where things stand
sections.key: Only about 12 traditional Indigenous languages are still strongly learned by children, per a 2019 national survey.
sections.b: Colonisation brought disease, dispossession and, for many decades, policies that separated families and discouraged or banned the use of Aboriginal languages in missions and schools. The effect was devastating. The 2020 National Indigenous Languages Report, based on a 2019 survey, found that about 120 traditional languages were still spoken, but only around 12 were being learned by children as a first language. Strong languages include some in Central Australia and Arnhem Land, such as Warlpiri, Pitjantjatjara and Yolŋu Matha varieties. In the 2021 Census, about 77,000 people reported speaking an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander language at home.

sections.key: Communities are reviving languages using elders' knowledge and old records, as with Kaurna in Adelaide.
sections.b: Languages that are no longer spoken are often described as 'sleeping', not dead, because they can be woken. Hebrew, used for centuries mainly in religious study, became an everyday spoken language again from the late 1800s. Māori revival, including Te Kōhanga Reo language nests from 1982, has had real success, as has Welsh. In Australia, Kaurna, the language of the Adelaide Plains, is being revived partly from records made by German missionaries around 1840. Wiradjuri, Dharug and many other languages are taught in community programs, schools and universities.

sections.key: Languages belong to their communities; follow local protocols and support community-led programs.
sections.b: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages belong to their communities, who decide how they are shared and taught. If you want to learn, look for programs run or endorsed by local language centres, and learn the traditional name of the Country where you live. Many councils and schools now use local-language place names and greetings. Some words, names or songs may be restricted, so follow guidance from community members. The United Nations has declared 2022–2032 the International Decade of Indigenous Languages, a reminder that this work is happening worldwide.

quiz.q: About how many living languages are there in the world?
quiz.e: Linguists count roughly 7,000, depending on where the line between language and dialect is drawn.

quiz.q: Which country has the most languages?
quiz.e: Papua New Guinea has around 840 languages, more than a tenth of the world's total.

quiz.q: Roughly what share of the world's languages are considered endangered?
quiz.e: Around 40% are endangered, usually because children are no longer learning them.

quiz.q: What is Kriol?
o: A sleeping language of the Adelaide Plains
A creole that is now the first language of thousands of Aboriginal people in northern Australia
The traditional language of the Torres Strait
quiz.e: Kriol is a creole, a full language that grew from a pidgin, spoken across northern Australia.

quiz.q: Kaurna, being revived today, is the traditional language of which area?
quiz.e: Kaurna revival draws partly on records made by German missionaries in Adelaide around 1840.

LESSONS.title: Grammar myths
LESSONS.hook: You were probably told never to split an infinitive or end a sentence with a preposition. Neither rule was ever part of English grammar. Here's where they came from, and what actually matters.

sections.key: Descriptive grammar records how people really use language; prescriptive grammar tells people how they should.
sections.b: Linguists distinguish two approaches. Descriptive grammar observes how fluent speakers actually use a language, the way a biologist describes an animal. By that standard, native speakers rarely make mistakes in their own everyday speech. Prescriptive grammar sets out rules for how people ought to write or speak, usually in formal settings. Some prescriptive rules are genuinely useful conventions. Others were invented by 18th and 19th-century writers who admired Latin, and they have been repeated by teachers ever since, even though great writers have ignored them for centuries.

sections.key: Splitting an infinitive, as in 'to boldly go', has never been a real grammatical error.
sections.b: An infinitive is the 'to' form of a verb, like 'to go'. Splitting it means putting a word in between: 'to boldly go', as Star Trek famously did. The supposed rule against this became popular in the 19th century, partly because in Latin the infinitive is a single word and can't be split. But English isn't Latin, and writers since the Middle Ages have split infinitives. Sometimes splitting reads better: 'to more than double sales' is clearer than any alternative. Modern style guides agree that it's fine, though some readers still notice.

sections.key: Ending a sentence with a preposition is natural English; the objection dates back to John Dryden.
sections.b: The idea that you can't end a sentence with a preposition, as in 'Who are you talking to?', is often traced to the poet John Dryden, who in 1672 criticised Ben Jonson for doing it. Dryden was again influenced by Latin, where this doesn't happen. In English, it's completely natural, and rewording often sounds stiff: 'To whom are you talking?' A famous joke attributed to Winston Churchill mocks the rule with 'This is the sort of English up with which I will not put', though there's no good evidence he said it.

sections.key: 'Literally' has been used as an intensifier for centuries, by writers such as Dickens and Twain.
sections.b: Using 'literally' to mean 'very much', as in 'I literally died laughing', drives some people up the wall. But this use goes back to at least the 1700s, and it appears in the work of Charles Dickens, Mark Twain and F. Scott Fitzgerald. Major dictionaries record it, usually with a note that some people object. Words that mean 'truly' often become intensifiers: 'very' comes from an old French word meaning 'true', and 'really' followed the same path. That said, in writing where precision matters, the figurative use can confuse.

sections.key: Many famous rules were one writer's preference, and singular 'they' dates back to the 1300s.
sections.b: The rule that 'less' is only for uncountable things (less water) and 'fewer' for countable ones (fewer bottles) seems to begin with Robert Baker in 1770, who said he merely preferred it. English speakers had used 'less' with countable nouns for about a thousand years. Using 'they' for one person of unknown gender, as in 'Someone left their umbrella', dates back to the 1300s and appears in Shakespeare and Jane Austen. Starting a sentence with 'And' or 'But' is also fine; the King James Bible does it constantly.

sections.key: Double negatives are non-standard in modern formal English, but they are not illogical.
sections.b: 'I didn't do nothing' is often called illogical, as if two negatives must cancel out. But language isn't arithmetic. Many languages, including Spanish, Italian and Russian, routinely stack negatives for emphasis, and Chaucer and Shakespeare did it in English too. Everyone understands exactly what the speaker means. The double negative became non-standard in written English over several centuries, and it now signals informal speech. So the real reason to avoid it in a job application is social, not logical: it sounds casual to many readers.

sections.key: Useful conventions are the ones that prevent ambiguity, like careful punctuation and clear modifiers.
sections.b: Some conventions genuinely help readers. Apostrophes distinguish 'its' (belonging to it) from 'it's' (it is). Commas can change meaning: 'Let's eat, Grandma' versus 'Let's eat Grandma'. Dangling modifiers cause confusion: 'Walking to work, the rain soaked me' suggests the rain was walking. Agreement between subject and verb helps readers track who is doing what. The test for any rule is simple: does following it make your meaning clearer, or does breaking it risk misunderstanding? Rules that pass the test are worth keeping.

sections.key: Good grammar means matching your language to your audience and purpose.
sections.b: Linguists talk about register: the style of language that suits a situation. Text messages to friends, a eulogy, a legal contract and a job application all call for different choices, and a skilled speaker switches between them without thinking. Formal writing still has conventions worth knowing, because some readers judge them. But correcting other people's everyday speech mostly signals social status, not superior logic. Aim for clarity and suitability, respect the conventions your audience expects, and don't let invented rules make your writing stiffer than it needs to be.

quiz.q: What does descriptive grammar do?
o: Tells people how they should speak
Records how people actually use language
quiz.e: Descriptive grammar observes real usage, while prescriptive grammar sets rules for how people ought to use language.

quiz.q: What reason is often given for the rule against split infinitives?
o: Latin infinitives are single words and can't be split
quiz.e: The rule is often said to be modelled on Latin, where infinitives are single words, but English infinitives are two words and have been split for centuries.

quiz.q: What is true about 'literally' used as an intensifier?
o: It has been used this way since at least the 1700s
quiz.e: Dickens, Twain and Fitzgerald used it; dictionaries record it, often noting that some people object.

quiz.q: How far back does singular 'they' go in English?
quiz.e: Singular 'they' dates back to the 1300s and appears in Shakespeare and Jane Austen.

quiz.q: Which grammar rule is most worth following?
o: Rules that prevent ambiguity, like careful punctuation
Never end a sentence with a preposition
quiz.e: Conventions that prevent misunderstanding, such as apostrophes and clear modifiers, genuinely help readers.

LESSONS.title: How to write clearly
LESSONS.hook: Clear writing isn't a talent you're born with. It's a handful of habits anyone can learn, and they'll make your emails, reports and messages easier to read and harder to ignore.

sections.key: Unclear writing usually comes from unclear thinking, so work out your main point before you start.
sections.b: Most muddled writing comes from muddled thinking. Before you write anything important, try to state your main point in one or two plain sentences, as if explaining it to a friend. If you can't, you're not ready to write yet. Then ask who your reader is, what they already know and what you want them to do. A note to a colleague, a complaint to a council and a report to a board need different amounts of detail. Knowing your point and your reader solves half of writing's problems before you type a word.

sections.key: Busy readers want the main point first, then the detail.
sections.b: Many of us were taught to build up to a conclusion, like a school essay. But busy readers skim, and they may never reach your last paragraph. So lead with what matters: the decision, request or key finding. 'Can you approve the budget by Friday?' beats three paragraphs of background followed by a question. Journalists call this the inverted pyramid, and the military calls it 'bottom line up front'. Useful subject lines and headings do the same job, telling readers what they're about to read before they commit time to it.

sections.key: Choose short, familiar words over long or fancy ones: 'use' not 'utilise', 'help' not 'facilitate'.
sections.b: Plain words are easier to read and more convincing. Write 'use' rather than 'utilise', 'start' rather than 'commence', 'about' rather than 'in relation to', and 'help' rather than 'facilitate'. Jargon has its place when every reader shares it, but it shuts others out. Plain language isn't dumbing down. The Australian Government Style Manual recommends it for all government writing, and studies of legal and medical documents show plain versions are understood better, even by experts. Readers rarely complain that something was too easy to understand.

sections.key: Aim for an average of around 15 to 20 words per sentence, with variety.
sections.b: Long sentences force readers to hold too much in their heads. Plain-language guides commonly suggest an average of around 15 to 20 words, with one main idea per sentence. That doesn't mean every sentence should be short, which would sound choppy. Mix lengths to keep a natural rhythm. When a sentence runs past about 30 words, look for a place to split it, often at an 'and', 'which' or 'however'. Shorter paragraphs help too, especially on phones, where a dense block of text looks like hard work.

sections.key: Active voice makes clear who did what; passive voice can hide responsibility.
sections.b: In the active voice, the doer comes first: 'The committee approved the plan.' In the passive, the action comes first and the doer may vanish: 'The plan was approved.' Active sentences are usually shorter, clearer and more direct. The passive can conveniently hide responsibility, as in the classic non-apology 'Mistakes were made.' That said, the passive isn't a crime. It's useful when the doer is unknown or unimportant, as in 'The bridge was built in 1932', or when you want to focus on what happened.

sections.key: Delete words that add nothing, and turn 'zombie nouns' back into verbs.
sections.b: Clutter creeps in everywhere: 'at this point in time' means 'now', 'due to the fact that' means 'because', and 'in order to' is usually just 'to'. Watch for words like 'very', 'really' and 'basically', which rarely add much. Another common problem is nominalisation, which the writing scholar Helen Sword calls 'zombie nouns': verbs turned into heavy nouns. 'We made a decision to conduct a review' becomes 'We decided to review'. William Strunk's classic advice, first published in 1918, still holds: 'Omit needless words.'

sections.key: In 1946, George Orwell offered six rules for clear writing, ending with 'break any of these rules' rather than write badly.
sections.b: In his 1946 essay 'Politics and the English Language', George Orwell argued that vague, inflated language helps people hide bad ideas. He offered six rules. Never use a metaphor or simile you're used to seeing in print. Never use a long word where a short one will do. If it's possible to cut a word out, always cut it out. Never use the passive where you can use the active. Never use a foreign phrase, scientific word or jargon if there's an everyday English equivalent. And break any of these rules sooner than say anything outright barbarous.

sections.key: Good writing is rewritten: leave a gap, read it aloud and cut ruthlessly.
sections.b: Almost no one writes clearly in a first draft. The philosopher Blaise Pascal apologised in 1656 for a long letter because he hadn't had time to make it shorter. When you can, leave a gap between drafting and editing, even an hour, so you read with fresh eyes. Read your draft aloud: you'll hear clumsy sentences and missing words that your eyes skip. Check that your main point is up front, cut anything that doesn't earn its place, and ask whether your reader will know what to do next.

quiz.q: What does 'bottom line up front' mean for your writing?
o: Put the key point or request first
Save the conclusion for the end
quiz.e: Busy readers skim, so lead with the decision, request or key finding, then add detail.

quiz.q: What average sentence length do plain-language guides commonly suggest?
quiz.e: Around 15 to 20 words on average, with variety, keeps writing clear without sounding choppy.

quiz.q: Which sentence is in the active voice?
quiz.e: In the active voice the doer comes first, making clear who did what.

quiz.q: What is a 'zombie noun'?
o: A verb turned into a heavy noun, like 'make a decision'
A noun used as an insult
quiz.e: Helen Sword's term for nominalisations; 'make a decision' is clearer as 'decide'.

quiz.q: What is the last of Orwell's six rules?
o: Break any of these rules sooner than say anything outright barbarous
quiz.e: Orwell ended by telling writers to break his rules rather than write something ugly or unclear.

LESSONS.title: How Australian law works
LESSONS.hook: Every day you live inside a system of rules built over 800 years, from English judges to the High Court in Canberra. Here's how it actually fits together.

sections.key: Australian law comes from parliaments (legislation) and from judges' decisions (common law).
sections.b: Australian law has two main sources. The first is legislation, also called statute law: Acts passed by the Commonwealth, state and territory parliaments, like road rules or the Fair Work Act. The second is common law, the body of principles built up by judges deciding cases over centuries. Australia inherited English common law when the British colony was founded in 1788. Where the two clash, legislation generally wins, because parliament can change or override the common law, as long as it stays within the limits of the Constitution.

sections.key: Under precedent, courts must follow the earlier decisions of higher courts in the same hierarchy.
sections.b: The common law runs on precedent. When a court decides a case, the core legal reasoning behind the decision becomes a rule that lower courts in the same system must follow in similar cases. This makes the law more predictable: lawyers can tell you how a dispute is likely to go by looking at how similar ones were decided. Precedent also lets law evolve. A famous example is Donoghue v Stevenson (1932), a Scottish case about a snail in a bottle of ginger beer, which shaped the modern law of negligence across the common law world, including Australia.

sections.key: Australia has one Commonwealth legal system plus separate systems for each state and territory.
sections.b: Because Australia is a federation, there isn't just one set of laws. The Commonwealth parliament makes laws on national subjects like tax, defence, immigration and trade. Each of the six states, and the two self-governing territories, the ACT and the Northern Territory, makes its own laws on most everyday matters, including most crimes, driving, property, schools and hospitals. That's why the penalty for the same offence, or the rules for renting a home, can differ between Sydney and Perth. Each state and territory also runs its own court system alongside the federal courts.

sections.key: Most cases start in local or magistrates courts; serious ones go to District, County or Supreme Courts.
sections.b: Courts are arranged like a ladder. At the bottom are the Local or Magistrates Courts, which handle the vast majority of criminal cases, from traffic offences to minor assaults, plus smaller civil claims. Most states then have an intermediate court, called the District Court in several states and the County Court in Victoria, for more serious crimes and larger claims. At the top of each state is the Supreme Court, which hears the most serious cases, such as murder, and appeals. The federal system includes the Federal Court and the Federal Circuit and Family Court, which handles family law.

sections.key: Criminal cases are brought by the state and need proof beyond reasonable doubt; civil cases need proof on the balance of probabilities.
sections.b: Law is split into two broad kinds of cases. In a criminal case, the state prosecutes someone for breaking the law, which is why cases are named like R v Smith, R standing for the Crown. Penalties include fines, community orders and prison, and guilt must be proved beyond reasonable doubt. In a civil case, one party, the plaintiff, sues another, the defendant, usually for money, called damages. The standard is lower: the balance of probabilities, meaning more likely than not. The same event, such as a car crash, can lead to both kinds of case.

sections.key: The prosecution must prove guilt; the accused doesn't have to prove innocence.
sections.b: A cornerstone of criminal law is the presumption of innocence. The prosecution carries the burden of proving every element of the offence, and the accused doesn't have to prove anything. Accused people generally have a right to silence, meaning refusing to answer police questions usually can't be used as evidence of guilt, although some laws create exceptions. Australian trials are adversarial: two sides present their cases while the judge acts as a neutral umpire. In Dietrich v The Queen (1992), the High Court held that a trial for a serious offence may be delayed if an accused person can't afford a lawyer and would otherwise face an unfair trial.

sections.key: A jury of 12 ordinary citizens decides the facts in serious criminal trials; the judge decides the law.
sections.b: Serious criminal trials are usually heard by a jury, typically 12 people chosen at random from the electoral roll. Jury service is a civic duty, although people can be excused for good reasons. The jury decides the facts and whether the accused is guilty; the judge rules on the law and, if there's a conviction, decides the sentence. What jurors discuss in the jury room must stay secret. Most states allow majority verdicts in some circumstances, but under section 80 of the Constitution, a jury trial for a serious Commonwealth offence needs a unanimous verdict. Juries are rare in civil cases.

sections.h: The High Court and getting help
sections.key: The High Court is Australia's final court of appeal and interprets the Constitution.
sections.b: The High Court of Australia, created by the Constitution and first sitting in 1903, sits at the top of the whole system. Its seven justices, based in Canberra, decide appeals from every other court and settle disputes about the Constitution. Appeals usually need special leave, so only important cases get heard. Since the Australia Act 1986, no appeals can go to Britain's Privy Council. Its decisions can reshape the nation: in Mabo (1992), it rejected the idea that Australia was 'terra nullius'. This lesson is general information only. If you have a legal problem, Legal Aid and community legal centres offer free or low-cost help, and a lawyer can advise on your situation.

quiz.q: When legislation and common law conflict, which usually wins?
quiz.e: Parliament can change or override the common law, subject to the Constitution.

quiz.q: Which court handles the vast majority of criminal cases?
quiz.e: Lower courts deal with most everyday matters.

quiz.q: What standard of proof applies in a civil case?
quiz.e: More likely than not is enough in civil cases.

quiz.q: In a jury trial, who usually decides the sentence after a conviction?
quiz.e: The jury decides guilt; the judge decides the law and sentence.

quiz.q: What changed with the Australia Act 1986?
o: Appeals to Britain's Privy Council ended
Common law was replaced by statute
quiz.e: Since 1986, the High Court is the final court of appeal.

LESSONS.title: The Australian Constitution
LESSONS.hook: A document written by colonial delegates in the 1890s still decides who can make which laws, and only the voters can change it.

sections.key: The Constitution took effect on 1 January 1901, when six colonies federated as the Commonwealth of Australia.
sections.b: Before 1901, Australia was six separate British colonies with their own parliaments, tariffs and even different railway gauges. Through the 1890s, delegates met at conventions to draft a constitution for a federation. Unusually for the time, it was approved by voters at colonial referendums and passed by the British Parliament as part of the Commonwealth of Australia Constitution Act 1900. The Commonwealth of Australia was born on 1 January 1901. The Constitution is short, around 128 sections, and it's freely available online. Reading its first chapters takes less time than most people expect.

sections.key: The first three chapters set up the Parliament, the Executive Government and the courts.
sections.b: The Constitution is organised into chapters. Chapter I creates the Parliament, made up of the King, represented by the Governor-General, the Senate and the House of Representatives. Chapter II covers the executive government, which puts laws into action. Chapter III establishes the High Court and other federal courts. Australia is a constitutional monarchy and a parliamentary democracy. The Senate gives each original state the same number of senators regardless of population, 12 each since 1984, protecting smaller states. The House of Representatives is based on population, and the party or coalition that controls it forms government.

sections.key: Section 51 lists the Commonwealth's law-making powers; the states keep the rest, and federal law wins in a conflict.
sections.b: Federation meant dividing law-making power. Section 51 lists about 40 subjects on which the Commonwealth parliament can make laws, including defence, taxation, trade between states, marriage, immigration, currency and postal services. A few, like coining money and raising armed forces, are effectively reserved for the Commonwealth. Everything not listed stays with the states, which is why they run police, schools, hospitals and most criminal law. Many areas overlap. When a valid Commonwealth law is inconsistent with a state law, section 109 says the Commonwealth law prevails and the state law is invalid to the extent of the inconsistency.

sections.key: Court decisions and control of income tax gave the Commonwealth far more power than the founders expected.
sections.b: The founders expected the states to remain powerful, but the balance has shifted towards the Commonwealth. In the Engineers' Case of 1920, the High Court began reading Commonwealth powers broadly. During World War II, the Commonwealth took over income tax, and the High Court upheld the scheme, which is why income tax is now collected federally. Section 96 lets the Commonwealth give states money on conditions, so it can shape areas like schools and hospitals it doesn't directly control. This gap between who raises money and who spends it is called vertical fiscal imbalance, and it drives constant federal and state negotiation.

sections.key: Law-making, executive and judicial power are separated, and judicial power is guarded most strictly.
sections.b: The Constitution separates the three arms of government: the legislature makes laws, the executive carries them out, and the judiciary interprets and applies them. In Australia, the legislature and executive are closely linked, because ministers must sit in parliament and answer to it, a system called responsible government. The separation of judicial power is much stricter. In the Boilermakers' Case (1956), the High Court held that federal courts can exercise only judicial power, and bodies that aren't courts can't exercise it. This protects judges' independence, so courts can rule against the government of the day without fear.

sections.key: Changes need a referendum passed by a double majority: a national majority and majorities in at least four states.
sections.b: The Constitution can only be changed by referendum under section 128. Parliament first passes a proposed change, then voters decide. It succeeds only with a double majority: a majority of voters nationally, and a majority of voters in at least four of the six states. Territory votes count towards the national total only. It's a high bar. Of 45 proposals put to voters since 1901, only eight have succeeded. The best known is 1967, when over 90% voted to count Aboriginal people in the census and let the Commonwealth make laws for them. Proposals in 1999 for a republic and in 2023 for an Indigenous Voice were not carried.

sections.key: Australia has no bill of rights, but the Constitution contains a few express rights and some implied ones.
sections.b: Unlike the United States, Australia has no national bill of rights. The Constitution contains only a handful of express rights: trial by jury for serious Commonwealth offences, limits on the Commonwealth making laws about religion, protection against discrimination based on which state you live in, and 'just terms' when the Commonwealth acquires property. In 1992, the High Court found an implied freedom of political communication, because a system where the people choose their parliament requires free discussion of politics. It isn't a general free speech right; it only limits laws that unduly burden political communication. Later cases have also protected the right to vote.

sections.key: Most rights in Australia come from ordinary laws and the common law, not the Constitution.
sections.b: Because the Constitution says so little about rights, most protections come from elsewhere. Federal laws such as the Racial Discrimination Act 1975 and the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 outlaw discrimination, and the common law protects things like personal liberty and fair hearings. Rights set out in ordinary laws can be changed or repealed by the parliament that passed them. Understanding the Constitution matters because enrolment and voting are compulsory at federal elections and referendums, so every adult citizen may be asked to change it. Before voting on a referendum, read the official Yes and No cases and look for independent explanations. This is general information only, not legal advice.

quiz.q: When did the Australian Constitution take effect?
quiz.e: Federation day, when the six colonies became one Commonwealth.

quiz.q: Under section 109, what happens when a valid Commonwealth law conflicts with a state law?
quiz.e: The state law is invalid to the extent of the inconsistency.

quiz.q: What does a referendum need to pass?
o: A two-thirds vote in parliament only
A national majority plus majorities in at least four states
quiz.e: This is called a double majority.

quiz.q: How are territory votes counted in a referendum?
quiz.e: Since a 1977 referendum, territory votes count in the national majority, but not towards the four-state requirement.

quiz.q: What did the High Court find in 1992?
o: A right to free legal aid
An implied freedom of political communication
quiz.e: It limits laws that unduly burden political discussion.

LESSONS.title: Contracts: the deals you make every day
LESSONS.hook: Your morning coffee, your phone plan and your job are all contracts. Knowing how they work helps you avoid nasty surprises.

sections.key: A contract is an agreement the law will enforce, and most people make several every day.
sections.b: A contract is simply an agreement that the law will enforce. You make them constantly: buying a coffee, tapping onto public transport, signing up for a streaming service, accepting a job or leasing a flat. Most are so routine you never think of them as legal events. In Australia, contract law comes mainly from the common law developed by judges, with legislation such as the Australian Consumer Law layered on top to protect consumers. For an agreement to be a binding contract, courts generally look for several ingredients: offer, acceptance, consideration, intention to create legal relations, capacity and reasonably certain terms.

sections.key: A contract forms when a clear offer is accepted on the same terms; a counter-offer cancels the original offer.
sections.b: Every contract starts with an offer: a clear promise to be bound on certain terms. Many things that look like offers aren't. Goods on a shelf and most advertisements are usually treated as an 'invitation to treat', an invitation for you to make an offer, which is one reason a shop usually isn't obliged to sell an item that was wrongly priced, though misleading pricing can breach consumer law. Acceptance must match the offer exactly. If you reply, 'I'll take it for $50 less', that's a counter-offer, which rejects the original offer. Acceptance normally has to be communicated, although actions, like starting the work requested, can count.

sections.key: Each side must give something of value; a bare promise of a gift usually isn't enforceable.
sections.b: Common law contracts need consideration: each side must give or promise something in exchange. You pay money; the café hands over coffee. This is why a simple promise to give someone a gift usually can't be enforced, because the other person hasn't provided anything in return. The consideration doesn't have to be fair or equal in value. A contract to sell a car for one dollar can be perfectly valid, although a court may look closely at whether there was pressure or deception. A formal document called a deed can make a promise binding without consideration, which is why deeds are common for guarantees.

sections.key: The parties must intend legal consequences and have the legal capacity to contract.
sections.b: Not every promise is meant to be legally binding. Courts presume that business deals are intended to create legal relations, but presume that family and social arrangements, like agreeing to cook dinner for a friend, are not. Either presumption can be overturned by evidence. The parties must also have capacity. People under 18 can often get out of contracts, although they can be bound for things like necessities and some beneficial arrangements, and the rules vary by state. A person who lacks mental capacity, or is severely intoxicated in a way the other party knew about, may be able to avoid a contract. Terms must also be certain enough to enforce.

sections.key: Most verbal contracts are binding, but some, like land sales, must be in writing, and writing is far easier to prove.
sections.b: A common myth is that a contract must be written and signed. Most contracts can be verbal, or formed through emails, text messages or clicking 'I agree' online. The problem with verbal contracts is proof: if a dispute arises, it's your word against theirs. Some contracts must be in writing to be enforceable, notably contracts for the sale of land and certain consumer credit contracts. For anything important, like building work, a loan to a friend or a business arrangement, put the key terms in writing, including the price, what's being delivered, deadlines and what happens if things go wrong.

sections.key: A breach can lead to damages, and a serious breach can let the other party end the contract.
sections.b: When someone fails to do what the contract requires, that's a breach. The usual remedy is damages: money intended to put you in the position you'd have been in if the contract had been properly performed, not to punish the other side. If the breach is serious, such as breaking an essential term, the innocent party may be entitled to end the contract. Occasionally, a court orders a party to actually perform, called specific performance, mostly for unique things like land. Contracts can also be set aside for misrepresentation, duress or unconscionable conduct. Time limits apply to claims, commonly six years in many states.

sections.key: In standard form contracts with consumers and small businesses, unfair terms can be declared void, and since 2023 using them can attract penalties.
sections.b: Many contracts, like phone plans, gym memberships and software licences, are standard form contracts: take it or leave it, with no real negotiation. The Australian Consumer Law protects consumers and small businesses from unfair terms in these contracts. A term may be unfair if it creates a significant imbalance between the parties, isn't reasonably necessary to protect the business, and would cause detriment. Examples include letting only one side cancel or change the price at will. A court can declare such a term void. Since November 2023, proposing or relying on unfair terms has also been illegal, with significant penalties available.

sections.key: There's no general cooling-off right, but specific laws give you one for door-to-door and phone sales and many property purchases.
sections.b: Many people believe every contract comes with a cooling-off period. It doesn't. Cooling-off rights exist only where a law or the contract itself creates them. Under the Australian Consumer Law, unsolicited sales, such as door-to-door or unexpected phone sales, carry a 10 business day cooling-off period. Most states give buyers of residential property a short cooling-off period, for example five business days in NSW, though usually not for auction sales. Before signing anything, read it fully, keep a copy, and never sign under pressure. This is general information only; for significant contracts, get advice from a lawyer, Legal Aid or a community legal centre.

quiz.q: Legally, what is a price tag on goods in a shop usually treated as?
quiz.e: You make the offer at the counter; the shop accepts it.

quiz.q: You reply to an offer, 'I'll take it for $50 less.' What have you made?
o: A counter-offer that rejects the original
quiz.e: A counter-offer cancels the original offer.

quiz.q: What do courts presume about casual family or social arrangements?
o: They're not intended to create legal relations
quiz.e: The presumption can be overturned by evidence.

quiz.q: Which of these must generally be in writing to be enforceable?
o: A contract for the sale of land
Hiring a plumber for an hour
quiz.e: Land contracts must be in writing.

quiz.q: What cooling-off period applies to unsolicited door-to-door sales under the Australian Consumer Law?
quiz.e: Unsolicited consumer agreements carry a 10 business day cooling-off period.

LESSONS.title: Your rights as a consumer
LESSONS.hook: 'No refunds' signs, 'take it up with the manufacturer', 'the warranty's expired'. Australian consumer law says otherwise more often than you think.

sections.key: The Australian Consumer Law has applied nationally since 2011, enforced by the ACCC and state fair trading agencies.
sections.b: Since 1 January 2011, consumers across Australia have been protected by one national law, the Australian Consumer Law, which sits in a schedule to the Competition and Consumer Act 2010. It applies the same way in every state and territory. It's enforced by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission, the ACCC, together with state and territory agencies such as NSW Fair Trading and Consumer Affairs Victoria. The law covers consumer guarantees, product safety, misleading conduct, unfair contract terms, unsolicited selling and more. You're generally a consumer if you buy goods or services normally used for personal or household purposes, or anything costing up to $100,000.

sections.key: Consumer guarantees apply automatically, can't be signed away, and cover goods and services.
sections.b: The heart of the law is a set of consumer guarantees. They apply automatically, whatever the receipt or store policy says, and businesses can't exclude them. Goods must be of acceptable quality, meaning safe, durable, free from defects and acceptable in appearance, for a reasonable time. They must be fit for any purpose you told the seller about, match their description or sample, and come with clear title. Services must be provided with due care and skill, be fit for purpose and be delivered within a reasonable time. What counts as reasonable depends on the item: a $2,000 fridge should last far longer than a $20 kettle.

sections.key: For a major failure you choose a refund or replacement; for a minor one the business may choose to repair.
sections.b: Your remedy depends on how serious the problem is. A failure is major if a reasonable consumer wouldn't have bought the item knowing about the problem, if it's unsafe, significantly different from its description, or substantially unfit for purpose and can't easily be fixed within a reasonable time. For a major failure, you can choose a refund or a replacement, or keep it and claim compensation for the drop in value. For a minor failure, the business can choose to repair, replace or refund. If it refuses or takes too long, you can get it fixed elsewhere and claim reasonable costs, or reject the goods.

sections.key: Change-of-mind refunds are optional, but 'no refunds' signs that deny your rights are illegal.
sections.b: Some common beliefs are wrong. You have no legal right to a refund just because you changed your mind; that's store policy, and many shops offer it voluntarily. But signs saying 'no refunds' or 'no refunds on sale items' are misleading if they suggest you have no rights when goods are faulty. The retailer can't send you to the manufacturer; you can deal directly with the business that sold you the item. You need proof of purchase, but that can be a bank statement or online order, not only the original receipt. And sale items are covered too, unless the defect was pointed out before you bought.

sections.key: Consumer guarantees often last longer than the manufacturer's warranty, so extended warranties may add little.
sections.b: A manufacturer's warranty against defects is a promise on top of your consumer guarantees, not a replacement for them. Your guarantee rights can continue after the warranty period ends, if a product fails sooner than a reasonable consumer would expect. That matters when you're offered an extended warranty at the checkout. It may give you some extra benefits, but much of what it covers you may already have under the law for free. Salespeople must not mislead you about your rights to sell you one. Before paying, ask exactly what it offers beyond the consumer guarantees, and read the terms carefully.

sections.key: Businesses must not mislead or deceive, and must generally show a single total price.
sections.b: The Australian Consumer Law bans misleading or deceptive conduct in trade. That includes false claims about a product's quality, origin or benefits, fake 'was' prices that inflate a discount, and fine print that contradicts the headline offer. Businesses must also generally display a single total price where they can, including compulsory fees, rather than hiding charges until the end, a practice called drip pricing. Large supermarkets must show unit prices, such as the price per 100 grams, so you can compare value. Unconscionable conduct, like exploiting someone who clearly doesn't understand a deal, is also prohibited, and the ACCC can take businesses to court over it.

sections.key: Scams impersonate trusted organisations and create urgency; pause, verify independently and report quickly.
sections.b: Scams are a major consumer threat. Common types include fake parcel delivery texts, calls impersonating banks, the ATO or police, investment schemes promising high returns, fake online shops, romance scams and fake invoices sent to businesses. They share warning signs: pressure to act immediately, unusual payment methods like gift cards or crypto, and requests for personal details or remote access to your device. If contacted unexpectedly, hang up and call the organisation back on a number you find yourself. If you've lost money or shared details, contact your bank straight away, then report it to Scamwatch, run by the ACCC's National Anti-Scam Centre. IDCARE offers free support.

sections.key: Complain to the business in writing first, then escalate to fair trading, an ombudsman or a tribunal.
sections.b: If something goes wrong, start with the business. Gather your proof of purchase, photos and any messages, explain the problem, and say which remedy you want under the consumer guarantees. Putting it in writing creates a record. If that fails, contact your state or territory fair trading agency, which can give advice and may help negotiate. Industry ombudsmen handle specific sectors for free, such as the Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman, energy and water ombudsmen, and the Australian Financial Complaints Authority. For money claims, state tribunals like NCAT or VCAT are cheaper than courts. Legal Aid and community legal centres can help; this lesson is general information only.

quiz.q: For a major failure, who chooses between a refund and a replacement?
quiz.e: Major failures give the consumer the choice.

quiz.q: Do you have a legal right to a refund if you simply change your mind?
o: Yes, if you have the receipt
No, change-of-mind refunds are up to store policy
quiz.e: Many shops offer them voluntarily, but the law doesn't require it.

quiz.q: A shop says 'take it up with the manufacturer'. What's the correct position?
o: You can deal with the retailer that sold it to you
quiz.e: The retailer can't pass you off to the manufacturer.

quiz.q: What happens to your consumer guarantee rights when a manufacturer's warranty expires?
o: They can continue for a reasonable time
quiz.e: Guarantees last as long as reasonable for that product.

quiz.q: Which is a common warning sign of a scam?
o: Pressure to pay immediately by gift card or crypto
A business giving you time to think
quiz.e: Urgency and unusual payment methods are red flags.

LESSONS.title: Your rights at work
LESSONS.hook: Minimum pay, leave, a safe workplace and protection from unfair sacking aren't favours from your boss. For most Australian workers, they're the law.

sections.key: The Fair Work Act 2009 covers most private-sector workers; the Fair Work Commission and Fair Work Ombudsman run the system.
sections.b: Most Australian employees are covered by the national workplace relations system under the Fair Work Act 2009. It covers nearly all private-sector workers, although some state public servants and local government workers, and many employees of sole traders and partnerships in WA, fall under state systems instead. Two bodies do the heavy lifting. The Fair Work Commission is the independent tribunal that sets minimum wages and awards and hears disputes such as unfair dismissal claims. The Fair Work Ombudsman gives free information and advice, helps resolve pay disputes and can take employers to court for breaking workplace laws.

sections.key: The National Employment Standards set minimum entitlements, such as leave and maximum hours, that no employer can undercut.
sections.b: The National Employment Standards, or NES, are a safety net that covers national system employees. An award, agreement or contract can't provide less. They include a maximum of 38 ordinary hours a week for full-time staff, plus reasonable additional hours; four weeks of paid annual leave, pro rata for part-timers; paid personal and carer's leave; compassionate leave; paid family and domestic violence leave; unpaid parental leave, with the right to request more; community service leave; long service leave; public holidays; and notice of termination and redundancy pay. The NES also give some employees the right to request flexible working arrangements.

sections.key: The Fair Work Commission sets the national minimum wage each year, and modern awards set minimum pay for particular industries.
sections.b: Every year, the Fair Work Commission reviews the national minimum wage, with changes usually starting on 1 July.
