Over the next two centuries it grew heavier and louder, gaining an iron frame and today's standard 88 keys. One of Cristofori's pianos, from 1720, survives in New York's Metropolitan Museum of Art.

sections.key: Electronic instruments, from the theremin to the synthesiser, make sound from electrical signals.
sections.b: The theremin, invented by the Russian scientist Leon Theremin around 1920, is played without being touched: moving your hands near two antennas changes its pitch and volume, giving the eerie sound of old science fiction films. In the 1960s, Robert Moog's synthesisers let musicians shape electronic sounds with knobs and patch cables. Australia has its own claim here: CSIRAC, one of the world's first stored-program computers, played music in the early 1950s. Since 1983, a standard called MIDI has let keyboards, drum machines and computers talk to each other, which is why a laptop can now stand in for a whole studio.

quiz.q: In the Hornbostel-Sachs system, what is a drum with a stretched skin?
quiz.e: Membranophones make sound with a stretched membrane, like a drum skin.

quiz.q: Which family does the saxophone belong to, and why?
o: Brass, because it is made of metal
Woodwind, because it uses a reed rather than buzzing lips
Strings, because it has a vibrating reed
quiz.e: Families are defined by how sound is started. The saxophone uses a single reed, so it is a woodwind.

quiz.q: What technique lets a yidaki player sustain an unbroken drone?
quiz.e: Players breathe in through the nose while pushing air out from the cheeks, so the sound never stops.

quiz.q: What did Cristofori's piano offer that the harpsichord did not?
o: Louder or softer notes depending on how hard you press
quiz.e: Its hammers let the player control volume by touch, hence the name pianoforte, 'soft-loud'.

quiz.q: What was unusual about CSIRAC?
o: It was the first synthesiser sold in shops
It was an early Australian computer that played music in the early 1950s
It was the first electric guitar
quiz.e: CSIRAC, one of the first stored-program computers, played music in the early 1950s.

LESSONS.title: A guide to classical music
LESSONS.hook: Three centuries, three giants and a lot of music that still turns up in films, ads and ringtones. Here is how to find your way in.

sections.key: 'Classical music' usually means the Western art music tradition, grouped into broad periods.
sections.b: In everyday speech, 'classical music' means the tradition of Western art music written for orchestras, choirs, soloists and small ensembles over roughly the last four centuries. Historians divide it into periods: the Baroque, about 1600 to 1750; the Classical period, about 1750 to 1820, which confusingly gives the whole tradition its name; and the Romantic period, about 1820 to 1900. Then came a burst of twentieth-century experiment. The dates are rough, since composers did not wake up one morning in a new era. Knowing the periods helps you hear why a piece sounds the way it does.

sections.key: Baroque music (about 1600–1750) is ornate and energetic, built on interweaving lines and a steady bass.
sections.b: Baroque music tends to be busy, decorated and driven by a steady rhythmic pulse. Underneath most pieces runs a continuous bass line, often played by a cello and a harpsichord filling in chords. Opera was born in Italy around 1600, and instrumental forms like the concerto flourished, pitting a soloist or small group against the orchestra. Antonio Vivaldi's The Four Seasons, published in 1725, is a set of four violin concertos that paint spring birdsong, summer storms and winter ice. George Frideric Handel's oratorio Messiah, first performed in Dublin in 1742, is still sung by choirs across Australia every Christmas.

sections.key: Bach (1685–1750) was the great master of counterpoint, weaving several independent melodies together.
sections.b: Johann Sebastian Bach spent his working life in Germany as a church musician and court composer, and was better known in his day as an organist than a composer. He wrote more than a thousand works, including the Brandenburg Concertos, the Mass in B minor and hundreds of church cantatas. His great skill was counterpoint: several independent melodies played at once that fit together perfectly, as in a fugue, where one theme enters again and again in different voices. After his death his music fell out of fashion, until Felix Mendelssohn revived his St Matthew Passion in 1829. Many musicians now consider him the greatest composer of all.

sections.key: The Classical period (about 1750–1820) prized clarity, balance and memorable tunes.
sections.b: After the dense layers of the Baroque, composers turned towards clarity: a clear melody on top, simpler accompaniment underneath, and balanced phrases like a question and answer. The harpsichord gave way to the new piano. This was the age of the symphony, a large orchestral work usually in four movements, and of the string quartet. Joseph Haydn wrote more than 100 symphonies and is often called the father of both forms. Composers also developed sonata form, a way of presenting two contrasting themes, developing them, and bringing them back, which shaped instrumental music for the next 150 years.

sections.key: Mozart (1756–1791) wrote over 600 works in a life of just 35 years.
sections.b: Mozart was born in Salzburg in 1756 and was touring Europe as a child prodigy by the age of six, performing for royalty alongside his sister Nannerl. In a life of only 35 years, he wrote more than 600 works, including 41 numbered symphonies, over 20 piano concertos and operas such as The Marriage of Figaro, Don Giovanni and The Magic Flute. His music can sound effortless, but it is full of subtle drama and wit. He died in Vienna in 1791 while working on his Requiem. Popular stories of a murderous rivalry with the composer Salieri, spread by the film Amadeus, are not supported by historians.

sections.key: Beethoven (1770–1827) kept composing as he went deaf and pushed music into the Romantic era.
sections.b: Beethoven was born in Bonn in 1770 and moved to Vienna, where he took lessons for a time from Haydn. In his late twenties he began to lose his hearing, and by his final years he was almost completely deaf. In 1802 he wrote a despairing letter to his brothers, now called the Heiligenstadt Testament, yet he kept composing. His Fifth Symphony opens with perhaps the most famous four notes in music, and his Ninth Symphony of 1824 broke convention by adding singers in its finale. His music is more personal and dramatic than earlier composers', and it opened the door to Romanticism.

sections.key: Romantic composers (about 1820–1900) used bigger orchestras to express intense emotion and national identity.
sections.b: Romantic composers valued personal feeling, drama and imagination over balance. Orchestras grew larger, pieces grew longer, and music was often linked to stories, landscapes or poems. Frédéric Chopin wrote intimate piano music; Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky wrote the ballets Swan Lake and The Nutcracker; Richard Wagner wrote operas lasting four or five hours; Johannes Brahms carried on Beethoven's symphonic tradition. Many composers drew on folk music to express national identity, such as Antonín Dvořák in Czech lands and Edvard Grieg in Norway. Much of today's film music, with its sweeping strings and big brass, grows directly out of this era.

sections.key: Start with short, famous pieces, listen actively, and try hearing an orchestra live.
sections.b: You don't need any training to enjoy classical music. Start with short, well-known pieces: a movement of Vivaldi's The Four Seasons, Mozart's Eine kleine Nachtmusik, the opening of Beethoven's Fifth, or Tchaikovsky's Nutcracker suite. Many are free on streaming services and on radio such as ABC Classic. Listen actively the first time, with no phone, and notice what repeats and what changes. If a piece grabs you, explore more by the same composer. Then try it live: the Sydney, Melbourne and other state symphony orchestras run affordable concerts, and hearing a full orchestra in person is a different experience from headphones.

quiz.q: Roughly when was the Baroque period?
quiz.e: The Baroque ran from about 1600 to 1750, ending around the time of Bach's death.

quiz.q: What is counterpoint, the technique Bach mastered?
o: Several independent melodies played at once that fit together
quiz.e: Counterpoint weaves independent melodic lines together, as in a fugue.

quiz.q: Which composer is often called the father of the symphony?
quiz.e: Joseph Haydn wrote more than 100 symphonies and shaped the form.

quiz.q: What do historians say about the story that Salieri murdered Mozart?
o: It is confirmed by Salieri's letters
It was proven in a Viennese court
It is not supported by historical evidence
quiz.e: The rivalry story was popularised by fiction, including the film Amadeus, but historians don't support it.

quiz.q: What was groundbreaking about Beethoven's Ninth Symphony?
o: It was the first symphony ever written
It added singers in the finale
It was written for harpsichord alone
quiz.e: Beethoven broke convention by bringing a choir and vocal soloists into the final movement.

LESSONS.title: From blues to hip hop
LESSONS.hook: Almost every song on your playlist can trace its family tree back to the blues, and to a few machines that changed how music was heard.

sections.key: The blues grew from African American communities in the US South around the turn of the twentieth century.
sections.b: The blues emerged in African American communities in the southern United States around the late 1800s and early 1900s, drawing on work songs, field hollers and spirituals rooted in the experience of slavery and its aftermath. Its most famous structure, the 12-bar blues, repeats a pattern of three chords over twelve bars, and its 'blue notes' bend slightly below the standard pitches of a Western scale. Musicians such as W.C. Handy, Bessie Smith and Robert Johnson helped spread it. The blues shaped jazz, rhythm and blues, rock and roll, soul and much of the popular music that followed.

sections.key: Recording turned music from a live-only event into something anyone could own and replay.
sections.b: For most of history, you could only hear music when someone played it in front of you. That changed in 1877, when Thomas Edison demonstrated the phonograph, recording sound as grooves on a tin foil cylinder. Flat gramophone discs followed, then radio in the 1920s, which brought music into millions of homes for free. For the first time, a singer in one city could be heard across the world, and styles spread and mixed faster than ever. Records also fixed a performance permanently, so one particular recording, rather than the written song, became the version people knew and loved.

sections.key: Rock and roll combined blues, country and gospel in the 1950s and made the electric guitar central.
sections.b: In the 1950s, rock and roll fused rhythm and blues with country music and gospel, driven by a strong backbeat on beats two and four. Black musicians such as Chuck Berry, Little Richard and Sister Rosetta Tharpe were central to its sound, and Elvis Presley became its biggest star. The electric guitar, amplified so it could compete with drums, became its signature instrument. Rock and roll was also a social shift: it was marketed directly to teenagers, who now had money to spend. In the 1960s, British bands such as the Beatles and the Rolling Stones sent it back across the Atlantic, reshaped.

sections.key: Magnetic tape, multitrack recording and the LP turned the studio into an instrument.
sections.b: After the Second World War, magnetic tape made recordings far easier to edit, and multitrack recorders let musicians record parts separately and layer them. The long-playing record, introduced in 1948, held around twenty minutes a side, encouraging artists to think in whole albums. By the late 1960s, the studio itself had become an instrument, with bands creating sounds that were difficult to play live. Portable cassettes arrived in the 1960s and the Walkman in 1979, making music personal and mobile. Compact discs followed in the early 1980s, then MP3 files, file sharing and, from the late 2000s, streaming services.

sections.key: Hip hop began at block parties in the Bronx, New York, in the 1970s.
sections.b: Hip hop grew out of block parties in the Bronx, New York, in the 1970s, largely among African American and Caribbean-born young people. A 1973 party where DJ Kool Herc played is often cited as its starting point. DJs extended the drum breaks of funk records by switching between two turntables, and MCs rhymed over the top. The culture is often described as having four elements: DJing, MCing, breakdancing and graffiti. Sampling, reusing fragments of existing recordings, became central to its sound. From a local scene it grew into one of the world's best-selling genres, including a strong Australian hip hop scene.

sections.key: Electronic dance music grew from disco, with house in Chicago and techno in Detroit in the 1980s.
sections.b: Disco in the 1970s built music for the dance floor around a steady four-on-the-floor kick drum. When disco faded in the United States, DJs and producers in Black and gay club scenes kept experimenting. In the mid-1980s, Chicago gave rise to house music and Detroit to techno, both built on affordable drum machines and synthesisers such as the Roland TR-808 and TB-303. The sound spread to Europe, fuelling the rave scene of the late 1980s and 1990s. Today electronic production techniques are everywhere, and many pop hits are made largely on a computer rather than with a live band.

sections.key: Australian music milestones include Johnny O'Keefe, AC/DC, Kylie Minogue and Yothu Yindi.
sections.b: Johnny O'Keefe's Wild One, in 1958, was one of the first Australian rock and roll hits. AC/DC, formed in Sydney in 1973 by brothers Malcolm and Angus Young, became one of the biggest rock bands in the world; their 1980 album Back in Black is among the best-selling albums ever. Kylie Minogue moved from the TV soap Neighbours to international pop stardom with The Loco-Motion in 1987. Yothu Yindi's Treaty, released in 1991 and sung partly in the Yolŋu language Gumatj, became a national hit, and singer Mandawuy Yunupingu was named Australian of the Year for 1992. The ABC's Countdown and triple j helped launch countless careers.

sections.key: Trace the family tree of the music you love to discover more of it.
sections.b: Almost every genre borrows from the ones before it, so following the family tree is a great way to find new music. If you like a modern artist, look up who they say influenced them, then listen to those artists. Liner notes and credits on streaming services show who wrote, produced and sampled each track. Many hip hop songs are built on samples of soul, funk and jazz records, which are worth hearing in full. Support local music too: live venues, community radio and triple j Unearthed are where many Australian artists get their start.

quiz.q: What is the 12-bar blues?
o: A song that must last exactly 12 minutes
A repeating pattern of three chords over twelve bars
A style played only on twelve-string guitar
quiz.e: The 12-bar blues repeats a set pattern of three chords over twelve bars.

quiz.q: Who demonstrated the phonograph in 1877?
quiz.e: Edison's phonograph recorded sound as grooves on a tin foil cylinder.

quiz.q: Where did hip hop begin?
o: The Bronx, New York, in the 1970s
quiz.e: Hip hop grew from Bronx block parties in the 1970s.

quiz.q: Which city is credited with house music in the mid-1980s?
quiz.e: House music came from Chicago; techno from Detroit.

quiz.q: What was notable about Yothu Yindi's Treaty?
o: It was the first Australian song played on radio
It was sung partly in the Yolŋu language Gumatj and became a national hit
It was recorded entirely on a synthesiser
quiz.e: Treaty (1991) brought Yolŋu language and Aboriginal perspectives into the national charts.

LESSONS.title: Music and the brain
LESSONS.hook: Music gives you no food, shelter or money, yet it can make your skin tingle and bring back memories you thought were lost. Why?

sections.key: Listening to music engages many brain areas at once, from hearing to movement to emotion.
sections.b: There is no single music centre in the brain. When you listen to a song, areas that process sound decode pitch and timbre, while regions involved in movement track the beat, which is why it's hard not to tap your foot. Memory areas recognise familiar tunes, and emotional and reward systems respond to how the music makes you feel. Playing an instrument adds fine motor control, reading and planning on top. This is one reason neuroscientists find music so useful to study: it connects perception, prediction, movement and feeling in a single everyday activity.

sections.key: Music stirs emotions partly by mimicking the voice and body, and partly by playing with our expectations.
sections.b: Music can make us feel sad, joyful, calm or pumped up, often within seconds. One explanation is that it borrows the cues of emotional speech and movement: happy music tends to be faster, higher and brighter, like excited speech, while sad music is slower, lower and softer. Another is expectation. Your brain constantly predicts what comes next, and composers delay, confirm or surprise those predictions to create tension and release. Culture matters too, but some features travel well: research comparing songs from many societies suggests people can often tell a lullaby from a dance song even in an unfamiliar musical tradition.

sections.key: Musical 'chills', or frisson, are tingling sensations many people feel at powerful moments in music.
sections.b: Many people know the feeling: a shiver down the spine or goosebumps at a key moment in a piece of music. Researchers call it frisson, or simply chills. It often arrives with something unexpected, like a sudden change in volume, a new voice entering, or a surprising chord, especially after a long build-up. Not everyone gets chills from music, and some studies suggest people who score high on openness to experience report them more often. Chills are a useful research tool, because they give scientists a clear, measurable moment of intense musical pleasure to study.

sections.key: Pleasurable music triggers dopamine release in the brain's reward system, even in anticipation of the peak.
sections.b: A 2011 study at McGill University in Montreal used brain scans to watch people listening to music that gave them chills. At the moment of peak pleasure, their brains released dopamine in the striatum, part of the reward system that also responds to food and other rewards. Interestingly, dopamine was also released in a different part of the striatum in the seconds before the peak, as listeners anticipated it. That helps explain why a favourite song's build-up can feel almost as good as the moment itself. Music is abstract, yet it taps into some of the brain's oldest reward machinery.

sections.key: Music is strongly tied to memory, especially music heard in our teens and early twenties.
sections.b: A few notes of an old song can transport you instantly to a particular summer, car trip or school dance. Music is closely bound up with autobiographical memory, and it tends to be tied to emotion, which helps memories stick. Studies consistently find that people remember and feel most strongly about music from their teens and early twenties, part of a wider pattern psychologists call the reminiscence bump. That's one reason many adults feel the best music was made when they were young. Songs also make words easier to remember, which is why children learn the alphabet with a tune.

sections.key: Musical memory is often relatively preserved in dementia, and personal music can improve mood and connection.
sections.b: Carers and researchers have long noticed that people with dementia, including some who struggle to recognise family members, can still sing along to songs from their youth. Musical memory seems to rely partly on brain areas that are affected relatively late in some forms of dementia such as Alzheimer's disease. Music does not cure dementia or reverse its progress. But there is reasonable evidence that personally meaningful music can lift mood, reduce agitation and help people connect with those around them. Many Australian aged-care homes now use personalised playlists, and registered music therapists work in hospitals and care settings.

sections.key: Listening to Mozart does not make you smarter; the famous 1993 finding was small, brief and hard to repeat.
sections.b: In 1993, a short paper in the journal Nature reported that university students who listened to ten minutes of a Mozart sonata did slightly better on a spatial reasoning task for about the next 10 to 15 minutes. The media turned this into 'Mozart makes babies smarter', and in 1998 the governor of the US state of Georgia proposed giving every newborn a classical music CD. Later studies struggled to repeat the result, and reviews found any effect was small and short-lived. The best explanation is simply that enjoyable music can briefly lift mood and alertness, and Mozart has no special power.

sections.h: Does learning an instrument make you smarter?
sections.key: Learning an instrument builds musical skills, but evidence it boosts general intelligence is mixed.
sections.b: Children who learn instruments often do better at school, but that doesn't prove the lessons caused it; families who pay for music lessons differ in many other ways. Studies that randomly assign children to music training have produced mixed results, and several reviews have found little evidence of broad gains in intelligence or grades. What is clear is that practice improves musical skills themselves, such as listening, timing and coordination, and that playing brings enjoyment, discipline and social connection at any age. So learn an instrument because you want to play music, and treat any other benefits as a bonus.

quiz.q: Which features tend to make music sound happy?
quiz.e: Happy-sounding music tends to share cues with excited speech: faster, higher and brighter.

quiz.q: What often triggers musical chills?
o: Something unexpected, like a sudden change or new voice
quiz.e: Chills often come with surprise, such as a sudden change after a build-up.

quiz.q: What did the 2011 McGill study find about dopamine and music?
o: It was released at peak pleasure and also in anticipation of it
Dopamine was released only while sleeping
Only classical music triggered any release
quiz.e: Dopamine was released both at the peak and in the build-up before it.

quiz.q: Music from which part of life do people tend to remember most strongly?
quiz.e: This is part of the reminiscence bump, when memories are especially vivid and lasting.

quiz.q: What is the best explanation for the original 'Mozart effect' result?
o: Mozart's music rewires the brain permanently
Enjoyable music briefly lifted mood and alertness
The students were all trained musicians
quiz.e: The small, brief effect is best explained by improved mood and arousal, not anything special about Mozart.

LESSONS.title: Why every culture tells myths
LESSONS.hook: Floods that drown the world, gods who build the sky from a giant's skull, heroes who leave home and come back changed. Almost every people on Earth has told stories like these. Here's why.

sections.key: To scholars, a myth is a traditional story, usually sacred, about gods, origins or the deep past, not simply a false belief.
sections.b: In everyday speech, a myth is something untrue, like the idea that goldfish have three-second memories. Scholars use the word differently. The Greek word mythos simply meant 'word' or 'story'. A myth, in this sense, is a traditional story, often sacred to the people who tell it, about gods, ancestors and how things came to be. It is usually set in a time before ordinary time, when the world was still being shaped. Calling a story a myth makes no claim about whether it is true. It describes what kind of story it is and the job it does.

sections.key: Myths explain origins, justify customs and rituals, teach values and give a community a shared identity.
sections.b: Myths answer the big questions: where did the world come from, why do we die, why are there seasons, why do we do things this way? They also hold societies together. The anthropologist Bronisław Malinowski, who studied the Trobriand Islanders in the early 1900s, argued that myths work like a 'charter' for a society, explaining and backing up its rules, rituals and ownership of land. Myths teach what counts as brave, shameful or sacred. And because they are shared, knowing the stories marks you as belonging to a people, much as knowing the songs and in-jokes of a family does.

sections.key: Creation myths follow a few recurring patterns: order from chaos, a divine body made into the world, an earth-diver, a cosmic egg or creation by word.
sections.b: Stories of how the world began take a handful of recurring shapes. In the Babylonian Enuma Elish, the god Marduk defeats the sea goddess Tiamat and splits her body to form the sky and the earth: order carved out of chaos. In many Native American traditions, an animal dives to the bottom of a great primeval sea and brings up mud that becomes land. In a Chinese story, the giant Pangu hatches from a cosmic egg and his body becomes mountains, rivers and stars. In the opening of Genesis, sacred to Jews and Christians, God creates by speaking: 'Let there be light'.

sections.key: Flood stories appear in many cultures, most famously in the Mesopotamian Epic of Gilgamesh, which closely parallels the story of Noah.
sections.b: In 1872, George Smith of the British Museum translated a clay tablet from ancient Nineveh and caused a sensation. It told of Utnapishtim, warned by a god to build a boat, save his family and animals, and ride out a world-destroying flood, then send out birds to find dry land. It was strikingly close to the story of Noah, and older than any surviving text of Genesis. Other cultures have floods too: in Greece, Deucalion and Pyrrha repopulate the world by throwing stones that become people; in India, Manu is warned by a fish. Early civilisations grew up beside flood-prone rivers, which may help explain why.

sections.key: Myths are sacred stories of gods and origins, legends are set in the human past, and folktales are told mainly to entertain.
sections.b: Folklorists often split traditional stories into three rough types, a scheme set out by the American scholar William Bascom in 1965. Myths are regarded as true and sacred by their tellers, feature gods, and are set in the remote past. Legends are set in the human, historical world and may have a real person at their core: King Arthur, Robin Hood or the many tales that grew up around Ned Kelly. Folktales, like Cinderella, are told mainly for entertainment, begin 'once upon a time' and could happen anywhere. The lines blur, and one culture's sacred myth can become another's bedtime story.

sections.key: Vladimir Propp found that Russian fairy tales are built from the same 31 plot 'functions', always in the same order.
sections.b: In 1928, the Russian folklorist Vladimir Propp analysed 100 Russian fairy tales and found they were built from a surprisingly small kit. He identified 31 recurring plot 'functions', such as the hero leaving home, being tested, receiving a magical helper, defeating the villain and finally marrying. Not every tale uses every function, but those that appear always come in the same order. He also found just seven character roles, including the hero, the villain, the donor who provides a magical gift, the helper and the false hero who claims the credit. His Morphology of the Folktale became influential worldwide after its English translation in 1958. Screenwriters and game designers still borrow his checklist to build stories that feel familiar.

sections.key: The Dreaming is not a set of old myths but a living system of law, knowledge and connection to Country for Aboriginal peoples.
sections.b: It would be wrong to file Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander knowledge under 'mythology' as if it were a thing of the past. For many Aboriginal peoples, the Dreaming is a living framework of law, kinship, ceremony and responsibility to Country. It tells how ancestral beings shaped the land, its creatures and its people, and it continues in the present. Each nation has its own words and knowledge: the Anangu of Uluru, for example, speak of Tjukurpa. Knowledge is carried in song, dance, art and songlines across the land, and some of it is restricted to particular people. Stories belong to their custodians and shouldn't be retold without permission.

sections.key: Myths live on in our language, films, psychology and art, and reading them well means asking what question each story answers.
sections.b: Myths never really went away. Marvel's Thor, the Percy Jackson books and countless films borrow gods and monsters directly. Psychology names ideas after them, like the Oedipus complex. We still speak of the Midas touch, a nemesis, a siren song, or being caught between Scylla and Charybdis. When you meet a myth, a few questions help: what problem is this story solving, who told it, and when? Compare versions, because most myths survive in several. Notice what it says about the values of the people who told it. And remember that stories that are 'just mythology' to one person may be sacred, living belief to someone else.

quiz.q: How do scholars use the word 'myth'?
o: A story that has been proven false
A traditional, often sacred story about gods, origins or the deep past
A historical account of a real battle
quiz.e: In the scholarly sense, calling something a myth describes its type, not whether it's true.

quiz.q: Which ancient text contains a flood story strikingly similar to Noah's?
quiz.e: George Smith's 1872 translation of the Gilgamesh flood tablet caused a sensation.

quiz.q: Which of these is best described as a folktale?
o: The creation of the world by Marduk
quiz.e: Folktales are told mainly to entertain and could happen 'once upon a time', anywhere.

quiz.q: What did Vladimir Propp find when he analysed Russian fairy tales?
o: They were all copied from Greek myths
They were built from recurring plot 'functions' in a fixed order
They had no features in common
They were all written by one author
quiz.e: Propp identified 31 functions and seven character roles.

quiz.q: Why is it misleading to call the Dreaming 'mythology'?
o: It is a living system of law, knowledge and connection to Country
It has no stories in it
quiz.e: For many Aboriginal peoples, the Dreaming continues in the present.

LESSONS.title: The gods of Olympus
LESSONS.hook: Jealous, vain, passionate and powerful: the Greek gods behaved like the most dramatic family you've ever met, and they left their names all over our language.

sections.key: In Hesiod's Theogony, the universe begins with Chaos, then Gaia (Earth) and Uranus (Sky), whose children are the Titans.
sections.b: The fullest Greek account of how the gods came to be is the Theogony, a poem by Hesiod from around 700 BC. First came Chaos, a yawning emptiness. Then came Gaia, the Earth, who gave birth to Uranus, the starry Sky. Their children were the Titans, a generation of huge and powerful gods. Uranus hated his children and trapped them inside the Earth. Gaia, in pain and fury, gave her youngest son, Cronus, a great sickle, and he used it to overthrow his father. The pattern was set: in Greek myth, sons topple fathers.

sections.h: Cronus, Zeus and the war of the Titans
sections.key: Zeus escaped being swallowed by his father Cronus, freed his siblings and defeated the Titans in a ten-year war.
sections.b: Cronus had been warned that one of his children would overthrow him, so he swallowed each one at birth. His wife Rhea saved the last, Zeus, by hiding him on Crete and handing Cronus a stone wrapped in baby clothes, which he swallowed instead. Grown up, Zeus forced his father to vomit up his brothers and sisters. They then fought the Titans for ten years in the Titanomachy. The Olympians won, and most Titans were locked in Tartarus, a pit deep beneath the underworld. The Titan Atlas was condemned to hold up the sky forever.

sections.key: The twelve Olympians ruled from Mount Olympus, each with their own domain, from Zeus's thunder to Poseidon's sea.
sections.b: The winning gods lived on Mount Olympus, Greece's highest mountain at nearly 2,920 metres. The usual twelve are Zeus, king of the gods and wielder of thunder; his wife Hera, goddess of marriage; Poseidon, god of the sea and earthquakes; Demeter, goddess of grain and harvest; Athena, goddess of wisdom and crafts; Apollo, god of music, prophecy and healing; his twin Artemis, goddess of the hunt; Ares, god of war; Aphrodite, goddess of love; Hephaestus, the blacksmith god; Hermes, the messenger; and Dionysus, god of wine, or in some lists Hestia, goddess of the hearth. Hades ruled the underworld.

sections.key: The Greek gods were immortal and powerful but showed very human flaws: jealousy, pride, lust and a thirst for revenge.
sections.b: Greek gods were not models of good behaviour. Zeus pursued countless lovers, mortal and divine, and Hera took furious revenge, often on the women and children involved rather than on Zeus. The gods fought among themselves, took sides in human wars and punished anyone who insulted them. In one story, told most famously by the Roman poet Ovid, the weaver Arachne boasted that she was more skilled than Athena, won or matched her in a contest, and was turned into a spider. The lesson for mortals was clear: never show hubris, the arrogant pride that challenges the gods.

sections.key: Famous myths explain why humans have fire, why the world holds suffering and why there are seasons.
sections.b: The Titan Prometheus stole fire from the gods for humans; Zeus had him chained to a rock where an eagle ate his liver every day. As a further punishment, Zeus sent Pandora, the first woman, with a jar that released evils into the world, leaving only hope inside. It was a jar, not a box: the box crept in through a translation slip in the 1500s. Another myth explains the seasons. When Hades carried off Persephone, her mother Demeter's grief made the crops fail. Because Persephone had eaten pomegranate seeds in the underworld, she must spend part of every year there, and the earth goes barren while she's away.

sections.key: Greek religion centred on rituals, sacrifices, festivals and oracles, not on a single holy book or creed.
sections.b: The Greeks had no single holy book and no fixed creed. Religion was about doing things properly: offering sacrifices, pouring wine for the gods, keeping festivals and honouring the patron god of your city, as Athens honoured Athena in the Parthenon. People consulted oracles for guidance. The most famous was at Delphi, where a priestess called the Pythia spoke for Apollo, and cities and kings sent envoys to ask her advice before wars and colonising expeditions. Her answers were famously ambiguous. Myths themselves came in many versions, told by different poets and playwrights, and nobody expected them all to agree.

sections.key: The Romans matched their own gods to the Greek ones, and the Roman names live on in our planets.
sections.b: When Rome came into contact with Greek culture, it identified its own gods with the Greek ones and absorbed many of their stories. Zeus became Jupiter, Hera became Juno, Poseidon became Neptune, Ares became Mars, Aphrodite became Venus, Hermes became Mercury, Athena became Minerva, Artemis became Diana, Hephaestus became Vulcan and Cronus became Saturn. Because Europe learned much of its mythology through Latin, the Roman names often stuck. Look up at night and the planets carry them: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn and Neptune. Saturday is Saturn's day, a trace of Rome in every weekend.

sections.key: Everyday words like panic, echo, titanic, cereal and volcano come from Greek and Roman gods and myths.
sections.b: The gods are hiding in plain sight in English. Panic comes from Pan, the goat-legged god of the wild, whose sudden shout could terrify travellers. Echo was a nymph who, cursed by Hera, could only repeat the last words spoken to her, and who faded away pining for Narcissus until only her voice remained. Titanic means huge, like the Titans. Cereal comes from Ceres, the Roman Demeter, and volcano from Vulcan's forge. Hermetic, meaning sealed, traces back to Hermes. Sports brand Nike is named for the goddess of victory. Knowing the myths turns ordinary words into little stories.

quiz.q: How did Rhea save the baby Zeus from Cronus?
o: She turned him into an eagle
She gave Cronus a stone wrapped in baby clothes
She hid him in the underworld
She asked Atlas to protect him
quiz.e: Cronus swallowed the stone, and Zeus grew up in hiding on Crete.

quiz.q: Who was the Greek god of the sea and earthquakes?
quiz.e: Poseidon was one of the three brothers, with Zeus and Hades, who divided the world.

quiz.q: What myth did the Greeks use to explain the seasons?
o: Persephone spending part of each year in the underworld
quiz.e: Demeter's grief while Persephone is away makes the earth barren.

quiz.q: What was the Roman name for Ares, god of war?
quiz.e: Many planets carry Roman god names, including Mars.

quiz.q: Where does the word 'panic' come from?
o: The god Pan, whose shout terrified travellers
quiz.e: Pan was the god of wild places, shepherds and flocks.

LESSONS.title: Greek heroes and their flaws
LESSONS.hook: They slew monsters, outwitted giants and sailed to the ends of the world. Yet almost every Greek hero was undone by something inside himself.

sections.key: A Greek hero was usually part divine and sought glory through extraordinary deeds, but was not necessarily good.
sections.b: The Greek word heros did not simply mean a good person. Heroes were extraordinary figures of the distant past, often with one divine parent, who performed deeds beyond ordinary humans. What drove them was kleos, glory: the fame that would keep their names alive after death. Many were violent, proud or reckless. Heroes were also worshipped. Across Greece, people made offerings at shrines and tombs believed to belong to heroes, hoping for their protection. Their stories were told and retold for centuries by poets and playwrights, which is why most exist in several, sometimes contradictory, versions.

sections.key: Heracles, son of Zeus, performed twelve labours as penance, including slaying the Nemean lion and the Hydra.
sections.b: Heracles, called Hercules by the Romans, was the son of Zeus and a mortal woman, Alcmene, which earned him the lifelong hatred of Zeus's wife Hera. She drove him into a madness in which he killed his own wife and children. To atone, he served King Eurystheus and performed twelve labours. He strangled the Nemean lion, whose hide no weapon could pierce, killed the many-headed Hydra, cleaned the filthy Augean stables in a day by diverting two rivers, and dragged Cerberus, the three-headed guard dog, up from the underworld. After his death, he was taken up to live among the gods.

sections.key: Perseus beheaded the Gorgon Medusa by watching her reflection, then rescued Andromeda from a sea monster.
sections.b: Perseus was the son of Zeus and Danaë, a princess locked away by her father. A scheming king sent the young Perseus to fetch the head of Medusa, a Gorgon whose gaze turned anyone to stone. The gods helped: Athena lent a polished shield, and he received winged sandals and a cap of invisibility. By watching Medusa's reflection in the shield, he cut off her head without meeting her eyes. On the way home he rescued the princess Andromeda, chained to a rock as an offering to a sea monster, and later used Medusa's head to turn the scheming king to stone.

sections.key: Theseus killed the Minotaur in the Labyrinth of Crete, finding his way out with Ariadne's thread.
sections.b: King Minos of Crete demanded that Athens regularly send seven young men and seven young women to be fed to the Minotaur, a half-bull, half-man monster kept in a maze called the Labyrinth. The Athenian prince Theseus volunteered to go. Minos's daughter Ariadne fell in love with him and gave him a ball of thread to unwind as he went in. He killed the Minotaur and followed the thread back out. But the story ends sadly. Theseus abandoned Ariadne on an island, then forgot to change his ship's black sails to white. His father Aegeus, thinking him dead, leapt into the sea, which is still called the Aegean.

sections.key: Jason sailed on the Argo to win the Golden Fleece, succeeding only with the help of the sorceress Medea.
sections.b: To reclaim his throne, Jason was set an impossible task: bring back the Golden Fleece from Colchis, at the far eastern end of the Black Sea, in what is now Georgia. He gathered a crew of heroes, the Argonauts, named after their ship the Argo, including Heracles and the musician Orpheus. In Colchis, the king's daughter Medea, a powerful sorceress, fell in love with Jason and helped him yoke fire-breathing bulls and get past the dragon guarding the fleece. Years later, Jason left Medea for a princess of Corinth. In Euripides' play Medea, first performed in 431 BC, her revenge is terrible.

sections.key: Achilles, the Iliad's central hero, chose a short, glorious life over a long, forgotten one.
sections.b: Achilles, son of the mortal king Peleus and the sea goddess Thetis, was the greatest Greek warrior at Troy. A prophecy gave him a stark choice: a long, obscure life at home or a short one with undying glory. He chose glory. Later writers say Thetis tried to keep him from the war by hiding him on the island of Skyros, dressed as a girl among the king's daughters, until Odysseus exposed him by laying out gifts with weapons among them. In the Iliad, grief over the death of his companion Patroclus drives him back into battle to kill the Trojan prince Hector. The famous story of his vulnerable heel comes from later writers, not Homer, but it gave us the Achilles tendon and the Achilles' heel.

sections.key: Odysseus won by cunning rather than strength, from the wooden horse to his disguised homecoming.
sections.b: Where Achilles was strength, Odysseus was brains. Tradition credits him with the idea of the wooden horse that got Greek soldiers inside Troy. Yet he was a reluctant warrior. To avoid being called up, he is said to have pretended to be mad, yoking an ox and a donkey together and sowing his fields with salt, until a recruiter laid his baby son Telemachus in front of the plough and Odysseus swerved. After his long journey home, he returned to Ithaca disguised as a beggar. Only his old dog Argos recognised him, wagging its tail before it died. Then he strung his great bow, which none of the suitors could manage, and shot an arrow through a row of twelve axe heads.

sections.key: Aristotle described the tragic hero as a person of high standing who falls through an error or flaw, often driven by hubris.
sections.b: In his Poetics, written in the 300s BC, the philosopher Aristotle analysed Greek tragedy. The ideal tragic hero, he said, is neither perfectly good nor wicked, but someone admirable who falls through hamartia, often translated as 'tragic flaw' but closer to 'error' or 'mistake'. Oedipus, who unknowingly kills his father and marries his mother, is the classic case. Pride, or hubris, is often the trigger. Watching the fall, Aristotle said, stirs pity and fear and brings catharsis, an emotional release. The idea runs through Shakespeare's Macbeth and modern stories alike: heroes are most interesting when their strengths and weaknesses are the same thing.

quiz.q: Why did Heracles perform his twelve labours?
o: To win the hand of a princess
To atone for killing his family in a Hera-sent madness
quiz.e: Hera's hatred drove him mad, and the labours were his penance.

quiz.q: How did Perseus avoid being turned to stone by Medusa?
o: He watched her reflection in a polished shield
He attacked while she slept in the dark
He was immune as a son of Zeus
quiz.e: Looking only at her reflection let him strike without meeting her gaze.

quiz.q: Which sea is named after Theseus's father?
quiz.e: Aegeus leapt into the sea when he saw black sails and believed Theseus dead.

quiz.q: What choice did Achilles make?
o: A long, quiet life at home
To abandon the war for wealth
A short life with undying glory
quiz.e: Achilles chose kleos, glory, over a long and forgotten life.

quiz.q: What did Aristotle call the error or flaw that brings down a tragic hero?
quiz.e: Hamartia is often translated 'tragic flaw' but is closer to 'error'.

LESSONS.title: Odin, Thor and the end of the world
LESSONS.hook: A one-eyed god who hanged himself for wisdom, a thunder god in a wedding dress, and a prophecy that the gods themselves will die. Norse myth is wilder than the movies.

sections.key: Most Norse myths survive in two Icelandic collections written in the 1200s, the Poetic Edda and Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda.
sections.b: The Norse peoples of Scandinavia told their myths aloud, so most of what we know was written down later, in Iceland, which officially adopted Christianity around the year 1000. The Poetic Edda is a collection of anonymous poems about gods and heroes, preserved mainly in a manuscript from around 1270. The Prose Edda was written around 1220 by the Icelandic chieftain and scholar Snorri Sturluson as a handbook for poets. These are precious sources, but they were recorded by Christians centuries after the conversion, so historians are careful. Rune stones, poems and archaeology help fill in the picture of what people actually believed.

sections.h: A world made from a giant
sections.key: In Norse myth, the world was made from the body of the giant Ymir, slain by Odin and his brothers.
sections.b: Before anything existed there was Ginnungagap, a vast gap between Muspelheim, a realm of fire, and Niflheim, a realm of ice. Where heat met frost, ice melted, and from the drops came Ymir, the first giant. A cosmic cow licked the salty ice and uncovered Buri, ancestor of the gods. Buri's grandsons, Odin and his brothers Vili and Vé, killed Ymir and built the world from him: his flesh became earth, his blood the sea, his bones the mountains and his skull the sky. They made the first humans, Ask and Embla, from two trees found on the shore.

sections.key: Yggdrasil is a giant ash tree that links the nine worlds of Norse myth, including Asgard, Midgard and Hel.
sections.b: At the centre of Norse cosmology stands Yggdrasil, an immense ash tree whose branches and roots connect nine worlds. These include Asgard, home of the gods; Midgard, the world of humans, joined to Asgard by the rainbow bridge Bifröst; Jotunheim, land of the giants; and Hel, realm of the dead. At the tree's roots sit the Norns, three women who shape the fates of gods and humans. The tree is under constant attack: a dragon called Nidhogg gnaws at its roots, deer nibble its leaves, and a squirrel named Ratatoskr runs up and down carrying insults between an eagle and the dragon.

sections.key: Odin, chief of the gods, sacrificed an eye and hung on Yggdrasil for nine nights to gain wisdom and the runes.
sections.b: Odin was king of the gods and god of wisdom, poetry, war and death. He was a restless seeker of knowledge and would pay any price for it. He gave one of his eyes for a drink from Mimir's well of wisdom. In one poem, he hangs on Yggdrasil for nine nights, wounded by a spear, 'myself given to myself', until he glimpses the runes and seizes them. Two ravens, Huginn and Muninn, meaning thought and memory, fly out each day to bring him news. He rides an eight-legged horse, Sleipnir, and gathers fallen warriors in Valhalla, chosen by his Valkyries.

sections.key: Thor, god of thunder, defended gods and humans against the giants with his hammer Mjölnir.
sections.b: Thor, Odin's son, was god of thunder and strength and the great defender of gods and humans against the giants. His weapon was the hammer Mjölnir, which always returned to his hand. He was probably the most popular god among ordinary people: many small Thor's hammer pendants have been found by archaeologists across Scandinavia. His myths are often funny. In one poem, a giant steals Mjölnir and demands the goddess Freyja as his bride. Thor goes instead, disguised in a bridal veil, alarms the giant by eating an entire ox and eight salmon, then grabs his hammer back when it is brought out to bless the 'bride'.

sections.key: Loki is a shape-shifting trickster who helps the gods and harms them, and who brings about the death of Baldr.
sections.b: Loki is the most slippery figure in Norse myth. Born of giants but living among the gods, he is clever, funny, spiteful and a shape-shifter. He gets the gods into trouble and then out of it; he is even the mother of Odin's horse Sleipnir, after turning himself into a mare. His children include the monstrous wolf Fenrir, the world-circling Midgard Serpent and Hel, ruler of the dead. His worst act is arranging the death of Baldr, the beloved god, using a dart of mistletoe. The gods bind him beneath a snake whose venom drips onto his face; his writhing causes earthquakes.

sections.key: Ragnarök is the prophesied final battle in which most gods die and the world is destroyed, before a new world rises.
sections.b: Norse myth is unusual because its gods know they will die. At Ragnarök, after three brutal winters with no summer between them, the bonds break. Fenrir breaks loose and swallows Odin. Thor kills the Midgard Serpent but staggers nine steps and falls dead from its venom. Loki and the god Heimdall kill each other, and the fire giant Surtr sets the world ablaze until it sinks into the sea. But that is not quite the end. In the poem Völuspá, a green new earth rises from the waters, some gods return, and other sources add two human survivors who repopulate the world. Scholars debate how much Christianity shaped this ending.

sections.key: Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday and Friday are named after Germanic gods closely related to Tyr, Odin, Thor and Frigg.
sections.b: The Anglo-Saxons who settled England shared many gods with the Norse, under slightly different names, and those gods still run your week. Tuesday is Tiw's day, after the war god the Norse called Tyr. Wednesday is Woden's day, the Old English name for Odin. Thursday is Thor's day. Friday is usually traced to Frigg, Odin's wife, though some link it to Freyja. The myths shaped modern storytelling too: J.R.R. Tolkien borrowed the names of his dwarves, and Gandalf, from a list in Völuspá, Wagner built his Ring operas on them, and Marvel turned Thor and Loki into film stars.

quiz.q: Who wrote the Prose Edda around 1220?
quiz.e: Snorri Sturluson wrote it in Iceland as a handbook for poets.

quiz.q: What is Yggdrasil?
o: The world tree connecting the nine worlds
quiz.e: Yggdrasil is an immense ash tree at the centre of Norse cosmology.

quiz.q: What did Odin give up for a drink from Mimir's well of wisdom?
quiz.e: Odin would pay any price for knowledge, including an eye.

quiz.q: Whose death did Loki arrange using a dart of mistletoe?
quiz.e: Baldr's death is Loki's worst act and leads to his punishment.

quiz.q: Which day of the week is named after Odin?
quiz.e: Wednesday is Woden's day, Woden being the Old English name for Odin.

LESSONS.title: Egypt's gods and the journey after death
LESSONS.hook: For well over a thousand years, Egyptians believed your heart would be weighed against a feather when you died. What happened next depended on how you'd lived.

sections.key: Ancient Egyptian religion lasted about 3,000 years, with many gods whose roles and stories changed and merged over time.
sections.b: Ancient Egyptian religion was not one fixed system. Over roughly 3,000 years it included hundreds of gods, many tied to particular towns, whose roles shifted and merged. The sun god Ra, for example, was later combined with Amun of Thebes as Amun-Ra. Gods were often shown with animal heads to signal their qualities: jackal-headed Anubis watched over the dead, ibis-headed Thoth was the god of writing and wisdom. Our sources include the Pyramid Texts, carved inside royal pyramids from around 2400 BC and among the oldest religious writings known, plus later coffin inscriptions, papyri and temple walls.

sections.h: Ra and the birth of the world
sections.key: Egyptians told of the world rising from primeval waters, and of the sun god Ra sailing across the sky by day and through the underworld by night.
sections.b: Egyptian creation stories begin with Nun, dark, endless waters. From them rose a mound of land, just as fields emerged each year as the Nile flood went down. In one version, from the city of Heliopolis, the creator god Atum produced Shu, air, and Tefnut, moisture, whose children were Geb, the earth, and Nut, the sky. The sun god Ra was central to daily life. By day he sailed across the sky in a boat; by night he journeyed through the underworld, fighting the chaos serpent Apep, to be reborn each dawn. Pharaohs called themselves the 'son of Ra'.

sections.key: Osiris, the good king, was murdered by his jealous brother Set, a story about order, chaos and death.
sections.b: The most important Egyptian myth concerns Osiris, a wise king who taught people farming and law. His brother Set, god of storms, deserts and disorder, was jealous. Egyptian texts only hint at the murder, but the fullest telling, by the Greek writer Plutarch around AD 100, describes Set tricking Osiris into lying in a beautifully made chest, slamming the lid and throwing it into the Nile. Later Set cut the body into pieces and scattered them across Egypt. The myth set good kingship against chaos, and gave Egyptians a way to think about death and what might lie beyond it.

sections.key: Isis restored Osiris and bore his son Horus, who defeated Set; the pharaoh was seen as a living Horus.
sections.b: Isis, Osiris's wife and sister, was the great goddess of magic and devotion. She searched Egypt for the pieces of her husband's body and, with her sister Nephthys and the god Anubis, put him back together, in effect making the first mummy. Osiris became ruler of the dead, and Isis conceived their son, Horus, whom she raised in hiding in the marshes of the Nile Delta. Grown up, Horus fought Set for the throne. He lost an eye in the struggle, which was restored; the Eye of Horus became a popular protective amulet. Each living pharaoh was identified with Horus.

sections.key: Egyptians believed a person had several parts, including the ka and ba, and needed a preserved body to live on after death.
sections.b: Egyptians saw a person as made of several parts. The ka was the life force, which needed food and drink offerings even after death. The ba, often shown as a bird with a human head, was the part that could move between the tomb and the world. Your name and your shadow mattered too. For these to survive, the body needed to be preserved. The goal was to become an akh, a transfigured spirit, and reach the Field of Reeds, an ideal version of Egypt with perfect harvests. Small servant figures called shabtis were buried with the dead to do farm work for them there.

sections.key: In the judgement of the dead, Anubis weighed the heart against the feather of Maat, and a heart heavy with wrongdoing was devoured by Ammit.
sections.b: The dead faced judgement in the Hall of Two Truths, pictured in the collection of spells we call the Book of the Dead. The deceased declared before a panel of divine judges the wrongs they had not committed: 'I have not stolen', 'I have not killed'. Then Anubis placed their heart on a scale against a feather representing Maat, the goddess of truth, justice and cosmic order, while Thoth recorded the result. A heart weighed down by wrongdoing was eaten by Ammit, a monster part crocodile, part lion and part hippopotamus. A balanced heart meant the person could go on to join Osiris.

sections.key: The heart stayed in the body under a protective scarab, and the Opening of the Mouth ritual let the dead breathe, eat and speak again.
sections.b: Mummification re-enacted what Isis and Anubis did for Osiris, and priests played the parts; the chief embalmer may have worn a jackal mask as Anubis. The brain was usually discarded, since Egyptians believed thinking happened in the heart. The heart itself was generally left in place, because it would be needed at the judgement. Over it lay a heart scarab, an amulet inscribed with a spell from the Book of the Dead begging the heart not to testify against its owner. Before burial, a priest performed the Opening of the Mouth, touching the mummy's face with sacred tools so the dead could breathe, eat and speak again in the afterlife.

sections.key: Egyptian myths still fascinate the world, and museums now think carefully about how they display ancient human remains.
sections.b: Since Howard Carter opened Tutankhamun's tomb in 1922, the world has been captivated by ancient Egypt, and a supposed 'curse' made great headlines, though historians find no evidence for it. The Eye of Horus appears on jewellery and tattoos, and Anubis, Ra and Osiris show up in films and games. Egyptians also mummified animals, from cats to ibises, in their millions as offerings. You can see Egyptian collections in Australia too, such as at the University of Sydney's Chau Chak Wing Museum. Many museums now treat mummies with extra care, remembering that each was once a person who expected eternal rest.

quiz.q: What did Ra do each night, according to Egyptian belief?
o: Journeyed through the underworld, fighting the serpent Apep
Weighed the hearts of the dead
quiz.e: Ra's nightly journey ended in rebirth at every dawn.

quiz.q: Who murdered Osiris?
quiz.e: Set, god of storms and disorder, was jealous of his brother.

quiz.q: What did the Eye of Horus become?
o: The name of the sun boat
quiz.e: Horus's restored eye symbolised protection and healing.

quiz.q: What was the heart weighed against in the judgement of the dead?
quiz.e: Maat stood for truth, justice and cosmic order.

quiz.q: Which organ was usually left inside the body during mummification?
quiz.e: The heart was needed for the weighing in the afterlife.

LESSONS.title: The five zones of the ocean
LESSONS.hook: Most of the living space on Earth is dark, cold and crushing, and we have seen almost none of it.

sections.key: The ocean covers about 71% of Earth and averages about 3,700 metres deep.
sections.b: The ocean covers about 71% of Earth's surface and holds around 97% of its water. Its average depth is roughly 3,700 metres, and because life can exist at every depth, the ocean makes up the vast majority of the living space on the planet. Scientists divide the water column into layers based mainly on how much sunlight reaches them. From top to bottom they are the sunlight, twilight, midnight, abyssal and hadal zones. Each has its own conditions, and the animals in each are shaped by the challenges of light, food, cold and pressure.

sections.key: The top 200 metres gets enough light for photosynthesis and holds most familiar sea life.
sections.b: The sunlight zone, or epipelagic zone, runs from the surface to about 200 metres. It is the only layer with enough light for photosynthesis, so it is where tiny drifting plants called phytoplankton grow. Phytoplankton produce roughly half of the oxygen made on Earth each year and form the base of almost every ocean food chain. This zone holds the life most people picture: coral reefs, kelp forests, tuna, turtles, dolphins and most commercial fisheries. It is also the warmest layer, heated by the sun and mixed by wind and waves.

sections.key: From 200 to 1,000 metres light fades to a dim blue, and many animals migrate up each night.
sections.b: Between about 200 and 1,000 metres lies the twilight zone, or mesopelagic zone. There is still faint blue light, but not enough for plants to grow. Many animals here, such as lanternfish, small squid and shrimp-like krill relatives, have large eyes and make their own light. Each night, vast numbers of them swim up towards the surface to feed in darkness, then sink back down at dawn to hide from predators. This daily commute, repeated across the world's oceans, is often described as the largest migration on Earth by numbers of animals.

sections.key: Below 1,000 metres there is no sunlight, the water is near freezing and food is scarce.
sections.b: From about 1,000 to 4,000 metres is the midnight zone, or bathypelagic zone. No sunlight reaches it at all; the only light comes from animals themselves. Temperatures sit around 2 to 4 degrees Celsius. With no plants, food mostly arrives as 'marine snow', a slow drift of dead plankton, droppings and other debris from above, along with the occasional carcass. Animals here tend to be slow-moving and energy-saving, with big mouths and stretchy stomachs so they can make the most of rare meals. Sperm whales dive into this zone to hunt squid.

sections.key: The abyssal plains lie at 4,000–6,000 metres; trenches plunge to about 11,000 metres.
sections.b: Below about 4,000 metres is the abyssal zone, named from a Greek word meaning 'bottomless'. Much of it is flat, muddy seafloor called the abyssal plain, covering a huge part of the planet. The deepest layer, the hadal zone, named after Hades, exists only in ocean trenches below about 6,000 metres. The deepest known point is the Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench, in the western Pacific, at roughly 11,000 metres. Surprisingly, life is found even there, including amphipods, sea cucumbers and microbes.

sections.key: Pressure rises by about one atmosphere every 10 metres; at the deepest point it is over 1,000 times surface pressure.
sections.b: Water is heavy. For every 10 metres you descend, pressure increases by roughly one atmosphere, the pressure of the air at sea level. At 1,000 metres it is about 100 times surface pressure; in the Challenger Deep it is more than 1,000 times, roughly the weight of a small car pressing on every square centimetre. Deep-sea animals cope because they lack air-filled spaces that would be crushed, and their proteins and cell membranes are adapted to work under pressure. Human visitors need thick-walled submersibles to survive.

sections.key: Only about a quarter of the seafloor is mapped in detail, and far less has ever been seen directly.
sections.b: People often say we know more about the surface of the Moon or Mars than about our own seafloor, and in terms of detailed maps that has been true. As of the mid-2020s, international mapping efforts such as the Seabed 2030 project had charted roughly a quarter of the seafloor at high resolution. The share that humans have actually seen, with cameras or in person, is far smaller, well under one per cent. New species are described from the deep sea every year, and scientists expect many more are waiting to be found.

sections.key: The deep ocean stores heat and carbon, supports fisheries and still holds undiscovered species.
sections.b: The ocean has absorbed around 90% of the extra heat trapped by greenhouse gases and roughly a quarter of the carbon dioxide humans release, slowing climate change on land. Much of that carbon is carried downward by marine snow and migrating animals. Fisheries feed billions of people, and deep-sea organisms have already yielded useful compounds for medicine and research. Australia manages one of the world's largest ocean territories, so decisions about fishing, marine parks and seabed mining matter here. Next time you look out from a beach, remember most of the ocean's life is out of sight below.

quiz.q: Roughly how much of the oxygen produced on Earth each year comes from ocean phytoplankton?
quiz.e: Phytoplankton in the sunlight zone produce roughly half of the oxygen made on Earth each year.

quiz.q: What happens in the twilight zone each night?
o: Huge numbers of animals rise towards the surface to feed
Animals migrate down to the trenches
quiz.e: Lanternfish, squid and others swim upward at night to feed, then sink at dawn: often called the largest migration on Earth.

quiz.q: What is 'marine snow'?
o: Ice that forms on the seafloor
A drift of dead plankton and debris sinking from above
quiz.e: Marine snow is sinking organic debris and a key food source in the dark zones.

quiz.q: About how much does water pressure increase for every 10 metres of depth?
quiz.e: Pressure rises about one atmosphere per 10 metres, so the deepest trench is over 1,000 atmospheres.

quiz.q: Where is the deepest known point in the ocean?
o: The Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench
quiz.e: The Challenger Deep, in the western Pacific's Mariana Trench, is roughly 11,000 metres deep.

LESSONS.title: Ocean currents: the planet's conveyor belt
LESSONS.hook: Rivers larger than any on land flow through the sea, carrying heat, food, plastic and even Nemo's dad.

sections.key: Ocean currents are continuous flows of water that move heat, nutrients and life around the globe.
sections.b: An ocean current is a steady, directional flow of seawater. Some are shallow and fast, others deep and slow, and the largest carry far more water than all the rivers on land combined. The Antarctic Circumpolar Current, which loops endlessly around Antarctica from west to east, moves over 100 times the flow of all the world's rivers put together. Currents shift heat from the tropics towards the poles, shape the climate of whole continents, carry larvae and nutrients that feed fisheries, and decide where floating things end up, from seeds to shipwreck debris.

sections.key: Surface currents are pushed by wind, bent by Earth's rotation and steered by coastlines.
sections.b: Currents in the upper few hundred metres are driven mainly by wind. Steady winds such as the trade winds drag the surface water along. Because Earth spins, moving water is deflected by what is called the Coriolis effect: to the left in the Southern Hemisphere and to the right in the Northern. Continents then block and redirect the flow. Together these forces create a predictable pattern of currents that sailors have used for centuries. Before engines, knowing the currents could shave weeks off a voyage, or strand a ship if ignored.

sections.key: Deep currents are driven by differences in temperature and saltiness, and a full loop takes around 1,000 years.
sections.b: Deep currents work differently. In the far North Atlantic and around Antarctica, seawater becomes very cold and salty, partly because sea ice leaves salt behind as it forms. That water is dense, so it sinks and spreads slowly along the ocean floor. Elsewhere, water rises to replace it. This density-driven circulation, called thermohaline circulation, links all the oceans in what is nicknamed the global conveyor belt. A single parcel of water can take around 1,000 years to complete the loop, carrying heat, oxygen and dissolved carbon as it goes.

sections.key: The Gulf Stream helps keep north-west Europe mild; scientists debate how much its wider system is slowing.
sections.b: The Gulf Stream carries warm water from the Gulf of Mexico up the east coast of North America and across the Atlantic. Along with prevailing winds, the wider current system it belongs to helps give Britain and north-west Europe milder winters than places at the same latitude in Canada. This system, called the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, may be weakening as melting ice adds fresh water that is less likely to sink. How much it has slowed, and whether it could approach a tipping point this century, is actively debated among scientists.

sections.key: The EAC carries warm tropical water south along Australia's east coast, and it is strengthening.
sections.b: Australia's best-known current is the East Australian Current, the one the turtles ride in the 2003 film Finding Nemo. It flows south from the Coral Sea along the coast of Queensland and New South Wales, carrying warm water and tropical fish larvae, which is why reef fish sometimes turn up around Sydney in late summer. Much of it peels away eastwards near the mid-north coast, forming large swirling eddies. As the climate warms, the current has been pushing further south, contributing to warming waters off Tasmania that have helped shrink its giant kelp forests dramatically.

sections.key: Unusually, a warm current flows south down Western Australia's coast, allowing corals far from the tropics.
sections.b: Most currents on the western side of continents flow towards the equator and carry cold water, which is why places like Peru and Namibia have chilly coastal seas. Western Australia is an exception. The Leeuwin Current carries warm, low-nutrient tropical water south along the WA coast and then around Cape Leeuwin towards the Great Australian Bight. It helps explain why coral reefs grow at Ningaloo and even at the Houtman Abrolhos Islands off Geraldton, well south of where you might expect. It also helps carry tropical marine life surprisingly far south.

sections.key: Huge circular currents called gyres trap floating plastic in 'garbage patches'.
sections.b: Where major currents connect, they form enormous rotating systems called gyres. There are five main subtropical gyres, in the North and South Pacific, North and South Atlantic and the Indian Ocean. Floating debris tends to collect towards their calm centres. The best known, the Great Pacific Garbage Patch between Hawaii and California, is not a solid island of rubbish but a vast area of scattered plastic, much of it tiny fragments, with discarded fishing gear making up a large share of its weight. In 1992, thousands of bath toys lost from a ship helped scientists track these currents for years.

sections.key: Currents affect Australian weather, fishing, swimming safety and where our rubbish ends up.
sections.b: Currents shape daily life more than most people realise. Shifts in Pacific currents and winds drive El Niño and La Niña, which strongly influence droughts, floods and bushfire seasons in eastern Australia. Upwelling, where currents bring cold, nutrient-rich water to the surface, supports rich fishing grounds. Closer to shore, rip currents are a leading cause of coastal drowning in Australia: if caught, stay calm, float and signal for help rather than fighting the flow. And plastic dropped on a beach can travel thousands of kilometres, so what we throw away rarely stays local.

quiz.q: What mainly drives surface ocean currents?
quiz.e: Winds push surface water, and the Coriolis effect and coastlines shape its path.

quiz.q: What makes deep water sink to drive the global conveyor belt?
o: It is warmer than surface water
It is cold and salty, and therefore dense
quiz.e: Cold, salty water is dense and sinks, driving the slow thermohaline circulation.

quiz.q: Which direction does the East Australian Current flow?
o: South along the east coast from the Coral Sea
quiz.e: The EAC carries warm tropical water south along Queensland and New South Wales.

quiz.q: Why is the Leeuwin Current unusual?
o: It is the fastest current on Earth
It carries warm water south along a western coastline
quiz.e: Most currents along western coastlines are cold and flow towards the equator; the Leeuwin is warm and flows south.

quiz.q: What is the Great Pacific Garbage Patch actually like?
o: A solid island you can walk on
A vast area of scattered, mostly small plastic pieces
quiz.e: It is a diffuse area of floating plastic, much of it small fragments and fishing gear, collected by a gyre.

LESSONS.title: Life in the deep sea
LESSONS.hook: In total darkness, near-boiling vents feed giant worms, fish carry their own lanterns, and a few humans have visited the very bottom.

sections.key: The deep sea is dark, cold and high-pressure, yet it is full of life.
sections.b: Below about 200 metres, sunlight fades, and below 1,000 metres it disappears entirely. The water is near freezing and the pressure is immense. For a long time, scientists assumed such a place would be almost lifeless. In the 1870s, the British research ship HMS Challenger dredged the deep seafloor during a voyage around the world and brought up thousands of previously unknown species, proving otherwise. Today we know the deep sea is home to an astonishing variety of animals and microbes, many of them still undescribed, living in ways that seem alien to us.

sections.key: In 1977, scientists discovered vents where life runs on chemical energy instead of sunlight.
sections.b: In 1977, scientists diving in the submersible Alvin near the Galápagos Islands found something no one expected: hot springs on the seafloor, surrounded by crowded communities of life. At these hydrothermal vents, seawater seeps into the crust, is heated by magma and gushes out loaded with minerals. Some vents, called black smokers, blast out water hotter than 350 degrees Celsius, kept from boiling by the enormous pressure. Instead of relying on sunlight, bacteria here get energy from chemicals such as hydrogen sulphide, a process called chemosynthesis, and whole food webs are built on them.

sections.key: Giant tube worms have no mouth or gut; bacteria living inside them make their food.
sections.b: The most famous vent animal is the giant tube worm, which can grow up to about two metres long, with a bright red plume sticking out of a white tube. It has no mouth and no gut as an adult. Instead, its body houses billions of bacteria that turn vent chemicals into food, and the worm's red plume, coloured by haemoglobin, collects what they need. Vents also host crabs, shrimp, clams and snails. Some scientists think life on Earth may have begun at vents like these, though this remains one of several competing ideas.

sections.key: Most deep-sea animals can make light, called bioluminescence, to hunt, hide and communicate.
sections.b: In the dark ocean, making your own light is normal rather than rare. Studies suggest around three-quarters of animals in the deep water column are bioluminescent, producing light through a chemical reaction or by hosting glowing bacteria. Most of it is blue, because blue light travels furthest through seawater. Animals use light to lure prey, startle predators, find mates, and even hide: some fish glow faintly on their bellies to match the dim light from above, erasing their silhouette. A few dragonfish produce red light that most other deep-sea animals cannot see, like a private torch.

sections.key: Female anglerfish dangle a glowing lure; in some species tiny males fuse permanently to females.
sections.b: Deep-sea anglerfish are the classic deep-sea monster, though most are smaller than a football. The female carries a fishing rod, a modified fin spine tipped with a glowing lure packed with light-producing bacteria. Curious prey swim close and are swallowed by a mouth full of needle-like teeth; the stomach can stretch to hold a meal almost as large as the fish itself. In some species, the males are tiny and, on finding a female in the vast darkness, bite on and fuse to her body permanently, sharing her blood supply and supplying sperm.

sections.h: The bottom of the Mariana Trench
sections.key: Crewed dives to the Challenger Deep began in 1960 and remain rare: only a few dozen people have been to the bottom.
sections.b: The Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench is roughly 11,000 metres deep, deep enough to swallow Mount Everest with more than two kilometres of water to spare. In 1960, Jacques Piccard and US Navy officer Don Walsh reached the bottom in the bathyscaphe Trieste, spending about 20 minutes there. Nobody returned until 2012, when filmmaker James Cameron made a solo dive in Deepsea Challenger, a submersible designed and built in Sydney. Since 2019, the explorer Victor Vescovo's submersible has made repeated dives, taking more people to the deepest point in the ocean.

sections.key: Most deep-sea exploration is now done by remotely operated and autonomous vehicles.
sections.b: Crewed dives are expensive and risky, so most deep-sea exploration uses robots. Remotely operated vehicles, tethered to a ship by a cable, carry cameras, lights and robotic arms. Autonomous vehicles map the seafloor with sonar on their own, and 'landers' are dropped with baited cameras and later float back up. In 2022, a team led by scientists from the University of Western Australia filmed a snailfish at about 8,300 metres off Japan, the deepest fish ever recorded. Research ships now often livestream their dives, so anyone can watch discoveries as they happen.

sections.key: The deep sea stores carbon and holds valuable minerals, and seabed mining is a live debate.
sections.b: The deep ocean is not just a curiosity. It stores enormous amounts of carbon, helping regulate the climate, and its organisms have produced enzymes and compounds used in medicine and research. It also holds metal-rich rocks called polymetallic nodules, containing cobalt, nickel and manganese used in batteries. Companies want to mine them, but many scientists warn that deep-sea ecosystems grow and recover extremely slowly, over decades to millions of years, and that we understand them too poorly to judge the damage. Whether and how to allow deep-sea mining is one of the big ocean debates of this decade.

quiz.q: What powers the food web at hydrothermal vents?
o: Bacteria using chemical energy, called chemosynthesis
Heat from the sun stored in rocks
quiz.e: Vent bacteria use chemicals like hydrogen sulphide for energy, supporting the whole community.

quiz.q: How does an adult giant tube worm get food?
o: It filters plankton with its mouth
Bacteria living inside its body make food from vent chemicals
quiz.e: Adult giant tube worms have no mouth or gut and depend on internal bacteria.

quiz.q: Why is most deep-sea bioluminescence blue?
o: Blue light travels furthest through seawater
Blue is the colour of the bacteria
quiz.e: Blue light penetrates water best, so it is the most useful colour in the deep.

quiz.q: Who first reached the bottom of the Challenger Deep, in 1960?
quiz.e: Piccard and Walsh reached the bottom in the Trieste in 1960; Cameron followed in 2012.

quiz.q: What is a major concern about deep-sea mining?
o: Deep-sea ecosystems recover very slowly and are poorly understood
quiz.e: Scientists warn that slow-growing, poorly studied deep-sea ecosystems could be lastingly damaged.

LESSONS.title: Sharks: fear versus facts
LESSONS.hook: Sharks are older than trees, come in more than 500 species and are far more at risk from us than we are from them.

sections.key: Sharks have existed for over 400 million years and survived several mass extinctions.
sections.b: Sharks appeared more than 400 million years ago, earlier than trees, which evolved roughly 385 million years ago, and long before dinosaurs. They have survived at least four of the five great mass extinctions. Their skeletons are made of cartilage, the flexible material in your nose and ears, rather than bone, which is why fossil sharks are mostly known from teeth. Sharks shed and replace teeth throughout life, sometimes thousands over a lifetime. The extinct megalodon, which died out around 3.6 million years ago, may have reached 15 metres or more.

sections.key: There are over 500 shark species, from palm-sized lanternsharks to the 12-metre-plus whale shark.
sections.b: There are more than 500 known species of shark, and most look nothing like the movie villain. The dwarf lanternshark is about 20 centimetres long and glows in the deep sea.
