Wobbegongs lie camouflaged on Australian reefs like shaggy rugs. The whale shark, the largest fish in the world, can exceed 12 metres yet feeds on plankton, and gathers each year at Ningaloo Reef in WA. The Greenland shark grows so slowly that a 2016 study estimated some live for several centuries, possibly around 400 years, making it the longest-lived known vertebrate.

sections.key: Some sharks lay eggs and others give birth to live pups; grey nurse shark embryos eat their siblings in the womb.
sections.b: Unlike most fish, which scatter huge numbers of tiny eggs, sharks produce a small number of large, well-developed young. Fertilisation happens inside the female. Some species lay eggs in tough cases; the Port Jackson shark, found around southern Australia, wedges its corkscrew-shaped egg cases into rocky crevices. Many others give birth to live pups, and hammerheads and bull sharks even nourish their young through a placenta-like connection. The grey nurse shark goes further: in each of the mother's two uteri, the first embryo to develop eats its smaller siblings and spare eggs, so a litter is usually just two pups, born every second year. Once born, pups get no parental care and must fend for themselves.

sections.key: Worldwide, unprovoked shark bites number in the dozens each year and fatalities are usually in single figures.
sections.b: Shark bites are frightening and heavily reported, but rare. Worldwide, researchers typically record somewhere around 50 to 80 confirmed unprovoked bites a year, with fatalities usually in single figures. Australia and the United States record the most. In Australia, a few people die from shark bites in a typical year, while well over a hundred people drown along the coast. Of more than 500 species, only a handful are responsible for most serious bites, chiefly the white shark, tiger shark and bull shark. Many bites are thought to be cases of mistaken identity or investigation.

sections.key: Humans kill an estimated 100 million sharks a year; many species are threatened.
sections.b: The danger runs overwhelmingly the other way. A widely cited 2013 study estimated that humans kill around 100 million sharks a year, through fishing, bycatch and the trade in shark fins. Because many sharks grow slowly, mature late and have few young, populations recover poorly. A major 2021 study found that numbers of oceanic sharks and rays had fallen by about 70% since 1970. Around a third of shark and ray species are now considered threatened with extinction. In Australia, the east coast population of the grey nurse shark is listed as critically endangered.

sections.key: As predators, sharks help keep ocean ecosystems balanced and healthy.
sections.b: Sharks play important roles as predators and scavengers. By removing sick and weak animals and changing where prey feed, they can shape entire ecosystems. When large sharks disappear, the effects can ripple down the food chain in ways that are hard to predict, sometimes allowing their prey to overgraze seagrass or reef communities. Tiger sharks, for example, are thought to help protect seagrass meadows in Shark Bay, WA, by keeping grazing turtles and dugongs on the move. Healthy shark populations are generally a sign of a healthy ocean.

sections.key: Australia uses nets, drumlines, drones and tagging, and the trade-offs are debated.
sections.b: Australian states use a mix of measures to reduce shark risk. Shark nets have been used at some Sydney beaches since 1937 and in Queensland since the 1960s, alongside baited drumlines. Critics point out that nets do not form a full barrier and catch many turtles, dolphins, rays and harmless sharks. Newer approaches include 'SMART' drumlines that alert crews when a shark is hooked so it can be tagged and released, drone and helicopter patrols, tagged-shark listening stations and public alert apps such as SharkSmart in NSW. Which mix works best remains debated.

sections.key: Swim at patrolled beaches, avoid dawn, dusk and murky water, and stay away from baitfish and fishing.
sections.b: You can lower an already small risk with a few habits. Swim at patrolled beaches between the red and yellow flags, and stay in groups. Avoid swimming at dawn, dusk or night, when many sharks feed more actively. Stay out of murky water, river mouths and canals, especially after heavy rain, which bull sharks favour. Keep clear of schools of baitfish, diving birds, seals, and people fishing or cleaning fish. Check local alerts or apps before heading in. And remember that rips, not sharks, are the far bigger danger at Australian beaches.

quiz.q: Which came first on Earth?
quiz.e: Sharks appeared over 400 million years ago, before trees and long before dinosaurs.

quiz.q: Why does a grey nurse shark usually give birth to only two pups?
o: It mates only once in its life
The first embryo in each uterus eats its developing siblings
It lays its eggs in rock crevices
Its pups are born fully grown
quiz.e: Each of the mother's two uteri usually produces just one surviving pup.

quiz.q: What does the whale shark mainly eat?
quiz.e: The world's largest fish is a filter feeder, eating plankton; it visits Ningaloo Reef each year.

quiz.q: Which three species cause most serious shark bites?
quiz.e: White, tiger and bull sharks account for most serious bites.

quiz.q: Roughly how many sharks do humans kill each year, according to a widely cited estimate?
quiz.e: A 2013 study estimated around 100 million sharks are killed each year.

LESSONS.title: Whales: giants of the sea
LESSONS.hook: The largest animal that has ever lived swims in our oceans, and humpbacks pass Australia's coast every winter singing songs that change each year.

sections.h: Mammals that returned to the sea
sections.key: Whales are mammals that evolved from land animals about 50 million years ago; their closest living relatives are hippos.
sections.b: Whales breathe air, are warm-blooded, give birth to live young and feed them milk. They evolved from four-legged land mammals roughly 50 million years ago, and fossils such as Pakicetus, a wolf-sized animal from what is now Pakistan, show early stages of that transition. Over millions of years their front limbs became flippers, their back legs shrank to tiny internal bones and their nostrils moved to the top of the head as blowholes. DNA studies show their closest living relatives are hippopotamuses. Whales, dolphins and porpoises together are called cetaceans.

sections.key: Baleen whales filter food through keratin plates; toothed whales, including dolphins, hunt with teeth and echolocation.
sections.b: Cetaceans fall into two groups. Baleen whales, such as blue, humpback, fin and southern right whales, have no teeth. Instead, hundreds of plates of baleen, made of keratin like your fingernails, hang from the upper jaw and strain krill and small fish from huge gulps of water. They have two blowholes. Toothed whales, a much larger group that includes sperm whales, orcas, dolphins and porpoises, have one blowhole and hunt individual prey. Most use echolocation, sending out clicks and reading the echoes to 'see' with sound.

sections.key: The blue whale is the largest animal known to have lived; the sperm whale has the largest brain.
sections.b: The blue whale is the largest animal known to have ever lived, larger than any dinosaur found so far. It can reach around 30 metres and well over 100 tonnes, and its heart alone can weigh around 180 kilograms. Pygmy blue whales feed in Australian waters, including off Perth and in the Bonney Upwelling off South Australia and Victoria. The sperm whale has the largest brain of any animal, and dives to depths of over a kilometre to hunt squid. Some bowhead whales in the Arctic are thought to live for more than 200 years.

sections.key: Humpbacks migrate each year between Antarctica and warm breeding waters off Queensland and WA.
sections.b: Every year, humpback whales travel between their feeding grounds in Antarctic waters and their breeding grounds in the tropics, one of the longest migrations of any mammal. Australia has two main populations. One travels up the east coast to the waters inside and near the Great Barrier Reef; the other heads up the west coast to the Kimberley. The northern migration runs roughly from May to August, and the return south, often with young calves, from about August to November. Headlands such as Cape Byron, North Stradbroke Island and Cape Naturaliste make excellent viewing spots.

sections.key: Commercial whaling nearly wiped out Australian humpbacks; the last station, in Albany, closed in 1978.
sections.b: Whaling was one of colonial Australia's earliest export industries, with whalers hunting southern right and sperm whales from the early 1800s. In the 20th century, stations such as Tangalooma on Moreton Island in Queensland and others in WA and NSW hunted humpbacks heavily. By the early 1960s, the east coast humpback population had collapsed to perhaps a few hundred animals, and the east coast stations closed in 1962 as catches dried up. Australia's last whaling station, at Cheynes Beach near Albany in WA, closed in 1978, and Australia went on to become a strong opponent of commercial whaling.

sections.key: Australian humpbacks have recovered to tens of thousands, and were removed from the threatened list in 2022.
sections.b: The International Whaling Commission agreed a moratorium on commercial whaling in 1982, which took effect in 1986. In 2014, the International Court of Justice ruled, in a case brought by Australia, that Japan's Antarctic whaling program was not for scientific purposes as claimed. Protected from hunting, humpbacks have made one of the great recoveries in wildlife conservation. The east coast population is now estimated in the tens of thousands, and in 2022 the Australian Government removed humpbacks from the national threatened species list. Other species, including blue whales, remain far below their pre-whaling numbers.

sections.key: Male humpbacks sing complex songs that change over time and spread between populations.
sections.b: Male humpbacks sing long, complex songs made of repeated phrases and themes, mostly on the breeding grounds. All males in a population sing roughly the same song, but it gradually changes over time. Researchers at the University of Queensland and elsewhere found that new songs can sweep eastward across the South Pacific, from eastern Australia to French Polynesia, over a year or two, a kind of cultural transmission rare outside humans. Why males sing is still debated, but it is probably linked to mating. Blue whale calls are among the loudest sounds made by any animal.

sections.key: Keep legal distances from whales, and report stranded or entangled whales to authorities.
sections.b: Australia is one of the best places in the world to watch whales, from shore, boats or planes. To protect them, there are legal approach distances: vessels must generally stay at least 100 metres from whales, with larger distances for mothers with calves in many states, and swimmers, jet skis and drones have their own limits. Rules vary slightly by state, so check before heading out. If you see a stranded, injured or entangled whale, do not try to free it yourself; call your state's wildlife or marine rescue hotline, as entangled whales can be extremely dangerous.

quiz.q: What are the closest living relatives of whales?
quiz.e: DNA studies show whales' closest living relatives are hippos.

quiz.q: What is baleen made of?
quiz.e: Baleen plates are keratin and strain food from the water.

quiz.q: Where do Australia's east coast humpbacks go to breed?
o: Waters inside and near the Great Barrier Reef
quiz.e: East coast humpbacks migrate north from Antarctica to breed in warm Queensland waters.

quiz.q: Where was Australia's last whaling station?
quiz.e: The Cheynes Beach station near Albany closed in 1978.

quiz.q: What is unusual about humpback whale songs?
o: Songs change over time and spread between populations
Every whale sings a completely different song
quiz.e: Songs evolve and can spread eastward across the South Pacific, a form of cultural transmission.

LESSONS.title: The Great Barrier Reef
LESSONS.hook: The largest structure built by living things on Earth is made by animals smaller than your fingernail, and it is under more pressure than ever.

sections.key: Corals are animals, tiny polyps related to jellyfish, that build limestone skeletons.
sections.b: Coral may look like rock or plants, but it is made of animals. Each coral is a colony of thousands of tiny polyps, soft-bodied creatures related to jellyfish and sea anemones. Each polyp has a ring of stinging tentacles for catching plankton at night, and builds a hard cup of calcium carbonate, or limestone, beneath itself. Over generations, colonies grow on the skeletons of those before them. Over thousands of years, this slow building, plus sand and rubble cemented together, creates reefs large enough to be seen from space.

sections.key: Microscopic algae living inside coral provide most of its food and its colour.
sections.b: Reef-building corals have a secret partner. Living inside their tissues are microscopic algae called zooxanthellae, which photosynthesise using sunlight and share the sugars they make with the coral, supplying most of its energy, often cited as up to about 90%. In return, the algae get shelter and nutrients. The algae also give coral much of its colour. This partnership is why reef-building corals grow in clear, shallow, sunlit tropical water. It is also the relationship that breaks down during bleaching, which is why heat stress is so dangerous.

sections.key: The reef stretches about 2,300 km, with around 3,000 reefs and hundreds of islands, and extraordinary biodiversity.
sections.b: The Great Barrier Reef stretches roughly 2,300 kilometres along the Queensland coast, from the Torres Strait to near Bundaberg, and its marine park covers an area larger than Italy. It is not one reef but around 3,000 individual reefs and hundreds of islands and cays. It supports over 400 kinds of hard coral, more than 1,500 species of fish, six of the world's seven species of marine turtle, dugongs, sharks and thousands of molluscs. Every spring, a few nights after a full moon, many corals spawn at once, a spectacle first documented by Australian scientists in the early 1980s.

sections.key: Reefs have grown here for hundreds of thousands of years; today's living reef formed after the last ice age.
sections.b: Coral reefs have grown along this coast for hundreds of thousands of years, dying back when sea levels fell during ice ages and regrowing when they rose. The living reef we see today began forming around 8,000 years ago, on top of older foundations, as rising seas flooded the continental shelf after the last ice age. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have lived alongside the reef throughout this time, and more than 70 Traditional Owner groups hold ongoing connections to its sea country. In 1770, James Cook's Endeavour ran aground on the reef near present-day Cooktown.

sections.key: When water is too warm for too long, corals expel their algae, turn white and may die.
sections.b: When sea temperatures stay even one or two degrees above the usual summer maximum for several weeks, the coral-algae partnership breaks down. The coral expels its algae and turns white, revealing its skeleton through clear tissue. This is bleaching. Bleached corals are not dead, and if temperatures fall soon enough they can regain their algae and recover. But if heat stress is severe or prolonged, they starve and die. The reef had mass bleaching events in 1998 and 2002, then in 2016, 2017, 2020, 2022, 2024 and 2025, with 2016 and 2017 killing a large share of shallow-water corals.

sections.key: Climate change is the biggest threat, alongside poor water quality, crown-of-thorns starfish and cyclones.
sections.b: Scientists and the reef's managers agree climate change is the greatest threat, through marine heatwaves that cause bleaching and through ocean acidification, which makes it harder for corals to build skeletons. Other pressures add up. Runoff from farms and land clearing carries sediment and fertiliser that cloud the water and can fuel outbreaks of crown-of-thorns starfish, which eat coral. Stronger cyclones smash reefs apart. Recovery between disturbances takes years, often a decade or more for slow-growing corals, and the gaps between events have been getting shorter. Parts of the reef have recovered well between events, but that resilience is being tested.

sections.key: Protected by a marine park since 1975 and World Heritage listed in 1981, with about a third of the park as no-take zones.
sections.b: The Great Barrier Reef Marine Park was created in 1975, following public campaigns against oil drilling and mining on the reef. In 1981, it was inscribed on the World Heritage List for its outstanding natural value. In 2004, the park was rezoned so that about a third of it became 'green zones', where fishing and collecting are banned, one of the largest such networks in the world. Crown-of-thorns control programs, efforts to cut farm runoff and research into heat-tolerant corals continue. UNESCO has several times considered listing the reef as 'in danger', a move Australian governments have argued against.

sections.key: Visit responsibly, never touch or stand on coral, and support action on climate and water quality.
sections.b: The reef supports tens of thousands of jobs and billions of dollars in tourism each year, and visiting it well can help. Choose operators with eco-certification, never touch, stand on or kick coral, and wear fins carefully when snorkelling. Follow zoning rules if fishing, and take all rubbish home. Some sunscreen ingredients can harm coral in lab studies, though their real-world impact is debated and small next to warming; a rash vest reduces the need for sunscreen anyway. The biggest help, experts agree, is reducing greenhouse emissions and improving water quality flowing from the land.

quiz.q: What are corals?
o: Colonies of tiny animals called polyps
quiz.e: Corals are colonies of polyps, animals related to jellyfish and anemones.

quiz.q: What do zooxanthellae provide to reef-building corals?
o: Most of their food energy and much of their colour
quiz.e: The algae photosynthesise and share sugars, supplying most of the coral's energy.

quiz.q: What happens during coral bleaching?
o: Heat-stressed coral expels its algae and turns white
quiz.e: Prolonged heat breaks the coral-algae partnership; corals can recover if temperatures fall in time.

quiz.q: When was the Great Barrier Reef World Heritage listed?
quiz.e: The reef was inscribed on the World Heritage List in 1981; the marine park dates from 1975.

quiz.q: What do experts identify as the biggest threat to the reef?
quiz.e: Climate change, through marine heatwaves and acidification, is the greatest threat.

LESSONS.title: Aristotle's rhetoric: ethos, pathos, logos
LESSONS.hook: Every ad you scroll past and every speech that moves you is using tools Aristotle catalogued about 2,300 years ago.

sections.h: The first great study of persuasion
sections.key: Aristotle's Rhetoric, written in the 300s BC, was the first systematic study of how persuasion works.
sections.b: In Athens in the 300s BC, citizens argued their own cases in court and voted directly in the assembly, so speaking well was a practical survival skill. Teachers called sophists charged fees to teach it, and critics like Plato worried they taught people to make the weaker argument look stronger. Aristotle took a different approach. In his Rhetoric he studied persuasion like a scientist studies animals, defining rhetoric as the ability to see the available means of persuasion in any given case. His framework is still taught in law schools, marketing courses and speechwriting workshops.

sections.key: Aristotle said speakers persuade through ethos (character), pathos (emotion) and logos (reasoning).
sections.b: Aristotle identified three 'modes of proof' that a speaker creates through the speech itself. Ethos is the credibility and character of the speaker: do we trust this person? Pathos is putting the audience into a particular emotional state: are we moved? Logos is the argument itself: does the reasoning and evidence hold up? He argued that good persuasion usually combines all three. A speech with perfect logic from someone we distrust falls flat, and pure emotion without reasons tends to fade once the feeling wears off.

sections.h: Ethos: why we trust a speaker
sections.key: Ethos rests on perceived good sense, good character and goodwill towards the audience.
sections.b: Aristotle thought ethos might be the most powerful mode of all. He said we trust speakers who show three qualities: practical wisdom, good moral character and goodwill towards us. Notice these are perceptions the speaker builds. Doctors in white coats, a tradie mentioning 20 years in the trade, and a politician rolling up their sleeves at a flood site are all building ethos. So is admitting a weakness, which signals honesty. Ethos can also be borrowed, which is why companies pay sports stars and celebrities to endorse their products.

sections.key: Pathos means stirring emotions like fear, pity, anger or hope so the audience is ready to act.
sections.b: Aristotle devoted a long section of the Rhetoric to emotions such as anger, fear, pity and confidence, because people judge differently when they feel differently. Pathos isn't automatically manipulation: a speech about a tragedy should make you feel something. It becomes a problem when emotion replaces reasons instead of accompanying them. Australia's graphic health warnings on cigarette packets, required since 2006 and enlarged under world-first plain packaging laws in 2012, are a deliberate use of pathos: the images are meant to make the risk feel real rather than abstract.

sections.h: Logos: the shape of an argument
sections.key: Logos is persuasion through reasoning, often using an enthymeme: an argument with an unstated premise.
sections.b: Logos covers facts, examples, statistics and logical steps. Aristotle noticed that everyday arguments rarely spell out every premise. He called these shortened arguments enthymemes. 'Buy this car, it has a five-star safety rating' leaves out the premise 'you want a safe car', which the audience fills in themselves. That participation is part of what makes enthymemes persuasive. It also makes them a place to hide weak assumptions. When you hear a punchy argument, try saying the missing premise out loud and asking whether you actually agree with it.

sections.key: Kairos is the Greek idea of the opportune moment: the same message can succeed or fail depending on timing.
sections.b: Kairos is often added to Aristotle's three, though it is really a broader Greek idea associated with earlier teachers such as Gorgias. It means the right moment, and the fitting message for that moment. A pitch for home insurance lands differently the week after a major storm. A joke that works at a barbecue can sink a eulogy. Advertisers chase kairos constantly, which is why sunscreen ads peak in summer and gym ads flood January. Good speakers ask not just 'what should I say?' but 'why now, and for this audience?'

sections.key: Aristotle divided speeches into deliberative (future), forensic (past) and epideictic (present, praise or blame).
sections.b: Aristotle sorted speeches by purpose. Deliberative speeches argue about the future: should we build the dam, pass the law, go to war? They appeal to advantage and harm. Forensic speeches, as in court, argue about the past: did the accused do it, and was it just? Epideictic, or ceremonial, speeches praise or blame in the present: eulogies, wedding toasts and award acceptances. Knowing which kind you're giving helps you choose your tools. A budget pitch at work is deliberative, so vivid praise alone won't carry it; you need costs and benefits.

sections.key: Naming ethos, pathos, logos and kairos helps you judge a message instead of just reacting to it.
sections.b: Try this with the next ad or speech you meet. Ethos: who is speaking, and why should I trust them? Is the credibility earned or borrowed? Pathos: what am I being made to feel, and does the feeling match the facts? Logos: what is the actual claim, what evidence supports it, and what premise is unstated? Kairos: why is this reaching me now? You'll find most effective messages lean on one mode more than the others. The skill cuts both ways: it makes you harder to fool and a clearer, fairer speaker yourself.

quiz.q: What does 'pathos' refer to in Aristotle's rhetoric?
quiz.e: Pathos is persuasion through emotion.

quiz.q: Which three qualities did Aristotle link to ethos?
o: Practical wisdom, good character and goodwill
quiz.e: We trust speakers who seem wise, good and on our side.

quiz.q: What is an enthymeme?
o: An argument with an unstated premise
quiz.e: The audience fills in the missing step.

quiz.q: What does 'kairos' mean?
quiz.e: The same message can succeed or fail depending on timing.

quiz.q: A eulogy at a funeral is which kind of speech?
quiz.e: Epideictic speeches praise or blame in the present.

LESSONS.title: Why stories persuade
LESSONS.hook: Facts tell, stories sell. There's real psychology behind why a good story can change a mind that statistics couldn't.

sections.key: Humans have told stories for tens of thousands of years; we remember and share information more easily in story form.
sections.b: Long before writing, people passed on knowledge through stories: where the water was, which plants were dangerous, who could be trusted. Aboriginal Australians have maintained oral traditions over many thousands of years, and some researchers argue certain stories preserve memories of real events such as sea-level rise. A story gives information a shape: someone wanted something, something got in the way, and something changed. That shape makes facts easier to remember and pass on. Psychologists note that a list of facts is quickly forgotten, while the same facts inside a narrative tend to stick.

sections.key: When we are 'transported' into a story, we tend to argue back less and absorb its message more.
sections.b: In 2000, psychologists Melanie Green and Timothy Brock described 'narrative transportation': the feeling of being carried away into a story. Their studies found that people who were more absorbed in a story were more likely to adopt beliefs consistent with it, and less likely to pick holes in it. When we read a list of arguments, we naturally counter-argue. When we're following a character, we're busy wondering what happens next. That's why stories can shift attitudes quietly, and why it's worth asking afterwards what a moving story was actually claiming.

sections.key: The identifiable victim effect: people give more to help one named person than to help a statistic.
sections.b: In a well-known 2007 study, Deborah Small, George Loewenstein and Paul Slovic asked people to donate to a charity. Some read about Rokia, a seven-year-old girl from Mali facing hunger. Others read statistics about millions of people facing food shortages in Africa. The Rokia group gave significantly more. Strikingly, adding the statistics to Rokia's story reduced donations. This 'identifiable victim effect' explains why charities lead with one person's story. It's also a reminder that our compassion doesn't scale well with numbers, which matters when big problems are at stake.

sections.key: Classic story structure moves from a setup, through rising tension and a turning point, to a resolution.
sections.b: In 1863, German writer Gustav Freytag described a pattern in dramatic plays, now called Freytag's pyramid: exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and resolution. Screenwriters often simplify it to three acts: setup, confrontation and resolution. The engine in every version is conflict. A character wants something and faces obstacles. 'I went to the shop and bought milk' isn't a story; 'the shop was closed and the baby was screaming' starts to become one. Without tension, there's no reason to keep listening, however interesting the facts.

sections.key: A 2016 computer analysis of over 1,300 novels found most stories follow one of six basic emotional arcs.
sections.b: Novelist Kurt Vonnegut liked to sketch stories as simple graphs, with the hero's fortune going up and down over time; his master's thesis on the idea was rejected by the University of Chicago. In 2016, researchers at the University of Vermont tested it, using computers to track the emotional tone of 1,327 novels from Project Gutenberg. They found six core arcs: rags to riches (a rise), tragedy (a fall), man in a hole (fall, then rise), Icarus (rise, then fall), Cinderella (rise, fall, rise) and Oedipus (fall, rise, fall). Judged by downloads, Icarus, Oedipus and a double 'man in a hole' were among the most popular shapes.

sections.key: In persuasive stories, the audience or customer should usually be the hero, and you the guide.
sections.b: A common mistake in business storytelling is casting yourself or your company as the hero. Audiences care most about their own problems. Marketing writers often borrow the hero's journey but reframe it: the customer is the hero with a problem, and the brand is the wise guide, like Obi-Wan Kenobi, who offers a plan. A bank ad that shows a young couple getting the keys to their first home follows this pattern. The bank barely appears. The story is about the couple, and the viewer imagines being them.

sections.key: At work, a short story built on situation, complication and resolution beats a pile of slides.
sections.b: You don't need a novel. A simple structure used by many consultants is situation, complication, resolution: here's where we are, here's what changed or went wrong, here's what we should do. Another is the 'story spine' from improv teacher Kenn Adams, popularised through Pixar's storytellers: once upon a time, every day, one day, because of that, until finally. A two-minute story about one real customer who struggled with your process can do more to win support for fixing it than twenty slides of complaint data.

sections.key: Pair a story with evidence, and ask whether a story is typical or just vivid.
sections.b: Because stories lower our guard, they can mislead as easily as they inform. A single dramatic anecdote about a rare side effect or a lucky investor can outweigh solid data in people's minds. When you're the audience, ask: is this story typical, or chosen because it's vivid? What would the numbers say? When you're the storyteller, use the story to open the door and the evidence to hold it open. The most persuasive, and most honest, communicators use both: a face that makes people care and facts that show the scale.

quiz.q: What did Green and Brock call the feeling of being absorbed in a story?
quiz.e: Absorbed readers counter-argue less.

quiz.q: In the Rokia study, what happened when statistics were added to her story?
quiz.e: The numbers seemed to dampen the emotional response.

quiz.q: What is the engine of every classic story structure?
quiz.e: Without a problem, there is no reason to keep listening.

quiz.q: Which basic story arc has a character fall into trouble and then climb out?
quiz.e: Man in a hole is a fall followed by a rise, one of six core arcs found in the 2016 study.

quiz.q: In persuasive business stories, who should usually be the hero?
quiz.e: The brand works best as the guide.

LESSONS.title: What makes a great speech
LESSONS.hook: A two-minute address at a cemetery, a hot August afternoon in Washington, a park in Redfern. Why some speeches outlive the people who gave them.

sections.key: Lincoln's Gettysburg Address of 1863 was only about 270 words, yet it redefined what the Civil War was for.
sections.b: On 19 November 1863, Abraham Lincoln spoke at the dedication of a military cemetery at Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, months after one of the bloodiest battles of the American Civil War. The main speaker, Edward Everett, spoke for about two hours. Lincoln spoke for about two minutes, roughly 270 words. He opened by reaching back to 1776, 'four score and seven years ago', and framed the war as a test of whether a nation built on equality could survive. He closed with a vision of 'a new birth of freedom'. Brevity made every word count.

sections.key: Churchill's 1940 speeches paired blunt honesty about disaster with defiant resolve.
sections.b: In May and June 1940, as Nazi Germany swept through Western Europe, new Prime Minister Winston Churchill gave a series of speeches to the House of Commons. He offered 'blood, toil, tears and sweat'. After the evacuation from Dunkirk, he called the campaign a colossal military disaster and warned that wars are not won by evacuations, then declared Britain would keep fighting on the beaches, in the fields and in the streets. His repetition of 'we shall fight' is a classic example of anaphora: repeating the opening words of successive phrases to build momentum.

sections.key: Martin Luther King Jr's 1963 'I Have a Dream' speech blended biblical cadence, American ideals and a partly improvised vision.
sections.b: On 28 August 1963, around 250,000 people gathered at the Lincoln Memorial for the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom. Martin Luther King Jr began with a prepared text, using the metaphor of America having given Black citizens a bad cheque marked 'insufficient funds'. Partway through, gospel singer Mahalia Jackson reportedly called out for him to tell them about the dream, and King moved into a passage he had used in earlier sermons. The repeated line 'I have a dream' turned an abstract demand for civil rights into vivid, concrete pictures of a fairer future.

sections.key: Paul Keating's 1992 Redfern speech was a landmark acknowledgement by a prime minister of the dispossession of Aboriginal people.
sections.b: On 10 December 1992, Prime Minister Paul Keating spoke in Redfern Park, Sydney, to launch Australia's part in the International Year of the World's Indigenous People. Delivered six months after the High Court's Mabo decision, the speech, largely written by Don Watson, stated plainly that non-Indigenous Australians had taken the land, brought the diseases and taken the children from their mothers. The power came from its use of 'we': rather than blaming a distant past, it asked listeners to imagine these things done to them. It is widely regarded as one of the most significant speeches in Australian history.

sections.key: Julia Gillard's 2012 speech in parliament went viral worldwide and prompted a dictionary to update a definition.
sections.b: On 9 October 2012, Opposition Leader Tony Abbott moved to remove the Speaker, Peter Slipper, over offensive text messages. Prime Minister Julia Gillard responded with a roughly 15-minute speech, speaking largely from notes, opening with the line that she would not be lectured about sexism and misogyny by this man. She listed remarks and incidents she saw as sexist. Reaction in Australia was divided at the time, partly because of the Slipper context, but the video spread globally. The Macquarie Dictionary soon broadened its definition of misogyny to include entrenched prejudice against women.

sections.key: Great speeches use repetition, rhythm, contrast and concrete images rather than abstract claims.
sections.b: Look across these speeches and patterns appear. Repetition: 'we shall fight', 'I have a dream'. Groups of three, like Lincoln's government 'of the people, by the people, for the people'. Contrast, setting what is against what could be. Concrete images: a bounced cheque, beaches and streets, children taken from their mothers. Speechwriters also write for the ear, not the eye: short sentences, strong verbs and deliberate pauses. Many of these devices were catalogued by ancient Greek and Roman teachers of rhetoric, which is why a speech from 1863 and one from 2012 can feel related.

sections.key: Every great speech met a moment of crisis or change and gave it words and meaning.
sections.b: None of these speeches worked in a vacuum. Lincoln spoke amid a war whose purpose people were questioning. Churchill spoke when invasion seemed possible. King spoke at the height of the civil rights movement. Keating spoke just after Mabo had overturned the legal fiction of terra nullius. Gillard spoke after months of heated public debate about how she was treated as the first female prime minister. The Greeks called this kairos: the right words at the right moment. A great speech names what an audience is already feeling and gives it a direction.

sections.key: Be brief, be concrete, use a memorable structure, and speak to the moment your audience is in.
sections.b: You're unlikely to address a nation, but the same lessons work at a wedding, a team meeting or a funeral. Be brief: Lincoln proved length isn't weight. Find one memorable line or image and build around it. Use repetition deliberately so listeners can follow without notes. Acknowledge hard truths, as Churchill and Keating did, because honesty builds trust. And speak to the moment: what is this room feeling right now? Finally, practise aloud. Many famous speeches were rehearsed, revised and borrowed from earlier drafts before their famous delivery.

quiz.q: Roughly how long was Lincoln's Gettysburg Address?
quiz.e: The main speaker before him spoke for about two hours.

quiz.q: Repeating 'we shall fight' at the start of phrases is an example of what?
quiz.e: Anaphora repeats the opening words of successive phrases.

quiz.q: Where did King deliver the 'I Have a Dream' speech?
quiz.e: It was the March on Washington, 1963.

quiz.q: What made Keating's Redfern speech distinctive?
o: It was only one minute long
It used 'we' to take responsibility for dispossession
quiz.e: It asked listeners to imagine these things done to them.

quiz.q: What change followed Gillard's 2012 speech?
o: The Macquarie Dictionary broadened its definition of misogyny
quiz.e: The definition was updated to include entrenched prejudice against women.

LESSONS.title: How to argue well
LESSONS.hook: Most arguments are two people defending their egos. Here's how to have the kind where someone actually learns something.

sections.key: The goal of a good argument is to find out what's true, not to beat the other person.
sections.b: Many of us treat arguments like sport: points scored, opponents defeated. But if you 'win' an argument while being wrong, you've lost the chance to learn. Writer Julia Galef calls the alternative the scout mindset: the aim is to see things as they are, rather than to defend a position like a soldier defending territory. In practice, this means going in curious. Ask yourself: what would I expect to see if I were wrong? What does this person know that I don't? The best arguments leave both people understanding more.

sections.key: A steelman is the strongest version of the other side's argument; a strawman is a weak caricature.
sections.b: A strawman is a distorted, weaker version of someone's view that's easy to knock down: 'So you think we should just let criminals go free?' A steelman is the opposite: the most charitable, strongest form of the argument. Steelmanning does two things. It shows the other person you've genuinely heard them, which lowers defensiveness. And it tests your own view properly: if your position only beats the weak version, it hasn't really won. A good check is whether the other person would say, 'Yes, that's exactly what I think.'

sections.key: Before criticising a view, restate it fairly, note agreements and say what you learned.
sections.b: Philosopher Daniel Dennett popularised a set of rules he attributed to the game theorist Anatol Rapoport. First, restate the other person's position so clearly and fairly that they wish they'd put it that way themselves. Second, list any points of agreement, especially ones that aren't widely shared. Third, mention anything you've learned from them. Only then should you offer criticism. It sounds slow, but it changes the whole temperature of a disagreement. People are far more open to your objections once they trust you actually understand their view.

sections.key: Attack ideas, not people; criticising the person instead of the argument is the ad hominem fallacy.
sections.b: In their 1981 negotiation classic Getting to Yes, Roger Fisher and William Ury advised separating the people from the problem. The same applies to arguments. 'That plan will blow the budget' is about the idea. 'You always come up with hopeless plans' is about the person, and guarantees defensiveness. Dismissing an argument because of who made it, rather than what it says, is the ad hominem fallacy. Programmer Paul Graham's 'hierarchy of disagreement' puts name-calling at the bottom and refuting the central point of an argument at the top. Aim high.

sections.key: Claims need evidence, and the burden of proof sits with whoever makes the claim.
sections.b: Confidence, repetition and volume feel persuasive but prove nothing. The person making a claim carries the burden of supporting it. Not all evidence is equal: a single anecdote is weaker than a large study, and a single study is weaker than a consistent body of research. Ask 'how do you know?' about your own beliefs as much as other people's. It also helps to agree on what evidence would count before you start. If neither of you can name anything that would change your mind, you're not arguing about facts, you're arguing about values or identity.

sections.key: Conceding good points builds credibility and makes the other person more willing to concede too.
sections.b: Many people fear that admitting any point weakens their case. Usually the opposite is true. Saying 'you're right about the cost, that's a real problem' shows you're being fair, which makes your other points more credible. It also invites reciprocity: people tend to return concessions, just as they return favours. Distinguish between the core of your view and its details. You can give ground on details, or admit uncertainty, without abandoning your main point. Arguments that never concede anything tend to harden into standoffs where nobody moves.

sections.key: Changing your mind in response to good evidence is a strength, and it usually happens gradually.
sections.b: Research published around 2010 suggested a 'backfire effect', where correcting people's false beliefs made them believe more strongly. Later, larger studies found this is rare: most people do shift, at least a little, when shown good evidence. Psychologist Philip Tetlock's research on forecasting found the most accurate predictors update their beliefs frequently in small steps, rather than lurching or refusing to budge. Try thinking in degrees of confidence rather than all or nothing: 'I'm now 60% sure instead of 90%' is a real and honest change of mind.

sections.key: Stay curious, ask questions, check understanding, and know when to pause an argument.
sections.b: Next time a disagreement starts, try a few habits. Ask questions before making statements: 'What makes you think that?' Summarise their view and check you've got it right. Look for the specific point where you actually disagree, as it's often narrower than it first seemed. Concede what's fair. Keep your tone about the idea. And recognise when emotions are too high for good thinking: 'Let's pick this up tomorrow' is not surrender. Online arguments with strangers rarely change minds; a calm, private conversation with someone who trusts you often does.

quiz.q: What is a steelman?
o: A weak caricature of an opposing view
The strongest version of the other side's argument
An insult disguised as a question
quiz.e: It's the opposite of a strawman.

quiz.q: Under Rapoport's rules, what should you do before criticising a view?
o: Restate it fairly, note agreements and say what you learned
Find a flaw in the speaker's character
quiz.e: Criticism comes last.

quiz.q: What is the ad hominem fallacy?
o: Attacking the person instead of the argument
quiz.e: It dismisses an argument because of who made it.

quiz.q: Who carries the burden of proof?
quiz.e: Claims need support from the person making them.

quiz.q: What did later research find about the 'backfire effect'?
o: It is rare; most people shift a little with good evidence
It was proven in every country
quiz.e: Larger studies found corrections usually work at least somewhat.

LESSONS.title: Body language: fact and fiction
LESSONS.hook: Crossed arms mean defensive, looking away means lying, and 93% of communication is non-verbal. Most of that is wrong.

sections.key: The claim that 93% of communication is non-verbal misreads narrow 1960s experiments.
sections.b: You may have heard that only 7% of communication is words, with 38% tone of voice and 55% body language. This comes from experiments by psychologist Albert Mehrabian in 1967. But his studies were narrow: listeners heard single words and judged whether the speaker liked or disliked them, when the words and tone clashed. Mehrabian has said his findings don't apply to communication in general. If 93% of meaning were non-verbal, you could follow a foreign-language film without subtitles. Body language matters, but words carry most of the content.

sections.h: What body language can tell you
sections.key: Body language gives useful clues about emotion and engagement, but only in context.
sections.b: Non-verbal signals do carry real information. A slumped posture, a tight jaw, a sudden stillness or a warm genuine smile can all hint at how someone feels. But a single signal is ambiguous. Crossed arms might mean defensiveness, or that the room is cold, or that it's comfortable. Experts suggest reading clusters of signals rather than one, and comparing them with the person's normal baseline. A usually chatty colleague going quiet tells you more than a naturally reserved person being quiet. Context always comes first.

sections.key: Studies show people detect lies at only about 54% accuracy, barely better than chance.
sections.b: A 2006 review of over 200 studies by Charles Bond and Bella DePaulo found people correctly identify lies and truths only about 54% of the time, only slightly better than tossing a coin. Police officers and other professionals generally do little better. The problem is that there's no reliable 'Pinocchio's nose'. Nervousness, fidgeting and hesitation show up in anxious truth-tellers too, and practised liars can appear calm. Researchers have found that focusing on the content of what someone says, such as consistency and checkable detail, works better than watching their body.

sections.key: The belief that liars avoid eye contact is common worldwide but not supported by evidence.
sections.b: A large international survey published in 2006 found that the belief 'liars avoid eye contact' was the most common lie-detection belief across dozens of countries. Yet studies find gaze aversion is not a reliable sign of lying. Some liars even hold more eye contact, knowing people watch for it. Popular claims that looking up and to one side reveals a lie, drawn from neuro-linguistic programming, have also been tested and not supported. Someone looking away may be thinking, shy, or following cultural norms. Judging honesty by eyes alone risks accusing the innocent.

sections.key: Early claims that 'power poses' change hormones failed to replicate; any effect on feelings appears small.
sections.b: In 2010, researchers Dana Carney, Amy Cuddy and Andy Yap reported that holding expansive 'power poses' for two minutes raised testosterone, lowered cortisol and increased risk-taking. Cuddy's 2012 TED talk on it became one of the most-watched ever. But a larger 2015 study failed to find the hormone or behaviour effects, and in 2016 Carney said she no longer believed the effects were real. Researchers still debate whether posture has small effects on how powerful people say they feel. Standing tall won't hurt you, but it's not a proven hormonal hack.

sections.key: Comfortable eye contact varies by person and culture; many Aboriginal communities see less direct eye contact as respectful.
sections.b: In many Western settings, moderate eye contact signals attention and confidence, while staring feels aggressive. One 2016 study found people's preferred length of mutual gaze averaged roughly three seconds, with wide individual differences. Culture matters a great deal. In many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities, avoiding direct eye contact, particularly with elders, can be a sign of respect rather than evasion. Similar norms exist in parts of Asia. Misreading this has caused real harm in settings like classrooms, job interviews and courtrooms, so avoid treating eye contact as a universal measure of honesty.

sections.key: Open, relaxed posture tends to signal approachability, while mirroring can reflect rapport.
sections.b: Some body language findings are more solid. People generally perceive an open posture, uncrossed arms, facing the person, relaxed shoulders, as warmer and more approachable. Nodding and leaning in signal that you're listening. When people get along, they often unconsciously mirror each other's posture and gestures. Deliberately copying someone can backfire if it's noticed, though. The most useful approach is not to perform a set of 'correct' gestures but to reduce distractions: put the phone away, face the person and let genuine attention show naturally.

sections.key: Treat body language as a question to ask, not an answer; never judge honesty from gestures alone.
sections.b: The practical lesson is humility. Body language offers hints, not verdicts. If you notice a change, like a friend going quiet or a client's arms folding, treat it as a prompt to check in: 'You seem unsure, what's on your mind?' That's better than silently deciding what they think. In high-stakes situations, like hiring, be wary of confident claims about reading people, as they can lead to bias. For your own presence, focus on being genuinely engaged. Authentic attention tends to show in your body without choreography.

quiz.q: What did Mehrabian's 1960s experiments actually study?
o: Judgements of liking from single words when words and tone clashed
quiz.e: He has said his findings don't apply to communication in general.

quiz.q: Roughly how accurately do people detect lies, according to a large review?
quiz.e: Only slightly better than chance.

quiz.q: Is avoiding eye contact a reliable sign of lying?
o: No, the evidence doesn't support it
quiz.e: Gaze aversion can reflect thinking, shyness or culture.

quiz.q: What happened when researchers tried to replicate the power posing hormone effects?
o: A larger study failed to find them
The effects were found only in athletes
quiz.e: One of the original authors later said she no longer believed them.

quiz.q: In many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities, less direct eye contact can signal what?
quiz.e: Eye contact norms vary widely by culture.

LESSONS.title: Renting in Australia
LESSONS.hook: About a third of Australian households rent. Knowing a few rules can save you hundreds of dollars and a lot of stress.

sections.key: Tenancy law is set by each state and territory, so the details depend on where you live.
sections.b: Roughly a third of Australian households rent their home. There's no single national tenancy law: each state and territory has its own act, rules and agencies, and they're updated regularly. The broad principles are similar, but notice periods, bond limits and repair rules differ. Your first move as a renter is to bookmark your local body: NSW Fair Trading, Consumer Affairs Victoria, the Residential Tenancies Authority in Queensland, Consumer and Business Services in South Australia, or Consumer Protection in Western Australia, for example. Tasmania, the ACT and the NT have their own equivalents.

sections.key: Strong applications include ID, proof of income, references and rental history; be wary of paying to apply.
sections.b: In a competitive market, a complete application stands out. Agents typically ask for photo ID, recent payslips or bank statements showing income, references from previous landlords or employers, and a rental ledger showing you paid rent on time. First-time renters can offer character references or a guarantor. Be cautious with your documents: send them through reputable platforms, and be alert to rental scams asking for money before you've inspected. Several states now ban agents from asking you to bid above the advertised rent, so check your state's current rules on bidding and fees.

sections.key: The bond is usually capped at around four weeks' rent and in most places must be lodged with a government bond authority.
sections.b: A bond is a security deposit that covers unpaid rent or damage at the end of your lease. It's commonly capped at about four weeks' rent, with some exceptions for high-rent properties. In most states and territories, the landlord or agent must lodge your bond with a government body, such as the Rental Bonds service in NSW or the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority in Victoria, within a set time. You should receive confirmation. The landlord can't simply keep it: at the end, it's returned unless both parties agree otherwise or a tribunal decides.

sections.key: The condition report records the property's state at move-in and is your best protection when claiming back your bond.
sections.b: At the start of a tenancy, the landlord or agent should give you a condition report describing each room. Don't sign it blindly. Walk through carefully, note every mark, stain, chip and fault, and return it with your comments within the deadline, which is usually a few days. Take dated photos or video too, and keep copies. At the end of the lease, the property is compared against this report. Without good records, a scratch that was already there can become a deduction from your bond.

sections.key: Tenants have rights to privacy and a safe home, and must pay rent on time and look after the property.
sections.b: As a tenant, you're entitled to quiet enjoyment, meaning reasonable peace and privacy. Landlords generally must give written notice before entering, and only for set reasons like inspections or repairs. In every state and the ACT, rent can now only be increased once every 12 months (the NT allows six), with written notice of about two months. Your responsibilities include paying rent on time, keeping the property reasonably clean, reporting damage promptly and not causing damage beyond fair wear and tear. Fair wear and tear, like faded curtains or worn carpet from normal use, isn't your cost.

sections.key: Several states now set minimum standards every rental must meet, and a tribunal can order repairs.
sections.b: Landlords must keep the property in reasonable repair, and several states now spell out minimum standards a rental must meet before anyone moves in. Depending on the state, these include being structurally sound and weatherproof, working locks on external doors, adequate lighting and ventilation, a working kitchen and bathroom, and privacy coverings on bedroom windows. New South Wales, Victoria and Queensland brought in standards like these between 2020 and 2024, and the ACT now requires ceiling insulation. If the landlord can't be reached in an emergency, tenants in most states can arrange urgent repairs themselves up to a set dollar limit and claim the cost back. Generally, don't stop paying rent over repairs: apply to your state's tribunal instead.

sections.key: Give proper written notice, expect a break fee if you leave a fixed term early, and attend the final inspection.
sections.b: A fixed-term lease runs for a set period, often 6 or 12 months; a periodic lease rolls on with no end date. To leave, you must give written notice, with required periods varying by state. Leaving a fixed-term lease early usually means paying a break fee or covering rent until a new tenant is found, depending on your state. Landlords must also give proper notice and, in several states, can no longer end leases without a valid reason. Before you go, clean thoroughly, compare the property with the condition report and attend the final inspection.

sections.key: Free tenant advice services and state tribunals exist to help resolve disputes; this lesson is general information only.
sections.b: Most disputes can be solved by calm, written communication. If that fails, each state has a tribunal that hears tenancy disputes cheaply, such as NCAT in NSW, VCAT in Victoria or QCAT in Queensland. Free advice is available from tenant services like Tenants' Union of NSW, Tenants Victoria and Tenants Queensland. Keep every email, receipt and photo; records win disputes. Tenancy laws change often, so check your state's official website for current rules. This lesson is general information only: for your specific situation, talk to a tenant advice service or a lawyer.

quiz.q: Who sets most tenancy rules in Australia?
quiz.e: Each state and territory has its own tenancy law.

quiz.q: In most states, where must a rental bond be lodged?
o: It is paid in cash to the agent
quiz.e: Landlords can't simply keep your bond.

quiz.q: Why is the condition report so important?
o: It records the property's state at move-in, protecting your bond
quiz.e: Note every mark and take dated photos.

quiz.q: Worn carpet from normal use is an example of what?
quiz.e: Fair wear and tear isn't the tenant's cost.

quiz.q: What should you generally do if a landlord won't fix repairs?
o: Fix everything and deduct it from rent
quiz.e: Withholding rent can put you in breach.

LESSONS.title: Dinosaurs: rulers of the Mesozoic
LESSONS.hook: They dominated the land for over 150 million years, left giant footprints in outback Queensland, and one branch of the family still visits your backyard.

sections.key: Dinosaurs are a specific group of land reptiles with legs held straight under the body; flying and swimming reptiles of the time were not dinosaurs.
sections.b: The word dinosaur, meaning 'terrible lizard', was coined by British anatomist Richard Owen in 1842. Scientifically, dinosaurs are a particular family of reptiles that walked with their legs held straight beneath the body, rather than sprawled out to the side like a lizard or crocodile. That rules out many famous prehistoric animals. Pterosaurs, the flying reptiles, were close cousins but not dinosaurs. Neither were the great marine reptiles such as plesiosaurs, ichthyosaurs and mosasaurs. And the sail-backed Dimetrodon, often sold in dinosaur toy sets, lived before the first dinosaurs and was actually closer to the ancestors of mammals.

sections.key: The age of dinosaurs, the Mesozoic Era, is split into the Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous periods, ending 66 million years ago.
sections.b: Dinosaurs lived through the Mesozoic Era, which geologists divide into three periods. The Triassic ran from about 252 to 201 million years ago; the first dinosaurs appeared around 230 million years ago, small and fast, in what is now Argentina and Brazil. The Jurassic, about 201 to 145 million years ago, brought giant long-necked sauropods and Stegosaurus. The Cretaceous, about 145 to 66 million years ago, saw flowering plants spread and gave us Tyrannosaurus and Triceratops. The time spans are staggering: T. rex lived closer in time to us than to Stegosaurus.

sections.key: Dinosaurs are traditionally split into 'lizard-hipped' saurischians and 'bird-hipped' ornithischians.
sections.b: Since the 1880s, scientists have sorted dinosaurs into two great branches based on the shape of their hip bones. The saurischians, or 'lizard-hipped' dinosaurs, include the meat-eating theropods, such as Tyrannosaurus and Velociraptor, and the huge plant-eating sauropods, such as Brachiosaurus. The ornithischians, or 'bird-hipped' dinosaurs, were plant-eaters, including Triceratops, Stegosaurus, armoured ankylosaurs and duck-billed hadrosaurs. Confusingly, birds evolved from the lizard-hipped branch, not the bird-hipped one. Some researchers have proposed rearranging this family tree, and the debate continues, but the two-branch system is still the one you'll find in most museums.

sections.key: T. rex reached about 12 metres long, the biggest sauropods perhaps 30 metres or more, but Velociraptor was only turkey-sized.
sections.b: Tyrannosaurus rex lived about 68 to 66 million years ago in western North America. Adults reached around 12 metres long and perhaps 8 tonnes, with one of the most powerful bites of any land animal. The largest sauropods, such as Argentinosaurus from South America, may have been 30 metres or more long and weighed 60 tonnes or more, though estimates from incomplete skeletons vary. Films have distorted some species: the real Velociraptor, from Mongolia, was roughly the size of a turkey and covered in feathers. Scientists have now named more than 1,000 non-bird dinosaur species, with dozens more described every year.

sections.key: Birds evolved from small feathered theropod dinosaurs, so scientists classify them as living dinosaurs.
sections.b: In 1861, quarry workers in Germany found Archaeopteryx, a roughly 150-million-year-old animal with feathered wings but also teeth, clawed fingers and a long bony tail. It hinted at a link between dinosaurs and birds. Since the 1990s, discoveries in north-eastern China have revealed dozens of feathered dinosaurs, many of which could not fly. Birds share features such as wishbones, hollow bones and similar egg-brooding behaviour with theropods like Velociraptor. Today scientists agree that birds are a branch of the dinosaur family tree. That makes the magpie on your fence, and the emu and cassowary, living dinosaurs.

sections.key: Central-west Queensland, especially around Winton, is Australia's richest dinosaur region, home to giant sauropods and the predator Australovenator.
sections.b: Australia's dinosaur fossils are rarer than those of North America, but the country has had a remarkable run of discoveries. Around Winton, in central-west Queensland, rocks roughly 95 million years old have yielded the long-necked sauropods Diamantinasaurus and Savannasaurus, and the agile predator Australovenator, nicknamed 'Banjo'. The Australian Age of Dinosaurs museum near Winton prepares many of these fossils. In 2021, scientists described Australotitan cooperensis, 'the southern titan', from near Eromanga in south-west Queensland. Estimated at 25 to 30 metres long, it is among the largest dinosaurs found in Australia. Queensland is also home to Muttaburrasaurus and the armoured Kunbarrasaurus.

sections.key: Lark Quarry preserves thousands of dinosaur footprints, and Victorian fossils show dinosaurs lived near the South Pole.
sections.b: At Lark Quarry, south-west of Winton, more than 3,000 small dinosaur footprints are preserved in rock around 95 million years old. They were long interpreted as a 'stampede' fleeing a large predator, though some researchers now argue the tracks were made by dinosaurs wading or swimming in shallow water, and the debate continues. In southern Victoria, sites such as Dinosaur Cove have yielded small dinosaurs like Leaellynasaura. About 110 million years ago, Australia sat much further south, joined to Antarctica, inside the polar circle. These dinosaurs coped with months of winter darkness, which tells us they were adaptable animals.

sections.key: Dinosaurs didn't live alongside humans, weren't all giants, and weren't slow, cold, swamp-bound failures.
sections.b: Popular culture gets a lot wrong. Humans and non-bird dinosaurs never met: the last of them died about 66 million years before our species appeared. Most dinosaurs were not giants; many were dog-sized or smaller. The old image of sluggish, cold-blooded creatures dragging their tails has been replaced by active, fast-growing animals, many with feathers, and their metabolism is still an active research question. Nor were they evolutionary failures: dinosaurs thrived for more than 150 million years and, through birds, are still here. Next time you visit a museum, look for feathers, posture and scale, and you'll see how far the science has moved.

quiz.q: Which of these was a true dinosaur?
quiz.e: Pterosaurs, plesiosaurs and Dimetrodon were ancient reptiles or relatives, but not dinosaurs.

quiz.q: Why is it said T. rex lived closer in time to us than to Stegosaurus?
o: Stegosaurus lived about 150 million years ago, T. rex about 66 million
They lived in the same period
T. rex lived in the Triassic
quiz.e: Around 80 million years separate Stegosaurus and T. rex, more than the 66 million years since T. rex.

quiz.q: What was the real Velociraptor like?
quiz.e: The Mongolian Velociraptor was small and feathered, unlike its film version.

quiz.q: Why do scientists call birds living dinosaurs?
o: They evolved from feathered theropod dinosaurs
They have scales on their legs
quiz.e: Birds are a branch of the theropod dinosaur family tree.

quiz.q: What is Australotitan cooperensis?
o: A small feathered predator from Winton
A giant sauropod from south-west Queensland
quiz.e: Described in 2021, it was a giant long-necked sauropod estimated at 25 to 30 metres long.

LESSONS.title: The day the dinosaurs died
LESSONS.hook: Sixty-six million years ago, a rock about 10 kilometres wide slammed into Mexico. Within a short time, around three-quarters of species on Earth were gone.

sections.key: About 66 million years ago, the Cretaceous ended in a mass extinction that wiped out around three-quarters of species, including all non-bird dinosaurs.
sections.b: Geologists had long noticed a sharp line in the rock record at the end of the Cretaceous period, about 66 million years ago. Below it are fossils of dinosaurs, ammonites and marine reptiles; above it, they are gone. This is the Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary, once called the K–T boundary. Around three-quarters of plant and animal species disappeared, including every non-bird dinosaur, the flying pterosaurs, and the great sea reptiles such as mosasaurs and plesiosaurs. It is one of the 'Big Five' mass extinctions in Earth's history, and the most recent. For over a century, its cause was a genuine mystery.

sections.key: In 1980, the Alvarez team found the boundary layer was rich in iridium, an element rare in Earth's crust but common in asteroids.
sections.b: In 1980, physicist Luis Alvarez, his geologist son Walter, and chemists Frank Asaro and Helen Michel published a bold idea. Studying a thin clay layer at the boundary near Gubbio, Italy, they found unusually high levels of iridium, a metal very rare in Earth's crust but much more common in asteroids and meteorites. The same spike soon turned up at sites in Denmark, New Zealand and elsewhere around the world. Their conclusion: a huge asteroid, around 10 kilometres wide, had struck Earth, and its vaporised debris settled over the whole planet. Many geologists were sceptical. The missing piece was the crater.

sections.key: The Chicxulub crater, about 180 kilometres wide and buried under Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula, was confirmed as the impact site in the early 1990s.
sections.b: The crater had actually been glimpsed in the late 1970s by geophysicists working for Mexico's state oil company, who noticed a giant buried ring structure. In 1991, researchers linked it to the extinction. Named after the nearby town of Chicxulub, the crater is about 180 kilometres across, mostly hidden beneath younger rock and the sea floor of the Gulf of Mexico. Dating shows it formed right at the boundary. Supporting evidence piled up: 'shocked' quartz grains that form only under extreme pressure, tiny glassy spherules of melted rock, and jumbled tsunami deposits around the Gulf. In 2016, an expedition drilled into the crater's peak ring.

sections.key: The impact caused fires, tsunamis and an 'impact winter' as soot and sulfur blocked sunlight and collapsed food chains.
sections.b: The asteroid released energy far greater than all the world's nuclear weapons combined. Near the site came huge tsunamis and earthquakes. Molten debris thrown into space rained back down, and it likely heated the air enough to ignite widespread fires. The biggest killer, though, was probably what followed. The target rocks were rich in sulfur, and the blast lofted sulfur aerosols, soot and dust high into the atmosphere. This blocked sunlight, cooled the planet sharply for years and shut down much of photosynthesis on land and in the oceans. When plants and plankton failed, the food chains built on them collapsed from the bottom up.

sections.key: Massive volcanic eruptions in India, the Deccan Traps, happened around the same time; scientists still debate how much they contributed.
sections.b: The asteroid is not the only suspect. Around the same time, enormous volcanic eruptions in India were pouring out lava that built the Deccan Traps, layers of rock more than a kilometre thick in places. Over hundreds of thousands of years, these eruptions released vast amounts of carbon dioxide and sulfur gases, which could have disrupted the climate. Some scientists argue the volcanoes were already stressing ecosystems before the impact, or even played a leading role. Others think the timing of the main eruptions doesn't fit. Most researchers today see the asteroid as the main trigger, but the exact role of the Deccan Traps remains genuinely contested.

sections.key: Survivors were mostly small animals that could shelter, eat varied food and live on detritus; no large land animals made it.
sections.b: Survival was not random. On land, nothing much bigger than about 25 kilograms is thought to have made it through. Small animals needed less food, bred quickly and could shelter in burrows or water. Freshwater creatures such as crocodiles, turtles and frogs fared relatively well, likely because their food webs relied on dead plant matter rather than fresh growth. Many mammals were small, burrowing, generalist eaters. Some birds survived too; one study suggested ground-dwelling birds did better than tree-dwellers because forests were devastated. In the oceans, the coiled-shell ammonites vanished, while sharks and many fish survived.

sections.key: With dinosaurs gone, mammals diversified rapidly, eventually leading to whales, horses, primates and us.
sections.b: Mammals had lived alongside dinosaurs for well over 100 million years, mostly as small, often nocturnal animals. With the large dinosaurs gone, they spread into empty roles. Within about 10 million years, mammals had evolved into many new forms, from early horses and primates to the ancestors of whales, which returned to the sea. Birds diversified dramatically too, becoming the only dinosaurs left. Flowering plants recovered and spread. Without that asteroid, it's quite possible that large dinosaurs would still dominate, and that mammals, including the primates that eventually led to humans, would have stayed small. Our existence owes something to a very bad day.

sections.key: Large asteroid impacts are extremely rare, and in 2022 NASA's DART mission showed we can nudge an asteroid's orbit.
sections.b: Asteroids of Chicxulub's size are thought to hit Earth roughly once every 100 million years or so, so the risk in any lifetime is tiny. Astronomers have found the great majority of near-Earth asteroids larger than a kilometre, and none are known to be on a collision course. Smaller objects are more common: the 2013 Chelyabinsk meteor in Russia injured over 1,000 people, mostly from shattered glass. In 2022, NASA's DART spacecraft deliberately crashed into a small asteroid called Dimorphos and shortened its orbit around a larger companion by about 32 minutes. For the first time in Earth's history, a species has shown it can deflect an asteroid.

quiz.q: Why was iridium at the boundary layer such an important clue?
o: It is rare in Earth's crust but common in asteroids
It is found in dinosaur bones
It shows the climate was warm
quiz.e: High iridium levels worldwide pointed to an extraterrestrial source.

quiz.q: Where is the Chicxulub crater?
quiz.e: The roughly 180-kilometre crater lies buried under the Yucatán Peninsula and Gulf of Mexico.

quiz.q: What was probably the biggest killer after the impact?
o: Sunlight being blocked, collapsing food chains
quiz.e: Soot, sulfur and dust blocked sunlight and shut down photosynthesis.

quiz.q: What are the Deccan Traps?
o: Huge volcanic rock layers in India from eruptions around that time
quiz.e: Their eruptions released gases that may have added to the crisis; their role is still debated.

quiz.q: Which animals tended to survive the extinction?
o: Small animals, and freshwater species like crocodiles and turtles
quiz.e: Small size, sheltering and detritus-based food webs helped survivors get through.

LESSONS.title: Ice Age giants and Australia's megafauna
LESSONS.hook: Rhino-sized wombat relatives, a marsupial 'lion' and a goanna the length of a car once roamed Australia. So where did they all go?

sections.key: Megafauna are large animals, often defined as over about 45 kilograms; the term usually refers to giants of the last Ice Age.
sections.b: Megafauna simply means 'big animals'. Scientists often use a cut-off of about 45 kilograms, though definitions vary. When people talk about 'the megafauna', they usually mean the giant mammals, birds and reptiles of the Pleistocene epoch, the period of repeated ice ages that ran from about 2.6 million to roughly 11,700 years ago. During this time every inhabited continent had a far richer cast of large animals than today. Over the last 50,000 years or so, a large share of them disappeared. Unlike the dinosaurs, these animals lived alongside humans, which makes their fate one of science's most interesting and debated questions.

sections.key: Woolly mammoths, woolly rhinos, cave bears, giant deer and sabre-toothed cats roamed the Northern Hemisphere.
sections.b: Across Europe, Asia and North America, the cold grasslands of the Ice Age supported woolly mammoths, woolly rhinoceroses and cave bears. The giant deer Megaloceros, sometimes called the Irish elk, carried antlers spanning up to about 3.5 metres. Sabre-toothed cats such as Smilodon hunted in the Americas. Early humans painted many of these animals on cave walls, as at Chauvet and Lascaux in France. Most mainland mammoths had died out by about 10,000 years ago, but a small population survived on Wrangel Island, off Siberia, until around 4,000 years ago, when the pyramids of Egypt were already standing.

sections.key: South America had elephant-sized ground sloths, while New Zealand's giant moa survived until a few hundred years after people arrived.
sections.b: South America had its own giants: ground sloths such as Megatherium, which could be as big as an elephant, and glyptodonts, armadillo relatives with domed shells the size of a small car. On islands, the story came much later. In New Zealand, the flightless moa, some species standing well over 2 metres tall with neck stretched, were hunted by Haast's eagle, the largest eagle known. Moa became extinct within roughly 200 years of Polynesian settlement, which began around 1300 AD. Madagascar lost its giant elephant birds, possibly the heaviest birds ever, after human arrival too. Island extinctions often closely follow the arrival of people.

sections.key: Diprotodon, a wombat relative about the size of a rhinoceros, was the largest marsupial that ever lived.
sections.b: Australia's megafauna were uniquely strange, dominated by giant marsupials. Diprotodon optatum, a distant relative of wombats, was the largest marsupial ever, roughly the size of a rhinoceros and weighing up to around 2.7 tonnes. Its fossils are found across much of the continent, and dozens of skeletons were recovered from the dry bed of Lake Callabonna in South Australia, where animals likely became trapped in mud. Other giants included Procoptodon goliah, a short-faced kangaroo around 2 metres tall that probably browsed on leaves, and the heavy, wombat-like Zygomaturus. There were also giant echidnas and a large horned land turtle, Ninjemys.

sections.key: Thylacoleo, the 'marsupial lion', had one of the strongest bites for its size of any mammal; Megalania was a giant goanna.
sections.b: Thylacoleo carnifex, the 'marsupial lion', was not a cat at all but a relative of wombats and koalas that became a formidable predator. Weighing roughly 100 kilograms or more, it had blade-like cheek teeth for slicing meat, a large hooked thumb claw, and is often described as having one of the most powerful bites relative to body size of any known mammal. Megalania, now usually called Varanus priscus, was a giant goanna, related to today's perentie and lace monitor. Size estimates vary a lot because skeletons are incomplete, but it may have reached around 4 to 7 metres long, making it among the largest land lizards known.

sections.key: Genyornis was a heavy, flightless bird around 2 metres tall, more closely related to ducks and geese than to emus.
sections.b: Genyornis newtoni was a massive flightless bird that stood about 2 metres tall and weighed perhaps 200 kilograms or more, far heavier than an emu. Despite appearances, it belonged to an extinct group called dromornithids, or mihirungs, whose closest living relatives are ducks and geese, not emus. Its relatives, sometimes nicknamed 'thunder birds', had lived in Australia for millions of years. Scientists have argued over burnt eggshell fragments, around 50,000 years old, that seemed to show early people cooking Genyornis eggs; a 2016 study proposed they came from a giant megapode instead, but a 2022 analysis of ancient proteins in the shells confirmed they belonged to Genyornis. It's a good example of how carefully evidence has to be read in this field.

sections.key: Scientists still debate whether humans, climate change, or a combination caused megafauna extinctions; the answer may differ by region.
sections.b: Most of Australia's megafauna appear to have disappeared by roughly 40,000 years ago, some time after people arrived on the continent, at least 50,000 years ago and possibly earlier. One view holds that human hunting, even at low levels, was enough to tip slow-breeding giants into decline, and that burning changed habitats. Another view points to climate: Australia was becoming drier and more variable. Many researchers now favour a combination, with emphasis differing by species and place. Dating fossils this old is difficult, which keeps the debate alive. Globally, the pattern is striking: big extinctions often follow human arrival, while Africa, where people evolved, kept more of its megafauna.

sections.key: Naracoorte Caves and Riversleigh together form a World Heritage-listed fossil site, and major museums display megafauna skeletons.
sections.b: You can see Australia's megafauna up close. The Naracoorte Caves in South Australia and the Riversleigh fossil fields in north-west Queensland were jointly World Heritage-listed in 1994 as the Australian Fossil Mammal Sites. At Naracoorte, animals fell through openings into the caves over hundreds of thousands of years, preserving an extraordinary record, and a reconstructed Thylacoleo stands among the fossils. State museums in Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane and Adelaide display Diprotodon skeletons and casts. The megafauna story also carries a lesson for today: large, slow-breeding animals are especially vulnerable to rapid change, whether from hunting, habitat loss or a shifting climate.

quiz.q: What was Diprotodon?
