quiz.e: Diprotodon was the largest marsupial ever, a distant relative of wombats.

quiz.q: Thylacoleo, the 'marsupial lion', was most closely related to which animals?
quiz.e: Despite its name, it was a vombatiform marsupial, like wombats and koalas.

quiz.q: Genyornis's closest living relatives are thought to be:
quiz.e: Genyornis was a dromornithid, a group related to ducks and geese.

quiz.q: What is the current scientific view on why Australia's megafauna disappeared?
o: Still debated: humans, climate or a combination
quiz.e: Many researchers favour a combination of human impacts and climate, and the debate continues.

quiz.q: What pattern appears on islands like New Zealand and Madagascar?
o: Giants survived longest where people lived longest
Large animals disappeared soon after humans arrived
Extinctions happened only during ice ages
quiz.e: Moa and elephant birds vanished soon after human settlement.

LESSONS.title: A tour of the solar system
LESSONS.hook: One star, eight planets, five recognised dwarf planets and countless icy leftovers, all born from a collapsing cloud 4.6 billion years ago.

sections.key: The solar system formed about 4.6 billion years ago when a cloud of gas and dust collapsed into the Sun and a spinning disc that built the planets.
sections.b: About 4.6 billion years ago, part of a giant cloud of gas and dust began to collapse under its own gravity. Most of the material fell to the centre and became hot and dense enough to start nuclear fusion: the Sun was born. The rest flattened into a spinning disc around it. Within that disc, dust grains stuck together into pebbles, then boulders, then bodies kilometres across, which collided and merged into planets. This is why the planets all orbit in roughly the same flat plane and the same direction. The Sun still holds about 99.8% of all the mass in the solar system.

sections.key: Near the Sun only rock and metal could condense, making small rocky planets; further out, ice let giant planets grow.
sections.b: The solar system has a clear pattern. The four inner planets, Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars, are small and rocky. The four outer planets are giants. The reason is temperature. Close to the young Sun, it was too hot for water and other ices to freeze, so only rock and metal could clump together, and there wasn't much of it. Beyond a boundary called the frost line, ice was plentiful, so planetary cores grew big enough to pull in huge amounts of gas. Jupiter and Saturn became gas giants; Uranus and Neptune, richer in ices, are often called ice giants.

sections.key: Mercury is the smallest planet, Venus the hottest, and Mars hosts Olympus Mons, a volcano about two and a half times the height of Everest.
sections.b: Mercury, closest to the Sun, is the smallest planet, with almost no atmosphere, so temperatures swing from about 430°C by day to around minus 180°C at night. Venus is actually hotter, at about 465°C, because its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat in a runaway greenhouse effect. It also spins backwards and so slowly that its day is longer than its year. Earth is the only world known to host life. Mars is a cold desert with ancient river valleys, evidence of past liquid water, and Olympus Mons, a volcano roughly 22 kilometres high, about two and a half times the height of Everest.

sections.key: Jupiter is more than twice as massive as all other planets combined; Saturn is less dense than water; Uranus rolls on its side.
sections.b: Jupiter is more than twice as massive as all the other planets put together. Its Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth that has raged for centuries. Saturn is famous for its rings, made mostly of chunks of water ice, and is so low in density that it would float in a big enough bathtub. Uranus is tipped over by about 98 degrees, so it effectively rolls around the Sun on its side, probably because of an ancient collision. Neptune, the farthest planet, has the fastest winds measured in the solar system, around 2,000 km/h. Saturn has well over 200 known moons and Jupiter nearly 100, with counts still rising.

sections.key: Shrink the Sun to the size of a door and Earth becomes a 5-cent coin about 215 metres away; Neptune is over 6 kilometres off.
sections.b: Space diagrams mislead because they can't show true distances. Earth is about 150 million kilometres from the Sun, a distance called an astronomical unit, and sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach us. Imagine shrinking the Sun to the height of a front door. Earth would be about the size of a 5-cent coin, roughly 215 metres away. Jupiter would be about a kilometre away, and Neptune over 6 kilometres. Voyager 1, launched in 1977 and the most distant human-made object, is now more than 160 times Earth's distance from the Sun. Canberra's Deep Space Communication Complex is the only station able to command its twin, Voyager 2.

sections.key: The asteroid belt lies between Mars and Jupiter; the icy Kuiper Belt lies beyond Neptune, with comets coming from even further out.
sections.b: Not everything became a planet. Between Mars and Jupiter lies the asteroid belt, millions of rocky bodies whose combined mass is only a few per cent of our Moon's. Jupiter's gravity likely stopped them from forming a planet. Despite science fiction, the belt is mostly empty space, and spacecraft cross it without trouble. Its largest member, Ceres, is a dwarf planet. Beyond Neptune, from about 30 to 50 times Earth's distance from the Sun, lies the Kuiper Belt, a vast ring of icy bodies including Pluto. Much further out, astronomers think a huge, spherical Oort Cloud supplies long-period comets, though it has never been directly observed.

sections.key: In 2006 the International Astronomical Union defined 'planet', and Pluto became a dwarf planet because it hasn't cleared its orbital neighbourhood.
sections.b: Pluto was discovered in 1930 by Clyde Tombaugh and named at the suggestion of an 11-year-old English schoolgirl, Venetia Burney. For decades it was the ninth planet. But from the 1990s astronomers found many similar icy bodies in the Kuiper Belt, and in 2005 they found Eris, roughly Pluto's size but more massive. Either there would be dozens of planets, or a definition was needed. In 2006 the International Astronomical Union ruled that a planet must orbit the Sun, be massive enough to be nearly round, and have cleared its orbital neighbourhood. Pluto fails the third test, so it became a dwarf planet. Some scientists still disagree.

sections.key: Five planets are visible to the naked eye: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn.
sections.b: You don't need a telescope to start exploring. Five planets are visible to the naked eye: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn. Venus is often the brightest point in the sky after the Moon, appearing as the 'evening star' after sunset or the 'morning star' before dawn. Planets usually shine steadily, while stars twinkle, and they all travel along roughly the same path the Sun and Moon follow. Even ordinary binoculars reveal Jupiter's four largest moons, first seen by Galileo in 1610. A free stargazing app will show which planets are up tonight from anywhere in Australia, and dark country skies make the view far better.

quiz.q: Why are the inner planets rocky and the outer ones giants?
o: Beyond the frost line ice was plentiful, letting large cores grow and gather gas
The Sun pushed gas outwards after the planets formed
The inner planets lost their rings
quiz.e: Cold outer regions had abundant ice, so cores grew big enough to capture gas.

quiz.q: Which is the hottest planet?
quiz.e: Venus's thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat, reaching about 465°C.

quiz.q: Which planet is so low in density it would float in water?
quiz.e: Saturn's average density is lower than that of water.

quiz.q: If the Sun were shrunk to the height of a front door, what would Earth be?
o: A grain of sand 20 kilometres away
quiz.e: Neptune would be over 6 kilometres away; the solar system is mostly empty space.

quiz.q: Why was Pluto reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006?
o: It hasn't cleared its orbital neighbourhood
It was found to be a moon of Neptune
quiz.e: Pluto shares its region of the Kuiper Belt with many other icy bodies.

LESSONS.title: Galaxies and the Milky Way
LESSONS.hook: On a dark night in outback Australia you can see our own galaxy's glowing core overhead, and two other galaxies with the naked eye.

sections.key: The Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy about 100,000 light-years across, with perhaps 100 to 400 billion stars.
sections.b: The Milky Way is our home galaxy, a vast system of stars, gas, dust and dark matter held together by gravity. It's a barred spiral: a central bar-shaped bulge of stars surrounded by a flat disc with spiral arms, all wrapped in a faint halo of old stars and globular star clusters. It is roughly 100,000 light-years across, meaning light takes about 100,000 years to cross it, and holds somewhere around 100 to 400 billion stars. The name comes from its appearance as a milky band across the sky; our word galaxy comes from the Greek for milk. In 1610 Galileo's telescope showed that band was made of countless stars.

sections.key: The Sun sits about 26,000 light-years from the centre and takes around 230 million years to orbit once.
sections.b: The Sun lies in a minor spiral arm, the Orion Arm, about 26,000 light-years from the galactic centre, roughly halfway out. We orbit the centre at about 800,000 km/h, yet a single lap takes around 230 million years, sometimes called a galactic year. Last time the Sun was in this spot, the earliest dinosaurs were only just appearing. At the very centre sits a supermassive black hole, Sagittarius A*, about 4 million times the mass of the Sun. In 2022 the Event Horizon Telescope collaboration released the first image of its glowing surroundings. Because we're inside the disc, we see the Milky Way edge-on, as a band.

sections.key: From Australia, the bright galactic centre passes high overhead on winter nights, and the dark dust clouds form the Emu in the Sky.
sections.b: Australians have one of the best views of our galaxy on Earth. The brightest part, towards the galactic centre in the constellations Sagittarius and Scorpius, rides high overhead on winter evenings in the Southern Hemisphere. Many Aboriginal cultures have long traced figures in the dark dust lanes, not just the stars. A widely known example is the Emu in the Sky, whose head is the dark Coalsack nebula beside the Southern Cross, with its neck and body stretching along the Milky Way. For many groups, its changing position through the year has been linked with the emu breeding season. Stories and meanings differ between Nations.

sections.key: Galaxies are broadly classed as spirals, ellipticals, lenticulars and irregulars.
sections.b: In the 1920s, American astronomer Edwin Hubble sorted galaxies by shape, and his scheme is still broadly used. Spiral galaxies, like ours, have flat discs with spiral arms where new stars form, and many have a central bar. Elliptical galaxies are smooth, rounded or egg-shaped collections of mostly older stars, with little gas for new stars; the largest known galaxies are giant ellipticals. Lenticular galaxies sit in between, with a disc but no clear spiral arms. Irregular galaxies have no tidy shape, often because gravity from neighbours has pulled them around. Collisions between galaxies are common over cosmic time and can transform one type into another.

sections.key: The Large and Small Magellanic Clouds are neighbouring galaxies, easily seen from Australia but not from most of the Northern Hemisphere.
sections.b: Look south on a dark, moonless night in Australia and you may spot two faint, fuzzy patches that look like torn-off pieces of the Milky Way. They are the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, separate dwarf galaxies about 160,000 and 200,000 light-years away. They are named after Ferdinand Magellan, whose crew recorded them during their voyage of 1519 to 1522, but they were known for thousands of years before that by Aboriginal people and others in the south. In 1987 a star exploded in the Large Magellanic Cloud. Supernova 1987A was visible to the naked eye and was studied closely by observatories in Australia and elsewhere.

sections.key: Andromeda, about 2.5 million light-years away, is the largest galaxy in our Local Group and is moving towards us.
sections.b: Our galaxy belongs to the Local Group, a gathering of dozens of galaxies, most of them small dwarfs. The largest member is the Andromeda Galaxy, a spiral about 2.5 million light-years away, often cited as the most distant object easily visible to the naked eye. From Australia it sits low in the northern sky, best seen from the north of the country. Andromeda's true nature was settled in the 1920s, when Hubble measured its distance and proved it lay far beyond the Milky Way. It is approaching us at about 110 kilometres per second. A merger in several billion years was long predicted; a 2025 study suggested the odds are closer to 50–50.

sections.key: The Milky Way grew partly by swallowing smaller galaxies, and it is pulling one apart right now.
sections.b: Big galaxies grow by merging with smaller ones, and the Milky Way is no exception. In 1994 astronomers discovered the Sagittarius Dwarf Galaxy on the far side of our galaxy's centre, being stretched into long streams of stars by the Milky Way's gravity. In 2018, data from the European Space Agency's Gaia spacecraft revealed that a sizeable galaxy, nicknamed Gaia-Enceladus or the Gaia Sausage, crashed into ours roughly 8 to 11 billion years ago; many stars in our galaxy's outer halo came from it. Even in such collisions, stars almost never hit one another, because the gaps between them are so vast. Many astronomers suspect Omega Centauri, a star cluster easily seen from Australia, is the leftover core of another swallowed galaxy.

sections.key: Galaxies spin too fast for their visible matter, suggesting invisible dark matter makes up about 85% of all matter.
sections.b: In the 1970s, American astronomer Vera Rubin and colleagues measured how fast stars orbit in spiral galaxies. Stars far from the centre moved just as fast as those closer in, far faster than the visible matter's gravity could hold. Something unseen was adding gravity. Astronomers call it dark matter, and it seems to make up about 85% of all matter in the universe, forming huge halos around galaxies. Nobody yet knows what it is, and a minority of physicists explore modified gravity instead. To see the Milky Way yourself, visit a dark site such as Warrumbungle National Park, Australia's first Dark Sky Park, and let your eyes adjust for 20 minutes.

quiz.q: What type of galaxy is the Milky Way?
quiz.e: It has a central bar-shaped bulge and spiral arms.

quiz.q: Roughly how long does the Sun take to orbit the galactic centre once?
quiz.e: This long orbit is sometimes called a galactic year.

quiz.q: The head of the Emu in the Sky is formed by:
o: The Coalsack, a dark dust cloud beside the Southern Cross
quiz.e: The Emu is traced in dark dust lanes, with its head at the Coalsack.

quiz.q: What are the Magellanic Clouds?
o: Gas clouds inside our solar system
Dwarf galaxies near the Milky Way, visible from the Southern Hemisphere
Weather features seen from the outback
quiz.e: They are separate dwarf galaxies about 160,000 and 200,000 light-years away.

quiz.q: What did Vera Rubin's measurements reveal that pointed to dark matter?
o: Stars in galaxies orbiting faster than visible matter can explain
Comets arriving from the Oort Cloud
quiz.e: Vera Rubin's rotation measurements showed galaxies needed extra, unseen mass.

LESSONS.title: Exoplanets: worlds beyond the Sun
LESSONS.hook: Thirty-odd years ago we knew of no planets around other stars like the Sun. Now we know of more than 6,000, and some might be able to hold liquid water.

sections.key: The first exoplanets were confirmed in the 1990s; the 1995 discovery of 51 Pegasi b around a Sun-like star won a Nobel Prize.
sections.b: An exoplanet is any planet orbiting a star other than the Sun. For centuries people wondered whether they existed, but they were too faint and too close to their bright stars to see. In 1992 astronomers confirmed planets orbiting a pulsar, the dead core of an exploded star. Then in 1995 Swiss astronomers Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz found 51 Pegasi b, a planet orbiting a Sun-like star, earning the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics. It was a surprise: a giant like Jupiter circling its star every four days. By 2025 the count of confirmed exoplanets passed 6,000, and it keeps climbing.

sections.key: When a planet passes in front of its star, the starlight dims slightly, revealing the planet's size and orbit.
sections.b: Most known exoplanets were found by the transit method. If a planet's orbit is lined up edge-on from our point of view, it passes in front of its star once each orbit, blocking a tiny fraction of the light. A Jupiter-sized planet dims a Sun-like star by about 1%; an Earth-sized one by only about one part in 10,000. Measuring how much the star dims reveals the planet's size, and the time between dips gives its orbit. The catch is that only planets with the right alignment transit, so for every one we catch, many more go unseen. Astronomers use statistics to account for them.

sections.key: A planet's gravity makes its star wobble, shifting its light slightly; this reveals the planet's mass.
sections.b: Planets don't simply orbit stars; both circle a shared centre of mass. A big planet makes its star wobble slightly, moving towards us and then away. That motion stretches and squeezes the star's light a tiny amount, the Doppler effect, which sensitive instruments called spectrographs can detect. This radial velocity, or wobble, method found 51 Pegasi b and hundreds of others. It gives an estimate of the planet's mass, so combining it with a transit reveals density: whether a world is rocky, watery or gassy. The Anglo-Australian Telescope at Siding Spring in New South Wales ran one of the longest-running wobble surveys. Direct imaging and microlensing find others.

sections.key: Kepler found thousands of planets, TESS surveys nearby bright stars, and JWST analyses exoplanet atmospheres.
sections.b: NASA's Kepler space telescope, launched in 2009, stared at one patch of sky containing about 150,000 stars, watching for transits. By the end of its mission in 2018 it had found more than 2,600 confirmed planets, and it showed that planets are common, likely outnumbering stars in our galaxy. Its successor, TESS, launched in 2018, scans most of the sky for planets around bright, nearby stars that are easier to study in detail. The James Webb Space Telescope, launched in 2021, can analyse starlight filtering through a planet's atmosphere. In 2022 it made a clear detection of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere of a hot giant called WASP-39b.

sections.key: The habitable zone is the range of distances from a star where liquid water could exist on a planet's surface; it doesn't guarantee life.
sections.b: Life as we know it needs liquid water, so astronomers look for planets in a star's habitable zone, sometimes called the Goldilocks zone: not too hot, not too cold for surface water to stay liquid. The zone's location depends on the star. Around a small, dim red dwarf, it sits very close in; around a bright star, far out. Being in the zone is no guarantee of life, or even water. Atmosphere matters enormously. Venus sits near the inner edge of the Sun's habitable zone but is scorching, while Mars sits within it but is frozen and dry. The zone is a starting point for searches, not a verdict.

sections.key: Exoplanets include scorching hot Jupiters, planets with two suns, and 'super-Earths' unlike anything in our solar system.
sections.b: Exoplanets have overturned expectations. Hot Jupiters are gas giants orbiting so close to their stars that their years last only days. Kepler-16b orbits two stars at once, so it would have two suns in its sky, like Tatooine in Star Wars. The most common planets found so far are 'super-Earths' and 'sub-Neptunes', sizes between Earth and Neptune, which don't exist in our solar system at all. The TRAPPIST-1 system, about 40 light-years away, has seven roughly Earth-sized planets, several in the habitable zone. The nearest known exoplanet, Proxima Centauri b, orbits the closest star to the Sun, about 4.2 light-years away.

sections.key: Astronomers look for 'biosignatures', such as oxygen with methane, in exoplanet atmospheres; no confirmed sign of life has been found.
sections.b: The ultimate question is whether any of these worlds host life. We can't visit them: even Proxima Centauri b would take over 70,000 years to reach at the speed of the Voyager probes. Instead, astronomers study atmospheres for biosignatures, gases that living things produce, such as oxygen, especially combined with methane, which shouldn't linger together without being constantly replenished. Claims need extreme care. In 2025 a team reported a possible hint of a sulfur compound linked to life on Earth in the atmosphere of K2-18b, but other scientists found the evidence weak, and it remains unconfirmed. So far, there is no confirmed evidence of life beyond Earth.

sections.key: Giant ground telescopes and future space missions aim to study Earth-like planets directly within the coming decades.
sections.b: The next leap will come from much bigger telescopes. Giant ground-based observatories under construction in Chile, including the Giant Magellan Telescope, in which Australian institutions are partners, and Europe's Extremely Large Telescope, are designed to study exoplanet atmospheres in far more detail. NASA is planning a future space telescope aimed at directly imaging Earth-like planets around Sun-like stars and checking their air for signs of life. You can take part too: citizen science projects such as Planet Hunters have let volunteers spot transits in real telescope data. Next time you see Alpha Centauri, the brighter Pointer to the Southern Cross, remember a planet orbits its small neighbour.

quiz.q: What made 51 Pegasi b such a landmark discovery in 1995?
o: It was the first planet found orbiting a Sun-like star
It was the first planet found with life
It was the first Earth-sized planet
It was found by the Kepler telescope
quiz.e: Mayor and Queloz's discovery won the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics.

quiz.q: How does the transit method detect planets?
o: By detecting a slight dip in starlight as a planet passes in front of its star
quiz.e: The size of the dip reveals the planet's size.

quiz.q: What does the wobble (radial velocity) method mainly reveal?
quiz.e: The star's wobble depends on the planet's mass.

quiz.q: What does it mean for a planet to be in the habitable zone?
o: It has oxygen in its air
Liquid water could exist on its surface
It is the same size as Earth
quiz.e: It's a range of distances where surface water could stay liquid, not a guarantee of life.

quiz.q: What is the current status of evidence for life on exoplanets?
quiz.e: Some claims have been made, but none is confirmed.

LESSONS.title: The world's religions
LESSONS.hook: Around three in four people on Earth identify with a religion. Knowing the basics of what they believe helps you understand your neighbours, the news and much of history.

sections.key: Most religions offer beliefs about ultimate reality, a moral code, rituals and a community.
sections.b: Religions differ enormously, but scholars notice some common threads. Most offer an account of ultimate reality, whether that is one God, many gods, or an impersonal truth. Most teach a way to live, with ideas about right and wrong, compassion and duty. Most have rituals such as prayer, meditation, festivals and ceremonies marking birth, marriage and death. And most create communities, from a village temple to a worldwide church. For many adherents, religion is less a list of beliefs than a whole way of life, shaping food, clothing, family and the calendar.

sections.key: Religions differ on God or gods, on what happens after death, and on how people should live.
sections.b: The differences are just as important. Judaism, Christianity and Islam are monotheistic, teaching that there is one God, and are often called the Abrahamic religions because they trace their roots to Abraham. Hinduism includes many deities, which many Hindus understand as forms of one divine reality. Buddhism does not centre on a creator God. Traditions also differ on what happens after death: some teach resurrection and judgement, others a cycle of rebirth. Each tradition also contains wide internal diversity, so it is always wise to ask individuals what they themselves believe.

sections.key: Christianity (about 2.3 billion) and Islam (about 2 billion) are the largest religions, followed by Hinduism (about 1.2 billion).
sections.b: Counting believers is difficult, so figures are rounded estimates, drawn mainly from large surveys by the Pew Research Center. Christianity is the largest religion, with roughly 2.3 billion people, or nearly three in ten people. Islam follows with about 2 billion. Hinduism has about 1.2 billion, most of them in India. Buddhism has several hundred million, depending on how it is counted. Judaism is much smaller, about 15 million, but deeply influential. Around 1.9 billion people describe themselves as having no religion, many of them in China, though that group includes people with spiritual beliefs.

sections.key: Sikhism, Jainism, Shinto, Taoism, the Baha'i Faith and many Indigenous traditions are also important.
sections.b: Beyond these five, many other traditions shape billions of lives. Sikhism, founded by Guru Nanak in the Punjab region around 500 years ago, has about 25 to 30 million followers and teaches devotion to one God, equality and service. Jainism, from India, emphasises non-violence towards all living things. Shinto in Japan honours kami, spirits found in nature and ancestors. Taoism and Confucianism have shaped Chinese culture for over 2,000 years. The Baha'i Faith, founded in the 1800s, teaches the unity of religions. Countless Indigenous traditions around the world connect spirituality to land and ancestors.

sections.key: Aboriginal spirituality, often called the Dreaming, links ancestral beings, Country, law and kinship.
sections.b: Aboriginal spiritual traditions are among the oldest continuous belief systems on Earth. They are often described in English as the Dreaming, though each language group has its own words, such as Tjukurpa in parts of Central Australia. In these traditions, ancestral beings shaped the land, animals and laws, and remain present in Country. Stories, songs, dances and art carry this knowledge, sometimes along songlines that cross the continent. Beliefs vary between hundreds of nations. Some knowledge is sacred and restricted, so it is shared only with the right people, and that protocol deserves respect.

sections.key: Many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people today combine traditional spirituality with Christianity.
sections.b: Torres Strait Islander spirituality has its own traditions, tied to the sea, the stars and totemic clan relationships. From the 1800s, Christian missions spread across both Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities, sometimes as part of harmful government policies, and sometimes forming lasting local churches. Today many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people are Christian, and many combine faith with traditional beliefs. Each year on 1 July, Torres Strait Islanders celebrate the Coming of the Light, marking the arrival of London Missionary Society missionaries on Erub (Darnley Island) in 1871, with church services, feasting and dance.

sections.key: At the 2021 Census, about 44% of Australians identified as Christian and about 39% reported no religion.
sections.b: The Census asks an optional question about religion, which makes it a useful long-term picture. In 1966, fewer than 1% of Australians reported no religion. By the 2021 Census, that figure had risen to about 39%, up from 30% in 2016. Christianity remained the largest group at about 44%, led by Catholics at about 20% and Anglicans at about 10%. Islam (about 3%), Hinduism (almost 3%) and Buddhism (over 2%) were the next largest, with Hinduism adding the most new followers, largely through migration. Results from the 2026 Census will show whether these trends continue.

sections.key: Ask rather than assume, use the terms adherents use, and remember that every tradition is diverse.
sections.b: Religion can be deeply personal, so a few habits help. Ask rather than assume: two Christians, Muslims or Buddhists may practise very differently. Use the names communities use for themselves, such as Latter-day Saints, or gurdwara for a Sikh place of worship. Separate what a religion teaches from the actions of individual followers, good or bad. Learn the key festivals of the people around you; wishing a colleague a happy Diwali, Eid or Hanukkah is usually warmly received. And remember that people without religion hold values and meaning too. Curiosity and respect open far more doors than debate.

quiz.q: Why are Judaism, Christianity and Islam often called the Abrahamic religions?
o: They were all founded in Egypt
They trace their roots to Abraham
They share a single holy book
They began in the same century
quiz.e: All three trace their spiritual ancestry to Abraham and teach belief in one God.

quiz.q: Which is the world's largest religion by number of adherents?
quiz.e: Christianity has roughly 2.3 billion adherents, followed by Islam with about 2 billion.

quiz.q: What is Tjukurpa?
o: A Central Australian word for what is often called the Dreaming
quiz.e: Tjukurpa is used in parts of Central Australia for the spiritual law and stories often called the Dreaming in English.

quiz.q: What does the Coming of the Light celebrate?
o: The arrival of missionaries on Erub in 1871
quiz.e: Held on 1 July, it marks the arrival of London Missionary Society missionaries in the Torres Strait in 1871.

quiz.q: Roughly what share of Australians reported no religion at the 2021 Census?
quiz.e: About 39% reported no religion in 2021, up from about 30% in 2016 and under 1% in 1966.

LESSONS.title: Hinduism
LESSONS.hook: The world's third-largest religion has no single founder, no single holy book and no single creed, yet it has shaped the lives of over a billion people for thousands of years.

sections.key: Hinduism has no single founder and grew over thousands of years in South Asia.
sections.b: Hinduism is often described as the world's oldest living major religion. Unlike many faiths, it has no single founder or date of origin. It grew over thousands of years in South Asia, drawing on the Vedic culture of northern India, whose earliest hymns date to roughly 1500 to 1200 BCE, and on many local traditions. The word Hindu originally came from outsiders naming people who lived beyond the Indus River. Many Hindus call their tradition Sanatana Dharma, often translated as the eternal way or eternal order.

sections.key: Hinduism is highly diverse, with major traditions devoted to Vishnu, Shiva or the Goddess.
sections.b: Hinduism is less a single system than a family of related traditions. Some Hindus focus devotion on Vishnu (Vaishnavism), others on Shiva (Shaivism), and others on the Goddess, called Devi or Shakti (Shaktism). Practice varies by region, language, caste background and family custom. Some Hindus emphasise philosophy, others devotion, ritual or service. Today there are about 1.2 billion Hindus, roughly 95% of them in India, with large communities in Nepal, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Mauritius, Fiji, the United Kingdom, the United States and Australia.

sections.key: Many Hindus believe in Brahman, the ultimate reality, and Atman, the eternal self within each being.
sections.b: A central idea in Hindu philosophy is Brahman, the ultimate reality underlying everything that exists. Each living being is believed to have an Atman, an eternal self or soul. Hindu schools of thought understand the relationship differently. The Advaita Vedanta school teaches that Atman and Brahman are ultimately one and the same. Other schools, especially devotional ones, see the soul as distinct from God while deeply connected through love. This range of views, from philosophical to devotional, sits comfortably within Hinduism and is part of its character.

sections.key: Dharma is duty and right living, karma is action and its consequences, samsara is rebirth, and moksha is liberation.
sections.b: Four ideas are key. Dharma means duty, righteousness or the right way of living, and it can differ by stage of life and role. Karma means action: Hindus believe actions have consequences that shape this life and future lives. Samsara is the cycle of birth, death and rebirth that the soul passes through. Moksha is liberation from that cycle, the ultimate spiritual goal. Classical texts also describe four aims of life: dharma, artha (prosperity), kama (pleasure and love) and moksha, suggesting a full human life balances all of them.

sections.key: Hindus honour many deities, including Vishnu, Shiva, Lakshmi, Durga and Ganesha, often seen as forms of one divine reality.
sections.b: Hindu worship includes many deities. Vishnu, the preserver, is believed to descend to Earth in forms called avatars, most famously Rama and Krishna. Shiva is associated with destruction and renewal, meditation and dance. Devi appears in many forms, including Lakshmi, goddess of prosperity, Parvati and the warrior goddess Durga. Ganesha, with his elephant head, is honoured as the remover of obstacles and is often worshipped before new beginnings. Many Hindus see these deities as different faces of one divine reality, and a family may have a favourite deity at home.

sections.key: Key Hindu texts include the Vedas, Upanishads, Ramayana, Mahabharata and the Bhagavad Gita.
sections.b: Hinduism has a vast body of sacred writing, much of it in Sanskrit. The Vedas are the oldest, collections of hymns and ritual knowledge passed down orally for centuries before being written. The Upanishads explore philosophical questions about Brahman and Atman. Two great epics are beloved across South Asia: the Ramayana, telling the story of Prince Rama, and the Mahabharata, one of the longest poems ever composed, at around 100,000 verses. Within the Mahabharata sits the Bhagavad Gita, a dialogue between Krishna and the warrior Arjuna about duty and devotion.

sections.key: Diwali, the festival of lights, celebrates the victory of light over darkness; Holi is the spring festival of colours.
sections.b: Worship, called puja, may take place at a home shrine or in a temple, and often involves offering flowers, food, light and incense before a sacred image called a murti. Diwali, the festival of lights, usually falls in October or November and celebrates the victory of light over darkness and good over evil. Families light oil lamps, share sweets and honour Lakshmi, and many recall Rama's return home. Holi, in spring, is famous for throwing coloured powder. Navaratri honours the Goddess over nine nights. Pilgrimage to sacred sites like Varanasi on the Ganges is also important.

sections.key: Hinduism added more followers than any other religion in Australia between 2016 and 2021, reaching almost 3% of the population.
sections.b: Hinduism is one of Australia's fastest-growing religions, rising to almost 3% of the population at the 2021 Census, largely through migration from India, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Fiji. Temples such as the Sri Venkateswara Temple at Helensburgh, south of Sydney, serve large communities, and Diwali celebrations draw big crowds in cities like Melbourne and Parramatta. If a Hindu colleague invites you to a celebration, it is polite to accept any sweets offered. At a temple, visitors usually remove shoes, dress modestly and may be asked not to bring in meat or leather items.

quiz.q: What do many Hindus call their own tradition?
quiz.e: Sanatana Dharma, often translated as the eternal way, is a name many Hindus use for their tradition.

quiz.q: In Hinduism, what is moksha?
o: Liberation from the cycle of rebirth
quiz.e: Moksha is liberation from samsara, the cycle of birth, death and rebirth.

quiz.q: Which deity is honoured as the remover of obstacles?
quiz.e: Ganesha, with his elephant head, is often worshipped before new beginnings.

quiz.q: Which are the oldest Hindu sacred texts?
quiz.e: The Vedas, hymns and ritual knowledge, were passed down orally for centuries before being written.

quiz.q: What does Diwali celebrate?
o: The victory of light over darkness
quiz.e: Diwali, the festival of lights, celebrates light over darkness and good over evil.

LESSONS.title: Judaism
LESSONS.hook: One of the world's oldest monotheistic religions, with only about 15 million adherents, yet its ideas helped shape both Christianity and Islam.

sections.key: Jews believe God made a covenant with Abraham, a special and lasting relationship with his descendants.
sections.b: Judaism traces its story to Abraham, who according to the Hebrew Bible left his home in Mesopotamia in response to God's call, perhaps around 4,000 years ago by traditional reckoning. Jews believe God made a covenant, a binding agreement, with Abraham: his descendants would be God's people, and they would be faithful to God. The covenant passed to his son Isaac and grandson Jacob, also called Israel, whose twelve sons became the ancestors of the twelve tribes of Israel. The idea of covenant, a relationship with obligations on both sides, is central to Jewish life.

sections.key: Jews remember the Exodus from slavery in Egypt, led by Moses, and the giving of the Torah at Mount Sinai.
sections.b: The central story of Jewish memory is the Exodus. According to the Torah, the Israelites were enslaved in Egypt until God called Moses to lead them to freedom. After their escape, at Mount Sinai, God gave Moses the Torah, including the Ten Commandments, renewing the covenant with the whole people. The Israelites then wandered in the desert for forty years before reaching the land of Canaan. Historians debate how these events relate to the archaeological record, but the story of liberation has been retold by Jews every year for millennia.

sections.key: The Torah is the five books of Moses; the wider Hebrew Bible is the Tanakh, and the Talmud records rabbinic discussion.
sections.b: Torah means teaching or instruction. In its narrowest sense it refers to the first five books of the Bible, from Genesis to Deuteronomy, handwritten on scrolls and read aloud in synagogues. The full Hebrew Bible is called the Tanakh, an acronym of its three parts: Torah, Nevi'im (Prophets) and Ketuvim (Writings). Jews also study the Talmud, a vast record of rabbinic debate and law compiled between about 200 and 500 CE. Jewish tradition values questioning and argument, and study is itself considered a form of worship.

sections.key: Jews believe in one God and in following God's commandments; the Shema declares that God is one.
sections.b: At the heart of Judaism is belief in one God, who created the world and is involved in human history. The Shema, a prayer recited morning and evening, begins: Hear, O Israel, the Lord is our God, the Lord is One. Tradition counts 613 commandments, or mitzvot, in the Torah, covering worship, ethics, food and daily life. The dietary laws, called kashrut, determine which foods are kosher. Judaism emphasises action and ethical living in this world, including justice and charity, more than detailed beliefs about the afterlife, on which views vary.

sections.key: Shabbat, the weekly day of rest, runs from Friday sunset to Saturday nightfall.
sections.b: Shabbat, the Sabbath, is a weekly day of rest from sunset on Friday to nightfall on Saturday, recalling that God rested on the seventh day of creation. It begins with lighting candles and a family meal with blessings over wine and a braided bread called challah. Many Jews attend synagogue services, where a rabbi, a teacher of Jewish law and tradition, may lead prayer and study. Observant Jews refrain from work on Shabbat, which traditionally includes cooking, travelling by car and using electrical devices. Others mark the day more simply.

sections.key: Key festivals include Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, Passover and Hanukkah; Bar and Bat Mitzvah mark religious adulthood.
sections.b: The Jewish calendar is lunisolar: lunar months, with a leap month added to keep festivals in their seasons. Rosh Hashanah, the new year, begins the High Holy Days, which end ten days later with Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, a day of fasting and prayer. Passover, or Pesach, retells the Exodus at a ritual meal called the Seder. Hanukkah, the eight-night festival of lights, recalls the rededication of the Temple in Jerusalem in the second century BCE. At 13, boys celebrate a Bar Mitzvah, and girls in many communities a Bat Mitzvah at 12 or 13.

sections.key: Major branches include Orthodox, Conservative and Reform (Progressive); Jewish history includes exile, diaspora and the Holocaust.
sections.b: Jewish history includes the destruction of the First Temple by the Babylonians in 586 BCE and of the Second Temple by the Romans in 70 CE, after which most Jews lived in diaspora, scattered across many lands. Communities developed distinct cultures, such as Ashkenazi in Europe and Sephardi and Mizrahi in the Mediterranean and Middle East. Persecution recurred over centuries, culminating in the Holocaust, in which about six million Jews were murdered. Today the main branches include Orthodox, Conservative and Reform (called Progressive in Australia), and many Jews are secular but culturally Jewish.

sections.key: About 100,000 Australians are Jewish, mostly in Melbourne and Sydney, with a presence dating back to the First Fleet.
sections.b: Jews have been in Australia since 1788, when a small number of Jewish convicts arrived on the First Fleet. Today about 100,000 Australians identify as Jewish, mostly in Melbourne and Sydney, including many Holocaust survivors and their descendants. Notable Jewish Australians include General Sir John Monash, commander in the First World War, and Sir Isaac Isaacs, the first Australian-born Governor-General. If you are invited to a Shabbat dinner or Seder, bring flowers or kosher wine, and ask your host about customs.

quiz.q: In Judaism, what is the covenant?
o: A binding relationship between God and the Jewish people
quiz.e: The covenant is the lasting agreement Jews believe God made with Abraham and his descendants.

quiz.q: What does the word Tanakh refer to?
o: The Hebrew Bible, from its three parts
quiz.e: Tanakh is an acronym of Torah, Nevi'im and Ketuvim, the three parts of the Hebrew Bible.

quiz.q: When does Shabbat take place?
quiz.e: Shabbat begins at sunset on Friday and ends at nightfall on Saturday.

quiz.q: Which festival retells the Exodus at a meal called the Seder?
quiz.e: Passover, or Pesach, remembers the Israelites' liberation from slavery in Egypt.

quiz.q: Which famous Australian general was Jewish?
quiz.e: Monash commanded the Australian Corps in 1918 and is one of Australia's most celebrated soldiers.

LESSONS.title: Buddhism
LESSONS.hook: A prince walked away from his palace to understand why people suffer. The path he taught now guides hundreds of millions, and its meditation practices have spread far beyond it.

sections.key: Siddhartha Gautama, born in Lumbini in present-day Nepal, gave up a life of luxury to seek an end to suffering.
sections.b: Buddhism began with Siddhartha Gautama, born into a ruling family at Lumbini, in present-day Nepal. His dates are debated, but many scholars place his life in the fifth century BCE. According to tradition, he grew up sheltered in luxury until, venturing out, he saw four sights: an old man, a sick man, a corpse and a wandering holy man. Shaken by the reality of ageing, sickness and death, he left his palace, his wife and his young son at about 29 to search for a way beyond suffering.

sections.key: After rejecting both luxury and extreme self-denial, Siddhartha found the Middle Way and became the Buddha.
sections.b: For several years Siddhartha practised extreme self-denial, fasting until he was close to death, but found it did not bring understanding. He concluded that the answer lay in a Middle Way between indulgence and harsh asceticism. Buddhists believe that, meditating under a tree at Bodh Gaya in India, he attained enlightenment, a complete understanding of the nature of suffering and how to end it. From then on he was called the Buddha, meaning the awakened one. He gave his first teaching at Sarnath and taught for about 45 years.

sections.key: Life involves suffering (dukkha), caused by craving; suffering can end, and the Eightfold Path is the way.
sections.b: The Buddha's first teaching set out the Four Noble Truths. First, life involves dukkha, often translated as suffering, but also meaning dissatisfaction or unease. Second, dukkha arises from craving and attachment: wanting things to be other than they are. Third, suffering can end; this ending is called nirvana. Fourth, there is a path that leads to it, the Noble Eightfold Path. Buddhists often compare the teaching to a doctor's approach: identify the illness, find its cause, confirm there is a cure, and prescribe the treatment.

sections.key: The Eightfold Path covers wisdom, ethical conduct and mental discipline, from right view to right concentration.
sections.b: The Noble Eightfold Path is a practical guide, often grouped into three areas. Wisdom includes right view and right intention. Ethical conduct includes right speech, right action and right livelihood, meaning earning a living without harming others. Mental discipline includes right effort, right mindfulness and right concentration. Right here means wise or skilful rather than obeying a rule. Many lay Buddhists also follow five precepts: avoiding killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech and intoxicants. The path is meant to be practised together, like strands of a single rope.

sections.key: Buddhists teach impermanence, non-self, karma and rebirth; many do not centre their practice on a creator God.
sections.b: Several ideas run through Buddhist teaching. Anicca, impermanence, holds that everything changes. Anatta, non-self, teaches that there is no fixed, unchanging self, only a flow of experiences. Buddhists also teach karma, that intentional actions shape future experience, and rebirth in a cycle called samsara, which ends with nirvana. Buddhism does not centre on a creator God, though many Buddhists honour buddhas, bodhisattvas and other beings. Buddhists take refuge in the Three Jewels: the Buddha, the Dharma (his teaching) and the Sangha (the community).

sections.key: Theravada is found mainly in Southeast Asia, Mahayana in East Asia, and Vajrayana in Tibet and the Himalayas.
sections.b: Over centuries, Buddhism spread across Asia and developed three broad traditions. Theravada, the way of the elders, is found mainly in Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Cambodia and Laos, and draws on scriptures preserved in the Pali language. Mahayana, the great vehicle, spread through China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam and emphasises the bodhisattva, who seeks enlightenment for the sake of all beings; Zen and Pure Land are Mahayana schools. Vajrayana, found in Tibet, Bhutan and Mongolia, uses ritual, chanting and visualisation. The Dalai Lama is its best-known figure.

sections.key: Meditation, such as calm-abiding and insight practice, is central to many Buddhist traditions.
sections.b: Meditation is central to many forms of Buddhism, though not every Buddhist meditates regularly. Two broad styles are often described: samatha, calm-abiding, which steadies the mind, often by focusing on the breath, and vipassana, insight, which observes thoughts and sensations to see their impermanent nature. Since the 1970s, secular mindfulness programs, inspired partly by Buddhist practice, have spread into hospitals, schools and workplaces. Many Buddhists welcome this, while others note that traditional meditation sits within an ethical and spiritual framework. Other practices include chanting, bowing, giving and festivals such as Vesak.

sections.key: About 2.4% of Australians identified as Buddhist at the 2021 Census; temples welcome respectful visitors.
sections.b: About 2.4% of Australians identified as Buddhist at the 2021 Census, many with roots in Vietnam, China, Sri Lanka, Thailand and other Asian countries, along with many Australian-born converts. Nan Tien Temple near Wollongong is one of the largest Buddhist temples in the Southern Hemisphere and welcomes visitors. When visiting a temple, it is customary to remove your shoes, dress modestly, avoid pointing your feet at Buddha images, and ask before taking photos. Many temples offer free introductory meditation classes, a good way to learn from practitioners directly.

quiz.q: Where was Siddhartha Gautama born?
quiz.e: Tradition places his birth at Lumbini, in present-day Nepal.

quiz.q: Buddhists often compare the Four Noble Truths to what?
quiz.e: Identify the illness, find its cause, confirm there is a cure, and prescribe the treatment.

quiz.q: Which of these is part of the Eightfold Path?
quiz.e: Right livelihood means earning a living without harming others.

quiz.q: Zen is a school within which Buddhist tradition?
quiz.e: Zen and Pure Land are schools within Mahayana Buddhism.

quiz.q: What is vipassana meditation?
o: Insight meditation that observes thoughts and sensations
quiz.e: Vipassana, or insight meditation, observes experience to see its impermanent nature.

LESSONS.title: Christianity
LESSONS.hook: The world's largest religion began with a Jewish teacher in a small Roman province. Two thousand years later, it shapes the calendar, laws and holidays of countries like Australia.

sections.key: Jesus was a Jewish teacher in Roman-ruled Judea, crucified around 30 CE; Christians believe he rose from the dead.
sections.b: Christianity centres on Jesus of Nazareth, a Jewish teacher who lived in Galilee and Judea, then under Roman rule. He was probably born around 4 BCE and was crucified in Jerusalem around 30 CE under the Roman governor Pontius Pilate. Most historians agree that Jesus existed, taught, gathered followers and was crucified. Christians believe much more: that he is the Son of God and the Messiah, and that he rose from the dead three days after his death. The title Christ comes from the Greek for anointed one, a translation of the Hebrew Messiah.

sections.key: Jesus taught love of God and neighbour, forgiveness and care for the poor, often through parables.
sections.b: According to the Gospels, Jesus taught that people should love God with all their heart and love their neighbour as themselves. He often taught through parables, short stories such as the Good Samaritan, in which a despised outsider helps a wounded traveller, and the Prodigal Son, about a father forgiving a wayward son. His Sermon on the Mount includes the Beatitudes, which bless the poor, the meek and the peacemakers, and the Lord's Prayer, still recited by Christians worldwide. He was known for welcoming outsiders, healing the sick and challenging religious authorities.

sections.key: The Christian Bible has two parts: the Old Testament, largely the Hebrew Bible, and the New Testament, with 27 books.
sections.b: The Christian Bible has two main parts. The Old Testament largely corresponds to the Hebrew Bible, shared with Judaism. The New Testament contains 27 books written in Greek in the first century or so after Jesus. It includes four Gospels, by Matthew, Mark, Luke and John, which tell of Jesus's life, death and resurrection; the Acts of the Apostles, on the early church; letters, many by the apostle Paul; and Revelation. Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include some additional Old Testament books. The Bible has been translated into more languages than any other book.

sections.key: Most Christians believe in one God as a Trinity, that Jesus is God made human, and that salvation comes through him.
sections.b: Most Christians believe in one God who exists as a Trinity: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. They believe that in Jesus, God became human, a belief called the incarnation, and that through his death and resurrection, people can be reconciled with God and receive eternal life. This is called salvation. Many churches summarise their beliefs in the Nicene Creed, first agreed at a church council in 325 CE. Most Christians practise baptism, a ritual of washing that marks entry into the faith, and Holy Communion, sharing bread and wine in memory of Jesus.

sections.key: Christianity spread across the Roman Empire and became its official religion in 380 CE.
sections.b: After Jesus's death, his followers, led by apostles such as Peter and Paul, spread the message across the Roman Empire. Early Christians were a small and sometimes persecuted minority. That changed under Emperor Constantine, who legalised Christianity in 313 CE, and in 380 CE it became the empire's official religion. Christianity had already become the state religion of Armenia, around 301, and of the Ethiopian kingdom of Aksum in the 330s. Over the following centuries it spread through Europe and beyond, and later, with European exploration and missions, to the Americas, Africa, Asia and Oceania. Today most Christians live outside Europe, with especially large and growing numbers in Africa and Latin America.

sections.key: The three largest branches are Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant, shaped by the split of 1054 and the Reformation of 1517.
sections.b: Christianity has many branches. In 1054, tensions between Rome and Constantinople led to the Great Schism, separating the Catholic Church in the west, led by the Pope in Rome, from the Eastern Orthodox churches, which include the Greek, Russian and Serbian Orthodox churches. In 1517, Martin Luther's criticisms of church practices helped spark the Protestant Reformation, which produced Lutheran, Anglican, Presbyterian, Baptist, Methodist and many other churches, and later the fast-growing Pentecostal movement. The Catholic Church is the largest, with over a billion members, more than half of all Christians.

sections.key: Christmas celebrates Jesus's birth; Easter, the most important Christian festival, celebrates his resurrection.
sections.b: Christmas, on 25 December, celebrates the birth of Jesus, though many Orthodox Christians celebrate on 7 January because they follow the older Julian calendar. For Christians, Easter is the most important festival. It is preceded by Lent, a season of about 40 days of reflection and often fasting. Holy Week includes Good Friday, remembering Jesus's crucifixion, and ends with Easter Sunday, celebrating his resurrection. Easter's date moves each year, falling on a Sunday between late March and late April, based on the spring full moon in the northern hemisphere.

sections.key: About 44% of Australians identified as Christian in 2021, with Catholics the largest group at about 20%.
sections.b: Christianity arrived with the First Fleet in 1788, whose chaplain, Richard Johnson, was Anglican. Catholic Irish convicts and settlers made Catholicism a major force, and today Catholics are the largest group, at about 20% of Australians in the 2021 Census, followed by Anglicans at about 10%. The Uniting Church formed in 1977 from Methodist, Congregational and most Presbyterian churches. Overall, about 44% of Australians identified as Christian in 2021, down from much higher levels in earlier decades. Mary MacKillop, canonised in 2010, is Australia's first saint, and church-run schools, hospitals and charities remain significant.

quiz.q: What does the title Christ mean?
quiz.e: Christ comes from the Greek for anointed one, translating the Hebrew word Messiah.

quiz.q: How many books are in the New Testament?
quiz.e: The New Testament has 27 books, including four Gospels, Acts, letters and Revelation.

quiz.q: What is the Christian belief in the Trinity?
o: That the Bible has three parts
One God as Father, Son and Holy Spirit
quiz.e: Most Christians believe in one God existing as Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

quiz.q: What event in 1517 helped spark the Protestant Reformation?
o: Martin Luther's criticisms of church practices
quiz.e: Martin Luther's criticisms of church practices, including his 95 theses, helped launch the Reformation.

quiz.q: Which festival do Christians generally regard as the most important?
quiz.e: Easter celebrates Jesus's resurrection, central to Christian belief.

LESSONS.title: Islam
LESSONS.hook: About one in four people on Earth is Muslim. The largest Muslim nation is not in the Middle East, and Muslims first reached Australia's shores long before the cameleers.

sections.key: Islam means submission to God; Muslims believe in one God and in prophets including Abraham, Moses, Jesus and Muhammad.
sections.b: The Arabic word Islam means submission, in the sense of submitting to the will of God, and a Muslim is one who submits. Allah is simply the Arabic word for God, and Arabic-speaking Christians use it too. The central belief of Islam is tawhid, the absolute oneness of God. Muslims believe God sent many prophets, including Adam, Abraham (Ibrahim), Moses (Musa) and Jesus (Isa), who is deeply honoured as a prophet. Muslims believe Muhammad was the final prophet. Like Jews and Christians, Muslims trace their faith to Abraham.

sections.key: Muhammad was born in Mecca around 570 CE; Muslims believe he began receiving revelations around 610 CE.
sections.b: Muhammad was born in Mecca, in the Arabian Peninsula, around 570 CE, and was orphaned young. He became a respected merchant. Muslims believe that around 610 CE, while meditating in a cave near Mecca, he received the first revelation from God through the angel Jibril (Gabriel). His message of one God met opposition in Mecca, and in 622 he and his followers moved to Medina. This journey, the Hijra, marks the start of the Islamic calendar. By his death in 632, much of Arabia had embraced Islam. Muslims often say peace be upon him after his name.

sections.key: Muslims believe the Qur'an is the word of God revealed to Muhammad; it has 114 chapters, called surahs, in Arabic.
sections.b: Muslims believe the Qur'an is the word of God, revealed to Muhammad over about 23 years. It has 114 chapters, called surahs, and was compiled into a single written text within a few decades of his death. Muslims regard the Arabic original as the true Qur'an; translations are seen as interpretations. Many Muslims memorise the entire text, earning the title hafiz. Alongside the Qur'an, Muslims draw on the hadith, reports of Muhammad's words and actions. Together these guide sharia, a broad framework for religious and ethical life, interpreted in varied ways by scholars.

sections.key: The Five Pillars are the declaration of faith, prayer, charity, fasting in Ramadan and pilgrimage to Mecca.
sections.b: Muslim practice rests on the Five Pillars. Shahada is the declaration of faith: there is no god but God, and Muhammad is the messenger of God. Salat is prayer five times a day, facing towards the Kaaba in Mecca. Zakat is giving to those in need, commonly 2.5% of savings above a set threshold each year. Sawm is fasting from dawn to sunset during the month of Ramadan. Hajj is the pilgrimage to Mecca, which every adult Muslim who is physically and financially able should make at least once in their lifetime.

sections.key: Ramadan is a month of fasting from dawn to sunset; Eid al-Fitr marks its end and Eid al-Adha falls during the Hajj.
sections.b: Ramadan is the ninth month of the Islamic lunar calendar. Because the lunar year is about 11 days shorter than the solar year, Ramadan moves earlier each year. During Ramadan, Muslims fast from dawn to sunset, avoiding food and drink, and focus on prayer, charity and reflection; children, the sick, travellers and pregnant women may be exempt. Each evening the fast is broken with a meal called iftar, often shared. The month ends with Eid al-Fitr, a joyful festival. Eid al-Adha, during the Hajj, honours Ibrahim's willingness to sacrifice his son at God's command.

sections.key: Most Muslims are Sunni, about 85–90%; Shia Muslims, about 10–15%, are a majority in Iran and Iraq.
sections.b: After Muhammad's death, his followers disagreed over who should lead the community. Those who became known as Sunni accepted Abu Bakr, a close companion, as the first caliph. Those who became Shia believed leadership belonged to Ali, Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law, and his descendants. The death of Ali's son Husayn at Karbala in 680 CE is mourned by Shia Muslims each year at Ashura. Today about 85 to 90% of Muslims are Sunni and 10 to 15% Shia, the majority in Iran and Iraq. Sufism, a mystical tradition, is found within both.

sections.key: During the Islamic Golden Age, scholars advanced algebra, optics, medicine and astronomy.
sections.b: From about the eighth to the thirteenth centuries, scholars in the Islamic world made major advances. In Baghdad, the House of Wisdom gathered and translated Greek, Persian and Indian works. Al-Khwarizmi wrote a founding text on algebra, a word that comes from Arabic, and his name gave us the word algorithm. Ibn al-Haytham used experiments to study light and vision. Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine was taught in European universities for centuries. The numerals we use today, first developed in India, reached Europe largely through Arabic texts, and many stars still carry Arabic names.

sections.h: Islam around the world and in Australia
sections.key: Indonesia has the world's largest Muslim population; about 3% of Australians were Muslim in 2021.
sections.b: Only about one in five Muslims is Arab. Indonesia has the largest Muslim population of any country, followed by Pakistan, India and Bangladesh. Contact with Australia is old: from at least the 1700s, Makassan sailors from Sulawesi, many of them Muslim, visited northern Australia to harvest trepang, or sea cucumber, trading with the Yolngu of Arnhem Land. From the 1860s, cameleers, known as Afghans though many came from British India, opened up the outback and built some of Australia's first mosques; the Ghan train is named after them. At the 2021 Census, about 3% of Australians were Muslim.

quiz.q: What does the word Islam mean?
quiz.e: Islam means submission, in the sense of submitting to the will of God.

quiz.q: What was the Hijra?
o: Muhammad's move from Mecca to Medina in 622
The first revelation in a cave
quiz.e: The Hijra, Muhammad's journey to Medina in 622, marks the start of the Islamic calendar.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the Five Pillars of Islam?
quiz.e: The Five Pillars are shahada, salat, zakat, sawm and hajj, the pilgrimage to Mecca.

quiz.q: Roughly what share of Muslims are Sunni?
quiz.e: About 85 to 90% of Muslims are Sunni and 10 to 15% are Shia.

quiz.q: Which country has the world's largest Muslim population?
quiz.e: Indonesia has more Muslims than any other country.

LESSONS.title: How rockets work
LESSONS.hook: A rocket doesn't push against the air. It throws mass out the back so fast that the rest of it has no choice but to go forward.

sections.key: Rockets work by Newton's third law: pushing gas out the back pushes the rocket forward.
sections.b: Every rocket relies on Isaac Newton's third law of motion: for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. Burning propellant creates hot gas at enormous pressure, and the engine's nozzle forces that gas out the back at several kilometres per second. Pushing all that mass backwards pushes the rocket forwards. You feel the same effect when a garden hose kicks in your hand or a balloon zips around the room as air rushes out. A rocket is simply a very large, very controlled version of that balloon.

sections.key: Rockets don't need air to push against, and they carry their own oxygen to burn fuel.
sections.b: A common myth is that rockets push against the air, so they couldn't work in space. In fact they work slightly better in a vacuum, because there is no air pressure resisting the exhaust. What rockets do need is oxygen to burn their fuel, and since space has none, they carry their own supply, called an oxidiser. Common pairings include refined kerosene with liquid oxygen, and liquid hydrogen with liquid oxygen. Solid rocket boosters mix fuel and oxidiser into a rubbery solid that burns like a giant firework.

sections.key: Most of a rocket's launch mass is propellant; the useful payload is only a few per cent.
sections.b: Getting to space is so demanding that a rocket is mostly a flying fuel tank. Typically around 85 to 90% of a large rocket's mass at lift-off is propellant, and the payload, the satellite or crew capsule it exists to carry, is often only a few per cent. A Falcon 9 weighs about 550 tonnes at lift-off yet can carry at most around 23 tonnes to low orbit, roughly 4% of its launch mass. The trouble is that every extra kilogram of fuel also has to be lifted, which needs yet more fuel.

sections.key: Tsiolkovsky worked out the theory; Goddard flew the first liquid-fuelled rocket in 1926.
sections.b: Rockets are old: the Chinese used gunpowder rockets in warfare by the 1200s. Modern spaceflight began with the Russian schoolteacher Konstantin Tsiolkovsky, who around 1903 published the equation linking a rocket's speed to its exhaust speed and fuel load, still called the rocket equation. In 1926 the American physicist Robert Goddard launched the first liquid-fuelled rocket in Massachusetts; it flew for about two and a half seconds. During World War II, Germany's V-2 became the first large guided ballistic missile, and its engineers later helped both the US and Soviet space programs.

sections.key: Rockets drop empty tanks and engines in stages so they don't carry dead weight to orbit.
sections.b: Because carrying empty tanks wastes energy, most rockets are built in stages stacked on top of one another. The large first stage does the heavy lifting through the thick lower atmosphere, then shuts down and falls away. A smaller second stage, now pushing a much lighter vehicle, carries on towards orbit, and some rockets add a third. Each time a stage drops off, the rocket sheds dead weight, so the remaining engines can accelerate it far more efficiently. Staging is the practical answer to the harsh arithmetic of the rocket equation.

sections.key: To stay in low orbit you must travel sideways at about 7.8 km/s, roughly 28,000 km/h.
sections.b: Reaching space is surprisingly easy: the commonly used boundary, the Kármán line, is only about 100 kilometres up. Staying there is the hard part. An object in orbit is constantly falling towards Earth, but moving sideways so fast that the ground curves away beneath it. In low Earth orbit that takes about 7.8 kilometres per second, roughly 28,000 km/h. That is why rockets lean over soon after launch and spend most of their effort gaining sideways speed rather than height. Launching eastwards also borrows a boost from Earth's own rotation.

sections.key: Landing and reflying boosters, pioneered by SpaceX from 2015, has cut launch costs.
sections.b: For most of the space age, rockets were used once and thrown away, like building a new airliner for every flight. The US Space Shuttle, flown from 1981 to 2011, was partly reusable, but refurbishing it proved slow and costly. In December 2015 SpaceX landed the first stage of a Falcon 9 orbital rocket upright after launch, and it now routinely lands and reflies boosters, some more than 30 times. Rocket Lab, founded in New Zealand, launches small satellites from the Mahia Peninsula. Cheaper launches have helped fuel today's boom in satellites.

sections.key: Woomera in South Australia launched WRESAT, Australia's first satellite, in 1967.
sections.b: Australia has a real place in rocket history. From 1947 the vast Woomera range in outback South Australia was used by Britain and Australia to test missiles and research rockets. In November 1967 WRESAT, Australia's first satellite, was launched from Woomera on a modified American rocket, making Australia one of the first handful of nations to launch a satellite from its own territory. The Australian Space Agency was set up in 2018, and several Australian companies are now developing launch vehicles and satellites. Next time you see a launch, you'll know it's Newton doing the work.

quiz.q: Which law explains how a rocket moves forward?
o: The law of conservation of mass
quiz.e: Pushing exhaust gas backwards produces an equal and opposite push forwards.

quiz.q: Why do rockets carry an oxidiser?
o: Because space has no oxygen to burn fuel
quiz.e: Burning needs oxygen, so rockets bring their own supply.

quiz.q: Why are rockets built in stages?
o: To make them easier to paint
So they can drop empty tanks and dead weight
quiz.e: Dropping empty stages lets the remaining engines accelerate a lighter vehicle.

quiz.q: Roughly how fast must something travel to stay in low Earth orbit?
quiz.e: Low orbit needs about 7.8 km/s, roughly 28,000 km/h, of sideways speed.

quiz.q: What was WRESAT?
o: Australia's first satellite, launched from Woomera in 1967
quiz.e: WRESAT was launched from Woomera, South Australia, in November 1967.

LESSONS.title: The Space Race
LESSONS.hook: In 1957 a metal ball the size of a beach ball started beeping overhead, and two superpowers began racing to the Moon.

sections.key: The Space Race was a Cold War rivalry between the US and USSR, closely tied to missiles.
sections.b: After World War II, the United States and the Soviet Union became rivals in the Cold War, a long standoff that stopped short of direct war between them. Space became a stage for that contest. Each side wanted to prove its political system produced better science and engineering, and the stakes were military as well as symbolic. A rocket powerful enough to put a satellite in orbit could also carry a nuclear warhead across the world. Much of the early space technology on both sides grew directly out of missile programs.

sections.key: On 4 October 1957 the USSR launched Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite.
sections.b: On 4 October 1957 the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the world's first artificial satellite. It was a polished metal sphere about 58 centimetres across, weighing roughly 84 kilograms, with four long antennas. It did little more than transmit a simple beeping radio signal, but anyone with the right receiver could hear it passing overhead about every 96 minutes. The launch shocked Americans, who had assumed they were technologically ahead. A month later Sputnik 2 carried a dog named Laika, the first animal to orbit Earth; she did not survive the flight.

sections.key: The US launched Explorer 1 in 1958 and created NASA the same year.
sections.b: The US answered quickly. On 31 January 1958 it launched its first satellite, Explorer 1, whose instruments detected the Van Allen radiation belts, bands of charged particles trapped by Earth's magnetic field. Later that year the government created NASA, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, to run a civilian space program. The shock of Sputnik also led to major new US spending on science and maths education. For the next few years, though, the Soviets kept claiming the headline firsts, including the first probe to reach the Moon's surface, Luna 2, in 1959.

sections.key: On 12 April 1961 Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space, orbiting Earth once in Vostok 1.
sections.b: On 12 April 1961 the Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin, a 27-year-old air force pilot, launched aboard Vostok 1 and became the first human in space. He orbited Earth once in a flight lasting about 108 minutes, then ejected from the capsule during descent and parachuted to the ground, as Vostok was designed for. His cheerful cry of 'Poyekhali!', meaning 'Let's go!', became famous. Gagarin became a global celebrity overnight. Tragically, he died in a jet training crash in 1968, aged just 34.

sections.key: Early crewed programs, Mercury and Vostok, proved people could survive and work in orbit.
sections.b: The first American in space, Alan Shepard, flew a 15-minute suborbital hop in a Mercury capsule on 5 May 1961. In February 1962 John Glenn became the first American to orbit Earth, circling it three times. As his capsule passed over Western Australia, the people of Perth famously switched on their lights, earning it the nickname 'City of Light'. Meanwhile the Soviet Vostok program kept setting records, and in June 1963 Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space, spending almost three days in orbit.

sections.key: In 1961 President Kennedy committed the US to landing a person on the Moon before the 1960s ended.
sections.b: Stung by Gagarin's flight, President John F. Kennedy told the US Congress in May 1961 that America should land a man on the Moon and return him safely before the decade was out. In a 1962 speech in Texas he added, 'We choose to go to the Moon in this decade and do the other things, not because they are easy, but because they are hard.' The goal turned the Space Race into a clear finish line. At its peak, NASA's Apollo effort employed roughly 400,000 people across government and industry.

sections.key: Gemini practised spacewalks, docking and long flights; Leonov made the first spacewalk in 1965.
sections.b: Before going to the Moon, astronauts had to master skills nobody had tried. On 18 March 1965 the Soviet cosmonaut Alexei Leonov made the first spacewalk, from Voskhod 2; his suit ballooned so much that he had to let air out to squeeze back inside. The US Gemini program, flying two-person crews in 1965 and 1966, practised spacewalks, flights of up to two weeks, and the first docking of two spacecraft in orbit. Behind the scenes, the Soviet program lost its brilliant chief designer, Sergei Korolev, who died in 1966.

sections.key: The US won the Moon race in 1969; by 1975 rivals were shaking hands in orbit.
sections.b: The race had real costs. In January 1967 a fire during a ground test of Apollo 1 killed three astronauts, and months later cosmonaut Vladimir Komarov died when Soyuz 1's parachute failed. The Soviets' giant N1 Moon rocket failed all four of its launch attempts. In July 1969 Apollo 11 landed on the Moon, effectively settling the race. By 1975 the mood had shifted: in the Apollo–Soyuz mission, American and Soviet crews docked and shook hands in orbit. That spirit later grew into the International Space Station.

quiz.q: Who was the first animal to orbit Earth, aboard Sputnik 2 in 1957?
quiz.e: Laika was launched a month after Sputnik 1; she did not survive the flight.

quiz.q: Who was the first human in space?
quiz.e: Yuri Gagarin orbited Earth in Vostok 1 on 12 April 1961.

quiz.q: Why was Perth nicknamed the 'City of Light' in 1962?
o: Residents switched on lights as John Glenn flew overhead
It had the first street lights in Australia
quiz.e: Perth's lights were visible to Glenn as he orbited above Western Australia.

quiz.q: Who made the first spacewalk?
quiz.e: Leonov stepped outside Voskhod 2 on 18 March 1965.

quiz.q: What was the Apollo–Soyuz mission of 1975?
o: A joint docking of US and Soviet spacecraft
The launch of the first space station
quiz.e: American and Soviet crews docked and shook hands in orbit, a symbol of easing tensions.

LESSONS.title: Apollo and the Moon landing
LESSONS.hook: In July 1969 about 600 million people watched two men walk on the Moon, and those pictures reached the world through a dish in a sheep paddock in New South Wales.

sections.key: Apollo 11 landed on the Moon on 20 July 1969 (US time); Armstrong and Aldrin walked on it.
sections.b: Apollo 11 launched from Florida on 16 July 1969 with three astronauts: Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin and Michael Collins. Four days later, on 20 July in US time and 21 July in Australia, Armstrong and Aldrin landed in the Sea of Tranquillity while Collins orbited above in the command module, Columbia. Hours later Armstrong stepped onto the surface and said, 'That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.' Aldrin followed about 20 minutes later. The pair spent roughly two and a half hours walking on the Moon.

sections.key: The Saturn V, about 110 metres tall, remains one of the most powerful rockets ever flown.
sections.b: Getting there took the Saturn V, a three-stage rocket about 110 metres tall, taller than a 30-storey building. Its five first-stage engines burned roughly 13 tonnes of propellant every second for about two and a half minutes. The first stage lifted the rocket through the atmosphere, the second pushed it almost to orbit, and the third reached orbit and later fired again to send the spacecraft towards the Moon. The Saturn V flew 13 times between 1967 and 1973 and never lost a crew or payload.

sections.key: Apollo used lunar orbit rendezvous: a small lander went down while the main ship waited in orbit.
sections.b: Rather than landing one huge spacecraft, NASA chose a plan called lunar orbit rendezvous. The command module stayed in orbit around the Moon, while a light, spidery lunar module called Eagle carried two astronauts down. The landing was tense: computer alarms flashed, and Armstrong had to steer past a boulder field by hand, touching down with less than a minute of landing fuel to spare by some estimates. Afterwards the lander's top half blasted off, docked with Columbia, and was left behind. Only the small command module returned, splashing down in the Pacific on 24 July.

sections.key: Parkes and Honeysuckle Creek in Australia relayed the TV pictures of the first moonwalk.
sections.b: Because Earth was turning, the Moon was above Australia when Armstrong stepped out, so Australian stations did vital work. The first TV images of his step came through the Honeysuckle Creek tracking station near Canberra. Minutes later, the CSIRO's 64-metre radio telescope at Parkes, in central-west New South Wales, took over and supplied the clearer pictures seen for most of the moonwalk. Strong gusts of wind buffeted the dish during the broadcast, beyond its normal safe limits, but staff kept it tracking. The story inspired the 2000 Australian film The Dish.

sections.key: Six Apollo missions landed; 12 astronauts walked on the Moon, the last in December 1972.
sections.b: Apollo 12 landed in November 1969, beside an older robotic probe. Apollo 13, in April 1970, never landed: an oxygen tank exploded on the way, and the crew survived by using the lunar module as a lifeboat, a famous feat of improvisation. Apollo 14 to 17 followed, and the last three carried a battery-powered buggy, the Lunar Roving Vehicle, to explore further. In all, six missions landed and 12 men walked on the Moon. The last, Apollo 17, left in December 1972, and no one has been back since.

sections.key: Apollo brought back about 382 kg of Moon rock, and its instruments revealed that the Moon has quakes.
sections.b: The six landings brought back about 382 kilograms of lunar rock and soil, which scientists around the world still study. Astronauts also set up instruments. Seismometers showed the Moon is not geologically dead: it has moonquakes, and vibrations ring on for a long time because the dry, cold rock barely dampens them. When the Apollo 12 crew deliberately crashed their lander's discarded upper stage into the surface, the Moon reverberated for nearly an hour, like a bell.
