NASA also kept some samples sealed for decades, waiting for better tools; in 2022 scientists opened one collected on Apollo 17 that had stayed vacuum-sealed since 1972.

sections.key: NASA's Artemis program aims to return people to the Moon, starting near its south pole.
sections.b: After five decades, humans are preparing to go back. NASA's Artemis program, named after Apollo's twin sister in Greek mythology, flew its first uncrewed test, Artemis I, around the Moon in late 2022. In April 2026 Artemis II, the first crewed flight, sent four astronauts, including a Canadian, around the Moon and back without landing. Later missions aim to land astronauts near the lunar south pole, where permanently shadowed craters may hold water ice that could supply drinking water, oxygen and even rocket fuel. China has also announced plans to land astronauts by 2030.

sections.key: The Moon landings are among the best-documented events in history, with independent evidence.
sections.b: Conspiracy theories claim the landings were faked, but the evidence is overwhelming. Around 400,000 people worked on Apollo, and the Soviet Union, which was tracking the missions and had every reason to expose a hoax, never disputed them. Moon rocks have been studied by scientists in many countries, including Australia. The laser mirrors still work. In 2009 and later, NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter photographed the landing sites, showing the lander bases, equipment and even the astronauts' footpaths. When you look at the Moon, you're looking at a place humans have walked.

quiz.q: Who stayed in lunar orbit during the Apollo 11 landing?
quiz.e: Collins piloted the command module Columbia while the others landed.

quiz.q: What role did the Parkes radio telescope play in Apollo 11?
o: It relayed TV pictures of the moonwalk
It guided the landing by radar
quiz.e: Parkes supplied the TV images seen for most of the moonwalk, after Honeysuckle Creek's first pictures.

quiz.q: What happened on Apollo 13?
o: It landed on the far side
An oxygen tank exploded, and the crew returned safely without landing
It was the last Moon landing
It carried the first lunar rover
quiz.e: The crew used the lunar module as a lifeboat and returned safely.

quiz.q: What did Apollo's seismometers reveal?
o: The Moon has a liquid water ocean
The Moon has no interior layers
quiz.e: The dry, cold rock lets vibrations ring on; one impact made the Moon reverberate for nearly an hour.

quiz.q: Why is the lunar south pole a target for Artemis?
o: Shadowed craters may hold water ice
quiz.e: Water ice could provide drinking water, oxygen and rocket fuel.

LESSONS.title: The International Space Station
LESSONS.hook: Right now, about 400 kilometres above you, people are eating, sleeping and doing experiments while circling Earth every hour and a half.

sections.key: The ISS orbits about 400 km up and has been continuously occupied since November 2000.
sections.b: The International Space Station is a large, crewed laboratory orbiting Earth at an altitude of about 400 kilometres, roughly the distance from Perth to Albany, but straight up. It travels at about 28,000 km/h, circling the planet roughly every 90 minutes, so its crew sees about 16 sunrises and sunsets a day. The first module was launched in November 1998, and astronauts have lived aboard continuously since 2 November 2000. That means a whole generation of people has grown up without a single day when humans weren't living in space.

sections.key: The ISS was assembled in orbit from modules, and is about the size of a football field.
sections.b: The station was far too big to launch in one go, so it was built in orbit over more than a decade from pieces carried up by US Space Shuttles and Russian rockets. Astronauts bolted modules together during hundreds of hours of spacewalks. The finished structure is about 109 metres across at its widest, roughly the length of a football field, and weighs around 420,000 kilograms. Huge solar arrays supply its electricity. Estimates of the total cost vary, but it is often described as the most expensive object ever built, well over US$100 billion.

sections.key: The ISS is a partnership of the US, Russia, Europe, Japan and Canada.
sections.b: The ISS is run by five space agencies: NASA of the United States, Roscosmos of Russia, the European Space Agency, the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency and the Canadian Space Agency. Each contributed hardware. Russia provides key modules and propulsion, Japan built the large Kibo laboratory, Europe the Columbus lab, and Canada the robotic arm, Canadarm2. Astronauts from more than 20 countries have visited. Australian-born astronaut Andy Thomas, from Adelaide, flew on four Space Shuttle missions, two of them to the ISS, the second after the Columbia disaster.

sections.key: Astronauts float because they are in free fall around Earth, not because there is no gravity.
sections.b: At the station's height, Earth's gravity is still about 90% as strong as on the ground. Astronauts float because the station and everything in it are in continuous free fall, falling around Earth together while moving sideways fast enough to keep missing it. Scientists call this microgravity. It makes daily life strange: water forms wobbling spheres, flames burn as round blue balls, and dropped tools drift away. Crew sleep in small cabins, zipped into sleeping bags fixed to the wall so they don't float into equipment during the night.

sections.key: Crews recycle nearly all their water, exercise about two hours a day and follow a tight schedule.
sections.b: Life aboard is carefully planned, with a typical crew of about seven people. Water is precious, so the station recycles moisture from air, washing and even urine; in 2023 NASA reported reaching about 98% water recovery. Food comes in pouches and cans, with fresh fruit a treat on resupply flights, and tortillas are popular because they don't make crumbs. Toilets use airflow instead of gravity. Crews talk with mission control around the clock, work on experiments and maintenance, and still find time to photograph Earth through the Cupola, a seven-windowed observation dome.

sections.key: Long stays in orbit affect eyes, blood and even gene activity, which is why NASA studies astronauts so closely.
sections.b: Weaker bones and muscles are only the start. Many astronauts on long missions develop swelling at the back of the eye and a slight flattening of the eyeball, a condition NASA calls spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome, and some need stronger glasses afterwards. Blood volume drops in orbit, so returning crew can feel faint when they first stand up. Radiation doses are far higher than on the ground. In NASA's Twins Study, astronaut Scott Kelly spent almost a year on the station while his identical twin, Mark, stayed on Earth. Researchers found changes in Scott's gene activity, gut bacteria and immune system, most of which returned to normal within months. Findings like these help plan trips to Mars.

sections.key: ISS research ranges from medicine and materials to physics, with thousands of experiments run.
sections.b: The ISS is above all a laboratory, and thousands of experiments have been run aboard. Microgravity lets scientists study things that are masked by gravity on Earth. Protein crystals can grow larger and more orderly, helping researchers understand molecules targeted by medicines. Flames, fluids and new materials behave differently, which improves models used on the ground. Crews have grown lettuce, chillies and flowers, and in 2015 astronauts ate lettuce grown on the station. A large particle detector on its exterior, the Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer, searches cosmic rays for clues about dark matter.

sections.key: You can often see the ISS from Australia with the naked eye; its future ends around 2030.
sections.b: You don't need a telescope to see the station. Shortly after dusk or before dawn, it appears as a bright, steady point of light gliding across the sky in a few minutes, without flashing like a plane. NASA's free Spot the Station service tells you when it will pass over your town. The ISS is ageing, and current plans are to retire it around 2030 and steer it into a remote part of the Pacific Ocean. Commercial space stations are being developed to replace it, and China already operates its own station, Tiangong.

quiz.q: About how long does the ISS take to orbit Earth?
quiz.e: At around 28,000 km/h, it laps Earth roughly every 90 minutes.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the five ISS partner agencies?
quiz.e: The partners are the US, Russia, Europe, Japan and Canada; China runs its own station.

quiz.q: How do candle flames behave in the ISS's microgravity?
o: They burn tall and yellow, as on Earth
quiz.e: Without gravity, hot air doesn't rise, so flames don't stretch into the familiar teardrop shape.

quiz.q: What did NASA's Twins Study compare?
o: Astronaut Scott Kelly, after almost a year in orbit, with his identical twin Mark on Earth
quiz.e: Researchers tracked changes in gene activity, gut bacteria and more, most of which faded within months of Scott's return.

quiz.q: How can you tell the ISS apart from a plane in the night sky?
o: It glides as a steady light without flashing
quiz.e: The ISS looks like a bright, steady moving point of light, with no flashing lights.

LESSONS.title: Telescopes: our eyes on the universe
LESSONS.hook: In 1610 a hand-made tube of lenses showed Galileo moons circling Jupiter. Today a mirror a million and a half kilometres away sees galaxies born soon after the Big Bang.

sections.key: In 1609–1610 Galileo used a telescope to discover Jupiter's moons, craters on the Moon and Venus's phases.
sections.b: The telescope was invented in the Netherlands around 1608, and within a year the Italian scientist Galileo Galilei had built his own, eventually reaching about 20 times magnification. Pointing it at the sky, he found mountains and craters on the Moon, countless stars in the Milky Way, and in January 1610 four moons orbiting Jupiter. He later saw that Venus shows phases like the Moon. These observations challenged the old belief that everything circled Earth and supported the idea that the planets orbit the Sun.

sections.key: A telescope's main job is to collect light, so larger mirrors see fainter, sharper detail.
sections.b: The most important feature of a telescope isn't magnification but its light-collecting area. A bigger lens or mirror gathers more light, revealing fainter objects, and can resolve finer detail. Early telescopes used lenses, but large lenses sag and blur colours, so in 1668 Isaac Newton built a reflecting telescope that used a curved mirror instead. Almost every big research telescope today is a reflector. Modern ground-based giants have mirrors around 8 to 10 metres across, and telescopes with mirrors of 25 to 40 metres are under construction.

sections.key: Earth's air blurs starlight, so observatories sit on high, dry mountains or go into space.
sections.b: Earth's atmosphere is a nuisance for astronomers. Moving air makes stars twinkle and blurs fine detail, and water vapour blocks some wavelengths. That is why major observatories sit on high, dry mountains such as Mauna Kea in Hawaii and the Atacama Desert in Chile. In Australia, Siding Spring Observatory near Coonabarabran in New South Wales hosts the 3.9-metre Anglo-Australian Telescope. Modern telescopes also use adaptive optics, deformable mirrors that change shape hundreds of times a second to cancel out atmospheric blurring.

sections.key: Launched in 1990, Hubble gave sharp views from orbit and helped measure the universe's age.
sections.b: The Hubble Space Telescope was launched in April 1990 aboard the Space Shuttle Discovery, orbiting about 540 kilometres up, above the blurring air. Its 2.4-metre mirror had been ground to slightly the wrong shape, making early images fuzzy, and astronauts fitted corrective optics in 1993. After that, Hubble became one of the most productive scientific instruments ever built. Its Deep Field images revealed thousands of galaxies in tiny patches of sky, and its measurements helped pin down the universe's age at about 13.8 billion years and show that its expansion is accelerating.

sections.key: JWST, launched in 2021, is a 6.5-metre infrared telescope about 1.5 million km from Earth.
sections.b: The James Webb Space Telescope launched on 25 December 2021. Its 6.5-metre mirror, made of 18 gold-coated hexagonal segments, had to fold up to fit inside the rocket and unfold in space. Webb observes mainly in infrared light, which passes through dust clouds and lets it see very distant galaxies whose light has been stretched to longer wavelengths by the expansion of the universe. It orbits around a point about 1.5 million kilometres from Earth, shaded by a sunshield about the size of a tennis court that keeps it extremely cold.

sections.key: Radio telescopes detect invisible radio waves from space; Parkes has operated since 1961.
sections.b: Visible light is only a small slice of what the universe sends us. In the 1930s the engineer Karl Jansky discovered radio waves coming from the Milky Way, launching radio astronomy. Radio telescopes are giant dishes or arrays of antennas that collect these faint signals. Australia is a world leader. The CSIRO's 64-metre Parkes dish, opened in 1961 and also known by its Wiradjuri name Murriyang, helped pinpoint the first identified quasar, has discovered a large share of the known pulsars, and its data revealed the first fast radio burst, a mysterious millisecond flash.

sections.key: The SKA, being built in Western Australia and South Africa, will be the largest radio observatory.
sections.b: The Square Kilometre Array is an international project to build the world's largest radio telescope, split between two sites with very little radio interference. SKA-Low, which listens to low frequencies, is being built in the Murchison region of Western Australia, on the traditional lands of the Wajarri Yamaji people, and will have around 131,000 antennas shaped like small metal Christmas trees. SKA-Mid, with about 200 dishes, is in South Africa's Karoo. Scientists hope the SKA will study the universe's first stars and galaxies and test theories of gravity.

sections.key: Binoculars and a dark sky reveal much more than most people expect.
sections.b: You don't need expensive gear to follow in Galileo's footsteps. A decent pair of binoculars shows craters on the Moon, Jupiter's four largest moons as tiny points, and star clusters like the Jewel Box in the Southern Cross. Get away from city lights and give your eyes 20 minutes to adjust to the dark. Free apps can identify what you're seeing. Australia's southern skies are superb, with the Magellanic Clouds, two neighbouring galaxies, visible to the naked eye. Many public observatories and astronomy clubs run affordable viewing nights.

quiz.q: In which country was the telescope invented, around 1608?
quiz.e: Within a year, Galileo had built his own and turned it on the sky.

quiz.q: What is the most important feature of a research telescope?
quiz.e: Bigger mirrors collect more light, revealing fainter objects and finer detail.

quiz.q: What went wrong with Hubble when it launched?
o: Its mirror was ground to the wrong shape
It was pointed at the Sun
quiz.e: Astronauts fitted corrective optics in 1993.

quiz.q: What kind of light does the James Webb Space Telescope mainly observe?
quiz.e: Infrared passes through dust and captures light from very distant galaxies.

quiz.q: Where is the low-frequency part of the Square Kilometre Array being built?
quiz.e: SKA-Low is in the Murchison region of WA; SKA-Mid is in South Africa.

LESSONS.title: Mars: the red frontier
LESSONS.hook: Mars once had rivers and lakes. Today it's a freezing desert patrolled by robots, and the most likely next destination for human footprints.

sections.key: Mars is about half Earth's width, with 38% of its gravity and a day of about 24 hours 40 minutes.
sections.b: Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun and about half Earth's diameter. Its surface gravity is about 38% of ours, so a 70-kilogram person would feel like they weighed about 27 kilograms. A Martian day, called a sol, lasts about 24 hours and 40 minutes, remarkably close to our own, but a Martian year takes 687 Earth days. Its distinctive red colour comes from iron oxide, essentially rust, in its dust and rocks. It has two small, lumpy moons, Phobos and Deimos, which may be captured asteroids.

sections.key: Mars's atmosphere is under 1% of Earth's pressure, mostly carbon dioxide, with an average near −60°C.
sections.b: Mars is a harsh place. Its atmospheric pressure is less than 1% of Earth's, and the air is made mostly of carbon dioxide, far too thin to breathe and too thin to keep liquid water stable on the surface for long. The average temperature is around −60°C, though a summer afternoon near the equator can briefly rise above 0°C. Mars has no global magnetic field, so harmful radiation from the Sun and deep space reaches the ground. Dust storms are common, and every few years some grow to cover almost the whole planet.

sections.key: Mars has Olympus Mons, the tallest volcano known, and the enormous canyon Valles Marineris.
sections.b: Mars holds some of the most spectacular landforms in the solar system. Olympus Mons is the largest known volcano, rising about 22 kilometres, about two and a half times the height of Mount Everest, and about 600 kilometres across. The canyon system Valles Marineris stretches about 4,000 kilometres, nearly as long as Australia is wide, and plunges up to about 7 kilometres deep. These features grew so large partly because Mars has lower gravity and no moving tectonic plates, so volcanoes stayed over the same hot spots for enormous lengths of time.

sections.key: Missions since the 1960s have mapped Mars; rovers Spirit and Opportunity far outlived their plans.
sections.b: Humans have been sending robots to Mars since the 1960s, and many early missions failed. NASA's Mariner 4 sent back the first close-up photos in 1965, showing a cratered, lifeless-looking surface. The Viking landers touched down in 1976 and tested soil for signs of life, with results most scientists read as inconclusive. The small Sojourner rover arrived in 1997. In 2004 the twin rovers Spirit and Opportunity landed, planned to last about 90 sols; Opportunity kept working for more than 14 years, driving over 45 kilometres before a dust storm ended it in 2018.

sections.key: Curiosity (2012) and Perseverance (2021) are car-sized, nuclear-powered rovers searching for habitable conditions.
sections.b: Curiosity landed in Gale Crater in August 2012, lowered to the ground by a rocket-powered 'sky crane'. Car-sized and powered by a nuclear battery, it confirmed that the crater once held a lake that could have supported microbes. Perseverance landed in Jezero Crater, an ancient river delta, in February 2021. It has been collecting rock samples in sealed tubes for possible return to Earth, but NASA's Mars Sample Return program lost its funding in early 2026, so no mission is currently approved to bring them home. Australian-born geologist Abigail Allwood leads one of its instruments, PIXL. Its companion helicopter Ingenuity made the first powered flight on another planet.

sections.key: Mars had liquid water long ago; today its water is mostly frozen in polar caps and underground ice.
sections.b: Orbiters and rovers have found dried riverbeds, ancient deltas, lakebed sediments and minerals that only form in water, strong evidence that liquid water flowed on Mars billions of years ago. The planet may have had a thicker atmosphere then, before much of it was stripped into space. Today, most of its water is frozen: the polar caps contain water ice topped seasonally by carbon dioxide frost, and ice lies buried beneath large areas of the surface. In 2008 NASA's Phoenix lander scraped up and confirmed water ice. Whether small amounts of liquid water exist today is still debated.

sections.key: A human Mars trip takes about 7 months each way, with a 2–3 year round mission.
sections.b: Earth and Mars line up favourably about every 26 months, so launch windows are limited. At best, a trip takes around six to nine months each way, and crews would likely need to stay a year or more waiting for the planets to realign, making a round mission two to three years. Radio messages take between about 3 and 22 minutes each way, so crews can't rely on real-time help from Earth. The biggest challenges include radiation exposure, landing heavy loads through the thin air, toxic perchlorate salts in the soil and the psychological strain of isolation.

sections.key: Future explorers plan to use Martian resources; Perseverance's MOXIE made oxygen from Martian air.
sections.b: Carrying everything from Earth would be impossibly expensive, so planners want to 'live off the land', a strategy called in-situ resource utilisation. Perseverance carried a toaster-sized experiment, MOXIE, which successfully produced oxygen from the carbon dioxide in Martian air, proof the idea can work. Buried ice could provide water, and combining it with carbon dioxide could make methane rocket fuel for the journey home. Several space agencies and companies have announced crewed Mars plans, but timelines have repeatedly slipped. Most experts expect the first human landing to be at least a decade or more away.

quiz.q: Why is Mars red?
o: Iron oxide, or rust, in its dust and rocks
Its atmosphere is made of red gas
quiz.e: Iron oxide in the soil and dust gives Mars its colour.

quiz.q: What is Olympus Mons?
o: The largest known volcano in the solar system
quiz.e: Olympus Mons rises about 22 km, about two and a half times the height of Everest.

quiz.q: How long was Opportunity originally planned to last?
quiz.e: It was planned for about 90 sols but kept working for over 14 years.

quiz.q: Where is most of Mars's water today?
o: In the atmosphere as rain clouds
Frozen in polar caps and underground ice
quiz.e: Mars's water is now mostly frozen at the poles and beneath the surface.

quiz.q: What did the MOXIE experiment on Perseverance achieve?
o: It flew the first Mars helicopter
It produced oxygen from Martian air
quiz.e: MOXIE turned carbon dioxide from the atmosphere into oxygen.

LESSONS.title: How computers actually work
LESSONS.hook: Every photo, message and game on your devices comes down to billions of tiny switches flicking on and off, billions of times a second.

sections.key: At heart, a computer is a vast collection of tiny electronic switches that are either on or off.
sections.b: Strip away the screen and the software, and a computer is a machine that stores and changes patterns of on and off. Each tiny switch represents a 1 (on) or a 0 (off). One switch can't do much, but billions of them, wired together cleverly and flipped in precise sequences, can add numbers, compare words, draw pictures and play music. Everything a computer appears to understand, from your bank balance to a cat video, is really a pattern of these switches. The genius is not in any single part, but in how simple parts are layered into something powerful.

sections.key: The transistor, invented at Bell Labs in 1947, is the electronic switch at the heart of every modern chip.
sections.b: Early computers used bulky vacuum tubes as switches. The American ENIAC, finished in 1945, used about 17,000 of them and weighed around 27 tonnes. Australia's first computer, CSIRAC, built in Sydney in 1949, was one of the world's earliest stored-program computers and is now held by Melbourne Museum. The breakthrough came in 1947, when John Bardeen, Walter Brattain and William Shockley at Bell Labs built the first transistor: a tiny solid-state switch, controlled by electricity itself, that needed no glowing filament and was far smaller, cooler and more reliable than a vacuum tube. The first transistor used germanium, but today's transistors are made from silicon, a material found in ordinary sand, which is why California's chip region became known as Silicon Valley.

sections.key: Transistors are combined into logic gates like AND, OR and NOT, which make simple yes-or-no decisions.
sections.b: A handful of transistors wired together makes a logic gate, a circuit that takes one or more on/off inputs and produces an output by a fixed rule. An AND gate outputs 1 only if both inputs are 1. An OR gate outputs 1 if either input is 1. A NOT gate flips its input. The maths behind this was worked out by the English mathematician George Boole in the 1850s, long before electronics existed. Combine enough gates and you can build a circuit that adds two numbers, then one that multiplies, compares and remembers. Every calculation your device performs is built from these tiny decisions.

sections.key: The CPU follows instructions one small step at a time, billions of times per second.
sections.b: The central processing unit, or CPU, is the part that actually carries out instructions. It works in a relentless loop: fetch the next instruction from memory, decode what it means, execute it, then move on. Each instruction is tiny, like 'add these two numbers' or 'jump to step 50 if this value is zero'. The trick is speed. A CPU running at 3 gigahertz ticks through about 3 billion clock cycles every second, and modern chips have several cores working side by side. Programs feel smooth and clever because millions of dull, simple steps happen faster than you can blink.

sections.key: RAM is fast, temporary working memory that is wiped when the power goes off.
sections.b: The CPU needs somewhere to keep the data it's working on right now. That's random-access memory, or RAM. Think of it as a workbench: fast to reach, but limited in size and cleared at the end of the day. RAM is volatile, meaning it loses everything when the power is cut, which is why unsaved work disappears in a blackout. When you open an app, it's copied from storage into RAM so the CPU can reach it quickly. If you open too many apps and RAM fills up, the computer has to shuffle data back and forth, and everything slows down.

sections.key: Storage, like an SSD or hard drive, keeps data permanently, even with the power off.
sections.b: Storage is the long-term filing cabinet. Older computers used hard disk drives, which store data magnetically on spinning platters read by a tiny arm, a bit like a record player. Most modern laptops and all smartphones use solid-state drives (SSDs), which store data in flash memory chips with no moving parts. SSDs are much faster, quieter and tougher when dropped. Storage is far larger than RAM but slower to reach, which is why a computer keeps what it's actively using in memory and everything else on the drive. When people say a phone has '256 gigabytes', they mean its storage.

sections.key: Moore's law observed that the number of transistors on a chip roughly doubled every two years.
sections.b: In 1965, Gordon Moore, who later co-founded Intel, noticed that the number of transistors that could fit on a chip was doubling at a steady rate. He later revised his estimate to about every two years, and the prediction became known as Moore's law. It isn't a law of physics, but it held remarkably well for decades, driving computers from room-sized machines to pocket devices. Today's top chips hold tens of billions of transistors. Progress has slowed as parts approach the size of a few dozen atoms, and engineers now also gain speed through smarter designs and specialised chips.

sections.key: Knowing the parts helps you buy wisely: CPU for speed, RAM for multitasking, storage for space.
sections.b: Understanding the basics makes tech choices easier. If a computer feels sluggish with many tabs open, more RAM often helps more than a faster CPU. If you keep running out of room for photos, you need more storage, or a cloud backup. An SSD is one of the best upgrades for an older computer still running a hard drive. And restarting a device genuinely helps, because it clears RAM of clutter from programs that didn't tidy up after themselves. Most of all, remember that behind every 'smart' device is a very fast, very obedient machine following simple instructions written by people.

quiz.q: What did Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley invent at Bell Labs in 1947?
quiz.e: The transistor, a small, reliable solid-state switch, replaced bulky, power-hungry vacuum tubes.

quiz.q: What does an AND gate do?
o: Outputs 1 only if both inputs are 1
quiz.e: An AND gate only outputs 1 when both of its inputs are 1.

quiz.q: Why does unsaved work vanish in a blackout?
o: RAM is volatile and loses data without power
quiz.e: RAM only holds data while powered, so anything not saved to storage is lost.

quiz.q: What does Moore's law describe?
o: The speed of the internet doubling yearly
Transistor counts on chips doubling roughly every two years
quiz.e: Gordon Moore observed transistor counts doubling regularly, later settling on about every two years.

quiz.q: What does a CPU running at 3 gigahertz do?
o: Completes about 3 billion clock cycles per second
quiz.e: Gigahertz measures clock speed: 3 GHz is about 3 billion cycles every second.

LESSONS.title: Binary: the language of computers
LESSONS.hook: With just two digits, 0 and 1, computers store every word you've typed, every song you've streamed and every photo you've taken.

sections.key: Computers use binary because their switches have two reliable states: on and off.
sections.b: We count in base ten, probably because we have ten fingers. Computers count in base two, or binary, using only 0 and 1. The reason is practical: a computer's transistors are switches, and it's easy and reliable to tell 'on' from 'off', but hard to reliably distinguish ten different voltage levels amid electrical noise. Two states are robust. The German mathematician Gottfried Leibniz published a description of binary arithmetic in 1703, centuries before electronic computers. He was fascinated that everything could be expressed with just 1 and 0. He had no idea how right he would turn out to be.

sections.key: In binary each place value doubles: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and so on, so 1011 means 11.
sections.b: In our decimal system, each column is worth ten times the one to its right: ones, tens, hundreds. In binary, each column is worth twice the one to its right: ones, twos, fours, eights, sixteens. So the binary number 1011 means one eight, no fours, one two and one one: 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11. Counting from zero goes 0, 1, 10, 11, 100, 101, 110, 111, 1000. It looks strange at first, but the logic is identical to decimal, just with a smaller set of digits. There's an old joke: there are 10 kinds of people, those who understand binary and those who don't.

sections.key: A bit is a single 0 or 1; a byte is 8 bits, which can represent 256 different values.
sections.b: A single binary digit is called a bit, short for 'binary digit'. One bit can only say yes or no. Group eight bits together and you get a byte, which can represent 256 different values, from 00000000 to 11111111, or 0 to 255. From there the units grow: a kilobyte is about a thousand bytes, a megabyte about a million, a gigabyte about a billion and a terabyte about a trillion. Confusingly, some systems count in powers of two, so a kilobyte can mean 1,024 bytes. Note that internet speeds are usually quoted in megabits per second, not megabytes, so 100 Mbps is about 12.5 megabytes per second.

sections.key: Text is stored by giving every character a number, using standards like ASCII and Unicode.
sections.b: Computers don't store letters, they store numbers that stand for letters. In the 1960s, the ASCII standard assigned numbers to 128 characters: capital A is 65, which in binary is 01000001, lowercase a is 97, and a space is 32. ASCII only covered English, so the Unicode standard was created to include the world's writing systems. It now defines more than 150,000 characters, from Chinese and Arabic to mathematical symbols and emoji. When you text a smiley face, you're really sending a code number that your friend's phone looks up and draws. Occasionally a garbled message appears when two systems disagree about the code.

sections.key: Digital images are grids of pixels, each stored as numbers for its red, green and blue levels.
sections.b: A digital photo is a grid of tiny coloured squares called pixels. Each pixel's colour is usually stored as three numbers, for how much red, green and blue light it contains, each from 0 to 255. That's one byte per colour, giving about 16.7 million possible colours. Pure red is 255, 0, 0; white is 255, 255, 255. A 12-megapixel phone photo contains about 12 million pixels, which would take roughly 36 megabytes stored raw. Formats like JPEG shrink files dramatically by discarding detail your eye is unlikely to notice, which is why saving the same photo again and again slowly degrades it.

sections.key: Sound is digitised by measuring the sound wave thousands of times per second and storing each measurement.
sections.b: Sound is a vibration, a smooth wave of changing air pressure. To store it, a microphone converts the wave into an electrical signal, and the computer measures that signal at regular intervals, a process called sampling. Audio CDs, introduced in the early 1980s, take 44,100 samples every second, each stored as a 16-bit number. Played back quickly enough, those measurements recreate a wave your ears hear as continuous. Formats like MP3 and those used by streaming services compress the data by removing sounds humans can barely hear, such as quiet tones masked by louder ones, cutting file sizes by around 90%.

sections.key: Programs are also stored as binary, so the same memory can hold data and the instructions that use it.
sections.b: Perhaps the most important idea in computing is that instructions themselves are numbers. A program is a long list of binary codes the processor recognises, such as 'add', 'compare' or 'jump'. Programmers rarely write in raw binary: they write in languages like Python or JavaScript, and special software translates their code into machine code. Storing programs in memory alongside data, an idea developed in the 1940s and associated with John von Neumann and others, means a computer can run completely different software without being rewired. The same laptop can be a typewriter, a cinema or a calculator, depending on which numbers it's running.

sections.key: Understanding bits and bytes helps you judge storage, download speeds and file sizes.
sections.b: Binary thinking has practical uses. When comparing internet plans, remember to divide megabits by eight to estimate megabytes per second. When a phone warns that storage is full, you'll know that videos, especially 4K ones, are usually the biggest culprits, since they're thousands of images per minute plus sound. You'll understand why compressed photos look blotchy when zoomed in, and why sending a 'high quality' file takes longer. Most of all, binary is a reminder that computers don't understand meaning: they shuffle numbers. The meaning comes from the people who designed the codes, and from you.

quiz.q: What is the binary number 1011 in decimal?
How many bits are in a byte?
quiz.e: A byte is 8 bits, allowing 256 different values.

quiz.q: What does Unicode do?
o: Assigns numbers to characters from the world's writing systems
quiz.e: Unicode gives every character a code number, covering more than 150,000 characters.

quiz.q: How is a pixel's colour usually stored?
o: As a word describing the colour
As red, green and blue values from 0 to 255
quiz.e: Each pixel usually stores red, green and blue levels, one byte each.

quiz.q: How many times per second does CD audio sample sound?
quiz.e: CD audio takes 44,100 samples per second, each a 16-bit number.

LESSONS.title: What's inside your smartphone
LESSONS.hook: The phone in your pocket holds more computing power than the machines that guided astronauts to the Moon, plus a dozen sensors you probably never think about.

sections.key: A smartphone is a full computer built around a single system-on-a-chip.
sections.b: A modern smartphone is a complete computer squeezed into a slab about 8 millimetres thick. Its heart is a system-on-a-chip, a single piece of silicon that combines the main processor, a graphics processor, memory controllers, image processing and, increasingly, specialised circuits for artificial intelligence. Squeezing it all together saves space and power. Around it sit RAM, flash storage, radios, cameras, speakers, a battery and a screen. The Apollo Guidance Computer that helped land astronauts on the Moon in 1969 had only about 4 kilobytes of working memory. A typical phone today is many thousands of times more powerful.

sections.key: Phones use sensors like accelerometers, gyroscopes and magnetometers to sense movement and direction.
sections.b: Your phone is packed with sensors. An accelerometer measures movement and gravity, which is how the screen knows to rotate and how your step count is estimated. A gyroscope detects rotation, making motion games and steady video possible. A magnetometer senses Earth's magnetic field and acts as a compass. A proximity sensor turns off the screen when you hold the phone to your ear, and an ambient light sensor adjusts brightness. Many phones also have a barometer, which measures air pressure and helps estimate which floor of a building you're on. Combined with satellite positioning, these sensors let maps track you smoothly.

sections.key: Most touchscreens detect tiny changes in an electrical field caused by your conductive finger.
sections.b: Almost all smartphones use capacitive touchscreens. Beneath the glass is a fine grid of transparent conductors carrying a small electrical charge. Your body conducts electricity, so when a finger comes close, it disturbs the electrical field at that point, and the phone calculates exactly where. Because the grid can sense many points at once, you can pinch and zoom, which the first iPhone popularised in 2007. This is also why ordinary gloves don't work: fabric doesn't conduct. Special touchscreen gloves have conductive thread in the fingertips. Wet screens misbehave for a similar reason, since water droplets also disturb the field.

sections.key: Phone cameras rely on software, combining several quick shots into one better photo.
sections.b: Phone camera sensors are tiny compared with those in professional cameras, so they capture less light. Manufacturers compensate with computational photography. When you press the shutter, the phone often captures several frames in quick succession, some darker and some brighter, then aligns and merges them to reduce blur, rescue shadows and keep bright skies from washing out. Portrait mode uses depth information to blur the background artificially, and night modes stack many exposures. Multiple lenses offer wide, standard and zoom views. The result is that much of a good phone photo is created by software decisions, not just by the lens.

sections.key: Lithium-ion batteries power phones; heat and time gradually reduce how much charge they hold.
sections.b: Phones run on lithium-ion batteries, which store a lot of energy for their weight and can be recharged hundreds of times. Their development earned John Goodenough, Stanley Whittingham and Akira Yoshino the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Charging moves lithium ions from one side of the battery to the other; using the phone moves them back. Over time, chemical wear means the battery holds less charge, often noticeably after two or three years. Heat speeds that wear, so avoid leaving a phone in a hot car. Many phones now offer optimised charging that pauses at around 80% to reduce strain.

sections.key: Your phone connects to a cellular network of towers, each covering an area called a cell.
sections.b: When you make a call or load a web page, your phone sends radio signals to the nearest mobile tower. Networks divide the landscape into areas called cells, each served by an antenna, which is where the name 'cellular' comes from. As you move, your phone is handed from one cell to the next without dropping the connection. The tower links into the carrier's fibre network and on to the wider internet. Each generation, from 3G to 4G to 5G, has brought more speed and capacity. Australia's major carriers switched off their 3G networks in 2023 and 2024, retiring some older phones.

sections.key: Besides mobile data, phones use Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, NFC and satellite positioning.
sections.b: A smartphone contains several separate radios. Wi-Fi connects to your home router, usually faster and cheaper than mobile data. Bluetooth links to earbuds, watches and cars over short distances. Near-field communication (NFC) works only within a few centimetres, which makes it suited to tap-and-pay: when you tap your phone at a checkout, it sends a one-time payment code rather than your actual card number. A satellite receiver picks up signals from GPS and other navigation systems to work out your location. Some recent phones can even send emergency text messages directly to satellites where there's no mobile coverage.

sections.key: Install updates, protect the battery from heat and review app permissions regularly.
sections.b: A few habits make a phone last longer and stay safer. Install software updates promptly, because they fix security holes as well as adding features. Keep the phone out of heat and avoid running the battery completely flat too often. A case and screen protector are cheap insurance against expensive repairs. Check which apps can use your location, camera and microphone, and turn off access that isn't needed. Use a screen lock with a PIN, fingerprint or face recognition. And when you're done with an old phone, back it up, erase it properly and recycle it through a program like MobileMuster.

quiz.q: Which sensor lets your phone act as a compass?
quiz.e: The magnetometer senses Earth's magnetic field.

quiz.q: Why don't ordinary gloves work on most touchscreens?
o: They're too thick to press the glass
quiz.e: Capacitive screens detect a conductive finger disturbing an electrical field; fabric doesn't conduct.

quiz.q: What gradually reduces a phone battery's capacity?
o: Chemical wear, sped up by heat
quiz.e: Lithium-ion batteries wear chemically over time, and heat accelerates it.

quiz.q: Where does the word 'cellular' come from?
o: Networks divided into areas called cells
Prison cells where early phones were tested
quiz.e: Networks divide coverage into cells, each served by an antenna.

quiz.q: What does NFC tap-and-pay send at the checkout?
quiz.e: Tap-and-pay sends a one-time code instead of your real card number.

LESSONS.title: Passwords, passkeys and staying locked
LESSONS.hook: Billions of stolen passwords circulate online, and if you reuse yours, one leak can open every door you have.

sections.key: Reusing a password means one breach can expose every account that shares it.
sections.b: The single biggest password mistake is reuse. Websites get breached all the time, and stolen email and password pairs are collected, traded and sold in huge lists. Criminals then run automated attacks called credential stuffing, trying those pairs on banks, email providers, shopping sites and streaming services. If you used the same password for an old gaming forum and your email, a breach of the forum hands them your email too. And your email is the master key: whoever controls it can reset passwords for almost everything else. Unique passwords mean a breach stays contained to one site.

sections.key: Attackers guess short and common passwords very quickly; length is the best defence.
sections.b: When criminals steal a database of scrambled passwords, they use powerful computers to guess billions of combinations, checking each against the stolen data. They start with the most likely: '123456', 'password', names, sports teams, keyboard patterns and dictionary words with a number on the end. Swapping letters for symbols, like 'P@ssw0rd', fools almost nobody, because cracking tools try those substitutions automatically. What really slows attackers is length. Each extra character multiplies the number of possible combinations, so a long password can take vastly longer to crack than a short, 'complex' one. That's why security advice has shifted from complexity to length.

sections.key: A passphrase of four or more random words is long, strong and easy to remember.
sections.b: A passphrase strings several random words together, such as 'crystal onion clay pretzel'. It's long, which makes it hard to crack, yet much easier to remember than a jumble of symbols. The Australian Cyber Security Centre recommends passphrases of four or more random words. The key word is random: song lyrics, famous quotes and your children's names are predictable and appear in cracking lists. One well-known method is to pick words using dice and a word list. Use passphrases for the few things you must type from memory, such as your computer login, your phone and your password manager.

sections.h: Can you trust a password manager?
sections.key: Good password managers encrypt your vault so that even the company running them can't read it.
sections.b: Handing every password to one app feels risky, so it's worth knowing how good ones protect you. Reputable password managers encrypt your vault on your own device, using a key derived from your master passphrase, before anything is synced. The company stores only scrambled data it can't read, an approach often called zero-knowledge. That design was tested in 2022, when criminals stole customer vault backups from LastPass: well-protected vaults stayed locked, but people with weak master passwords were left exposed. So choose a strong, unique master passphrase, turn on multi-factor authentication for the vault, and set up recovery or emergency-access options in case you're ever locked out.

sections.key: Security questions are weak passwords in disguise; give random answers and store them in your password manager.
sections.b: Many accounts let you reset a password by answering questions like your mother's maiden name or your first pet, which can quietly undo all your careful password work. The answers are often public or guessable. When Google researchers analysed users' security answers in 2015, they found an attacker had nearly a one-in-five chance of guessing English speakers' answer to 'What is your favourite food?' in a single try. The answer: pizza. Around 40% of users also couldn't remember their own answers when needed. Inventing an answer only helps if it's truly random, because people often pick the same predictable fakes. Treat each answer like a password: generate a random one and save it in your password manager.

sections.key: Passkeys replace passwords with a cryptographic key on your device that can't be phished or reused.
sections.b: Passkeys are a newer technology designed to replace passwords altogether, backed by Apple, Google, Microsoft and the industry group the FIDO Alliance. When you create a passkey, your device makes a matching pair of cryptographic keys. The website stores the public key; the private key stays protected on your devices and is never shared with the website. To sign in, you just unlock your device with your face, fingerprint or PIN. Because there's no password to type, there's nothing to steal in a breach, nothing to reuse, and a fake website can't trick you, since the passkey only works with the real site. Where it's offered, it's worth using.

sections.key: Breach-checking services show whether your email has appeared in known data leaks.
sections.b: You can check whether your email address has appeared in known data breaches using Have I Been Pwned, a free service created by Australian security researcher Troy Hunt. Many password managers also warn you about reused, weak or leaked passwords. If you find you've been caught up in a breach, change that password immediately, plus any account where you reused it, and turn on multi-factor authentication. Watch for scam messages that mention details from the breach, since criminals use leaked information to sound convincing. If identity documents were exposed, IDCARE, Australia's national identity and cyber support service, offers free help.

sections.key: Start with your email: unique passphrase, MFA on, then move outwards to banking and the rest.
sections.b: You don't have to fix everything at once. Start with your main email account: give it a unique passphrase and turn on multi-factor authentication, because it's the key to resetting everything else. Then do the same for banking, myGov and social media. Set up a password manager and let it replace old passwords gradually as you log in to each site. Switch to passkeys wherever they're offered. Write down recovery codes and keep them somewhere safe offline. Finally, keep your devices updated. These few steps put you ahead of most attackers, who prefer easy targets and will simply move on.

quiz.q: What is credential stuffing?
o: Guessing passwords one letter at a time
Trying stolen email and password pairs on many other sites
Filling a form with fake data
quiz.e: Criminals test leaked username and password pairs across many sites, exploiting reuse.

quiz.q: What makes a password hardest to crack?
quiz.e: Each extra character multiplies the combinations; symbol swaps are tried automatically.

quiz.q: What is one well-known way to choose truly random words for a passphrase?
o: Use lines from your favourite song
Roll dice and look the numbers up in a word list
Pick the first words that come to mind
quiz.e: Dice take human habits out of the choice; lyrics, names and words that 'feel random' are more predictable than they seem.

quiz.q: What did a 2015 Google study find about the security question 'What is your favourite food?'
o: An attacker could guess many people's answer, pizza, nearly one time in five
It was the hardest question to guess
quiz.e: Common answers make security questions easy to guess, so use random answers stored in a password manager.

quiz.q: Why can't passkeys be phished by a fake website?
o: They only work with the genuine site they were created for
quiz.e: A passkey is tied to the real website, so a lookalike site can't use it.

LESSONS.title: Phishing: don't take the bait
LESSONS.hook: Most cyber attacks don't start with genius hackers breaking code. They start with a message that convinces a real person to click.

sections.key: Phishing is a fake message designed to trick you into giving away information, money or access.
sections.b: Phishing is when criminals pretend to be someone you trust, like your bank, a delivery company, the tax office or your boss, to trick you into clicking a link, opening an attachment, handing over details or sending money. The name, spelled with 'ph' in the style of early phone hackers, comes from the idea of fishing: cast enough bait and someone will bite. It began in the 1990s with emails aimed at internet account holders, and it remains one of the most common ways attacks begin, because fooling a person is often far easier than breaking through security technology.

sections.key: Phishing arrives by email, text (smishing), phone call (vishing), social media and even QR codes.
sections.b: Phishing has spread well beyond email. Scam text messages, sometimes called smishing, often claim a parcel is waiting, a toll is unpaid or an account is locked. Phone scams, or vishing, use a live voice, sometimes a spoofed caller ID showing a real bank's number. Social media messages may come from hacked friends' accounts. Fake QR codes stuck over real ones in car parks can lead to lookalike payment pages. Increasingly, scammers use AI to write flawless messages or imitate voices. Some attacks are generic blasts to millions; others, called spear phishing, are carefully tailored to one person or business using details found online.

sections.key: Phishing works by triggering urgency, fear, curiosity or greed so you act before you think.
sections.b: Phishing messages are designed to push emotional buttons. Urgency: 'Your account will be closed in 24 hours.' Fear: 'Suspicious activity detected' or 'You owe unpaid tax.' Curiosity: 'Is this you in this photo?' Greed or hope: 'You've won a gift card' or 'Claim your refund.' Authority: a message that seems to come from a manager, police or government. All of these aim at the same thing: getting you to act quickly, before your careful thinking catches up. Once you recognise that pressure itself is a warning sign, many scams become much easier to see through.

sections.key: Watch for mismatched links and senders, unexpected requests, pressure, and requests for codes or payment.
sections.b: Common red flags include: a sender address or phone number that doesn't quite match the organisation; links that lead to odd web addresses, like 'mybank-secure-login.co' instead of the real site; an unexpected attachment or invoice; a generic greeting; pressure to act immediately; and any request for passwords, one-time codes, card details or remote access to your computer. On a computer, hover over a link to preview its real destination. Be careful, though: modern scams can look polished, use your name and appear in the same message thread as genuine texts. The absence of red flags doesn't prove a message is safe.

sections.key: Scammers impersonate suppliers or bosses to redirect payments to their own bank accounts.
sections.b: Businesses are prime targets for a scam called business email compromise. Criminals hack or imitate a supplier's email account, then send a convincing message saying their bank details have changed. The next invoice gets paid into the scammer's account. Others pose as a senior manager urgently asking staff to transfer money or buy gift cards. Home buyers are targeted too, with fake emails from 'conveyancers' giving new account details for a deposit. The defence is simple but must be firm: always verify any change of bank details by phoning the person on a number you already have, never the one in the email.

sections.key: Never use the contact details in a suspicious message; go to the organisation yourself.
sections.b: The single most useful habit is to verify independently. If a message claims to be from your bank, don't click its link or call its number. Instead, open your banking app, type the bank's address into your browser yourself, or phone the number on the back of your card. The same goes for the tax office, myGov, delivery companies and toll roads. If a friend or relative messages from a new number asking for money, call them on their old number. Genuine organisations won't mind you checking. The ACCC's Scamwatch sums it up as three steps: stop, check, protect.

sections.key: Act fast: contact your bank, change passwords, turn on MFA and report it.
sections.b: If you think you've fallen for phishing, act quickly and don't be embarrassed; smart people are caught every day. If you gave out card or bank details or sent money, call your bank immediately using its official number, as it may be able to stop payments. If you entered a password, change it straight away, along with any account using the same one, and turn on multi-factor authentication. If you installed software or gave someone remote access, disconnect from the internet and get trusted help. For identity theft, IDCARE offers free support. The Australian Cyber Security Hotline, 1300 CYBER1, can also advise.

sections.key: Report scams to Scamwatch and cybercrime to ReportCyber, which helps protect others.
sections.b: Reporting helps authorities warn others and disrupt scammers. In Australia, report scams to Scamwatch, run by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission, at scamwatch.gov.au. Report cybercrime, such as hacked accounts or online fraud, through ReportCyber at cyber.gov.au, run by the Australian Signals Directorate's Australian Cyber Security Centre. You can also report scam messages to the organisation being impersonated, and most email and messaging apps have a 'report' or 'block' button. If money was lost, contact your bank first. Even a report that doesn't recover your money can help stop the same scam reaching someone else.

quiz.q: What is 'smishing'?
quiz.e: Smishing is phishing delivered by SMS text message.

quiz.q: Why do phishing messages often create urgency?
o: To make you act before thinking carefully
quiz.e: Urgency and fear push people to act quickly, before careful thinking catches up.

quiz.q: An email from a supplier says their bank details have changed. What should you do?
o: Reply to the email to confirm
Phone the supplier on a number you already have
Click the link to update records
quiz.e: Always verify changes by phoning a number you already know, never one in the email.

quiz.q: You realise you've typed your email password into a fake login page. What should you do first?
o: Wait to see if anything happens
Change that password straight away, plus anywhere you reused it, and turn on MFA
Reply to the phishing email to complain
Delete the email and do nothing else
quiz.e: Acting fast locks the criminal out before they can use the password or reset your other accounts.

quiz.q: Where do Australians report cybercrime such as hacked accounts?
quiz.e: ReportCyber, run by the Australian Cyber Security Centre, takes cybercrime reports.

LESSONS.title: Your data and your privacy
LESSONS.hook: Every tap, search and purchase leaves a trace. Here's who collects it, what happened when big companies lost it, and what rights you have.

sections.key: Many free services are paid for with data about you, used mainly to target advertising.
sections.b: Many of the most popular online services, from search engines to social media, are free to use. They make money largely by selling advertising, and ads are worth more when they're targeted at the right people. That means detailed knowledge about you, such as your age, location, interests, habits and purchases, has real commercial value. There's an old saying online: if you're not paying for the product, you are the product. That's a simplification, since data also improves services and fights fraud, but it's a useful reminder that 'free' usually involves a trade, even if you never see the price.

sections.key: Cookies, tracking pixels, app data, location and device fingerprinting build a picture of you.
sections.b: Tracking happens in many ways. Cookies are small files websites store in your browser; third-party cookies, placed by advertisers, can follow you across many sites. Tracking pixels, tiny invisible images in emails and web pages, report when you open or view something. Apps may collect your location, contacts and usage patterns. Device fingerprinting identifies you from your device's unique combination of settings, even without cookies. Loyalty cards link purchases to your identity. Separately, data brokers gather and trade information from many sources to build profiles. Individually each piece seems harmless; combined, they can reveal a surprising amount about your life.

sections.key: In 2022 the Optus breach exposed personal details of roughly 10 million current and former customers.
sections.b: In September 2022, telecommunications company Optus revealed a cyber attack that exposed personal information of around 10 million current and former customers, among the largest data breaches in Australian history. Details included names, dates of birth, phone numbers and addresses, and for many people, driver's licence or passport numbers. Millions had to replace identity documents, and governments and banks increased monitoring for fraud. The incident sparked national debate about why companies were keeping so much data, sometimes about customers who had left years earlier, and it helped drive tougher privacy penalties passed later that year. Legal and regulatory action followed.

sections.key: The 2022 Medibank breach exposed data of about 9.7 million people, including some health claims information.
sections.b: Weeks after Optus, in October 2022, health insurer Medibank was hit by a cyber attack affecting data of about 9.7 million current and former customers. Along with personal details, criminals accessed health claims information for many people. Medibank refused to pay the ransom demanded, in line with government advice, and the criminals published some of the stolen data online. In 2024, the Australian Government imposed cyber sanctions on a Russian man it identified as responsible. The breach showed how sensitive health information can be exploited, and why storing less data, and protecting it well, matters so much.

sections.key: The Privacy Act 1988 and its 13 Australian Privacy Principles govern how organisations handle personal information.
sections.b: In Australia, the main law is the Privacy Act 1988. It includes 13 Australian Privacy Principles that set rules for how personal information is collected, used, stored, disclosed and kept secure. It applies to federal government agencies and to most businesses and not-for-profits with annual turnover above $3 million, plus some smaller ones, such as health service providers. States and territories have their own laws for their agencies. The Act is overseen by the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC). It has been updated several times, including reforms in 2022 and 2024, and further changes have been under discussion.

sections.key: You can generally ask to see and correct your information, and must be told of serious breaches.
sections.b: Under the Privacy Act, you generally have the right to know why an organisation is collecting your personal information and how it will be used. You can ask to access the information held about you and request that incorrect information be corrected. You can often choose not to identify yourself, where that's practical, and opt out of direct marketing. Since 2018, the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme has required covered organisations to notify you and the OAIC when a breach is likely to cause serious harm. If you're unhappy with how your information was handled, complain to the organisation first, then to the OAIC.

sections.key: Review app permissions, ad and tracking settings, and share less information by default.
sections.b: You can reduce tracking without going off the grid. On your phone, review which apps can access your location, contacts, camera and microphone, and switch off anything unnecessary. On iPhones, you can ask apps not to track you across other apps; Android has similar ad privacy settings. In your browser, block third-party cookies or use a privacy-focused browser. Check social media privacy settings, and think twice before posting your birthday, address or holiday dates publicly. When a form asks for information, ask whether it's really needed. Data you never hand over can't be leaked, sold or misused later.

sections.key: If your data is breached, follow the company's advice, change passwords, watch accounts and beware of follow-up scams.
sections.b: If you're told your data was caught in a breach, read the notice carefully to see exactly what was exposed. Change affected passwords and turn on multi-factor authentication. If identity documents were exposed, follow advice about replacing them; some agencies can issue new licence numbers. Consider a free credit ban through Australia's credit reporting bodies if you're worried about identity fraud, and watch bank statements closely. Be especially wary of follow-up scam messages using your leaked details. IDCARE provides free support. This is general information only: for a specific legal problem, talk to a lawyer or community legal centre.

quiz.q: What can third-party cookies do?
o: Follow your activity across many websites
quiz.e: Advertisers use third-party cookies to track you across different sites.

quiz.q: What happened in the 2022 Optus breach?
o: Personal details of around 10 million current and former customers were exposed
The mobile network was permanently shut down
quiz.e: Names, birth dates, contact details and many ID numbers were exposed.

quiz.q: How did Medibank respond to the ransom demand in 2022?
quiz.e: Medibank refused to pay, and criminals published some stolen data.

quiz.q: Which businesses does the Privacy Act generally cover?
o: Most businesses with turnover above $3 million, plus some smaller ones
quiz.e: It covers federal agencies and most businesses with turnover over $3 million, plus some smaller ones like health providers.

quiz.q: What does the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme require?
o: Companies to delete all data yearly
Notification of breaches likely to cause serious harm
Customers to report breaches to police
quiz.e: Covered organisations must notify affected people and the OAIC about serious breaches.

LESSONS.title: Hacking: myth and reality
LESSONS.hook: Forget the hoodie in a dark room typing green code. Real hacking is often slower, stranger and much more human than the movies suggest.

sections.key: The word 'hacker' began as praise for clever tinkering, not a label for criminals.
sections.b: The word 'hacker' traces back to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in the late 1950s and 1960s, where members of a model railway club used 'hack' to describe a clever, playful solution to a technical problem. Early hackers were enthusiasts who loved understanding systems deeply and making them do unexpected things. Only later, as computers spread and break-ins made headlines in the 1980s, did the word come to mean someone who gets into systems without permission. Many in the security world still use it in the original sense, which is why you'll meet proud, law-abiding 'hackers' working for banks and governments.

sections.key: White hats hack with permission to improve security; black hats break in illegally; grey hats sit in between.
sections.b: Borrowing from old Western films, the security world describes hackers by hat colour. White hats are ethical hackers who test systems with permission, find weaknesses and help fix them. Many work as penetration testers, paid to attack an organisation's defences before criminals do. Black hats break into systems illegally, for money, data, disruption or bragging rights. Grey hats fall in between: they might probe a system without permission but then report the flaw rather than exploit it. Even with good intentions, accessing a computer system without authorisation is a crime in Australia under Commonwealth and state laws.

sections.key: Most attacks exploit known weaknesses: unpatched software, reused passwords and misconfigured systems.
sections.b: Real attacks are rarely feats of pure genius. Many criminals use automated tools to scan the internet for computers running outdated software with publicly known security flaws, then exploit whichever ones haven't been patched. Others use leaked passwords, poorly configured cloud storage left open to the world, or accounts without multi-factor authentication. A 'zero-day' is a flaw unknown to the software maker, so no fix exists yet; these are rare and valuable, and more often used by well-resourced groups, including some linked to governments. For most people and businesses, the threat is opportunistic attackers looking for an easy way in.

sections.key: Social engineering manipulates people rather than machines, and is behind a large share of attacks.
sections.b: Often the easiest way into a system is through a person. Social engineering means manipulating people into giving up access or information: a phishing email, a phone call pretending to be IT support, a fake courier who tailgates staff through a secure door, or a USB stick left in a car park labelled 'salaries'. The American hacker Kevin Mitnick, once one of the FBI's most wanted, became famous for talking his way into systems rather than cracking code, and later worked as a security consultant. Technology can't fully fix this, which is why training people to pause and verify matters so much.

sections.key: Ransomware locks or steals an organisation's data and demands payment, often in cryptocurrency.
sections.b: Ransomware is malicious software that encrypts an organisation's files so they can't be used, then demands payment, usually in cryptocurrency, for the key. Many modern gangs also steal data first and threaten to publish it, called double extortion. In 2017, the WannaCry attack spread worldwide within days, disrupting parts of Britain's National Health Service. Hospitals, councils, schools and businesses of all sizes are targets. Paying offers no guarantee of recovery and funds further crime, which is why governments generally advise against it. Since 2025, larger Australian businesses must report ransomware payments to the government. Good offline backups are the best defence.

sections.key: Bug bounty programs pay ethical hackers to find and report security flaws responsibly.
sections.b: Many companies now invite hackers to attack them, within rules. Bug bounty programs offer rewards to anyone who finds a security flaw and reports it privately so it can be fixed before criminals find it. Netscape ran one of the first in 1995. Today, large technology companies, banks and governments run programs, and payouts for serious flaws can reach tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars. The practice of reporting privately and giving the company time to fix a problem before going public is called responsible or coordinated disclosure. It has turned many curious tinkerers into a valuable, legitimate line of defence.

sections.key: Attackers range from lone opportunists to organised criminal gangs and state-backed groups.
sections.b: Attackers vary widely. At one end are opportunists using ready-made tools bought online. In the middle are organised criminal groups that operate like businesses, with specialists, customer support for victims paying ransoms, and even affiliate schemes where they rent their ransomware to others. At the far end are groups linked to governments, which may pursue espionage, theft of intellectual property or disruption of critical infrastructure. Hacktivists attack for political causes. In Australia, the Australian Signals Directorate works to defend against serious cyber threats and publishes an annual cyber threat report summarising the trends it sees.

sections.key: Most attacks can be blocked by basics: updates, MFA, unique passwords, backups and a healthy pause.
sections.b: The good news is that most attacks target easy weaknesses, so basic hygiene defeats a large share of them. Keep devices and apps updated, since patches close the holes attackers scan for. Use unique passwords or passkeys, and turn on multi-factor authentication. Keep backups, including one that isn't permanently connected, so ransomware can't reach it. Be sceptical of unexpected messages and verify requests independently. If hacking fascinates you, there are legal ways to learn: capture-the-flag competitions, practice labs designed for training, and university and TAFE cybersecurity courses. Australia needs more skilled defenders, and curiosity is where they start.

quiz.q: Where did the word 'hacker' originally come from?
o: Enthusiasts at MIT describing clever technical solutions
quiz.e: It began at MIT as praise for clever, playful problem-solving.

quiz.q: What is a white hat hacker?
o: An ethical hacker who tests systems with permission
Someone who writes viruses for fun
quiz.e: White hats test systems with permission to help fix weaknesses.

quiz.q: What is social engineering?
o: Manipulating people into giving access or information
quiz.e: Social engineering targets people rather than machines.

quiz.q: What is the best defence against ransomware?
quiz.e: Backups that ransomware can't reach let you restore without paying.

quiz.q: What does a bug bounty program do?
o: Pays people to find and report security flaws responsibly
quiz.e: Bug bounties reward ethical hackers for privately reporting flaws.

LESSONS.title: The Mechanical Turk: a chess machine with a secret
LESSONS.hook: For over 80 years, a turbaned automaton beat chess players across Europe and America. The truth inside its cabinet still echoes through modern AI.

sections.key: In 1770 Wolfgang von Kempelen unveiled a chess-playing ‘machine’ at the Habsburg court in Vienna.
sections.b: Wolfgang von Kempelen was a Hungarian-born engineer and civil servant serving Empress Maria Theresa. In 1770 he presented her court with something astonishing: a life-sized figure dressed in Ottoman-style robes and a turban, seated behind a large wooden cabinet with a chessboard on top. Kempelen claimed it could play chess against any challenger. Audiences watched the figure's mechanical arm reach out, grasp a piece and move it, sometimes nodding or shaking its head when an opponent made an illegal move. It usually won. Kempelen himself seemed slightly embarrassed by its fame, dismissing it as a trifle, and for years he reportedly kept it packed away. But the public could not get enough of the machine that seemed to think.

sections.key: Each demonstration began by opening the cabinet to show gears, as if proving nothing was hidden.
sections.b: Before every game the operator performed a careful ritual. He opened the cabinet's doors one at a time, shining a candle inside to reveal a dense tangle of cogs, wheels and levers. He lifted the figure's robes to show more machinery. Only then did he wind the device with a key, and the clicking of clockwork filled the room. The routine was brilliant theatre. By showing the audience the inside of the cabinet piece by piece, never all at once, it convinced most onlookers they had seen everything. The whirring was real, but it was mostly there for effect. People came away certain that the machine contained only machinery, which was exactly what they were meant to believe.

sections.key: A strong human chess player hid in the cabinet, sliding on a seat to stay out of sight.
sections.b: The secret was simple and daring: a skilled chess player was hidden inside. The interior was cleverly arranged so the operator could slide along on a moving seat as different doors were opened, staying behind panels and fake machinery. Above his head, each chess piece on the board carried a magnet, which tugged on small metal markers beneath the board so he could follow the game. He worked out his moves on a small pegboard of his own, and steered the Turk's arm with a system of levers. A candle provided light, with smoke escaping through the figure's turban. Over the decades, a series of strong players worked as operators, cramped and sweating in the dark.

sections.key: The Turk toured Europe and America for decades and is said to have played some very famous opponents.
sections.b: In the 1780s the Turk toured Europe, including Paris and London. Accounts say it played Benjamin Franklin in Paris. After Kempelen's death in 1804, it was bought by Johann Nepomuk Maelzel, a showman and inventor best remembered for promoting the metronome. Under Maelzel it is said to have played Napoleon in 1809, and stories claim the emperor tested it with illegal moves until the figure swept the pieces off the board. Some of these tales were embroidered in the retelling, so it is wise to hold them loosely. Maelzel took the Turk to the United States in 1826, where it toured cities for years and drew large paying crowds.

sections.key: Writers including Edgar Allan Poe argued that a human must be hidden inside.
sections.b: Not everyone was fooled. Several writers published theories about how the trick worked, and in 1836 Edgar Allan Poe wrote an essay called ‘Maelzel's Chess-Player’ arguing that a person must be concealed inside. Poe made a sharp point: a true machine would win every game, yet the Turk sometimes lost. Some of his other reasoning was wrong, but his central conclusion was right. After Maelzel died in 1838, the Turk ended up in a museum in Philadelphia, where it was destroyed by fire in 1854. Only afterwards did a son of its last owner publish a detailed account of the secret, confirming what the sceptics had long suspected.

sections.key: In 2005 Amazon named a crowd-work platform after the Turk, openly embracing its trick.
sections.b: The Turk's name came back to life in 2005, when Amazon launched a service called Amazon Mechanical Turk. It lets businesses post small online tasks that are easy for people but hard for computers, such as describing a photo, checking whether two products are the same or transcribing a blurry receipt. Thousands of workers around the world complete these tasks for small payments. Amazon described the idea as ‘artificial artificial intelligence’: like the original Turk, it looks like a computer doing the work, but humans are quietly inside. Platforms like this became a major source of the labelled data that later trained machine learning systems, including image recognisers.

sections.key: Much of today's AI still depends on hidden human labour, and on our willingness to be impressed.
sections.b: The Turk's lesson is still relevant. Modern AI systems learn from huge amounts of data that people have created, sorted and labelled, often low-paid workers in many countries. Humans also rate chatbot answers to teach them which responses are helpful, and moderate the disturbing content that filters miss. Some start-ups have been caught presenting services as automated while staff did much of the work behind the scenes. None of this means AI is fake. It means the line between machine and human effort is often blurrier than it looks. Like eighteenth century audiences, we tend to see intelligence where clever presentation invites us to, so it pays to ask who, or what, is really doing the work.

quiz.q: How did the Mechanical Turk really play chess?
o: A hidden human player operated it from inside the cabinet
Kempelen signalled moves from the audience
quiz.e: A strong chess player hid inside, following the game with magnets and steering the arm with levers.

quiz.q: Why did the operator open the cabinet's doors one at a time?
o: To let the machine cool down
To convince audiences they had seen everything inside
To check the candle was lit
quiz.e: Showing the interior piece by piece let the hidden player shift position while the audience believed nothing was concealed.

quiz.q: What point did Edgar Allan Poe make about the Turk?
o: A true machine would never lose, yet the Turk sometimes did
quiz.e: Poe argued that a genuine machine would win every time, so occasional losses suggested a human mind inside.

quiz.q: What does Amazon Mechanical Turk do?
o: Lets businesses pay people to do small tasks computers struggle with
quiz.e: Amazon called it ‘artificial artificial intelligence’: humans quietly doing work that appears automated.

quiz.q: What is a modern parallel to the Turk's secret?
o: AI systems relying heavily on hidden human labour such as data labelling
Chess programs that refuse to lose
quiz.e: AI learns from data that people create and label, and humans rate and moderate its output behind the scenes.

LESSONS.title: Where the word ‘robot’ came from
LESSONS.hook: The word ‘robot’ is barely a century old. It was born in a Czech play about manufactured workers who rise up against their makers.

sections.key: The word ‘robot’ first appeared in Karel Čapek's 1920 play R.U.R.
sections.b: In 1920 the Czech writer Karel Čapek published a play called R.U.R., short for Rossum's Universal Robots. It premiered in Prague in January 1921 and was soon performed in New York, London and beyond, carrying a new word into dozens of languages.
