The play is set in a factory on a remote island that mass-produces artificial workers. They are cheap, tireless and obedient, and the world's economy comes to depend on them. Human beings, freed from labour, grow idle and stop having children. Eventually the robots rebel and wipe out almost all of humanity. A science fiction warning about technology and work arrived, complete with its own vocabulary.

sections.key: ‘Robot’ comes from the Czech ‘robota’, meaning forced or drudging labour.
sections.b: Čapek credited his brother Josef, a painter and writer, with suggesting the word. Karel had been planning to call the creatures ‘labori’, from the Latin for work, but felt it sounded too bookish. Josef proposed ‘roboti’. It came from the Czech word ‘robota’, which means drudgery or forced labour, and historically referred to the unpaid work serfs owed to their landlords. The choice was pointed. Čapek's robots are not simply machines; they are a new servant class, created only to work. The name carried a hint of exploitation from the very start, and that is part of why the story of robots rebelling against their owners felt so natural to audiences.

sections.key: Čapek's original robots were made of synthetic flesh, closer to what we would now call androids.
sections.b: If you picture R.U.R.'s robots as clanking metal figures, you are picturing a later idea. Čapek's robots were assembled from an artificial organic material, a kind of synthetic protoplasm, mixed in vats and shaped into bodies. They looked almost human and were built in factories like any other product. In modern terms they resemble biological androids more than mechanical machines. The image of the robot as a metal man came mostly from later films, magazine covers and toys of the 1920s and 1930s, such as the gleaming robot in Fritz Lang's 1927 film Metropolis. Over time the word ‘robot’ shifted to mean any machine that senses, decides and acts in the world.

sections.key: People built lifelike moving machines long before anyone called them robots.
sections.b: The dream is ancient. Greek myths described bronze guardians like Talos, said to patrol the island of Crete. In the first century AD, Hero of Alexandria wrote about devices driven by water, air and weights, including self-opening temple doors. In 1206 the engineer Ismail al-Jazari, working in what is now Turkey, described intricate water-powered automata, including a band of mechanical musicians. In eighteenth century Switzerland, Pierre Jaquet-Droz and his collaborators built ‘The Writer’, a doll-sized boy who dips a quill in ink and writes a programmable message. It still works and is displayed in a museum in Neuchâtel. These machines were marvels of clockwork, though none could sense or respond to the world.

sections.key: Science fiction writer Isaac Asimov coined ‘robotics’ and imagined robots built with safety rules.
sections.b: In the 1940s the American writer Isaac Asimov grew tired of stories where robots always turned on their creators. He imagined robots designed with built-in safeguards, which he set out as the Three Laws of Robotics in his 1942 story ‘Runaround’. In short: a robot must not harm a human or allow one to come to harm through inaction; it must obey human orders unless that conflicts with the first law; and it must protect itself unless that conflicts with the first two. Asimov also coined the word ‘robotics’. Many of his best stories are actually about the laws failing in unexpected ways, an early insight into how hard it is to turn values into rules.

sections.key: The Unimate arm, installed at a General Motors plant in 1961, began the age of industrial robots.
sections.b: Real robots arrived in factories rather than living rooms. The American inventor George Devol patented a programmable arm, and businessman Joseph Engelberger helped turn it into a product. In 1961 their machine, the Unimate, went to work at a General Motors plant in New Jersey. It lifted hot pieces of die-cast metal and stacked them, a dangerous and unpleasant job. It looked nothing like Čapek's humanoids, just a heavy arm bolted to the floor, but it could be reprogrammed for different tasks. Today millions of industrial robots weld, paint, pack and assemble around the world, mostly doing repetitive work in carefully controlled environments rather than walking among us.

sections.key: A century on, Čapek's themes of labour, control and rebellion still shape how we talk about AI.
sections.b: It is remarkable how much of today's debate was already present in a play from 1920. R.U.R. asked what happens to people when machines do all the work, who profits from artificial labour, and whether created beings could ever deserve rights. Its robot uprising became a template repeated in countless films. Many researchers think that template distorts public thinking, since real risks from AI tend to be less dramatic, involving errors, bias, misuse and economic disruption rather than armies of rebellious machines. Even so, Čapek's choice of a word meaning forced labour was a sharp reminder that technology is never only about machines. It is also about the people who build them, own them and live alongside them.

quiz.q: What does the Czech word ‘robota’ mean?
quiz.e: ‘Robota’ meant drudgery or forced labour, such as the unpaid work serfs owed their landlords.

quiz.q: In R.U.R., what happens to the robots' makers?
o: The robots rebel and wipe out almost all of humanity
quiz.e: Čapek's play ends with the robots rising up against the humans who made them.

quiz.q: What were Čapek's original robots made of?
o: An artificial organic material, like synthetic flesh
quiz.e: They were biological creations, closer to what we would now call androids than to metal machines.

quiz.q: What is notable about many of Asimov's robot stories?
o: They explore how the Three Laws fail in unexpected ways
They show robots always obeying perfectly
They have no humans in them
quiz.e: Asimov used the laws as a source of puzzles, revealing how hard it is to turn values into rules.

quiz.q: What job did the first Unimate robot do?
o: Lifting and stacking hot die-cast metal parts
quiz.e: Installed at a General Motors plant in 1961, it handled hot metal castings, a dangerous task for people.

LESSONS.title: Will machines take our jobs? What history says
LESSONS.hook: People have feared that machines would make human work obsolete for over 200 years. The real story is more surprising, and more uncomfortable, than either side admits.

sections.key: Between 1811 and 1816, English textile workers smashed machines that threatened their livelihoods.
sections.b: In 1811, in the English Midlands and north, groups of skilled textile workers began breaking into workshops at night and smashing machinery. They signed their letters in the name of ‘General Ludd’ or ‘King Ludd’, a mythical leader. The movement spread through Nottinghamshire, Yorkshire and Lancashire. The government responded harshly, sending thousands of soldiers, making machine-breaking a capital crime in 1812, and hanging or transporting many Luddites, some of them to Australia. Today ‘Luddite’ is an insult meaning someone who hates technology. Historians point out that is unfair. The Luddites were not opposed to machines as such. They objected to machines being used to cut wages, employ unskilled labour and produce shoddier goods.

sections.key: For some workers, mechanisation brought decades of hardship before things improved.
sections.b: It is tempting to say the Luddites were simply wrong, since Britain went on to become far richer. But for many workers the suffering was real and long-lasting. Hand-loom weavers are the classic example. Once relatively well-paid craftspeople, they saw their wages collapse over several decades in the early nineteenth century as power looms took over, and many families sank into poverty. Economic historians still debate how quickly ordinary workers' living standards rose during the Industrial Revolution, and some argue wages lagged behind productivity for a long time. The lesson is that new technology can make a society richer overall while leaving particular people, towns and trades much worse off for a generation or more.

sections.key: Machines replaced most farm work, yet people found new kinds of jobs.
sections.b: Consider farming. Around 1900, roughly two in five American workers worked on farms, and the share in Australia was also large. Today it is a small fraction in both countries, thanks to tractors, harvesters, fertilisers and better crops. If you had told a farmer in 1900 that most farm jobs would vanish, they might have predicted mass unemployment. Instead, people moved into factories, offices, shops, schools and hospitals, doing jobs that had barely existed before. Rising productivity made food cheaper, which left people with more money to spend on other things, which created demand for new kinds of work. Over the long run, this pattern has repeated again and again.

sections.key: Economists warn against assuming there is only a fixed amount of work to go around.
sections.b: A common mistake in debates about automation is called the lump of labour fallacy. It is the idea that there is a fixed amount of work in an economy, so if machines do more of it, there must be less left for people. History suggests the amount of work is not fixed. When technology makes something cheaper, people often buy more of it, and the savings get spent elsewhere, creating new jobs. New technologies also create entirely new industries, from car repair to web design. Of course, avoiding this fallacy does not guarantee everything will work out. It just means ‘machines do more, so humans do less’ is too simple.

sections.key: Cash machines spread widely, yet the number of US bank tellers did not collapse for decades.
sections.b: Automated teller machines spread through banks from the 1970s onwards. It seemed obvious that human tellers would disappear. Yet the economist James Bessen found that in the United States, the number of bank teller jobs held up and even grew for decades after ATMs arrived. Cheaper branches meant banks opened more of them, and tellers shifted towards customer service and selling financial products. The full story has a twist, though. Teller numbers did eventually fall, mainly as online and mobile banking spread. The ATM puzzle shows that automation usually changes the tasks within jobs before it removes jobs, and that the effects can play out in unexpected ways over long periods.

sections.key: Most technologies automate particular tasks, reshaping jobs rather than simply deleting them.
sections.b: Many economists find it useful to think of a job as a bundle of tasks. A lawyer drafts documents, researches cases, advises clients and argues in court. Technology tends to automate some of those tasks while leaving others, and sometimes making the remaining ones more valuable. Spreadsheets automated a great deal of calculation, yet the number of accountants and analysts grew, because their time shifted to interpreting numbers and advising people. The economist John Maynard Keynes, writing in 1930, popularised the phrase ‘technological unemployment’ but also predicted that his grandchildren might work around 15 hours a week. Neither mass unemployment nor the 15-hour week arrived. Instead, the mix of what people do kept changing.

sections.key: AI reaches into thinking work, and economists genuinely disagree about how this time will unfold.
sections.b: Past waves of automation mostly replaced muscle and routine tasks. AI can now draft text, write code, summarise documents and analyse images, reaching into work that once seemed safely human. Some economists expect the familiar pattern: disruption, then new jobs and higher living standards. Others worry the change could be faster and broader than before, giving workers less time to adapt, or could concentrate gains among a small number of companies. Honest forecasters admit deep uncertainty. What history does teach clearly is that how a society handles the transition matters enormously, through education, retraining, safety nets and who shares in the gains. The Luddites' real question, who benefits from new machines, has never gone away.

quiz.q: What did the Luddites mainly object to?
o: Machines being used to cut wages and lower quality
quiz.e: Historians argue the Luddites targeted the way machines were used against workers, not technology itself.

quiz.q: What happened to many hand-loom weavers during the Industrial Revolution?
o: Their wages collapsed over decades as power looms spread
quiz.e: Mechanisation made Britain richer overall but left many weavers' families in poverty for a generation or more.

quiz.q: What is the lump of labour fallacy?
o: The mistaken idea that there is a fixed amount of work to share
The belief that heavy jobs are best automated
A rule about maximum working hours
The idea that robots are lazy
quiz.e: The amount of work is not fixed: cheaper goods and new industries tend to create new demand and new jobs.

quiz.q: What happened to US bank teller numbers after ATMs spread?
o: They fell to zero within five years
They held up and even grew for decades, before later falling with online banking
quiz.e: Cheaper branches meant more branches, and tellers shifted to service and sales, until online banking changed things again.

quiz.q: Why do economists often think in terms of tasks rather than jobs?
o: Because technology usually automates some tasks in a job, reshaping it
Because tasks are easier to tax
Because all tasks are automated at once
quiz.e: A job is a bundle of tasks; automating some can shift people's time to others, as spreadsheets did for accountants.

LESSONS.title: How spam filters learned to fight junk mail
LESSONS.hook: Every day, filters quietly throw away enormous amounts of junk email before you ever see it. Their story is one of the first great victories of everyday machine learning.

sections.key: In 1978 a marketer sent an unsolicited advertisement to hundreds of users of the early internet.
sections.b: On 3 May 1978, Gary Thuerk, a marketing manager at the computer company Digital Equipment Corporation, sent a message to several hundred users of ARPANET, the network that grew into the internet. It invited them to presentations of the company's new computers. Back then, ARPANET was meant for government and research use, and the reaction was swift and angry. An official reminded users it was not to be used for advertising. Thuerk later said the message led to some sales, which is exactly why unsolicited mass email never went away. When email reached the general public in the 1990s, sending a million messages cost almost nothing, and a tiny response rate could still turn a profit.

sections.key: The name comes from a Monty Python sketch where the word drowns out everything else.
sections.b: In a 1970 episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus, a couple try to order breakfast in a café where almost every dish contains Spam, the canned meat. A group of Vikings in the café keep bursting into song, chanting ‘Spam, Spam, Spam’ until no one can hear anything else. Early internet users, many of them Python fans, borrowed the word for floods of repetitive, unwanted messages that drowned out real conversation in chat rooms and discussion forums. The name stuck. A notorious 1994 case, when two lawyers advertised their immigration services to thousands of Usenet discussion groups at once, helped bring both the practice and the word to wider attention.

sections.key: Early filters used hand-written rules, which spammers quickly learned to dodge.
sections.b: The first defence against spam was a list of rules. Block email containing certain phrases, such as ‘make money fast’. Block messages written in all capitals. Block known spam senders. These rules worked briefly, but spammers adapted almost instantly. They misspelled words, swapped letters for numbers, hid text inside images, and constantly changed the addresses they sent from. Meanwhile, rigid rules caught innocent messages, such as a doctor's email that happened to mention a medicine name. Writing rules by hand turned into an endless game of catch-up. The problem needed a system that could learn from examples and keep updating itself as the junk changed.

sections.key: In 2002 a widely read essay showed that simple probability could filter spam remarkably well.
sections.b: In 2002 the programmer Paul Graham published an essay called ‘A Plan for Spam’. He described a filter based on Bayesian probability, an approach that researchers had also been exploring. Instead of fixed rules, the filter looks at a collection of emails already sorted into spam and genuine mail. For each word, it calculates how much more often it appears in one pile than the other. A new email is then scored by combining the evidence from its most telling words. Words like ‘unsubscribe’ or ‘winner’ might push it towards spam, while your colleague's name or a project's jargon pushes it the other way. The approach was simple, effective and personal, because it learned from your own mail.

sections.key: Every time you mark a message as spam or not spam, you help train the filter.
sections.b: Spam filtering is a classic example of supervised machine learning: learning from examples labelled with the right answer. When you click ‘report spam’ or rescue a message from the junk folder, you supply exactly those labels. Large email providers combine signals from vast numbers of users, so a new scam campaign reported by early recipients can be blocked for everyone else within a short time. Modern filters look far beyond words. They check where a message came from, how that sender has behaved before, whether links lead to known scam sites, and whether the email passes technical checks proving it really came from the domain it claims, using standards with names like SPF, DKIM and DMARC.

sections.key: Filters must balance catching junk against wrongly hiding real email.
sections.b: Every filter makes two kinds of mistakes. A false negative lets spam into your inbox, which is annoying. A false positive sends a real message to the junk folder, which can be far worse if it is a job offer, a bill or a message from a friend. Filters can be tuned to be stricter or more relaxed, but reducing one kind of error usually increases the other. Most email providers lean towards letting a little spam through rather than losing genuine mail. That is why it is worth checking your junk folder occasionally, especially when you are waiting for something important, such as a booking confirmation or a password reset.

sections.h: An arms race that never ends
sections.key: Spam and phishing keep evolving, so filters are only one layer of protection.
sections.b: Spammers and filter builders are locked in an arms race. As filters improved, many criminals moved from selling dodgy products to phishing, crafting emails that impersonate banks, delivery companies or government agencies to steal passwords and money. Some now use AI to write fluent, personalised messages without the spelling mistakes that once gave scams away. Laws help too. Australia's Spam Act 2003, enforced by the Australian Communications and Media Authority, requires commercial messages to have consent, identify the sender and include a way to unsubscribe. But no filter is perfect. The best final layer is you: slow down, check the sender, and never click a link in an unexpected message asking you to log in or pay.

quiz.q: Where does the word ‘spam’ for junk messages come from?
o: An acronym for ‘sending pointless advertising mail’
A Monty Python sketch where the word drowns out conversation
The first company to send junk mail
quiz.e: In the sketch, Vikings chanting ‘Spam’ drown everything out, much like floods of unwanted messages.

quiz.q: Why did hand-written spam rules struggle?
o: Spammers quickly adapted, and rigid rules blocked innocent emails
They worked perfectly but were too expensive
quiz.e: Spammers misspelled words and changed tactics, while fixed rules caught genuine messages.

quiz.q: How does a Bayesian spam filter judge an email?
o: By the length of the subject line
By asking the sender to confirm
By combining evidence from words that appear more in spam or genuine mail
By the time it was sent
quiz.e: It learns from already sorted emails which words point towards spam and which towards genuine mail.

quiz.q: What happens when you click ‘report spam’?
o: You provide a labelled example that helps train the filter
quiz.e: Your clicks are labels, the raw material of supervised learning, and help protect other users too.

quiz.q: Why do email providers usually lean towards letting some spam through?
o: Wrongly hiding a real email can be worse than seeing some junk
quiz.e: A false positive can bury an important message, so providers accept a little spam to avoid that.

LESSONS.title: Clever Hans and the AI that learned the wrong lesson
LESSONS.hook: A horse that seemed to do maths, and computers that seemed to diagnose disease, turned out to be solving a different problem altogether. Here's how AI can be right for the wrong reasons.

sections.key: In early 1900s Berlin, a horse named Clever Hans appeared to answer maths questions by tapping his hoof.
sections.b: In the early 1900s, a retired German schoolteacher named Wilhelm von Osten toured Berlin with his horse, Hans. Ask Hans to add five and three, and he would tap his hoof eight times. He seemed to handle fractions, dates and even spelling. Crowds were amazed, and von Osten genuinely believed his horse could think. In 1904 a commission of experts examined Hans and found no sign of deliberate trickery. Then the psychologist Oskar Pfungst ran careful experiments. When the questioner did not know the answer, or Hans could not see them, his accuracy collapsed. Hans was not counting. He was reading tiny, unconscious changes in posture and expression that told him when to stop tapping.

sections.key: AI systems can find shortcuts in their data that produce correct answers without real understanding.
sections.b: Clever Hans had learned something genuinely impressive, just not what people thought. Machine learning systems do the same. A model is trained to get the right answer on its examples, and it will use whatever patterns help, whether or not they are the ones we intended. If some accidental feature in the data happens to line up with the right answers, the model may latch on to it, because that is often easier than learning the real thing. Researchers call this shortcut learning. Unlike specification gaming, where a system exploits a badly worded goal, shortcut learning happens even when the goal is sensible. The data quietly offers an easier path, and the model takes it.

sections.key: A deliberately flawed experiment showed an image classifier could judge animals by their backgrounds.
sections.b: In 2016 a team of researchers wanted to show how easily a classifier could fool people. They trained a model to tell wolves from huskies, deliberately choosing photos in which the wolves had snow behind them and the huskies did not. The model performed well on similar photos. But when the researchers used a tool to highlight which parts of each image mattered, it became clear the model was largely looking at the snow, not the animal. It was effectively a snow detector. They then showed the results to volunteers, many of whom trusted the model until they saw the explanation. The experiment was a warning: high accuracy alone does not tell you what a system has learned.

sections.key: Medical image models have learned to recognise hospitals and pen marks instead of disease.
sections.b: Shortcut learning becomes serious in medicine. In a 2018 study, researchers found that deep learning models trained on chest X-rays could identify which hospital an image came from, using subtle clues such as markings and equipment. Because some hospitals had sicker patients, the hospital itself helped predict disease, and the models performed worse when tested on X-rays from elsewhere. In 2019, dermatologists reported that a skin cancer classifier was more likely to call a mole cancerous if it had been marked with a surgical skin marker, which doctors often draw on suspicious spots. In both cases the system had partly learned to recognise doctors' habits rather than the disease itself.

sections.h: A famous story that may be a myth
sections.key: The often-told tale of a tank-spotting AI that really detected weather is probably not true.
sections.b: For decades, AI lectures have repeated a story about an early neural network trained to spot camouflaged tanks in photos. It did perfectly in testing but failed in the field, because, the story goes, all the tank photos had been taken on cloudy days and the network had learned to detect the weather. It is a perfect parable, but researchers who have tried to trace it have found no solid evidence it ever happened. Versions differ in the details, the dates and even the country. It is best treated as an illustrative legend. The good news is that we no longer need it, because real, well-documented examples of shortcut learning are now plentiful.

sections.key: Testing on genuinely new data and asking what the model is looking at can reveal hidden shortcuts.
sections.b: Pfungst exposed Clever Hans by changing the conditions: he hid the questioner and used questions nobody in the room knew the answer to. AI researchers use similar tricks. The most important is testing a model on data from different sources than it was trained on, such as X-rays from another hospital or photos from another country. If performance drops sharply, a shortcut may be to blame. Researchers also use explanation tools that highlight which parts of an input influenced a decision, and they deliberately alter images or text to see whether irrelevant changes flip the answer. Collecting more varied training data, where accidental patterns no longer line up with the answers, makes shortcuts harder to learn.

sections.key: When an AI seems brilliant, it is worth asking what else could explain its success.
sections.b: The deepest lesson of Clever Hans is about us, not the horse. Von Osten was honest, and the experts who first examined Hans were not fools. They simply did not ask what else might explain the results. When a review in 2021 examined dozens of published AI models for diagnosing COVID-19 from chest scans, it found none ready for clinical use, with many suffering from flaws including biased or mismatched data. Impressive accuracy figures can hide a narrow trick. Whenever you hear that an AI can detect something remarkable, it is worth thinking like Pfungst: what exactly was it tested on, and could it be picking up on something other than what we think?

quiz.q: How did Clever Hans really get his answers right?
o: He was reading unconscious cues from the people around him
His owner used a hidden signal on purpose
quiz.e: Pfungst showed Hans reacted to tiny, unintended changes in posture and expression that told him when to stop tapping.

quiz.q: What is shortcut learning in AI?
o: Training a model faster by skipping data
A model using accidental patterns in data that happen to predict the answer
quiz.e: Models take whatever path predicts the answers, even if it's not the one we intended.

quiz.q: What did the 2018 chest X-ray study find?
o: Models could identify which hospital an X-ray came from, which helped predict disease
X-rays cannot be used by AI
Models only worked on broken bones
quiz.e: Hospital clues correlated with disease rates, so models did worse on X-rays from other hospitals.

quiz.q: What is the status of the famous ‘tank in cloudy weather’ story?
o: It was proven in a military report
It is the first documented case of AI
There is no solid evidence it happened, so it's best treated as a legend
quiz.e: Researchers who traced the story found no reliable source, though real examples of shortcut learning now exist.

quiz.q: What is one of the best ways to catch a shortcut?
o: Test it on data from different sources than its training data
Ask the model if it is cheating
quiz.e: If accuracy drops sharply on genuinely new data, the model may have relied on a shortcut.

LESSONS.title: How computers learned to understand speech
LESSONS.hook: Talking to a phone feels effortless now, but getting a machine to hear words took seventy years of clever engineering. Here is how ‘wreck a nice beach’ became ‘recognise speech’.

sections.key: Spoken words run together, vary between speakers and change with context.
sections.b: When you listen to someone talk, you hear separate words. But the sound itself is mostly a continuous stream with no clear gaps between words. Each speech sound, or phoneme, changes shape depending on the sounds around it, a blending called coarticulation. Accents, age, speed, mood, background noise and microphone quality all change the signal further. Different phrases can sound almost identical: ‘recognise speech’ and ‘wreck a nice beach’ is a classic example engineers use. People resolve these puzzles effortlessly using knowledge of language and context. A computer starts with nothing but a fast-changing sequence of air pressure measurements, sampled thousands of times a second, and must somehow work out what was meant.

sections.key: The first recognisers in the 1950s and 1960s could understand only digits and a handful of words.
sections.b: In 1952 researchers at Bell Laboratories in the United States built a system nicknamed Audrey. It could recognise spoken digits from zero to nine, mostly when spoken clearly by a voice it had been tuned for. It filled a rack of electronics. A decade later, at the 1962 Seattle World's Fair, IBM demonstrated the Shoebox, a device that understood 16 spoken words, including the digits and commands like ‘plus’ and ‘minus’, and could do simple sums. These early machines matched the sound patterns of whole words against stored templates. That worked for a tiny vocabulary and a single careful speaker, but it could never scale up to everyday conversation.

sections.key: Recognisers analyse speech as a spectrogram, a picture of which frequencies are present over time.
sections.b: A key step in nearly every speech system is turning raw sound into something more useful. The audio is chopped into tiny overlapping slices, each lasting a few hundredths of a second. For each slice, the system measures how much energy is present at different frequencies, low rumbles through to high hisses. Laid side by side, these measurements form a spectrogram, a kind of picture of sound in which time runs left to right and pitch runs bottom to top. Vowels show up as distinctive bands, and sounds like ‘s’ appear as high-frequency fuzz. Trained experts can learn to read some words from spectrograms by eye, and machines learn to read them far faster.

sections.key: From the 1970s, probability-based models beat attempts to hand-code linguistic rules.
sections.b: In the 1970s the United States defence research agency DARPA funded a major speech understanding programme. One of its standout results, a Carnegie Mellon University system called Harpy, could handle a vocabulary of around a thousand words. Over the following years, researchers at IBM and elsewhere championed a statistical approach built on hidden Markov models. Instead of hand-writing rules about how language works, these models calculate probabilities: how likely a stretch of sound is to be a particular phoneme, and how likely one word is to follow another. Given enough recorded speech to learn from, statistics proved more reliable than expert rules. The approach dominated speech recognition for roughly three decades.

sections.key: Consumer dictation arrived in the 1990s, and voice assistants went mainstream in the 2010s.
sections.b: In 1997 Dragon Systems released Dragon NaturallySpeaking, one of the first products that let ordinary people dictate continuous speech on a home computer, rather than pausing between every word. It needed training on the user's voice and a quiet room, but it was a real milestone, especially for people unable to type easily. Accuracy was still frustrating for many users. The next big leap came around 2010 to 2012, when teams at universities and technology companies showed that deep neural networks could cut error rates substantially. Combined with huge amounts of recorded speech and cloud computing, this made smartphone voice assistants and automatic video captions practical for millions of people.

sections.key: Smart speakers listen locally for a short trigger phrase before sending audio anywhere.
sections.b: A common worry about smart speakers is that they are constantly recording everything. In normal operation, they work in two stages. A small, low-power model running on the device itself listens continuously, but only for a short wake word, such as the assistant's name. Only when it thinks it has heard that phrase does the device start recording the request and, typically, send it to powerful computers elsewhere for full recognition. The wake word detector is deliberately simple, so it sometimes triggers by mistake on similar sounds, accidentally capturing snippets of conversation. Most devices let you review and delete recordings and mute the microphone, which is worth knowing if privacy matters to you.

sections.key: Speech recognition still works better for some accents, ages and voices than others.
sections.b: Speech systems learn from the recordings they are trained on. If those recordings mostly feature certain accents, they work best for people who sound like that. Studies have found commercial systems making noticeably more errors for some groups, including speakers of particular dialects, people with strong regional or non-native accents, children, older adults and people with speech impairments. This matters more as voice becomes a way to access services, from banking to medical transcription. Developers are collecting more diverse speech data and letting systems adapt to individual voices, but equal accuracy for everyone remains an unfinished job.

quiz.q: Why is speech hard for computers to recognise?
o: Words run together and sounds change with speaker and context
Computers cannot process sound at all
quiz.e: Speech is a continuous stream where sounds blend, and accents, noise and context all change the signal.

quiz.q: What is a spectrogram?
o: A list of all words in a language
A picture showing which frequencies are present in sound over time
quiz.e: Time runs left to right and frequency bottom to top, turning sound into an image a system can analyse.

quiz.q: What approach dominated speech recognition from around the 1980s?
o: Statistical models based on probability, such as hidden Markov models
quiz.e: Probability-based models learned from recorded speech and proved more reliable than expert-written rules.

quiz.q: How does a smart speaker normally decide when to start recording a request?
o: It records everything all the time
It only works when you press a button
It waits for a phone call
A small on-device model listens for a wake word first
quiz.e: Only after detecting the wake word does it record the request and usually send it on for full recognition.

quiz.q: Why can speech recognition work worse for some people?
o: Some voices are too quiet to record
Training data has often under-represented certain accents, ages and voices
It is designed only for one language
quiz.e: Systems work best for voices like those in their training data, so diverse data is key to fairness.

LESSONS.title: How AI learns: walking downhill in the fog
LESSONS.hook: Behind almost every modern AI lies one surprisingly simple idea: take a small step in the direction that makes your mistakes smaller, then repeat it billions of times.

sections.key: Gradient descent is like finding your way down a mountain in thick fog by always stepping downhill.
sections.b: Imagine you are standing on a mountainside in dense fog. You cannot see the valley, but you want to reach the lowest point. A sensible strategy is to feel the slope beneath your feet, take a step in whichever direction goes downhill most steeply, then feel again and repeat. You will gradually descend, even without ever seeing the whole landscape. This is the core idea of gradient descent, the method used to train nearly all modern neural networks. The mountain represents how wrong the model is, and every position on it is a different setting of the model's internal numbers. Learning means walking downhill towards fewer mistakes.

sections.key: A loss function turns a model's errors into a single number that training tries to shrink.
sections.b: Before a model can improve, it needs a way to measure how badly it is doing. This measure is called the loss function. Suppose a model predicts house prices. For each house in the training data, you compare its prediction with the real price, and the loss combines those errors into one number. A big loss means poor predictions; a small loss means good ones. For a language model, the loss measures how surprised the model was by the actual next word in its training text. Choosing the loss is a crucial design decision, because the model will become very good at whatever it measures, which is not always exactly what we want.

sections.key: The gradient tells you how to adjust each of the model's parameters to reduce the loss.
sections.b: A neural network is controlled by parameters, also called weights, which you can picture as knobs. A small model might have thousands; today's largest have billions or more. Each combination of knob settings gives a different loss. The gradient is a mathematical object, from calculus, that tells you for every knob at once which way to turn it, and how strongly, to increase the loss fastest. So you turn every knob a little in the opposite direction. That single step lowers the loss slightly. The French mathematician Augustin-Louis Cauchy described this method back in 1847, long before computers. What changed was the scale at which it could be applied.

sections.key: The learning rate controls how big each step is, and getting it wrong can ruin training.
sections.b: How far should you step each time? This is controlled by a setting called the learning rate. If it is too small, training crawls, taking far too long to get anywhere useful. If it is too large, you overshoot the valley, leap up the opposite slope and may bounce around wildly or even climb higher. Picture taking giant strides on that foggy mountain: you might jump straight over the low point. Engineers spend a lot of effort tuning the learning rate, and common practice is to change it during training, often starting with larger steps and gradually shrinking them, so the model can settle into a good spot.

sections.key: Training can stall in places that aren't the lowest point, though in practice good solutions are usually found.
sections.b: Real loss landscapes are not smooth bowls. They are full of dips, ridges, plateaus and saddle points, places that slope down in some directions and up in others. In theory, walking downhill could trap you in a small hollow, a local minimum, far above the true lowest point. For a long time this was a major worry about neural networks. In practice, very large networks seem to train well anyway. Researchers have found that in landscapes with millions of dimensions, there is usually some direction still leading down, and many low points are roughly equally good. Exactly why training works so reliably is still an active area of research.

sections.key: Stochastic gradient descent uses small random batches of data, making training fast and practical.
sections.b: Calculating the exact slope would mean checking every single example in the training data before taking each step. With millions or billions of examples, that is painfully slow. Instead, nearly all training uses stochastic gradient descent, where stochastic means involving randomness. Each step uses a small, randomly chosen batch of examples, perhaps a few hundred, to estimate the slope. The estimate is noisy, so the path down the mountain wobbles, but each step is quick, and the wobble can even help the model avoid getting stuck. Over many passes through the data, those many small, imperfect steps add up to steady improvement. Clever variations on this method power most modern AI training.

sections.key: Backpropagation is the efficient method for working out the gradient in a deep network.
sections.b: There is one more problem. In a deep network with many layers, how do you work out how each of millions of weights contributed to the final error? The answer is backpropagation. It starts with the error at the output, then works backwards through the network, layer by layer, using the chain rule from calculus to share out responsibility for the mistake. Versions of the idea were developed by several people, but a 1986 paper by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton and Ronald Williams made it widely known for training neural networks. Backpropagation calculates the slope; gradient descent takes the step. Together, repeated over enormous datasets, they are the engine of today's deep learning.

quiz.q: What does a loss function do?
o: Turns a model's errors into a single number to be reduced
Chooses which language a model speaks
quiz.e: The loss measures how wrong the model is, and training aims to make it as small as possible.

quiz.q: What does the gradient tell you?
o: How many parameters a model has
How each parameter should change to increase the loss fastest
quiz.e: Training then nudges every parameter the opposite way, lowering the loss a little each step.

quiz.q: What can happen if the learning rate is too large?
o: The model overshoots and may bounce around or get worse
quiz.e: Giant steps can leap past the valley, like striding straight over the low point on a foggy mountain.

quiz.q: What makes gradient descent ‘stochastic’?
o: It uses the whole dataset for every step
Each step uses a small random batch of examples
quiz.e: Random mini-batches give quick, noisy estimates of the slope, which add up to steady progress.

quiz.q: What is backpropagation's job?
o: Efficiently working out how each weight contributed to the error
Testing the model on new data
quiz.e: It works backwards from the output using the chain rule, giving gradient descent the slope it needs.

LESSONS.title: Words as maps: how AI captures meaning
LESSONS.hook: Computers only understand numbers. So how can a machine know that ‘puppy’ is close to ‘dog’ and far from ‘spreadsheet’? The answer is to give every word a place on a giant map.

sections.key: Words that appear in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings.
sections.b: In 1957 the British linguist J. R. Firth wrote a line that has become a motto for language AI: ‘You shall know a word by the company it keeps.’ The idea, known as the distributional hypothesis, is that you can learn a lot about a word's meaning from the words that surround it. Consider an unfamiliar word in sentences like ‘the wombok was crisp and fresh’ and ‘she chopped the wombok for the stir-fry’. Even if you have never heard it, you can guess it is a vegetable. Words like ‘coffee’ and ‘tea’ appear near similar words, such as ‘cup’, ‘hot’ and ‘morning’. A computer can exploit exactly this pattern, given enough text.

sections.key: Giving each word an arbitrary ID number tells a computer nothing about meaning.
sections.b: The simplest way to feed words to a computer is to number them: ‘aardvark’ is word 1, ‘abacus’ is word 2, and so on. But these numbers carry no meaning. Word 500 is not more similar to word 501 than to word 40,000. To a system built this way, ‘cat’ and ‘kitten’ are as unrelated as ‘cat’ and ‘carburettor’. Anything it learns about one word cannot transfer to another. A better approach would represent each word so that words with related meanings get related numbers. That way, if a model learns that ‘dog’ goes with ‘bark’ and ‘walk’, it can guess something sensible about ‘puppy’ too.

sections.h: A map with hundreds of directions
sections.key: An embedding gives each word a list of numbers, placing it as a point in a high-dimensional space.
sections.b: The solution is called an embedding. Each word is represented by a list of numbers, often a few hundred long. You can think of each list as coordinates, placing the word at a point on an enormous map. On an ordinary map, two numbers, latitude and longitude, give a position. An embedding uses hundreds of dimensions, which we cannot picture, but the mathematics works the same way. Words used in similar contexts end up close together. ‘Sydney’, ‘Melbourne’ and ‘Brisbane’ cluster in one region, while ‘happy’, ‘glad’ and ‘cheerful’ cluster in another. Crucially, these positions are not chosen by people. The model learns them from huge amounts of text.

sections.key: A 2013 method called word2vec showed embeddings could capture relationships through arithmetic.
sections.b: In 2013 a team at Google led by Tomas Mikolov released word2vec, a fast method for learning embeddings from billions of words. It trained a simple network to predict words from their neighbours, and the embeddings emerged as a by-product. Researchers then noticed something striking. Directions on the map seemed to carry meaning. Take the position of ‘king’, subtract ‘man’, add ‘woman’, and the nearest word was ‘queen’. Similar tricks related countries to capitals and verbs to their past tenses. The famous examples were somewhat selected, and the arithmetic works less neatly in general than headlines suggested, but it showed that meaning had been captured in geometry, learned entirely from patterns in text.

sections.key: Embeddings absorb the stereotypes present in the text they learn from.
sections.b: Because embeddings learn from human writing, they also learn human prejudices. In 2016 researchers showed that word2vec embeddings trained on news articles completed analogies such as ‘man is to computer programmer as woman is to homemaker’. In 2017 another team found that embeddings reproduced many associations measured in psychological tests of human bias, linking some names, genders and groups with pleasant or unpleasant words. The embeddings were not programmed to be biased. They faithfully mapped the patterns in the language they were fed. This matters because embeddings are used inside search engines, recruitment tools and recommendation systems, where such associations can quietly shape real decisions about real people. Researchers have developed methods to measure and reduce these effects.

sections.key: Modern models create embeddings that change depending on the surrounding sentence.
sections.b: The original word embeddings had a weakness: each word got one fixed position. But many words have several meanings. ‘Bank’ means something different in ‘river bank’ and ‘bank loan’; ‘bat’ could be an animal or cricket gear. A single point on the map has to blur these together. From around 2018, new models, soon dominated by the transformer design, began producing contextual embeddings, where a word's position is recalculated for each sentence, taking every surrounding word into account. Today's chatbots work this way. Text is broken into pieces called tokens, each token starts with an embedding, and many layers then refine those embeddings, mixing in context until the model has a rich representation of the whole passage.

sections.key: Embeddings now represent images, songs and documents, powering search and recommendations.
sections.b: The embedding idea spread far beyond single words. Whole sentences and documents can be embedded, so a search engine can find pages that match the meaning of your question even if they share no exact words with it. Songs, products and films can be embedded based on who enjoys them, helping recommendation systems suggest similar items. Some systems embed images and text into the same shared space, so a photo of a beach lands near the words ‘sand and waves’, which lets you search your photo library by description. Whenever an app finds things that are ‘similar’ in a way that feels like understanding, there is a good chance it is measuring distances on a learned map.

quiz.q: What is the distributional hypothesis?
o: Words are distributed randomly in text
A word's meaning can be learned from the words around it
Every language has the same words
quiz.e: As Firth put it, ‘You shall know a word by the company it keeps.’

quiz.q: Why don't simple word ID numbers capture meaning?
o: The numbers are arbitrary, so related words get unrelated numbers
quiz.e: Word 500 is no closer in meaning to word 501 than to any other, so nothing learned transfers between related words.

quiz.q: What famous result showed word2vec embeddings capturing relationships?
o: King minus man plus woman landed near queen
quiz.e: Directions on the learned map seemed to encode relationships, though the trick works less neatly than headlines suggested.

quiz.q: Why did early word embeddings show gender stereotypes?
o: They were trained on random letters
They learned the patterns present in human-written text
quiz.e: Embeddings faithfully map the associations in their training text, including prejudiced ones.

quiz.q: What problem do contextual embeddings solve?
o: Words with several meanings, like ‘bank’, getting a single blurred position
quiz.e: Contextual embeddings recalculate each word's position using the surrounding sentence.

LESSONS.title: Expert systems: when AI ran on rules
LESSONS.hook: In the 1980s, the future of AI was supposed to be computers stuffed with the knowledge of human experts. Businesses spent fortunes on it. Then the boom went bust.

sections.key: Expert systems tried to capture a specialist's knowledge as a large set of if-then rules.
sections.b: Early AI researchers tried to build general problem-solvers, programs that could reason about anything. Progress was slow. In the 1960s and 1970s, some researchers, notably Edward Feigenbaum at Stanford University, argued for a different approach: forget general intelligence and focus on deep knowledge of one narrow field. Interview human experts, write down what they know as hundreds or thousands of rules, and let a computer apply them. A rule might read: if the patient has a fever and a stiff neck, then consider meningitis. A separate piece of software, called the inference engine, chained these rules together to reach conclusions. These programs became known as expert systems, and for a time they were the face of AI.

sections.key: One of the first expert systems helped chemists identify unknown molecules.
sections.b: One of the earliest successes was DENDRAL, a project begun at Stanford in 1965 involving Feigenbaum, the geneticist Joshua Lederberg and the chemist Carl Djerassi. Chemists use a technique called mass spectrometry, which smashes molecules apart and measures the fragments. Working back from fragments to the original structure is a hard puzzle. DENDRAL encoded chemists' knowledge about how molecules tend to break, generating and ranking possible structures. It performed well enough to be used in real research, and some of its results appeared in scientific papers. Its lesson for AI was influential: in this case, a program's power came less from clever general reasoning than from the specialised knowledge packed into it.

sections.key: MYCIN diagnosed blood infections and recommended antibiotics, but was never used on real patients.
sections.b: In the 1970s, Edward Shortliffe and colleagues at Stanford built MYCIN, an expert system for identifying bacteria causing serious blood infections and recommending antibiotics. It contained several hundred rules, each carrying a ‘certainty factor’ to handle the fact that medical evidence is rarely clear-cut. A doctor answered its questions about the patient, and MYCIN produced a ranked diagnosis and treatment advice. In a formal evaluation, experts judged its recommendations to be as good as, or better than, those of infectious disease specialists. Yet MYCIN was never used in hospitals. Reasons included the time it took to answer its many questions, the computers of the day, and unresolved questions of responsibility if it was wrong.

sections.key: Because they followed explicit rules, expert systems could show exactly why they reached a conclusion.
sections.b: One great strength of expert systems was transparency. If a doctor asked MYCIN why it wanted to know something, it could display the rule it was trying to apply. If asked how it had reached a conclusion, it could list the chain of rules that led there. Users could check the reasoning step by step and spot faulty logic. This contrasts sharply with modern neural networks, whose decisions emerge from millions or billions of learned numbers that even their designers cannot easily interpret. Today, researchers in the field of explainable AI are trying to recover some of that old clarity, especially for high-stakes uses like medicine, lending and law.

sections.key: In the 1980s, companies and governments invested heavily, and one system saved its company millions a year.
sections.b: By the early 1980s, expert systems had left the laboratory. A famous example was XCON, developed with Carnegie Mellon University for Digital Equipment Corporation. It configured complex computer orders, working out which cables, cabinets and components a customer's system needed, a job that had produced costly errors. XCON grew to thousands of rules, and the company estimated it saved tens of millions of dollars a year. Success stories like this sparked a boom. Companies set up AI departments, start-ups sold specialised hardware and software, and in 1982 Japan launched its ambitious Fifth Generation Computer project, prompting rival government programmes in Britain, Europe and the United States.

sections.key: Extracting and maintaining expert knowledge proved slow, costly and fragile.
sections.b: The trouble was getting knowledge in. Experts often cannot fully explain what they do, because much of their skill is intuition built over years. Interviewing them and turning their answers into rules was painstaking, a problem Feigenbaum called the knowledge acquisition bottleneck. Systems also became hard to maintain: adding a new rule could clash with existing ones in unexpected ways. And expert systems were brittle. Step slightly outside their narrow domain, or give them a situation their rules did not anticipate, and they could fail badly, with no common sense to fall back on. A medical rule system knew nothing about the world beyond its rules, not even that patients are people.

sections.key: The market crashed in the late 1980s, but rule-based systems quietly live on.
sections.b: By the late 1980s, expectations had run far ahead of results. The market for specialised AI computers collapsed around 1987, as ordinary desktop machines became powerful enough to do the job more cheaply. Funding was cut, companies folded, and the field entered what became known as the second AI winter. Yet expert systems never disappeared. Rule-based software still checks insurance claims, flags suspicious bank transactions, calculates tax and guides call centre staff, though rarely under the AI label. Their story also shaped modern thinking. Machine learning rose partly as an answer to the knowledge bottleneck: rather than asking experts to write down rules, let computers learn patterns directly from data.

quiz.q: How did expert systems represent knowledge?
o: As large sets of if-then rules gathered from human experts
quiz.e: An inference engine chained these hand-written rules together to reach conclusions.

quiz.q: Why was MYCIN never used in hospitals despite performing well?
o: Practical issues like time, the computers of the day and questions of responsibility
Doctors could not read its output
quiz.e: Evaluations rated its advice highly, but practical and responsibility questions kept it out of clinical use.

quiz.q: What was a key strength of expert systems compared with modern neural networks?
o: They could explain the rules behind their conclusions
quiz.e: MYCIN could show which rule it was applying and how it reached a conclusion, step by step.

quiz.q: What was the knowledge acquisition bottleneck?
o: Too few users buying the systems
The difficulty of extracting experts' knowledge and turning it into rules
quiz.e: Experts often can't fully explain their intuitive skills, so building rules was slow and painstaking.

quiz.q: How did machine learning respond to the problems of expert systems?
o: By letting computers learn patterns from data instead of hand-written rules
quiz.e: Learning from data sidestepped the bottleneck of writing every rule by hand.

LESSONS.title: The bitter lesson: why scale keeps winning
LESSONS.hook: For seventy years, researchers have tried to make AI smarter by teaching it what humans know. Again and again, they were beaten by simpler methods with more computing power. One famous essay asked what that means.

sections.key: In 2019 Rich Sutton argued that general methods using computation beat human-crafted knowledge.
sections.b: In March 2019 the computer scientist Rich Sutton, a pioneer of reinforcement learning, published a short essay called ‘The Bitter Lesson’. Its argument was simple and provocative. Looking back over decades of AI research, he wrote, the biggest lesson is that general methods which make the most of computation, chiefly search and learning, ultimately win by a large margin. Researchers repeatedly tried to build in their own understanding of a problem, such as how chess masters think or how language works. This helped in the short term and felt satisfying. But in the long run it plateaued, and was overtaken by methods that simply scaled up with more computing power. Sutton later shared computing's highest honour, the Turing Award, with Andrew Barto.

sections.key: Because computing power has grown exponentially for decades, methods that use it well keep improving.
sections.b: The engine behind the bitter lesson is the long, steady fall in the cost of computation. For decades the number of transistors on a chip roughly doubled every couple of years, a trend known as Moore's law, and specialised chips for AI have since added further gains. A method that gets better when given more computation will therefore keep improving year after year, almost automatically. A method that depends on carefully hand-crafted human knowledge improves only as fast as researchers can write that knowledge down. Over a few years the difference may be small. Over decades it becomes overwhelming. Sutton's point was that researchers, focused on short-term results, kept underestimating this compounding effect.

sections.key: Game-playing AI moved from encoding expert insight to massive search and self-taught learning.
sections.b: Chess was the first clear example. Many researchers hoped to win by capturing how grandmasters understand the board. Instead, IBM's Deep Blue beat Garry Kasparov in 1997 largely through enormous search, examining huge numbers of positions per second, combined with expert-tuned evaluation. Researchers who had pursued human-like approaches were disappointed. Go repeated the story with a twist. In 2016 DeepMind's AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol, having learned partly from human games and partly from playing itself. The following year AlphaGo Zero learned purely from self-play, with no human games at all apart from the rules, and became stronger still. Human knowledge, it seemed, had been a helpful crutch that was eventually not needed.

sections.key: In both fields, learning from data overtook systems built on expert theories.
sections.b: The same pattern played out elsewhere. In speech recognition, early systems tried to apply linguistic knowledge about how words and sounds work. Statistical methods that learned probabilities from recorded speech pulled ahead from the 1970s, and deep neural networks took over in the 2010s. In computer vision, researchers spent years hand-designing features, carefully engineered methods for detecting edges, corners and textures. Then in 2012, a deep network that learned its own features from over a million labelled images beat them decisively. Each time, the experts' knowledge was genuine and hard-won. It just turned out to matter less than a general learning method with enough data and computation.

sections.key: Research around 2020 found that language models improve smoothly and predictably as they grow.
sections.b: Researchers later found that this pattern can be surprisingly predictable. In 2020 a team at OpenAI reported scaling laws for language models: as you increase the model's size, the amount of training data and the computation used, the model's error falls along a smooth curve called a power law. This meant labs could forecast how good a bigger model would be before training it. In 2022 researchers at DeepMind refined these results with a model nicknamed Chinchilla, showing that many large models had been trained on too little data for their size, and that balancing parameters and data gives better results for the same computing budget. Scaling became a deliberate strategy rather than a lucky accident.

sections.key: Many researchers argue scale alone has limits and that built-in structure still matters.
sections.b: The bitter lesson has thoughtful critics. One point is that successful methods do contain human insight. Convolutional networks for vision build in the idea that a pattern means the same thing wherever it appears in an image, and that idea came from people. Others note practical limits: high-quality data is finite, and training ever larger models consumes vast amounts of money, electricity and chips. Some researchers argue that current systems still struggle with reliable reasoning, learning from few examples and understanding the physical world, and that new ideas, not just more scale, will be needed. Whether scaling will keep delivering, and for how long, is one of the most hotly debated questions in the field.

sections.key: The lesson is bitter because it suggests our own understanding is less useful to machines than we hoped.
sections.b: Why ‘bitter’? Because the lesson cuts against what makes research rewarding. It is deeply satisfying to understand a problem and build that understanding into a machine. The bitter lesson suggests that, in the long run, this effort is often wasted, and that the best thing researchers can do is build general methods that discover knowledge for themselves. Sutton argued we should stop trying to build in how we think we think. Whether or not he is fully right, the essay captures something important about the past decade of AI: its biggest leaps came less from elegant theories of intelligence than from learning methods, data and computation scaled to a size earlier generations could barely imagine.

quiz.q: What was the central claim of Sutton's ‘The Bitter Lesson’?
o: AI research has made no progress
General methods that leverage computation beat approaches built on human knowledge in the long run
Human experts should design all AI rules
Computers will never beat humans at games
quiz.e: Sutton argued that search and learning, scaled with computation, repeatedly overtook hand-crafted knowledge.

quiz.q: Why do methods that use computation keep improving over time?
o: The cost of computation has fallen steadily for decades
quiz.e: As computing gets cheaper and more powerful, methods that scale with it improve almost automatically.

quiz.q: What was special about AlphaGo Zero?
o: It learned purely from self-play, without human games
It was programmed with grandmaster rules
quiz.e: Starting from just the rules, it became stronger than the version that learned from human games.

quiz.q: What did scaling laws show about language models?
o: Only data matters, not model size
Error falls smoothly and predictably as size, data and computation increase
quiz.e: This let labs forecast a larger model's performance, and Chinchilla later showed data and size must be balanced.

quiz.q: Which is a common criticism of the bitter lesson?
o: Successful methods still contain human insight, and scale faces limits of data, cost and energy
AI cannot use data at all
quiz.e: Critics note built-in ideas like convolution came from people, and question how far scaling alone can go.

LESSONS.title: The Rosetta Stone: cracking the code of the pharaohs
LESSONS.hook: For fourteen centuries nobody on Earth could read an Egyptian hieroglyph. Then a broken slab of stone and a stubborn young Frenchman changed everything.

sections.key: The Rosetta Stone was found by French soldiers in 1799, built into the remains of an old fort.
sections.b: In July 1799, during Napoleon Bonaparte's invasion of Egypt, French soldiers were rebuilding a crumbling fort near the town of Rashid, which Europeans called Rosetta, in the Nile Delta. An officer named Pierre-François Bouchard noticed that one dark block reused in the walls was covered in writing. It was a broken slab of granodiorite a little over a metre tall, and it carried three bands of text. Napoleon had brought scholars as well as soldiers, and they quickly realised its importance. When the British defeated the French in Egypt, the stone was handed over under the terms of surrender in 1801. It has been displayed in the British Museum in London since 1802, and it remains one of the most visited objects there.

sections.key: The stone repeats a single decree in hieroglyphs, Demotic and ancient Greek, which made it a key for translation.
sections.b: The text itself is surprisingly ordinary. It is a decree issued by a council of priests at Memphis in 196 BC, praising the young king Ptolemy V and listing the honours to be paid to him. What made it extraordinary was the format. The decree was carved three times: in hieroglyphs, the sacred picture script of temples and tombs; in Demotic, the everyday cursive script of Egyptian scribes; and in ancient Greek, the language of the ruling Ptolemaic court. Scholars in 1799 could read Greek perfectly well. If the three texts said the same thing, then the Greek could act as a crib for the other two. In theory the code was cracked. In practice it would take more than twenty years.

sections.key: Knowledge of hieroglyphs died out in late antiquity, and later scholars wrongly assumed every sign was a symbol.
sections.b: Hieroglyphs had been used for over three thousand years, but as Egypt became part of the Greek and then Roman and Christian world, fewer and fewer people learnt them. The last known hieroglyphic inscription was carved at the temple of Philae in AD 394. After that the knowledge vanished. For centuries European scholars believed hieroglyphs were mystical symbols, each picture standing for a deep idea, rather than a working writing system. One seventeenth century scholar, Athanasius Kircher, published elaborate translations that turned out to be pure invention. This assumption was the real barrier. As long as people looked for hidden philosophy in every owl and reed, they could never see that many of the signs simply spelt out sounds, like letters.

sections.key: The breakthrough began with royal names, which were written inside oval rings called cartouches.
sections.b: In some places the hieroglyphs were enclosed in an oval ring, now called a cartouche. Scholars suspected these held royal names. The English polymath Thomas Young, a physicist and doctor, worked on the stone in the 1810s and showed that the cartouche matched the name Ptolemy in the Greek text. He correctly identified several sounds. But Young still believed sound signs were used mainly for foreign names. Then a second inscription helped. An obelisk from Philae carried the names Ptolemy and Cleopatra, which share the letters p, t, o and l. If the same signs appeared in the same positions in both cartouches, that was strong evidence of an alphabet-like system. The pieces were falling into place.

sections.key: Jean-François Champollion proved that hieroglyphs mixed sound signs and meaning signs, even in native Egyptian words.
sections.b: Jean-François Champollion was a French linguist who had studied languages obsessively since boyhood, including Coptic, the late form of the Egyptian language still used in Christian church services. In 1822 he looked at cartouches copied from temples such as Abu Simbel. One began with a sun disc. In Coptic, the word for sun was 're'. The cartouche ended with signs he already read as 's', and in between was a sign he linked to the Coptic word for birth, 'mise'. Together they spelt Ramesses, a truly Egyptian pharaoh, not a Greek one. That was the leap: sound signs were used throughout the script. A family story says he rushed to his brother's office, cried that he had done it, and collapsed.

sections.key: Hieroglyphs combine signs for sounds, signs for whole words and silent signs that clarify meaning.
sections.b: Champollion announced his results in a famous letter in September 1822, and the decades that followed confirmed and refined them. Hieroglyphic writing turned out to be a clever mixture. Some signs stand for a single consonant, some for two or three consonants together, and some for a whole word. Many words end with a silent sign called a determinative, which tells the reader what kind of thing is meant. A walking pair of legs might mark a verb of movement, while a seated man marks a person. Vowels were usually not written at all, which is why modern scholars still argue over how names were pronounced. Once this system was understood, temple walls, tomb paintings and papyri could finally speak again.

quiz.q: Why was the Rosetta Stone so useful for decoding hieroglyphs?
o: It contained a dictionary of hieroglyphic signs
It repeated the same decree in a script scholars could already read
It was written by Champollion's teachers
It showed pictures beside each word
quiz.e: The decree was carved in hieroglyphs, Demotic and ancient Greek. Because scholars could read the Greek, it acted as a crib for the two Egyptian scripts.

quiz.q: What mistaken belief held back the decipherment of hieroglyphs for centuries?
o: That hieroglyphs were written right to left only
That every sign was a mystical symbol rather than part of a working script
That hieroglyphs were a form of Greek
That only priests could pronounce them
quiz.e: Scholars such as Athanasius Kircher treated each sign as a symbol of a deep idea. Seeing that many signs stood for sounds was the real breakthrough.

quiz.q: What is a cartouche?
o: An oval ring enclosing a royal name
A Greek translation of a hieroglyph
A silent sign at the end of a word
quiz.e: Cartouches are oval rings around royal names. Comparing the names Ptolemy and Cleopatra in cartouches helped show that some signs stood for sounds.

quiz.q: How did Champollion read the name Ramesses?
o: He found it in the Greek text of the Rosetta Stone
He used his knowledge of Coptic to read a sun sign and other sound signs
Thomas Young sent him the answer
He guessed it from the shape of the cartouche
quiz.e: In Coptic the word for sun was 're'. Reading the sun disc together with other sound signs gave Ra-mes-ses, proving sound signs were used in native Egyptian names too.

quiz.q: What is a determinative in hieroglyphic writing?
o: A sign that marks the start of a sentence
A silent sign that shows what kind of thing a word refers to
quiz.e: Determinatives are not pronounced. They clarify meaning, such as walking legs for movement, which helps readers tell apart words that share the same consonants.

LESSONS.title: 1066: the year England changed hands
LESSONS.hook: In a single autumn, England's king fought two invasions, marched hundreds of kilometres and died on a ridge in Sussex. The country that came out the other side would never be the same.

sections.h: A king dies, three men want his crown
sections.key: When Edward the Confessor died childless in January 1066, three powerful men claimed the English throne.
sections.b: Edward the Confessor died on 5 January 1066 without children, leaving no obvious heir. The English council quickly chose Harold Godwinson, the richest and most powerful earl in the kingdom, and he was crowned the very next day. Two other men believed the crown was theirs. William, Duke of Normandy, a distant relative of Edward, claimed that Edward had promised him the throne years earlier and that Harold had sworn an oath to support him. Across the North Sea, Harald Hardrada, King of Norway and one of the most famous warriors of his age, claimed it through an older agreement between earlier kings. Both began preparing invasions. Harold had to guard a long coastline without knowing who would strike first.

sections.key: Harold crushed the Norwegian invasion at Stamford Bridge, only to hear that William had landed in the south.
sections.b: Harold spent the summer waiting for William on the south coast, but the Normans were held in port by unfavourable winds. In September, with supplies running low, Harold sent much of his army home. Almost immediately Harald Hardrada landed in the north with a large fleet, joined by Harold's own exiled brother, Tostig. They defeated the northern earls at Fulford, near York, on 20 September. Harold marched north astonishingly fast and caught the Norwegians by surprise at Stamford Bridge on 25 September. It was a crushing victory. Hardrada and Tostig were both killed, and the age of great Viking invasions of England is often said to end there. Three days later, on 28 September, William's army landed at Pevensey in Sussex.

sections.key: At Hastings on 14 October 1066, the English shield wall held for hours before it finally broke.
sections.b: Harold raced south again and took up a strong position on a ridge about ten kilometres from Hastings, where the town of Battle stands today. His soldiers formed a shield wall, a dense line of overlapping shields bristling with spears and the feared long-handled Dane axes. William's army combined archers, heavy infantry and mounted knights. All day on 14 October the Normans attacked uphill, and all day the wall held. At one point a rumour spread that William was dead, and he reportedly lifted his helmet to show his face to his men. Norman accounts describe retreats, some panicked and some possibly feigned, that lured English soldiers down from the ridge where they could be cut off. Slowly the line thinned.

sections.key: Harold died late in the battle, but whether an arrow in the eye killed him is still debated.
sections.b: By evening Harold was dead, along with his brothers Gyrth and Leofwine and much of the English nobility. Without its leaders the remaining army collapsed. The most famous image of Harold's death comes from the Bayeux Tapestry, which shows a figure grasping an arrow near his eye beneath the words saying Harold the king is killed. Historians still debate what it shows. The figure may be Harold, or Harold may be the man next to him being cut down by a mounted knight, or both images may be him at different moments. The tapestry was also restored in the nineteenth century, which may have altered the arrow. What is certain is that the last Anglo-Saxon king crowned in England fell at Hastings.

sections.key: The Bayeux Tapestry is a seventy metre embroidery, probably made in England within a few decades of the battle.
sections.b: The Bayeux Tapestry is not technically a tapestry at all. Tapestries are woven, while this is embroidery, with coloured woollen threads stitched onto long strips of linen. It is around seventy metres long and about half a metre tall, and tells the story of 1066 like a comic strip, from Harold's visit to Normandy to the battle itself. It was most likely commissioned by Bishop Odo of Bayeux, William's half-brother, and many historians think it was made by English embroiderers, who were famous across Europe for their needlework. It includes over six hundred people, horses, ships, a sighting of what we now know was Halley's Comet, and even a few rude figures in the margins. Its final section is lost.

sections.key: The Normans replaced the English elite, built castles everywhere and left a lasting mark on the English language.
sections.b: William was crowned in Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day 1066, but conquest took years. Rebellions in the north were met with the Harrying of the North in 1069 and 1070, a campaign of deliberate destruction that caused famine across a huge region. Within a generation almost every great English landholder had been replaced by a Norman or other Frenchman. Castles of earth and timber, then stone, appeared across the country, including the Tower of London. At Christmas 1085 William ordered the Domesday Book, an extraordinary survey of who owned what across most of England. French became the language of the court for centuries, which is why English often has paired words: cow and beef, pig and pork, sheep and mutton.

quiz.q: Who was crowned king of England immediately after Edward the Confessor died?
quiz.e: Harold Godwinson, England's most powerful earl, was chosen by the English council and crowned the day after Edward's death in January 1066.

quiz.q: Why was Harold's army under such strain at Hastings?
o: It had just fought and won a major battle in the north
It had been at sea for weeks
It was made up only of foreign mercenaries
quiz.e: Harold had marched north to defeat Harald Hardrada at Stamford Bridge on 25 September, then hurried south to face William, who landed three days after that battle.

quiz.q: What was the English army's main formation at Hastings?
o: A shield wall on a ridge
A line of archers in front of the infantry
quiz.e: The English formed a dense shield wall on a ridge. It held for hours before Norman attacks and retreats, real and possibly feigned, gradually wore it down.

quiz.q: Why is the Bayeux Tapestry technically misnamed?
o: It is embroidered rather than woven
quiz.e: Tapestries are woven. The Bayeux Tapestry is embroidery, with woollen threads stitched onto linen, probably by English embroiderers.

quiz.q: Why does English have pairs of words like cow and beef?
o: French became the language of the Norman ruling class
They were created by the Domesday Book
quiz.e: After 1066 the elite spoke French for generations. English words often survived for the animal, while French-derived words such as beef and pork came to mean the meat.

LESSONS.title: Cleopatra: the last pharaoh
LESSONS.hook: She has been painted as a seductress for two thousand years, mostly by her enemies. The real Cleopatra was a scholar-queen fighting to keep her country alive.

sections.key: Cleopatra belonged to a Macedonian Greek dynasty that had ruled Egypt for nearly three centuries.
sections.b: Cleopatra VII was born in 69 BC, but her family story begins with Alexander the Great. After Alexander died, one of his generals, Ptolemy, took control of Egypt and founded a dynasty. For nearly three hundred years Ptolemies ruled from Alexandria, the glittering Greek city on the Mediterranean coast. They presented themselves to Egyptians as pharaohs, but they spoke Greek and often married their own siblings to keep power in the family. Cleopatra was the seventh queen of that name. Here is a perspective worth sitting with: she lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid of Giza. To her, the pyramids were already ancient monuments, more than two thousand years old.

sections.key: Ancient writers were most struck by Cleopatra's intelligence, languages and conversation, not her looks.
