sections.b: Hollywood made Cleopatra a famous beauty, but the ancient evidence points elsewhere. The Greek writer Plutarch, who drew on earlier sources, said her beauty was not in itself incomparable, but that her presence was captivating, her conversation charming and her voice delightful. He also reported that she spoke many languages and could talk to foreign envoys without interpreters. According to Plutarch, she was the first of her dynasty to bother learning Egyptian, the language of the people she ruled. Her coins show a strong hooked nose and a firm chin, though coin portraits were also political images. She was educated in Alexandria, one of the great centres of learning in the ancient world, and she ruled as a skilled, calculating politician.

sections.key: Cleopatra won back her throne by allying with Julius Caesar, who arrived in Alexandria in 48 BC.
sections.b: Cleopatra came to power around 51 BC as co-ruler with her younger brother, Ptolemy XIII, but his advisers soon drove her out. She raised an army and the siblings were at war when Julius Caesar arrived in Alexandria in 48 BC, chasing his Roman rival Pompey. Cleopatra needed to reach Caesar without being caught by her brother's men. Plutarch says she was smuggled into the palace by boat at dusk, hidden inside a bag for bedding, the origin of the later legend about a carpet. Caesar took her side. After months of fighting in the city, Ptolemy XIII drowned while fleeing, and Cleopatra was restored to the throne. She later bore a son, Ptolemy Caesar, nicknamed Caesarion.

sections.key: After Caesar's murder, Cleopatra allied with Mark Antony, the most powerful Roman in the East.
sections.b: Cleopatra was living in Rome when Caesar was assassinated in 44 BC, and she quickly returned to Egypt. Rome's power was now split, and Mark Antony controlled the eastern provinces. In 41 BC he summoned her to Tarsus, in modern Turkey. Plutarch describes her arriving on a barge with a gilded stern, purple sails and silver oars, dressed as the goddess Aphrodite. Whatever the exact details, it was political theatre, and it worked. Antony and Cleopatra became partners in power and in private, and she had three children with him. In 34 BC, at a ceremony in Alexandria, Antony handed territories to Cleopatra and her children. In Rome, his rival Octavian used this as proof that Antony had betrayed Rome to a foreign queen.

sections.key: Defeated by Octavian at Actium in 31 BC, Antony and Cleopatra both took their own lives.
sections.b: War between Octavian and the partners came in 31 BC. At the naval Battle of Actium, off western Greece, their fleet was beaten, and Cleopatra and Antony escaped back to Egypt. A year later Octavian's armies closed in on Alexandria. Antony, believing Cleopatra was already dead, stabbed himself and died soon after. Cleopatra died in August 30 BC, aged thirty-nine, rather than be paraded through Rome as a captive. The famous story says she was bitten by an asp, a venomous Egyptian snake smuggled to her in a basket of figs. Yet even Plutarch admitted that nobody knew the truth of how she died, and some historians think poison is more likely. Caesarion was later killed on Octavian's orders.

sections.key: Most of what we know about Cleopatra comes from Roman writers who saw her as a dangerous enemy.
sections.b: With Cleopatra's death, Egypt became a Roman province, and three thousand years of rule by pharaohs came to an end. Octavian soon took the name Augustus and became Rome's first emperor. Because Octavian had won, his version of the story dominated. Roman poets portrayed Cleopatra as a drunken, power-hungry foreign queen who had bewitched a Roman hero. Later came Shakespeare's tragic lover and Hollywood's glamorous icon. Historians today try to look past these images and see a ruler who spent her whole reign trying to keep Egypt independent in the shadow of an expanding Rome, using money, diplomacy and alliances. Her tomb has never been found, and searches for it in and around Alexandria continue.

quiz.q: Which dynasty did Cleopatra belong to?
o: A native Egyptian family from Thebes
The Ptolemies, descended from one of Alexander the Great's generals
quiz.e: Cleopatra was a Ptolemy, part of a Macedonian Greek dynasty founded by Alexander's general Ptolemy, which ruled Egypt for nearly three centuries.

quiz.q: What did Plutarch say was most striking about Cleopatra?
o: Her conversation, presence and command of languages
quiz.e: Plutarch wrote that her beauty was not in itself incomparable, but that her presence, conversation and voice were captivating, and that she spoke many languages.

quiz.q: According to Plutarch, how did Cleopatra reach Julius Caesar in the palace?
o: Hidden in a bedding bag carried in by boat
On a royal barge with silver oars
quiz.e: Plutarch says she was carried in hidden in a bag for bedding. The famous carpet is a later retelling of this story.

quiz.q: What does the ancient evidence say about the asp story?
o: It is proven by her tomb
It is the traditional story, but even Plutarch said nobody knew how she really died
quiz.e: The asp is the traditional account, but Plutarch himself admitted the truth was unknown. Some historians think poison is more likely.

quiz.q: Why do historians treat ancient accounts of Cleopatra with caution?
o: They were written mostly by her Roman enemies or their supporters
They were all written in Egyptian
They were written by her children
quiz.e: Octavian won the war, so Roman writers shaped her image as a dangerous foreign seductress. Modern historians look past that propaganda to the political ruler.

LESSONS.title: The real life of a medieval knight
LESSONS.hook: Forget cranes lifting clanking men onto horses. Real knights were trained athletes, expensive to equip, and often far less chivalrous than the stories suggest.

sections.h: From page to squire to knight
sections.key: A noble boy's path to knighthood traditionally took well over a decade of training.
sections.b: Becoming a knight was not a matter of simply buying a sword. In the classic pattern, a boy from a noble family was sent at around seven to serve in another lord's household as a page. He learnt manners, riding, basic weapon handling and how to serve at table. At around fourteen he became a squire, attached to a knight whose armour he cleaned, whose horses he tended and whom he followed onto the battlefield. If he proved himself, he might be dubbed a knight around the age of twenty-one, sometimes in a solemn ceremony and sometimes in a hurry on the eve of battle. The ages varied a great deal, but the idea was constant: knighthood was earned through years of service.

sections.key: Armour, weapons and especially warhorses made knighthood extraordinarily costly.
sections.b: A knight was in many ways a very expensive piece of military equipment. He needed armour, a sword, a lance, a shield, squires and servants, and above all horses. The finest warhorses, called destriers, were specially bred, trained for the noise and violence of battle, and could cost many times the price of an ordinary horse. A knight also needed riding horses for travel and pack horses for baggage. This is why knights were usually supported by land. In return for military service, a lord granted them estates whose peasants produced the income to pay for all this. The cost was so heavy that, by the 1200s, the English crown was ordering qualified landowners to take up knighthood, and many paid fines to avoid it.

sections.key: A full suit of plate armour weighed roughly twenty to twenty-five kilograms, spread across the whole body.
sections.b: Films often show knights hoisted onto their horses by cranes, helpless if they fell. That image is a myth, popularised in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Early knights wore mail, made from thousands of small interlinked iron rings. Full plate armour appeared later and reached its peak in the 1400s. A complete suit typically weighed around twenty to twenty-five kilograms, less than the load carried by many modern soldiers, and because it was spread across the body rather than hanging from the shoulders, a fit man could run, mount a horse and get up after a fall. The real cost was stamina. Modern experiments with volunteers in replica armour found that walking and running took roughly twice as much energy.

sections.h: Heraldry: a logo on your shield
sections.key: Coats of arms began as a practical way to identify knights whose faces were hidden by helmets.
sections.b: Once knights began wearing helmets that covered the whole face in the twelfth century, there was a practical problem. In the chaos of battle or a tournament, how could anyone tell who was who? The answer was heraldry. Knights painted bold, simple designs on their shields and later on the cloth surcoats worn over their armour, which is where the phrase coat of arms comes from. Designs used strong colours and shapes that were easy to recognise at a distance: lions, eagles, crosses, stripes and chevrons. Over time arms became hereditary, passed down through families, and specialists called heralds kept track of them. Many modern flags, sports badges and company logos still borrow the visual language of medieval heraldry.

sections.key: Medieval tournaments began as chaotic mock battles and later became more controlled jousting contests.
sections.b: Tournaments started in the eleventh and twelfth centuries as something close to real war. Teams of knights charged each other across open countryside in a mêlée, capturing opponents and holding them for ransom. People were injured and killed, and the Church repeatedly condemned them. For a skilled but landless knight, though, they were a path to fortune. William Marshal, an English knight of the late twelfth century, reportedly captured hundreds of opponents in his tournament career and rose to become one of the most powerful men in England. Later tournaments became more organised and theatrical, with jousting, in which two knights charged each other with lances, often separated by a barrier. Champions became celebrities, and spectators watched from decorated stands.

sections.h: Chivalry: the ideal and the reality
sections.key: Chivalry was a genuine ideal of honour and service, but knights often fell far short of it in war.
sections.b: Chivalry described an ideal knight: brave, loyal to his lord, generous, courteous and devoted to the Church. Poets and romances about King Arthur and his knights spread these values, and many knights took them seriously. Rules of conduct also had practical benefits for the knights themselves. A captured noble was usually worth more alive, for ransom, than dead. But chivalry mostly applied between knights. Ordinary soldiers and peasants often received no such mercy. Medieval armies regularly practised the chevauchée, a raid that deliberately burned villages and crops to ruin an enemy's economy. The gap between the ideal and reality was obvious even to people at the time, and many medieval writers criticised knights for their cruelty and greed.

quiz.q: What was the traditional order of training on the path to knighthood?
quiz.e: A noble boy typically began as a page in another lord's household, became a squire in his teens, and might be dubbed a knight around twenty-one.

quiz.q: Why were knights usually granted land?
o: To grow food for their horses only
Because knights were forbidden to use money
Because the income from land paid for their very costly equipment and horses
quiz.e: Armour, weapons and warhorses were extremely expensive. Land worked by peasants produced the income that let a knight meet his military obligations.

quiz.q: What is true about a full suit of plate armour?
o: It weighed about 100 kg and needed a crane
It weighed roughly 20 to 25 kg and a fit man could run and mount a horse in it
It was so light it made no difference to stamina
It was only worn for parades
quiz.e: Plate armour was heavy but well distributed. Knights could move freely, though modern experiments show it roughly doubled the energy needed to walk or run.

quiz.q: Why did heraldry develop?
o: To identify knights whose faces were hidden by helmets
To show how much land a knight owned
To mark which knights had been on crusade
quiz.e: Once full face helmets appeared, knights needed bold designs on shields and surcoats so they could be recognised in battle and tournaments.

quiz.q: Which statement best describes chivalry in practice?
o: Knights showed mercy to everyone they fought
It was invented in the nineteenth century
It was a real ideal, but mostly applied between knights and was often ignored in war
It banned knights from fighting at all
quiz.e: Chivalry was taken seriously as an ideal, but its protections mostly applied to fellow nobles. Raids that burned villages and crops were common practice.

LESSONS.title: Tutankhamun: the tomb that time forgot
LESSONS.hook: He was a minor king who died as a teenager. That is exactly why his tomb survived, and why its discovery in 1922 stunned the world.

sections.key: Tutankhamun took the throne as a child around 1332 BC and died about nine years later.
sections.b: Tutankhamun ruled Egypt for only about nine or ten years in the fourteenth century BC, coming to the throne at around eight or nine years old. He was born into turbulent times. His father was very probably Akhenaten, the pharaoh who had abandoned Egypt's traditional gods to worship a single sun disc, the Aten. The boy was originally named Tutankhaten, meaning living image of the Aten. Early in his reign, guided by powerful advisers, the court restored the old gods, and the young king's name was changed to Tutankhamun, honouring the god Amun. He died at around eighteen or nineteen. To the Egyptians who came after, he was a footnote, and later kings even left his name off official lists.

sections.key: Howard Carter spent years searching the Valley of the Kings, funded by the wealthy Lord Carnarvon.
sections.b: By the early twentieth century, most archaeologists believed the Valley of the Kings, the royal burial ground near ancient Thebes, had given up all its secrets. Howard Carter, an English archaeologist who had worked in Egypt since he was a teenager, disagreed. Small finds bearing Tutankhamun's name convinced him that the king's tomb was still out there. His sponsor was George Herbert, the fifth Earl of Carnarvon, a wealthy aristocrat with a passion for Egyptology. Year after year, Carter's workers cleared tonnes of rubble with little to show for it. By 1922, Carnarvon was ready to stop paying. Carter persuaded him to fund one final season, and turned his attention to a patch of ground near the tomb of Ramesses VI.

sections.key: In November 1922, Carter's team uncovered a hidden staircase leading to a nearly intact royal tomb.
sections.b: On 4 November 1922, a few days into the new season, workers uncovered a stone step cut into the bedrock. More steps followed, leading down to a sealed doorway stamped with royal seals. Carter covered it up again and sent a telegram to Carnarvon in England. When Carnarvon arrived, the team cleared the passage and reached a second doorway. On 26 November, Carter made a small hole and held up a candle. As he later recalled, when Carnarvon asked whether he could see anything, he replied that he could see wonderful things. In the flickering light were gilded couches, statues, chests and chariots, piled together in a room no one had entered for more than three thousand years.

sections.key: Thieves broke in soon after the burial, but the tomb was resealed and then hidden under later debris.
sections.b: Tutankhamun's tomb was not untouched. Evidence showed that robbers broke in at least once, and probably twice, not long after the burial. They took small, easily carried valuables, such as oils and metal objects, before officials discovered the break-in, tidied up hastily and resealed the tomb. Then luck intervened. Over time the entrance was buried under flood debris and the rubble and huts of workers digging later tombs, including that of Ramesses VI, so the entrance was forgotten. The tomb itself was small, possibly a private tomb adapted in a hurry after his unexpected death. Yet it held over five thousand objects. Recording, conserving and removing them took Carter and his team about a decade.

sections.key: Beyond the famous golden mask, the tomb was crammed with everyday objects that reveal how an Egyptian king lived.
sections.b: The best known treasure is the funerary mask, made of gold inlaid with glass and semi-precious stones and weighing about ten kilograms. The king's body lay inside three nested coffins, the innermost made of solid gold and weighing over a hundred kilograms. These were themselves enclosed within a stone sarcophagus and four gilded wooden shrines. But many of the most revealing objects were ordinary. There were chariots, bows, walking sticks, board games, linen underwear, sandals, jars of food and wine, and a lock of hair that belonged to his grandmother, Queen Tiye. There were even two tiny mummified daughters, stillborn babies buried with their father. Together these objects let historians see an Egyptian royal life in unusual detail.

sections.key: Lord Carnarvon's death in 1923 sparked rumours of a curse, but the evidence does not support one.
sections.b: In April 1923, just months after the opening, Lord Carnarvon died in Cairo from an infection that began with an infected mosquito bite, which he had accidentally nicked while shaving. Newspapers, competing for stories, spread the idea of a pharaoh's curse, and novelists such as Arthur Conan Doyle encouraged it. No curse inscription was found in the tomb. Howard Carter, who spent the most time inside, lived until 1939. Later studies comparing people who were present at the tomb's opening with others found no sign that they died earlier. How Tutankhamun himself died is still debated. Scans and DNA studies have pointed to a broken leg, a foot deformity and evidence of malaria, but no single cause is agreed.

quiz.q: Why was Tutankhamun's original name changed?
o: He was adopted by a foreign king
The court restored Egypt's traditional gods, and his name was changed to honour Amun
He was named after Howard Carter
His original name was considered unlucky after his death
quiz.e: Born Tutankhaten, honouring the Aten, he was renamed Tutankhamun when the court returned to the traditional gods after Akhenaten's religious upheaval.

quiz.q: What nearly ended Howard Carter's search?
o: Lord Carnarvon was ready to stop funding it
quiz.e: After years of little success, Carnarvon was ready to stop paying. Carter persuaded him to fund one last season, which led to the discovery in November 1922.

quiz.q: Why did Tutankhamun's tomb survive mostly intact?
o: It was never found by robbers
It was guarded by soldiers for centuries
After an early robbery it was resealed, and its entrance was later buried under debris
It was hidden inside a pyramid
quiz.e: Robbers broke in soon after the burial, but officials resealed it. Later flood debris and workers' rubble from other tombs hid the entrance for millennia.

quiz.q: Which of these was found in the tomb?
o: Everyday objects such as sandals, board games and linen underwear, as well as gold
Papyrus maps of the Valley of the Kings
quiz.e: Alongside the golden mask and coffins were thousands of ordinary objects, which reveal far more about daily royal life than treasure alone.

quiz.q: What does the evidence say about the curse of Tutankhamun?
o: Everyone who entered the tomb died within a year
A curse inscription was found on the door
It was a newspaper sensation not supported by evidence
Carter died the day the tomb was opened
quiz.e: Carnarvon died of an infection, no curse inscription was found, Carter lived until 1939, and studies found no early deaths among those present.

LESSONS.title: Hannibal: the general who crossed the Alps
LESSONS.hook: He marched elephants over the Alps and destroyed Roman armies one after another. So why did Rome, not Hannibal, win the war?

sections.key: Rome and Carthage fought three wars over control of the western Mediterranean.
sections.b: In the third century BC, two great powers faced each other across the Mediterranean. Rome was a rising land power that had brought most of Italy under its control. Carthage, a wealthy trading city founded by Phoenicians in what is now Tunisia, dominated sea trade, with territory in North Africa, Spain, Sardinia and Sicily. The Romans called the Carthaginians Poeni, which is why their wars are known as the Punic Wars. The first, from 264 to 241 BC, was fought largely at sea over Sicily. Rome, which had barely had a navy, built fleets almost from scratch and won. Carthage lost Sicily and paid a huge indemnity. Many Carthaginians, especially the powerful Barca family, wanted revenge.

sections.key: Hannibal grew up in Carthaginian Spain, where his family built a new power base after the first war.
sections.b: After the first war, Hamilcar Barca led Carthaginian armies into Spain, conquering territory rich in silver mines and fighting men. His son Hannibal grew up in military camps there. The ancient historians Polybius and Livy tell a famous story: before leaving for Spain, the nine-year-old Hannibal asked to come along, and his father made him swear at an altar never to be a friend of Rome. Whether or not every detail is true, Hannibal took command of the army in Spain in 221 BC, at about twenty-six. In 219 BC he besieged and captured Saguntum, a Spanish city allied with Rome. Rome demanded that Carthage hand him over. Carthage refused, and the Second Punic War began in 218 BC.

sections.key: Hannibal marched from Spain over the Pyrenees and the Alps to invade Italy by land.
sections.b: Rome controlled the sea, so Hannibal decided to attack overland, which no one expected. In 218 BC he led his army from Spain across the Pyrenees, through southern Gaul and over the Rhône, with war elephants ferried across on rafts. Then, late in the year, he crossed the Alps. The journey took about fifteen days in the mountains, through snow, landslides and ambushes by local tribes. Polybius, who wrote within living memory and claimed to have walked the route, says Hannibal reached Italy with about twenty thousand infantry and six thousand cavalry, a fraction of the force that had left Spain. Most of the elephants died soon after. Which pass he used is still debated by historians today.

sections.key: At Cannae in 216 BC, Hannibal encircled and destroyed a much larger Roman army.
sections.b: Hannibal defeated the Romans at the Trebia river in 218 BC, then ambushed an entire army in fog beside Lake Trasimene in 217. Rome responded with a new strategy under Quintus Fabius Maximus, who avoided pitched battle and shadowed Hannibal instead, earning the nickname Cunctator, the delayer. Frustrated Romans abandoned this approach. In 216 BC, at Cannae in southern Italy, a huge Roman army attacked. Hannibal placed his weakest troops in the centre, which bent backwards under pressure as planned, drawing the Romans in. His heavy infantry then closed in from both sides while his cavalry struck from behind. The Romans were surrounded and slaughtered. Ancient sources give figures of fifty thousand or more dead, and military academies still study the battle.

sections.key: Rome refused to negotiate, most of its allies stayed loyal and Hannibal could never take the city itself.
sections.b: After Cannae, many expected Rome to surrender. It did not. The Senate refused to discuss peace, raised new legions, and returned to Fabius's careful strategy. Hannibal hoped Rome's Italian allies would desert in large numbers. Some, including the city of Capua, did, but most of central Italy stayed loyal and kept supplying men and money. Hannibal lacked siege equipment and reinforcements to attack Rome directly, and Carthage sent him little help. He remained in Italy for about fifteen years, undefeated in major battle yet unable to finish the war. Meanwhile a brilliant young Roman general, Publius Cornelius Scipio, conquered Carthaginian Spain and then invaded North Africa, forcing Carthage to recall Hannibal to defend his home city.

sections.key: Scipio defeated Hannibal at Zama in 202 BC, and Rome destroyed Carthage itself in 146 BC.
sections.b: In 202 BC, Scipio and Hannibal met at the Battle of Zama in North Africa. Scipio had learnt from his enemy, opening lanes in his lines for Hannibal's charging elephants to pass through harmlessly, and his cavalry won the day. Carthage surrendered, gave up its fleet and its overseas empire, and paid Rome heavy tribute. Scipio was honoured with the name Africanus. Hannibal led Carthage's government for a time, then fled into exile in the East, and around 183 BC took poison rather than be handed to the Romans. In the Third Punic War, Rome besieged and destroyed Carthage in 146 BC. The popular story that the Romans sowed the ground with salt, however, appears to be a modern invention.

quiz.q: What were Rome and Carthage mainly competing over?
quiz.e: The Punic Wars were a struggle over the western Mediterranean, beginning with a fight over Sicily in the First Punic War.

quiz.q: Why did Hannibal invade Italy over the Alps?
o: Rome controlled the sea, so an overland attack was unexpected
The Alps were the shortest route
His elephants could not travel by ship
Carthage had no ships at all
quiz.e: Rome dominated the sea after the First Punic War, so Hannibal chose a long, dangerous land route that the Romans did not expect.

quiz.q: How did Hannibal win at Cannae?
o: He used his elephants to break the Roman centre
He poisoned the Roman water supply
He let his centre bend back, then closed in from both sides and the rear
He waited for the Romans to run out of food
quiz.e: Hannibal's centre gave way deliberately, drawing the Romans in, while his heavy infantry and cavalry surrounded them. It remains a classic encirclement.

quiz.q: Which factor most helped Rome survive Hannibal's victories?
o: Hannibal never won a major battle
Most of Rome's Italian allies stayed loyal and Rome refused to negotiate
Carthage sent Hannibal no soldiers at all from the start
quiz.e: Rome kept raising armies, refused to make peace, and most allies kept supplying men and money, while Hannibal lacked the means to take Rome.

quiz.q: What is true about the story that Rome sowed salt on Carthage?
o: It is recorded by Polybius as an eyewitness
It appears to be a modern invention
It is why Tunisia has salt lakes
It happened after the First Punic War
quiz.e: Rome did destroy Carthage in 146 BC, but the salting story is not found in the ancient sources and appears to be a modern addition.

LESSONS.title: Joan of Arc and the Hundred Years' War
LESSONS.hook: A teenage peasant girl from a village in eastern France told a prince that God had sent her to save his kingdom. Astonishingly, she very nearly did.

sections.h: A war longer than a lifetime
sections.key: The Hundred Years' War was a long series of conflicts between England and France from 1337 to 1453.
sections.b: The Hundred Years' War actually lasted 116 years, from 1337 to 1453, with long truces in between. At its heart was a question of inheritance. English kings, descended from French nobility, held lands in France and claimed the French crown itself. England won famous victories at Crécy in 1346, Poitiers in 1356 and Agincourt in 1415, where Henry V's outnumbered army, with its longbowmen, defeated a much larger French force. By the 1420s France was in desperate trouble. The powerful Duke of Burgundy had sided with England, and the Treaty of Troyes in 1420 declared that the English king would inherit the French throne, disinheriting the French heir, Charles, known as the Dauphin. Much of northern France, including Paris, was under English and Burgundian control.

sections.key: Joan, a peasant girl from Domrémy, said saints spoke to her and told her to help the Dauphin.
sections.b: Joan was born around 1412 in Domrémy, a village in north-eastern France, the daughter of a farming family. She could not read or write. From the age of about thirteen, she later said, she heard voices and saw visions of saints, especially Saint Michael, Saint Catherine and Saint Margaret. Their message grew increasingly clear: she must go to the Dauphin, drive the English out and see him crowned. In early 1429, at around seventeen, she persuaded a local garrison commander to give her an escort, cut her hair short, dressed in men's clothing for the journey and rode across hostile country to the Dauphin's court at Chinon. What exactly she experienced is unknowable, but her conviction was absolute.

sections.key: After theologians examined her, the Dauphin sent Joan with an army to relieve the besieged city of Orléans.
sections.b: Charles was cautious, and he had good reason. A young woman claiming divine instructions could be a saint, a fraud or an agent of the devil, and backing the wrong one would be disastrous. A later tradition says he hid among his courtiers to test her and she picked him out at once. More certainly, he had her questioned for weeks by churchmen at Poitiers, who found nothing wrong in her faith or conduct. The situation was desperate enough to take a chance. The city of Orléans, the key to southern France, had been under English siege since late 1428. Charles provided Joan with armour, a banner and a place with an army sent to bring supplies and break the siege.

sections.key: Joan helped lift the siege of Orléans in May 1429, and Charles was crowned at Reims that July.
sections.b: Joan arrived at Orléans at the end of April 1429. She did not command the army in a formal sense, but her presence electrified the soldiers and townspeople, and she pushed for bold attacks where commanders had hesitated. She was wounded by an arrow between the neck and shoulder during one assault but returned to the fight. On 8 May the English abandoned the siege. More victories followed, including the Battle of Patay in June, where English archers were caught before they could prepare their defences. Joan then urged Charles to make the dangerous journey to Reims, the traditional site where French kings were crowned. On 17 July 1429 he was crowned Charles VII, with Joan standing nearby holding her banner.

sections.key: Captured in 1430, Joan was tried for heresy by a pro-English Church court in Rouen.
sections.b: After the coronation, Joan's fortunes turned. An attack on Paris failed, and the king grew more interested in negotiation than war. In May 1430, while defending the town of Compiègne, she was pulled from her horse and captured by Burgundian soldiers, who sold her to the English. There is no evidence that Charles made any serious attempt to rescue her. In 1431 she was tried for heresy in Rouen by a Church court led by Pierre Cauchon, a bishop allied with the English. The English needed her condemned, since that would suggest Charles had been crowned with the devil's help. The surviving records show an illiterate young woman answering trick questions from learned men with remarkable sharpness and courage.

sections.key: Joan was burned at the stake in 1431, aged about nineteen, and was declared innocent in a retrial in 1456.
sections.b: One major charge against Joan was that she wore men's clothing, which her accusers treated as a sin against divine law. Under pressure she signed a statement renouncing her claims and agreed to wear women's dress, but days later she resumed men's clothing, and the court declared her a relapsed heretic. On 30 May 1431, in the market square of Rouen, she was burned at the stake. She was about nineteen. Within a generation the war she had helped turn ended, as French armies took back Normandy and Gascony. By 1453 England held only Calais. A retrial authorised by the Pope declared the original verdict null in 1456. Joan was made a saint in 1920 and is a patron saint of France.

quiz.q: What did the Treaty of Troyes in 1420 do?
o: Declared that the English king would inherit the French throne
Made Joan of Arc a commander
quiz.e: The treaty disinherited the Dauphin Charles and named the English king as heir to France, putting the French cause in deep trouble.

quiz.q: Why did Charles have Joan questioned by churchmen at Poitiers?
o: To decide whether she was genuine or a fraud or heretic before trusting her
quiz.e: Backing a false prophet could be disastrous, so theologians examined her for weeks. They found nothing wrong, and Charles sent her to Orléans.

quiz.q: Why was the coronation at Reims so important?
o: It was where Joan was born
It was the traditional place where French kings were crowned, strengthening Charles's claim
quiz.e: Being crowned at Reims gave Charles VII the traditional legitimacy of a French king, a powerful answer to English claims.

quiz.q: Who captured Joan at Compiègne in 1430?
o: Burgundian soldiers, who sold her to the English
quiz.e: Burgundian forces, allied with England, captured her and handed her over to the English for payment.

quiz.q: What happened in 1456?
o: A retrial declared her original conviction null
quiz.e: A retrial authorised by the Pope overturned her conviction in 1456. She was canonised much later, in 1920.

LESSONS.title: Hadrian's Wall: life on the edge of an empire
LESSONS.hook: For nearly three hundred years, soldiers from across the Roman world guarded a stone wall in the rain of northern Britain. The letters they left behind are astonishingly human.

sections.key: Hadrian ordered the wall around AD 122 as part of a policy of securing the empire's borders.
sections.b: Hadrian became Roman emperor in AD 117, when the empire was at its largest extent. Rather than pursue endless conquest, he chose to consolidate, giving up some recently won territory and strengthening the frontiers. He spent much of his reign travelling the provinces, and around AD 122 he visited Britain. His biography, written centuries later, says he built a wall to separate the Romans from the barbarians. Construction began soon after. The wall ran across the narrow neck of northern Britain for about 118 kilometres, from Wallsend on the River Tyne in the east to Bowness-on-Solway in the west. It was built mainly by soldiers of the three legions stationed in Britain, who were skilled builders as well as fighters.

sections.key: The wall was a whole military system of forts, milecastles, turrets, roads and ditches.
sections.b: Hadrian's Wall was not just a line of stone. In its eastern part it was built of stone up to about three metres thick; the western section was first built of turf and later rebuilt in stone. Every Roman mile, roughly 1.5 kilometres, there was a small fort called a milecastle, with a gateway through the wall, and between each pair of milecastles stood two watchtowers called turrets. In front ran a deep ditch. Behind it the Romans dug another huge earthwork known as the vallum, a ditch flanked by mounds that marked off a military zone. Later, around fifteen larger forts were added along the wall itself, such as Housesteads, each holding hundreds of soldiers, with a military road connecting them.

sections.key: The wall probably controlled movement, trade and taxation as much as it kept out invaders.
sections.b: It is tempting to see Hadrian's Wall as a fortress line built to stop invading hordes, but most historians think its purpose was more complicated. Soldiers did not usually fight from the top of walls; they fought in the open. The wall's many gateways suggest that people were expected to pass through, under supervision. Its main jobs were probably controlling who crossed, collecting customs duties on goods, preventing small-scale raids and cattle rustling, and watching the tribes to the north. It was also a statement. A massive stone barrier stretching from coast to coast announced the power and reach of Rome. Historians still debate how much each purpose mattered, and the answer may have changed over its long life.

sections.key: The wall was garrisoned by auxiliary troops recruited from across the empire, from the Low Countries to Syria.
sections.b: The legionaries who built the wall were mostly moved elsewhere once it was finished. It was garrisoned by auxiliaries, soldiers recruited from the empire's provinces who became Roman citizens after their service. Inscriptions show units from what are now Belgium, the Netherlands, Germany, Spain and beyond. At the fort of Arbeia, in modern South Shields, there was even a unit of bargemen from the Tigris river in Mesopotamia. A tombstone found there was set up by Barates, a man from Palmyra in Syria, for his wife Regina, a freed slave from the British Catuvellauni tribe. It is carved with an inscription in Latin and a line in Palmyrene Aramaic. The northern frontier was one of the most multicultural places in Roman Britain.

sections.key: Wooden writing tablets found at Vindolanda preserve the everyday letters of soldiers and their families.
sections.b: Just south of the wall lies Vindolanda, a fort that predates Hadrian's Wall. From 1973, archaeologists there led by Robin Birley began finding thin wooden tablets, preserved in waterlogged, oxygen-free soil, covered in ink handwriting from around AD 100. They include duty reports, supply lists and private letters. One soldier is sent socks, sandals and two pairs of underpants. Another note dismissively calls the locals Brittunculi, little Britons. The most famous is a birthday invitation from Claudia Severa to her friend Sulpicia Lepidina, the wife of the fort's commander. Most of it was written by a scribe, but a few warm lines at the end appear to be in Claudia's own hand, among the earliest known examples of Latin handwriting by a woman.

sections.key: Hadrian's Wall lies entirely in England and was never the border with Scotland.
sections.b: A common myth is that Hadrian's Wall marks the border between England and Scotland. It does not. The whole wall lies within England, and in places the modern border is up to about a hundred kilometres to the north. Around AD 142, Hadrian's successor Antoninus Pius pushed further into what is now Scotland and built the turf Antonine Wall, but it was abandoned within about twenty years and the army returned to Hadrian's line. The wall was garrisoned until Roman rule in Britain ended in the early fifth century. Afterwards, much of its stone was taken to build farms, churches and roads. Even so, long stretches still stand, and since 1987 it has been listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

quiz.q: What was Hadrian's general policy for the empire's frontiers?
quiz.e: Hadrian preferred to secure and defend the empire's existing borders rather than keep expanding. The wall was part of that policy.

quiz.q: What was a milecastle?
o: A town built every hundred miles
A small fort with a gateway placed roughly every Roman mile along the wall
A stone marker showing distance to Rome
quiz.e: Milecastles were small fortlets about every Roman mile, each with a gateway, with two turrets between each pair.

quiz.q: What does the wall's large number of gateways suggest about its purpose?
o: It was never meant to be crossed
It was designed mainly for tourists
People were expected to cross under supervision, so it controlled movement and trade
quiz.e: Gateways indicate controlled passage. Many historians think the wall regulated movement and customs as much as it stopped attacks.

quiz.q: Why did the Vindolanda tablets survive for nearly two thousand years?
o: They were stored in a Roman library
Waterlogged, oxygen-free soil preserved the wood
They were copied by medieval monks
quiz.e: Wet, oxygen-poor conditions slowed decay, preserving thin wooden tablets with their ink writing from around AD 100.

quiz.q: Which statement about Hadrian's Wall today is true?
o: It is the modern border between England and Scotland
It was built after the Antonine Wall
quiz.e: The wall is wholly in England, in places far south of the modern border. Long stretches survive, and it is a World Heritage Site.

LESSONS.title: Myths about the Middle Ages
LESSONS.hook: Flat Earth, no baths, and everyone dead by thirty. Much of what people think they know about medieval life was invented or exaggerated centuries later.

sections.h: Myth: they thought the Earth was flat
sections.key: Educated medieval Europeans knew the Earth was round; the flat Earth myth was largely a nineteenth century creation.
sections.b: One of the most persistent ideas about the Middle Ages is that people believed the Earth was flat, and that Columbus had to prove otherwise. Educated medieval Europeans knew perfectly well that the Earth was a sphere. Ancient Greek scholars had shown this, and medieval writers such as the English monk Bede in the eighth century took it for granted. A popular thirteenth century textbook on astronomy, known as De sphaera, taught a spherical Earth in universities for centuries. Kings were even shown holding an orb, a globe symbolising their rule. The argument over Columbus's voyage was about the size of the Earth, and his critics were right that it was larger than he claimed. The flat Earth myth spread mostly in the 1800s.

sections.key: Low average life expectancy was driven by child deaths; adults who survived childhood often lived into their fifties and sixties.
sections.b: You may have heard that medieval people lived to around thirty. Estimates of average life expectancy at birth in that range are plausible, but averages can mislead. A huge share of children died in infancy or early childhood from disease, and these deaths pulled the average down sharply. If a family had one child who died as a baby and another who lived to sixty, their average is about thirty, yet no one died at thirty. People who survived childhood had a reasonable chance of reaching their fifties or sixties, and some lived much longer. Old people were a normal part of medieval communities. Dangers for adults were real, including childbirth, plague, war and accidents, but thirty was not old age.

sections.key: Medieval people valued cleanliness, and many towns had public bathhouses.
sections.b: Medieval people did not have modern plumbing, but they were not indifferent to dirt. Washing hands before and after meals was expected etiquette, and people washed their faces and bodies with water from basins. Soap was made and sold across Europe. Many towns had public bathhouses, often called stews in England, where people bathed in warm water and socialised. These became associated with prostitution, and many closed in the sixteenth century, partly because of fears that they spread disease, including syphilis. Ironically, some later periods, with their suspicion of bathing in water, may have been less fond of a good wash than the Middle Ages. Medieval medical writers also offered plenty of advice on hygiene, from cleaning teeth to washing hair.

sections.key: There is little reliable evidence that chastity belts were actually used in the Middle Ages.
sections.b: The image of a crusading knight locking his wife into an iron chastity belt is a favourite of comedies and tourist museums. Historians, however, find almost no reliable evidence that this happened. The earliest known mentions are a handful of references and drawings from the fifteenth century, several of which seem to be jokes or satire about jealous husbands. Many of the metal belts once displayed in museums have since been identified as much later creations, some made in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, and several institutions have withdrawn them or relabelled them. Wearing one for long periods would also have caused serious infections. Most historians now consider the medieval chastity belt to be largely a myth, invented or embellished by later generations.

sections.h: Myth: they drank beer because water was deadly
sections.key: Medieval people did drink water; ale was popular as food, drink and calories rather than as a safety measure.
sections.b: Another common claim is that medieval people drank only beer and wine because all water was dangerous. Historians who have studied the evidence argue this is greatly exaggerated. People knew that some water sources were dirty and preferred clean springs, wells and rivers, and towns invested in fountains and pipes to bring fresh water. Monastic rules and medical writings refer to drinking water, sometimes recommending it. Ale was extremely popular, but for other reasons. It was a valuable source of calories for hard physical work, it was cheap, and people enjoyed it. Much everyday ale was relatively weak. The picture of a society too frightened of water to drink it is mostly a modern assumption, not something medieval sources describe.

sections.key: The great European witch hunts took place mainly in the early modern period, from about 1450 to 1750.
sections.b: When people picture witch trials, they often imagine the Middle Ages. In fact, the large-scale witch hunts of Europe happened mostly afterwards, in the early modern period, peaking roughly between 1560 and 1630. Before then, many Church authorities had been sceptical about witches' powers, and an early medieval Church text, the Canon Episcopi, even treated the idea of witches flying at night as an illusion. Belief in organised, devil-worshipping witches grew in the fifteenth century, helped by books such as the Malleus Maleficarum, published in 1486 and spread by the new printing press. Estimates suggest that roughly forty to sixty thousand people were executed for witchcraft in Europe. Many were hanged rather than burned, depending on local law.

sections.key: Historians now rarely use the term ‘Dark Ages’, because the medieval period saw real advances in learning and technology.
sections.b: The Italian scholar Petrarch, in the fourteenth century, helped popularise the idea that the centuries after Rome's fall were a time of darkness compared with classical antiquity. The label stuck, but most historians now avoid it. The early medieval period does have fewer written sources in some regions, which makes it darker to us in the sense of being harder to see. But the medieval centuries also produced the first European universities, such as Bologna, Paris and Oxford, soaring Gothic cathedrals, mechanical clocks, eyeglasses and the spread of windmills. Monasteries copied and preserved many classical texts. Meanwhile, scholars in the Islamic world, Byzantium and China were making major advances. The Middle Ages were not a pause in history.

quiz.q: What was the real argument about Columbus's voyage?
o: The size of the Earth, which Columbus underestimated
Whether ships could sail west at all
quiz.e: Educated people knew the Earth was round. Columbus's critics argued correctly that the Earth was larger than he claimed, making Asia much further away.

quiz.q: Why does a low average medieval life expectancy not mean people died at thirty?
o: High child mortality pulled the average down, while many adults lived to their fifties or sixties
quiz.e: Averages combine many infant deaths with long adult lives. Someone who survived childhood had a good chance of living well beyond thirty.

quiz.q: What do historians say about medieval chastity belts?
o: They were standard for crusaders' wives
There is little reliable evidence they were used, and many museum examples are later creations
They were invented by the Romans
quiz.e: Early references look like satire, and many surviving belts were made centuries later. Most historians regard medieval use as largely a myth.

quiz.q: When did the major European witch hunts mostly take place?
o: In the early Middle Ages, around AD 800
In the early modern period, peaking roughly 1560 to 1630
quiz.e: The great witch hunts were mainly early modern, after the Middle Ages, helped by printed books such as the Malleus Maleficarum.

quiz.q: Why do most historians avoid the term ‘Dark Ages’?
o: The period produced universities, cathedrals and new technologies
There are no sources from the period
quiz.e: The medieval period saw universities, Gothic cathedrals, mechanical clocks, eyeglasses and much more, so ‘dark’ is misleading.

LESSONS.title: The Library of Alexandria: what really happened
LESSONS.hook: It is the most famous lost library in history, supposedly destroyed in a single catastrophic fire. The truth is slower, stranger and more of a warning.

sections.h: A library for a whole world
sections.key: The Ptolemaic kings founded the Library in the early third century BC as part of a research institution called the Mouseion.
sections.b: After Alexander the Great's death, his general Ptolemy took Egypt and made Alexandria his capital. Early in the third century BC, Ptolemy I or his son Ptolemy II founded the Mouseion, a temple to the Muses that functioned as a kind of research institute, and with it the Library. The Ptolemies wanted Alexandria to outshine Athens as the centre of Greek culture, and they paid scholars to live, work and dine together at royal expense. The goal of the Library was ambitious: to collect every important book written in Greek, along with translations of works from other cultures. A later tradition holds that the Hebrew scriptures were first translated into Greek there, producing the version known as the Septuagint.

sections.key: The Ptolemies collected aggressively, reportedly copying books from ships and keeping the Athenian originals of classic plays.
sections.b: The Ptolemies went to remarkable lengths to fill their shelves. The Roman-era physician Galen, writing centuries later, told two famous stories. In one, ships arriving at Alexandria's harbour were searched for books, which were taken to be copied; the owners received the copies and the Library kept the originals. In the other, Ptolemy III borrowed the official Athenian texts of the great tragedians Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides, leaving an enormous deposit of fifteen talents of silver as security. He then kept the originals, sent back copies and cheerfully forfeited the deposit. These stories may be exaggerated, but they capture the Library's hunger. Books were written on papyrus scrolls, and a single long work might fill dozens of them.

sections.key: Ancient estimates of the Library's size vary wildly, from tens of thousands to around seven hundred thousand scrolls.
sections.b: Nobody knows how many books the Library held. Ancient writers give figures ranging from around forty thousand to seven hundred thousand scrolls, and these numbers were often written long after the fact, by authors who had no way of checking. Counting was also complicated by duplicates and by the fact that a single work could fill many scrolls. Modern scholars generally treat the higher figures with scepticism, while agreeing that the collection was the largest of its time in the Greek world. Its main rival was the library of Pergamon, in modern Turkey. A story told by Pliny the Elder claims that rivalry over papyrus supplies encouraged Pergamon to develop parchment, made from animal skin, though historians doubt this neat explanation.

sections.key: Alexandria's scholars measured the Earth, catalogued literature and edited the texts of Homer.
sections.b: The Library mattered less for its shelves than for the people who worked there. Eratosthenes, one of its chief librarians, estimated the circumference of the Earth by comparing the angle of the Sun's shadow at Alexandria and at Syene, far to the south, on the same day. His result was remarkably close to the true value, though historians debate exactly how close because his units of length are uncertain. The poet Callimachus compiled the Pinakes, a huge catalogue of Greek authors and works, often described as an ancestor of the library catalogue. Scholars such as Zenodotus and Aristarchus produced careful editions of Homer, comparing different copies to remove errors. Alexandria also became a great centre of medicine, mathematics and astronomy.

sections.key: Julius Caesar's war in Alexandria in 48 BC caused a fire that destroyed books, but how many, and where, is unclear.
sections.b: The most famous story about the Library's destruction involves Julius Caesar. In 48 BC, besieged in Alexandria during the civil war involving Cleopatra and her brother, Caesar set fire to ships in the harbour. Several ancient writers say the blaze spread and burned books. The Roman philosopher Seneca mentions forty thousand books lost. But the sources disagree about what burned. Some historians think the fire mainly destroyed warehouses near the docks holding scrolls awaiting export or cataloguing, rather than the Library itself. What is clear is that scholarly activity in Alexandria continued afterwards. The geographer Strabo worked in the city a couple of decades later and wrote about the Mouseion, while saying nothing about a destroyed library.

sections.key: The Library most likely declined over centuries through political purges, war, lost funding and the natural decay of papyrus.
sections.b: Rather than one dramatic ending, the evidence points to a long decline. As early as 145 BC, King Ptolemy VIII expelled many intellectuals from Alexandria, including the head librarian Aristarchus, scattering scholars to other cities. Under Roman rule royal patronage disappeared. In the AD 270s, fighting under the emperor Aurelian devastated the palace quarter where the Library probably stood. Meanwhile there was a quieter enemy. Papyrus is fragile, and in Alexandria's damp coastal air scrolls rotted and had to be recopied regularly. A library that loses its funding and its staff loses its books without any fire at all. By late antiquity, the great Library seems to have faded away, and no source clearly describes its final end.

sections.key: Stories blaming Christian mobs or the Arab conquest for burning the Library are not supported by reliable evidence.
sections.b: Later writers have blamed whichever villain suited their argument. In AD 391, Christians destroyed the Serapeum, a temple in Alexandria that had housed a smaller daughter library, but it is unclear whether it still held many books by then. The murder of the philosopher Hypatia in 415 was a terrible event, but it had nothing to do with destroying a library. A story claims that after the Arab conquest of 642, the Caliph Umar ordered the books burned to heat the city's bathhouses for six months. This story first appears in sources written more than five centuries later, and most historians reject it. The real lesson of Alexandria may be that knowledge usually dies through neglect, not one great fire.

quiz.q: What was the Mouseion?
o: A temple to the Muses that functioned as a royal research institution
A school for scribes run by Roman emperors
quiz.e: The Mouseion, from which the word museum derives, housed and paid scholars under Ptolemaic patronage, with the Library as part of it.

quiz.q: Why should ancient figures for the Library's size be treated with caution?
o: They were all written by Caesar
They vary enormously and were often written long afterwards without any way to check
quiz.e: Estimates range from about 40,000 to 700,000 scrolls, often given by much later authors, and complicated by duplicates and multi-scroll works.

quiz.q: What did Eratosthenes estimate using the Sun's shadow?
quiz.e: By comparing shadow angles at Alexandria and Syene on the same day, Eratosthenes estimated the Earth's circumference with impressive accuracy.

quiz.q: According to the evidence, what most likely ended the Library?
o: A single fire started by Caesar
A long decline through purges, war, lost funding and decaying papyrus
quiz.e: The evidence points to centuries of decline, including expelled scholars, lost royal funding, war damage and the need to keep recopying fragile scrolls.

quiz.q: Why do most historians reject the story that the Caliph Umar ordered the books burned?
o: It first appears in sources written more than five centuries after the event
Umar was not alive in the seventh century
The story was invented by Strabo
quiz.e: The tale first appears centuries later, long after the Library had already faded, so it is not regarded as reliable evidence.

LESSONS.title: The day the Mona Lisa vanished
LESSONS.hook: In 1911 a handyman walked out of the Louvre with the world's most famous painting under his smock. Strangely, the theft is a big part of why it became so famous.

sections.key: The Mona Lisa was stolen on 21 August 1911, a day the Louvre was closed to the public.
sections.b: Mondays were cleaning days at the Louvre, when the galleries were shut and workmen moved freely through the halls. On the morning of 21 August 1911, a man in a white workman's smock lifted Leonardo da Vinci's portrait off its hooks in the Salon Carré. The painting is small, about 77 by 53 centimetres, and painted on a thin panel of poplar wood rather than canvas. The thief carried it to a service stairwell, removed the heavy frame and protective glass box, and slipped the panel under his clothing. Accounts differ on whether he had hidden in a storeroom overnight or simply arrived that morning among the staff. Either way, he walked out into the Paris streets, and nobody stopped him.

sections.key: The empty wall went unremarked for more than a day, because paintings were often moved for photography.
sections.b: The next morning, a painter named Louis Béroud arrived to sketch in the Salon Carré and found four iron pegs where the Mona Lisa should have been. Guards assumed it had been taken away by the museum's photographers, which happened regularly. Only after Béroud pushed them to check did the truth sink in. The museum closed for a week, and police searched every corner of its vast buildings. They found the empty frame and glass case in the stairwell, but the painting itself was gone. The newspapers erupted. The scandal cost the museum's director his job, and the story spread across the world, with the missing picture reproduced on front pages in country after country.

sections.key: The investigation swept up famous names, including the poet Guillaume Apollinaire and the young Pablo Picasso.
sections.b: With few leads, police followed some strange trails. A shady acquaintance of the poet Guillaume Apollinaire had earlier stolen small ancient Iberian statuettes from the Louvre, and Picasso had ended up with two of them. When the press reported the link, Apollinaire was arrested and spent several days in jail, and Picasso was questioned by a magistrate. Both were cleared of any connection to the Mona Lisa. Meanwhile, rumours flourished: that a wealthy collector had ordered the theft, that the German Kaiser was behind it, or that the museum had lost it through sheer incompetence. The real thief had actually been interviewed by police early on, at his lodgings, and had not raised suspicion.

sections.key: The thief, Vincenzo Peruggia, kept the painting hidden in his small Paris room for more than two years.
sections.b: The man behind it was Vincenzo Peruggia, an Italian craftsman who had worked at the Louvre and had helped install the very glass cases meant to protect its paintings. He knew the building, and the staff knew him. For more than two years he kept the Mona Lisa in a trunk with a false bottom in his room in Paris. In late 1913 he wrote to an art dealer in Florence, Alfredo Geri, offering to return the painting to Italy. Geri arranged a meeting at a hotel along with Giovanni Poggi, director of the Uffizi Gallery. After examining the panel and checking the Louvre's markings on the back, they alerted police, and Peruggia was arrested.

sections.key: Peruggia claimed he wanted to bring Leonardo's masterpiece home to Italy, though he also hoped for a reward.
sections.b: At his trial in Florence, Peruggia argued that he had acted out of patriotism. He believed, wrongly, that Napoleon had looted the painting from Italy. In fact, Leonardo had taken it to France himself and it had passed into the French royal collection long before Napoleon was born. Peruggia's story struck a chord with many Italians, and he received a fairly light sentence of a little over a year, of which he served only about seven months. Historians note that he had also asked for money, so his motives were probably mixed. Before going home, the Mona Lisa was put on display in Florence, Rome and Milan, drawing enormous crowds, and returned to the Louvre in early 1914.

sections.h: How a theft made a superstar
sections.key: The theft turned a respected masterpiece into a global celebrity.
sections.b: Before 1911, the Mona Lisa was admired by art lovers, but it was not obviously the most famous painting on Earth. The theft changed that. For two years, the story ran in newspapers worldwide, with photographs of the portrait printed again and again. During its absence, visitors even queued at the Louvre to stare at the empty space on the wall. When it came back, it returned as a celebrity. Art historians often point to the theft as a turning point in the painting's fame, alongside Leonardo's reputation and the picture's genuinely remarkable technique, such as the soft, smoky blending called sfumato. Today it sits behind protective glass and is seen by millions of visitors every year.

quiz.q: Why could the thief move freely through the Louvre that day?
o: It was a public holiday with huge crowds
It was a Monday, when the museum was closed for cleaning
The painting was being moved to another wing
quiz.e: On Mondays the Louvre was closed and workmen moved around the galleries, so a man in a smock looked ordinary.

quiz.q: Why didn't guards raise the alarm straight away?
o: They assumed photographers had taken the painting
They were in on the plot
A copy had been hung in its place
The room had been locked for repairs
quiz.e: Paintings were often removed to be photographed, so the empty wall did not seem alarming at first.

quiz.q: Which famous artist was questioned during the investigation?
quiz.e: Picasso had acquired statuettes stolen from the Louvre by an acquaintance of Apollinaire, so he was questioned, but he was cleared.

quiz.q: What was wrong with Peruggia's claim about Napoleon?
o: Napoleon had paid for the painting
Leonardo himself had taken the painting to France long before Napoleon
The painting had never left Florence
Napoleon had tried to destroy it
quiz.e: Leonardo brought the portrait to France, and it entered the French royal collection centuries before Napoleon.

quiz.q: What effect did the theft have on the painting's reputation?
o: It made people doubt it was genuine
It made the painting a worldwide celebrity
It led the Louvre to sell it
quiz.e: Two years of worldwide headlines and photographs helped turn the Mona Lisa into the most famous painting in the world.

LESSONS.title: The Bayeux Tapestry: 1066 in wool
LESSONS.hook: A strip of linen nearly 70 metres long tells the story of the Norman conquest of England like a medieval comic strip. And technically, it isn't even a tapestry.

sections.key: The Bayeux Tapestry is an embroidery, stitched in coloured wool on linen.
sections.b: A true tapestry has its picture woven into the fabric on a loom. The Bayeux Tapestry was made differently. Its images were stitched with coloured woollen yarn onto a long band of plain linen, which makes it an embroidery. It is roughly 68 metres long but only about half a metre tall, made from several pieces of linen joined together. The embroiderers used only a handful of colours, mainly shades of red, yellow, green and blue, yet they created hundreds of people, horses, ships, buildings and animals. Short Latin captions run above the scenes, naming people and places. Read from left to right, it unfolds like a film reel, which is why it is often called the world's oldest comic strip.

sections.key: It was probably commissioned by Bishop Odo, William the Conqueror's half-brother, and stitched in England in the 1070s.
sections.b: No document records who ordered the embroidery, but most historians think it was Odo, Bishop of Bayeux, half-brother of William the Conqueror. Odo appears prominently in the scenes, and the cathedral at Bayeux was consecrated in 1077, a likely occasion for such a gift. Strangely for a French treasure, it was probably made in England. The style of the drawings and some of the spelling in the captions suggest English craftspeople, possibly working in Canterbury, which was famous for its needlework. English embroidery was admired across Europe at the time. So the story of England's conquest may have been stitched by the conquered themselves, working for one of the new Norman rulers.

sections.key: The story begins with Harold Godwinson making a solemn promise to Duke William of Normandy.
sections.b: The embroidery opens in England with the old king, Edward the Confessor, and his powerful nobleman Harold Godwinson. Harold sails to France, is captured, and ends up at the court of William, Duke of Normandy. He even joins William on a military campaign in Brittany. Then comes the key scene: Harold swears an oath with his hands on holy relics. The embroidery does not spell out the promise, but Norman sources claimed he swore to support William's claim to the English throne. When Edward died in January 1066 and Harold took the crown himself, the Normans could present him as an oath breaker. The tapestry, in other words, is telling the story from the winners' point of view.

sections.key: The embroidery shows Halley's Comet as an omen, then the huge effort of building an invasion fleet.
sections.b: Soon after Harold is crowned, people point up at a star with flaming tails. This is Halley's Comet, which really did appear in the spring of 1066 and was widely seen as an omen. The tapestry then shows something often skipped in history books: the logistics of invasion. Trees are felled, ships are built, and men carry armour, swords, spears and barrels of wine down to the boats. Horses are loaded aboard and the fleet crosses the Channel. Once landed, the Normans build a fort and cook a feast. These everyday scenes are priceless to historians, offering rare pictures of eleventh century clothing, weapons, tools, ships and food.

sections.key: The climax is the battle of 14 October 1066, ending with the death of King Harold.
sections.b: The battle scenes are crowded and violent. Norman cavalry charge at English soldiers standing in a shield wall on a hill. Bodies, severed heads and fallen horses fill the lower border. At one point William lifts his helmet to show his men he is still alive, after a rumour spread that he had been killed. Then comes the famous scene of Harold's death, under the caption saying that King Harold is killed. One figure appears to clutch an arrow in his eye, and another is cut down by a mounted knight. Historians still debate which figure is Harold, and some believe the arrow was altered or added during nineteenth century restoration work. The final section of the embroidery is missing.

sections.key: The fragile embroidery has survived fires, revolutions and wars, and has often been used as propaganda.
sections.b: The first known written record of the embroidery is a 1476 inventory of Bayeux Cathedral, where it was hung around the nave on certain feast days. During the French Revolution it was nearly cut up to cover military wagons, until a local official rescued it. Napoleon put it on display in Paris in the early 1800s while he was planning his own invasion of England. During the Second World War, Nazi researchers studied it as a supposed celebration of Germanic warriors, and it was moved to the Louvre in 1944 for safekeeping. Today it is displayed in a museum in Bayeux, in low light and under careful climate control, to protect its ancient wool and linen.

quiz.q: Why is the Bayeux Tapestry technically not a tapestry?
o: It is embroidered with wool on linen rather than woven on a loom
It is printed with wooden blocks
quiz.e: A tapestry is woven; this work is stitched onto linen, which makes it an embroidery.

quiz.q: Where was the embroidery most likely made?
quiz.e: The drawing style and caption spellings point to English makers, probably working for Bishop Odo.

quiz.q: Why is Harold's oath so important in the story?
o: It shows Harold being crowned by the Pope
It lets the Normans portray Harold as an oath breaker when he takes the throne
It ends the war between England and France
It shows William promising land to Harold
quiz.e: Norman sources said Harold swore to support William's claim, so his coronation could be framed as a broken oath.

quiz.q: What does the 'star with flaming tails' in the embroidery represent?
quiz.e: Halley's Comet appeared in 1066 and was seen as an omen.

quiz.q: What do historians debate about the famous death scene?
o: Whether the battle happened at all
Which figure is Harold, and whether the arrow was altered in later restoration
Whether the scene was added in the 1900s
quiz.e: It is unclear which figure is Harold, and restoration work may have changed the arrow.

LESSONS.title: How the movies began
LESSONS.hook: A bet about a galloping horse, a peephole machine and a café screening in Paris led to the most popular art form of the twentieth century. And one of the first feature films was Australian.

sections.key: In 1878 Eadweard Muybridge photographed a running horse and settled a long argument about how horses move.
sections.b: For centuries, painters showed galloping horses with legs stretched out front and back like a rocking horse. Nobody could see clearly enough to know. In California, the businessman Leland Stanford hired the photographer Eadweard Muybridge to find out whether all four hooves ever left the ground at once. In 1878, Muybridge set up a row of cameras along a track, triggered one after another as the horse raced past. The pictures showed that the hooves did all leave the ground, but when they were tucked up underneath the body, not stretched out. Muybridge then put his sequences on a spinning disc and projected them, so audiences watched the horse appear to run. Moving pictures had begun.

sections.h: Why still pictures seem to move
sections.key: Film is a series of still frames shown fast enough that the brain blends them into motion.
sections.b: A film strip is simply a long row of photographs, each slightly different from the last. Shown quickly enough, the brain stops seeing separate pictures and perceives smooth movement. For a long time this was explained by persistence of vision, the idea that each image lingers on the retina. Most researchers now think that explanation is incomplete. The illusion mainly comes from how the brain's visual system detects motion, filling in movement between closely spaced images, a related effect psychologists call apparent motion. Early silent films ran at varied speeds, often around 16 to 20 frames per second. When sound arrived in the late 1920s, 24 frames per second became the standard, and it is still common today.

sections.key: Thomas Edison's team built the Kinetoscope, a box in which one person at a time watched a short film.
sections.b: In the United States, Thomas Edison's laboratory took up the challenge, with much of the work done by his assistant William Kennedy Laurie Dickson. They used long strips of flexible celluloid film with holes punched along the edges so a mechanism could pull them through smoothly. Their Kinetoscope, shown to the public in 1894, was a wooden cabinet with a viewing hole on top. One customer at a time peered in to watch a film lasting less than a minute: a strongman flexing, dancers, a sneeze. Kinetoscope parlours opened in New York and other cities. Edison believed individual viewing would be more profitable than projecting films for crowds, a decision that let rivals take the lead in projection.

sections.key: On 28 December 1895, Auguste and Louis Lumière held a paid public film screening in Paris.
sections.b: In Lyon, France, the brothers Auguste and Louis Lumière ran a successful photographic business. They designed the Cinématographe, a light, hand-cranked machine that could film, develop prints and project them onto a screen. On 28 December 1895, in a room beneath the Grand Café in Paris, they showed a programme of short films to a paying audience. The films were scenes from life: workers leaving the Lumière factory, a baby being fed, a gardener squirted by his own hose. A famous story claims that viewers of their film of a train arriving at a station panicked and fled. Historians have found little reliable evidence for this, and it is probably an exaggeration that grew in the retelling.

sections.key: Filmmakers soon discovered tricks and editing, turning simple recordings into stories.
sections.b: One spectator at an early Lumière show was Georges Méliès, a Paris stage magician. He began making films and discovered that stopping the camera, changing something and starting again could make people vanish or transform. His 1902 film A Trip to the Moon, with its rocket lodged in the eye of the moon's face, became one of the most famous images of early cinema. In the United States, The Great Train Robbery of 1903, directed by Edwin S. Porter, told an action story across separate scenes and locations. Audiences learned to follow shots joined together, accepting that a cut could jump in space and time. Cinema was becoming a language of its own.

sections.key: The Story of the Kelly Gang, made in Melbourne in 1906, is widely regarded as the world's first feature-length narrative film.
sections.b: Most early films lasted a few minutes. Then, in 1906, a team in Melbourne, including members of the Tait family of concert promoters, filmed the story of the bushranger Ned Kelly. The Story of the Kelly Gang ran for about an hour, far longer than almost anything made before, and it toured Australia, New Zealand and Britain with great success. It is widely considered the first feature-length narrative film anywhere in the world. Sadly, most of it has been lost, because early nitrate film was fragile and highly flammable. Only fragments survive, carefully restored by the National Film and Sound Archive. In 2007 the film was added to UNESCO's Memory of the World Register.

sections.key: Synchronised sound in the late 1920s transformed the industry within a few years.
sections.b: Silent films were rarely silent. Cinemas hired pianists, organists or whole orchestras, and some had narrators or sound effects. But recording dialogue that matched the actors' lips was hard. In 1927 Warner Bros released The Jazz Singer, which included synchronised songs and a few lines of spoken dialogue. Audiences were thrilled, and within a few years most studios had switched to sound. The change was brutal for some. Actors whose voices did not suit the microphone lost careers, cinema musicians lost jobs, and cameras were temporarily trapped in soundproof booths. Yet sound also opened new forms, such as the musical. In barely three decades, moving pictures had gone from a scientific curiosity to a global art.

quiz.q: What did Muybridge's photographs reveal about galloping horses?
o: Their hooves never all leave the ground
All four hooves leave the ground, but tucked under the body
Horses gallop with legs stretched out front and back
Only the front legs leave the ground
quiz.e: The hooves do all leave the ground at once, but when gathered underneath, not stretched out like a rocking horse.

quiz.q: What became the standard frame rate when sound films arrived?
quiz.e: Sound required a fixed speed, and 24 frames per second became the standard in the late 1920s.

quiz.q: What is the truth about audiences fleeing from the Lumières' train film?
o: It is well documented in police reports
There is little reliable evidence, so it is probably exaggerated
It caused the film to be banned
quiz.e: Historians have found little solid evidence for the panic story, which likely grew in the retelling.

quiz.q: What technique did Georges Méliès use to make people vanish on screen?
o: Stopping the camera, changing the scene and restarting
quiz.e: Méliès, a magician, discovered that stopping and restarting the camera created magical transformations.

quiz.q: Why is The Story of the Kelly Gang famous?
o: It was the first colour film
It was the first film with sound
It is widely regarded as the first feature-length narrative film
It was the first film shown in a cinema
quiz.e: Made in Melbourne in 1906, it ran about an hour, far longer than earlier films.

LESSONS.title: Frida Kahlo: painting her own reality
LESSONS.hook: A teenage bus crash left her in pain for life. From her bed, with a mirror above her, Frida Kahlo began painting the face that would become one of the most recognised in art.

sections.key: Frida Kahlo was born in 1907 in Coyoacán, near Mexico City, and grew up in the house now known as the Blue House.
sections.b: Magdalena Carmen Frida Kahlo was born on 6 July 1907 in Coyoacán, then a village on the edge of Mexico City. Her father was a photographer of German origin and her mother was Mexican. Later in life Frida often gave her birth year as 1910, the year the Mexican Revolution began, linking herself to the birth of modern Mexico. At about six she caught polio, which left her right leg thinner than the left. She was bright and rebellious, and in 1922 she became one of a small number of girls admitted to the elite National Preparatory School, where she planned to study medicine. Art was not yet her ambition.

sections.key: In 1925 a crash between a bus and a streetcar left her with terrible injuries and lifelong pain.
sections.b: On 17 September 1925, the bus Frida was riding in collided with a streetcar in Mexico City. She was eighteen. A metal handrail pierced her body, and she suffered fractures to her spine, pelvis, collarbone, ribs and right leg. Doctors were not sure she would survive. She did, but she spent months confined to bed and lived with pain for the rest of her life, undergoing many operations over the years. During her recovery, her mother had a special easel made so she could paint lying down, and a mirror was fitted above her bed. With her own reflection as the most available subject, she began painting self-portraits. Medicine gave way to art.

sections.key: Her marriage to the muralist Diego Rivera was passionate, stormy and central to her life and work.
sections.b: In 1928 Frida showed her paintings to Diego Rivera, already the most famous painter in Mexico and a leader of the mural movement, which covered public walls with scenes of Mexican history and workers' lives. He encouraged her, and they married in 1929. He was about twenty years older and much larger, and her parents reportedly compared the match to an elephant marrying a dove. Both had many affairs, and Rivera's affair with Frida's sister Cristina hurt her deeply. They divorced in 1939 and remarried in 1940. They travelled together to the United States, where Rivera painted murals, and their circle included artists, writers and political figures, among them the exiled Russian revolutionary Leon Trotsky.

sections.key: More than a third of her paintings are self-portraits, full of personal and Mexican symbolism.
sections.b: Kahlo made around 55 self-portraits, more than a third of her known paintings. She painted herself with her strong joined eyebrows and faint moustache, refusing to soften them. She often wore traditional Tehuana dresses from southern Mexico, with long skirts, embroidered blouses and flowers in her hair, celebrating Indigenous Mexican culture. Her paintings are small and detailed, influenced by Mexican folk art and the little devotional paintings called retablos. They are also frank about pain, miscarriage, surgery and heartbreak.
