In The Two Fridas, painted in 1939 around the time of her divorce, two versions of herself sit hand in hand, their exposed hearts joined by a single vein. Her body and her feelings were her central subject.

sections.key: The Surrealists claimed her as one of their own, but she rejected the label.
sections.b: In 1938 the French writer André Breton, leader of the Surrealist movement, visited Mexico and was enchanted by her work, which seemed to him dreamlike and strange. He helped arrange an exhibition for her in Paris in 1939. While she was there, the Louvre bought her self-portrait The Frame, making her the first twentieth century Mexican artist in its collection. The work is now held at the Pompidou Centre. Kahlo, however, was not comfortable being called a Surrealist. She said, in effect, that she did not paint dreams but her own reality. Her strange images, such as roots growing from her body or a broken stone column in place of her spine, were ways of showing real experiences.

sections.key: Her health declined in the 1950s, but she attended her first solo exhibition in Mexico from her bed.
sections.b: Kahlo's health grew worse through the 1940s and 1950s. She wore a series of supportive corsets, some of which she painted on, and had several spinal operations. In 1953, part of her right leg was amputated because of gangrene. That same year, she had her first solo exhibition in Mexico, at a gallery in Mexico City. Her doctors told her not to attend, so she arrived by ambulance and was carried in on her four poster bed, which had been installed in the gallery, and received guests lying down. She died at the Blue House on 13 July 1954, aged 47. Rivera later gave the house to the nation, and it opened as a museum in 1958.

sections.h: From cult figure to global icon
sections.key: Decades after her death, Kahlo became one of the most famous artists in the world.
sections.b: During her lifetime Kahlo was often seen mainly as Rivera's wife. That changed from the 1970s onwards, as feminist art historians, Mexican American artists and a 1983 biography by Hayden Herrera brought her work to a wide audience. A Hollywood film about her life followed in 2002. Her face now appears on everything from tote bags to fridge magnets, a phenomenon sometimes called Fridamania, which some critics feel risks reducing her to a brand. Her paintings have become hugely valuable. In 2021 her self-portrait Diego and I sold at auction for about 35 million US dollars, at the time a record for a Latin American artist. Mexico treats her works as national artistic heritage.

quiz.q: How did Kahlo begin painting self-portraits?
o: While bedridden after her accident, using a mirror fitted above her bed
She copied her father's photographs of her
Diego Rivera asked her to paint them
quiz.e: Her mother had a special easel made and a mirror installed so Frida could paint while lying down.

quiz.q: Who was Diego Rivera?
o: Mexico's most famous muralist, whom she married
Her art dealer in New York
quiz.e: Rivera was a leader of the Mexican mural movement; they married in 1929, divorced in 1939 and remarried in 1940.

quiz.q: What do Kahlo's Tehuana dresses represent in her paintings?
o: A celebration of Indigenous Mexican culture
Her time living in the United States
quiz.e: The dresses come from southern Mexico and expressed her pride in Indigenous Mexican identity.

quiz.q: How did Kahlo respond to being called a Surrealist?
o: She rejected it, saying she painted her own reality, not dreams
She founded her own Surrealist group
quiz.e: Though André Breton championed her, she insisted her images came from her real life.

quiz.q: How did Kahlo attend her first solo exhibition in Mexico in 1953?
o: She sent Diego in her place
She arrived by ambulance and received guests from her bed
quiz.e: Against medical advice, she was carried in on her four poster bed, which had been set up in the gallery.

LESSONS.title: Michelangelo and the Sistine Chapel ceiling
LESSONS.hook: A sculptor who didn't want the job spent four years painting a chapel ceiling twenty metres above the floor. He didn't do it lying on his back, either.

sections.key: Pope Julius II hired Michelangelo to paint the ceiling, though he thought of himself as a sculptor.
sections.b: In 1508, Michelangelo Buonarroti was in his early thirties and already famous for his marble David in Florence and his Pietà in Rome. He thought of himself first and foremost as a sculptor. Pope Julius II, a forceful and warlike pope, had earlier hired him to carve a grand tomb, but then turned his attention to decorating the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in the Vatican, built by his uncle, Pope Sixtus IV. Michelangelo had little experience of fresco painting and accepted the commission reluctantly. The chapel walls were already covered with frescoes by leading painters such as Botticelli and Perugino. The ceiling, painted as a starry sky, was about to be transformed.

sections.key: The ceiling is a fresco, painted onto fresh plaster in sections small enough to finish before it dried.
sections.b: Fresco means fresh in Italian. In true fresco, the painter applies pigments mixed with water onto a layer of wet lime plaster. As the plaster dries, a chemical reaction locks the colour into the wall itself, making it extremely durable. The catch is speed. Each day, only as much plaster as could be painted before it set was laid, and these daily patches are called giornate, from the Italian for a day's work. Mistakes could not simply be painted over; the plaster had to be chipped away and redone. Michelangelo's team transferred his designs to the plaster using full-size drawings called cartoons, either by pricking holes along the lines or by pressing them into the soft surface.

sections.key: Michelangelo painted standing on a scaffold and leaning back, not lying flat as the legend says.
sections.b: A popular image shows Michelangelo lying on his back for years, paint dripping onto his face. In reality, he designed a wooden scaffold that bridged the chapel just below the ceiling, leaving the floor below free for services. He and his assistants worked standing up, with heads tilted back and arms raised. It was still punishing. Michelangelo wrote a comic poem, with a little sketch in the margin, complaining about his aching neck, bent back and the paint dripping onto his face. Nor did he work entirely alone, as another myth claims. He had assistants to grind pigments, prepare plaster and help with some painting, although he did the great majority of the figures himself.

sections.key: The centre of the ceiling shows nine scenes from the Book of Genesis, surrounded by prophets, sibyls and ancestors.
sections.b: The ceiling is about 40 metres long and 13 metres wide, and it holds more than 300 figures. Down the centre run nine scenes from Genesis, from God separating light from darkness, through the creation of Adam and Eve and their expulsion from Eden, to the story of Noah. Around them sit huge figures of Old Testament prophets and the sibyls, prophetesses from the classical world, symbolising that the whole world awaited Christ. Muscular nude youths called ignudi perch on painted architecture that looks three-dimensional but is entirely an illusion. Interestingly, Michelangelo painted the scenes in reverse story order, starting near the entrance with Noah, and his figures grew larger and bolder as he went.

sections.key: The near-touching fingers of God and Adam became one of the most reproduced images in the world.
sections.b: The best known scene shows Adam reclining on the earth, his arm lifted limply, as God sweeps towards him surrounded by figures in a billowing red cloak. Their fingertips almost meet, leaving a tiny gap charged with tension. Life is about to pass from creator to creature. The scene has been copied, parodied and reproduced endlessly. Some writers have pointed out that the shape around God resembles a human brain and have suggested Michelangelo, who had studied anatomy by dissecting corpses, hid it there deliberately. It is an intriguing idea, but there is no evidence he intended it, and many art historians treat it as a modern reading rather than a hidden message.

sections.key: Over twenty years later Michelangelo painted The Last Judgment on the altar wall.
sections.b: The ceiling was unveiled in 1512 and stunned everyone who saw it. More than two decades later, Michelangelo returned to the chapel to paint The Last Judgment across the entire wall behind the altar, working from 1536 to 1541. It shows Christ raising the saved towards heaven while the damned tumble down to hell, a swirling mass of hundreds of mostly naked bodies. Some church officials were scandalised by the nudity. After Michelangelo's death, the painter Daniele da Volterra was hired to paint drapery over some figures, earning the mocking nickname Il Braghettone, the breeches maker. Some of these coverings were left in place even during modern restoration, as part of the painting's history.

sections.key: A major restoration from 1980 to 1994 revealed bright colours hidden under candle soot and old varnish.
sections.b: For centuries, smoke from candles and incense, along with layers of glue and varnish added in earlier restorations, darkened the ceiling. People came to think of Michelangelo's colours as sombre and muddy. Between 1980 and 1994, a team of Vatican restorers cleaned the ceiling and The Last Judgment. Underneath the grime were vivid pinks, greens, oranges and blues. The results were controversial. Some critics argued the restorers had removed final touches Michelangelo himself had added, while others welcomed the brilliant colours as his true intention. Today the chapel receives millions of visitors a year, and it is still used for its most famous purpose: the conclave in which cardinals elect a new pope.

quiz.q: What did Michelangelo consider his main art form?
quiz.e: He saw himself as a sculptor and accepted the ceiling commission reluctantly.

quiz.q: Why did fresco painters work in daily sections called giornate?
o: The pope only allowed one section a day
The paint had to be applied before the plaster dried
The chapel was open only on certain days
Pigments were too expensive to buy in bulk
quiz.e: Colour is locked in as wet plaster dries, so only a day's worth was laid at a time.

quiz.q: How did Michelangelo actually paint the ceiling?
o: Lying on his back on a platform
Standing on a scaffold he designed, leaning backwards
From the floor using very long brushes
On canvas panels later attached to the ceiling
quiz.e: He worked standing with his head tilted back, which still caused him great strain.

quiz.q: What is the status of the idea that a brain is hidden in The Creation of Adam?
o: It is confirmed by Michelangelo's letters
It is an intriguing modern reading with no evidence it was intended
It was revealed by the 1980s restoration
quiz.e: Some writers see a brain shape, but there is no evidence Michelangelo meant it.

quiz.q: What did the 1980 to 1994 restoration reveal?
o: Bright colours under centuries of soot and varnish
That the ceiling was painted by Raphael
quiz.e: Cleaning removed grime and old varnish to reveal vivid colours, though some critics disputed the results.

LESSONS.title: The Stradivarius mystery
LESSONS.hook: Violins made in a small Italian town three centuries ago sell for millions of dollars. But when top players are blindfolded, can they actually tell the difference?

sections.key: Antonio Stradivari made string instruments in Cremona, Italy, from the 1660s until his death in 1737.
sections.b: Cremona, in northern Italy, was the heart of violin making for generations. The Amati family established the craft there in the 1500s, and the Guarneri family also worked in the town. Antonio Stradivari was born around 1644 and may have trained with Nicolò Amati. He worked for an extraordinary length of time, making violins, violas, cellos, guitars and harps until he died in 1737, in his early nineties. Estimates suggest he made around a thousand or more instruments, and roughly 650 are thought to survive today, though the numbers are approximate. Experts generally regard the instruments from about 1700 to 1720 as his golden period, when his designs were at their most refined.

sections.h: How a violin makes its sound
sections.key: A violin's sound comes from the vibrating strings driving a thin wooden box that amplifies and shapes the tone.
sections.b: A string on its own makes only a faint sound. The bow drags the string, which vibrates, and those vibrations pass through the bridge into the violin's body. The top plate is usually spruce and the back is usually maple, each carved to just a few millimetres thick. Inside, a small wooden dowel called the sound post connects top and back, and a strip of wood called the bass bar runs under the top. The whole body vibrates and the f-shaped holes let sound out. Tiny differences in wood density, thickness and arching change which frequencies are boosted, which is why makers obsess over every curve. Varnish protects the wood and can subtly affect how it vibrates.

sections.key: Researchers have proposed many explanations for Stradivari's sound, from cold-climate wood to chemical treatments.
sections.b: Because the instruments are so prized, people have long searched for a lost secret. One theory points to the climate. Stradivari's working life overlapped with the Maunder Minimum, a period of low solar activity during the cooler era known as the Little Ice Age, and some researchers have suggested that slow-growing trees produced unusually dense, even wood. Another line of research has found evidence that the wood may have been treated with minerals or chemicals, perhaps to protect against woodworm, which could have changed its properties. Others focus on the varnish. None of these ideas has been proven to be the decisive secret, and many experts think his skill as a craftsman and designer matters more than any single ingredient.

sections.key: In controlled blind tests, experienced violinists could not reliably tell old Italian violins from good new ones.
sections.b: From 2010, the French acoustics researcher Claudia Fritz and American violin maker Joseph Curtin ran a series of careful experiments. In the first, published in 2012, experienced violinists wore modified welder's goggles so they could not see which instrument they were playing. They tried violins by Stradivari and Guarneri alongside high quality new ones. Players could not reliably tell old from new, and the single most preferred instrument was a new one. A larger follow-up with leading soloists, published in 2014, found similar results. Later tests with audiences in concert halls found listeners often thought the new violins projected better. These studies do not prove old violins are poor, only that their superiority is far less obvious than legend suggests.

sections.key: Rarity, history and the players' own experience all add to the value of old Italian instruments.
sections.b: If blindfolded players struggle to pick them, why do Stradivari violins remain so valuable? Part of the answer is that they are rare historical objects, like Old Master paintings, and their value reflects scarcity, craftsmanship and provenance as much as sound. Many have names and long histories, passing through the hands of famous musicians. Some violinists also argue that lab tests cannot capture what it feels like to live with an instrument for years, learning its responses in large halls. Belief may play a part too. Knowing you are playing a three hundred year old masterpiece can change how you play and how listeners hear. Researchers continue to debate how much of the magic is acoustic and how much is psychological.

sections.key: Top Stradivari instruments have sold for many millions of dollars, and many are owned by foundations and loaned to players.
sections.b: In 2011, a Stradivari violin known as the Lady Blunt sold for about 15.9 million US dollars, with the proceeds going to relief efforts after the earthquake and tsunami in Japan. Few working musicians could ever afford such prices, so many of the finest instruments are owned by banks, foundations, governments or wealthy collectors, who lend them to talented performers. In Australia, for example, some leading players perform on historic Italian instruments on loan. A few Stradivari violins are kept almost unplayed in museums, such as the Messiah violin at the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford, which is prized partly because it looks nearly new. Most, though, are still played, which many musicians feel is what they were made for.

quiz.q: Roughly when is Stradivari's 'golden period' usually dated?
quiz.e: Experts generally regard his instruments from around 1700 to 1720 as his finest.

quiz.q: What role does the body of a violin play?
o: It vibrates with the strings, amplifying and shaping the sound
It produces sound independently of the strings
It keeps the violin in tune
quiz.e: Vibrations pass through the bridge into the wooden body, which boosts and colours the sound.

quiz.q: What does the 'Little Ice Age' theory propose?
o: Cold made the varnish set harder
Stradivari stored his violins in ice
Slow-growing trees in a cool period produced dense, even wood
Cold winters forced him to work faster
quiz.e: Some researchers suggest the cool climate produced unusually dense wood, though it is not proven to be the secret.

quiz.q: What did Fritz and Curtin's blind tests find?
o: Players could not reliably tell old Italian violins from good new ones
Audiences could not hear any violins clearly
quiz.e: Blindfolded experts often could not tell them apart, and some preferred new instruments.

quiz.q: Why are many top Stradivari instruments loaned to performers?
o: Most musicians cannot afford their multi-million-dollar prices
They must be played daily to stay legal
quiz.e: Owners such as foundations and banks lend them to talented players who could never buy one.

LESSONS.title: The night The Rite of Spring caused an uproar
LESSONS.hook: In Paris in 1913, a new ballet about an ancient sacrifice provoked jeers, shouting and scuffles in the audience. Within a year, its music was being cheered.

sections.key: The Rite of Spring was created by Sergei Diaghilev's Ballets Russes, a Russian company based in Paris.
sections.b: In the years before the First World War, the most exciting dance company in Europe was the Ballets Russes, run by the Russian impresario Sergei Diaghilev. He had a gift for bringing together brilliant artists: composers, painters, dancers and choreographers. His star dancer was Vaslav Nijinsky, famous for his astonishing leaps. Diaghilev's young composer was Igor Stravinsky, who had already scored hits in Paris with The Firebird in 1910 and Petrushka in 1911. For their next project, Stravinsky worked with the painter and expert on ancient Russian culture Nicholas Roerich on an idea about pagan rituals in prehistoric Russia. Nijinsky would choreograph. The result premiered on 29 May 1913 at the new Théâtre des Champs-Élysées in Paris.

sections.key: The ballet depicts ancient spring rituals ending with a young woman dancing herself to death.
sections.b: The Rite of Spring, in French Le Sacre du printemps, has no conventional plot or romance. It presents a series of rituals among ancient Slavic tribes celebrating the arrival of spring. In the first part, young people perform dances of the earth, rival tribes compete, and a wise elder blesses the ground. In the second part, a young woman is chosen from among the maidens to be sacrificed so that spring will return. In the final scene, called the Sacrificial Dance, she dances in a frenzy until she dies, watched by the elders. It was a stark, primal subject, far removed from the graceful fairy tales and swans most ballet audiences expected.

sections.key: Stravinsky's score used clashing chords, pounding irregular rhythms and an orchestra pushed to extremes.
sections.b: The music opens with a bassoon playing a folk-like melody so high in its range that many listeners at first could not identify the instrument. Soon the orchestra builds into layers of overlapping tunes. Then comes a famous passage where strings hammer the same harsh chord again and again, with accents falling in unpredictable places, so the listener cannot settle into a regular beat. Elsewhere the time signature changes almost every bar. Stravinsky used a very large orchestra, with extra woodwinds, brass and percussion, to create sounds that were savage and thrilling. Many of the melodies were based on or inspired by Russian folk tunes, but they were reshaped into something entirely new and startling.

sections.key: Nijinsky's choreography rejected classical ballet's grace in favour of stamping, hunched, inward-turned movements.
sections.b: Classical ballet prized elegance: turned-out feet, lifted bodies and the illusion of weightlessness. Nijinsky did the opposite. His dancers turned their toes inwards, hunched their shoulders, jumped heavily and landed with a thud, and stamped in rhythmic groups. Roerich's costumes were heavy, colourful smocks inspired by old Russian peasant dress. To many in the audience, it looked ugly or even ridiculous, and to others it was daringly modern. The dancers themselves found the music extremely hard to follow because of its constantly shifting rhythms. Nijinsky's original choreography was performed only a handful of times and then largely lost, until it was carefully reconstructed for the Joffrey Ballet in 1987 from notes, drawings and memories.

sections.key: The premiere was interrupted by laughter, shouting and arguments, though accounts differ on how violent it became.
sections.b: Soon after the curtain rose, parts of the audience began to laugh, whistle and jeer, while others shouted back in defence of the work. The noise became so loud that the dancers struggled to hear the orchestra, and Nijinsky stood on a chair in the wings shouting the counts to them. Stravinsky left his seat and went backstage. Exactly what happened is hard to pin down. Many famous descriptions were written years or even decades later, and they contradict each other. Some describe fist fights and objects being thrown, and stories circulated of police being called. Historians generally agree there was a real uproar, but they caution that the legend of a full-scale riot has probably grown in the retelling.

sections.key: Within a year, The Rite of Spring was cheered in the concert hall, and it is now a cornerstone of twentieth century music.
sections.b: The ballet was performed only a few more times in 1913. But in April 1914, the music was played as a concert piece in Paris without dancers, and this time it was a triumph, with Stravinsky reportedly carried from the hall on admirers' shoulders. Freed from the startling choreography, audiences could focus on the score's raw power. The Rite became one of the most influential works of the century, shaping later classical music, jazz and film scores. In 1940, Walt Disney used it in the film Fantasia, set to scenes of the early Earth and dinosaurs. Today it is a regular part of orchestral programmes, and dozens of choreographers have created their own versions of the ballet.

quiz.q: Who composed The Rite of Spring?
quiz.e: Stravinsky wrote the score; Diaghilev ran the company, Nijinsky choreographed and Roerich designed it.

quiz.q: What happens in the ballet's final scene?
o: A chosen young woman dances until she dies
quiz.e: In the Sacrificial Dance, the chosen maiden dances herself to death so spring will return.

quiz.q: Why did the opening of the score puzzle listeners?
o: A bassoon played so high that many could not recognise it
The orchestra was hidden behind a curtain
quiz.e: The bassoon's unusually high register made it hard for listeners to identify.

quiz.q: What do historians say about the famous 'riot' at the premiere?
o: It is fully documented by police records
There was a real uproar, but many accounts were written much later and the legend has grown
It happened at a different ballet
quiz.e: The disturbance was real, but contradictory, later accounts mean details such as fights and police are uncertain.

quiz.q: How was the music received when played as a concert piece in 1914?
quiz.e: Without the dancing, audiences cheered the score, and Stravinsky was reportedly carried out on admirers' shoulders.

LESSONS.title: The Bauhaus: the school that designed the modern world
LESSONS.hook: A German art school lasted only fourteen years before the Nazis shut it down. Yet its ideas are in your kitchen chairs, your fonts and the buildings you walk past every day.

sections.h: A new school after the war
sections.key: Walter Gropius founded the Bauhaus in Weimar in 1919 to unite art and craft.
sections.b: In 1919, just after the First World War, the architect Walter Gropius founded a new school in Weimar, Germany, by merging an art academy with a school of arts and crafts. He called it the Staatliches Bauhaus, roughly meaning state house of building. Gropius believed the old split between fine artists and craftspeople was harmful. Painters looked down on furniture makers, while industry churned out poorly designed products. At the Bauhaus, students would learn both artistic principles and hands-on skills in workshops for metal, wood, textiles, pottery, printing and more. The long-term goal was building, bringing all the arts together. Germany was poor, politically divided and recovering from defeat, and the school hoped to help shape a better society.

sections.key: Every student began with a preliminary course that stripped away habits and explored materials, shape and colour.
sections.b: New students did not start in a specialist workshop. First they took the preliminary course, developed by the painter Johannes Itten and later run by László Moholy-Nagy and Josef Albers. The aim was to unlearn old academic habits and experiment directly with materials. Students explored the textures of wood, glass, paper and metal, studied contrasts of light and dark, and built structures from folded paper to see what it could do. Albers later became famous for his studies of how colours change appearance depending on the colours beside them. Teachers also included the painters Paul Klee and Wassily Kandinsky, who taught theories of form and colour. It was one of the most remarkable teaching staffs ever gathered.

sections.key: Bauhaus workshops designed simple, functional objects meant to be mass-produced, many of which are still made today.
sections.b: Over time the Bauhaus shifted from handcraft towards designing prototypes for industry. In the metal workshop, Marianne Brandt designed elegant teapots, tea infusers and lamps, and she became one of the most successful designers of the school. Marcel Breuer, a student who became a teacher, designed a tubular steel armchair in the mid 1920s, later named the Wassily chair after Kandinsky; he said he was inspired by the light steel tubes of his bicycle. In the weaving workshop, artists such as Anni Albers and Gunta Stölzl developed new textiles. Herbert Bayer designed clean typefaces using only lower case letters. Many Bauhaus designs, including chairs and lamps, are still manufactured and sold today, nearly a century later.

sections.key: The Bauhaus promised equality, but many women students were steered into the weaving workshop.
sections.b: The Bauhaus officially welcomed students regardless of sex, and in its first year more women than men applied. Gropius and the school's leaders soon worried about this, and many women were pushed towards the weaving workshop, which was seen as more suitable for them, rather than architecture or metalwork. The women turned that limitation into an achievement. Under Gunta Stölzl, who became the first female master at the school, the weaving workshop became one of the most commercially successful parts of the Bauhaus, producing modern textiles for industry. Some women, such as Marianne Brandt, did break into other workshops. Their work has been increasingly recognised by historians and museums in recent decades.

sections.key: In 1925 the school moved to Dessau, into a striking glass and concrete building designed by Gropius.
sections.b: The Bauhaus was always politically controversial. Conservative and nationalist politicians in Weimar saw it as foreign, left-wing and a waste of public money, and cut its funding. In 1925 the school moved to the industrial city of Dessau. Gropius designed a new building for it, completed in 1926, with a huge glass curtain wall on the workshop wing, flat roofs and separate wings for teaching, workshops and student studios, linked by a bridge. It became an icon of modern architecture. Gropius stepped down in 1928. The architect Hannes Meyer led the school next, followed in 1930 by Ludwig Mies van der Rohe. The Bauhaus buildings in Weimar and Dessau are now UNESCO World Heritage sites.

sections.key: Under Nazi pressure the Bauhaus moved to Berlin in 1932 and closed for good in 1933.
sections.b: As the Nazi Party gained power, the Bauhaus became a target. The Nazis attacked it as un-German, associated with communism and degenerate modern art. In 1932, after the Nazis won control of the local council in Dessau, the school was forced out. Mies van der Rohe tried to keep it going as a private school in an old telephone factory in Berlin, but police raided it, and in 1933 the staff decided to close it. Many Bauhaus figures left Germany. Some members, including Jewish students and those with left-wing politics, suffered persecution, and some were killed in the Holocaust. In its fourteen years, the school had perhaps around 1,250 students, a small number for such huge influence.

sections.key: Bauhaus teachers spread its ideas across the world, shaping architecture, design education and everyday objects.
sections.b: The closure scattered Bauhaus ideas worldwide. Gropius taught at Harvard and Mies van der Rohe led the architecture school at what became the Illinois Institute of Technology in Chicago, designing glass and steel towers that defined the modern skyline. Moholy-Nagy founded the New Bauhaus in Chicago in 1937. Josef and Anni Albers taught at Black Mountain College in North Carolina, influencing a generation of American artists. Architects trained in the Bauhaus style helped build the White City of Tel Aviv, now a World Heritage site. A common myth credits the Bauhaus with the slogan form follows function, but that phrase came from the American architect Louis Sullivan in the 1890s. Still, the idea suits the Bauhaus well.

quiz.q: What was Walter Gropius's central aim for the Bauhaus?
o: To unite fine art and craft, working towards building
To produce luxury goods for royalty
quiz.e: Gropius wanted to break down the barrier between artists and craftspeople, with architecture as the ultimate goal.

quiz.q: What was the purpose of the preliminary course?
o: To teach students to copy Old Masters
To unlearn old habits and explore materials, form and colour
To choose the best students for architecture
quiz.e: Taught by Itten, Moholy-Nagy and Albers, it encouraged direct experiment with materials.

quiz.q: What did Marcel Breuer say inspired his tubular steel chair?
quiz.e: Breuer said the light steel tubing of his bicycle gave him the idea.

quiz.q: Why did the Bauhaus close in 1933?
o: Nazi pressure and police raids forced it to shut
quiz.e: The Nazis attacked the school as un-German; after it was forced from Dessau and raided in Berlin, the staff closed it.

quiz.q: Who actually coined the phrase 'form follows function'?
quiz.e: The American architect Louis Sullivan used the phrase in the 1890s, before the Bauhaus existed.

LESSONS.title: How music learned to be written down
LESSONS.hook: For most of history, music lived only in memory. The squiggles, lines and dots that now let anyone read a song were invented bit by bit over a thousand years.

sections.key: For most of human history, music was passed on by ear and memory, not written notation.
sections.b: Every culture has made music, but very few wrote it down in a way that recorded precise pitches and rhythms. Melodies were learned by listening and copying, passed from teacher to student and parent to child. Some ancient societies did develop notation. A clay tablet from the ancient city of Ugarit, in modern Syria, dating to around 1400 BCE, contains instructions for a hymn, and the ancient Greeks used letter symbols for pitch. But these systems were limited or lost. In medieval Europe, the Christian church's huge repertoire of chant, now often called Gregorian chant, was learned by heart. Training a singer to know it all could take many years.

sections.key: In the ninth century, monks began writing small marks called neumes above texts to show the shape of a melody.
sections.b: From around the ninth century, scribes began adding little marks above the Latin words in chant books. These signs, called neumes, showed whether the melody went up or down and how notes were grouped on each syllable. They worked as memory aids for singers who already knew the tune. What they could not do was show exactly how high or low a note was, or how long it lasted. A singer who had never heard a chant could not learn it from early neumes alone. Different regions developed their own styles of neumes. Gradually, scribes started placing them at different heights on the page, so their position hinted at pitch, a crucial step towards modern notation.

sections.key: Around 1030, the monk Guido of Arezzo promoted a system of lines showing exact pitch.
sections.b: The breakthrough is usually credited to Guido of Arezzo, an Italian Benedictine monk and teacher active in the early eleventh century. Building on earlier experiments, he championed writing notes on and between horizontal lines, each representing a fixed pitch, and marking certain lines with letters, which evolved into today's clefs. With this staff, a singer could read a melody they had never heard. Guido claimed that his methods let young singers learn in a short time what had previously taken many years. His four-line staff is still used for chant, and the five-line staff became standard later. It was a revolution: music could now travel across distance and time on parchment alone.

sections.h: Where do re mi comes from
sections.key: The syllables used to sing scales come from a Latin hymn that Guido used as a teaching tool.
sections.b: Guido also gave singers a memory trick. He used a Latin hymn to Saint John the Baptist in which each of the first six lines began one step higher than the last. The first syllables of those lines were ut, re, mi, fa, sol and la. By learning the hymn, students could fix the sound of each step in their minds. Over the centuries, ut was replaced in most countries by do, which is easier to sing. A seventh syllable, si, was added later, and in the nineteenth century English teachers changed it to ti so that every syllable began with a different letter. This system, called solfège, is still used to teach singing around the world.

sections.key: Later medieval musicians invented note shapes that showed how long each note should last.
sections.b: Showing pitch was only half the problem. As composers wrote music for several voices singing different lines at once, called polyphony, singers needed to know exactly how long each note lasted so they stayed together. In the thirteenth century, theorists such as Franco of Cologne set out rules in which the shape of a note indicated its duration. This system, called mensural notation, developed over the following centuries. Notes gradually changed from black squares and diamonds to the round open and filled heads used today. Bar lines, which divide music into regular units, only became common in the seventeenth century. Time signatures, rests and ties followed, building the toolkit modern musicians take for granted.

sections.key: Printed sheet music, from 1501 onwards, spread music across Europe and helped create a market for composers.
sections.b: Copying music by hand was slow and expensive. In 1501, the Venetian printer Ottaviano Petrucci published the Odhecaton, a collection of songs and generally regarded as the first book of polyphonic music printed using movable type. His method required several passes through the press, one for the staff lines and others for the notes and text, and it was difficult, but the results were beautiful. Cheaper methods soon followed. Printed music allowed compositions to spread quickly across Europe and helped create a market of amateur musicians who bought music to play at home. By the nineteenth century, sheet music for the piano had become a big business, much like the recorded music industry later.

sections.key: Standard notation is not the only system; tablature, graphic scores and other traditions record music differently.
sections.b: Western staff notation is powerful, but it is not universal. Lute players in the Renaissance used tablature, which shows where to put the fingers rather than which notes sound, and modern guitar tabs work the same way. Many traditions in India, China, Indonesia and elsewhere have their own notation systems, and plenty of musicians in jazz, folk and popular music learn mainly by ear. Notation also leaves a lot out. It struggles to capture subtle timing, tone colour and improvisation, which is why two performances of the same score can sound so different. In the twentieth century, some composers created graphic scores, using drawings, shapes and instructions to give performers freedom rather than exact notes.

quiz.q: What was the main limitation of early neumes?
o: They were written only in Greek
They did not show exact pitch or length, so they only reminded singers of tunes they knew
They could only be read by bishops
They recorded rhythm but not melody
quiz.e: Early neumes showed the general rise and fall of a melody but not precise pitches or durations.

quiz.q: What did Guido of Arezzo's staff make possible?
o: Reading a melody you had never heard before
quiz.e: Lines representing fixed pitches let singers read unfamiliar melodies directly from the page.

quiz.q: Where do the syllables ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la come from?
o: The names of six Italian towns
The first syllables of lines of a Latin hymn
quiz.e: Each line of a hymn to Saint John began one step higher, and its first syllable named that step.

quiz.q: Why did composers need notation for rhythm?
o: To keep several voices singing different lines together
Because the church banned slow music
To make music easier to print
quiz.e: In polyphony, singers needed exact note lengths to stay coordinated.

quiz.q: What does guitar tablature show?
o: Where to place the fingers rather than which notes sound
The exact rhythm of every note
quiz.e: Like Renaissance lute tablature, guitar tab shows finger positions on the instrument.

LESSONS.title: Vermeer: the mystery of light
LESSONS.hook: Barely three dozen paintings, almost no letters, no surviving drawings. Johannes Vermeer painted quiet rooms full of light, and art detectives are still arguing about how he did it.

sections.key: Johannes Vermeer lived and worked in the Dutch city of Delft from 1632 to 1675, leaving few records behind.
sections.b: Johannes Vermeer was baptised in Delft, in the Dutch Republic, in October 1632. His father was a weaver who also dealt in art, and Johannes took over the business. In 1653 he married Catharina Bolnes, from a Catholic family, and he probably converted to Catholicism himself. They had a large family, with eleven children surviving when he died. He joined the local painters' guild and was respected enough to serve as one of its heads. Yet he left almost no personal records: no diaries, no surviving letters about his art, and not a single drawing that can confidently be attributed to him. Nearly everything known about him comes from legal and financial documents.

sections.key: Vermeer produced very few paintings, with only around 34 to 37 now attributed to him.
sections.b: The Dutch Golden Age was a time of enormous artistic output, with painters producing thousands of works for a busy market. Vermeer was the opposite. Scholars attribute only about 34 to 37 surviving paintings to him, and the exact count is still debated, as some attributions are disputed. He seems to have worked very slowly, perhaps producing only a few paintings a year. A local collector, Pieter van Ruijven, appears to have bought many of them, which may have given Vermeer some freedom to work carefully. His most famous paintings show one or two figures, often women, in quiet domestic interiors, reading letters, pouring milk, playing music or weighing pearls, lit by soft daylight.

sections.key: Many of Vermeer's interiors use light from a window on the left, rendered with extraordinary subtlety.
sections.b: A striking number of Vermeer's interiors show a room lit by a window on the left side of the picture. He paid close attention to how daylight behaves. In The Milkmaid, light falls across a whitewashed wall that is not plain white at all, but full of subtle shifts, with tiny nail holes and marks. Shadows are not simply darker; they often contain colour, picking up reflections from nearby surfaces. He also used tiny dots of light paint, sometimes called pointillé, to suggest the sparkle of light on bread, metal or fabric. These dots look rather like the blurred highlights seen through an out-of-focus lens, a detail that has fuelled debate about how he worked.

sections.key: Vermeer used costly natural ultramarine generously, even mixed into shadows and underlayers.
sections.b: Natural ultramarine was made from the semi-precious stone lapis lazuli, mined in what is now Afghanistan, and it was more expensive than many other pigments. Many painters reserved it for important details, such as the robes of the Virgin Mary. Vermeer used it remarkably freely. It appears in the famous blue and yellow headscarf of the Girl with a Pearl Earring and the apron of The Milkmaid. Technical studies have also found ultramarine mixed into shadows and underlayers, where it helps create cool, luminous tones. This lavish use of costly materials is puzzling for an artist who ended his life in debt, and it remains part of the mystery of his working methods and finances.

sections.key: Some researchers argue Vermeer used a camera obscura, an optical device, but there is no documentary proof.
sections.b: A camera obscura is a darkened box or room in which a lens projects an image of the scene outside onto a surface. The device was known in Vermeer's time, and Delft was home to the pioneering microscope maker Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, who later served as trustee of Vermeer's bankrupt estate, though there is no evidence the two men ever discussed optics. In 2001 the architectural historian Philip Steadman argued that the geometry of several Vermeer rooms fits what one would expect from a camera obscura. That same year, the artist David Hockney suggested optical aids were widely used by Old Masters. Many art historians remain sceptical. No document mentions Vermeer owning such a device, and even if he used one, the painting itself still required immense skill.

sections.key: A 2013 documentary tested whether optics could explain Vermeer's precision, sharpening but not settling the debate.
sections.b: In the documentary Tim's Vermeer, released in 2013, the American inventor Tim Jenison tried to recreate The Music Lesson. He built a full-size copy of the room and used a lens and a small angled mirror to compare the projected scene with his own painting, matching colours and tones point by point. After many months of slow work, he produced a strikingly close copy despite having no training as a painter. Supporters saw this as evidence that Vermeer could have used a similar method. Critics pointed out that showing something is possible does not prove that Vermeer did it, and that Vermeer's genius lies in choices of composition, colour and mood that no device can supply.

sections.key: Vermeer died in debt and was largely forgotten for two centuries before a French critic championed him.
sections.b: In 1672, France invaded the Dutch Republic, and the art market collapsed. Vermeer's income dried up. He died in December 1675, aged 43, leaving his family deeply in debt; his widow later said the stress of financial ruin had contributed to his death. Over the following centuries his name faded, and some of his paintings were sold under other artists' names. In the 1860s, the French critic Théophile Thoré-Bürger published enthusiastic articles about him and helped restore his reputation. Since then his fame has soared. The Girl with a Pearl Earring has become one of the best known paintings in the world, and a major Vermeer exhibition in Amsterdam in 2023 sold out completely.

quiz.q: Why is so little known about Vermeer's working methods?
o: His studio was destroyed in a fire
He left no diaries, letters about his art or confirmed drawings
He worked under a false name
quiz.e: Almost all evidence about him comes from legal and financial documents, not personal records.

quiz.q: Roughly how many paintings are attributed to Vermeer today?
quiz.e: He worked slowly, and only around 34 to 37 surviving paintings are attributed to him.

quiz.q: What are the tiny dots of light paint in Vermeer's work often compared to?
o: Blurred highlights seen through an out-of-focus lens
quiz.e: The pointillé highlights resemble out-of-focus lens effects, which feeds the debate about optical aids.

quiz.q: Why was Vermeer's use of ultramarine surprising?
o: It was a cheap pigment nobody valued
It was very expensive, yet he used it freely, even in shadows
quiz.e: Made from lapis lazuli, ultramarine was costly, yet Vermeer used it generously.

quiz.q: What is the status of the theory that Vermeer used a camera obscura?
o: Plausible to some researchers but unproven, with no documentary evidence
quiz.e: Researchers such as Philip Steadman argue for it, but no document shows Vermeer used one.

LESSONS.title: Jainism: the path of harming nothing
LESSONS.hook: Some monks sweep the ground before every step so they won't crush an insect. Behind that gesture lies one of the world's oldest and most demanding ideas: that every living thing has a soul.

sections.key: Jainism is an Indian religion centred on non-violence, self-discipline and the liberation of the soul.
sections.b: Jainism grew up in the Ganges plain of northern India, in the same restless era that produced the Buddha. Its most famous teacher, Mahavira, is usually dated to the sixth or fifth century BCE, and he and the Buddha are often described as contemporaries. Jains do not regard Mahavira as the founder, though. In their tradition he is the twenty-fourth and last Tirthankara of our age, a ‘ford-maker’ who crossed the river of rebirth and showed others the way across. His predecessor, Parshvanatha, is widely accepted by historians as a real figure who lived a few centuries earlier. Today there are roughly four to five million Jains, most of them in India, with communities in Britain, North America, East Africa and Australia.

sections.key: Jains believe countless souls are bound to bodies by karma, which they understand as a fine, sticky matter.
sections.b: At the heart of Jain teaching is the jiva, the soul. Every soul is, by nature, perfectly knowing, perceiving and blissful. The problem is that souls are weighed down by karma. In many religions karma is a kind of moral law of cause and effect, but in Jainism it is pictured as an extremely fine substance that clings to the soul whenever we act with passion, greed or violence. That build-up keeps the soul trapped in the cycle of birth and death. Souls are found not only in humans and animals but in plants, and even in tiny beings in earth, water, fire and air. The goal of life is to stop new karma from attaching and to burn away the old, until the soul rises free.

sections.key: Non-violence, or ahimsa, is the central Jain value and shapes daily life in remarkable detail.
sections.b: Because so many beings have souls, the Jain duty not to harm reaches further than in almost any other tradition. Jains are strict vegetarians, and many also avoid root vegetables such as onions, garlic and potatoes, because pulling them up kills the whole plant and the small creatures living in the soil around it. Traditionally many avoid eating after sunset, when insects could fall unseen into food. Monks and nuns may carry a soft brush to clear the ground before they sit or walk, and some wear a cloth over the mouth to avoid harming tiny beings in the air. Non-violence also covers words and thoughts. Harsh speech and hateful intentions count as harm too, so ahimsa is as much a discipline of the mind as of the body.

sections.key: Jain thinkers taught that truth has many sides, and that no single viewpoint captures all of it.
sections.b: One of Jainism's most admired ideas is anekantavada, often translated as ‘many-sidedness’ or ‘non-absolutism’. Reality is complex, Jain philosophers argued, and any statement about it is true only from a particular standpoint. To illustrate this, Jains, like Buddhists and Hindus, tell the story of the blind men and the elephant. One touches the trunk and says an elephant is like a snake; another feels a leg and insists it is like a tree. Each is partly right and each is wrong to think he has the whole truth. Jain logicians built this into a careful system for qualifying statements with words like ‘in some respect’. Many modern Jains see it as a natural partner to ahimsa: intellectual humility as a form of non-violence.

sections.key: Jainism's two main branches differ over monastic clothing and some points of scripture.
sections.b: Jain monks and nuns take five great vows: non-violence, truthfulness, not stealing, chastity and non-possession. How far to take non-possession helped divide the community into two main traditions. Digambara monks, whose name means ‘sky-clad’, give up even clothing and go naked as a sign of complete detachment, carrying little more than a peacock-feather brush and a water pot. Digambaras also hold that a woman must be reborn as a man before reaching liberation. The Svetambara, or ‘white-clad’, tradition allows monks and nuns to wear simple white robes and teaches that women can attain liberation. The two branches also disagree over which ancient scriptures survived. Lay Jains follow gentler versions of the same vows, adapted to working and family life.

sections.key: Jain temples are famous for their marble craftsmanship, and the yearly festival of Paryushana is devoted to forgiveness.
sections.b: Jain temples contain images of the Tirthankaras, usually shown seated in meditation or standing perfectly still, and worshippers honour them as models rather than as gods who grant favours. Some temples are breathtaking, such as the intricately carved white marble of Dilwara at Mount Abu and the many-pillared temple at Ranakpur in Rajasthan. At Shravanabelagola in Karnataka a granite statue of Bahubali, around 17 metres tall and more than a thousand years old, is anointed with milk, saffron and flowers in a great ceremony held roughly every twelve years. The most important annual festival is Paryushana, a period of fasting and reflection. It ends with Jains asking one another's forgiveness with the phrase ‘Micchami Dukkadam’, roughly ‘may my wrongs be forgiven’.

sections.h: A small faith with long reach
sections.key: Jain ideas of non-violence influenced Gandhi and live on in charity, business and animal care.
sections.b: Jains are a small minority even in India, yet their influence is wide. Mohandas Gandhi grew up in Gujarat, where Jain ideas were part of everyday life, and he counted a Jain thinker, Shrimad Rajchandra, among his most important spiritual guides. Gandhi's strategy of non-violent resistance drew on many sources, but ahimsa was close to its heart. Jain communities are also known for trade, banking and generous philanthropy, partly because many farming and fishing jobs risk harming living things. Some run hospitals for animals and birds, including a well-known bird hospital at a Jain temple in Old Delhi. In an age worried about animal welfare and the environment, an ancient rule of harming as little as possible has found new admirers far beyond India.

quiz.q: How do Jains regard Mahavira?
o: As the founder who invented Jainism
As the last of 24 Tirthankaras of this age
As a disciple of the Buddha
quiz.e: In Jain tradition Mahavira is the 24th Tirthankara, a teacher who rediscovered and taught the path, not its inventor.

quiz.q: How is karma understood in Jainism?
o: As fine matter that clings to the soul
As a reward handed out by a creator god
As an illusion with no real effect
As a debt owed to one's ancestors
quiz.e: Jains picture karma as a subtle substance that binds the soul and must be stopped and burned away.

quiz.q: Why do many Jains avoid onions and potatoes?
o: They are thought to cause anger
They were forbidden by a medieval king
Uprooting them kills the plant and creatures in the soil
They are too expensive for monks
quiz.e: Pulling up root vegetables destroys the whole plant and harms small beings living in the earth.

quiz.q: What does anekantavada teach?
o: Truth has many sides and each viewpoint is partial
The world is entirely an illusion
quiz.e: Many-sidedness holds that reality is complex and statements are true only from a given standpoint.

quiz.q: What does ‘Digambara’ mean?
quiz.e: Digambara monks are ‘sky-clad’, renouncing clothing entirely; Svetambaras are the ‘white-clad’.

LESSONS.title: Ireland's gods, heroes and fairy mounds
LESSONS.hook: Before St Patrick, Ireland had shining gods who vanished into the hills, a hero who could fight an army alone, and a giant who supposedly built a causeway to Scotland.

sections.key: Most Irish myths survive because medieval Christian scribes wrote them down.
sections.b: The pre-Christian Irish did not leave written scriptures. Their lore was carried in memory by poets and druids, people trained for years to recite genealogies, laws and tales. What we have now comes mostly from manuscripts copied by monks between roughly the eighth and fifteenth centuries, long after Ireland had become Christian. That makes the stories wonderful but tricky. The scribes preserved them with obvious affection, yet they also reshaped them, turning old gods into ancient kings and fitting Irish history into a biblical timeline. Scholars sort the tales into groups, often called the Mythological Cycle, the Ulster Cycle, the Fenian Cycle and the Cycles of the Kings. Together they form one of the richest bodies of early medieval literature in Europe.

sections.key: The medieval ‘Book of Invasions’ tells Ireland's history as a series of peoples arriving one after another.
sections.b: A medieval text known as the Lebor Gabála Érenn, the ‘Book of the Taking of Ireland’, set out a grand legendary history. Ireland, it says, was settled in waves. First came groups led by Cessair and Partholón, then the people of Nemed, then the Fir Bolg. Each struggled against the Fomorians, a monstrous race often linked with the sea. Then came the Tuatha Dé Danann, the ‘peoples of the goddess Danu’, a race of skilled and magical beings who arrived wrapped in mist. Finally the Milesians, ancestors of the Irish themselves, sailed from Spain. The book was compiled largely in the eleventh century and blends older tradition with learned invention, so historians treat it as legend rather than a record of real migrations.

sections.key: The Tuatha Dé Danann were Ireland's old gods, remembered as a magical people who retreated into the hills.
sections.b: The Tuatha Dé include figures many scholars see as former gods. The Dagda, the ‘good god’, owned a cauldron that never ran empty, a club that could kill with one end and restore life with the other, and a harp that commanded the seasons. Lugh was master of every art and craft, and led the Tuatha Dé to victory over the Fomorians at the second battle of Mag Tuired. Brigid was linked with poetry, healing and smithcraft, and her name lives on in St Brigid, Ireland's beloved saint. The Morrígan was a goddess of war and fate who could take the form of a crow. When the Milesians won Ireland, the Tuatha Dé withdrew into the sídhe, the ancient mounds, and became the fairy folk of later folklore.

sections.h: Cú Chulainn, the Hound of Ulster
sections.key: The Ulster Cycle's great hero won his name as a boy and defended a province alone.
sections.b: The boy Sétanta was the nephew of King Conchobar of Ulster. Arriving late to a feast at the house of the smith Culann, he was attacked by Culann's ferocious guard dog and killed it. Seeing the smith's grief, the boy offered to act as his hound until a new one could be raised, and so he became Cú Chulainn, ‘Culann's Hound’. In battle he could be seized by a terrifying frenzy, the ríastrad, in which his body twisted into a monstrous shape. In the epic Táin Bó Cúailnge, the ‘Cattle Raid of Cooley’, Queen Medb of Connacht invades Ulster to seize a prize bull. The Ulster warriors lie helpless under a curse, so the teenage Cú Chulainn holds back her army single-handed, fighting a long series of duels at a river ford.

sections.key: Cú Chulainn's final stand, tied to a standing stone, became a lasting symbol of courage.
sections.b: Irish heroes lived under geasa, sacred prohibitions that could not be broken without disaster. Cú Chulainn was bound never to eat dog meat, yet also never to refuse hospitality. Before his last battle he was offered dog meat by three old women, and either choice meant breaking a geis. Weakened, he fought on. Mortally wounded, he tied himself to a standing stone so that he could die on his feet, facing his enemies. They dared not approach until a crow, the sign of the Morrígan, landed on his shoulder. The image proved powerful in modern times. A bronze statue of the dying Cú Chulainn stands in Dublin's General Post Office as a memorial to those who fought in the 1916 Easter Rising.

sections.key: Fionn mac Cumhaill led a band of hunter-warriors, and gained his wisdom from a magical salmon.
sections.b: The Fenian Cycle follows Fionn mac Cumhaill, often anglicised as Finn McCool, and his roving war band, the Fianna. As a youth Fionn served a poet who had spent seven years trying to catch the Salmon of Knowledge. When it was finally caught, Fionn was told to cook it but not to taste it. He burnt his thumb on the skin, sucked it to ease the pain, and received all the fish's wisdom. Afterwards he could summon knowledge by putting his thumb to his mouth. Later folklore turned Fionn into a giant. In one popular tale he builds the Giant's Causeway in Northern Ireland as a road to Scotland, a playful story about a landscape actually formed by cooling volcanic lava.

sections.h: Swans and the Land of Youth
sections.key: Tales of the children of Lir and of Oisín in Tír na nÓg are among Ireland's best-loved stories.
sections.b: Two tales of time and loss still move readers. In the Children of Lir, a jealous stepmother turns four children into swans, condemned to spend nine hundred years on the lakes and seas of Ireland. They keep their human voices and sing so beautifully that people come to listen. When the spell finally breaks, they become withered old people and soon die, often comforted in Christian retellings by baptism. In another story, Fionn's son Oisín rides away with Niamh to Tír na nÓg, the Land of Youth. After what seems three years he visits home, warned never to touch the ground. He finds that around three hundred years have passed. When he slips from his horse, he instantly ages into a very old man.

quiz.q: Who wrote down most surviving Irish myths?
quiz.e: Monastic scribes copied the tales into manuscripts, sometimes reshaping them in the process.

quiz.q: What happened to the Tuatha Dé Danann after the Milesians arrived?
o: They withdrew into the ancient mounds and became the fairy folk
quiz.e: Defeated, they retreated into the sídhe and live on in folklore as the fairy people.

quiz.q: How did Cú Chulainn get his name?
o: He offered to guard a smith's house after killing its hound
He hunted the hound of a rival king
He could turn into a dog
quiz.e: Having killed Culann's guard dog, the boy offered to take its place, becoming ‘Culann's Hound’.

quiz.q: What sign told Cú Chulainn's enemies that he was dead?
o: His sword fell from his hand
A crow landed on his shoulder
quiz.e: A crow, associated with the Morrígan, settled on him, and only then did his enemies approach.

quiz.q: How did Fionn gain the Salmon of Knowledge's wisdom?
o: He sucked a thumb burnt on the salmon's skin
He ate the whole fish in secret
A druid gave him its bones
He swam with it in the River Boyne
quiz.e: Burning his thumb while cooking, he put it in his mouth and absorbed the salmon's wisdom.

LESSONS.title: King Arthur: how a legend was built
LESSONS.hook: There may never have been a King Arthur. Yet over a thousand years, writers in Wales, England and France assembled Camelot, the Round Table and the Holy Grail piece by piece.

sections.key: Arthur's story is set in the obscure centuries after Roman rule ended in Britain.
sections.b: Roman authority in Britain collapsed in the early fifth century. Over the following two hundred years, Anglo-Saxon groups settled much of what became England, while Britons held out in the west and north. Written records from this period are extremely thin, which is exactly why legends could flourish. A British monk named Gildas, writing in the sixth century, described a British victory over the Saxons at a place called Mount Badon. Tellingly, Gildas does not mention any Arthur. The earliest possible reference comes from a Welsh poem, Y Gododdin, which praises one warrior by saying he was brave, ‘though he was no Arthur’. Its date is uncertain and the line may have been added later. From these faint traces, a towering figure would grow.

sections.key: Ninth and tenth century Welsh texts first present Arthur as a war leader against the Saxons.
sections.b: Around 830, a Latin work called the Historia Brittonum, traditionally linked to a monk named Nennius, listed twelve battles fought by Arthur, a ‘leader of battles’, ending with Badon. Some of the battle sites are impossible to locate, and one passage has him carrying an image of the Virgin Mary into combat. A later Welsh chronicle, the Annales Cambriae, records Badon and also the battle of Camlann, ‘in which Arthur and Medraut fell’. Medraut would later become the treacherous Mordred. Early Welsh poems and tales show a rather different Arthur, leading a band of heroes against giants, witches and a monstrous boar. Most historians today think there is not enough evidence to say whether a real Arthur existed, though the debate continues.

sections.key: Geoffrey of Monmouth's history, written around 1136, turned Arthur into a conquering king of Europe.
sections.b: The Arthur most people know was really launched by Geoffrey of Monmouth, a cleric in Oxford. His History of the Kings of Britain, completed around 1136, claimed to be translated from an ancient British book, a claim most scholars doubt. Geoffrey gave Arthur a dramatic biography. Merlin's magic lets Uther Pendragon visit Igerna at Tintagel, and Arthur is conceived. As king, Arthur defeats the Saxons, conquers much of Europe and challenges Rome itself. While he is away, his nephew Mordred seizes the throne and Guinevere. Arthur returns, kills Mordred and is mortally wounded, then carried to the island of Avalon for his wounds to be healed. The book was a medieval sensation, surviving in more than two hundred manuscripts.

sections.h: French knights and a famous table
sections.key: French and Anglo-Norman poets added the Round Table, Lancelot and the romance of chivalry.
sections.b: Writers across the Channel took Geoffrey's warrior king and dressed him in the courtly fashions of their day. In 1155 the Norman poet Wace retold Geoffrey's history in French verse and introduced the Round Table, a seating arrangement where no knight could claim the place of honour. Later in the twelfth century, Chrétien de Troyes wrote a series of romances that shifted attention from Arthur to his knights. He gave us the earliest surviving story of Lancelot's love for Queen Guinevere, and he first mentioned Camelot as Arthur's court. In these tales Arthur often sits at home while knights ride out on quests, rescue ladies, fight strange champions and struggle to balance loyalty, love and honour.

sections.key: The Holy Grail began as a mysterious dish and became the cup of the Last Supper.
sections.b: Chrétien's unfinished poem Perceval, written around the 1180s, introduced a strange object called a graal, a serving dish carried in a procession at the castle of a wounded king. Chrétien died before explaining it, and that mystery invited others to finish the story. Soon afterwards Robert de Boron identified the Grail as the vessel used by Christ at the Last Supper, in which Joseph of Arimathea caught his blood. Robert's work is also among the earliest to include the sword in the stone, proving young Arthur's right to rule. Later French prose romances made the Grail quest a spiritual test that most knights failed. Only the pure knight Galahad, Lancelot's son, finally achieves it.

sections.h: Malory and the bones at Glastonbury
sections.key: Thomas Malory's 1485 book shaped the English legend, while a convenient ‘discovery’ of Arthur's grave shaped belief.
sections.b: In 1191, monks at Glastonbury Abbey announced that they had found the grave of Arthur and Guinevere, complete with a lead cross naming Avalon. The abbey had been badly damaged by fire a few years earlier and needed funds and pilgrims, and many historians suspect the find was staged. Still, it helped tie Avalon to Glastonbury in popular imagination. Nearly three centuries later Sir Thomas Malory, a knight who wrote at least part of his work while in prison, gathered the French and English stories into one great English prose narrative. William Caxton printed it in 1485 as Le Morte d'Arthur. Malory's version, with its tragic ending of broken loyalties, became the main source for nearly every later retelling in English.

sections.key: Arthur keeps returning because each age reshapes him to answer its own questions.
sections.b: Legend held that Arthur did not truly die but would return in Britain's hour of need, and in a sense he has kept returning. Alfred, Lord Tennyson's Idylls of the King made him a model of Victorian duty. T. H. White's The Once and Future King, completed in the 1950s, used him to think about power after two world wars, and inspired the musical Camelot and Disney's The Sword in the Stone. Monty Python made him absurd; other modern writers made him a gritty post-Roman warlord. The survival of the legend says less about a historical general than about the stories people need. Arthur stands for the hope of a just ruler, and for the sadness when even good kingdoms fall.

quiz.q: What is notable about Gildas's account of the battle of Mount Badon?
o: He does not mention Arthur at all
quiz.e: Gildas, the closest writer to the period, mentions the victory at Badon but names no Arthur.

quiz.q: Which writer, around 1136, made Arthur a conqueror of much of Europe?
quiz.e: Geoffrey's History of the Kings of Britain created the grand royal biography of Arthur.

quiz.q: Who introduced the Round Table into the legend?
quiz.e: The Norman poet Wace first mentions the Round Table in his French verse history of 1155.

quiz.q: In Chrétien's original poem, what was the Grail?
quiz.e: Chrétien's graal was a dish; Robert de Boron later identified it with the cup of the Last Supper.

quiz.q: Why do many historians doubt the 1191 Glastonbury ‘discovery’?
o: No one ever saw the grave
The abbey needed money and pilgrims after a fire
quiz.e: The fire-damaged abbey had strong reasons to attract visitors, so the find looks suspiciously convenient.

LESSONS.title: The great pilgrimages
LESSONS.hook: Every year millions of people walk, pray and queue for days to reach a single sacred place. Pilgrimage is one of the oldest things humans do, and it is booming.

sections.key: Pilgrimage joins a physical journey to an inner one, and is found in almost every faith.
sections.b: A pilgrimage is a journey to a place believed to be holy, made for religious or spiritual reasons. It can be undertaken to fulfil a duty, to give thanks, to ask for healing or forgiveness, to honour the dead, or simply to be near something sacred. Almost every major tradition has pilgrimage sites: Jerusalem for Jews, Christians and Muslims; Mecca for Muslims; the Ganges for Hindus; Bodh Gaya, where the Buddha is said to have awakened, for Buddhists; the Golden Temple at Amritsar for Sikhs. The hardship is often part of the point. Walking long distances, fasting or sleeping rough strips away daily comforts, and many pilgrims say the road itself changes them as much as the destination.

sections.key: The pilgrimage to Mecca is a duty for every Muslim who is physically and financially able, once in a lifetime.
sections.b: The Hajj is one of the Five Pillars of Islam. It takes place over several days in the Islamic month of Dhu al-Hijjah, and in recent years has drawn somewhere between one and a half and two and a half million pilgrims. Before arriving, pilgrims enter a state of ritual purity called ihram. Men wear two plain, unstitched white cloths, so that rich and poor stand dressed alike before God. Pilgrims circle the Kaaba, the cube-shaped shrine at the heart of the Great Mosque, seven times anticlockwise. The most important moment is the day spent standing in prayer on the plain of Arafat. Pilgrims also throw pebbles at pillars in Mina, remembering Abraham's rejection of temptation. The festival of Eid al-Adha follows, celebrated by Muslims worldwide.

sections.key: A Hindu festival of sacred bathing that ranks among the largest gatherings of people on Earth.
sections.b: Hindu tradition tells how gods and demons churned the cosmic ocean to obtain amrita, the nectar of immortality. As the pot, or kumbha, was carried away, drops spilled at four places on Earth: Prayagraj, Haridwar, Ujjain and Nashik. The Kumbh Mela rotates among these sites, and the largest gatherings, held at Prayagraj where the Ganges and Yamuna meet, attract crowds counted in the tens of millions over several weeks. Pilgrims believe bathing in the river at auspicious times washes away sins. Processions of ascetics, including the naked, ash-smeared Naga sadhus, rush into the water at dawn. Organising the festival means building a temporary city with roads, bridges, hospitals and police stations. UNESCO recognised it as intangible cultural heritage in 2017.

sections.key: Medieval Christians walked across Europe to the tomb of St James; today hundreds of thousands still do.
sections.b: According to tradition, the remains of St James the Apostle were discovered in north-western Spain in the ninth century, and a great cathedral rose at Santiago de Compostela. By the Middle Ages it was one of Christianity's most important pilgrimage destinations, alongside Rome and Jerusalem. Pilgrims walked from all over Europe along routes now known as the Camino, or Way. The scallop shell became their symbol, and today yellow arrows and shell markers still guide walkers. The modern revival has been spectacular, with hundreds of thousands of people a year arriving, some deeply religious, others seeking time to think. Those who walk at least the final 100 kilometres, or cycle 200, can receive a certificate called the Compostela.

sections.key: Many Hindus hope to die or be cremated in Varanasi, believing it offers release from rebirth.
sections.b: Varanasi, also called Kashi or Benares, stands on the banks of the Ganges and is among the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world. For Hindus it is the city of Shiva and one of the holiest places on Earth. Pilgrims descend the stone steps known as ghats to bathe in the river at sunrise, and each evening priests perform the spectacular aarti ceremony with flames and bells. Many Hindus believe that dying in Varanasi, or having one's ashes placed in the Ganges there, brings moksha, liberation from the cycle of birth and death. At the Manikarnika ghat cremation fires burn day and night. Some elderly people travel to the city specifically to spend their final days there.

sections.key: A Japanese Buddhist circuit of 88 temples traces the footsteps of the monk Kūkai.
sections.b: On the Japanese island of Shikoku, a pilgrimage route links 88 Buddhist temples in a loop of roughly 1,200 kilometres. It honours Kūkai, also known as Kōbō Daishi, a ninth-century monk who founded the Shingon school of Buddhism and was born on the island. Traditional pilgrims, called henro, wear white clothing, a conical sedge hat and carry a staff, which is said to represent Kūkai himself walking beside them. Many hats carry the words ‘we two, travelling together’. Walking the whole circuit usually takes between one and two months, though many people now travel by bus or car, or complete it in sections over years. Local residents traditionally offer pilgrims small gifts of food or money, a custom called osettai.

sections.key: Mass travel and modern logistics have made pilgrimage bigger, while raising new challenges.
sections.b: Cheaper travel has transformed pilgrimage. Journeys that once took months now take hours, and numbers have grown enormously. That brings pressure. Saudi Arabia allocates Hajj places by country through a quota system and has built vast infrastructure to move crowds safely, yet crushes and extreme heat remain serious dangers at several crowded sites. Popular Camino routes face overcrowding, and local towns worry about the effect on housing and daily life. Meanwhile new kinds of pilgrimage have appeared. Many Australians and New Zealanders travel to Gallipoli for Anzac Day dawn services, and visitors file past the graves of musicians and writers. Whether religious or not, people still seem to need special places where they feel connected to something larger than themselves.

quiz.q: What do male pilgrims wear on the Hajj?
quiz.e: The simple ihram cloths mean rich and poor stand dressed alike.

quiz.q: Which moment is considered the high point of the Hajj?
o: Standing in prayer on the plain of Arafat
quiz.e: The day of standing at Arafat is the central rite of the pilgrimage.

quiz.q: According to Hindu tradition, why are the four Kumbh Mela sites holy?
o: The Buddha taught at each one
Drops of the nectar of immortality fell there
They are where four rivers end
quiz.e: Drops of amrita spilled at Prayagraj, Haridwar, Ujjain and Nashik as the pot was carried away.

quiz.q: What is the traditional symbol of pilgrims on the Camino de Santiago?
quiz.e: The scallop shell has marked Camino pilgrims since the Middle Ages and still guides walkers.

quiz.q: Whom do pilgrims on Shikoku believe walks beside them?
quiz.e: The pilgrim's staff represents Kūkai, and hats read ‘we two, travelling together’.

LESSONS.title: Día de Muertos: a festival for the dead
LESSONS.hook: Each year at the start of November, families across Mexico build glowing altars and lay paths of orange petals so that their dead can find the way home. It is a celebration, not a horror show.

sections.key: Day of the Dead is a family celebration of remembrance, not a spooky festival.
sections.b: Día de Muertos, the Day of the Dead, is often lumped together with Halloween because the dates are close and both involve skulls. The spirit is very different. Halloween plays with fear; Día de Muertos is about love and remembrance. Families believe that for a short time their departed relatives return to visit, and the living prepare to welcome them as honoured guests. The main days are 1 and 2 November. In many places the first day is dedicated to children who have died, sometimes called los angelitos, the little angels, and the second to adults. Customs vary greatly from region to region, and Indigenous communities often keep some of the most distinctive traditions.

sections.key: The festival blends Indigenous Mexican traditions of honouring the dead with Catholic feast days.
sections.b: Long before the Spanish arrived, peoples of Mesoamerica, including the Aztecs, held ceremonies honouring the dead. Death was seen as part of a cycle rather than a final end, and the Aztec underworld, Mictlan, was ruled by Mictlantecuhtli and his consort Mictecacihuatl. After the Spanish conquest in the sixteenth century, missionaries promoted the Catholic feasts of All Saints' Day and All Souls' Day on 1 and 2 November. Over centuries, local practices and Catholic customs wove together. Exactly how much of today's festival comes directly from pre-Hispanic religion is debated by historians, as some features developed much later. What is clear is that the result is something uniquely Mexican, neither simply Indigenous nor simply European.

sections.key: Home altars called ofrendas hold photographs, favourite foods and objects to welcome returning souls.
sections.b: The heart of the celebration is the ofrenda, an altar built in homes, and sometimes in schools, offices and public squares. It usually has several tiers covered in cloth and decorated with papel picado, delicate tissue paper cut into intricate patterns. Photographs of the dead take pride of place, along with things they loved in life: a favourite dish, a bottle of tequila, cigarettes, sweets, toys for children. Candles light the way, and copal incense perfumes the air. Many families include water to quench the souls' thirst after their long journey, and salt for purification. Building the ofrenda is a family task, and telling stories about the people pictured is part of the point. Remembering keeps the dead present.

sections.key: Bright orange marigolds and special breads and sugar skulls are the festival's signature foods and flowers.
sections.b: The flower of the season is the cempasúchil, a vivid orange marigold whose name comes from the Nahuatl language. Its strong colour and scent are believed to help guide souls, and families scatter petals in paths leading from the street, or the cemetery, to the altar. Bakeries fill with pan de muerto, a soft, sweet bread often flavoured with orange blossom and decorated with strips of dough shaped like bones. Sugar skulls, called calaveras de azúcar, are moulded from sugar and decorated with coloured icing, sometimes with a person's name written across the forehead. Rather than being morbid, the skulls are cheerful and bright. They express a familiar attitude: death comes to everyone, so it may as well be met with a smile.

sections.key: Many families spend the night beside their relatives' graves, cleaning, decorating and sharing food.
sections.b: In many towns, people go to the cemetery to clean and decorate the graves of their family. Tombs are washed, weeds are pulled, and graves are covered with marigolds, candles and offerings. In some communities families keep vigil through the night, eating, praying, telling stories and sometimes listening to musicians. The island of Janitzio in Lake Pátzcuaro, Michoacán, is famous for its candlelit vigil, when local Purépecha fishermen cross the lake in canoes carrying lights. The atmosphere surprises many visitors. It can be solemn, but it is also warm and social, closer to a family reunion than a funeral.
