The dead are spoken to directly, welcomed back and gently farewelled until the following year.

sections.h: La Catrina and the joking dead
sections.key: An elegant skeleton drawn by a satirical printmaker became one of the festival's most famous symbols.
sections.b: Skeletons dressed as living people have long been used in Mexico to poke fun at the powerful. Around the early 1910s the printmaker José Guadalupe Posada made an etching of a skeleton woman in a grand feathered hat, mocking Mexicans who imitated European fashions while forgetting their roots. Decades later the painter Diego Rivera placed her in his 1947 mural Dream of a Sunday Afternoon in the Alameda Central, dressed in finery beside a young version of himself, and she became known as La Catrina. Today people dress as Catrinas with painted skull faces. The joking tradition also lives on in calaveras literarias, humorous rhyming poems that imagine friends, politicians and celebrities being carried off by Death.

sections.key: UNESCO recognised the festival in 2008, and films and new traditions have spread it worldwide.
sections.b: In 2008 UNESCO inscribed the Indigenous festivity dedicated to the dead on its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, recognising its importance to Mexican identity. The festival keeps changing. The 2015 James Bond film Spectre opened with an invented Day of the Dead parade in Mexico City; the following year the city staged a real one, and it has become an annual event. Pixar's 2017 film Coco, which was made with extensive cultural consultation, introduced the ofrenda and the marigold bridge to audiences around the world. Some Mexicans worry about commercialisation, while others welcome the attention. Either way, the central message survives: the people we love are not truly gone while we remember them.

quiz.q: On which days is Día de Muertos mainly celebrated?
quiz.e: The main days are 1 and 2 November, often for children and then for adults.

quiz.q: Which Catholic feasts became woven into the festival?
o: All Saints' Day and All Souls' Day
quiz.e: Missionaries promoted All Saints' and All Souls' Days, which merged with Indigenous traditions.

quiz.q: Why are marigold petals scattered towards the altar?
o: To guide souls with their colour and scent
To mark where children should sit
quiz.e: The cempasúchil's strong colour and scent are believed to help souls find their way.

quiz.q: Who first created the image that became La Catrina?
quiz.e: Posada etched the satirical skeleton lady; Diego Rivera later made her famous in a mural.

quiz.q: What inspired Mexico City's large Day of the Dead parade?
o: A parade invented for a James Bond film
quiz.e: After Spectre showed a fictional parade in 2015, the city began staging a real one in 2016.

LESSONS.title: The Bahá'í Faith: one God, one humanity
LESSONS.hook: Born in nineteenth-century Persia amid persecution and exile, the Bahá'í Faith teaches that all the great religions come from the same source. One of its temples stands among the gum trees of Sydney's northern beaches.

sections.key: The Bahá'í story begins with a young merchant in Shiraz who announced a new age in 1844.
sections.b: In 1844, in the Persian city of Shiraz, a young merchant named Siyyid ‘Alí-Muhammad declared that he was the Báb, meaning ‘the Gate’. He taught that a new era of revelation was beginning and that he was preparing the way for a far greater messenger to come. His message spread quickly, and so did opposition from religious and political authorities. Thousands of his followers were killed. The Báb himself was imprisoned and, in 1850, executed by firing squad in Tabriz. Bahá'í accounts relate that the first volley only cut the ropes binding him, and that a second regiment carried out the execution. Bahá'ís regard the Báb as a messenger of God in his own right and as the forerunner of their faith's founder.

sections.key: The faith's founder spent four decades as a prisoner and exile, writing the texts at its heart.
sections.b: Mírzá Husayn-‘Alí, born in 1817 to a noble Persian family, became a follower of the Báb and took the title Bahá'u'lláh, ‘the Glory of God’. In 1852 he was thrown into a notorious underground prison in Tehran known as the Black Pit. Bahá'ís believe that there he first received the revelation of his mission. Released, he was banished to Baghdad, then to Constantinople, Adrianople and finally the prison city of Akka, in what is now Israel. In 1863, in a Baghdad garden called Ridván, he announced to his companions that he was the messenger the Báb had foretold. Over the following decades he wrote thousands of tablets and several books. He died in 1892 near Akka, where his shrine is the holiest place on Earth for Bahá'ís.

sections.key: Bahá'ís believe God has sent a series of messengers, each suited to the needs of their time.
sections.b: A central Bahá'í teaching is that there is one God, who has revealed truth to humanity in stages. Messengers such as Abraham, Moses, Krishna, Zoroaster, the Buddha, Jesus and Muhammad are seen as teachers from the same divine school, each bringing guidance suited to the age in which they appeared. Their spiritual truths are eternal, while their social laws were designed for particular times and places. The Báb and Bahá'u'lláh are regarded as the most recent of these messengers, though not the last; Bahá'ís believe revelation will continue in the far future. This view leads Bahá'ís to treat other religions with deep respect, seeing the divisions between them as the result of human interpretation rather than of the founders' teachings.

sections.key: Bahá'í principles include equality of women and men, universal education and harmony between science and religion.
sections.b: If there is one God and one unfolding religion, Bahá'ís reason, then there is one human family, and the great task of this age is to unite it. From this flow principles that sounded radical in the nineteenth century. Bahá'ís teach the full equality of women and men, compulsory education for all children, and the elimination of prejudice of every kind, whether of race, class, nation or religion. They hold that true science and true religion cannot conflict, since both seek truth; if a religious belief contradicts reason, it should be reconsidered. Bahá'u'lláh also called for world peace, a global system of governance and an international auxiliary language that everyone would learn alongside their mother tongue.

sections.key: Bahá'í communities are run by elected councils, chosen by secret ballot with no candidates or campaigning.
sections.b: The Bahá'í Faith has no priests or ministers. After Bahá'u'lláh, leadership passed to his son ‘Abdu'l-Bahá, who travelled to Europe and North America to spread the teachings, and then to his grandson Shoghi Effendi. Since 1963 the faith has been governed by the Universal House of Justice, a nine-member council based in Haifa, Israel. Local and national communities elect their own nine-member spiritual assemblies. The elections are unusual. There are no nominations, no candidates and no campaigning; each voter prays and writes down the names of those they believe best suited to serve. Community life centres on the Nineteen-Day Feast, held at the start of each month of the Bahá'í calendar, which has nineteen months of nineteen days.

sections.key: Bahá'í temples are open to people of every faith, and the one in Sydney is among the oldest.
sections.b: Bahá'í Houses of Worship share some features: they are nine-sided, crowned with a dome, and open to everyone regardless of religion. Services are simple readings and prayers from the scriptures of many faiths, often sung by a choir without instruments, and there are no sermons. The temple in New Delhi, completed in 1986 and shaped like a lotus flower of white marble petals, has become one of India's most visited buildings. Sydney's House of Worship, in bushland at Ingleside, was dedicated in 1961. The faith's world centre spreads across Haifa and Akka, including the Shrine of the Báb surrounded by nineteen garden terraces on Mount Carmel. These Bahá'í holy places were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2008.

sections.key: Spread across almost every country, Bahá'ís still face serious persecution in Iran, where the faith began.
sections.b: From a small Persian movement, the Bahá'í Faith has spread to almost every country and territory, with followers estimated in the millions, though figures vary widely. Some of its largest communities are in India and parts of Africa and the Pacific. In the land of its birth, however, the faith remains under heavy pressure. Bahá'ís are the largest non-Muslim religious minority in Iran, but the Iranian government does not recognise their religion. Since the 1979 revolution, hundreds have been executed, while many others have been imprisoned, barred from university or had property confiscated, according to the United Nations and human rights groups. Bahá'ís have generally responded without violence, in keeping with teachings that forbid them from involvement in partisan politics.

quiz.q: What did the title ‘the Báb’ mean?
quiz.e: The Báb, meaning ‘the Gate’, said he was preparing the way for a greater messenger.

quiz.q: Where is the holiest place on Earth for Bahá'ís?
o: The Lotus Temple in New Delhi
The shrine of Bahá'u'lláh near Akka
quiz.e: Bahá'u'lláh's shrine at Bahjí, near Akka, is the faith's holiest site.

quiz.q: What does ‘progressive revelation’ mean in Bahá'í belief?
o: God reveals truth in stages through a series of messengers
Each nation has its own separate god
quiz.e: Bahá'ís see figures such as Moses, the Buddha, Jesus and Muhammad as messengers of one God for different ages.

quiz.q: How are Bahá'í spiritual assemblies chosen?
o: By secret ballot with no candidates or campaigning
By public debate between nominated candidates
quiz.e: Voters prayerfully write down names without nominations or campaigns.

quiz.q: What shape do all Bahá'í Houses of Worship share?
quiz.e: Every House of Worship has nine sides and a dome, and welcomes people of all faiths.

LESSONS.title: Enuma Elish: Babylon's war in heaven
LESSONS.hook: Long before Genesis was written down, Babylonians told how the world was made from the split body of a sea goddess. Their creation epic is also a brilliant piece of political propaganda.

sections.key: Enuma Elish is the Babylonian creation epic, named after its opening words.
sections.b: Ancient Mesopotamian texts were known by their first words, and this one begins ‘Enuma elish’, meaning ‘When on high’. It opens with a world before the sky was named and the earth had a name, when nothing existed but water. The poem fills seven clay tablets written in Akkadian cuneiform. Most surviving copies date from the first millennium BCE, but the poem is older. Many scholars think it was composed in the late second millennium BCE, perhaps around the time of King Nebuchadnezzar I, who brought Marduk's statue back to Babylon in the twelfth century BCE, though others argue for earlier dates. It is not a neutral account of creation. It tells how one god became king of all the others.

sections.key: Copies found in the ruins of an Assyrian royal library caused a sensation in Victorian Britain.
sections.b: In the mid-nineteenth century, excavations at Nineveh, in modern Iraq, uncovered the remains of the library of Ashurbanipal, a seventh-century BCE Assyrian king who collected texts from across his empire. Tens of thousands of clay tablets and fragments were shipped to the British Museum. Among them were pieces of Enuma Elish. In 1876 the self-taught Assyriologist George Smith, who had already found a Babylonian flood story in the Epic of Gilgamesh, published a translation in his book The Chaldean Account of Genesis. Victorian readers were astonished to learn that Mesopotamians had told their own story of creation, centuries before much of the Hebrew Bible was written down. Further copies discovered since have filled most of the gaps.

sections.key: The first gods were born from the mingling of Apsu, the fresh waters, and Tiamat, the salt sea.
sections.b: In the beginning there were two primal beings: Apsu, the fresh water beneath the earth, and Tiamat, the salty sea, often imagined as female and sometimes linked with a sea dragon. Their waters mingled, and generations of gods were born. The younger gods were noisy and restless, and their racket disturbed Apsu's rest. He resolved to destroy them, despite Tiamat's protests. The wise god Ea, a god of fresh water and magic, discovered the plot. He cast a spell that put Apsu to sleep, killed him and built his own home upon Apsu's body. There, in that freshwater dwelling, Ea and his wife Damkina had a son. He was Marduk, a dazzling god with four eyes and four ears, mightier than all his elders.

sections.key: Provoked to vengeance, Tiamat created monsters and made the god Kingu her commander.
sections.b: Tiamat at first had refused to harm her children, but after Apsu's death other gods urged her to strike back. She gave birth to an army of monsters, including serpents with venom for blood, dragons, scorpion-men and raging demons. She chose the god Kingu as her new husband and commander, and fastened to his chest the Tablet of Destinies, which gave its holder supreme authority over the universe. The other gods were terrified. Ea and then the sky god Anu went out to face her and turned back. Finally the assembly turned to young Marduk. He agreed to fight on one condition: if he won, his word would decide destinies, and he would be supreme among the gods.

sections.h: The battle and the making of the world
sections.key: Marduk slew Tiamat and made the sky and earth from the two halves of her body.
sections.b: Armed with a bow, a mace, a net and the winds, Marduk rode out in a storm chariot. When Tiamat opened her mouth to swallow him, he drove in an evil wind that swelled her body, then shot an arrow that split her heart. He caught her helpers in his net and took the Tablet of Destinies from Kingu. Then he began to build. He split Tiamat's body in two like a fish for drying, raising one half to form the sky and laying out the other as the earth. From her eyes flowed the Tigris and Euphrates. He set the stars and constellations, fixed the calendar, and gave the moon its phases. The cosmos was ordered from the body of chaos.

sections.key: People were created from the blood of the rebel god Kingu so that the gods could rest.
sections.b: With the world built, the gods faced a problem: someone had to do the endless labour of maintaining it. Marduk proposed creating a new being. The gods identified Kingu as the one who had stirred up Tiamat's rebellion, and he was put to death. From his blood Ea fashioned humankind, who were given the gods' work so that the gods could be free. This is a striking view of humanity's purpose. People exist to serve the gods by tending temples, offering food and keeping order. In gratitude, the gods built Babylon and its great temple, the Esagila, as Marduk's home. The poem ends with the gods proclaiming Marduk's fifty names, each praising a different aspect of his power.

sections.key: The epic promoted Babylon and its god, and has long been compared with the Bible.
sections.b: Enuma Elish raised Marduk, the patron god of Babylon, above older and more famous gods, mirroring Babylon's own rise to power. It was recited during the Akitu, the great new year festival of Babylon. When the Assyrians adopted the poem, some versions simply replaced Marduk with their own national god, Ashur, showing how clearly it was understood as a statement of power. The epic has also been compared with the opening of Genesis, which likewise begins with primeval waters and a separation of sky from earth. Some scholars link the Hebrew word tehom, ‘the deep’, to Tiamat. How far the biblical writers knew or responded to this tradition is still debated, but the comparison illuminates both texts.

quiz.q: Where does the name ‘Enuma Elish’ come from?
o: Its opening words, meaning ‘When on high’
The city where it was found
A title given by George Smith
quiz.e: Mesopotamian texts were named after their first words; ‘Enuma elish’ means ‘When on high’.

quiz.q: What did Apsu and Tiamat represent?
quiz.e: Apsu was the fresh water under the earth and Tiamat the salt sea; their mingling produced the gods.

quiz.q: What did Marduk demand before agreeing to fight Tiamat?
o: To become supreme among the gods
To be given the city of Nineveh
quiz.e: He agreed to fight only if his word would fix destinies and he would rule the gods.

quiz.q: How did Marduk create the sky and the earth?
o: From the two halves of Tiamat's body
quiz.e: He split Tiamat in two, raising one half as the sky and laying the other out as the earth.

quiz.q: Why were humans created, according to the epic?
o: To rule the world in the gods' place
To do the gods' labour so the gods could rest
quiz.e: Humans, made from Kingu's blood, were given the gods' work of maintaining the world.

LESSONS.title: The Aztec gods and the Fifth Sun
LESSONS.hook: The Mexica believed they lived under the fifth sun the gods had made, and that it moved only because gods had given their lives. Their religion was built around keeping it in the sky.

sections.key: The people we call the Aztecs called themselves the Mexica and founded Tenochtitlan on a lake island.
sections.b: The name ‘Aztec’ was popularised much later. The people who built the great city of Tenochtitlan called themselves the Mexica, and their name lives on in Mexico. According to their own traditions, they migrated south from a homeland called Aztlan, guided by their patron god Huitzilopochtli. He promised them they would know their new home when they saw an eagle perched on a cactus growing from a rock. They found that sign on a marshy island in Lake Texcoco, where they founded Tenochtitlan, traditionally in 1325. The image of the eagle on the cactus is now at the centre of Mexico's flag. Within two centuries the island had become one of the largest cities in the world, linked to the shore by causeways.

sections.key: The Mexica believed the world had been created and destroyed four times before the present age.
sections.b: In Mexica cosmology, time moved in great ages called Suns. Each Sun was a separate creation, ruled by a different god, and each ended in catastrophe. In one widely told version, the first world was destroyed by jaguars, the second by tremendous winds, the third by a rain of fire and the fourth by a flood. Accounts differ about the order and details, since our sources were written after the Spanish conquest and draw on different traditions. The present age was the Fifth Sun, called Nahui Ollin, ‘Four Movement’. It too was destined to end, many believed, in terrible earthquakes. This sense that the world was fragile, and could fail, shaped much of Mexica religious life.

sections.h: The gods who leapt into the fire
sections.key: The Fifth Sun began when two gods sacrificed themselves in a great fire at Teotihuacan.
sections.b: After the fourth world ended, the gods gathered in darkness at Teotihuacan, an ancient city that was already in ruins when the Mexica arrived and which they regarded as sacred. Someone had to become the new sun by leaping into a great fire. The proud and wealthy god Tecciztecatl volunteered but lost his nerve four times. Then the humble, sickly god Nanahuatzin jumped without hesitating and rose as the sun. Ashamed, Tecciztecatl followed and also became a sun. Because two suns would be too bright, a god threw a rabbit into the second one's face, dimming it into the moon, which is why the Mexica saw a rabbit in the moon. Even then the sun would not move until the other gods gave their own lives.

sections.key: The great temple of Tenochtitlan had twin shrines for the god of war and the sun and the god of rain.
sections.b: At the heart of Tenochtitlan stood the Templo Mayor, a huge stepped pyramid topped by two shrines. One honoured Huitzilopochtli, the Mexica's own patron, a god of the sun and war. The other honoured Tlaloc, an ancient god of rain and fertility worshipped across Mesoamerica long before the Mexica. Together they represented war and agriculture, the twin foundations of the empire. Huitzilopochtli's birth story was famous. His mother Coatlicue became pregnant miraculously at the hill of Coatepec. Her daughter Coyolxauhqui and four hundred sons, outraged, plotted to kill her. Huitzilopochtli was born fully armed, defeated his siblings and cast his dismembered sister down the hill, an event the temple's design itself recalled.

sections.key: The feathered serpent and the god of the smoking mirror were powerful rivals in Mexica myth.
sections.b: Quetzalcoatl, the Feathered Serpent, was among the oldest and most widely honoured gods of Mesoamerica. Associated with wind, learning, priesthood and the morning star, he was said in some stories to have retrieved human bones from the underworld and given people life with his own blood. His great rival was Tezcatlipoca, the ‘Smoking Mirror’, a mysterious, powerful god of night, fate and sorcery, often shown with an obsidian mirror in place of a foot. In one cycle of tales they alternately create and destroy the earlier Suns. In another, Tezcatlipoca tricks Quetzalcoatl, ruler of the legendary city of Tollan, into disgrace, and Quetzalcoatl departs towards the east, promising, in some versions, to return.

sections.key: Because gods had died to set the sun moving, the Mexica believed humans owed a debt paid in offerings and blood.
sections.b: The logic of Mexica sacrifice followed from their myths. The gods had given their lives to create and power the Fifth Sun, so humans owed a debt that had to be repaid. Worshippers offered incense, food, flowers and their own blood, drawn with cactus spines or bone points. Most dramatically, priests sacrificed human beings, many of them war captives, at ceremonies across the ritual year. Spanish accounts of the scale were sometimes exaggerated, and historians long debated them, but archaeology has confirmed that sacrifice was real and significant. Since 2015, excavations in Mexico City have uncovered parts of the Huei Tzompantli, a great rack and tower built with the skulls of hundreds of individuals, near the Templo Mayor.

sections.key: The story that the Mexica thought Cortés was Quetzalcoatl is now widely doubted.
sections.b: Spanish forces led by Hernán Cortés conquered Tenochtitlan in 1521, with tens of thousands of Indigenous allies. A famous story claims the emperor Moctezuma believed Cortés was the returning Quetzalcoatl. Many historians now doubt this, since the story appears mainly in sources written decades after the conquest, shaped by both Spanish and Indigenous writers trying to explain what had happened. The Mexica religion itself was suppressed, its temples demolished and a cathedral built near the ruins. Yet much survived. In 1978 electricity workers in Mexico City uncovered a huge carved stone of the dismembered Coyolxauhqui, leading to the full excavation of the Templo Mayor. Today more than a million and a half people in Mexico still speak Nahuatl, the Mexica language.

quiz.q: What sign told the Mexica where to found their city?
o: An eagle perched on a cactus
A jaguar drinking from a spring
quiz.e: Huitzilopochtli promised them an eagle on a cactus, now shown on Mexico's flag.

quiz.q: Which god leapt first into the fire to become the sun?
quiz.e: The humble Nanahuatzin jumped without hesitating; proud Tecciztecatl followed and became the moon.

quiz.q: Which two gods had shrines on top of the Templo Mayor?
quiz.e: The twin shrines honoured Huitzilopochtli, god of sun and war, and Tlaloc, god of rain.

quiz.q: Why did the Mexica believe offerings and sacrifice were necessary?
o: To win favour with the Spanish
To repay the gods who had died to create and move the sun
To stop the lake from flooding
quiz.e: Humans owed a debt to the gods who gave their lives for the Fifth Sun.

quiz.q: Why do many historians doubt that Moctezuma thought Cortés was Quetzalcoatl?
o: Quetzalcoatl was unknown to the Mexica
The story appears mainly in sources written decades later
Cortés denied it in his letters
quiz.e: The tale is largely found in later accounts shaped by efforts to explain the conquest.

LESSONS.title: The orishas: Yoruba gods of two continents
LESSONS.hook: From the cities of south-western Nigeria to the beaches of Brazil and the streets of Havana, millions of people honour the orishas, divine forces of thunder, rivers, iron and the sea.

sections.key: Yoruba religion developed among one of West Africa's largest peoples and centres on the orishas.
sections.b: The Yoruba are one of Africa's largest ethnic groups, numbering tens of millions, mostly in south-western Nigeria and neighbouring Benin and Togo. Their traditional religion is often called Ìṣẹ̀ṣe, meaning tradition or origin. It recognises a supreme creator, Olodumare, who is vast and distant and not usually approached directly. Instead, people relate to the orishas, divine beings who act as intermediaries and each govern particular forces of nature and areas of life. Some are seen as forces present since creation, others as deified ancestors and kings. There is also àṣẹ, the vital power that makes things happen, which flows through gods, people, words and objects. Today many Yoruba are Christian or Muslim, but traditional practice and its influence remain strong.

sections.key: In Yoruba tradition, dry land was first made at the sacred city of Ile-Ife.
sections.b: One widely told creation story begins with the world as water and marsh. Olodumare sends the orisha Obatala down from the sky on a golden chain, carrying a snail shell full of earth and a bird, often described as a hen or cockerel. Obatala pours out the earth, and the bird scratches and scatters it, spreading dry land. In some versions Obatala becomes drunk on palm wine and falls asleep, and his rival Oduduwa completes the task instead. Obatala is also said to shape human bodies from clay, and some traditions explain disabilities as the result of his drunkenness, which is why Obatala's followers avoid palm wine and protect people with disabilities. The place where land first appeared is Ile-Ife, still regarded as a sacred city.

sections.key: Each orisha has its own domain, colours, foods, stories and devotees.
sections.b: The orishas are vivid personalities. Obatala, associated with white cloth and coolness, stands for purity, wisdom and calm judgement. Ogun is the orisha of iron, tools and war, honoured by blacksmiths, hunters and, today, drivers and mechanics. Shango, lord of thunder and lightning, is remembered as a fiery king of the city of Oyo, and his symbol is a double-headed axe. Oshun, orisha of sweet waters, love, beauty and fertility, is linked with the Osun River, and her sacred grove at Osogbo is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Yemoja is a great mother associated with water and motherhood. Eshu, or Elegba, the trickster messenger, guards crossroads and carries offerings, and must be honoured first in many ceremonies.

sections.key: The Ifá system of divination preserves a huge body of verse used to guide decisions.
sections.b: When facing a serious decision, illness or trouble, a person may consult a babalawo, a priest of Ifá. Ifá is linked with Orunmila, the orisha of wisdom and destiny. The babalawo casts a divining chain, or manipulates sacred palm nuts, to produce one of 256 possible patterns called odu. Each odu is associated with a large collection of memorised verses, stories and proverbs. The priest recites them, and the client and priest together interpret which passage speaks to the situation, often followed by recommended offerings. Training takes many years. UNESCO has recognised the Ifá divination system as part of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, and its verses are treasured as a vast store of Yoruba history, values and wisdom.

sections.key: Enslaved Yoruba people carried their faith to the Americas, where it took new forms.
sections.b: During the Atlantic slave trade, especially in its final decades, large numbers of Yoruba people were captured and taken to the Americas, particularly to Cuba and Brazil. Forbidden from openly practising their religion and pressured to become Catholic, many found ways to keep the orishas alive. Over time, each orisha came to be associated with a Catholic saint with similar imagery or qualities. Shango was linked in Cuba with St Barbara, whose symbols include lightning, and Oshun with the Virgin of Charity, Cuba's patron. Historians and practitioners still discuss how far this was a disguise and how far a genuine blending. Out of these experiences grew new religions, including Santería, also called Lucumí, in Cuba and Candomblé in Brazil.

sections.key: In Cuba and Brazil, orisha religions developed their own ceremonies of drumming, dance and initiation.
sections.b: In Cuban Santería, initiated priests and priestesses are dedicated to a particular orisha who is believed to ‘rule their head’. New initiates traditionally dress all in white for a year. Ceremonies feature sacred batá drums, songs in a liturgical form of Yoruba, and dances in which devotees may be possessed by an orisha. Brazil's Candomblé, particularly strong in the city of Salvador in Bahia, is organised around houses called terreiros, often led by women, and also uses drumming, dance and possession. Yoruba spellings shifted across the ocean: Yemoja became Yemayá in Cuba and Iemanjá in Brazil, where she became queen of the sea. Both religions were long stigmatised and sometimes persecuted, but have gained recognition and many followers.

sections.key: Orisha traditions now shape public festivals and have followers around the world.
sections.b: In Brazil, Iemanjá is celebrated far beyond Candomblé. On 2 February in Salvador, huge crowds carry flowers, perfume and gifts to the sea in her honour. On New Year's Eve many Brazilians, whatever their religion, dress in white and toss flowers into the waves or jump seven waves for good luck, customs linked to her. Orisha imagery shapes Cuban music, Brazilian carnival and contemporary art. Migration has spread these religions to the United States, Europe and beyond, and some African Americans have looked to orisha worship as a way to reconnect with African heritage. Meanwhile, in Nigeria, the annual Osun-Osogbo festival draws thousands of devotees and visitors to the sacred grove each August.

quiz.q: In Yoruba religion, who is Olodumare?
quiz.e: Olodumare is the supreme creator, usually approached through the orishas rather than directly.

quiz.q: How was dry land first created, in one widely told Yoruba story?
o: Shango split the sea with lightning
Obatala poured earth from a shell and a bird scattered it
A giant turtle rose from the water
quiz.e: Obatala descended on a chain with earth in a snail shell and a bird spread it at Ile-Ife.

quiz.q: Which orisha is associated with iron, tools and those who work with them?
quiz.e: Ogun is the orisha of iron and is honoured by smiths, hunters, drivers and mechanics.

quiz.q: How many possible patterns, or odu, can Ifá divination produce?
quiz.e: The system produces 256 odu, each linked to memorised verses and stories.

quiz.q: With which Catholic saint was Shango associated in Cuba?
quiz.e: St Barbara's imagery of lightning made her a natural match for Shango, the thunder orisha.

LESSONS.title: How the Bible became a book
LESSONS.hook: The Bible was not written at once, nor agreed on in a single meeting. It grew over a thousand years, and Christians still do not all have the same list of books.

sections.key: The Bible is a collection of writings from many authors, centuries and genres.
sections.b: The word Bible comes from the Greek ta biblia, ‘the books’. It is a library rather than a single work, containing law, history, poetry, prophecy, proverbs, letters and visions, written mostly in Hebrew and Greek, with some Aramaic. Its writing is usually thought to span more than a thousand years. A canon is the official list of books a community accepts as scripture, from a Greek word for a measuring rod. Different communities settled on different canons. The Jewish Bible contains 24 books. Protestant Bibles have 66, Catholic Bibles 73, and Eastern Orthodox and Oriental churches more again. How those lists formed is a long story, and scholars continue to debate some of its details.

sections.key: The Hebrew Bible took shape in three parts, with the Torah recognised first.
sections.b: Jewish scripture is called the Tanakh, an acronym of its three parts: Torah (the Teaching, the five books of Moses), Nevi'im (the Prophets) and Ketuvim (the Writings, including Psalms, Proverbs and Job). Scholars generally think the Torah was recognised as authoritative first, probably by around the fifth or fourth century BCE, and the Prophets next. The Writings remained more open for longer. Rabbinic texts record debates over whether books like Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs belonged, and the list seems to have been broadly settled in the early centuries CE. Christian Old Testaments in Protestant Bibles contain the same material, counted as 39 books rather than 24 because books like Samuel, Kings and the twelve minor prophets are divided differently.

sections.key: The Septuagint, a Greek translation made in Egypt, included extra books that later divided Christians.
sections.b: From the third century BCE, Jews in Alexandria, many of whom spoke Greek, translated their scriptures into Greek, beginning with the Torah. A legend in the Letter of Aristeas says seventy-two scholars completed the work in seventy-two days, which is why the translation is called the Septuagint, from the Latin for seventy. The Greek collections that circulated also included texts not later accepted in the Jewish canon, such as Tobit, Judith, Wisdom of Solomon, Sirach and books of Maccabees. Early Christians, who mostly read the scriptures in Greek, used the Septuagint widely. Those extra books, which Catholics and Orthodox call deuterocanonical and Protestants call the Apocrypha, became a lasting point of difference between Christian traditions.

sections.key: Scrolls found near Qumran from 1947 pushed the manuscript record of the Hebrew Bible back about a thousand years.
sections.b: In 1947 Bedouin shepherds exploring caves near Qumran, on the north-western shore of the Dead Sea, found jars holding ancient scrolls. Over the next decade around 900 manuscripts, most surviving only as fragments, were recovered from eleven caves. Dating mostly from the third century BCE to the first century CE, they include copies or fragments of every book of the Hebrew Bible except Esther. Before this, the oldest complete Hebrew Bible manuscripts were medieval, such as the Leningrad Codex of about 1008 CE. The Great Isaiah Scroll, roughly a thousand years older, proved remarkably close to the medieval text. Other scrolls, though, show variant versions, revealing that in that era some biblical books still circulated in more than one form.

sections.key: Early Christians gradually sorted widely trusted writings from disputed ones over several centuries.
sections.b: The earliest New Testament writings are the letters of Paul, usually dated to the 50s CE. Most scholars date the four gospels to roughly 70 to 100 CE, though dates are debated. Many other writings circulated too. In the mid-second century a teacher named Marcion proposed a scripture made up only of an edited Luke and ten letters of Paul, rejecting the Jewish scriptures entirely. Many scholars think his challenge pushed other Christians to define their own collection more clearly. By around 200 CE the four gospels and Paul's letters were widely accepted. Some books stayed disputed for longer, including Hebrews, James, 2 Peter, Jude and Revelation, while others, like the Shepherd of Hermas, were read in some churches but eventually left out.

sections.key: A popular myth says the Council of Nicaea chose the Bible's books; it did not.
sections.b: A widely repeated claim, popularised by novels such as The Da Vinci Code, holds that the Emperor Constantine and the Council of Nicaea in 325 CE picked which books made it into the Bible. There is no evidence for this. The council's surviving decisions concern the nature of Christ, the date of Easter and church discipline, not the canon. The process was slower and more spread out. In 367 CE Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, wrote an Easter letter that is the earliest known list matching the 27 books of today's New Testament. Regional councils at Hippo in 393 and Carthage in 397 endorsed similar lists. Even then, some churches, notably in Syria and Ethiopia, continued to use somewhat different collections.

sections.key: Protestants separated out the Apocrypha, Catholics affirmed it, and some churches kept even larger canons.
sections.b: The question reopened in the sixteenth century. Martin Luther, following the Hebrew canon for the Old Testament, placed the deuterocanonical books in a separate section between the Testaments in his 1534 German Bible, describing them as useful to read but not equal to scripture. In 1546 the Catholic Council of Trent formally affirmed them as fully canonical. Most Protestant Bibles later dropped them altogether. Eastern Orthodox churches accept further books, such as 1 Esdras and 3 Maccabees. The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church has the largest canon, usually counted at around 81 books, including 1 Enoch and Jubilees. Even the chapters and verses are late additions: chapter divisions date from the thirteenth century and New Testament verse numbers from 1551.

quiz.q: What is a ‘canon’ of scripture?
o: The official list of books a community accepts
quiz.e: A canon, from a word for a measuring rod, is the accepted list of scriptural books.

quiz.q: Why do Catholic and Protestant Bibles differ in length?
o: Catholics include books found in Greek collections that Protestants call the Apocrypha
Catholics removed the letters of Paul
Protestants include the Dead Sea Scrolls
quiz.e: Books like Tobit and Sirach, preserved in Greek collections, are canonical for Catholics but not for most Protestants.

quiz.q: What did the Great Isaiah Scroll reveal?
o: Isaiah had been completely rewritten in the Middle Ages
The book of Isaiah was originally in Greek
Its text was remarkably close to medieval manuscripts a thousand years younger
Isaiah was not part of the Hebrew Bible
quiz.e: The scroll, about a thousand years older than medieval copies, matched them closely.

quiz.q: What did the Council of Nicaea in 325 CE actually deal with?
o: Choosing the books of the New Testament
The nature of Christ, the date of Easter and church discipline
quiz.e: Nicaea's decisions concerned doctrine and church matters; it did not set the canon.

quiz.q: Which church has the largest biblical canon?
quiz.e: The Ethiopian canon is usually counted at around 81 books, including 1 Enoch and Jubilees.

LESSONS.title: Blood types: why your blood has a label
LESSONS.hook: For centuries, giving someone blood was a gamble that often killed them. Then a Viennese doctor mixed a few test tubes and discovered why.

sections.key: Early transfusions were dangerous because nobody knew that blood comes in incompatible types.
sections.b: In 1667 the French physician Jean-Baptiste Denys transfused lamb's blood into human patients. A few seemed to survive, but after one man died the practice was banned in France, and transfusion fell out of favour for well over a century. From 1818 the English obstetrician James Blundell tried again, this time using human blood, notably for women bleeding heavily after childbirth. Some patients recovered remarkably. Others suffered fever, back pain, dark urine and death, and no one could predict which would happen. Doctors of the 1800s were left with a frustrating puzzle. The same procedure that rescued one dying patient killed the next, and the reason lay hidden in the blood itself, invisible to the microscopes of the day.

sections.key: In 1901 Karl Landsteiner showed that mixing some people's blood makes it clump, and identified the first blood groups.
sections.b: In 1901 Karl Landsteiner, working in Vienna, took blood from himself and his colleagues and separated it into red cells and serum, the liquid part. Then he mixed each person's serum with every other person's red cells. Sometimes nothing happened. Sometimes the red cells clumped together into sticky clusters, a reaction called agglutination. From the pattern he sorted people into groups, which became known as A, B and O. A year later two of his colleagues found the rarer fourth group, AB. The clumping explained the old disasters: incompatible donor cells were being attacked and destroyed inside the patient. Landsteiner's work made safe transfusion possible, and in 1930 it earned him the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

sections.key: Your blood type depends on which sugar markers, called antigens, coat your red blood cells.
sections.b: Every red blood cell is studded with molecules on its surface. In the ABO system, the important ones are chains of sugars. Type A cells carry the A antigen, type B cells carry B, type AB cells carry both, and type O cells carry neither. The twist is that your plasma usually contains antibodies against whichever antigens you lack. Someone with type A blood has anti B antibodies, and someone with type O has both anti A and anti B. These antibodies appear in early childhood, probably because gut bacteria carry similar sugar molecules that train the immune system. If incompatible blood is transfused, those antibodies latch onto the foreign cells and can trigger a severe, sometimes fatal, reaction.

sections.key: The Rh factor is a second major blood group system, and it matters greatly in pregnancy.
sections.b: The plus or minus after your blood type refers to another system, discovered in 1940 by Landsteiner and Alexander Wiener. They named it after the rhesus monkeys used in their experiments, and the name stuck even though the human antigen later proved to be different. People whose cells carry the main Rh antigen, called D, are Rh positive; those without it are Rh negative. This became vital in pregnancy. If an Rh negative mother carries an Rh positive baby, she can make antibodies that attack the red cells of that baby or a later one, a condition called haemolytic disease of the newborn. Since the late 1960s, injections of anti D antibodies have prevented most of these cases.

sections.key: O negative red cells can be given to almost anyone, which makes them precious in emergencies.
sections.b: Because type O negative red cells carry no A, B or D antigens, the recipient's antibodies have nothing to attack. That is why O negative is called the universal donor for red cells, and why ambulances and emergency departments rely on it when there is no time to test a patient's blood. At the other end, people with AB positive blood can receive red cells of any ABO and Rh type, because they make no anti A or anti B antibodies. For plasma the rules flip: AB plasma contains no ABO antibodies, so it can be given to anyone. Even with these shortcuts, hospitals still crossmatch blood whenever they can, testing donor and patient samples together before a planned transfusion.

sections.key: Scientists now recognise more than 40 blood group systems, and blood type does not shape your personality.
sections.b: ABO and Rh are the systems that matter most for everyday transfusion, but they are far from the whole story. Researchers have identified more than 40 blood group systems and hundreds of individual antigens, which is why people with rare combinations sometimes need specially matched donors. In Australia, roughly four in ten people are O positive, making it the most common type, while O negative is carried by fewer than one in ten. AB negative is the rarest, at around one per cent. One popular idea deserves retiring. In Japan and some other countries, blood type is often linked to personality, much like star signs. Careful studies involving large numbers of people have found no meaningful connection.

quiz.q: What did Karl Landsteiner observe when he mixed serum from one person with red cells from another?
quiz.e: Landsteiner saw agglutination, or clumping, in some combinations. The pattern revealed the A, B and O groups.

quiz.q: Why does a person with type A blood react badly to type B red cells?
o: Their plasma contains anti B antibodies
Type B cells carry no antigens
quiz.e: People usually carry antibodies against the ABO antigens they lack, so type A plasma contains anti B antibodies that attack type B cells.

quiz.q: What problem did anti D injections largely prevent?
quiz.e: An Rh negative mother can make antibodies against an Rh positive baby's red cells. Anti D injections stop her immune system from becoming sensitised.

quiz.q: Why is O negative blood used in emergencies when there is no time to test?
o: It clots faster than other types
It is the most common type in Australia
Its red cells lack A, B and D antigens
quiz.e: With no A, B or D antigens on its red cells, O negative blood gives the recipient's antibodies nothing to target.

quiz.q: What have large studies found about blood type and personality?
o: Type O people are more confident
Type AB people are more creative
The link only applies in Japan
quiz.e: Despite the popular belief, careful research has not found any meaningful link between blood type and personality.

LESSONS.title: How a cut heals
LESSONS.hook: Slice your finger and your body launches a carefully timed rescue operation, from emergency plugging to months of quiet rebuilding.

sections.key: Within seconds, blood vessels narrow and platelets begin plugging the hole.
sections.b: The moment skin is cut, the damaged blood vessels tighten, reducing the flow of blood to the area. Tiny cell fragments called platelets, which drift through the blood in huge numbers, touch the exposed tissue and become sticky. They clump together into a soft plug and release chemicals that call in more platelets. At the same time a chain of clotting proteins in the plasma switches on, step by step, until a protein called fibrinogen is converted into long strands of fibrin. These strands weave through the platelet plug like a net, trapping red cells and turning liquid blood into a solid clot. As the surface of that clot dries out, it becomes the familiar crusty scab.

sections.key: Redness, heat, swelling and pain are signs that the clean-up crew has arrived.
sections.b: Around two thousand years ago the Roman writer Celsus described the four classic signs of inflammation: redness, heat, swelling and pain. They are not signs that something is going wrong. Damaged cells release chemical alarms that widen nearby blood vessels, bringing extra blood that makes the area red and warm. The vessel walls become leakier, so fluid and immune cells seep into the tissue, causing swelling. Within hours, white blood cells called neutrophils arrive to kill bacteria. They are followed by macrophages, large cells that swallow debris, dead cells and germs. Macrophages also release signals that tell the next wave of repair cells to get to work, which makes them the managers of healing.

sections.key: Over the following days, new blood vessels, collagen and skin cells fill and close the wound.
sections.b: After a few days, the wound enters its building phase. Cells called fibroblasts move in and start producing collagen, the tough protein that gives skin its strength. New capillaries sprout into the area to supply oxygen and nutrients. Together they form granulation tissue, the pink, slightly bumpy surface you may see in a healing graze. Meanwhile, skin cells at the edges of the wound multiply and crawl across the gap, sliding underneath the scab until they meet in the middle. Some fibroblasts transform into specialised cells that can contract, gently pulling the wound edges closer together. When the new skin is complete, the scab is no longer needed and eventually falls away.

sections.key: Scar tissue keeps changing for a year or more, but it never fully matches the original skin.
sections.b: The final phase is the slowest. The first collagen laid down is hastily arranged, and over the following months the body breaks it down and replaces it with stronger, better organised fibres. A scar that looked red and raised often fades and flattens over a year or more. Even so, scar tissue never becomes perfect skin. It typically regains at most around 80 per cent of the original strength, and it usually lacks hair follicles and sweat glands. Curiously, researchers have found that wounds in early foetuses can heal without any scar at all. Understanding exactly how they do it is one of the long-standing goals of wound research.

sections.key: Keeping a wound clean and moist usually helps it heal faster than leaving it to dry in the air.
sections.b: Many of us grew up hearing that cuts should be left uncovered so they can breathe. In 1962 a British researcher named George Winter tested this on pigs, whose skin is similar to ours. Shallow wounds covered with a plastic film, which kept them moist, healed considerably faster than wounds left exposed to the air. A dry scab, it turns out, is a barrier that new skin cells must tunnel underneath. A moist surface lets them glide across more easily. Winter's work helped launch modern wound dressings, from simple hydrocolloid patches to specialised hospital products. The practical lesson for small cuts is to clean them gently and keep them covered.

sections.key: Smoking, diabetes, poor nutrition and infection can all delay repair.
sections.b: Healing needs a good blood supply, oxygen and raw materials, so anything that interferes with those slows the process. Smoking narrows blood vessels and reduces oxygen delivery. Diabetes can damage circulation and nerves, which is why people with diabetes are advised to check their feet carefully. Protein and vitamin C are essential for making collagen. Sailors with scurvy, caused by a lack of vitamin C, were recorded as having old, long healed wounds break open again. Healing also slows with age. Get medical help for wounds that are deep, gaping, very dirty or caused by animal bites, or that show signs of spreading infection. For severe bleeding, apply firm pressure and call 000.

quiz.q: What protein forms the net of strands that turns liquid blood into a clot?
quiz.e: Clotting proteins convert fibrinogen into fibrin, whose strands weave through the platelet plug and trap blood cells.

quiz.q: Why does an injured area become red and warm?
o: Nearby blood vessels widen and bring in more blood
Bacteria produce heat as they grow
quiz.e: Damaged cells release chemicals that widen vessels. Extra blood flow produces the redness and warmth of inflammation.

quiz.q: Which cells produce the collagen that rebuilds the wound?
quiz.e: Fibroblasts move into the wound and lay down collagen, forming granulation tissue together with new capillaries.

quiz.q: How does a mature scar compare with the original skin?
o: It is stronger than the original
It is identical once fully healed
It is weaker and usually lacks hair follicles
quiz.e: Scar tissue usually regains at most about 80 per cent of the original strength and lacks hair follicles and sweat glands.

quiz.q: What did George Winter's 1962 experiment show?
o: Moist, covered wounds healed faster than exposed ones
Wounds heal fastest in direct sunlight
quiz.e: Winter found that wounds kept moist under film healed faster, because new skin cells can move more easily across a moist surface.

LESSONS.title: Your teeth: the hardest part of you
LESSONS.hook: Your teeth are coated in the toughest material your body makes, yet a bag of lollies can slowly dissolve it. Here is how they work and how to keep them.

sections.key: Teeth have a hard outer shell of enamel, a living layer of dentine and a soft pulp inside.
sections.b: A tooth is built like a fortress. The outer layer of the crown is enamel, the hardest substance in the human body. It is about 96 per cent mineral, mostly crystals of a calcium phosphate called hydroxyapatite. Beneath it lies dentine, which is softer and full of microscopic tubes. That is why a worn or cracked tooth can feel sensitive to cold. At the centre is the pulp, a soft core of nerves and blood vessels that keeps the tooth alive. The root is anchored into the jawbone by tiny fibres called the periodontal ligament. Enamel has one great weakness. It contains no living cells, so once it is lost, the body cannot grow it back.

sections.key: Humans grow 20 baby teeth, then 32 adult teeth that must last the rest of their lives.
sections.b: Most mammals, including us, get two sets of teeth. Children have 20 baby teeth, which usually start appearing at around six months. Even then, the adult teeth are already forming deep in the jaw. From about the age of six, the baby teeth loosen and fall out as the permanent teeth push up from below. A full adult set has 32 teeth: incisors for cutting, canines for tearing, premolars and molars for grinding. The last four molars, known as wisdom teeth, usually arrive between the late teens and mid twenties, if they arrive at all. Unlike sharks, which replace teeth throughout their lives, we get no third set.

sections.key: Mouth bacteria turn sugar into acid, and that acid dissolves enamel.
sections.b: Your mouth is home to hundreds of species of bacteria, which live in a sticky film called plaque. Some of them, including a species called Streptococcus mutans, feed on sugars and release acid as waste. When the surface of a tooth becomes acidic enough, roughly below a pH of 5.5, minerals start to dissolve out of the enamel. Saliva fights back. It neutralises acid and supplies calcium and phosphate that can rebuild early damage. Trouble starts when the attacks come too often for saliva to keep up. That is why how often you eat sugar matters more than the total amount. Sipping soft drink all afternoon is harder on teeth than having one with lunch.

sections.h: The mystery of the brown stain
sections.key: Fluoride was discovered when a dentist investigated mottled teeth that rarely decayed.
sections.b: In the early 1900s a young dentist named Frederick McKay moved to Colorado Springs and noticed that many locals had brown stains on their teeth. Over years of investigation he found the stained teeth were strangely resistant to decay, and the cause was eventually traced to naturally high levels of fluoride in the water. Researchers then worked out that a much lower level could reduce decay without staining. In 1945 Grand Rapids, Michigan, became the first city to add fluoride to its water supply deliberately. In Australia, the Tasmanian town of Beaconsfield led the way in 1953. Fluoride helps enamel rebuild into a form called fluorapatite, which resists acid better than the original.

sections.key: Gum disease starts with plaque and, left untreated, can destroy the bone that holds teeth in place.
sections.b: Healthy teeth can still be lost if the gums and bone around them fail. Plaque that is not removed along the gumline irritates the gums, causing gingivitis, with redness, swelling and bleeding when you brush. At this stage the damage is reversible with good cleaning. Plaque left in place hardens into tartar, which a toothbrush cannot remove. Over time, ongoing inflammation can progress to periodontitis, in which pockets form between gums and teeth and the supporting bone is gradually destroyed. Teeth can loosen and eventually fall out. Researchers have found links between gum disease and conditions such as diabetes and heart disease, though how much one directly causes the other is still being studied.

sections.key: People have cleaned their teeth for thousands of years, but the modern toothbrush is surprisingly recent.
sections.b: Ancient peoples cleaned their teeth with chew sticks, twigs frayed at one end, and the miswak stick is still widely used in parts of the Middle East, Africa and Asia. Bristle brushes made with hog hair appeared in China centuries ago. In England, a man named William Addis began mass producing toothbrushes in the late 1700s; popular accounts say he came up with the idea while in prison. The first nylon bristle brushes went on sale in 1938, replacing animal hair. Today, dental authorities, including in Australia, recommend brushing twice a day with fluoride toothpaste, cleaning between the teeth, and spitting out rather than rinsing, so some fluoride stays on the enamel.

quiz.q: Why can't the body repair enamel that has been lost?
quiz.e: Enamel is almost entirely mineral and has no living cells, so the body cannot regrow it once it is gone.

quiz.q: How many teeth are in a full adult set?
quiz.e: Adults have 32 teeth, including four wisdom teeth. Children have 20 baby teeth.

quiz.q: Why is sipping a sugary drink all afternoon worse than drinking it with a meal?
o: Repeated acid attacks give saliva no time to repair enamel
Sugar becomes more acidic over time
quiz.e: Frequent sugar keeps the mouth acidic. Saliva needs time between attacks to neutralise acid and rebuild minerals.

quiz.q: What clue led to the discovery of fluoride's benefits?
o: Teeth that glowed under ultraviolet light
Children who never lost baby teeth
Brown stained teeth that rarely decayed
quiz.e: Frederick McKay noticed that mottled, stained teeth in Colorado Springs resisted decay, which was traced to fluoride in the water.

quiz.q: What is true of gingivitis?
o: It always leads to tooth loss
It is reversible with good cleaning
quiz.e: Gingivitis, the early stage of gum disease, can be reversed by removing plaque. Untreated, it can progress to periodontitis.

LESSONS.title: How your voice works
LESSONS.hook: Every word you speak begins as a buzz from two tiny folds of tissue in your throat. The rest is shaped by your body like a musical instrument.

sections.key: Your voice is made in the larynx, where two vocal folds sit across the airway.
sections.b: Sitting at the top of your windpipe is the larynx, or voice box, a structure of cartilage, muscle and ligament. The bump at the front of the neck, often called the Adam's apple, is part of its largest cartilage, and it tends to stick out more in men. Inside, stretched across the airway, are two vocal folds. They are often called vocal cords, but they are not strings. Each is a layered band of muscle and ligament covered in soft, moist membrane. When you breathe, the folds swing apart to let air through. When you swallow, they snap shut, helping to stop food and drink going down the wrong way. When you speak, they come together and vibrate.

sections.key: Air from your lungs forces the vocal folds open and shut hundreds of times every second.
sections.b: To make a sound, muscles bring the vocal folds together. Air pushed up from the lungs builds pressure beneath them until it forces them apart and a puff escapes. The folds then spring back together, helped by their own elasticity and the drop in pressure as air rushes between them, and the cycle repeats. This happens remarkably fast. A typical adult man's speaking voice vibrates at around 100 to 120 cycles per second, and a typical woman's at around 200. Tighter, thinner folds vibrate faster and produce higher notes, which is how you change pitch. Push more air through and the sound gets louder. On its own, though, this buzz sounds nothing like speech.

sections.key: Your throat, mouth and nose act as a resonating chamber that turns a buzz into words.
sections.b: The raw buzz from the larynx travels up through the throat, mouth and nose, which together form the vocal tract. Like the body of a guitar, this space strengthens some frequencies and weakens others. By moving your tongue, lips, jaw and soft palate you change its shape, and with it the sound. Vowels depend mainly on tongue and lip position; say ‘ee’ then ‘oo’ and feel the difference. Consonants come from briefly blocking or narrowing the airflow with the lips, teeth or tongue. Whispering shows the two systems working separately. When you whisper, your vocal folds do not vibrate at all, yet you can still form clear words using the air rushing through your mouth.

sections.key: Puberty, hormones and age all reshape the voice box and the sounds it makes.
sections.b: Children of both sexes have similar voices because their larynxes are similar in size. At puberty, testosterone makes the larynx grow and the vocal folds lengthen and thicken, especially in boys. Longer, heavier folds vibrate more slowly, and many male voices drop by around an octave. During the change, boys may find their voice cracks unpredictably as the muscles adjust to a rapidly changing instrument. Girls' voices deepen too, but only slightly. Voices keep changing throughout life. In older age, vocal folds can thin and lose some muscle, which can make a voice sound weaker or breathier. Hormonal changes around menopause can also lower a woman's voice a little.

sections.key: Your recorded voice sounds strange because you normally hear yourself partly through your bones.
sections.b: Most people wince when they hear a recording of their own voice. There is a physical reason. When others hear you, the sound reaches them only through the air. When you hear yourself speak, sound also travels to your inner ears through the bones of your skull. Bone conduction carries lower frequencies well, so the voice in your head sounds deeper and fuller than the one everyone else hears. A recording captures only the air carried version, which can sound thin and unfamiliar. Psychology may add to the discomfort, because the voice is so tied to our sense of self. The voice on the recording, though, is much closer to what other people actually hear.

sections.key: Vocal folds can be strained by overuse, and lasting hoarseness should be checked by a doctor.
sections.b: Because the vocal folds collide many times every second, heavy use takes a toll. Teachers, singers, coaches and call centre workers are among those most likely to develop voice problems. Repeated strain can cause swelling or small, callus-like growths called vocal nodules, which make the voice rough or tired. Common advice includes resting your voice when it is sore, avoiding habitual shouting or straining to be heard over noise, staying well hydrated and not smoking. Whispering is not necessarily restful, as many people strain while doing it. Hoarseness from a cold usually settles within a week or two, but hoarseness lasting more than about three weeks should be checked by a doctor.

quiz.q: What happens to the vocal folds when you swallow?
o: They close to help protect the airway
quiz.e: The folds snap shut during swallowing, which helps stop food and drink from entering the airway.

quiz.q: How do you raise the pitch of your voice?
o: By tightening and thinning the vocal folds
quiz.e: Tighter, thinner folds vibrate faster, producing higher notes. More air mainly makes the sound louder.

quiz.q: What is unusual about whispering?
o: The vocal folds do not vibrate
quiz.e: In a whisper the folds stay still. Words are formed by air rushing through the shaped mouth and throat.

quiz.q: Why do many male voices drop at puberty?
o: Testosterone makes the vocal folds longer and thicker
quiz.e: Testosterone causes the larynx to grow and the folds to lengthen and thicken, so they vibrate more slowly.

quiz.q: Why does your voice sound deeper to you than on a recording?
o: You also hear it through the bones of your skull
Your ears are tuned to high sounds
quiz.e: Bone conduction carries lower frequencies to your inner ear, so your own voice sounds fuller in your head than in the air.

LESSONS.title: Water and thirst: how much do you really need?
LESSONS.hook: Eight glasses a day sounds like ancient wisdom, but its origins are murkier than you might think. Your body has a far better guide built in.

sections.key: Water makes up roughly half to 60 per cent of an adult's body weight.
sections.b: Water is the most abundant substance in your body. In a typical adult it accounts for roughly 50 to 60 per cent of body weight, and in newborn babies the share is higher still, at around 75 per cent. People with more muscle tend to carry more water, because muscle holds more water than fat does. About two thirds of it sits inside your cells, and the rest bathes the spaces between cells or flows as blood plasma. Water dissolves nutrients, carries waste to the kidneys, cushions joints and the brain, and spreads heat around the body. Almost every chemical reaction that keeps you alive takes place in it, which is why your body guards its water levels so carefully.

sections.key: You lose water constantly through urine, sweat and breath, and food supplies a good share of what you take in.
sections.b: Even on a quiet day you are always losing water. Most leaves as urine, but a surprising amount escapes unnoticed as sweat evaporating from your skin and as water vapour in every breath you exhale. More is lost in faeces. A sedentary adult in a mild climate typically loses around two and a half litres a day, and far more during hard exercise or hot weather. To balance this, water comes in from drinks, from food and in a small amount from the chemical reactions that burn fuel inside your cells. Food matters more than many people realise. Fruit, vegetables, soups, rice and pasta are full of water, and food can supply roughly a fifth of a typical intake.

sections.key: There is no good evidence that everyone needs eight glasses of plain water a day.
sections.b: The rule of eight glasses a day is repeated everywhere, but nobody has found solid scientific evidence behind it. One often-cited origin is a 1945 recommendation from a United States nutrition board, which suggested about two and a half litres of water a day for adults. The same advice added that most of this is already contained in prepared foods, a detail that was quietly forgotten. Australian guidelines suggest typical fluid intakes from drinks of around 2.6 litres for men and 2.1 litres for women, but these are averages for healthy people, not targets everyone must hit. Tea, coffee, milk and other drinks all count. The mild diuretic effect of caffeine is small in regular drinkers.

sections.key: The brain monitors how concentrated your blood is and adjusts thirst and urine to match.
sections.b: Deep in the brain, the hypothalamus contains sensors that track how concentrated your blood is. When you lose water, the blood becomes slightly saltier, and these sensors respond in two ways. They make you feel thirsty, and they prompt the pituitary gland to release antidiuretic hormone, also called vasopressin. This hormone tells the kidneys to reabsorb more water, so your urine becomes smaller in volume and darker in colour. When you drink plenty, the hormone falls and the kidneys release more dilute urine. The system is sensitive, responding to changes of only a few per cent. For most healthy people, drinking when thirsty and noticing pale straw-coloured urine is a reliable guide.

sections.key: Older adults, babies and people working in heat are more vulnerable to dehydration.
sections.b: Thirst works well for most healthy adults, but not for everyone. The thirst response tends to weaken with age, so older people can become dehydrated without feeling particularly thirsty, especially when they are unwell. Babies and young children lose fluid quickly through fever, vomiting or diarrhoea and cannot fetch a drink for themselves. People doing hard physical work or exercise in Australian summer heat can sweat out more than a litre an hour. Early signs of dehydration include thirst, dark urine, headache, tiredness and dizziness. Heat stroke is a medical emergency. If someone in the heat becomes confused, collapses or stops making sense, call 000 and start cooling them while you wait.

sections.h: Too much of a good thing
sections.key: Drinking far more than you need can dangerously dilute the sodium in your blood.
sections.b: It is possible to drink too much water. If you take in fluid much faster than your kidneys can remove it, the sodium in your blood becomes diluted, a condition called hyponatraemia. Water moves into cells, including brain cells, which can swell. Symptoms range from nausea and headache to confusion, seizures and, rarely, death. Endurance athletes are among those at risk, particularly slower runners who drink at every station for hours. A study of Boston Marathon runners, published in 2005, found that around one in eight had low blood sodium at the finish, and weight gain from drinking too much was the strongest predictor. Many sports doctors now advise athletes to drink to thirst rather than forcing fluids.

quiz.q: Roughly what share of an adult's body weight is water?
quiz.e: Water makes up roughly 50 to 60 per cent of an adult's body weight, and an even higher share in newborn babies.

quiz.q: Which of these is a source of water that people often overlook?
o: Food such as fruit, vegetables and soups
quiz.e: Food can provide roughly a fifth of daily water intake, and the body also makes a little water when burning fuel.

quiz.q: What detail of the 1945 recommendation was later forgotten?
o: It was meant for soldiers only
Most of the water is contained in prepared foods
quiz.e: The advice said most of the suggested amount is already in food, a caveat that disappeared as the ‘eight glasses’ idea spread.

quiz.q: What does antidiuretic hormone do when you are low on water?
o: It tells the kidneys to keep more water
quiz.e: Antidiuretic hormone, or vasopressin, makes the kidneys reabsorb water, producing smaller amounts of darker urine.

quiz.q: What is hyponatraemia?
o: Dangerously diluted sodium in the blood
A shortage of red blood cells
A kidney infection caused by dehydration
quiz.e: Drinking far more water than the kidneys can clear dilutes blood sodium, which can make cells, including brain cells, swell.

LESSONS.title: Fever: why your body turns up the heat
LESSONS.hook: A fever is not your body losing control of its temperature. It is a deliberate decision, and one that animals have been making for hundreds of millions of years.

sections.key: In a fever, the brain deliberately raises the temperature it aims to maintain.
sections.b: Your body temperature is controlled by the hypothalamus, a small region at the base of the brain that works much like a thermostat. During an infection, immune cells release signalling molecules, including cytokines such as interleukin 1 and interleukin 6. These trigger the production of a substance called prostaglandin E2, which acts on the hypothalamus and raises its set point. Suddenly your normal temperature feels too cold. You shiver, your skin turns pale as blood vessels narrow to save heat, and you reach for a blanket, all to warm yourself up to the new target. When the fever breaks and the set point drops again, the opposite happens. You feel hot, flush and sweat heavily.

sections.key: Normal body temperature is a range, not a single number, and it changes throughout the day.
sections.b: The figure of 37 degrees Celsius traces back largely to the German physician Carl Wunderlich, who in 1868 published an analysis of an enormous number of armpit temperature readings. His work helped make the thermometer a standard medical tool. Modern measurements suggest the average is often a little lower, commonly somewhere around 36.5 to 36.8 degrees, though it depends on the person and where the temperature is measured. Your temperature also rises and falls with your body clock, usually lowest in the early morning and highest in the late afternoon or evening. Age, activity and, for women, the menstrual cycle shift it too. Some researchers have even found evidence that average temperatures have drifted down since Wunderlich's day.

sections.key: Cold-blooded animals give themselves a fever by seeking warmth, which suggests fever is ancient and useful.
sections.b: In the 1970s the physiologist Matthew Kluger ran experiments with desert iguanas, which cannot make their own body heat and instead control their temperature by moving between warm and cool spots. When infected with bacteria, the lizards chose warmer places, raising their temperature by around two degrees, a so-called behavioural fever. Lizards kept at cooler temperatures were much more likely to die. Similar behaviour has since been seen in fish, insects and other animals. Because fever appears across so many branches of the animal kingdom, and producing it costs a lot of energy, most scientists conclude it evolved because it helps fight infection. A costly trait that useless would likely have been lost long ago.

sections.key: Higher temperatures boost parts of the immune system and make life harder for some germs.
sections.b: Fever seems to help in several ways. Many immune processes run faster at higher temperatures, including the movement of white blood cells and the production of some defensive molecules. Some bacteria and viruses multiply less efficiently when their surroundings are warmer, and the body also restricts the iron that many bacteria need to grow. History offers a grim illustration of heat's power. In 1917 the Austrian psychiatrist Julius Wagner-Jauregg deliberately infected patients with neurosyphilis, a then incurable brain infection, with malaria to induce high fevers. Some patients improved, and he received the Nobel Prize in 1927. The treatment was dangerous and was abandoned once penicillin arrived, but it showed fever could attack a disease.

sections.key: A fever is controlled by the brain, whereas heat stroke is the body failing to shed heat.
sections.b: A fever and heat stroke can both produce a high temperature, but they are very different. In a fever, the brain has raised its set point and the body is still regulating carefully around it. Fevers from infection rarely climb much above about 41 degrees, because the system keeps working. In heat stroke, the set point has not changed. Instead, the body is absorbing or producing heat faster than it can get rid of it, perhaps during hard work in a heatwave, and its temperature keeps rising out of control. Medicines that lower fever work on the set point, so they do not treat heat stroke. Heat stroke is an emergency: call 000 and begin cooling the person immediately.

sections.key: Most fevers are harmless, but some warning signs need urgent medical attention.
sections.b: Most fevers are the body doing its job and pass within a few days. Medicines that lower temperature mainly make people feel more comfortable and do not cure the underlying illness, so follow the label or ask a pharmacist. Some situations, however, call for prompt medical help. Babies under three months old with a fever should be seen by a doctor urgently. Seek help quickly for anyone with a fever who also has a stiff neck, a rash that does not fade when pressed, difficulty breathing, severe drowsiness or confusion. Young children sometimes have a seizure with a fever, called a febrile convulsion. These are frightening but usually harmless. Call 000 if a seizure lasts more than five minutes.

quiz.q: Why does a person with a rising fever shiver and feel cold?
o: Their blood has lost heat to the infection
The brain has raised its target temperature
The infection has damaged their nerves
Their muscles are too weak to stay warm
quiz.e: The hypothalamus raises its set point, so normal body temperature suddenly feels too cold and the body works to warm up.

quiz.q: What do modern measurements say about normal body temperature?
o: It is exactly 37 degrees for everyone
It never changes during the day
It is a range, often a little below 37 degrees
It is always higher in the morning
quiz.e: Normal temperature varies by person, time of day and measurement site, and the average is often a little below 37 degrees.

quiz.q: What did Matthew Kluger's experiments with desert iguanas show?
o: Infected lizards sought warmth, and cooler lizards died more often
quiz.e: Infected iguanas raised their temperature by moving somewhere warmer, and those kept cool had higher death rates.

quiz.q: Why did Julius Wagner-Jauregg infect patients with malaria?
o: To induce fevers that attacked neurosyphilis
quiz.e: He used malaria-induced fevers to treat neurosyphilis, an approach abandoned once penicillin became available.

quiz.q: Why don't fever-reducing medicines treat heat stroke?
o: Heat stroke is not caused by a raised set point
Heat stroke involves a low temperature
quiz.e: These medicines lower the brain's set point. In heat stroke the set point is unchanged; the body simply cannot shed heat.

LESSONS.title: Reflexes: when your spine decides first
LESSONS.hook: Touch a hot pan and your hand is gone before you feel the pain. That split-second move is made without your brain's permission.

sections.key: The idea that the body can react automatically goes back at least to René Descartes.
sections.b: In his book Treatise of Man, published in 1664 after his death, the French philosopher René Descartes included a famous drawing of a boy with his foot near a fire. Descartes imagined that the heat tugged on tiny threads inside the nerves, opening valves in the brain that sent spirits back to the muscles to pull the foot away. The details were wrong, but the core idea was striking. Some actions might happen mechanically, like clockwork, without any conscious choice. Over the following centuries, scientists discovered that many of these automatic responses do not even need the brain. They are handled lower down, in the spinal cord, by circuits we now call reflex arcs.

sections.key: Tapping below the kneecap triggers one of the simplest circuits in the nervous system.
sections.b: When a doctor taps the tendon just below your kneecap, your lower leg kicks forward. In 1875 two German neurologists, Wilhelm Erb and Carl Westphal, independently described this reflex, and it has been tested ever since. The tap briefly stretches the large quadriceps muscle at the front of the thigh. Stretch sensors inside the muscle, called muscle spindles, fire signals along a sensory nerve into the spinal cord. There, the sensory neuron connects directly to a motor neuron, which sends a command straight back to the same muscle, telling it to contract. With only one connection in the chain, it is called a monosynaptic reflex. Its job in everyday life is to help keep you upright.

sections.key: Every reflex arc has a sensor, an incoming nerve, a processing point, an outgoing nerve and a muscle.
sections.b: A reflex arc has five basic parts. A receptor detects a change, such as stretch, heat or pressure. A sensory neuron carries the signal to the spinal cord or brainstem. A processing step links that signal to an outgoing motor neuron, sometimes through extra nerve cells called interneurons. Finally a muscle or gland responds. The British physiologist Charles Sherrington spent decades mapping these circuits and coined the word synapse for the gap between nerve cells. He showed that reflexes coordinate muscles in pairs. When the quadriceps contracts during the knee jerk, signals simultaneously relax the hamstrings behind the thigh so they do not fight the movement. Sherrington shared the Nobel Prize in 1932.

sections.key: The withdrawal reflex moves you away from harm and shifts your balance at the same time.
sections.b: Step on a sharp object and your foot lifts before you have time to think.
