In conversation we tend to copy each other's facial expressions, tone of voice, speech rhythms and posture, mostly without realising. Swedish psychologist Ulf Dimberg measured tiny electrical signals in facial muscles while people looked at pictures of faces. Smiling faces triggered slight activity in the muscles that pull the mouth into a smile, and angry faces triggered the frowning muscles, within a fraction of a second. In some experiments the faces were flashed so briefly that people did not consciously see them, yet their muscles still responded. Mimicry seems to help social life run smoothly: people who are subtly mirrored often report liking their partner more, and shared expressions signal that we are on the same wavelength.

sections.key: Copying an expression may nudge your own emotions, though the effect is smaller than once claimed.
sections.b: How does copying a face turn into feeling the emotion? One idea is facial feedback: signals from our own muscles influence how we feel. A famous 1988 study by Fritz Strack and colleagues had people hold a pen either between their teeth, forcing a smile-like expression, or between their lips, preventing one, and reported that the 'smilers' found cartoons funnier. But in 2016 a large replication involving 17 labs found no effect. That led to a bigger collaboration, the Many Smiles project, published in 2022, which tested several methods across many countries. It found that deliberately mimicking smiling faces or posing a smile could make people feel slightly happier, but the pen method did not reliably work. Facial feedback seems real, but modest.

sections.key: One person's mood can ripple through a team and affect how well the group works.
sections.b: In a 2002 study, organisational psychologist Sigal Barsade of the Yale School of Management ran a set of group exercises in which volunteers negotiated how to share a pool of money. Unknown to them, one member was a trained actor who behaved with either cheerful enthusiasm, warm calm, irritable hostility or depressed sluggishness. The actor's mood spread to the others, and groups with a cheerful actor reported more cooperation and less conflict. Other research has found that the moods of leaders are especially contagious, since people watch those in charge closely. This matters in workplaces from offices to hospital wards to building sites, where a calm supervisor can steady a tense shift. Emotions are not just private states; they are part of a team's working conditions.

sections.key: A famous study suggested happiness spreads through social networks, but critics challenged the interpretation.
sections.b: In 2008 Nicholas Christakis and James Fowler analysed data from the Framingham Heart Study, a long-running study of residents of a town in Massachusetts that also recorded who was friends, neighbours or relatives with whom. They reported that people's happiness was linked with that of their friends, their friends' friends and even their friends' friends' friends, and that a happy friend living nearby was associated with a higher chance of being happy. The findings drew wide attention, but other researchers pointed out problems. People tend to befriend others like themselves, and friends share environments, such as the same suburb, job market or bad winter. Those factors can make happiness cluster without anything spreading. Many researchers think some contagion likely occurs, but the size of these network effects is still debated.

sections.key: A controversial Facebook experiment found that the emotional tone of news feeds slightly affected what people posted.
sections.b: In 2014 researchers from Facebook and Cornell University published a study involving about 689,000 Facebook users. For one week in 2012, the company quietly tweaked their news feeds to show fewer posts containing positive words, or fewer containing negative words. Users who saw fewer positive posts then wrote slightly fewer positive words and slightly more negative words themselves, and the reverse happened in the other group. The effects were very small for any individual, but the study suggested contagion could happen through text alone, without faces or voices. It also sparked a storm of criticism, because users had not knowingly agreed to have their emotions manipulated. The episode became a landmark case in debates about research ethics and the influence of social media platforms.

sections.key: Knowing about contagion helps you choose what you catch and what you pass on.
sections.b: Emotional contagion is not a flaw. It helps us connect, empathise and coordinate. But knowing about it gives you some choices. Notice when your mood shifts after time with certain people, places or feeds, and ask whether the feeling belongs to you or whether you have simply caught it. People in caring and frontline roles, such as nurses, teachers, paramedics and police, are constantly exposed to others' distress and anger, so deliberate decompression after a shift, through exercise, a chat with a trusted mate or time outdoors, can stop it piling up. Contagion also works in your favour. A calm voice can lower the temperature of a tense room, and spending time with steady, warm people is one of the simplest ways to borrow some of their steadiness.

quiz.q: What did studies of newborn babies show about emotional contagion?
o: Newborns cried more at another baby's crying than at other noises of similar loudness
Newborns only respond to their mother's voice
Newborns laugh when other babies cry
quiz.e: Babies only a day or two old cried more in response to another baby's crying, suggesting we are tuned in to others' feelings from birth.

quiz.q: What did Ulf Dimberg's research show about facial mimicry?
o: People only copy faces they consciously notice
Facial muscles respond to others' expressions within a fraction of a second, even to faces not consciously seen
Mimicry only happens between close friends
People copy angry faces with smiles
quiz.e: Dimberg found rapid matching muscle activity in response to smiling and angry faces, even when the faces were flashed too quickly to be consciously seen.

quiz.q: What happened when the famous pen-in-mouth facial feedback study was tested in a large replication?
o: It found no reliable effect for the pen method
It showed smiling makes people sadder
quiz.e: A 17-lab replication in 2016 found no effect, and the later Many Smiles project found small effects from posed smiles but not reliably from the pen method.

quiz.q: In Barsade's 2002 study, what spread through the groups?
o: The mood of a trained actor planted in each group
A preference for one negotiation strategy
quiz.e: A hidden actor displayed different moods, and that mood spread to the rest of the group, affecting cooperation and conflict.

quiz.q: What was a major criticism of the claim that happiness spreads through social networks?
o: Friends tend to be similar and share environments, which can make happiness cluster without spreading
Happiness cannot be measured at all
The data came from social media
quiz.e: Similar people befriend each other and share circumstances, so happiness can cluster in networks without truly passing from person to person.

LESSONS.title: Emotional labour: when feelings are part of the job
LESSONS.hook: Flight attendants smile through turbulence; debt collectors scowl on cue. In 1983 a sociologist showed that many jobs sell not just our time and effort, but our feelings.

sections.key: Sociologist Arlie Hochschild coined ‘emotional labour’ for managing your feelings as part of paid work.
sections.b: In 1983 Arlie Russell Hochschild, a sociologist at the University of California, Berkeley, published The Managed Heart: Commercialization of Human Feeling. She argued that many jobs demand more than physical or mental effort. Workers are also required to produce particular emotional states in themselves and, through them, in customers. She called this emotional labour. A flight attendant must seem calm and warm so that passengers feel safe and welcome. A nurse must appear composed in front of frightened families. A funeral director must convey quiet sympathy, again and again, day after day. Hochschild's insight was that these feelings had become part of what the employer sells, and therefore something the employer tries to manage, train and monitor, just as it manages speed or accuracy.

sections.key: Hochschild studied how Delta Air Lines trained flight attendants to produce warmth on demand.
sections.b: Much of Hochschild's research focused on flight attendants at Delta Air Lines in the late 1970s and early 1980s. She sat in on training sessions and interviewed staff. Trainees were encouraged to think of the cabin as their living room and passengers as guests in their home, and to imagine that a rude passenger might be frightened of flying or going through something difficult. The aim was for warmth to look genuine, because airlines competed partly on friendly service. Hochschild contrasted this with debt collectors, whose job required the opposite: suppressing sympathy and projecting suspicion or sternness to pressure people into paying. In both cases, she argued, workers were being asked to bend their own feelings into a shape that suited the company's goals.

sections.key: Workers can fake the expected emotion on the outside, or try to genuinely feel it inside.
sections.b: Hochschild borrowed two ideas from the theatre, drawing on the Russian director Konstantin Stanislavski. In surface acting, you put on the expected expression without changing what you feel, smiling at a rude customer while seething underneath. In deep acting, you try to actually summon the feeling, for example by reframing the customer as anxious rather than nasty, or by recalling something that makes you feel warm. Later researchers, notably Blake Ashforth and Ronald Humphrey in 1993, pointed out a third possibility: sometimes workers simply feel what the job requires, such as genuine compassion for a patient, with no acting needed. Hochschild also described feeling rules, the often unspoken norms about what we should feel in a situation, such as happiness at a wedding or grief at a funeral.

sections.key: Research consistently links surface acting with emotional exhaustion and lower job satisfaction.
sections.b: Hochschild worried that long-term emotional labour could estrange people from their own feelings, leaving them unsure which emotions were really theirs. Later quantitative research has tested parts of this idea. A useful concept is emotional dissonance: the gap between what you feel and what you must display. Psychologist Alicia Grandey, in an influential 2000 paper, framed emotional labour as a form of emotion regulation, connecting it with laboratory research showing that suppressing feelings takes effort. Meta-analyses pooling many workplace studies, such as one by Ute Hülsheger and Anna Schewe in 2011, found that surface acting was fairly consistently associated with emotional exhaustion, lower job satisfaction and more stress symptoms. Deep acting showed weaker and more mixed links with strain, and was sometimes associated with better performance.

sections.key: Emotional labour is concentrated in service, care and frontline work, and falls unevenly.
sections.b: Hochschild estimated that roughly a third of American workers had jobs involving substantial emotional labour, and about half of working women did, reflecting how many women worked in service and caring roles. Classic examples include retail and hospitality staff, call centre workers, nurses, teachers, childcare workers, paramedics, police and social workers. Some roles demand constant positivity, others composure in the face of distress or hostility, and some, such as corrections or security work, require projecting calm authority while staying alert to danger. Status matters too. Workers lower in the hierarchy are often expected to absorb rudeness without responding, while customers or managers face few such rules. Research has also found that customer mistreatment is a significant stressor for frontline staff, made worse when workers feel they cannot respond or set limits.

sections.key: ‘Emotional labour’ is now widely used for unpaid relationship and household work, a stretch its creator has questioned.
sections.b: In the 2010s the phrase escaped academic journals and took on a broader life online. People began using it for the unpaid work of remembering birthdays, organising family schedules, noticing that the household is running low on things, and soothing everyone's moods, a load often carried disproportionately by women. Related terms such as the mental load describe the invisible planning behind running a home. These are real and important issues, and research on the division of household labour is extensive. But Hochschild herself has said in interviews that she thinks the term has sometimes been stretched to cover almost any chore, blurring her original focus on managing feelings, especially for a wage. When you meet the phrase, it helps to ask which meaning is intended.

sections.key: Autonomy, support and genuine recovery time reduce the toll of emotionally demanding work.
sections.b: Emotional labour cannot be removed from many jobs, and it is not inherently harmful; many people find meaning in comforting, calming or helping others. Research points to factors that make it more sustainable. Workers with more autonomy, including some freedom over how they express themselves, tend to suffer less strain. Supportive supervisors and colleagues help, as does a workplace culture that backs staff when customers become abusive. Deep acting through reframing, such as reminding yourself that an angry caller is probably scared or overwhelmed, may cost less than gritting your teeth behind a fixed smile. Finally, recovery matters. Studies of psychological detachment, by researchers such as Sabine Sonnentag, suggest that genuinely switching off from work during time off helps people recover from demanding jobs.

quiz.q: What did Arlie Hochschild mean by ‘emotional labour’?
o: Physical work that causes emotional stress
Managing your own feelings and displays as part of paid work
quiz.e: Hochschild used the term for managing one's feelings to produce the emotional displays a job requires, which employers then train and monitor.

quiz.q: A call centre worker smiles and sounds cheerful while feeling furious inside. What is this called?
quiz.e: Surface acting means displaying the required emotion without changing what you feel. Deep acting tries to actually generate the feeling.

quiz.q: How did Hochschild contrast debt collectors with flight attendants?
o: Debt collectors were required to suppress sympathy and project sternness
Debt collectors performed no emotional labour at all
Debt collectors were trained to be warmer than flight attendants
Debt collectors were paid to cry with customers
quiz.e: Flight attendants manufactured warmth, while debt collectors suppressed sympathy and projected suspicion. Both were shaping feelings to suit their employer.

quiz.q: What have meta-analyses generally found about surface acting?
o: It has no effect on workers
It is consistently linked with emotional exhaustion and lower job satisfaction
It improves wellbeing more than deep acting
quiz.e: Pooled studies link surface acting with exhaustion, lower satisfaction and stress symptoms. Deep acting shows weaker, mixed links with strain.

quiz.q: Which factor does research suggest helps make emotionally demanding work more sustainable?
o: Banning workers from speaking to colleagues
Requiring a fixed smile at all times
quiz.e: Autonomy, supportive supervisors and colleagues, and real recovery time away from work all reduce the toll of emotional labour.

LESSONS.title: Shackleton and the Endurance
LESSONS.hook: His ship was crushed by ice and his men were stranded at the bottom of the world. What happened next became the most famous survival story in polar history.

sections.key: After the South Pole was reached, Ernest Shackleton set out to make the first crossing of the whole continent.
sections.b: By 1914 the race to the South Pole was over. Roald Amundsen had arrived first and Robert Falcon Scott had died on the return journey. Ernest Shackleton, an Anglo-Irish explorer who had already come close to the Pole himself, wanted a new prize: the first crossing of Antarctica on foot, from the Weddell Sea to the Ross Sea, roughly 2,900 kilometres. He called it the Imperial Trans-Antarctic Expedition. His ship, Endurance, was a sturdy wooden vessel built in Norway. It sailed from England in August 1914, just as the First World War broke out. Shackleton offered his ship and crew to the war effort, but the Admiralty told him to carry on. A second ship would land a party on the far side to lay supply depots.

sections.h: The advertisement that probably never ran
sections.key: The famous ‘men wanted for hazardous journey’ newspaper advert is almost certainly a myth.
sections.b: You may have seen a quote said to be Shackleton's recruiting advertisement, promising small wages, bitter cold, constant danger and a doubtful safe return. It is a wonderful piece of writing, but researchers have searched the newspaper archives of the period and found no trace of it. It seems to have appeared in print only decades later, and no original has ever turned up. The real recruitment was less romantic. Thousands of people reportedly wrote asking to join, and Shackleton picked men through interviews that could be famously quick and quirky. He valued temperament as much as skill, looking for people who would stay cheerful under strain. That instinct for character would turn out to matter far more than he could have guessed.

sections.key: Endurance was frozen into the Weddell Sea pack ice and slowly crushed over the following months.
sections.b: Endurance left the whaling station at South Georgia in December 1914 and pushed south into the Weddell Sea, one of the iciest stretches of ocean on Earth. In January 1915, within sight of the Antarctic coast, the pack ice closed around her. The 28 men could only wait as the ship drifted with the ice through the long polar winter. They kept routines, exercised the sled dogs, played football on the floes and held concerts. But the pressure of the moving ice grew, and the hull groaned and buckled. In October 1915 Shackleton ordered everyone off the ship and onto the ice. Endurance finally slipped beneath the surface in November. The crossing of Antarctica was over. The new goal was simply to get every man home alive.

sections.key: For months the crew camped on drifting sea ice, hauling lifeboats and hoping the ice would carry them north.
sections.b: With their ship gone, the men lived in tents on the moving ice, first at a spot they called Ocean Camp and later at Patience Camp. They had salvaged three lifeboats, food, tools and a few personal items. Shackleton made a point of keeping spirits up and of keeping possible troublemakers close to him. Food ran short, and as the months passed the sled dogs had to be shot. The expedition photographer, Australian Frank Hurley, had taken hundreds of glass plate photographs, but they were too heavy to carry. He kept a small selection and smashed the rest so he would not be tempted to go back for them. In April 1916 the ice began breaking up, and the men finally took to the boats.

sections.key: After a harrowing boat journey, the crew reached solid ground for the first time in about 16 months.
sections.b: The three small boats spent around a week battling freezing spray, rough seas and exhaustion. Some men suffered frostbite, and many could barely stand. Around mid April 1916 they landed on Elephant Island, a bleak, rocky outpost off the tip of the Antarctic Peninsula. It was the first time they had stood on land since leaving South Georgia well over a year earlier. But the island was far from any shipping route, and nobody knew they were there. Waiting for rescue meant almost certain death. Shackleton decided that a small party would take the strongest lifeboat and try to reach help. The other 22 men, led by his deputy Frank Wild, would shelter under two upturned boats and survive on penguins and seals.

sections.h: The voyage of the James Caird
sections.key: Six men sailed a 7 metre lifeboat about 1,300 kilometres across the Southern Ocean to South Georgia.
sections.b: On 24 April 1916, Shackleton and five companions set out in the James Caird, a lifeboat less than 7 metres long that the ship's carpenter had strengthened and partly decked over. Their target was South Georgia, about 1,300 kilometres away across some of the stormiest seas on the planet. Navigation fell to Frank Worsley, Endurance's New Zealand captain, who could take sun sightings with his sextant only a handful of times in the whole voyage, often while being thrown about by huge waves. The men were permanently soaked, chipped ice off the boat so it would not capsize, and rode out a hurricane force storm. After about 16 days they landed on South Georgia. It is still regarded as one of the greatest small boat journeys ever made.

sections.key: Shackleton, Worsley and Crean crossed South Georgia's unmapped peaks, and in August 1916 every man on Elephant Island was rescued.
sections.b: There was one cruel problem. They had landed on the wrong side of South Georgia, and the whaling stations were on the far coast. With the boat too battered to sail around, Shackleton, Worsley and Tom Crean set off across the island's unmapped glaciers and mountains with screws in their boots for grip, a rope and almost no rest. After about 36 hours they staggered into the Stromness whaling station in May 1916. Shackleton then made several attempts to reach Elephant Island but was turned back by ice. On 30 August 1916, the Chilean tug Yelcho, commanded by Luis Pardo, finally got through. All 22 men were alive. Sadly, the expedition's separate Ross Sea party on the other side of Antarctica lost three men.

sections.key: In 2022 explorers found Endurance on the seabed, remarkably well preserved, about 3,000 metres down.
sections.b: For more than a century, Endurance lay somewhere beneath the Weddell Sea, which is so choked with ice that searching for it seemed nearly impossible. In March 2022 an expedition using an icebreaker and underwater robots finally located the wreck about 3,000 metres down. The images were astonishing. The wooden hull was largely intact, and the name ENDURANCE could still be read across the stern. The cold water and the absence of the wood-eating creatures found in warmer seas had protected it. The wreck is a protected historic site under the Antarctic Treaty and is being left undisturbed. Shackleton's expedition failed at everything it set out to do, yet it is remembered for something rarer: a leader who brought his whole ship's crew home.

quiz.q: What was the original goal of Shackleton's 1914 expedition?
o: To be first to the South Pole
To make the first crossing of Antarctica on foot
To map the coast of South Georgia
To find a sea route through Antarctica
quiz.e: The Pole had already been reached, so Shackleton aimed to cross the whole continent from the Weddell Sea to the Ross Sea.

quiz.q: What do historians conclude about the famous ‘men wanted’ advertisement?
o: It ran in The Times in 1913
Shackleton wrote it but never published it
No original has ever been found and it is probably a myth
It was written by Frank Hurley
quiz.e: Searches of period newspapers have found no trace of it, and it appears only in much later publications.

quiz.q: Why did Frank Hurley smash most of his glass plate photographs?
o: They had been ruined by seawater
They were too heavy to carry, so he kept only a selection
He was unhappy with their quality
quiz.e: Weight mattered on the ice, so he kept a small selection and broke the rest to avoid being tempted to retrieve them.

quiz.q: Who navigated the James Caird to South Georgia?
quiz.e: Worsley, the New Zealand captain, navigated with only a few sextant sightings in terrible conditions.

quiz.q: How many of the men left on Elephant Island survived to be rescued?
quiz.e: The Yelcho reached the island on 30 August 1916 and every one of the 22 men was alive.

LESSONS.title: The safety lift: how Otis made skyscrapers possible
LESSONS.hook: Lifting people up a shaft was easy. Convincing them they would not plunge to their deaths was the hard part, and one man did it by cutting his own rope.

sections.key: People had used rope hoists for thousands of years, but they were too risky to trust with passengers.
sections.b: Lifting things with ropes and pulleys is ancient. Builders hauled stone with cranes and windlasses, mines raised ore up shafts, and in Rome's Colosseum, wooden lifts worked by teams of men raised wild animals from tunnels beneath the arena into the light. By the early nineteenth century, factories and warehouses used steam-powered hoists to move heavy goods between floors. What they did not do, at least not often, was carry people. The reason was simple. Ropes, made of hemp in those days, wore out and snapped, and when they did, the platform and everything on it fell straight down the shaft. A broken rope on a goods hoist meant smashed crates. On a passenger lift it would mean funerals.

sections.key: In 1852 Elisha Otis devised a brake that stopped a hoist from falling if its rope broke.
sections.b: Elisha Graves Otis was an American mechanic and tinkerer from Vermont who had tried his hand at several businesses, from building wagons to running a sawmill. In 1852 he was working at a bedstead factory in Yonkers, New York, and was asked to help install a hoist to lift heavy equipment to an upper floor. Worried about what would happen if the rope failed, he devised a safety brake. He attached a strong wagon spring to the top of the platform, linked to the hoisting rope. While the rope was taut, the spring was held in. If the rope broke and the tension vanished, the spring snapped outwards and its ends caught in ratchet teeth cut into the guide rails on either side of the shaft.

sections.key: At an 1854 exhibition in New York, Otis stood on his platform and had the rope cut in front of a crowd.
sections.b: A clever brake is useless if nobody trusts it, and Otis understood showmanship. In 1854, at a large exhibition held in New York's Crystal Palace, he built an open lift platform high above the crowd and rode it upwards, sometimes with goods stacked around him. Then he had an assistant cut the only rope holding him up with an axe. The platform dropped a few centimetres and stopped dead as the brake caught in the rails. Otis is said to have doffed his hat and announced, ‘All safe, gentlemen, all safe.’ Whether or not those were his exact words, the stunt worked. Orders began to arrive, and the company he founded would grow into one of the biggest lift makers in the world.

sections.key: In 1857 the first commercial passenger safety lift opened in a New York department store.
sections.b: On 23 March 1857, an Otis passenger lift went into service in the E. V. Haughwout Building, a five storey cast iron store on Broadway in New York that sold china, glassware and silver. It was powered by a steam engine in the building and climbed at a gentle pace of about twelve metres a minute, slow enough to feel very safe. The store's owner saw it as a novelty to attract wealthy shoppers to the upper floors. The building still stands. Elisha Otis did not live to see what his invention would become. He died in 1861, and his sons took over the business, which went on to install lifts in buildings around the world, including the Eiffel Tower.

sections.key: Safe lifts made tall buildings practical and flipped the value of top floors from cheapest to most expensive.
sections.b: Before lifts, buildings were limited by how many stairs people were willing to climb, usually around five or six storeys. The top floors were the least desirable, often rented cheaply to servants, poor tenants or struggling artists. Safe lifts changed that. Combined with new steel frames, which could carry much more weight than thick masonry walls, they made it possible to build upwards, and the skyscraper was born. Chicago's ten storey Home Insurance Building, finished in 1885, is often called the first. Electric lifts soon replaced steam and hydraulic ones. Werner von Siemens demonstrated an electric lift in Germany in 1880. The view, the quiet and the distance from street noise made the top floors the most prestigious addresses in town.

sections.h: How a modern lift stays safe
sections.key: Today's lifts have several separate protections, which is why deadly falls are extremely rare.
sections.b: Most modern traction lifts hang from several steel cables, and each one alone is strong enough to hold the car. A heavy counterweight on the other end balances the car, so the motor only has to lift the difference. If the car ever goes too fast, a device called an overspeed governor trips and triggers safety brakes that clamp onto the guide rails, a descendant of Otis's original idea. Buffers at the bottom of the shaft cushion the car as a last resort. The most famous survival story came in 1945, when a bomber crashed into New York's Empire State Building and operator Betty Lou Oliver's lift fell around 75 storeys. She survived, partly because the trailing cables and compressed air helped slow the fall.

sections.key: Very tall towers need new tricks, such as sky lobbies and lighter cables.
sections.b: In very tall towers, steel cable becomes a problem, because the longer the cable, the more it weighs, until much of the motor's effort goes into lifting the cable itself. Supertall buildings get around this with sky lobbies, where passengers change from one lift to another partway up, and engineers have developed lighter cables made with carbon fibre. Lifts have also become smarter. Destination dispatch systems ask you to choose your floor before you board, then group passengers going to similar floors. And if you ever get stuck, the advice is calm and simple: press the alarm or intercom button, stay inside the car and wait for trained help. Never try to climb out, and if someone has a medical emergency, call 000.

quiz.q: Why were early hoists rarely used for passengers?
o: If the rope snapped, the platform fell straight down
quiz.e: Hemp ropes wore out and broke, and nothing stopped the platform falling.

quiz.q: How did Otis's safety brake work?
o: A parachute opened under the platform
When the rope lost tension, a spring snapped out and caught in teeth on the guide rails
quiz.e: The taut rope held the spring in; when tension vanished, the spring engaged ratchet teeth in the rails.

quiz.q: What did Otis do at the 1854 New York exhibition?
o: Had the rope holding his platform cut while he stood on it
quiz.e: His platform dropped only a few centimetres before the brake caught, proving it worked.

quiz.q: How did safe lifts change the value of a building's top floors?
o: Top floors became illegal to rent
They went from cheapest to most prestigious
quiz.e: Without stairs to climb, the views and quiet made upper floors desirable.

quiz.q: What does an overspeed governor do?
o: Triggers brakes on the rails if the car moves too fast
Opens the doors in an emergency
quiz.e: If the car exceeds a safe speed, the governor trips and the safety brakes clamp onto the rails.

LESSONS.title: The tin can: food that keeps
LESSONS.hook: An army needed food that would not rot, so a French government offered a prize. The answer sits in your pantry today, and for decades nobody knew why it worked.

sections.key: In the 1790s France offered a cash reward for a better way to preserve food for its armies and navy.
sections.b: For most of history, keeping food meant drying it, salting it, smoking it, pickling it or packing it in sugar. These methods worked, but they changed the taste and texture, and armies on the move still struggled to eat well. Soldiers and sailors suffered from poor diets and disease. In the 1790s, during the wars of the French Revolution, the French government announced a prize for anyone who could find a practical way to preserve food. The famous saying that ‘an army marches on its stomach’ is usually attributed to Napoleon, though nobody can prove he said it. Whoever coined it, the idea was true, and the challenge attracted a Parisian confectioner with a lot of patience and a very practical mind.

sections.key: Appert sealed food in glass bottles and heated them in boiling water, winning the prize in 1810.
sections.b: Nicolas Appert was a cook, brewer and confectioner who spent about fifteen years experimenting. His method was simple to describe. He packed food into thick glass bottles, sealed them tightly with cork and wax, and then heated the sealed bottles in boiling water for a carefully judged time. Soups, vegetables, fruit, meat and milk all went in. Samples sent to sea with the French navy came back still edible months later. In 1810 the government awarded him the prize of 12,000 francs on condition that he publish his method, which he did in a book explaining the art of preserving foods. He used some of the money to expand his business, often described as the world's first commercial cannery, although his containers were bottles, not cans.

sections.key: Appert didn't know about microbes; Louis Pasteur's work decades later explained his success.
sections.b: Appert believed that heat somehow drove out a corrupting quality in the air, and that sealing kept it from returning. He had the method right and the reason wrong. The real explanation came half a century later, when Louis Pasteur and others showed that food spoils mainly because of microorganisms, such as bacteria, yeasts and moulds. Heating kills most of them, and a proper seal stops new ones getting in. Without microbes, the food inside can last for years. This is a lovely example of technology running ahead of science. People often learn that something works long before anyone can explain it, and the explanation then lets engineers improve the method, for example by working out the precise temperatures and times needed for different foods.

sections.key: In England, Peter Durand patented the idea of using tin-plated iron containers in 1810.
sections.b: Glass was heavy and broke easily, especially on ships and battlefields. In 1810, the same year Appert won his prize, an Englishman named Peter Durand was granted a patent for preserving food in containers including tin-plated iron canisters. Durand does not seem to have manufactured them himself. Instead, the engineer Bryan Donkin and his partners set up a canning works in London around 1812 and began supplying the Royal Navy and polar explorers. The word ‘tin’ was always a little misleading. The cans were made of iron, and later steel, coated with a thin layer of tin to stop rust. Early cans were made by hand, with each one soldered shut, and a skilled worker could make only a modest number in a day.

sections.key: The can opener wasn't invented until almost fifty years after the can.
sections.b: Here is one of the oddest gaps in the history of invention. Early cans were thick and heavy, and the instructions on some reportedly suggested opening them with a chisel and hammer. Soldiers reportedly used bayonets, knives or even gunfire. The first patented can opener in the United States, a lever-type blade, came from Ezra Warner in 1858, almost half a century after the can itself. The familiar design with a rotating cutting wheel that rolls around the rim appeared in 1870, patented by William Lyman. Why the delay? Cans only became thinner and easier to open as manufacturing improved and steel replaced heavier iron, so a handy opener simply wasn't practical until the cans themselves changed. Ring-pull lids came much later, in the twentieth century.

sections.h: Cans on expeditions and in wars
sections.key: Canned food fed explorers and armies, though early cans were not always safe.
sections.b: Canned food soon went everywhere people could not easily get fresh supplies. Polar expeditions packed it in huge quantities. Sir John Franklin's doomed 1845 Arctic expedition carried thousands of cans, and some researchers have suggested lead from the soldered seams contributed to the crew's decline. Historians still debate how much it mattered compared with cold, scurvy and starvation. During the American Civil War, canned food reached soldiers on a large scale, and many took the habit home. By the late nineteenth century, factories using machines and pressure cookers called retorts were turning out cans by the million. Lead solder was eventually phased out, and modern cans are often lined to protect both the food and the metal.

sections.key: Modern canning is very safe, but damaged, swollen or leaking cans should be thrown out.
sections.b: Today canned food is among the safest and cheapest ways to store nutritious food for long periods, and it keeps many nutrients surprisingly well. Canned tomatoes, beans and fish are kitchen staples around the world. Most cans are now made of steel or aluminium, and both are highly recyclable. The one serious danger is a rare but dangerous bacterium called Clostridium botulinum, which can grow without oxygen if a can is poorly processed or damaged. So food safety advice is simple: do not use cans that are swollen, bulging, leaking, badly dented along the seams, or that spurt when opened. In a suspected case of food poisoning with serious symptoms, such as trouble breathing or swallowing, call 000.

quiz.q: What did Nicolas Appert actually use to preserve food?
o: Sealed glass bottles heated in boiling water
quiz.e: Appert sealed food in glass bottles and heated them; tin cans came from English developments.

quiz.q: Why does heating sealed food stop it spoiling?
o: It drives the air out of the food
It kills microorganisms, and the seal keeps new ones out
It changes the food's chemistry into sugar
quiz.e: Pasteur's later work showed spoilage is mainly caused by microbes, which heat kills.

quiz.q: What were ‘tin’ cans mostly made of?
o: Iron, later steel, coated with tin
quiz.e: A thin coating of tin stopped the iron or steel underneath from rusting.

quiz.q: Roughly how long after the tin can did a patented can opener appear?
quiz.e: Ezra Warner's opener was patented in 1858, nearly half a century after Durand's 1810 patent.

quiz.q: Which can should you throw out rather than eat from?
o: One that is swollen or bulging
One that is past its best-before date by a day
quiz.e: Swelling can signal bacterial growth inside, including the bacterium that causes botulism.

LESSONS.title: Spectacles: the invention that extended working lives
LESSONS.hook: Nobody knows who invented glasses, and one famous inventor turns out to be a fake. But this medieval gadget quietly changed what people could do after forty.

sections.key: Most people lose the ability to focus up close in their forties, a condition called presbyopia.
sections.b: Inside your eye sits a flexible lens that changes shape to focus on things at different distances. As we age, that lens slowly stiffens. By somewhere around the mid forties, most people find that small print starts to blur unless they hold it at arm's length. This is called presbyopia, from the Greek for ‘old eye’. Before spectacles, there was nothing to be done. A scribe copying manuscripts, a jeweller, a weaver or a scholar might find their working life cut short just as they reached the peak of their skill. It is hard to overstate what it meant when a simple pair of curved pieces of glass could hand those years back.

sections.key: Before glasses, people used polished lumps of glass or crystal laid on the page to magnify text.
sections.b: The magnifying power of curved glass and crystal had been noticed long before spectacles. Ancient writers mentioned that a glass globe filled with water made letters look bigger. The great Arab scholar Ibn al-Haytham, working around the year 1000, studied how light passes through curved surfaces, and his work on optics was later translated into Latin and read in Europe. By the medieval period, some readers were using ‘reading stones’, rounded pieces of glass or rock crystal placed directly on a page to enlarge the letters beneath. They helped, but you had to slide them along the line, and they were no use for sewing, carving or any task where you needed your hands free and your eyes on the work.

sections.key: Spectacles appeared in northern Italy in the late thirteenth century, but their inventor is unknown.
sections.b: The best early evidence comes from a sermon. In 1306, a Dominican friar named Giordano da Pisa told a congregation in Florence that it was not yet twenty years since the art of making eyeglasses had been discovered, and that he had met the man who first made them. Frustratingly, he did not record the man's name. That places the invention in northern Italy in the 1280s. The region had skilled glassworkers, especially around Venice, where guild rules from around 1300 mention lenses for reading. The first spectacles had two convex lenses, thicker in the middle, set in frames riveted together, and were perched on the nose or held up to the eyes. Paintings from the following century show scholars wearing them.

sections.key: The claim that a Florentine named Salvino degli Armati invented glasses rests on a fabricated tomb inscription.
sections.b: For a long time, many books named Salvino degli Armati of Florence as the inventor of spectacles. The evidence was a tomb inscription describing him as their inventor. Historians later examined the story and concluded that it was a seventeenth-century invention, created with the help of a local antiquarian keen to give Florence the credit. The inscription's wording did not fit the period it claimed to come from, and there is no reliable earlier record of Salvino as an inventor. It is a useful reminder that history has its own fakes. A satisfying story with a name, a date and a plaque can travel for centuries, even when the honest answer is simply that we do not know.

sections.key: Concave lenses for short sight came later, and Johannes Kepler finally explained how lenses correct vision.
sections.b: The first spectacles helped with close work, which is why they spread among older readers. People who were short-sighted, struggling with distant objects, needed something different: concave lenses, thinner in the middle, which spread light out before it enters the eye. These appeared later, with clear evidence by the fifteenth century. Spectacle makers worked largely by trial and error, without a proper theory of how the eye focused. That came in 1604, when the astronomer Johannes Kepler showed that the eye forms an image on the retina at the back, and that spectacles work by shifting where the light comes to a focus so that it lands on the retina properly. Lens makers' skills also fed directly into the invention of the telescope and microscope.

sections.key: Side arms, bifocals and contact lenses each solved a practical problem in turn.
sections.b: For centuries, the hardest part of wearing glasses was keeping them on. People tried ribbons, leather straps and frames that pinched the nose. Rigid side arms resting on the ears became common in the eighteenth century, and the London optician Edward Scarlett is often credited with popularising them around the 1720s. Benjamin Franklin, tired of swapping between two pairs, described his ‘double spectacles’ in a 1784 letter, with each lens split into a top half for distance and a bottom half for reading. These became known as bifocals. In 1888 the German doctor Adolf Fick described glass lenses placed directly on the eye. Comfortable soft contact lenses arrived in the 1960s, thanks to the Czech chemist Otto Wichterle.

sections.key: Glasses extended skilled working lives and today remain one of the most effective health tools on Earth.
sections.b: It is easy to overlook glasses because they are everywhere, but their effect has been enormous. In medieval and early modern Europe, they allowed scholars, clerks, merchants and craftspeople to keep doing detailed work for decades longer. Some historians argue that this was a small but real boost to learning and productivity, especially after the printing press made books cheaper and reading more common. The need is still huge. The World Health Organization estimates that around a billion people worldwide have vision impairment that could have been prevented or has yet to be addressed, much of it simple short sight or presbyopia. A cheap pair of reading glasses can still keep someone working, reading and independent, just as it did seven centuries ago.

quiz.q: What is presbyopia?
o: Short sight caused by too much reading
An age-related loss of the ability to focus up close
quiz.e: As the eye's lens stiffens with age, usually noticeable around the mid forties, close focus becomes harder.

quiz.q: What is the best early evidence for when spectacles were invented?
o: A painting by Leonardo da Vinci
A 1306 sermon saying the art was not yet twenty years old
quiz.e: Friar Giordano da Pisa's sermon places the invention in northern Italy in the 1280s.

quiz.q: Why do historians reject Salvino degli Armati as the inventor of spectacles?
o: He lived after spectacles were common
The tomb inscription naming him appears to be a seventeenth-century fabrication
quiz.e: The inscription's wording didn't fit its supposed era and there is no reliable earlier record of his invention.

quiz.q: What kind of lens helps someone who is short-sighted?
quiz.e: Concave lenses spread light out, moving the focus back onto the retina for distant objects.

quiz.q: What did Benjamin Franklin describe in his 1784 letter?
o: Split ‘double spectacles’ for distance and reading
quiz.e: Each lens had a distance half and a reading half, the idea behind bifocals.

LESSONS.title: Matthew Flinders: the man who named Australia
LESSONS.hook: He sailed all the way around the continent, was locked up for six and a half years, and published his great work the day before he died. Then his grave was lost under a railway station.

sections.h: A boy who read Robinson Crusoe
sections.key: Matthew Flinders joined the Royal Navy as a teenager and learned his trade under William Bligh.
sections.b: Matthew Flinders was born in 1774 in Donington, Lincolnshire, the son of a surgeon. He later said that reading Robinson Crusoe made him want to go to sea, and he joined the Royal Navy at fifteen. His big early break was sailing with Captain William Bligh on Bligh's second breadfruit voyage to the Pacific, in the early 1790s, where he sharpened his skills in navigation and chart making. In 1795 he arrived in the young colony of New South Wales aboard HMS Reliance. On board was a ship's surgeon about his own age, George Bass. The two quickly became friends and shared an appetite for exploring the unknown coastline around them, often in tiny boats.

sections.key: In 1798 and 1799 Flinders and Bass sailed around Van Diemen's Land, proving a strait separated it from the mainland.
sections.b: Europeans had long wondered whether Van Diemen's Land, now Tasmania, was joined to the Australian mainland. Bass had already sailed south in a whaleboat and suspected a strait existed, judging by the strong swell rolling in from the west. In 1798 and 1799, Flinders and Bass took the small sloop Norfolk all the way around the island, settling the question. The passage between Tasmania and Victoria was named Bass Strait, at Flinders' suggestion. The discovery mattered practically too. Ships sailing from Britain could now take a shorter route through the strait rather than going all the way around Tasmania's south coast, saving days on the long voyage to Sydney, though the strait's storms and reefs made it dangerous.

sections.key: From 1801 to 1803 Flinders made the first known circumnavigation of the Australian continent.
sections.b: Back in England, Flinders persuaded Sir Joseph Banks and the Admiralty to back a full survey of the continent's coastline, much of which was still unmapped by Europeans. He sailed in 1801 in HMS Investigator, with scientists and artists on board, including the botanist Robert Brown and the botanical artist Ferdinand Bauer. Flinders carefully charted the south coast, including Spencer Gulf and Gulf St Vincent, then sailed north along the east coast and around Cape York into the Gulf of Carpentaria. By then the Investigator was rotting so badly that he had to cut short the detailed survey and hurry back to Sydney around the west coast. He arrived in June 1803, completing the first known voyage all the way around Australia.

sections.key: Bungaree, a Kuring-gai man, sailed with Flinders, and so did a famous ship's cat called Trim.
sections.b: Flinders did not sail alone. Bungaree, an Aboriginal man from the Broken Bay area north of Sydney, joined him on earlier coastal work and then on the Investigator. He helped communicate with Aboriginal groups along the coast, and Flinders praised his good nature and courage. By sailing on the Investigator, Bungaree is regarded as the first person born in Australia to circumnavigate the continent. The other famous crew member was Trim, a black cat with white paws, born on board an earlier ship. Trim was a lively, clever cat who reportedly learned tricks and roamed the decks fearlessly. Flinders later wrote an affectionate tribute to him. Statues of Trim now sit near statues of Flinders, including outside the State Library of New South Wales.

sections.key: Flinders was wrecked, then held captive by the French on Mauritius for six and a half years.
sections.b: In 1803 Flinders set off for England as a passenger aboard HMS Porpoise, which struck a reef far off the Queensland coast, now called Wreck Reef. The survivors camped on a sandbank while Flinders took a ship's cutter, a small open boat, back to Sydney to organise a rescue. He then continued towards England in the tiny schooner Cumberland, which was leaking badly, and in December 1803 put in at Mauritius, then a French colony. Britain and France were at war again, and the governor, Charles Decaen, suspected him of spying. Flinders was detained for six and a half years. He used the time to work on his charts and journals. Trim, who had stayed with him, vanished on the island.

sections.key: Flinders championed the name Australia, which Governor Macquarie began using officially in 1817.
sections.b: Released in 1810, Flinders finally reached England, in poor health, and spent his last years preparing his account of the voyages. The continent was known by various names, including New Holland and Terra Australis, the ‘southern land’. Flinders preferred a shorter form, Australia, which he felt was more pleasing to the ear. He was not the first person to use the word, but he was its most influential champion. His book, A Voyage to Terra Australis, used Australia in its text, though his publishers kept the older name in the title. Governor Lachlan Macquarie of New South Wales read his work and began using Australia in official correspondence from 1817. The book was published on 18 July 1814. Flinders died the next day, aged forty.

sections.key: Flinders' grave was lost for nearly two centuries until archaeologists found it under London's Euston station in 2019.
sections.b: Flinders was buried in a cemetery in London, but over the following decades the burial ground was cleared and built over during the expansion of Euston railway station. His exact resting place was lost, and a story grew that he lay beneath one of the platforms. In 2019, archaeologists excavating the site for the new High Speed 2 rail project found a coffin with a lead breastplate bearing his name, among tens of thousands of burials. It was one of the few that could be identified so clearly. In 2024 his remains were reburied in his home village of Donington, Lincolnshire. In Australia his name lives on in places such as Flinders Street in Melbourne, the Flinders Ranges and Flinders University.

quiz.q: What did Flinders and Bass prove in 1798 and 1799?
o: That New Zealand was two islands
That Van Diemen's Land was an island
That a river crossed the continent
That the Gulf of Carpentaria was a strait
quiz.e: Sailing the Norfolk around it proved a strait, now Bass Strait, separated Tasmania from the mainland.

quiz.q: Why did Flinders have to rush the end of the Investigator voyage?
quiz.e: The Investigator was so decayed he abandoned the detailed survey and hurried back to Sydney around the west coast.

quiz.q: Who is regarded as the first Australian-born person to circumnavigate the continent?
quiz.e: Bungaree, a Kuring-gai man from the Broken Bay area, sailed with Flinders on the Investigator.

quiz.q: Why was Flinders detained on Mauritius?
o: He had lost his ship's papers in a storm
The French governor suspected him of spying while Britain and France were at war
quiz.e: Governor Decaen held him for six and a half years amid the Napoleonic Wars.

quiz.q: Where were Flinders' remains found in 2019?
quiz.e: Archaeologists working on the HS2 rail project identified his coffin by its lead breastplate.

LESSONS.title: Zheng He and the treasure fleets
LESSONS.hook: Decades before Columbus, a Chinese admiral led some of the largest fleets the world had ever seen across the Indian Ocean. Then China stopped sending them.

sections.key: Zheng He was a Muslim boy from Yunnan who was captured, served a Ming prince and rose to command vast fleets.
sections.b: Zheng He was born around 1371 in Yunnan, in southwest China, into a Muslim family originally named Ma. His father and grandfather had reportedly made the pilgrimage to Mecca. When Ming armies conquered Yunnan, the boy was captured, castrated, as was common for captive boys entering royal service, and sent to serve in the household of a prince, Zhu Di. He grew into a tall, capable soldier and adviser and helped Zhu Di win a bloody civil war to seize the throne in 1402. Zhu Di became the Yongle Emperor, one of the most ambitious rulers in Chinese history. He rewarded his loyal eunuch with a new surname, Zheng, and later gave him command of an enterprise on a scale the world had rarely seen.

sections.key: Between 1405 and 1433, Zheng He led seven expeditions across Southeast Asia and the Indian Ocean.
sections.b: The first voyage set out in 1405. Chinese records describe a fleet of over 300 ships carrying around 27,000 people: sailors, soldiers, interpreters, doctors, craftsmen and officials. Over seven voyages, ending in 1433, the fleets visited ports across what are now Vietnam, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Sri Lanka, then pressed on to India's Calicut, a hub of the spice trade, and Hormuz at the entrance to the Persian Gulf. Later voyages sent detachments to Arabia and down the coast of East Africa, to places such as Mogadishu and Malindi. Some crew visited Mecca. The fleets sailed with the monsoon winds, which reverse with the seasons across the Indian Ocean, so the timing of each voyage followed a reliable rhythm.

sections.h: How big were the treasure ships?
sections.key: Old records describe ships over 120 metres long, but historians and engineers debate whether that is realistic.
sections.b: The largest vessels in the fleet were called treasure ships. A later Ming source gives their size in a way that works out at roughly 120 to 140 metres long, which would make them some of the biggest wooden ships ever built, many times longer than Columbus's Santa Maria. Some historians accept these figures, pointing to a huge rudder post found at a Nanjing shipyard site. Many others are sceptical. Wooden hulls of that length tend to flex and leak, and later texts may have exaggerated. A common middle view is that the biggest ships were perhaps around 60 to 75 metres long, still enormous for their day. What nobody disputes is that the fleets as a whole were vast and impressively organised.

sections.key: The voyages mainly displayed Ming power and drew rulers into China's tribute system, though force was sometimes used.
sections.b: The fleets did not set out to found colonies. Their main purpose was to show the might and wealth of the new emperor, gather tribute, and bring foreign rulers into the Chinese system in which they acknowledged the emperor's supremacy and received generous gifts and trade in return. Envoys from dozens of states came back with the fleets to visit the Ming court. That does not mean the voyages were entirely peaceful. The soldiers on board fought on several occasions, including against a pirate leader near Palembang in Sumatra and in a conflict in Sri Lanka, where a local king was captured and taken to China. Zheng He's fleets were floating diplomacy backed by an unmistakable threat of force.

sections.key: In 1414 a giraffe from East Africa arrived in China and was celebrated as a mythical qilin.
sections.b: One of the most charming results of the voyages was a giraffe. In 1414, envoys from Bengal brought one to China; it had originally come from Malindi on the East African coast. Courtiers declared it a qilin, a gentle creature from Chinese legend whose appearance was said to signal a wise and virtuous ruler. A court painting shows the giraffe led by a handler, along with a poem of praise for the emperor. More animals followed in later years, including zebras, ostriches and oryx. For the Yongle Emperor, whose seizure of power had been violent and controversial, there was obvious political value in having heaven's approval walk into the palace on four very long legs.

sections.key: After the 1430s the Ming court turned away from great ocean voyages, for reasons historians still debate.
sections.b: Zheng He probably died around 1433, during or soon after the seventh voyage, and he may have been buried at sea. No fleet on that scale ever sailed again. Historians point to several reasons. The voyages were extremely expensive, and the court faced costly pressures on land, especially from Mongol forces on the northern frontier and the building of the new capital at Beijing. Confucian officials were often hostile to the powerful palace eunuchs who ran the voyages, and saw them as a wasteful vanity. Later Ming governments also restricted private overseas trade for long periods. A story claims that officials deliberately destroyed the voyage records, though how much was lost and why is still debated. Either way, China's great age of ocean expeditions closed.

sections.key: Zheng He did not reach America, but he is honoured today across Asia as a symbol of seafaring and cultural exchange.
sections.b: Zheng He's story has attracted some wild claims. A popular book published in 2002 argued that his fleets discovered America and sailed around the world in 1421. Historians have firmly rejected this, as there is no credible evidence for it in Chinese or other records, or in archaeology. The real story needs no exaggeration. Around Southeast Asia, temples and shrines remember him, including in Malacca, Semarang and Surabaya, and he is a respected figure among both Chinese and Muslim communities. In modern China he has become a symbol of peaceful maritime exchange. It is worth remembering the contrast he offers. Decades before Portuguese ships reached India, Chinese fleets had crossed the same ocean, and then chose not to come back.

quiz.q: How did Zheng He come to serve the Ming court?
o: He was a merchant who bought a position
He was captured as a boy and placed in the household of a prince
He was the son of the emperor
quiz.e: Captured when Ming armies took Yunnan, he served Zhu Di, who became the Yongle Emperor.

quiz.q: Which of these places did Zheng He's fleets reach?
o: Hormuz and the East African coast
quiz.e: The fleets sailed to India, Hormuz and later to East African ports like Mogadishu and Malindi.

quiz.q: What is the debate about the treasure ships?
o: Whether they really were up to 120 metres or more long
Whether they were made of iron
quiz.e: Old records imply huge sizes, but many historians and engineers think the largest were closer to 60 to 75 metres.

quiz.q: Why was the giraffe's arrival politically useful to the emperor?
o: It proved China could conquer Africa
It was used to pay a debt
It was a gift to Mongol leaders
It was hailed as a qilin, a sign of a virtuous ruler
quiz.e: Courtiers linked it to the legendary qilin, implying heaven approved of the emperor's reign.

quiz.q: What do historians say about the claim that Zheng He discovered America in 1421?
o: There is no credible evidence for it
It is proven by a map in Beijing
It was confirmed by DNA studies
quiz.e: The claim has been firmly rejected because no reliable records or archaeology support it.

LESSONS.title: How railways invented time zones
LESSONS.hook: Once every town set its clocks by its own sun. Then trains arrived, timetables turned into chaos, and the world had to agree on what time it was.

sections.h: When every town had its own noon
sections.key: Before railways, towns kept local solar time, so clocks differed from place to place.
sections.b: For most of history, time was local. Noon was when the Sun stood highest in the sky, and because the Earth turns, that moment arrives slightly later the further west you go. Each town set its clocks by its own sun, often checked with a sundial and kept by a church or town hall clock. The differences were real but small: in England, Bristol's clocks ran about ten minutes behind London's. When the fastest way to travel was by horse, nobody cared. A coach journey took so long that a few minutes' disagreement between towns made no practical difference. Watches were expensive anyway, and most people lived by bells, daylight and habit rather than precise minutes.

sections.key: Fast trains and timetables made dozens of local times confusing and even dangerous.
sections.b: Railways changed the scale of the problem. Suddenly people could cover in hours what once took days, and timetables needed to be precise to the minute. If each station ran on its own local time, a timetable became a puzzle, and passengers missed connections. Worse, on single track lines, where trains travelling in opposite directions had to pass at set places, confusion over time could cause collisions. The telegraph made a solution possible, because a time signal could now be sent along wires almost instantly. Railway companies became, in effect, the keepers of the clock. They began running their whole networks on a single standard time, whatever the sundial in a particular town might say.

sections.key: British railways adopted Greenwich time in the 1840s, and it became the legal time across Great Britain in 1880.
sections.b: In Britain, the Great Western Railway began using London time across its network in 1840. Other companies followed, and by around 1848 most British railways had adopted Greenwich Mean Time, based on observations at the Royal Observatory in Greenwich. People called it railway time. Not everyone was happy. Some towns kept two times for a while, and a few public clocks were given two minute hands, one showing local time and one showing London time. Gradually, as people came to depend on trains, the rest of daily life followed the railway clock. In 1880 Parliament made Greenwich Mean Time the legal standard across Great Britain. A local idea of time had given way to a national one.

sections.key: On 18 November 1883, North American railways switched from dozens of local times to a handful of time zones.
sections.b: North America faced a far bigger problem. The United States spans so much longitude that railways were using dozens of different times, and a big station might display several clocks at once. On 18 November 1883, the railways of the United States and Canada switched to a system of standard time zones, each roughly an hour apart. In many towns, clocks were reset at noon, so people experienced noon twice that day, once by the old local time and once by the new standard time. That is why it is remembered as the day of two noons. The change was organised by the railways, not the government. The United States did not make time zones official in federal law until 1918.

sections.key: In 1884 an international conference chose Greenwich as the prime meridian, the starting line for world longitude.
sections.b: Standard zones need a starting point. In 1884 delegates from about twenty five countries met in Washington DC for the International Meridian Conference. They chose the meridian passing through the Royal Observatory at Greenwich as zero degrees longitude. Practical reasons favoured it, as most of the world's shipping already used charts based on Greenwich. The Canadian railway engineer Sandford Fleming was one of the great champions of a worldwide system of time based on a single meridian. Not everyone agreed. France abstained in the vote and kept using the Paris meridian for its own purposes for decades. The conference did not actually impose time zones around the world, but it gave countries a shared reference to build their own on.

sections.key: The Australian colonies adopted standard time in 1895, and South Australia later moved to a half-hour zone.
sections.b: In Australia, each colony had kept its own local time, and travellers crossing borders by train faced the same headaches as everyone else. In 1895 the colonies agreed on standard times based on Greenwich: Eastern, Central and Western. South Australia first chose nine hours ahead of Greenwich, but in 1899 it moved to nine and a half hours, a choice that has been debated ever since. The Northern Territory, then administered by South Australia, followed. Half-hour zones like this are unusual but not unique: India uses one, and Nepal goes further with a quarter-hour offset. Daylight saving complicates the picture today. Queensland, Western Australia and the Northern Territory don't use it, so in summer the mainland runs on five different times.

sections.key: Modern civil time is based on atomic clocks, while time zones remain a mix of geography and politics.
sections.b: Greenwich Mean Time has largely been replaced as the world's reference by Coordinated Universal Time, or UTC, which is kept by a network of highly accurate atomic clocks. Because the Earth's spin is slightly irregular, leap seconds have occasionally been added to keep UTC close to the Sun, but in 2022 international scientists voted to stop adding them by 2035. Time zones themselves are decided by governments, and politics often beats geography. China, which spans the width of five standard zones, uses just one official time, so in its far west the Sun can rise very late by the clock. Spain sits mostly west of Greenwich but uses Central European Time. The railway engineers' solution still governs every phone and laptop.

quiz.q: What determined the time in a town before standard time?
o: The position of the Sun, so each town had its own local time
A national clock in the capital
quiz.e: Noon was when the Sun was highest, so towns east and west of each other kept slightly different times.

quiz.q: Which invention made a single standard time practical across a network?
quiz.e: The telegraph could carry a time signal along wires almost instantly.

quiz.q: Why is 18 November 1883 called ‘the day of two noons’?
o: Clocks were reset at noon, so many towns had noon twice
The Sun rose twice in the Arctic
Two different calendars were in use
quiz.e: When North American railways switched to standard zones, many towns reset their clocks at local noon.

quiz.q: What did the 1884 International Meridian Conference decide?
o: That every country must use GMT
That time zones should be exactly one hour apart worldwide
That France would host the prime meridian
That longitude zero would run through Greenwich
quiz.e: It chose Greenwich as the prime meridian; countries still set their own time zones.

quiz.q: Which change did South Australia make in 1899?
o: It moved to a half-hour zone, nine and a half hours ahead of Greenwich
quiz.e: SA first chose nine hours ahead of Greenwich, then shifted to nine and a half in 1899.

LESSONS.title: Lewis and Clark: across a continent
LESSONS.hook: In 1804 a small army party set out to cross North America to the Pacific and back. They found no easy river route, but they mapped a continent and depended on the people who already lived there.

sections.key: After the Louisiana Purchase, President Jefferson sent an expedition to explore the west and look for a water route to the Pacific.
sections.b: In 1803 the United States bought the vast Louisiana Territory from France, roughly doubling the size of the young country, for about fifteen million dollars. President Thomas Jefferson had already been planning an expedition into the west, and now it had added urgency. He wanted to know what the land held, from plants and animals to rivers and mountains, and to make contact with the Native nations who lived there. Above all, he hoped to find a practical water route, by river and a short overland carry, linking the Missouri to the Pacific. Many still dreamed of a Northwest Passage across the continent. To lead the effort he chose his personal secretary, an army captain named Meriwether Lewis.

sections.key: Lewis chose William Clark as co-leader, and their party of soldiers, boatmen and others left near St Louis in May 1804.
sections.b: Lewis asked his former army comrade William Clark to share command, and the two worked as genuine equals, although the army officially ranked Clark lower. Lewis spent months preparing, studying botany, astronomy and medicine and buying supplies, from rifles and gunpowder to scientific instruments and thousands of gifts for Native leaders. The expedition, known as the Corps of Discovery, included about thirty to forty soldiers and boatmen, with numbers changing along the way. Among them was York, an enslaved man owned by Clark, and Lewis's large Newfoundland dog, Seaman. In May 1804 the party set off up the Missouri River from their winter camp near St Louis, in a keelboat and two smaller boats, rowing, poling and hauling against the current.

sections.key: The Corps spent its first winter among the Mandan and Hidatsa, where it hired Charbonneau and Sacagawea.
sections.b: By late 1804 the expedition had travelled well over two thousand kilometres up the Missouri to the villages of the Mandan and Hidatsa people, in what is now North Dakota. These were busy trading towns of earth lodges, and the Corps built a small fort nearby to survive a bitterly cold winter. Only one member of the party died on the entire journey, Sergeant Charles Floyd, in August 1804, probably of a burst appendix. At the Mandan villages the captains hired a French-Canadian trader, Toussaint Charbonneau, as an interpreter. One of his wives was Sacagawea, a young Shoshone woman who had been captured by Hidatsa raiders as a girl. In February 1805 she gave birth to a son, Jean Baptiste, who travelled the rest of the way as a baby.

sections.key: Sacagawea was not the expedition's guide, but her skills and presence mattered enormously.
sections.b: Sacagawea is often pictured leading the Corps across the mountains, pointing the way. The truth is more interesting. She was not hired as a guide and did not know most of the route. Her value lay elsewhere. She spoke Shoshone, the language of the people from whom the expedition badly needed horses, and she recognised landmarks in her home region, such as Beaverhead Rock in what is now south-western Montana. Clark noted that a woman travelling with the party signalled peaceful intentions to the nations they met, because war parties did not travel that way. In August 1805 the Corps met a Shoshone band whose chief, Cameahwait, turned out to be Sacagawea's brother. The meeting helped secure the horses they needed to cross the mountains.

sections.key: The Rocky Mountains proved far wider and harder than expected, and the Corps nearly starved crossing them.
sections.b: The expedition's first great obstacle was the Great Falls of the Missouri, where it took about a month to carry boats and supplies around a series of waterfalls. Then came the Rockies. Jefferson had hoped for a short portage between rivers, but the mountains were range after range. In September 1805 the Corps crossed the Bitterroot Mountains along a steep trail in early snow, with little game to hunt. They were reduced to eating candles and some of their horses. Starving and sick, they came down into the lands of the Nez Perce, who fed them and helped them build canoes. The crossing ended the dream of an easy water route across the continent.

sections.key: The Corps reached the Pacific in November 1805, and everyone, including York and Sacagawea, voted on where to winter.
sections.b: The Corps paddled down the Snake and Columbia rivers and in November 1805 reached the Pacific coast, where Clark wrote of the ocean in his journal with famously creative spelling. They had to decide where to spend the winter, and the captains put the question to the whole party. York's view and Sacagawea's were recorded alongside the soldiers', an extraordinary moment for an enslaved man and a Native woman in that era, though it changed nothing about their status afterwards. They built Fort Clatsop, near today's Astoria in Oregon, and endured a wet, miserable winter, with rain recorded on most days. In March 1806 they started for home. The return journey included a deadly clash with Blackfeet warriors, the only fight of the journey in which people were killed.

sections.key: The Corps returned in 1806 with maps and descriptions of many species, but its legacy for Native nations was painful.
sections.b: The Corps arrived back in St Louis in September 1806, after more than two years away, to a public that had largely given them up for dead. Their journals and Clark's maps transformed knowledge of the west, and they described well over a hundred animals and plants new to science, including the grizzly bear, prairie dog and western species of trout. But the expedition also opened the way for fur traders, settlers and the US government, and over the following century Native nations along the route lost much of their land and many lives. The fates of the travellers were mixed. Lewis died from gunshot wounds in 1809, most likely suicide. Clark did not free York for around a decade. Sacagawea is thought to have died young, around 1812, though some Shoshone traditions say she lived into old age.

quiz.q: What did Jefferson most hope the expedition would find?
o: A practical water route to the Pacific
A site for a new capital
quiz.e: He hoped rivers and a short overland carry would link the Missouri to the Pacific.

quiz.q: How many members of the Corps died during the expedition?
quiz.e: Sergeant Charles Floyd died in 1804, probably of appendicitis; he was the only death.

quiz.q: What was Sacagawea's most important role?
o: She was the official guide for the whole route
She interpreted Shoshone, recognised landmarks near her homeland, and signalled peaceful intent
quiz.e: She was not the guide, but her language skills, local knowledge and presence were vital.

quiz.q: Who helped the starving Corps after they crossed the Bitterroot Mountains?
quiz.e: The Nez Perce fed them and helped them build canoes for the journey down to the Pacific.

quiz.q: What was remarkable about the vote on where to winter in 1805?
o: It was decided by the President
York and Sacagawea had their views recorded alongside the soldiers'
They voted to sail home by sea
quiz.e: An enslaved man and a Native woman were included, though their status did not change afterwards.

LESSONS.title: Into the Challenger Deep
LESSONS.hook: The deepest point in the ocean lies nearly 11 kilometres down, under pressure that could crush a submarine. Two men first reached it in 1960 in a craft held up by petrol.

sections.key: The Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench is the deepest known point in Earth's oceans, nearly 11 kilometres down.
sections.b: In the western Pacific, east of the Philippines and south west of Guam, lies the Mariana Trench, a curved scar on the seafloor more than 2,500 kilometres long. It forms where one tectonic plate dives beneath another. At its southern end is the Challenger Deep, the deepest known place in the world's oceans. Estimates of its depth vary slightly between surveys, but it is close to 11,000 metres, or about 10,900 metres by most recent measurements. Put Mount Everest at the bottom, and its summit would still sit more than two kilometres underwater. The trench is named after HMS Challenger, a British ship whose round-the-world scientific voyage in the 1870s took a sounding there, and a later survey ship of the same name pinpointed the deep in 1951.

sections.key: At the bottom, water pressure is more than a thousand times that at the surface.
sections.b: Every ten metres of seawater adds roughly another atmosphere of pressure. At the bottom of the Challenger Deep, the pressure is more than a thousand times what we feel at sea level, roughly equivalent to more than a tonne pressing on every square centimetre. An ordinary submarine would be crushed long before it got there. Any vessel carrying people needs a cabin that can resist this squeeze, which in practice means a thick, strong sphere, since a sphere spreads pressure evenly. The trouble is that such a sphere is extremely heavy and sinks like a stone. The question for engineers was not only how to get down, but how to float back up again.

sections.key: Auguste Piccard's bathyscaphe used a huge float filled with petrol to provide buoyancy at extreme depths.
sections.b: The solution came from the Swiss physicist Auguste Piccard, who had already flown balloons into the stratosphere. He realised the same principle could work in water. His bathyscaphe, meaning ‘deep boat’, was essentially an underwater balloon. A large float filled with petrol was attached above a small, thick steel crew sphere. Petrol is lighter than water and compresses very little, so it keeps providing lift even under enormous pressure. To descend, the craft carried tonnes of iron pellets as ballast, held in place by electromagnets. To come back up, the crew released the pellets and the petrol float carried them to the surface. Piccard and his son Jacques built the bathyscaphe Trieste in Italy in the 1950s, and the US Navy later bought it.

sections.key: Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh became the first people to reach the bottom of the Challenger Deep.
sections.b: On 23 January 1960, Jacques Piccard and US Navy lieutenant Don Walsh squeezed into the Trieste's cramped sphere, only about two metres across inside, and began their descent. It took nearly five hours. Partway down, they heard a loud crack, and later found that an outer window had fractured, though the inner structure held. Finally they settled onto the seabed, nearly 11 kilometres down. They spent only around twenty minutes on the bottom. Their landing stirred up a cloud of fine sediment that made photographs impossible. Piccard reported seeing a flatfish through the porthole, but many biologists now doubt this, since fish are not thought to survive at that depth. The ascent took over three hours, and both men returned to a hero's welcome.

sections.key: After 1960 no one returned to the Challenger Deep in person for more than fifty years.
sections.b: It seems astonishing, but after the Trieste's dive, no human went back to the bottom of the Challenger Deep for fifty-two years. Ocean science moved on in other directions.
