Historians who dig into old cookbooks and newspapers often find gradual change rather than one inventor. What makes a food iconic is less its birth than the memories, rituals and pride people build around it.

quiz.q: What did historian Helen Leach find about the pavlova?
o: It was invented in Perth in 1935
New Zealand recipes called pavlova date to the late 1920s, and similar meringue cakes existed earlier overseas
quiz.e: Leach found late-1920s New Zealand recipes, earlier than the Perth claim, and older meringue cakes abroad.

quiz.q: Why can't a business normally sell ‘Anzac cookies’?
o: The word Anzac is protected by law, and approval generally requires the name Anzac biscuits
Only the army may bake them
quiz.e: Commercial use of ‘Anzac’ needs approval, and products must stay true to the traditional biscuit.

quiz.q: Who is the lamington named after?
quiz.e: Lamingtons are named after Lord Lamington, Queensland's governor from 1896 to 1901, though their inventor is uncertain.

quiz.q: What inspired Frank McEncroe's Chiko Roll?
quiz.e: McEncroe based his sturdy deep-fried roll on Chinese spring rolls and launched it in 1951.

quiz.q: Where did the name Tim Tam come from?
o: A racehorse that won the 1958 Kentucky Derby
quiz.e: Ian Norris named the biscuit after Tim Tam, the 1958 Kentucky Derby winner.

LESSONS.title: Cooking by degrees: the science of precise temperature
LESSONS.hook: A few degrees can turn silky meat into shoe leather. Understanding exactly what heat does to proteins explains sous vide, perfect eggs and why chefs swear by thermometers.

sections.key: Heat changes the shape of proteins, and each protein changes at its own temperature.
sections.b: Proteins are long chains folded into specific shapes. When they are heated, the chains vibrate harder until the weak bonds holding their shape give way. They unfold, a process called denaturation, and then tangle and bond with neighbouring proteins, a process called coagulation. That is what turns a runny egg white into a solid white, or translucent raw prawn flesh into firm, opaque meat. The crucial detail is that different proteins denature at different temperatures, and those temperatures are often only a few degrees apart. Most traditional cooking blasts food with heat far hotter than the target, like a 200 degree oven for meat that should finish around 55 to 60 degrees. Precise cooking starts from a different question: what temperature do I want the food to reach?

sections.key: Egg white and yolk proteins set at different temperatures, so precise heat creates textures impossible by boiling.
sections.b: An egg shows how much a few degrees matter. Egg white is a mix of proteins. One of them, ovotransferrin, begins setting at roughly 62 degrees, which makes the white turn milky and tender. The most abundant, ovalbumin, needs closer to 80 degrees to set firm. The yolk thickens at around 65 degrees and becomes fully firm by the low 70s. Boiling water, at 100 degrees, overshoots everything, so you rely on timing to stop the heat in time. Hold an egg at a steady 63 to 65 degrees for about an hour, though, and you get a yolk like thick custard and a soft, barely set white. Japanese cooks have long made onsen tamago this way, gently cooking eggs in hot springs.

sections.key: Meat firms as its proteins set, squeezes out juice at higher temperatures and turns tender as collagen melts.
sections.b: Meat is mostly water held inside muscle proteins, wrapped in connective tissue made largely of collagen. As meat heats up, the muscle protein myosin begins to set at around 50 degrees, and the meat firms but stays juicy; that is roughly the rare range. As it climbs through the 60s, other proteins, including actin at roughly 66 degrees or above, contract and squeeze out moisture, and meat becomes noticeably drier. Collagen behaves differently. It shrinks at around 60 degrees, but given enough time at higher temperatures, it slowly breaks down into gelatin, which gives braised meat its silky, falling-apart texture. That is the cook's dilemma: tender cuts want low temperatures, while tough, collagen-rich cuts need long cooking times.

sections.key: Sous vide, cooking vacuum-sealed food in precisely heated water, was developed in France in the 1970s.
sections.b: Sous vide is French for ‘under vacuum’. Food is sealed in a plastic bag, usually with the air removed, and cooked in a water bath held at an exact temperature. Its modern culinary use is usually traced to 1974, when the chef Georges Pralus developed it for foie gras for the restaurant of the Troisgros brothers in Roanne. Cooked conventionally, the expensive liver lost much of its weight as fat melted out, but gentle, controlled heat greatly reduced the loss. Around the same time, the food scientist Bruno Goussault researched sous vide for large-scale catering and spent decades training chefs. Once costly lab equipment, immersion circulators became affordable home gadgets in the 2010s, bringing restaurant precision into ordinary kitchens.

sections.key: Water transfers heat far faster than air, which is why a hot water bath cooks evenly and gently.
sections.b: You can briefly put your hand into a 200 degree oven without injury, but never into a pot of boiling water at 100 degrees. The difference is heat transfer. Water is denser than air and carries heat to a surface much faster, so it delivers its energy efficiently and evenly. In sous vide, the bath is set to the final temperature you want, say 56 degrees for medium-rare steak. Because the water can never be hotter than that, the food cannot overcook in the usual sense. The whole piece, from edge to centre, reaches the same doneness, with none of the grey, overcooked band you get under a pan-seared crust. The catch is that no browning happens at such low temperatures, so cooks finish with a quick, very hot sear.

sections.key: Killing bacteria depends on both temperature and time, so a lower temperature held longer can be just as effective.
sections.b: Food safety guidance usually gives a single number, such as cooking poultry until the centre reaches 75 degrees, which kills harmful bacteria such as Salmonella almost instantly. But bacterial death actually depends on both temperature and time. At lower temperatures, bacteria still die, just more slowly. Food scientists have published tables showing that holding food at a lower temperature for long enough achieves the same reduction as a brief moment at a higher one. That is how sous vide cooks can safely serve chicken that is juicier than conventional cooking allows. However, these methods need accurate equipment, correct holding times and an understanding of the science. For everyday cooking at home, follow the official temperature guidance, and use a probe thermometer to check.

sections.key: Low temperature cooking carries real food safety risks, and a thermometer is the most useful tool for cooking precisely.
sections.b: Precise low temperature cooking has risks that conventional cooking avoids. Inside a sealed, airless bag, bacteria that thrive without oxygen, such as Clostridium botulinum, can be a hazard if food is held too long at too low a temperature or cooled slowly afterwards. Cooking below about 55 degrees for long periods is particularly risky, and cooked food should be eaten promptly or chilled quickly in iced water and refrigerated. Pregnant people, young children, older adults and those with weakened immunity are generally advised to avoid lightly cooked meat, fish and eggs. The simplest takeaway for any cook is the probe thermometer. Once you know the internal temperature, you are no longer guessing, and dry chicken and overcooked steak become far rarer.

quiz.q: What happens when proteins denature during cooking?
o: They unfold as heat breaks the weak bonds holding their shape
quiz.e: Heat breaks weak bonds so proteins unfold, then they bond with neighbours and coagulate, changing texture.

quiz.q: Why does an egg held at about 64°C have a custardy yolk and a soft white?
o: Its proteins set at different temperatures, and only some reach their setting point
Low heat removes water from the yolk
quiz.e: Some white proteins and the yolk partly set around 62 to 65°C, while ovalbumin needs nearer 80°C.

quiz.q: Why do tough, collagen-rich cuts need long cooking?
o: Collagen only converts slowly into gelatin over time
Collagen is a type of fat
quiz.e: Collagen slowly breaks down into gelatin, giving braises their silky, tender texture.

quiz.q: Why can't food overcook in a sous vide bath in the usual sense?
o: The water is set at the final temperature, so food cannot get hotter than that
Food cooks from the inside out
The water is constantly cooled with ice
quiz.e: The bath is held at the target temperature, so the whole piece reaches that doneness and no further.

quiz.q: How can a lower cooking temperature still make food safe?
o: Holding it there long enough kills bacteria as effectively as a brief higher temperature
quiz.e: Bacterial death depends on time and temperature together, so lower temperatures need longer holding times.

LESSONS.title: 1816: the year without a summer
LESSONS.hook: A mountain in Indonesia blew itself apart, and a year later it snowed in New England in June. Here is how one eruption chilled half the world.

sections.key: In April 1815 Mount Tambora produced the largest eruption in recorded history.
sections.b: Mount Tambora sits on the island of Sumbawa, in what is now Indonesia. After rumbling for days, it exploded with enormous force around 10 and 11 April 1815. The blasts were heard more than 2,000 kilometres away, and some colonial officials on distant islands reportedly mistook them for cannon fire and sent troops to investigate. Columns of ash and rock rose into the stratosphere, and glowing avalanches of hot gas and debris swept down the slopes, wiping out villages. When it was over, the mountain had lost well over a kilometre of height, leaving a caldera around six kilometres wide. Volcanologists rate it a 7 on the Volcanic Explosivity Index, a level reached only a handful of times in the past few thousand years.

sections.key: The eruption and the famine that followed killed tens of thousands of people.
sections.b: The immediate eruption killed many thousands of people on Sumbawa, buried under ash or caught by the scorching flows. Yet the larger toll came afterwards. Ash smothered crops and fouled water across Sumbawa and the neighbouring island of Lombok, and livestock died in great numbers. Starvation and disease followed for months. Exact numbers are impossible to know, because records from the region were patchy, but estimates of the total death toll commonly run to tens of thousands, and some researchers argue it was higher still. Among the losses was a small local kingdom, Tambora, whose people and language were largely wiped out. Later archaeologists digging in the ash found houses, pottery and human remains, earning the site a nickname as the ‘Pompeii of the East’.

sections.key: Sulphur gas, not ash, was what cooled the planet.
sections.b: Ash falls out of the air within days or weeks, so it was not ash that changed the world's weather. The real culprit was sulphur dioxide. Tambora blasted huge quantities of it into the stratosphere, more than ten kilometres up, where there is no rain to wash it out. There it reacted with water to form tiny droplets of sulphuric acid, known as sulphate aerosols. Winds spread this haze around the globe over the following months. The droplets reflected a share of incoming sunlight back into space, so less warmth reached the ground. Scientists estimate global average temperatures dropped by somewhere around half a degree, which sounds small but was enough to upset growing seasons across the Northern Hemisphere. The effect lingered for a year or more.

sections.key: In 1816 summer frosts and cold rains ruined harvests in North America and Europe.
sections.b: The strangest year was 1816. In New England and eastern Canada, snow fell in early June, and killing frosts returned in July and August, destroying corn and other crops. Farmers who had planted several times watched each attempt fail. In western Europe the summer was cold and relentlessly wet. Harvests failed across Britain, Ireland, France and the German lands, grain prices soared, and there were food riots in several countries. Switzerland suffered such hunger that it became one of the worst years in its modern history. Typhus spread through a weakened, hungry population in Ireland. Many New England families gave up on their rocky farms and moved west. People at the time had no idea why the weather had turned so savage.

sections.key: A gloomy holiday in Switzerland produced two of the great horror stories.
sections.b: In June 1816 a group of young English writers rented houses beside Lake Geneva, including the poet Lord Byron, Percy Bysshe Shelley, Mary Godwin, soon to be Mary Shelley, and Byron's doctor, John Polidori. Storms and endless rain kept them indoors at the Villa Diodati, so Byron proposed that each of them write a ghost story. Mary's idea grew into Frankenstein, published in 1818. Polidori's effort became The Vampyre, an early and influential vampire tale. Byron wrote a bleak poem called Darkness, imagining the Sun going out. It is a lovely irony that two monsters of modern fiction owe something to a volcano none of the writers had heard of, on an island on the far side of the world.

sections.key: The link between Tambora and the cold year was only firmly made a century later.
sections.b: For a long time the cold of 1816 was simply a puzzle. Some people at the time blamed sunspots, while others had their own theories. In the early twentieth century, the American scientist William Humphreys argued that volcanic dust and gases could cool the climate, and Tambora became the prime suspect. Later evidence clinched it. Ice cores drilled in Greenland and Antarctica contain a sharp spike of sulphate in layers from around 1815 and 1816, the chemical fingerprint of the eruption falling as acid snow at both ends of the planet. The story is a little more complicated than one volcano, though. Another large eruption, still unidentified, occurred around 1808 or 1809, and the Sun was in a quiet phase, so Tambora struck an already cool world.

quiz.q: What actually cooled the climate after Tambora erupted?
o: Sulphate droplets in the stratosphere reflecting sunlight
Steam from the eruption forming thick clouds
quiz.e: Sulphur dioxide reached the stratosphere and formed sulphate aerosols that reflected sunlight. Ash falls out of the sky within days or weeks.

quiz.q: How do volcanologists rate the Tambora eruption on the Volcanic Explosivity Index?
quiz.e: Tambora rates a 7, a level reached only a handful of times in the past few thousand years.

quiz.q: Which of these happened in 1816?
o: Snow fell in New England in June
The Thames froze for the last time
Europe had record drought and heat
Australia had its coldest winter ever recorded
quiz.e: New England saw June snow and summer frosts, while western Europe suffered a cold, wet summer and failed harvests.

quiz.q: Which famous novel began during the gloomy summer of 1816?
quiz.e: Mary Shelley began Frankenstein at Lake Geneva when bad weather kept Byron's party indoors telling ghost stories.

quiz.q: What evidence in ice cores links Tambora to the cold years?
o: Layers of volcanic glass from Indonesia
A spike of sulphate in layers from around 1815 and 1816
quiz.e: Sulphate from the eruption fell as acid snow in Greenland and Antarctica, leaving a sharp chemical spike in the ice.

LESSONS.title: Reading the clouds
LESSONS.hook: Every cloud has a name, and most have a message about the weather to come. A young pharmacist worked out how to read them over two hundred years ago.

sections.h: The man who named the clouds
sections.key: Luke Howard's simple Latin names, proposed in 1802, are still used today.
sections.b: Before the early 1800s, clouds were thought too fleeting to classify. Then an English pharmacist and keen amateur weather watcher named Luke Howard gave a talk in London in 1802, published the following year, called On the Modifications of Clouds. He borrowed the idea from naturalists who sorted plants and animals into families, and proposed a few basic Latin names. Cirrus means a curl or wisp of hair. Cumulus means a heap. Stratus means a layer or sheet. Nimbus refers to rain. These could be combined, so a heaped rain cloud became cumulonimbus. The scheme was so clear that it spread across Europe. The German writer Goethe admired Howard so much he wrote poems in his honour. Modern meteorology still builds on his names.

sections.key: Clouds form when rising air cools until its water vapour condenses onto tiny particles.
sections.b: Air always holds some invisible water vapour, and warm air can hold more than cold air. When a parcel of air rises, the pressure around it drops, so it expands and cools. Eventually it cools to its dew point, the temperature at which it can no longer hold all its vapour. The excess condenses into droplets, or ice crystals if it is cold enough. But water needs something to condense onto. The air is full of microscopic specks of sea salt, dust, smoke and pollen, called condensation nuclei, and each droplet forms around one. Air can be forced upwards in several ways: by the Sun heating the ground, by wind pushing it over mountains, or by a mass of cold air sliding underneath warm air.

sections.key: A cloud can weigh hundreds of tonnes but stays up because its droplets are tiny.
sections.b: A modest fair weather cumulus cloud about a kilometre across holds a surprising amount of water. With around half a gram of liquid in every cubic metre, a cubic kilometre of cloud contains roughly 500 tonnes of water, about the weight of a hundred elephants. So why does it not fall? The answer is that the weight is spread across billions upon billions of droplets, each typically a hundredth of a millimetre or so across. Droplets that small fall incredibly slowly through the air, and gentle rising air currents easily hold them up. Rain begins only when droplets collide and merge, or when ice crystals grow at the expense of droplets, until they become heavy enough to fall faster than the air is rising.

sections.key: Clouds are grouped by their height and by whether they spread out in sheets or pile up in heaps.
sections.b: Today's official system, set out in the World Meteorological Organization's International Cloud Atlas, recognises ten main cloud types grouped by height. High clouds, roughly five kilometres up or more, are made of ice crystals: wispy cirrus, patchy cirrocumulus and milky sheets of cirrostratus. Middle clouds carry the prefix alto, such as altocumulus, which forms rows of puffy patches, and altostratus, a grey veil through which the Sun looks like a smudged coin. Low clouds include stratus, a flat grey blanket that can sit on hilltops as fog, stratocumulus in lumpy layers, and nimbostratus, the thick, dark sheet behind a long day of steady rain. Cumulus and cumulonimbus are special because they can stretch from low levels to great heights.

sections.key: Cumulonimbus can tower more than ten kilometres high and brings storms, hail and lightning.
sections.b: On a hot, humid afternoon, a small cumulus cloud can keep growing as warm, moist air surges upwards inside it. As water vapour condenses, it releases heat, which makes the air rise even faster. A towering cloud like this is called cumulus congestus. If it keeps going, it becomes a cumulonimbus, the thunderstorm cloud, whose top can reach twelve kilometres or more, and higher still in the tropics. When the rising air hits the stable layer at the base of the stratosphere, it can rise no further and spreads sideways into a flat anvil shape. Inside, strong updrafts and downdrafts toss raindrops and ice about, building hail and separating electrical charges. Cumulonimbus clouds bring downpours, damaging winds, lightning and, occasionally, tornadoes.

sections.key: Watching how clouds change over a few hours can tell you what weather is coming.
sections.b: Clouds are not perfect forecasters, but their patterns carry real information. High cirrus streaks that gradually thicken into a pale sheet of cirrostratus, sometimes with a halo around the Sun or Moon, often mean a warm front and its rain are approaching within a day or so. Cumulus that stay small and flat-topped on a sunny morning suggest a settled day, but cumulus that swell into tall, cauliflower towers by midday warn of afternoon storms. Lens-shaped lenticular clouds hovering near mountains signal strong winds aloft. Clouds still hold surprises. In 2017 the International Cloud Atlas added a new feature called asperitas, a dramatic, wave-like underside first championed by members of the public in the Cloud Appreciation Society.

quiz.q: What does the cloud name ‘cumulus’ mean?
quiz.e: Luke Howard chose cumulus, Latin for heap, for the puffy, piled-up clouds. Stratus means layer and cirrus a curl of hair.

quiz.q: What do cloud droplets need in order to form?
o: Tiny particles such as dust or sea salt to condense onto
quiz.e: Water vapour condenses around microscopic condensation nuclei like salt, dust and smoke once air cools to its dew point.

quiz.q: Why does a cloud holding hundreds of tonnes of water not fall?
o: Clouds are lighter than air because they are made of steam
The weight is spread among tiny droplets that fall very slowly and are held up by rising air
The Earth's magnetic field supports them
quiz.e: Each droplet is minute, so it sinks extremely slowly and gentle updrafts keep it aloft until droplets merge into raindrops.

quiz.q: What causes the flat ‘anvil’ top of a thunderstorm cloud?
o: Strong winds cutting the top off
Rising air reaching the stable base of the stratosphere and spreading sideways
Ice crystals melting at the top
quiz.e: Updrafts cannot punch far into the stable stratosphere, so the cloud spreads out horizontally into an anvil.

quiz.q: Thin cirrus gradually thickening into cirrostratus with a halo often signals what?
o: A warm front and rain approaching
A guaranteed week of fine weather
quiz.e: Thickening high cloud is a classic sign that a warm front and its rain are on the way, often within a day or so.

LESSONS.title: Tornadoes: the most violent winds on Earth
LESSONS.hook: Tornadoes produce the fastest winds measured near the ground, yet they are small, brief and still not fully understood. Here is what we do know.

sections.key: A tornado is a violently rotating column of air reaching from a storm cloud to the ground.
sections.b: A tornado is a column of rapidly spinning air that is in contact with both the ground and the base of a thunderstorm cloud. Many are visible as a funnel because falling pressure inside causes moisture to condense, and dust and debris thicken the shape. Some, though, are almost invisible until they hit something, and others are hidden behind curtains of rain. Most tornadoes are fairly modest, lasting a few minutes and travelling a few kilometres. A small fraction become monsters, hundreds of metres wide, staying on the ground for an hour or more and carving a path of destruction tens of kilometres long. Their small size and short lives are part of what makes them so hard to study and forecast precisely.

sections.key: The strongest tornadoes come from supercells, thunderstorms with a rotating updraft.
sections.b: Most powerful tornadoes form in a special kind of thunderstorm called a supercell. The ingredients are warm, moist air near the ground, cooler, drier air above, something to lift the air, and wind shear, meaning winds that change speed and direction with height. Wind shear can set the lower atmosphere rolling horizontally, like a pencil spinning on a desk. When a strong updraft tilts that rolling air upright, the whole updraft begins to rotate. This rotating column, several kilometres wide, is called a mesocyclone. Under the right conditions, a much narrower and more intense vortex develops beneath it and touches down. Exactly why some supercells produce tornadoes while most do not is still an active area of research.

sections.key: The United States has more tornadoes than anywhere else, because of its unusual geography.
sections.b: The United States records on the order of a thousand or more tornadoes in a typical year, far more than any other country. Its geography is the reason. Warm, humid air flows north from the Gulf of Mexico, dry air descends from the Rocky Mountains and the desert south west, and cold air sweeps down from Canada, all meeting over the flat central plains with no east to west mountain range to keep them apart. The region from Texas to South Dakota is nicknamed Tornado Alley, and the south east also sees many deadly tornadoes. The worst in American history, the Tri-State Tornado of 1925, killed nearly 700 people across Missouri, Illinois and Indiana. Bangladesh, however, suffered the deadliest tornado on record, in 1989.

sections.key: Tornadoes are rated by the damage they cause, because their winds are rarely measured directly.
sections.b: Tornado winds are almost impossible to measure with ordinary instruments, which are usually destroyed or simply not in the right place. In 1971 the Japanese American meteorologist Ted Fujita created a scale that estimated wind speed from the damage left behind. The United States replaced it in 2007 with the Enhanced Fujita scale, which runs from EF0, peeling shingles and breaking branches, to EF5, where well built houses are swept off their foundations. EF5 winds are estimated at over 320 kilometres per hour. Portable Doppler radar has since allowed scientists to chase storms and measure winds inside them. During the Oklahoma tornado outbreak of May 1999, a truck-mounted radar recorded winds of around 480 kilometres per hour, among the highest wind speeds ever measured on Earth.

sections.key: Australia does get tornadoes, though they are usually weaker and less frequent than in America.
sections.b: Many Australians are surprised to learn that tornadoes happen here too. They are reported every year, most often in the south west of Western Australia, along the eastern seaboard and in parts of inland New South Wales and Queensland, and some are spawned by tropical cyclones as they come ashore. Most are short-lived and weak, but there have been destructive ones, such as the tornado that tore through Bucca in Queensland in 1992. A common confusion is worth clearing up. The ‘willy-willy’ of outback folklore is usually a dust devil, a spinning column of air that forms on hot, clear days from heated ground, not from a storm. Dust devils are mostly harmless curiosities, while true tornadoes need a thunderstorm overhead.

sections.key: Shelter low, inside and away from windows; opening windows to ‘equalise pressure’ is a myth.
sections.b: Safety advice for tornadoes is simple and well established. Take warnings seriously, and in Australia follow the Bureau of Meteorology's severe thunderstorm warnings and call 000 in a life-threatening emergency. If a tornado approaches, go to the lowest floor of a sturdy building and get into a small interior room, such as a bathroom or hallway, with as many walls as possible between you and the outside. Stay away from windows, and cover your head and neck. Cars and caravans offer poor protection. One old myth deserves retiring. People were once told to open windows so the house would not explode from low pressure. In fact houses are destroyed by wind and flying debris, and time spent opening windows is time not spent sheltering.

quiz.q: What is a mesocyclone?
o: A rotating updraft inside a supercell thunderstorm
A cyclone that forms in mid-latitudes
The calm eye of a tornado
quiz.e: Wind shear tilted upright by a strong updraft makes the updraft rotate. This broad rotating column is the mesocyclone, from which strong tornadoes can form.

quiz.q: Why does the central United States get so many tornadoes?
o: It has the hottest summers on Earth
Contrasting air masses meet over flat plains with no east to west mountains to separate them
It lies on a tectonic plate boundary
quiz.e: Humid Gulf air, dry western air and cold Canadian air collide over the plains, creating ideal conditions for supercells.

quiz.q: How is a tornado's rating on the Enhanced Fujita scale usually decided?
o: By counting how long it lasts
By the colour of the funnel
quiz.e: Because winds are rarely measured directly, EF ratings are estimated from the damage the tornado leaves behind.

quiz.q: What is the outback ‘willy-willy’ usually?
o: A dust devil formed from hot ground, not a storm
quiz.e: Willy-willies are usually dust devils, which form on hot clear days. True tornadoes need a thunderstorm above them.

quiz.q: Why should you NOT open windows when a tornado approaches?
o: Houses are destroyed by wind and debris, not pressure, and it wastes time you need for sheltering
It increases the risk of lightning
quiz.e: The pressure myth has been debunked. The priority is to get to a small interior room on the lowest floor, away from windows.

LESSONS.title: Antarctica: the continent of extremes
LESSONS.hook: The coldest, windiest, highest and driest continent holds most of the world's ice, and lakes hidden kilometres beneath it.

sections.key: Antarctica is almost twice the size of Australia and holds about 90 per cent of the world's ice.
sections.b: Antarctica covers about 14 million square kilometres, nearly twice the area of Australia. Almost all of it lies under an ice sheet that averages around two kilometres thick and in places is more than four kilometres deep. That ice holds roughly 90 per cent of all the ice on Earth and about 70 per cent of its fresh water. If it all melted, which would take many thousands of years, global sea levels would rise by close to 60 metres. The ice is so heavy that it presses the rock beneath it down into the Earth's mantle. Because of the ice sheet's thickness, Antarctica has the highest average elevation of any continent. Beneath the ice lie mountain ranges, valleys and even volcanoes.

sections.key: Russia's Vostok Station recorded −89.2°C in 1983, the lowest air temperature ever measured.
sections.b: On 21 July 1983, at Russia's Vostok Station on the high East Antarctic plateau, thermometers recorded an air temperature of −89.2°C, the coldest ever directly measured on Earth's surface. Satellites have since detected even colder snow surfaces in hollows on the plateau, below −90°C. At those temperatures, exposed skin freezes in moments and breath can crackle. Antarctica is colder than the Arctic for several reasons. It is a high landmass rather than a frozen ocean, so it does not benefit from the relative warmth of seawater beneath it. Its bright white surface reflects most incoming sunlight. And for months each winter, the Sun does not rise at all over much of the continent, so heat simply radiates away into space.

sections.key: Despite all that ice, Antarctica's interior receives less precipitation than many hot deserts.
sections.b: A desert is defined by how little precipitation falls, not by heat, and by that measure much of Antarctica is a desert. Cold air holds very little moisture, so the high interior receives only a few centimetres of water equivalent each year, as fine snow and ice crystals. The ice sheet has built up not because it snows heavily but because almost nothing melts, so tiny amounts accumulated over hundreds of thousands of years. Some places are drier still. The McMurdo Dry Valleys are largely free of ice and snow, scoured by fierce winds, and parts are thought to have seen little or no rain for a very long time. Scientists use them to test equipment and ideas for exploring Mars.

sections.key: Cold, heavy air pouring off the ice plateau creates some of the strongest winds on the planet.
sections.b: Antarctica's interior is a vast dome of ice, and the air above it becomes intensely cold and dense. Gravity pulls this heavy air downhill towards the coast, where it can accelerate into ferocious winds called katabatic winds, from a Greek word meaning going down. Some coastal places are battered by them almost constantly. The Australian geologist Douglas Mawson experienced this during his Australasian Antarctic Expedition of 1911 to 1914. His base at Cape Denison in Commonwealth Bay was so wind-lashed that he titled his account of the expedition The Home of the Blizzard. Expedition members learned to walk bent almost horizontally into gusts. The same journey saw Mawson's harrowing solo trek back to base after both his companions died.

sections.key: The Antarctic Treaty of 1959 set the continent aside for peace and science.
sections.b: Seven countries, including Australia, claim parts of Antarctica, and Australia's claim, the Australian Antarctic Territory, is the largest at about 42 per cent of the continent. Yet these claims are effectively frozen. In 1959, at the height of the Cold War, twelve nations signed the Antarctic Treaty, which came into force in 1961. It bans military activity and nuclear explosions, guarantees freedom of scientific research and requires countries to share their findings. A later agreement, the Madrid Protocol of 1991, banned mining and set strict environmental rules. More than fifty countries have now joined the treaty system. Australia runs three permanent research stations on the continent, Casey, Davis and Mawson, and a fourth on sub-Antarctic Macquarie Island.

sections.key: Hundreds of liquid lakes lie beneath the ice, and the largest land animal is a tiny insect.
sections.b: One of Antarctica's great surprises is that liquid water lies far beneath the ice. Radar surveys have found hundreds of subglacial lakes, kept from freezing by the insulating ice above and by heat rising from the Earth below. The largest known is Lake Vostok, buried under about four kilometres of ice, which Russian drillers reached in 2012. Some of these lakes are linked by rivers flowing under the ice sheet. On the surface, life clings mostly to the coasts. Penguins, seals and seabirds feed in the rich surrounding ocean, and emperor penguins remarkably breed through the dark winter on the sea ice. There are no native land mammals. The largest animal living permanently on land is a wingless midge only a few millimetres long.

quiz.q: Roughly how much would sea levels rise if all of Antarctica's ice melted?
quiz.e: Antarctica's ice sheet holds enough water to raise global sea levels by close to 60 metres, though full melting would take many thousands of years.

quiz.q: Why is Antarctica colder than the Arctic?
o: It is closer to the Sun's shadow
It is a high landmass rather than a frozen ocean, and its white surface reflects sunlight
It has more volcanoes cooling the air
It spins faster than the North Pole
quiz.e: The Arctic is a frozen ocean warmed slightly by the sea beneath, while Antarctica is a high, reflective continent.

quiz.q: What are katabatic winds?
o: Cold, dense air flowing downhill off the ice plateau
Winds caused by the Earth's rotation alone
quiz.e: Katabatic means going down. Heavy, cold air drains off the high interior towards the coast, sometimes at great speed.

quiz.q: What does the Antarctic Treaty system do?
o: Divides Antarctica equally among all nations
Bans military activity and mining while protecting scientific research
Gives Australia full ownership of the continent
Allows oil drilling with a permit
quiz.e: The 1959 treaty bans military activity and guarantees scientific freedom, and the 1991 Madrid Protocol bans mining.

quiz.q: What is the largest animal living permanently on land in Antarctica?
o: A wingless midge a few millimetres long
quiz.e: Penguins and seals depend on the sea. The largest true land-dweller is a tiny flightless midge.

LESSONS.title: Everest: the roof of the world
LESSONS.hook: The highest mountain on Earth is still rising, and its summit is made of rock that formed at the bottom of an ancient sea.

sections.key: Everest's official height is 8,848.86 metres, agreed by Nepal and China in 2020.
sections.b: Mount Everest sits on the border between Nepal and the Tibet region of China. Measuring it has always been tricky, partly because its peak is capped with snow that changes depth, and partly because the two countries used different methods. For decades Nepal and China quoted slightly different figures. In December 2020 they jointly announced a new official height of 8,848.86 metres, based on satellite positioning and surveyors carrying equipment to the summit. At that height the air pressure is only about a third of what it is at sea level, so each breath delivers far less oxygen. Above about 8,000 metres lies what climbers call the death zone, where the human body slowly deteriorates and cannot acclimatise.

sections.key: The rock at Everest's top contains fossils of sea creatures, because it formed on an ocean floor.
sections.b: The very top of Everest is made of limestone that formed hundreds of millions of years ago on the floor of a shallow sea. Geologists have found fossils of marine creatures such as trilobites and crinoids, also called sea lilies, in this rock. How did a seabed end up nearly nine kilometres in the sky? The answer lies in plate tectonics. Long ago, India was a separate landmass drifting north across an ocean called the Tethys. When India collided with Asia, sediments from the ocean floor were crumpled, stacked and pushed upwards. The great Himalayan range is the result of that crash, which is still going on. India continues to push north by a few centimetres every year.

sections.key: The Himalaya are being pushed up by a few millimetres each year, while erosion wears them down.
sections.b: The collision between India and Asia began around 50 million years ago, though geologists still debate the exact timing. It has not stopped. Precise satellite measurements show that parts of the Himalaya are being pushed upwards by a few millimetres each year. At the same time, ice, landslides, rivers and frost shatter the rock and carry it away, so the height we see is a constant tug of war between uplift and erosion. Earthquakes are part of the same process. The devastating Nepal earthquake of April 2015 was caused by the Indian plate sliding beneath Asia. It also shifted the land around Everest slightly, one reason the mountain was measured again a few years later.

sections.key: Everest was named after a surveyor who reportedly objected to the honour.
sections.b: The mountain has had local names for centuries. In Tibetan it is Chomolungma, often translated as goddess mother of the world, and in Nepali it is Sagarmatha. To the British surveyors of the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India, it was simply Peak XV. Calculations completed around 1852, in which the Indian mathematician Radhanath Sikdar is often credited with a key role, showed it to be the highest mountain on Earth. The Surveyor General, Andrew Waugh, proposed naming it after his predecessor, Sir George Everest. Everest himself reportedly objected, arguing that his name could not easily be written or pronounced by local people. The name was officially adopted in 1865 anyway. Fittingly, he pronounced his own surname ‘Eve-rest’.

sections.key: Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay reached the summit on 29 May 1953.
sections.b: British expeditions attempted Everest from the Tibetan side in the 1920s. In 1924 George Mallory and Andrew Irvine vanished high on the mountain, and whether they reached the top before dying remains one of mountaineering's enduring mysteries. Mallory's body was found in 1999, but the camera they may have carried has never been recovered. After Nepal opened its borders, a British expedition led by John Hunt tried the southern route in 1953. On 29 May, the New Zealand beekeeper Edmund Hillary and the Sherpa mountaineer Tenzing Norgay stood on the summit. The news reached London on the morning of Queen Elizabeth II's coronation. Since then, thousands of people have climbed Everest, though it remains genuinely dangerous, and hundreds have died trying.

sections.key: Measured in other ways, Mauna Kea and Chimborazo can claim titles of their own.
sections.b: Everest's summit is the highest point above sea level, but there are other ways to measure a mountain. Mauna Kea in Hawaii rises about 4,200 metres above the sea, yet most of the volcano is hidden underwater. Measured from its base on the ocean floor, it stands around 10,000 metres, taller than Everest. Then there is Chimborazo, a volcano in Ecuador only about 6,260 metres above sea level. Because the Earth spins, it bulges slightly at the equator, and Chimborazo sits near the top of that bulge. As a result, its summit is the point on Earth's surface farthest from the planet's centre, roughly two kilometres farther out than Everest's. Which mountain is biggest depends on the question you ask.

quiz.q: Why are there marine fossils near the summit of Everest?
o: The rock formed on an ancient sea floor and was pushed up when India collided with Asia
Sea levels were once nine kilometres higher
quiz.e: The summit limestone formed in the Tethys Ocean, and the India–Asia collision crumpled and lifted it into the sky.

quiz.q: What is happening to the height of the Himalaya today?
o: They are rising by a few millimetres a year, while erosion wears them down
They stopped changing millions of years ago
They are rising by several metres a year
quiz.e: India is still pushing into Asia, lifting the range a few millimetres a year, while erosion constantly removes rock.

quiz.q: What was Everest called by the British surveyors before it was named?
quiz.e: It was catalogued as Peak XV until calculations showed it was the world's highest mountain.

quiz.q: Who were the first people confirmed to reach the summit of Everest?
quiz.e: Hillary and Tenzing reached the top on 29 May 1953. Whether Mallory and Irvine made it in 1924 remains unknown.

quiz.q: Why is Chimborazo's summit farther from Earth's centre than Everest's?
o: It is taller above sea level
It sits near the equator, where the Earth bulges outwards
It is a volcano that is still growing
It stands on the ocean floor
quiz.e: The spinning Earth bulges at the equator, so Chimborazo's summit is the farthest point from the planet's centre.

LESSONS.title: Kati Thanda–Lake Eyre: Australia's sometimes sea
LESSONS.hook: For most of its life it is a blinding sheet of salt. Then, every so often, distant floods turn it into Australia's largest lake and birds arrive from hundreds of kilometres away.

sections.key: Kati Thanda–Lake Eyre lies about 15 metres below sea level in outback South Australia.
sections.b: In the arid north of South Australia lies Kati Thanda–Lake Eyre, the lowest natural point on the Australian continent, about 15 metres below sea level. It has two names. Kati Thanda comes from the Arabana people, the traditional owners, for whom the lake and its surrounds hold deep cultural significance, and the dual name was formally adopted in 2012. Lake Eyre honours Edward John Eyre, the English-born explorer who saw parts of it in 1840. Most of the time the lake is dry, a vast flat crust of salt that glares white under the sun. It is made up of two main parts, Lake Eyre North, much the larger, and Lake Eyre South, joined by a narrow channel.

sections.h: A drain for a sixth of a continent
sections.key: The lake sits at the bottom of one of the world's largest inland drainage basins.
sections.b: Water flows downhill, and in central Australia much of it flows towards Kati Thanda. Its catchment, the Lake Eyre Basin, covers about 1.2 million square kilometres, roughly one sixth of Australia, stretching across parts of Queensland, the Northern Territory, South Australia and New South Wales. It is one of the largest internally draining basins in the world, which means none of its water ever reaches the sea. Rivers such as the Diamantina, the Georgina and Cooper Creek wander slowly across this immense, flat landscape, spreading into channels the locals call the Channel Country. Floodwater can take months to travel from Queensland to the lake, and most of it evaporates or soaks into the ground along the way.

sections.key: The lake fills only occasionally, and filling completely is rare, happening a few times a century.
sections.b: Because the basin is so dry and the evaporation so intense, it takes truly exceptional rains to deliver serious water to Kati Thanda. Small floods reach the lake fairly often, but a significant filling happens only every several years, and filling it close to capacity happens only a few times in a century. The great floods of the 1950s and 1974 were among the biggest on record. When it is full, it becomes the largest lake in Australia, covering around 9,500 square kilometres. Even then it is shallow, mostly just a few metres deep. As the water spreads over the salt crust, it dissolves salt and turns progressively saltier, and the shallow water can glow pink from salt-loving algae and microbes.

sections.key: Floods trigger a boom of fish, shrimp and birds, including pelicans flying in from the coast.
sections.b: When water arrives, the desert erupts with life. Eggs of tiny crustaceans, such as brine shrimp, that have lain dormant in the dry mud hatch within days. Fish washed down the rivers multiply in the fresher water. Then the birds come. Pelicans, silver gulls, terns, ducks and other waterbirds arrive in huge numbers, many to breed on islands in the lake. Australian pelicans appear to fly hundreds of kilometres from the coast to reach the water, and exactly how they detect that the lake has filled remains a mystery. Breeding can be a race against time. As the lake shrinks and salt rises, fish die off and the food runs out, and colonies may be abandoned before all the chicks fledge.

sections.h: A speed record on the salt
sections.key: In 1964 Donald Campbell set a world land speed record on the lake's dry bed.
sections.b: The lake's flat, hard salt surface once attracted record breakers. In 1964 the British driver Donald Campbell brought his jet-turbine car, Bluebird CN7, to Lake Eyre. His attempt was plagued by bad luck, as unusual rain softened the salt and delayed his runs for weeks. On 17 July 1964, on a surface still damp and far from ideal, he finally set a world land speed record of about 648 kilometres per hour, or 403 miles per hour. Later that same year he set a water speed record in Western Australia, becoming the only person to break both records in the same year. His father, Malcolm Campbell, had also held both records, and the Bluebird name ran through the family's machines.

sections.key: The basin is one of the world's last great unregulated river systems.
sections.b: Many of the world's great river systems have been dammed and drained for irrigation, but the rivers of the Lake Eyre Basin still largely flow as they always have, in irregular boom and bust cycles. This makes the basin one of the largest unregulated, dryland river systems left on Earth. That natural pattern drives everything, from fish breeding to the cattle stations of the Channel Country, whose pastures green after floods. Much of the region also sits above part of the Great Artesian Basin, a huge underground water reserve that feeds natural springs, such as the mound springs near the lake's southern edge. Protecting this system has become a priority for scientists, pastoralists and the Aboriginal communities who have cared for it for tens of thousands of years.

quiz.q: Roughly how far below sea level is the lowest part of Kati Thanda–Lake Eyre?
quiz.e: The lake's lowest point is about 15 metres below sea level, the lowest natural point in Australia.

quiz.q: What does it mean that the Lake Eyre Basin is ‘internally draining’?
o: Its water flows underground to the ocean
Its water never reaches the sea
It drains into the Murray River
It is fed only by rainfall on the lake itself
quiz.e: Water in the basin flows towards the lake and then evaporates or soaks away, never reaching the ocean.

quiz.q: How often does the lake fill close to its full capacity?
o: Only a few times a century
quiz.e: Small floods reach the lake fairly often, but filling close to capacity happens only a few times each century.

quiz.q: What is still not fully understood about pelicans at Lake Eyre?
o: How they detect, from far away, that the lake has filled
Whether they can swim in salt water
quiz.e: Pelicans arrive from hundreds of kilometres away when the lake fills, and how they know remains a mystery.

quiz.q: What did Donald Campbell achieve on Lake Eyre in 1964?
o: The first sailing race on the lake
quiz.e: Campbell set the land speed record on the salt in July 1964, then took the water speed record later that year in Western Australia.

LESSONS.title: Supervolcanoes: the truth about Yellowstone
LESSONS.hook: A few volcanoes have erupted on a scale that dwarfs anything in recorded history. Are they overdue to do it again? The real answer is calmer than the headlines.

sections.key: A supereruption ejects more than 1,000 cubic kilometres of material in one event.
sections.b: Volcanologists measure eruptions on the Volcanic Explosivity Index, which runs from 0 to 8. Each step up represents roughly ten times more erupted material. An eruption rated 8, the top of the scale, blasts out more than 1,000 cubic kilometres of ash, pumice and rock. For comparison, the 1980 eruption of Mount St Helens produced around one cubic kilometre. A volcano capable of a VEI 8 eruption has become known as a supervolcano, a popular rather than strictly scientific term that spread widely through television documentaries around the year 2000. Supervolcanoes rarely look like classic cone-shaped mountains. Instead, their eruptions empty such a vast underground magma reservoir that the ground collapses, leaving an enormous depression called a caldera.

sections.key: Yellowstone has had three giant caldera-forming eruptions, two of them supereruptions.
sections.b: Yellowstone National Park, mostly in the American state of Wyoming, sits above one of the world's best known volcanic systems. Over the past 2.1 million years, it has produced three huge caldera-forming eruptions. The first, about 2.1 million years ago, was the largest, ejecting around 2,500 cubic kilometres of material. The second, about 1.3 million years ago, was much smaller. The third, about 631,000 years ago, produced around 1,000 cubic kilometres and formed the caldera seen in the park today. Ash from these eruptions blanketed much of North America. Between and since these giants, Yellowstone has erupted many times on a smaller scale, mostly as slow-moving lava flows. The most recent lava flow was roughly 70,000 years ago.

sections.key: Yellowstone sits over a hotspot, and a trail of older calderas stretches across Idaho.
sections.b: Yellowstone is far from any plate boundary, so why is it volcanic? The leading explanation is a hotspot, a plume of unusually hot rock rising from deep within the Earth's mantle. The plume stays roughly in place while the North American plate slides slowly south west over it. As a result, the volcanic activity has appeared to march north east over millions of years, leaving a line of older, worn down calderas across the Snake River Plain of southern Idaho. Yellowstone is simply the current location. The heat is also what powers its famous hydrothermal features. Yellowstone contains more than half of the world's active geysers, including Old Faithful, which erupts on a fairly predictable schedule, typically every hour or two.

sections.key: No. Volcanoes do not erupt on a timetable, and the risk in any given year is very small.
sections.b: A common claim online is that Yellowstone is overdue for a supereruption, because the gaps between its big eruptions average around 700,000 years. This reasoning does not hold up. Three events are far too few to establish a pattern, the gaps between them were quite different, and volcanoes do not work like clocks. Studies of the magma beneath Yellowstone suggest the reservoir is mostly solid crystal mush, with only a modest fraction of molten rock, far less than would likely be needed for a supereruption. The United States Geological Survey monitors the area closely with seismometers, GPS and gas sensors. It considers a future supereruption possible but highly unlikely in any given year, and judges smaller lava flows or steam explosions much more likely.

sections.key: The Toba supereruption, about 74,000 years ago, was once blamed for nearly wiping out humanity.
sections.b: The largest eruption of the past couple of million years happened at Toba, on the Indonesian island of Sumatra, about 74,000 years ago. It ejected something like 2,800 cubic kilometres of material and left a caldera now filled by Lake Toba, about 100 kilometres long. In the 1990s, some researchers proposed that Toba caused a volcanic winter so severe that it pushed early humans to the brink of extinction, a genetic bottleneck. The idea became famous, but newer evidence has weakened it. Archaeological sites in India and South Africa suggest people living through the eruption carried on making tools and finding food. Many scientists now think Toba's climate effects were real but shorter or more patchy than once feared.

sections.key: New Zealand's Lake Taupō fills the caldera of the youngest known supereruption.
sections.b: The world's most recent supereruption happened not far from Australia. About 25,500 years ago, the Taupō volcano in the North Island of New Zealand produced the Oruanui eruption, ejecting more than 1,000 cubic kilometres of material. Ash fell over much of New Zealand and as far as the Chatham Islands. Lake Taupō, New Zealand's largest lake, now fills part of the collapsed caldera. Taupō erupted again around 232 CE, in the Hatepe eruption, one of the most violent of the past few thousand years, though not on a super scale. It remains an active system that scientists watch carefully. Like Yellowstone, its quiet beauty, with hot springs and steaming vents, sits on top of an extraordinary history.

quiz.q: What defines a supereruption on the Volcanic Explosivity Index?
o: Any eruption that lasts more than a year
An eruption ejecting more than 1,000 cubic kilometres of material
An eruption that produces lava flows over 100 kilometres long
Any eruption that kills more than 10,000 people
quiz.e: A VEI 8 eruption ejects more than 1,000 cubic kilometres, about a thousand times more than Mount St Helens in 1980.

quiz.q: Why is there a line of old calderas across southern Idaho?
o: Yellowstone used to be several separate volcanoes on a plate boundary
The North American plate has moved over a stationary hotspot
quiz.e: As the plate drifted south west over the mantle hotspot, volcanic activity appeared to move north east, leaving older calderas behind.

quiz.q: Why is the claim that Yellowstone is ‘overdue’ misleading?
o: Volcanoes do not erupt on regular timetables, and three events are too few to define a pattern
Its eruptions happen exactly every 100,000 years
quiz.e: Eruption gaps vary, volcanoes are not clocks, and current evidence suggests the magma reservoir is mostly solid crystal mush.

quiz.q: What has newer evidence suggested about the Toba eruption's effect on humans?
o: It definitely wiped out most humans outside Africa
People in places like India and South Africa appear to have carried on living through it
It caused humans to migrate to Australia
It had no effect on climate at all
quiz.e: Archaeological sites suggest people coped, weakening the once-popular idea of a near-extinction bottleneck.

quiz.q: Where was the world's most recent known supereruption?
quiz.e: The Oruanui eruption at Taupō, about 25,500 years ago, is the youngest known supereruption.

LESSONS.title: When the Sahara was green
LESSONS.hook: Ten thousand years ago, people fished, swam and herded cattle across land that is now the world's largest hot desert. A wobble in Earth's orbit explains how.

sections.key: Rock art and fossils show the Sahara once had lakes, grasslands and large animals.
sections.b: Today the Sahara covers around nine million square kilometres of North Africa, an area larger than Australia, and much of it receives almost no rain. Yet scattered across it are clues to a very different past. Rock paintings and engravings in places such as Tassili n'Ajjer in Algeria show giraffes, elephants, rhinoceroses, hippopotamuses and herds of cattle, sometimes with people hunting or tending them. Fossilised bones of crocodiles and fish lie in what is now bare sand. Ancient shorelines mark the edges of vanished lakes. Mega-Lake Chad, a huge ancestor of today's shrunken Lake Chad, once covered hundreds of thousands of square kilometres. Scientists call this wetter period the African Humid Period, which lasted roughly from 11,000 to 5,000 years ago.

sections.key: A cave in the Egyptian desert contains famous paintings that appear to show people swimming.
sections.b: In 1933 the Hungarian desert explorer László Almásy, later fictionalised in the novel and film The English Patient, visited a rock shelter in the remote Gilf Kebir plateau of south western Egypt. On its walls were small painted human figures with their arms and legs stretched out, apparently swimming. The site became known as the Cave of Swimmers. Almásy suggested the paintings showed that the area had once held water, an idea that seemed outlandish at the time in one of the driest places on Earth. Researchers still debate what the figures actually represent, and some suggest they may have spiritual meaning rather than showing literal swimming. But the wider evidence confirms that the region was once far wetter than it is now.

sections.key: Slow changes in Earth's orbit strengthened summer sunshine and pulled the monsoon rains north.
sections.b: The main driver of the green Sahara was astronomical. The Earth's axis slowly wobbles, like a spinning top, in a cycle of roughly 20,000 to 26,000 years called precession. This changes the time of year when Earth is closest to the Sun. Around 10,000 years ago, the Northern Hemisphere was closest to the Sun during its summer, so summers in North Africa received noticeably more sunshine than today. Stronger summer heating over the land drew the West African monsoon much further north, carrying rain deep into what is now desert. Feedbacks then amplified the change. Plants and lakes darkened the landscape and recycled moisture into the air, helping the rains persist. The opposite process eventually dried the region out.

sections.key: Fishers and herders lived across the wet Sahara, leaving graves, pottery and harpoons behind.
sections.b: People moved into the Sahara as it greened. At Gobero, in Niger, archaeologists working from 2000 onwards uncovered graves belonging to communities who lived beside an ancient lake. Their remains were found with bone harpoons, fish hooks and pottery, along with bones of fish, turtles and crocodiles. One moving burial held a woman and two children, apparently laid to rest together. Across the region, people made some of the world's early pottery and, later, took up cattle herding as conditions became drier and less predictable. Rock art shows people with herds and dogs. This was not a single culture but many groups, adapting over thousands of years to a landscape that kept slowly changing around them.

sections.key: The Sahara became a desert again around 5,000 years ago, though how fast is still debated.
sections.b: As Earth's orbit continued its slow cycle, summer sunshine in North Africa weakened and the monsoon retreated south. The lakes shrank, the grasslands thinned and the Sahara became desert again, around 5,000 years ago. Scientists still debate how quickly this happened. Some evidence from ocean sediments, which record dust blown off Africa, suggests a fairly abrupt shift over a few centuries. Other records, from lakes and pollen, suggest a more gradual drying that varied from place to place. The people living there had to adapt, and many appear to have moved towards more reliable water, including the Nile Valley. Some archaeologists have suggested this migration played a part in the rise of early Egyptian civilisation, though that link remains a hypothesis.

sections.key: The Sahara has turned green many times, and its dust still feeds the Amazon today.
sections.b: The green period of 11,000 to 5,000 years ago was not unique. Sediment records show the Sahara has swung between desert and grassland many times over hundreds of thousands of years, roughly in step with the precession cycle. These green corridors may have opened routes for animals and early humans to move out of Africa. Even as a desert, the Sahara shapes the planet. Winds lift hundreds of millions of tonnes of dust each year and carry it across the Atlantic. Much of it comes from the Bodélé Depression in Chad, the dried bed of the old mega-lake. Satellite studies suggest this dust delivers phosphorus and other nutrients to the Amazon rainforest, helping fertilise one of Earth's richest ecosystems.

quiz.q: Which of these is evidence that the Sahara was once green?
o: Ancient tree rings in the sand
Rock art showing hippos, giraffes and cattle
quiz.e: Rock art at sites like Tassili n'Ajjer, plus fossils of crocodiles and fish, show the Sahara once had water and grasslands.

quiz.q: What mainly caused the green Sahara?
o: A change in ocean salt levels
Earth's orbital wobble boosting summer sunshine and pulling the monsoon north
quiz.e: Precession gave North Africa stronger summer sunshine, drawing the West African monsoon rains far further north.

quiz.q: What did archaeologists find at Gobero in Niger?
o: Graves of lakeside people with harpoons, fish hooks and pottery
quiz.e: Gobero's burials sat beside an ancient lake and included fishing tools and the bones of fish, turtles and crocodiles.

quiz.q: What do scientists still debate about the end of the green Sahara?
o: Whether it happened in the last century
quiz.e: Some records suggest an abrupt shift over centuries, others a gradual drying that varied by place.

quiz.q: How does Saharan dust affect South America today?
o: It causes frequent dust storms in Brazil
It helps fertilise the Amazon rainforest with nutrients such as phosphorus
It blocks rainfall over the Amazon
It has no effect because it never crosses the Atlantic
quiz.e: Dust, much of it from Chad's Bodélé Depression, crosses the Atlantic and delivers nutrients to the Amazon.

LESSONS.title: Monsoons: the seasons of rain
LESSONS.hook: For billions of people, the most important weather event of the year is the arrival of the monsoon. Its rains decide harvests, rivers and even history.

sections.h: A wind, not just a rain
sections.key: A monsoon is a seasonal reversal of winds, which brings a wet season and a dry season.
sections.b: The word monsoon comes, through Portuguese and Dutch, from the Arabic mawsim, meaning season. People often use it to mean heavy rain, but strictly a monsoon is a pattern of winds that reverses direction with the seasons. In a monsoon climate, winds blow in from the ocean for part of the year, carrying moisture and bringing a long wet season. For the rest of the year, they blow from the land, bringing dry weather. Monsoons affect South Asia, East and South East Asia, West Africa, northern Australia and parts of the Americas. The South Asian monsoon is the largest and most famous, and it shapes the lives and livelihoods of well over a billion people.

sections.key: Land heats faster than sea, drawing moist ocean air inland in summer.
sections.b: The basic driver is simple. Land heats up and cools down much faster than the ocean. In late spring and summer, the land warms strongly, and the hot air above it rises, creating lower pressure near the ground. Cooler, moist air flows in from the ocean to replace it. As that humid air is lifted, by heating or by mountains, it cools and drops its moisture as rain. In winter the pattern reverses, as the land becomes cooler than the sea. The real picture is more complicated, because the monsoon is also tied to the seasonal migration of the tropical rain belt, called the Intertropical Convergence Zone, which follows the Sun's strongest heating north and south through the year.

sections.key: The South West monsoon arrives in Kerala around the start of June and brings most of India's yearly rain.
sections.b: Each year the India Meteorological Department watches for the monsoon to arrive on the coast of Kerala, at India's southern tip, typically around 1 June. Over the following weeks, the rains push north and usually cover almost the whole country by early to mid-July. The South West monsoon delivers roughly three quarters of India's annual rainfall in just four months. The Himalaya and the high Tibetan Plateau play a crucial role. The plateau heats strongly in summer, helping power the circulation, while the mountains act as a wall that keeps the moisture over the subcontinent. A good monsoon fills reservoirs, recharges groundwater and feeds rice and other crops. A weak one can mean drought, falling harvests and rising food prices.

sections.key: Monsoon winds hitting hills in north east India produce some of the highest rainfall ever recorded.
sections.b: Some of the wettest places on Earth are in the Khasi Hills of Meghalaya, in north east India. Here monsoon winds loaded with moisture from the Bay of Bengal are forced up steep slopes and wring out torrential rain. The village of Mawsynram averages close to 12 metres of rain a year, among the highest averages anywhere. Nearby Cherrapunji holds a famous record. In the twelve months from August 1860 to July 1861, it received more than 26 metres of rain. People in the region have adapted in remarkable ways. Some Khasi villages have grown living bridges by training the roots of rubber fig trees across rivers over many years, creating structures that grow stronger with age.

sections.key: For centuries, sailors timed voyages across the Indian Ocean to the monsoon winds.
sections.b: Long before engines, the monsoon's predictable winds were a gift to sailors. Because the winds blow reliably one way for part of the year and the other way later, a ship could sail across the Arabian Sea and return months later when the winds reversed. Arab, Indian, Persian, African and later Greek and Roman merchants used this pattern to trade across the Indian Ocean. A first century guidebook in Greek, the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, describes ports and trade goods along these routes. Spices, pepper, textiles, gems and gold moved between East Africa, Arabia, India and South East Asia. The rhythm of the monsoon shaped where port cities grew and how cultures and religions spread around the ocean's rim.

sections.key: Northern Australia's wet season is driven by its own monsoon.
sections.b: Australia has a monsoon too. Across the Top End, the Kimberley and Cape York, the year divides into a wet season, roughly from November or December to March, and a long dry season. During the wet, moist north westerly winds flow in from the warm seas to the north, bringing heavy rain, thunderstorms and high humidity, while tropical cyclones can form offshore. The monsoon does not rain constantly. It arrives in bursts, with active phases of widespread rain separated by breaks. First Nations peoples of the north recognise many more seasons than two, based on detailed knowledge of weather, plants and animals. The wet season floods rivers and wetlands such as those in Kakadu, triggering a flush of life.

quiz.q: What does the word ‘monsoon’ originally mean?
quiz.e: It comes from the Arabic mawsim, meaning season, because the winds reverse with the seasons.

quiz.q: What is the basic driver of a summer monsoon?
o: Land heating faster than sea, drawing moist ocean air inland
Cold air sinking over the ocean
quiz.e: Hot land creates low pressure, and moist ocean air flows in, rising and dropping rain.

quiz.q: Roughly what share of India's annual rainfall comes from the South West monsoon?
quiz.e: The South West monsoon delivers roughly three quarters of India's annual rain in about four months.

quiz.q: Why are places like Mawsynram and Cherrapunji so wet?
o: They sit next to the ocean at sea level
Moist monsoon winds are forced up steep hills, where they cool and drop rain
quiz.e: Moisture from the Bay of Bengal is pushed up the Khasi Hills, wringing out enormous rainfall.

quiz.q: How did monsoon winds help ancient trade?
o: They pushed ships across the Pacific
Their reliable seasonal reversal let ships sail out and return months later
They kept the Indian Ocean calm all year
quiz.e: Sailors timed voyages so the winds carried them one way, then waited for the reversal to sail home.

LESSONS.title: Ice cores: reading Earth's frozen diary
LESSONS.hook: Drill deep into Antarctica and you pull up ancient air, volcanic fallout and the planet's temperature history, layer by layer, going back 800,000 years.

sections.key: Snow that never melts piles up year after year, preserving a record of the atmosphere.
sections.b: In the coldest parts of Greenland and Antarctica, snow falls and never melts. Each year's snow is buried by the next, slowly compressing into a granular material called firn and then, deeper down, into solid ice. The result is an archive stacked in time, with the youngest ice at the top and the oldest near the bedrock, which can be more than three kilometres down. To read it, scientists drill out cylinders of ice, called cores, usually around ten centimetres across, in sections a few metres long. The work is slow, cold and exacting. Cores are logged, cut and shipped frozen to laboratories, where each centimetre can be analysed for chemicals, dust, gas and the makeup of the water itself.

sections.key: In places with heavy snowfall, annual layers can be counted like tree rings.
sections.b: Where snow falls heavily, as in parts of Greenland, each year leaves a distinct layer, because summer and winter snow differ in texture, dust and chemistry. Scientists can count these layers, much like tree rings, back for tens of thousands of years. Deeper down, the ice is squeezed thin and flows, so layers become too fine to count, and ages are estimated using models of how ice flows, combined with known markers. Some of the most useful markers are volcanic. Large eruptions leave sharp spikes of sulphate and sometimes ash in the ice of both hemispheres. The eruption of Tambora in 1815, for example, appears clearly in cores from Greenland and Antarctica, helping scientists tie different records to the same calendar.

sections.key: Tiny bubbles trapped in the ice are real samples of the past atmosphere.
sections.b: The most remarkable treasure in ice cores is air. As firn turns to ice, the spaces between grains close off and trap small bubbles of the atmosphere. In laboratories, scientists crush or melt samples under vacuum and measure the gases inside, including carbon dioxide and methane. There is one subtlety. Air keeps circulating through the porous firn until it is sealed, typically at depths of several tens of metres, so the trapped air is younger than the ice around it, sometimes by thousands of years in slow-snowfall areas. Scientists correct for this gap. Australian researchers made a major contribution with cores from Law Dome, near Casey Station, where high snowfall gives a detailed record of carbon dioxide over the past two thousand years.

sections.key: The ratio of heavy to light water molecules reveals past temperatures.
sections.b: Ice itself holds a record of temperature. Water molecules come in slightly different versions, because some contain heavier isotopes, such as oxygen-18 instead of the common oxygen-16, or deuterium, a heavier form of hydrogen. As moist air travels towards the poles and cools, the heavier molecules tend to rain or snow out first. The colder the conditions, the fewer heavy molecules remain in the snow that eventually falls on the ice sheet. By measuring the ratio of heavy to light isotopes in each layer, scientists can reconstruct how temperature changed over time. This isotope thermometer, developed in large part by the Danish scientist Willi Dansgaard from the 1950s onwards, is one of the foundations of modern climate science.

sections.key: Antarctica's deepest cores show ice ages and warm periods tracking carbon dioxide closely.
sections.b: The longest continuous ice core record comes from Dome C, high on the East Antarctic plateau, drilled by the European Project for Ice Coring in Antarctica, known as EPICA. It reaches back about 800,000 years. The record shows eight full cycles of ice ages and warmer interglacial periods. Through all of them, carbon dioxide and temperature rise and fall together. During cold glacial periods, carbon dioxide sat around 180 parts per million, and during warm interglacials it rose to around 280 to 300. The ice cycles themselves are paced by changes in Earth's orbit, with carbon dioxide acting as a powerful amplifier. For comparison, by the mid-2020s atmospheric carbon dioxide had passed 420 parts per million, far outside the range seen in the entire ice core record.

sections.key: Greenland ice reveals abrupt climate swings and even ancient metal smelting.
sections.b: Greenland cores revealed something unsettling. During the last ice age, temperatures over Greenland repeatedly jumped by several degrees, in some cases up to around ten degrees or more, within just decades, before slowly cooling again. These swings, known as Dansgaard–Oeschger events, showed that climate can change abruptly, not only gradually. The ice also records human history. Lead from mining and smelting drifted north and settled in Greenland's snow, and studies have tracked rises in lead pollution during the height of the Roman Empire and dips during times of war and plague. Ice cores even preserve traces of past wildfires, desert dust storms and changes in sea ice, making them one of the richest archives of the Earth system.

sections.h: The hunt for the oldest ice
sections.key: Scientists are now drilling for ice more than a million years old.
sections.b: The 800,000-year record leaves a big puzzle. About a million years ago, the rhythm of ice ages changed from cycles of roughly 41,000 years to longer, more intense cycles of about 100,000 years, and nobody is certain why. Older ice could help explain it. Finding it is hard, because at the bottom of the ice sheet, heat from the Earth can melt the oldest layers, and flowing ice scrambles them. Teams have used radar to search for sites where ancient ice survives. A European project called Beyond EPICA announced in early 2025 that it had drilled to bedrock at Little Dome C, recovering ice believed to be well over a million years old. Separately, scientists have found scattered fragments of ice more than two million years old in Antarctica's blue ice areas.

quiz.q: Why is the air in ice core bubbles younger than the ice around it?
o: Bubbles rise through the ice over time
Air keeps circulating through porous firn until it is sealed tens of metres down
Modern air leaks in during drilling
Bacteria produce new gases inside the ice
quiz.e: The firn stays open to the atmosphere until bubbles close off at depth, so trapped air is younger than the surrounding ice.

quiz.q: How do isotope ratios in ice reveal past temperatures?
o: Colder conditions leave fewer heavy water molecules in the snow
Heavy isotopes glow under ultraviolet light
quiz.e: Heavy molecules rain or snow out first as air cools, so snow formed in colder conditions has fewer of them.

quiz.q: What range did carbon dioxide stay within over the 800,000-year ice core record?
quiz.e: Glacial periods were around 180 ppm and interglacials around 280 to 300 ppm. By the mid-2020s, levels had passed 420 ppm.

quiz.q: What did Dansgaard–Oeschger events show?
o: That ice ages end only very gradually
That climate can shift abruptly, by several degrees within decades
That Greenland was never covered in ice
quiz.e: Greenland cores revealed sudden warmings during the last ice age, proving climate can change rapidly.

quiz.q: How do large volcanic eruptions help scientists date ice cores?
o: They melt the ice, leaving visible gaps
They leave sulphate spikes that appear in both Greenland and Antarctic ice
They stop snow falling for several years
quiz.e: Sulphate and ash from big eruptions like Tambora mark the same moment in ice from both hemispheres, linking records together.

LESSONS.title: Ireland's Great Hunger, 1845–1852
LESSONS.hook: A microscopic organism destroyed one crop, and within a few years Ireland had lost a quarter of its people. The blight was natural. The scale of the disaster was not.

sections.key: By the 1840s millions of poor Irish people depended almost entirely on the potato.
sections.b: In the early 1840s Ireland had around eight and a half million people, many of them tenant farmers and labourers renting tiny plots from landlords, some of whom lived in England. Wheat, oats, cattle and butter were grown for rent and sale, but the poorest families lived on potatoes. An acre of potatoes could feed a family for much of a year, and the crop grew well in damp, poor soil. Many relied on a single variety, the high yielding but vulnerable ‘lumper’. An adult labourer might eat several kilograms of potatoes a day, with a little buttermilk. It was a diet that kept people alive and surprisingly healthy, as long as the harvest never failed. That one dependency left about a third of the population exposed.

sections.key: A water mould from the Americas turned potato fields black and rotten almost overnight.
sections.b: In 1845 a disease now known as Phytophthora infestans, a fungus-like water mould, reached Europe, most likely carried from the Americas. It spread through Ireland in the late summer of that year. Leaves blackened, the plants collapsed and potatoes rotted in the ground or in storage, giving off a sickening smell. Roughly a third to a half of the 1845 crop was lost. Worse followed. In 1846 the blight destroyed most of the harvest, and families who had eaten their seed potatoes to survive had little to plant in 1847. Blight returned in later years too. Other countries in Europe suffered from the same disease in the mid 1840s, but nowhere else was so large a share of the population so completely dependent on the crop.

sections.key: Government relief existed, but it was shaped by a belief that the market and local taxes should carry the burden.
sections.b: Prime Minister Robert Peel's government quietly bought maize from America in 1845 to sell cheaply and keep prices down. When Lord John Russell's government took over in 1846, it leaned heavily on the idea that the state should not interfere with trade. Starving people were offered work on public projects such as roads, often for wages too low to buy food, sometimes building roads that led nowhere. In 1847 soup kitchens briefly fed around three million people a day, and they worked. Yet they were wound down within months, and responsibility shifted to Ireland's workhouses and local property taxes. A rule called the Gregory clause denied relief to anyone holding more than a quarter acre of land, forcing many to give up their homes to qualify.

sections.key: Ireland kept exporting food during the famine, a fact that still stirs anger and debate.
sections.b: One of the most painful facts of the famine is that grain, cattle, butter and other produce continued to be shipped out of Ireland while people starved.
