Landlords needed rent, farmers sold crops to pay it, and armed guards sometimes escorted food convoys past hungry crowds. Historians debate how much difference keeping that food would have made. From 1847 more grain was coming into Ireland than leaving, and the potato's loss was so vast that exports alone could not have filled the gap. But most agree the deeper problem was choice, not supply. A wealthy empire had the means to keep people alive and instead treated the crisis as a chance to reform Irish agriculture. Senior Treasury official Charles Trevelyan came to symbolise that hard-hearted outlook.

sections.key: Most famine victims died not of starvation alone but of diseases that spread among weakened people.
sections.b: Hunger made people vulnerable, and disease did much of the killing. Typhus, relapsing fever and dysentery swept through crowded workhouses, roadsides and cabins. Scurvy appeared as diets collapsed. Landlords, facing unpaid rents and rising local taxes, evicted hundreds of thousands of tenants, often tearing down cottages so families could not return. Whole communities in the west, especially in counties such as Mayo, Galway and Cork, were devastated. Around one million people died between 1845 and 1852, although exact numbers are uncertain because so many deaths went unrecorded. Irish speakers called it An Gorta Mór, the Great Hunger. The worst year, 1847, became known as Black ’47, and mass graves from that period are still being identified today.

sections.key: Over a million people emigrated, many on crowded, disease-ridden ships.
sections.b: For many families the only hope was to leave. Well over a million people emigrated during the famine years, mostly to Britain, the United States and Canada. Some crossed the Atlantic in overcrowded, poorly supplied vessels that became known as coffin ships. At the quarantine station on Grosse Île in Canada, thousands died of typhus in 1847 alone. Australia received famine emigrants too. Between 1848 and 1850 an assisted scheme brought more than four thousand Irish orphan girls from workhouses to Sydney, Melbourne and Adelaide, where many found work as servants and later married and raised families. Emigration became a habit that lasted generations. Ireland's population kept falling for decades, and the island still holds fewer people today than it did before the famine.

sections.key: The famine reshaped Irish identity, politics and the global Irish diaspora.
sections.b: The Great Hunger left marks everywhere. The Irish language, strongest among the rural poor who suffered most, declined sharply. Bitterness towards British rule hardened and fed later campaigns for land reform and independence. Irish communities abroad, from Boston to Melbourne, carried the memory with them and became politically powerful. Acts of kindness were remembered too. In 1847 the Choctaw Nation in America, who had themselves recently been forced from their lands, sent money to help the starving Irish, a gift honoured today by a sculpture in County Cork. Historians still argue over blame, but most now see the famine as a natural disaster made far deadlier by poverty, a harsh land system and government decisions that put economic doctrine ahead of human lives.

quiz.q: Why were so many Irish people exposed when the potato crop failed?
o: They had never grown potatoes before
The poorest relied almost entirely on potatoes for food
Ireland imported all of its potatoes
quiz.e: The poorest third of the population lived almost entirely on potatoes, often a single variety, so losing the crop meant losing nearly all their food.

quiz.q: What caused the potato blight?
o: A water mould called Phytophthora infestans
quiz.e: The blight was caused by Phytophthora infestans, a fungus-like water mould that probably arrived from the Americas.

quiz.q: What happened to the soup kitchens of 1847?
o: They fed millions but were closed within months
quiz.e: Soup kitchens fed around three million people a day and worked, but the government wound them down quickly and shifted the burden to workhouses.

quiz.q: What killed most famine victims?
o: Diseases such as typhus and dysentery
quiz.e: Hunger weakened people, but fevers and other diseases spreading through crowded places did much of the killing.

quiz.q: Where did a scheme send more than four thousand Irish orphan girls between 1848 and 1850?
quiz.e: An assisted emigration scheme brought Irish workhouse orphan girls to Australian cities, where many worked as servants and later raised families.

LESSONS.title: The Christmas Truce of 1914
LESSONS.hook: Five months into the most industrial war yet fought, enemy soldiers climbed out of their trenches, shook hands and sang carols together. Then they went back to killing each other.

sections.h: A war that was meant to be short
sections.key: By December 1914 the hope of a quick war had died in the mud of the Western Front.
sections.b: When the First World War began in August 1914, many on both sides expected it to be over by Christmas. Instead the German advance into France was stopped at the Marne in September, and both armies dug in. By winter a line of trenches ran from the Belgian coast to the Swiss border. On the British part of the front, around Flanders, opposing trenches were sometimes only fifty to a few hundred metres apart. Soldiers lived in freezing water, surrounded by rats and the unburied dead of the autumn battles. Snipers made raising your head deadly. Yet the closeness had a strange side effect. Men could hear the enemy talking, coughing and singing, and they began to see them as people in the same miserable situation.

sections.key: Even before Christmas, informal habits had grown up that reduced the killing.
sections.b: Long before the famous truce, small unofficial understandings had appeared along quiet parts of the line. Each side might avoid shelling the other at breakfast time, or let men fetch water or bring in wounded without being shot. Historians call this the ‘live and let live’ system. It was never ordered by anyone. It grew from shared exhaustion and a simple logic: if you hold your fire, they might hold theirs. Officers knew it happened and often looked the other way. In December 1914 Pope Benedict XV called for a pause in fighting over Christmas, but the warring governments ignored him. What happened next came not from leaders but from ordinary soldiers acting on their own.

sections.key: On Christmas Eve, German soldiers lit small trees and sang carols, and the British answered.
sections.b: On Christmas Eve 1914, British soldiers in several sectors were astonished to see lights appearing along the German trenches. German troops had placed small Christmas trees, decorated with candles, on their parapets. Then came singing, including the carol ‘Stille Nacht’, Silent Night. British soldiers replied with their own carols, and the two sides applauded each other across no man's land. Shouted conversations followed, helped by the fact that some Germans had worked in Britain before the war and spoke English. Here and there, a few brave men walked out unarmed into the open ground. When nobody fired, others followed. By Christmas morning, along stretches of the front, soldiers who had been trying to kill each other days earlier were standing together in the frozen mud.

sections.key: Soldiers swapped gifts and buried their dead, and some kicked a ball about.
sections.b: Letters home describe an extraordinary day. Men exchanged cigarettes, tobacco, chocolate, plum puddings, sausages, buttons and badges as souvenirs. They showed each other photographs of wives and children. Barbers cut enemy hair. Most importantly, both sides used the calm to recover and bury the bodies that had lain between the lines, and in some places they held joint burial services. Football is the most famous part of the story. Several soldiers wrote about kickabouts with the enemy, sometimes with a makeshift ball, and these accounts seem genuine. But the idea of a single organised match with a final score is much harder to prove. Historians think informal games happened in a few places, not one grand fixture played across the front.

sections.key: The truce was patchy, and in many places the shooting never stopped.
sections.b: It is easy to imagine the whole front falling silent, but that did not happen. The truce was strongest in sectors held by British and German troops, especially around Ypres in Belgium. It occurred in some French and Belgian sectors too, but less often, perhaps because those soldiers were fighting on their own invaded soil. In other places fighting continued and men were killed on Christmas Day. Some truces lasted only a few hours, others until New Year or beyond. By some estimates around one hundred thousand soldiers took part in one way or another, but nobody knows the true figure. Many soldiers felt uneasy, and some officers were furious. Not every man who wrote home that week described peace.

sections.key: Commanders moved to make sure the truce was not repeated.
sections.b: High commands on both sides saw the truce as a threat to discipline. If soldiers came to like their enemies, how could they be ordered to kill them? In the following years strict orders forbade fraternisation, and artillery bombardments were sometimes deliberately scheduled for Christmas. Small, local pauses still happened in 1915, but nothing on the scale of 1914 occurred again. The war grew far more brutal, with poison gas, the Somme and Verdun, and the old mood of shared misery hardened into hatred and grim endurance. When British newspapers printed soldiers' letters and photographs of the truce in January 1915, readers were amazed. The story spread because it seemed almost impossible, a moment of human decency in a machine built for slaughter.

sections.key: The truce shows that ordinary people can recognise a shared humanity even in total war.
sections.b: The Christmas truce has become one of the most retold stories of the First World War, featured in songs, films, advertisements and memorials. Some versions are heavily romanticised, and it is worth remembering how limited and brief it really was. Yet the core is well documented in hundreds of letters and diaries. It reveals something important about how wars work. Armies depend on soldiers being willing to see the other side as an enemy, and that willingness can falter when men meet face to face. The truce did not end the war or even shorten it. Its power lies in a simple, uncomfortable question it leaves behind: if the men in the trenches could stop, why couldn't those in charge?

quiz.q: Why were soldiers able to hear each other across the lines?
o: Opposing trenches were often very close together
quiz.e: In parts of Flanders, opposing trenches were sometimes only tens of metres apart, close enough to hear voices and singing.

quiz.q: What was the ‘live and let live’ system?
o: Informal habits of holding fire that grew up on quiet sectors
A medical program for the wounded
quiz.e: Without any orders, soldiers developed unspoken understandings, such as not firing at mealtimes, that reduced the killing.

quiz.q: What did German soldiers place on their parapets on Christmas Eve 1914?
quiz.e: Germans set out small decorated trees with candles and sang carols such as Silent Night, and British troops answered with carols of their own.

quiz.q: What do historians conclude about football during the truce?
o: There was one official match with a recorded score
Informal kickabouts probably happened in a few places
Football was banned by the Pope
quiz.e: Soldiers' letters describe kickabouts, but evidence for a single organised match with a final score is weak.

quiz.q: How did commanders respond in later years?
o: They made the truce an annual event
They forbade fraternisation and discouraged repeats
They signed a formal Christmas ceasefire
They sent soldiers home every Christmas
quiz.e: Commanders saw the truce as a threat to discipline and issued orders against fraternisation, so nothing on the 1914 scale happened again.

LESSONS.title: The Titanic: one night that changed the sea
LESSONS.hook: On a calm, moonless night in April 1912, the largest ship afloat struck an iceberg and sank in under three hours. The rules that keep ships safe today were written in its wake.

sections.key: Titanic was the largest moving object people had ever built, designed for comfort and size rather than speed.
sections.b: RMS Titanic was built in Belfast by the shipyard Harland and Wolff for the White Star Line, and launched in 1911. About 269 metres long, it was briefly the largest ship in the world. White Star competed with its rival Cunard not on speed but on size and luxury. First class passengers enjoyed a swimming pool, a gymnasium, Turkish baths and grand staircases. Third class, or steerage, was far plainer but still better than on many ships of the time. Below the waterline the hull was divided into sixteen compartments by watertight bulkheads. The ship could stay afloat with any two flooded, and even with the first four flooded. That design gave people great confidence.

sections.key: The idea that White Star loudly advertised Titanic as unsinkable is mostly a later exaggeration.
sections.b: A popular belief says Titanic was famously promoted as unsinkable, tempting fate. The truth is more ordinary. A trade journal described the White Star ships' watertight design as making them ‘practically unsinkable’, and that phrase echoed in the press and in passengers' minds. But it was not a central advertising slogan, and the boldest versions of the claim spread mostly after the disaster, when the irony made it irresistible. Many people at the time did believe that large modern ships were very safe, and that confidence mattered. It helped explain why the ship carried too few lifeboats, why ice warnings were not taken seriously enough, and why some passengers at first refused to leave the warm ship for a small boat on a freezing sea.

sections.key: Titanic received several warnings about ice but kept up a high speed through the night.
sections.b: Titanic left Southampton on 10 April 1912, called at Cherbourg in France and Queenstown in Ireland, and headed for New York with over two thousand people aboard. On 14 April, the ship's wireless operators, employed by the Marconi company, received a series of warnings from other ships about ice ahead. Not all of them reached the bridge, partly because the operators were busy sending passengers' private messages. Captain Edward Smith altered course slightly but kept the ship moving at about 22 knots, close to its top speed, as was normal practice at the time. The sea was flat calm and there was no moon, which made icebergs harder to spot because no waves broke around their base. The lookouts in the crow's nest had no binoculars.

sections.key: The iceberg opened too many compartments, and Titanic sank in about two hours and forty minutes.
sections.b: At about 11.40 pm on 14 April, lookout Frederick Fleet spotted an iceberg dead ahead. The officer on watch ordered a hard turn and the ship began to swing, but too late. The iceberg scraped along the starboard side below the waterline, buckling plates and popping rivets along a long stretch of hull. It was not one huge gash but a series of openings. Water poured into the first five or six compartments, more than the design could survive. Thomas Andrews, the ship's designer, who was aboard, told the captain the ship would sink. As the bow went down, water spilled over the tops of the bulkheads from one compartment into the next. At about 2.20 am on 15 April, Titanic broke apart and sank.

sections.key: Titanic legally carried lifeboats for only about half the people aboard, and many were launched half full.
sections.b: Titanic carried twenty lifeboats, with room for about 1,178 people. That was more than the outdated British rules required, which were based on a ship's weight rather than the number of people aboard, but it was only enough for about half of the roughly 2,200 passengers and crew. Early boats were lowered well below capacity, as crew were unsure of the davits and passengers hesitated to leave. The rule of women and children first was applied strictly on one side of the ship. Survival rates were starkly unequal. Most first class passengers survived, while around three quarters of third class passengers died. More than 1,500 people lost their lives, many in water around minus two degrees, where death could come within minutes.

sections.h: Rescue, and a ship that didn't come
sections.key: Carpathia raced to help, while a much closer ship, Californian, failed to respond.
sections.b: Titanic's wireless operators sent distress calls, including the new signal SOS. The Cunard liner Carpathia, more than 100 kilometres away, turned and steamed at full speed through the ice, arriving about an hour and a half after Titanic sank. It picked up around 700 survivors from the lifeboats. Another ship, the Californian, had stopped for the night in the ice much closer. Its crew saw rockets in the distance but did not understand what they meant, and its only wireless operator had switched off his set and gone to bed. The inquiries that followed criticised Californian's captain, though debate about exactly how close it was continues. Among those who died were the ship's eight musicians, who played on deck as the boats were loaded.

sections.key: The disaster led to international rules on lifeboats, radio watches and ice patrols that still shape shipping.
sections.b: Inquiries in the United States and Britain prompted the first International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea, known as SOLAS, agreed in London in 1914. Ships would have to carry enough lifeboat places for everyone aboard and hold lifeboat drills. Wireless rooms on passenger ships were to be staffed around the clock, so no distress call went unheard. The International Ice Patrol was created to track icebergs in the North Atlantic, and it still operates today. The wreck itself lay undiscovered until 1985, when a team led by Robert Ballard and Jean-Louis Michel found it nearly four kilometres down, broken in two. Its slow decay on the seabed reminds us how a confident age learned humility the hard way.

quiz.q: How many flooded compartments could Titanic survive?
quiz.e: The design could stay afloat with any two compartments flooded or the first four, but the iceberg opened five or six.

quiz.q: What is the truth about the ‘unsinkable’ claim?
o: It was White Star's main advertising slogan
A trade journal called the design ‘practically unsinkable’, and the claim grew after the disaster
The captain announced it at departure
Nobody ever used the word before 1985
quiz.e: The phrase ‘practically unsinkable’ came from a trade journal, and the boldest versions of the myth spread mostly after the sinking.

quiz.q: What kind of damage did the iceberg cause?
o: A series of openings along the hull below the waterline
A hole in the top deck
quiz.e: The iceberg buckled plates and popped rivets, creating a series of openings rather than one giant tear.

quiz.q: Why did Titanic have so few lifeboats?
o: Lifeboats had not yet been invented
Outdated rules based lifeboat numbers on ship weight, not people aboard
quiz.e: British regulations were based on tonnage and badly outdated, so Titanic legally carried boats for only about half of those aboard.

quiz.q: Which international agreement was a direct result of the disaster?
o: The Safety of Life at Sea convention (SOLAS)
The Law of the Sea treaty of 1982
quiz.e: The first SOLAS convention of 1914 required enough lifeboats for all, round-the-clock radio watches and other safety measures.

LESSONS.title: Dunkirk: the miracle of 1940
LESSONS.hook: In nine days in 1940, an army that seemed doomed was carried home across the English Channel. Britain called it a miracle. Churchill warned that wars are not won by evacuations.

sections.key: A rapid German breakthrough in May 1940 cut off the British army and many French troops against the sea.
sections.b: On 10 May 1940 Germany attacked the Netherlands, Belgium and France. Allied commanders expected the main thrust through Belgium, and sent their best troops north to meet it, including most of the British Expeditionary Force. But the real blow came further south. German tanks pushed through the hilly, wooded Ardennes, which the French had thought too difficult for armour, and crossed the Meuse. Moving with astonishing speed, they reached the English Channel near Abbeville on 20 May. Hundreds of thousands of British, French and Belgian soldiers were now caught in a shrinking pocket, with Germans on one side and the sea on the other. The only realistic way out was through the port of Dunkirk and the long sandy beaches beside it.

sections.key: German tanks paused outside Dunkirk for several days, a decision historians still debate.
sections.b: On 24 May, with German armour only a short distance from Dunkirk, the advance halted. The order came from senior German commanders and was confirmed by Hitler. Why it was given is still argued over. Tanks needed maintenance after their dash across France, the marshy ground around Dunkirk was poor tank country, and commanders feared an Allied counterattack. Hermann Göring, head of the Luftwaffe, also claimed his air force could finish the trapped army alone. Whatever the reasons, the pause lasted around three days. It gave the Allies precious time to strengthen the defensive perimeter around the town, where British and especially French troops held off attacks while the evacuation began. Without that pause, the story might have ended very differently.

sections.key: The evacuation was planned in tunnels beneath Dover Castle and began on 26 May.
sections.b: The rescue was organised by Vice-Admiral Bertram Ramsay from rooms deep in the cliffs below Dover Castle. Its codename, Operation Dynamo, is said to come from the room that had once housed an electrical generator. When it began on 26 May, planners hoped to save perhaps 45,000 men in two days before the Germans closed in. The conditions were terrible. Dunkirk's docks had been wrecked by bombing, oil tanks burned and black smoke hung over the town. The beaches sloped so gently that large ships could not get close to shore. Men waited for days on the sand under air attack, queuing in long lines into the sea. Ramsay's staff worked almost without sleep, improvising as the situation changed hour by hour.

sections.h: The mole and the little ships
sections.key: Most soldiers left from a long harbour breakwater, while small boats ferried others from the beaches.
sections.b: The famous image of Dunkirk is a flotilla of pleasure boats, fishing vessels and yachts crossing the Channel. These ‘little ships’ were real and heroic, many crewed by naval reservists or their owners, and they were vital for carrying men from the shallow beaches out to larger ships offshore. But most soldiers were actually taken off from the East Mole, a long concrete and timber breakwater protecting the harbour. It was never designed for ships to tie up against, yet destroyers and passenger ferries came alongside and loaded thousands of men at a time. In all, many hundreds of vessels took part, from warships to Thames barges. The Royal Navy's destroyers did the heaviest lifting and paid a high price, with several sunk.

sections.key: The air battle and the rearguard made the escape possible, often out of sight of the men on the beach.
sections.b: Soldiers waiting on the beaches were bombed and strafed by German aircraft, and many angrily asked where the Royal Air Force was. In fact the RAF was flying hard, but much of its fighting took place inland or above the clouds, intercepting bombers before they reached the coast. It lost many aircraft and pilots. On the ground, the defence of the perimeter was just as important. British units fought delaying actions, and French troops held the line until the very end, allowing others to escape. When the evacuation finished on 4 June, tens of thousands of French soldiers who had protected the beaches were left behind and taken prisoner. Their sacrifice is often forgotten in the British telling of the story.

sections.key: About 338,000 Allied troops were rescued, far more than anyone had dared to hope.
sections.b: When Operation Dynamo ended, around 338,000 Allied soldiers had been carried to England, including well over 100,000 French troops, many of whom were quickly shipped back to continue fighting in France. Compared with the original hope of 45,000, the result seemed miraculous. But the losses were heavy. Many ships were sunk, and the British army abandoned almost all its heavy equipment: tens of thousands of vehicles, hundreds of tanks, guns and huge stores of ammunition. France itself fell within weeks, signing an armistice on 22 June. Britain now stood without major allies in Western Europe. Yet it still had the core of a trained army, the men who would later form the backbone of forces that fought in Africa, Italy and Normandy.

sections.key: Churchill used Dunkirk to rally Britain while insisting it was a disaster, not a triumph.
sections.b: On 4 June Winston Churchill, who had become prime minister less than a month earlier, spoke to the House of Commons. He called the rescue a miracle of deliverance but warned that wars are not won by evacuations, and described the campaign as a colossal military disaster. The same speech ended with his famous promise that Britain would fight on the beaches, the landing grounds, the fields and the streets, and would never surrender. Dunkirk gave Britain a story of ordinary people pulling together in a crisis, later called the Dunkirk spirit. Historians today stress the complexities: the German pause, the French rearguard, the Royal Navy's central role. But the essential truth remains that an army was saved, and Britain stayed in the war.

quiz.q: How did German forces trap the Allied armies in May 1940?
o: By breaking through the Ardennes and racing to the Channel
By a long siege of Paris
quiz.e: German tanks pushed through the Ardennes, which the French had thought unsuitable for armour, and reached the Channel on 20 May.

quiz.q: Why do historians still debate the German halt order of 24 May?
o: Its reasons were mixed, including tank maintenance, poor ground and Göring's promises
It was ordered by the French
quiz.e: Several factors are suggested, from worn-out tanks and marshy terrain to fears of counterattack and Göring's claims, and their weight is still argued.

quiz.q: How many men did planners originally hope to evacuate?
quiz.e: Ramsay's planners hoped to save perhaps 45,000 men in two days, so the final total seemed miraculous.

quiz.q: Where were most soldiers actually taken off?
o: From the East Mole, a long harbour breakwater
quiz.e: The little ships were vital on the beaches, but most men boarded destroyers and ferries at the East Mole.

quiz.q: How did Churchill describe the campaign in his speech of 4 June 1940?
o: As a colossal military disaster, despite the rescue
quiz.e: Churchill called the rescue a miracle but warned that wars are not won by evacuations and that the campaign was a colossal military disaster.

LESSONS.title: The Panama Canal: cutting a continent in two
LESSONS.hook: For centuries people dreamed of a shortcut between the Atlantic and Pacific. The first attempt ended in disaster. The second succeeded only after doctors worked out what was really killing the workers.

sections.key: Before the canal, ships sailing between the American coasts had to go all the way around South America.
sections.b: Panama is a narrow strip of land, at its slimmest under 80 kilometres wide, linking North and South America. On one side lies the Caribbean and the Atlantic, on the other the Pacific. Yet for a ship sailing from New York to San Francisco, that strip forced a voyage around Cape Horn, at the stormy southern tip of South America, of more than 20,000 kilometres. Spanish explorers had imagined a canal as early as the 1500s. During the California Gold Rush, a railway was built across Panama in the 1850s, and thousands of travellers crossed it, despite deadly tropical diseases. The prize was obvious. A canal would cut the New York to San Francisco voyage by roughly 13,000 kilometres and reshape world trade.

sections.key: The builder of the Suez Canal tried to dig a sea-level canal through Panama and failed catastrophically.
sections.b: In 1881 a French company led by Ferdinand de Lesseps began work. De Lesseps was a national hero who had built the Suez Canal through flat Egyptian desert, and he insisted Panama could be done the same way, as a canal at sea level with no locks. Panama was nothing like Suez. Its mountains, landslides, heavy rains and the flooding Chagres River defeated the plan. Worse, yellow fever and malaria killed workers in enormous numbers. Estimates suggest around 20,000 people died during the French years, many of them labourers from the Caribbean. By 1889 the company had gone bankrupt, ruining many small French investors. A corruption scandal followed, and the half-dug ditches were left to the jungle.

sections.h: America steps in, and Panama is born
sections.key: The United States backed Panama's independence from Colombia to secure the canal route.
sections.b: At the start of the twentieth century, the United States wanted a canal for trade and to move its navy quickly between oceans. President Theodore Roosevelt bought the French company's assets, but Colombia, which then ruled Panama, rejected the treaty terms offered. In November 1903 a revolt in Panama declared independence, and US warships made sure Colombian troops could not land to stop it. Within about two weeks the new Panamanian government's representative, a Frenchman named Philippe Bunau-Varilla, signed a treaty giving the United States control of a Canal Zone across the country, in perpetuity. Many Panamanians resented the deal from the start. The way the United States had acquired the route became a source of tension in Latin America for decades.

sections.key: Controlling mosquitoes, which spread yellow fever and malaria, made the canal possible.
sections.b: The Americans began work in 1904, and at first yellow fever returned and workers fled. The breakthrough came from medicine. Doctors had recently confirmed, building on the Cuban physician Carlos Finlay's theory and Walter Reed's experiments in Cuba, that yellow fever was spread by mosquitoes, while malaria was carried by a different mosquito. Dr William Gorgas, the chief sanitary officer, launched a vast campaign. Teams drained swamps, spread oil on standing water, fumigated buildings, screened windows and installed piped water so people no longer stored it in open barrels. By 1906 yellow fever had been eliminated from the zone, and malaria deaths fell sharply. It was one of the great public health victories in history, and without it the canal would likely have failed again.

sections.key: Instead of digging to sea level, engineers built a dam and lifted ships over the land using locks.
sections.b: The American chief engineer John Stevens, and later George Goethals, abandoned the sea-level idea. Instead they dammed the Chagres River at Gatun, creating what was then the largest artificial lake in the world. Ships would climb from the ocean through a series of giant locks, sail across the lake around 26 metres above sea level, then descend through more locks on the other side. The hardest work was the Culebra Cut, a passage through the mountainous spine of the isthmus, where repeated landslides buried months of digging. Steam shovels, railways and dynamite moved vast quantities of earth and rock. The locks themselves were triumphs of concrete and engineering, their huge gates driven by electric motors. On 15 August 1914, the cargo ship SS Ancon made the first official transit.

sections.key: Tens of thousands of Caribbean workers did the hardest jobs, under a system of segregated pay.
sections.b: The canal is often told as a story of American engineers, but most of the labour came from the Caribbean, especially Barbados and Jamaica. These workers did the most dangerous jobs, in the Culebra Cut and with dynamite. The canal zone ran a segregated system. White American employees were paid in gold on the ‘gold roll’, while most black and non-American workers were paid less, in silver, on the ‘silver roll’, with poorer housing and food. Over 5,000 workers died during the American construction years, according to official records, a far lower toll than the French era but still grim. Their descendants remain an important part of Panama's population, and their role is now more widely recognised.

sections.key: Panama took full control of the canal at the end of 1999.
sections.b: Resentment of the Canal Zone, a slice of US-run territory cutting through the middle of Panama, grew through the twentieth century. In 1964 riots over the right to fly the Panamanian flag in the zone left more than twenty people dead. In 1977 US President Jimmy Carter and Panama's leader Omar Torrijos signed treaties agreeing to transfer the canal. On 31 December 1999 Panama took full control. Since then it has run the canal profitably and opened a set of larger locks in 2016 to take bigger ships. The canal still depends on rain to fill Gatun Lake, and in 2023 a severe drought forced limits on the number of ships that could pass, a reminder that even great engineering relies on nature.

quiz.q: Why did the French effort to build the canal fail?
o: A sea-level design, difficult terrain and deadly diseases overwhelmed it
quiz.e: De Lesseps insisted on a sea-level canal like Suez, but mountains, floods and disease defeated the project, and the company went bankrupt in 1889.

quiz.q: How did the United States gain control of the canal route?
o: It backed Panama's 1903 independence from Colombia and signed a treaty for a Canal Zone
It won a war against France
quiz.e: After Colombia rejected its terms, the US supported Panama's revolt and quickly gained a Canal Zone by treaty.

quiz.q: What breakthrough made construction possible?
o: Controlling the mosquitoes that spread yellow fever and malaria
quiz.e: Once it was confirmed that mosquitoes spread these diseases, Gorgas's sanitation campaign eliminated yellow fever from the zone by 1906.

quiz.q: How do ships cross the high ground of Panama?
o: By rising through locks to an artificial lake and descending again
By sailing at sea level the whole way
quiz.e: Engineers dammed the Chagres River to form Gatun Lake, and locks lift ships about 26 metres up to it and back down.

quiz.q: When did Panama take full control of the canal?
quiz.e: The 1977 treaties set the handover, which took place at the end of 1999.

LESSONS.title: Bismarck and the making of Germany
LESSONS.hook: In 1860 there was no country called Germany, just dozens of separate states. Eleven years later a German empire was proclaimed in a French palace, built by one man's three wars.

sections.key: Before 1871, German speakers were divided among dozens of separate kingdoms, duchies and free cities.
sections.b: After Napoleon's defeat in 1815, the German lands were organised into the German Confederation, a loose association of 39 states. They ranged from great powers such as the Austrian Empire and the Kingdom of Prussia to tiny duchies and free cities like Hamburg. Austria, ruled by the Habsburgs, dominated the Confederation, while Prussia, in the north, was growing rich through industry and the Zollverein, a customs union that removed trade barriers between many German states but excluded Austria. Many liberals and nationalists dreamed of a single German nation. In the revolutions of 1848, an elected parliament in Frankfurt tried to create one, and failed. The question remained: would Germany be united by speeches and votes, or by force?

sections.key: Bismarck came to power in 1862 and made clear he would use force, not parliaments, to settle Germany's future.
sections.b: Otto von Bismarck was a Prussian landowner from the conservative Junker class, a brilliant, bad-tempered and ruthless diplomat. In 1862 King Wilhelm I of Prussia was locked in a struggle with the Prussian parliament, which refused to fund his plans to enlarge the army. Wilhelm appointed Bismarck as his chief minister to break the deadlock. Bismarck simply carried on collecting taxes and spending them without parliament's approval. In a famous speech to a parliamentary committee, he declared that the great questions of the day would not be decided by speeches and majority votes, the mistake of 1848, but by iron and blood. The phrase, usually remembered as ‘blood and iron’, came to define his career and, for many, the character of the new Germany.

sections.key: Bismarck used short, carefully isolated wars against Denmark, Austria and France to unite Germany under Prussia.
sections.b: Bismarck's genius lay in fighting one enemy at a time, while making sure no other power joined in. In 1864, Prussia and Austria together defeated Denmark over the duchies of Schleswig and Holstein. Bismarck then used arguments over running those duchies to provoke Austria. In 1866 the Prussian army, using railways, telegraphs and fast-firing breech-loading rifles, crushed Austria at Königgrätz in a war lasting only weeks. Bismarck insisted on mild peace terms, so Austria would not seek revenge, but it was pushed out of German affairs. Prussia annexed several states and formed the North German Confederation. Only the southern German states, including Bavaria, remained outside. Bismarck believed a war against France would bring them in.

sections.key: Bismarck edited a royal telegram to make France feel insulted, helping provoke the war he wanted.
sections.b: In 1870 a crisis erupted when a relative of the Prussian king was offered the Spanish throne. France, fearing encirclement, protested, and the candidacy was withdrawn. But France pressed further, and its ambassador approached King Wilhelm at the spa town of Ems to demand a promise it would never be renewed. Wilhelm politely declined and sent Bismarck a telegram describing the meeting. Bismarck shortened it before releasing it to the press so that it sounded as if the king had curtly snubbed the ambassador. As he hoped, the French public was outraged. France declared war in July 1870, appearing to be the aggressor. The southern German states, bound to Prussia by defensive alliances, joined the fight, as Bismarck had planned.

sections.key: After crushing France, Germany was declared an empire in the Hall of Mirrors in January 1871.
sections.b: The Franco-Prussian War went disastrously for France. At Sedan in September 1870, Emperor Napoleon III was captured with his army, and his regime collapsed. Paris was besieged through a bitter winter. On 18 January 1871, while the siege continued, German princes gathered in the Hall of Mirrors at the palace of Versailles, and Wilhelm I was proclaimed German Emperor, or Kaiser. The choice of setting was a deliberate humiliation of France. The peace treaty forced France to pay a large indemnity and to give up Alsace and much of Lorraine. The new Germany was a federal empire dominated by Prussia, with Bismarck as chancellor. French resentment over the lost provinces would poison relations between the two countries for decades.

sections.key: Bismarck fought Catholics and socialists, yet also created the world's first national social insurance system.
sections.b: As chancellor, Bismarck saw enemies of the new empire everywhere. In the 1870s he waged the Kulturkampf, a struggle against the power of the Catholic Church, which backfired by strengthening Catholic political loyalty. He then turned on the growing socialist movement, banning its organisations from 1878. Yet alongside repression came a remarkable innovation. To win workers away from socialism, Bismarck introduced national health insurance in 1883, accident insurance in 1884, and old age and disability pensions in 1889. Workers, employers and the state shared the costs. It was the first system of its kind in the world, and it became a model for social insurance in many other countries. His motives were conservative, but the legacy proved lasting.

sections.key: Bismarck kept the peace through a complex web of alliances, which his successors failed to maintain.
sections.b: After 1871 Bismarck declared Germany satisfied. His aim was to prevent a war that could destroy what he had built, especially a two-front war against France and Russia. He hosted the Congress of Berlin in 1878, presenting himself as an honest broker, and wove a network of treaties: the Dual Alliance with Austria-Hungary in 1879, later the Triple Alliance with Italy, and a secret Reinsurance Treaty with Russia in 1887. In 1888 the young Wilhelm II came to the throne, and he clashed with the old chancellor. Bismarck was forced to resign in 1890. The treaty with Russia was not renewed, and Russia soon allied with France. The isolation Bismarck had feared was beginning to take shape, setting the stage for 1914.

quiz.q: What was the Zollverein?
o: A customs union removing trade barriers between many German states
quiz.e: The Zollverein was a customs union, led by Prussia and excluding Austria, which boosted trade and Prussian influence.

quiz.q: What made Bismarck's three wars so effective?
o: He fought all his enemies at once
He isolated each enemy diplomatically and fought short wars
He relied entirely on naval power
quiz.e: Bismarck ensured each opponent stood alone, and Prussia's modern army won quick victories against Denmark, Austria and France.

quiz.q: What did Bismarck do with the Ems Telegram?
o: Edited it to make the king's response sound like an insult to France
quiz.e: By shortening the telegram, Bismarck made the exchange sound like a snub, provoking France into declaring war.

quiz.q: Where was the German Empire proclaimed in 1871?
o: The Hall of Mirrors at Versailles
quiz.e: Wilhelm I was proclaimed German Emperor in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, a deliberate humiliation of defeated France.

quiz.q: What lasting innovation did Bismarck introduce in the 1880s?
o: The world's first national social insurance system
quiz.e: To undercut socialism, Bismarck created health, accident and old age insurance, the first national system of its kind.

LESSONS.title: 1848: the year Europe caught fire
LESSONS.hook: In a few weeks of 1848, revolutions broke out in dozens of cities across Europe. Kings fled, ministers resigned and constitutions were promised. Within two years almost all of it had been undone.

sections.key: Hunger, economic crisis and new ideas created the conditions for revolution across Europe.
sections.b: After Napoleon's defeat in 1815, Europe's great powers tried to restore order under conservative monarchs. The Austrian chancellor, Prince Klemens von Metternich, became the symbol of this system, with censorship, secret police and a deep suspicion of change. But beneath the surface pressures were building. Liberals wanted constitutions, elected parliaments and a free press. Nationalists wanted peoples such as Germans, Italians, Hungarians and Poles to govern themselves. Industrialisation was creating a new urban working class living in grim conditions. Then, in the mid 1840s, disaster struck. Potato blight and poor grain harvests sent food prices soaring, followed by a financial crisis and mass unemployment in 1847. Hungry, angry crowds and frustrated middle class reformers were a combustible mix.

sections.key: The overthrow of France's king in February 1848 set off revolutions everywhere.
sections.b: The first major uprising of 1848 came in January in Palermo, Sicily, but it was Paris that ignited the continent. King Louis-Philippe's government had banned a series of political banquets used by reformers to campaign for a wider vote. In February, protests turned into street fighting, barricades went up and soldiers fired on a crowd. Within days the king abdicated and fled to England. A provisional government declared the Second Republic, introduced voting rights for all adult men, abolished slavery in French colonies and created national workshops to provide jobs for the unemployed. News travelled fast by rail, telegraph and newspaper. To liberals and radicals across Europe, the message seemed clear: if Paris could do it, so could they.

sections.key: In March 1848 revolution spread to Vienna, Berlin, Milan, Budapest and many other cities.
sections.b: What followed became known as the Springtime of Peoples. In March, students and workers rose in Vienna, and Metternich, the great defender of the old order, resigned and fled, reportedly disguised. In Berlin, after deadly barricade fighting, King Frederick William IV of Prussia promised a constitution and saluted the bodies of fallen revolutionaries. In Milan, citizens drove out the Austrian army during the Five Days. Hungary, led by Lajos Kossuth, won sweeping self-government from Austria. Revolts or reforms swept through dozens of German and Italian states, while in Prague, Czech leaders called for their own rights. The speed was astonishing. In a matter of weeks, governments that had seemed immovable gave way to demands that a year earlier would have meant prison.

sections.key: German liberals elected a national parliament to unite Germany, but it had no real power.
sections.b: In May 1848 an elected assembly met in St Paul's Church in Frankfurt to create a united, constitutional Germany. Its members were mostly educated professionals: lawyers, professors, civil servants. They debated long and earnestly, drawing up a list of basic rights, including freedom of speech and equality before the law. But they faced hard questions. Should Germany include German-speaking Austria and its many non-German peoples, or leave Austria out? And the parliament had no army or money of its own. In 1849 it finally offered the crown of a united Germany to Frederick William IV of Prussia. He refused to accept a crown offered by an elected assembly rather than by fellow princes. The parliament soon dissolved, and its remnant was dispersed by troops.

sections.key: Divisions among revolutionaries and the loyalty of armies allowed the old rulers to strike back.
sections.b: The revolutions of 1848 failed for several connected reasons. Middle class liberals wanted constitutions and order, while workers wanted jobs and social change, and the two soon feared each other. In Paris, the closure of the national workshops sparked the bloody June Days uprising, crushed by the army with thousands killed. Nationalities quarrelled too: Hungarians demanded freedom from Austria while denying it to Croats and Romanians within Hungary. Above all, the armies mostly stayed loyal to their monarchs. In late 1848 Austrian troops retook Vienna, and the young Franz Joseph became emperor. In 1849 Russian troops helped Austria crush Hungary. In France, voters elected Louis-Napoleon Bonaparte president, and in 1851 he seized power and soon declared himself emperor.

sections.key: Although the revolutions were defeated, some major changes lasted.
sections.b: It is tempting to call 1848 the turning point where history failed to turn, but some changes endured. In the Austrian Empire, peasants were freed from compulsory labour owed to landlords, the remnants of serfdom, and this reform was never reversed. Prussia kept a constitution and parliament, although a limited one. Denmark became a constitutional monarchy in 1849, the Netherlands adopted a more liberal constitution in 1848, and Switzerland adopted a federal constitution that laid the foundations of its modern state. Piedmont-Sardinia kept its constitution and later led the unification of Italy. The year also showed rulers that ignoring public opinion was dangerous, and they increasingly used nationalism for their own purposes, as Bismarck later did in Germany.

sections.key: Defeated revolutionaries spread their ideas across the world, while new political movements took shape.
sections.b: Many revolutionaries fled into exile. Thousands of Germans, known as Forty-Eighters, emigrated to the United States, where many became journalists, politicians and soldiers, and some later fought for the Union in the American Civil War. In Britain, the Chartist movement for working-class voting rights held a huge meeting in London in April 1848, but it fizzled out without revolution. Coincidentally, The Communist Manifesto by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels was published in February 1848, just as the revolutions began, though it had little influence on events that year. Its later impact was enormous. For historians, 1848 remains a fascinating case study in how revolutions spread quickly, why unity is so hard to keep, and why winning a crowd is not the same as winning a state.

quiz.q: What economic troubles helped trigger the revolutions?
o: Crop failures, high food prices and a financial crisis
The end of the slave trade
quiz.e: Potato blight and poor harvests drove up food prices in the mid 1840s, followed by financial crisis and unemployment in 1847.

quiz.q: What did France's new Second Republic introduce in 1848?
o: Voting rights for all adult men
quiz.e: The provisional government declared a republic, introduced universal male suffrage and abolished slavery in French colonies.

quiz.q: Why did the Frankfurt Parliament fail to unite Germany?
o: It had no army or money, and Prussia's king refused its crown
quiz.e: Without power of its own, the parliament depended on princes, and Frederick William IV refused a crown offered by an elected assembly.

quiz.q: Which factor most helped the old rulers regain control?
o: The armies mostly stayed loyal to their monarchs
quiz.e: Loyal armies, along with divisions between liberals, workers and rival nationalities, allowed monarchs to crush the uprisings.

quiz.q: Which change in the Austrian Empire outlasted the revolutions?
o: The end of compulsory peasant labour for landlords
quiz.e: The abolition of the remnants of serfdom in the Austrian Empire was never reversed, even after the revolutions were defeated.

LESSONS.title: Australia's Vietnam War
LESSONS.hook: It was Australia's longest war of the twentieth century and its most divisive. Young men were chosen for it by a lottery of birthdays, and many came home to silence.

sections.key: Fear of communism spreading through Asia, and the wish to keep the United States close, drew Australia in.
sections.b: After the Second World War, Australian leaders worried about the rise of communism in Asia, especially after the communist victory in China in 1949 and the Korean War. A popular idea, the domino theory, held that if one country fell to communism its neighbours would follow, one after another, until the threat reached Australia's doorstep. Vietnam had been divided in 1954 into a communist North and a non-communist South, and an insurgency was growing in the South, supported by the North. Australia also wanted to strengthen its alliance with the United States, formalised in the ANZUS treaty of 1951, as Britain's power in the region faded. In 1962 the Menzies government sent a small team of thirty military advisers to South Vietnam.

sections.key: In 1965 Australia committed combat troops, and later a task force based at Nui Dat.
sections.b: The advisers of the Australian Army Training Team Vietnam, known as the Team, trained South Vietnamese troops and became some of the most decorated Australian units of the war. In April 1965 Prime Minister Robert Menzies announced that an infantry battalion would be sent, saying South Vietnam had requested help, a claim later questioned by historians. The battalion served alongside American forces. From 1966 Australia ran its own 1st Australian Task Force, based at Nui Dat in Phuoc Tuy province, south-east of Saigon. There the army focused on patrolling the jungle and villages to cut the insurgents off from local support. Australian troops became known for slow, patient, careful patrolling, partly learned from earlier experience in Malaya, rather than heavy firepower.

sections.key: National service selected twenty-year-old men by drawing birth dates, and conscripts could be sent to Vietnam.
sections.b: In 1964 the government introduced a new scheme of national service. Twenty-year-old men had to register, and a lottery drew birth dates from a barrel. If your birthday was drawn, you could be called up for two years of military service. From 1965 the law allowed these conscripts, often called nashos, to be sent overseas, including to Vietnam. Around 15,000 national servicemen served there, and some of them were killed. The randomness troubled many Australians. A young man's future, and perhaps his life, could depend on whether a marble bearing his birth date came out of a barrel. Some refused to register or to serve, and a few were jailed. The ballot made the war deeply personal for families across the country.

sections.key: In August 1966, a single company of Australians fought a much larger enemy force in a rubber plantation.
sections.b: On 18 August 1966, D Company of the 6th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment, about 105 men, was patrolling near Nui Dat in a rubber plantation called Long Tan. In a tropical downpour they ran into a far larger force of Viet Cong and North Vietnamese troops. For several hours the Australians, along with three New Zealand artillery observers, fought off repeated attacks, helped by intense artillery fire from the base and an ammunition drop by helicopter. As darkness fell, armoured personnel carriers arrived and the attackers withdrew. Eighteen Australians were killed. Enemy losses were far higher, though exact numbers are disputed. The Battle of Long Tan became the best-known Australian action of the war, and 18 August is now marked as Vietnam Veterans Day.

sections.key: As the war dragged on, opposition grew into some of the largest protests in Australian history.
sections.b: At first many Australians supported the war, but doubts grew as it dragged on without victory, particularly after the Tet Offensive of 1968 showed the enemy was far from beaten. Television brought images of the fighting into lounge rooms. Groups such as Save Our Sons, formed by mothers of possible conscripts, campaigned against the ballot. In May 1970 the Moratorium marches brought huge crowds into city streets around Australia. In Melbourne, led by Labor politician Jim Cairns, crowds were estimated at between 70,000 and 100,000 people, filling the city centre. Supporters of the war saw protesters as disloyal, and many protesters saw the government as sending young men to die for an unwinnable cause. The divide split families, churches and friendships.

sections.key: Australian combat troops withdrew in 1971, and the Whitlam government ended conscription in 1972.
sections.b: As the United States began reducing its forces, Australia followed. The task force left Phuoc Tuy in late 1971, and the last advisers left soon after. In December 1972 the newly elected Whitlam Labor government ended conscription, freed men jailed for refusing to serve and withdrew the remaining personnel. Altogether, almost 60,000 Australians served in Vietnam, and around 520 died, with thousands wounded. For the Vietnamese, the cost was vastly greater. Estimates of Vietnamese deaths during the war vary widely, but most run into the millions, civilians and soldiers alike. In April 1975, North Vietnamese forces captured Saigon and the country was reunified under communist rule. Australia later resettled tens of thousands of Vietnamese refugees.

sections.key: Many veterans returned to indifference or hostility, and recognition came only years later.
sections.b: Unlike soldiers returning from the world wars, most Vietnam veterans came home individually or in small groups, often flying in quietly, and were expected to slip back into ordinary life. Some were abused by protesters, while some older veterans' organisations were slow to welcome them. Many struggled with what is now recognised as post-traumatic stress, and concerns grew about the health effects of chemical defoliants such as Agent Orange, investigated by a Royal Commission in the 1980s. Recognition came slowly. In October 1987, tens of thousands of Vietnam veterans marched through Sydney in a Welcome Home parade, an emotional moment for many. A national memorial was dedicated in Canberra in 1992. The war's lessons about alliances, conscription and public trust are still debated today.

quiz.q: What was the domino theory?
o: A plan to build railways in Asia
The idea that if one country fell to communism its neighbours would follow
quiz.e: The domino theory held that communism would spread from country to country, a fear that drove Australian involvement.

quiz.q: How were national servicemen selected?
o: By a ballot of birth dates
quiz.e: Birth dates were drawn from a barrel, and twenty-year-old men whose birthdays were chosen could be conscripted.

quiz.q: Why is 18 August marked as Vietnam Veterans Day?
o: It is the date of the fall of Saigon
It is the anniversary of the Battle of Long Tan
It is the day conscription ended
It is when the first advisers arrived
quiz.e: On 18 August 1966, D Company 6RAR fought the Battle of Long Tan, now the best-known Australian action of the war.

quiz.q: What were the Moratorium marches of 1970?
quiz.e: The May 1970 Moratorium marches brought enormous crowds into Australian cities to oppose the war and conscription.

quiz.q: When did Vietnam veterans receive a national Welcome Home parade in Sydney?
quiz.e: The Welcome Home parade in October 1987 came many years after most veterans had returned quietly to civilian life.

LESSONS.title: Apartheid: rise and fall
LESSONS.hook: For more than four decades, South Africa's laws sorted every person by race and decided where they could live, work, love and vote. Then, against most predictions, the system was dismantled without the all-out civil war many had feared.

sections.key: Racial discrimination in South Africa long predated apartheid, which made it total and systematic.
sections.b: South Africa's black majority had faced discrimination for centuries under Dutch and then British colonial rule. When the Union of South Africa was formed in 1910, most black South Africans were denied the vote. The Natives Land Act of 1913 restricted black land ownership to a small fraction of the country, and pass laws controlled where black people could travel and work. In 1912, educated black leaders founded the organisation that became the African National Congress, or ANC, to fight for rights. The word apartheid, meaning apart or separateness in Afrikaans, came into political use in the 1940s. It described a plan to push segregation much further, turning a patchwork of discriminatory practices into a complete legal system governing every part of life.

sections.key: After 1948 the National Party passed laws classifying everyone by race and separating them by law.
sections.b: In 1948 the National Party, drawing its support mainly from white Afrikaners, won the election and began building apartheid. The Population Registration Act of 1950 classified every South African into racial groups, broadly white, coloured, Indian and black African, with officials sometimes deciding a person's category through humiliating tests. Marriage and sexual relationships across racial lines were banned. The Group Areas Act assigned separate residential areas to each group, and whole communities, such as District Six in Cape Town and Sophiatown in Johannesburg, were bulldozed and their residents forcibly moved. Separate and unequal schools, hospitals, beaches, buses and even park benches followed. Bantu Education was designed to prepare black children for lives as labourers. Pass laws required black adults to carry identity documents everywhere.

sections.key: Apartheid's planners tried to strip black South Africans of citizenship by assigning them to separate ‘homelands’.
sections.b: The most ambitious part of apartheid was the homeland system. The government divided black South Africans into ethnic groups and assigned each to a territory, or Bantustan, often scattered fragments of poor land. The aim was to declare these homelands independent, so that black people would become citizens of them rather than of South Africa, leaving a white-ruled state with no black citizens at all. Four homelands, including Transkei, were declared independent, though almost no other country recognised them. Millions of people were forcibly moved to these areas in the 1960s and 1970s, often to places with few jobs or services. Black workers who needed jobs in cities became migrants in their own country, living in hostels far from their families.

sections.key: Peaceful protest was met with bullets and bans, pushing the resistance towards armed struggle.
sections.b: Through the 1950s the ANC and its allies led mass nonviolent campaigns, and in 1955 adopted the Freedom Charter, declaring that South Africa belonged to all who lived in it. On 21 March 1960 at Sharpeville, police opened fire on a crowd protesting the pass laws, killing 69 people, many shot in the back. The government banned the ANC and other groups. Leaders including Nelson Mandela concluded that peaceful protest alone was failing, and in 1961 an armed wing, Umkhonto we Sizwe, began a sabotage campaign. In 1964, after the Rivonia trial, Mandela and others were sentenced to life imprisonment, and many were sent to Robben Island. Inside South Africa, open opposition was largely silenced for more than a decade.

sections.key: School students rising up in 1976 began a wave of resistance that never fully stopped.
sections.b: On 16 June 1976, thousands of school students in Soweto, near Johannesburg, marched against a rule forcing them to be taught some subjects in Afrikaans, a language many saw as the language of their oppressors. Police opened fire. A photograph of the dying twelve-year-old Hector Pieterson, carried by another student, travelled around the world. Unrest spread across the country, and hundreds of people were killed in the months that followed. The Black Consciousness movement, led by Steve Biko, urged black South Africans to reject feelings of inferiority. Biko died in police custody in 1977 after severe beatings. In the 1980s township protests, strikes and boycotts grew, and the government declared states of emergency, detaining many thousands of people without trial.

sections.key: Sanctions and boycotts isolated South Africa, and sporting bans hit white South Africans hard.
sections.b: International pressure grew steadily. The United Nations condemned apartheid, and many countries imposed trade, arms and financial sanctions, especially in the 1980s. Banks refused new loans and companies pulled out, damaging an already struggling economy. Sport mattered deeply to many white South Africans, and sporting boycotts struck at their sense of belonging in the world. South Africa was excluded from the Olympics for decades. In Australia, a 1971 tour by South Africa's Springbok rugby team sparked large protests and clashes, and later governments of both major parties took strong anti-apartheid positions in the Commonwealth. Historians debate how much sanctions themselves forced change, compared with internal resistance and economic decline, but together they made apartheid increasingly costly to keep.

sections.key: In 1990 the government unbanned the ANC and released Mandela, opening tense negotiations.
sections.b: By the late 1980s, many in the government realised apartheid could not survive. On 2 February 1990, President F. W. de Klerk announced to parliament that the ANC and other banned organisations would be legalised. Nine days later, on 11 February, Nelson Mandela walked out of prison after 27 years. Negotiations over a new constitution followed, interrupted by violence that killed thousands of people, including clashes between the ANC and the Inkatha Freedom Party and attacks by those trying to wreck the talks. In 1993 the assassination of popular ANC leader Chris Hani brought the country close to the brink, but Mandela's appeal for calm held. That year Mandela and de Klerk were jointly awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.

sections.key: South Africa's first fully democratic election brought Mandela to the presidency.
sections.b: On 27 April 1994, South Africans of every race voted together for the first time. Millions of people queued for hours, sometimes in lines stretching for kilometres, many casting the first vote of their lives. The ANC won about 62 per cent of the vote, and on 10 May Mandela was inaugurated as president, leading a government of national unity that included de Klerk as a deputy president. A new constitution, adopted in 1996, included one of the world's most extensive bills of rights. The country set up a Truth and Reconciliation Commission to hear testimony about the crimes of the apartheid years. The legal system of apartheid was gone, though its economic legacy of deep inequality remains a major challenge today.

quiz.q: What did the Population Registration Act of 1950 do?
o: Classified every South African into a racial group
Created the national census of farms
quiz.e: The Act classified every person by race, the foundation on which all other apartheid laws rested.

quiz.q: What was the goal of the homeland system?
o: To give black South Africans more farmland
To strip black South Africans of South African citizenship
To build new cities for all races
To prepare for a world war
quiz.e: Planners hoped to make black people citizens of nominally independent homelands, leaving white-ruled South Africa without black citizens.

quiz.q: What happened at Sharpeville on 21 March 1960?
o: Police killed 69 people protesting the pass laws
The first democratic election was held
quiz.e: Police fired on protesters at Sharpeville, killing 69, after which the government banned the ANC.

quiz.q: What sparked the Soweto uprising of 1976?
o: A rule forcing students to be taught some subjects in Afrikaans
quiz.e: Students marched against compulsory Afrikaans teaching, and police fired on them, sparking unrest across the country.

quiz.q: When did South Africa hold its first fully democratic election?
quiz.e: On 27 April 1994, South Africans of all races voted together for the first time, and Mandela became president.

LESSONS.title: Mao's China: the Great Leap and the Cultural Revolution
LESSONS.hook: Mao Zedong set out to transform China into a modern socialist power within a generation. Two of his campaigns caused one of the deadliest famines in history and a decade of political terror.

sections.key: In 1949 the Communists won China's civil war and set out to remake society from top to bottom.
sections.b: On 1 October 1949, Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic of China in Beijing, after the Communist Party won a long civil war against Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists, who retreated to Taiwan. China had endured decades of foreign invasion, warlords and civil war, and many Chinese welcomed peace and the promise of national strength. The new government moved fast. Land reform in the early 1950s took land from landlords and gave it to peasants, but it was carried out through mass ‘struggle sessions’ in which landlords were publicly denounced, and many were killed. Estimates of deaths in land reform and related campaigns range from several hundred thousand to several million. Private businesses were nationalised, and a Soviet-style planned economy began to take shape.

sections.key: Mao invited open criticism in 1956 and 1957, then punished hundreds of thousands who spoke up.
sections.b: In 1956 Mao encouraged intellectuals to speak freely with the slogan ‘let a hundred flowers bloom, let a hundred schools of thought contend’. After hesitation, criticism poured in, attacking officials, the party's privileges and even its right to rule. Mao abruptly reversed course. In 1957 he launched the Anti-Rightist Campaign, and roughly 550,000 people, many of them teachers, writers, scientists and engineers, were labelled ‘rightists’. Many lost their jobs and were sent to labour camps or the countryside for years. Historians still debate whether Mao planned the trap from the start or reacted to criticism that went further than he expected. Either way, the lesson was clear to everyone: honest criticism was dangerous. That silence would have disastrous consequences in the years ahead.

sections.key: From 1958, Mao tried to make China an industrial power almost overnight through mass mobilisation.
sections.b: In 1958 Mao launched the Great Leap Forward, aiming to overtake Britain in steel production within about fifteen years and to prove that mass enthusiasm could beat Soviet-style caution. Hundreds of millions of peasants were organised into vast people's communes, where private plots were abolished and families ate in communal canteens. Millions of small backyard furnaces were built to make steel, consuming pots, pans and tools, while much of what they produced was useless. Farmers were pulled from fields to work on furnaces and dams. Pseudo-scientific farming methods such as very close planting and deep ploughing were imposed. A campaign against the Four Pests killed huge numbers of sparrows, and crop-eating insects flourished, adding to the harm.

sections.key: Inflated harvest reports led the state to seize grain that farmers needed to survive.
sections.b: Local officials, terrified of being labelled rightists, reported fantastic harvests that never existed. The state then took a share of grain based on those false figures, leaving many villages with little or nothing to eat, while China continued to export grain. In 1959, at a party conference at Lushan, Defence Minister Peng Dehuai privately criticised the Leap in a letter to Mao. Mao denounced and purged him, and the campaign was pushed even harder. The result was a catastrophic famine between 1959 and 1961. Estimates of excess deaths vary widely, from around fifteen million to more than forty million, with many demographers putting the figure at around thirty million. It is among the deadliest famines in recorded history, and largely caused by policy.

sections.key: Pragmatic leaders repaired the damage, but Mao feared the revolution was losing its way.
sections.b: By the early 1960s, other leaders, especially head of state Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping, quietly reversed many Leap policies. They allowed private plots and markets again and used material incentives, and food production slowly recovered. Mao stepped back from day-to-day economic management but grew suspicious. He believed the party was becoming a new privileged elite, and that the Soviet Union, which he now regarded as having betrayed true communism, showed how a revolution could decay. He also resented the loss of his own authority. Meanwhile his image was being built into a cult of personality, helped by Defence Minister Lin Biao, whose army published Quotations from Chairman Mao, the famous Little Red Book, in the mid 1960s.

sections.key: In 1966 Mao unleashed millions of young Red Guards against party officials, teachers and tradition.
sections.b: In 1966 Mao launched the Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution, calling on young people to attack ‘bourgeois’ influences within the party and society. Students formed groups of Red Guards. At huge rallies in Tiananmen Square, millions waved the Little Red Book and cheered Mao. Red Guards humiliated, beat and sometimes killed teachers, officials and neighbours accused of being class enemies. They ransacked homes, burned books and smashed temples and historic sites as part of a campaign against the ‘Four Olds’: old customs, culture, habits and ideas. Liu Shaoqi was purged and died in custody in 1969. Deng Xiaoping was sent to work in a tractor factory. Rival Red Guard factions fought each other, sometimes with weapons, and the army had to restore order.

sections.key: Millions of urban youths were sent to the countryside, and political violence continued for a decade.
sections.b: From 1968, with the Red Guards out of control, Mao sent millions of young urban people, an estimated sixteen to seventeen million over the following years, ‘up to the mountains and down to the countryside’ to learn from peasants. Many lost their education and spent years in harsh rural poverty, an experience that shaped a whole generation, including China's later leader Xi Jinping. Political turmoil continued. In 1971 Lin Biao, by then Mao's chosen successor, died in a plane crash in Mongolia, after apparently fleeing China following a failed plot, though the details remain murky. Estimates of the number of people killed during the Cultural Revolution vary widely, from hundreds of thousands to two million or more, with many millions more persecuted.

sections.key: Mao's successors arrested his radical allies, turned to reform and gave a carefully limited verdict on his rule.
sections.b: Mao died on 9 September 1976. Within a month, the radical leaders known as the Gang of Four, including his widow Jiang Qing, were arrested. By the late 1970s Deng Xiaoping had emerged as China's paramount leader and launched the reforms that opened China's economy to markets and the world. In 1981 the Communist Party issued an official resolution that called the Cultural Revolution a catastrophe responsible for the most severe setbacks since 1949, and acknowledged Mao's mistakes. Yet it insisted his contributions outweighed his errors, and his portrait still hangs over Tiananmen Square. Open research into these years remains restricted in China, and archives are hard to access, which is why historians' estimates of the human toll still vary so much.

quiz.q: What happened after the Hundred Flowers campaign invited criticism?
o: The critics were rewarded with promotions
Hundreds of thousands were labelled rightists and punished
quiz.e: Mao reversed course with the Anti-Rightist Campaign of 1957, branding around 550,000 people rightists and teaching everyone that criticism was dangerous.

quiz.q: Why did the state take so much grain during the Great Leap Forward?
o: Procurement was based on hugely inflated harvest reports
The Soviet Union demanded it all
quiz.e: Officials afraid of punishment reported fantastic harvests, and the state took grain based on those false figures, leaving villages starving.

quiz.q: Which statement best reflects estimates of the Great Leap famine death toll?
o: Estimates range widely, from about fifteen to more than forty million
Exactly ten million, according to official records
quiz.e: Historians and demographers disagree, but estimates range from about fifteen to more than forty million, with many around thirty million.

quiz.q: What were the ‘Four Olds’ that Red Guards attacked?
o: Old customs, culture, habits and ideas
Old weapons, tools, coins and books
quiz.e: Red Guards targeted old customs, culture, habits and ideas, destroying temples, books and historic sites.

quiz.q: What did the Communist Party's 1981 resolution conclude about Mao?
o: The Cultural Revolution was a catastrophe, but Mao's contributions outweighed his errors
He should be removed from all memorials
The Great Leap was a success
quiz.e: The resolution condemned the Cultural Revolution and acknowledged Mao's mistakes, while maintaining that his contributions were greater.

LESSONS.title: Backing up: never lose your photos again
LESSONS.hook: In 1998, a single mistyped command wiped out most of Pixar's Toy Story 2. What saved the film was a backup nobody knew existed.

sections.key: Even experts lose data, and the copy that saves you is often the one you didn't plan.
sections.b: In 1998, partway through making Toy Story 2, someone at Pixar ran a command that began deleting the film's files. Characters, sets and animation disappeared from the shared drives as staff watched. Worse, the studio's regular backups turned out not to have been working properly. The film was rescued because Galyn Susman, a technical director working from home after having a baby, had a fairly recent copy of the project on her home computer. The machine was carefully wrapped and driven back to the studio, and most of the work was restored. The story is told and retold in technology circles for a simple reason: if a world-class studio can come that close to disaster, so can your phone full of family photos.

sections.key: Files are lost to hardware failure, theft, accidents, malware and simple human error.
sections.b: Data rarely vanishes in dramatic ways. A phone is dropped in the surf, a laptop is stolen from a car, a hard drive quietly fails after a few years, or you delete a folder while tidying up and empty the bin. Fires, floods and break-ins take computers and the backup drive sitting right beside them. Then there is malicious software, especially ransomware, which scrambles your files and demands payment to unlock them. Storage is also less permanent than it feels. Every drive eventually fails, and cheap USB sticks and memory cards can corrupt without warning. The question is never whether something will go wrong with a device you own, but whether you will lose anything when it does.

sections.key: Keep three copies of what matters, on two different kinds of storage, with one copy kept offsite.
sections.b: The most widely quoted rule of thumb, popularised by photographer Peter Krogh, is 3-2-1. Keep at least three copies of anything important: the original plus two backups. Store them on at least two different kinds of storage, such as your computer's internal drive and an external drive, so a single type of failure cannot take them all. And keep at least one copy offsite, somewhere physically separate, so a fire, flood or burglary at home leaves something behind. Today the offsite copy is usually a cloud backup service, but a drive kept at a relative's house or your workplace also counts. The rule is not magic, but it forces you to think about every way your data could be destroyed at once.

sections.key: A syncing service copies your mistakes everywhere, instantly, unless it also keeps old versions.
sections.b: Many people assume their files are safe because they live in iCloud, Google Drive, OneDrive or Dropbox. These services are wonderful, but most of them are built mainly to sync: to keep the same files identical across all your devices. That means if you delete a folder, or overwrite a document with the wrong version, the change can spread to every device within seconds. A true backup is a separate copy that your everyday mistakes cannot reach. Many sync services do keep deleted files and older versions for a limited time, which helps, so it is worth learning how long yours keeps them and how to restore them. Treat sync as convenience, and make sure something else is your safety net.

sections.key: Keep at least one backup disconnected, so malware on your computer cannot reach it.
sections.b: Ransomware is software that encrypts your files so you cannot open them, then demands payment, often in cryptocurrency, for the key. Paying is no guarantee you will get your files back, and it funds the criminals. The best defence is a recent backup the malware cannot touch. If your external drive is permanently plugged in, ransomware can encrypt it along with everything else. So many experts suggest keeping a backup drive unplugged except while a backup is running, or using a cloud service that keeps older versions you can roll back to.
