Carroll himself publicly denied this in 1896, calling the story utterly false. Another common claim is that the Hatter was inspired by hat makers poisoned by the mercury used to treat felt. Mercury poisoning in the hat trade was real, and the phrase mad as a hatter existed before the book, but there is no evidence Carroll was making a point about it. Scholars have also debated Carroll's friendships with children, which were common in Victorian society but are viewed very differently today. The relationship with the Liddell family cooled in 1863 for reasons nobody fully knows, because the relevant pages of his diary were later cut out.

sections.key: The original handwritten Alice crossed the Atlantic and came back as a gift.
sections.b: Alice Liddell grew up, married and became Mrs Alice Hargreaves. In 1928, needing money after her husband's death, she sold the handwritten Alice's Adventures Under Ground at auction in London. It went to an American dealer and then to private collectors in the United States. After the Second World War, a group of American donors led by Luther Evans, the Librarian of Congress, bought it and gave it back to Britain in 1948, as a gesture of thanks for Britain's role in the war. It is now held by the British Library. Dodgson followed Alice with Through the Looking-Glass, published at the end of 1871, which gave the world Tweedledum, Tweedledee and the Jabberwock. He died in 1898, still a quiet Oxford don.

quiz.q: How did the Alice story first come into being?
o: It was a commission from Macmillan
It was improvised aloud on a rowing trip
It was adapted from a German fairy tale
It was written for a school magazine
quiz.e: Dodgson made up the story on 4 July 1862 while rowing with the Liddell sisters, then wrote it down at Alice's request.

quiz.q: Where did the pen name Lewis Carroll come from?
o: A character in a Dickens novel
A Latinised, reversed version of his own first names
The name of an Oxford street
quiz.e: Charles Lutwidge was Latinised as Carolus Ludovicus, then reversed and anglicised into Lewis Carroll.

quiz.q: Why are copies of the 1865 first edition so rare?
o: Most were destroyed in a warehouse fire
Tenniel was unhappy with the printing, so the edition was withdrawn
quiz.e: Tenniel complained about poor print quality. The run was withdrawn and reprinted, so only about two dozen 1865 copies survive.

quiz.q: What does the book actually call the character we know as the Mad Hatter?
quiz.e: In the text he is simply the Hatter. The 'Mad Hatter' label was popularised by readers and adaptations.

quiz.q: What did Carroll say about the story that Queen Victoria asked for his next book and got a maths text?
o: He said it happened to his brother
He publicly denied it as false
quiz.e: In 1896 Carroll publicly stated the story was false, although it is still often repeated.

LESSONS.title: Ern Malley: the poet who never lived
LESSONS.hook: In 1944 an Australian magazine hailed the discovery of a brilliant dead poet. He had been invented in a single afternoon by two bored soldiers.

sections.key: Angry Penguins was a bold young magazine championing modernist art and poetry.
sections.b: In the early 1940s, Australian art and literature were split between traditionalists and a younger crowd excited by modernism, the experimental style of writers such as T. S. Eliot and painters like Picasso. At the centre of the Australian avant-garde was a magazine called Angry Penguins, co-founded in Adelaide in 1940 by Max Harris, who was then still a teenager. It was supported by Melbourne patrons John and Sunday Reed, whose circle included the painters Sidney Nolan and Albert Tucker. The magazine published surrealist-influenced poetry and passionately argued that Australia needed to break with old forms. To its critics, much of this new poetry looked like pretentious nonsense that anyone could produce. Two of those critics decided to test that idea.

sections.key: James McAuley and Harold Stewart wrote the poems by deliberately stitching together random phrases.
sections.b: James McAuley and Harold Stewart were young poets who disliked modernism and preferred traditional craft. In 1943 both were serving in the army in Melbourne. According to their own account, they wrote an entire body of work in a single afternoon. They opened books at random, including a dictionary, a collected Shakespeare, a dictionary of quotations and an American report on draining swamps to control mosquitoes, and wove the phrases into sixteen poems. They deliberately included nonsense, false allusions and clumsy lines. Then they invented an author: Ern Malley, a mechanic and insurance salesman who had supposedly died young of illness in 1943, leaving his poems unpublished. The whole collection was titled The Darkening Ecliptic.

sections.key: Max Harris believed he had found a lost genius and published him lavishly.
sections.b: The poems were posted to Harris with a covering letter from Ethel Malley, Ern's supposedly grieving sister, who said she did not understand them but wondered if they were any good. Harris was thrilled. He believed he had discovered a major Australian poet who had died unrecognised, and he devoted a special issue of Angry Penguins to Ern Malley in 1944, with a cover painting by Sidney Nolan inspired by the poems. Not everyone was convinced, and some readers suspected a joke from the start. Within weeks, journalists began investigating who Ethel and Ern really were. In June 1944 the press revealed the truth, and McAuley and Stewart explained their experiment, declaring that the poems were deliberately meaningless.

sections.key: The hoax made Harris a national laughing stock and led to an obscenity prosecution.
sections.b: The story was a sensation, and newspapers across the country mocked Harris and modernism together. Worse was to come. South Australian police charged Harris with publishing indecent material, pointing to lines in the Ern Malley poems and other contributions to the magazine. The trial in Adelaide in 1944 became famous for its absurdity, as a police detective was asked to explain why certain words and images were immoral, and admitted he did not know what some of them meant. Harris was convicted and fined five pounds. Angry Penguins survived only a few more years. For a while, the episode seemed to prove exactly what the hoaxers had intended: that modernist poetry could not tell genuine art from random words.

sections.h: The poet who outlived his makers
sections.key: Many readers came to believe the fake poems were genuinely good.
sections.b: Then something unexpected happened. Over the following decades, many critics and poets argued that Ern Malley's poems were actually striking, with vivid images and an odd emotional power, regardless of how they were made. Sidney Nolan returned to Ern Malley in his art for years, and the American poet John Ashbery was among those who admired the poems. Some suggested that McAuley and Stewart, despite themselves, had poured real talent and feeling into the work. The poems have stayed in print ever since, which is more than can be said for most of the serious verse of 1944. The hoax also inspired later writing, including Peter Carey's 2003 novel My Life as a Fake.

sections.key: The Ern Malley affair raises lasting questions about authorship, intention and meaning.
sections.b: Does a poem's value depend on what its author intended? McAuley and Stewart said their poems meant nothing, yet readers kept finding meaning in them. That tension has made Ern Malley one of the most discussed literary hoaxes in the world, studied far beyond Australia. It also shows how chance can be creative: surrealist artists themselves had used random methods to escape habit. Some historians argue the hoax set back Australian modernism by years, making editors and audiences wary of experiment. Max Harris, for his part, went on to a long career as a bookseller, publisher and columnist, and never fully disowned Ern. The fictional poet, born as a joke, became one of the best known names in Australian poetry.

quiz.q: What kind of art did Angry Penguins champion?
quiz.e: Angry Penguins, edited by Max Harris, promoted modernist and surrealist-influenced art and writing.

quiz.q: How did McAuley and Stewart say they wrote the Ern Malley poems?
o: Over ten years of careful drafting
By stitching together random phrases from books in one afternoon
By copying an unknown poet's diary
quiz.e: They said they opened books at random, including a dictionary and a report on mosquito control, and combined phrases in a single afternoon.

quiz.q: Who supposedly sent the poems to Max Harris?
quiz.e: A letter from 'Ethel Malley', the invented sister, accompanied the poems.

quiz.q: What happened to Harris after the hoax was revealed?
o: He was fined for publishing indecent material
He sued the hoaxers and won
quiz.e: South Australian police prosecuted him for indecency, and he was convicted and fined five pounds.

quiz.q: Why do the Ern Malley poems remain famous today?
o: They were proven to be by T. S. Eliot
Many readers found them genuinely powerful despite their origin
They are taught as examples of bad grammar
quiz.e: Many critics and poets came to admire the poems, raising lasting questions about whether intention determines artistic value.

LESSONS.title: Pen names: why writers hide
LESSONS.hook: George Orwell, Mark Twain and George Eliot were not real names. Behind every pen name is a reason, from prejudice to privacy to a bit of mischief.

sections.key: Some of the most famous names in literature were invented.
sections.b: A pen name, also called a pseudonym or nom de plume, is a name an author publishes under instead of their own. The practice is ancient and widespread. The French writer Voltaire was born François-Marie Arouet. Lewis Carroll was Charles Dodgson. George Orwell was born Eric Arthur Blair. Australian readers know Henry Handel Richardson, author of The Fortunes of Richard Mahony, but the writer was in fact Ethel Florence Lindesay Richardson. Writers have adopted pen names to escape prejudice, to protect their families, to keep a day job, to separate different kinds of writing, or simply because they liked the sound of something better. Each disguise tells a small story about the pressures writers faced in their time.

sections.key: The Brontë sisters published as men to be judged on their writing alone.
sections.b: In 1846 three sisters living in a parsonage in Yorkshire published a book of poems under the names Currer, Ellis and Acton Bell. It sold only a handful of copies. The following year, Jane Eyre by Currer Bell became a sensation, and Wuthering Heights by Ellis Bell and Agnes Grey by Acton Bell appeared soon after. The authors were Charlotte, Emily and Anne Brontë. They kept their own initials but chose names that were not obviously female, because, as Charlotte later explained, they had noticed critics treated women writers with prejudice. Reviewers speculated wildly about whether the Bells were one person or several, and men or women. Charlotte and Anne eventually revealed themselves to their London publisher in 1848.

sections.key: Mary Ann Evans wanted to be taken seriously and to protect her private life.
sections.b: Mary Ann Evans was already a respected editor and translator when she turned to fiction in the 1850s. She chose the name George Eliot for several reasons. Female novelists were often assumed to write light romances, and she wanted her work judged as serious literature. She also lived openly with the writer George Henry Lewes, who was married and could not obtain a divorce, a scandalous arrangement in Victorian England. A male pen name kept attention on the books rather than on her life. Her identity became known within a few years of her first novel's success, but she kept the name. Middlemarch, published in instalments in 1871 and 1872, is often ranked among the greatest novels in English.

sections.key: Some pen names carry hidden meanings from the writer's life.
sections.b: Samuel Clemens worked as a Mississippi riverboat pilot before he became a writer. On the river, crew members called out depth readings, and 'mark twain' meant the second mark on the line: two fathoms, about 3.7 metres, deep enough for a steamboat to pass safely. Clemens began signing his newspaper writing Mark Twain in 1863. Eric Blair adopted the name George Orwell in 1933 for his first book, Down and Out in Paris and London, partly to spare his family embarrassment about his time living in poverty. George was a solidly English name, and the River Orwell in Suffolk was one he knew. Both disguises became so famous that their real names now sound like the pseudonyms.

sections.key: Established authors sometimes use new names to escape their own fame.
sections.b: Pen names are not only for beginners. Stephen King published several novels as Richard Bachman, partly because publishers then believed releasing more than about one book a year by the same author would saturate the market. A bookshop worker who noticed the similarities researched copyright records, and King was exposed in 1985. J. K. Rowling's initials were themselves a kind of disguise: her publisher suggested that boys might be reluctant to read a book by a woman, and she borrowed the K from her grandmother Kathleen. In 2013 she published a crime novel, The Cuckoo's Calling, as Robert Galbraith. It had modest sales until her authorship leaked, after which it shot up the bestseller lists overnight.

sections.key: Some modern authors use pen names to keep the focus on the work itself.
sections.b: The Italian novelist who writes as Elena Ferrante has kept her real identity officially private since her first novel in 1992, even as her Neapolitan novels became international bestsellers. She has said in interviews that books, once written, do not need their authors. Journalists have tried to unmask her, prompting fierce debate about whether readers have any right to know. Pen names raise interesting questions. Does knowing an author's gender, background or reputation change how we read? The Galbraith experiment suggests that names strongly influence sales, if not quality. Today, pen names are also common in genre fiction, where authors may write romance under one name and thrillers under another so loyal readers know what to expect.

quiz.q: Why did the Brontë sisters publish as Currer, Ellis and Acton Bell?
o: Their father forbade them to write
They believed critics were prejudiced against women writers
Their publisher was based in America
quiz.e: Charlotte later explained they chose names that were not obviously female because critics treated women writers with prejudice.

quiz.q: Which of these was a reason Mary Ann Evans used the name George Eliot?
o: To hide that she was a member of parliament
To avoid confusion with her sister
To be judged as a serious novelist and keep attention off her private life
Because her real name was too long to print
quiz.e: She wanted her work treated as serious literature, and her relationship with the married George Henry Lewes was a scandal at the time.

quiz.q: What did the riverboat call 'mark twain' mean?
quiz.e: It marked a depth of two fathoms, about 3.7 metres, which was safe for a steamboat.

quiz.q: What happened when it was revealed that Robert Galbraith was J. K. Rowling?
o: Sales of The Cuckoo's Calling soared
quiz.e: The novel had modest sales until the leak, then jumped to the top of bestseller lists, showing how much a name affects sales.

quiz.q: Who was the Australian author behind the name Henry Handel Richardson?
quiz.e: The author of The Fortunes of Richard Mahony was Ethel Florence Lindesay Richardson, writing under a male pen name.

LESSONS.title: Dracula: the theatre manager's monster
LESSONS.hook: The world's most famous vampire was created by a busy Irish theatre manager who never set foot in Transylvania. Much of what we think we know about Dracula isn't in the book.

sections.key: Bram Stoker spent most of his career managing a theatre, writing in his spare time.
sections.b: Abraham 'Bram' Stoker was born in Dublin in 1847. As a small child he was so ill that he could barely walk, and he later wrote that he spent his early years in bed listening to his mother's stories, including grim memories of a cholera epidemic. He recovered completely and became a champion athlete at Trinity College Dublin. He worked as a civil servant at Dublin Castle while writing theatre reviews for free. One of his reviews praised the actor Henry Irving, the two became friends, and in 1878 Stoker moved to London to become business manager of Irving's Lyceum Theatre. He held the job for around 27 years, handling everything from finances to tours, and wrote fiction in the gaps.

sections.key: Stoker built on a century of vampire folklore and fiction.
sections.b: Vampires did not begin with Stoker. Eastern European folklore told of the restless dead returning to harm the living, and reports of vampire panics in the 1700s spread across Europe. In 1819 John Polidori's story The Vampyre gave the creature an aristocratic, seductive character. In the 1840s the cheap serial Varney the Vampire thrilled readers for years. In 1872 the Irish writer Sheridan Le Fanu published Carmilla, about a female vampire, which scholars widely see as an influence on Stoker. What Stoker added was scale and method. He spent several years researching and planning, filling notebooks with ideas, and fused folklore, modern technology and Victorian anxieties into a single sweeping thriller that would eventually overshadow everything that came before it.

sections.key: Stoker's villain was originally called Count Wampyr; he found the name Dracula in a library book.
sections.b: Stoker's working notes, which survive, show that his vampire began as Count Wampyr. In 1890 Stoker holidayed in Whitby, a fishing town in Yorkshire with a ruined abbey on the cliff. In the local library he read an 1820 book about Wallachia and Moldavia which mentioned a ruler called Dracula and claimed the word meant devil in the local language. Stoker seized the name. The historical figure behind it was Vlad III of Wallachia, known as Vlad the Impaler, but scholars point out that Stoker seems to have known very little about him beyond the name. Whitby itself found its way into the novel: Dracula comes ashore there when a ship runs aground in a storm, and he leaps onto land in the shape of a large dog.

sections.key: Dracula is told through diaries, letters and recordings, which makes it feel like evidence.
sections.b: Dracula, published in May 1897, has no single narrator. Instead it is assembled from journals, letters, newspaper cuttings, a ship's log and telegrams. This form, called an epistolary novel, makes the story feel like a case file of real evidence. It was also strikingly modern. Dr Seward records his diary on a phonograph, and Mina Harker types up and organises the documents on a typewriter, cross-referencing them to track the Count. The heroes use trains, telegrams and blood transfusions. Stoker set an ancient monster against the newest technology of the 1890s, and much of the tension comes from that clash. The heroes win less through strength than through information, teamwork and careful paperwork.

sections.key: Several famous vampire rules come from films, not from Stoker's novel.
sections.b: Readers who come to the novel from films are often surprised. Stoker's Count can walk around London in daylight; the sun weakens his powers but does not destroy him. The idea that sunlight kills a vampire was popularised by the 1922 German silent film Nosferatu. The Count of the novel is first described as an old man with a long white moustache, who grows younger as he feeds. The suave figure in evening dress and cape owes much to the stage adaptations and to Bela Lugosi's performance in the 1931 Hollywood film. Garlic, crucifixes and a stake through the heart do appear in the book, but Stoker freely invented and mixed his rules.

sections.h: The widow and the stolen film
sections.key: Florence Stoker fought to protect the book, and the most famous pirate copy barely survived.
sections.b: Dracula sold steadily but did not make Stoker rich, and he died in 1912 with modest means. His widow, Florence, relied on the rights to the book. Nosferatu, released in Germany in 1922, was an unauthorised adaptation that changed the names, so Count Dracula became Count Orlok, but kept the story's shape. Florence Stoker sued for copyright infringement, and a German court ordered copies of the film destroyed. Fortunately for film history, some prints survived abroad, and Nosferatu is now considered a masterpiece. Florence later licensed an official stage version, which led to the 1931 film. Through more than a century of adaptations, Dracula became one of the most portrayed characters in screen history.

quiz.q: What was Bram Stoker's main job for most of his career?
o: Business manager of the Lyceum Theatre
quiz.e: Stoker managed Henry Irving's Lyceum Theatre in London for around 27 years and wrote fiction alongside the job.

quiz.q: What was Stoker's vampire originally called in his notes?
quiz.e: His notes show the name Count Wampyr; he found 'Dracula' in a library book in Whitby.

quiz.q: How is the novel Dracula told?
o: Through a single narrator, Jonathan Harker
Through diaries, letters, cuttings and recordings
quiz.e: It is an epistolary novel, assembled from documents, which makes it feel like a case file.

quiz.q: In the novel, what does sunlight do to Dracula?
o: Weakens his powers but doesn't destroy him
quiz.e: Stoker's Count walks in daylight with reduced powers. Lethal sunlight was popularised by the 1922 film Nosferatu.

quiz.q: Why did Florence Stoker sue the makers of Nosferatu?
o: It was an unauthorised adaptation of Dracula
It used her husband's name in the credits
It was filmed in her house
quiz.e: Nosferatu adapted the story without permission. A court ordered copies destroyed, but some prints survived.

LESSONS.title: Charles Dickens and the cliffhanger
LESSONS.hook: Dickens wrote his novels a few chapters at a time, while readers waited for each new instalment. A secret childhood trauma shaped almost everything he wrote.

sections.h: The boy in the blacking factory
sections.key: A painful childhood experience gave Dickens a lifelong sympathy for poor children.
sections.b: Charles Dickens was born in Portsmouth in 1812, the son of a navy pay clerk who was hopeless with money. In 1824, when Charles was twelve, his father was imprisoned for debt in the Marshalsea prison in London, and much of the family moved in with him, as was common at the time. Charles was sent to work in a warehouse near the Thames, pasting labels onto pots of boot blacking for about ten hours a day. The job lasted perhaps a year, but he felt abandoned and humiliated. He told almost no one. The full story became public only after his death, when his friend John Forster published his biography. The echoes run through his novels, full of orphans, debtors and cruel institutions.

sections.key: A job as a reporter trained Dickens's ear, and a comic serial made him famous at 24.
sections.b: Dickens had little formal schooling, but he taught himself shorthand and became a fast, skilled reporter, including in the press gallery of parliament. He watched people closely and listened to how they spoke. His humorous sketches of London life appeared under the pen name Boz. In 1836 a publisher asked him to write text to accompany a series of comic sporting illustrations. Dickens took control of the project, which became The Pickwick Papers. Sales started slowly, but when the witty Cockney servant Sam Weller appeared, the story took off. By the end of its run, each monthly part was selling tens of thousands of copies. Dickens was in his mid-twenties and already the most popular author in Britain.

sections.key: Dickens published most of his novels in instalments, writing as he went.
sections.b: Most of Dickens's novels first appeared in parts rather than as complete books. The typical format was a monthly instalment of about 32 pages with two illustrations, costing one shilling, usually running for nineteen or twenty months. Some novels, such as Oliver Twist, ran in magazines. This format made fiction affordable for more people, since buying a part a month was easier than paying for a whole book. It also shaped how Dickens wrote. He often stayed only a few instalments ahead of publication, ended parts on moments of suspense and could adjust stories in response to readers' reactions. Families and neighbours gathered to read new instalments aloud, so a single copy might reach many listeners.

sections.h: Little Nell and the waiting crowds
sections.key: Dickens's readers became intensely involved with his characters, sometimes to the point of legend.
sections.b: The Old Curiosity Shop, published weekly in 1840 and 1841, followed the doomed child Little Nell. As her death approached, readers begged Dickens to spare her. A famous story says crowds on a New York wharf shouted to arriving ships, asking whether Little Nell was dead. The tale is widely repeated, but historians note it is poorly documented and may be embellished. What is certain is that the novel was enormously popular on both sides of the Atlantic and that many readers grieved openly. Later critics found the death scene sentimental. Oscar Wilde reportedly joked that one would need a heart of stone to read it without laughing, though like many Wilde lines its exact source is uncertain.

sections.h: A Christmas Carol and the pirates
sections.key: Dickens fought for fair pay and helped shape the modern idea of Christmas.
sections.b: In 1843, short of money, Dickens wrote A Christmas Carol in about six weeks. He insisted on an expensive edition with gilt edges and colour illustrations at a low price, so although it sold out quickly, his profits were disappointing. The story nonetheless helped popularise an image of Christmas centred on family, generosity and feasting. Dickens was also furious about piracy. Before international copyright agreements, American publishers could reprint British books without paying the author a penny. On his first visit to the United States in 1842, he spoke out about it and was criticised in the American press for raising the subject. The United States did not offer meaningful copyright protection to foreign authors until 1891, two decades after his death.

sections.key: Dickens became a star performer, reading his own work to vast audiences.
sections.b: From the late 1850s, Dickens gave paid public readings of his work, playing every character with different voices and gestures. Audiences in Britain and America packed halls to see him. The tours earned him a fortune but exhausted him, especially his violent reading of the murder of Nancy from Oliver Twist, which left him drained. In June 1865 he survived a serious railway accident at Staplehurst in Kent, when a train he was travelling on crashed on a bridge under repair. He helped tend the injured and dying, then remembered his manuscript and climbed back into the carriage to retrieve it. He was shaken for the rest of his life. He died in 1870, five years to the day after the crash, leaving The Mystery of Edwin Drood unfinished.

quiz.q: What happened to Dickens at the age of twelve?
o: He won a scholarship to Oxford
He was sent to work in a blacking warehouse while his father was in debtors' prison
quiz.e: His father was imprisoned in the Marshalsea for debt, and Charles pasted labels on blacking pots, an experience he kept secret.

quiz.q: Which character helped turn The Pickwick Papers into a hit?
quiz.e: Sales were slow until the witty servant Sam Weller appeared, after which the monthly parts sold tens of thousands of copies.

quiz.q: Why did monthly instalments matter for readers?
o: They made fiction more affordable, a part at a time
They were only sold to libraries
quiz.e: A shilling a month was easier to afford than a whole book, and one copy was often read aloud to many people.

quiz.q: What problem did Dickens campaign against in the United States?
o: The pirating of British books without paying authors
quiz.e: Without international copyright, American publishers reprinted his books freely. He criticised this on his 1842 visit.

quiz.q: How should we treat the story of New York crowds asking whether Little Nell was dead?
o: As a widely repeated tale that is poorly documented
As something Dickens invented for advertising
As a scene from the novel itself
quiz.e: The novel was hugely popular, but historians note the wharf story is poorly sourced and may be embellished.

LESSONS.title: Invented languages: from Esperanto to Klingon
LESSONS.hook: People have built entire languages from scratch, hoping to unite the world, deepen a fantasy, or just for fun. Most failed. A few took on lives of their own.

sections.key: Inventing languages goes back at least nine centuries.
sections.b: Constructed languages, often called conlangs, are languages consciously designed by a person rather than evolving naturally in a community. One of the earliest recorded is the Lingua Ignota, or unknown language, created by the German abbess Hildegard of Bingen in the twelfth century, which included around a thousand invented words. In the 1600s, philosophers such as John Wilkins in England tried to build perfectly logical languages, where every word's form would reveal its meaning, sorting all of reality into categories. These schemes were brilliant and unusable. Historians have counted hundreds of attempts over the centuries. Their makers have had three main motives: to help people from different nations communicate, to explore ideas about logic and thought, or to bring a fictional world to life.

sections.key: A German priest's language briefly became a worldwide craze, then collapsed.
sections.b: In 1879 Johann Martin Schleyer, a Catholic priest in southern Germany, published Volapük, a language intended for international use. He said the idea came to him during a sleepless night. Its name came from distorted English roots: vol from world and pük from speak. In the 1880s it spread astonishingly fast, with clubs, journals and international congresses, and supporters claimed a very large following, though such numbers are hard to verify. But Volapük was difficult, with complex grammar and words so altered from their sources that they were hard to recognise. When reformers proposed simplifying it, Schleyer insisted on keeping control, and the movement split. Within a few years most of its followers had moved to a new rival.

sections.key: Zamenhof designed Esperanto to be easy and to promote peace between peoples.
sections.b: That rival was Esperanto. Its creator, Ludwik Lejzer Zamenhof, grew up in Białystok, then part of the Russian Empire, where Poles, Jews, Germans and Russians lived side by side, often with mistrust. He believed a shared neutral language could reduce hatred. An eye doctor by profession, he published his project in 1887 under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, meaning one who hopes. Esperanto was designed to be learnt quickly: spelling is phonetic, grammar has very few exceptions, nouns end in o and adjectives in a. Its vocabulary draws mostly on European languages. Estimates of speakers today vary enormously, from tens of thousands of fluent users to perhaps a couple of million with some knowledge, and a small number of people have grown up speaking it from birth.

sections.key: Esperanto survived hostility from dictators and the rise of English.
sections.b: Esperanto's internationalism made it suspicious to authoritarian regimes. In Nazi Germany it was attacked as a Jewish conspiracy, partly because Zamenhof was Jewish, and the movement was suppressed. In the Soviet Union under Stalin, many Esperantists were arrested in the purges of the late 1930s, accused of contact with foreigners. Zamenhof's own children were killed in the Holocaust. Even so, the language survived, holding world congresses, publishing original literature and translations, and later thriving online. It never became the global second language its founder hoped for; English largely took that role for reasons of power and economics rather than design. Still, it remains by far the most successful international language ever created, with a living community more than a century after its birth.

sections.key: J. R. R. Tolkien invented languages and then created a world for them to live in.
sections.b: J. R. R. Tolkien was a professional philologist, an expert in the history of languages, and he invented languages from his teenage years onwards. He called the hobby his secret vice in a 1931 lecture. For Tolkien, the languages came before the stories: he later explained that he built his mythology partly to give his languages a world and a history in which they could exist. His two main Elvish languages were modelled on real ones he loved. Quenya drew on the sounds of Finnish, while Sindarin was influenced by Welsh. He also worked out how they had changed over thousands of years of imagined history. This depth helps explain why Middle-earth feels so ancient: its names carry the weight of invented centuries.

sections.key: Film and television made professional language invention a career.
sections.b: In 1984 the linguist Marc Okrand developed the Klingon language for the film Star Trek III, building on a few words used earlier in the series. He deliberately gave it unusual features to make it sound alien, including a basic word order of object, verb, subject, which is rare among human languages. The Klingon Dictionary followed in 1985, and devoted fans have since translated works including Hamlet. Later, the linguist David J. Peterson created Dothraki and High Valyrian for the television series Game of Thrones, and other languages for many productions. These languages have consistent grammar and vocabulary, which is why fans can learn them. Some have even appeared in mainstream language learning apps, a sign of how seriously the art is now taken.

quiz.q: What was Hildegard of Bingen's Lingua Ignota?
o: One of the earliest recorded invented languages
quiz.e: In the twelfth century the abbess Hildegard created the Lingua Ignota, with around a thousand invented words.

quiz.q: Why did Volapük decline so quickly?
o: It was banned by the Pope
It was difficult, and its creator resisted reforms, splitting the movement
Its creator died before publishing it
quiz.e: Volapük's complex grammar and distorted vocabulary made it hard, and Schleyer's insistence on control split the movement.

quiz.q: What does 'Esperanto' mean?
quiz.e: Zamenhof published under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, meaning one who hopes, and the name stuck to the language.

quiz.q: Which real language inspired the sound of Tolkien's Quenya?
quiz.e: Tolkien modelled Quenya on Finnish, and Sindarin on Welsh.

quiz.q: What unusual feature did Marc Okrand give Klingon to make it sound alien?
quiz.e: Object-verb-subject order is rare among human languages, so it helps Klingon feel alien.

LESSONS.title: Sign languages: real languages, not gestures
LESSONS.hook: Sign languages have their own grammar, history and even accents. They are not universal, and they are not English on the hands.

sections.key: Sign languages are full natural languages, not mime or a code for spoken words.
sections.b: Many hearing people assume sign language is one universal system of gestures, or simply a spoken language spelled out with the hands. Neither is true. There are many sign languages around the world; one widely used reference catalogue lists well over a hundred. They arise naturally wherever deaf people form communities, and they differ from each other as spoken languages do. British Sign Language and American Sign Language, for example, are not mutually intelligible, even though both countries speak English. Each sign language has its own vocabulary and grammar, which are not copied from the spoken language around it. Fingerspelling, where words are spelled letter by letter, exists but is used mainly for names and borrowed terms, not for everyday conversation.

sections.key: American Sign Language descends largely from French Sign Language.
sections.b: Why is American Sign Language so different from British? The answer is a historical accident. In 1815 Thomas Hopkins Gallaudet, an American minister, travelled to Britain to learn how to teach deaf children, but the schools he visited were secretive about their methods. Instead he met teachers from the Paris school for the deaf, which welcomed him, and studied there with Laurent Clerc, a deaf teacher. Clerc agreed to come to America, and in 1817 they founded what is now the American School for the Deaf in Hartford, Connecticut. The French signs Clerc brought mixed with local sign systems used by American deaf people. The result was ASL, which still shares many signs with French Sign Language. Gallaudet University in Washington, DC, is named in his honour.

sections.key: On Martha's Vineyard, hearing and deaf people shared a sign language for generations.
sections.b: On the island of Martha's Vineyard, off Massachusetts, a hereditary form of deafness was unusually common from the 1700s into the early 1900s, especially in certain villages. As a result, a local sign language developed, and many hearing islanders learnt it too. Deaf people married, worked, voted and joined in community life much like anyone else, and hearing residents sometimes signed to each other even when no deaf person was present. The anthropologist Nora Ellen Groce documented this history in a 1985 book whose title reports what older residents told her: that everyone there spoke sign language. The case suggests that deafness becomes a disability largely when society cannot communicate with deaf people. As the island became less isolated, the local sign language died out.

sections.key: In 1880 educators voted to ban sign language from deaf schools, with effects lasting a century.
sections.b: In 1880, an international congress of educators of the deaf met in Milan. Almost all delegates were hearing, and they voted overwhelmingly in favour of oralism, the method of teaching deaf children only through speech and lip-reading, and against using sign language in classrooms. Over the following decades, schools in many countries followed this approach. Deaf children were often punished for signing, and some deaf teachers lost their jobs. Many deaf adults later described their schooling as deeply damaging, with years spent drilling speech instead of learning. Yet sign languages survived in dormitories, playgrounds and deaf clubs, passed from child to child. In 2010 an international congress on deaf education, held in Vancouver, formally rejected the Milan resolutions and apologised for their effects.

sections.key: Linguist William Stokoe showed that signs have structure, just like spoken words.
sections.b: For a long time even scholars thought sign was mere gesture. That changed with William Stokoe, a hearing English teacher at Gallaudet College in Washington. In 1960 he published a study showing that ASL signs can be broken into a small set of meaningful building blocks, such as handshape, location and movement, much as spoken words are built from a limited set of sounds. Change one element and you change the meaning, exactly as changing a sound turns pat into bat. Later researchers found rich grammar, including the use of space to track who did what to whom, and facial expressions as grammar: raised eyebrows, for example, can mark a yes or no question. Studies also found that damage to the brain's left hemisphere disrupts signing much as it disrupts speech.

sections.key: Australia's sign language belongs to the same family as British and New Zealand Sign Language.
sections.b: The sign language of Australia's deaf community is Auslan, a name formed from Australian Sign Language that came into wide use in the 1980s. Auslan descends mainly from British Sign Language, brought by deaf immigrants and teachers in the 1800s, with influence from Irish Sign Language through Catholic schools. Linguists group British, Australian and New Zealand Sign Language as closely related members of one family, and like British signers, Auslan users fingerspell with two hands, while ASL uses one. Auslan has regional variation too, with northern and southern dialects. It was recognised as a community language in Australia's national language policy of 1987, and today it is taught in some schools and TAFEs, and interpreters appear at many public events and emergency broadcasts.

quiz.q: Are British Sign Language and American Sign Language mutually intelligible?
o: Yes, because both countries speak English
quiz.e: Sign languages are not based on the local spoken language, so BSL and ASL are quite different.

quiz.q: Why does ASL share many signs with French Sign Language?
o: A deaf French teacher, Laurent Clerc, helped found the first permanent US deaf school
ASL was invented by a French linguist in 1960
Both copied a Latin sign system
quiz.e: Clerc came to America with Thomas Gallaudet in 1817, and French signs blended with local signing to form ASL.

quiz.q: What does the Martha's Vineyard story suggest?
o: When a community shares sign language, deafness is far less disabling
Sign languages cannot survive on islands
Hearing people cannot learn to sign
quiz.e: Because many hearing islanders signed, deaf residents took part fully in community life.

quiz.q: What did the 1880 Milan congress decide?
o: To make sign language compulsory in schools
To favour speech-only teaching and exclude sign language
To create one universal sign language
quiz.e: The mostly hearing delegates voted for oralism, leading to decades of bans on signing in classrooms.

quiz.q: Which sign language is Auslan most closely related to?
quiz.e: Auslan descends mainly from BSL, and together with New Zealand Sign Language forms one language family.

LESSONS.title: What your eyes and brain do when you read
LESSONS.hook: Reading feels smooth and effortless, but your eyes are jumping, stopping and skipping all the time. And your brain is using circuits that evolved for something else.

sections.h: A new trick for an old brain
sections.key: Writing is too recent for evolution to have produced a reading brain.
sections.b: Humans have been speaking for at least tens of thousands of years, probably far longer, but writing was invented only around 5,000 years ago, and mass literacy is barely a few centuries old. That is far too recent for evolution to have produced a brain built for reading. So how do we do it? The neuroscientist Stanislas Dehaene has proposed a theory called neuronal recycling. Learning to read repurposes brain circuits that originally evolved for other jobs, such as recognising objects and faces, and links them to the brain's language areas. In children learning to read, brain scans show a region on the underside of the left hemisphere becoming increasingly tuned to written letters and words.

sections.key: A specific region becomes specialised for recognising written words.
sections.b: That region is often called the visual word form area, sitting in the left fusiform gyrus, near areas that respond to faces and objects. In skilled readers it responds strongly to letters and words in a familiar script, and much less to unfamiliar symbols. It helps us recognise a word whether it is written in capitals, lower case or different fonts, an impressive feat of pattern recognition. Damage to this area, for example from a stroke, can cause a condition in which a person can still write but struggles to read back what they have just written. Research also suggests that learning to read changes the brain in other ways, including how it processes spoken sounds, which partly explains why reading and phonics are so closely linked.

sections.h: Your eyes jump, they don't glide
sections.key: Reading is a rapid series of jumps and pauses, not a smooth sweep.
sections.b: If you watch someone's eyes as they read, you will see they do not move smoothly along the line. They make quick jumps called saccades, separated by brief pauses called fixations. In English, a typical fixation lasts roughly a quarter of a second, and a typical jump covers around seven to nine letters. During the jump itself, you take in almost no useful visual information; the brain stitches the pauses together so that reading feels continuous. Readers skip many short, predictable words, such as the and of, and land more often on longer content words. About one jump in ten or so goes backwards, as the reader checks something. Researchers study all this with eye trackers, which record exactly where and when the eyes stop.

sections.key: You only see clearly a few letters at a time, and the window points in your reading direction.
sections.b: Sharp vision covers only a tiny part of what your eyes see, so at each fixation you can identify only a handful of letters clearly. Clever experiments, in which text on a screen changes depending on where the reader is looking, have measured this window. For English readers it extends roughly three or four letters to the left of the fixation point and about fourteen or fifteen to the right, because that is where the next words are. For readers of Hebrew, which runs right to left, the window is reversed. Information from the edge of the window helps the brain plan the next jump and get a head start on the next word. Reading, in short, is constant prediction.

sections.key: Research shows that reading much faster usually means understanding much less.
sections.b: Typical silent reading speeds for adults are roughly 200 to 300 words per minute, varying with the text and the reader. Speed reading courses have long promised thousands of words per minute, often by claiming you can stop hearing words in your head or take in whole lines at a glance. A major 2016 review of the research, with the eye-movement scientist Keith Rayner as lead author, concluded that these claims do not hold up. The limiting factor is not the eyes but the brain's speed in recognising words and understanding language. Pushing much faster forces a trade-off: comprehension drops. Speed reading techniques are essentially skimming, which is a useful skill for finding information but not a shortcut to deep understanding. Becoming a faster reader comes mainly from reading more.

sections.key: A famous internet text about jumbled words was not based on Cambridge research and only partly true.
sections.b: You may have seen a message claiming that, according to research at Cambridge University, it doesn't matter what order the letters in a word are, as long as the first and last letters are right. Matt Davis, a scientist at a Cambridge brain research unit, investigated and found no such study at Cambridge. The text is readable partly because of how it was written: many words are short and unscrambled, function words are intact, and the jumbled letters are often close to their correct positions. Scrambling longer words more thoroughly makes text much harder to read, and research shows jumbled letters still slow readers down noticeably. The meme does capture something real, though: the brain uses context and letter identity flexibly, not strictly one letter after another.

sections.key: A famous story suggests silent reading was once rare, but historians are more cautious.
sections.b: In his Confessions, written around 400 CE, Saint Augustine described his surprise at seeing Bishop Ambrose of Milan reading silently, his eyes moving over the page while his voice was still. This passage was long taken as proof that almost everyone in the ancient world read aloud. Reading aloud was certainly common, partly because ancient texts were often written without spaces between words, which made them harder to read silently. But historians now point to other ancient sources showing silent reading was known, and argue Augustine's surprise may have had other causes. What is clearer is that word spacing, which spread in European manuscripts during the early Middle Ages, made silent, private reading easier and much more widespread.

quiz.q: What does the neuronal recycling theory propose?
o: Reading uses brain circuits that evolved for other tasks
Humans evolved a reading gene 5,000 years ago
Neurons are replaced each time we learn a word
Reading uses only the right hemisphere
quiz.e: Writing is too recent for evolution to shape, so reading repurposes circuits such as those for recognising objects.

quiz.q: What are saccades?
o: Quick jumps of the eyes between fixations
Backward reading of a whole page
quiz.e: Saccades are the rapid jumps between fixations. We take in almost no useful information during the jump itself.

quiz.q: Why does an English reader's attention window extend further to the right?
o: The right eye is usually stronger
That is where the upcoming words are
Letters on the left are smaller
quiz.e: The window points in the direction of reading, which is why it is reversed for readers of Hebrew.

quiz.q: What did a major 2016 review conclude about speed reading?
o: Big gains in speed generally cost comprehension
It is impossible to read faster than 100 words per minute
quiz.e: The bottleneck is language processing in the brain, so going much faster mostly means understanding less.

quiz.q: What did a Cambridge scientist find about the scrambled letters meme?
o: It was based on a famous Cambridge study
There was no such Cambridge study, and the claim is only partly true
It was written by a Cambridge professor in 1903
quiz.e: Matt Davis found no such study. Scrambled text is readable only under certain conditions and still slows readers down.

LESSONS.title: Banned books: the trials that changed what we can read
LESSONS.hook: Popes, customs officers and courts have all tried to stop people reading certain books. Again and again, the ban made the book more famous.

sections.key: For four centuries the Catholic Church kept an official list of forbidden books.
sections.b: In 1559, under Pope Paul IV, the Catholic Church published the Index Librorum Prohibitorum, the Index of Prohibited Books. Catholics were forbidden to read or own listed works without permission. The Index grew out of anxiety about the printing press and the Protestant Reformation, which spread new ideas faster than authorities could control them. Over time it included works by figures such as the astronomer Galileo, the philosopher René Descartes and many others whose ideas were judged dangerous to faith or morals. Galileo's Dialogue, which defended the idea that the Earth moves around the Sun, stayed on the list for around two centuries. The final edition appeared in 1948, and the Index was formally abolished in 1966, ending its legal force.

sections.key: James Joyce's novel was banned in the United States until a landmark 1933 ruling.
sections.b: James Joyce's Ulysses, set in Dublin over a single day in 1904, broke many rules of the novel, including frank descriptions of sex and the body. When episodes appeared in an American magazine, The Little Review, the editors were prosecuted for obscenity in 1921 and fined. No publisher in Britain or America would take the full book, so it was published in Paris in 1922 by Sylvia Beach, owner of the bookshop Shakespeare and Company. Copies were smuggled into other countries and seized by customs. In 1933 the publisher Random House deliberately arranged for a copy to be seized to provoke a test case. Judge John M. Woolsey ruled that the book, read as a whole, was not obscene, and it was legally published in the United States in 1934.

sections.key: A famous 1960 trial in Britain opened the door to frank literature.
sections.b: D. H. Lawrence's Lady Chatterley's Lover, about an affair between an aristocrat's wife and a gamekeeper, was privately printed in Florence in 1928 and banned in Britain in its full form for decades. In 1959 a new British law allowed a book's literary merit to be considered as a defence against obscenity. Penguin Books tested it in 1960 by announcing a cheap, unabridged paperback, and was prosecuted. The defence called around 35 witnesses, including novelists, critics and clergy, to argue for the book's value. The chief prosecutor famously asked the jury whether it was a book they would want their wives or servants to read, a question that made the prosecution seem hopelessly out of touch. The jury acquitted Penguin, and the paperback sold millions of copies within months.

sections.key: For much of the twentieth century, Australia had one of the strictest censorship regimes in the Western world.
sections.b: Australian censorship was run largely through customs, which seized imported books at the border, alongside state obscenity laws. For decades the list of banned titles was itself kept confidential for long periods, so readers often did not know what they were missing. Works by authors such as James Joyce, D. H. Lawrence and many others were banned at various times, as were political works judged subversive. Lady Chatterley's Lover remained banned in Australia for several years after the British trial. Pressure for change grew through the 1960s. In 1970, Penguin Australia secretly printed Philip Roth's banned novel Portnoy's Complaint locally and distributed it, provoking prosecutions in several states. Around the same time, the federal customs minister Don Chipp began dramatically loosening the system, moving toward a classification approach.

sections.key: Censorship has sometimes gone far beyond bans to violence against books and authors.
sections.b: On 10 May 1933, Nazi-organised students in Berlin and other German cities burnt tens of thousands of books by Jewish, left-wing and other authors deemed un-German. More than a century earlier the German poet Heinrich Heine, whose own works were among those burnt, had written in a play that where books are burnt, people will eventually be burnt too. In 1989 Iran's supreme leader, Ayatollah Khomeini, issued a fatwa calling for the death of Salman Rushdie over his novel The Satanic Verses, which many Muslims considered blasphemous. Rushdie spent years in hiding. His Japanese translator, Hitoshi Igarashi, was murdered in 1991, and others connected to the book were attacked. In 2022, Rushdie himself was stabbed at a public lecture in New York state and lost the sight of one eye.

sections.key: Banning a book often draws more attention to it than it would otherwise receive.
sections.b: Censors face a stubborn problem: forbidding a book advertises it. The Lady Chatterley trial turned a little-read novel into a bestseller, and Ulysses gained a glamorous reputation partly because readers had to smuggle it. Today, book bans more often take the form of challenges to books in school and public libraries, where parents or groups ask for titles to be removed. Organisations such as the American Library Association track these challenges, which in recent years have frequently targeted books about race, gender and sexuality. People still argue about where the line falls between protecting children and restricting ideas. Many libraries celebrate an annual Banned Books Week, inviting readers to discover the books others tried to keep from them, and to decide for themselves.

quiz.q: When was the Catholic Church's Index of Prohibited Books abolished?
quiz.e: First published in 1559, the Index had its final edition in 1948 and was abolished in 1966.

quiz.q: How did Ulysses become legal in the United States?
o: A judge ruled in 1933 that, read as a whole, it was not obscene
It was reclassified as a medical text
quiz.e: Random House arranged a test case, and Judge John M. Woolsey ruled in the book's favour.

quiz.q: What change in British law made the Lady Chatterley trial possible?
o: A 1959 law allowing literary merit as a defence
A law requiring juries to read every book
quiz.e: The Obscene Publications Act 1959 allowed literary merit to be considered, which Penguin tested in 1960.

quiz.q: What did Penguin Australia do with Portnoy's Complaint in 1970?
o: Secretly printed and distributed it in defiance of the ban
quiz.e: Penguin Australia printed it locally and distributed it, provoking prosecutions and adding pressure for reform.

quiz.q: What is a common effect of banning a book?
o: It often attracts more attention and readers
quiz.e: Bans tend to advertise books; the Lady Chatterley trial turned the novel into a bestseller.

LESSONS.title: Does your language shape how you think?
LESSONS.hook: Do Inuit really have hundreds of words for snow? Does a language without left and right change how you see the world? The truth is stranger and more subtle than the myths.

sections.key: Benjamin Lee Whorf argued that the structure of a language shapes the way its speakers think.
sections.b: Benjamin Lee Whorf was a chemical engineer who worked for a fire insurance company in Connecticut, and studied linguistics in his spare time, partly under the anthropologist Edward Sapir. In his job he noticed that workers were careless near drums labelled empty, even though empty petrol drums can be full of explosive vapour. The word empty, he suggested, was shaping their behaviour. In the 1930s he went further, arguing that languages carve up reality differently and that speakers of very different languages think about the world in fundamentally different ways. This became known as the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis, though neither man ever stated it as a formal hypothesis, and the label was applied by others after their deaths.

sections.key: Linguists distinguish between language determining thought and merely influencing it.
sections.b: It helps to separate two claims. The strong version, sometimes called linguistic determinism, says language sets the limits of thought: if your language has no word for something, you cannot think about it. The weak version, linguistic relativity, says language nudges what you notice, remember and pay attention to, without imprisoning you. The strong version is almost certainly false. People can think about things they have no words for, babies and animals reason without language, and we constantly invent new words for new ideas, which would be impossible if words had to come first. Translation, while imperfect, is always possible to a meaningful degree. The live scientific question is about the weak version: how much, and in what ways, does language nudge thought?

sections.key: Claims about Hopi time and Inuit snow words became cautionary tales.
sections.b: Whorf claimed the Hopi language of Arizona had no words or grammatical forms referring to time as we understand it, so Hopi speakers saw the world differently. In 1983 the linguist Ekkehart Malotki published a large study documenting extensive time expressions in Hopi, including words for days, seasons and units of time. Then there is the claim that Inuit have dozens or hundreds of words for snow. It grew from a modest remark by the anthropologist Franz Boas, who mentioned four distinct root words, and was exaggerated with each retelling. Linguists Laura Martin and Geoffrey Pullum debunked the inflation in the 1980s. Inuit languages build long words from many parts, so counting words is misleading, and English has plenty of snow words too.

sections.h: The language without left or right
sections.key: Speakers of some Aboriginal languages use compass directions for everything, and track direction constantly.
sections.b: Some of the strongest evidence for linguistic relativity comes from Australia. In Guugu Yimithirr, from the Cape York region of Queensland, speakers do not use words like left, right, in front or behind to describe where things are. Instead they use cardinal directions, roughly north, south, east and west, even at small scales: there is an ant on your northern leg. Research by the linguists John Haviland and Stephen Levinson found that speakers kept remarkably accurate track of direction at all times, even indoors or after travelling, because their language demands it. In experiments where people turned around and recreated arrangements of objects, speakers of such languages tended to preserve compass direction, while English and Dutch speakers preserved left and right.

sections.key: Language can speed up colour discrimination and may be needed for exact counting.
sections.b: Russian has two basic colour terms for what English calls blue: goluboy for lighter blues and siniy for darker blues. In a 2007 study, Russian speakers were slightly faster at telling apart two shades when they fell on different sides of that boundary, while English speakers showed no such advantage. The effect disappeared when participants had to repeat numbers silently at the same time, suggesting language was actively involved. Numbers offer a more dramatic case. The Pirahã people of the Amazon have no words for exact numbers, only terms meaning roughly small and larger amounts. In several experiments they matched small sets accurately but struggled with exact quantities beyond about three, though results varied with the task. Researchers concluded that number words may be a cognitive tool for exact quantities.

sections.key: How we picture time can follow the direction of writing or the words we use for it.
sections.b: Asked to arrange pictures showing a sequence, such as a person ageing, English speakers tend to lay them out from left to right, while speakers of Hebrew and Arabic, written right to left, often go right to left. Research by Lera Boroditsky and Alice Gaby with Kuuk Thaayorre speakers, from Pormpuraaw on Cape York, found they tended to arrange time from east to west, whichever way they were facing, like the sun's path. In the Aymara language of the Andes, the word for the past is linked to the front and the future to the back: you can see what has already happened, while the future is unseen behind you. Speakers' gestures match, pointing forward for the past. These findings show how flexible human thinking about time can be.

sections.key: Language nudges thought in measurable ways, but some celebrated findings have not held up.
sections.b: Most researchers now accept a modest form of linguistic relativity. Language does not trap anyone's mind, but it guides attention, makes some distinctions easier to notice and remember, and provides tools, like number words, that extend what we can do. Caution is still essential. Some well-publicised findings, such as experiments suggesting that grammatical gender changes how people describe objects, have proved difficult to replicate, and other claims linking grammar to behaviours like saving money remain contested. Critics such as the psychologist Steven Pinker argue that thought largely runs on something deeper than any particular language. Learning another language, then, may not rewire your mind, but it can show you distinctions you never noticed, and a different way of standing in the world.

quiz.q: What observation from Whorf's insurance work inspired his thinking?
o: Workers ignored fire alarms written in English
Workers were careless around drums labelled empty that were full of vapour
Fires were more common in bilingual factories
quiz.e: He suggested the word 'empty' shaped behaviour, even though the drums held explosive vapour.

quiz.q: Which version of the Sapir-Whorf idea is almost certainly false?
o: The weak version, that language nudges attention
The strong version, that language sets the limits of thought
quiz.e: People think about things they lack words for and invent new words, so language cannot strictly limit thought.

quiz.q: What happened to the claim that Inuit have hundreds of words for snow?
o: It was confirmed by Franz Boas
It was an exaggeration of a modest remark, debunked by linguists
It was found to apply only to Hopi
It was proved in a 2007 experiment
quiz.e: Boas mentioned four roots; retellings inflated it, and Laura Martin and Geoffrey Pullum exposed the myth.

quiz.q: How do Guugu Yimithirr speakers usually describe where things are?
o: Using compass directions such as north and east
quiz.e: They use cardinal directions even at small scales, and research found they track direction with remarkable accuracy.

quiz.q: What did the Pirahã number studies suggest?
o: Pirahã speakers cannot see small sets of objects
Exact number words may be a tool needed for exact quantities
Counting is innate in all humans
Pirahã has the largest number vocabulary in the world
quiz.e: Without exact number words, Pirahã speakers struggled to match exact quantities above about three.

LESSONS.title: The pigeonhole principle: the simplest idea that proves surprising things
LESSONS.hook: If you have more pigeons than holes, some hole holds two pigeons. That is the whole idea, and it can prove that two people in Sydney have exactly the same number of hairs.

sections.key: If more items go into fewer boxes, at least one box must hold more than one item.
sections.b: Imagine ten pigeons flying home to nine pigeonholes. However they arrange themselves, at least one hole must end up with two birds. There is no clever trick, no probability and no calculation involved. It simply cannot be otherwise. This is the pigeonhole principle, and it may be the most obvious statement in all of mathematics. Yet mathematicians love it, because it lets you prove that something must exist without ever finding it. You do not need to know which hole is crowded, only that one is. The German mathematician Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet used the idea in the 1830s and 1840s, and in German it became known as the Schubfachprinzip, the drawer principle. The English name is thought to refer to the small compartments in old desks and mail sorters rather than to actual birds.

sections.key: Count the possible categories, add one, and a match is guaranteed.
sections.b: Here is the principle at its most practical. Your drawer holds a jumble of black socks and grey socks, the power is out, and you need a matching pair. How many socks must you grab to be certain? The answer is three. There are only two colours, so two socks might be one of each, but a third sock has to match one of them. The colours are the pigeonholes and the socks are the pigeons. The same thinking works for anything. With 367 people in a room, at least two must share a birthday, because there are only 366 possible dates, counting 29 February. Notice the difference between certainty and likelihood. A shared birthday becomes likely with just 23 people, but only 367 makes it a guarantee.

sections.key: Sometimes the principle proves a fact that sounds impossible to check.
sections.b: A typical human head has somewhere around 100,000 hairs, and estimates usually range up to about 150,000. Nobody has anything close to a million. Now consider Sydney, home to more than five million people. Make a pigeonhole for every possible hair count, from zero for the completely bald up to one million, giving just over a million holes. Then place each Sydneysider in the hole matching their exact number of hairs. There are far more people than holes, so at least two residents must have precisely the same number of hairs on their heads. In fact, the principle guarantees that some hair count is shared by at least five people. Nobody could ever find them by counting, yet we know for certain that they exist.

sections.key: Spread n items across k boxes and some box must hold at least n divided by k, rounded up.
sections.b: The principle has a stronger version, which tells you not just that some box is shared but how crowded it must be. Suppose 100 people attend a conference and are each born on one of the seven days of the week. Divide 100 by 7 and you get about 14.3, so at least one weekday must be the birthday of 15 or more of them. The rule is to divide the number of items by the number of boxes and round up. With 10 pigeons and 3 holes, some hole has at least 4. This version is how you can prove that among any 13 people, at least two were born in the same month, and among any 25, at least three were.

sections.key: At any gathering, at least two people have shaken the same number of hands.
sections.b: Here is a lovely puzzle. At a party, people shake hands with some of the other guests but never with themselves or twice with the same person. Prove that two guests have shaken exactly the same number of hands. Say there are 20 guests. Each person's count could be anything from 0 to 19, which looks like 20 possible values for 20 people, just enough to all be different. But look closer. If someone shook nobody's hand, then nobody can have shaken all 19 other hands. So the values 0 and 19 cannot both appear. That leaves only 19 usable pigeonholes for 20 guests, and two people must share a count. The trick is a common one: first show there are fewer real options than there appear to be.

sections.h: Why no app can shrink every file
sections.key: Counting alone proves that perfect lossless compression of every possible file is impossible.
sections.b: The pigeonhole principle sets hard limits in computing. Compression software such as zip shrinks files and later restores them exactly. Could a cleverer program shrink every possible file, even by a single bit? Counting says no. There are 1,024 different files that are exactly 10 bits long, but only 1,023 different files that are shorter, including the empty one. If every 10-bit file were squeezed into something shorter, two of them would have to share the same compressed version, and the program could not know which original to restore. So any lossless method that shrinks some files must leave others the same size or make them bigger. Real compression works because everyday files, like text and photos, are full of patterns, while truly random data cannot be squeezed.

sections.key: When something feels like it must happen, ask whether you can count the boxes.
sections.b: The principle teaches a habit of mind. Many claims that sound mysterious become clear once you ask how many possibilities there are and how many things must fit into them. It explains why hash functions, which turn any amount of data into a short fingerprint, must sometimes give two different inputs the same fingerprint, so security depends on making such collisions extraordinarily hard to find rather than impossible. It explains why a short PIN can only have so many combinations. It also guards against faulty reasoning, because the principle guarantees only that a match exists, not where it is or how many there are. Professional mathematicians use far more sophisticated versions in number theory and combinatorics, but each one starts with the same simple picture of crowded pigeonholes.

quiz.q: You have only black and grey socks in a dark drawer. How many must you take to be sure of a matching pair?
quiz.e: With only two colours, two socks could differ, but a third must match one of them.

quiz.q: Why must two Sydney residents have exactly the same number of hairs?
o: There are more residents than possible hair counts
quiz.e: With just over a million possible hair counts and more than five million people, some count must be shared.

quiz.q: If 10 pigeons go into 3 holes, what is the most you can say for certain?
o: Some hole has at least 4 pigeons
quiz.e: 10 divided by 3 is about 3.3, which rounds up to 4, so at least one hole must hold 4 or more.

quiz.q: In the handshake puzzle with 20 guests, why are there really only 19 possible counts?
o: Counts of 0 and 19 cannot both occur
Everyone shakes at least one hand
Handshakes always come in pairs of 10
quiz.e: If someone shook nobody's hand, nobody can have shaken everyone's, so only 19 values are available for 20 people.

quiz.q: What does the pigeonhole principle prove about compression?
o: All files can be shrunk by half
No method can shrink every possible file without loss
quiz.e: There are fewer shorter files than longer ones, so some files would have to share a compressed form.

LESSONS.title: The clever maths hiding in A4 paper
LESSONS.hook: Fold an A4 sheet in half and you get a smaller sheet of exactly the same shape. That is no accident: it rests on a single number, the square root of 2.

sections.key: Most rectangles change shape when you cut them in half.
sections.b: Take an ordinary rectangle and cut it in half across its long side. Usually the two halves have a different shape from the original. A square cut in half becomes two long, thin strips. A sheet twice as long as it is wide becomes two squares. This is a nuisance for printers, publishers and office workers, because a page designed for one size will not shrink neatly onto the next size down. Margins end up lopsided and enlarged copies leave gaps. The question is whether there is a rectangle that keeps its exact proportions every time you halve it. There is, and only one shape works. Most of the world now uses it every day without giving it a second thought, every time someone loads a printer or slips a letter into an envelope.

sections.key: A sheet whose long side is about 1.414 times its short side keeps its shape when halved.
sections.b: Call the short side 1 and the long side r. When you fold the sheet in half, the old short side becomes the new long side, and the new short side is r divided by 2. For the shape to stay the same, the ratio of long to short must be unchanged, so r divided by 1 must equal 1 divided by r over 2. Rearranged, that means r squared equals 2, so r is the square root of 2, about 1.414. Check it with A4, which measures 210 by 297 millimetres. Divide 297 by 210 and you get 1.414, almost exactly the square root of 2. Fold it in half and you get A5, 148 by 210 millimetres, with the very same proportions.

sections.key: A0 has an area of one square metre, and every A size is half the one before.
sections.b: The A series begins with A0, a sheet with an area of one square metre and sides in the ratio of the square root of 2. Its measurements are 841 by 1,189 millimetres, which multiply to 999,949 square millimetres, as close to one square metre as whole millimetres allow. Halve A0 and you get A1. Halve that for A2, then A3, then A4, which is one sixteenth of a square metre. This gives a neat bonus for anyone posting letters. Paper weight is sold in grams per square metre, so a standard 80 gram office sheet of A4 weighs one sixteenth of 80 grams, which is exactly 5 grams. Count the pages in an envelope and you can estimate its weight before you reach the post office.

sections.h: A German idea, two centuries in the making
sections.key: The idea was suggested in the 1780s, used in revolutionary France and standardised in Germany in 1922.
sections.b: In 1786 the German scientist and writer Georg Christoph Lichtenberg noted in a letter that a sheet with sides in the ratio of the square root of 2 could be halved again and again without changing shape. A few years later, revolutionary France, busy rationalising everything from weights to calendars, used the same ratio for some official paper sizes in a 1798 law on stamp duty. The idea then faded until the German engineer Walter Porstmann built a full system around it, starting from one square metre. Germany adopted his standard, DIN 476, in 1922. Other countries followed over the decades, and in 1975 it became the international standard ISO 216. Australia uses it, as do most nations, but the United States and Canada mostly stick with older inch-based sizes such as Letter.

sections.key: The 141% and 71% buttons on a copier are the square root of 2 and its reciprocal.
sections.b: Look at the zoom buttons on an office photocopier and you may see two strange-looking settings: 141% and 71%. They are the square root of 2 in disguise. To enlarge an A4 page so it fills an A3 sheet, the area must double, so each side must grow by a factor of the square root of 2, which is about 1.414, or 141%. To shrink A4 down to A5, each side shrinks by 1 divided by the square root of 2, about 0.707, or 71%. Because every sheet in the series has the same shape, the copy fits perfectly with no awkward white strip down one side. Two A4 pages placed side by side also shrink exactly onto one A4 sheet, which is how booklets and handouts are made.

sections.key: B and C sizes fill the gaps, and C envelopes are designed to hold A sheets.
sections.b: The system has two companion series. B sizes sit between A sizes. B4, for example, measures 250 by 353 millimetres, larger than A4 but smaller than A3, and each side is the geometric mean of its neighbours, found by multiplying them and taking the square root. B sizes are used for posters, passports and some books. The C series, mostly used for envelopes, sits between the A and B sizes, so a C envelope is just a little larger than the matching A sheet. A C4 envelope holds an A4 sheet flat, while a C5 envelope takes A4 folded once in half. The popular DL envelope, 110 by 220 millimetres, is made for an A4 sheet folded into thirds. A whole family of sizes fits together because of one number.

sections.key: The golden ratio is famous, but the square root of 2 is the ratio that actually runs the office.
sections.b: People often assume that elegant rectangles must follow the golden ratio, about 1.618, which is said to appear in art and architecture, though many of those claims are exaggerated. The golden rectangle has its own neat trick: cut a square off one end and the remaining piece is another golden rectangle. That is beautiful mathematics, but it is not what you need for paper. When you fold a sheet, you halve it rather than trim off a square, and only the square root of 2 survives halving. Compare US Letter, 8.5 by 11 inches, with a ratio of about 1.29. Fold it in half and the shape changes noticeably. A4 is a quiet reminder that a simple equation, solved properly, can make countless everyday jobs a little easier.

quiz.q: What is the ratio of the long side to the short side of A4 paper?
quiz.e: 297 divided by 210 is about 1.414, the square root of 2, the only ratio that survives halving.

quiz.q: Why does a standard 80 gram sheet of A4 weigh about 5 grams?
o: A4 is one sixteenth of a square metre
A4 is one tenth of a square metre
Paper is sold by the sheet
Each A size is one third of the last
quiz.e: A0 is one square metre and A4 is A0 halved four times, so it weighs one sixteenth of 80 grams.

quiz.q: Who built the full A-series system that Germany adopted in 1922?
quiz.e: Walter Porstmann's DIN 476 standard later became the international standard ISO 216.

quiz.q: Why does a photocopier use 141% to enlarge A4 onto A3?
o: A3 is 41% longer than A4 on one side only
Doubling the area means multiplying each side by the square root of 2
quiz.e: A3 has twice the area of A4, so each side grows by about 1.414, which is 141%.

quiz.q: Which envelope holds an A4 sheet without folding?
quiz.e: C sizes are slightly larger than the matching A size, so C4 holds A4 flat, while C5 takes A4 folded once.

LESSONS.title: Every shuffle is history: the astonishing size of 52!
LESSONS.hook: Shuffle a pack of cards properly and you have almost certainly created an order that no one in history has ever held. The maths behind that claim is simple and staggering.

sections.key: The number of ways to arrange things is found by multiplying down from the total.
sections.b: How many ways can you arrange three books on a shelf? Any of the three can go first, either of the remaining two can go second, and the last one fills the final spot.
