That is 3 × 2 × 1, which makes 6 arrangements. With four books it is 4 × 3 × 2 × 1, or 24. This multiplying-down pattern is called a factorial and is written with an exclamation mark, so 4! means 24. The notation was introduced by the French mathematician Christian Kramp in 1808, and it suits the numbers, because factorials grow at an exclamation-worthy pace. Ten books can be arranged in 3,628,800 different ways. A shelf of twenty books has more than two quintillion possible orders.

sections.key: A standard deck can be ordered in about 8 × 10 to the power of 67 ways.
sections.b: Now apply the idea to a pack of 52 playing cards. The top card can be any of 52, the next any of the remaining 51, and so on down to the last card. Multiply them all together and you get 52!, a number roughly 8 followed by 67 zeros. Written out, it is 68 digits long, beginning 8065. That number is hard to imagine, so try this. Suppose every one of the eight billion people alive today had been shuffling a deck once every second since the Big Bang, about 13.8 billion years ago. Together they would have produced roughly 3.5 × 10 to the power of 27 shuffled decks. That sounds like a lot, but it is less than a billionth of a billionth of a billionth of all possible orders.

sections.key: A properly shuffled deck is very likely in an order never seen before.
sections.b: Because the number of possible orders dwarfs the number of shuffles that have ever taken place, a well-shuffled deck is almost certainly unique in history. The odds that it matches any earlier shuffle, anywhere, are vanishingly small. There is an important catch hidden in the word ‘well’. A brand-new pack comes out of the box in a set order, and a couple of lazy shuffles leave much of that order intact. Decks shuffled badly are far more likely to repeat known patterns. Casinos take shuffling seriously for exactly this reason. The claim of uniqueness is about thoroughly randomised decks, where every one of those 52! orders is equally likely, not about a pack someone has given one quick riffle.

sections.key: Mathematicians showed that about seven riffle shuffles are needed to mix a deck well.
sections.b: So how many shuffles does it take? In 1992 the mathematicians Dave Bayer and Persi Diaconis published a famous analysis of the riffle shuffle, where you split the deck in two and let the halves fall together. They showed that the deck stays noticeably ordered for the first few shuffles, then becomes well mixed quite suddenly, at around seven shuffles. Beyond that, extra shuffles add little. Diaconis is an unusual figure in maths. He left home as a teenager to travel as a magician and only later became a celebrated professor of statistics. Other shuffling styles are much weaker. The overhand shuffle, where small clumps of cards are slid from one hand to the other, mixes so slowly that one analysis suggested it would take thousands of shuffles to randomise a deck.

sections.key: Eight perfect riffle shuffles return a deck to exactly its starting order.
sections.b: A perfect shuffle is not random at all. Skilled magicians can cut a deck into two exact halves of 26 and interleave them perfectly, one card from each side in turn. In the version called the out-shuffle, the top card stays on top. Do this once and the deck looks mixed. Keep going, and something surprising happens. After exactly eight perfect out-shuffles, a 52-card deck returns to its original order. Magicians use the predictability of perfect shuffles to make a pack look thoroughly mixed while secretly knowing where every card is. The lesson for everyone else is that mixing depends on randomness. A shuffle that is too precise is really just a permutation, a fixed rearrangement, and doing a fixed rearrangement enough times can bring you back to where you began.

sections.key: When order does not matter, you divide out the repeats, which gives combinations.
sections.b: Sometimes order does not matter. A five-card poker hand is the same hand whatever order you pick the cards up in. To count hands, start with 52 × 51 × 50 × 49 × 48 ordered ways to deal five cards, then divide by 5!, the 120 ways of rearranging the same five cards. That gives 2,598,960 possible poker hands. The same idea measures lotteries. A game where you choose 6 numbers from 45 has 8,145,060 possible combinations, so a single entry has about a one in eight million chance of the top prize. Counting like this is called combinatorics. It sounds abstract, but it tells you plainly how long the odds are, and why it is unwise to treat a lottery ticket as a plan rather than a bit of entertainment.

sections.key: Huge numbers of combinations are what make good passwords and encryption keys hard to guess.
sections.b: The explosive growth of possibilities is not just a party fact; it protects you every day. A four-digit PIN has only 10,000 possibilities, which is why banks lock a card after a few wrong guesses. A long password made of several random words has vastly more, because each extra word multiplies the total. Modern encryption relies on keys chosen from so many possibilities that trying them all would take longer than the age of the universe, even with enormous computing power. The same principle that makes a shuffled deck unique makes a properly chosen key unguessable. There is a practical takeaway: when you want something to be hard to guess, length and genuine randomness matter far more than clever substitutions, like swapping the letter o for a zero.

quiz.q: What does 4! equal?
quiz.e: 4! means 4 × 3 × 2 × 1, which is 24.

quiz.q: Roughly how many ways can a 52-card deck be ordered?
quiz.e: 52! is about 8 followed by 67 zeros, a 68-digit number.

quiz.q: According to Bayer and Diaconis, about how many riffle shuffles mix a deck well?
quiz.e: The deck stays noticeably ordered for a few shuffles, then becomes well mixed at around seven.

quiz.q: What happens after eight perfect out-shuffles of a 52-card deck?
o: It returns to its original order
The top card moves to the bottom
quiz.e: A perfect shuffle is a fixed rearrangement, and eight of them bring a 52-card deck back to the start.

quiz.q: Why do you divide by 5! when counting poker hands?
o: Because the order of the five cards does not matter
Because only five players can play
quiz.e: The same five cards can be picked up in 120 orders, so dividing by 5! counts each hand once.

LESSONS.title: The averaging trap: when rates don't add up
LESSONS.hook: Drive somewhere at 60 km/h and back at 40, and your average speed is not 50. Averages of rates fool almost everyone, and the mistake shows up in fuel bills, class sizes and bus stops.

sections.key: Averaging two speeds over equal distances does not give the average speed.
sections.b: You drive 60 kilometres to visit a friend at a steady 60 km/h, then crawl home through roadworks at 40 km/h. What was your average speed? Nearly everyone says 50 km/h, but that is wrong. The trip there took one hour. The trip home took an hour and a half, because 60 kilometres at 40 km/h is 1.5 hours. You covered 120 kilometres in 2.5 hours, which is 48 km/h. The slow leg drags the average down more than the fast leg lifts it, because you spend longer travelling slowly. Average speed is always total distance divided by total time. The moment you average the speeds themselves, you quietly give the fast leg and the slow leg equal weight, even though you spent far more time on the slow one.

sections.key: Some average-speed targets cannot be reached no matter how fast you go.
sections.b: This trap leads to a famous brain teaser. A cyclist rides one kilometre up a steep hill at 30 km/h and wants to average 60 km/h over the full two-kilometre trip, up and back down. How fast must she go downhill? Intuition suggests 90 km/h, to balance out the 30. But to average 60 km/h over two kilometres, the whole trip must take two minutes. The climb alone, one kilometre at 30 km/h, has already used up those two minutes. She would need to come down in no time at all, which means travelling infinitely fast. The target is impossible. Puzzles like this show why it pays to translate rates back into the real quantities behind them, such as distances and times, before doing any averaging at all.

sections.key: For equal distances at different speeds, the right average is called the harmonic mean.
sections.b: There is a proper tool for this job. For two speeds over equal distances, the correct average is the harmonic mean: divide 2 by the sum of the reciprocals of the speeds. For 60 and 40 km/h, the reciprocals are 1/60 and 1/40, which add to 1/24. Two divided by 1/24 is 48, matching the earlier answer. The harmonic mean is always less than or equal to the ordinary average, and it leans towards the smaller number. It appears whenever you average rates over a fixed amount of something, such as kilometres per hour over fixed distances or price per item over a fixed budget. A simpler rule of thumb is enough for most people: if in doubt, add up the totals and divide, rather than averaging the rates.

sections.key: Litres per 100 kilometres shows real savings far more honestly than kilometres per litre.
sections.b: In 2008 the researchers Richard Larrick and Jack Soll published a study in the journal Science about what they called the ‘MPG illusion’. Americans measure fuel economy in miles per gallon, and people assume that a bigger improvement in that number saves more fuel. Australia mostly uses litres per 100 kilometres, which avoids the trap. Compare two upgrades. Replacing a thirsty car that uses 20 litres per 100 kilometres with one using 15 saves 5 litres every 100 kilometres. Replacing an efficient car that uses 6 litres with one using 4 saves only 2 litres. In kilometres per litre, the first upgrade goes from 5 to about 6.7, while the second leaps from about 16.7 to 25. The second looks far more impressive, yet the first saves more than twice as much fuel.

sections.key: The average class size and the class size the average student experiences are different numbers.
sections.b: Imagine a small college with just two classes, one of 10 students and one of 90. The college can truthfully report an average class size of 50. Now ask each student how big their class is. The 10 students in the small class answer 10, but the 90 in the large class answer 90. Average those 100 answers and you get 82. Both numbers are correct, but they measure different things. Most students are in the crowded class, so the typical student experience is far more cramped than the official average. The same effect means that, on average, people's friends have more friends than they do, a result called the friendship paradox. Popular people appear in many friend lists, so they are overrepresented when you look at anyone's friends.

sections.key: If you arrive at random, you are more likely to land in a long gap between buses.
sections.b: Buses on your route come on average every 10 minutes, so you might expect to wait about 5 minutes. But buses often bunch up. Suppose the gaps alternate between 5 minutes and 15 minutes. That still averages 10, but if you arrive at a random moment, you are three times as likely to land in a 15-minute gap as a 5-minute one, simply because it lasts three times as long. Your expected wait works out to 6.25 minutes, longer than the 5 minutes you would wait if the buses were perfectly regular. Statisticians call this the inspection paradox. Whenever you sample something by stumbling into it, whether a gap between buses, a queue or a class, longer and bigger things are more likely to be the ones you find.

sections.key: Before averaging anything, ask what is being counted and whose point of view it is.
sections.b: These traps share a cause: an average is only meaningful if you know what it is an average of. A few questions protect you. First, are you averaging rates? If so, go back to the totals, such as distance and time, or fuel and kilometres, and divide those instead. Second, who is doing the counting? An average across classes, buses or businesses can differ wildly from the average experienced by the people inside them. Third, would a different unit tell a different story? Kilometres per litre and litres per 100 kilometres carry identical information, but one makes savings easy to see. None of this requires advanced maths, just the patience to ask what lies behind the number before you trust it to describe your own life.

quiz.q: You drive 60 km at 60 km/h and return the same 60 km at 40 km/h. What is your average speed?
quiz.e: 120 km in 2.5 hours is 48 km/h, because you spend more time on the slow leg.

quiz.q: A cyclist climbs 1 km at 30 km/h. Why can she never average 60 km/h over the 2 km round trip?
o: The climb alone uses up all the time allowed
quiz.e: Averaging 60 km/h over 2 km allows two minutes, and the climb has already taken two minutes.

quiz.q: Which car swap saves more fuel over 100 km?
o: It depends on the price of petrol
quiz.e: Going from 20 to 15 saves 5 litres per 100 km, compared with only 2 litres for the other swap.

quiz.q: A college has one class of 10 and one of 90. What average class size do its students experience?
quiz.e: 10 students report 10 and 90 report 90, which averages to 82 across all 100 students.

quiz.q: Why do randomly arriving passengers tend to wait longer when buses bunch up?
o: They are more likely to arrive during a long gap
quiz.e: Long gaps take up more of the clock, so a random arrival is more likely to fall in one.

LESSONS.title: The doomsday rule: find the weekday of any date in your head
LESSONS.hook: A mathematician named John Conway could tell you the day of the week for any date in history in a couple of seconds. His method is easy to learn, and it starts with 4 April.

sections.h: A party trick with a grim name
sections.key: Every year, a set of easy-to-remember dates all fall on the same day of the week.
sections.b: In the early 1970s the British mathematician John Horton Conway, famous for inventing the Game of Life, devised a way to work out the weekday of any date mentally. He built on an earlier method by Lewis Carroll, the author of Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, who was also a mathematician. Conway's trick rests on a striking fact. In any given year, a whole collection of memorable dates always land on the same weekday. Conway called that weekday the year's ‘doomsday’. The name sounds ominous, but it means nothing sinister, just the anchor day for that year. Once you know a year's doomsday and remember the anchor dates, finding the weekday of any other date in that year takes only a little counting forwards or backwards.

sections.key: 4/4, 6/6, 8/8, 10/10 and 12/12 always share a weekday, along with a few others.
sections.b: Here are the dates that always fall on the doomsday. First the even months, which are easy: 4 April, 6 June, 8 August, 10 October and 12 December, or 4/4, 6/6, 8/8, 10/10 and 12/12. For the odd months, a popular American mnemonic is ‘I work 9 to 5 at 7-Eleven’. That gives 9 May and 5 September, plus 11 July and 7 November. Australians writing dates day first can simply remember that the pairs swap. The last day of February is always a doomsday, as is 14 March, celebrated as Pi Day in the United States. For January, use 3 January in ordinary years and 4 January in leap years. In 2026, every one of these dates is a Saturday.

sections.key: Find the nearest anchor date, then step by weeks and count the remaining days.
sections.b: Now put the anchors to work. In 2026 the doomsday is Saturday. What day is Christmas? The nearest anchor is 12 December, a Saturday. Add a week and 19 December is also Saturday, then 26 December is too. Christmas, the day before, is a Friday. What about Australia Day, 26 January 2026? In an ordinary year, 3 January is a doomsday, so it is Saturday. Then 10, 17, 24 and 31 January are Saturdays, so 26 January is a Monday. With a little practice you jump to the nearest anchor and count only a few days. Because the anchors are spread through the year, no date is ever more than a couple of weeks from one, so even awkward dates take just a moment.

sections.key: Each year the doomsday moves forward one day, or two after a leap day.
sections.b: Doomsdays shift in a predictable way. A normal year has 365 days, which is 52 weeks and one day, so the doomsday moves forward by one weekday. A leap year has an extra day, so the jump after 29 February is two. In 2026 the doomsday is Saturday. In 2027 it moves to Sunday. Then 2028 is a leap year, so its doomsday jumps two places to Tuesday, because 29 February 2028 falls before 4 April and pushes everything along. To handle any year in a century, start from a known anchor. For the 1900s it is Wednesday and for the 2000s it is Tuesday. Add the number of years past the century, plus the number of leap years in that stretch, and count forward that many weekdays, ignoring complete weeks.

sections.h: A worked example: the Moon landing
sections.key: Working out a date from 1969 takes three quick steps.
sections.b: Let us test the method on a famous date. Neil Armstrong stepped onto the Moon on 20 July 1969, by American time. The anchor for the 1900s is Wednesday. The year is 69 years into the century, and in that time there were 17 leap years, since 69 divided by 4 is 17 with some left over. Add them: 69 plus 17 makes 86. Remove complete weeks: 86 divided by 7 is 12 weeks with 2 left over. Count two days on from Wednesday and the doomsday for 1969 is Friday. Now the anchor for July is 11 July, so that was a Friday, and so was 18 July. That makes 20 July a Sunday. In eastern Australia, the clocks were well into the next day, so viewers here watched on Monday 21 July.

sections.key: The calendar's rules make it repeat exactly every 400 years.
sections.b: The doomsday method works because the calendar follows fixed rules. Most countries use the Gregorian calendar, introduced by Pope Gregory XIII in 1582 and adopted gradually around the world. A year is a leap year if it is divisible by 4, except century years, which are only leap years if divisible by 400. So 1900 was not a leap year but 2000 was. These rules create a cycle of 400 years containing 146,097 days, which happens to be exactly 20,871 weeks. That means the calendar repeats perfectly every 400 years, with every date on the same weekday as four centuries earlier. A quirky consequence is that, across that cycle, the 13th of the month falls on a Friday slightly more often than on any other day of the week.

sections.key: Speed comes from repetition, and the payoff is a deeper feel for how the calendar works.
sections.b: Conway became remarkably fast at the method and reportedly had his computer quiz him with random dates when he logged in, timing his answers. He died in April 2020, during the early months of the COVID-19 pandemic, but the method remains popular with puzzle fans and memory competitors. To learn it, start small. Learn the current year's doomsday and the anchor dates, then check yourself against a calendar using birthdays and holidays. Once that feels easy, add the year-to-year shift, and later the century anchors. Beyond the party trick, the method teaches a useful idea from mathematics called modular arithmetic, which is the arithmetic of remainders. Weekdays cycle every seven, just as hours on a clock cycle every twelve, and many real-world patterns run in such repeating loops.

quiz.q: Which of these dates always falls on the same weekday as 4 April in the same year?
quiz.e: 4/4, 6/6, 8/8, 10/10 and 12/12 always share the year's doomsday.

quiz.q: If 12 December 2026 is a Saturday, what day is 25 December 2026?
quiz.e: 19 and 26 December are also Saturdays, so 25 December is the day before, a Friday.

quiz.q: The doomsday for 2027 is Sunday. Why is the doomsday for 2028 Tuesday rather than Monday?
quiz.e: 29 February 2028 adds an extra day before the anchor dates, so the doomsday jumps two places.

quiz.q: Which of these years was not a leap year?
quiz.e: Century years are leap years only if divisible by 400, so 1900 was not but 2000 was.

quiz.q: What branch of maths does the doomsday rule rely on?
o: Modular arithmetic, the arithmetic of remainders
quiz.e: Weekdays repeat every seven days, so the method works with remainders after dividing by 7.

LESSONS.title: Logarithms: the invention that turned multiplying into adding
LESSONS.hook: In 1614 a Scottish nobleman published tables that saved astronomers years of drudgery. For the next 350 years, his idea sat in the pocket of every engineer as the slide rule.

sections.key: Before calculators, multiplying large numbers by hand was slow and full of errors.
sections.b: Picture an astronomer around 1600, working out the orbit of a planet. Each step requires multiplying and dividing long numbers, often with seven or more digits, and a single slip ruins weeks of work. Navigators plotting positions at sea and surveyors mapping land faced the same burden. Adding two large numbers is quick and fairly safe, but multiplying them by hand means many rows of partial products and a lot of carrying. Mathematicians had long wondered whether there was a way to turn hard multiplication into easy addition. A clue came from patterns in powers. Since 2 × 2 × 2 is 8 and 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 is 16, multiplying 8 by 16 means adding the counts of twos, 3 plus 4, to get 7 twos, which is 128.

sections.key: Napier published the first tables of logarithms in 1614 after about twenty years of work.
sections.b: John Napier was a Scottish landowner, the Laird of Merchiston near Edinburgh, who also wrote a fiercely argued book on the biblical Book of Revelation. Mathematics was his passion, and he spent around two decades developing what he called logarithms, a word he built from Greek roots meaning ratio and number. In 1614 he published them in a Latin book usually known by its short title, the Descriptio, short for a description of the wonderful rule of logarithms. The book contained tables pairing numbers with their logarithms. To multiply two numbers, you looked up their logarithms, added them, and looked up which number had that total as its logarithm. Napier's version was not quite the logarithm used today, but the essential trick, turning multiplication into addition, was there.

sections.key: A logarithm answers the question: what power do I raise the base to, to get this number?
sections.b: The modern idea is easiest with base 10. The logarithm of 100 is 2, because 10 squared is 100. The logarithm of 1,000 is 3. In-between numbers have in-between logarithms. The logarithm of 2 is about 0.301, and the logarithm of 8 is about 0.903. Now watch the magic. Add those two logarithms and you get about 1.204. Look up which number has a logarithm of 1.204 and the answer is 16, which is exactly 2 × 8. Multiplication has become addition, and division becomes subtraction. Raising a number to a power becomes simple multiplication, and finding a square root becomes halving. With a good book of tables, a calculation that once took an hour could be done in minutes, with far less room for mistakes.

sections.key: Henry Briggs travelled to Scotland to meet Napier and went on to produce practical base 10 tables.
sections.b: Napier's book thrilled the English mathematician Henry Briggs, a professor in London, who travelled to Scotland in 1615 to meet him. The two agreed that logarithms would be far more convenient if they were based on 10, so that the logarithm of 10 was 1 and of 100 was 2. Napier died in 1617, and Briggs carried out the enormous labour of calculating the new tables by hand, publishing them in stages, including a large volume in 1624 covering numbers up to 20,000 and from 90,000 to 100,000. Others filled the gap soon after. These common logarithms became a standard tool. Students were still using printed books of log tables in classrooms, including in Australia, until electronic calculators became cheap and common in the 1970s.

sections.key: Logarithms arrived just in time to help Johannes Kepler finish his great planetary tables.
sections.b: One of the first scientists to seize on the new tool was the German astronomer Johannes Kepler. He had already worked out that planets move in ellipses, but turning that insight into tables predicting planetary positions years ahead required staggering amounts of arithmetic. Kepler studied Napier's work, wrote his own account of how logarithms worked and used them in completing the Rudolphine Tables, published in 1627. Those tables predicted planetary positions far more accurately than anything before them, and they helped persuade astronomers that Kepler's ideas, and the Sun-centred picture of the solar system, were correct. Kepler even dedicated a book to Napier, not knowing at first that Napier had died. Logarithms did not create the scientific revolution, but they made its endless calculations bearable.

sections.key: Placing two logarithmic scales side by side turned multiplication into sliding a ruler.
sections.b: Soon after Napier, the English mathematician Edmund Gunter drew a ruler marked with a logarithmic scale, so that distances along it represented logarithms. Using dividers, users could add lengths and so multiply numbers. In the 1620s and 1630s, the clergyman William Oughtred had the clever idea of sliding two such scales against each other, which did the adding automatically. This was the slide rule. Over the following centuries it became the engineer's constant companion. Slide rules helped design bridges, ships, aircraft and the rockets of the space age, and engineers on NASA's Apollo program used them. A good slide rule gave answers to about three significant figures, which is accurate enough for most engineering. Pocket electronic calculators replaced them almost overnight in the 1970s, ending three and a half centuries of service.

sections.key: Logarithms still describe how we measure sound, earthquakes, acidity and growth.
sections.b: Calculators made log tables obsolete, but logarithms themselves are everywhere. They are the natural way to handle quantities that span huge ranges or grow by multiplying. The decibel scale for sound is logarithmic, so every 10 decibels means ten times the sound intensity. Earthquake magnitude scales are logarithmic too, as is the pH scale for acidity, where each step is a tenfold change. In finance and biology, logarithms help describe compound growth and halving. Your own senses seem to work in a roughly logarithmic way, noticing proportional changes rather than absolute ones, so an extra candle brightens a dark room far more than a sunny one. The idea Napier spent twenty years refining still shapes how scientists see the world, long after its original purpose disappeared.

quiz.q: Using powers of 2, why does 8 × 16 equal 128?
o: 3 twos plus 4 twos makes 7 twos, and 2 to the power of 7 is 128
quiz.e: 8 is 2 to the power of 3 and 16 is 2 to the power of 4, so adding the powers gives 2 to the power of 7.

quiz.q: In what year did John Napier publish his tables of logarithms?
quiz.e: Napier published his Descriptio in 1614 after about twenty years of work.

quiz.q: If the logarithm of 2 is about 0.301 and the logarithm of 8 is about 0.903, what number has a logarithm of about 1.204?
quiz.e: Adding logarithms multiplies the numbers, so the answer is 2 × 8, which is 16.

quiz.q: What change did Henry Briggs and Napier agree on?
quiz.e: Base 10 logarithms made the logarithm of 10 equal 1, which was far more convenient for calculation.

quiz.q: How does a slide rule multiply numbers?
o: By sliding two logarithmic scales so their lengths add
By storing answers in a table
quiz.e: Lengths along the scales represent logarithms, and adding them multiplies the numbers.

LESSONS.title: Ramanujan: the clerk who wrote to Cambridge
LESSONS.hook: A largely self-taught clerk in Madras posted pages of strange formulas to a famous English mathematician. They were so astonishing that they changed both men's lives.

sections.h: A boy and a borrowed book
sections.key: Ramanujan taught himself advanced mathematics, largely from a single dense book of results.
sections.b: Srinivasa Ramanujan was born on 22 December 1887 in Erode, in southern India, and grew up in the town of Kumbakonam. As a teenager he came across a book by George Shoobridge Carr, a summary of several thousand mathematical results, mostly given without proofs. Ramanujan worked through it on his own, filling notebooks with his own discoveries. His obsession had a cost. He won a scholarship to college but neglected his other subjects, failed his exams and lost the scholarship. For several years he lived in poverty, working on mathematics with little guidance. Eventually, with the help of supporters who recognised his talent, he found a job as a clerk at the Madras Port Trust in 1912, which gave him a small wage and time to keep working.

sections.key: In 1913 Ramanujan wrote to G. H. Hardy at Cambridge, enclosing pages of extraordinary results.
sections.b: In January 1913 Ramanujan wrote to Godfrey Harold Hardy, one of the leading mathematicians in England, at Trinity College, Cambridge. He enclosed pages packed with formulas, many of them about infinite series and fractions, offered without proof. Hardy received many letters from cranks, and at first he was tempted to dismiss it. But as he and his colleague John Littlewood studied the pages, they realised they were looking at something remarkable. Some results were already known, a few were wrong, but many were new and astonishing. Hardy later wrote that some of the formulas must be true, because if they were not true, no one would have had the imagination to invent them. He set about bringing Ramanujan to Cambridge, though travelling overseas raised difficult questions for a devout Brahmin.

sections.key: Ramanujan arrived in 1914 and produced brilliant work, but struggled with cold, food and illness.
sections.b: Ramanujan sailed for England in 1914, arriving shortly before the outbreak of the First World War. He and Hardy formed one of the great partnerships in mathematical history, although they were very different people. Hardy insisted on rigorous proofs, while Ramanujan seemed to arrive at results by intuition, sometimes saying they came to him from the goddess Namagiri, his family deity. Hardy had to teach him the discipline of proof without crushing his originality. Life in wartime Cambridge was hard for him. He was a strict vegetarian, wartime food was scarce, the climate was cold and he was far from his family. Even so, his output was extraordinary, and in 1918 he was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society, one of the first Indians to receive that honour.

sections.key: Ramanujan saw at once that 1729 is the smallest number that is a sum of two cubes in two ways.
sections.b: The most famous story about Ramanujan comes from Hardy himself. Visiting his friend in hospital, Hardy mentioned that he had arrived in taxi number 1729, which he thought a rather dull number. Ramanujan replied that, on the contrary, it was very interesting. It is the smallest number that can be written as the sum of two cubes in two different ways. Check it: 1 cubed is 1 and 12 cubed is 1,728, which add to 1,729. Also, 9 cubed is 729 and 10 cubed is 1,000, which add to 1,729 as well. Numbers with this property are now called taxicab numbers in honour of the story. It captures something real about Ramanujan, who seemed to know individual numbers the way other people know old friends.

sections.key: Ramanujan and Hardy found a formula to estimate how many ways a number can be split into sums.
sections.b: One of their greatest achievements concerns partitions, the number of ways to write a whole number as a sum of positive whole numbers. The number 4 has five partitions: 4, 3 plus 1, 2 plus 2, 2 plus 1 plus 1, and 1 plus 1 plus 1 plus 1. The counts explode as numbers grow. The number 200 has 3,972,999,029,388 partitions, a figure the mathematician Percy MacMahon worked out painstakingly by hand. Hardy and Ramanujan found a formula that estimated such values with astonishing accuracy, and it was later refined into an exact formula. Ramanujan also spotted hidden patterns. The partition counts of 4, 9, 14, 19, 24 and so on, every fifth number, are always divisible by 5. Those counts begin 5, 30, 135, 490 and 1,575.

sections.key: Ramanujan fell seriously ill, returned to India in 1919 and died the following year, aged 32.
sections.b: By 1917 Ramanujan was seriously ill, and he spent long periods in hospitals and nursing homes in England. At the time doctors suspected tuberculosis, but historians and doctors still debate the cause, and some later studies have suggested a liver infection called amoebiasis. In 1919 he returned to India, weak but still working, and produced new ideas about strange functions he called mock theta functions. He died on 26 April 1920, aged just 32. His notebooks have kept mathematicians busy ever since. In 1976 the American mathematician George Andrews found a bundle of his later papers, now called the ‘lost notebook’, in the library of Trinity College. Researchers spent decades proving the results it contained, and some of his ideas have since found uses in modern physics.

sections.key: His formulas still help calculate pi and inspire research, and India celebrates his birthday.
sections.b: Ramanujan's influence reaches well beyond pure mathematics. In 1914 he published remarkably fast formulas for calculating pi, and in the 1980s computer scientists used one of his series to compute pi to millions of digits. Since 2012 India has celebrated his birthday, 22 December, as National Mathematics Day. His life has been told in Robert Kanigel's 1991 biography The Man Who Knew Infinity, later made into a film. His story is also a warning about lost talent. He was discovered partly by luck, through supporters in India and a single letter that happened to reach the right reader. Hardy, looking back, rated Ramanujan's natural genius above anyone he had known, and wondered how much more he might have achieved with an earlier, fuller education.

quiz.q: Why did Ramanujan lose his college scholarship?
o: He neglected his other subjects and failed exams
quiz.e: His passion for mathematics led him to neglect other subjects, and he failed his exams.

quiz.q: What did Hardy say about some of Ramanujan's formulas?
o: They must be true because no one could have imagined them otherwise
They were too simple to matter
quiz.e: Hardy felt some results were so strange that nobody could have invented them unless they were true.

quiz.q: Which pair of cube sums shows why 1729 is special?
quiz.e: 1729 equals 1 cubed plus 12 cubed and also 9 cubed plus 10 cubed.

quiz.q: How many partitions does the number 4 have?
quiz.e: 4, 3+1, 2+2, 2+1+1 and 1+1+1+1 make five partitions.

quiz.q: What was found in the library of Trinity College in 1976?
o: The ‘lost notebook’ of his later work
quiz.e: George Andrews discovered Ramanujan's later papers, now called the lost notebook.

LESSONS.title: I cut, you choose: the maths of fair sharing
LESSONS.hook: Two children and one cake have a perfect solution that is thousands of years old. Add more children and mathematicians needed until 2016 to finish the job.

sections.key: One person divides and the other chooses, so neither has reason to complain.
sections.b: Two siblings, one slice of cake, and an argument brewing. The classic solution is simple: one cuts, the other chooses. The cutter has every reason to make the two pieces equal in their own eyes, because they will get whichever piece is left. The chooser can then take the piece they prefer. Neither can reasonably complain. The idea is ancient. In the Book of Genesis, Abraham proposes dividing the land between himself and his nephew Lot and lets Lot choose which part to take. Mathematicians admire divide-and-choose because it works even when people value things differently. One sibling may care about the icing and the other about the size. Nobody needs to agree on what fair means, and nobody needs to trust anybody else's judgement.

sections.key: A share can be proportional, meaning at least your fair fraction, or envy-free, meaning you prefer it to anyone else's.
sections.b: Mathematicians who study fair division separate two ideas. A division is proportional if each of n people receives what they consider at least one nth of the total. A division is envy-free if nobody would rather swap their share for someone else's. With two people, these are the same thing: if you think your piece is at least half, you cannot prefer the other half. With three or more, they come apart. You might think your piece is a fair third, yet feel that someone else got a better piece than you did. Envy-free is the stronger and more satisfying standard, because it removes resentment entirely. It is also much harder to achieve, which is why even the three-person cake puzzled mathematicians until around 1960.

sections.key: A simple method guarantees everyone at least a fair share, but it does not prevent envy.
sections.b: In the 1940s the Polish mathematician Hugo Steinhaus and his colleagues Stefan Banach and Bronisław Knaster studied how to share fairly among many people. One of their methods is called the last diminisher. The first person cuts a slice they consider a fair share. The slice is passed around, and anyone who thinks it is too big may trim it down. The last person to touch the slice takes it. Everyone else continues with the rest of the cake. Each person can always guarantee themselves at least their fair fraction by trimming whenever a slice looks too generous. The method is proportional, but it is not envy-free. Someone might still believe that a later slice, cut from the remainder, was bigger and better than their own.

sections.key: In about 1960, two mathematicians independently found an envy-free method for three people.
sections.b: Around 1960, John Selfridge and John Conway, the mathematician behind the Game of Life, each found an envy-free method for three people. Neither published at first, so it spread by word of mouth and is now called the Selfridge–Conway procedure. Roughly, it works like this. The first person cuts the cake into three pieces they consider equal. The second person may trim the biggest piece to tie with the second biggest, setting the trimmings aside. Then the third person picks first, the second picks next and must take the trimmed piece if it is still available, and the first person takes what remains. A clever second round shares out the trimmings in a similar way. At the end, nobody prefers anyone else's total. It takes at most five cuts.

sections.key: Envy-free methods for any number of people were found in 1995, and a bounded one only in 2016.
sections.b: For four or more people, the problem became notoriously difficult. In 1995 the political scientist Steven Brams and the mathematician Alan Taylor published an envy-free procedure for any number of people. But it had a strange flaw. For some cakes and some preferences, the number of cuts it needed had no upper limit, so you could not say in advance when it would finish. Finding a method guaranteed to end within a fixed number of steps remained an open problem until 2016, when the computer scientists Haris Aziz and Simon Mackenzie found one. Their method always finishes, but the number of steps it may need is so astronomically large that nobody would use it at a party. The result is a proof that fairness is possible, not a practical recipe.

sections.key: Fair division maths can set rents for rooms of different quality so that no housemate envies another.
sections.b: Fair division is not just about cake. Housemates sharing a place with a big sunny room, a small room and a room near the noisy road face the same problem in reverse: they must divide a rent bill as well as rooms. In 1999 the mathematician Francis Su published a method, building on work by others, that uses a result called Sperner's lemma to show that there is always a way to set the rents so that each person prefers their own room at its price. Online tools based on these ideas now help people split rent, share chores and divide shared costs. Chores are a reminder that fairness flips when the thing being shared is unpleasant. With dirty jobs, the chooser picks the smallest burden, and the cutter adjusts accordingly.

sections.h: Fairness at the bottom of the sea
sections.key: An international treaty uses a version of divide-and-choose to share deep-sea mining sites.
sections.b: The most surprising use of divide-and-choose may be in international law. Under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, agreed in 1982, a company or country wanting to mine minerals from the deep seabed beyond national borders proposes an area large enough for two mining operations, split into two parts of similar estimated value. The International Seabed Authority then chooses one of the parts to reserve for future mining by the Authority itself or by developing countries, and the applicant may work the other. The applicant has every reason to divide fairly, just like the child cutting the cake. It is a striking example of a nursery rule turned into a tool of diplomacy, and it shows that good mechanisms, rather than trust or goodwill, can make sharing work.

quiz.q: Why does ‘I cut, you choose’ encourage the cutter to be fair?
o: The cutter gets whichever piece is left
quiz.e: Because the chooser picks first, the cutter's best strategy is to make both pieces equal in their own eyes.

quiz.q: What does it mean for a division to be envy-free?
o: Everyone gets exactly the same size
Nobody would rather have someone else's share
Everyone gets at least one nth
The pieces are all cut by one person
quiz.e: Envy-free means each person prefers, or is happy with, their own share over anyone else's.

quiz.q: What is a weakness of the last diminisher method?
o: It does not guarantee anyone a fair share
Someone may still envy a share given out later
It only works for two people
quiz.e: It is proportional, guaranteeing a fair fraction, but it does not prevent envy.

quiz.q: What did Aziz and Mackenzie achieve in 2016?
o: A bounded envy-free method for any number of people
A method using only one cut
Proof that fair division is impossible
quiz.e: Their method always finishes within a fixed number of steps, though that number is astronomically large.

quiz.q: In deep-sea mining under the Law of the Sea, who chooses which part of the area is reserved?
quiz.e: The applicant divides the area in two and the Authority chooses one part to reserve.

LESSONS.title: The maths of queues: why lines get long so suddenly
LESSONS.hook: A café that is busy most of the time can run smoothly, then a few extra customers turn it into a long wait. Queueing theory explains why, and how to fix it.

sections.key: Queueing theory began in 1909 with Agner Erlang's work on telephone exchanges.
sections.b: In the early 1900s telephone companies faced an expensive puzzle. Every call needed a line through the exchange. Too few lines and callers heard a busy signal; too many and costly equipment sat idle. Agner Krarup Erlang, a Danish mathematician working for the Copenhagen Telephone Company, tackled the problem with probability. In 1909 he published a paper on telephone conversations and probability, followed by further work that let engineers calculate how many lines they needed for a given level of service. His work founded queueing theory, the mathematics of waiting. A unit of telephone traffic, the erlang, is still named after him. The same maths now runs call centres, hospital emergency departments, supermarket checkouts, traffic lights and the computer servers that handle internet requests.

sections.key: Queues form even when there is enough capacity on average, because arrivals bunch up.
sections.b: Suppose a coffee cart can serve 30 customers an hour and, on average, 24 arrive each hour. You might think there would never be a queue, since the barista has spare capacity. In reality, customers do not arrive at neat, evenly spaced intervals. Some minutes bring nobody; then three people turn up together. Service times vary too, because one person wants a flat white and the next orders five complicated drinks. When several customers arrive close together, a queue forms, and the time the barista spends idle during quiet moments cannot be saved up for later. Lost idle time is gone for good. This is the key insight of queueing theory. Variability, not just the average workload, is what creates waiting, and waiting can build up even when a system looks comfortably under capacity.

sections.key: As a system gets close to full capacity, waiting times shoot up dramatically.
sections.b: Queueing models reveal a striking curve. In a classic model of a single server with random arrivals and random service times, the average wait in the queue depends on utilisation, the fraction of time the server is busy. At 50 per cent utilisation, the average wait equals about one typical service time. At 80 per cent it is four service times. At 90 per cent it is nine, and at 95 per cent it is nineteen. Plotted on a graph, the line stays fairly flat, then bends sharply upward like a hockey stick. That is why a café can cope well for most of the morning, then suddenly be swamped when just a few extra customers arrive. It is also why a system run at nearly full capacity, with no slack, is fragile.

sections.key: A single queue feeding several servers usually beats separate lines for each server.
sections.b: Think of a supermarket with a separate line at every checkout. You pick one, and the person in front has a problem with a price, while the line beside you races ahead. Now think of a bank or airport using one snaking queue that feeds several counters, with the person at the front going to whichever counter frees up first. The average wait is usually shorter with a single queue, and, just as importantly, the waits are far more even. Nobody gets stuck behind one slow transaction while other servers sit idle. Mathematicians call this the benefit of pooling. Separate lines can still make sense when space is tight or when express lanes help speed up small purchases, but pooling is one of the most reliable lessons of queueing theory.

sections.key: The average number in a system equals the arrival rate multiplied by the average time each spends there.
sections.b: One of the most useful results in the field is beautifully simple. Little's law, proved by the American researcher John Little in 1961, says that the average number of items in a stable system equals the rate at which they arrive multiplied by the average time each one stays. If a café gets 20 customers an hour and each stays for half an hour, then on average 20 × 0.5, or 10 customers are inside at any moment. The law works almost regardless of the details. It applies to customers in shops, patients in a hospital ward, cars on a motorway or tasks waiting on a computer. Managers use it in reverse, too. Knowing how many people are typically present and how fast they arrive tells you how long each one is staying.

sections.key: The experience of waiting depends on psychology as much as on the clock.
sections.b: Queueing maths measures minutes, but people judge waits by how they feel. In 1985 the business researcher David Maister wrote an influential essay on the psychology of waiting lines. Among his principles were that unoccupied time feels longer than occupied time, that uncertain waits feel longer than known ones, and that unexplained waits feel longer than explained ones. Unfair waits, such as watching someone push in, feel longer than fair ones. This explains many familiar features of modern life. Theme parks post estimated waiting times at the start of a line. Apps show your position in a call queue or how far away your rideshare is. Businesses place screens and menus where people queue. None of this shortens the wait, but it can make it feel noticeably more bearable.

sections.key: Leave slack, reduce variability and pool resources, whether you run a shop or a calendar.
sections.b: Queueing theory offers practical advice well beyond shops. Planning your own week works like a queue. If your schedule is packed at 95 per cent of your available time, any small delay causes knock-on chaos, just as the hockey-stick curve predicts. Leaving some slack is not laziness; it is what keeps the whole system flowing. Reducing variability helps too. Booking appointments, staggering arrivals and preparing for predictable busy periods all smooth out the bunching that creates queues. Pooling shared resources, such as one shared inbox for a team rather than separate ones, spreads work more evenly. And when you are the one waiting, it helps to remember that a long line is rarely about one slow person. It is usually mathematics at work.

quiz.q: Who founded queueing theory with work on telephone exchanges?
quiz.e: Erlang, working for the Copenhagen Telephone Company, published his first work on the subject in 1909.

quiz.q: Why can a queue form even when a server has spare capacity on average?
o: Arrivals and service times vary, and idle time cannot be saved
quiz.e: Randomness bunches arrivals together, and time lost being idle in quiet moments is gone for good.

quiz.q: In the classic single-server model, how does the average wait at 90% utilisation compare with 50%?
quiz.e: The wait is about one service time at 50% and about nine service times at 90%.

quiz.q: A clinic sees 6 patients an hour, each staying 2 hours on average. By Little's law, how many are there on average?
quiz.e: Little's law multiplies the arrival rate by the time in the system: 6 × 2 = 12.

quiz.q: According to David Maister, which of these makes a wait feel longer?
o: Being told the reason for it
Knowing how long it will be
quiz.e: Maister argued that unfair waits, like seeing someone push in, feel longer, while explained, occupied and known waits feel shorter.

LESSONS.title: Calculus without fear: the maths of change
LESSONS.hook: Calculus has a fearsome reputation, but its two big ideas can be grasped with a speedometer and an odometer. Its invention also sparked one of the bitterest feuds in science.

sections.key: Calculus answers how fast something is changing and how much has built up over time.
sections.b: Strip away the symbols and calculus asks two questions. First, how fast is something changing at this exact moment? Second, if you know how fast something is changing, how much has it added up to over time? Every car carries a picture of both ideas. The speedometer shows how fast your distance is changing right now. The odometer adds up all those changing speeds into a total distance travelled. The first idea is called differentiation, and its result is a derivative. The second is integration, and its result is an integral. These two operations sit at the heart of physics, engineering, economics and biology, anywhere things change smoothly. The genius of calculus is that it handles constant change, where ordinary arithmetic only works with fixed values.

sections.key: Ancient Greek paradoxes showed that thinking about infinitely small steps is genuinely tricky.
sections.b: The ideas behind calculus troubled thinkers long before anyone named it. Around the fifth century BCE, the Greek philosopher Zeno of Elea devised paradoxes about motion. In one, the swift Achilles can never catch a tortoise with a head start, because each time he reaches where the tortoise was, it has moved a little further on. In another, a moving arrow is at rest at every instant, so how can it move at all? Zeno's puzzles exposed a real difficulty: how can an infinite number of steps add up to a finite result? Today we can answer him. Add a half, a quarter, an eighth and so on forever, and the total gets ever closer to exactly 1. An infinite sum can have a finite value.

sections.key: Archimedes found areas and volumes by squeezing shapes between ever-finer approximations.
sections.b: In the third century BCE, Archimedes of Syracuse came remarkably close to integral calculus. To find the area of a circle, he trapped it between polygons drawn inside and outside it, then doubled the number of sides again and again. With 96-sided polygons, he showed that pi lies between 223/71 and 22/7, which is between about 3.1408 and 3.1429. His approach, now called the method of exhaustion, squeezed an unknown quantity between approximations that could be made as close as you liked. He used similar reasoning to find the area under a curve called a parabola and the volume of a sphere, which he was so proud of that he wanted a sphere and cylinder carved on his tomb. What he lacked was a general method that worked for every problem.

sections.h: Newton, Leibniz and a bitter feud
sections.key: Newton and Leibniz each invented calculus independently, then their supporters fought over who came first.
sections.b: In the mid-1660s, while Cambridge was closed by plague, the young Isaac Newton developed what he called the method of fluxions, but he kept it largely to himself for years. In Germany, Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz developed his own version in the 1670s and published first, in 1684. A bitter priority dispute followed, with Newton's supporters accusing Leibniz of plagiarism. In 1712 the Royal Society, of which Newton was president, issued a report that ruled in Newton's favour. Newton himself secretly drafted much of it. Historians now agree that the two men invented calculus independently. Leibniz's notation, such as dy/dx for a derivative and the long S symbol for an integral, proved clearer and won out, while British mathematicians, sticking loyally to Newton's dots, fell behind continental Europe for a century.

sections.key: A derivative finds the speed at an instant by measuring change over ever-shorter intervals.
sections.b: Drop a ball, and the distance it falls in metres is about 4.9 multiplied by the time in seconds squared, ignoring air resistance. How fast is it moving at exactly one second? Speed is distance divided by time, but at a single instant no time passes. So take short intervals. From 1 to 1.1 seconds, the ball falls from 4.9 metres to about 5.93, an average speed of 10.29 metres per second. From 1 to 1.01 seconds, the average is about 9.85. As the interval shrinks towards zero, the average speed closes in on exactly 9.8 metres per second. That limit is the derivative. On a graph, it is the slope of the curve at a single point, found by zooming in until the curve looks like a straight line.

sections.key: An integral adds up countless thin slices to find a total, such as distance or area.
sections.b: Integration runs the other way. If you drive at a steady 60 km/h for two hours, you travel 120 kilometres. On a graph of speed against time, that is the area of a rectangle, 60 high and 2 wide. But real driving involves constantly changing speed, so the graph is a wavy line. To find the distance, slice the area under it into thin vertical strips, each almost a rectangle, and add them up. The thinner the strips, the better the answer, and in the limit of infinitely thin strips, you get the exact area, which is the integral. This is Archimedes' squeezing idea made general. Engineers use integrals to find the total force on a dam wall, the volume of a fuel tank or the energy used over a day.

sections.key: Differentiation and integration are opposites, which turns hard area problems into easy ones.
sections.b: The deepest discovery of calculus is that its two halves undo each other. If you integrate a speed to get distance, then differentiate that distance, you get the speed back. This link is called the fundamental theorem of calculus, and Newton and Leibniz each grasped it. Earlier mathematicians, including Isaac Barrow, Newton's teacher at Cambridge, had glimpsed the connection, but the two founders turned it into a working method. Its power is enormous. Instead of slicing an area into thousands of strips, you can often find a formula whose derivative is the curve you care about, and the area follows almost instantly. Problems that once took Archimedes' genius became routine exercises. This single connection is why calculus spread so quickly through science in the following century.

sections.key: Calculus worked for over a century before mathematicians fully explained why.
sections.b: Early calculus had an embarrassing weakness. Newton and Leibniz reasoned with quantities that were infinitely small yet not quite zero, which critics found hard to swallow. In 1734 the Irish philosopher George Berkeley mocked these vanishing quantities as ‘ghosts of departed quantities’. Calculus kept producing correct answers in astronomy and engineering, but its foundations were shaky. In the nineteenth century, mathematicians including Augustin-Louis Cauchy and Karl Weierstrass rebuilt the subject on the idea of a limit, defined precisely without any mysterious infinitesimals. Their definitions answered Zeno at last. Today calculus underpins weather forecasting, rocket trajectories, medical scanners, economic models and the training of artificial intelligence systems, which adjust millions of settings by following derivatives downhill towards smaller errors. The maths of change runs much of the modern world.

quiz.q: In a car, which instrument is a picture of integration?
quiz.e: The odometer adds up changing speeds over time into a total distance, which is what an integral does.

quiz.q: What did Archimedes prove about pi using 96-sided polygons?
quiz.e: Squeezing the circle between inner and outer polygons showed pi lies between about 3.1408 and 3.1429.

quiz.q: Who secretly drafted much of the 1712 Royal Society report on the calculus dispute?
quiz.e: Newton was president of the Royal Society and drafted much of the report that ruled in his own favour.

quiz.q: A falling ball's distance is 4.9 × t squared. What is its speed at exactly 1 second?
quiz.e: Average speeds over shrinking intervals close in on 9.8 m/s, which is the derivative at 1 second.

quiz.q: What does the fundamental theorem of calculus say?
o: Every curve is a straight line
Differentiation and integration undo each other
quiz.e: Integrating then differentiating gets you back where you started, linking the two halves of calculus.

LESSONS.title: Dollar Bill and the day Australia went decimal
LESSONS.hook: On one Monday in 1966, a whole nation swapped pounds, shillings and pence for dollars and cents. Almost nobody wanted it called the dollar at first.

sections.key: Before 1966 Australians did their sums in a system based on twelves and twenties.
sections.b: For most of its history Australia counted money the British way. A pound was worth 20 shillings, and each shilling was worth 12 pence, so a pound held 240 pennies. Prices were written in a clumsy shorthand such as £2 7s 6d, and adding up a shopping bill meant constant carrying of twelves and twenties. Australia had issued its own pound since 1910, but the arithmetic was inherited from medieval England. By the 1950s businesses, banks and schools were complaining. Children spent hours learning to convert pence into shillings, and the new adding machines and early computers suited tens far better. Many countries had long since gone decimal, and a government committee set up in 1959 recommended Australia follow.

sections.key: The government's first choice of name, the ‘royal’, was so unpopular it was quietly dropped.
sections.b: Choosing a name proved harder than doing the maths. The public sent in thousands of suggestions, from the austral and the kanga to the emu and the ming, a cheeky nod to Prime Minister Robert Menzies' nickname. In 1963 the government announced that the new unit would be called the royal. The reaction was swift and scornful. Newspapers mocked it, and many people felt it sounded old-fashioned for a young country building its own identity. Within months the government backed down and settled on the dollar, a name already used in the United States, Canada and elsewhere, and short enough to say easily. The fuss is a reminder that money is not just maths. It carries national pride.

sections.key: The switch happened on a single day, backed by a huge public education campaign.
sections.b: The changeover was set for Monday 14 February 1966, nicknamed C-Day. To prepare people, the Decimal Currency Board ran one of the biggest public information campaigns Australia had seen. Its star was a cartoon character called Dollar Bill, and a catchy jingle sung to the tune of the bush ballad ‘Click Go the Shears’ explained the change on radio and television. The conversion rule was simple: ten shillings became one dollar, so one pound became two dollars. Banks closed briefly beforehand to prepare, and thousands of cash registers and machines had to be converted or replaced. Old and new money circulated side by side for a while, with shopkeepers giving change in decimal currency to drain the old coins from circulation.

sections.key: The new coins carried Australian wildlife, a design that has lasted for decades.
sections.b: The coin designs came from Stuart Devlin, a young Australian designer who later became a famous silversmith in London. Instead of kings and coats of arms on every coin, he chose native animals. The one cent showed a feathertail glider, the two cent a frilled-neck lizard, the five cent an echidna, the ten cent a lyrebird and the twenty cent a platypus. The fifty cent carried the national coat of arms. The monarch stayed on the other side, as is still the custom. These designs became so familiar that they have stayed largely unchanged through many decades, even as portraits of the monarch were updated. For many Australians, the platypus on the twenty is as recognisable as any flag.

sections.h: The coin worth more than its face
sections.key: The first round fifty cent coin contained so much silver it was worth melting down.
sections.b: One coin did not last long. The original 1966 fifty cent piece was round and made of 80 per cent silver. That seemed reasonable at first, but the world price of silver climbed during the 1960s, and soon the metal inside the coin was worth more than fifty cents. People began hoarding them rather than spending them, a textbook case of what economists call Gresham's law: when two kinds of money circulate, the one with more valuable content tends to disappear into drawers, leaving the cheaper one in use. The government withdrew the round coin and in 1969 introduced the distinctive twelve-sided fifty cent piece, made of copper and nickel, which is still in use today.

sections.key: Australia kept innovating, pioneering polymer banknotes and later scrapping its smallest coins.
sections.b: The story did not stop in 1966. In 1988, for the bicentenary of European settlement, the Reserve Bank issued a ten dollar note printed on plastic polymer instead of paper. It was developed in Australia, partly to defeat counterfeiters, since a clear window and other features were very hard to copy. By 1996 Australia had become the first country with a full series of polymer notes, and the technology has since spread to many countries. Meanwhile inflation slowly shrank the value of small coins. In 1992 the one and two cent coins were withdrawn, and cash totals have been rounded to the nearest five cents ever since. Card payments, of course, are still charged to the exact cent.

quiz.q: Under the old system, how many pence made up one pound?
quiz.e: A pound held 20 shillings and each shilling held 12 pence, so a pound was 240 pence.

quiz.q: What name did the government first announce for the new currency in 1963?
quiz.e: The government announced the royal, but public mockery led it to switch to the dollar.

quiz.q: What was the conversion rule on C-Day?
quiz.e: Ten shillings equalled one dollar, so one pound became two dollars.

quiz.q: Why did the round 1966 fifty cent coin disappear from circulation?
o: It was too easy to forge
It was too heavy to carry
Its silver came to be worth more than fifty cents
quiz.e: Rising silver prices meant the metal was worth more than the face value, so people hoarded the coins, an example of Gresham's law.

quiz.q: What happened to Australia's one and two cent coins in 1992?
o: They were withdrawn and cash totals rounded to five cents
They were redesigned with new animals
quiz.e: The coins were withdrawn and cash totals have since been rounded to the nearest five cents.

LESSONS.title: Why the Aussie dollar rises and falls
LESSONS.hook: In 2001 an Australian dollar bought less than 50 US cents. A decade later it bought more than a US dollar. Here is what moves a currency.

sections.key: An exchange rate is simply the price of one currency in terms of another.
sections.b: When you hear that the Australian dollar is ‘at 65 US cents’, it means one Australian dollar can be swapped for 65 American cents. An exchange rate is a price, and like other prices it is set by supply and demand. Every day, importers, exporters, tourists, investors and banks buy and sell currencies, and the trading in currency markets is enormous, measured in trillions of US dollars a day worldwide. If more people want Australian dollars, perhaps to buy Australian iron ore or Australian bonds, the price rises. If more people want to sell them, it falls. The Australian dollar is one of the most heavily traded currencies in the world, often nicknamed the Aussie.

sections.key: Australia let its currency float freely in December 1983, one of the biggest economic reforms in its history.
sections.b: It was not always this way. For decades Australia's currency was pegged, first to the British pound, then to the US dollar, and from 1974 to a basket of currencies that officials adjusted. The government and Reserve Bank effectively decided the rate, and strict controls limited how much money could flow in or out of the country. Defending the peg became increasingly difficult as money sloshed around the world. In December 1983 the Hawke government, with Treasurer Paul Keating, floated the dollar and removed most exchange controls, letting the market set the price. It was a dramatic shift. Since then the Reserve Bank has only occasionally stepped into the market, usually during periods of severe disorder.

sections.key: The Aussie dollar often moves with the prices of the minerals and farm goods Australia exports.
sections.b: Australia sells huge quantities of iron ore, coal, gas, gold, wheat and beef to the world. When those commodity prices climb, foreign buyers need more Australian dollars to pay for them, and the currency tends to rise. That is why traders call the Aussie a commodity currency. The mining boom of the 2000s is the clearest example. China's rapid industrialisation drove up demand for Australian iron ore and coal, and the dollar climbed from a low of under 48 US cents in 2001 to above parity, more than one US dollar, in late 2010, peaking in 2011. When commodity prices later fell, the dollar fell with them. The link is not perfect, but it is strong enough to watch.

sections.key: Higher interest rates can attract investors, pushing a currency up.
sections.b: Commodities are only part of the story. Investors constantly move money around the world looking for the best return. If Australian interest rates are higher than those in the United States or Japan, investors can earn more by holding Australian dollar deposits or bonds, so they buy Australian dollars to do it. This tends to push the currency up. One famous strategy, the carry trade, involves borrowing in a low interest currency, such as the Japanese yen for much of recent history, and investing in a higher interest one. It can be profitable for years and then unwind suddenly when markets panic. That is one reason the Aussie often falls sharply during global crises, as nervous investors rush to safer currencies.

sections.key: A strong dollar helps importers and travellers, while a weak one helps exporters and tourism.
sections.b: Whether a high dollar is good news depends on who you are. When the Aussie is strong, overseas holidays are cheaper, imported cars and electronics cost less, and Australians can buy foreign shares more cheaply. But exporters suffer, because their goods become more expensive for foreign buyers, and local manufacturers struggle to compete against cheaper imports. Universities and tourism operators also feel it, since Australia becomes a pricier place to study or visit. A weak dollar flips these effects. Overseas trips hurt, but farmers, miners and tour operators gain. This is why the exchange rate works as a kind of shock absorber for the economy, cushioning the blow when commodity prices or global conditions change.

sections.key: Comparing burger prices is a playful way to ask whether a currency is overvalued.
sections.b: If a currency is fairly priced, the same basket of goods should cost roughly the same everywhere once you convert the money. Economists call this idea purchasing power parity. In 1986 The Economist magazine turned it into a light-hearted gauge called the Big Mac index, comparing the price of the burger in different countries. If a Big Mac costs much more in Switzerland than in the United States after conversion, the Swiss franc looks overvalued by burger logic. The index is deliberately simple, since local wages, rents and taxes all affect burger prices. But it captures a real idea. In the long run exchange rates tend to drift towards levels that make prices broadly comparable, even if they stray widely in the short term.

quiz.q: What is an exchange rate?
o: The price of one currency in terms of another
The interest rate set by the central bank
A fixed rate set by the United Nations
quiz.e: An exchange rate is a price, set by supply and demand for currencies.

quiz.q: What happened to the Australian dollar in December 1983?
o: It was pegged to the US dollar
It was floated and the market set its price
It was linked to the price of gold
quiz.e: The Hawke government, with Treasurer Paul Keating, floated the dollar and removed most exchange controls.

quiz.q: Why is the Aussie called a commodity currency?
o: It often moves with the prices of the resources Australia exports
It is backed by gold reserves
It can only be used to buy commodities
quiz.e: When prices for iron ore, coal and other exports rise, demand for Australian dollars rises too.

quiz.q: How can higher Australian interest rates affect the dollar?
o: They can attract foreign investors, pushing the dollar up
They force the dollar back to parity
quiz.e: Investors seeking better returns buy Australian dollars to hold higher yielding deposits and bonds.

quiz.q: Who generally benefits from a weak Australian dollar?
quiz.e: A weak dollar makes Australian goods and holidays cheaper for foreigners, helping exporters and tourism.

LESSONS.title: Bank runs: when everyone wants their money at once
LESSONS.hook: Your bank does not keep your savings in a vault. Usually that is fine. When everyone turns up at once, it can be catastrophic.

sections.key: Banks lend out most of the money deposited with them, keeping only a fraction on hand.
sections.b: When you deposit money in a bank, it does not sit in a box with your name on it. Banks take deposits that customers can withdraw at any moment and use them to fund loans that will not be repaid for years, such as mortgages and business loans. They keep only a small portion as cash and reserves, betting, sensibly, that not everyone will want their money on the same day. This arrangement is the heart of banking and it is genuinely useful, turning idle savings into homes and businesses. But it creates a built-in fragility. A bank can be perfectly sound, with good loans that will be repaid, and still be unable to hand everyone their money back immediately.

sections.key: A run can topple a healthy bank simply because people fear it will fall.
sections.b: Imagine a rumour spreads that your bank is in trouble. Even if you think the rumour is false, you have a problem. If other people believe it and withdraw their money, the bank may run out of cash, and those who wait could lose out. So the rational move is to join the queue. Everyone reasons the same way, and the fear becomes reality. Economists Douglas Diamond and Philip Dybvig described this trap in a famous 1983 model, showing how a bank run can be a self-fulfilling prophecy. Their work helped earn them a share of the 2022 Nobel Prize in economics, alongside Ben Bernanke, who studied how bank failures deepened the Great Depression.

sections.key: Australia suffered one of history's great banking crises after a property bubble burst.
sections.b: Australia knows this story well. In the 1880s Melbourne boomed on gold wealth and borrowed British money, and land prices soared in a speculative frenzy. Dozens of building societies and land banks lent freely against property. When the bubble burst at the end of the decade, borrowers defaulted and many of these institutions collapsed. In 1893 the crisis reached the major banks. Depositors rushed to withdraw their money, and many of the colonies' major banks suspended payments within a few weeks. Some reopened after being reorganised, but savings were frozen or lost and the colonies plunged into a deep depression that lasted for much of the decade. Melbourne took years to recover.

sections.key: Banks fight runs by explaining that the money is safe, just tied up in loans.
sections.b: The classic film It's a Wonderful Life, released in 1946, contains one of the clearest explanations of a bank run ever filmed. When panicked customers crowd into George Bailey's building and loan company demanding their savings, he explains that their money is not in a safe. It is in Joe's house and the Kennedys' house, lent out so neighbours could buy homes. If everyone insists on withdrawing at once, the whole community suffers. Bailey calms the crowd by asking each person to take only what they need. Real banks rely on something similar but more powerful: a central bank willing to lend them cash against good assets in an emergency, acting as a lender of last resort.

sections.key: Governments now insure deposits so that ordinary savers have no reason to run.
sections.b: The most effective cure for bank runs has been deposit insurance. After thousands of American banks failed in the early 1930s, the United States created the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation in 1933, promising savers they would get their money back up to a limit. With that guarantee in place, there was little reason to panic, and large-scale runs became rare. Australia introduced its Financial Claims Scheme during the global financial crisis in 2008. As of the mid-2020s it protects deposits up to 250,000 dollars per account holder at each authorised bank, building society or credit union. Because the guarantee exists, the need to use it is far less likely. Confidence itself is the protection.

sections.key: Modern runs can happen in hours, driven by phones and social media.
sections.b: Runs have not disappeared. In September 2007 queues formed outside branches of Britain's Northern Rock, one of the first visible signs of the global financial crisis and the first run on a British bank in well over a century. In March 2023 California's Silicon Valley Bank collapsed in a run of startling speed. Many of its customers were tech firms with deposits far above the insured limit, and as worries spread through group chats and social media, they tried to pull tens of billions of dollars in a single day using banking apps. There were no queues outside, just a flood of online transfers. The bank was closed by regulators within roughly two days, showing how quickly modern panic can spread.

quiz.q: Why can a sound bank still be unable to pay all depositors at once?
o: It keeps all deposits in gold
Most deposits have been lent out in long-term loans
Banks are not allowed to hold cash
Deposits are held by the government
quiz.e: Banks lend most deposits as long-term loans and keep only a fraction available as cash.

quiz.q: What did Diamond and Dybvig show about bank runs?
o: They only happen to badly run banks
They can be self-fulfilling, toppling even healthy banks
They are caused by high interest rates
They cannot happen once a country has a central bank
quiz.e: Their 1983 model showed that fear of a run can rationally cause one, even at a sound bank.

quiz.q: In It's a Wonderful Life, where does George Bailey say the depositors' money is?
o: In a vault in New York
Lent out in their neighbours' homes
quiz.e: He explains the money is lent out to neighbours for their houses, not sitting in a safe.

quiz.q: What does Australia's Financial Claims Scheme do?
o: Guarantees deposits up to a limit at authorised institutions
Lends money to first home buyers
quiz.e: It protects deposits, as of the mid-2020s up to 250,000 dollars per account holder at each authorised institution.

quiz.q: What made the 2023 run on Silicon Valley Bank unusual?
o: It was extraordinarily fast, driven by online transfers and social media
It was stopped by deposit insurance alone
quiz.e: Customers tried to pull tens of billions of dollars in a day using apps, with panic spreading online.

LESSONS.title: The Medici: the bankers who built a Renaissance
LESSONS.hook: A family of Florentine money-changers became bankers to the Pope, patrons of genius and rulers of a city. Their tricks still shape finance today.

sections.key: Banking in Renaissance Italy began with money-changers working at benches in the street.
sections.b: In the 1300s Italian cities such as Florence, Venice and Genoa were the trading hubs of Europe, awash with coins from dozens of different states. Merchants needed someone to weigh, test and swap these coins, and to move money safely across long distances. Money-changers set up at tables, and the Italian word for such a bench, banco, gave us the word bank. A banker who could not pay was said to be banca rotta, a broken bench, the root of our word bankrupt. In 1397 Giovanni di Bicci de' Medici founded the Medici Bank in Florence. Within a few decades it would become the most powerful bank in Europe.

sections.key: The Medici grew rich by managing the finances of the Catholic Church.
sections.b: The Medici's greatest client was the papacy. The Church collected revenues from all over Christian Europe, from England to Poland, and needed a way to move that money to Rome without carting chests of silver across the Alps. The Medici, with their network of trusted agents, could do it. For long stretches of the 1400s they served as the main bankers to the Pope, a relationship that brought enormous profits and political influence. Their Rome branch was often the most profitable in the company. The connection lasted well beyond the bank itself. In the following century two members of the family became popes themselves, Leo X and Clement VII, a sign of how deeply the family had woven itself into the Church.

sections.key: The Church banned charging interest, so bankers earned it through currency exchange instead.
sections.b: There was an awkward problem. The Church condemned usury, which in that era meant charging interest on a loan, as a sin. So how could a bank make money? The answer was the bill of exchange. A merchant in Florence might hand over florins and receive a document payable months later in another currency, say in Bruges or London. The rates used at each end were set so that the banker made a profit, but on paper the deal was an exchange of currencies, not a loan.
