quiz.e: The magnet bent its track like an electron's but in the opposite direction, and the lead plate showed which way it was travelling.

quiz.q: How does annihilation compare with nuclear fission?
o: Annihilation converts all the mass into energy; fission converts less than one per cent
quiz.e: When matter meets antimatter, their whole mass becomes energy, the most complete conversion known.

quiz.q: How does a PET scan use antimatter?
o: It fires antiprotons into the body
It stores antimatter in the scanner
It turns body tissue into antimatter
It detects the paired gamma rays from positrons annihilating with electrons
quiz.e: Positrons from a radioactive tracer annihilate with electrons, and detectors trace the opposite-pointing gamma rays back to their source.

quiz.q: What is the matter–antimatter mystery?
o: Why the universe is made almost entirely of matter when equal amounts should have formed
Why positrons are heavier than electrons
Why antimatter can't be made in labs
quiz.e: A small excess of matter somehow survived the Big Bang, and known effects are far too small to explain it.

LESSONS.title: The snail in the bottle: how negligence law was born
LESSONS.hook: A woman in a Scottish café sipped a ginger beer and claimed she found a rotting snail in it. Her lawsuit changed the law for almost everyone in the English-speaking world.

sections.key: A ruined drink in 1928 led to one of the most famous court cases ever decided.
sections.b: On the evening of 26 August 1928, May Donoghue met a friend at the Wellmeadow Café in Paisley, near Glasgow. Her friend bought her an ice cream float, made with ginger beer from a dark, opaque glass bottle. Mrs Donoghue drank some of it. When the rest was poured out, she later said, the decomposed remains of a snail slid into her glass. She claimed the sight, and what she had already swallowed, made her ill with shock and gastroenteritis. Nobody could see through the bottle, so nobody could have spotted the snail beforehand. It sounds like a small, unpleasant accident. Yet the question it raised would travel all the way to the highest court in Britain and reshape the law for nearly a century.

sections.key: Mrs Donoghue had no contract with anyone, so the old law seemed to leave her with no remedy.
sections.b: At the time, if a faulty product hurt you, your main legal route was usually to sue the person who sold it to you for breaching your contract. But Mrs Donoghue had not bought the drink. Her friend had, so she had no contract with the café owner. The café owner had not made the drink or sealed the bottle either. The obvious target was the manufacturer, David Stevenson, whose name was on the bottle. The trouble was that she had no contract with him at all. Earlier cases suggested that a manufacturer owed nothing to a stranger who consumed its goods, except in a few special situations, such as inherently dangerous items. On the law as many understood it, she had nowhere to go.

sections.h: All the way to the Lords
sections.key: The House of Lords decided only whether she had a case in law, not whether there really was a snail.
sections.b: Mrs Donoghue had little money, and she was allowed to sue as a pauper, which meant she did not have to pay the usual court costs. Her lawyer, Walter Leechman, took on the manufacturer. The case reached the House of Lords, then Britain's highest court, which gave its decision in May 1932. Importantly, the judges were not deciding whether a snail had really been in the bottle. They were answering a preliminary question: assuming everything she said was true, did the law give her a claim? By a narrow majority of three to two, the Lords said yes. A manufacturer who sells products in a form meant to reach the consumer unchanged owes that consumer a duty to take reasonable care.

sections.key: Lord Atkin's neighbour principle became the foundation of the modern law of negligence.
sections.b: The most famous judgment came from Lord Atkin, who reached for a Bible story. In the parable of the Good Samaritan, a lawyer asks Jesus, ‘Who is my neighbour?’ Atkin gave a legal answer. You must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions that you can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure your neighbour. And your neighbour, in law, is anyone so closely and directly affected by what you do that you ought to have them in mind. This was a broad principle rather than a narrow rule about ginger beer. It suggested that a general duty of care could exist between strangers, wherever harm was foreseeable and the relationship close enough. Lawyers call this the neighbour principle, and it is still taught to almost every first year law student.

sections.key: To win a negligence claim you generally need a duty of care, a breach of that duty and harm caused by the breach.
sections.b: Donoghue v Stevenson gave shape to negligence, the area of law dealing with careless harm. In broad terms, a person suing for negligence must show three things. First, the other side owed them a duty of care. Second, the other side breached that duty by falling below the standard of a reasonable person in their position. Third, the breach actually caused them harm of a kind the law recognises. These ideas now sit behind claims about car crashes, medical mistakes, slippery supermarket floors and unsafe buildings. Courts have spent decades refining where duties begin and end, because a duty that stretched forever would make everyone liable for everything. Many places, including Australian states, have also passed laws limiting some claims and damages.

sections.h: The case that went around the world
sections.key: Courts across the common law world, including Australia, adopted the principle within a few years.
sections.b: A Scottish decision about a Paisley café could easily have stayed local. Instead, it spread quickly. In the mid 1930s, an Australian case reached the Privy Council in London, then the final court of appeal for Australia. Dr Richard Grant had developed severe dermatitis from woollen underwear made by Australian Knitting Mills, which contained irritating chemicals left over from manufacturing. Relying on the principle from Donoghue v Stevenson, the Privy Council found the manufacturer liable. Courts in Canada, New Zealand and elsewhere followed similar paths. Later, governments built consumer protection laws on top of these foundations, giving people statutory rights against makers of unsafe goods. The snail had travelled a very long way from Scotland.

sections.key: No court ever decided whether the snail existed, because the case settled out of court.
sections.b: Here is the twist. After the House of Lords ruled that Mrs Donoghue had a claim, the case was supposed to return to the Scottish courts for a trial on the facts. But David Stevenson died before that could happen, and the claim was settled out of court. So no judge ever ruled on whether there really was a snail in the bottle. Some sceptics have wondered about it ever since. In a sense it does not matter. The case is remembered not for its facts but for its principle. Today a memorial marks the site of the old café in Paisley, and lawyers from around the world have visited it to pay tribute to a woman, a bottle and a possibly imaginary snail.

quiz.q: Why couldn't Mrs Donoghue simply sue for breach of contract?
o: Contracts were not enforceable in Scotland
Her friend bought the drink, so she had no contract with anyone
quiz.e: She had not bought the ginger beer herself, so she had no contract with the café or the manufacturer.

quiz.q: What did the House of Lords actually decide in 1932?
o: That a snail was definitely in the bottle
That the café owner must go to prison
That, if her story was true, she had a valid claim in law
That ginger beer should be sold in clear bottles
quiz.e: The Lords answered a preliminary legal question, assuming her facts were true, and ruled 3 to 2 that a duty of care existed.

quiz.q: In Lord Atkin's neighbour principle, who counts as your ‘neighbour’?
o: Anyone so closely and directly affected by your actions that you ought to have them in mind
Only people who live next door
Only people you have a contract with
quiz.e: Atkin's legal neighbour is anyone closely and directly affected by your acts, whose harm you could reasonably foresee.

quiz.q: Which three elements does a negligence claim generally need?
o: A contract, a signature and a witness
A duty of care, a breach of that duty and harm caused by it
quiz.e: Negligence broadly requires a duty, a breach of the expected standard of care, and harm caused by that breach.

quiz.q: Why did no court ever rule on whether the snail existed?
o: The manufacturer died and the case was settled out of court
Snails could not be used as evidence
quiz.e: David Stevenson died before the trial on the facts, and the claim was settled, so the snail was never proven or disproven.

LESSONS.title: Habeas corpus: the right not to simply vanish
LESSONS.hook: Two Latin words protect you from being locked away without reason. They have stood up to kings, slave owners and presidents.

sections.key: Habeas corpus is a court order demanding that a jailer justify why a person is being held.
sections.b: Habeas corpus is Latin for ‘you shall have the body’. It is the name of a writ, a formal order from a court, directed at whoever is holding a prisoner, whether a jailer, a soldier or a government official. The writ commands them to bring the person before the court and show a lawful reason for the detention. If they cannot, the judge can order the prisoner released. The idea is simple but powerful. It does not decide whether someone is guilty. It asks a more basic question: is there any legal authority to hold this person at all? That makes it a check on power itself. Without it, a government could make people disappear into cells with no charge, no trial and no end date.

sections.key: The writ grew out of medieval English courts and the promise in Magna Carta of no imprisonment without lawful judgment.
sections.b: Habeas corpus did not appear in a single moment. Versions of the writ existed in English courts by the 1200s, at first mostly as a tool for bringing people to court rather than for freeing them. Over time, judges began using it to examine whether detentions were lawful. It drew strength from a famous promise in Magna Carta of 1215: that no free man would be imprisoned except by the lawful judgment of his peers or by the law of the land. That promise was often broken in practice, but it became a powerful ideal. Over the following centuries, as courts and Parliament wrestled with the Crown over who held power, habeas corpus slowly became the practical tool for turning that ideal into reality.

sections.key: Clashes with Charles I and later kings led Parliament to strengthen the writ in the Habeas Corpus Act of 1679.
sections.b: In 1627, King Charles I jailed several knights who refused to pay a forced loan he had demanded without Parliament's consent. They sought habeas corpus, but the jailer's only answer was that they were held by the king's special command. The court refused to release them. Outrage over the Five Knights' Case helped produce the Petition of Right in 1628, which declared such imprisonment unlawful. Arguments continued for decades, and in 1679 Parliament passed the Habeas Corpus Act, which set deadlines and penalties to stop officials dodging the writ. According to an account by Bishop Gilbert Burnet, the act squeaked through the House of Lords only because a very large lord was jokingly counted as ten votes. Historians treat that story with caution.

sections.key: In 1772 an English court used habeas corpus to stop an enslaved man being shipped away by force.
sections.b: One of the most dramatic uses of the writ came in 1772. James Somerset had been enslaved in Virginia and brought to England by Charles Stewart, a customs official. Somerset escaped, was recaptured and was put aboard a ship bound for Jamaica, where he would be sold. Supporters, including the campaigner Granville Sharp, sought habeas corpus. The case came before Lord Mansfield, the senior judge of the King's Bench. Mansfield ruled that there was no law in England allowing a master to force Somerset out of the country, and he was freed. The decision did not abolish slavery, which continued in British colonies for decades, but it was widely celebrated and became a landmark in the long struggle against slavery.

sections.key: In emergencies governments have suspended habeas corpus, and those moments have always been controversial.
sections.b: Because habeas corpus limits government power, governments under pressure have sometimes tried to switch it off. Britain's Parliament suspended it several times, for example in the 1790s amid fears of revolution spreading from France. The framers of the United States Constitution included the writ but allowed suspension only in cases of rebellion or invasion when public safety required it. In 1861, at the start of the American Civil War, President Abraham Lincoln suspended it in some areas. Chief Justice Roger Taney argued in the Merryman case that only Congress had that power, and Lincoln largely ignored him. Congress later authorised suspension. Ever since, lawyers and historians have debated how far emergencies justify setting aside this ancient safeguard.

sections.key: Habeas corpus remains part of the legal toolkit in Australia and across the common law world.
sections.b: English colonists carried habeas corpus around the world, and it remains part of the law in countries including Australia, New Zealand, Canada, India and the United States. In Australia, superior courts such as the state Supreme Courts and the High Court can issue it. In practice, many detentions are now reviewed through other routes, such as bail hearings, appeals and judicial review, so the old writ is used less often than its fame suggests. But it still matters most when other protections fail. It has been invoked over immigration detention, mental health detention and wartime imprisonment. Its enduring message is that power must always answer one question in court: by what lawful authority is this person being held?

quiz.q: What does a writ of habeas corpus require?
o: That a prisoner be found guilty or innocent immediately
That the person holding a prisoner bring them to court and justify the detention
That a prisoner be given a lawyer
That a trial be held before a jury
quiz.e: The writ orders the jailer to produce the prisoner and show a lawful reason for holding them.

quiz.q: Which 1215 document promised no imprisonment except by lawful judgment or the law of the land?
quiz.e: Magna Carta's promise became an ideal that habeas corpus later helped put into practice.

quiz.q: What did the Five Knights' Case of 1627 help produce?
quiz.e: When the court refused to release the knights, Parliament responded with the Petition of Right.

quiz.q: What did Lord Mansfield decide in James Somerset's case?
o: That slavery was abolished across the British Empire
That Somerset must be returned to Virginia
That Somerset should be sold in England instead
That no English law allowed Somerset to be forcibly removed from the country
quiz.e: Mansfield freed Somerset, though slavery continued in British colonies for decades afterwards.

quiz.q: When does the US Constitution allow habeas corpus to be suspended?
o: During rebellion or invasion when public safety requires it
quiz.e: The Constitution permits suspension only in cases of rebellion or invasion, as Lincoln's actions in 1861 tested.

LESSONS.title: The 1967 referendum: what it really changed
LESSONS.hook: More than 90 per cent of Australians voted Yes in 1967, the biggest win in referendum history. Yet many people still believe it did things it never did.

sections.key: On 27 May 1967 Australians voted overwhelmingly to change the Constitution regarding Aboriginal people.
sections.b: Changing Australia's Constitution is notoriously hard. A proposal must pass Parliament and then win a double majority: a majority of voters nationally, and majorities in at least four of the six states. Only a handful of the more than 40 proposals put to the people have ever passed. On 27 May 1967 one question about Aboriginal people won about 91 per cent of the national vote and carried every state. No referendum before or since has come close. The result is remembered as a turning point in Australian history, and the date now marks the start of National Reconciliation Week. But to understand why it mattered, it helps to know exactly which words were removed, and also what the vote did not do.

sections.key: The referendum deleted a phrase from the race power and removed section 127 entirely.
sections.b: The 1901 Constitution mentioned Aboriginal people only twice, and both times to exclude them. Section 51, which lists the subjects the federal Parliament can make laws about, gave it power over ‘the people of any race, other than the aboriginal race in any State’, for whom special laws were deemed necessary. That left laws about Aboriginal people to the states. Section 127 said that in reckoning the numbers of the people of the Commonwealth, or of a state, ‘aboriginal natives shall not be counted’. The 1967 referendum removed the words ‘other than the aboriginal race in any State’ from section 51, and deleted section 127 altogether. Those two changes were the entire legal effect of the vote.

sections.h: Myth one: the right to vote
sections.key: The referendum did not give Aboriginal people the vote; that had already happened through ordinary laws.
sections.b: One of the most common beliefs about 1967 is that it gave Aboriginal people the right to vote. It did not. Voting rights are set mainly by ordinary laws passed by parliaments, not by the Constitution. Some Aboriginal people had been able to vote in a few colonies since the 1850s and 1890s, although many were later excluded. The Commonwealth Electoral Act was amended in 1962 to give all Aboriginal people the right to vote in federal elections. The states moved at different speeds, and Queensland was the last to grant state voting rights, in 1965. So by the time of the referendum, Aboriginal Australians could already vote everywhere, even though many still faced real barriers in practice.

sections.h: Myth two: citizenship and ‘flora and fauna’
sections.key: The vote did not create citizenship, and there was never a law classifying Aboriginal people as flora and fauna.
sections.b: Another myth is that the referendum made Aboriginal people citizens. Australian citizenship was created in 1949, and Aboriginal people born in Australia were covered by it, although in practice many were still denied rights through state laws controlling where they lived, worked and married. A third persistent myth says Aboriginal people were managed under a ‘Flora and Fauna Act’ until 1967. Historians and fact checkers have found no such law, at federal or state level. The myth probably spread because it captured how dehumanising the real treatment felt, but it is not accurate. Correcting these myths does not shrink the referendum's importance. It shows that its power was partly symbolic, and partly about which government held responsibility.

sections.key: A decade of grassroots activism by Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal campaigners built the case for Yes.
sections.b: The referendum did not come from nowhere. Through the late 1950s and 1960s, groups such as the Federal Council for the Advancement of Aborigines and Torres Strait Islanders gathered petitions, held meetings and lobbied politicians. Faith Bandler, an activist of South Sea Islander heritage, was one of the campaign's best known leaders, alongside Aboriginal figures such as Joe McGinness and many others. Events like the 1965 Freedom Ride through country New South Wales, led by Charles Perkins and university students, exposed segregation in pools, pubs and cinemas. By the time Parliament put the question, it had support from across the major parties, and there was no organised No case. That unusual unity helps explain the record result.

sections.key: The referendum gave the federal Parliament power to make laws for Aboriginal people, opening a new era of national policy.
sections.b: Removing the exclusion from section 51 meant the Commonwealth, not just the states, could now make laws specifically for Aboriginal people. Over the following years, the federal government created new agencies and programs, and in 1976 Parliament passed the Aboriginal Land Rights (Northern Territory) Act. The deletion of section 127 meant Aboriginal people would be included in official population counts. Yet the change was neutral on its face. The race power lets the Commonwealth make laws about people of any race, and courts have since debated whether those laws must be for a group's benefit. Many campaigners felt that real progress came more slowly than the 1967 euphoria promised. Even so, the vote remains a landmark of national goodwill.

quiz.q: What is the ‘double majority’ needed to change Australia's Constitution?
o: Both houses of Parliament voting twice
A national majority of voters plus majorities in at least four of the six states
A majority in every state and territory
quiz.e: A proposal needs a majority nationally and a majority in at least four states.

quiz.q: What did section 127, deleted in 1967, say?
o: That Aboriginal people could not vote
That Aboriginal people could not own land
That Aboriginal people were not citizens
That Aboriginal natives should not be counted in reckoning the population
quiz.e: Section 127 excluded Aboriginal people from official population counts, and the referendum removed it.

quiz.q: When did all Aboriginal people gain the right to vote in federal elections?
quiz.e: An amendment to the Commonwealth Electoral Act in 1962 gave the federal vote, five years before the referendum.

quiz.q: What did historians find about the supposed ‘Flora and Fauna Act’?
o: It was repealed by the referendum
It was replaced by the Citizenship Act
quiz.e: No federal or state law classified Aboriginal people as flora and fauna, though the myth reflected real mistreatment.

quiz.q: What was the main legal effect of changing section 51?
o: It allowed the federal Parliament to make laws specifically for Aboriginal people
quiz.e: Removing the exclusion gave the Commonwealth power to legislate for Aboriginal people, not only the states.

LESSONS.title: Gerrymandering: winning by drawing the lines
LESSONS.hook: You can lose the popular vote and still win the election, if someone has drawn the map cleverly enough. Meet the strange art of the gerrymander.

sections.key: The word comes from an 1812 cartoon mocking a district shaped like a monster.
sections.b: In 1812, the Massachusetts legislature redrew the boundaries of its state senate districts. The new map was designed to help the governing party, and Governor Elbridge Gerry signed it into law. One district north of Boston snaked around in such a strange, twisting shape that critics said it looked like a salamander. A newspaper, the Boston Gazette, published a cartoon turning the district into a winged, clawed beast and named it the ‘Gerry-mander’. The insult stuck, and the word entered the language. Interestingly, Gerry's name was pronounced with a hard G, like Gary, but the word is now almost always said with a soft G, like Jerry. Gerry himself reportedly disliked the plan, but his name is forever attached to it.

sections.key: Gerrymanders work by concentrating opponents' votes in a few seats or spreading them thinly across many.
sections.b: In systems where each electorate elects one member, the boundaries of electorates matter enormously. Imagine a region with ten seats, where two parties each have half the voters. Draw the lines one way and each party wins five seats. Draw them another way and one party can win seven or eight. There are two classic tricks. Packing means cramming as many of your opponent's supporters as possible into a few seats, which they win by huge, wasteful margins. Cracking means splitting their remaining supporters thinly across many seats, so they fall just short everywhere. The opponent's votes are not taken away. They are simply arranged so that many of them make no difference. With modern data and computers, these techniques can be applied with remarkable precision.

sections.h: Malapportionment: a cousin of the gerrymander
sections.key: Unequal numbers of voters in each seat can distort results just as powerfully as odd shapes.
sections.b: A related trick is malapportionment, where some electorates have many more voters than others. If country seats have half as many voters as city seats, each country vote counts roughly double. This was historically common, partly from a genuine belief that rural areas needed extra representation, and partly because it helped whoever drew the map. Britain once had ‘rotten boroughs’, tiny constituencies with a handful of voters that still elected members of Parliament, until reforms from 1832 began to sweep them away. In the United States, Supreme Court decisions in the 1960s, especially Reynolds v Sims in 1964, required state legislative districts to have roughly equal populations, a principle known as one person, one vote.

sections.key: Several Australian states once used heavily weighted maps, before reforms moved boundary drawing to independent bodies.
sections.b: Australia has its own chapters in this story. In South Australia, rural seats were for decades given far more weight than Adelaide seats, a system that kept Thomas Playford's government in power for a long time and was nicknamed the Playmander. In Queensland, a zonal system first introduced in 1949 by a Labor government was later reshaped under Country Party and National Party governments, and critics called it the Bjelkemander after Premier Joh Bjelke-Petersen. Both systems were criticised for letting parties win government with fewer votes than their rivals. After the Fitzgerald Inquiry into corruption in the late 1980s, Queensland moved to boundaries drawn by an independent commission with roughly equal enrolments. Other states have also moved towards equal weighting over time.

sections.key: Federal electorates are drawn by the independent Australian Electoral Commission under rules set by law.
sections.b: Today, boundaries for federal elections in Australia are drawn not by politicians but by the Australian Electoral Commission, an independent statutory body. When population shifts or the number of seats in a state changes, a redistribution is held. Committees propose new boundaries, the public and political parties can lodge objections, and the final decision rests with an independent commission. The law requires electorates in a state to have close to the same number of voters, within set tolerances, while also considering communities of interest, transport links and physical features. States and territories run similar independent processes for their own elections. Parties still argue about individual decisions, but the design keeps the pencil out of the hands of those who benefit.

sections.key: In many US states legislators still draw the lines, and courts have struggled with how to respond.
sections.b: In the United States, district lines for Congress and state legislatures are usually drawn by state legislatures, so whichever party controls a state can shape its map. Both major parties have been accused of gerrymandering where they hold power. Some states have handed the job to independent or bipartisan commissions, often after citizen ballot initiatives. Courts remain involved where maps are challenged on grounds such as racial discrimination. But in Rucho v Common Cause in 2019, the US Supreme Court held that claims of partisan gerrymandering were political questions that federal courts could not resolve, leaving them to states and Congress. Researchers have developed measures such as the efficiency gap, which counts wasted votes, to try to detect unfair maps objectively.

quiz.q: Where does the word ‘gerrymander’ come from?
o: A Dutch word for a crooked fence
A cartoon mocking a district signed into law by Governor Elbridge Gerry
A British politician named Gerald Mander
quiz.e: An 1812 Boston Gazette cartoon turned a salamander shaped district into the ‘Gerry-mander’.

quiz.q: What is ‘packing’ in gerrymandering?
o: Concentrating opponents' supporters in a few seats they win by huge margins
Adding fake voters to the roll
Stuffing ballot boxes with extra votes
Holding elections on a busy day
quiz.e: Packing wastes the opponent's votes by piling them into a few overwhelmingly safe seats.

quiz.q: What is malapportionment?
o: Electorates with very unequal numbers of voters
Counting votes in the wrong order
quiz.e: When seats have unequal numbers of voters, votes in the smaller seats effectively count for more.

quiz.q: What nickname was given to South Australia's rurally weighted system?
quiz.e: It was named after Premier Thomas Playford, whose government benefited from it for decades.

quiz.q: Who draws federal electorate boundaries in Australia?
o: The governing party in each state
quiz.e: Redistributions are handled by the AEC and independent committees, with chances for public objection.

LESSONS.title: Diplomatic immunity: why ambassadors can't be arrested
LESSONS.hook: A diplomat can park illegally, refuse to answer police and walk free from a courtroom. There is a surprisingly old and sensible reason why.

sections.key: Protecting envoys is one of the oldest rules of international relations, because without it no one could negotiate.
sections.b: For thousands of years, rulers have needed a way to talk to their rivals, even during wars. That only works if messengers can travel safely. Ancient Greek heralds, Roman envoys and ambassadors in many other civilisations were treated as protected, often with religious overtones. Harming an envoy was seen as a grave offence. One famous example comes from the early 1200s, when Mongol envoys sent by Genghis Khan to the Khwarazmian Empire in Central Asia were mistreated, and at least one was executed. Genghis Khan responded with a devastating invasion from 1219. The lesson has been learned again and again. If envoys can be arrested, jailed or killed, diplomacy collapses, and the only remaining way to settle disputes is force.

sections.key: In 1708 the arrest of Russia's ambassador in London led Britain to pass a law protecting diplomats.
sections.b: In 1708, Andrey Matveyev, the ambassador of Tsar Peter the Great, was about to leave London when he was dragged from his coach and briefly locked up over unpaid debts owed to local merchants. Peter was furious and demanded that the offenders be punished severely. The British government was embarrassed, but under English law the creditors had done nothing illegal. To repair the relationship, Parliament passed the Diplomatic Privileges Act of 1708, which made it unlawful to arrest ambassadors or seize their goods. Queen Anne's government sent a formal apology to Moscow. It is a good example of how international law often grows: an awkward incident exposes a gap, and states create rules so it does not happen again.

sections.key: Modern diplomatic immunity is set out in a 1961 treaty that almost every country has joined.
sections.b: Today the main rules are found in the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations of 1961, one of the most widely accepted treaties in the world. Australia gives effect to it through its Diplomatic Privileges and Immunities Act of 1967. Under the convention, diplomatic agents cannot be arrested or detained, and they are immune from the host country's criminal courts. They are also immune from most civil and administrative cases, with some exceptions, such as private property deals or business activities unrelated to their official work. Their families generally share these protections. The diplomatic bag, used to send documents and items between an embassy and its home government, must not be opened or detained. Separate, narrower rules protect consular officials, under a 1963 convention.

sections.key: Contrary to popular belief, embassies remain part of the host country, but local authorities cannot enter without permission.
sections.b: Films often say that stepping into an embassy means stepping onto foreign soil. That is a myth. An embassy in Canberra stands on Australian territory, and in general Australian law applies there. What the Vienna Convention does is make the premises inviolable. Police and other officials of the host country may not enter without the consent of the head of the mission, even with a warrant, and the host country has a special duty to protect the building from intrusion or damage. That is why people sometimes seek refuge inside embassies: not because they have left the country, but because local authorities cannot simply walk in and take them. In practice the effect can look similar, but the legal reasoning is quite different.

sections.key: When immunity is abused, the host country's main weapon is to expel the diplomat.
sections.b: Immunity does not mean diplomats are above the law. The Vienna Convention says they must respect local laws, and it is designed to protect their work, not their personal convenience. When they break the rules, the host country has options. It can ask the sending country to waive immunity so the person can be prosecuted, which sometimes happens. Or it can declare the diplomat persona non grata, Latin for an unwelcome person, which means they must leave. The most notorious case came in London in April 1984, when shots fired from the Libyan embassy killed Police Constable Yvonne Fletcher during a protest outside. Britain could not enter or prosecute, so after a siege it expelled the diplomats and broke off relations with Libya.

sections.key: Immunity exists because the alternative, governments harassing each other's envoys, would be worse for everyone.
sections.b: When a diplomat escapes punishment for something serious, people understandably ask why the system exists at all. The answer is reciprocity. Every country has diplomats posted abroad, including in places with unreliable courts or hostile governments. If a host country could arrest foreign diplomats on any charge, real or invented, governments could use them as hostages or bargaining chips. Immunity ensures that ambassadors can report honestly, negotiate freely and deliver unwelcome messages without fear. Because every state benefits, nearly all of them follow the rules most of the time, even when relations are tense. The occasional injustice is the price of keeping open the channels that can stop disputes from turning into wars.

quiz.q: Why have societies protected envoys for thousands of years?
o: Because diplomacy cannot work if messengers can be harmed
quiz.e: Without safe messengers, rivals cannot negotiate, leaving force as the only option.

quiz.q: What prompted Britain's Diplomatic Privileges Act of 1708?
o: The arrest of Russia's ambassador over unpaid debts
The murder of a British envoy in Spain
quiz.e: Peter the Great's ambassador was arrested for debt, and Parliament passed the act to repair relations.

quiz.q: What is the legal status of an embassy in Canberra?
o: It is part of the foreign country's territory
It is international territory belonging to the UN
It is Australian territory, but local authorities cannot enter without permission
It has no legal status at all
quiz.e: Embassies are inviolable, not foreign soil. Police need the head of mission's consent to enter.

quiz.q: What does declaring a diplomat ‘persona non grata’ mean?
o: They must leave the host country
They are put on trial immediately
quiz.e: It means ‘unwelcome person’, and it is the host country's main response to serious abuse.

quiz.q: What is the main argument for keeping diplomatic immunity?
o: Reciprocity: without it, governments could harass or hold each other's envoys hostage
quiz.e: Every state has diplomats abroad, so all benefit from rules that stop envoys being used as bargaining chips.

LESSONS.title: The Geneva Conventions: rules for the worst of times
LESSONS.hook: Even war has laws. They began with a Swiss businessman who stumbled onto a battlefield and could not forget what he saw.

sections.key: Henry Dunant's experience of a bloody 1859 battle inspired the modern laws of war.
sections.b: In June 1859, a Swiss businessman named Henry Dunant travelled to northern Italy hoping to meet the French emperor Napoleon III about a business venture. He arrived just after the Battle of Solferino, where French and Sardinian forces had fought the Austrian army. Tens of thousands of soldiers lay dead or wounded, and the armies had nowhere near enough medical help. Dunant helped organise local villagers, many of them women, to care for the wounded of both sides, insisting that all were brothers. Back home, he wrote a short book, A Memory of Solferino, published in 1862. It described the suffering in vivid detail and proposed two ideas: trained volunteer relief groups, and an international agreement to protect the wounded and those caring for them.

sections.h: The Red Cross and the first convention
sections.key: Dunant's ideas led to the founding of the Red Cross in 1863 and the first Geneva Convention in 1864.
sections.b: Dunant's book caused a sensation across Europe. In 1863 he and four other citizens of Geneva formed a committee that became the International Committee of the Red Cross. A year later, in August 1864, the Swiss government hosted a diplomatic conference, and twelve states signed the first Geneva Convention. It was short, but revolutionary. Wounded and sick soldiers had to be cared for regardless of which side they belonged to. Ambulances, military hospitals and medical staff were to be treated as neutral and protected. A distinctive emblem would mark them: a red cross on a white background, the reverse of the Swiss flag. For the first time, states had agreed in a permanent treaty to limit the suffering of war.

sections.h: A sad ending, a late honour
sections.key: Dunant fell into poverty and obscurity, but was later awarded the first Nobel Peace Prize.
sections.b: Dunant's own story did not end happily for many years. His business ventures in Algeria failed, he went bankrupt in the 1860s, and the scandal forced him out of the organisation he had helped create. He drifted through Europe in poverty and eventually settled in the small Swiss town of Heiden, where he lived quietly in a hospital home. In the 1890s a journalist rediscovered him, and his story spread again. In 1901 Dunant shared the very first Nobel Peace Prize with the French peace campaigner Frédéric Passy. He reportedly spent little of the prize money on himself. He died in 1910. Today his birthday, 8 May, is celebrated as World Red Cross and Red Crescent Day.

sections.h: Four conventions after a world war
sections.key: After the horrors of the Second World War, the rules were rewritten and expanded in 1949.
sections.b: The original treaty was updated several times, including in 1906 and 1929, but the Second World War exposed its limits. Millions of prisoners of war died in captivity, and civilians suffered mass killings, deportations and starvation under occupation. In 1949 states agreed on four new Geneva Conventions. The first protects wounded and sick soldiers on land. The second does the same for those wounded, sick or shipwrecked at sea. The third sets out how prisoners of war must be treated, including humane conditions and protection from torture and public curiosity. The fourth, which was entirely new, protects civilians in enemy hands and in occupied territory. Every country in the world has since ratified the 1949 conventions, which makes them truly universal.

sections.key: Modern humanitarian law rests on ideas such as distinction, proportionality and humane treatment.
sections.b: Two Additional Protocols were added in 1977, strengthening protections for civilians and for victims of civil wars. Together with other treaties, such as the Hague Conventions governing weapons and tactics, they form what is called international humanitarian law. A few principles run through it. Distinction means combatants must distinguish between military targets and civilians, and may only target the former. Proportionality means an attack is unlawful if the expected harm to civilians would be excessive compared with the concrete military advantage. People who are no longer fighting, such as the wounded, the sick and those who surrender, must be treated humanely. These rules do not decide whether a war is justified. They apply equally to all sides, whatever the cause.

sections.key: Breaking the rules can be a war crime, and some serious breaches can be prosecuted by any country.
sections.b: The red cross emblem is protected by law and must not be misused, even for decoration or advertising. The red crescent has also been used since the 1870s, and in 2005 states adopted a third emblem, the red crystal, with no religious or national associations. Enforcement is the hardest part. The conventions require states to search for and prosecute people accused of grave breaches, such as wilful killing, torture or taking hostages, whatever their nationality. Australia does this through its own legislation, including the Geneva Conventions Act 1957. Since the 1990s, international tribunals and the International Criminal Court have also tried war crimes. Violations still happen far too often, but the rules give victims a standard and the world a way to judge.

quiz.q: What inspired Henry Dunant to campaign for the wounded?
o: Seeing the aftermath of the Battle of Solferino in 1859
Serving as a soldier in the Crimean War
Working as a nurse in London
quiz.e: Dunant saw thousands of wounded soldiers left with little care and wrote A Memory of Solferino.

quiz.q: Why is the Red Cross emblem a red cross on white?
o: It is the flag of the Vatican
It was chosen by Napoleon III
It reverses the colours of the Swiss flag
It represents the blood of soldiers
quiz.e: The emblem honoured Switzerland, where the movement and first convention began, by reversing its flag.

quiz.q: What did the Fourth Geneva Convention of 1949 newly protect?
o: Civilians in enemy hands and occupied territory
quiz.e: The fourth convention was entirely new, responding to the suffering of civilians in the Second World War.

quiz.q: What does the principle of proportionality require?
o: That both sides use the same weapons
That expected civilian harm not be excessive compared with the military advantage
That armies be the same size
That wars last only a set length of time
quiz.e: An attack is unlawful if civilian harm would be excessive relative to the concrete military advantage expected.

quiz.q: Do the Geneva Conventions decide whether a war is justified?
o: No, they apply equally to all sides regardless of the cause
Yes, only defending sides are protected
Only the United Nations can decide that under the conventions
quiz.e: Humanitarian law regulates how wars are fought, not whether they are justified, and binds every side.

LESSONS.title: Lindy Chamberlain and the dingo: a wrongful conviction
LESSONS.hook: A baby vanished from a tent near Uluru, and her mother was convicted of murder. It took decades, and a chance discovery, to prove the truth.

sections.key: On 17 August 1980, nine week old Azaria Chamberlain disappeared from a campground tent.
sections.b: In August 1980, Michael and Lindy Chamberlain, a pastor and his wife from Mount Isa, were camping near Uluru with their three children. On the night of 17 August, their nine week old daughter Azaria was asleep in the family tent. Lindy said she heard a cry, went to check, and saw a dingo leaving the tent. Azaria was gone. Campers and rangers searched through the night, but she was never found. A week later, some of her clothing, including a bloodied jumpsuit, was discovered near a dingo den. Dingoes had been seen around the campground, and some had been bold with visitors. Yet from the start, many Australians found the idea of a dingo taking a baby hard to believe.

sections.key: Public suspicion grew, fed by rumours about the family's religion and Lindy's calm manner.
sections.b: The Chamberlains were Seventh day Adventists, and wild rumours spread that Azaria's name meant ‘sacrifice in the wilderness’, which was false, and that her death was some kind of ritual. Lindy's composure in public was read by many as coldness, as if a grieving mother must behave in a particular way. A first coroner's inquest, in 1981, found that a dingo had taken the baby, and the coroner criticised the police investigation. But investigators kept working, now on the theory of murder. Further forensic tests were carried out, the first finding was quashed, and a second inquest led to Lindy being charged with murder and Michael with being an accessory after the fact. Their trial in Darwin in 1982 became a national obsession.

sections.key: The prosecution relied on scientific evidence that seemed powerful but was later shown to be deeply flawed.
sections.b: There was no body, no confession, no clear motive and no witness to any killing. The prosecution's case rested heavily on science. Experts testified that tests showed foetal blood, the kind found in young babies, in the family's car, including a spray pattern under the dashboard. A forensic expert argued that marks on the jumpsuit looked like a bloody handprint and that damage to the clothing was made by a cutting instrument, not a dingo's teeth. The prosecution suggested Lindy had cut Azaria's throat in the car. The jury, faced with confident experts, convicted. In October 1982 Lindy was sentenced to life imprisonment with hard labour, and Michael received a suspended sentence. Appeals, including to the High Court, failed.

sections.key: In 1986 a missing piece of clothing was found by chance near a dingo lair, and Lindy was released.
sections.b: Lindy had always said Azaria had been wearing a small matinee jacket, which had never been found. In early 1986, an English tourist, David Brett, fell to his death while climbing Uluru. While searching for his remains, police found the jacket half buried near a dingo lair, in an area not easily reached. It supported Lindy's account. Within days she was released from prison, having served more than three years. The government then set up a Royal Commission, led by Justice Trevor Morling. His 1987 report found serious problems with the forensic evidence. Most strikingly, the supposed spray of foetal blood under the dashboard was shown to be a sound deadening compound applied when the car was made.

sections.key: The convictions were quashed in 1988, and a coroner finally confirmed in 2012 that a dingo took Azaria.
sections.b: Morling concluded that the convictions could not be justified on the evidence. In September 1988, the Northern Territory Court of Criminal Appeal quashed the convictions of both Lindy and Michael. In 1992 the Chamberlains received compensation of about 1.3 million dollars for their wrongful imprisonment and legal costs. Yet the official cause of death remained uncertain. A third inquest, in 1995, returned an open finding. Only at a fourth inquest, in June 2012, did the Northern Territory coroner, Elizabeth Morris, formally find that Azaria had been taken and killed by a dingo, and the death certificate was changed. More than 30 years after that night, the family's account was finally recognised in law as the truth.

sections.key: The Chamberlain case changed how Australian courts and scientists think about forensic evidence.
sections.b: The case is now studied as a warning about wrongful convictions. Experts had presented uncertain results with too much confidence, and some tests were poorly done or misread. The jury had little way to know. In the years that followed, Australian forensic science moved towards stricter standards, accreditation and more careful presentation of evidence in court. The case also showed how media coverage and public prejudice can shape a trial, as people judged Lindy by her manner and religion rather than the facts. Later attacks by dingoes on children, including a fatal attack on Fraser Island, now K'gari, in 2001, ended any lingering doubt that dingoes can be dangerous. Above all, the case reminds us that a conviction is only as strong as its evidence.

quiz.q: What did the first coroner's inquest, in 1981, find?
o: That the cause of death could never be known
That a dingo had taken Azaria
quiz.e: The first inquest found a dingo had taken the baby, but that finding was later quashed.

quiz.q: What was the prosecution's case mainly based on?
quiz.e: With no body or confession, the case relied heavily on expert forensic testimony that later proved flawed.

quiz.q: What discovery led to Lindy's release in 1986?
o: Azaria's matinee jacket was found near a dingo lair
A dingo was caught on camera
A police officer confessed to errors
quiz.e: The jacket, found by chance during a search for a fallen climber, supported Lindy's account.

quiz.q: What did the supposed ‘foetal blood’ spray under the dashboard turn out to be?
o: A sound deadening compound applied during manufacture
quiz.e: The Morling Royal Commission found the spray was a factory compound, not blood.

quiz.q: When was a dingo officially found responsible for Azaria's death?
quiz.e: Coroner Elizabeth Morris made the finding in June 2012, and the death certificate was changed.

LESSONS.title: Marbury v Madison: how courts got the power to strike down laws
LESSONS.hook: A row over an undelivered job letter gave judges one of the greatest powers in modern government. The judge who did it managed to win by appearing to lose.

sections.key: In 1801 an outgoing president rushed to fill new judicial posts with his own supporters.
sections.b: In the United States election of 1800, President John Adams and his Federalist Party lost to Thomas Jefferson and his Democratic Republicans. Before handing over power in March 1801, Adams and the outgoing Congress created a batch of new judicial posts, and Adams filled them with Federalists. Critics called them the midnight judges, because the appointments were made in the final days and hours of his term. One of the appointees was William Marbury, a businessman named as a justice of the peace for the District of Columbia. His commission, the official document of appointment, was signed and sealed. But in the last minute rush, the Secretary of State's office failed to deliver it. That Secretary of State was John Marshall, who had just become Chief Justice.

sections.h: A lawsuit in the highest court
sections.key: Jefferson's administration refused to deliver the commission, so Marbury went straight to the Supreme Court.
sections.b: When Jefferson took office, his new Secretary of State, James Madison, refused to hand over the undelivered commissions. Marbury and several others sued. Relying on a section of the Judiciary Act of 1789, they went directly to the Supreme Court, asking it to issue a writ of mandamus, an order commanding an official to do his legal duty. The case put Chief Justice Marshall in an awkward spot. If he ordered Madison to deliver the commission, the Jefferson administration would probably ignore him, exposing the Court as powerless. If he backed down, he would seem to concede that the executive could ignore the law. The young Court, with little prestige, faced a political trap. Marshall's way out was brilliant.

sections.key: Marshall ruled Marbury was entitled to his job, but that the Court could not order it, because the law was unconstitutional.
sections.b: In February 1803, Marshall delivered the Court's opinion. First, he said, Marbury had a right to his commission, and Madison's refusal was a violation of that right. Second, the law should provide a remedy. Third, and here was the twist, the Supreme Court could not provide it. The section of the Judiciary Act that let Marbury bring his case directly to the Supreme Court had tried to expand the Court's original jurisdiction beyond what the Constitution allowed. When an ordinary law conflicts with the Constitution, Marshall reasoned, the Constitution must win, and the law is void. So Marbury lost. Jefferson got the result he wanted. But the Court had claimed something far bigger: the power to declare acts of Congress unconstitutional.

sections.key: The decision established judicial review, the power of courts to strike down laws that breach the constitution.
sections.b: Marshall's reasoning was straightforward. A written constitution is the supreme law, deliberately placed above ordinary laws. If Congress could pass any law it liked regardless of the Constitution, then the Constitution's limits would be meaningless. Someone must decide whether a law conflicts with it, and Marshall argued that this job belonged to judges. In one of the most quoted lines in American law, he wrote that it is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is. This is judicial review. The Constitution itself had not spelled it out clearly, though some founders had discussed the idea. Marshall turned it into settled doctrine, using a case where his ruling handed his political opponents a short term win.

sections.key: The Supreme Court did not strike down another federal law for over half a century.
sections.b: For a power so important, judicial review was used sparingly at first. After Marbury, the Supreme Court did not strike down another act of Congress until 1857, in the infamous Dred Scott decision, which held that Black Americans could not be citizens and helped push the country towards civil war. That is a reminder that judicial review is a tool, and courts can use it badly as well as well. Over time the power grew. In the 20th century, the Court struck down laws on everything from segregated schools to campaign spending. Because judges are unelected, debates continue about how boldly they should use this power, and when they should defer to elected lawmakers. Those debates are as old as the decision itself.

sections.key: Australia's High Court has used judicial review since Federation, while Britain's courts traditionally cannot strike down Acts of Parliament.
sections.b: The idea spread to many countries with written constitutions. Australia's framers built a federal system in which the Commonwealth's powers are limited, so it was taken for granted that the High Court would decide whether laws stayed within those limits. In the 1951 Communist Party case, Justice Fullagar wrote that in our system the principle of Marbury v Madison is accepted as axiomatic, meaning self-evident. The United Kingdom is different. Under the doctrine of parliamentary sovereignty, British courts cannot strike down an Act of Parliament. Since the Human Rights Act 1998 they can declare a law incompatible with protected rights, but it is up to Parliament to decide whether to change it. Different systems, different answers to the question of who has the final word.

quiz.q: Why was William Marbury's commission never delivered?
o: It was lost in the post
It was not delivered in the rush at the end of Adams's term
quiz.e: The commission was signed and sealed, but the outgoing administration failed to deliver it in time.

quiz.q: What did Marbury ask the Supreme Court to issue?
o: A writ of mandamus ordering Madison to deliver the commission
quiz.e: Mandamus is an order commanding an official to perform a legal duty.

quiz.q: Why did Marbury ultimately lose?
o: He had no right to the commission
The law letting him sue directly in the Supreme Court was unconstitutional
quiz.e: Marshall held the relevant section of the Judiciary Act unlawfully expanded the Court's original jurisdiction.

quiz.q: When did the Supreme Court next strike down an act of Congress after Marbury?
quiz.e: Judicial review lay largely unused against Congress until the infamous Dred Scott decision of 1857.

quiz.q: What can British courts do with an Act they find incompatible with protected human rights?
o: Ignore it in all future cases
Declare it incompatible, leaving Parliament to decide what to do
quiz.e: Parliamentary sovereignty means UK courts cannot strike down Acts, but can issue declarations of incompatibility.

LESSONS.title: Common law and civil law: the world's two great legal families
LESSONS.hook: Most of the world's legal systems descend from one of two ancestors: medieval English judges, or the law books of ancient Rome. Which one you live under shapes how courts work.

sections.key: Most countries' legal systems belong mainly to either the common law or the civil law tradition.
sections.b: If you are arrested in Sydney, Paris, Tokyo or Chicago, the courtroom you end up in will look and work differently. Much of that difference comes from history. Most of the world's legal systems belong largely to one of two great families. The common law tradition grew from medieval England and spread through the British Empire, to places such as Australia, the United States, Canada, New Zealand and India. The civil law tradition grew from Roman law, revived in medieval Europe and organised into national codes. It is found across most of continental Europe, Latin America and much of Asia and Africa. Counted by number of countries, civil law is the more widespread. Both traditions aim for justice, but they take different routes.

sections.key: ‘Civil law’ has two meanings: a legal tradition, and non-criminal cases such as contract disputes.
sections.b: Before going further, it helps to clear up a confusing piece of vocabulary. In everyday Australian usage, civil law means the part of law dealing with disputes between people or organisations, such as contracts, negligence and family matters, as opposed to criminal law, where the state prosecutes offences. That is not what civil law means in this lesson. Here it refers to a whole legal tradition, the one descended from Roman law and built around written codes. A civil law country has both criminal and non-criminal cases, just as a common law country does. When lawyers compare legal systems, they usually say civil law tradition or civilian systems to make the meaning clear. Keep both meanings in mind, and the rest becomes much easier to follow.

sections.key: The common law grew from royal judges travelling England and building law case by case.
sections.b: After the Norman conquest of 1066, English kings gradually built a national system of royal courts. Under Henry II, who reigned from 1154 to 1189, royal judges were sent travelling on circuits around the country, hearing cases in the king's name. Over time they developed rules that applied across the whole realm, a law common to all of England, which is where the name comes from. Rather than starting from a grand written code, the common law grew case by case. Judges looked at how earlier cases had been decided and followed them. This principle, known as precedent, means that a decision of a higher court binds lower courts in similar cases. Parliament can override judge made law with statutes, but much of the law began in courtrooms.

sections.key: Civil law grew from Emperor Justinian's law books, rediscovered in medieval Italy and later turned into national codes.
sections.b: In the 530s, the Eastern Roman emperor Justinian ordered his lawyers to collect and organise centuries of Roman law. The result, later called the Corpus Juris Civilis, or Body of Civil Law, was a vast compilation of legal rules and expert opinions. For centuries it was largely forgotten in Western Europe. Then, in the late 1000s, scholars in Bologna, in Italy, began studying it closely, and Roman law became the basis of university legal education across Europe. Many centuries later, nations turned these ideas into tidy national codes. The most influential was France's Civil Code of 1804, often called the Napoleonic Code. Germany's Civil Code of 1900 was another giant, later influencing countries as different as Japan and Greece.

sections.key: Common law trials tend to be adversarial, while civil law trials are often more inquisitorial, with judges leading the inquiry.
sections.b: The traditions also differ in how trials work. Common law systems are usually adversarial. Two sides, each with its own lawyers, present evidence and question witnesses, while a judge acts like an umpire and, in serious criminal cases, a jury often decides the facts. Civil law systems are usually described as more inquisitorial. Judges, sometimes including an investigating judge before trial, take a more active role in gathering evidence and questioning witnesses, and written files matter more. Juries are less common, although some countries use lay judges who sit alongside professionals. Judges in civil law countries are often career officials who train specifically for the role, rather than experienced lawyers appointed later in life, as is common in Australia.

sections.key: Many places mix traditions, and in practice the two families have grown closer over time.
sections.b: Real legal systems are rarely pure. Scotland and South Africa have mixed systems combining civil law roots with common law influences. In Canada, Quebec uses a civil code for private law, while the other provinces follow common law. In the United States, Louisiana's private law shows its French and Spanish heritage. Many countries also blend in religious law or customary law. And the two great families have drifted closer. Common law countries now rely on huge volumes of statutes, so much of their law is written down much like a code. Meanwhile, courts in civil law countries often follow earlier decisions of higher courts in practice, even where they are not formally bound. Two old family trees, but with branches increasingly intertwined.

quiz.q: In this lesson, what does ‘civil law’ refer to?
o: A legal tradition descended from Roman law and built around codes
quiz.e: Civil law has two meanings. Here it means the Roman derived tradition, not non-criminal cases.

quiz.q: Where does the name ‘common law’ come from?
o: Law that applied in common land only
A law common to the whole realm, developed by royal judges
Laws shared with the Roman Empire
quiz.e: Royal judges travelling England created rules common to the entire kingdom.

quiz.q: What is precedent?
o: The rule that higher court decisions bind lower courts in similar cases
The order in which cases are heard
The first law passed by a parliament
quiz.e: Following earlier decisions lets common law develop consistently case by case.

quiz.q: Which 1804 code became especially influential in the civil law world?
o: The French Civil Code, or Napoleonic Code
quiz.e: The Napoleonic Code organised French law and influenced legal systems around the world.

quiz.q: Which of these has a civil code for private law within a mostly common law country?
quiz.e: Quebec, reflecting its French heritage, uses a civil code for private law within Canada.

LESSONS.title: The Communist Party case: when the High Court said no
LESSONS.hook: In 1950, at the height of the Cold War, the Australian Parliament banned the Communist Party. Within months, the High Court struck the law down, in one of its most important decisions.

sections.key: In 1950 the Menzies government passed a law to dissolve the Communist Party of Australia.
sections.b: By 1950 the Cold War was deepening. The Soviet Union had tested an atomic bomb, communists had won the civil war in China, and in June 1950 the Korean War began, with Australian forces soon involved. At home, there were fears about communist influence in trade unions, sharpened by a major coal strike in 1949. Robert Menzies' Liberal and Country Party coalition had won the 1949 election promising to ban the Communist Party of Australia, which was then a legal political party. In 1950 Parliament passed the Communist Party Dissolution Act. The opposition Labor Party, which controlled the Senate, was divided over the bill but eventually allowed it to pass. Almost as soon as the act took effect in October, it was challenged in the High Court.

sections.key: The act dissolved the party, let the government declare other groups and people, and relied on Parliament's own statements of fact.
sections.b: The act was sweeping. It declared the Communist Party of Australia dissolved and its property forfeited to the Commonwealth. It allowed the Governor General, acting on government advice, to declare other organisations unlawful if they were linked to communism and considered a threat to security or defence. It also allowed individuals to be declared, which barred them from Commonwealth jobs and from holding office in certain trade unions. Crucially, the act began with a series of recitals, statements in which Parliament itself declared that communists were engaged in activities aimed at overthrowing the system of government by violence and that the law was needed for defence. Declared people had only limited ability to challenge the government's conclusions in court.

sections.key: The Communist Party and several unions challenged the law, with Labor's deputy leader arguing for one union.
sections.b: The Communist Party and a number of trade unions argued that the act was beyond the powers of the federal Parliament. The case attracted enormous attention, partly because of who appeared in it. Dr H. V. Evatt, Labor's deputy leader and a former High Court judge, appeared as a barrister for the Waterside Workers' Federation, one of the challenging unions, a decision that was politically controversial at the time. The Commonwealth relied mainly on the defence power in section 51 of the Constitution, which lets Parliament make laws about the defence of the Commonwealth, and on its power to protect the Constitution and the government itself. The central question was whether Parliament could simply declare that a threat existed, and thereby give itself the power to act.

sections.h: The stream cannot rise above its source
sections.key: Six of the seven judges held that Parliament could not make its own law valid by declaring the facts that justified it.
sections.b: In March 1951, the High Court ruled the act invalid by six votes to one, with Chief Justice Latham dissenting. The majority's key point concerned the recitals. In a federation with limited powers, whether a law falls within a head of power is a question for the courts, not for Parliament to decide about itself. Justice Fullagar captured it with a memorable image: a stream cannot rise higher than its source. Parliament cannot expand its power simply by reciting that the facts justify it. Since Australia was not formally at war, the defence power did not support such drastic measures against named groups in peacetime, at least not in this form. Without the recitals, the law could not be connected to any power the Constitution gave.

sections.h: The rule of law as an assumption
sections.key: Justice Dixon wrote that the Constitution assumes the rule of law, an idea still cited today.
sections.b: The most celebrated judgment came from Justice Owen Dixon, later Chief Justice and widely regarded as one of Australia's greatest judges. He observed that history and not only ancient history shows that it is often governments, not just private groups, that undermine democratic institutions. He also said the Constitution was framed in accordance with traditional conceptions, some of which it simply assumes, and that among these the rule of law forms an assumption. In other words, the Constitution takes for granted that government is subject to law, enforced by independent courts. Dixon's words have been quoted in many later cases. They help explain why Australian courts insist that the limits on government power are ultimately for judges, not ministers, to determine.

sections.key: The government then asked voters to give Parliament the power, and the referendum narrowly failed.
sections.b: The Menzies government was not finished. After winning a double dissolution election in April 1951, it took the question to the people. A referendum in September 1951 asked voters to give the Commonwealth power to deal with communists and communism. Evatt, by then Labor leader, campaigned strongly against it, arguing that it endangered civil liberties. Early polls suggested the proposal would pass, but support fell during the campaign. In the end, just under half of voters said Yes, and the proposal carried only three states, Queensland, Western Australia and Tasmania, short of the double majority required. The Communist Party continued as a legal party. It never became a major force in elections, and in the early 1990s it dissolved itself.

sections.key: The case is a landmark on judicial review, the separation of powers and the limits of emergency laws.
sections.b: Lawyers still treat the Communist Party case as one of the most important decisions in Australian constitutional law. It confirmed that the High Court, not Parliament, decides the limits of federal power, applying the principle of judicial review inherited from Marbury v Madison. It showed that national security concerns, however sincerely held, do not automatically expand constitutional power, especially in peacetime. It linked the Constitution to the rule of law. And the referendum that followed showed the other check in the system, the voters, choosing not to grant the power the courts had denied. The case is frequently cited when courts consider modern laws dealing with terrorism, organised crime and security, where the same old question returns: who decides the limits of government?

quiz.q: What role did the ‘recitals’ play in the Communist Party Dissolution Act?
o: They listed the names of party members
They were Parliament's own statements of fact claiming the law was needed for defence
They set out the penalties for joining the party
They gave the High Court special powers
quiz.e: The recitals declared a communist threat, aiming to connect the law to the defence power.

quiz.q: What did Justice Fullagar mean by ‘a stream cannot rise higher than its source’?
o: Parliament cannot expand its own power just by declaring facts that justify a law
Laws must be passed in order
quiz.e: Whether a law falls within constitutional power is for courts to decide, not for Parliament to declare.

quiz.q: What was the High Court's vote in the Communist Party case?
o: Unanimous in favour of the act
6 to 1 against the act, with Latham CJ dissenting
quiz.e: Six judges found the act invalid; Chief Justice Latham dissented.

quiz.q: What did Justice Dixon say the Constitution assumes?
quiz.e: Dixon wrote that the rule of law forms an assumption of the Constitution.

quiz.q: What happened at the 1951 referendum on banning communism?
o: It narrowly failed, carrying only three states
It was cancelled by the High Court
It passed but was never used
quiz.e: Just under half of voters said Yes and only three states carried it, so it failed the double majority.

LESSONS.title: Eclipses: the cosmic coincidence
LESSONS.hook: For a few minutes, day turns to night, the temperature drops and stars appear at noon. It happens because of one of the luckiest coincidences in the solar system.

sections.key: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon but also about 400 times farther away, so they look almost the same size.
sections.b: Hold your thumb at arm's length and it can hide a whole building. The Moon does the same trick with the Sun. The Sun is roughly 400 times the Moon's diameter, yet it also sits roughly 400 times farther from us. The result is that both discs appear almost exactly the same size in our sky, about half a degree across. No other planet in the solar system has a moon that matches its sun so neatly. When the Moon passes directly between Earth and the Sun, it can cover the blinding disc completely while leaving the Sun's faint outer atmosphere, the corona, glowing around the edges like a silver crown. It is a pure accident of geometry, and we happen to live in the right era to enjoy it.

sections.key: Because the Moon's orbit is slightly oval, some solar eclipses are total and others leave a ring of fire.
sections.b: The Moon's orbit is not a perfect circle. When an eclipse happens while the Moon is near its closest point to Earth, it looks big enough to cover the Sun entirely, giving a total eclipse. When it happens near the farthest point, the Moon looks slightly too small, and a bright ring of sunlight surrounds it. This is an annular eclipse, from the Latin annulus, meaning ring. Anyone standing outside the narrow central path sees only a partial eclipse, with a bite taken out of the Sun. The path of totality is usually only about 100 to 200 kilometres wide, racing across Earth's surface faster than a jet airliner. That is why eclipse chasers travel the world to stand in exactly the right strip of land.

sections.key: The Moon's orbit is tilted about five degrees, so it usually passes above or below the Sun.
sections.b: The Moon goes around Earth roughly once a month, so you might expect an eclipse at every new moon. The catch is that the Moon's orbit is tilted by about five degrees compared with Earth's path around the Sun. Most months the new moon slides just above or below the Sun in our sky and nothing happens. Eclipses can only occur when a new or full moon lines up with one of the two points where the orbits cross. These alignments come around in 'eclipse seasons' roughly every six months. Ancient astronomers in Babylon noticed that eclipses repeat in a cycle of about 18 years and 11 days, now called the saros, which let them predict eclipses long before anyone understood orbits.

sections.key: During a total lunar eclipse the Moon turns red because Earth's atmosphere bends sunset-coloured light onto it.
sections.b: A lunar eclipse is the reverse arrangement: Earth passes between the Sun and the full Moon, and our planet's shadow falls across the lunar surface. You might expect the Moon to vanish completely, but it usually glows a deep copper or blood red instead. The reason is our atmosphere. Sunlight skimming past the edge of Earth is bent inwards towards the Moon, and on its way through the air most of the blue light is scattered out, the same process that makes sunsets red. In effect, the Moon is lit by every sunrise and sunset on Earth at once. Unlike solar eclipses, lunar eclipses can be seen by anyone on the night side of the planet, and they are completely safe to watch with the naked eye.

sections.key: Measurements during a total eclipse in 1919 supported Einstein's prediction that gravity bends light.
sections.b: Einstein's general theory of relativity predicted that the Sun's gravity should bend starlight passing close to it, by about twice the amount older physics suggested. Normally the Sun's glare makes those nearby stars impossible to see. A total eclipse offered the chance. In May 1919, British expeditions organised by Arthur Eddington and Frank Dyson photographed stars around the darkened Sun from the island of Príncipe off West Africa and from Sobral in Brazil. Comparing the star positions with photographs taken months earlier, they reported shifts that matched Einstein rather than Newton. The news made headlines around the world and turned Einstein into a celebrity almost overnight. Historians still discuss how precise those early measurements really were, but many later, more accurate tests have confirmed the result.

sections.key: Never look at a partial solar eclipse without proper eclipse glasses; only totality itself is safe to view directly.
sections.b: Even when most of the Sun is covered, the remaining sliver is intense enough to damage the retina, and because the retina has no pain receptors you may not notice until afterwards. Ordinary sunglasses are nowhere near dark enough. Safe options include certified eclipse glasses or solar viewers meeting the ISO 12312-2 standard, or an indirect method such as a pinhole projector, where you look at an image of the Sun cast onto paper. Never look through binoculars, a camera or a telescope without a proper solar filter fitted to the front. The one exception is the brief period of totality, when the Sun is completely hidden and it is safe to look. The moment the first bead of sunlight reappears, the glasses must go back on.

sections.key: A total solar eclipse will cross Australia, including Sydney, on 22 July 2028.
sections.b: Any single spot on Earth sees a total solar eclipse only rarely, on average once every few centuries, so it is a big event when one passes over a major city. On 22 July 2028 the path of totality will sweep across Australia from the Kimberley in Western Australia, through the Northern Territory and Queensland, and down to New South Wales, passing directly over Sydney. It will be one of the very few times a total eclipse has crossed a large Australian city in the modern era. Enjoy it while the coincidence lasts. The Moon is slowly drifting away from Earth by about four centimetres a year, and in the very distant future it will look too small to ever cover the Sun completely again.

quiz.q: Why do the Sun and Moon look almost the same size in our sky?
o: They are actually the same size
The Sun is about 400 times larger but also about 400 times farther away
The Moon is closer to the Sun than Earth is
quiz.e: The Sun is roughly 400 times wider than the Moon and roughly 400 times more distant, so their apparent sizes almost match.

quiz.q: What causes an annular eclipse, with a ring of sunlight around the Moon?
o: The Moon is near the farthest point of its orbit and looks slightly too small
Clouds cover part of the Sun
The Moon is closer than usual
quiz.e: When the Moon is near its farthest point from Earth it appears slightly smaller than the Sun, leaving a bright ring visible.

quiz.q: Why don't we get a solar eclipse at every new moon?
o: The Moon is too small most months
The Moon's orbit is tilted about five degrees, so it usually passes above or below the Sun
quiz.e: The Moon's orbit is tilted relative to Earth's, so the three bodies only line up during eclipse seasons roughly every six months.

quiz.q: Why does the Moon often turn red during a total lunar eclipse?
o: Dust on the Moon reflects red light
Earth's atmosphere bends reddened sunlight onto it
The Moon heats up and glows
quiz.e: Sunlight passing through Earth's atmosphere loses most of its blue light and is bent towards the Moon, like the light of every sunrise and sunset at once.

quiz.q: When is it safe to look at a solar eclipse without eye protection?
o: During the partial phases if most of the Sun is covered
Only during totality, when the Sun is completely covered
quiz.e: Only the brief total phase is safe to view directly. Even a thin sliver of the Sun can damage the retina, so certified eclipse glasses are needed at all other times.

LESSONS.title: Comets: dirty snowballs from the deep
LESSONS.hook: For thousands of years comets were seen as omens of doom. Then one astronomer predicted a comet's return, died before he could see it, and was proved right.

sections.key: Before science explained them, comets were widely feared as signs of disaster or change.
sections.b: A comet appears suddenly, hangs in the sky for weeks with a ghostly tail, then fades away. To many ancient cultures that unpredictability made them frightening. Chinese astronomers kept careful records of comets for more than two thousand years, often linking them to political upheaval.
