Finally they gather observations and use induction to judge whether the evidence supports the idea. Then the cycle starts again. You can do the same with everyday puzzles. When you land on an explanation, ask what else could explain the facts, what your idea predicts, and whether you've checked.

quiz.q: Which kind of reasoning was Holmes mostly using when he guessed Watson had been in Afghanistan?
quiz.e: Holmes was inferring the most plausible explanation for a set of clues, which is abduction, not a guaranteed deduction.

quiz.q: What makes a deductive argument ‘sound’?
o: It is convincing to most people
It is based on many observations
It is valid and its premises are true
quiz.e: A valid argument with a false premise can reach a false conclusion. Soundness requires both correct structure and true premises.

quiz.q: What did the black swans seen in 1697 show about induction?
o: A conclusion based on many observations can be overturned by one new one
Swans migrate to Australia each year
Deduction is more reliable than observation
quiz.e: Countless sightings of white swans didn't prove all swans were white. One new observation was enough to overturn the generalisation.

quiz.q: ‘If it rained, the lawn would be wet. The lawn is wet, so it rained.’ What's wrong with this?
o: Nothing, it is a valid deduction
It relies on too few observations
It affirms the consequent, ignoring other possible causes
quiz.e: A wet lawn fits rain, but also a sprinkler or dew. Treating a possible explanation as certain is the fallacy of affirming the consequent.

quiz.q: In the scientific cycle, what role does deduction usually play?
o: Working out what should happen if a hypothesis is true
Coming up with the first guess
quiz.e: Deduction turns a hypothesis into testable predictions, which observations can then support or undermine.

LESSONS.title: The framing effect: same facts, different choices
LESSONS.hook: Would you choose a treatment with a 90 per cent survival rate? What about one with a 10 per cent death rate? They're identical, yet the wording changes what people choose.

sections.key: Describing the same options as lives saved or lives lost flipped people's choices.
sections.b: In 1981 the psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman published a now-famous problem. Imagine a disease outbreak expected to kill 600 people. One group of participants chose between two programs. With Program A, 200 people will be saved. With Program B, there's a one-third chance all 600 are saved and a two-thirds chance no-one is saved. Most chose A, the sure thing. A second group got the same choice in different words. With Program C, 400 people will die. With Program D, there's a one-third chance nobody dies and a two-thirds chance all 600 die. Now most chose D, the gamble. Yet A and C describe exactly the same outcome, as do B and D.

sections.h: Gains feel safe, losses invite a gamble
sections.key: People tend to avoid risk when thinking about gains, and take risks to avoid sure losses.
sections.b: The outbreak problem revealed a pattern that Kahneman and Tversky built into their prospect theory. When outcomes are described as gains, such as lives saved, people tend to be cautious and prefer a certain result. When the same outcomes are described as losses, such as deaths, people become more willing to gamble to avoid a sure loss. Part of the reason is loss aversion: losses tend to feel more painful than equivalent gains feel good, with many studies putting the ratio at roughly two to one, though estimates vary. Logically, the wording should make no difference, because the numbers are identical. Psychologically, the frame sets the reference point against which everything else is judged.

sections.key: Even physicians' choices shifted depending on whether outcomes were framed as survival or death.
sections.b: You might hope experts would see through framing. In a 1982 study published in the New England Journal of Medicine, Barbara McNeil and colleagues, including Tversky, asked people to choose between surgery and radiation therapy for lung cancer. Surgery carried a higher risk of dying during or soon after treatment, but better long-term survival. When the results were presented as chances of surviving, surgery looked more attractive than when the very same results were described as chances of dying. The effect appeared among patients, among students, and among physicians. Since then, many guides to communicating medical risk have encouraged presenting figures in more than one way, for example giving both survival and death rates together.

sections.key: Labels that highlight the positive side make products seem better, even after tasting them.
sections.b: Framing is everywhere in shopping. In a 1988 study, Irwin Levin and Gary Gaeth asked people to evaluate minced beef described either as ‘75 per cent lean’ or ‘25 per cent fat’. It was the same meat, but people rated the ‘lean’ version as better quality and less greasy. Interestingly, the gap shrank when people actually tasted the beef, though it didn't vanish. Marketers know this well. Yoghurt is ‘95 per cent fat free’ rather than ‘5 per cent fat’. A fee might be presented as a ‘discount for paying cash’ instead of a ‘surcharge for paying by card’. None of these descriptions is false. They simply choose which side of the same coin you see first.

sections.key: In politics and news, choosing which aspect of an issue to emphasise can shift opinions.
sections.b: There's a second, broader kind of framing. Instead of describing the same numbers in two ways, it highlights different aspects of an issue. In a 1997 study by Thomas Nelson, Rosalee Clawson and Zoe Oxley, Americans read a news story about a planned rally by the Ku Klux Klan. When the story framed it as a matter of free speech, readers were more tolerant of the rally going ahead than when the same event was framed as a threat to public order. Debates about tax, immigration, crime and climate are full of these frames. Is a policy ‘tax relief’ or a ‘cut to services’? Each phrase invites you to think about one side of the trade-off and quietly forget the other.

sections.key: Restate choices in more than one way and convert percentages into real numbers before deciding.
sections.b: You can't avoid frames, because every description has to start somewhere. But you can learn to notice them. When you face an important choice, deliberately flip the wording: if you're told nine out of ten customers are satisfied, remind yourself that one in ten isn't. If a deal is framed as avoiding a loss, ask how it looks as a plain gain. Turn percentages into concrete counts, such as ‘out of 100 people like me, how many?’ This makes risks much easier to compare. Be especially wary when someone else has chosen the frame for you and stands to gain from your decision. And when you present information to others, giving both frames is often the fairest thing you can do.

quiz.q: In the outbreak problem, why is the switch in people's choices surprising?
o: The programs had genuinely different outcomes
Programs A and C described exactly the same outcome
The second group was given more information
quiz.e: Saving 200 of 600 is the same as 400 dying. Only the wording changed, yet the majority preference reversed.

quiz.q: When outcomes are framed as losses, people tend to:
o: Choose whichever option is listed first
quiz.e: Facing a sure loss feels so painful that people often prefer a risky option that might avoid it altogether.

quiz.q: Who was influenced by framing in the 1982 lung cancer study?
o: Nobody, once the numbers were explained
quiz.e: Physicians were affected too, which is why presenting risks in more than one frame is often recommended.

quiz.q: What happened in the minced beef study when people actually tasted the meat?
o: The framing effect shrank but didn't disappear
Tasting made them reject both samples
quiz.e: Direct experience reduced the influence of the label, but the ‘lean’ description still gave the beef an edge.

quiz.q: Which is a good way to defuse a frame?
o: Restate the choice the other way and convert percentages into counts
quiz.e: Seeing both versions and using concrete counts strips away the emotional pull of a single framing.

LESSONS.title: The wisdom of crowds: when many guesses beat experts
LESSONS.hook: In 1906 hundreds of people guessed the weight of an ox. Hardly anyone was spot on, but together they were astonishingly close. Here's why, and when crowds turn foolish.

sections.key: Francis Galton found that a crowd's middle guess was remarkably close to an ox's true weight.
sections.b: In 1906 the scientist Francis Galton visited a livestock fair in Plymouth, England. Visitors could pay a small fee to guess the weight of an ox once it had been slaughtered and dressed, with prizes for the closest entries. Galton, who was not a great admirer of ordinary people's judgement, collected the 787 legible tickets afterwards and analysed them. The guesses were all over the place. But the middle value, the median, was 1,207 pounds, about 547 kilograms. The actual weight was 1,198 pounds, so the crowd was out by less than one per cent. Later analyses found the average of the guesses was even closer. Galton published the result in Nature in 1907 under the title ‘Vox Populi’, the voice of the people.

sections.key: When people's mistakes are independent, overestimates and underestimates tend to cancel each other out.
sections.b: How can a crowd of non-experts beat almost every individual in it? Each guess contains two parts: some genuine information and some error. One person might overestimate because the ox looks bulky, while another underestimates because they're thinking of a smaller breed. If those errors point in different directions, they tend to cancel out when you average them, while the useful information adds up. The result is an estimate that is often better than most of the individual guesses, and sometimes better than an expert's. But this only works if people bring different knowledge and make their mistakes independently. If everyone shares the same blind spot, averaging simply produces a confident version of the same error.

sections.key: Combining many judgements works in plenty of everyday settings, from quiz shows to forecasts.
sections.b: The idea was popularised by the journalist James Surowiecki in his 2004 book The Wisdom of Crowds. One of his examples came from the quiz show Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? Contestants who were stuck could phone a friend they had chosen for being smart, or poll the studio audience. By Surowiecki's account, the chosen friends gave the right answer about 65 per cent of the time, while the audience's most popular answer was right about 91 per cent of the time. Similar principles underpin many tools today, from averaging the forecasts of several economists to combining many runs of weather models, and the product ratings that pool the experiences of thousands of buyers.

sections.key: Crowds are wise when they are diverse, independent, decentralised and properly combined.
sections.b: Surowiecki argued that wise crowds need four ingredients. Diversity: people should bring different information and perspectives, not all the same views. Independence: each person's judgement should be their own, rather than copied from those around them. Decentralisation: people should be able to draw on local and specialised knowledge. And aggregation: there must be some way of combining all the private judgements into one answer, such as an average, a vote or a market price. Take away any of these and the magic fades. A room of people who all read the same article, or who call out their guesses one after another, is less a crowd of independent minds than one opinion repeated many times.

sections.key: Social influence can make crowds more confident without making them more accurate.
sections.b: Independence is the fragile ingredient. In a 2011 study, Jan Lorenz and colleagues in Switzerland asked groups to estimate factual quantities, such as crime figures, over several rounds. Some groups were shown what the others had guessed before answering again. Seeing others' answers narrowed the range of guesses and made people more confident, but the group's estimates did not become more accurate. The crowd had lost its diversity without gaining any wisdom. On a larger scale, similar dynamics help explain stock market bubbles, fads and panic buying, where people react to each other rather than to independent information. A crowd that copies itself doesn't cancel out its errors. It can amplify them.

sections.key: Averaging two separate guesses of your own can improve your accuracy.
sections.b: You can even borrow the effect for yourself. In 2008 Edward Vul and Harold Pashler asked people to answer factual questions, then unexpectedly asked them to guess again. The average of a person's two guesses was more accurate than either guess alone, and the benefit was larger when the second guess came three weeks later rather than straight away. The delay helped because it made the second guess more independent of the first. Researchers call this the crowd within. A practical version: when you estimate something important, such as how long a job will take, make a guess, then assume your first answer was wrong, think about why, and make a second estimate. Then average the two.

quiz.q: What was striking about the guesses at the Plymouth fair?
o: The median guess was within about one per cent of the true weight
The butchers' guesses were by far the best
quiz.e: Individual guesses varied widely, but the middle value of all 787 was only nine pounds off the actual weight.

quiz.q: Why does averaging many guesses work?
o: Independent errors tend to cancel out
People guess more carefully in groups
Large numbers are easier to estimate
quiz.e: When errors point in different directions, they offset each other, leaving the shared genuine information.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of Surowiecki's conditions for a wise crowd?
quiz.e: Wise crowds need diversity, independence, decentralisation and aggregation. Everyone agreeing is not required, and can be a warning sign.

quiz.q: What did Lorenz and colleagues find when people saw others' guesses?
o: Guesses narrowed and confidence rose, without the group becoming more accurate
quiz.e: Social influence reduced diversity and boosted confidence, but didn't improve the collective estimate.

quiz.q: In Vul and Pashler's study, when did a second guess help most?
o: When it was made three weeks later
When a friend made it instead
When it copied the first guess
quiz.e: A delay made the second guess more independent of the first, so averaging the two cancelled out more error.

LESSONS.title: Small samples, big surprises: the law of small numbers
LESSONS.hook: The places with the lowest cancer rates and the highest ones share the same surprising feature. Understanding why will change how you read every ranking and review.

sections.key: Both the healthiest and unhealthiest-looking places on a map are often the ones with the fewest people.
sections.b: Imagine a map of the United States showing kidney cancer rates county by county. The counties with the lowest rates are mostly rural and sparsely populated. It's tempting to explain this: fresh air, clean water, active lives, fewer pollutants. Now look at the counties with the highest rates. They are also mostly rural and sparsely populated. Suddenly the explanations sound less convincing, since rural life can't be both protective and harmful. This example, discussed by the statistician Howard Wainer and later by Daniel Kahneman in his book Thinking, Fast and Slow, has a simple answer. Small counties don't have unusual health. They have small populations, and small numbers bounce around far more than large ones.

sections.key: The smaller the sample, the more likely it is to produce extreme results by chance.
sections.b: Think of flipping coins. Toss a fair coin four times and getting all heads is not unusual: it happens about one time in sixteen. Toss it 400 times and getting all heads is practically impossible. Results from small samples are naturally more variable, so they are much more likely to land at the extremes, both very high and very low. A county with a few thousand residents might record no cases of a rare cancer for years, then an unusual cluster, purely by chance. A city of a million people will almost always land close to the national average. So whenever you rank places, schools or hospitals of very different sizes, the small ones will tend to crowd both the top and the bottom of the list.

sections.key: Even people trained in statistics tend to ignore sample size when it matters.
sections.b: In the early 1970s Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman posed a question. A town has two hospitals. In the larger one about 45 babies are born each day, and in the smaller one about 15. Roughly half of all babies are boys, but the exact share varies from day to day. Over a year, each hospital records the days when more than 60 per cent of the babies born were boys. Which hospital recorded more such days? Most people said about the same. The right answer is the smaller hospital, because with only 15 births a day, lopsided results are much more common. In an earlier paper titled ‘Belief in the law of small numbers’, they had shown that even research psychologists trusted small samples too much.

sections.key: Uncertainty in an average shrinks only with the square root of the sample size.
sections.b: The maths behind this traces back to the 1700s and the French-born mathematician Abraham de Moivre. In modern terms, the typical wobble in an average shrinks in proportion to the square root of the number of things being averaged. That has a sobering consequence. To halve the uncertainty in an estimate, you don't need twice as much data; you need four times as much. To cut it to a tenth, you need a hundred times more. Howard Wainer has called this ‘the most dangerous equation’, not because it's complicated, but because ignoring it has led to so many costly mistakes. It explains why tiny trials, small surveys and short track records can be so misleading.

sections.key: Policies based on small-sample rankings can end up chasing patterns that are really noise.
sections.b: Wainer's favourite cautionary tale involves American education. From the late 1990s, reformers noticed that small schools were overrepresented among the top performers on test results. Major funders, including the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, invested heavily in creating smaller schools and breaking up big ones. But as Wainer and colleagues pointed out, small schools were also overrepresented among the worst performers. Their results were simply more variable, because each year's scores came from fewer students. Evaluations of the small-schools push produced mixed results, and the Gates Foundation later shifted its education strategy. Whatever the other merits of smaller schools, the striking rankings had been at least partly an illusion created by sample size.

sections.key: Before trusting an extreme result, check how many cases it's based on.
sections.b: Once you know this, you'll see it everywhere. A new café with five reviews averaging five stars may be no better than an established one averaging 4.6 from 2,000 reviews. A footballer who scores in each of their first three games isn't necessarily a star. A small study reporting a dramatic effect is more likely to be a fluke than a large study reporting a modest one. A useful habit is to mentally pull extreme results from small samples back towards the average until more evidence comes in. Statisticians have formal versions of this idea, sometimes called shrinkage. And when you hear that a small town is the best or worst place for something, your first question should be: how many people live there?

quiz.q: What do US counties with the lowest and the highest kidney cancer rates often have in common?
o: They are close to large cities
They share the same water supply
They are all on the coast
quiz.e: Small populations produce more variable rates, so they land at both extremes by chance.

quiz.q: In the hospital problem, which hospital records more days when over 60 per cent of babies are boys?
quiz.e: With only 15 births a day, lopsided results happen far more often than with 45 births a day.

quiz.q: To halve the uncertainty in an average, roughly how much more data do you need?
quiz.e: Uncertainty shrinks with the square root of sample size, so halving it takes four times the data.

quiz.q: Why were small schools overrepresented among the top performers?
o: Their results varied more because each was based on fewer students
quiz.e: Small schools also crowded the bottom of the rankings. Their extreme results were largely a product of small samples.

quiz.q: A new café has five reviews, all five stars. What's the most sensible view?
o: It's definitely the best café in town
The rating is uncertain, so mentally pull it back towards average
Ignore all reviews from now on
quiz.e: With so few reviews, an extreme average is likely to drift as more come in. Treat it as promising, not proven.

LESSONS.title: Piltdown Man: the fake fossil that fooled science for 40 years
LESSONS.hook: For four decades, a skull from an English gravel pit was hailed as a key link in human evolution. It was a forgery, and the reasons experts believed it are the real lesson.

sections.key: In 1912 bones from a Sussex gravel pit were announced as an ancient human ancestor.
sections.b: In December 1912 Charles Dawson, a solicitor and keen amateur fossil collector, and Arthur Smith Woodward, a leading geologist at the British Museum (Natural History), presented a sensational find to the Geological Society of London. From a gravel pit near Piltdown in Sussex came fragments of a skull and part of a jawbone with two worn teeth, along with animal fossils and crude stone tools. Woodward's reconstruction showed a creature with a large, humanlike braincase and an apelike jaw. It was given the scientific name Eoanthropus dawsoni, ‘Dawson's dawn man’. Newspapers celebrated the find as the earliest Englishman, and many experts accepted Piltdown as a vital link between apes and humans.

sections.h: It told experts what they expected
sections.key: Piltdown fitted the popular belief that big brains evolved first.
sections.b: Part of Piltdown's power was that it confirmed what many scientists already thought. A common view at the time was that humans had become human through intelligence, so a large brain must have evolved before other human features, such as upright walking or smaller teeth. Piltdown seemed to show exactly that: a big brain paired with an ape's jaw. National pride may also have played a part. Important fossils had been found in Germany, such as the Neanderthal remains and the Heidelberg jaw, and France had its Cro-Magnon skeletons. Britain had little of comparable importance. A find that matched both scientific expectation and national hopes faced far less scrutiny than it deserved.

sections.key: The parts that could have exposed the fake were missing, and few researchers saw the original bones.
sections.b: Looking back, there were warning signs. The jaw was broken in exactly the places that would have shown whether it truly belonged with the skull: the joint where jaw meets skull and the chin were both missing. Some scientists, especially in the United States and France, argued from early on that the skull and jaw came from different creatures. But most researchers were given plaster casts rather than access to the original fossils, which were closely guarded at the British Museum. Casts could not show details, such as tool marks or staining, that might have raised suspicion. Later finds, including a canine tooth in 1913 and fragments Dawson said he found at a second site, seemed to settle the debate.

sections.key: Because Piltdown seemed authentic, a genuine African fossil was sidelined for years.
sections.b: The forgery did real damage. In 1924 the Australian-born anatomist Raymond Dart, working in South Africa, identified a small fossil skull from a quarry at Taung. In 1925 he argued in Nature that this ‘Taung Child’ belonged to an early human relative, which he named Australopithecus africanus. It had the opposite combination to Piltdown: a small, apelike brain but humanlike teeth and signs of upright posture. Many leading experts dismissed it, partly because it clashed with Piltdown's big-brain-first story. It took more than two decades, and many further fossil discoveries in Africa, before Dart's view was widely accepted. We now know that upright walking came long before large brains.

sections.key: New dating methods and careful examination proved the bones were a recent fake.
sections.b: As more genuine fossils emerged, Piltdown looked increasingly out of place. In 1949 Kenneth Oakley applied a new fluorine test, which helps estimate how long bones have been buried by measuring the fluorine they absorb from groundwater. The Piltdown bones contained surprisingly little, suggesting they were far younger than claimed. In 1953 Oakley, together with Joseph Weiner and Wilfrid Le Gros Clark, announced the truth. The jaw came from an orangutan. Its teeth had been filed down to look humanlike. The skull belonged to a modern human who had lived only centuries earlier, and the bones had been stained to look ancient. Under a microscope, the file marks on the teeth were plain to see.

sections.key: Suspicion fell on many people, but a 2016 study points strongly to Dawson.
sections.b: For decades, people argued over who had planted the fakes. Suspects included Woodward; the Jesuit priest and scientist Pierre Teilhard de Chardin, who found the canine tooth; and even Arthur Conan Doyle, the creator of Sherlock Holmes, who lived nearby. In 2016 a team led by Isabelle De Groote published a detailed re-examination using DNA analysis and CT scanning. The evidence suggested the jaw and teeth from both sites came from a single orangutan, and that the same methods had been used throughout, including packing bones with gravel and putty. That pointed to a single forger, and Dawson, who has also been linked to other dubious finds, was by far the most likely culprit.

sections.key: Be most careful with evidence that tells you exactly what you hoped to hear.
sections.b: Piltdown wasn't exposed because science is infallible; it was exposed because science keeps testing. Better methods and new evidence eventually revealed what expectation had hidden. But the story offers lessons well beyond fossils. Be extra careful with evidence that confirms exactly what you, your team or your country hoped to find. Ask whether anyone has examined the original data, rather than a summary or a copy. Notice when crucial pieces of evidence are conveniently missing. And remember that the anomaly that doesn't fit, like the Taung Child, may turn out to be the real discovery. When an idea seems to explain everything you expected, that's a moment to look harder, not to relax.

quiz.q: Why did Piltdown Man fit what many experts expected?
o: It had a large brain with an apelike jaw, matching the idea that big brains evolved first
It was found alongside written records
It looked exactly like a modern human
It came from Africa, as Darwin had predicted
quiz.e: Piltdown seemed to confirm the popular theory that intelligence came first in human evolution, which lowered experts' guard.

quiz.q: Why were most researchers unable to spot the forgery early on?
o: The fossils were lost for decades
They mostly worked from plaster casts rather than the original bones
The bones were kept in Africa
No-one was allowed to publish about them
quiz.e: Casts hid the file marks and staining that close examination of the originals would later reveal.

quiz.q: What was Raymond Dart's Taung Child?
o: A genuine early human relative that experts long dismissed
quiz.e: The Taung Child was real, but because it contradicted Piltdown's story, it took decades to be widely accepted.

quiz.q: What did Oakley's fluorine test reveal?
o: The bones were millions of years old
The skull belonged to an ape
The bones were far younger than claimed
quiz.e: The bones had absorbed too little fluorine to be ancient, the first strong clue that Piltdown was a recent fake.

quiz.q: What did the 2016 re-examination suggest?
o: Arthur Conan Doyle was the forger
A single forger, most likely Dawson, was responsible
The bones were genuine after all
quiz.e: Consistent methods and DNA from a single orangutan pointed to one forger, and Dawson was the most likely candidate.

LESSONS.title: The lady tasting tea: how to design a fair test
LESSONS.hook: A scientist claimed she could taste whether the milk or the tea went into the cup first. Working out how to test her claim properly helped shape the modern experiment.

sections.h: A cup of tea at Rothamsted
sections.key: A casual claim at afternoon tea inspired Ronald Fisher's thinking about how to test ideas.
sections.b: In the early 1920s, at the Rothamsted agricultural research station north of London, the statistician Ronald Fisher offered a colleague a cup of tea. Dr Muriel Bristol, a scientist who studied algae, declined because he had poured the milk in after the tea. She preferred milk first, and insisted she could taste the difference. Fisher was sceptical. According to later accounts from people who were there, a test was quickly arranged, and she reportedly identified the cups correctly. The story might have been forgotten, but Fisher used it to open a chapter of his 1935 book The Design of Experiments. Behind a light-hearted example lay a serious question: how do you fairly test a claim?

sections.key: A fair test starts by asking what pure guessing would produce, an idea called the null hypothesis.
sections.b: Fisher's key move was to start by assuming the claim is false. Suppose Bristol has no ability at all and is simply guessing. This assumption is now called the null hypothesis. If we can work out what results guessing would produce, we can ask whether her actual performance is surprising by comparison. Fisher's proposed design used eight cups: four with milk poured first and four with tea first, presented in random order. She would be told there were four of each and asked to pick out the four milk-first cups. If she got them all right, would that be convincing? That depends on how easily a guesser could do the same, which turns out to be a question of counting.

sections.key: There are 70 ways to choose four cups from eight, so a pure guesser gets them all right only once in 70.
sections.b: How many different ways can you choose four cups out of eight? The answer is 70. Only one of those choices is completely correct, so someone guessing at random has a 1 in 70 chance of a perfect score, about 1.4 per cent. That's unlikely enough that a perfect result would be reasonable evidence of real skill. But what about getting three right and one wrong? There are 16 ways to do that, so the chance of scoring at least three out of four by luck is 17 in 70, about 24 per cent. That's far too common to prove anything. Fisher's point was that you should decide what result would count as convincing before you run the test.

sections.key: Random order stops hidden patterns or clues from masquerading as skill.
sections.b: Why insist the cups be served in random order? Imagine the four milk-first cups were all prepared first and served first. They might be slightly cooler, or the taster might pick up on a pattern. Any success could then come from those clues rather than from tasting the milk. Fisher argued that randomisation is the most reliable protection against hidden factors like these, including ones nobody has thought of. He also stressed keeping everything else the same: the same cups, the same tea and the same amount of milk. Fisher developed many of these ideas through crop experiments at Rothamsted, where treatments were assigned to plots of land at random so that differences in soil couldn't bias the results.

sections.key: Too small a test can never give convincing evidence, however good the taster is.
sections.b: Fisher's framework also reveals why the number of trials matters. With six cups, three of each, there are only 20 ways to choose, so even a perfect score has a 1 in 20 chance of happening by luck, or five per cent. With just four cups, two of each, a guesser gets a perfect score one time in six. A test that small could never convince anyone, however genuine the skill. Fisher suggested treating results that would happen by chance less than about one time in 20 as worth taking seriously, a convention that later hardened into the famous 0.05 threshold for statistical significance. He saw it as a rough guide to which results deserve attention, not a magic line between truth and falsehood.

sections.key: Fisher's principles underpin modern clinical trials, field trials and online A/B tests.
sections.b: The ideas in Fisher's tea example now run through modern research. A drug trial assigns patients to treatment or placebo at random, works out in advance how many participants are needed, and asks how likely the observed results would be if the drug did nothing. Farmers test crop varieties in randomised plots. Technology companies run what they call A/B tests, randomly showing different versions of a web page to different users to see which works better. Even if you never calculate a probability, the core questions are worth carrying with you. What would I expect to see if this claim were false? Could something other than the claimed cause explain the result? And was the test big enough to tell?

sections.key: A brilliant method doesn't protect its inventor from wishful thinking.
sections.b: Fisher was one of the most influential statisticians of the twentieth century and a major figure in genetics. Yet his story carries a warning too. In the late 1950s, as evidence mounted that smoking caused lung cancer, Fisher publicly argued that the link might not be causal. He suggested that some inherited factor could make people both more likely to smoke and more likely to develop cancer. Asking about a hidden common cause is a legitimate question, but the evidence that smoking itself was responsible soon became overwhelming. Fisher was a keen pipe smoker and had acted as a consultant to the tobacco industry. Good methods matter, but so does honesty about what you want to be true.

quiz.q: What is the null hypothesis in the tea test?
o: That she can always tell the difference
That she has no ability and is simply guessing
That the cups were poured incorrectly
quiz.e: The null hypothesis assumes no real effect. The test then asks whether her results would be surprising if that were true.

quiz.q: With eight cups, four of each, what's the chance a pure guesser picks all four milk-first cups correctly?
quiz.e: There are 70 ways to choose four cups from eight, and only one of them is entirely correct.

quiz.q: Why should the cups be served in random order?
o: So hidden clues or patterns can't be mistaken for skill
To reduce the number of cups needed
So the taster can't drink too much tea
quiz.e: Randomisation protects against hidden factors, such as temperature or serving order, that could otherwise explain a good score.

quiz.q: Why would a test with only four cups, two of each, be unconvincing?
o: The tea would go cold before the end
Fisher's maths only works with eight cups
Small tests are always biased against the taster
A guesser would get a perfect score one time in six
quiz.e: With only six possible choices, even a perfect result could easily happen by luck, so it couldn't demonstrate real skill.

quiz.q: What did Fisher argue about smoking and lung cancer?
o: That smoking was clearly the main cause
That an inherited factor might explain the link instead
That lung cancer rates weren't really rising
That no further research was needed
quiz.e: Fisher proposed a hidden common cause. The question was fair, but the evidence soon showed smoking itself was responsible.

WORDS.blank: Profit alone shouldn't be the only ___ for judging a company's success.

WORDS.def: To have an intense feeling of longing for something or someone.
ex: After months overseas, she yearned for a good flat white.
He yearned to see his grandchildren again before the year was out.
WORDS.origin: From Old English giernan, 'to desire'.
WORDS.blank: After years in the city, he would often ___ for the quiet of the farm.

WORDS.def: The amount of profit or return produced by an investment, or, as a verb, to produce a result or to give way.
ex: The term deposit offers a decent yield compared to a regular savings account.
The talks finally began to yield results after weeks of stalemate.
WORDS.origin: From Old English gieldan, 'to pay, repay'.
WORDS.blank: Investors were disappointed by the fund's low ___ last quarter.

WORDS.def: A wooden frame used to join two draught animals for pulling, or, figuratively, something that binds or burdens a person.
ex: The bullocks were fitted with a wooden yoke to pull the cart.
She finally felt free of the yoke of her old job.
WORDS.origin: From Old English geoc, related to Latin iugum.
WORDS.blank: The colony eventually threw off the ___ of foreign rule.

WORDS.def: Occurring every day; ordinary and commonplace to the point of dullness.
ex: She found poetry in the quotidian rhythm of the 7:42 train into Flinders Street.
The novel lingers on quotidian details: burnt toast, school lunches, the bins on a Tuesday night.
WORDS.origin: From Latin quotidianus, from quotidie 'every day' (quot 'how many' + dies 'day').
WORDS.blank: After a month of travel, he was oddly glad to return to the ___ routine of commuting, cooking and sleeping.

WORDS.def: Showing a casual, carefree lack of concern, especially where worry would be expected.
ex: He strolled into the exam ten minutes late with an insouciant grin.
Her insouciant shrug suggested the parking fine was the least of her worries.
WORDS.origin: From French, in- 'not' + soucier 'to worry, care', from Latin sollicitare 'to disturb'.
WORDS.blank: Despite the storm warnings, the surfer remained ___, waxing his board as the sky turned black.

WORDS.def: A manuscript page scraped or washed and written over, with traces of the earlier text still visible; by extension, anything bearing layers of its own history.
ex: Multispectral imaging revealed lost works of Archimedes hidden beneath the prayers of a medieval palimpsest.
The old terrace in Fitzroy is a palimpsest of painted signs, each fading through the next.
WORDS.origin: Via Latin from Greek palimpsestos 'scraped again', from palin 'again' + psen 'to rub smooth'.
WORDS.blank: Under ultraviolet light the parchment proved to be a ___, with an older Greek text beneath the Latin.

WORDS.def: Having a strong spiritual or religious quality; suggesting the presence of something divine or awe-inspiring.
ex: At dawn, Uluru glowing red felt almost numinous to the silent crowd.
The cathedral's vast, dim nave produced a numinous hush.
WORDS.origin: From Latin numen, numinis 'divine power, nod of the gods'; popularised by Rudolf Otto's The Idea of the Holy (1917).
WORDS.blank: Standing alone among the ancient redwoods, she felt a ___ sense of being in the presence of something holy.

WORDS.def: Impossible to escape or avoid, however hard one struggles.
ex: Rising sea levels are an ineluctable concern for low-lying Pacific nations.
The tragedy moves with ineluctable logic towards its final scene.
WORDS.origin: From Latin ineluctabilis, from in- 'not' + eluctari 'to struggle out of'.
WORDS.blank: Ageing is ___: no diet, cream or surgery can hold it off forever.

WORDS.def: An unfilled space or gap, especially a missing section in a manuscript, argument or body of knowledge.
ex: The thesis fills a lacuna in research on early colonial Tasmania.
A water-damaged lacuna in the diary leaves three crucial days unexplained.
WORDS.origin: From Latin lacuna 'pool, pit, gap', from lacus 'lake'.
WORDS.blank: Scholars have long puzzled over the ___ in the poem, where an entire stanza was torn from the page.

WORDS.def: Deliberately faithless and treacherous; betraying trust.
ex: The perfidious adviser sold the campaign's strategy to the rival party.
'Perfidious Albion' was a long-standing French jibe at supposed English treachery.
WORDS.origin: From Latin perfidiosus, from perfidia 'treachery', from per- 'away from' + fides 'faith'.
WORDS.blank: The ___ ally signed the treaty in the morning and invaded by nightfall.

WORDS.def: The appearance of being true or real, especially in fiction or art.
ex: The film's verisimilitude owes much to shooting on location in outback Queensland.
Small, precise details lend a story verisimilitude.
WORDS.origin: From Latin verisimilitudo, from verisimilis 'probable', literally 'like the truth' (verum 'true' + similis 'like').
WORDS.blank: The novelist interviewed retired detectives to give her crime scenes greater ___.

WORDS.def: Deliberately inoffensive and bland, so as to avoid provoking any reaction; (originally) relieving pain.
ex: The press release was a page of anodyne corporate phrases that said nothing at all.
He gave an anodyne answer about 'learning from the process'.
WORDS.origin: Via Latin from Greek anodunos 'painless', from an- 'without' + odune 'pain'.
WORDS.blank: Fearing a backlash, the minister replaced her fiery speech with a few ___ remarks about working together.

WORDS.def: Denoting a past period remembered as idyllically happy and peaceful.
ex: He spoke wistfully of the halcyon summers of his youth on the Mornington Peninsula.
Those were the halcyon days before mortgages and deadlines.
WORDS.origin: From Greek alkuon 'kingfisher'; in legend the bird calmed the sea to nest on it around the winter solstice, the 'halcyon days'.
WORDS.blank: Grandma still talks about the ___ days of the 1960s, when the whole street left their doors unlocked.

WORDS.def: (Especially of fabric) so light, delicate and fine that it is almost transparent.
ex: A diaphanous curtain stirred in the sea breeze.
The dragonfly's diaphanous wings caught the afternoon light.
WORDS.origin: From medieval Latin diaphanus, from Greek diaphanes 'see-through', from dia 'through' + phainein 'to show'.
WORDS.blank: The bride wore a ___ veil of silk so fine you could read print through it.

WORDS.def: Vanishing gradually from sight or memory; fading away almost as soon as it appears.
ex: The evanescent glow of the aurora australis faded before she could find her camera.
Fame on social media is evanescent.
WORDS.origin: From Latin evanescere 'to disappear', from e- 'out' + vanescere 'to vanish' (vanus 'empty').
WORDS.blank: The scent of the jasmine was ___, gone the moment the wind changed.

WORDS.def: A person who is self-indulgently devoted to luxury and sensual pleasure.
ex: A true sybarite, he booked the spa, the degustation and the penthouse in a single weekend.
The resort markets itself to sybarites who never want to lift a finger.
WORDS.origin: From Sybaris, an ancient Greek city in southern Italy whose citizens were famed for their luxury.
WORDS.blank: Only a committed ___ would insist on silk sheets and champagne while camping.

WORDS.def: Travelling from place to place, especially working or living in a series of locations for short periods.
ex: As a peripatetic music teacher, she visits six schools across the Riverina each week.
His peripatetic childhood, following his father's mining jobs, meant nine schools in ten years.
WORDS.origin: From Greek peripatetikos, from peripatein 'to walk up and down'; applied to Aristotle's school, which taught in a covered walkway of the Lyceum.
WORDS.blank: The ___ surgeon flew between remote clinics in the Kimberley, never staying more than a week.

WORDS.def: A person who confidently gives opinions on matters beyond their knowledge or expertise.
ex: The comment section was full of ultracrepidarians explaining virology to virologists.
A celebrity turned ultracrepidarian, he now lectures economists on monetary policy.
WORDS.origin: From Latin ultra crepidam 'beyond the sandal', from Pliny's story of the painter Apelles telling a cobbler who criticised more than a sandal to stick to his trade; used by William Hazlitt in 1819.
WORDS.blank: The footballer was an ___, offering his views on quantum physics and climate science with equal confidence.

WORDS.def: A state of disuse, especially of a law or custom that is no longer observed or enforced.
ex: The old statute against Sunday trading had long fallen into desuetude.
The tradition of formal calling cards has passed into desuetude.
WORDS.origin: From Latin desuetudo, from desuescere 'to become unaccustomed', from de- 'away' + suescere 'to grow used to'.
WORDS.blank: No one had been prosecuted under the archaic law for a century, and judges agreed it had fallen into ___.

WORDS.def: The legal right to use and enjoy the income or produce of another's property, without owning it and without damaging or diminishing its substance.
ex: Under the will, she held a usufruct of the farm for life, after which it passed to her nephews.
The usufruct let him keep the rents from the building but not sell it.
WORDS.origin: From Latin usufructus, from usus et fructus 'use and enjoyment (of the fruits)'.
WORDS.blank: He could harvest the orchard's apples under his ___, but he could not fell the trees or sell the land.

WORDS.def: A paid position that requires little or no work but brings status or income.
ex: Critics called the ambassadorship a sinecure for retired politicians.
His board seat was a sinecure: four meetings a year and a generous fee.
WORDS.origin: From Latin sine cura 'without care', originally a church benefice without the 'cure' (care) of souls.
WORDS.blank: The so-called advisory role was a ___, paying a full salary for one lunch a month.

WORDS.def: (Of speech or writing) using too many words and therefore tediously long.
ex: The judge criticised the prolix submissions, which ran to four hundred pages.
Her early drafts were prolix, but the editor cut them to the bone.
WORDS.origin: From Latin prolixus 'poured forth, extended', from pro- 'forward' + liquere 'to be liquid'.
WORDS.blank: The report was so ___ that its key finding was buried on page ninety.

WORDS.def: A state of serene calm and freedom from mental disturbance, prized as the goal of life by Epicureans and Sceptics.
ex: Epicurus taught that ataraxia comes from limiting desires and banishing fear of the gods.
After a week offline in the Daintree, he felt something close to ataraxia.
WORDS.origin: From Greek ataraxia 'impassiveness', from a- 'not' + tarassein 'to disturb'.
WORDS.blank: The Epicureans sought ___, an untroubled calm of mind, rather than wild pleasure.

WORDS.def: A person or thing that is the centre of attention or admiration.
ex: The young Matilda was the cynosure of every scout at the national championships.
Her gold gown made her the cynosure of the Logies red carpet.
WORDS.origin: Via Latin from Greek kunosoura 'dog's tail', the name for the constellation Ursa Minor, which contains the Pole Star used for guidance.
WORDS.blank: The moment the champion walked in, she became the ___ of the room, every eye turning to her.

WORDS.def: A confused, jumbled mixture of things, often used scornfully of ideas or claims.
ex: The defence's story was a farrago of half-truths and invented alibis.
The website was a farrago of conspiracy theories and miracle cures.
WORDS.origin: From Latin farrago 'mixed fodder for cattle', from far 'spelt, grain'.
WORDS.blank: The so-called evidence was a ___ of rumours, misquotes and outright fabrications.

WORDS.def: Only just begun and so not yet fully formed or developed; rudimentary.
ex: The policy was still inchoate, a few bullet points on a whiteboard.
Her inchoate fears took shape only when the letter arrived.
WORDS.origin: From Latin inchoatus, past participle of incohare 'to begin'.
WORDS.blank: At this stage the plan is ___, more a vague ambition than a strategy.

WORDS.def: Serving no practical purpose or result; superfluous.
ex: Once the new law passed, the old clause became otiose.
The editor struck out every otiose adjective.
WORDS.origin: From Latin otiosus 'at leisure, unemployed', from otium 'leisure'.
WORDS.blank: With automatic backups in place, the nightly manual copy is now ___ and can be dropped.

WORDS.def: Written or said to promote a particular point of view, especially a controversial one, rather than to present the facts fairly.
ex: The documentary's tendentious editing left out every inconvenient interview.
Reviewers dismissed the history as tendentious, more pamphlet than scholarship.
WORDS.origin: Early 20th century, from 'tendency' modelled on German tendenziös; ultimately from Latin tendere 'to stretch, aim'.
WORDS.blank: The so-called independent review was ___, written to justify a decision already made.

WORDS.def: The near-straight-line alignment of three celestial bodies, such as the Sun, Earth and Moon at new or full moon.
ex: Spring tides occur at syzygy, when the pull of the Sun and Moon combine.
A total solar eclipse is a particularly precise syzygy.
WORDS.origin: Via late Latin from Greek suzugia 'a yoking together', from suzugos 'yoked'.
WORDS.blank: Eclipses can happen only at ___, when the Sun, Earth and Moon fall into line.

WORDS.def: The moment in a drama when a character makes a critical discovery or recognises the truth of their situation.
ex: Oedipus's anagnorisis, realising he has killed his father, is the model Aristotle admired.
The film's anagnorisis comes when the detective sees her own handwriting on the note.
WORDS.origin: From Greek anagnorisis 'recognition', from anagnorizein 'to recognise'; analysed in Aristotle's Poetics.
WORDS.blank: In Aristotle's terms, the play's ___ comes when the king finally recognises the beggar as his lost son.

WORDS.def: Showing steady, careful and persevering diligence.
ex: Years of sedulous practice turned a shy student into a concert pianist.
The archivist's sedulous cataloguing saved the collection from chaos.
WORDS.origin: From Latin sedulus 'zealous, careful', perhaps from se dolo 'without guile'.
WORDS.blank: Thanks to her ___ attention to every receipt, the audit found nothing amiss.

WORDS.def: Unattractive and objectionable; off-putting and repellent.
ex: His rebarbative manner alienated even his allies.
The brutalist car park was condemned as rebarbative.
WORDS.origin: From French rebarbatif, from se rebarber 'to face each other beard to beard', from barbe 'beard'.
WORDS.blank: Critics found the building ___: a grim slab of raw concrete that seemed designed to repel visitors.

WORDS.def: A salary, fee or other payment received from employment or holding an office.
ex: The directors' emoluments are disclosed in the annual report.
Judges' emoluments are set by an independent tribunal.
WORDS.origin: From Latin emolumentum, probably originally 'payment to a miller for grinding corn', from emolere 'to grind out'.
WORDS.blank: The annual report lists each director's ___, including salary, bonus and superannuation.

WORDS.def: Relating to or consisting of money.
ex: Members of parliament must declare any pecuniary interest in matters they vote on.
The penalty was purely pecuniary: a fine, with no jail time.
WORDS.origin: From Latin pecuniarius, from pecunia 'money', from pecu 'cattle', the earliest form of wealth.
WORDS.blank: Councillors with a ___ interest in the development, such as shares in the builder, had to leave the room.

WORDS.def: The misappropriation of money by a person entrusted with looking after it, such as a trustee or treasurer.
ex: The club treasurer's defalcation came to light during the annual audit.
Bankruptcy does not wipe out debts arising from a trustee's defalcation.
WORDS.origin: From medieval Latin defalcare 'to lop off', from falx, falcis 'sickle'.
WORDS.blank: The trustee's ___ left the estate $2 million short when the beneficiaries finally checked the accounts.

WORDS.def: A literary or artistic assistant, especially one who writes from dictation or copies manuscripts.
ex: Blind by then, Milton dictated Paradise Lost to a series of amanuenses.
She served as the composer's amanuensis, writing out the scores he sang to her.
WORDS.origin: From Latin (servus) a manu 'slave at hand(writing)' + -ensis 'belonging to'.
WORDS.blank: Unable to hold a pen after the stroke, the novelist dictated her final book to an ___.

WORDS.def: A self-taught person, especially one who has mastered a subject without formal instruction.
ex: An autodidact, he learned Mandarin from library books and podcasts.
Ramanujan was largely an autodidact before he wrote to Hardy.
WORDS.origin: From Greek autodidaktos 'self-taught', from autos 'self' + didaskein 'to teach'.
WORDS.blank: Never having attended university, the brilliant ___ taught herself calculus from secondhand textbooks.

WORDS.def: Having the iridescent, shimmering lustre of mother-of-pearl.
ex: The inside of the abalone shell was smooth and nacreous.
Nacreous clouds glow in pastel colours high in the polar stratosphere after sunset.
WORDS.origin: From nacre 'mother-of-pearl', via French from Italian naccaro, probably of Arabic origin.
WORDS.blank: Polar stratospheric clouds are also called ___ clouds for their shimmering mother-of-pearl colours.

WORDS.def: Stubbornly or wilfully disobedient to authority, especially to the orders of a court.
ex: The judge found the witness contumacious for refusing three times to answer.
A contumacious refusal to pay the fine led to a warrant.
WORDS.origin: From Latin contumax, contumacis 'stubborn, insolent'.
WORDS.blank: Having ignored three court orders to produce the documents, the director was held in contempt for ___ conduct.

questions.q: What is the only positive whole number that is exactly twice the sum of its digits?
Which war did the Peace of Westphalia (1648) bring to an end?
questions.e: It also helped establish the modern idea of sovereign states.

questions.q: What does the Chandrasekhar limit describe?
o: The maximum mass of a stable white dwarf, about 1.4 solar masses
The speed at which galaxies recede
The size of the observable universe
The minimum mass of a planet
questions.e: Above it, a white dwarf can't support itself against gravity.

questions.q: Which language family does Finnish belong to?
questions.e: Along with Estonian and Hungarian, unlike most European languages.

questions.q: Who proved Fermat's Last Theorem, announced in 1993 and completed in 1994?
questions.e: It had resisted proof for over 350 years.

questions.q: What do Gödel's incompleteness theorems show?
o: Every true statement can be proved
Any consistent system capable of basic arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove
questions.e: Published by Kurt Gödel in 1931.

questions.q: Which enzyme unwinds the DNA double helix during replication?
questions.e: Polymerase builds the new strands; ligase joins fragments.

questions.q: In 1952 Michael Ventris deciphered the Linear B script. What language did it turn out to record?
questions.e: The clay tablets were Mycenaean palace records, written centuries before Homer.

questions.q: What does Gresham's law state?
questions.e: People hoard more valuable coins and spend debased ones.

questions.q: What are telomeres?
o: Protective caps on the ends of chromosomes that shorten as cells divide
questions.e: Hobart-born Elizabeth Blackburn shared the 2009 Nobel Prize in Medicine for discovering how they are protected.

questions.q: What is a Lagrange point?
o: The centre of a black hole
A spot where the pull of two large bodies and orbital motion balance, so a small object can keep its position
The lowest point of an orbit
The edge of the solar system
questions.e: Every pair, such as the Sun and Earth, has five. Space telescopes are often parked near them.

questions.q: Who composed The Rite of Spring, whose 1913 Paris premiere caused a near-riot?
questions.e: Its dissonance and rhythms shocked the audience.

questions.q: Which metal has the highest melting point?
questions.e: About 3,422°C, which is why it is used in rocket nozzles and was used for light-bulb filaments.

questions.q: What is a 'hapax legomenon'?
o: A word that appears only once in a text or body of writing
questions.e: They can make ancient words very hard to translate.

questions.q: Which of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World stood at Alexandria?
questions.e: It stood over 100 metres tall by some estimates.

questions.q: What is the most abundant protein in the human body?
questions.e: It's a major component of skin, bone, tendons and ligaments.

questions.q: Which moon of Saturn has a thick nitrogen-rich atmosphere and liquid methane lakes?
questions.e: Europa and Io orbit Jupiter.

questions.q: In what year was the Treaty of Waitangi signed in New Zealand?
questions.e: Between the British Crown and many Māori chiefs.

questions.q: Who painted The Garden of Earthly Delights?
questions.e: A strange, crowded triptych from around 1500.

questions.q: Which mineral sits at 1, the softest, on the Mohs hardness scale?
questions.e: Diamond sits at 10.

questions.q: What does the Drake equation estimate?
o: The number of detectable alien civilisations in our galaxy
The mass of a black hole
questions.e: Frank Drake wrote it in 1961. Most of its factors, like how often life arises, are still unknown.

questions.q: Which philosopher wrote the Critique of Pure Reason (1781)?
questions.e: Kant was 'awakened from his dogmatic slumber' by Hume.

questions.q: In economics, what is a 'Giffen good'?
o: A good whose demand rises as its price rises, due to poverty
questions.e: A rare exception to the usual law of demand.

questions.q: Leonhard Euler's 1736 solution to the Seven Bridges of Königsberg problem founded which branch of maths?
questions.e: He proved no walk could cross each of the city's seven bridges exactly once, by reducing the map to points and lines.

questions.q: Which is the only sea with no coastline?
questions.e: It lies in the North Atlantic, bounded by ocean currents rather than land, and is named after its floating Sargassum seaweed.

questions.q: What does the Latin legal phrase 'habeas corpus' literally mean?
questions.e: It protects against unlawful detention.

questions.q: The Hanseatic League, a powerful medieval trading network, was centred on which sea?
questions.e: Merchant towns such as Lübeck, Hamburg and Riga dominated northern European trade from the 1200s to the 1400s.

questions.q: What is the smallest prime number greater than 100?
questions.e: 101 has no divisors other than 1 and itself.

questions.q: Which physicist predicted antimatter in 1928, from an equation combining quantum mechanics and relativity?
questions.e: The positron, the electron's antimatter twin, was found by Carl Anderson in 1932.

questions.q: The Voynich manuscript is famous for what?
o: Being written in an unknown script that no one has deciphered
Containing Leonardo da Vinci's secret notes
questions.e: Its vellum dates to the early 1400s. The strange text and drawings of unknown plants still baffle cryptographers.

questions.q: How many prime numbers are there below 100?
questions.e: There are 168 primes below 1,000, and they thin out steadily as numbers grow.

questions.q: What is special about 1729, the 'taxicab number'?
o: It is the first number whose digits sum to a perfect cube
It is the largest known perfect number below 10,000
It is the smallest number divisible by every number from 1 to 12
It is the smallest number that is the sum of two positive cubes in two different ways
questions.e: 1729 = 1³ + 12³ = 9³ + 10³, as Ramanujan pointed out when G. H. Hardy arrived in taxi number 1729.

questions.q: What is the Riemann hypothesis about?
o: Where the non-trivial zeros of the zeta function lie
How many dimensions a sphere can be smoothly bent into
Whether there are infinitely many twin primes
Whether every even number above 2 is the sum of two primes
questions.e: Posed in 1859, it would pin down how the primes are distributed, and it is one of the Clay Millennium Prize problems.

questions.q: Why was the proof of the four colour theorem (1976) a landmark?
o: It was proved wrong after being accepted for a century
It was the first major theorem proved with essential help from a computer
It was proved by a teenager
It was the first proof ever published by two mathematicians together
questions.e: Kenneth Appel and Wolfgang Haken had a computer check almost 2,000 configurations, which sparked debate about what counts as a proof.

questions.q: How many regular convex polyhedra (Platonic solids) exist?
questions.e: Tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron and icosahedron: Euclid's Elements ends by proving there can be no others.

questions.q: Does the harmonic series 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4 + ... add up to a finite number?
questions.e: It grows incredibly slowly: the first million terms add up to only about 14.4.

questions.q: Which book, written in 1202, helped bring Hindu-Arabic numerals into use in Europe?
questions.e: It also contains the rabbit-breeding puzzle that gives us the Fibonacci sequence.

questions.q: What does Emmy Noether's theorem (1918) connect?
o: Symmetries in nature with conservation laws
questions.e: For example, the laws of physics not changing over time is exactly why energy is conserved.

questions.q: Since 1983, how has the metre been defined?
o: By a platinum-iridium bar kept near Paris
By the distance light travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second
As one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator
By a wavelength of light from krypton-86
questions.e: Fixing the speed of light as an exact number made the metre depend on the second.

questions.q: What is Cherenkov radiation?
o: Light given off when a charged particle moves through a medium faster than light travels in that medium
X-rays emitted when electrons suddenly slow down
questions.e: It causes the eerie blue glow in the water around nuclear reactor cores.

questions.q: What does the Pauli exclusion principle state?
o: You cannot know a particle's position and momentum exactly at once
Every action has an equal and opposite reaction
Energy can be neither created nor destroyed
No two identical fermions can occupy the same quantum state at once
questions.e: It forces electrons into successive shells, which gives the periodic table its structure and keeps matter from collapsing.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of magnetic flux density?
questions.e: The gauss is the older CGS unit: 1 tesla equals 10,000 gauss, and an MRI scanner typically runs at 1.5 to 3 tesla.

questions.q: What did the Michelson-Morley experiment of 1887 famously fail to detect?
o: The bending of starlight by the Sun
questions.e: Its null result was later explained by special relativity: light's speed is the same for every observer.

questions.q: Albert Einstein received the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics chiefly for what?
o: His explanation of the photoelectric effect
questions.e: The prize was actually handed over in 1922, and his work showed light behaves as particles, a foundation of quantum theory.

questions.q: Which element has the highest electronegativity?
questions.e: On the Pauling scale fluorine scores about 3.98, which is why it reacts with almost everything.

questions.q: Mendeleev predicted the properties of 'eka-silicon' before it was discovered. What is it called today?
questions.e: Clemens Winkler found it in 1886, and its measured properties closely matched Mendeleev's forecast.

questions.q: What does it mean for a molecule to be 'chiral'?
o: It cannot be superimposed on its mirror image
It contains a ring of six carbon atoms
It has no overall electric charge
questions.e: The word comes from the Greek for hand, since left and right hands are the classic example.

questions.q: What does the Haber-Bosch process manufacture?
questions.e: By fixing nitrogen from the air for fertiliser, it now helps feed a large share of the world's population.

questions.q: In 1807, Humphry Davy used electrolysis to isolate which two elements for the first time?
questions.e: He went on to isolate several more, including calcium and magnesium, the following year.

questions.q: Photo 51, the X-ray image that revealed DNA's helical shape, was made in whose lab?
questions.e: It was taken in 1952 by her PhD student Raymond Gosling, and Watson saw it without her knowledge.

questions.q: Which enzyme copies RNA into DNA, the trick used by retroviruses like HIV?
questions.e: It was discovered independently by Howard Temin and David Baltimore in 1970.

questions.q: What are Okazaki fragments?
o: Short stretches of DNA made on the lagging strand during replication
Fragments of cell membrane left after cell division
Tiny RNA molecules that silence genes
Pieces of broken chromosome that cause mutations
questions.e: DNA polymerase can only build in one direction, so one strand must be copied in pieces, later joined by DNA ligase.

questions.q: Where in a eukaryotic cell does the Krebs (citric acid) cycle take place?
questions.e: Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm, then its products move into mitochondria to be fully broken down.

questions.q: Genetically, fungi are more closely related to which group?
questions.e: Fungi and animals share a common ancestor, and fungal cell walls are made of chitin, like insect exoskeletons, not cellulose.

questions.q: In 1796, Edward Jenner showed he could protect against smallpox using material from which disease?
questions.e: The word vaccine comes from vacca, Latin for cow.

questions.q: In the 1840s, Ignaz Semmelweis sharply cut deaths from childbed fever in Vienna by introducing what?
o: Handwashing with a chlorinated lime solution
questions.e: Many doctors rejected his idea, and it only won acceptance after germ theory arrived decades later.

questions.q: Which organ produces most of the hormone erythropoietin, which drives red blood cell production?
questions.e: This is why people with serious kidney disease often develop anaemia.

questions.q: Howard Florey, who shared the 1945 Nobel Prize for turning penicillin into a usable drug, was born in which country?
questions.e: Born in Adelaide in 1898, he shared the prize with Alexander Fleming and Ernst Chain.

questions.q: John Snow's 1854 study, which traced an outbreak to the Broad Street pump in London, concerned which disease?
questions.e: He persuaded officials to remove the pump's handle, and his maps helped found modern epidemiology.

questions.q: Which Ottoman sultan captured Constantinople in 1453?
questions.e: He was only 21, and he made the city his new capital.

questions.q: Which Carthaginian general crossed the Alps with war elephants in 218 BCE?
questions.e: It was an opening move of the Second Punic War, and he then won crushing victories in Italy, including Cannae.

questions.q: Which female pharaoh of Egypt's 18th Dynasty built the great temple at Deir el-Bahari?
questions.e: She was often shown with a false beard, the traditional symbol of a pharaoh's authority.

questions.q: Who led the Haitian Revolution until his capture by the French in 1802?
questions.e: He died in a French prison in 1803, the year before Haiti declared independence.

questions.q: The Congress of Vienna (1814-15) redrew the map of Europe after the defeat of whom?
questions.e: Its balance of power helped Europe avoid a general war for about a century.

questions.q: The Taiping Rebellion (1850-1864), one of the deadliest civil wars in history, was fought in which country?
questions.e: Its leader, Hong Xiuquan, claimed to be the younger brother of Jesus, and the war killed tens of millions.

questions.q: In which year was the last Western Roman emperor, Romulus Augustulus, deposed?
questions.e: The Germanic general Odoacer deposed him, while the Eastern Roman Empire carried on for nearly another thousand years.

questions.q: The Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) divided newly claimed lands outside Europe between which two powers?
questions.e: Its dividing line is the reason Brazil speaks Portuguese while most of Latin America speaks Spanish.

questions.q: Whose book Leviathan (1651) described life without government as 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short'?
questions.e: He wrote it in exile in Paris during the upheaval of the English Civil War, arguing that people accept a strong ruler in exchange for security.

questions.q: In which language did the Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius write his Meditations?
questions.e: Greek was the language of philosophy for educated Romans, and he wrote the notes for himself, not for publication.

questions.q: Which philosopher, a follower of Jeremy Bentham, wrote the essay Utilitarianism?
questions.e: Mill refined Bentham's idea by arguing some pleasures, like those of the intellect, are higher than others.

questions.q: Which school of philosophy did Zeno of Citium found in Athens around 300 BCE?
questions.e: It is named after the Stoa Poikile, the painted porch where Zeno taught.

questions.q: Who wrote The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money (1936)?
questions.e: It argued governments could spend to fight unemployment during a slump, reshaping economics after the Great Depression.

questions.q: In game theory, what is a Nash equilibrium?
o: The outcome that gives all players the greatest total reward
A situation where every player picks a strategy at random
A game in which one player's gain exactly equals another's loss
A set of strategies where no player can do better by changing theirs alone
questions.e: The prisoner's dilemma shows it can leave everyone worse off than if they had cooperated.

questions.q: When economists say demand for a product is 'price elastic', what do they mean?
o: The price can rise without any change in sales
The quantity bought changes proportionally more than the price does
Buyers switch products only when prices fall
Demand rises and falls with the seasons
questions.e: Luxuries and goods with close substitutes tend to be elastic, while essentials like petrol tend to be inelastic in the short run.

questions.q: What does 'quantitative easing' involve?
o: A country fixing its currency to the US dollar
A government cutting taxes to boost spending
A bank reducing its lending to control inflation
A central bank creating money to buy assets such as government bonds
questions.e: It is used when interest rates are already near zero, and the Reserve Bank of Australia used it from 2020.

questions.q: The Great Vowel Shift, from about 1400 to 1700, changed the pronunciation of which language?
questions.e: Spelling had largely settled before it finished, which is why English vowels rarely sound the way they are written.

questions.q: Which language of Spain and France is a 'language isolate', with no proven relatives?
questions.e: It is widely thought to predate the arrival of Indo-European languages in western Europe.

questions.q: In linguistics, what is a 'phoneme'?
o: A word borrowed from another language
The smallest unit of sound that can change a word's meaning
A letter that is written but not spoken
The smallest unit of meaning in a word
questions.e: In English, /p/ and /b/ are separate phonemes because 'pat' and 'bat' mean different things.

questions.q: What does Grimm's law describe?
o: Regular consonant shifts from Proto-Indo-European into the Germanic languages
The order in which children learn speech sounds
How fairy tales spread between cultures
questions.e: It explains pairs like Latin pater and English father, where p shifted to f. Jacob Grimm, the fairy-tale collector, stated it in 1822.

questions.q: What is a 'creole' language?
o: A language that grew from a pidgin and became a community's first language
A language that has no written form
A secret language used by traders
A dialect spoken only in cities
questions.e: Kriol, spoken by many Aboriginal people across northern Australia, is an example.

questions.q: Who painted Las Meninas (1656)?
questions.e: The painter included himself at his easel, and the king and queen appear only as a reflection in a mirror.

questions.q: What is true fresco (buon fresco)?
o: Painting with oils on stretched canvas
Painting with pigment on wet lime plaster so it becomes part of the wall
Painting with egg yolk on wooden panels
questions.e: Fresco is Italian for fresh, and Michelangelo painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling this way.

questions.q: Who sculpted The Ecstasy of Saint Teresa in Rome?
questions.e: The marble figure sits in a theatrical chapel lit by a hidden window, a showpiece of Baroque drama.

questions.q: Hokusai's The Great Wave off Kanagawa comes from which print series?
o: One Hundred Famous Views of Edo
The Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō
questions.e: Mount Fuji sits small in the background, dwarfed by the wave. The series used the imported pigment Prussian blue.

questions.q: How many semitones make up a perfect fifth?
questions.e: The two notes vibrate in a frequency ratio of roughly 3:2, one of the most consonant intervals.

questions.q: Which composer developed the twelve-tone technique in the early 1920s?
questions.e: It treats all twelve notes of the chromatic scale as equals, arranged in a fixed series called a tone row.

questions.q: Who composed The Well-Tempered Clavier?
questions.e: Its two books each contain a prelude and fugue in all 24 major and minor keys.

questions.q: Which Russian writer's comic novel Dead Souls follows a swindler buying up the names of dead serfs?
questions.e: Chichikov plans to mortgage the 'souls' as if they were still alive. Gogol burned much of the second volume shortly before he died in 1852.

questions.q: Who guides Dante through Hell and Purgatory in the Divine Comedy?
questions.e: Beatrice takes over at the summit of Purgatory and leads him through Paradise, since Virgil, as a pagan, cannot enter Heaven.

questions.q: James Joyce's Ulysses takes place over a single day in Dublin. Which one?
questions.e: It is said to be the day of Joyce's first outing with Nora Barnacle, and fans celebrate it each year as Bloomsday.

questions.q: Which novel opens: 'Happy families are all alike; every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way'?
questions.e: Leo Tolstoy published it in instalments in the 1870s.

questions.q: In which Shakespeare play does Portia say 'The quality of mercy is not strained'?
questions.e: She says it while disguised as a young lawyer, pleading with Shylock in court.

questions.q: What is the longest continental mountain range in the world?
questions.e: It runs about 7,000 km, though the mostly underwater mid-ocean ridge system is far longer.

questions.q: About how deep is the Challenger Deep, the deepest known point in the ocean?
questions.e: It lies in the Mariana Trench, and Mount Everest placed inside it would still sit about 2 km underwater.

questions.q: Which is the largest landlocked country in the world?
questions.e: It is the ninth-largest country overall and borders the Caspian Sea, which is itself landlocked.

questions.q: Which river flows through or along the borders of more countries than any other?
questions.e: It touches 10 countries on its way from Germany's Black Forest to the Black Sea, passing four capital cities.

questions.q: In criminal law, what does 'mens rea' mean?
o: Let the matter speak for itself
questions.e: Most crimes need both mens rea and actus reus, the guilty act.

questions.q: Which legal doctrine did the High Court of Australia overturn in Mabo v Queensland (No 2) in 1992?
questions.e: It recognised native title for the Meriam people of Mer (Murray Island) in the Torres Strait.

questions.q: What does the legal principle of 'stare decisis' require?
o: Courts follow the precedents set by earlier decisions
The accused is presumed innocent until proven guilty
Both sides must be heard before judgement
A person cannot be tried twice for the same crime
questions.e: The Latin means roughly 'to stand by things decided', and it is central to common law systems.

questions.q: In AD 212, which Roman emperor granted citizenship to almost all free men across the empire?
questions.e: The historian Cassius Dio claimed it was partly a tax grab, since only citizens paid the inheritance tax.

riddles.q: A man looks at a portrait and says: 'Brothers and sisters I have none, but that man's father is my father's son.' Who is in the portrait?
riddles.e: 'My father's son' is himself, so the man's father is him: it's his son.
Each term describes the one before: 111221 is 'three 1s, two 2s, one 1', so 312211.

riddles.q: Two ropes each take exactly an hour to burn, but they burn unevenly. How can you time exactly 45 minutes?
o: Light rope A at both ends and rope B at one end; when A burns out, light B's other end
Burn one rope, then half of the other
riddles.e: Lit at both ends, A finishes in 30 minutes. B then has 30 minutes of burning left; lit at both ends, that takes 15 more.

riddles.q: How many times do a clock's hour and minute hands overlap in a full 24-hour day?
riddles.e: The minute hand laps the hour hand 11 times every 12 hours, not 12, so 22 times a day.

riddles.q: Eight identical-looking balls include one that is slightly heavier. What is the fewest weighings on a balance scale that guarantees finding it?
riddles.e: Weigh 3 against 3. If they balance, weigh the last 2 against each other. If not, take the heavier 3 and weigh 1 against 1.

riddles.q: On an island, knights always tell the truth and knaves always lie. A says: 'We are both knaves.' What are A and B?
o: A is a knave, B is a knight
A is a knight, B is a knave
riddles.e: A knight couldn't say it, so A lies; then 'both knaves' is false, so B is a knight.

riddles.q: Four cards show A, K, 4 and 7. Each has a letter on one side and a number on the other. To test the rule 'If a card has a vowel on one side, it has an even number on the other', which cards must you turn over?
riddles.e: Turn A (it must hide an even number) and 7 (it must not hide a vowel). The 4 can't break the rule whatever is behind it.

riddles.q: Three switches downstairs control one bulb upstairs. You may go upstairs once. How do you find the right switch?
o: Turn one on for minutes, off, turn a second on, then go up and check light and warmth
riddles.e: On = second switch; off but warm = first; off and cold = third.

riddles.q: Which English word contains all five vowels, a, e, i, o and u, exactly once and in alphabetical order?
riddles.e: Abstemious is the other well-known example.

riddles.q: Which English word sounds exactly the same after you remove four of its five letters?
riddles.e: Remove u, e, u, e and you are left with Q, pronounced the same.

riddles.q: What letter comes next: M, V, E, M, J, S, U, ?
riddles.e: They are the planets in order from the Sun, ending with Neptune.

riddles.q: What letter comes next: T, F, S, E, T, ?
riddles.e: Two, four, six, eight, ten, twelve: the first letters of the even numbers.

riddles.q: A game show has three doors: a car behind one, goats behind two. You pick a door. The host, who knows where the car is and always opens an unpicked goat door, opens one and offers you a switch. If you always switch, what is your chance of winning the car?
riddles.e: Your first pick is right 1/3 of the time, so switching loses then; the other 2/3 of the time the host's forced reveal leaves the car behind the remaining door, so switching wins 2/3.

riddles.q: Consider all two-child families that have at least one boy. Assuming each child is independently equally likely to be a boy or a girl, what fraction of those families have two boys?
