riddles.e: The equally likely families are BB, BG, GB and GG; ruling out GG leaves three, and only one of them (BB) has two boys.

riddles.q: Ignoring leap years and assuming all 365 birthdays are equally likely, what is the smallest group in which the chance that at least two people share a birthday exceeds 50%?
riddles.e: With 23 people there are 253 possible pairs, and the probability that all birthdays differ drops to about 49.3%, so a shared birthday is slightly more likely than not.

riddles.q: On an island, knights always tell the truth and knaves always lie. A says: 'B is a knave.' B says: 'A and I are the same type.' What are they?
o: A is a knave, B is a knight
A is a knight, B is a knave
riddles.e: If A were a knave, B would be a knight, but then B's true statement would make them the same type, a contradiction. So A is a knight and B a knave, whose claim of 'same type' is duly false.

riddles.q: Exactly one of three suspects is guilty, and exactly one of their statements is true. A: 'I am innocent.' B: 'A is guilty.' C: 'I am innocent.' Who is guilty?
riddles.e: If A were guilty, B and C would both be telling the truth; if B were guilty, A and C would both be truthful. Only C guilty leaves exactly one true statement (A's).

riddles.q: Two guards stand at a fork: one road is safe. One guard always tells the truth, the other always lies, and you don't know which is which. With one question to one guard, what is a sure way to choose the safe road?
o: Ask 'Which road is safe?' and take it
Ask 'Are you the truthful guard?' and decide from the answer
Ask 'Which road would the other guard say is safe?' and take that one
Ask 'Which road would the other guard say is safe?' and take the other one
riddles.e: Whichever guard you ask, the answer passes through exactly one lie, so it always names the dangerous road; take the opposite one.

riddles.q: Among 12 identical-looking coins, one is counterfeit and is either heavier or lighter, you don't know which. What is the minimum number of uses of a balance scale that guarantees finding the fake and whether it is heavy or light?
riddles.e: There are 24 possibilities (12 coins times heavy or light). Two weighings give only 3 x 3 = 9 outcomes, while three give 27, and a known scheme does it in three.

riddles.q: Using a balance scale where weights may go in either pan, what is the fewest whole-kilogram weights needed to weigh every whole number of kilograms from 1 to 40?
riddles.e: Weights of 1, 3, 9 and 27 kg work, since each can sit on the load side, the other side, or off the scale. Three weights can give at most (27 minus 1) / 2 = 13 distinct positive values, too few.

riddles.q: A farmer must ferry a wolf, a goat and a cabbage across a river. The boat carries him plus one item. Left alone, the wolf eats the goat and the goat eats the cabbage. What is the minimum number of one-way crossings?
riddles.e: Goat over, return, wolf over, bring the goat back, cabbage over, return, goat over: 7 crossings. Fewer is impossible because the goat must be brought back once.

riddles.q: Four people must cross a bridge at night with one torch. At most two cross at once, carrying the torch, at the slower person's pace. They take 1, 2, 5 and 10 minutes. What is the shortest total time?
riddles.e: 1 and 2 cross (2), 1 returns (1), 5 and 10 cross together (10), 2 returns (2), 1 and 2 cross (2): 17. Having the 1-minute person escort everyone takes 19.

riddles.q: What is the angle between the hour and minute hands of an analogue clock at exactly 3:15?
riddles.e: The minute hand points at the 3 (90 degrees), but the hour hand has moved a quarter of the way from 3 to 4, an extra 7.5 degrees, to 97.5 degrees.

riddles.q: A clock takes 5 seconds to strike six o'clock, timed from the first chime to the last. At the same rate, how long does it take to strike twelve?
riddles.e: Six chimes have five gaps, so each gap is 1 second. Twelve chimes have eleven gaps, taking 11 seconds.

riddles.q: In a non-leap year, 1 January falls on a Monday. On what day does 31 December fall?
riddles.e: 365 days is 52 weeks plus 1 day, so day 365 is the same weekday as day 1. The next 1 January is then a Tuesday.

riddles.q: What is the greatest number of Friday the 13ths that can occur in a single calendar year?
riddles.e: Every year has at least one and at most three. For example, a common year starting on a Thursday has them in February, March and November.

riddles.q: What number comes next: 2, 3, 5, 9, 17, 33, ?
riddles.e: Each term is double the previous one minus 1 (equivalently, the gaps double: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32), so 33 x 2 minus 1 = 65.

riddles.q: What number comes next: 61, 52, 63, 94, 46, ?
riddles.e: These are the squares 16, 25, 36, 49 and 64 written backwards. The next square, 81, reversed is 18.

riddles.q: Why are the digits arranged in this order: 8, 5, 4, 9, 1, 7, 6, 3, 2, 0?
o: They follow the order of keys on a phone keypad
Their English names are in alphabetical order
Each is the previous one minus 3, wrapping round
They are ordered by how many strokes it takes to write them
riddles.e: Eight, five, four, nine, one, seven, six, three, two, zero: the English names run in alphabetical order.

riddles.q: A bat and a ball cost $1.10 in total. The bat costs $1.00 more than the ball. How much does the ball cost?
riddles.e: If the ball is x, the bat is x + 1.00, so 2x + 1.00 = 1.10 and x = 0.05. A 10-cent ball would make the bat $1.10 and the total $1.20.

riddles.q: A patch of lily pads doubles in size every day. It takes 48 days to cover the whole lake. On which day did it cover half the lake?
riddles.e: It doubles each day, so it was half the size the day before it was full: day 47.

riddles.q: If 5 machines take 5 minutes to make 5 widgets, how long would 100 machines take to make 100 widgets?
riddles.e: Each machine makes one widget in 5 minutes, so 100 machines working in parallel make 100 widgets in the same 5 minutes.

riddles.q: Three guests pay $30 for a room. The manager realises it costs $25 and sends the porter with $5. The porter keeps $2 and gives each guest $1 back. Each has now paid $9: 3 x $9 = $27, plus the porter's $2 makes $29. Where is the missing dollar?
o: There is none: the $2 is part of the $27, so adding it is wrong
riddles.e: The guests' $27 equals the $25 room plus the porter's $2. The $2 should be subtracted from $27, not added; $27 + $3 refunded = $30 is the correct tally.

riddles.q: Which common English word contains three consecutive pairs of double letters?
riddles.e: Book-keeper: oo, kk, ee appear back to back. Committee and Mississippi have double letters, but never three pairs in a row.

riddles.q: Which nine-letter word can lose one letter at a time, staying a real English word at every step, all the way down to a single letter?
riddles.e: Startling, starting, staring, string, sting, sing, sin, in, I.

riddles.q: Consider all rolls of two fair dice that show at least one six. What fraction of those rolls show two sixes?
riddles.e: Of the 36 equally likely outcomes, 11 contain at least one six (6 + 6 minus the double-counted 6 and 6), and only one of them is a double six.

riddles.q: Three boxes hold two gold coins, two silver coins, and one of each. You pick a box at random and draw a coin at random from it: it is gold. What is the probability the other coin in that box is gold?
riddles.e: There are three equally likely gold coins you could have drawn, and two of them sit in the gold-gold box, so the chance is 2/3, not 1/2.

riddles.q: Three logicians walk into a bar. The bartender asks: 'Does everyone want a drink?' The first says 'I don't know.' The second says 'I don't know.' The third says 'Yes!' What can you conclude?
o: Only the third wants a drink
None of them knows what the others want
The first two do not want a drink
riddles.e: If the first didn't want one, he would answer 'No'; 'I don't know' shows he does. The same goes for the second, so the third, who also wants one, can answer 'Yes'.

riddles.q: A dark drawer holds 10 black socks and 10 white socks. What is the fewest you must take out, without looking, to be certain of getting a pair of black socks?
riddles.e: In the worst case you draw all 10 white socks first, then need 2 black ones: 12 in total. Three guarantees a matching pair, but not a black one.

riddles.q: 'The day before yesterday I was 25. Next year I will turn 28.' This is true if today is which date?
riddles.e: With a 31 December birthday and today 1 January: on 30 December the speaker was 25, turned 26 on 31 December, turns 27 this year and 28 next year.

riddles.q: You drive 60 km at 30 km/h. How fast must you drive the 60 km back to average 60 km/h for the whole round trip?
riddles.e: Averaging 60 km/h over 120 km takes exactly 2 hours, but the first leg alone has already used 2 hours, so no finite speed works.

GK.q: Which country has the longest coastline in the world?
GK.e: Canada's coastline runs over 200,000 km, thanks to its tens of thousands of Arctic islands.

GK.q: What is the largest lake in Africa?
GK.e: Shared by Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania, it's the world's largest tropical lake and a main source of the White Nile.

GK.q: Which African country has the largest population?
GK.e: Nigeria has more than 220 million people, and Lagos is one of the biggest cities in Africa.

GK.q: What is the capital of Canada?
GK.e: Ottawa, in Ontario, is Canada's capital.

GK.q: What is the smallest country in the world by area?
GK.e: Vatican City covers less than half a square kilometre.

GK.q: What is Africa's highest mountain?
GK.e: Kilimanjaro, a dormant volcano in Tanzania, rises about 5,895 metres, and you can walk to the top without climbing gear.

GK.q: What is the largest hot desert in the world?
GK.e: The Sahara covers much of North Africa.

GK.q: Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?
GK.e: Neil Armstrong stepped onto the Moon on 20 July 1969 (21 July in Australia).

GK.q: In 1868, the Meiji Restoration ended centuries of rule by shoguns in which country?
GK.e: Power returned to the emperor, and Japan industrialised at astonishing speed over the following decades.

GK.q: Who was the first emperor of Rome?
GK.e: Augustus became the first emperor in 27 BC. Julius Caesar was never emperor.

GK.q: In which year did the Titanic sink?
GK.e: It sank on its first voyage in April 1912.

GK.q: Which English king was executed in 1649, after losing a civil war to Parliament?
GK.e: After his trial and beheading, England was briefly a republic, until the monarchy returned in 1660.

GK.q: Which civilisation built Machu Picchu?
GK.e: The Inca built it in the 15th century in the Andes of Peru.

GK.q: Which of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World is still standing?
GK.e: The Great Pyramid is the only one left.

GK.q: What is the chemical symbol for gold?
GK.e: Au, from the Latin aurum. Ag is silver.

GK.q: On the Celsius scale, roughly what is absolute zero, the coldest possible temperature?
GK.e: It is −273.15°C, or 0 kelvin. It can be approached but never quite reached. (−459°F is the same point in Fahrenheit.)

GK.q: Which gas makes up most of Earth's atmosphere?
GK.e: Nitrogen is about 78%; oxygen about 21%.

GK.q: Which part of a cell releases energy from food?
GK.e: Mitochondria are often called the cell's powerhouse.

GK.q: What is the pH of pure water at 25°C?
GK.e: Pure water is neutral, pH 7.

GK.q: What is the hardest natural substance?
GK.e: Diamond, a form of carbon, is the hardest natural material.

GK.q: What force keeps the planets in orbit around the Sun?
GK.e: The Sun's gravity holds the planets in their orbits.

GK.q: What does CPU stand for?
GK.e: The CPU is the chip that carries out a computer's instructions.

GK.q: Who co-founded Apple with Steve Wozniak?
GK.e: Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak founded Apple in 1976, with Ronald Wayne.

GK.q: What does the 'HTTP' in web addresses stand for?
GK.e: It's the protocol browsers use to fetch web pages.

GK.q: Which two digits does binary code use?
GK.e: Binary uses only 0 and 1.

GK.q: In which year was the first iPhone released?
GK.e: Apple released the first iPhone in 2007.

GK.q: Which company owns the Android operating system?
GK.e: Google bought Android Inc. in 2005.

GK.q: Which planet is closest to the Sun?
GK.e: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun.

GK.q: What is the largest planet in our solar system?
GK.e: Jupiter is more than twice as massive as all the other planets combined.

GK.q: Which planet is known as the Red Planet?
GK.e: Iron oxide (rust) in its soil makes Mars look red.

GK.q: Which is the only planet in our solar system not named after a Greek or Roman god?
GK.e: 'Earth' comes from Old English eorþe, meaning ground or soil. Uranus is named after the Greek sky god.

GK.q: Which planet has the shortest day?
GK.e: Jupiter spins once in just under 10 hours, even though it is the largest planet.

GK.q: What is the name of our galaxy?
GK.e: We live in the Milky Way.

GK.q: Which bird lays the largest egg?
GK.e: An ostrich egg weighs about 1.4 kg, as much as roughly two dozen chicken eggs.

GK.q: What is the fastest land animal?
GK.e: Cheetahs can sprint at around 100 km/h.

GK.q: What is a group of crows called?
GK.e: A murder of crows. The phrase appears in English lists of animal group names from the 1400s.

GK.q: How many legs does a spider have?
GK.e: Spiders are arachnids, with eight legs.

GK.q: Which of these mammals lays eggs?
GK.e: Platypuses and echidnas are monotremes: egg-laying mammals.

GK.q: What is a baby kangaroo called?
GK.e: Baby kangaroos (and other marsupials) are called joeys.

GK.q: Which bird can fly backwards?
GK.e: Hummingbirds can hover and fly backwards.

GK.q: What is the largest organ of the human body?
GK.e: Your skin is your largest organ.

GK.q: Which part of your body gets most of its oxygen straight from the air rather than from blood?
GK.e: The cornea has no blood vessels, which keeps it clear. It absorbs oxygen dissolved in your tears.

GK.q: Which blood type is the universal red-cell donor?
GK.e: O negative red cells can be given to almost anyone.

GK.q: Where is the smallest bone in your body?
GK.e: The stapes, in the middle ear, is about 3 millimetres long.

GK.q: How many chambers does the human heart have?
GK.e: Two atria and two ventricles.

GK.q: Which vitamin does your blood need in order to clot?
GK.e: The K comes from 'Koagulation', the German spelling of coagulation. Leafy greens are a good source.

GK.q: Which country has the most Portuguese speakers?
GK.e: Brazil has over 200 million people, about 20 times Portugal's population.

GK.q: Día de los Muertos, the Day of the Dead, is a famous celebration from which country?
GK.e: Around 1–2 November, families build altars with marigolds, photos and favourite foods to welcome back the spirits of loved ones.

GK.q: How many strings does a standard guitar have?
GK.e: A standard guitar has six strings.

GK.q: Origami, the art of paper folding, is most associated with which country?
GK.e: The word origami is Japanese: ori 'folding', kami 'paper'.

GK.q: In which city is the Colosseum?
GK.e: Rome's Colosseum was completed in 80 AD.

GK.q: What is the currency of Japan?
GK.e: The yen.

GK.q: What does GDP stand for?
GK.e: GDP is the total value of goods and services produced in a country.

GK.q: What is Australia's central bank?
GK.e: The Reserve Bank of Australia sets the cash rate.

GK.q: What is it called when prices fall across the economy?
GK.e: Deflation is a general fall in prices.

GK.q: If supply of a product falls but demand stays the same, what usually happens to its price?
GK.e: Scarcer goods with steady demand get more expensive.

GK.q: In a 'bear market', share prices are generally...
GK.e: A bear market is a sustained fall, usually 20% or more.

GK.q: What is the currency of most European Union countries?
GK.e: 21 of the 27 EU countries use the euro; Bulgaria became the latest in January 2026.

GK.q: What is the capital of Australia?
GK.e: Canberra was chosen as a compromise between Sydney and Melbourne.

GK.q: How many states does Australia have?
GK.e: Six states, plus territories including the ACT and NT.

GK.q: The Twelve Apostles rock stacks stand off the coast of which state?
GK.e: They line the Great Ocean Road. Despite the name there were never twelve, and waves have toppled some of them.

GK.q: Where is Uluru?
GK.e: Uluru is in the Northern Territory.

GK.q: After Sydney, which is Australia's oldest capital city?
GK.e: Hobart was founded in 1804, the year after a first settlement at nearby Risdon Cove.

GK.q: Who is the longest-serving Prime Minister in Australian history?
GK.e: Menzies led the country for over 18 years in total, from 1939 to 1941 and again from 1949 to 1966.

GK.q: What is the largest marsupial?
GK.e: Male red kangaroos can stand about 1.8 metres tall.

GK.q: What is the world's largest sand island, off Queensland, now officially called?
GK.e: Formerly Fraser Island, it officially took back its Butchulla name, K'gari, meaning 'paradise', in 2023.

GK.q: How many players does a soccer team have on the field?
GK.e: Eleven, including the goalkeeper.

GK.q: In which sport do Australia and England contest the Ashes?
GK.e: The Ashes is a cricket Test series.

GK.q: How often are the Summer Olympics held?
GK.e: Every four years.

GK.q: Which city hosted the 2000 Summer Olympics?
GK.e: Sydney hosted in 2000.

GK.q: In tennis, what is a score of zero called?
GK.e: Zero is 'love' in tennis.

GK.q: Which country had won the most men's Rugby World Cups as of 2023?
GK.e: South Africa's 2023 win was its fourth title.

GK.q: What kind of race is the Melbourne Cup?
GK.e: A horse race held on the first Tuesday of November.

GK.q: Who painted the Mona Lisa?
GK.e: Leonardo da Vinci, in the early 1500s.

GK.q: Who painted The Scream?
GK.e: The Norwegian artist made several versions from 1893. One sold for about US$120 million in 2012.

GK.q: Who painted The Birth of Venus?
GK.e: Botticelli painted it in Florence in the 1480s. It hangs in the city's Uffizi Gallery.

GK.q: What are the three primary colours in traditional painting?
GK.e: Red, yellow and blue. (Screens use red, green and blue light.)

GK.q: Salvador Dalí is best known for which art movement?
GK.e: Surrealism, with dreamlike images like melting clocks.

GK.q: Who designed the Sydney Opera House?
GK.e: Danish architect Jørn Utzon.

GK.q: Who wrote Romeo and Juliet?
GK.e: Shakespeare, in the 1590s.

GK.q: Who wrote the novel 1984?
GK.e: George Orwell published it in 1949.

GK.q: Which novel opens with 'It was the best of times, it was the worst of times'?
GK.e: Charles Dickens's 1859 novel is set in London and Paris during the French Revolution.

GK.q: Which novel opens with the line 'Call me Ishmael'?
o: The Old Man and the Sea
GK.e: Herman Melville's Moby-Dick (1851).

GK.q: Who wrote the Harry Potter books?
GK.e: J. K. Rowling.

GK.q: Who wrote War and Peace?
GK.e: Published in the 1860s, it follows several aristocratic families through Napoleon's invasion of Russia.

GK.q: Which Australian author has won the Booker Prize twice?
GK.e: He won in 1988 for Oscar and Lucinda and in 2001 for True History of the Kelly Gang. (J. M. Coetzee, now an Australian citizen, has also won twice.)

GK.q: Which is the largest country in the world by area?
GK.e: Russia covers about 17 million square kilometres, over twice the size of Australia.

GK.q: Which continent has the most countries?
GK.e: Africa has 54 countries recognised by the United Nations.

GK.q: The Strait of Gibraltar separates Europe from which continent?
GK.e: At its narrowest it's only about 14 km between Spain and Morocco.

GK.q: What is the world's deepest lake?
GK.e: Siberia's Lake Baikal is over 1,600 metres deep and holds roughly a fifth of the world's unfrozen fresh surface water.

GK.q: Counting its overseas territories, which country has the most time zones?
GK.e: With territories scattered around the globe, France spans 12 time zones.

GK.q: Which ship carried the Pilgrims from England to America in 1620?
GK.e: Its passengers founded Plymouth Colony, in what is now Massachusetts.

GK.q: Mansa Musa, often called one of the richest people in history, ruled which West African empire?
GK.e: His 1324 pilgrimage to Mecca reportedly handed out so much gold that its value in Cairo fell for years.

GK.q: Who was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize?
GK.e: Marie Curie shared the 1903 Physics prize, then won Chemistry in 1911.

GK.q: The temple complex of Angkor Wat, the world's largest religious monument, is in which country?
GK.e: Built by the Khmer Empire in the early 1100s as a Hindu temple, it later became Buddhist and now appears on Cambodia's flag.

GK.q: Who was the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic?
GK.e: Amelia Earhart made the flight in 1932.

GK.q: Which pigment gives human skin, hair and eyes their colour?
GK.e: People have roughly the same number of melanin-making cells. Skin colour depends on how much melanin those cells produce.

GK.q: At sea level, at what temperature does water boil?
GK.e: 100°C, though it boils at lower temperatures up mountains where air pressure is lower.

GK.q: What is the most abundant metal in Earth's crust?
GK.e: Aluminium makes up about 8% of the crust by mass. Only oxygen and silicon are more abundant overall.

GK.q: Roughly how fast does sound travel through air?
GK.e: About 343 metres per second. To estimate a storm's distance, count the seconds between lightning and thunder and divide by 3 for kilometres.

GK.q: What does 'VPN' stand for?
GK.e: A VPN encrypts your connection and routes it through another server, which is useful on public Wi-Fi.

GK.q: What does 'AI' stand for?
GK.e: Artificial intelligence: computers doing tasks that normally need human thinking.

GK.q: What is a CAPTCHA test designed to check?
o: That you're a human, not a bot
GK.e: The name stands for 'Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart'.

GK.q: What does 'URL' stand for?
GK.e: A URL is the address of a resource on the web.

GK.q: What is 'phishing'?
o: A way to speed up Wi-Fi
Fake messages that trick you into giving away information
A type of computer virus scanner
GK.e: Phishers pose as banks, delivery companies or government agencies to steal logins and money.

GK.q: How many planets are in our solar system?
GK.e: Eight. Neptune, the farthest, takes about 165 years to orbit the Sun once.

GK.q: After the Sun, which star is closest to Earth?
GK.e: Proxima Centauri is about 4.2 light-years away.

GK.q: Which planet has the most prominent ring system?
GK.e: Saturn's rings are made mostly of chunks of ice and rock.

GK.q: In 2003, which country became the third to launch a person into space on its own rocket?
GK.e: Yang Liwei orbited Earth in Shenzhou 5, after the Soviet Union and the United States, both in 1961.

GK.q: What is a 'shooting star'?
o: A star falling from the sky
A small space rock burning up in Earth's atmosphere
GK.e: Most are no bigger than a grain of sand. Any piece that survives to reach the ground is called a meteorite.

GK.q: What is the tallest animal?
GK.e: Giraffes can grow to over 5 metres tall.

GK.q: What do we call an animal that eats only plants?
GK.e: Herbivores like kangaroos and koalas eat plants.

GK.q: What is a group of lions called?
GK.e: A pride usually includes several related females, their cubs and a few males.

GK.q: What is the largest living lizard?
GK.e: Komodo dragons can reach about 3 metres and live on a handful of Indonesian islands.

GK.q: Koalas mainly eat the leaves of which trees?
GK.e: Gum leaves are low in energy, which is one reason koalas sleep around 18 to 22 hours a day.

GK.q: What do red blood cells carry around your body?
GK.e: They use a protein called haemoglobin to carry oxygen from your lungs.

GK.q: Which organs filter your blood to make urine?
GK.e: Your two kidneys filter around 180 litres of blood plasma a day.

GK.q: What is the longest bone in the human body?
GK.e: The femur is also one of the strongest bones.

GK.q: Roughly how much of an adult's body weight is water?
GK.e: Around 60%, though it varies with age and body composition.

GK.q: What are the tiny air sacs in your lungs, where oxygen passes into your blood, called?
GK.e: You have hundreds of millions of them, with a combined surface area of around 70 square metres.

GK.q: Which instrument usually has 88 keys?
GK.e: 52 white keys and 36 black keys.

GK.q: Which country gave the Statue of Liberty to the United States?
GK.e: It was a gift from the people of France, dedicated in 1886.

GK.q: Swahili is widely spoken in which part of the world?
GK.e: It is an official language of Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda, and tens of millions more speak it as a second language.

GK.q: Chinese New Year is also known as what?
GK.e: It follows the lunar calendar, so the date changes each year.

GK.q: What is 'stagflation'?
o: High inflation combined with weak growth and high unemployment
A long period of stable prices
GK.e: The word blends 'stagnation' and 'inflation'. Many economies suffered it after the 1970s oil shocks.

GK.q: What is 'bracket creep'?
o: When tax brackets are cut every year
When pay rises push more of your income into higher tax brackets, even if they only keep up with inflation
A slow rise in interest rates
When prices creep up after a sale
GK.e: Australia's income tax thresholds aren't automatically indexed to inflation, so governments periodically cut taxes to hand some of it back.

GK.q: What is 'shrinkflation'?
o: When prices fall because demand shrinks
When a product gets smaller but its price stays the same
When the economy shrinks during inflation
GK.e: A chocolate block that quietly drops from 200 g to 180 g at the same price is a hidden 11% price rise.

GK.q: What does 'ASX' stand for?
GK.e: It's Australia's main stock exchange, based in Sydney.

GK.q: If a savings account pays interest, who pays whom?
GK.e: The bank pays you for letting it use your money.

GK.q: Which is Australia's largest state by area?
GK.e: Western Australia covers about a third of the continent.

GK.q: Which Australian state is an island?
GK.e: Tasmania is a bit smaller than Ireland, and more than 40% of it is protected in parks and reserves.

GK.q: What is Australia's national floral emblem?
GK.e: National Wattle Day is celebrated on 1 September.

GK.q: What is Australia's largest lake (when it fills)?
GK.e: In South Australia, it's usually a dry salt pan and fills completely only rarely.

GK.q: In 1943, who became the first woman elected to the federal House of Representatives?
GK.e: At the same election Dorothy Tangney became the first woman in the Senate. Edith Cowan had been the first woman in any Australian parliament, in WA in 1921.

GK.q: How many players does a netball team have on court?
GK.e: Seven, each restricted to certain zones of the court.

GK.q: In golf, what is one stroke under par called?
GK.e: An eagle is two under and an albatross three under.

GK.q: How long is a marathon?
GK.e: The odd distance was standardised after the 1908 London Olympics.

GK.q: In which sport would you see a slam dunk?
GK.e: A slam dunk is when a player jumps and pushes the ball straight down through the hoop.

GK.q: Cathy Freeman won gold at the Sydney 2000 Olympics in which event?
GK.e: She won the 400 m final in front of about 110,000 people.

GK.q: Which Dutch artist painted Girl with a Pearl Earring?
GK.e: Vermeer painted it around 1665.

GK.q: Which Dutch artist painted The Night Watch?
GK.e: Completed in 1642, it's more than 4 metres wide and hangs in Amsterdam's Rijksmuseum.

GK.q: Which Australian artist painted a famous series about Ned Kelly?
GK.e: Nolan painted the series in the 1940s, showing Kelly in his black box-like helmet.

GK.q: Pablo Picasso co-founded which art movement?
GK.e: He developed Cubism with Georges Braque in the early 1900s.

GK.q: Who wrote To Kill a Mockingbird?
GK.e: Published in 1960, it won the Pulitzer Prize.

GK.q: Which Charles Dickens story features Ebenezer Scrooge?
GK.e: Published in 1843, it helped shape how Christmas is celebrated.

GK.q: Who wrote the poem 'My Country', which includes 'I love a sunburnt country'?
GK.e: Mackellar wrote it while homesick in England; it was first published in 1908.

GK.q: Who wrote and illustrated The Magic Pudding?
GK.e: Published in 1918, it's about a grumpy pudding that never runs out.

GK.q: Who wrote Frankenstein?
GK.e: She began it as a teenager; it was published in 1818 and is often called the first science-fiction novel.

GK.q: Which river flows through Baghdad, the capital of Iraq?
GK.e: Baghdad was founded beside the Tigris in 762 as the grand new capital of the Abbasid caliphs.

GK.q: What is the longest river in Europe?
GK.e: The Volga runs about 3,500 km through Russia and empties into the Caspian Sea, which has no outlet to the ocean.

GK.q: Which country is home to the Atacama Desert, one of the driest places on Earth?
GK.e: Its dry, clear skies make it one of the best places in the world for astronomers to build large telescopes.

GK.q: The Danube River empties into which sea?
GK.e: The Danube passes through or along ten countries, more than any other river in the world.

GK.q: Which continent has no permanent human population?
GK.e: Only scientists and support staff live there, rising to a few thousand in summer and dropping sharply in winter.

GK.q: Mount Kosciuszko, the highest mountain on the Australian mainland, is in which state?
GK.e: Polish explorer Paweł Strzelecki named it in 1840 after the Polish-Lithuanian hero Tadeusz Kościuszko.

GK.q: Which strait separates Asia from North America?
GK.e: At its narrowest it is only about 82 km wide, and two small islands in the middle sit on opposite sides of the International Date Line.

GK.q: Which line of latitude passes through the Queensland city of Rockhampton?
GK.e: The Tropic slowly shifts as Earth's tilt changes, so Rockhampton's marker spire no longer sits exactly on the line.

GK.q: The city of Istanbul sits on both sides of which strait, dividing Europe from Asia?
GK.e: The Bosphorus links the Black Sea to the Sea of Marmara, and ships have used it for thousands of years.

GK.q: Which small kingdom is completely surrounded by South Africa?
GK.e: Every part of Lesotho lies above about 1,400 m, giving it the highest lowest point of any country.

GK.q: Which mountain range forms the border between France and Spain?
GK.e: The tiny country of Andorra is tucked high in the Pyrenees between the two.

GK.q: Which sea lies between Australia and New Zealand?
GK.e: It is named after Dutch explorer Abel Tasman, the first European known to reach New Zealand, in 1642.

GK.q: Not counting continental Australia, what is the world's largest island?
GK.e: Most of Greenland is buried under an ice sheet that is up to about 3 km thick.

GK.q: What is the Pacific 'Ring of Fire'?
o: A coral reef system around Polynesia
A horseshoe-shaped belt of volcanoes and earthquake zones
A chain of undersea hot springs near Hawaii
GK.e: It traces the edges of tectonic plates around the Pacific, where most of the world's earthquakes happen.

GK.q: Victoria Falls lies on which African river?
GK.e: Locally it is called Mosi-oa-Tunya, meaning 'the smoke that thunders', after its huge clouds of spray.

GK.q: What is the name of the line of 0° longitude?
GK.e: An international conference in 1884 chose the line through the Royal Observatory at Greenwich, London.

GK.q: Lake Titicaca, one of the highest large lakes in the world, lies on the border of Peru and which country?
GK.e: It sits about 3,800 m above sea level, and the Uros people live on floating islands woven from reeds.

GK.q: The shore of which body of water is the lowest point on dry land?
GK.e: Its shore is more than 400 m below sea level and keeps getting lower as the water level falls.

GK.q: Which country contains most of the Amazon rainforest?
GK.e: Around 60% of the Amazon lies in Brazil, with the rest spread across eight other countries and territories.

GK.q: What is a fjord?
o: A sandbar across a river mouth
A long, narrow sea inlet carved by a glacier
GK.e: Milford Sound in New Zealand is actually a fjord, despite its name.

GK.q: Which river forms much of the border between the United States and Mexico?
GK.e: In Mexico the same river is called the Río Bravo del Norte.

GK.q: Darwin is closer to which Asian capital than it is to Canberra?
GK.e: Jakarta is about 2,700 km from Darwin, while Canberra is more than 3,000 km away.

GK.q: What is the largest of North America's Great Lakes?
GK.e: Lake Superior is so big it could hold all the water of the other four Great Lakes, with room to spare.

GK.q: The name 'Nullarbor' comes from Latin. What does it mean?
GK.e: The Eyre Highway across the Nullarbor includes a 146.6 km stretch with no curves, Australia's longest straight road.

GK.q: Which two countries share the longest international border in the world?
GK.e: Including the Alaska section, the border runs for about 8,900 km.

GK.q: Mount Everest sits on the border between Nepal and which other country?
GK.e: A joint Nepal-China survey in 2020 measured its height at 8,848.86 m.

GK.q: Which Asian country is made up of more than 7,000 islands, with Manila as its capital?
GK.e: The islands are commonly grouped into three main regions: Luzon, the Visayas and Mindanao.

GK.q: In 1770, which navigator charted Australia's east coast aboard HMS Endeavour?
GK.e: He first landed at Kamay (Botany Bay), named for the many new plants his botanists collected there.

GK.q: Genghis Khan founded which empire?
GK.e: At its height it became the largest connected land empire in history, stretching from Korea to Eastern Europe.

GK.q: The Rosetta Stone was the key to reading which ancient writing?
GK.e: It carries the same decree in hieroglyphs, Demotic script and ancient Greek, and Jean-François Champollion cracked it in 1822.

GK.q: Which Australian prime minister disappeared while swimming at Cheviot Beach, Victoria, in December 1967?
GK.e: He had been prime minister for less than two years, and his body was never found.

GK.q: Cleopatra VII, the last active ruler of Ptolemaic Egypt, belonged to a royal family of what origin?
GK.e: Her family had ruled Egypt for nearly 300 years, yet she is said to be the first of them to learn the Egyptian language.

GK.q: Around 1440, who developed a printing press with movable metal type in Europe?
GK.e: Movable type already existed in China and Korea, but Gutenberg's press spread rapidly and transformed European learning.

GK.q: Which Roman city was buried by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 CE?
GK.e: The ash preserved the town so well that archaeologists have found bread still in its ovens.

GK.q: The Gallipoli peninsula, where Anzac troops landed on 25 April 1915, is in which modern country?
GK.e: The date of the landing is now marked each year as Anzac Day in Australia and New Zealand.

GK.q: Who was the first President of the United States?
GK.e: He is the only president who never lived in the White House, which was finished after his term ended.

GK.q: In 1453, Constantinople fell to which empire?
GK.e: Sultan Mehmed II used enormous cannons to break the city's ancient walls, ending the Byzantine Empire.

GK.q: Which English king agreed to the Magna Carta in 1215?
GK.e: A few of its clauses, including the right to justice without delay, are still part of English law.

GK.q: Mahatma Gandhi's 1930 Salt March was a protest against which ruling power in India?
GK.e: He and his followers walked about 390 km to the sea to make salt, defying a British tax on it.

GK.q: In what year did the First Fleet arrive at Sydney Cove?
GK.e: More than 1,000 people made the voyage of about eight months from England in eleven ships.

GK.q: The Terracotta Army was buried to guard the tomb of which Chinese ruler?
GK.e: Farmers digging a well near Xi'an stumbled upon it in 1974, and the soldiers' faces vary so much that no two seem alike.

GK.q: In what year did Nelson Mandela become President of South Africa?
GK.e: He was elected after spending 27 years in prison, and won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1993.

GK.q: How long did the Hundred Years' War between England and France actually last?
GK.e: It ran from 1337 to 1453, with long pauses between the fighting.

GK.q: Which ancient people invented cuneiform, one of the earliest writing systems?
GK.e: They wrote by pressing a wedge-shaped reed into wet clay, and 'cuneiform' means 'wedge-shaped'.

GK.q: Who led the first expedition to reach the South Pole, in 1911?
GK.e: His Norwegian team used dog sleds and beat Scott's British party by about five weeks.

GK.q: In 1893, which country became the first self-governing nation to give women the vote in national elections?
GK.e: South Australia soon went a step further, passing a law in 1894 that also let women stand for parliament.

GK.q: The first voyage around the world, from 1519 to 1522, was led at the start by which explorer, who died before it ended?
GK.e: Magellan was killed in the Philippines, and Juan Sebastián Elcano brought the last ship home to Spain.

GK.q: Which people built Tenochtitlan, the city on whose ruins Mexico City now stands?
GK.e: It was built on an island in Lake Texcoco and linked to the shore by long causeways.

GK.q: The Black Death, which swept Europe from 1347, was caused by what?
o: Plague bacteria spread largely by fleas
GK.e: It killed perhaps a third or more of Europe's population within a few years.

GK.q: Which country has more ancient pyramids than Egypt?
GK.e: The kingdom of Kush built over 200 steep-sided pyramids there, many at the royal city of Meroë.

GK.q: The Kokoda Track campaign of 1942 was fought in which present-day country?
GK.e: Australian troops were supported by Papuan carriers who carried supplies and the wounded over rugged mountains.

GK.q: Which British monarch reigned from 1837 to 1901, giving her name to an era?
GK.e: Both the state of Victoria and the state of Queensland were named in her honour.

GK.q: What is the chemical symbol for iron?
GK.e: It comes from 'ferrum', the Latin word for iron, which also gives us the word 'ferrous'.

GK.q: Which gas do plants take in from the air to make food through photosynthesis?
GK.e: The oxygen plants give off actually comes from splitting water molecules, not from the carbon dioxide.

GK.q: Which gas gives the classic red-orange glow of old advertising signs?
GK.e: Other gases in the tubes make other colours, and the name comes from the Greek word for 'new'.

GK.q: What does DNA stand for?
GK.e: Unwound, the DNA in just one of your cells would stretch about 2 metres.

GK.q: Roughly how fast does light travel in a vacuum?
GK.e: That is fast enough to circle Earth about seven and a half times in one second.

GK.q: Who discovered X-rays in 1895?
GK.e: One of his first X-ray pictures showed the bones of his wife's hand, wedding ring and all. He won the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901.

GK.q: What type of rock forms when lava or magma cools and hardens?
GK.e: Granite and basalt are both igneous rocks, and the word comes from the Latin for 'fire'.

GK.q: Which metal is a liquid at room temperature?
GK.e: Gallium comes close: it melts at about 30°C, so it can turn liquid in your hand.

GK.q: What is the SI unit of electrical resistance?
GK.e: It is named after German physicist Georg Ohm, and its symbol is the Greek letter omega (Ω).

GK.q: Which Adelaide-educated scientist shared the 1915 Nobel Prize in Physics with his father, at just 25?
GK.e: The Braggs used X-rays to work out how atoms are arranged in crystals. He is still the youngest person to win the physics prize.

GK.q: What colour does blue litmus paper turn in an acid?
GK.e: Litmus dye is made from lichens and has been used to test acids for centuries.

GK.q: In science, what is a 'half-life'?
o: Half the lifespan of a living cell
The time for half of a radioactive sample to decay
The time a battery takes to lose half its charge
Half the time an element takes to melt
GK.e: Carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5,730 years, which is why it is used to date ancient remains.

GK.q: What is the chemical formula for table salt?
GK.e: It is made of sodium, a metal that reacts violently with water, and chlorine, a poisonous gas.

GK.q: The ozone layer, which absorbs harmful UV rays, is found in which layer of the atmosphere?
GK.e: After the 1987 Montreal Protocol phased out ozone-damaging chemicals, the ozone hole has slowly begun to recover.

GK.q: Which colour of visible light has the longest wavelength?
GK.e: Just beyond red is infrared, which we can't see but can feel as heat.

GK.q: Which scientist coined the word 'cell' in 1665 after looking at thin slices of cork under a microscope?
GK.e: The tiny boxes reminded him of the small rooms, or cells, that monks lived in.

GK.q: Bronze is an alloy made mainly from copper and which other metal?
GK.e: It was so important it gave its name to a whole era, the Bronze Age.

GK.q: What is it called when a solid turns directly into a gas without becoming a liquid?
GK.e: Dry ice (frozen carbon dioxide) does this, which is why it makes spooky fog instead of puddles.

GK.q: Which particle in an atom's nucleus has no electric charge?
GK.e: James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932, and won the Nobel Prize for it three years later.

GK.q: What does a seismometer measure?
o: Ground shaking, such as from earthquakes
GK.e: Seismometers are so sensitive they can detect large earthquakes on the other side of the world.

GK.q: In Einstein's equation E = mc², what does 'c' stand for?
GK.e: Because c is squared, a tiny amount of mass holds an enormous amount of energy.

GK.q: Australians Barry Marshall and Robin Warren won a Nobel Prize for showing that most stomach ulcers are caused by what?
GK.e: To prove it, Marshall drank a culture of the bacteria and soon developed stomach inflammation.

GK.q: Why can't sound travel through outer space?
o: There is no air or other matter to carry it
GK.e: Sound is a vibration passed from particle to particle, so in a near-vacuum there is nothing to vibrate.

GK.q: Which scientist described three famous laws of motion in 1687?
GK.e: He published them in a book usually called the Principia, which also set out his law of gravity.

GK.q: What is ordinary glass mainly made from?
GK.e: The silica in sand melts at around 1,700°C, so soda is added to lower the melting point.

GK.q: In chemistry, what does a catalyst do?
o: Changes a liquid into a gas
Makes a reaction produce more heat
Speeds up a reaction without being used up
GK.e: Enzymes in your body are natural catalysts, and cars use catalytic converters to clean exhaust.

GK.q: What kind of energy is stored in a stretched rubber band?
GK.e: When you let go, that stored energy turns into movement energy as the band flies off.

GK.q: What was the first video ever uploaded to YouTube, in April 2005?
o: A co-founder at the zoo talking about elephants
GK.e: Titled 'Me at the zoo', the 19-second clip shows co-founder Jawed Karim at San Diego Zoo.

GK.q: What does 'RAM' stand for in computing?
GK.e: RAM is temporary working memory, so everything in it is lost when the power goes off.

GK.q: Which Australian research organisation developed technology that became key to fast Wi-Fi?
GK.e: Its Wi-Fi patents earned it hundreds of millions of dollars in licence fees from tech companies.

GK.q: Australian scientist David Warren invented which device for aircraft?
GK.e: Despite the nickname, flight recorders are painted bright orange so they are easier to find after a crash.

GK.q: Who is often called the first computer programmer, for her 1840s notes on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine?
GK.e: She also imagined that such machines might one day create music, not just do sums.

GK.q: What does 'GPS' stand for?
GK.e: Your device works out where it is using timing signals from at least four satellites at once.

GK.q: What does 'USB' stand for?
GK.e: USB was introduced in the mid-1990s to replace a tangle of different plugs and ports.

GK.q: Which company created the Windows operating system?
GK.e: Microsoft was founded in 1975 by childhood friends Bill Gates and Paul Allen.

GK.q: What does 'PDF' stand for?
GK.e: Adobe launched it in 1993 so a document looks the same on any device or printer.

GK.q: What does 'LED' stand for?
GK.e: The 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics went to the inventors of the blue LED, which made bright white LED lighting possible.

GK.q: Who was granted the first patent for the telephone, in 1876?
GK.e: His first words on it were reportedly 'Mr Watson, come here, I want to see you.'

GK.q: What is 'open-source' software?
o: Software whose code anyone can view, use and change
Software that is free to download but locked
GK.e: Linux, which powers most of the world's web servers and Android phones, is open source.

GK.q: What does 'QR' stand for in 'QR code'?
GK.e: QR codes were invented in Japan in 1994 to track car parts in factories.

GK.q: What was the first item sold on eBay, back when it was called AuctionWeb in 1995?
GK.e: It sold for US$14.83. When founder Pierre Omidyar checked, the buyer said he collected broken laser pointers.

GK.q: What does 'Moore's law' predict?
o: Computers become half as expensive every year
Batteries last twice as long every decade
The number of transistors on a chip doubles about every two years
GK.e: Gordon Moore, later a co-founder of Intel, first predicted a yearly doubling in 1965, then revised it to every two years in 1975.

GK.q: Which inventor is famous for pioneering alternating current (AC) electricity systems?
GK.e: The SI unit of magnetic flux density, the tesla, is named in his honour.

GK.q: What does 'SIM' stand for in 'SIM card'?
GK.e: The card stores the details that let your mobile network recognise your account.

GK.q: What is 'cloud computing'?
o: Storing and running things on remote servers over the internet
GK.e: 'The cloud' is really huge data centres full of servers, and some are built in cool climates to help keep them cool.

GK.q: Which symbol did Ray Tomlinson choose for email addresses when he sent the first network email in 1971?
GK.e: He chose it because it was rarely used and neatly meant 'at' a particular computer.

GK.q: Which Scottish inventor gave the first public demonstration of a working television in 1926?
GK.e: His early television was mechanical, using a spinning disc with holes to scan the picture.

GK.q: Australian Graeme Clark pioneered which medical device?
GK.e: The first implant of his multi-channel device took place in Melbourne in 1978.

GK.q: What is a 'pixel'?
o: One of the tiny dots that make up a digital image
GK.e: The word is short for 'picture element'.

GK.q: In mobile networks like 4G and 5G, what does the 'G' stand for?
GK.e: The first generation of mobile phones in the 1980s could only make voice calls.

GK.q: What is two-factor authentication?
o: Using a second proof of identity, like a code, as well as your password
Changing your password twice a year
GK.e: Even if someone steals your password, they usually can't get in without the second factor.

GK.q: What does 'HTML' stand for?
GK.e: HTML describes the structure of web pages, while CSS controls how they look.

GK.q: During World War II, what did Germany's Enigma machine do?
GK.e: Codebreakers at Bletchley Park, including Alan Turing, cracked its codes and shortened the war.

GK.q: Which company released the Walkman portable cassette player in 1979?
GK.e: It changed music forever by letting people carry their own soundtrack wherever they went.

GK.q: The word 'modem' is short for what?
GK.e: A modem turns digital data into signals that can travel over phone or cable lines, and back again.

GK.q: Which planet is the hottest in our solar system?
GK.e: Its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat, keeping the surface around 465°C, hotter than Mercury.

GK.q: What was the name of the first artificial satellite, launched in 1957?
GK.e: It was a metal ball about 58 cm wide that sent out simple radio beeps anyone could pick up.

GK.q: Who was the first person to travel into space, in 1961?
GK.e: His flight aboard Vostok 1 made one orbit of Earth and lasted about 108 minutes.

GK.q: Which planet rotates on its side, with an axis tilted about 98°?
GK.e: Because of this tilt, each pole gets about 42 years of sunlight followed by 42 years of darkness.

GK.q: What does a light-year measure?
GK.e: It is the distance light travels in a year, about 9.46 trillion km.

GK.q: Which NSW radio telescope helped broadcast TV pictures of the Apollo 11 moonwalk to the world in 1969?
GK.e: The Honeysuckle Creek station near Canberra carried the very first steps, then Parkes took over with clearer pictures.

GK.q: What is Jupiter's Great Red Spot?
GK.e: The storm is wider than Earth and has been watched through telescopes for well over 150 years.

GK.q: Triton, a large moon that orbits in the opposite direction to its planet's spin, belongs to which planet?
GK.e: Its backwards orbit suggests Triton was captured from the Kuiper Belt rather than forming alongside Neptune.

GK.q: Which planet has the most known moons?
GK.e: Saturn has well over 200 confirmed moons, far more than Jupiter, and astronomers keep finding small new ones.

GK.q: What is the largest moon in the solar system?
GK.e: Ganymede, which orbits Jupiter, is bigger than the planet Mercury.

GK.q: What causes Earth's seasons?
o: Earth's changing distance from the Sun
GK.e: Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January, during Australia's summer and the northern winter.

GK.q: Why do we always see the same side of the Moon from Earth?
o: It spins once for every orbit of Earth
It does not spin at all
Earth's shadow hides the other side
The other side has no light
GK.e: This is called tidal locking, and the far side gets just as much sunlight as the near side.

GK.q: What is the Sun mostly made of?
GK.e: Every second the Sun fuses around 600 million tonnes of hydrogen into helium.

GK.q: Which space telescope, launched in 2021, has a gold-coated mirror made of 18 hexagonal segments?
GK.e: Its main mirror is 6.5 m across, so it had to fold up to fit inside its rocket.

GK.q: How many astronauts walked on the Moon during the Apollo missions from 1969 to 1972?
GK.e: Six Apollo missions landed, each carrying two moonwalkers while a third astronaut stayed in orbit.

GK.q: What is the Kuiper Belt?
o: A region of icy objects beyond Neptune
The belt of asteroids between Mars and Jupiter
A band of stars in the Milky Way
GK.e: Pluto is one of its best-known members, and many short-period comets come from there.

GK.q: In 2006, what was Pluto reclassified as?
GK.e: Pluto was discovered in 1930 by American astronomer Clyde Tombaugh, who was just 24 at the time.

GK.q: Olympus Mons, one of the tallest volcanoes known in the solar system, is on which planet?
GK.e: It rises about 22 km, roughly two and a half times the height of Mount Everest.

GK.q: Which way does a comet's tail point?
GK.e: The Sun's radiation and the solar wind push the gas and dust outwards, so the tail can even lead the comet.

GK.q: Who was the first woman to travel into space, in 1963?
GK.e: She orbited Earth 48 times over nearly three days aboard Vostok 6.

GK.q: Launched in 1977, which spacecraft became the first to reach interstellar space in 2012?
GK.e: It carries a gold-plated record with sounds and images from Earth, in case anyone ever finds it.

GK.q: What is a supernova?
o: A huge explosion of a star
GK.e: Supernova 1987A, in the Large Magellanic Cloud, was easily seen from the Southern Hemisphere.

GK.q: Which planet takes the shortest time to orbit the Sun?
GK.e: A year on Mercury lasts just 88 Earth days, so you'd have a birthday about every three months.

GK.q: What is the official name of the constellation known as the Southern Cross?
GK.e: It is the smallest of the 88 official constellations, yet it appears on the Australian flag.

GK.q: Roughly how long does the Moon take to go through its full cycle of phases?
GK.e: The full cycle takes about 29.5 days, and the word 'month' comes from 'moon'.

GK.q: The main asteroid belt lies between which two planets?
GK.e: Despite films showing crowded rocks, the asteroids are so spread out that spacecraft pass through easily.

GK.q: Roughly how long does a spacecraft in low Earth orbit, like the International Space Station, take to circle Earth once?
GK.e: That means astronauts on board see around 16 sunrises and sunsets every day.

GK.q: Which planet has the most extreme winds measured in the solar system, reaching over 2,000 km/h?
GK.e: These are the fastest winds measured in the solar system, remarkable for a planet that gets so little heat from the Sun.

GK.q: What is the largest animal alive today?
GK.e: A blue whale can grow to around 30 m long, longer than two buses parked end to end.

GK.q: How many hearts does an octopus have?
GK.e: Its blood is blue, because it uses a copper-based molecule to carry oxygen.

GK.q: Which Australian animal is the largest living carnivorous marsupial?
GK.e: Devils have one of the strongest bites for their size of any mammal and can crunch through bone.

GK.q: In emus, which parent sits on the eggs until they hatch?
GK.e: The male sits on the nest for about eight weeks, rarely eating or drinking.

GK.q: What is a baby echidna called?
GK.e: Echidnas lay eggs, and the puggle hatches inside its mother's pouch.

GK.q: What word describes animals that are most active at dawn and dusk?
GK.e: Many kangaroos and wallabies are crepuscular, which is why drivers need extra care at those times.

GK.q: Which is the only group of mammals capable of true flight?
GK.e: Gliders only glide, while bats flap their wings, and they make up about a fifth of all mammal species.

GK.q: The thylacine, or Tasmanian tiger, was what kind of animal?
GK.e: Despite its stripes and dog-like looks, it carried its young in a pouch, and unusually the males had a pouch too.

GK.q: What is a group of owls called?
GK.e: The name is thought to come from owls' old reputation for wisdom.

GK.q: Why do snakes flick their tongues in and out?
o: To smell by collecting scent particles
GK.e: The tongue delivers scents to a special organ in the roof of the mouth called the Jacobson's organ.

GK.q: Which sea animal has no brain, heart or bones?
GK.e: Jellyfish have drifted through the oceans for more than 500 million years.

GK.q: Which Australian bird is famous for mimicking sounds like chainsaws and camera shutters?
GK.e: The superb lyrebird appears on the Australian 10 cent coin.

GK.q: What is the hard case a caterpillar forms before it becomes a butterfly?
GK.e: Inside the chrysalis, the caterpillar's body breaks down and rebuilds itself into a butterfly.

GK.q: Which animals are humans' closest living relatives?
GK.e: Humans share about 98.8% of their DNA with chimpanzees.

GK.q: In seahorses, which parent gives birth?
o: Neither, they lay eggs on reefs
GK.e: The female places her eggs in the male's pouch, and he carries them until the babies are born.

GK.q: Sharks can sense the tiny electric fields of hidden prey using organs called what?
GK.e: These jelly-filled pores on the snout can detect incredibly faint electric signals from muscles.

GK.q: Which land mammal has the longest pregnancy?
GK.e: Elephant pregnancies last about 22 months, and a newborn calf can weigh around 100 kg.

GK.q: The axolotl, a salamander from Mexico, is famous for which ability?
GK.e: It can regrow limbs and even parts of its heart and brain, and keeps its frilly gills as an adult.

GK.q: Which bird reaches the highest speeds of any animal when diving for prey?
GK.e: In a steep dive, called a stoop, it can exceed 300 km/h.

GK.q: Baleen, which some whales use to filter food, is made of what?
GK.e: Keratin is the same protein found in your hair and fingernails.

GK.q: Which is the largest species of penguin?
GK.e: Male emperors huddle through the Antarctic winter, each balancing an egg on its feet.

GK.q: What gives flamingos their pink colour?
o: Pigments in the food they eat
GK.e: Their diet of algae and small shrimp is rich in carotenoids, the same pigments that colour carrots.

GK.q: Tardigrades, tiny animals about half a millimetre long, are famous for what?
GK.e: Nicknamed 'water bears', they can dry out completely and revive years later when water returns.

GK.q: How do honeybees tell other bees where to find food?
o: By leaving a trail of wax
GK.e: Karl von Frisch shared a Nobel Prize in 1973 partly for decoding what the dance means.

GK.q: What is the largest living reptile?
GK.e: 'Salties' live across northern Australia and Southeast Asia, and large males can exceed 6 m.

GK.q: Scientists found that some dung beetles use what to steer at night?
GK.e: It was the first animal shown to navigate using the Milky Way.

GK.q: How many bones are in the adult human body?
GK.e: Babies are born with about 300 bones, and many fuse together as they grow.

GK.q: Why do your fingertips go wrinkly after a long bath?
o: Your skin simply soaks up water and swells
Your nerves tell blood vessels to narrow, puckering the skin
Your skin loses its natural oils
The water dissolves the top layer of skin
GK.e: Fingers with damaged nerves don't wrinkle. Some studies suggest the wrinkles help us grip wet objects.

GK.q: What is the largest internal organ in the human body?
GK.e: The liver can regrow to full size even after a large part of it has been removed.

GK.q: What is the largest muscle in the human body?
GK.e: This buttock muscle helps keep you upright and powers you up stairs and hills.

GK.q: Which part of the brain mainly coordinates balance and smooth movement?
GK.e: Its name means 'little brain', yet it holds more than half of all the brain's nerve cells.

GK.q: How many teeth does a full set of adult teeth have, including wisdom teeth?
GK.e: Children have 20 baby teeth, which start falling out around age six.

GK.q: What is the coloured part of your eye called?
GK.e: Iris patterns are so unique that your left and right eyes don't even match each other.

GK.q: Which vitamin does your skin make when exposed to sunlight?
GK.e: Vitamin D helps your body absorb calcium to build strong bones.

GK.q: Which blood cells help fight infection?
GK.e: Your body makes billions of new white blood cells every day in the bone marrow.

GK.q: Which bone is the only one in the human body not joined to any other bone?
GK.e: This small U-shaped bone in the neck supports the tongue and helps you swallow.

GK.q: Which mineral sits at the centre of haemoglobin, helping it hold on to oxygen?
GK.e: Iron is also what makes blood red.

GK.q: What connects muscles to bones?
GK.e: Ligaments, by contrast, connect one bone to another.

GK.q: Roughly how long is the adult small intestine?
GK.e: It is folded tightly inside your belly, and its lining has a huge surface area to absorb food.

GK.q: What is the name for the body's natural roughly 24-hour cycle of sleeping and waking?
GK.e: 'Circadian' comes from Latin words meaning 'about a day'.

GK.q: Which pea-sized gland is often called the body's 'master gland'?
GK.e: It sits at the base of the brain and sends out hormones that control many other glands.

GK.q: What does the snail-shaped cochlea in your inner ear do?
o: Turns sound vibrations into nerve signals
GK.e: Tiny hair cells inside it respond to different pitches, and once damaged they don't grow back.

GK.q: What is the common name for the patella?
GK.e: Babies' kneecaps are mostly soft cartilage, which slowly hardens into bone in early childhood.

GK.q: What is the main job of platelets in the blood?
GK.e: Platelets are tiny fragments of cells, and each one lasts only about a week to ten days.

GK.q: Roughly how many of the adult body's bones are in the hands and feet combined?
GK.e: Each hand has 27 bones and each foot has 26, giving 106 in total.

GK.q: What causes goosebumps?
GK.e: In our furry ancestors this puffed up the fur for warmth or to look bigger.

GK.q: What does the diaphragm help you do?
GK.e: Hiccups happen when the diaphragm suddenly spasms and the vocal cords snap shut.

GK.q: Roughly how much blood does an average adult have?
GK.e: The heart pumps roughly that whole amount around the body about once every minute at rest.

GK.q: What is a typical normal body temperature for a healthy person?
GK.e: It naturally rises and falls a little through the day and is usually lowest in the early morning.

GK.q: What is the hardest substance in the human body?
GK.e: The cells that make enamel are lost once a tooth comes through, so enamel can't regrow.

GK.q: What are the body's smallest blood vessels called?
GK.e: Their walls are just one cell thick, letting oxygen and nutrients pass through to tissues.

GK.q: Which small organ stores bile, which helps digest fat?
GK.e: Bile is made by the liver, and the gallbladder squeezes it into the gut after a fatty meal.

GK.q: When you hit your 'funny bone', what are you actually knocking?
GK.e: The ulnar nerve runs close to the skin at the elbow, which is why a bump causes that tingling jolt.

GK.q: What type of joint is your shoulder?
GK.e: Its range of movement makes the shoulder the most mobile joint, but also one of the easiest to dislocate.

GK.q: In what year did Australia's six colonies federate to form the Commonwealth of Australia?
GK.e: The new nation's Constitution came into force on 1 January 1901, and Melbourne served as the temporary seat of government.

GK.q: The Eureka Stockade rebellion of 1854 took place on the goldfields near which town?
GK.e: Miners were protesting against costly mining licences, and their blue and white Southern Cross flag is still a famous symbol.

GK.q: Quokkas, famous for their 'smiling' photos, live mainly on which island?
GK.e: Dutch explorer Willem de Vlamingh thought they were giant rats, so he named the island 'rat nest'.

GK.q: Which language has the most native speakers in the world?
GK.e: Mandarin has around 900 million native speakers, far more than any other language.

GK.q: Diwali, celebrated by Hindus, Sikhs and Jains, is known as the festival of what?
GK.e: Families light rows of small clay oil lamps called diyas to symbolise light winning over darkness.

GK.q: Paella originally comes from which region of Spain?
GK.e: The original Valencian version used rabbit, chicken and beans rather than seafood.

GK.q: Kimchi, a spicy fermented vegetable dish, is a staple food of which country?
GK.e: Kimjang, the communal autumn making of kimchi, is on UNESCO's list of Intangible Cultural Heritage.

GK.q: The Guru Granth Sahib is the holy scripture of which religion?
GK.e: Sikhs treat it as a living Guru, and hymns from it are sung throughout the day at the Golden Temple in Amritsar.

GK.q: During Ramadan, many Muslims fast between which times each day?
GK.e: The fast is often broken at sunset with dates and water, in a meal called iftar.

GK.q: The tango dance first developed in which part of the world?
GK.e: It grew up in the late 1800s in the working-class neighbourhoods of Buenos Aires and Montevideo.

GK.q: The Hindi-language film industry known as Bollywood is based mainly in which city?
GK.e: The name blends Bombay, the city's former name, with Hollywood.

GK.q: What is traditionally mixed into sushi rice to give it a tangy flavour?
GK.e: Sushi began as a way of preserving fish in fermented rice, and vinegar later replaced the slow fermentation.

GK.q: Oktoberfest is held every year in which city?
GK.e: It began in 1810 as a celebration of the wedding of Bavaria's Crown Prince Ludwig and Princess Therese.

GK.q: What is Esperanto?
o: A language invented to be easy to learn internationally
The ancient language of the Basques
GK.e: It was published in 1887 by L. L. Zamenhof, who hoped a shared second language would help people get along.

GK.q: The sitar is a stringed instrument closely linked with the classical music of which country?
GK.e: Ravi Shankar made the sitar famous in the West, and taught George Harrison of the Beatles to play it.

GK.q: Which 1927 film is famous as the first feature-length 'talkie' with synchronised dialogue?
GK.e: Most of the film is actually silent with title cards, with only a few scenes of synchronised singing and speech.

GK.q: Samba music and dance are most closely linked with the Carnival of which country?
GK.e: In Rio de Janeiro, samba schools compete in a purpose-built parade venue called the Sambadrome.

GK.q: How many nights does the Jewish festival of Hanukkah last?
GK.e: The special Hanukkah candle holder has nine branches: one for each night plus a helper candle used to light the others.

GK.q: Haggis is a traditional dish from which country?
GK.e: It is served on Burns Night each January, when Robert Burns's poem 'Address to a Haggis' is recited.

GK.q: Hangul is the alphabet used to write which language?
GK.e: It was created in the 15th century under King Sejong the Great so that ordinary people could learn to read.

GK.q: What is the traditional Japanese tea ceremony called?
GK.e: The ceremony centres on matcha, a powdered green tea whisked with hot water in a bowl.

GK.q: Flamenco music and dance are most associated with which region of Spain?
GK.e: Flamenco blends influences from the region's Roma people with Spanish, Moorish and Jewish traditions.

GK.q: Which composer wrote the set of violin concertos called The Four Seasons?
GK.e: Each concerto was published with a short poem describing the scenes the music paints, such as birdsong and storms.

GK.q: Which composer wrote his Ninth Symphony while almost completely deaf?
GK.e: Its final movement, known as the 'Ode to Joy', is now used as the anthem of Europe.

GK.q: The Cannes Film Festival is held each year in which country?
GK.e: Its top prize is the Palme d'Or, meaning 'Golden Palm'.

GK.q: What was Walt Disney's first full-length animated feature film?
o: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs
GK.e: Released in 1937, it was nicknamed 'Disney's Folly' by doubters before becoming a huge hit.

GK.q: Traditional Italian risotto is made with which grain?
GK.e: Short-grain varieties such as Arborio release starch as they cook, giving risotto its creamy texture.

GK.q: The French croissant is thought to have developed from the kipferl, a crescent-shaped pastry from which country?
GK.e: This is why French bakers call croissants and similar pastries 'viennoiserie', meaning things from Vienna.

GK.q: What does the Japanese word 'tsunami' literally mean?
GK.e: Fishers returning home would find their harbours devastated by waves they had barely noticed out at sea.

GK.q: Afrikaans, which developed from Dutch, is mainly spoken in which country?
GK.e: It grew from the Dutch spoken by settlers at the Cape from the 1600s, mixed with other languages over time.

GK.q: What is the Vietnamese Lunar New Year festival called?
GK.e: Songkran is the Thai New Year, famous for its good-natured water fights.

GK.q: The saxophone is made of brass, but which family of instruments does it belong to?
GK.e: It counts as a woodwind because its sound comes from a reed, and it was invented by Adolphe Sax in the 1840s.

GK.q: Who wrote The Wealth of Nations, published in 1776?
GK.e: His famous phrase 'invisible hand' appears only once in the whole book.

GK.q: What did John Maynard Keynes argue governments should do during a recession?
o: Cut spending to balance the budget
GK.e: His 1936 book The General Theory shaped how many governments responded to downturns for decades.

GK.q: What is a 'Veblen good'?
o: A product people want more of as its price rises, because it signals status
A basic item people buy no matter the price
A product that gets cheaper when made in bulk
A service the government provides for free
GK.e: It's named after economist Thorstein Veblen, who coined 'conspicuous consumption'. Luxury handbags and watches are classic examples.

GK.q: What is a monopoly?
o: A market with only one seller
A group of countries that trade freely
A market with only one buyer
GK.e: The board game Monopoly grew out of The Landlord's Game, designed to show the problems of concentrated land ownership.

GK.q: What does 'CPI', the most common measure of inflation, stand for?
GK.e: In Australia, the Australian Bureau of Statistics calculates CPI by tracking the prices of a basket of everyday goods and services.

GK.q: Which country was the first to use paper money widely?
GK.e: Paper money spread in China around 1,000 years ago, and Marco Polo later marvelled at it in his travel accounts.

GK.q: What is compound interest?
o: Interest that goes down over time
A fixed fee paid once a year
Interest charged only on late payments
Interest earned on both your original money and past interest
GK.e: Over long periods compounding snowballs, which is why starting to save early makes such a difference.

GK.q: The 'tulip mania' of the 1630s took place in which country?
GK.e: Some rare bulbs reportedly sold for more than a house, though historians now think its wider damage was exaggerated.

GK.q: What does it mean when a government runs a budget deficit?
o: It spends more than it collects in a year
It collects more than it spends in a year
It has paid off all its debts
GK.e: The gap is usually covered by borrowing, which adds to government debt. The opposite is a budget surplus.

GK.q: In finance, what does 'IPO' stand for?
GK.e: An IPO is when a company first sells its shares to the public on a stock exchange.

GK.q: The idea that 'bad money drives out good' is named after which person?
GK.e: Gresham was a 16th-century English financier, and his 'law' explains why people hoard coins with more precious metal in them.

GK.q: David Ricardo is famous for which idea about trade?
GK.e: His classic example showed England and Portugal both gaining by specialising in cloth and wine.

GK.q: What did Thomas Malthus famously warn about in 1798?
GK.e: Farming productivity rose faster than he expected, but his ideas influenced Charles Darwin's thinking on natural selection.

GK.q: Which two institutions were created at the 1944 Bretton Woods conference?
o: The WTO and the United Nations
The IMF and the World Bank
The European Central Bank and the IMF
GK.e: The conference was held at a hotel in New Hampshire, with delegates from 44 Allied nations.

GK.q: A 'technical recession' is commonly defined as what?
o: Two quarters in a row of shrinking GDP
A fall in share prices of 20%
GK.e: It's a rule of thumb, and economists often look at broader measures such as jobs and spending too.

GK.q: The Wall Street Crash that helped trigger the Great Depression happened in which year?
GK.e: The worst days came in late October, remembered as Black Thursday and Black Tuesday.

GK.q: What is a 'monopsony'?
o: A market with only one seller
A market with only one buyer
GK.e: A single big employer in a small town can act like one, because workers have few other places to sell their labour.

GK.q: Which currency uses the symbol £?
GK.e: The £ sign comes from a fancy letter L, standing for 'libra', a Roman unit of weight.

GK.q: When Australia switched to decimal currency in 1966, which currency did the dollar replace?
GK.e: The changeover was promoted with a catchy television jingle featuring a cartoon character called Dollar Bill.

GK.q: In 1988, Australia became the first country to issue banknotes made from what?
GK.e: The first was a $10 note marking the bicentenary, and polymer notes last much longer than paper ones.

GK.q: Which country printed a 100 trillion dollar banknote during severe hyperinflation in the late 2000s?
GK.e: The worst hyperinflation ever recorded was in Hungary in 1946, when prices roughly tripled every day.

GK.q: What is barter?
o: Selling shares on the stock market
Paying for things by credit card
Swapping goods or services without using money
GK.e: Barter still happens today, for example when neighbours swap garden produce or skills.

GK.q: What does the law of 'diminishing marginal utility' describe?
o: Workers become less productive with age
Each extra unit of something brings less satisfaction
Costs rise as a business grows
GK.e: Your first slice of pizza usually feels much more rewarding than your fifth.

GK.q: What does 'GDP per capita' measure?
o: The income of the average worker after tax
The total wealth of a country's richest people
The amount a government spends per person on health
A country's economic output divided by its population
GK.e: It's often used to compare living standards, though it says nothing about how income is shared.

GK.q: Which international organisation, founded in 1995, sets trade rules and settles trade disputes between countries?
GK.e: It replaced an earlier agreement called GATT, which had governed world trade since 1948.

GK.q: What is the Gini coefficient used to measure?
GK.e: A score of 0 means everyone has the same income, while a score of 1 means one person has it all.

GK.q: Which economist popularised the term 'creative destruction'?
GK.e: He described how new innovations sweep away old industries, as streaming did to video rental shops.

GK.q: Milton Friedman is best known for which school of economic thought?
GK.e: Monetarists argue that controlling the money supply is the key to keeping inflation in check.

GK.q: Who was Australia's first Prime Minister?
GK.e: After leaving politics in 1903, Barton became one of the first judges of the High Court of Australia.

GK.q: The Great Barrier Reef lies off the coast of which state?
GK.e: Stretching more than 2,000 km, it's the largest structure on Earth built by living things.

GK.q: In 1902, Australian women won which rights in federal elections?
o: The right to vote and to stand for parliament
Only the right to stand for parliament
The right to vote in local councils only
GK.e: Most Aboriginal people were excluded, and all Indigenous Australians only gained the federal vote in 1962.

GK.q: The 1967 referendum, passed with over 90% of the vote, changed the Constitution so that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people would be...
o: Given the right to vote for the first time
GK.e: It remains one of only eight referendums ever passed out of the dozens put to Australians.

GK.q: The High Court's 1992 Mabo decision overturned which legal idea?
GK.e: Eddie Mabo came from Mer (Murray Island) in the Torres Strait, and the case recognised native title for the first time.

GK.q: Which two animals appear on Australia's coat of arms?
GK.e: The shield between them carries the badges of the six states.

GK.q: Which body of water separates Tasmania from mainland Australia?
GK.e: George Bass and Matthew Flinders sailed around Tasmania in 1798 and 1799, proving it was an island.

GK.q: Which explorers made the first recorded European crossing of the Blue Mountains in 1813?
GK.e: Earlier attempts had failed by following the valleys, while this group succeeded by following the ridges.

GK.q: What were Burke and Wills attempting on their ill-fated 1860 to 1861 expedition?
o: To cross Australia from south to north
To find gold in Western Australia
GK.e: They reached the tidal mangroves near the Gulf of Carpentaria, but both men died on the return journey.

GK.q: What is the upper house of Australia's federal parliament called?
GK.e: Each state elects the same number of senators, no matter its population.

GK.q: What is the maximum term of the federal House of Representatives in Australia?
GK.e: It's one of the shortest terms among the world's democracies, while every state now has four-year terms.

GK.q: Which Australian city was largely destroyed by Cyclone Tracy on Christmas Day 1974?
GK.e: Most of the city's homes were destroyed and most residents were evacuated, leading to much stronger building codes.

GK.q: Which is Australia's smallest state?
GK.e: Victoria is the smallest mainland state. The ACT is smaller still, but it's a territory rather than a state.

GK.q: Which Australian bird is famous for its loud 'laughing' call?
GK.e: The laughing kookaburra is the largest member of the kingfisher family.

GK.q: What was the main purpose of the Snowy Mountains Scheme, built between 1949 and 1974?
o: To generate hydro-electricity and supply water for irrigation
To build a railway to Canberra
To mine coal in the Alps
GK.e: More than 100,000 people from over 30 countries worked on it, many of them post-war migrants.

GK.q: Who commanded the First Fleet and became the first Governor of New South Wales?
GK.e: 26 January, when Phillip raised the British flag at Sydney Cove, is now Australia Day.

GK.q: What are the three colours of the Aboriginal flag?
GK.e: Designed by Harold Thomas, it represents the people, the red earth and the sun, and was first flown in Adelaide in 1971.

GK.q: Kakadu National Park, famous for ancient rock art, is in which state or territory?
GK.e: It's World Heritage listed for both its natural and cultural values, a rare combination.

GK.q: What is Australia's national anthem?
GK.e: It became the anthem in 1984, and in 2021 the line 'young and free' was changed to 'one and free'.

GK.q: Which country hosted the first modern Olympic Games in 1896?
GK.e: The Games were held in Athens, as a nod to the ancient Olympics held in Greece.

GK.q: How many rings are on the Olympic flag?
GK.e: Pierre de Coubertin chose the colours because every nation's flag contained at least one of them, with the white background.

GK.q: Which country hosted and won the first FIFA World Cup in 1930?
GK.e: Only 13 teams took part, and most European teams stayed away because of the long sea voyage.

GK.q: Which tennis Grand Slam tournament is played on clay courts?
GK.e: Its home, Roland-Garros, is named after a French aviator who died in the First World War.

GK.q: Which golf course in Scotland is known as 'the home of golf'?
GK.e: Golf has been played on the links at St Andrews for about 600 years.

GK.q: In cricket, what does 'LBW' stand for?
GK.e: A batter can be given out LBW if the ball hits their leg when it would otherwise have hit the stumps.

GK.q: How many players are on the field for each team in rugby union?
GK.e: Rugby league, which split from rugby union in 1895, uses 13 players per side.

GK.q: In which sport do players talk about the 'hammer', the 'house' and 'sweeping'?
GK.e: Many curling stones are made from granite quarried on Ailsa Craig, a small island off Scotland.

GK.q: Basketball was invented in 1891 by James Naismith, who came from which country?
GK.e: He invented the game in Springfield, Massachusetts, using peach baskets as the first hoops.

GK.q: How many points is a touchdown worth in American football?
GK.e: After a touchdown, the team can try for one or two extra points.

GK.q: What is the maximum possible break in a standard game of snooker?
GK.e: It requires potting all 15 reds, each followed by the black, then all six colours in order.

GK.q: The Stanley Cup is awarded in which sport?
GK.e: It was donated by Lord Stanley, a Governor General of Canada, and first awarded in 1893.

GK.q: In the Tour de France, what colour jersey does the overall leader wear?
GK.e: Yellow was the colour of the paper of L'Auto, the newspaper that founded the race in 1903.

GK.q: Sumo wrestling is the traditional national sport of which country?
GK.e: The highest rank a sumo wrestler can reach is yokozuna, meaning grand champion.

GK.q: How long is an Olympic swimming pool?
GK.e: Olympic pools also have ten lanes, though only the middle eight are used in races.

GK.q: How many points is a try worth in rugby union?
GK.e: In early rugby a try scored no points at all, it only earned the chance to 'try' a kick at goal.

GK.q: In Australian rules football, how many points is a goal worth?
GK.e: A behind is worth one point, and a match score such as 12.8 (80) shows goals, behinds and total.
